Notice is hereby given pursuant to the Antitrust Procedures and Penalties Act,
15 U.S.C. 16(b)-(h)
, that the Response of the United States to Public Comments on the Proposed Final Judgment in
United States of America et al.
v.
RealPage et al.,
Civil Action No. 24-cv-00710, regarding Defendant Willow Bridge Property Company, LLC, has been filed in the United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina, together with the comments. Copies of the public comments and the United States' Response are also available for inspection on the Antitrust Division's website at
http://www.justice.gov/​atr
.
Suzanne Morris,
Deputy Director Civil Enforcement Operations, Antitrust Division.
In the United States District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Plaintiff, vs.
WILLOW BRIDGE PROPERTY COMPANY, LLC,
Defendant.
No. 1:24-cv-00710
Response of Plaintiff United States to Public Comments on the Proposed Final Judgment
Pursuant to the requirements of the Antitrust Procedures and Penalties Act (the “APPA” or “Tunney Act”),
15 U.S.C. 16(b)-(h)
, the United States submits this response to the two public comments received regarding the proposed Final Judgment as to Defendant Willow Bridge Property Company, LLC (Doc. 200-1).
[
1
]
After careful consideration of the submitted comments, the United States continues to believe that the proposed Final Judgment will provide an effective and appropriate remedy for the antitrust violations alleged in the Complaint.
After this response and the public comments have been published in the
Federal Register
pursuant to 15 U.S.C § 16(d), the United States will move the Court to enter the proposed Final Judgment.
I. Procedural History
On August 23, 2024, the United States, along with several States (“Plaintiffs”), filed a civil antitrust Complaint against RealPage, Inc. (“RealPage”) (Doc. 1). On January 7, 2025, Plaintiffs amended their civil Complaint (the “Complaint”) to add Willow Bridge Property Company, LLC (“Willow Bridge”) and five other landlords as Defendants (Doc. 47) alleging that Willow Bridge's agreements with RealPage and other landlords to share information and align pricing violate Section 1 of the Sherman Act,
15 U.S.C. 1
. The Complaint seeks to enjoin Defendants from sharing and exploiting competitively sensitive data.
On July 6, 2026, the United States filed a proposed Final Judgment (Doc. 200-1) as to Willow Bridge, which is designed to remedy the loss of competition alleged in the Complaint due to Willow Bridge's conduct, and a Stipulation and Proposed Order (Doc. 200), in which Willow Bridge consented to entry of the proposed Final Judgment after compliance with the requirements of the Tunney Act.
[
2
]
Also on the same date, the United States filed a Competitive Impact Statement describing the proposed Final Judgment as to Willow Bridge. (Doc. 202)
The United States arranged for the publication of the Complaint, proposed Final Judgment, and Competitive Impact Statement in the
Federal Register
on July 16, 2026, see
15 U.S.C. 16(b)-(c)
;
91 FR 43
,
774
(July 16, 2026), and caused notice regarding the same, together with directions for the submission of written comments relating to the proposed Final Judgment, to be published in the
Washington Post
and the
Greensboro News and Record
from July 14 to July 21, 2026. The 60-day period for public comment has now ended. The United States received two comments in response, which are described below and attached as Exhibits 1 & 2 hereto.
II. The Complaint and The Proposed Final Judgment
The Complaint alleges that, by unlawfully sharing its confidential and competitively sensitive information with RealPage for use in its and competing landlords' pricing, Willow Bridge violated Section 1 of the Sherman Act,
15 U.S.C. 1
. Under their licensing agreements with RealPage, Willow Bridge and competing landlords have provided RealPage with daily, competitively sensitive, nonpublic information for use in RealPage's revenue management software relating to the landlords' leasing businesses, including details like how many leases have been renewed, for what terms, and at what price. The transactional data that Willow Bridge and other landlords have agreed to provide to RealPage includes current, forward-looking, granular, and highly competitively sensitive information. RealPage has
(
printed page 70899)
used Willow Bridge's competitively sensitive, nonpublic information to influence rental prices and other recommendations across rental properties managed by competing landlords. Willow Bridge's rental prices and related recommendations were likewise influenced by its competitors' competitively sensitive, nonpublic information obtained from RealPage. In each relevant market, RealPage and participating landlords, including Willow Bridge, have sufficient market power, including market and data penetration, to harm renters and the competitive process through this unlawful sharing of confidential and competitively sensitive information. Moreover, Willow Bridge and other landlords can achieve any procompetitive objective of revenue management software without sharing this kind of information.
The Complaint also alleges that Willow Bridge and other landlords, by adopting and using RealPage's revenue management software, agreed with RealPage to align their pricing and thereby violate Section 1 of the Sherman Act,
15 U.S.C. 1
. RealPage has entered into agreements with Willow Bridge and its competing landlords relating to how to price rental units, including through the licensing of its revenue management software—AI Revenue Management (“AIRM”), YieldStar, and Lease Rent Options (“LRO”)—to landlords, and the provision by landlords of their competitively sensitive, nonpublic transactional data to RealPage for training and running its revenue management software. Adoption and use of RealPage's revenue management software by Willow Bridge and other landlords have the likely effect of causing competing landlords to employ the same or very similar strategies, processes, and decisions relating to their pricing of rental units. Willow Bridge and other landlord users understand this likely effect, which here dampens the competitive process that benefits renters.
The proposed Final Judgment imposes several requirements and restrictions on Willow Bridge that address the United States' anticompetitive concerns regarding Willow Bridge's conduct alleged in the Complaint. Specifically:
i. Willow Bridge must not license or use any revenue management product that uses third-party nonpublic data to recommend or set prices;
ii. Willow Bridge must not license or use any revenue management product that pools information from Willow Bridge properties that have different owners;
iii. Willow Bridge must not disclose, solicit, or use competitively sensitive information from competitors that can be used to set rental prices or generate pricing;
iv. Willow Bridge must cooperate in this civil antitrust proceeding (
United States et al.
v.
RealPage et al.
);
v. Willow Bridge must adopt a written antitrust compliance policy and designate a chief antitrust compliance officer who will train Willow Bridge employees on the policy;
vi. Willow Bridge must allow the United States to inspect its documents and to interview its employees to ensure compliance with the Final Judgment;
vii. If Willow Bridge uses a revenue management product, Willow Bridge will be subject to a monitor unless Willow Bridge obtains a certification that meets certain requirements, including an affirmation that the product complies with all required limitations regarding use of competitors' competitively sensitive data; and
viii. If, in the future, the Court finds that Willow Bridge has violated the terms of the proposed Final Judgment, Willow Bridge will be subject to a court-appointed monitor.
Under the terms of the Stipulation and Order, Willow Bridge must abide by and comply with the provisions of the proposed Final Judgment until it is entered by the Court or until the time for all appeals of any Court ruling declining entry of the proposed Final Judgment has expired.
The United States and Willow Bridge have stipulated that the proposed Final Judgment may be entered by the Court after compliance with the APPA. Entry of the proposed Final Judgment will terminate this action with respect to the United States' claims against Willow Bridge, except that the Court will retain jurisdiction to construe, modify, or enforce the provisions of the proposed Final Judgment and to punish violations thereof by Willow Bridge.
III. Standard of Judicial Review
The Clayton Act, as amended by the APPA, requires that proposed consent judgments in antitrust cases brought by the United States be subject to a 60-day comment period, after which the Court shall determine whether entry of the proposed Final Judgment “is in the public interest.”
15 U.S.C. 16(e)(1)
. In making that determination, the Court, in accordance with the Tunney Act as amended in 2004, is required to consider:
(A) the competitive impact of such judgment, including termination of alleged violations, provisions for enforcement and modification, duration of relief sought, anticipated effects of alternative remedies actually considered, whether its terms are ambiguous, and any other competitive considerations bearing upon the adequacy of such judgment that the court deems necessary to a determination of whether the consent judgment is in the public interest; and
(B) the impact of entry of such judgment upon competition in the relevant market or markets, upon the public generally and individuals alleging specific injury from the violations set forth in the complaint including consideration of the public benefit, if any, to be derived from a determination of the issues at trial.
15 U.S.C. 16(e)(1)(A)
& (B). In considering these statutory factors, the Court's inquiry is necessarily a limited one, as the government is entitled to “broad discretion to settle with the defendant within the reaches of the public interest.”
United States
v.
Microsoft Corp.,
56 F.3d 1448, 1461 (D.C. Cir. 1995);
United States
v.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.,
No. 25-CV-00951-PCP, 2026 WL 2349970, at *16 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 12, 2026);
United States
v.
U.S. Airways Grp., Inc.,
38 F. Supp. 3d 69, 75 (D.D.C. 2014) (explaining that the “court's inquiry is limited” in Tunney Act settlements);
United States
v.
InBev N.V./S.A.,
No. 08-1965 (JR), 2009 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 84787, at *3 (D.D.C. Aug. 11, 2009) (noting that a court's review of a consent judgment is limited and only inquires “into whether the government's determination that the proposed remedies will cure the antitrust violations alleged in the complaint was reasonable, and whether the mechanism to enforce the final judgment are clear and manageable”);
United States
v.
Keyspan Corp.,
763 F. Supp. 2d 633, 637-38 (S.D.N.Y. 2011);
see SEC
v.
Citigroup Global Markets Inc.,
673 F.3d 158, 168 (2d Cir. 2012) (“We are bound in such matters to give deference to an executive agency's assessment of the public interest.”).
As the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit has held, under the APPA, a court considers, among other things, the relationship between the remedy secured and the specific allegations in the government's complaint, whether the proposed Final Judgment is sufficiently clear, whether its enforcement mechanisms are sufficient, and whether it may positively harm third parties.
See Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1458-62;
United States
v.
Apple, Inc.,
889 F. Supp. 2d 623, 631 (S.D.N.Y. 2012) (citing
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1458, 1461-62). With respect to the adequacy of the relief secured by the proposed
(
printed page 70900)
Final Judgment, a court may “not make de novo determination of facts and issues.”
United States
v.
W. Elec. Co.,
993 F.2d 1572, 1577 (D.C. Cir. 1993) (quotation marks omitted);
see also Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1460-62;
United States
v.
Alcoa, Inc.,
152 F. Supp. 2d 37, 40 (D.D.C. 2001);
United States
v.
Enova Corp.,
107 F. Supp. 2d 10, 16 (D.D.C. 2000);
InBev,
2009 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 84787, at *3. Instead, “[t]he balancing of competing social and political interests affected by a proposed antitrust consent decree must be left, in the first instance, to the discretion of the Attorney General.”
W. Elec. Co.,
993 F.2d at 1577 (quotation marks omitted). “The court should bear in mind the
flexibility
of the public interest inquiry: the court's function is not to determine whether the resulting array of rights and liabilities is one that will
best
serve society, but only to confirm that the resulting settlement is within the
reaches
of the public interest.”
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1460 (quotation marks omitted);
see also United States
v.
Deutsche Telekom AG,
No. 19-2232 (TJK), 2020 WL 1873555, at *7 (D.D.C. Apr. 14, 2020). More demanding requirements would “have enormous practical consequences for the government's ability to negotiate future settlements,” contrary to congressional intent.
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1456. “The Tunney Act was not intended to create a disincentive to the use of the consent decree.”
Id.
[
3
]
“Because enforcement by consent decree is an alternative to enforcement by trial or abandonment of the litigation altogether and often reflects the United States's assessment of litigation risk, a proposed settlement does not need to replicate the full relief that [the] United States sought in its complaint.”
Hewlett Packard Enter.,
2026 WL 2349970, at *17. The United States' predictions about the efficacy of the remedy are to be afforded deference by the Court.
See, e.g., Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1461 (recognizing courts should give “due respect to the Justice Department's . . . view of the nature of its case”);
United States
v.
Iron Mountain, Inc.,
217 F. Supp. 3d 146, 152-53 (D.D.C. 2016) (“In evaluating objections to settlement agreements under the Tunney Act, a court must be mindful that [t]he government need not prove that the settlements will perfectly remedy the alleged antitrust harms[;] it need only provide a factual basis for concluding that the settlements are reasonably adequate remedies for the alleged harms.”) (internal citations omitted);
United States
v.
Republic Servs., Inc.,
723 F. Supp. 2d 157, 160 (D.D.C. 2010) (noting “the deferential review to which the government's proposed remedy is accorded”);
United States
v.
Archer-Daniels-Midland Co.,
272 F. Supp. 2d 1, 6 (D.D.C. 2003) (“A district court must accord due respect to the government's prediction as to the effect of proposed remedies, its perception of the market structure, and its view of the nature of the case”). In determining whether a proposed settlement is in the public interest, a district court “is not permitted to reject the proposed remedies merely because the court believes other remedies are preferable.”
United States
v.
Morgan Stanley,
881 F. Supp. 2d 563, 567 (S.D.N.Y. 2012) (quoting
United States
v.
Abitibi-Consol. Inc.,
584 F. Supp. 2d 162, 165 (D.D.C. 2008)). The ultimate question is whether “the remedies [obtained by the Final Judgment are] so inconsonant with the allegations charged as to fall outside of the `reaches of the public interest.' ”
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1461 (
quoting W. Elec. Co.,
900 F.2d at 309).
Moreover, the Court's role under the APPA is limited to reviewing the remedy in relationship to the violations that the United States has alleged in its complaint and does not authorize the Court to “construct [its] own hypothetical case and then evaluate the decree against that case.”
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1459;
see also U.S. Airways,
38 F. Supp. 3d at 75 (noting that the court must simply determine whether there is a factual foundation for the government's decisions such that its conclusions regarding the proposed settlements are reasonable);
United States
v.
Keyspan Corp.,
763 F. Supp. 2d 633 637-38 (S.D.N.Y. 2011) (“The Court's function is not to determine whether the proposed [d]ecree results in the balance of rights and liabilities that is the one that will best serve society, but only to ensure that the resulting settlement is `within the reaches of the public interest.'” (quoting
United States
v.
Alex. Brown & Sons, Inc.,
963 F. Supp. 235, 238 (S.D.N.Y. 1997));
InBev,
2009 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 84787, at *20 (“the `public interest' is not to be measured by comparing the violations alleged in the complaint against those the court believes could have, or even should have, been alleged”). Because the “court's authority to review the decree depends entirely on the government's exercising its prosecutorial discretion by bringing a case in the first place,” it follows that “the court is only authorized to review the decree itself,” and not to “effectively redraft the complaint” to inquire into other matters that the United States did not pursue.
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1459-60.
See also Heckler
v.
Chaney,
470 U.S. 821, 832 (1985) (quoting U.S. Const. art. II, § 3) (recognizing that the decision about which claims to bring “has long been regarded as the special province of the Executive Branch.”).
In its 2004 amendments to the APPA, Congress made clear its intent to preserve the practical benefits of using consent judgments proposed by the United States in antitrust enforcement,
Public Law 108-237
§ 221, and added the unambiguous instruction that “[n]othing in this section shall be construed to require the court to conduct an evidentiary hearing or to require the court to permit anyone to intervene.”
15 U.S.C. 16(e)(2)
;
see also U.S. Airways,
38 F. Supp. 3d at 76 (indicating that a court is not required to hold an evidentiary hearing or to permit intervenors as part of its review under the Tunney Act). This language explicitly wrote into the statute what Congress intended when it first enacted the Tunney Act in 1974. As Senator Tunney explained: “[t]he court is nowhere compelled to go to trial or to engage in extended proceedings which might have the effect of vitiating the benefits of prompt and less costly settlement through the consent decree process.” 119 Cong. Rec. 24,598 (1973) (statement of Sen. Tunney). “A court can make its public interest determination based on the competitive impact statement and response to public comments alone.”
U.S. Airways,
38 F. Supp. 3d at 76 (citing
Enova Corp.,
107 F. Supp. 2d at 17).
IV. Summary of Public Comments and the United States' Response
The United States received two public comments in response to the proposed Final Judgment. The comments were submitted by private individuals, whom the United States will refer to by each individual's initials: MC (“MC Comment”) and JD (“JD Comment”).
A. The MC Comment
MC's comment requests that the United States consider whether the proposed Final Judgment adequately addresses the role of pricing algorithms in renewal pricing, including situations where renewal prices offered are materially higher than prices quoted to prospective tenants for the same apartment unit, and “whether monitoring under the decree should
(
printed page 70901)
examine the differences between renewal and new-tenant prices.”
[
4
]
The terms of the proposed Final Judgment with Willow Bridge do not make a distinction between renewal pricing and new-tenant pricing. Therefore, the limitations imposed on the use, disclosure, pooling, combination, or training of Nonpublic Data apply equally to recommendations regarding renewal pricing and new-tenant pricing generated by revenue management software.
[
5
]
Furthermore, the Complaint did not allege anticompetitive conduct related to differences between renewal pricing and new-tenant pricing. (
See, e.g.,
Doc. 47, ¶ 62 (“Every morning, the landlord's property manager chooses whether to accept the floor plan price recommendation, keep the previous day's rent, or override the recommendation. These options are the same for new leases and renewal leases.”) & ¶ 107 (“Specifically, he urged the group to `push up new and renewal pricing where demand [is] solid' and warned against over-relying on concessions. They were instead to `trust the science' of YieldStar.”).) MC's requests therefore are not relevant to the United States' claims and not germane to Tunney Act review.
The fact that Willow Bridge may choose to price its apartment units differently to existing tenants and prospective tenants does not, in of itself, present a competitive concern, absent evidence that such a pricing strategy uses Nonpublic Data shared by Willow Bridge's competitors or aligns with the pricing strategy used by Willow Bridge's competitors in a local rental market. The terms of the proposed Final Judgment ensure that any differential pricing of renewals and new leases by Willow Bridge is not a result of the types of anticompetitive conduct alleged in the Complaint.
MC further requests that the United States consider whether the proposed Final Judgment should require Willow Bridge to provide notification to tenants on a property's use of “automated revenue management systems.”
[
6
]
Such a requirement would go beyond addressing the United States' claims regarding the sharing of competitively sensitive data among landlords and the use of revenue management software to align their pricing. The use of an “automated revenue management system” or software with a rental property, standing alone, does not raise competitive concerns. What matters is whether such a system or software is being trained on or otherwise uses Nonpublic Data shared by Willow Bridge's competitors and whether such a system or software, during operation, “automates” pricing recommendations and/or decision-making for Willow Bridge and its competitors who are also using the system or software. The proposed Final Judgment effectively addresses such scenarios associated with Willow Bridge's use of an “automated revenue management system.” More is therefore not required.
Finally, MC requests that the United States consider whether the proposed Final Judgment should require Willow Bridge to provide “meaningful human review” of renewal prices.
[
7
]
Similar to MC's other requests, this request questions whether a landlord like Willow Bridge should be allowed to use revenue management software, and specifically software that may automatically generate pricing recommendations for renewals and new leases. As explained above, the United States' Complaint does not allege that Willow Bridge's use of a revenue management system or software, standing alone, is anticompetitive. What matters is whether such a system or software is being trained on or otherwise uses Nonpublic Data shared by Willow Bridge's competitors and whether such a system or software, during operation, “automates” pricing recommendations and/or decision-making for Willow Bridge and its competitors who are also using the system or software. The proposed Final Judgment effectively addresses such scenarios associated with Willow Bridge's use of revenue management software, and a requirement of “meaningful human review” is neither relevant nor necessary to address the competitive concerns raised by the Complaint.
B. The JD Comment
JD first requests that the United States investigate whether their specific rental property uses a RealPage or other third-party revenue management product and whether their specific property's rental prices were calculated with the use of competitively sensitive information.
[
8
]
JD further requests that the United States explain “whether potentially affected renters will have any process to learn whether their property or its data was within the investigation or remedial program.”
[
9
]
A renter can “evaluate whether the decree protects that renter.”
[
10
]
In the United States' judgment, the type of process requested by JD is not necessary. The proposed Final Judgment applies to
all
conventional multifamily rental properties, located within the United States or its territories, that are serviced by Willow Bridge (defined as “Willow Bridge Properties”).
[
11
]
It therefore would apply to JD's specific rental property if it is a Willow Bridge Property. As for JD's request for any investigative information specific to their rental property, the United States is prohibited by statute from disclosing these materials.
[
12
]
The United States notes, however, that the Complaint identifies multiple geographic markets in Appendices A & B, which the public may consult to understand the scope and extent of the competitive harms being addressed by the proposed Final Judgment.
JD also requests that the proposed Final Judgment require independent technical verification of third-party revenue management products.
[
13
]
Although the proposed Final Judgment does not require independent technical verification, it requires third-party revenue management providers to provide certifications that the software complies with the terms of the proposed Final Judgment.
[
14
]
Furthermore, the United States has the right to obtain and inspect the code and pseudocode of Willow Bridge's proprietary revenue management software.
[
15
]
JD recommends that the United States require Willow Bridge's internal annual audit to include a “statistically and operationally meaningful sample.”
[
16
]
The proposed Final Judgment requires an internal audit of employees “engaged in or overseeing Willow Bridge's revenue management of multifamily rental properties in the United States and its territories,” and at least 12 “randomly selected, local, regional, or supervisory employees who manage property operations.”
[
17
]
This is sufficient to capture the scope and diversity of Willow Bridge's revenue management operations, and there is no need to expand or otherwise modify the
(
printed page 70902)
audit requirement. Importantly, the proposed Final Judgment provides the United States broad rights to ensure compliance with the Final Judgment. These include access to “electronic copies of all books, ledgers, accounts, records, data, and documents” and to Willow Bridge's employees for interviews relating to any matters contained in the Final Judgment.
[
18
]
JD also requests that Willow Bridge be required to provide a public annual compliance report. The compliance report should include, according to the commenter, “the number of properties and units under each category of revenue-management product” and information regarding compliance and corrective actions.
[
19
]
An annual compliance report of this nature is not necessary. Moreover, such a report would be at odds with the proposed Final Judgment's prohibitions against public disclosure of information and documents obtained pursuant to any of its provisions.
[
20
]
Disclosure would also create a risk that competitively sensitive information relating to Willow Bridge will be made public which could lead to coordination among competing landlords.
JD recommends that the proposed Final Judgment make “unmistakably clear” that structured datasets containing competitors' nonpublic information may not be accessed, used, combined, retained without controls, and require “documented segregation, access restriction, deletion or defensible inaction, and testing to prevent legacy data from entering recommendations or model training.”
[
21
]
The proposed Final Judgment already includes such a provision. Paragraph VI.C. of states that Willow Bridge must not “use or access, as part of setting rental prices or generating rental pricing recommendations for any Willow Bridge property, any External Nonpublic Data . . . including such data derived from any RealPage Revenue Management Product.”
[
22
]
JD also points to the definition of “Willow Bridge Property” and notes that it excludes “student, affordable, age-restricted or senior, and military housing.”
[
23
]
The commenter requests that if “operational differences justify particular exceptions, those exceptions should be narrowly tailored.” The United States' Complaint alleges a product market for conventional multifamily conventional housing that does not include student, age-restricted, and military housing (Doc. 47, ¶ 183). This portion of the commenter's request is therefore outside the scope of the Complaint and is not subject to Tunney Act consideration.
JD proposes that early termination of the Final Judgment by the United States should be based on a “reasoned public determination,” and involve a process that includes “public notice.”
[
24
]
The proposed Final Judgment already provides that a request for early termination would involve a public notice to the Court (and to Willow Bridge) that continuation of the Final Judgment is no longer necessary or in the public interest.
[
25
]
JD questions the proposed Final Judgment's cap of 15 employees and 60 total hours for cooperation with the litigation.
[
26
]
This comment fails to recognize that cooperation is not the only way that the United States can develop evidence. In any investigation or litigation, the United States always has procedural tools to compel the production of documents and testimony.
[
27
]
The cap in the proposed Final Judgment, which is the product of a negotiated settlement, does not in any way hamstring the United States' ability to obtain discovery in its litigation against any other defendant in this action.
Finally, JD asks why the proposed Final Judgment does not include any monetary relief.
[
28
]
The proposed Final Judgment does not provide for restitution because it is not one of the remedies sought by the United States in its Complaint.

https://www.justice.gov/​atr/​webform/​pcsf-citizen-complaint
).
V. Conclusion
After careful consideration of the public comments, the United States continues to believe that the proposed Final Judgment provides an effective and appropriate remedy for the antitrust violations alleged in the Complaint against Willow Bridge and is therefore in the public interest. The United States will move this Court to enter the proposed Final Judgment after the comments and this response are published in a manner approved by the Court, as required by
15 U.S.C. 16(d)
.

The proposed judgment contains meaningful protections. It broadly restricts the use and disclosure of competitors' nonpublic, property-specific information; limits revenue-management products that pool data across different owners; prohibits agreements with other property managers or owners to use a product; restricts price floors, automatic acceptance, and financial incentives tied to accepting recommendations; bars participation in RealPage meetings; preserves Department inspection rights; and provides contempt and cost-shifting remedies. These are material safeguards.
The public-interest question, however, is whether those safeguards can be verified and enforced across Willow Bridge's national operating footprint. The Competitive Impact Statement states that Willow Bridge manages more than 240,000 units. Against that scale, several provisions appear too dependent on self-reporting, vendor assurances, small samples, and nonpublic oversight.
1. Require Independent Technical Verification and an Initial Monitoring Period
The proposed judgment permits Willow Bridge to use a third-party revenue-management product if the provider certifies that the product meets the decree's requirements. It also appears to permit use of a RealPage product without a separate certification if a final judgment is entered against RealPage. A monitoring trustee is not automatic: monitoring is principally tied to use of an uncertified product or a judicial finding of a violation.
Vendor certification is useful evidence, but it is not independent verification. The alleged conduct involved data flows, model training, product settings, information exchanges, and operational practices that can change after a certification is issued. Reliance on a separate judgment against RealPage also does not establish that Willow Bridge's configuration and use of a product are compliant in practice.
I ask the Department to require:
—independent technical validation before initial use and after material product, model, data-source, or configuration changes;
—testing of actual data inputs, model-training data, access controls, recommendation settings, overrides, and outputs—not only review of a vendor's written representations; and
—an independent monitoring trustee for at least the first two years, with risk-based authority to examine products and practices whether or not a violation has already been proved.
If the Department believes these protections are unnecessary, its response should explain how vendor certification and a contingent monitor provide equivalent assurance.
2. Scale the Audit Program to Willow Bridge's Footprint and Risk
The proposed judgment requires an annual audit of revenue-management personnel and at least 12 randomly selected local, regional, or supervisory property-operations employees. A minimum sample of 12 employees is difficult to reconcile with a company managing more than 240,000 units. Random selection alone can also miss markets, properties, transition periods, or teams presenting the greatest risk.
The final judgment should require a statistically and operationally meaningful sample tied to the number of properties, units, markets, products, and owners involved. The sample should include risk-based selections, not merely random ones, and should test management transitions, complaints, unusual override patterns, product changes, and markets where multiple competing properties use the same software. The audit should examine owners' instructions and approvals when those instructions affect product use or pricing practices.
3. Add Public, Aggregated Compliance Reporting
The proposed judgment gives the Department access to significant nonpublic information, but it does not appear to require a public annual compliance report. Monitoring reports are generally protected from disclosure, and the public may never learn whether a monitor was appointed, what products were used, whether violations were detected, or whether corrective action occurred.
Confidential business information should remain protected. But confidentiality does not require complete public opacity. The final judgment should require an annual public report stating, in aggregated and noncommercial terms:
—the number of properties and units using each category of revenue-management product;
—the number and type of audits, technical tests, complaints, and substantiated violations;
—the general nature and completion status of corrective actions;
—whether a monitoring trustee is serving and the scope of completed review; and
—whether the Department has granted, rejected, or conditioned any request affecting compliance.
Public reporting would allow affected renters and the Court to assess whether the decree is functioning without disclosing rents, algorithms, personal data, or competitively sensitive information.
4. Clarify Legacy-Data Controls and the Housing-Category Exclusions
The proposed judgment requires Willow Bridge to identify certain structured datasets containing competitors' nonpublic information, but states that the identification provisions do not apply to data maintained in OneSite, Yardi Voyager, or other property-management software. The final judgment should make unmistakably clear that this storage-location language is not permission to access, use, combine, retain without controls, or repurpose prohibited information. It should require documented segregation, access restriction, deletion or defensible inactivation, and testing sufficient to prevent legacy data from entering recommendations or model training.
The definition of “Willow Bridge Property” also excludes student, affordable, age-restricted or senior, and military housing. The public record should explain why residents and owners in those sectors do not require the decree's core protections against competitor data exchange and cross-owner pooling. The judgment should also clarify that an otherwise conventional multifamily property is not excluded merely because individual households use tenant-based rental assistance. If operational differences justify particular exceptions, those exceptions should be narrowly tailored; the core information-sharing prohibitions should apply wherever the competitive risk exists.
5. Condition Any Early Termination on a Public Compliance Record
The proposed judgment lasts five years but permits termination after three years upon notice by the United States. Early termination should require a reasoned public determination based on completed independent testing, a record of corrective action, and the absence of unresolved material violations. The Department should provide public notice before early termination and give the Court and the public a meaningful opportunity to assess the compliance record.
(
printed page 70905)
6. Explain the Limits of the Remedy and Cooperation Provisions
The proposed judgment requires cooperation but caps voluntary interviews under that provision at 15 employees and 60 total hours. Formal discovery and civil investigative demands remain available. Even so, given the alleged duration, nationwide scope, and technical nature of the conduct, the Department should explain why those ceilings are appropriate for voluntary cooperation, or replace them with a reasonable-necessity standard.
The Competitive Impact Statement also recognizes that private parties may pursue damages and that the proposed judgment will have no prima facie effect in private litigation. The settlement contains no restitution or monetary relief for renters. I recognize that a Tunney Act review is not an individual claims process and that the Court's role is not to rewrite the government's case. Still, the Department should explain why forward-looking relief without monetary redress is adequate in light of the complaint's allegations and what public compliance information will allow potentially affected renters to understand whether the challenged practices have actually stopped.
Requested Disposition
I respectfully ask the Department to modify the proposed Final Judgment to include the safeguards above before entry. At minimum, the Department's response to public comments should address each concern with enough specificity for the Court to evaluate whether the decree's verification, transparency, duration, coverage, and cooperation provisions are adequate for a company of Willow Bridge's scale.
The decree should not depend on the public simply trusting the participants and vendors whose future conduct it is designed to constrain. Durable relief requires independent testing, proportionate auditing, limited but meaningful transparency, and a public basis for any early termination.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, DHS.
ACTION:
Notification of enforcement of regulation.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard will enforce security zones for the Protection of Military Cargo from November 8 through November 12, 2026, to provide for the security of life and vessels on navigable waterways during this event. Our regulation for Protection of Military Cargo within the Captain of the Port Zone Puget Sound, WA identifies the security zones for this event in the Blair Waterway and Sitcum Waterway in Commencement Bay, WA. During the enforcement periods, the operator of any vessel in the regulated area must comply with directions from the Captain of the Port or a designated representative.
DATES:
The regulations in
33 CFR 165.1321
will be enforced for the security zones identified in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section below for the dates and times specified.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this notification of enforcement, call or email LT Anthony Pinto, Sector Puget Sound Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 206-217-6051, email
sectorpugetsoundWWM@uscg.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Coast Guard will enforce security zones in
33 CFR 165.1321
for the Blair Waterway Security Zone (
33 CFR 165.1321(c)(1)
) and the Sitcum Waterway Security Zone ((c)(2)), for military outloads from 12:01 a.m. on November 8, 2026, through 11:59 p.m. on November 12, 2026. This action is being taken to provide for the security of life and vessels on navigable waterways during this 5-day event. Our regulation for Protection of Military Cargo within the Captain of the Port Zone Puget Sound, WA, § 165.1321, specifies the location of the regulated area for the Military Outloads which encompasses portions of the Blair Waterway and Sitcum Waterway in Commencement Bay, WA. During the enforcement periods, as reflected in § 165.1321(d), if you are the operator of a vessel in the regulated area, you must comply with directions from the Captain of the Port or any Designated Representative to enter, move within, or exit the security zones. Vessels 20 meters or greater in length should seek permission from the COTP or a Designated Representative at least 4 hours in advance. Vessels less than 20 meters in length should seek permission at least 1 hour in advance. VTS Puget Sound may be reached on VHF channel 14.
In addition to this notification of enforcement in the
Federal Register
, the Coast Guard plans to provide notification of this enforcement period via the Local Notice to Mariners.
Michael J. Hunt,
Captain, U.S. Coast Guard, Captain of the Port, Sector Puget Sound.

AGENCY:
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of denials.
SUMMARY:
FMCSA announces its decision to deny applications from 16 individuals who requested an exemption from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs) prohibiting persons with a clinical diagnosis of epilepsy or any other condition that is likely to cause a loss of consciousness or any loss of ability to operate a commercial motor vehicle (CMV) from operating CMVs in interstate commerce.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ms. Christine A. Hydock, Chief, Medical Programs Division, FMCSA, DOT, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001; (202) 366-4001;
fmcsamedical@dot.gov
.
Office hours are from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation
A. Viewing Comments
To view comments, go to
www.regulations.gov
.
Insert the docket number, (FMCSA-2026-0036) in the keyword box and click “Search.” Next, choose the only notice listed, and click “Browse Comments.” If you do not have access to the internet, you may view the docket online by visiting Dockets Operations in Room W58-213 of the DOT West Building, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
B. Privacy Act
In accordance with
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(6)
, DOT solicits comments from the public on the exemption requests. DOT posts these comments, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov
,
as described in the system of records notice DOT/ALL-14 FDMS (Federal Docket Management System), which can be reviewed under the “Department Wide System of Records Notices” link at
https://www.transportation.gov/​individuals/​privacy/​privacy-act-system-records-notices
.
The comments are posted without edit and are searchable by the name of the submitter.
II. Legal Basis
FMCSA has authority under
49 U.S.C. 31136(e)
and
31315(b)
to grant exemptions from the FMCSRs. FMCSA must publish a notice of each exemption request in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(a)
). The Agency must provide the public an opportunity to inspect the information relevant to the application, including the applicant's safety analysis. The Agency must provide an opportunity for public comment on the request.
The Agency reviews the application, safety analyses, and public comments submitted and determines whether granting the exemption would likely achieve a level of safety equivalent to, or greater than, the level of safety that would be achieved absent such exemption, pursuant to the standard set forth in
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(1)
. The Agency must publish its decision in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(b)
). If granted, the notice will identify the regulatory provision from which the applicant will be exempt, the effective period, and all terms and conditions of
(
printed page 70981)
the exemption (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(1)
). If the exemption is denied, the notice will explain the reason for the denial (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(2)
). The exemption may be renewed (
49 CFR 381.300(b)
).
III. Background
The physical qualification standard for drivers regarding seizures and loss of consciousness provides that a person is physically qualified to drive a CMV if that person has “no established medical history or clinical diagnosis of epilepsy or any other condition which is likely to cause the loss of consciousness or any loss of ability to control” a CMV (
49 CFR 391.41(b)(8)
). To assist in applying this standard, FMCSA publishes guidance for medical examiners (MEs) in the form of medical advisory criteria in Appendix A to 49 CFR part 391.
[
1
]
In 2007, FMCSA published recommendations from a Medical Expert Panel (MEP) that FMCSA tasked to review the existing seizure disorder guidelines for MEs.
[
2
]
The MEP performed a comprehensive, systematic literature review, including evidence available at the time. The MEP issued recommended criteria to evaluate whether an individual with a history of epilepsy, a single unprovoked seizure, or a provoked seizure should be allowed to drive a CMV.
On January 15, 2013, FMCSA began granting exemptions, on a case-by-case basis, to individual drivers from the physical qualification standard regarding seizures and loss of consciousness in
49 CFR 391.41(b)(8)
(
78 FR 3069
). The Agency considers the medical advisory criteria, the 2007 MEP recommendations, and each individual's medical information and driving record in deciding whether to grant the exemption.
On March 17, 2026, FMCSA published a notice announcing receipt of applications from 17 individuals requesting an exemption from the epilepsy and seizure disorders prohibition in
49 CFR 391.41(b)(8)
and requested comments from the public (
91 FR 12893
). The public comment period ended on April 16, 2026, and five comments were received.
IV. Discussion of Comments
FMCSA received five comments on these exemption applications. One commenter advocated balanced and individualized regulations that prioritize both public safety and the equal opportunity for individuals to drive when their seizures are well-managed. In response to this comment, FMCSA finds that its seizure exemption process adequately balances the Agency's mission of improving public safety on the nation's roadways with the opportunity for otherwise ineligible individuals to present evidence of why they should nonetheless be permitted to drive CMVs.
Two comments were in support of granting an exemption to Mr. Sparkman and one comment was in support of granting an exemption to Donte Watkins, both listed in this notice. Although FMCSA received comments in support of Mr. Sparkman's and Mr. Watkins' Federal seizure exemption applications, FMCSA evaluates each application considering the medical advisory criteria, the 2007 MEP recommendations, and each individual's medical information and driving record in deciding whether to grant the exemption as stated above. In both cases, the information provided in the comments did not alter FMCSA's evaluation of the medical evidence the individuals submitted with their applications.
The last comment was out of scope for this notice.
V. Basis for Exemption Determination
The Agency conducted an individualized assessment of each applicant's medical information, including the root cause of the respective seizure(s) and medical information about the applicant's seizure history, the length of time that has elapsed since the individual's last seizure, the stability of each individual's treatment regimen, and the duration of time on or off of anti-seizure medication. In addition, the Agency reviewed the treating clinician's medical opinion related to the ability of the driver to safely operate a CMV with a seizure history and each applicant's certified driving record from their State Driver Licensing Agency (SDLA). The information obtained from each applicant's driving record provides the Agency with details regarding any moving violations or reported crash data, which demonstrates whether the driver has a safe driving history and is an indicator of future driving performance. If the driving record revealed a crash, FMCSA requested and reviewed the related police reports and other relevant documents, such as the citation and conviction information. A summary of each applicant's seizure history was discussed in the March 17, 2026,
Federal Register
notice (
91 FR 12893
) and will not be repeated in this notice.
VI. Conclusion
Based upon its evaluation of the 17 exemption applications, FMCSA has determined that the following 16 applicants do not satisfy the eligibility criteria or meet the terms and conditions of the Federal exemption and granting these exemptions would not provide a level of safety that would be equivalent to, or greater than, the level of safety that would be obtained by complying with
49 CFR 391.41(b)(8)
. Therefore, the 16 applicants in this notice have been denied exemptions from the physical qualification standards in
49 CFR 391.41(b)(8)
.
Each applicant has, prior to this notice, received a letter of final disposition regarding his or her exemption request. Those decision letters fully outlined the basis for the denial and constitute final action by the Agency. This notice summarizes the Agency's recent denials as required under
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(6)(c)
by publishing names and reasons for denial.
The following 16 applicants do not meet the minimum time requirement for being seizure-free, either on or off anti-seizure medication:

Kyle Benner (PA)
Devin Brockington (MD)
Wendy Cook (OR)
Caedmon Cunningham (KS)
Steven Ernest (ME)
Chauncy Gibson (GA)
Matthew Heller (NY)
Michael S. Miller (CA)
Michael George Murray (NY)
Brandon Petruzzi (MA)
Scott Pontious (OH)

Ryen Seyfried (NY)
Jeffrey Sparkman (KY)
Donte Watkins (NC)

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This action, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
, proposes to amend regulations issued to carry out a marketing order as defined in
7 CFR 900.2(j)
. This proposed rule is issued under the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, as amended (
7 U.S.C. 601-674
) (the Act), amending Marketing Order No. 986 (
7 CFR part 986
) (the Order), which regulates the handling of pecans grown in Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Mexico, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Texas. The Council locally administers the Order and is comprised of growers and handlers of pecans operating within the production area, as well as one accumulator member and one public member.
This proposed action is exempt from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) review process required by
Executive Order 12866
. This proposed rule would amend existing Marketing Order No. 986, as amended (
7 CFR part 986
), “Pecans Grown in the States of Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Mexico, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Texas,” and is necessary for the continued operation of the Order. Additionally, this proposed action is exempt from the requirements of
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” pursuant to section 5(c).
This proposed rule has been reviewed under
Executive Order 13175
, “Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments,” which requires Federal agencies to consider whether their rulemaking actions would have Tribal implications. The Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS) has determined this proposed rule is unlikely to have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes.
This proposed rule has been reviewed under
Executive Order 12988
, “Civil Justice Reform.” This proposed rule is not intended to have a retroactive effect.
This proposed rule would eliminate regional and size designations for sheller members, modify the nomination process for sheller members, adjust the requirements of the inter-handler transfer report form, and establish a late fee and interest charges for unpaid assessments. In addition, this proposed rule would make administrative corrections to §  986.178 to remove an inadvertently duplicated paragraph and a paragraph that was previously incorporated under §  986.177(b).
Section 986.45 of the Order establishes Council membership, with two sheller seats currently allocated to each of the three regions as defined in § 986.33: Eastern, Central, and Western. Section 986.45(b)(2) provides that each region is represented by two sheller seats, with one seat allocated to a sheller who handles more than 12.5 million pounds of pecans per year, and one seat allocated to a sheller handling 12.5 million pounds or less of pecans per year. Each member has an alternate. Section 986.45(c) also authorizes the Council to recommend, with the approval of the Secretary, changes to the requirements for grower and sheller seats to accommodate changes within the industry.
Section 986.46 of the Order outlines the nomination procedures for the Council and § 986.46(b)(8) authorizes the Council to recommend, subject to the approval of the Secretary, changes to the member nomination process. Section 986.58 authorizes the Council to recommend, with the approval of the Secretary, reapportionment and reestablishment of the regions specified in § 986.33.
The Council and Order's activities are funded through handler assessments as authorized in § 986.61. Each handler in the production area pays a pro rata share based on their weight of inshell pecans handled. Section 986.61(g) authorizes the Council, with the approval of the Secretary, to establish a late payment and/or interest charge when assessments are not paid on time. The current assessment rates and due
(
printed page 70810)
dates are codified in §§ 986.161 and 986.177, respectively, of the Order's rules and regulations. Assessments are due at the time of reporting and monthly reports are due on the 10th day of the month following the month the pecans were handled.
Section 986.62 provides for the inter-handler transfers of pecans and allows for the transferring handler to shift the reporting and payment of assessments for these pecans to the receiving handler. Under § 986.162, handlers are required to file reports the month following the first transfer between two handlers to indicate a transfer was completed during the season, regardless of the frequency of transfers or weight transferred.
Pursuant to the authorities listed above, the Council recommended revising the rules and regulations under the Order. The Council met on August 14, 2025, and unanimously recommended, with a vote of 14 in favor and none opposed, to eliminate the regional and size designation requirements for sheller seats and modify the nomination process to reflect these changes; to revise the inter-handler transfer report from an annual to monthly submission and include information on the weight and type of inshell of pecans transferred; and to establish a five percent one-time late fee for unpaid assessments and a one percent monthly interest charge on any outstanding balances. The Council recommended these changes to increase sheller representation on the Council, improve data collection accuracy, and encourage timely payment of assessments.
During the original promulgation of the Order in 2016 (
81 FR 51298
, August 4, 2016), representative membership was a principal issue. As a result, Council membership structure was established to represent distinctive production areas as well as maintain a balance between grower and handler interests. To represent handlers, the Order included six regional seats for shellers and one at-large seat for accumulators. Understanding the dynamic nature of the industry, the Order included provisions for reapportionment and reestablishment if needed in the future.
Since the current membership requirements were established in 2016, the pecan industry has experienced consolidation and change, particularly among shelling operations. As of August 2025, fewer than 30 shellers remain in business, down from 50 in 2016. Due to the decline in the number of shellers, the Council has experienced challenges filling sheller member positions during its nomination cycles, resulting in several vacancies on the Council over the last few years.
When sheller seat vacancies occur, the Council believes it lacks the benefit of additional perspectives in its deliberations. The Council considered solutions to resolve the issue of sheller vacancies, including reducing the weight of inshell pecans required to be considered a large sheller. However, after reviewing the breakdown of active shellers, the Council determined this adjustment would not fully address the problem and that there would still be a shortage of eligible shellers to fill available seats.
At the August 14, 2025, meeting, the Council indicated that many of the remaining shellers now source pecans from multiple regions, operating multiple facilities with some in multiple regions. These changes make the regional affiliations for sheller members required under the Order less applicable. Further, the distribution of shellers throughout the regions is not uniform, making filling seats in some regions more challenging.
During its discussions, the Council also determined that the large and small designations on the sheller seats reduced the number of candidates available for nomination. Because there are fewer large shellers than small, the Council reported that it was difficult finding enough large shellers to fill all the available large sheller member and alternate seats. Consequently, the Council determined that the three regions and size distinctions are no longer representative of the sheller portion of the industry and impede the Council's nominations process.
Accordingly, this proposal would combine the three sheller regions into one sheller region, which would consist of all states within the production area, and remove the large and small sheller seat allocations. All six sheller seats would be open to any qualified sheller, regardless of location or size. This is similar to the accumulator seat on the Council, which is an at-large position that is not limited by location or size. The Council believes these proposed changes would help increase participation on the Council and ensure full sheller representation. During Council discussions on August 14, 2025, it was noted the National Pecan Shellers Association had also expressed support for the proposal.
Implementing these changes would require changes to the sheller member nomination process. Therefore, this proposal would adjust the nomination process to reflect one region with six sheller member seats and six alternate seats. All shellers would be able to nominate and vote on all seats regardless of their size or location. To implement this proposed change, the Council also recommended staggering the initial terms of the new sheller seats, with half serving two-year terms of office and the other half serving the full four-year term of office, so that half of the sheller seats will be up for nomination every two years. Accordingly, this proposed rule would add §§ 986.145 and 986.146 to the administrative provisions under the Order's rules and regulations to establish a single region for sheller seats and a modified nomination process, respectively.
Because the grower segment of industry has not experienced the same level of changes that the sheller segment has, these changes would pertain solely to the sheller seats and nomination process. Thus, the proposal would not redefine the existing regions for growers or modify the grower nomination qualifications and process.
The Order also authorizes specific reporting requirements, with handlers reporting pecans received, shipped, and in inventory to the Council to provide valuable aggregated data to the industry. Assessments are paid according to the reports of pecans received by handlers. The Order's inter-handler transfer provisions allow handlers to shift responsibility for reporting and payment of assessments to another handler when transferring loads of pecans. Having this flexibility has been particularly useful for small entities selling to larger handlers.
The inter-handler transfer provides a way to document the transfer of pecans, ensure transferred pecans are reported as received, and that the associated assessments are paid. Council members agreed these provisions are useful to handlers of all sizes, particularly when lots of pecans need to be redistributed to meet customer needs. Without this record, it would be difficult for the Council to verify which pecans have already been reported and assessed.
Currently, the Order requires the inter-handler transfer form, APC Form #4, to be submitted once during the season, in the month following the initial transfer between the handlers involved. In practice, however, the Council reported the submission of this report is frequently delayed. This creates difficulty for the Council when verifying assessments due and completing handler compliance audits, as there may have been transfers that have not yet been reported. Further, because the current reporting requirement does not include the weight
(
printed page 70811)
or type of inshell pecans transferred, the Council must conduct additional follow-up with handlers to determine if the proper assessments are being paid and to ensure the transferred pecans are not being overreported when tracking industry inventory.
During discussions on the issue, the Council reflected on the original intent of the inter-handler transfer report and determined that a monthly report documenting the handler parties involved, as well as the weight and type of inshell pecans transferred, would ensure proper and more accurate accounting of pecans handled and assessments paid. The Council anticipates this proposed change to § 986.162 would enable handlers to better maintain complete records, as required under the Order, as well as assist Council staff in identifying reporting discrepancies. Additionally, because transfers typically occur from November to February, for many handlers, this monthly reporting requirement would only apply to about four months of the year. The Council also noted that the proposed change would not be overly burdensome for handlers and their operations, as the report is completed using readily available information. Accordingly, on August 14, 2025, the Council unanimously recommended making the inter-handler transfer report due monthly and requiring that the weight and type of inshell pecans transferred be reported.
Regarding the timely payment of assessments, the Council reported that some handlers are repeatedly late in paying assessments. Chronic late payments increase administrative burden, disrupt cash flow, and force the Council to devote additional staff resources to collections. Currently, there are no consequences for late payments unless a full compliance case is filed with USDA for consideration of civil penalties, as would be warranted and appropriate under the Act. Although it does not wish to create a financial burden on the industry, the Council believes it is unfair to handlers paying on time to allow handlers who are late submitting their payments to incur no penalty.
To address this, the Council discussed adding a five percent one-time late fee for each occurrence of unpaid assessments that are 30 days past due, as well as a one percent monthly interest charge on the outstanding balance until paid. While late payment penalties and interest fees might be more burdensome on small handlers that are already experiencing cash flow problems, just as assessments are based on a pro rata share of the program's cost, the Council believes the proposed penalties should also apply proportionally. While it is an additional cost, the Council agreed this type of penalty would ensure fairness for all handlers, promote on-time assessment payments, and reduce Council resources spent managing delinquent handlers. The proposed late fee and interest charge would also be consistent with those in place for the industry's Federal research and promotion program. After discussing various options, including extending the allowable payment period, the Council unanimously recommended on August 14, 2025, implementing a five percent one-time late fee for each occurrence of assessments that are 30 days past due and a one percent monthly interest charge on the outstanding balance until paid. These requirements would be codified in a new § 986.163 of the Order's administrative provisions.
Additionally, this rule would also make administrative corrections to §  986.178. A final rule published in the
Federal Register
on April 8, 2020 (
85 FR 19651
,
19654
), made changes to several reporting requirements prescribed under the Order, and inadvertently duplicated a paragraph in §  986.178 and failed to remove language from this section that was incorporated under §  986.177(b). This rule would remove paragraph (b) from §  986.178, which was inadvertently duplicated from paragraph (a) in the section, as well as remove paragraph (c), which was previously consolidated under §  986.177(b). These corrections are administrative in nature and would not have an effect on the other changes proposed in this rulemaking and would not alter reporting requirements.
Therefore, this proposed rule would revise the rules and regulations under the Order by eliminating the regional and size designation requirements for sheller seats and modifying the nomination process to reflect these changes; revising the inter-handler transfer report from an annual to monthly submission and to include information on the weight and type of inshell pecans transferred; and establishing a five percent one-time late fee for unpaid assessments and a one percent monthly interest charge on any outstanding balances. The proposal would also include administrative corrections to §  986.178 to remove an inadvertently duplicated paragraph and a paragraph that was previously incorporated under §  986.177(b).
Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis
Pursuant to requirements set forth in the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
), AMS has considered the economic impact of this proposed rule on small entities. Accordingly, AMS has prepared this initial regulatory flexibility analysis.
The purpose of the RFA is to fit regulatory actions to the scale of businesses subject to such actions in order that small businesses will not be unduly or disproportionately burdened. Marketing orders issued pursuant to the Act are unique regulations in that they are brought about through group action of typically small entities acting on their own behalf.
There are approximately 4,500 growers of pecans in the production area and approximately 110 handlers subject to regulation under the Order. At the time this analysis was prepared, the Small Business Administration (SBA) defined small agricultural growers as those having annual receipts equal to or less than $3,750,000 (North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code 111335, Tree Nut Farming) (
13 CFR 121.201
). Small agricultural service firms a were defined by the SBA as those having annual receipts equal to or less than $34,000,000 (NAICS code 115114, Postharvest Crop Activities).
Based on data from the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), the average annual grower price for pecans utilized for processing during the 2023-2024 season was approximately $1.77 per pound. With a total utilization of 264,980,000 pounds for the 2023-2024 fiscal year, the total 2023-2024 value of the crop utilized for processing is estimated at $469,014,600 ($1.77 per pound multiplied by $264,980,000 pounds). Dividing the crop value by the estimated number of pecan growers yields an estimated average receipt per grower of $104,225 ($469,014,600 divided by 4,500 pecan growers). Thus, the majority of growers would be classified as small entities.
Based on AMS Market News shipping point and terminal market data for 2024 and 2025, AMS has determined a grower to handler price markup estimate of 25 percent. Adding this margin to the average grower price of $1.77 for in-shell pecans yields an estimated handler price of $2.21 per pound ($1.77 per pound multiplied by 0.25 equals $0.44, added to $1.77). With a total 2023-2024 utilization of 264,980,000 pounds, the total value of handled pecans for the fiscal year was $585,605,800 ($2.21 per pound multiplied by 264,980,000 pounds). Dividing this figure by the number of
(
printed page 70812)
handlers yields an estimated average annual handler receipt of $5,323,689 ($585,605,800 divided by 110 pecan handlers). Thus, the majority of handlers would be classified as small entities.
This proposed rule would eliminate regional and size designations for sheller members, modify the nomination process for sheller members, adjust the requirements of the inter-handler transfer report form, and establish a late fee and interest charges for unpaid assessments. In addition, this proposed rule would include administrative corrections to §  986.178 to remove an inadvertently duplicated paragraph and a paragraph that was previously incorporated under §  986.177(b). At its August 14, 2025, meeting, the Council unanimously voted 14 in favor, and none opposed to recommend the proposed changes.
Apart from imposing late fees and interest charges for unpaid assessments, it is not anticipated that this proposed rule would result in any additional cost for the industry. This proposed rule would combine the three sheller regions into one region and remove the designated seats for small and large shellers. While this proposal would modify the nomination process for sheller seats, it would not prohibit any qualified sheller, regardless of size or location, from seeking nomination on the Council. The Council believes this change would help increase sheller representation and participation and create opportunities for more shellers to serve on the Council. Grower seats and regions would remain unchanged.
The proposed rule would also modify the reporting requirements for inter-handler transfers. Rather than be submitted annually, the report would instead be submitted monthly and would include the weight and type of inshell pecans transferred. While this could increase the reporting burden for some handlers, this change would contribute to ensuring the Council's monthly industry reports are accurate and assist with program compliance, which would be beneficial to the industry. Additionally, because transfers typically occur from November to February, the monthly reporting requirement for handlers would apply to about four months of the year. The Council also noted that the proposed change would not be overly burdensome for handlers and their operations, as the report is completed using readily available information. The Council anticipates this change would enable handlers to better maintain complete records, as required under the Order, as well as assist Council staff in identifying reporting discrepancies.
Finally, the proposed rule would add a five percent one-time late fee on assessments that are more than 30 days past due and a one percent monthly interest charge on the outstanding balance until paid. However, these additional costs would only apply to those handlers who are not timely complying with the Order's assessment requirements. Handler assessments represent a pro rata share of the costs of operating the Order and are applied based on the weight of inshell pecans handled. Similarly, the penalties for delinquent assessments would be proportional to the weight of inshell of pecans handled and assessments due. The Council anticipates that establishing these penalties would help deter nonpayment of assessments.
The Council considered alternatives to the recommended changes made at its August 14, 2025, meeting. Regarding sheller membership, the Council previously recommended removing the regional distinctions but leaving the large and small seat designations. However, Council records indicated such a change would not solve the issue of repeated vacancies, as few remaining shellers meet the large sheller definition.
In reviewing the inter-handler transfer provisions, the Council considered removing the inter-handler transfer reporting requirement altogether but determined that small handlers may have difficulty complying with the additional reporting and tracking of assessments due on their own. The Council also considered leaving the report unchanged but found with more frequent reporting and the inclusion of the weight and type of inshell pecans transferred, the Council could improve its compliance processes and industry reports.
When discussing penalties for delinquent assessments, the Council considered changing the due dates for assessments, applying a longer period before assessing penalties, or not taking any additional action. However, the Council determined that these alternatives would not encourage timely payments or resolve the issue of unpaid assessments. For these reasons, the Council rejected all other alternatives.
Council meetings are widely publicized throughout the pecan industry. All interested persons are invited to attend meetings and participate in Council deliberations. Like all Council meetings, the August 14, 2025, meeting was a public meeting and all entities, both large and small, were able to express their views on these issues. Finally, interested persons are invited to submit comments on this proposed rule, including the regulatory and informational impacts of this action on small businesses.
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. chapter 35
), the Order's information collection requirements have been previously approved by OMB and assigned OMB No. 0581-0291, “Federal Marketing Order for Pecans.” This proposed rule would require changes to the Council's existing forms. Specifically, the proposed rule would make nominal adjustments to two sheller nomination forms, Forms SC-308 and SC-310, and the inter-handler transfer form, APC Form #4. The proposed changes to the sheller nomination forms would not increase the reporting burden. For the inter-handler transfer report, the changes would be minor and the currently approved burden for the form would be minimally increased by the proposed changes. The revised forms have been submitted to OMB for approval.
This proposed rule, if finalized, may impose some additional reporting or recordkeeping requirements on either small or large pecan handlers. However, the Council anticipates the changes to APC Form #4 and the inter-handler transfer reporting requirements would help ensure the Council's monthly industry reports are accurate and assist with program compliance, which would be beneficial to the industry. Additionally, because transfers typically occur from November to February, for many handlers, this monthly reporting requirement would only apply to about four months of the year. The Council also noted that the proposed change would not be overly burdensome for handlers and their operations, as the report is completed using readily available information. The Council anticipates this change would enable handlers to better maintain complete records, as required under the Order, as well as assist Council staff in identifying reporting discrepancies. As with all Federal marketing order programs, reports and forms are periodically reviewed to reduce information requirements and duplication by industry and public sector agencies.
AMS is committed to complying with the E-Government Act to promote the use of the internet and other information technologies to provide increased opportunities for citizen access to Government information and services and for other purposes.
AMS has not identified any relevant Federal rules that duplicate, overlap, or conflict with this proposed rule.
(
printed page 70813)
After consideration of all relevant material presented, including the information and recommendations submitted by the Council and other available information, AMS has determined that this proposed rule would be consistent with and would effectuate the purposes of the Act.
A 30-day comment period is provided to allow interested persons to respond to this proposed rule. All written comments timely received will be considered before a final determination is made on this action.
