AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Proposed rule, request for comments.
SUMMARY:
NMFS proposes to amend regulations that prohibit commercial fishing in the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument Expansion (PRIMNM Expansion), which comprises waters of the U.S. exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between 50 to 200 nautical miles (nmi; 93 to 370 kilometers (km)) around Johnston Atoll and Wake and Jarvis Islands. This action is necessary to conform fishing regulations with Presidential Proclamation 10918 of April 17, 2025—Unleashing American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific, as amended by Presidential Proclamation 11035 of June 11, 2026—Restoring American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific, and in light of a court order. Fisheries in the PRIMNM Expansion would be regulated pursuant to existing fishing regulations under the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act), the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Convention Implementation Act (WCPFCIA), the South Pacific Tuna Act (SPTA), and other applicable laws, that apply to all U.S. commercial fishing vessels but were superseded and made inapplicable when the commercial fishing prohibition for the PRIMNM Expansion was established. The proposed rule supports the long-term sustainability of U.S. fisheries and provides for the proper care and management of the PRIMNM and PRIMNM Expansion and the objects of historic or scientific interest therein, as directed by Proclamation 10918, as amended by Proclamation 11035.
DATES:
NMFS must receive comments by December 9, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
A plain language summary of this proposed rule is available at
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​NOAA-NMFS-2026-2410
.
You may submit comments on this document, identified by NOAA-NMFS-2026-2410, by either of the following methods:
Electronic Submission:
Submit all electronic public comments via the Federal e-Rulemaking Portal. Visit
https://www.regulations.gov
and type NOAA-NMFS-2026-2410 in the Search box, Click the “Comment” icon, complete the required fields, and enter or attach your comments.
Mail:
Submit written comments to Sarah Malloy, Regional Administrator, NMFS Pacific Islands Regional Office (PIRO), 1845 Wasp Blvd. Bldg. 176, Honolulu, HI 96818.
Instructions:
Comments sent by any other method, to any other address or individual, or received after the end of the comment period, may not be considered by NMFS. All comments received are a part of the public record and will generally be posted for public viewing on
https://www.regulations.gov
without change. All personal identifying information (
e.g.,
name, address), confidential business information, or otherwise sensitive information submitted voluntarily by the sender will be publicly accessible. NMFS will accept anonymous comments (enter “N/A” in the required fields if you wish to remain anonymous). NMFS has voluntarily prepared an environmental assessment (EA) that discusses the impact on the quality of the human environment as a result of this proposed rule and the resumption of commercial fishing under applicable regulations in PRIMNM Expansion. The EA, and other supporting documents referenced in this rule are available at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jarad Makaiau, NMFS PIRO Sustainable Fisheries, 808-725-5000.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Since the 1980s, NMFS and the Western Pacific Fishery Management Council (Council) have managed fisheries in the U.S. EEZ in the Western Pacific through five species-based fishery management plans (FMP) consistent with the provisions of the Magnuson-Stevens Act—the Bottomfish and Seamount Groundfish FMP, the Crustaceans FMP, the Precious Corals FMP, the Coral Reef Ecosystems FMP, and the Pelagic FMP. Pursuant to section 303(a) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, an FMP, FMP amendment and the issuance of implementing regulations, or modification to regulations under section 303(c) are undertaken when necessary and appropriate for the conservation and management of the fishery to prevent overfishing and rebuild overfished stocks, and to protect, restore, and promote the long-term health and stability of the fishery, consistent with the Magnuson-Stevens Act's National Standards. NMFS, in cooperation with the Council, implements or amends FMP regulations that prevent overfishing while achieving on a continuing basis the optimum yield from each fishery for the U.S. fishing industry when the best scientific information available indicate it is necessary or appropriate.
In 2009, the Council recommended, and NMFS approved the restructuring of the five species-based FMPs by incorporating the conservation and management measures of the species-based FMPs into five place-based fishery ecosystem plans (FEP)—the American Samoa FEP, the Hawaii FEP, the Marianas FEP, the Pacific Remote Islands Area FEP (PRIA FEP) and the Pelagics FEP (
75 FR 2198
, January 14, 2010). In developing these FEPs, NMFS also prepared an environmental impact statement that evaluated the potential environmental effects of fishing under the five place-based FEPs.
The PRIA FEP governs fishing in the U.S. EEZ (0 to 200 nmi; 0 to 370 km) around the Pacific Remote Island Areas (PRIA) of Baker, Jarvis, Wake and Howland Islands, Kingman Reef, and Johnston and Palmyra Atolls and establishes conservation and management measures for coral reef fish, bottomfish, crustacean, and precious coral fisheries, including permit and reporting requirements, marine protected areas, gear restrictions, at-sea observer requirements and other measures to ensure sustainable fishing. Since 2010, the PRIA FEP has been amended three times and NMFS has evaluated the potential environmental effects of fishing under the amended FEP consistent with the Magnuson-Stevens Act, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and other applicable laws.
Similarly, the Pelagics FEP establishes conservation and management measures for pelagic fisheries and includes limited access programs, gear restrictions, protected species mitigation measures, prohibited area management and other measures to ensure sustainable fishing. Since 2010, the Pelagics FEP has been amended 12 times and NMFS has evaluated the potential environmental effects of
(
printed page 70828)
fishing under the amended FEP consistent with the Magnuson-Stevens Act, NEPA, ESA and other applicable laws. Regulations implementing the PRIA FEP and Pelagics FEP are found at
50 CFR part 665 subparts E
and
F
, respectively. General Magnuson-Steven Act regulations prohibiting the use of any gear or participation in a fishery not on the list of authorized fisheries and gear under a fishery management plan are also found at
50 CFR 600.725
.
In addition, U.S. fisheries for highly migratory species (HMS), including tunas and billfish in the U.S. EEZ around the PRIA, and on the adjacent high seas are also subject to regulations implementing the WCPFCIA, the SPTA and other applicable laws. Regulations implementing conservation and management measures pursuant to these Acts are found in
50 CFR 300 subparts D
and
O
, respectively. When these regulations were codified, NMFS likewise evaluated the potential environmental effects of fishing for HMS consistent with the WCPFCIA, the SPTA, NEPA, ESA and other applicable laws.
On January 6, 2009, Presidential Proclamation 8336 established the PRIMNM for the purpose of protecting objects of historic or scientific interest identified in the proclamation, including corals, fish, shellfish, marine mammals, seabirds, water birds, land birds, insects, and vegetation not found elsewhere (
74 FR 1565
, January 12, 2009). At that time, the PRIMNM comprised the waters and submerged and emergent lands of Wake Island, Baker Island, Howland Island, Jarvis Island, Johnston Atoll, Kingman Reef, and Palmyra Atoll seaward to a distance approximately 50 nmi (93 km) from the mean low water line around each island, reef, and atoll. Proclamation 8336 directed the Secretaries of Commerce and the Interior to prohibit commercial fishing within the boundaries of the PRIMNM and authorized the Secretaries to permit non-commercial fishing, including recreational fishing in the PRIMNM. The proclamation also directed the Secretaries to take appropriate action pursuant to their respective authorities under the Antiquities Act and the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and such other authorities as may be available to implement this proclamation, to regulate fisheries, and to provide for the proper care and management of the monument. Proclamation 8336 had the effect of making the existing regulations authorizing and regulating sustainable commercial fishing in the U.S. EEZ in the PRIMNM inapplicable (
50 CFR 665 subparts E
and
F
). The Council did not, however, recommend nor did NMFS take action to amend those regulations, and they remain codified in the Code of Federal Regulations.
On June 3, 2013, NMFS published a final rule establishing requirements for fishing in the PRIMNM (
78 FR 32996
). Specifically, the final rule added regulatory provisions to codify the non-discretionary prohibition on commercial fishing and established new management measures for non-commercial fishing, including recreational fishing, including permit and reporting requirements and other discretionary measures NMFS, with input from the Council, deemed necessary and appropriate to regulate non-commercial fishing in the PRIMNM (
78 FR 32996
, June 3, 2013;
78 FR 39583
, July 2, 2013).
On September 25, 2014, Presidential Proclamation 9173 expanded the boundaries of the PRIMNM around Wake Island, Johnston Atoll, and Jarvis Island to the seaward limit of the U.S. EEZ to establish the PRIMNM Expansion (
79 FR 58645
, September 29, 2014). The purpose of the PRIMNM Expansion was to provide an expanded area for the protection of objects of scientific interest identified in the proclamation, including seamounts, deep sea corals, sea turtles, seabirds, and other migratory species. Proclamation 9173 directed the Secretaries of Commerce and the Interior to prohibit commercial fishing within the boundaries of the PRIMNM Expansion and authorized the Secretaries to permit non-commercial fishing and provide a process to ensure recreational fishing continues to be managed as a sustainable activity in the PRIMNM and PRIMNM Expansion. The proclamation also directed the Secretaries to take appropriate action pursuant to their respective authorities under the Antiquities Act and the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and such other authorities as may be available to implement the proclamation, to regulate fisheries, and to provide for the proper care and management of the monument. Proclamation 9173 had the effect of making the existing regulations authorizing and regulating sustainable commercial fishing in the U.S. EEZ in the PRIMNM Expansion inapplicable (
50 CFR 665 subparts E
and
F
). The Council did not, however, recommend nor did NMFS take action to amend those regulations, and they also remain codified in the Code of Federal Regulations.
On March 25, 2015, NMFS published a final rule establishing requirements for fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion (
80 FR 15694
). Specifically, the final rule added regulatory provisions to codify the non-discretionary prohibition on commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion and established new management measures for non-commercial fishing, including recreational fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion, including permit and reporting requirements among other discretionary measures NMFS, with input from the Council, deemed necessary and appropriate to regulate non-commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion.
On April 17, 2025, Presidential Proclamation 10918—Unleashing American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific (
90 FR 16987
, April 22, 2025) provided that a prohibition on commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion “is not, at this time, necessary for the proper care and management of the Monument or the objects of historic or scientific interest therein” and declared the “section entitled `Management of the Marine National Monument' in Proclamation 9173 is deleted and replaced” with a provision that includes direction that the Secretary of Commerce not prohibit commercial fishing. Specifically, Proclamation 10918 provides: “Between 50 to 200 nautical miles from the landward boundaries of the Monument, the Secretary of Commerce shall not prohibit commercial fishing within the boundaries of the Monument and the Monument Expansion in those areas where the Monument and Monument Expansion is coterminous with the Exclusive Economic Zone of the United States.” Proclamation 10918 also directed the Secretaries of Commerce and the Interior to take appropriate action pursuant to their respective authorities under the Antiquities Act, the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and such other authorities as may be available to implement the proclamation, to regulate fisheries, and to provide for the proper care and management of the PRIMNM Expansion.
On April 25, 2025, due to inquiries from the regulated fishing industry on whether fishermen could fish in the PRIMNM Expansion given Proclamation 10918, NMFS issued a letter to the regulated community notifying fishermen that regulations implementing the prohibition on commercial fishing in Proclamation 9173 are no longer effective. NMFS further indicated it planned to expeditiously initiate rulemaking to bring fishing regulations into compliance with Proclamation 9173 as amended by Proclamation 10918. NMFS's letter was subsequently challenged in court by various
(
printed page 70829)
individuals and environmental groups in
Kapa'a
v.
Trump,
794 F. Supp. 3d 793 (D. Haw. 2025). The U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii found the plaintiffs were “entitled to participate in a notice and comment” process on whether commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion would be appropriately managed to provide for the proper care and management of monument resources (
Kapa'a,
794 F. Supp. 3d at 823).
At its 206th meeting held March 24-26, 2026, in Honolulu, the Council considered management alternatives to amend fisheries regulations at
50 CFR part 665
to restore commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion consistent with Presidential Proclamation 10918. Before making final recommendations, the Council provided opportunity for public testimony and comment (
91 FR 11046
, March 6, 2026). The public comments received reflected both support and opposition to the resumption of commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion.
After considering public comments, the Council recommended revising commercial fishing prohibitions to authorize commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion subject to the regulatory requirements that had been superseded and made inapplicable by commercial fishing prohibitions established in Presidential Proclamation 9173.
Before the Council transmitted its proposed regulations for Secretarial review pursuant to Section 303(c) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, on June 11, 2026, the President issued Proclamation 11035, “Restoring American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific,” (
91 FR 36741
, June 17, 2026). Proclamation 11035 amended Proclamation 10918 “to clarify that the proclamation itself removes monument-based prohibitions on commercial fishing and agency rulemaking is intended to amend or repeal inconsistent regulations.” Accordingly, NMFS has no discretion and must “amend or repeal existing regulations that are inconsistent with this proclamation's removal of monument-based prohibitions on commercial fishing” (
91 FR 36742
, June 17, 2026). Thus, notice and comment rulemaking to amend monument-based prohibitions on commercial fishing would not be necessary. However, out of an abundance of caution and in light of an Order by the U.S. District Court for the District of Hawaii in
Kapa'a
v.
Trump,
NMFS is providing the public with prior notice and an opportunity to comment on this proposed rule. NMFS is also requesting public comment on whether the resumption of commercial fishing under the Council and NMFS's existing regulations and restrictions provide for the proper care and management of the PRIMNM and monument resources, consistent with Proclamation 10918.
Consistent with the directives in Proclamations 10918, as amended by Proclamation 11035, this proposed rule would amend Magnuson-Stevens Act regulations at
50 CFR 665 subpart H
(§§ 665.930-665.936) that prohibit commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion. When finalized, commercial fisheries operating in the PRIMNM Expansion will be subject to existing fishing regulations and restrictions at
50 CFR 665 subpart A
(§§ 665.1-665.20), implementing general requirements for fisheries in the Western Pacific;
50 CFR 665 subpart E
(§§ 665.598-665.669) and
50 CFR subpart F
(§§ 665.798-665.819), implementing the PRIA FEP and Pelagics FEP, respectively;
50 CFR 600.725
, implementing Magnuson-Stevens Act general prohibitions;
50 CFR 300 subpart D
(§§ 300.30-300.46), implementing the SPTA and subpart O (§§ 300.210-300.230), implementing WCPFCIA.
Under the proposed action, commercial fishing shoreward of 50 nmi (93 km) around Wake Island, Johnston Atoll and Jarvis Island in the PRIMNM will continue to be prohibited by regulations at
50 CFR 665 subpart H
(§§ 665.933-665.934) implementing the PRIMNM, consistent with Presidential Proclamation 10918, as amended by Presidential Proclamation 11035. For this reason, NMFS anticipates only longline and purse seine fishing for highly migratory species such as tunas and billfish would resume in the PRIMNM Expansion because the habitat to support non-pelagic species managed under the PRIA FEP, including bottomfish, crustacean, coral reef and precious corals are found entirely within 50 nmi (93 km) from shore, which will remain closed to commercial fishing.
NMFS anticipates the resumption of commercial fishing by pelagic longline and purse seine vessels in the PRIMNM Expansion under the proposed action would have no effect on terrestrial resources, coral reefs, shallow water coral reef ecosystem resources, reef fish, shellfish, and outer reef slope communities because these monument resources are found entirely within 12 nmi (22 km) from the shoreline, well within the 50 nmi (93 km) boundary where commercial fishing will remain prohibited and are spatially separated from commercial fishing activities. Similarly, NMFS does not anticipate the resumption of commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion would result in adverse impacts to seamounts, deep sea coral communities and demersal habitats because pelagic fishing gear is deployed in the water column within 985 ft (300 m) of the surface and does not come into contact with the ocean floor. As such, commercial fishing activities are spatially separated from these resources and unlikely to affect them.
In addition, reverting to existing management measures for resuming commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion is in accordance with the Magnuson-Stevens Act, ESA of 1973, and Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 (MMPA). NMFS evaluates the impacts of fishing activity on the population of target stocks and protected species throughout the entirety of their range. Under the proposed action, NMFS expects the combined amount of catch of target stocks and other marketable fishery resources by longline and purse seine fisheries within the PRIMNM Expansion would remain within historical levels and would not cause a change in the sustainability of fish populations throughout their range as currently assessed in accordance with the Magnuson-Stevens Act and other domestic and international requirements.
Similarly, NMFS expects the shift of fishing effort by longline and purse seine fishing vessels from the high seas into the PRIMNM Expansion would result in a negligible change in the amount of fishery interactions over the range of ESA-listed species, including sea turtles, sharks and rays, marine mammals, and seabirds. And we anticipate interactions would remain within the levels that do not exceed thresholds established under ESA consultations. Based on ESA consultations and analyses, the overall effects on protected species are expected to be negligible.
NMFS expects a likely minor, beneficial impact to fisheries operations and management. For longline and purse seine vessels, the proposed action would restore 2.04 percent and 1.55 percent of historical fishing areas, respectively. The longline and purse seine fisheries will also experience minor beneficial impacts due to reduced competition with foreign fleets, which are prohibited from fishing in U.S. waters of the PRIMNM Expansion and access to fishing areas closer to home ports, reducing transit times and overall fuel and operational costs.
NMFS estimates up to a maximum of 6 percent of the total effort of the purse seine fishery to shift to the Jarvis Island
(
printed page 70830)
EEZ and up to a maximum of 6 percent of the total effort of longline fisheries to shift to the Johnston Atoll from areas currently accessible to the fisheries. Because the functional restraints, including catch and effort limits and limited entry permits on the fisheries will not change as a result of this action, NMFS expects negligible impacts on fisheries catch and effort and target fish populations.
Thus, NMFS expects the resumption of commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion would not result in a substantial increase in vessel traffic or fishing gear entering the PRIMNM Expansion and is expected to have negligible effects on monument resources, given the limited increase in fishing activity expected, and spatial protective boundary within 50 nmi (93 km). Additionally, Federal protections under current laws governing vessel operations, marine pollution, refuge management, and gear management and disposal would limit impacts by vessels operating in the PRIMNM Expansion.
NMFS also expects resumption of commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion would have negligible effects on activities managed under authorities other than the Magnuson-Stevens Act, as directed by Proclamation 10918. This is because within the PRIMNM Expansion, transiting of maritime vessels, including innocent passage is the primary non-fishing activity that occurs in this area, and NMFS anticipates transiting vessels would avoid vessels actively engaged in fishing so as to avoid collisions.
To the extent that other non-fishing activities may occur, they would be subject to management by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. NMFS believes that the commercial fishing that would resume under the proposed action would not interfere with other non-fishing activities managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
NMFS further expects impacts on cultural resources would be negligible due to the geographic separation from fishing activities and land-based practices and the low likelihood of encounters between cultural practitioners and voyagers and fishing vessels in the PRIMNM Expansion. Since the establishment of the PRIMNM Expansion, zero cultural practitioners have sought Special Use Permits for cultural activities.
Finally, NMFS expects the resumption of commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion under the proposed action would result in minor beneficial impacts on fishery economics, as vessels could save cost on fuel by fishing closer to home ports instead of on the high seas and purse seine vessels may avoid daily access fees required for fishing in foreign EEZs adjacent to the PRIMNM Expansion.
As discussed above, regulations at
50 CFR 665 subpart A
(§§ 665.1-665.20),
50 CFR 665 subpart E
(§§ 665.598-665.669);
50 CFR subpart F
(§§ 665.798-665.819);
50 CFR 600.725
;
50 CFR 300 subpart D
(§§ 300.30-300.46); and
50 CFR 300 subpart O
(§§ 300.210-300.230) provide the conservation and management measures developed and evaluated under the Magnuson-Stevens Act and other applicable law, including NEPA, the ESA, and MMPA. Under these existing regulations and restrictions, NMFS believes that commercial fisheries operating in the PRIMNM and PRIMNM Expansion would be appropriately managed and that monument resources would receive proper care and management, consistent with the direction in Proclamation 10918.
NMFS invites public comment on whether these existing regulations and restrictions appropriately manage commercial fishing and would provide for the proper care and management of monument resources in the PRIMNM and PRIMNM Expansion, consistent with the proclamation.
NMFS will consider public comments on this proposed rule and will announce the final rule in the
Federal Register
. NMFS must receive any comments by the date provided in the
DATES
.
Classification
Magnuson-Stevens Act
NMFS is proposing this rule pursuant to 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act to carry out section 303(a)(1)(C). This action is necessary to ensure that MSA regulations implementing the PRIA FEP and Pelagics FEP are carried out consistent with Presidential Proclamation 10918, as amended by Proclamation 11035, directing the removal of monument-based prohibitions on commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion. Accordingly, this proposed rule would amend those regulations that are inconsistent with Proclamation 10918, as amended by Proclamation 11035. The Assistant Administrator for Fisheries, NOAA has determined that this rule is consistent with, and conforms to Presidential Proclamation 10918, as amended by Proclamation 11035, the Antiquities Act, the PRIA and Pelagics FEPs, other provisions of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and other applicable laws.
NEPA
This proposed action is to bring Magnuson-Stevens Act implementing regulations in conformity with applicable law—specifically Presidential Proclamation 10918—as amended by Proclamation 11035, which removed prohibitions on commercial fishing described in Presidential Proclamation 9173, and specified that agency rulemaking is intended to amend inconsistent regulations. NMFS has voluntarily prepared an EA that discusses the impact on the quality of the human environment as a result of this rule and the resumption of commercial fishing under applicable regulations in the PRIMNM Expansion. NMFS considered two alternatives: the proposed action to amend regulations that restrict commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion, which would restore commercial fishing under existing regulations and taking no action which would maintain existing commercial fishing prohibitions in the PRIMNM Expansion.
A copy of the EA is available from NMFS (See
ADDRESSES
).
Executive Order 12866
This proposed rule has been determined to be significant for purposes of
Executive Order 12866
section 3(f). However, it has not been found to be economically significant under section 3(f)(1) because it would not likely result in an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more, or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local, or tribal governments or communities.
Executive Order 14192
This proposed rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action because it would amend regulations that prohibit commercial fishing between 50 to 200 nautical miles (nmi; 93 to 370 kilometers (km)) around Johnston Atoll and Wake and Jarvis Islands and restore access to these areas for U.S. commercial fishermen.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Senior Lead Counsel for Regulation of the Department of Commerce certified to the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration that this proposed rule, if adopted, would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The proposed rule would amend regulations under the Magnuson-Stevens Act that prohibit commercial
(
printed page 70831)
fishing between 50 to 200 nmi (93 to 370 km) around Wake Island, Johnston Atoll and Jarvis Island in the PRIMNM Expansion. This action, which would expand areas open to commercial fishing by over 300,000 square nmi (1,030,000 square km), is necessary to conform U.S. fishing regulations with Presidential Proclamation 10918 of April 17, 2025—Unleashing American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific, and Presidential Proclamation 11035 of June 11, 2026—Restoring American Commercial Fishing in the Pacific, and in light of the U.S. District Court of Hawaii's Order in
Kapa'a
v.
Trump,
794 F. Supp. 3d 793 (D. Haw. 2025), which found the plaintiffs were entitled to participate in a notice and comment process on whether commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion would be appropriately managed to provide for the proper care and management of monument resources.
The proposed action would apply to all fisheries managed under the PRIA FEP and Pelagics FEP, as well as the U.S. purse seine and longline vessels operating under the SPTA and the WCPFCIA. However, given the remote location of the monument and considerable distance from U.S. ports, the fisheries affected are essentially limited to longline and purse seine fisheries; the areas between 50 to 200 nmi (93 to 370 km) around Wake Island, Johnston Atoll and Jarvis Island that would be reopened by this action (hereafter the PRIMNM Expansion) are generally inaccessible to small boat fisheries managed under the Pelagics FEP. While the proposed action would apply to as many as 224 longline vessels and 40 purse seine vessels, given recent fishing activities, it would likely affect only the 163 permitted and active longline vessels and 13 licensed and active purse seine vessels. The Hawaii and American Samoa longline fisheries are limited entry fisheries. The Hawaii longline fishery is capped at 164 vessels with 149 currently permitted. The American Samoa longline fishery is capped at 60 vessels with 20 currently permitted. Six of those 20 current permit holders are dual permitted so they also possess current Hawaii longline vessel permits. The purse seine fleet is limited to a total of 40 licenses under the SPTA, with 13 active licensed vessels. There has historically been only very limited fishing by the Pelagics FEP small boat fisheries and none by the PRIA FEP fisheries within the PRIMNM Expansion. This is because habitat to support species managed under the PRIA FEP, including bottomfish, crustacean, coral reef fish and precious corals are found entirely within 50 nmi (93 km) from shore, which will remain closed to commercial fishing.
NMFS has established a small business size standard for businesses, including their affiliates, whose primary industry is commercial fishing (see
50 CFR 200.2
). A business primarily engaged in commercial fishing (North American Industry Classification System code 11411) is classified as a small business if it is independently owned and operated, is not dominant in its field of operation (including its affiliates), and has combined annual receipts not in excess of $11 million for all its affiliated operations worldwide. Based on available information, NMFS believes that most of the affected fish harvesting businesses are small entities under the NMFS standard, as they are engaged in the business of fish harvesting, independently owned or operated, are not dominant in their field of operation, and have annual gross receipts not in excess of $11 million. In 2025, the Hawaii longline fishery earned $109 million fleetwide ($731,543 per vessel on average) while the American Samoa longline fishery earned approximately $3 million ($150,000 per vessel on average). With regard to the purse seine fleet, the majority, but not all vessels, could be considered small entities. For the 11 vessels that operated between 2022 and 2024 and were still active in 2025, the average per vessel revenue was almost $10 million. Seven of those 11 vessels could be considered small entities with estimated revenues of less than $11 million. Even though this proposed action may apply to a substantial number of entities, based on our analysis the implementation of this action would not result in significant adverse economic impacts on individual entities.
The primary benefit for fishermen under the proposed action is a modest increase in the available U.S. EEZ waters where U.S. fishing vessels do not have to compete with foreign fleets for access to fish. This benefit primarily applies to longline fleets based in Hawaii, where the majority of U.S. EEZ waters are closed due to the longline exclusion zone around the main Hawaiian Islands (
50 CFR 665.806(a)(2)
) and prohibitions on commercial fishing in the PRIMNM (
50 CFR 665.933
), Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument (
50 CFR 404
) and Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary (
15 CFR 922 subpart W
—Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary). From the purse seine fishery perspective, the major benefit is related to avoiding costs associated with fishing in the EEZs of foreign nations that, under the SPTA, charge daily access fees for fishing activity. These access fees range from $10,000 to $13,000 per day, depending on the EEZ or groups of EEZs that are fished. Considered relative to daily average revenue for purse seine vessels ($68,000), these fees are about 14 to 19 percent of daily revenue, on days that these vessels fish in the EEZs of foreign nations that charge daily access fees.
The amount of annual effort shifted to the action area from current fishing locations under the proposed action is expected to range from 0 to about 6 percent of overall fleetwide effort in both the longline and purse seine fisheries given past fishing in the action area prior to the initial commercial fishery prohibitions in 2009 and further expansion of fishing restrictions in 2014. In longline fisheries, deep- and shallow-set fisheries combined averaged 22,020 sets over the last 5 years (2020-2024). This suggests that the number of sets that could shift to areas that open as a result of implementing the proposed action could range from 0 to 1,321 longline sets fleetwide. For purse seine fisheries, the number of sets has averaged 1,753 in the last 5 years (2020-2024). Implementing the proposed action could shift the number of purse seine sets in these waters ranging from 0 to 105 sets fleetwide.
With regard to longline vessels, there could potentially be some savings in fuel costs associated with this anticipated switched effort; however, both Johnston Atoll and Jarvis Island are far from Honolulu relative to where the majority of longline effort is concentrated. The anticipated fuel cost differences for shifted effort under the proposed action are difficult to estimate, but fuel represents about 50 percent of the total costs of a fishing trip and therefore does represent a substantial portion of operating costs.
For purse seine vessels, a similar magnitude minor shift in effort under the proposed action may affect fuel costs. In general, purse seine fishing is concentrated in the productive skipjack tuna fishing waters to the west and south of the PRIMNM Expansion; inside the EEZs of countries party to the South Pacific Tuna Treaty. Transit distances to Jarvis Island from the center of purse seine effort would be significant, but the lack of daily access fees in the PRIMNM Expansion may increase the economic value of reopened areas around Jarvis Island. If we assume that all effort shifted to the PRIMNM Expansion under the proposed action moved from areas where a daily access fee was required, the total savings fleetwide could be as high as $1,367,340. Based
(
printed page 70832)
on 13 currently licensed and active purse seine vessels, each vessel could save up to $105,180 per year in access fees, or roughly 1 percent of a vessel's average annual revenue of $10 million. Revenue gains would be on the higher end of the potential range if purse seine vessels decide to fully transition away from foreign EEZs upon reopening commercial fishing in the PRIMNM Expansion, and closer to zero if they do not. Because fishing location choice is based on many factors, and fishermen are unlikely to fully transition away from foreign EEZs, the fleet-wide revenue gain as a result of the expanded locations available for commercial fishing as a result of this proposed action, would likely be less than $1,367,340, and individual vessel revenue gains would be lower than $105,180 (
i.e.,
lower than 1 percent).
The proposed action does not duplicate, overlap, or conflict with other Federal rules and is not expected to have a significant impact on small entities, organizations or government jurisdictions. The proposed action also will not place a substantial number of small entities at a significant competitive disadvantage nor disproportionately flow to large entities because the expansion of fishing areas would provide minor benefits to all entities without regard to the size of each individual entity.
For the reasons above, NMFS does not expect the proposed action to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
As a result, an initial regulatory flexibility analysis is not required, and none has been prepared.
Paperwork Reduction Act
This proposed rule contains no information collection requirements under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995.
Coastal Zone Management Act
Because this proposed rule affects fisheries that occur outside the coastal zone of any State and will not have reasonably foreseeable effects on any coastal use or resource, NMFS is not required to coordinate with State agencies under section 307 of the Coastal Zone Management Act.
ESA
Fishing activities conducted pursuant to this rule will not affect endangered and/or threatened species or critical habitat under the ESA in a manner that would result in effects that have not previously been considered in current ESA section 7 consultations.
Under the proposed rule, NMFS anticipates only longline and purse seine fishing for HMS such as tunas and billfish would be resumed in the PRIMNM Expansion because the habitat to support non-pelagic species such as bottomfish, crustacean, coral reef and precious corals are found entirely within 50 nmi (93 km) from shore, which will remain closed to commercial fishing.
NMFS previously evaluated the potential impact of longline and purse seine fisheries on ESA-listed species and designated critical habitat in areas of the Pacific Ocean where fishing vessels fish and transit on their way to fishing grounds. NMFS determined these fisheries are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of ESA-listed species or result in adverse modification of designated critical habitat.
NMFS does not expect that resuming commercial longline and purse seine fishing under existing fishing regulations in the PRIMNM Expansion would cause an effect on endangered and/or threatened species or critical habitat beyond that considered in applicable consultations for these fisheries. This conclusion is reached in part because there is no designated critical habitat for ESA-listed species in the PRIMNM Expansion for pelagic longline and purse seine fisheries to affect. Additionally, some ESA-listed species such as corals are only found in shallow nearshore waters around the islands and well within 50 nmi (93 km) of shore where commercial fishing remains prohibited. This buffer provides spatial separation that prevents their exposure to fishing activities occurring 50 to 200 nmi (93 to 370 km) offshore.
Many of the ESA-listed species, such as sea turtles, sharks and manta rays are highly migratory, and the PRIMNM Expansion represents just a small fraction of their range. For this reason, existing ESA consultations account for the potential population level impacts of fishing activities on ESA-listed species that may visit the PRIMNM Expansion but are exposed to fishing activities throughout their range.
Historically, annual fishing effort in the PRIMNM waters prior to monument designation represented up to a maximum of 6 percent of total fishing effort for longline and purse seine fisheries. As both longline and purse seine fisheries are limited entry fisheries with maximum caps on the number of vessels that can fish, we expect that fishing in the restored areas of the PRIMNM Expansion will reflect effort by existing vessels shifting from currently open fishing areas into the PRIMNM, as opposed to additional increased fishing effort.
Therefore, the shift in some fishing effort from outside the PRIMNM Expansion into the PRIMNM Expansion is expected to result in a negligible change in the amount of fishery interactions over the range of ESA-listed species and would remain within the levels considered and analyzed in the current ESA section 7 consultations for these fisheries. The results of the ESA consultations for Pacific Island longline and purse seine fisheries are detailed in the EA developed for this action (see
ADDRESSES
).
Executive Order 13175
NMFS has determined that this action would not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes; therefore, consultation with Tribal officials under
E.O. 13175
is not required, and the requirements of sections (5)(b) and (5)(c) of
E.O. 13175
also do not apply. A Tribal summary impact statement under section (5)(b)(2)(B) and section (5)(c)(2) of
E.O. 13175
is not required and has not been prepared.

ACTION:
Notice and request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Transportation (DOT) invites public comments about our intention to request Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval to renew the information collection approved under OMB Control No. 2105-0529, Procedures for Transportation Drug and Alcohol Testing Program. The information to be collected will be used to document tests conducted and actions taken to ensure safety in the workplace or is otherwise necessary to collect under the Omnibus Transportation Employee Testing Act of 1991, which requires DOT to implement a drug and alcohol testing program in various transportation-related industries. DOT is required to publish this notice in the
Federal Register
in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
OMB Control Number:
2105-0529.
Title:
Procedures for Transportation Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Programs.
Form Numbers:
DOT F 1385; DOT F 1380.
Type of Review:
Clearance of a renewal of an information collection.
Background:
Under the Omnibus Transportation Employee Testing Act of 1991, DOT is required to implement a drug and alcohol testing program in various transportation related industries. This specific requirement is elaborated in
49 CFR part 40
, Procedures for Transportation Workplace Drug and Alcohol Testing Programs (Part 40). This request for a renewal of the information collection for the program includes 45 burden items related to the overall program and two official DOT forms: the U.S. Department of Transportation Alcohol Testing Form (ATF) [DOT F 1380] and the DOT Drug and Alcohol Testing Management Information System (MIS) Data Collection Form [DOT F 1385].
The ATF includes the employee's name, the type of test taken, the date of the test, and the name of the employer. Data on each test conducted, including test results, is necessary to document that the tests were conducted and is used to take action, when required, to ensure safety in the workplace.
The MIS form includes employer specific drug and alcohol testing information such as the reason for the test and the cumulative number of test results for the negative, positive, and refusal tests. No employee specific data is collected. The form has fields for data related to urine and oral fluid drug testing. The MIS data is used by each of the affected DOT Agencies (
i.e.,
Federal Aviation Administration, Federal Transit Administration, Federal Railroad Administration, Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, and the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration) and the United States Coast Guard when calculating their industry's annual random drug and/or alcohol testing rate.
DOT will request OMB approval to revise the MIS Data Collection Form. Specifically, in Section I of the form, “Employer”, in the line for PHMSA—Pipeline, DOT will remove the text “: (Check) Gas Gathering_ Gas Transmission_ Gas Distribution_ Transport Hazardous Liquids_ Transport Carbon Dioxide_”. Because pipeline operators submit other reports to PHMSA, PHMSA already knows the types of pipelines they operate; therefore, collecting this data element on the MIS form is unnecessary. Furthermore, contractors to pipeline operators who must submit an MIS form are not operators and are confused by the options because the `type of pipeline' does not apply to them. Removing this data element will not hinder the data collection effort or alter the form's burden estimate. In the Paperwork Reduction Act Notice section of the form, DOT will replace the text ‘Suite W62-300’ with ‘Rm W75-211’ to reflect the new office location.
Respondents:
The information will be collected from transportation employers, Department representatives, and a variety of service agents. Estimated total number of respondents is 2,383,126.
Frequency:
The information will be collected annually.

Surface Transportation Board
[Docket No. EP 791]
AGENCY:
Surface Transportation Board.
ACTION:
Statement of Board Policy.
SUMMARY:
The Surface Transportation Board (STB or Board) is issuing this policy statement on the scope of its jurisdiction over transportation by rail carriers and on preemption of conflicting state and federal laws under the ICC Termination Act of 1995
(
printed page 70957)
(ICCTA). The policy statement provides an overview of the Board's jurisdiction and preemption through a review of existing legal precedent, discussing many commonly occurring questions. The Board intends the policy statement to serve as a useful tool for the public to review, in one place, concise explanations from the Board about its jurisdiction and application of preemption, which the Board anticipates will reduce confusion and facilitate the efficient resolution of disputes.
DATES:
This policy statement will be final on November 9, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Amanda Gorski at (202) 915-8453. If you require accommodation under the Americans with Disabilities Act, please call (202) 245-0245.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Congress granted the Board exclusive jurisdiction over rail transportation and preempted conflicting federal or state laws in ICCTA.
See generally
49 U.S.C. 10501
. ICCTA embodies Congress's recognition of the need to regulate railroad operations at the federal level. Broadly, it provides that the Board has jurisdiction over rail transportation that is part of the interstate rail network. In ICCTA, Congress included an expansive preemption provision, the purpose of which is to ensure the free flow of interstate commerce, including by preventing patchwork regulation and eliminating unduly burdensome state laws, and by providing a nationally uniform, efficient national rail network to meet the needs of the public and national defense. On September 19, 2025, the Board received a letter from a coalition of six railroad and shipper organizations (Coalition)
[
1
]
requesting that the Board issue guidance on the scope and application of federal preemption. Coalition Letter (Sept. 19, 2025),
https://www.stb.gov/​wp-content/​uploads/​Coalition-Letter-on-ICCTA-Preemption_​FINAL.pdf
.
Board members issued a joint response letter on September 24, 2025, noting the Coalition's views and stating that the Board was considering issuing a policy statement on preemption. Letter from Board Members Fuchs, Hedlund, & Schultz (Sept. 24, 2025),
https://www.stb.gov/​wp-content/​uploads/​Preemption-Letter-Final.pdf
.
Over the 30 years since ICCTA's enactment, the Board and the courts have issued many decisions addressing the scope of the Board's jurisdiction over transportation by rail carriers and the preemptive effect of ICCTA when presented with potentially conflicting state, local, or federal regulations. While those decisions are generally consistent, they are numerous, have not always used the same terminology or analytical approaches, and may contain technical language unfamiliar to the general public. The Board therefore views it as important to set forth its considered, longstanding view of its jurisdiction over rail transportation and the application of ICCTA preemption. This policy statement is non-exhaustive but explores a significant number of questions that are frequently presented to the Board and to courts interpreting and applying ICCTA. Although any future case that comes before the Board (or a court) will be evaluated on the specific facts, circumstances, and laws presented in that case, the Board anticipates that the policy statement will serve the public by summarizing for stakeholders existing precedent. The policy statement will promote collaboration by reducing uncertainty about the scope of the Board's jurisdiction and ICCTA preemption and describing how the Board has analyzed frequently occurring questions. The Board thus aims to proactively prevent disputes regarding the Board's jurisdiction and ICCTA preemption, and when disputes do arise, for the policy statement to serve as a useful tool for the public and courts in resolving such disputes, potentially lowering litigation costs for carriers, shippers, and state and local governments. In turn, this action would, as appropriate, potentially support economic growth by better facilitating the avoidance or removal of undue or inappropriate impediments to rail transportation serving domestic manufacturing, agriculture, and energy facilities, among other critical aspects of the economy.
By addressing key concepts and authorities in one consolidated, synthesized document, the policy statement provides benefits to stakeholders and the general public. The policy statement will lower costs by reducing the time and resources necessary to process and evaluate a breadth of topics relevant to the Board's jurisdiction and preemption. It will allow a wide array of users to quickly reference and read about their individual areas of interest. And it synthesizes precedents and provides guidance on the Board's jurisdiction and preemption—including processes for rail carrier licensing and the proper forum for adjudicating disputes—in a practical way that is not necessary, or possible, when resolving individual matters before the Board. By reducing these incremental costs, the policy statement is considered a deregulatory action under
Executive Order 14192
,
Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.
I. Executive Summary
This policy statement explains how the Board and state and federal courts have interpreted the Board's authority over rail transportation and the preemption of state and local laws under ICCTA.
[
2
]
Congress' framework, set forth in ICCTA, has been interpreted in ways that ensure the uniform federal regulation over interstate rail transportation, which is critical to the American economy. Individual cases must be decided based on the facts, circumstances, and applicable law in each case, and this policy statement supports that endeavor by setting forth the Board's general perspective on its jurisdiction and ICCTA preemption.
The policy statement begins with an explanation of the long-recognized need for uniform rail regulation at the federal level, including under the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution, the passage of the Interstate Commerce Act in 1887, and subsequent federal legislation, culminating in the passage of ICCTA and the creation of the Board in the 1990s. In enacting the statutory provision most relevant to preemption—
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
—Congress included two key, interrelated components: (1) broad, exclusive jurisdiction over transportation by rail carriers (including certain related activity), and (2) that the remedies provided under ICCTA expressly preempt the remedies provided under federal and state law. The policy statement explains and analyzes numerous elements of the statute.
Regarding jurisdiction, the Board discusses the definitions of “transportation” and “rail carrier” (with attention to both freight and passenger rail carriers), and provides an explanation of three categories of track that the Board has recognized (common carrier, ancillary, and private) and how each is viewed for jurisdictional purposes. In analyzing the preemption provision, the policy statement identifies the broad scope of
(
printed page 70958)
“regulations” that may be preempted—including those from both state and local authorities and those that may take the form of less-direct methods of regulation. The policy statement also explains that preemption extends beyond economic regulation and may apply when ICCTA does not provide an alternative remedy. The Board and courts may both be proper forums for disputes regarding the Board's jurisdiction and ICCTA preemption, with courts often referring preemption issues to the Board, consistent with the Board's expertise on such matters.
The policy statement next explores the analytical preemption framework that the Board applies when considering state or local regulations. The policy statement explains that what courts often call express preemption is typically analyzed, under ICCTA, as “categorical” preemption, and what is often called implied preemption is typically analyzed as “as-applied” preemption. The policy statement then explains that the categorical analysis is employed where state or local laws attempt to regulate rail transportation matters or when regulations (such as permitting) can be used to prevent rail transportation. It further explains that the “as-applied” analysis is used when a regulation may unreasonably burden or interfere with rail transportation or discriminate against rail carriers. The policy statement then analyzes and synthesizes precedents on complete takings of rail property by state or local governments, as well as the indirect regulation of rail transportation through regulation of shippers in ways that may limit common carrier rail service. The policy statement then addresses a number of commonly occurring preemption questions, summarizing the preemption analysis applied and the results of Board and court decisions. The non-exhaustive list of preemption fact patterns includes: (1) abandonment of rail property interests, (2) complete taking of rail carrier property, (3) utilities and pipelines within the right-of-way, (4) blocked crossings, (5) pedestrian or road crossings of rail lines, (6) locomotive idling, (7) environmental permitting, zoning ordinances, and land use laws, (8) noise, smoke, appearance, and other nuisance-related claims, (9) design, construction, or maintenance of rail infrastructure, (10) breach of contract, and (11) routing of traffic.
The policy statement also discusses the analysis that applies in considering whether a federal law is preempted by ICCTA. The Board explains the harmonization analysis that applies to give effect to both federal laws where possible. The policy statement then discusses two illustrative federal law regimes that have been the subject of harmonization analysis in past decisions—federal rail safety laws (including the Federal Railroad Safety Act (FRSA)) and federal environmental laws (including the Clean Air Act (CAA) and Clean Water Act (CWA)).
The Board is not making any binding determinations in this policy statement. Indeed, this policy statement is not exhaustive and should not be interpreted to predetermine the outcome of any particular dispute that may come before the agency, in which the Board would consider the specific facts, circumstances, and arguments presented. Instead, it compiles principles from certain existing cases to help parties understand how the Board and courts have approached frequently occurring questions concerning the Board's jurisdiction and ICCTA preemption. Where this policy statement identifies areas in which the Board provides a refinement to its prior analysis, such as complete takings and regulations directed at rail customers, the discussion below explains the basis for the refinement. The Board intends that this policy statement will serve as a reference document that can be used to promote growth in the rail industry and collaboration between rail carriers, shippers, and communities to proactively develop solutions to rail-related concerns.
Nevertheless, railroads should not use ICCTA preemption as an excuse to be unresponsive to local public officials. Consistent with the rail transportation policy of the United States government (set forth at
49 U.S.C. 10101
), railroads, as regulated entities, should seek to engage in good communication, information sharing and cooperation with the communities they serve and operate within. State and local governments may have legitimate interests in the development of, among other things, passenger rail and trails within rights of way where allowed, for the benefit of both rail carriers and local communities. Local government officials who believe that a railroad has been unresponsive may seek assistance from the Board's Office of Public Assistance, Governmental Affairs, and Compliance (OPAGAC) to facilitate improved communications.
II. Historically Recognized Need for Uniform Federal Rail Regulation
The Surface Transportation Board was created on January 1, 1996 by ICCTA,
Public Law 104-88
, 109 Stat. 803 (1995), as the successor to the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC) (1887-1995). The Board is the federal agency that is responsible for the economic regulation of various modes of surface transportation, primarily freight rail. Its responsibilities include oversight of railroad rates, practices, and service issues, as well as rail restructuring transactions including mergers, line sales, line construction, and line abandonments. The Board also has jurisdiction over certain passenger rail matters, the intercity bus industry, household goods carriers' tariffs, rate regulation of non-contiguous domestic water transportation (marine freight shipping involving the mainland United States, Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other U.S. territories and possessions), and pipeline carriers transporting commodities other than water, gas, or oil. While questions can arise regarding the scope of the Board's authority over each of these other transportation modes, this policy statement discusses rail transportation, which is the primary focus of the Board's statutory obligations.
Congress and the courts long have recognized a need to uniformly regulate rail transportation at the federal level. As an inherently interstate mode of transportation, “[r]ailroads have been subject to comprehensive federal regulation for [more than] a century.”
United Transp. Union
v.
Long Island R.R.,
455 U.S. 678, 687 (1982);
see also
Interstate Commerce Act, ch. 104, 24 Stat. 379 (1887). Even before Congress enacted the Interstate Commerce Act in 1887, the Supreme Court had established that a state's regulation of railroad rates unconstitutionally interfered with interstate commerce.
See Wabash, St. Louis & Pac. Ry.
v.
Illinois,
118 U.S. 557, 577 (1886). In 1887, Congress created the ICC to oversee a “comprehensive regulatory regime over the rail industry.” Paul Stephen Dempsey,
The Rise & Fall of the Interstate Com. Comm'n,
95 Marq. L. Rev. 1151, 1161 (2012);
see also
Interstate Commerce Act Sec. 11, 24 Stat. 383. And since that time, the Supreme Court has “frequently invalidated attempts by the States to impose on common carriers obligations that are plainly inconsistent with the plenary authority of the [ICC] or with congressional policy as reflected in the [Interstate Commerce Act].”
Chi. & NW Transp. Co.
v.
Kalo Brick & Tile Co.,
450 U.S. 311, 318 (1981) (citing
Tex. & Pac. Ry.
v.
Abilene Cotton Oil Co.,
204 U.S. 426, 446 (1907);
Transit Comm'n
v.
United States,
289 U.S. 121, 129 (1933)). Indeed, the Interstate Commerce Act is “among the most pervasive and comprehensive federal regulatory
(
printed page 70959)
schemes.”
Chi. & NW Transp. Co.,
450 U.S. at 318.
In response to significant financial concerns experienced by the railroad industry in the 1970s, Congress substantially amended the Interstate Commerce Act by enacting “two major pieces of legislation of a generally deregulatory thrust”: the Railroad Revitalization and Regulatory Reform Act of 1976, Public Law 94-210, and the Staggers Rail Act of 1980 (Staggers Act), Public Law 96-448.
Balt. Gas & Elec. Co.
v.
United States,
817 F.2d 108, 112-13 (D.C. Cir. 1987). Together, these laws were intended to reduce unnecessary regulation and help restore the financial stability of the railroad industry.
Congress carried that deregulatory thrust forward in 1995, when it enacted ICCTA as a means of “extending exclusive Federal jurisdiction” over rail transportation. H.R. Rep. No. 104-311, at 82, 95 (1995),
as reprinted in
1995 U.S.C.C.A.N. 793, 793-94, 807 (“There is a long history behind the termination of the [ICC] beginning with [the Staggers Act], which began the substantial economic deregulation of the surface transportation industry . . . .”). And through ICCTA, Congress further expanded federal uniformity by preempting certain areas of state authority over rail activity that previously existed.
See Fla. E. Coast Ry.
v.
City of W. Palm Beach,
266 F.3d 1324, 1337-38 (11th Cir. 2001) (explaining that “[t]he pre-ICCTA statute expressly authorized regulation of certain railroad activities to be undertaken concurrently by the federal and state governments, while still other regulation would be the exclusive province of state law.”). At the same time, in further deregulating the rail industry, Congress did not intend for states and local governments to replace federal regulation with a patchwork of differing state and local rail regulations.
See
S. Rep. No. 104-176, at 6 (1995) (noting that nothing in ICCTA “should be construed to authorize States to regulate railroads in areas where Federal regulation has been repealed . . . .”).
Indeed, in ICCTA, Congress reaffirmed that “the direct and complete pre-emption of State economic regulation of railroads” was necessary to preserve “the uniformity of Federal standards” and prevent “the balkanization and subversion of the Federal scheme of minimal regulation for this intrinsically interstate form of transportation.” H.R. Rep. No. 104-311, at 95-96. Subjecting the interstate rail network to varying state regulations “would greatly undermine the industry's ability to provide the `seamless' service that is essential to its shippers,” and would weaken the rail industry's “efficiency and competitive viability.” S. Rep. No. 104-176, at 6. In this way, preemption is consistent with the national rail transportation policy to promote a “safe and efficient rail transportation system,”
49 U.S.C. 10101(3)
, and “ensure the development and continuation of a sound rail transportation system with effective competition among rail carriers and with other modes, to meet the needs of the public and the national defense,”
49 U.S.C. 10101(4)
.
III. The Jurisdiction and Preemption Provisions of
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
The scope of the Board's exclusive jurisdiction over transportation by rail carriers is set forth in
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
. The statute also contains an express preemption provision. Taken together, the statutory provisions governing jurisdiction and preemption establish the framework for the Board's analysis.
The statute provides that the “jurisdiction of the Board over (1) transportation by rail carriers, and the remedies provided in [Part A of Subtitle IV of Title 49] with respect to rates, classifications, rules (including car service, interchange, and other operating rules), practices, routes, services, and facilities of such carriers; and (2) the construction, acquisition, operation, abandonment, or discontinuance of spur, industrial, team, switching, or side tracks, or facilities, even if the tracks are located, or intended to be located, entirely in one State, is exclusive.”
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
. Furthermore, “[e]xcept as otherwise provided in [Part A of Subtitle IV of Title 49], the remedies provided under this part with respect to regulation of rail transportation are exclusive and preempt the remedies provided under Federal or State law.”
Id.
These provisions of section 10501 work together to ensure the free flow of interstate commerce by preventing a patchwork of different state and local regulations.
E.g., Tenth Ave. Neighbors—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36654, slip op. at 3-4 (STB served May 8, 2024) (citing
Tubbs—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35792, slip op. at 5 (STB served Oct. 31, 2014),
aff'd sub nom. Tubbs
v.
STB,
812 F.3d 1141 (8th Cir. 2015));
see also Elam
v.
Kan. City S. Ry.,
635 F.3d 796, 804 (5th Cir. 2011) (recognizing that a purpose of ICCTA was to create a “[f]ederal scheme of minimal regulation for this intrinsically interstate form of transportation”);
Fayus Enters.
v.
BNSF Ry.,
602 F.3d 444, 452 (D.C. Cir. 2010) (ICCTA reflected a Congressional effort to prevent the “balkanization” of railroad-related laws);
U.S. Env't Prot. Agency—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.
(
EPA Declaratory Ord.
), FD 35803, slip op. at 7 (STB served Dec. 30, 2014) (“The courts and the Board have emphasized the importance of national uniformity in laws governing rail transportation when interpreting [section] 10501(b).”). Since ICCTA was enacted, it has been observed that “[i]t is difficult to imagine a broader statement of Congress' intent to preempt state regulatory authority over railroad operations.”
City of Auburn
v.
United States,
154 F.3d 1025, 1030 (9th Cir. 1998) (quoting
CSX Transp. Inc.
v.
Ga. Pub. Serv. Comm'n,
944 F. Supp. 1573, 1581 (N.D. Ga. 1996)).
From this established statutory structure, disputes have arisen about both the jurisdictional and preemption aspects of ICCTA. Two preliminary jurisdictional questions have guided the analysis of whether regulation under local, state, or another federal law may be subject to ICCTA preemption. First, is the activity at issue “transportation by rail carrier” as part of the interstate rail network or related to the construction, acquisition, operation, abandonment or discontinuance of spur, industrial, team, switching, or side tracks (collectively, commonly referred to as “ancillary track” or “excepted track”), or facilities? And second, does the local, state, or federal action constitute regulation of such activity? If the answer to both questions is yes, then the Board and courts apply a preemption analysis to determine whether ICCTA preempts such regulation.
[
3
]
Though the steps are straightforward, the case-specific analysis required to determine preemption is often fact-intensive and detailed. Questions can arise in each stage of the inquiry: what activities constitute “transportation”; is the actor a “rail carrier,” or operating on behalf of a rail carrier; are the railroad tracks or facilities part of the interstate rail network or a shipper's private facilities; what types of actions by local and state governments (or other actors) are considered “regulation”; when does a state or local regulation “unreasonably interfere” with rail transportation; to what extent does preemption cover lawsuits for damages allegedly caused by rail carrier operations? The analysis below addresses these and other related questions and summarizes existing precedent on the Board's jurisdiction and ICCTA preemption.
(
printed page 70960)
A. Transportation by Rail Carrier or Related to Ancillary/Excepted Track or Facilities
The threshold question in any preemption analysis is whether the activity at issue falls within the Board's jurisdiction. As specified, under
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
, the Board has jurisdiction over “transportation by rail carriers.” Whether a particular activity constitutes “transportation by rail carrier” is a case-by-case, fact-specific determination.
E.g., Town of Smithtown—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 3 (STB served Feb. 23, 2024) (citing
Padgett
v.
STB,
804 F.3d 103, 108 (1st Cir. 2015);
Town of Milford—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 34444, slip op. at 2 (STB served Aug. 12, 2004)). The same is true for determining whether railroad tracks and facilities are subject to the Board's jurisdiction.
See, e.g.,
Ne. La. Multimodal Dist.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36809, slip op. at 5-6 (STB served Sept. 15, 2025) (describing factors considered in distinguishing between common carrier/mainline (10901) and ancillary/excepted (10906) track));
Tri-City R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36037, slip op. at 5 (STB served June 1, 2017) (describing hallmarks of private track).
To determine whether a particular activity is subject to the Board's jurisdiction and, potentially, preemption under
49 U.S.C. 10501
, both the “transportation” and “by rail carrier” prongs of the standard must be satisfied. The Board has held that preemption does not apply to non-transportation activities by rail carriers.
See, e.g., Grafton & Upton R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36696, slip op. at 10 (STB served Nov. 15, 2023) (stating that “the taking of the [rail carrier's property] via eminent domain would likely not be preempted if it is developed for purposes unrelated to rail transportation.”). Likewise, transportation activities by non-rail carriers generally are not preempted.
See, e.g., Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4-5 (holding that application of state and local regulations to transloading facility would not be preempted where the facility was owned by a non-carrier that was not affiliated with the carrier; not acting as the carrier's agent; and not subject to the carrier's exertion of control over operations).
1. Transportation
The Board has jurisdiction over transportation in the United States, including, but not limited to,
[
4
]
(1) between a place in a state and a place in another state, and (2) between a place in a state and another place in the same state, as long as that intrastate transportation is “part of the interstate rail network.”
49 U.S.C. 10501(a)(2)
. Rail carriers that operate exclusively in one state—as many short line railroads
[
5
]
often do—are thus generally subject to the Board's jurisdiction if they connect to the interstate rail network.
See Great Redwood Trail Agency—Adverse Aban.—Mendocino Ry. in Mendocino Cnty., Cal.,
AB 1305 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 9-10 (STB served Feb. 19, 2026) (acknowledging that a rail carrier solely transporting shipments between points within the same state could be subject to the Board's jurisdiction). As used in ICCTA, “transportation” includes not just the act of moving freight or passengers by rail but also broadly encompasses equipment, facilities, and services related to that movement. Specifically, transportation “includes a locomotive, car, vehicle, vessel, warehouse, wharf, pier, dock, yard, property, facility, instrumentality, or equipment of any kind related to the movement of passengers or property, or both, by rail, regardless of ownership or an agreement concerning use; and services related to that movement, including receipt, delivery, elevation, transfer in transit, refrigeration, icing, ventilation, storage, handling, and interchange of passengers and property.”
49 U.S.C. 10102(9)
. This list is non-exhaustive, as “use of the word `include' indicates the list is illustrative rather than comprehensive.”
Del Grosso
v.
STB,
898 F.3d 139, 142 (1st Cir. 2018).
Proceedings before the Board and courts have made clear that the broad definition of “transportation” includes transloading and related operations when performed or operated by, or under the auspices of, a rail carrier.
See, e.g.,
Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4-5 (stating that “the Board's jurisdiction extends to rail-related activities that take place at transload facilities if the activities are offered by a rail carrier, either directly or through its agent, or if a rail carrier exerts control over a third-party's operations”). Additionally, conducting activities such as making repairs to rail equipment and the construction and operation of excepted track constitute “transportation” because they involve facilities, instrumentalities, and equipment related to the movement of property (tracks and rail equipment) and services related to that movement (repairs and operation of tracks and rail equipment).
See Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 10-11.
Though expansive, the definition of “transportation” has its limits.
Emerson
v.
Kan. City S. Ry.,
503 F.3d 1126, 1129 (10th Cir. 2007);
see also Del Grosso
v.
STB,
804 F.3d 110, 119 (1st Cir. 2015) (stating that courts and the Board have rejected interpretations of “transportation” that extend beyond activities relating to the movement of “passengers or property” by rail). As the courts have recognized, “regulation of activities that occur before or after `transportation' and are incidental to such transportation may not be preempted.”
Delaware
v.
STB,
859 F.3d 16, 21-22 (D.C. Cir. 2017);
see also Emerson,
503 F.3d at 1130-32 (holding that a railroad's disposal of railway ties into a wastewater drainage ditch adjacent to its tracks was not “transportation,” and thus state tort claims related to the disposal were not preempted).
As one example, “manufacturing and commercial transactions that occur on property owned by a railroad that are not part of or integral to the provision of rail service are not embraced within the term `transportation.' ”
Del Grosso,
898 F.3d at 142 (quoting
New England Transrail, LLC—Constr., Aquis. & Operation Exemption—in Wilmington & Woburn, Mass.
(
New England Transrail
), FD 34797, slip op. at 10 (STB served July 10, 2007));
see also Fla. E. Coast Ry.,
266 F.3d at 1327, 1336 (a third party's aggregate distribution business operating in a rail yard was not “transportation”);
New England Transrail,
FD 34797, slip op. at 14-15 (shredding of construction debris at a transloading facility before loading the material onto railcars was not “transportation”);
Town of Milford,
FD 34444, slip op. at 1-2 (cutting and welding steel in a rail yard after rail transportation had occurred but before the steel was loaded onto trucks was not “transportation”).
(
printed page 70961)
2. Rail Carrier
Under ICCTA, a “rail carrier,” is defined as “a person providing common carrier railroad transportation for compensation, but does not include street, suburban, or interurban electric railways not operated as part of the general system of rail transportation.”
49 U.S.C. 10102(5)
. The term “railroad” includes “a bridge, car float, lighter, ferry, and intermodal equipment used by or in connection with a railroad; the road used by a rail carrier and owned by it or operated under an agreement; and a switch, spur, track, terminal, terminal facility, and a freight depot, yard, and ground, used or necessary for transportation.”
49 U.S.C. 10102(6)
. The common carrier obligation requires that rail carriers “providing transportation or service subject to the jurisdiction of the Board under [Part A of Subtitle IV of Title 49] shall provide the transportation or service on reasonable request.”
49 U.S.C. 11101(a)
. Thus, as the Supreme Court has recognized, rail carriers are required to provide transportation “to any person or commodity,” and “cannot decline to provide [such] transport based on the product or commodity to be carried.”
Seven Cnty. Infrastructure Coal.
v.
Eagle Cnty.,
605 U.S. 168, 191 n.6 (2025). This includes products ranging from crude oil,
id.,
to hazardous substances,
Riffin
v.
STB,
733 F.3d 340, 346-47 (D.C. Cir. 2013), to agricultural products, construction materials, and retail goods.
The Board and courts have also interpreted the term “rail carrier” broadly, such that activities do not necessarily need to be conducted directly by the rail carrier in order for preemption to apply. Rather, the transportation must be performed “by, or under the auspices of, a rail carrier.”
Del Grosso—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35652, slip op. at 2 & n.4 (STB served July 31, 2017) (collecting cases);
City of Alexandria—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35157, slip op. at 2 (STB served Feb. 17, 2009). The Board has stated that, for example, at transload facilities, “the Board's jurisdiction extends to rail-related activities that take place at transload facilities if the activities are offered by a rail carrier, either directly or through its agent, or if a rail carrier exerts control over a third-party's operations.”
Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4. As discussed in more detail below, certain cases have held that indirect regulation that burdens common carrier rail service implicates preemption.
a. Freight Rail Carriers
The Board has jurisdiction over freight rail carriers engaged in interstate transportation, as well as intrastate transportation that is “part of the interstate rail network.”
49 U.S.C. 10501(a)(2)
. The Board classifies freight rail carriers into three categories based on annual operating revenues, with Class I carriers being the largest, Class II in the middle, and Class III the smallest.
See
49 CFR 1201
. Class II and III carriers are commonly referred to as short line railroads. Short line railroads frequently operate within the Board's jurisdiction because, even when they operate only within one state, they often connect with Class I carriers and serve as part of the interstate rail network by handling the first or last segment (sometimes referred to as “first mile/last mile service”) as part of a longer journey.
Whether a freight operator is considered a rail carrier within the Board's jurisdiction is not always immediately clear. The Board (as did the ICC before it) issues decisions authorizing transactions that, if consummated, confer rail carrier status. Typically, the Board-issued document is a decision approving the potential rail carrier's authority for construction,
[
6
]
acquisition, and/or operation (under
49 U.S.C. 10901
or
10502
), often in the form of a notice of exemption in the case of acquisition and operation transactions (under
49 CFR 1150.31
).
[
7
]
Although these decisions are maintained in agency records, they may not be readily accessible, particularly when the agency's approval was issued decades ago. Moreover, the Board's licensing structure is permissive. Only when the entity consummates a Board-authorized acquisition or operation does it become a “rail carrier” under the Board's jurisdiction.
See Mendocino Ry.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36868, slip op. at 3-4 (STB served Sept. 26, 2025) (citing
Middletown & N.J. R.R.—Lease & Operation Exemption—Norfolk S. Ry.,
FD 35412, slip op. at 4-5 (STB served Mar. 27, 2013)). And once the transaction is consummated, no separate notice of consummation is required to be filed with the Board. At this time, the Board does not maintain a registry, list, or website of licensed rail carriers, nor does it provide a physical or digital license document.
[
8
]
Additionally, a rail carrier does not automatically lose its common carrier status by stopping its rail service over a line. By statute, Board authorization is needed to terminate the common carrier obligation generally through a line sale, abandonment, or discontinuance.
See, e.g.,
Middletown,
FD 35412, slip op. at 4;
see also Strohmeyer—Acquis. & Operation Exemption—Valstir Indus. Track in Middlesex & Union Cntys., N.J.,
