FD 35527, slip op. at 2 & n.5 (STB served Oct. 20, 2011) (discussing the mechanisms a railroad may employ to excuse itself, permanently or temporarily, from its common carrier obligations) (citing
Pejepscot Indus. Park, Inc.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
6 S.T.B. 886, 898 (2003)). Therefore, regardless of how much time has passed since a shipper last requested common carrier service, a rail carrier remains within the Board's jurisdiction until the Board, in its sole authority, authorizes its removal and that authorization is consummated.
When questions concerning a rail carrier's status cannot be resolved through the review of public decisions, parties often seek assistance from the Board.
[
9
]
The Board's Rail Customer and Public Assistance (RCPA) program can assist in resolving disputes, explain the Board's jurisdiction and procedures, and informally answer questions based on the Staff's knowledge and experience.
[
10
]
Additionally, the Board has discretionary authority under
5 U.S.C. 554(e)
and
49 U.S.C. 1321
to
(
printed page 70962)
issue a declaratory order to eliminate controversy or remove uncertainty.
See, e.g.,
Bos. & Me. Corp.
v.
Town of Ayer,
330 F.3d 12, 14 n.2 (1st Cir. 2003);
Delegation of Auth.—Declaratory Ord. Procs.,
5 I.C.C.2d 675 (1989). For example, the Board recently received a request from a rail carrier to confirm its status as a common carrier subject to the Board's jurisdiction, which was disputed during legal challenges by local municipalities and state agencies.
See Mendocino Ry.,
FD 36868, slip op. at 1. The Board reviewed prior decisions related to the requesting rail carrier—including past Board decisions granting a common carrier obligation to the rail carrier's predecessor, and subsequently granting the rail carrier authority to purchase the line—and determined that the rail carrier was a common carrier subject to the Board's jurisdiction and therefore, if applicable, entitled to the benefits of federal preemption for its transportation activities under
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
.
See id.
at 1-4.
b. Passenger Rail Carriers
The Board also has jurisdiction over certain passenger rail operations. While the Board generally has jurisdiction over “transportation”—including equipment or services related to the movement of passengers as well as property,
see
49 U.S.C. 10102(9)
—by a “rail carrier,” not all passenger rail operations fall within the Board's jurisdiction. The definition of “rail carrier” specifically excludes “street, suburban, or interurban electric railways not operated as part of the general system of rail transportation.”
49 U.S.C. 10102(5)
. Additionally, except in limited circumstances,
[
11
]
the Board “does not have jurisdiction under this part over . . . public transportation provided by a local government authority.”
49 U.S.C. 10501(c)(2)(A)
. This exclusion generally applies to “regular, continuing shared-ride surface transportation services that are open to the general public or open to a segment of the general public defined by age, disability, or low income,” with certain exceptions, when provided by a local governmental authority.
[
12
]
49 U.S.C. 5302(15)
. Additionally, the National Railroad Passenger Corporation (Amtrak) is treated separately under ICCTA. Although Amtrak is part of the interstate rail network, Congress limited the Board's jurisdiction over Amtrak to specific statutory provisions, including to address directed service (
49 U.S.C. 11123
), equipment trusts (
id.
11301), pooling (
id.
11322(a)), withholding taxes (
id.
11502), and liability (
id.
11706).
See
49 U.S.C. 24301(c)
.
[
13
]
Whether a passenger rail service solely within one state is part of the interstate rail network is a fact-specific determination based on the totality of the circumstances.
Tex. Cent. R.R. & Infrastructure, Inc.—Pet. for Exemption—Passenger Rail Line Between Dallas & Houston, Tex.,
FD 36025, slip op. at 7 (STB served July 16, 2020);
Cal. High-Speed Rail Auth.—Constr. Exemption—in Merced, Madera & Fresno Cntys., Cal.,
FD 35724, slip op. at 11-15 (STB served June 13, 2013). It has also long been the agency's position that it does not have jurisdiction over purely intrastate passenger service, even if that service is performed by a licensed rail carrier.
See, e.g.,
Napa Valley Wine Train, Inc.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
7 I.C.C.2d 954, 969 (1991). However, questions can arise when an intrastate passenger line connects to the interstate rail network, as such service may indeed be subject to the Board's jurisdiction.
See, e.g.,
Tex. Cent. R.R.,
FD 36025, slip op. at 12 (finding that a proposed intrastate passenger rail line would be subject to the Board's jurisdiction because it was connected to the interstate rail system via through-ticketing arrangements and transfer service). The Board examines multiple factors in determining whether a particular passenger service is under its jurisdiction, such as whether the proposed service has a through-ticketing arrangement or whether it shares a station with an interstate carrier, although no single factor is dispositive.
See, e.g.,
id.,
slip op. at 7;
Cal. High-Speed Rail Auth.,
FD 35724, slip op. at 11-15.
3. Classifications of Rail Track
Whether an activity falls within the definition of “transportation by rail carrier” will sometimes depend, in whole or in part, on the legal status of the rail line or track on which service is being provided. Again, the Board recognizes three categories of track: common carrier (or mainline),
[
14
]
ancillary (or excepted),
[
15
]
and private. The first two (common carrier and ancillary) are subject to the Board's jurisdiction, whereas private track is not.
a. Common Carrier/Mainline Rail Lines
The Board has exclusive jurisdiction over rail lines over which a rail carrier provides “common carrier” service to shippers.
49 U.S.C. 10501(a)-(b)
;
id.
11101;
see Allied Erecting & Dismantling Co.
v.
STB,
835 F.3d 548, 550 (6th Cir. 2016). No one may build an extension to a common carrier rail line, build additional lines, provide transportation over an extended or additional line, or abandon a line without Board authorization.
49 U.S.C. 10901(a)
,
10903
;
see Allied Erecting & Dismantling Co.,
835 F.3d at 550.
[
16
]
b. Ancillary/Excepted Tracks
The Board often refers to spur, industrial, team, switching, or side tracks, or facilities interchangeably as “ancillary” or “excepted” tracks. “Ancillary” because such tracks and facilities are used for loading cars, track switching, and other activities that are incidental, or
ancillary,
to the provision of common carrier service,
see Nicholson
v.
ICC,
711 F.2d 365, 367-68 & n.11 (D.C. Cir. 1983); “excepted” because under
49 U.S.C. 10906
, the construction, acquisition, operation, abandonment, or discontinuance of such tracks and related facilities is
excepted
from the Board's licensing authority. Thus, while spur, industrial, team, switching, or side tracks, or facilities, are within the Board's exclusive jurisdiction, they can be added to or removed from the interstate rail network without authorization from the Board.
See N.Y.C. Econ. Dev. Corp.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36467, slip op. at 5 (STB served June 11, 2021);
Tri-City R.R.,
FD 36037, slip op.
(
printed page 70963)
at 4. Even though the Board does not license ancillary track (as it does common carrier rail lines), such track is under the Board's exclusive jurisdiction and therefore is subject to federal preemption.
See
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)(2)
. There is no bright-line test to distinguish between common carrier rail lines and ancillary tracks. Instead, the Board considers various indicia when determining whether a track is excepted under section 10906, including a track's relationship to the rail system, intended use, physical characteristics, and history.
See, e.g.
, Oakland Glob. Rail Enter.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36168, slip op. at 8 & n.8 (STB served Mar. 15, 2019).
[
17
]
A track segment that constitutes a carrier's entire rail system cannot be considered ancillary track (because it is not “ancillary” to other track of the carrier), and therefore is not excepted under
49 U.S.C. 10906
.
Effingham R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.—Constr. at Effingham, Ill.,
FD 33468, slip op. at 5 (STB served Sept. 18, 1998).
c. Private Track
Private track is track typically built and maintained by a shipper (or for a shipper at the shipper's expense), and operated by the shipper or its contractor to serve its own operations and move its own goods.
E.g., B. Willis, C.P.A., Inc.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
6 S.T.B. 280, 281 (2002),
aff'd sub nom. B. Willis, C.P.A., Inc.
v.
STB,
51 Fed. App'x 321 (D.C. Cir. 2002). Where the shipper does not hold out to provide common carrier railroad service over the line to other shippers for compensation, neither the construction of the track nor the operations require Board approval.
See B. Willis, C.P.A., Inc.,
6 S.T.B. at 285;
see also Devens Recycling Ctr.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 34952, slip op. at 3 (STB served Jan. 10, 2007) (finding no jurisdiction over operations conducted on private track used exclusively to serve the track owner pursuant to a contractual arrangement with the owner). When track is constructed and operated in a manner that does not constitute common carriage, the agency has held that it is not subject to the Board's jurisdiction.
See B. Willis, C.P.A., Inc.,
6 S.T.B. at 285. The agency has stated that private track need not serve only one shipper and can include private service to numerous shippers within a single location—such as an industrial park—as long as the carrier is not providing common carrier service.
Cf. TGS Cedar Port R.R.—Operation Exemption—in Chambers Cnty., Tex.,
FD 36627, slip op. at 1 (STB served Apr. 1, 2024) (noting that carrier previously operated 1.28 miles of private track within an industrial park without needing Board authority until conversion to common carrier service). Because such track is not subject to the Board's jurisdiction, construction and removal of such track is not covered by federal preemption. However, as discussed in further detail below, the Board is providing in this policy statement clarification regarding instances where state or local regulation of construction of or operations over private track may be considered to interfere with “transportation by rail carrier” and thus could be subject to preemption.
B. Regulation of Rail Transportation and the Preemption of Remedies
ICCTA contains an express preemption provision, providing that “[e]xcept as otherwise provided in [Part A of Subtitle IV of Title 49], the remedies provided under this part with respect to regulation of rail transportation are exclusive and preempt the remedies provided under Federal or State law.”
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
. The plain meaning of “regulation” is “managing or governing,”
Fla. E. Coast Ry.,
266 F.3d at 1331 (citing Black's Law Dictionary 1286 (6th ed. 1990)) (citation modified), or “controlling by rule or restriction,”
Union Pac. R.R.
v.
Chi. Transit Auth.,
647 F.3d 675, 679 n.2 (7th Cir. 2011). ICCTA thus bars states from “exercising control . . . over rail transportation as it is defined in
49 U.S.C. 10102(9)
.”
Id.
(citation modified).
ICCTA's use of “State” encompasses both state and local law, and it is well established that ICCTA preempts local as well as state regulation.
Padgett,
804 F.3d at 107 (citation modified). This can include, among other things, certain state or local building permits, zoning ordinances, and environmental and land use permitting requirements.
See, e.g.,
Wash. & Idaho Ry.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36017, slip op. at 4 (STB served Mar. 17, 2017) (noting that state or local permitting or preclearance requirements, including building permits, zoning ordinances, and environmental and land use permitting requirements may be subject to preemption).
“Regulation” does not simply mean laws passed by a legislature or rules enacted by a regulatory agency, and can, in appropriate circumstances, include common-law tort claims that similarly regulate rail transportation and certain related activity. Legal actions asserting eminent domain, adverse possession, easements, and other property rights have, as appropriate, been deemed “regulation” for purposes of analyzing ICCTA preemption.
See, e.g.,
Tri-City R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35915, slip op. at 7 (STB served Sept. 14, 2016) (collecting cases);
see also Edwards
v.
CSX Transp., Inc.,
983 F.3d 112, 121 (4th Cir. 2020) (holding that “regulation” need not “be by way of public rule”). Tort actions may also be considered “regulation” for purposes of ICCTA in certain circumstances “because damages awarded under state tort laws can manage or regulate a railroad as effectively as the application of any other type of state statute or regulation.”
Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 4. Thus, ICCTA's “preemptive reach can encompass common-law tort actions, in addition to statutes and ordinances.”
Edwards,
983 F.3d at 121-22 (collecting cases) (recognizing that ICCTA's preemption clause “in no way distinguishes between statutory prohibitions and common-law duties”). Indeed, the statute's “all-encompassing language” does not “permit the federal statute to be circumvented by allowing liability to accrue under state common law.”
Ezell
v.
Kan. City S. Ry.,
866 F.3d 294, 299-300 (5th Cir. 2017). It has been noted that “[o]f course, not
all
common-law claims against railroads are preempted.”
Edwards,
983 F.3d at 122. Rather, common law claims are subject to the same preemption analyses as are other forms of “regulation,” such as state and local laws.
While “the core of ICCTA preemption is `economic regulation,'”
Fayus Enters.,
602 F.3d at 451, such as state laws governing the setting of rates and rules and practices related to rail transportation or service, “ICCTA `does not preempt only explicit economic regulation.'”
Id.
(quoting
N.Y.
Susquehanna & W. Ry.
v.
Jackson,
500 F.3d 238, 252 (3d Cir. 2007));
accord City of Auburn,
154 F.3d at 1030. And as the Board has recognized, any such limitation would be “contrary to the statutory text and unworkable in practice.”
Friends of the Aquifer,
5 S.T.B. 880, 884 n.8 (2001). Additionally, given the broad language of section 10501(b)(2) (granting the Board exclusive jurisdiction over construction, acquisition, operation, abandonment, or discontinuance of rail lines), the distinction between “economic” and “environmental” regulation begins to blur.
See City of Auburn,
154 F.3d at 1031. “For if local authorities have the ability to impose `environmental'
(
printed page 70964)
permitting regulations on the railroad, such power will in fact amount to `economic regulation' if the carrier is prevented from constructing, acquiring, operating, abandoning, or discontinuing a line.”
City of Auburn,
154 F.3d at 1031.
The remedies that the Board may impose are set forth throughout the Board's governing statute, covering issues such as competition and access (
49 U.S.C. 11102
), rates (
id.
10702(1)), licensing (
id.
10901-10910), and the economic relationship between shippers and carriers (
id.
10702(2)). Section 10501(b) expressly states that “the remedies provided under [
49 U.S.C. 10101-11908
] with respect to regulation of rail transportation are exclusive and preempt the remedies provided under Federal or State law.” And so ICCTA preemption may apply even though a remedy may not exist under the Interstate Commerce Act for all instances where a state or local law is preempted.
14500 Ltd. LLC—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35788, slip op. at 5 (STB served June 5, 2014) (“Although [section] 10501(b) states that `the remedies provided under this part with respect to rail transportation are exclusive,' that does not mean that a remedy must exist under the Interstate Commerce Act for all instances where a state or local law is preempted under [section] 10501(b)”.);
Norfolk S. Ry.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35701, slip op. at 6 (STB served Nov. 4, 2013).
A notable instance where the Board does not have regulatory authority (but still has jurisdiction) is with respect to ancillary or excepted track. As noted above, Congress provided the Board with exclusive jurisdiction over the “construction, acquisition, operation, abandonment, or discontinuance of spur, industrial, team, switching, or side tracks,”
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)(2)
, while simultaneously stating that “[t]he Board does not have authority” over the licensing of these activities,
49 U.S.C. 10906
.
See also Pace
v.
CSX Transp., Inc.,
613 F.3d 1066, 1068-69 (11th Cir. 2010) (finding state law claims relating to side track preempted even though Board does not actively regulate such track);
Port City Props.
v.
Union Pac. R.R.,
518 F.3d 1186, 1188 (10th Cir. 2008) (stating that Congress intended to remove Board authority over the construction, operation, and abandonment of side tracks “while still preempting state jurisdiction over them”). Accordingly, even though the Board does not authorize construction or abandonment of ancillary track, state and local governments are prohibited from regulating such activities.
See
49 U.S.C. 10906
. For example, this means that states and localities are barred from requiring an environmental permit for construction of ancillary track, despite no environmental review being conducted by the Board.
The principle applies to other “transportation” activities that the Board does not directly regulate.
See Del Grosso,
804 F.3d at 114 (“Whether or not the Board is exercising its regulatory authority over the transportation, state and local laws governing such transportation are generally preempted.”). ICCTA preemption can apply “without regard to whether or not the Board actively regulates the particular activity involved.”
Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 4 (holding that a state law damages claim alleging improper design, construction, and maintenance of a rail carrier's main line track was preempted even though the Board does not directly regulate these issues).
[
18
]
For example, although the Board does not regulate how long carriers may idle locomotives, a state or local law seeking to impose its own regulation on how long locomotives may idle would nonetheless be preempted.
See Pet. of Norfolk S. Ry. for Expedited Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35949, slip op. at 4-5 (STB served Feb. 25, 2016),
aff'd sub nom. Delaware,
859 F.3d at 21-22.
ICCTA preempts not only direct regulation but may also preempt indirect regulation that affects a rail carrier's ability to provide common carrier operations to its customers.
See Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4 n.7 (collecting cases);
City of Alexandria,
FD 35157, slip op. at 2 (holding that ICCTA preempted local regulation of trucks serving a transloading facility operated by rail carrier's contractor). Such laws conflict with Congress's purpose in codifying the common carrier obligation because a rail carrier's ability to provide service and a shipper's right to receive service on reasonable request are two sides of the same coin.
C. Proper Forum for Disputes Concerning Board Jurisdiction and ICCTA Preemption
The Board's exclusive “jurisdiction” should not be confused with traditional subject-matter jurisdiction to hear and resolve a dispute. The Board's “jurisdiction” essentially confers a broad and exclusive “authority to regulate” (except where specifically stated otherwise,
e.g.,
ancillary track). But the Board does not have exclusive “subject-matter jurisdiction” to resolve disputes about whether a particular activity is preempted. It is well-established that the Board and courts have concurrent jurisdiction to resolve preemption questions.
E.g., Ne. La. Multimodal Dist.,
FD 36809, slip op. at 4;
see also Adrian & Blissfield R.R.
v.
Vill. of Blissfield,
550 F.3d 533, 539 n.4 (6th Cir. 2008). Actions implicating ICCTA preemption therefore may be originated either at the Board or in court.
[
19
]
Because jurisdiction is concurrent, the Board often has exercised its discretion not to address questions that have already been litigated by the parties and decided by a court.
See, e.g.,
City of N. Chi.,
FD 36619, slip op. at 4 n.3 (declining to issue declaratory order where “the preemption question posed by [the petition for declaratory order] has already been decided by the [referring] court”).
In addition to resolving disputes filed directly with the Board, the Board generally accepts referrals from courts grappling with questions regarding the extent of the Board's jurisdiction and preemption under ICCTA. Courts have sought the Board's input in a variety of ways, including dismissing a judicial proceeding without prejudice while the Board resolves an issue,
e.g., Tri-City R.R.,
FD 35915, slip op. at 4 n.4; staying a judicial proceeding while the parties seek a determination from the Board,
e.g., Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 1; or referring a question to the Board for resolution,
e.g., Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 5. And some courts have retained jurisdiction while referring a preemption determination to the Board, despite retaining concurrent jurisdiction to resolve the issue.
See, e.g.,
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 5. Particularly when the threshold question is whether the Board has jurisdiction at all—such as where the parties dispute whether an entity qualifies as a “rail carrier” under ICCTA, or whether a segment of track is excepted (jurisdictional) or private (non-jurisdictional), or whether a
(
printed page 70965)
jurisdictional track has been abandoned and therefore is no longer subject to the Board's jurisdiction as a matter of federal law—the Board's expertise and unique responsibility for ensuring uniform national rail standards may be utilized.
Cf. In re Metro. Transp. Auth.,
32 A.D.3d 943, 946 (N.Y. App. Div. 2006) (When “questions exist with regard to whether the track at issue is a spur and, if so, whether its apparent nonuse is sufficient to result in an abandonment, . . . [s]uch matters are properly addressed to the [Board]”). For example, some courts have directed the parties, during litigation, to seek guidance from the Board on the jurisdictional status of track.
See, e.g.,
Brookhaven Rail Terminal—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35819, slip op. at 4 (STB served Aug. 30, 2016) (determining Board's jurisdiction over track subject to litigation);
Pinelawn Cemetery—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35468, slip op. at 8 (STB served Apr. 21, 2015) (same).
IV. ICCTA Preemption Analysis for State and Local Laws
There is a well-settled framework, grounded in Supreme Court precedent, that guides the analysis of whether a federal law preempts state (or local) law. In relevant part, federal preemption of state law can either be express or implied.
[
20
]
Although courts (particularly the federal courts) regularly describe the Board's preemption framework using these established terms, the Board historically has not, electing instead to use the terms “categorical” and “as-applied.” The Board takes this opportunity to clarify where these concepts overlap: Express preemption is generally analyzed as “categorical” ICCTA preemption,
[
21
]
and implied preemption is generally
[
22
]
analyzed as “as-applied” ICCTA preemption. As described in more detail below, “categorical” preemption addresses state or local action that, by its nature, manages or governs rail transportation, whereas “as-applied” preemption addresses action that does so in its particular operation or effect. Each term is defined in more depth below.
A. Constitutional Framework for Preemption Analysis
Under our constitutional structure, the federal government is responsible for regulating interstate commerce.
See King Cnty.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
1 S.T.B. 731, 735 (1996) (citing Supreme Court precedent and stating that “under the Commerce and Supremacy Clauses of the United States Constitution, direct regulation of interstate commerce by the states is prohibited”);
see also Mo. Pac. R.R.
v.
Stroud,
267 U.S. 404, 408 (1925) (“It is elementary and well settled that there can be no divided authority over interstate commerce, and that the acts of Congress on that subject are supreme and exclusive.”). Federal preemption flows from the United States Constitution's Supremacy Clause, which makes federal law “the supreme Law of the Land.” U.S. Const., art. VI, cl. 2. The Supremacy Clause empowers Congress to enact federal laws that supersede state law by means of an express provision in a federal statute or by implication.
See id.;
see also Arizona,
567 U.S. at 398-99. Congress can show preemptive intent either expressly through the statute's language or impliedly through its purpose and structure.
Altria Grp., Inc.
v.
Good,
555 U.S. 70, 76 (2008);
Franks Inv. Co.
v.
Union Pac. R.R.,
593 F.3d 404, 407 (5th Cir. 2010) (en banc). Congress established a uniform federal regulatory framework governing the regulation of rail transportation through ICCTA, which both expressly and impliedly preempts state regulation.
E.g., Edwards,
983 F.3d at 121 (recognizing that ICCTA's provisions “produce both express and implied preemptive effects”).
ICCTA contains an express preemption provision, stating that “[e]xcept as otherwise provided in [Part A of Subtitle IV of Title 49], the remedies provided under this part with respect to regulation of rail transportation are exclusive and preempt the remedies provided under Federal or State law.”
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
. When a “statute contains an express pre-emption clause, [courts] do not invoke any presumption against pre-emption,” instead following the statute's “plain wording.”
See Puerto Rico
v.
Franklin Cal. Tax-Free Tr.,
579 U.S. 115, 125 (2016) (citation modified);
CSX Transp., Inc.
v.
Easterwood,
507 U.S. 658, 664 (1993);
see also Arizona,
567 U.S. at 399 (“There is no doubt that Congress may withdraw specified powers from the States by enacting a statute containing an express preemption provision.”). As relevant to interstate commerce, “States are precluded from regulating conduct in a field that Congress, acting within its proper authority, has determined must be regulated by its exclusive governance.”
Id.
“A principal purpose of this express federal preemption is to prevent a patchwork of local and state regulations from unreasonably interfering with interstate commerce.”
Tenth Ave. Neighbors,
FD 36654, slip op. at 3-4. In the Board's parlance, such state laws are categorically preempted.
See, e.g.,
Wichita Terminal Ass'n—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35765, slip op. at 6 (STB served June 23, 2015) (stating that certain actions are “expressly or categorically preempted under [section] 10501(b)”).
The breadth of this grant of exclusive jurisdiction, in conjunction with the preemption provision, also forms a basis for implied preemption. Congress stated its intent to “reflect the direct and complete pre-emption of State economic regulation of railroads,” and “extend[ ] exclusive Federal jurisdiction” to areas where state jurisdiction was previously reserved. H.R. Rep. No. 104-311, at 95. And through ICCTA, Congress affirmed that “the Federal policy of occupying the entire field of economic regulation of the interstate rail transportation system” was “intended to address and encompass all such regulation and to be completely exclusive.”
Id.
The Board considers contrary state law to be preempted on an as-applied basis.
See, e.g.,
Franks Inv. Co.,
593 F.3d at 414 (“We adopt the [Board's] as-applied preemption analysis as appropriate for implied preemption under the ICCTA.”). This rule also follows longstanding precedent, predating ICCTA, holding that the Interstate Commerce Act “preempts state laws that could operate to unreasonably burden interstate commerce.”
Tex. Dep't of Transp.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord. Regarding Highway Constr. In Tarrant Cnty, Tex.,
FD 32589, slip op. at 4 (ICC served Feb. 7, 1995);
see also Reguls. Governing Fees for Servs. Performed in Connection with Licensing & Related Servs.,
l I.C.C.2d 60, 81 (1984) (evaluating whether state regulatory actions were “an unreasonable burden on interstate commerce”).
(
printed page 70966)
B. ICCTA Preemption Framework
When faced with a question about whether ICCTA preempts a state or local law, the Board and courts first determine whether to apply a categorical preemption analysis or an as-applied preemption analysis based on the nature of the regulation. Whether preemption is categorical or as-applied does not turn merely on whether the potentially preempted regulation is directed at rail carrier transportation specifically (such as limiting railroad operating hours) or instead is of general applicability (like zoning ordinances). Both sorts of regulations may be preempted either categorically or as-applied, depending on whether the regulation intrudes on a matter directly regulated by the Board—for example, reasonable rail rates and practices—and not on the entity subject to the regulation.
[
23
]
It is the Board's long-established policy to analyze preemption in a way that seeks to prevent a patchwork of state and local regulation from interfering with rail transportation within the Board's jurisdiction.
See Tenth Ave. Neighbors,
FD 36654, slip op. at 3-4 (recognizing that “[a] principal purpose of this express federal preemption is to prevent a patchwork of local and state regulations from unreasonably interfering with interstate commerce”);
CSX Transp., Inc.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 11 (STB served March 14, 2005) (stating that “[s]ection 10501(b) is intended to prevent a patchwork of local regulation from unreasonably interfering with interstate commerce,” and that the regulation at issue “would unreasonably interfere with interstate commerce, and if permitted to exist, would likely lead to further piecemeal attempts by other localities to regulate rail shipments”).
1. Categorical Preemption Analysis
State or local laws are preempted categorically if they may reasonably be understood to manage or govern transportation by a rail carrier or certain related activities, including by foreclosing or restricting the railroad's ability to conduct its own operations.
See Delaware,
859 F.3d at 18 (ICCTA preempts “all state laws that may reasonably be said to have the effect of managing or governing rail transportation.”);
Wichita Terminal Ass'n,
FD 35765, slip op. at 6. Categorical preemption typically applies to: (1) laws that directly regulate transportation by rail carriers, and (2) generally applicable permitting or preclearance laws when imposed on rail transportation.
ICCTA “prevent[s] states or localities from intruding into matters that are directly regulated by the Board (
e.g.,
railroad rates, services, construction, and abandonment).”
14500 Ltd. LLC,
FD 35788, slip op. at 3;
see also Ass'n of Am. R.Rs.
v.
S. Coast Air Quality Mgmt. Dist.,
No. 06-CV-1416, 2007 WL 2439499, at *7 (C.D. Cal. Apr. 30, 2007) (holding that rules directly regulating rail operations, such as idling, are preempted regardless of whether they are considered undue or unreasonable),
aff'd,
622 F.3d 1094 (9th Cir. 2010). Categorical preemption “also prevents states or localities from imposing requirements that, by their nature, could be used to deny a railroad's ability to conduct rail operations or proceed with activities that the Board has authorized, such as a construction or abandonment,” or to maintain its facilities.
14500 Ltd. LLC,
FD 35788, slip op. at 3-4 & n.5. Therefore, “state law preclearance or permitting requirements that could be used to deny or unreasonably delay a rail carrier's ability to conduct rail operations typically are categorically preempted.”
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 7 (collecting cases). Some examples include building permits, zoning ordinances, and environmental and land use permitting requirements.
E.g., Jie Ao—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35539, slip op. at 5 (STB served June 6, 2012). The Board and courts have long recognized that “[i]f local authorities have the ability to impose `environmental' permitting regulations on the railroad, such power will in fact amount to `economic regulation' if the carrier is prevented from constructing, acquiring, operating, abandoning, or discontinuing a line.”
City of Auburn,
154 F.3d at 1031 (affirming Board finding of preemption of state and local environmental permitting laws as applied to rail construction project).
Additionally, categorical preemption applies regardless of the stated purpose of the law.
See Borough of Riverdale—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.—N.Y. Susquehanna & W. Ry.,
4 S.T.B. 380, 388 n.16 (1999) (noting that “even health and safety regulation is preempted where Congress intended to preempt all state and local law”). Moreover, it “does not depend on whether the practical application of the statute or regulation is narrowly tailored.”
Delaware,
859 F.3d at 22. The categorical “preemption analysis is addressed not to the reasonableness of the particular state or local action, but rather to the act of regulation itself.”
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 3 (STB served May 3, 2005);
see also Green Mountain R.R.
v.
Vermont,
404 F.3d 638, 644 (2d Cir. 2005) (stating that “the focus is the act of regulation itself, not the effect of the state regulation in a specific factual situation”) (citation modified). Some limited fact-finding may be needed to determine “whether the state or local action falls within a category subject to categorical preemption.”
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 35832, slip op. at 5. But if it does, a regulation that has the effect of managing or governing transportation by rail carrier is preempted “regardless of its practical effect.”
Delaware,
859 F.3d at 19. And state permitting or preclearance requirements are categorically preempted “without requiring a factual analysis of their effect on transportation.”
See, e.g.,
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 7 (collecting cases);
see also Green Mountain R.R.,
404 F.3d at 644 (“[W]hat is preempted here is the permitting process itself, not the length or outcome of that process in particular cases.”).
2. As-Applied Preemption Analysis
Even when a state or local law is not categorically preempted, it may be preempted under the “as-applied” analysis if it either: (1) unreasonably burdens or interferes with transportation by rail carriers, or (2) discriminates against rail carriers.
a. Unreasonable Burden or Interference
State and local laws are preempted “as applied” if they unreasonably burden or interfere with current—or future—rail transportation. This is “a fact-specific determination based on the circumstances of each case.”
See, e.g.,
Wichita Terminal Ass'n,
FD 35765, slip op. at 6 (citation omitted). An as-applied analysis includes a comprehensive analysis of the likely impact of the proposed law's application to current rail operations.
See, e.g.,
Tri-City R.R.,
FD 35915, slip op. at 8 (analyzing length, location, and configuration of track, its uses, and potential alternative locations for operations). The Board and courts also consider interference with planned or potential future rail operations. Certain state actions may be preempted even when no current rail operations exist on tracks within the Board's jurisdiction, based on potential future use (for example, when a line is
(
printed page 70967)
railbanked or when a rail carrier intends to develop a property for rail use).
See, e.g.,
id.
(analyzing future operations and effects of increases in rail traffic);
Jie Ao,
FD 35539, slip op. at 5 (analyzing effects on future reactivation of railbanked line, even though “there are currently no specific plans to reactivate this property,” including impacts on potential rail-related construction, track bed stabilization, drainage, and maintenance).
Because ICCTA was established to prevent a patchwork of differing state and local regulations, the unreasonable-burden analysis also requires consideration of ripple effects across the broader interstate rail network. Accordingly, the analysis considers not only the facts of a single case, but also the potential impact on the interstate rail network as a whole, guarding against a “patchwork” of “potentially differing standards” as trains travel across the network.
See Wichita Terminal Ass'n,
FD 35765, slip op. at 10;
see also Norfolk S. Ry.,
FD 35701, slip op. at 4-6 (finding that state inverse condemnation claims based on dust, vibration, and noise were preempted and explaining that absent preemption “all railroads on the interstate rail network could be subject to inverse condemnation actions from adjacent landowners throughout the country based on the effects of normal railroad operations”). “The interstate rail network could not function properly if states and localities could impose their own potentially differing standards for” rail operations, nor if state regulations could “interfer[e] with the railroad's ability to uniformly design, construct, maintain, and repair its railroad line.”
Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 5.
Again, ICCTA preemption has its limits. Federal law does not preempt local and state application of laws having a “more remote or incidental effect on rail transportation.”
N.Y. Susquehanna & W. Ry.,
500 F.3d at 252. Therefore, ICCTA's “preemption provision does not prevent state and local governments from imposing appropriate health and safety regulations and exercising their police powers” in appropriate circumstances.
Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4. In addition, the Board has held that condemnations of railroad property, under generally applicable state eminent domain law for “routine non-conflicting uses, such as non-exclusive easements for at-grade road crossings . . . are not preempted so long as they would not impede rail operations or pose undue safety risks.”
Wichita Terminal Ass'n,
FD 35765, slip op. at 6. Additionally, the enforcement of “generally applicable, non-discriminatory regulations” like “[e]lectrical, plumbing and fire codes” that have only an “incidental” effect on rail transportation may be permissible.
See Green Mountain R.R.,
404 F.3d at 643, 645;
Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4. And again, ICCTA preemption reaches “transportation” by “rail carrier.”
But states “cannot use their police powers to indirectly regulate matters reserved to the Board . . . .”
Soo Line R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35850, slip op. at 5 (STB served Dec. 23, 2014). Although pre-ICCTA, the Interstate Commerce Act explicitly preserved the states' “police power” to impose “reasonable intrastate transportation” requirements,
49 U.S.C. 10501(c)
(1994), this “disclaimer regarding residual State police powers [was] eliminated as unnecessary [in ICCTA], in view of the Federal policy of occupying the entire field,” H.R. Rep. No. 104-311, at 95-96. “Although States retain the police powers reserved by the Constitution, the Federal scheme of economic regulation and deregulation is intended to address and encompass all such regulation and to be completely exclusive.”
Id.
at 96. Thus, “states are not free to impose any requirements they wish in the name of their police power.”
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 4-5 (STB served May 3, 2005). Although certain decisions have referred to a “police power exception” to ICCTA preemption,
see Grafton & Upton R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35752, slip op. at 9 (STB served Sept. 19, 2014), what matters is not that the state or locality is exercising “police powers” as such, but that it is enforcing “generally applicable, non-discriminatory regulations” like “[e]lectrical, plumbing and fire codes” that have only an “incidental” effect on rail transportation—and even then, such regulations “must not have the effect of foreclosing or restricting the railroad's ability to conduct its operations or otherwise unreasonably burdening interstate commerce,” or they may be preempted.
See Green Mountain R.R.,
404 F.3d at 643, 645;
Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4 (ICCTA “does not prevent state and local governments from . . . exercising their police powers so long as” they do not regulate, unreasonably burden, or discriminate against rail carriers).
b. Discrimination Against Rail Transportation.
State laws and regulations that discriminate against rail transportation may also be preempted on an as-applied basis. The ICC long held that, “in areas not governed by [f]ederal legislation, [s]tates and their subdivisions may make reasonable regulations affecting commerce under our jurisdiction so long as they are uniformly applied and do not discriminate against or constitute an undue burden on or an obstruction of commerce, in accordance with standard preemption principles.”
Appls. for Operating Auth.—Motor Passenger Carriers,
133 M.C.C. 62, 86-87 (I.C.C. 1982) (discussing motor carriers);
see also
City of Auburn,
154 F.3d at 1029 n.6 (“Before 1980, the ICC was empowered to preempt state regulation of intrastate lines only when an intrastate rate set by the state unjustly discriminated against or imposed an undue burden on interstate commerce.”). Thus “state and local entities can enforce in a non-discriminatory manner” local laws passed under their police powers.
Riverdale,
4 S.T.B. at 389;
see also Green Mountain R.R.,
404 F.3d at 643 (noting that certain “non-discriminatory regulations” would not be preempted);
Delaware,
859 F.3d at 18-19 (same, after conducting extensive survey of precedent);
City of Milwaukie—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35625, slip op. at 4 (STB served Mar. 25, 2013) (noting that such regulations can apply to rail carrier transportation “if they are applied without discrimination”).
Courts have recognized that “[t]he non-discriminatory prong is particularly useful in determining whether a state is regulating principally to discriminate against a specific industry.”
N.Y.
Susquehanna & W. Ry.,
500 F.3d at 254. “[F]or a state regulation to pass muster, it must address state concerns generally, without targeting the railroad industry.”
Id.; see also
BNSF Ry.
v.
Cal. Dep't of Tax & Fee Admin.,
904 F.3d 755, 761, 768 (9th Cir. 2018) (concluding that ICCTA would preempt use of traditional state police powers to impose a fee on shipment of hazardous materials in California, where the fee would apply only to shipments “by rail”). But even so, a regulation addressing state concerns generally—which may include a fee or other charge on rail carriers or transportation by rail—cannot be used “as pretext for interfering with or curtailing rail service.”
N.Y.
Susquehanna & W. Ry.,
500 F.3d at 254;
see also BNSF Ry.
v.
Town of Cicero, Ill.,
592 F. Supp. 3d 716, 729 (N.D. Ill. 2022) (finding that the rail carrier adequately showed that a local sewer ordinance regulated railroad transportation because it singled out and targeted railroads for a rate higher than the rate paid by other commercial and industrial
(
printed page 70968)
properties).
[
24
]
To assess preemption in this context, the Board and courts look to whether the law “is being applied in a discriminatory manner, or being used as a pretext for frustrating or preventing a particular activity.”
Joint Pet. for Declaratory Ord.—Bos. & Me. Corp.,
5 S.T.B. 500, 509 (2001). Though not all state regulations that apply specifically to railroads are impermissibly discriminatory, such regulations may be preempted in at least two circumstances: (1) when the regulation requires something of the railroad that it does not require of other modes of transportation or similarly situated entities, or (2) when the regulation could be used to target railroads in order to cause indefinite delays to railroad operations.
See Adrian & Blissfield R.R.,
550 F.3d at 541-42.
As in other forms of preemption analysis, laws can be discriminatory whether or not they specifically mention rail carriers. For example, a law of general applicability passed to protect health and safety by imposing quantity, duration, and location restrictions on the storage of certain substances was found discriminatory as applied to a rail carrier's transloading facility.
See Vt. Ry.
v.
Town of Shelburne,
287 F. Supp. 3d 493, 494 (D. Vt. 2017),
aff'd,
918 F.3d 82 (2d Cir. 2019). In that instance, the court held that the timing of the passage of the ordinance (during litigation between the town and rail carrier), threshold limits, and commodities affected would, in practice, uniquely apply to the transload facility and not others who may be similarly situated, and as such, “these provisions clearly target and discriminate against the [rail carrier]'s facility.”
Id.
at 500-01. For these reasons (as well as unreasonable burden), the ordinance was preempted.
Id.
at 505. Conversely, in
Adrian & Blissfield R.R.,
an ordinance requiring rail carriers to construct, or pay for the construction of sidewalk crossings over their tracks was found non-discriminatory.
See Adrian & Blissfield R.R.,
550 F.3d at 539. In that case, the court first held that the ordinance did not regulate rail transportation.
See id.
at 540 & n.6. It went on to “apply the as-applied-preemption analysis,” including the prohibition on laws that “discriminate against railroads.”
Id.
at 541 (citation omitted). The court deemed the ordinance was non-discriminatory because (1) it “addresse[d] a general state concern”; (2) there was “no evidence” that the ordinance could be used pretextually to interfere with rail operations; and (3) the state was not “requir[ing] something of the Railroad that it does not require of similarly situated entities.”
Id.
at 541-42.
3. Complete Takings—Refocused Categorical Approach
When state or local law is used in an attempt to entirely dispossess a rail carrier of its property rights—such as through a private claim for adverse possession, or a state's use of eminent domain—the Board and court precedents have been unclear about whether categorical or as-applied analysis should govern.
[
25
]
See, e.g.,
Jie Ao,
FD 35539, slip op. at 1 (holding that “state law adverse possession claim is federally preempted, regardless of whether this case is analyzed as `categorical' preemption [or] as `as applied' preemption”). And as courts have recognized, “[t]he more a property action excludes a rail carrier and takes a property for a conflicting use, the more likely the action will be preempted.”
Norfolk S. Ry.
v.
Dille Rd. Recycling, LLC,
94 F.4th 517, 524, 527 (6th Cir. 2024) (discussing a “spectrum” of easement claims where “routine, nonexclusive easements . . . are generally not preempted,” but those “that are exclusive or deemed adverse possession by another name are often preempted”). While this policy statement is not adopting a definitive approach that resolves all cases, there are strong policy arguments that state and local law claims seeking to take exclusive possession of any portion of a validly held railroad right-of-way, or to take rail carrier property that the rail carrier uses—or plans to use—to support rail transportation (
i.e.,
property falling within the definition of “transportation” under
49 U.S.C. 10102(9)
) would be better reviewed under the categorical preemption analysis.
[
26
]
And there are also strong policy arguments that claims involving more routine, non-conflicting uses—such as non-exclusive easements for at-grade road crossings, subterranean water or sewer lines, and related claims—are best assessed using an as-applied analysis as the Board does currently.
State or local regulation that seeks to take exclusive control of rail carrier rights-of-way or other property can take many different forms, including but not limited to claims for eminent domain, condemnation, or adverse possession, among others. “The agency's broad and exclusive jurisdiction over railroad operations and activities prevents application of state law claims that would take rail property for another, conflicting use, including adverse possession claims that would interfere with rail use, present or future.”
14500 Ltd. LLC,
FD 35788, slip op. at 4. Using state law for these purposes “is exercising control—the most extreme type of control—over rail transportation as it is defined in section 10102(9).”
Wis. Cent. Ltd.
v.
City of Marshfield,
160 F. Supp. 2d 1009, 1013 (W.D. Wis. 2000). This type of taking “is a permanent action, and `it can never be stated with certainty at what time any particular part of a right of way may become necessary for railroad uses.'”
City of Lincoln
v.
STB,
414 F.3d 858, 862 (8th Cir. 2005) (quoting
Midland Valley R.R.
v.
Jarvis,
29 F.2d 539, 541 (8th Cir. 1928)). Further, such actions “would foreclose [the rail carrier]'s development of the property for rail `transportation' purposes.”
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 11.
For rail carrier property within the Board's jurisdiction, only upon abandonment does the underlying property become “ordinary property” subject to the application of state law.
See, e.g.,
Hayfield N. R.R.
v.
Chi. & NW
(
printed page 70969)
Transp. Co.,
467 U.S. 622, 633-34 (1984). Rail lines under the Board's jurisdiction remain available for common carrier service upon reasonable request.
49 U.S.C. 11101(a)
. Even where the Board has authorized discontinuance of service over a rail line, such that there is no extant common carrier obligation, the line remains available for the reinstitution of service in the future.
See, e.g.,
Preseault
v.
ICC,
494 U.S. 1, 5 n.3 (1990) (stating that “discontinuance” authority allows a railroad to cease operating a line for an indefinite period while preserving the rail corridor for possible reactivation of service in the future). The common carrier obligation is not permanently extinguished until the line has been removed from Board jurisdiction via Board-authorized abandonment.
See id.
Permitting the use of state law for acquiring exclusive control of rail carrier property would contravene this statutory scheme. As the Board has explained, it would allow for the taking of “railroad [right-of-way] all over the country for non-rail use, even though the Board has not authorized the [right-of-way] to be permanently removed from the nation's rail system under Title 49.”
Jie Ao,
FD 35539, slip op. at 7. This is an “untenable result [that] would undermine interstate commerce and the strong federal policy in favor of retaining rail property in the national rail network, where possible.”
Id.
(citing
49 U.S.C. 10904
,
10907
&
16 U.S.C. 1247(d)
). Subjecting Board-jurisdictional rail line or excepted track to adverse possession, eminent domain, or condemnation claims under state law would thus “have the effect of managing or governing rail transportation,”
Skidmore
v.
Norfolk S. Ry.,
1 F.4th 206, 215 (4th Cir. 2021), and “would amount to regulation of rail transportation because [they] would confer exclusive control to [someone other than the rail carrier] over property that is part of the national rail network.”
Jie Ao,
FD 35539, slip op. at 3. With this backdrop, the Board has previously observed that “[n]either the Board nor the courts . . . have found that cities can entirely take from a railroad land the railroad has slated for present or future rail use.”
Norfolk S. Ry.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.
(
Ala. Great S.
), FD 35196, slip op. at 5 (STB served Mar. 1, 2010).
[
27
]
And the Board has held that ICCTA “preempts state law eminent domain and adverse possession claims for exclusive possession of part of a railroad right-of-way or other railroad property that could affect present or future rail transportation.”
Ohio Rail Dev. Comm'n—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36822, slip op. at 7 (STB served Mar. 30, 2026). As summarized by the Fourth Circuit:
Indeed, allowing an individual landowner to wrest exclusive control of land within the national rail corridor away from a railroad could expose a rail carrier to death by a thousand cuts. Rail carriers would either have to be hyper-vigilant about fending off adverse possession claims along countless miles of tracks, or risk losing ownership interests in land that is (or might be) necessary to conduct business and comply with federal regulations. Because maintaining a unified federal mechanism for governing the national rail network is an issue of overwhelming national importance, federal law must preempt [state or local] quiet title claims.
Skidmore,
1 F.4th at 217.
One critical aspect of the Board's categorical preemption analysis is that such regulations are preempted without requiring a factual analysis of their effect on transportation and whether any interference may be unreasonable. With respect to claims for possession of rights-of-way subject to the Board's jurisdiction, once the threshold determination is made that the scope of the sought-after property right would exclude rail use, there are strong arguments that the analysis should be at its end. Such claims may be categorically preempted without a detailed inquiry into their effect on present or future operations and whether interference is unreasonable.
Cf. Green Mountain R.R.,
404 F.3d at 644 (applying categorical preemption to permitting of transloading construction and stating that “what is preempted here is the permitting process itself, not the length or outcome of that process in particular cases”);
see also Wis. Cent. Ltd.,
160 F. Supp. at 1013-14 (holding that condemnation was preempted without an inquiry as to interference). The Board recognizes that condemnation claims, including those involving non-exclusive easements, have often been analyzed under the as-applied framework.
See e.g.,
City of Lincoln,
414 F.3d at 860. In the Board's view, there are compelling policy considerations that the as-applied framework is ill-suited to address condemnation or similar claims that would foreclose rail use of rail property and rights-of-way (or portions thereof) that are subject to the Board's jurisdiction and must remain available for common carrier service. These types of takings are arguably more severe incursions on activities within the Board's exclusive jurisdiction than others that have been long recognized as categorically preempted. If a state entity is categorically prohibited from enforcing a zoning law or other preclearance requirement to prevent the construction of a rail carrier's facility on its property, it makes little sense to find that the state entity would be subject to a less rigorous as-applied framework if it were instead to seek to take the property outright through condemnation. Moreover, consideration of such exclusive takings under the as-applied preemption framework may result in patchwork regulation of standards concerning present and future rail service, contrary to the uniform licensing framework established in ICCTA. Parties contending that such rights-of-way no longer serve any bona fide rail purpose have historically directed that contention to the Board through an adverse abandonment proceeding.
[
28
]
In prior cases, rail carriers defending against actions to take their property have been required to set forth extensive analysis of the current and potential future uses of the property for rail operations.
See, e.g.,
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696 (STB served Nov. 15, 2023);
14500 Ltd. LLC,
FD 35788 (STB served June 5, 2014);
Ala. Great S.,
FD 35196 (STB served Mar. 1, 2010). Where an action to take rail property would exclude rail use on a portion of the rail property or rights-of-way subject to the Board's jurisdiction, that consequence is ascertainable at the outset and therefore may warrant categorical treatment without further inquiry.
See Jie Ao,
FD 35539, slip op. at 5-7
; see also Wis. Cent. Ltd.,
160 F. Supp. 2d at 1013-14 (categorically preempting condemnation of rail property and stating that “the nature of the preempted state regulation is irrelevant”);
Soo Line R.R.,
827 F. Supp. 2d at 1022 (same and noting that “factual `as applied' arguments concerning whether the proposed easement would unreasonably interfere with [the rail carrier]'s activities are not relevant”).
It may be reasonable to conclude that certain other takings claims would not be appropriate for a categorical analysis.
(
printed page 70970)
As noted above, there are strong arguments that non-exclusive easements, such as for crossings, warrant an as-applied preemption analysis that looks to the degree of interference with rail operations. Similarly, claims to take land under a right-of-way or under other rail property, such as for laying subterranean utility or broadband lines or similar facilities, may be analyzed under the as-applied framework. Subject to the facts and circumstances in particular cases, such non-exclusive uses may be permissible, or may unreasonably interfere with interstate rail transportation if, for example, they are placed in locations that undermine the integrity of the rail right-of-way, or are installed in a manner, or for a duration, that prevents or materially interferes with rail operations.
4. Shipper and Receiver Rights to Common Carrier Rail Service
The Board recognizes that private investment in rail infrastructure—by carriers and customers alike—is critical to maintaining and improving the expansive interstate rail network for existing customers, extending its reach to new customers, and ensuring its competitiveness with other modes of transportation. Rail transportation—unlike modes such as trucking and water carriage, which rely heavily on public infrastructure maintained by public entities (such as roads, waterways, and ports)—operates almost exclusively on privately owned and developed infrastructure. Such projects are time and labor intensive, and require high levels of coordination—and, frequently, co-investment—between rail carriers and potential customers seeking common carrier rail service.
Although the Board's jurisdiction extends only to “transportation” by, or under the auspices of, a “rail carrier,” the application of state and local regulations nominally to rail customers implicates ICCTA in certain situations.
It has been long recognized that “ICCTA preempts both direct and indirect regulation that affects a railroad's ability to conduct common carrier operations.”
Smithtown,
FD 36575 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 4 n.7 (collecting cases). Thus, for example, a local ordinance and permit restricting truck transportation “regulate[d] `transportation by a rail carrier,' as defined by the ICCTA,” because they “directly impact[ed] [the rail carrier]'s ability to move goods shipped by rail.”
Norfolk S. Ry.
v.
City of Alexandria,
608 F.3d 150, 158-59 (4th Cir. 2010). Preemption applied even though the ordinance and permit “regulate[d] only the trucks leaving the [railroad's transloading] Facility, not the trans-loading process itself,” and did not directly “regulate any aspect of the movement of trains [or] the unloading or transloading of trains.”
Id.
at 159. Likewise, ICCTA does not permit “regulation of the interstate freight rail network under the guise of local regulations directed at the shippers who would use the network,” which would “create the patchwork of conflicting local regulations that Congress sought to avoid in the Interstate Commerce Act.”
Bos. & Me. Corp.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35749, slip op. at 5 (STB served July 19, 2013). Shippers have “rights provided by federal law to ask for and receive common carrier rail service from” rail carriers under the Board's jurisdiction, and so even regulations “directed solely at” a shipper would create a “fundamental conflict between” the shipper's right to request, and a rail carrier's right to provide, common carrier rail service under ICCTA.
Id.
at 4. Such state and local regulations conflict with Congress's purpose in codifying the common carrier obligation, because rail carriers' ability to provide service and shippers' right to receive service on reasonable request are two sides of the same coin.
Cf. Engine Mfrs. Ass'n
v.
S. Coast Air Quality Mgmt. Dist.,
541 U.S. 246, 255 (2004) (“[T]reating sales restrictions and purchase restrictions differently for pre-emption purposes would make no sense,” because the “right to sell . . . is meaningless in the absence of a purchaser's right to buy . . . .”).
The point at which activities no longer constitute “transportation by rail carrier” and certain related activities, and thus fall outside the Board's jurisdiction, can be difficult to discern in some situations—particularly for activities involving the loading and unloading of rail cars on shipper-owned track—and the Board's precedents in this area have not always been entirely consistent. In
Boston & Maine,
FD 35749, slip op. at 4-5, the Board suggested that state regulation of a customer's private, non-jurisdictional track would be preempted if it impacted common carrier service. On the other hand, in
SEA-3, Inc.—Petition for Declaratory Order
(
SEA-3
), FD 35853, slip op. at 6-7 (STB served Mar. 17, 2015), the Board determined that a city's challenge to a zoning decision allowing an existing rail customer to increase its use of rail common carrier service by constructing additional rail berths at its transloading facility was not preempted. And, in
Valero Refining Co.—Petition for Declaratory Order
(
Valero
), FD 36036, slip op. at 2, 6 (STB served Sept. 20, 2016), the Board held that it did not have jurisdiction over an existing rail customer's construction of an off-loading facility designed to receive common carrier unit train service. In
Valero,
state and local authorities denied a permit for construction of the project, based at least in part on the impacts of increased common carrier service, as well as impacts of the commodity likely to be carried in that service.
See id.
at 2.
[
29
]
Thus, the Board provides here a modified analytical framework that, subject to the arguments and facts presented in particular proceedings, may inform an evaluation of whether regulations nominally directed at rail customers are, in practice and in legal effect, regulations of transportation by rail carriers that are preempted by ICCTA. The potential framework begins with a fact-specific threshold inquiry consisting of two questions. First, is the facility or project at issue developed or used to receive or tender common carrier rail service—a transload, off-loading, or similar facility whose function is the interchange of traffic with a rail carrier? Second, does the state or local action restrict, condition, or dictate common carrier service to that facility, such as the volume, frequency, timing, configuration, or commodity mix of common carrier service? Where the answer to both is yes, the action may regulate transportation by rail carrier in practical effect, and the categorical or as-applied framework, as appropriate, would apply depending on the nature of the regulation. A regulation that, for
(
printed page 70971)
example, caps the rail traffic a facility may receive binds the carrier as surely as one addressed to the carrier by name: the carrier cannot lawfully tender the service, the shipper cannot lawfully receive it, and the common carrier obligation of
49 U.S.C. 11101(a)
—and the shipper's correlative right to service on reasonable request—is displaced by local command.
See Boston & Maine,
FD 35749, slip op. at 4-5;
cf. Engine Mfrs. Ass'n,
541 U.S. at 255. Where either answer is no—such as where the object of the regulation is the facility's non-rail activities, not the receipt or tender of rail service—section 10501(b) is not implicated (unless the action discriminates against rail transportation, which is an independent basis for analyzing preemption).
This potential framework would refine the principle recognized in
Boston & Maine
—state or local action directed at a rail customer implicates section 10501(b) where it operates, in practical effect, on the common carrier service the customer receives.
See Bos. & Me.,
FD 35749, slip op. at 4-5. The threshold inquiry clarifies the limit and scope of this principle, and its rationale is evident from the examples of
SEA-3
and
Valero.
In
SEA-3,
a city sought to use state and local regulations to prevent an already rail-served customer from increasing its facility from three to eight rail berths. If the construction was not allowed to occur, the result from the local regulation would be no different than a locality limiting or directing a rail carrier's execution of its common carrier obligations. In practice, it would dictate that only three, and not eight, cars could be sent to the customer at any given time. And to provide the same amount of product, the common carrier must make three trips, rather than one, to the customer facility, and must also change its operational schedule, yard storage, and any number of other operational decisions accordingly. Similarly, in
Valero,
the refusal by state and local officials to grant permission for construction not only dictated the number of cars and type of service (unit train vs. manifest) that the carrier could provide, but also imposed restrictions on the types of commodities that the rail carrier could tender to its customer, thus preventing the rail carrier from being able to fulfill its common carrier obligation. These types of decisions are ordinarily within the decision-making control of rail carriers in providing service to their customers, but were implicated by local regulation of rail customers in both cases.
SEA-3
and
Valero
read “transportation by rail carrier” to ask what is the stated object of the regulation, whereas a better reading might ask what was regulated in effect. The Board recognizes that rail service provided by a common carrier remains transportation by rail carrier even when the restriction on such service is addressed to the customer and takes this opportunity to reemphasize that principle.
To be sure, rail customers are not directly under the Board's jurisdiction. And the Board expects that much regulation of rail customers' facilities is, and should remain, beyond the Board's jurisdiction. For example, a zoning ordinance would likely be preempted if it prevented a rail carrier from developing a transload facility. By contrast, ICCTA would not prevent enforcement of that same ordinance against a private business developing a manufacturing facility with an incidental rail component, or against the portions of the facility unrelated to the receipt or tender of common carrier rail service, unless there was evidence that the ordinance was being applied in a discriminatory manner against rail transportation. Likewise, if the construction projects in
SEA-3
and
Valero
implicated local zoning or environmental ordinances, the ordinances' application to these customers would not implicate ICCTA to the extent that they apply to portions of the project unrelated to receiving common carrier rail service. And, in any event, many local ordinances—such as electrical, fire, plumbing, and others—would still apply, just as they do to rail carrier facilities.
C. Commonly Arising State and Local Preemption Issues
There are numerous types of state laws or regulations that frequently result in litigation about preemption. Below is a list of common situations, and a summary of how such issues have been analyzed for preemption purposes. It should be noted that the list is not exhaustive, and that there are additional precedents on many of the issues discussed below, that at times come to differing conclusions based on the facts of the particular case. Moreover, the Board here does not take a position on how any potential future case that may come to the Board (or a court analyzing preemption) will, or should be, resolved. Rather, this list is meant to inform the public about relevant existing precedents on certain topics, in the hopes that this information will help parties proactively resolve disputes at an early stage.
1. Abandonment of Rail Property Interests
As long as the Board retains jurisdiction over rail rights-of-way, only the Board can grant abandonment authority, and state law abandonment claims are preempted.
Grantwood Vill.
v.
Mo. Pac. R.R.,
95 F.3d 654, 658 (8th Cir. 1996). For example, state laws providing that an easement used for rail purposes can be abandoned simply through non-use, or where the rail carrier has removed track and ties, have been found to be federally preempted.
Great Walton R.R.,
AB 1242 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 6-8, 13 (STB served Feb. 27, 2026) (finding that ancillary track was not abandoned and remained subject to the Board's jurisdiction and that, therefore, a prior state court ruling that the easement for the track had been abandoned under state law was preempted);
see also Ala. R.R.—Aban. Exemption—in Escambia, Conecuh, & Monroe Cntys., Ala.,
AB 1324X, slip op. at 2 n.4 (STB served Oct. 24, 2022) (stating that a state court's “assertion of jurisdiction” to find that railroad abandoned a rail line right-of-way as a matter of “state law” is “flatly inconsistent with the Board's exclusive and plenary authority over the abandonment of rail lines”);
Jackson Cnty.—Acquis. & Operation Exemption—Union Pac. R.R.,
FD 35982, slip op. at 5, 7 (STB served July 31, 2019) (rejecting argument that rail line was “abandoned under Missouri law when the tracks and ties were removed” because it is “well settled” that the Board has exclusive jurisdiction over abandonment). Federal preemption of state abandonment laws applies both to common carrier/mainline track and ancillary/excepted track.
Great Walton R.R.,
AB 1242 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 6-7 (STB served Feb. 27, 2026).
[
30
]
It should be noted that preemption may apply to forestall eviction or removal of the rail carrier from rail property even in situations where a rail carrier voluntarily agreed to a time-limited property interest.
See Fillmore & W. Freight Serv., LLC—Emergency Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35813, slip op. at 3 (STB served Mar. 12, 2015) (“It is well settled that, without abandonment or
(
printed page 70972)
discontinuance authority from the Board, the enforcement of a state or local order that would prevent operation over a railroad line is precluded.”);
see also Pinelawn Cemetery,
FD 35468, slip op. at 9-11 (“[E]ven if the state court were to find that the 1904 Lease was not renewed, Pinelawn could not use that ruling to evict the Railroads from the property.”).
2. Complete Takings of Rail Carrier Property
Takings of rail property can come in many different forms, including but not limited to claims for eminent domain, condemnation, adverse possession, prescriptive easement, or quiet title, among others. The Board and courts have recognized that state law actions which “would remove the land at issue from the national railway system and deprive [a common carrier] of the ability to use the land to support its rail transportation operations” are typically preempted.
Skidmore,
1 F.4th at 214-15 (holding that state actions for quiet title and an exclusive prescriptive easement were preempted);
see also City of Lincoln,
414 F.3d at 862 (same for eminent domain claim);
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 1 (same for eminent domain claim);
14500 Ltd. LLC,
FD 35788, slip op. at 4-5 (same for claims of adverse possession and exclusive prescriptive easement);
Jie Ao,
FD 35539, slip op. at 6-7 (same for adverse possession claim).
But see Girard,
979 N.E.2d at 1287 (holding that an eminent domain claim was not preempted where the carrier claimed a speculative future need for rail service, but the railroad property had remained vacant for 15 years, and the carrier appeared to undermine its own claim by entering into an agreement to sell the property for purposes unrelated to rail transportation).
[
31
]
Although Board and court decisions have at times reviewed such exclusive takings under the “as-applied” standard, others have found preemption “regardless of whether th[e] case is analyzed as `categorical' preemption [or] as `as applied' preemption . . . .”
Jie Ao,
FD 35539, slip op. at 1. Synthesizing these analyses, takings of exclusive control of rail property and rights-of-way are best understood as categorically preempted, whereas non-exclusive takings may be reviewed under an as-applied approach.
The Board and courts have recognized that removal of part of the right-of-way or a railroad's property, including of currently unused property, could foreclose or unduly restrict present or future transportation by the rail carrier.
E.g., Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 7. Rail carriers defending such cases have elaborated on the operational issues that may be raised by the removal of rail property, even when it is not being used directly. For example, rail carriers have expressed the importance of the property and rail yard to their overall network (
14500 Ltd. LLC
); the necessity to conduct maintenance or handle derailments (
City of Lincoln
); maintenance of retaining walls; and the placement of signal towers (
Ala. Great S.
). Carriers have also highlighted the potential of future use, such as for the planned construction of a transload facility (
Grafton & Upton,
Docket No. FD 36696); available capacity to accommodate future traffic growth (
14500 Ltd. LLC, Ala. Great S.
); and the ability to conduct maintenance including slope stabilization (
Jie Ao
). Accordingly, a broad array of present or future transportation-related uses could support a finding that attempts to take rail property are categorically preempted.
Such cases can sometimes present complex policy issues. For example, in
Wisconsin Central Ltd.,
a city and state department of transportation sought to condemn rail property in order to realign a highway in an effort to reduce traffic accidents. 160 F. Supp. 2d at 1011. And in
City of Lincoln,
the town sought to take a strip of rail property to improve its storm drainage system and complete a commuter trail for pedestrians and bicyclists that would connect campuses at a state university. 414 F.3d at 859;
see also Ala. Great S.,
FD 35196, slip op. at 4 (condemnation for creation of a public park with amphitheater, children's playground, and other features). Notwithstanding these worthy public purposes, both actions were held to be preempted by ICCTA.
3. Utilities and Pipelines Within the Right-of-Way
The Board and courts typically view actions seeking condemnation for the purposes of constructing overhead or underground utilities, such as water or sewer lines or wire crossings, under the as-applied framework. The Board has determined that “routine, non-conflicting uses such as non-exclusive easements for at-grade road crossings, wire crossings, sewer crossings, etc., are not preempted so long as they would not impede rail operations or pose undue safety risks.”
Maumee & W. R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 34354, slip op. at 2 (STB served Mar. 3, 2004);
see also City of Lincoln,
414 F.3d at 863 (addressing storm sewer project and noting that “it is well established that nonconflicting, nonexclusive easements across railroad property are not preempted if they do not hinder rail operations or pose safety risks”). Relevant considerations include whether the facility will be placed in a location that would impair the railroad's use of the right-of-way (such as by undermining the integrity of underlying real property) or whether the timing and duration of the activity would hinder the rail carrier's operations. The Board has also focused on whether the crossings would be on the surface level or underground, and the amount of access to the right-of-way that would be conferred.
See, e.g.,
City of N. Chi.,
FD 36619, slip op. at 3-4 (acknowledging that a state court had already determined that a condemnation action for a water main easement crossing under rail property was preempted but providing guidance explaining that in cases where preemption is found the state court may be able to craft a remedy that avoids unreasonable interference with rail operations and would thus not be preempted);
E. Ala. Ry.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35583, slip op. at 6-7 (STB served Mar. 9, 2012) (holding that condemnation for construction of underground water and sewage lines was not preempted).
4. Blocked Crossings
State and local laws that limit a rail carrier's ability to block at-grade road crossings have been found to be preempted in the courts, regardless of whether the regulations apply to moving or stationary trains. These laws generally attempt to regulate the amount of time that a train may block a road crossing and contain a variety of terms related to the amount of time the train may block a crossing; whether the train is moving or stopped; the permissible reasons for doing so; and various penalties. Although the Board itself has not had occasion to rule on any blocked crossings law outside of the permitting process—and thus has never resolved the issue of whether ICCTA preemption or FRSA preemption should apply as it pertains to blocked crossings—courts that have applied ICCTA preemption have regularly found such laws preempted. Anti-blocking laws have been found to be preempted by ICCTA because they “purport[ ] to regulate rail transportation by dictating how railroads conduct their operations at crossings,”
CSX Transp., Inc.
v.
Williams,
No. 3:16CV2242, 2017 WL 1544958, at *2 (N.D. Ohio Apr. 28,
(
printed page 70973)
2017), including train speed and length, scheduling, the performance of federally mandated air brake tests, the coupling and uncoupling of cars, switching, repairs, safety checks, and waiting for tracks to clear.
See BNSF Ry.
v.
Hiett,
22 F.4th 1190, 1194 (10th Cir. 2022) (“[M]any factors determine the time that a train will block a grade crossing, including the train's speed and length, whether the side track intersects the grade crossing, when a railroad schedules a train to pass, and the time required to comply with federally mandated tests and procedures.”),
cert. denied sub nom. City of Edmond
v.
BNSF Ry.,
142 S. Ct. 2835 (2022);
Elam,
635 F.3d at 807. Because such regulations dictate rail operations directly, courts have uniformly found them preempted, and their reasoning aligns with the Board's categorical framework.
See, e.g.,
Hiett,
22 F.4th at 1194 (finding a blocked crossing statute preempted, explaining that “it too effectively regulates rail operations—a task the ICCTA reserves for the STB”);
Elam,
635 F.3d at 807 (finding a blocked crossing statute completely preempted because the statute directly attempted to manage the carrier's switching operations, including the carrier's decisions as to train speed, length, and scheduling);
Williams,
2017 WL 1544958, at *2 (finding a blocked crossing statute categorically preempted because it purported “to regulate rail transportation by dictating how railroads conduct their operations at crossings”).
In 2022, and again in 2024, the United States Supreme Court declined to review, respectively, a federal circuit court and a state supreme court decision invalidating state blocked-crossing laws as federally preempted, leaving those decisions in place.
See City of Edmond,
142 S. Ct. 2835 (2022);
Ohio
v.
CSX Transp., Inc.,
144 S. Ct. 545 (2024).
5. Pedestrian or Road Crossings of Rail Lines
State or local laws that dictate where track crossings must be constructed or closed are evaluated for preemption on an as-applied basis. Non-exclusive easements for at-grade road crossings may be considered routine, non-conflicting uses of rail carrier property.
See Wichita Terminal Ass'n,
FD 35765, slip op. at 6 (citation omitted). State actions related to such crossings are therefore permissible if the actions do not unreasonably burden or interfere with rail transportation.
Id.
at 7. Because the Board utilizes an as-applied preemption analysis, such cases require a factual analysis of the specific crossing at issue.
E.g., Franks Inv. Co.,
