593 F.3d at 415 (requiring evidence about specific crossings at issue, rather than general evidence about crossings, in denying as-applied preemption challenge to crossing case). Such evidence can include the location of the crossing, present or future operational impacts on the rail carrier, and potential alternatives.
See, e.g.
, Wichita Terminal Ass'n,
FD 35765, slip op. at 9 (analyzing proposed crossing's potential impacts on traffic, capacity, and operations);
Tri-City R.R.,
FD 35915, slip op. at 8-9 (same, including switching and storage operations, as well as present and future impacts). For example, in
Wichita Terminal Association,
FD 35765, the Board found that a state court order requiring construction of a road crossing over tracks at a specific location was preempted. At the same time, however, the Board noted that it did “not conclude that any crossing . . . necessarily would be preempted,” suggesting that an alternative location for a crossing may not impose the same burden or interference with rail transportation.
Id.
at 10-11;
see also City of Ozark—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36104, slip op. at 5-6 (STB served July 28, 2017) (holding that, based on facts presented, the city's effort to force reinstallation of a removed at-grade crossing would unreasonably interfere with present and future railroad operations and cause undue safety risks under an as-applied preemption analysis). And a court has found that a state statute requiring pedestrian crossings over rail tracks was not preempted where operational impacts were limited by giving the railroads discretion as to the manner of construction.
See Adrian & Blissfield R.R.,
550 F.3d at 542.
6. Locomotive Idling
State or local laws that regulate idling trains have been found to be categorically preempted. These regulations may include restrictions on the amount of time, hours, reasons for, or location of idling, including record-keeping requirements. Unlike generally applicable building codes, such regulations specifically target railroads and directly regulate rail operations.
E.g., Ass'n of Am. R.Rs.,
2007 WL 2439499, at *7 (holding that rules related to railroad idling were categorically preempted). These laws place the state or local regulator, rather than the railroad, in the position to “mak[e] operational decisions about when, where, and how long locomotives could idle.”
Delaware,
859 F.3d at 22. Therefore, regardless of the purpose of the state or local law, and regardless of whether the state or locality has attempted to narrowly tailor the law or provide exceptions, idling-related laws have been found to be categorically preempted. For example, in
Delaware,
a state statute generally prohibiting idling in residential neighborhoods at night was categorically preempted, even though the statute only prohibited “non-essential” idling and contained exemptions for certain enumerated purposes, because the statute directly managed railroad operations regardless of its practical effect.
See id.
7. Environmental Permitting, Zoning Ordinances, and Land Use Laws
State or local permitting or preclearance requirements, including building permits, zoning ordinances, and environmental and land use permitting requirements, have been found to be categorically preempted as to rail carrier transportation and related infrastructure because ICCTA “prevents states and localities from imposing requirements that, by their nature, could be used to deny a rail carrier the ability to conduct rail operations.”
Soo Line R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35850, slip op. at 4 (STB served Dec. 23, 2014). Otherwise, states or localities could interfere with interstate commerce by denying, or indefinitely delaying, approval of rail projects or operations approved by the Board and subject to its exclusive jurisdiction.
See Green Mountain R.R.,
404 F.3d at 643;
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 7 (collecting cases);
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 35832, slip op. at 4 (recognizing that state or local authority to “deny or unreasonably delay” construction and maintenance “would irreconcilably conflict with the Board's authorization of those facilities and operations”). For example, the Board has held that a local conservation commission's order seeking to impose environmental permitting requirements on the construction of a rail carrier's transload facility was categorically preempted.
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 12. However, state and local regulations that have a “more remote or incidental effect on rail transportation,” have been found not to be preempted.
N.Y. Susquehanna & W. Ry.,
500 F.3d at 252 (internal citation omitted). Resolution of issues regarding such remote or incidental effects may require discussion and cooperation between communities and rail carriers.
See Joint Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
5 S.T.B. at 508 (noting that some environmental requirements, such as requiring carriers to share their plans with the community or to submit environmental monitoring or testing information for an appropriate
(
printed page 70974)
period of time after operations begin, may not be preempted).
8. Noise, Smoke, Appearance, and Other Nuisance-Related Claims
State or local regulation of nuisance-related issues, such as noise caused by rail operations,
[
32
]
smoke, appearance of rail property, and other related matters have been found to be categorically preempted when related to activities under the Board's jurisdiction. These issues may also arise in litigation raising state or common law claims for nuisances caused by rail operations.
See, e.g.,
Pace,
613 F.3d at 1068-69 (holding that a lawsuit alleging that construction and operation of side track caused an increase in noise and smoke that made land unusable was preempted). Such state or local actions can directly regulate, and potentially provide remedies for, rail carrier operations under the Board's exclusive jurisdiction and thus may be preempted by ICCTA, even though ICCTA provides no remedy.
See, e.g.,
Friberg
v.
Kan. City S. Ry.,
267 F.3d 439, 443 (5th Cir. 2001) (holding that state tort claims related to trains on a railroad's side tracks blocking access to plaintiff's property were preempted, explaining that “it is beyond peradventure that regulation of [the railroad's] train operations, as well as the construction and operation of the [railroad's] side tracks, is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the STB . . . .”);
Lange—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35037, slip op. at 4 (STB served Jan. 28, 2008) (stating that remedies for nuisance claims are preempted);
Joint Pet. for Declaratory Ord.
5 S.T.B. at 510 (holding that a local ordinance declaring an automobile unloading facility to be a “noisome trade” was preempted) However, such claims may not be preempted if they do not directly implicate subject matter within the Board's jurisdiction.
See Emerson,
503 F.3d at 1130-32 (holding that a railroad's disposal of railway ties into a wastewater drainage ditch adjacent to its tracks was not “transportation” under ICCTA and thus state tort claims related to flooding of adjoining property were not preempted).
9. Design, Construction, or Maintenance of Rail Infrastructure
State law regulations, including tort claims, that dictate the design, construction or maintenance of rail lines and rail transportation facilities under the Board's jurisdiction have been found to be categorically preempted.
See CSX Transp. Inc.,
FD 35832, slip op. at 4-5 (collecting cases). Common cases include claims for damages caused by flooding or other events that claimants assert were caused by rail carrier infrastructure decisions, such as the design of bridges or embankments, materials used in construction, maintenance of culverts, and related operational decisions.
E.g., Edwards,
983 F.3d at 122 (preempting flooding damage claims).
But see Emerson,
503 F.3d at 1130-32 (holding that state tort claim related to flooding on plaintiffs' property allegedly caused by a railroad's disposal of railway ties into a wastewater drainage ditch adjacent to its tracks was not preempted because the railroad's disposal did not qualify as “transportation” under ICCTA);
Hatcher—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35581, slip op. at 5-8 (STB served Sept. 21, 2012) (holding that state tort claims related to flooding and damage to plaintiffs' property allegedly caused by defendant railroads' blocking drainage infrastructure near the rail line during salvage operations following Board-authorized abandonment of the rail line were not preempted). As the Board has recognized, such claims can “unduly burden interstate commerce and amount to impermissible state regulation of [a rail carrier]'s operations by interfering with the railroad's ability to uniformly design, construct, maintain, and repair its railroad line. The interstate rail network could not function properly if states and localities could impose their own potentially differing standards for these important activities, which are an integral part of, and directly affect, rail transportation.”
Tubbs—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35792, slip op. at 5 (STB served Oct. 31, 2014),
aff'd,
812 F.3d 1141 (8th Cir. 2015).
[
33
]
However, claims based on violation of FRA's regulations and standards would be subject to the federal harmonization analysis.
See Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 7 (declining to preempt, under ICCTA, claims based on uniform federal regulations under the FRSA).
10. Breach of Contract
Under
49 U.S.C. 10709
, Congress has expressly provided that contracts between rail carriers and purchasers of rail services to provide such services are not subject to the rail provisions of 49 U.S.C. subtitle IV (Part A). Because Part A of subtitle IV includes the preemption provision at
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
, enforcement of such contracts in court is not preempted. Additionally, actions under state law for breach of a contract between a rail carrier and other parties are generally not preempted. As the Fourth Circuit has explained, “[v]oluntary agreements between private parties,” and the “enforcement” of such contracts, “are not presumptively regulatory acts.”
PCS Phosphate Co.
v.
Norfolk S. Corp.,
559 F.3d 212, 218-19 (4th Cir. 2009) (explaining how the “history and purpose of ICCTA . . . suggest that such agreements do not fall into the core of economic regulation that the ICCTA was intended to preempt.”). The Board has stated that “voluntary agreements must be seen as reflecting the carrier's own determination and admission that the agreements would not unreasonably interfere with interstate commerce.”
Twp. of Woodbridge, N.J.
v.
Consol. Rail Corp.,
5 S.T.B. 336, 340 (2000);
see also Joint Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
5 S.T.B. at 508 (“[P]reemption provisions should not be used to shield a carrier from its own commitments . . . .”). However, depending on the facts and circumstances of a specific case and the degree to which a voluntary agreement unreasonably interferes with interstate rail operations, certain agreements may be subject to an as-applied preemption analysis.
See Woodbridge,
5 S.T.B. at 340 (declining to find enforceable agreement preempted where, among other things, there was not evidence that enforcement of the agreement would unreasonably interfere with the railroad's operations);
see also PCS Phosphate,
559 F.3d at 221 (“This is not to say that a voluntary agreement could never constitute an `unreasonable interference' with rail transportation, but the facts of this case indicate that any interference is not unreasonable . . . .”).
11. Routing of Traffic
The Board and courts have found that ICCTA categorically preempts state and local laws that seek to regulate when and where particular commodities can be carried by rail.
See, e.g.,
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 5 (STB served May 3, 2005). In one example, the District of Columbia passed a law banning transportation of certain classes of hazardous commodities within an area of the District without a permit from the DC. Department of Transportation.
CSX Transp., Inc.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 2 (STB served Mar. 14, 2005). The Board found that such regulation “plainly” fell within the
(
printed page 70975)
types of actions categorically preempted under section 10501(b), explaining that to the extent the DC law “would require a permit to move certain rail traffic through protected parts of the City, it is directly covered by the categorical preemption against state and local permitting processes.”
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 5 (STB served May 3, 2005). “And to the extent that the D.C. Act would otherwise ban the specified movements, it would directly conflict with the Board's authority over rail operations, including matters such as routing over which any state action is expressly preempted by section 10501(b).”
Id.
(noting that other federal regulatory regimes may also apply in a complementary fashion).
V. ICCTA Harmonization Analysis for Federal Law
By its terms, ICCTA's express preemption provision applies to federal, as well as state, law.
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
. When, however, the question presented is the interaction between ICCTA and another federal law, the express or implied preemption framework flowing from the Supremacy Clause is inapplicable. The Board therefore does not utilize its categorical/as-applied framework in such cases, and instead follows the tests set forth in the federal courts to analyze whether the laws can be harmonized and, if not, whether the later-enacted law repealed the other by implication. These federal-federal conflicts have mostly arisen in the realms of rail safety and environmental regulation, but the Board would apply similar principles to other potentially conflicting federal laws.
A. Constitutional Framework for Harmonization Analysis
“When confronted with two Acts of Congress allegedly touching on the same topic,” the Board
[
34
]
and courts are “not at liberty to pick and choose among congressional enactments and must instead strive to give effect to both.”
Epic Sys. Corp.
v.
Lewis,
584 U.S. 497, 510 (2018) (citation modified). When there is an apparent conflict between ICCTA and another federal law, the Board or a court “must strive to harmonize the two laws, giving effect to both laws if possible.”
Ass'n of Am. R.R.s
v.
S. Coast Air Quality Mgmt. Dist.,
622 F.3d 1094, 1097 (9th Cir. 2010). However, if there is a “positive repugnancy” or an “irreconcilable conflict” between the laws, the question becomes whether the later-enacted statute repealed the earlier-enacted statute to the extent of the conflict.
Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co.
v.
Epstein,
516 U.S. 367, 381 (1996);
Radzanower
v.
Touche Ross & Co.,
426 U.S. 148, 155 (1976);
see also Joint Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
5 S.T.B. at 509 n.28. Whether one law “displaces the other” requires “a clearly expressed congressional intention.”
Epic Sys. Corp.,
584 U.S. at 510. And where “there is no clear intention otherwise, a specific statute will not be controlled or nullified by a general one, regardless of the priority of enactment.”
Crawford Fitting Co.
v.
J.T. Gibbons, Inc.,
482 U.S. 437, 445 (1987) (citation modified). Thus, the statutes are harmonized by giving effect to the more specific statute.
See generally Patten
v.
District of Columbia,
9 F. 4th 921, 926 (D.C. Cir. 2021) (“In seeking to harmonize [disparate] statutes . . . [w]e are guided by the `old and familiar rule' that `the specific governs the general,' which is `particularly true' where `Congress has enacted a comprehensive scheme and has deliberately targeted specific problems with specific solutions.'”) (quoting
RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC
v.
Amalgamated Bank,
566 U.S. 639, 645-46 (2012)).
The Board conducts this analysis against the backdrop of the expansive, exclusive, and specific jurisdiction that ICCTA grants over transportation by rail carriers, which is the manifestation of Congress's intent to ensure uniform federal regulation.
Ass'n of Am. R.R.s,
FD 36369, slip op. at 14 (“Congress clearly intended that [section] 10501(b) preempt laws that create an irreconcilable conflict with the free flow of interstate commerce by imposing a patchwork of regulation on interstate rail transportation.”). ICCTA will often be the more specific statute insofar as it applies specifically to the rail industry, although there are numerous other federal laws related to the rail industry, and the Board would accord appropriate weight to the specificity of those laws in any harmonization analysis.
35
See Pittsburgh & Lake Erie R.R.
v.
Ry. Lab. Executives' Ass'n,
491 U.S. 490, 511 (1989) (discussing harmonization of the Railway Labor Act and Interstate Commerce Act).
B. Examples of Harmonization of ICCTA and Other Federal Laws
The analytical framework for harmonization described above would apply in any Board analysis of another federal law for a determination of ICCTA preemption. There are two illustrative examples of federal laws that the Board has previously addressed—related to rail safety and environmental laws—that are discussed in more detail below. The Board could apply a similar analysis when presented with questions about the preemptive effect of ICCTA when harmonization with another federal law is required.
1. Harmonization With FRSA
Congress enacted the FRSA in 1970 “to promote safety in every area of railroad operations.”
49 U.S.C. 20101
. FRSA instructed the Secretary of Transportation, who has delegated this power to the FRA, to “prescribe regulations and issue orders for every area of railroad safety.”
Id.
20103(a);
49 CFR 1.89(a)
. Under the FRSA preemption provision, Congress provided that “[l]aws, regulations, and orders related to railroad safety . . . shall be nationally uniform to the extent practicable.”
49 U.S.C. 20106(a)(1)
. To ensure “[n]ational uniformity of regulation” in this area, FRSA preempts state law obligations aimed at a “subject matter” addressed in regulations issued thereunder.
Id.
20106(a)(2);
see also Duluth, Winnipeg & Pac. Ry.
v.
City of Orr,
529 F.3d 794, 796 (8th Cir. 2008) (FRSA “generally preempt[s] state laws covering the same subject matter” as Department of Transportation (DOT) or Department of Homeland Security (DHS) standards).
Nonetheless, in some limited situations, FRSA might lead to the patchwork of rail regulations that ICCTA is designed to avoid, because FRSA contains a narrow savings clause permitting states to regulate where FRA has not yet issued rail safety
[
36
]
regulations covering “the subject matter of the State requirement.” 49 U.S.C.
(
printed page 70976)
20106(a)(2);
Duluth, Winnipeg & Pac. Ry.,
529 F.3d at 796 (stating that FRSA “creates a narrow exception to preemption through its savings clause”). FRSA also allows states to “adopt or continue in force an additional or more stringent” rail safety law or regulation, but only if it “(A) is necessary to eliminate or reduce an essentially local safety or security hazard; (B) is not incompatible with a law, regulation, or order of the United States Government; and (C) does not unreasonably burden interstate commerce.”
49 U.S.C. 20106(a)(2)
. Courts have interpreted the “essentially local” safety hazard requirement narrowly to address “local situations which are not statewide in character and not capable of being adequately encompassed within national uniform standards.”
Nat'l Ass'n of Regul. Util. Comm'rs
v.
Coleman,
542 F.2d 11, 14-15 (3d Cir. 1976);
see also Duluth, Winnipeg & Pac. Ry.,
529 F.3d at 798 (collecting cases). And notably, the exception directly requires that such regulations must be “not incompatible” with federal laws.
In 2007, Congress enacted an amendment clarifying the savings clause in section 20106.
See
49 U.S.C. 20106(b)
;
see also Bates
v.
Mo. & N. Ark. R.R.,
548 F.3d 634, 637 (8th Cir. 2008). The amendment specifically provided that nothing within section 20106 “shall be construed to preempt an action under State law seeking damages for personal injury, death, or property damage” alleging that a party: (A) failed to comply with an applicable Federal standard of care established by DOT or DHS; (B) failed to comply with its own plan, rule, or standard that it created pursuant to an applicable DOT or DHS regulation or order; or (C) failed to comply with a State law, regulation, or order that is not incompatible with the provisions of section 20106(a)(2) described above.
49 U.S.C. 20106(b)
.
By contrast, ICCTA expressly overrides “remedies provided under [other] Federal . . . law[s]” to the extent of a conflict.
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
. ICCTA was enacted more recently (1995) than the authority at section 20103 and the savings clause at section 20106(a)(2).
See In re Fed.-Mogul Global Inc.,
684 F.3d 355, 374 (3d Cir. 2012) (citation omitted) (declining “to limit the preemptive scope” of a statute based on the existence of an older, narrower provision covering a closely related topic). And if there is a potential conflict with the tort law clarification to the FRSA savings clause, enacted in 2007 at section 20106(b), the Board could take note of the timing.
See Lundeen
v.
Can. Pac. R.R.,
532 F.3d 682, 688 (8th Cir. 2008) (“This `clarifying' amendment reflected Congress's disagreement with the manner in which the courts . . . had interpreted [section] 20106 to preempt state law causes of action whenever a federal regulation covered the same subject matter as the allegations of negligence in a state court lawsuit.”).
The Board has said that ICCTA and FRSA should be harmonized to give effect to both.
See, e.g.,
Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 7. ICCTA primarily applies to rail transportation and operations, and FRSA primarily applies to rail safety. Although “the ICCTA preemption provision can be read to cover virtually everything related to rail transportation and . . . rail safety-related claims will almost always touch on rail transportation and operations,”
Waneck—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36167, slip op. at 5 (STB served Oct. 31, 2018),
[
37
]
the Board has long recognized that ICCTA “does not preempt valid safety regulation under [FRSA].”
Green Mountain R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 34052, slip op. at 6 n.8 (STB served May 28, 2002). The agencies have exercised their authority in complementary fashion, and when their responsibilities overlap, they have “coordinate[d] and cooperate[d] with each other as appropriate.”
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 10 (STB served Mar. 14, 2005);
see also Tyrrell
v.
Norfolk S. Ry.,
248 F.3d 517, 523 (6th Cir. 2001) (stating that the Board's and FRA's “complementary exercise of their statutory authority accurately reflects Congress's intent for the ICCTA and FRSA to be construed
in pari materia”
). And the Board “does not usurp or interfere with the role of other federal agencies in regulating railroad safety and security and hazardous materials transportation under other federal regulatory statutes.”
CSXT Transp., Inc.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 7 (STB served May 3, 2005).
Applying these principles, the Board has determined that ICCTA applies to operation and construction-related claims, including state-law tort claims alleging that a rail line was designed, constructed, and maintained in a way that caused flooding-related property damage.
See Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 6-7. Conversely, FRSA applies to primarily safety-related claims, including state-law tort claims related to a collision between a train and a tour bus at a railroad crossing,
see Waneck,
FD 36167, slip op. at 4 (STB served May 25, 2018), and state regulation of the clearance distance between tracks,
see Tyrrell,
248 F.3d at 522-24. The Board has stated that “the states' ability to act with respect to railroad/highway crossings (including grade separations) remains undisturbed so long as their action does not unreasonably interfere with railroad operations or interstate commerce, and does not constitute regulation of the railroad's operations.” Br. of Surface Transp. Bd. as Amicus Curiae,
Iowa, Chi. & E. R.R.
v.
Wash. Cnty.,
384 F.3d 557 (8th Cir. 2004) (No. 03-3136), 2004 WL 6395939, at *21-23 (discussing whether law about redesign and replacement of bridges at crossing for safety reasons was subject to ICCTA preemption). And, as discussed above, the Board found that both ICCTA and FRSA applied to a local safety-related regulation limiting the shipment of hazardous materials because it affected both safety and the railroad's ability to carry certain commodities.
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 5-7 (STB served May 3, 2005).
Thus, ICCTA and FRSA can typically be harmonized. However, issues may arise when a state or local safety-related law which may not be preempted under FRSA may still be preempted under ICCTA because such laws effectively manage or govern rail transportation and thus directly conflict with the Board's exclusive jurisdiction. Some courts have suggested that only FRSA preemption can apply to at least some safety-related issues.
See, e.g.
, Island Park, LLC
v.
CSX Transp.,
559 F.3d 96, 107 (2d Cir. 2009) (stating that the “federal statutory scheme places principal federal regulatory authority for rail safety with the FRA, not the [Board],” and so “FRSA provides the appropriate basis for analyzing whether a state law, regulation or order affecting rail safety is pre-empted by federal law”);
Tyrrell,
248 F.3d at 522-23. And the Board has partially endorsed the same view in non-binding guidance.
See Waneck,
FD 36167, slip op. at 5 (STB served Oct. 31, 2018). However, as the Office of the Solicitor General recently argued to the Supreme Court in a case about whether states could regulate blocked crossings, “FRSA cannot be read to create a loophole in the ICCTA that would permit a patchwork of state and local regulation over rail transportation simply because the regulations also happen to touch on `safety-related' matters.” OSG Amicus Brief, 2023 WL 8112708, at *13;
see also Ohio
v.
CSX Transp., Inc.,
144 S. Ct. 545 (2024) (denying Ohio's certiorari petition). This is also consistent with the savings clause's requirement that state regulations that are in addition to or more stringent than DOT or DHS
(
printed page 70977)
rules governing the same subject matter must relate to an “essentially local” hazard, be “not incompatible with” other federal laws, and “not unreasonably burden interstate commerce.”
See
49 U.S.C. 20106(a)(2)(B)
. Thus, even if FRSA alone does not preempt a state or local railroad safety regulation, ICCTA preemption may still apply if upholding the state or local regulation addresses a generally-applicable concern, would be inconsistent with ICCTA, or would otherwise unreasonably burden rail transportation.
2. Harmonization With Federal Environmental Laws
The Board has stated that ICCTA preemption is implicated when the relevant state activity was undertaken pursuant to regulations passed under the auspices of federal environmental statutes. This dynamic has arisen in two situations. First, ICCTA preemption may apply to the extent the state regulations would cause a “patchwork of regulations” burdening interstate commerce.
See EPA Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35803, slip op. at 8. In
EPA Declaratory Ord.,
the Board concluded that ICCTA would likely preempt a California air quality district's rules related to railroad locomotive idling and recordkeeping—even if those rules were approved by EPA under the CAA as part of California's state implementation plan “because of the potential patchwork of regulations that could result.”
Id.
The Board noted that it must consider “not only the impact of the District's rules . . . but the fact that other states and local districts throughout the country could follow suit and adopt their own emission rules . . . leading to the lack of uniformity of regulation that Congress intended to preclude in [section] 10501(b).”
EPA Declaratory Ord.,
FD 35803, slip op. at 8;
see also id.
at 10 (“[A]llowing states and localities to create a variety of complex regulations governing how an instrument of interstate commerce is operated, equipped, or kept track of (even if federalized under the CAA) would directly conflict with the goal of uniform national regulation of rail transportation.”).
The Board applied the same principle in
AAR Declaratory Order
to conclude that the CWA's National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permitting program and discharge prohibition “would likely be preempted by [ICCTA] if applied to discharges incidental to the operation of rail cars in transit.”
AAR Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36369, slip op. at 1. Because the program was “based on state-specific permitting requirements” and “individual permit writers . . . have discretion to impose [standards] more stringent than EPA guidelines,” applying the program would be “likely to result in a patchwork of differing regulations” that would “be incompatible with [ICCTA's] purpose of ensuring uniform regulation of rail transportation.”
Id.
at 11-12;
see also id.
at 13-14 (stating that ICCTA was “arguably the more specific statutory provision,” and that, to the extent the NPDES permitting program was “incompatible with the purpose” of ICCTA, the later-enacted statute (ICCTA) should “be given effect”).
Thus, similar to the unreasonable-burden prong of as-applied preemption, the analysis is cumulative: if applying another federal law or allowing claims thereunder would, in the aggregate, interfere with Congress's uniform regulatory scheme, ICCTA preemption is implicated. This suggests two important distinctions: between federal laws with one uniform federal standard and those that permit a patchwork of state-promulgated requirements; and between state laws passed under color of federal law that apply to instrumentalities of interstate commerce in motion
[
38
]
versus those applying to stationary structures. In
AAR Declaratory Order,
the Board asserted that “[t]o the extent that EPA could issue a nationwide general permit for incidental discharges from rail cars in transit that includes uniform requirements for the states, such a nationwide general permit would not create a patchwork of differing regulations and could therefore potentially be harmonized with [section] 10501(b).”
AAR Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36369, slip op. at 16. The Board also focused on the fact that “rail cars in transit are inherently instrumentalities of interstate commerce.”
Id.
at 15. Although “subjecting them to differing regulatory requirements as they pass from one state to the next is likely to be incompatible with the free flow of interstate commerce that Congress envisioned when enacting [section] 10501(b)[,] . . . non-discriminatory application to . . . stationary facilities owned or operated by railroads” may not be.
Id.
Instead, such stationary facility applications under the color of federal law “are generally not preempted because, although they may differ from state to state, they do not typically conflict with [section] 10501(b)'s goal of preventing differing regulations from interfering with the free flow of interstate commerce.”
Id.
Additionally, ICCTA preemption is implicated if a federal “statute or regulation is being applied in a discriminatory manner, or being used as a pretext for frustrating or preventing a particular activity.”
Joint Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
5 S.T.B. at 509. In
Joint Petition for Declaratory Order,
the Board concluded that the local governments were “simply using [federal environmental law] as a pretext to do what Congress expressly precluded: interfere with interstate commerce by imposing a local permitting or environmental process as a prerequisite to the railroad's ability to conduct its operations.”
Id.
The local concerns appeared unfounded because neither EPA nor the state environmental regulator had expressed any concerns, and the record showed that substantial pollution was “unlikely.”
Id.
at 509-10.
This is necessarily a “fact-bound” analysis in which the regulator's stated concerns “need to be reviewed individually” to determine whether they have a reasonable basis.
Id.
at 508-09. As in the preemption context, this aspect of the analysis furthers the congressional scheme by ensuring that seemingly neutral regulatory measures are not being used to target or obstruct rail operations.
VI. Conclusion
This policy statement sets forth the Board's perspective on the state of the law as of the time of its issuance, acknowledging that new precedents from the Board and courts will further develop the law on STB jurisdiction and preemption. Although forthcoming cases will be evaluated based on their facts, circumstances, and proffered arguments, the Board intends for this policy statement to be beneficial and informative to the public about the Board's jurisdiction and ICCTA preemption, and to encourage the smooth flow of interstate commerce via the nation's rail network.

                         When Board authorization is required for certain projects, the Board must consider, among other things, the potential environmental and historic impacts of the construction and operation of a proposed rail line pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969,
42 U.S.C. 4321-4370m-11
, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act,
54 U.S.C. 300101
et seq.,
the Board's environmental rules at
49 CFR part 1105
, and related environmental laws.
Back to Citation
17.
    
                         Parties that are uncertain whether a particular track is considered a common carrier rail line or ancillary track (or private track) often request a determination from the Board.
See, e.g.,
Ne. La. Multimodal Dist.,
FD 36809;
N.Y.C. Econ. Dev. Corp.,
FD 36467.
Back to Citation
18.
    
                         Although the Board's statute has a provision on “rights and remedies of persons injured by rail carriers,”
49 U.S.C. 11704
, this provision “only applies to claims for violations of the Interstate Commerce Act,” and does not create a general cause of action.
See City of N. Chi.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36619, slip op. at 4 n.3 (STB served May 18, 2023);
see also 14500 Ltd. LLC,
FD 35788, slip op. at 5 (explaining that section 11704 and the Interstate Commerce Act do not address or provide any remedies for state law property issues).
Back to Citation
19.
    
                         The Board takes no position regarding whether a preemption related claim may be initiated originally in state or federal court, or whether a claim can be removed to federal court. As the Board has acknowledged, “[t]he Board is not the proper forum for deciding the extent of a court's jurisdiction.”
Waneck—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 36167, slip op. at 4 (STB served May 25, 2018) (citing
Lopez-Elias
v.
Reno,
209 F.3d 788, 791 (5th Cir. 2000) (noting that the determination of a court's jurisdiction is exclusively for the court to decide)).
Back to Citation
20.
    
                         The Board recognizes that federal preemption analysis involves many nuances beyond whether preemption is express or implied. For example, implied preemption can be broken down into “field preemption” and “conflict preemption.”
See Arizona
v.
United States,
567 U.S. 387, 399 (2012). For purposes of this policy statement, the Board believes it is sufficient to analogize “as-applied” preemption to implied preemption without further elaboration on whether field preemption, conflict preemption, or both are the basis for the analysis.
Back to Citation
21.
    
                         Categorical preemption is also sometimes referred to as “per se” or “facial” preemption.
See, e.g.
, Soo Line R.R.
v.
City of St. Paul,
827 F. Supp. 2d 1017, 1020 (D. Minn. 2010);
CSX Transp., Inc.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
FD 34662, slip op. at 4-5 (STB served May 3, 2005).
Back to Citation
22.
    
                         It should be noted that at least one circuit court has determined that “as-applied” preemption is a form of express, rather than implied, preemption.
See City of Ozark,
v.
Union Pac. R.R.,
843 F.3d 1167, 1171 (8th Cir. 2016). Numerous other circuit court cases have interpreted the Board's “as-applied” analysis as a form of implied preemption.
E.g., Edwards,
983 F.3d at 121;
Ezell,
866 F.3d at 299.
Back to Citation
23.
    
                         Moreover, a Board or court holding that a state law of general applicability is preempted, either categorically or as-applied, does not invalidate the state law. Instead, the ICCTA preemption determination means that the law is preempted only in its application to activities within the Board's exclusive jurisdiction under
49 U.S.C. 10501(b)
. Thus, a zoning ordinance that is categorically preempted when used to manage jurisdictional rail carrier transportation may still be applied generally to other industries.
Back to Citation
24.
    
                         In general, a fee is discriminatory if it treats railroads differently than other modes without sufficient justification.
Cf. Ala. Dept. of Revenue
v.
CSX Transp., Inc.,
575 U.S. 21, 27, 30 (2015) (discussing discriminatory taxes under the Railroad Revitalization and Regulation Reform Act of 1976 (4R Act),
49 U.S.C. 11501(b)(4)
);
Union Pac. R.R.
v.
Wis. Dep't. of Revenue,
940 F.3d 336, 337 (7th Cir. 2019) (finding a tax “singl[ing] out railroads as part of an isolated and targeted group” unlawful under the 4R Act).
Back to Citation
25.
    
                         State laws governing the acquisition of property by a rail carrier generally are not preempted.
See, e.g.,
Grafton & Upton R.R.
v.
STB,
177 F.4th 1234, 1240 (D.C. Cir. 2026) (“ICCTA does not preempt generally applicable state property laws that `do not unreasonably interfere with railroad operations or the Board's regulatory programs.'”) (quoting
CSX Transp.,
FD 35832, slip op. at 4);
Great Walton R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.,
AB 1242 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 7, 11 (STB served June 9, 2020) (leaving it to rail carrier to establish its interest in the underlying real property under state law);
see also Allegheny Valley R.R.—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.—William Fiore,
FD 35388, slip op. at 4 & n.4 (STB served Apr. 25, 2011) (explaining that disputes over the “size, location, and nature of property rights” are most appropriately decided by courts applying state law and that “[p]roof of ownership . . . cannot be inferred from our approval to acquire and operate the rail line”);
Tongue River R.R.—Constr.& Operation—W. Alignment,
FD 30186 (Sub-No. 3) et al., slip op at 16 n.50 (STB served Oct 9, 2007) (“The applicant [in rail construction cases] is responsible for acquiring the land necessary to build the line.”). Relatedly, the Board's jurisdiction generally does not preempt rail carrier efforts to acquire property under state eminent domain law, including where a state denies a carrier condemnation request.
See Great Walton R.R.,
AB 1242 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 7 (STB served June 9, 2020);
see also Great Redwood Trail Agency,
AB 1305 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 14 (“[R]ail carriers are generally responsible for acquiring the land necessary to support their operations, including to the extent permitted by condemnation.”).
Back to Citation
26.
    
                         As noted above, limited fact-finding may be needed to determine “whether the state or local action falls within a category subject to categorical preemption.”
CSX Transp., Inc.,
FD 35832, slip op. at 5.
Back to Citation
27.
But see Girard
v.
Youngstown Belt Ry.,
979 NE2d 1273, 1287 (Ohio 2012) (subsequently holding that eminent domain claim was not preempted).
Back to Citation
28.
    
                         Although the Board has granted adverse abandonment of rail carrier property in certain limited circumstances, applicants bear a heavy burden.
See Colo. Landowners—Adverse Aban.—Great W. Ry. of Colo. in Weld Cnty, Colo.,
AB 857 (Sub-No. 2), slip op. at 5 (STB served July 30, 2025). The Board considers matters such as whether active shippers would lose service, whether there is any potential for continued rail service, whether the carrier has taken reasonable steps to attract traffic or rehabilitate or utilize an inoperable line, and the carrier's judgment about the need for, and usefulness of, the line.
See id.
at 6-7 (summarizing the state of the Board's precedent on adverse abandonments).
Back to Citation
29.
    
                         The Board has been made aware that Valero abandoned the rail transload terminal project following the Board's decision and announced its intent to cease refining operations at the facility in 2026,
see
Valero,
Valero Announces Notice to the California Energy Commission Regarding its Benicia, California, Refinery
(Apr. 16, 2025),
https://investorvalero.com/​news/​news-details/​2025/​Valero-Announces-Notice-to-the-California-Energy-Commission-Regarding-its-Benicia-California-Refinery/​default.aspx
,
and Valero's website indicates that full idling of all processing units at this facility was completed in April 2026,
see
Valero,
Benicia Refinery,
https://www.valero.com/​about/​locations/​benicia-refinery
(last visited Sept. 30, 2026). Additionally, although the Board has not revisited
Valero
in the decade since its issuance, the Board is aware that state and local restrictions on rail-served facilities have been promulgated and upheld as beyond the Board's jurisdiction in numerous circumstances.
See, e.g.,
Montana
v.
City of Portland,
No. 3:23-cc-00219-YY, 2024 WL 1007865, at *1, 12 (D. Or. Feb. 26, 2024) (finding local ordinance restricting the construction of bulk fossil fuel terminals was, among other things, not preempted because plaintiffs did not allege they were rail carriers or performing activities on behalf of or under the auspices of a rail carrier),
rep. & recommendation adopted in part, rejected in part,
No. 3:23-CV-00219-YY, 2024 WL 3326230 (D. Or. July 5, 2024).
Back to Citation
30.
    
                         A Board determination that a state court ruling finding a rail line has been abandoned under state law is preempted does not affect the state court's ruling on who has title to the property. The Board has acknowledged that it is “well settled that the interpretation of deeds and the determination of who owns good title to property are issues of state law” that are most appropriately decided by state courts.
Great Walton R.R.,
AB 1242 (Sub-No. 1), slip op. at 6 n.8 (STB served Feb. 27, 2026) (citing
Cent. Kan. Ry.—Aban. Exemption—in Marion & McPherson Cntys., Kan.,
AB 406 (Sub-No. 6X), slip op. at 2 (STB served May 8, 2001)).
Back to Citation
31.
    
                         In
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, the Board analyzed
Girard,
distinguished it on the facts presented, and for that reason, determined that “[t]he Board need not decide whether to endorse the court's analysis in
Girard.
”
Grafton & Upton,
FD 36696, slip op. at 8.
Back to Citation
32.
    
                         Although not enforced by the Board, the Board notes that under the Noise Control Act of 1972, other federal agencies have established and enforce standards related to railroad noise which preempt state or local standards. 
                        See
42 U.S.C. 4916
;
40 CFR part 201
;
49 CFR part 210
.
Back to Citation
33.
    
                         The Board determined in
Tubbs
that the state law claims were preempted regardless of whether they were analyzed as “categorical” or “as-applied,”
Tubbs,
FD 35792, slip op. at 4, though on appeal, the Eighth Circuit utilized the as-applied framework,
see generally Tubbs,
812 F.3d. 1141.
Back to Citation
34.
    
                         The Board has previously affirmed that it, as well as the courts, can engage in this federal-federal harmonization and implied repeal analysis.
Ass'n of Am. R.R.s—Pet. for Declaratory Ord.
(
AAR Declaratory Ord.
), FD 36369, slip op. at 9, 12 (STB served Dec. 30, 2020). This is because “[t]he statute requires, in certain circumstances, the preemption of other federal laws and does not prohibit the Board from opining on its interpretation of the other federal laws to determine where ICCTA preemption applies.”
Id.
at 9.
Back to Citation
35.
    
                         At the time of this writing, these include, but are not limited to, the Railroad Retirement Act of 1974 (
45 U.S.C. 231
et seq.
); the Railway Labor Act (
45 U.S.C. 151
et seq.
); the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act (
45 U.S.C. 351
et seq.
); and the Federal Employers' Liability Act (
45 U.S.C. 51
et seq.
).
Back to Citation
36.
    
                         Certain state and local regulations that impact rail carriers may in reality be related to public safety, rather than rail safety, which could impact the Board's analysis of its jurisdiction and harmonization with FRSA. 
                        See 
                         Br. for United States as Amicus Curiae,
Ohio
v.
CSX Transp., Inc.,
No. 22-459, OSG Amicus Brief, 2023 WL 8112708, at *14 (U.S. Nov. 21, 2023) [hereinafter OSG Amicus Brief] (“It is debatable whether a blocked-crossing statute . . . is `related to
railroad
safety,'
49 U.S.C. 20106(a)(1)
(emphasis added), given that [the] safety-related concerns principally involve the safety of emergency-services users and other members of the public—not the safety of railroads and railroad operations.”).
Back to Citation
37.
    
                         Note, however, that the
Waneck
opinion described itself as “purely advisory guidance.”
Id.
at 4.
Back to Citation
38.
    
                         The Board notes that a significant percentage of rail cars are owned by separate leasing companies or directly by shippers, rather than the rail carriers themselves. 
                        See 
                         Pet. 5-7, July 26, 2021,
Pet. for Rulemaking to Adopt Rules Governing Priv. Railcar Use by R.Rs.,
EP 768. This disparate ownership structure may amplify the effects of patchwork regulation as compliance costs are imposed on many different entities, ranging from large rail carriers and manufacturers to small shippers that own their own small fleets.
Back to Citation

AGENCY:
Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
We are advising the public that the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service has received a petition from Pioneer Hi-Bred International, Inc. seeking a determination of nonregulated status for COR-ØØ121-4 maize (corn), which has been developed using genetic engineering to express the IPD083Cb protein for protection against certain susceptible lepidopteran pests and the phosphomannose isomerase protein that was used as a selectable marker. We are making the petition and draft plant pest risk assessment available for public review and comment.
DATES:
We will consider all comments that we receive on or before January 8, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by either of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
www.regulations.gov
.
Enter APHIS-2026-1288 in the Search field. Select the Documents tab, then select the Comment button in the list of documents.
Postal Mail/Commercial Delivery:
Send your comment to Docket No. APHIS-2026-1288, Regulatory Analysis and Development, PPD, APHIS, 5601 Sunnyside Avenue #AP760, Beltsville, MD 20705.
The petition, draft plant pest risk assessment, and any comments we receive on this docket may be viewed at
www.regulations.gov
,
or in our reading room, which is located in 1620 of the USDA South Building, 14th Street and Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC. Normal reading room hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 799-7039 before coming.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mr. Alan Pearson, Biotechnology Regulatory Services, APHIS, USDA, 5601 Sunnyside Avenue, AP100-3-WS-1151, Beltsville, MD 20705; (301) 851-3944; email:
alan.pearson@usda.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the authority of the plant pest provisions of the Plant Protection Act (
7 U.S.C. 7701
et seq.
), the regulations in
7 CFR part 340
, “Introduction of Organisms and Products Altered or Produced Through Genetic Engineering Which Are Plant Pests or Which There Is Reason to Believe Are Plant Pests,” regulate, among other things, the introduction (importation, interstate movement, or release into the environment) of organisms and products altered or produced through genetic engineering that are plant pests or that there is reason to believe are plant pests. Such organisms and products are considered “regulated articles.”
Section 340.6(a) of the regulations provides that any person may submit a petition to the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) seeking a determination that an article should not be regulated under
7 CFR part 340
. Paragraphs (b) and (c) of § 340.6 describe the form that a petition for a determination of nonregulated status must take and the information that must be included in the petition.
APHIS has received a petition (APHIS Petition Number 26-084-01p) from Pioneer Hi-Bred International, Inc. seeking a determination of nonregulated status for COR-ØØ121-4 maize (corn), referred to as COR121 maize, which has been developed using genetic engineering to express the IPD083Cb protein for protection against certain susceptible lepidopteran pests and the phosphomannose isomerase protein that was used as a selectable marker. The petition states that the information provided indicates that COR121 maize is unlikely to pose a plant pest risk and therefore should not be regulated under APHIS' regulations in
7 CFR part 340
.
As part of our decision-making process regarding the organism's regulatory status, APHIS prepared a draft plant pest risk assessment (PPRA) to assess the plant pest risk of the organism. APHIS' draft PPRA compared the pest risk posed by COR121 maize with that of the unmodified variety from which it was derived. The draft PPRA concluded that COR121 maize is unlikely to pose an increased plant pest risk compared to the unmodified corn.
Paragraph (d) of § 340.6 provides that APHIS will publish a notice in the
Federal Register
providing 60 days for public comment on petitions for a determination of nonregulated status. In accordance with § 340.6(d), we are publishing this notice to inform the public that APHIS will accept written comments regarding the petition and draft PPRA from interested or affected persons for a period of 60 days from the date of this notice. The petition and draft PPRA are available for public review and comment, and copies are available as indicated under
ADDRESSES
and from the individual listed under the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this notice. We are particularly interested in receiving comments regarding biological or ecological issues, and we encourage the submission of scientific data, studies, or research to support your comments.
After the comment period closes, APHIS will review and evaluate any information received during the comment period and any other relevant information. Based upon available information, APHIS will respond to the petitioner either approving or denying the petition. APHIS will post its regulatory determination on its website and publish a notice of availability in the
Federal Register
.

AGENCY:
Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Treasury; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Board).
ACTION:
Proposed rule; withdrawal.
SUMMARY:
FinCEN and the Board (collectively, the “Agencies”) are withdrawing the joint notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) published on October 27, 2020, that proposed modifying the threshold in the Agencies' rules implementing the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) requiring financial institutions to collect and retain information on certain funds transfers and transmittals of funds. The NPRM would have reduced this threshold from $3,000 to $250 for funds transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the United States. FinCEN additionally proposed reducing from $3,000 to $250 the threshold in FinCEN's rule requiring financial institutions to transmit to other financial institutions in the payment chain information on funds transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the United States. The NPRM also would have clarified the meaning of “money” as used in the Agencies' rules to specify that the rules apply to domestic and cross-border transactions involving convertible virtual currency (CVC) and digital assets that have legal tender status to a recipient. The Agencies will not take further action on this NPRM.
DATES:
FinCEN and the Board are withdrawing the NPRM published at
85 FR 68005
(October 27, 2020), as of November 9, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
FinCEN
: The FinCEN Regulatory Support Section by submitting an inquiry at
www.fincen.gov/​contact
.
Board
: Evan Winerman, Deputy Associate General Counsel, (202) 872-7578, Legal Division, Board of
(
printed page 70825)
Governors of the Federal Reserve System, 20th Street and Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20551. Users of Telecommunication Device for Deaf (TDD) only, call (202) 263-4869.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Certain Federal regulations—often referred to as the “Recordkeeping Rule” and “Travel Rule”—collectively require banks and nonbank financial institutions to collect, retain, and transmit information on funds transfers and transmittals of funds in amounts of $3,000 or more.
[
1
]
The Recordkeeping Rule, which requires banks and nonbank financial institutions to collect and retain information related to funds transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the United States, is jointly issued by both the Board and FinCEN. The Travel Rule, which requires banks and nonbank financial institutions to transmit information on funds transfers and transmittals of funds that begin or end outside the United States, is issued by FinCEN.
On October 27, 2020, FinCEN and the Board published a joint NPRM that proposed modifying the Recordkeeping Rule to reduce the threshold at which banks and nonbank financial institutions must collect and retain certain information from $3,000 to $250.
[
2
]
FinCEN additionally proposed to modify the Travel Rule to change the threshold at which banks and nonbank financial institutions must transmit information from $3,000 to $250.
[
3
]
The Agencies also proposed clarifying the meaning of “money” in these rules by revising the definitions of “payment order” and “transmittal order” to specify that the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule apply to domestic and cross-border transactions involving CVC or any digital asset having legal tender status to a recipient.
[
4
]
II. Summary of Public Comments
The Agencies received nearly 3,000 comments on the proposal from depository institutions, money services businesses, trade associations, individuals, and others.
[
5
]
Commenters generally opposed the proposal to reduce the thresholds applicable to the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule for international transactions. Many comments argued that a threshold of $250 would impose a significant regulatory burden on financial institutions, particularly smaller financial institutions; would disrupt the ability of consumers to send remittances overseas (and could potentially drive consumers into less regulated marketplaces); would significantly increase the number of transactions subject to the provisions of the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule; and would increase the liability exposure of financial institutions required to maintain personally identifiable information. Many comments also noted that some potentially illicit transactions under the $3,000 threshold were already being reported to FinCEN through Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs). A number of commenters asserted that the Agencies did not provide sufficient analysis or data to justify the proposed reduction in the threshold. Several commenters stated that, rather than decrease the threshold, the Agencies should adopt a higher threshold due to the effects of inflation since the original threshold was adopted in 1995.
Commenter sentiment was mixed with respect to the proposal to specify that the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule apply to CVC transactions. In general, companies that provide CVC-related services (and related trade associations) opposed this aspect of the proposal, while some depository institutions, money services businesses, and related trade associations supported this aspect of the proposal. Commenters opposed to this aspect of the proposal stated that implementing the proposal would be challenging (
e.g.,
due to technological limitations and the lack of an international messaging standard for CVC transactions), that the proposal would inhibit CVC innovation, and that the Agencies should improve coordination with other regulators who were, at that time, simultaneously developing rules affecting the CVC industry.
Many commenters offered more general comments on the proposal, including that the proposal would constitute an unwarranted invasion of privacy or an unreasonable search and seizure in violation of the Fourth Amendment. Many commenters also stated that the comment period on the proposal was insufficient, and that, if the Agencies finalize the proposal, the proposed implementation period should be extended.
III. Withdrawal of NPRM
The Agencies have reconsidered the proposal in light of the public comments received and have determined to withdraw the joint NPRM for two primary reasons. First, more than five years have passed since the issuance of the NPRM, and the Agencies believe that additional feedback from the public would be useful before the Agencies adopted any amendments to the Recordkeeping Rule or Travel Rule that are similar to the proposed amendments. The proposal is being withdrawn to provide certainty to the public that no final rule will be issued without an additional opportunity for public comment.
Second, and relatedly, the Agencies believe that there have been significant recent developments in the CVC industry since the proposal was issued. For example, CVC markets have continued to mature, and new legal frameworks are emerging.
[
6
]
The Agencies believe that any future, potential amendments to the Recordkeeping Rule and Travel Rule related to CVC should be considered in light of these recent developments to ensure that such amendments are fit for purpose.
[
7
]
Because the Agencies no longer intend to issue a final rule with respect to this proposal, the NPRM published at
85 FR 68005
is hereby withdrawn.
Jimmy L. Kirby,
Deputy Director, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.
Jointly issued by:
By order of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.
Benjamin McDonough,
Secretary of the Board.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The IRS, in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)
), provides the general public and Federal agencies with an opportunity to comment on proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps the IRS assess the impact and minimize the burden of its information collection requirements. Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and/or included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record, and viewable on relevant websites. For this reason, please do not include in your comments information of a confidential nature, such as sensitive personal information. Comments are invited on: (a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information shall have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the collection of information; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology; and (e) estimates of capital or start-up costs and costs of operation, maintenance, and purchase of services to provide information.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Abstract
Title I of The Patent Law Treaties Implementation Act of 2012
[
1
]
(PLTIA) amended the patent laws to implement the provisions of the Geneva Act of the Hague Agreement Concerning International Registration of Industrial Designs (hereafter “Hague Agreement”). The Hague Agreement is an international registration system which offers the possibility of obtaining protection for up to 100 industrial designs in designated member countries and intergovernmental organizations (referred to as “Contracting Parties”) by filing a single international design application either directly with the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) or indirectly through the office of an applicant's Contracting Party. The United States is a Contracting Party to
(
printed page 70867)
the Hague Agreement, which took effect with respect to the United States on May 13, 2015. The Hague Agreement is administrated by the International Bureau (IB) of WIPO located in Geneva, Switzerland.
Under the Hague Agreement, a U.S. applicant can file an international design application indirectly through the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO), which will forward the application to the IB upon satisfaction of certain requirements, or directly with the IB. All international design applications are subject to the following fees: (1) a basic fee, (2) a publication fee, and (3) in respect of each Contracting Party designated for protection, either a standard or individual designation fee. An international design application is also subject to an additional per word fee where the description exceeds 100 words. A transmittal fee is also required for international design applications filed indirectly through the USPTO. The fees required by the IB may be paid either directly to the IB in Swiss currency or through the USPTO as an office of indirect filing in U.S. dollars. If applicants want to pay the required fees through the USPTO as an office of indirect filing, the fees must be paid no later than the date of payment of the transmittal fee. The fees will then be forwarded to the IB after conversion to Swiss currency.
Where the U.S. is designated, the applicant will be required to pay a first part U.S. designation fee to the IB. The first part U.S. designation fee, established in Swiss currency, is based on the combined amounts of the basic filing fee (
37 CFR 1.16(b)
), search fee (§ 1.16(l)), and examination fee (§ 1.16(p)) for a design application. See § 1.1031(f)(1). Upon issuance of a notice of allowance by the USPTO, payment of a second part U.S. designation fee (
i.e.,
the issue fee) will be required. See § 1.1031(f)(2). The second part U.S. designation fee may be paid either directly to the USPTO in U.S. dollars or through the IB in Swiss currency.
The IB examines international design application for compliance with the applicable formal requirements under the Hague Agreement. If the applicable requirements are satisfied, the IB registers the international design to the International Register. Thereafter, the IB will publish the international registration in the International Designs Bulletin based on the publication timing selected by the applicant. The IB will provide a copy of the publication of the international registration to each Contracting Party designated by the application.
A designated Contracting Party may or may not perform a substantive examination of the international design registration. The USPTO will perform a substantive examination for patentability of the international design application, as in the case of regular U.S. design applications.
This information collection covers all the necessary information required for an international design application that is filed either through the USPTO as an office of indirect filing or directly with the IB. The information in this collection is used to register industrial designs under the provisions of the Hague Agreement. The USPTO manages two forms in this information collection, and the rest are forms managed by the IB.

Items in this information collection may be submitted as electronic submissions. Applicants may also submit the information in paper form by mail, fax, or hand delivery.

Drawing Costs
The USPTO estimates that the costs to produce design drawings can range from $50 to $350 per sheet. Taking the average of this range, the USPTO estimates that it can cost $200 per sheet to produce design drawings. On average, 10 sheets of drawings are submitted for an application resulting in an average cost of $2,000 to produce the design drawings. The USPTO estimates that 140 respondents will file international design applications indirectly through the USPTO for transmission to the IB. The USPTO further estimates that it will receive approximately 3,870 international design applications from the IB where applicants have designated the U.S., accompanied by payment of the first part of the designated fee for substantive examination by the USPTO. The USPTO estimates that all of the 4,010 design applications will be submitted with drawings. Overall, the costs associated with submitting these drawings are estimated to be $8,020,000.
Postage Costs
Although the USPTO prefers that the items in this information collection be submitted electronically, responses may be submitted by mail through the United States Postal Service. The USPTO estimates that 1% of the 5,633 items in this information collection will be submitted in the mail, resulting in 56 mailed items. The USPTO estimates that the average postage cost for a mailed submission, using a Priority Mail legal flat-rate envelope, will be $13.25. Therefore, the USPTO estimates the total mailing costs for this information collection is $742.
IV. Request for Comments
The USPTO is soliciting public comments to:
(a) Evaluate whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
(b) Evaluate the accuracy of the Agency's estimate of the burden of the collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(c) Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
(d) Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who intend to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses.
All comments submitted in response to this notice are a matter of public record. The USPTO will include or summarize each comment in the request to OMB to approve this information collection. Before including an address, phone number, email address, or other personally identifiable information (PII) in a comment, be advised that the entire comment—including PII—may be made publicly available at any time. While one may request in a comment to withhold PII from public view, the USPTO cannot guarantee that it will be able to do so.

SUMMARY:
KPT Energy LLC (the Applicant or KPT Energy) has applied for renewed authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to Canada pursuant to the Federal Power Act.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 9, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Comments or requests for more information should be addressed
(
printed page 70873)
by electronic mail to
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Marina Fennel, (240) 702-6156,
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The United States Department of Energy (DOE) regulates electricity exports from the United States to foreign countries in accordance with section 202(e) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) (
16 U.S.C. 824a(e)
) and regulations thereunder (
10 CFR 205.300
). Sections 301(b) and 402(f) of the DOE Organization Act (
42 U.S.C. 7151(b)
and
7172(f)
) transferred this regulatory authority, previously exercised by the now-defunct Federal Power Commission, to DOE.
Section 202(e) of the FPA provides that an entity which seeks to export electricity must obtain an order from DOE authorizing that export (
16 U.S.C. 824a(e)
). On January 8, 2026, the authority to issue such orders was delegated to the DOE's Assistant Secretary for the Office of Electricity by Redelegation Order No. S3-DEL-OE1-2026.
On July 24, 2026, KPT Energy filed an application (Application or App.) with DOE for authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to Canada for a term of five years.
KPT Energy is a Delaware limited liability company “with its principal place of business in Toronto, Canada.” App at 1. KPT Energy is “formed to be a power marketer engaging in the purchase and sale of physical and/or virtual energy in wholesale electricity markets.” App. at 2. KPT Energy is directly and wholly owned by KPT Energy LP, which is wholly and directly owned by KPT Energy Holdings Inc. KPT Energy Holdings Inc. is directly owned by DTFC Holdings Inc. and Boof & Doof Corp., both organized under the laws of Canada. App. at 1-2. KPT Energy states that “neither KPT Energy nor its affiliates own or operate generation or transmission facilities, nor do they have a franchised electric power service area” and that it is “not seeking authorization to export power on behalf of, or in conjunction with, any partners or partnerships.” KPT energy affirms it will “make all necessary commercial arrangements and will obtain any and all other regulatory approvals required in order to schedule and deliver power exports.”
Id.
at 4.
The existing international transmission facilities to be utilized by the Applicant have been previously authorized by Presidential permits issued pursuant to
Executive Order 10485
, as amended, and are appropriate for open access transmission by third parties.
See
App. at Exhibit A.
Procedural Matters:
Any person desiring to be heard in this proceeding should file a comment to the Application at
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.
Comments concerning KPT Energy's Application should be clearly marked with OE Docket No. EA-532. Comments will be posted along with the relevant application on the program website at
www.energy.gov/​oe/​pending-applications
.
A final decision will be made on the requested authorization after the environmental impacts have been evaluated consistent with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) of 1969, as amended (
42 U.S.C. 4321
,
et seq.
), the DOE NEPA regulations at
10 CFR part 1021
, and the DOE's Implementing Procedures (June 2026) and after DOE evaluates whether the proposed action will have an adverse impact on the sufficiency of supply or reliability of the United States electric power supply system.
Copies of this Application are available on the program website at
www.energy.gov/​oe/​pending-applications
or by emailing
Electricity.Exports@hq.doe.gov
.

Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information (including each proposed extension or reinstatement of an existing collection of information) and to allow 60 days for public comment on the proposed action. Interested persons are invited to send comments regarding our burden estimates or any other aspect of this collection of information, including the necessity and utility of the proposed information collection for the proper performance of the agency's functions, the accuracy of the estimated burden, ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected, and the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology to minimize the information collection burden.
DATES:

ADDRESSES:
When commenting, please reference the document identifier or OMB control number. To be assured consideration, comments and recommendations must be submitted in any one of the following ways:
1.
Electronically.
You may send your comments electronically to
http://www.regulations.gov
. Follow the instructions for “Comment or Submission” or “More Search Options” to find the information collection document(s) that are accepting comments.
2.
By Regular Mail.
You may mail written comments to the following address: CMS, Office of Strategic Operations and Regulatory Affairs, Division of Regulations Development, Attention: Document Identifier: __/OMB Control Number: __, Room C4-26-05, 7500 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, Maryland 21244-1850.

.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Contents
This notice sets out a summary of the use and burden associated with the following information collections. More detailed information can be found in each collection's supporting statement and associated materials (see
ADDRESSES
).
Under the PRA (
