We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
CMS received many comments on its reading of the statute to aggregate all dosage forms and strengths of a drug with the same active moiety and the same holder of a NDA or of a biological product with the same active ingredient and the same holder of a BLA, for the purposes of identifying potential qualifying single source drugs as proposed at § 429.125(b). Many commenters disagreed with CMS' approach to identifying a qualifying single source drug and asserted that the proposal at § 429.125(b) contradicts the statute and stated that they do not believe that CMS has the statutory authority to aggregate qualifying single source drugs across multiple NDAs/BLAs. These commenters claimed that the statute defines a qualifying single source drug in reference to a distinct NDA or BLA, and some of these commenters stated that it would be reasonable and appropriate that such a definition would align with the FDA's approval and licensure processes under section 505(c) of the FD&C Act or section 351(a) of PHS Act. A few commenters claimed that the statute defines a qualifying single source drug by reference to the definition of a “covered Part D drug” at section 1860D-2(e) of the Act, which in turn cross-references the definition of a “covered outpatient drug” at section 1927(k)(2) of the Act. The commenter asserted that, under section 1927(k)(2) of the Act, whether a single source drug is a distinct “covered outpatient drug” is based on whether the product is approved pursuant to a distinct NDA or BLA, and the only exception to this rule is for line extensions. A few commenters asserted that the reference to “payment under Part B” in section 1192(e)(1) of the Act requires CMS to identify a qualifying single source drug exclusively by reference to how the CMS identifies the drug for payment purposes and asserted that CMS has long interpreted section 1847A of the Act as identifying distinct single source drugs payable under Part B by reference to whether they have distinct NDAs or BLAs. Some commenters stated that CMS' failure to limit the identification of a potential qualifying single source drug to products approved or licensed under a distinct NDA/BLA will be detrimental to future innovation and patient access to medications and limit manufacturers from researching follow-on innovations such as extended release formulations and new indications, including indications for rare diseases.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their input. As discussed in responses to similar comments in the revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026, the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, and the Negotiation Program Guidance, section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act directs CMS to “use data that is aggregated across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the drug, such as an extended release formulation, and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of the drug” for purposes of determining whether a qualifying single source drug is a negotiation-eligible drug. Identifying potential qualifying single source drugs on the basis of active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component, as applicable, permits us to effectuate these statutory directives. We use “active ingredient” and “active moiety” (or, for vaccines for infectious disease(s), “antigen component”) as markers for active substances that remain constant across changes in strength, dosage form, or release mechanism. These terms also comport with the ordinary meaning of “drug”. See, for example, Drug, Black's Law Dictionary (12th ed. 2024) (“A substance intended for use in diagnosis, cure, treatment, or prevention of disease.”); Drug, Merriam-Webster's Collegiate Dictionary (12th ed. 2025) (“[A] substance used as a medication or in the preparation of medication”). We adopted this approach in guidance for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027 and 2028, and this final rule to ensure that a new dosage form, strength, or new formulation of a drug with the same “active ingredient”, “active moiety”, or “antigen component”, but that received a new FDA approval or licensure, would not avoid or delay eligibility for negotiation contrary to these statutory provisions. Indeed, complying with the statutory requirement to identify a qualifying single source drug using data that is aggregated across different dosage forms and strengths and new formulations has the effect of reducing manufacturer incentives to engage in “product hopping,” as well as counteracting the effects of existing “product hopping” on the Negotiation Program. Ensuring that drug and biological products are not inappropriately excluded from, or delayed from inclusion in, the Negotiation Program based on modest or minor modifications is consistent with the purpose of the statute, which is to ensure that the Negotiation Program delivers benefits to the Medicare program and its beneficiaries. Similarly, section 1196(a)(2) of the Act directs CMS to establish procedures “to compute and apply the maximum fair price across different strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of such drug.” In addition, section 1194(e)(1)(D) of the Act instructs CMS, for purposes of the negotiation process discussed in further detail in subpart F of this final rule, to consider, among other information, “applications and approvals under section 505(c) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or section 351(a) of the Public Health Service Act,” in the plural, for the “drug,” in the singular. The aggregation rules under sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act are clear and are designed to ensure that the Negotiation Program delivers benefits to the Medicare program and its beneficiaries in accordance with statute. Because different dosage forms and strengths, as well as different formulations, containing the same active moiety/active ingredient may be approved or licensed under multiple NDAs or BLAs, the suggestion from commenters to define a qualifying single
(
printed page 72212)
source drug in reference to a distinct NDA or BLA is inconsistent with sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. Contrary to the views of some commenters, sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act require the aggregation of data across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the drug, and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of the drug, thereby necessarily establishing that the statutory selection and negotiation procedures apply more broadly than to a distinct NDA or BLA.
For these same reasons, we disagree that the references in section 1192(e)(1) of the Act to the definition of a “covered Part D drug” and to payment which “may be made under part B” require CMS to identify a qualifying single source drug with respect to a distinct NDA or BLA. This language in section 1192(e)(1) of the Act sets forth one of multiple statutory criteria that CMS must use to identify qualifying single sources drugs. Specifically, section 1192(e)(1) of the Act requires that a qualifying single source drug that is a drug as set forth in section 1192(e)(1)(A) of the Act or that is a biological product as set forth in section 1192(e)(1)(B) of the Act must be “a covered part D drug (as defined in section 1860D-2(e))” or “a drug or biological product for which payment may be made under part B of title XVIII” or both. Were we to accept the commenters' view that this statutory language requires CMS to identify a qualifying single source drug with respect to a distinct NDA or BLA, we would fail to give full effect to the aggregation rules under sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. Under our understanding of the statutory language, section 1192(e) of the Act, including its references to a “covered Part D drug” and to payment which “may be made under part B”, sets forth the qualifying conditions for drug and biological products; these qualifying conditions do not supersede nor conflict with—and, to the contrary, must be read in concert with—the aggregation rules under sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. Unlike the views offered by some commenters, our understanding of the statutory language gives full effect to all relevant provisions of the statute, including sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1192(e), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act; we are applying an interpretation of the statute that follows the statutory criteria for the identification of a qualifying single source drug under section 1192(e) of the Act and, consistent with sections 1192(d)(3)(B), 1194(e)(1)(D), and 1196(a)(2) of the Act, gives effect to the statutory policy that a drug that may be selected for negotiation includes multiple dosage forms and strengths and formulations of that drug.
Comment:
A commenter expressed appreciation for CMS' consistent approach to the identification of potential qualifying single source drugs. This commenter stated that section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act clarifies the intent of policymakers to apply negotiated prices across dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug, which the commenter asserted necessitates the approach CMS proposes in the rule for identifying potential qualifying single source drugs. This commenter stated that the approach proposed by CMS will prevent gaming and abuse of the Negotiation Program that may occur if manufacturers were able to prevent a high-revenue product from qualifying for negotiation through product hopping and obtaining new NDAs and BLAs, effectively resetting the clock on the statutory 7- and 11-year periods before a drug or biological product may qualify for selection.
Response:
We thank the commenter for the support. We agree that the statutory requirement to identify a qualifying single source drug using data that is aggregated across different dosage forms and strengths, as described in the proposed rule, is expected to reduce incentives for pharmaceutical manufacturers to engage in “product hopping.” This ensures that the Negotiation Program selects drugs for negotiation that have high total expenditures under Part B and Part D of the Medicare program regardless of variations like differences in formulation or packaging.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS provide greater transparency regarding its methodologies for identifying the active moiety/active ingredient in a potential qualifying single source drug, stating that public sources cited by CMS (such as, but not limited to, RxNorm, OpenFDA, FDALabel, DailyMed, and FDA's Active Ingredient-Active Moiety Relationship/Bases of Strength file) aggregate and display FDA information, as well as other data, for secondary purposes, such as clinical terminology standardization, drug information directories, and labeling repositories, and the classifications in these sources do not necessarily track the regulatory distinctions that are determinative for FDA's active moiety/active ingredient identification. The commenter recommended that CMS use NDA and BLA approvals, approved labeling, and Orange Book and Purple Book data, as the primary and binding sources for identifying active moieties/active ingredients, with supplementary databases such as RxNorm, OpenFDA, FDALabel, and DailyMed used only to confirm, and never to override, those records. The commenter requested that CMS publish an analytic plan describing what information from each public source will be used and how CMS will reconcile differences that may arise between the sources, stating that without a defined hierarchy specifying which sources will be used in the event of conflict, manufacturers will have insufficient information about how CMS will treat their products. The commenter also requested that any FDA consultation undertaken to resolve a naming or classification question should be disclosed to the affected manufacturer, with a defined opportunity for the manufacturer to respond, and the consultation—including the information provided to FDA, the FDA division consulted, and FDA's response—should be documented in the administrative record.
Response:
We appreciate the input. We maintain that manufacturers have sufficient notice of the information we use to identify active moieties/active ingredients, as described in this final rule. Because information on active moiety/active ingredient names are not always standardized across systems, we believe that using a combination of public sources, including those cited by CMS (for example, FDA's Active Ingredient-Active Moiety Relationship/Basis of Strength file, OpenFDA, FDALabel, RxNorm, and DailyMed), in addition to FDA consultation, as applicable, is the best way to accurately identify active moieties/active ingredients. We consider the body of information across sources together, which we believe produces a more accurate and complete identification than relying on any one source alone. This holistic, non-hierarchical approach preserves our ability to incorporate FDA feedback to ensure accurate identification of the active moiety/active ingredient consistent with the statute. Where these sources conflict or CMS seeks additional clarity, we may consult FDA. We recognize that some fields within these sources are not fully standardized because the sources themselves draw on multiple, non-uniform inputs. To that end, CMS incorporates RxNorm to provide normalized names and unique identifiers for medicines and drugs, consistent with RxNorm's stated goal to
(
printed page 72213)
provide such normalization.

Further, RxNorm incorporates FDA's approved labeling information in the form of FDA SPL. FDA's SPL is a published standard used by FDA for processing and managing labeling and labeling changes. In response to the request that CMS use NDA and BLA approvals, FDA approved labeling, and Orange Book and Purple Book data, we reiterate that our proposal referred to FDA and FDA-derived sources such as FDALabel, DailyMed, and OpenFDA. Further, in addition to FDA's SPL, OpenFDA incorporates many other FDA sources such as Orange Book, Drugs@FDA and the NDC Directory. Lastly, FDA's Active Ingredient-Active Moiety Relationship/Basis of Strength file is an FDA publication. Therefore, we believe our proposal already incorporates the sources suggested by the commenter and do not believe it is necessary to add these additional FDA sources to the non-exhaustive list of sources already identified. In response to the request that CMS publish an analytic plan, we believe this final rule provides sufficient detail on how CMS identifies active moieties/active ingredients. Our approach is holistic and sensitive to drug-specific details rather than a rigid assessment of data fields. In response to the request that CMS disclose any FDA consultation to the affected manufacturer, we note that section 1192(e) of the Act sets forth the requirements for the identification of qualifying single source drugs and does not require nor contemplate that CMS disclose such consultations to manufacturers.

After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing § 429.125(a) and (b) as proposed, but with a technical modification to § 429.125(b)(4) to improve organizational clarity that is discussed in the next section of this final rule. We direct readers to the discussion in section II.B.6.a.1. of this final rule for our consideration of public comments received on the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) as well as our summary of the aforementioned technical modification to § 429.125(b)(4).
(1) Fixed Combination Drugs
At proposed § 429.125(b)(4), for the purpose of identifying potential qualifying single source drugs and subject to the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) to clarify our treatment of new formulations, we proposed that if a drug is a fixed combination drug (defined in proposed § 429.20) with two or more active moieties, active ingredients, or, for vaccines for infectious disease(s), antigen components, the distinct combination of active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components would generally be treated as one active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component. Therefore, all formulations with this distinct combination offered by the same NDA/BLA holder would be aggregated across all dosage forms and strengths of the fixed combination drug (that is, all formulations and dosage forms and strengths of this distinct combination would be considered the same potential qualifying single source drug and, if applicable, CMS would aggregate total expenditures for all such formulations and dosage forms and strengths when determining whether such drug is a negotiation-eligible drug or selected drug). Under this proposal, a product containing only one (but not all) of the active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components that is offered by the same NDA/BLA holder would generally not be aggregated with the formulations of the fixed combination drug and would be considered a separate potential qualifying single source drug. For example, a corticosteroid inhaler would not be aggregated with a fixed combination inhaler from the same NDA/BLA holder that contains the same corticosteroid combined with a long-acting beta agonist. In this example, the corticosteroid inhaler would be considered as a separate potential qualifying single source drug from the fixed combination inhaler.
In the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028, we stated our belief that treating distinct combinations of active moieties/active ingredients as one active moiety/active ingredient for the purpose of identifying potential
(
printed page 72214)
qualifying single source drugs is generally appropriate. However, we acknowledged that there may exist fixed combination drugs for which one of the active ingredients or active moieties contained is not biologically active against the disease state(s) the drug is indicated for and thus does not result in a clinically meaningful difference. We solicited comments on whether the addition of drugs payable under Part B may impact the fixed combination drug policy described in the draft guidance. In particular, we solicited comments on how CMS might consider grouping such fixed combination drug products with products containing at least one but not all of the active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s) into the same potential qualifying single source drug for both drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D, including input on terminology that could facilitate the effectuation of such a policy.
We received many comments in response to this previous comment solicitation. Some commenters supported a modification to the fixed combination drug policy as a way to close a loophole for manufacturers to avoid selection by making minor changes to existing drugs, specifically citing the addition of hyaluronidase to drugs payable under Part B. Other commenters opposed such a modification, citing concerns that CMS lacks the statutory authority to do so, that the approach described in the comment solicitation does not align with how FDA regulates and reviews the approvals of fixed combination drugs, or that CMS would not be able to apply a consistent definition to the terminology described in the comment solicitation, including the terms “biologically active against the disease state” or “clinically meaningful difference.” Some commenters raised concerns that the modification would potentially harm patients and discourage the innovation of pharmaceutical manufacturers. In the Negotiation Program Guidance, we stated that, due to the complexity and scope of the issue as noted in the stakeholder comments, we believed additional time would be necessary to develop objective policy criteria if we were to finalize such a policy, and thus did not make a change to the fixed combination drug policy in the Negotiation Program Guidance. We stated our intent to address the program integrity risk posed by certain fixed combination drugs and that we were continuing to consider appropriate policy to potentially propose in rulemaking for initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years.
In the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36258
), we stated that, since publishing the Negotiation Program Guidance, we have continued to consider program integrity risks posed by certain fixed combination drugs. Specifically, we stated that we were aware of a program integrity risk in which, under Negotiation Program policies for identifying qualifying single source drugs set forth in guidance with respect to previous initial price applicability years, a manufacturer may avoid selection of a qualifying single source drug or, in the case that a qualifying single source drug becomes a selected drug, avoid the application of the MFP, by marketing a new formulation of the qualifying single source drug that includes, in addition to the active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) in the original product, an active moiety, antigen component, or active ingredient, such as hyaluronidase, that enables an alternative route of administration for the shared active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) in the original product. Under the general fixed combination drug policy set forth in guidance with respect to previous initial price applicability years, including, for example, section 30.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028, we explained that we were aware that such a manufacturer may avoid having all dosage forms and strengths of a drug, including the new formulation of such drug, with its active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) included in a qualifying single source drug in instances in which a new formulation differs from other formulations of the qualifying single source drug based on the inclusion of an additional active moiety/active ingredient/antigen component that enables an alternative route of administration for the shared active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s).
We explained that, in this scenario, we were concerned that application of CMS' general fixed combination drug policy would be in tension with statutory requirements under sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act because we would not aggregate together the original product and the new formulation containing the additional active moiety/active ingredient/antigen component, even though these may be appropriately understood as different formulations of the same drug under sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act.

First, application of the general fixed combination drug policy to such products would be in tension with section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act in the course of drug selection because we would not treat the original product and the new formulation containing the additional active moiety/active ingredient/antigen component as one qualifying single source drug. Thus, when determining whether a qualifying single source drug is a negotiation-eligible drug, as proposed at § 429.115(a), we would calculate the combined total expenditures under Part B and Part D separately for the original product and the new formulation. We stated our belief that separately calculating total expenditures for such products under these circumstances may be inconsistent with the statutory direction at section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act to use data that is aggregated across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the drug, in determining whether a qualifying single source drug is a negotiation-eligible drug. Because under the general fixed combination drug policy we would evaluate the original product and the new formulation separately during the drug selection process, the time since approval or licensure (determined as proposed at § 429.125(c)) for the new formulation would likely be later than for the original product, thereby extending the years before which the new formulation could potentially be selected and, if selected and if an MFP is agreed to, be subject to an MFP. We explained that this dynamic presents program integrity risks because evaluating the time since approval or licensure separately for the original product and the new formulation and splitting combined total expenditures under Part B and Part D between such products could lead to a scenario where the original product or the new formulation or both are never selected or are not selected until a future initial price applicability year, which would reduce or delay the ability of the Negotiation Program to negotiate MFPs
(
printed page 72215)
for high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products.
Second, if the original product is selected for negotiation, and a negotiated MFP is agreed upon for that drug, the general fixed combination drug policy may be in tension with section 1196(a)(2) of the Act, which directs CMS to apply the MFP across different strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulations or package size or package type of such drug, because the MFP would not apply to the new formulation. We explained that this dynamic presents further program integrity risks. If the new formulation is not part of the selected drug, then the Primary Manufacturer would be able to market the new formulation without the new formulation being subject to MFP effectuation requirements, thereby creating a new incentive for the Primary Manufacturer to drive patient utilization toward the new formulation and circumvent the application of the MFP to the original product for such patients.
To address these program integrity risks, and to clarify how CMS interprets sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act as applied to new formulations of a drug, including in the context of fixed combination drugs, we proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) a policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations: if CMS determines that a fixed combination drug with two or more active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or, for a vaccine for infectious disease(s), antigen component(s), shares one or more active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) with another drug or biological product(s) with the same NDA/BLA holder, and such products differ in active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) due to the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), CMS would, for purposes of identifying the potential qualifying single source drug under proposed § 429.125(b)(1) and (b)(2), use all dosage forms and strengths of the drug or biological product with the shared moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) and the same NDA/BLA holder. In other words, we would identify the potential qualifying single source drug as including all dosage forms and strengths with the shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) that is offered by the same NDA/BLA holder. An example is the inclusion of active ingredient X with a different active ingredient Y, where active ingredient X creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for active ingredient Y. In the described example and as set forth in proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), CMS would identify the potential qualifying single source drug using all dosage forms and strengths of the drug or biological product that contain active ingredient Y and share the same BLA holder.

We proposed the policy at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) because the program integrity concerns this policy would address relate primarily to biological products that are more likely payable under Part B, and drugs were not selected based on total expenditures under Part B until initial price applicability year 2028. The program integrity concerns raised by fixed combination drugs that are new formulations have not yet impacted drug selection but may soon do so as more drugs with significant total expenditures under Part B become qualifying single source drugs and negotiation-eligible drugs. We stated that we did not believe that significant reliance interests have arisen around the fixed combination policy established in Negotiation Program guidance for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, as incentives for pharmaceutical manufacturers to develop new formulations like the ones we proposed to address in this policy long predate the Negotiation Program. In the absence of this proposed policy, however, pharmaceutical manufacturers may have increased incentives under Negotiation Program policy to drive patient utilization toward new formulations that would be treated as distinct qualifying single source drugs, and if selected, as distinct selected drugs.
The proposal incorporated previous feedback from commenters that raised concerns about how we would operationalize terms used in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028, such as “biologically active against the disease state”. We stated that we understood from these commenters' concerns the importance of developing a modification to the general fixed combination drug policy that is narrowly tailored to the development of new formulations that pose program integrity concerns and does not group products together under the same potential qualifying single source drug beyond what the statute permits. Additionally, we stated that we understood the importance of developing criteria that allow the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations to be operationalized in a consistent and objective manner over a large set of active moieties/active ingredients/antigen components. We stated our belief that the terminology proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would achieve both these goals.
First, we stated our belief that the criteria proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) can be operationalized in a consistent and objective manner using public sources. Specifically, we proposed to use public sources such as, but not limited to, RxNorm, OpenFDA, FDALabel, DailyMed, and FDA's Active Ingredient-Active Moiety Relationship/Basis of Strength file to identify the active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) of the drug or biological products, as described in section II.B.6.a. of this final rule, and to use public sources such as, but not limited to, Orange Book, Purple Book, Drugs@FDA, and DailyMed to identify the routes of administration of the fixed combination drug and the drug or biological product with the same NDA/BLA holder that shares one or more active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) with the fixed combination drug. We stated that we may also consult with FDA, as appropriate. We solicited comments on recommended approaches to inform CMS identification of active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) that enable an alternative route of administration for co-administered active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s), including what types of information or descriptions we should look for within product labeling when identifying such cases.
Second, we stated that focusing on active moieties/active ingredients/antigen components that enable an alternative route of administration would reduce the number of products qualifying for the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations as compared to the previous language citing active moieties/active ingredients not biologically active against the disease state(s) for which the drug is indicated. For example, we stated our belief that
(
printed page 72216)
the terminology proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would currently only impact biological products licensed under BLAs.
We explained that, in developing this proposed policy, CMS also considered other feedback from commenters on our prior proposal to modify our fixed combination drug policy. As we noted in the Negotiation Program Guidance, many commenters raised concerns that a modification to CMS' fixed combination drug policy would not align with how FDA regulates and reviews the approvals of fixed combination drugs. We considered this feedback but maintain that the language at proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) clarifies how CMS would comply with sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act for fixed combination drugs that are new formulations, and the commenters' suggestion that CMS must treat fixed combination drugs in the same manner as what such commenters assert is how the FDA may treat such products under FDA authorities is not persuasive in this instance. Identifying such products as a single potential qualifying single source drug reflects CMS' proposed interpretation of sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act and would solely be for the purpose of implementing the Negotiation Program.
We noted that we also considered comments on how a modification to CMS' fixed combination drug policy would potentially impact pharmaceutical innovation. Although a few of the previous commenters stated a modification to the fixed combination drug policy would potentially harm patients by discouraging the innovation of pharmaceutical manufacturers, another commenter noted that manufacturers already have substantial financial motivations beyond the Negotiation Program to pursue the development of new formulations—including new formulations that are fixed combination drugs—to delay generic or biosimilar competition. We agreed with this latter argument and noted further our belief that the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would effectuate sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act, address the program integrity concerns in the Negotiation Program that we and commenters have identified, while not meaningfully impacting incentives for innovation. We also reiterated our statement in the Negotiation Program Guidance that we are committed to a negotiation process that recognizes the clinical benefit of products, including products with different dosage forms and strengths, formulations or routes of administration from other products that are aggregated as part of the same qualifying single source drug, and we directed readers to proposed § 429.510(e) and section II.F.3.d.1. of the Negotiation Program proposed rule for discussion of CMS' approach to adjusting the starting point for an initial offer based on section 1194(e)(2) factors, which include factors related to clinical benefit as compared to therapeutic alternatives.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and recommended finalizing. Many commenters agreed with CMS that the proposed policy is important for addressing a program integrity risk in which manufacturers may develop minor reformulations of existing drugs to avoid selection of a qualifying single source drug or, in the case that a qualifying single source drug becomes a selected drug, avoid the application of the MFP. A few commenters remarked that the inclusion of a component that enables a different route of administration, including the addition of hyaluronidase to enable subcutaneous administration, largely represents a repackaging of the existing product and should not transform the existing drug into a new one for purposes of Medicare pricing. Some commenters stated that the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is appropriately tailored to address this scenario. A commenter stated that the proposal appropriately balances program integrity concerns while preserving the existing framework for other fixed combination drugs, which will appropriately balance the goals of reducing Medicare drug costs and encouraging biosimilar competition. A commenter stated that the proposal is consistent with existing CMS policy, such as Medicaid line extension rules, establishing that minor product modifications should not allow manufacturers to avoid the consequences of competition or price regulation. A few commenters stated that the proposal is consistent with the statutory mandate at sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act to aggregate data across dosage forms and strengths of a drug, including new formulations.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS withdraw the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations and instead treat a product approved under a distinct NDA/BLA, including a fixed combination drug, as a unique qualifying single source drug. Many of these commenters stated that the modification to CMS' fixed combination drug policy would contradict statute because, in their view, statute requires CMS to identify qualifying single source drugs in reference to a distinct NDA or BLA, and FDA approves or licenses fixed combination products separately from products with a single active moiety/active ingredient. In their view, CMS' existing aggregation framework already contradicts statute, and the commenters contended that the proposed policy worsens that asserted contradiction. Many commenters stated that the proposal would result in premature negotiation-eligibility for products that would qualify for the criteria proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) because 7- or 11-years, as applicable, would not have elapsed between that product's own approval or licensure and the selected drug publication date.
Some commenters disagreed with CMS' statement in the proposed rule (
91 FR 36258
) that certain fixed combination drugs that are new formulations may be appropriately understood as different formulations of the same drug under sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act; these commenters asserted instead that these statutory provisions are fully satisfied by aggregating expenditures and applying the MFP across the dosage forms and strengths (including new formulations such as an extended-release formulation) that are marketed under a qualifying single source drug's unique NDA or BLA. A few commenters stated that the fixed combination drug policy is unmoored from statute because statute says nothing about route of administration as a basis for determining whether products should be aggregated into the same qualifying single source drug. A couple of commenters stated that, if Congress intended CMS to aggregate fixed combination drug products with products containing only a subset of their active moieties/active ingredients, it would have done so expressly as it did for line extensions under the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program and Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' feedback. In response to the commenters that asserted that the statute requires CMS to identify qualifying single source drugs in reference to a distinct NDA or BLA, we direct readers to our response to
(
printed page 72217)
comments on this topic in section II.B.6.a. of this final rule. In response to comments stating that the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would result in premature negotiation-eligibility for products that qualify for the proposal, we refer readers to our discussion in section B.6.b. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36261
) and this final rule describing how CMS identifies the date of approval or licensure, as applicable, for a potential qualifying single source drug with more than one FDA application, including a fixed combination drug that qualifies for the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i).
We disagree with the commenters who stated that a fixed combination drug described in proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) should not be aggregated under the same qualifying single source drug pursuant to section 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act and that route of administration should not be used as a component of qualifying single source drug identification. The proposed policy is consistent with the statutory directives. Section 1196(a)(2) of the Act requires that CMS establish “procedures to compute and apply the maximum fair price across different strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of the drug.” Likewise, section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act requires CMS to use data that is “aggregated across dosage forms and strengths of the drug,
including
new formulations of the drug,
such as
an extended release formulation” (emphasis added). The terms “including” and “such as” in section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act make clear that the extended release example is illustrative, not exhaustive. That example, however, illustrates how our proposed policy is consistent with these statutory aggregation directives. With respect to extended release formulations, these directives reflect the understanding that such formulations are new formulations of the same underlying drug, albeit ones that are delivered through a modified release mechanism. Here too, fixed combination drugs in which an additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component enables an alternative route of administration for its co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) is likewise best understood as part of the same underlying drug as the product with only the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), albeit with an alternative route of administration enabled by the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component. Just as CMS may aggregate extended release formulations under our statutory directives—even though FDA may approve or license those formulations under a separate NDA or BLA from the original formulation—CMS may also consider a fixed combination drug as part of the same qualifying single source drug as the product with the co-administered active moiety(s), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), even if FDA approves or licenses the fixed combination drug under a separate NDA or BLA. Finally, including a fixed combination drug described in proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) with the original product in the same potential qualifying single source drug, pursuant to sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act, is consistent with commonly held and plain language understandings of what constitutes the same underlying drug, as evidenced, at least in part, by how the pharmaceutical and financial industries generally view these products. For example, manufacturers commonly market products that meet the criteria of the proposed policy, including formulations of a drug with hyaluronidase, under the same branding as the original, non-hyaluronidase formulation. Similarly, filings (for example, filings with the SEC) pertaining to the marketing of the fixed combination drug and the original formulation commonly refer to and calculate the products' sales and contributions to revenue in the collective. Accordingly, we believe the proposed policy reflects the best understanding of the statutory aggregation directives. Similarly, we disagree with the commenters analogizing to the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program and Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program line extension provisions to argue that the policy is not authorized under the statute. For the same reasons previously discussed, we believe the proposed policy accords with the best reading of the statutory aggregation provisions, and the lack of even more granular statutory language singling out these types of drugs does not undermine that conclusion.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that the proposed modification for fixed combination drugs would violate the holding of
Loper Bright
because, in their view, CMS does not apply the single, best meaning of statute. These commenters stated that CMS is interpreting statute differently beginning in initial price applicability year 2029 than it did in prior initial price applicability years, as well as interpreting the same statutory text differently depending on the category of drug or biological product. A few commenters asserted that the proposed modification is arbitrary and capricious because it singles out products with an additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration without providing sufficient statutory, scientific, and regulatory basis for doing so. A few commenters asserted that CMS does not adequately explain its rationale for aggregating products that contain an additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration, while continuing to treat as separate products that add a new active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that does not create a new formulation and enable an alternative route of administration. One of these commenters stated that CMS did not identify evidence demonstrating that products that contain an additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration present a greater program integrity risk than other fixed combination drug products that would be aggregated as a unique qualifying single source drug under the general policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4).
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' perspectives. However, we disagree that the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would not apply the best meaning of the statute or that it applies an inconsistent interpretation of the statute. Our proposal reflects our consistent interpretation of the statutory provisions requiring aggregation across dosage forms and strengths, inclusive of new formulations. Generally, and as relevant here, we have applied these statutory directives by identifying qualifying single source drugs as all dosage forms and strengths, including new formulations, with shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s). Our proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) continues to identify qualifying single source drugs on the basis of shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), consistent with this interpretation of the statutory aggregation directives. Proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) marks a specific application of this interpretation to products with multiple active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components as compared to prior policy. While prior policy always treated each unique combination of
(
printed page 72218)
active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components as distinct potential qualifying single source drugs, proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) reflects our determination that for a narrow, limited set of products—that for which the addition of a distinct active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component enables an alternative route of administration, as compared to a product without such additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component but with otherwise shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s)—the new product would most appropriately be understood as a new formulation of the original product under section 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. For the reasons discussed in our proposed rule and in this final rule, including in the previous comment response, we believe our interpretation of this statute, and the application thereof represented by this proposed policy, reflects the best reading of the relevant statutory provisions. We disagree with the contention that we interpret the same statutory text differently depending on the category of drug or biological product; rather, the general fixed combination drug policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4) and the proposed policy for new formulations at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) apply the same interpretation of sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act to different categories of fixed combination drugs, only one of which fits the statutory description of a new formulation of the same drug. We also note that the proposed policy applies equally to all fixed combination drugs that meet the criteria set forth at proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), and likewise, the general fixed combination drug policy applies equally to all fixed combination drugs that do not meet these criteria.
We disagree with commenters who argued that proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i) demonstrates that CMS is interpreting statute differently beginning in initial price applicability year 2029 than it did in prior initial price applicability years. As previously explained, proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i) is consistent with our longstanding interpretation of the statutory aggregation directives. Rather, our proposed application of this interpretation with respect to products meeting the criteria at proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i) is reflective of concerns that our prior policy, if applied to these products, could produce results that are inconsistent with our interpretation and create program integrity risks. We have long heard concerns from interested parties that, under the general fixed combination drug policy, certain fixed combination drugs could pose program integrity risks to the Negotiation Program. In comments on the initial guidance for initial price applicability year 2026
[
38
]
and draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and MFP effectuation for 2026 and 2027,
[
39
]
interested parties raised concerns that the general fixed combination drug policy creates program integrity risks in which CMS would treat an original formulation and a fixed combination drug that is a new formulation as separate qualifying single source drugs, which could result in certain drugs not being selected, being selected later than statutorily required, or avoiding application of the MFP if utilization shifts to the fixed combination drug product that is a new formulation of the original formulation. Those guidance documents established policy for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027 in which we selected drugs based on total expenditures under Part D. Because the fixed combination drug program integrity risks primarily relate to biological products that are more likely payable under Part B, we did not believe it necessary for the implementation of the statute to establish a policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations at that time. In accordance with section 1192(a) of the Act, CMS was required to select drugs based on total expenditures under Part B and Part D beginning in initial price applicability year 2028. Therefore, when establishing policy for initial price applicability year 2028, we took the opportunity to solicit comments on our treatment of fixed combination drugs since initial price applicability year 2028 was the first initial price applicability year in which we identified and selected drugs based on total expenditures under Part B. Given the complexity of the issue, we deemed it prudent to take more time to evaluate policy options and stated our intent to address this program integrity risk in rulemaking beginning in initial price applicability year 2029. As we noted in the proposed rule (
91 FR 36259
), the program integrity concerns raised by fixed combination drugs that are new formulations have not yet impacted drug selection but may soon as more drugs with significant total expenditures under Part B become qualifying single source drugs and negotiation-eligible drugs. We therefore believe it necessary at this point to address the program integrity risk posed by certain fixed combination drugs in this rule. The proposed policy thus does not represent an inconsistent interpretation of statute across initial price applicability years but rather an updated policy applying the statute's aggregation requirements in response to the identification of a specific program integrity risk, input from interested parties, and the aggregation issues raised, largely, by the incorporation of total expenditures under Part B into the drug selection process beginning in initial price applicability year 2028.
Finally, commenters asserted that CMS did not adequately explain its rationale for aggregating fixed combination drugs that include an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration in accordance with proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i). We disagree and refer readers to the robust discussion in the proposed rule (
91 FR 36258
through
36259
) of our program integrity concerns related to certain fixed combination drugs, which the proposal at §  429.125(b)(4)(i) specifically and narrowly targets. We also refer readers to our response to comments earlier in this section explaining why fixed combination drugs described in proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i) are reasonably understood as new formulations comparable to extended-release formulations. Finally, we refer readers to comments summarized earlier in this section, which agreed that the inclusion of a component that enables a different route of administration, including the addition of hyaluronidase to enable subcutaneous administration, largely represents a repackaging of the existing product and should not be considered as a separate qualifying single source drug under the Negotiation Program.
Comment:
Some commenters disagreed with CMS' statement in the proposed rule that the criteria proposed at §  429.125(b)(4)(i) can be operationalized in a consistent and objective manner using public sources. A few commenters asserted that the public sources cited by CMS in the proposed rule—such as RxNorm, OpenFDA, FDALabel, DailyMed, and FDA's Active Ingredient-Active Moiety Relationship/Basis of Strength file—do not address how CMS will determine whether an added ingredient creates a new formulation or enables an alternative route of administration. Some commenters stated that CMS does
(
printed page 72219)
not have the expertise to determine whether an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component creates a new formulation or enables an alternative route of administration, and that such expertise sits at FDA instead. A couple of commenters stated that CMS effectively acknowledges that it lacks a framework for determining whether an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration via its solicitation for comments on approaches to inform CMS' identification of such components. A commenter supported CMS' proposed approach to operationalizing proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i), stating that the approach is a practical and administrable way to address program integrity risks.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback. We agree with the commenter that stated that our approach to operationalizing proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is practicable and administrable, and we disagree with commenters' concerns about the potential for inconsistent operationalization of proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i). As we stated in the proposed rule (
91 FR 36259
), our proposal incorporated feedback from previous commenters that raised concerns about how we would operationalize terms used in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028, such as “biologically active against the disease state,” which we used to articulate the nature of the issue underlying our concern. In the proposed rule, we proposed to identify fixed combination drugs that qualify for the policy identified at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) using criteria that are available in public sources. To provide additional transparency, we take this opportunity to provide further information about how CMS will use these public sources in a consistent and objective manner.
We will identify the active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components in a fixed combination drug consistent with how we identify active moieties, active ingredients, and antigen components generally under § 429.125(b) for purposes of identifying potential qualifying single source drugs. Specifically, and as described in section II.B.6.a. of the proposed rule, we will use public sources such as, but not limited to, RxNorm, OpenFDA, FDALabel, DailyMed, and FDA's Active Ingredient-Active Moiety Relationship/Basis of Strength file to identify the active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), and antigen component(s) of drugs, biological products, and vaccines for infectious disease(s), as applicable. We will identify any fixed combination drug that shares one or more active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component with another drug, biological product, or vaccine for infectious disease(s), as applicable, with the same NDA/BLA holder. Consistent with section II.B.6.a.1. of the proposed rule, we will use public sources such as, but not limited to, Orange Book, Purple Book, Drugs@FDA, and DailyMed to identify the route(s) of administration for the fixed combination drug and the drug or biological product with the same NDA/BLA holder that shares one or more active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) with such fixed combination drug. To provide further information on additional public sources we may use, as requested by commenters, we affirm in this final rule that we may also use public sources including, but not limited to, FDA SPL resources such as FDALabel to identify the route(s) of administration.
Then we will identify active ingredients, active moieties, and antigen components, as applicable, that, when co-administered with one or more other active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), enable an alternative route of administration for such co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s). Our determination that a fixed combination drug contains a CMS-identified route-enabling active ingredient, active moiety, or antigen component that meets the criteria proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is a product-specific evaluation, which may include consideration of whether the original product and the fixed combination drug have different routes of administration and whether the information or descriptions within product labeling for such product indicate that the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component enables the alternative route of administration. We may also consult with FDA, as appropriate, about the information contained in these public sources. We will consider this information holistically to determine whether the fixed combination drug is best understood under sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act and proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) as a new formulation of the drug or biological product with the same NDA/BLA holder that shares one or more active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) with such fixed combination drug, and therefore should be aggregated into the same qualifying single source drug as the drug or biological product with the same NDA/BLA holder that shares one or more active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) with the fixed combination drug. We believe this determination falls squarely within CMS' expertise and aligns with the directives at sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act.
Comment:
Some commenters opposed finalizing the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations but made the following recommendations about how CMS should operationalize the policy were it to be finalized. A few commenters recommended that the determination as to whether a fixed combination drug qualifies for the proposed policy should be made in consultation with FDA, the patient community, and using product-specific evidence that the additional component exists solely to enable a different route of administration. A commenter recommended that any such input from the public should be narrow and time-limited so that it does not delay the drug selection process or convert CMS' identification of qualifying single source drugs into a broader adjudicatory proceeding. A commenter asked that the burden of demonstrating that a product is not subject to proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) should sit with CMS and manufacturers, not with patients. A couple of commenters urged CMS to apply the proposed policy prospectively only to products approved or licensed after the effective date of the final rule. A few commenters stated that CMS should give affected manufacturers, patients, caregivers, and clinicians advance notice that CMS intends to apply proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) to a product and create an appeals process. A commenter asked CMS to clarify how aggregation under proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would operate if the two products carry different FDA-approved indications, and how CMS would treat a product under the proposed policy if the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component is separately licensed and marketed. A commenter recommended that when CMS determines that a product qualifies for the proposed policy, CMS should publish the relevant NDA or BLA, NDC and HCPCS mapping, shared and added components, route of administration, and FDA sources supporting its conclusion.
Response:
We appreciate the suggestions. We refer readers to our
(
printed page 72220)
immediate previous response and to the discussion in section II.B.6.a.1. of this final rule for details on how CMS intends to operationalize proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i). There, we detail the public sources and processes we will use to implement the proposed policy. We affirm that we will use product-specific information to implement the proposed policy and may consult with FDA about information contained in the public sources described previously. We also take this opportunity to clarify for these commenters that nothing in the text of proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) suggests that the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component must exist
solely
to enable an alternative route of administration; rather, the regulatory text states that the additional component “creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s)”.
We affirm that CMS' implementation of the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) will not modify the timing of the drug selection process nor require interested parties to demonstrate that a product does or does not qualify for the proposed policy. While we appreciate the suggestions, we decline to create an advance notice or appeals process or to consult interested parties such as patients. Section 1192(e) of the Act sets forth the requirements for the identification of qualifying single source drugs and does not require nor contemplate engagement with patients or with manufacturers via an advance notice or appeals process. Additionally, an advance notice or appeals process and patient consultation is operationally infeasible due to the time constraints required to meet statutory deadlines and the complexity of the preparation that must be undertaken in advance of the publication of the selected drug list by the selected drug publication date. We also decline to apply the proposed policy prospectively only to products approved or licensed after the effective date of the final rule due to the program integrity risks that currently marketed fixed combination drugs that are new formulations pose to the Negotiation Program. Further, prospective-only application of the proposed policy would be inconsistent with the statutory directives at sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. In response to the commenter's requested clarifications, we affirm that FDA-approved indications are not considered for purposes of aggregation in the drug selection process, and we reiterate that a qualifying single source drug can include dosage forms and strengths and formulations approved or licensed under different NDA/BLAs. In response to the commenter's suggestion that we publish certain information for products that qualify for the proposed policy, we refer readers to our discussion in section II.B.1. of this final rule and § 429.100, which affirms that, for a selected drug identified under proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), we will publish the shared active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s) identified under proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), plus any additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component included in new formulations of such selected drug. Additionally, for all selected drugs, including those identified under proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), we will publish the NDC-11s CMS identifies in accordance with § 429.100(c)(1) and the corresponding NDC-9s and HCPCS codes (as applicable). We decline to publish the routes of administration and NDA(s)/BLA(s) because this information is publicly available. We also decline to publish FDA sources supporting our conclusion that a fixed combination drug is a new formulation because we believe this final rule provides sufficient detail on our operationalization process, including public sources that we may consult.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed views on whether proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) appropriately targets drug and biological products that pose true program integrity risks to the Negotiation Program. A few commenters supported the proposed policy but stated that CMS should modify the proposal to broaden the scope of products that the provision would target, or at minimum retain flexibility to broaden the proposal in the future based on new fact patterns. These commenters expressed concern that, under the language at proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), manufacturers could still avoid or delay selection and application of the MFP by adding an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component to an existing qualifying single source drug to create a new formulation that is not different from the original product in a clinically meaningful way but does not meet the proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) criteria because: (1) the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component leaves the route of administration unchanged for the new formulation; or (2) the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component is not the sole enabler of the alternative route of administration (for example, because the change in route of administration may also depend on factors such as excipients, device design, or stabilizers). To address the first scenario, a couple of commenters recommended that CMS evaluate whether a fixed combination drug is a new formulation using the clinically meaningful difference standard that CMS used to articulate its program integrity concerns related to fixed combination drugs in the draft guidance for initial price applicability year 2028 and manufacturer effectuation of the MFP in 2026, 2027, and 2028. To address the second scenario, a commenter recommended that CMS modify the text of proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) to require that the relevant active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component “creates a new formulation and
helps to
enable an alternative route of administration . . .”, and another commenter recommended that CMS define “enables” to mean that the added component materially enables or materially facilitates the alternative route of administration for the shared component. In contrast, some commenters expressed concern that the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would impact more products than would be appropriate but did not provide specific examples. Similar to the prior commenters, these commenters recommended that CMS consider whether the added active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component creates a clinically meaningful different product from the original product, but in contrast to the prior commenters' view, they believed that fewer drugs would qualify for the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) if CMS were to employ a clinically meaningful difference standard.
Response:
We appreciate the support and suggestions. We acknowledge the concern that manufacturers could still avoid or delay selection, or if selected, avoid application of the MFP, by including an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component in an existing qualifying single source drug that may be considered to result in a new formulation but does not meet the criteria proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i). With respect to the first scenario, in which a manufacturer includes an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component in an existing qualifying single source drug to create a new formulation that leaves the route of administration unchanged, we acknowledge that the proposed policy would not reach such a product. As we explained previously and in the
(
printed page 72221)
proposed rule (
91 FR 36259
), the proposed policy addresses the specific program integrity concern of which we are currently aware. We acknowledge commenters' concern that broader criteria—such as language in the Negotiation Program Guidance citing active moieties/active ingredients not biologically active against the disease state(s) for which the drug is indicated—could more comprehensively address program integrity risks across a wider range of product modification strategies. As noted in the proposed rule (
91 FR 36260
), we considered this approach. Commenters did not provide examples of fixed combination drugs that would not qualify for proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) but, they believe, should qualify. We continue to believe proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is appropriately tailored to the program integrity risks with the general fixed combination drug policy and the specific elements of the policy that are in tension with section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act, which directs CMS to aggregate across dosage forms and strengths, including new formulations of the drug, and section 1196(a)(2) of the Act, which directs CMS to apply the MFP across different strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulations or package size or package type of such drug. We will continue to monitor the Negotiation Program for evidence of program integrity risks that are in tension with sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act and which pose program integrity risks beyond those addressed by proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), and we may consider additional modifications to our fixed combination drug policy in the future.
With respect to the second scenario, in which the change in route of administration depends not only on the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component but also on other product features such as excipients, device design, injection volume, concentration, or stabilizers, we take this opportunity to clarify that the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component need not be the sole enabler of the alternative route of administration in order for a product to qualify for proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i). A product may qualify for the proposed policy if the added component creates a new formulation and enables the alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component, even if other product features also contribute to making the alternative route possible. We believe this reading is consistent with proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and addresses the concern raised by these commenters. Requiring the additional component to be the sole enabler of the alternative route of administration would be inconsistent with the purpose of the proposed policy and could allow manufacturers to avoid aggregation by arguing that the alternative route of administration also depended on other product features. We believe the existing regulatory text, as clarified herein, is sufficiently clear, and we do not believe a modification to the regulatory text or definition of “enables” is necessary at this time.
In response to the commenters who expressed concern that the scope of products that would be impacted by the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is too broad, we respectfully disagree. We note that commenters generally understood the scope of the products affected by proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) to be fixed combination drug products that contain hyaluronidase, or a hyaluronidase variant, which aligns with our general expectation of the scope of this policy and the example provided in section VI.C.1. of the Negotiation Program proposed rule. As we previously stated, proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) narrowly addresses the program integrity risks with the general fixed combination drug policy and responds to previously received input summarized in the revised guidance for initial price applicability year 2026, final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, and the Negotiation Program Guidance in which interested parties raised concerns about such program integrity risks.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) because, in their view, it conflicts with FDA's regulatory framework. Many commenters explained that FDA evaluates fixed combination drugs as distinct medicines and requires separate applications, clinical trials, and demonstrations of safety and effectiveness, and therefore, CMS should not disregard FDA's determination that a fixed combination drug constitutes a separate drug. A few commenters raised concerns that overriding FDA's determinations would introduce substantial uncertainty and send conflicting messages to interested parties by subjecting products to different standards within different parts of the federal government. Some commenters appeared to interpret the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) to mean that CMS would be determining the clinical efficacy of an additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component and stated that it would be incorrect for CMS to assume that the additional component added to enable an alternative route of administration lacks meaningful clinical activity or value, and moreover, that the scientific expertise to make such a determination lies with FDA, not CMS. A commenter pointed to CMS' decisions in the calendar year (CY) 2021 Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) final rule and CY 2022 PFS final rule to not finalize proposals involving clinical evaluation of drugs approved under section 505(b)(2) of the FD&C Act as evidence that CMS has conceded that it does not have the scientific expertise to make such determinations. Some commenters asserted that CMS' continued reliance on
21 CFR 300.50
undermines the logic of the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i), explaining that, in their view, CMS incorporates FDA's definition of a fixed combination drug at
21 CFR 300.50
but disregards FDA's judgements embedded within that definition regarding an active ingredient's contribution to the product's overall safety and effectiveness.
Response:
We appreciate the input but disagree with the commenters' suggestion that CMS' treatment of fixed combination drugs when identifying qualifying single source drugs for purposes of the Negotiation Program must, in every instance, align with how FDA treats fixed combination drugs for purposes of
21 CFR 300.50
. The proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) does not disregard, diminish, or otherwise impact FDA's judgments embedded within
21 CFR 300.50
regarding an active moiety's, active ingredient's, or antigen component's contribution to a fixed combination drug's safety and efficacy: nothing in the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) suggests that an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component may not contribute to the safety and efficacy of a fixed combination drug in accordance with FDA's determination at
21 CFR 300.50
. As we noted previously, the proposed policy is solely for the purpose of the Negotiation Program and identifies a specific, narrow category of fixed combination drugs—those in which the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component enables an alternative route of administration and creates a new formulation for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s)—that are appropriately understood as new formulations of the same drug under
(
printed page 72222)
sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act.
To the commenters who appeared to interpret proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) to mean that CMS would be determining the clinical efficacy of the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component included in a fixed combination drug, we reiterate that a fixed combination drug would meet the criteria in proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) if such additional component enables an alternative route of administration and creates a new formulation for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s). That is, the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) does not include an evaluation of the clinical efficacy of such additional component. For this same reason, we disagree with the suggestion that our proposal to define a fixed combination drug as having the meaning set forth in
21 CFR 300.50
undermines the logic of the proposed policy. The proposed policy does not contradict
21 CFR 300.50
but rather narrowly modifies how we will treat certain fixed combination drugs for purposes of achieving the Negotiation Program's statutory requirements. Similarly, we disagree with the commenter's suggestion that CMS' decisions with respect to payment policies for drugs approved under section 505(b)(2) of the FD&C Act undermine the proposed policy. The discussion in the PFS rulemakings to which the commenter referred addressed distinct statutory schemes and did not relate to the type of determinations we proposed here.
Comment:
A commenter raised concerns that combining distinct formulations, such as a new formulation that is a fixed combination drug and an original formulation, under the same qualifying single source drug could increase the MFP. This commenter recommended that CMS ensure the MFP reflects the value of each product individually and should avoid an approach under which the added value of a new formulation increases the MFP for the original formulation.
Response:
Sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act direct CMS to identify a qualifying single source drug, and to negotiate a single MFP for that drug, inclusive of its dosage forms, strengths, and formulations. The proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) gives full effect to these statutory directives. We decline to adopt this suggestion as it would be in conflict with the directive at section 1196(a)(2) of the Act to establish procedures to compute and apply the MFP across different strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of such drug. We direct readers to our discussion of the application of the MFP across dosage forms and strengths in section II.H.1. of this final rule and at § 429.700.
Comment:
