A commenter raised objections to CMS' implementation of policies related to the identification and selection of fixed combination drugs in prior initial price applicability years. A commenter stated that that largest untapped savings for American patients do not lie in redefining what counts as a drug but rather in pharmaceutical benefit manager reform.
Response:
These comments are out of scope for this final rule.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that fixed combination drugs that are subcutaneous formulations of injectable drugs offer meaningful clinical value, including reduced infusion times, improved adherence, better tolerability, reduced caregiver burden, patient preference for subcutaneous administration, and the benefits and convenience of administering drugs at home or in more accessible practice sites. These commenters stated that CMS' proposal would discount those benefits. Many commenters highlighted that subcutaneous formulations offer benefits to and improve health equity access for underserved patient populations or patients that reside in rural geographic areas where barriers to health care resources may exist, noting that CMS' proposal could result in these patients losing access to beneficial treatment options. A few commenters noted the benefits of subcutaneous formulations, specifically the use of long-acting injectables, for patients with mental health conditions and the providers that serve those communities. Many commenters noted the clinical distinctiveness of subcutaneous products as compared to products that are administered via infusion, stating that a shared active ingredient alone is an incomplete measure of clinical equivalence, noting the differences in bioavailability, safety profiles, differences in tolerability, and dosing and monitoring requirements among products that share an active ingredient. Some commenters recommended that CMS preserve separate qualifying single source drug treatment for products that provide genuine improvements in safety, effectiveness, tolerability, adherence, or delivery, and develop transparent and objective criteria to distinguish genuine clinical innovation from efforts primarily to avoid negotiation eligibility. Some commenters stated that patient choice and individualized care are afforded by the existence of multiple formulations, which allow patients and providers to select the option best suited to individual circumstances, mobility, comorbidities, and access constraints. These commenters recommended that CMS incorporate long-term patient access into its final policy rather than applying an aggregation standard that sacrifices future treatment options for short-term expenditure reductions.
Response:
We thank commenters for their input on the clinical value of fixed combination drugs that are subcutaneous formulations of injectable drugs and the benefits those formulations may offer to patients. We acknowledge the concerns commenters raised about the clinical value of subcutaneous formulations and the potential consequences of this policy for patients. Our determination that a fixed combination drug meeting the criteria at proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is not a distinct qualifying single source drug rests on the statutory aggregation requirements at sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act, not on an assessment of the clinical characteristics of any particular route of administration. The Negotiation Program is designed to address high-expenditure, single source drugs that lack generic or biosimilar competition. If we were to apply the general fixed combination drug policy to a fixed combination drug that includes an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), and such fixed combination drug has the same NDA/BLA holder as another drug or biological product containing those same co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), the fixed combination drug would be treated as a distinct qualifying single source drug, resetting the negotiation eligibility clock of that formulation. That outcome would create a significant program integrity risk inconsistent with the statutory purpose of the IRA. The proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) addresses a discrete and well-defined category of products. It reaches only those products whose distinction from the original drug is an added active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables a different route of administration. It does not apply to other types of fixed combination drugs that contain active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen
(
printed page 72223)
components that do not meet such criteria and which continue to retain their status as distinct qualifying single source drugs, where applicable, under proposed § 429.125(b)(4). Regarding commenters' concerns about clinical distinctiveness, we note that clinical differences across formulations do not on their own provide a basis for separate qualifying single source drug treatment under the statute. As discussed earlier, sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act direct CMS to aggregate across dosage forms, strengths, and new formulations of a drug. These aggregation requirements operate notwithstanding the clinical differences that may exist between different dosage forms and strengths and formulations. For example, an extended release formulation may offer real benefits over an immediate-release formulation in dosing frequency and adherence, yet the statute directs CMS to consider it within the scope of the same drug. The same logic applies to the exception proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i). Differences in bioavailability, tolerability, or patient population between a subcutaneous and an intravenous formulation do not, by themselves, take a product outside the statute's aggregation directives. This does not mean we discount those differences. Rather, it means they are weighed at a different point in the statutory framework. Section 1194(e)(2) of the Act and § 429.505(d)(3)(iii) ensures we consider comparative clinical effectiveness to therapeutic alternatives outside the selected drug, not between formulations aggregated within the same selected drug, in the course of the negotiation process rather than in selecting drugs under section 1192 of the Act. The clinical value a subcutaneous formulation offers remains part of that selected drug's overall profile; however, it is accounted for when we assess the drug's benefits relative to competing therapeutic alternatives under section 1194(e)(2) of the Act and through other categories of information we consider under section 1194(e)(1) of the Act.
We also disagree that proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) sacrifices future treatment options in favor of short-term expenditure reductions. The policy does not restrict the development, approval, or marketing of new formulations, including subcutaneous formulations; it determines only whether such a formulation is aggregated with other products under the same qualifying single source drug or as a separate one for purposes of the Negotiation Program. We further note that patients and providers retain the ability to choose among available formulations of a qualifying single source drug or selected drug, as applicable, consistent with individual clinical circumstances, as discussed previously, regardless of whether those formulations are aggregated under the same qualifying single source drug or selected drug, as applicable.
Regarding commenters' concerns about health equity and access for rural and underserved patients, we share the goal of ensuring that Medicare beneficiaries have access to clinically appropriate treatment options. Consistent with section 1196(a)(2) of the Act and as discussed in II.H.1. of this final rule and at § 429.700, the MFP applies to the qualifying single source drug as a whole, including all dosage forms and strengths. We do not anticipate that this policy will steer patients away from subcutaneous formulations. The policy is intended to ensure that the Negotiation Program can reach high-expenditure drugs regardless of whether a manufacturer has introduced a new formulation with an alternative route of administration. The policy affects only the identification of qualifying single source drugs for purposes of the Negotiation Program. It does not alter FDA approval or licensure status, formulary requirements, or prescribing authority. We also considered but decline to adopt commenters' recommendation that we preserve separate qualifying single source drug treatment for products that provide genuine improvements in safety, effectiveness, tolerability, adherence, or delivery. The policy described at proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) covers a limited scope of fixed combination drugs where the additional active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component serves to create a new formulation and enable an alternative route of administration.
Comment:
Many commenters stated the proposed fixed combination drug policy would disincentivize future investments in post-approval innovations of drug products due to the potential for reduced expected returns on separately patented, independently developed products, and as a result would chill long term research and development planning, with some of these commenters recommending that CMS establish a more transparent and predictable regulatory framework to allow manufacturers to develop future investment roadmaps. Many commenters noted the technical and regulatory complexity of developing subcutaneous formulations of drugs, including the requirements to establish separate clinical programs, pharmacokinetic evaluations, manufacturing practices and full FDA review of new to market formulations and stated that CMS' proposal discounts those investments and the resulting patient benefits. Many commenters stated that this proposal would have chilling effects beyond subcutaneous product development and could result in discouraged development in areas such as pediatric formulations, rare disease therapies, inhaled anti-infectives and other delivery and adherence improvements to formulations of drug products, and they stated that legitimate innovation in those areas would be penalized. A few commenters stated that the proposal would negatively impact the U.S. intellectual property and innovation ecosystem by stripping economic value and practical benefits from separately patented delivery improvements. Some commenters questioned whether CMS' approach to fixed combination drugs is clear enough to offset the potential chilling effect on pharmaceutical investment and believed manufacturers would need a more predictable regulatory and investment framework to develop future roadmaps. Some commenters stated that the proposal does not appropriately distinguish between evasive product development and true innovative product development and recommended that CMS develop objective, transparent criteria to make that distinction rather than applying a blanket aggregation standard. A commenter stated that the proposal would discourage the development and availability of both intravenous and subcutaneous formulations, leaving patients with fewer treatment choices. A commenter suggested that the sequential development of intravenous products first and subcutaneous products to follow is rational and beneficial to patients, and CMS' proposal would penalize this development pathway without distinguishing it from evasive reformulation strategies. A commenter stated the proposal risks eroding U.S. biopharmaceutical leadership, shifting research and development investment away from the United States. Some commenters stated that the economic impacts of the proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) would reduce the time to recover distinct research and development costs including the post-development costs for a subcutaneous product's development, such as clinical trials, manufacturing, and FDA review, because newer therapies would inherit the older product's negotiation timeline and could be subject to price negotiation
(
printed page 72224)
as soon as they enter the market. Some commenters noted that developing subcutaneous formulations requires significant post-approval investment, including in separate clinical programs, pharmacokinetic evaluations, manufacturing, and FDA evaluation, and stated that the proposal would indirectly penalize that investment and signal to the industry that patient-centered improvements to existing drugs will not be appropriately valued. Many commenters noted that the policy would disproportionately harm small biotechnology companies, start-ups, and delivery-technology platform companies whose business models depend on innovations related to combination therapy innovation and that the proposal could foreclose continued development of those patient-centric innovations. Some commenters stated that the uncertainty created by the proposal could have a chilling effect on long-term planning because manufacturers cannot rationally commit resources to develop a product that may collapse into an earlier product's negotiation framework and recommended that CMS distinguish genuine delivery innovation from evasive reformulation and establish a more transparent and predictable framework for manufacturers to assess their investment decisions in advance.
Response:
We thank commenters for their input and have carefully considered these comments in developing this final rule. The scope of the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is limited to fixed combination drugs that differ from the original drug due to the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), such as the addition of hyaluronidase to enable subcutaneous administration of an existing intravenous product. It does not apply to other types of fixed combination drugs that contain active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components that do not meet such criteria. Notably, commenters did not identify specific examples of fixed combination drugs that would qualify for proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), but should not, supporting CMS' analyses that the modification we proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is appropriately tailored to the program integrity risks it is designed to address. Its application is limited to fixed combination drugs that differ from the original drug due to the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s). It does not apply to other types of fixed combination drugs that contain active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components that do not meet such criteria, which remain eligible, where applicable, for separate qualifying single source drug treatment under proposed § 429.125(b)(4). Regarding the question of the potential chilling effects beyond subcutaneous product development, we note that the policy applies only to the narrow category of fixed combination drugs described under proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i). Regarding commenters' concerns about the impact of the policy on the U.S. intellectual property and innovation ecosystem, we note that the policy intends to effectuate the statutory requirements of the Negotiation Program, which is designed to address high-expenditure, single source drugs that lack generic or biosimilar competition. The statute establishes a predictable framework under which certain drugs become eligible for selection based on total expenditure under Part B and Part D and the length of time they have been on the market without facing generic or biosimilar competition. Treating a new formulation as a distinct qualifying single source drug with a new negotiation eligibility clock would be in tension with sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act.
We also note that some commenters' projections of reduced innovation are highly dependent on assumptions regarding manufacturer, investor, and market responses whose magnitude and direction are inherently uncertain. These same uncertainties apply to commenters' predictions regarding the specific effect of proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) on the development of subcutaneous and other alternative formulations. Researchers have found no association between drug prices and R&D investment levels, noting that treatment costs reflect what the market will bear rather than the cost of R&D.
[
40
]
Recent empirical evidence further demonstrates that R&D spending, biotech equity investment, and business development activity all increased in the 6 quarters following IRA enactment compared to the 6 quarters prior, suggesting the biopharmaceutical industry has remained robust and continued investing in innovation despite the IRA's prospective effect on future drug prices.
[
41
]
This evidence undercuts the premise that the proposed policy will meaningfully depress investment in drug innovation, specifically given that the industry has continued to invest robustly even as broader IRA drug pricing provisions have been implemented. Commenters' analyses of potential impacts on innovation may not fully account for the range of ways in which manufacturers may adapt to changing market conditions, including by continuing to pursue alternative route of administration innovation for reasons independent of Negotiation Program timing, such as competitive differentiation, patient demand, and anticipated generic or biosimilar entry. Regarding the commenter who stated that the sequential development of intravenous products first and subcutaneous products to follow is rational and beneficial to patients, as discussed previously, projections of the policy's impact on manufacturers' investment and formulation sequencing decisions are inherently uncertain, and the proposed policy will be only one of many factors manufacturers consider in such decisions. We further reiterate that the proposed policy would apply only where the fixed combination drug differs from the original drug because of the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s).
Regarding commenters' concerns about the disproportionate impact of the policy on small biotechnology companies, start-ups, and delivery-technology platform companies, consistent with proposed § 429.440, we note that the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36281-36285
) and this final rule include a Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030. That provision establishes a temporary floor for the MFP for eligible small biotech drugs, providing additional protection for qualifying smaller manufacturers. On the question of investment uncertainty and the recommendation that we distinguish
(
printed page 72225)
genuine delivery innovation from evasive reformulation and establish a more transparent and predictable framework, the proposed policy at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) itself provides clear and defined criteria for qualifying single source drug aggregation purposes.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that CMS' program integrity concerns are speculative and that CMS provided no evidence that manufacturers are developing fixed combination drug products to avoid the Negotiation Program. These commenters stated that CMS did not have a sufficient basis or justification to deviate from the established interpretation that all fixed combination drugs are distinct qualifying single source drugs and recommended that CMS retain the established interpretation. Some commenters noted that hyaluronidase-based subcutaneous formulations have been on market since before the IRA was enacted and that CMS' suggestion that these new formulations are being developed to avoid selection in the Negotiation Program or application of the MFP is not supported by evidence. A few commenters noted real-world product development examples to illustrate that products were not developed to circumvent the Negotiation Program, highlighting the clinical validation, years of formulation work, and significant investment required for subcutaneous product development, stating that CMS' proposal would sweep in products developed years before the IRA and that represent legitimate innovation. A commenter noted that if CMS believes program integrity concerns exist, the appropriate remedy is to bring that concern to Congress rather than altering how CMS identifies qualifying single source drugs.
Response:
We thank commenters for their input. We disagree that our program integrity concerns are speculative. The use of reformulation strategies to extend market exclusivity and delay competition is well documented in peer-reviewed literature
[
42
]
and reflects broader industry dynamics that are not unique to any single manufacturer.
[
43
]
Further, we stated in the Negotiation Program Guidance that we intended to address this specific program integrity risk associated with fixed combination drugs that are new formulations in rulemaking. We also disagree that the pre-IRA market history of hyaluronidase-based subcutaneous formulations undermines the program integrity rationale for this policy. The program integrity risk identified by CMS does not depend on when a particular formulation was developed or approved, or on any manufacturer's intent in developing it. A program integrity risk can arise where a generally applicable policy does not fully capture the nuances of specific situations, not only from intentional fraud, abuse, or bad conduct. Absent the proposal at § 429.125(b)(4)(i), a product that CMS has determined constitutes a new formulation of an existing drug under sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act would not be aggregated with that existing drug for purposes of identifying a qualifying single source drug and applying the MFP. As discussed in the proposed rule (
91 FR 36260
), the program integrity concerns raised by fixed combination drugs that are new formulations have not yet impacted drug selection but may soon as more drugs with significant total expenditures under Part B become qualifying single source drugs and negotiation-eligible drugs. CMS is addressing that vulnerability through the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations to ensure that these formulations are properly aggregated and selected consistent with the statute so that the Negotiation Program achieves its intended statutory aims. Regarding the commenter who stated that the appropriate remedy for program integrity concerns is Congressional action, we disagree that Congressional action is the sole recourse to address our program integrity concerns. The policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is based on and consistent with the statutory directives at sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. It does not alter CMS' general framework for identifying qualifying single source drugs but rather is applicable only to a discrete type of product that CMS has determined constitutes a new formulation under the statute's aggregation provisions and that would otherwise be treated as a separate qualifying single source drug under the general fixed combination drug policy.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that CMS should evaluate the total cost of treatment associated with a therapy, not acquisition price alone, noting that subcutaneous formulations can reduce facility administration expenses, staffing, monitoring, transportation costs, and caregiver burden. These commenters recommended that CMS assess total treatment costs, healthcare resource use, and long-term market effects before adopting classifications that discourage resource-saving improvements. A few commenters stated that by implementing proposed §  429.125(b)(4)(i), CMS would undermine its intended savings goals because the additional costs and burden associated with the administration of intravenous products—including facility fees, nursing time, and monitoring costs—would offset any acquisition price reduction achieved through negotiation. Some commenters suggested that the proposed policy would discourage more convenient treatment options and create more reliance on infusion centers and other resource-intensive care sites.
A few commenters believed that, if finalized, the proposal would set precedents affecting other Medicare reimbursement contexts, specifically the actions of Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) and coverage decisions related to intravenous and subcutaneous formulations. These commenters recommended that CMS codify in regulatory text that aggregation under § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is solely for purposes of the Negotiation Program and creates no presumption regarding clinical interchangeability, coverage, or preferred route of administration in any other Medicare policy context. A commenter raised concerns that a broader qualifying single source drug definition might cause Part D plans to place selected drugs on less favorable formulary tiers or impose utilization management restrictions and requested that CMS issue explicit guidance to Part D plans prohibiting utilization management restrictions on selected drugs solely on the basis of route of administration.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback. On the question of total treatment costs and the potential for the policy to undermine our savings goals, we note that the Negotiation Program selects drugs based on total expenditures under Part B and Part D, which represent a significant and direct cost to Medicare and its beneficiaries. We recognize that site-of-care costs, facility fees, nursing time, and monitoring costs are relevant considerations in the broader assessment of treatment value. Regarding commenters' concerns about infusion capacity and the potential for the policy to discourage more convenient treatment options and the potential to steer patients toward higher-cost infusion settings, the policy
(
printed page 72226)
proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) does not restrict the availability of subcutaneous or intravenous formulations. Prescribers and patients retain the ability to select from available formulations best suited to individual clinical circumstances, mobility, comorbidities and access constraints. Regarding commenters' concerns that the policy would set precedents affecting other Medicare reimbursement contexts, specifically the actions of MACs and coverage decisions related to intravenous and subcutaneous formulations, the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) reflects the Negotiation Program's statutory directives regarding aggregation and applies solely for purposes of the Negotiation Program. Regarding the commenter who recommended that we issue explicit guidance to Part D plans prohibiting utilization management restrictions on selected drugs solely on the basis of route of administration, consistent with our policies proposed at § 423.120(b)(2)(vii) and (viii), Part D plan sponsors are required to include each Part D drug that is a selected drug with an MFP in effect on their formularies, inclusive of the exception that permits Part D plan sponsors to remove such a selected drug if the removal would be permitted under the successor regulation at § 423.120(e)(2)(i), (f)(2), (3), and (4). We refer readers to section III.A. of the Negotiation Program proposed rule and this final rule for further discussion of CMS' use of its comprehensive formulary review process to assess any practices that may undermine beneficiary access to selected drugs and ensure that Part D plan sponsors comply with existing statutory and regulatory restrictions on formulary design.
Comment:
Some commenters recommended that CMS examine the full range of impacts of the proposed policy—including effects on patients, infusion providers, access, competitive market forces, Medicare spending, and future innovation—before finalizing any policy change. A few commenters stated that an exclusive focus on immediate negotiation expenditures would overlook treatments that were delayed, narrowed, or never developed and recommended that CMS evaluate the dynamic effects of delayed or never-pursued treatments and recognize that program performance should be measured through patient-centered outcomes and long-term innovation, not solely through immediate reductions in Medicare expenditures. A few commenters recommended that CMS monitor the impact of the proposed policy and commit to reconsidering the policy if evidence after implementation shows reduced development of meaningful improvements, fewer treatment choices, or disproportionate access effects. A commenter recommended that CMS address program integrity concerns through objective, individualized, and evidence-based review rather than categorical aggregation.
Response:
We thank commenters for their recommendations. We share commenters' interest in ensuring that the Negotiation Program operates effectively, efficiently, and in compliance with Federal law while serving the best interests of Medicare beneficiaries. The proposed policy was developed with the input of comments from patients, clinicians, healthcare providers, manufacturers, and other interested parties. The comments we received reflect the breadth and depth of that engagement. We have carefully considered all of that input in developing this final rule. We appreciate commenters' recommendation that we monitor the impacts of the policy and commit to reconsidering it if implementation evidence shows reduced development of meaningful improvements, fewer treatment choices, or disproportionate access effects. We will assess the real-world impacts as the policy described at proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is implemented, including program integrity risks, and we will remain engaged with patients, clinicians, and other affected communities as we consider future rulemaking. Regarding the commenter who recommended that we address program integrity concerns through objective, individualized, and evidence-based review, not categorical aggregation, the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is only applicable where a fixed combination drug differs from a drug or biological product with the same NDA/BLA holder due to the inclusion of an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s). For all other fixed combination drugs not subject to the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i), we reiterate that, where applicable, we continue to treat it as a distinct qualifying single source drug under the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4).
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that CMS engage patients, clinicians, healthcare providers, and innovators in further evaluating the clinical, economic, and patient-centered impacts of the proposed change before adopting a final policy, stating that the agency cannot adequately assess the real-world consequences of reshaping the pricing framework governing subcutaneous therapies without meaningful input from the communities most directly affected. A commenter stated that some of the most meaningful effects of a formulation change may not be captured by product labeling or administrative data and that patient and clinician input should be indispensable before finalizing the proposal. A commenter asked CMS to explore further with the wider patient community and subject matter experts the degree to which application of an MFP on a qualifying single source drug that includes a fixed combination drug constitutes a deterrent for investment and research into novel indications.
Response:
We thank commenters for their input, and we share commenters' commitment to ensuring that Medicare beneficiaries have access to clinically appropriate treatment options and that the real-world consequences of our policies are fully understood. The policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) was developed through a notice-and-comment rulemaking process that provided patients, clinicians, healthcare providers, manufacturers, and other interested parties a meaningful opportunity to submit input on the proposed change. We have carefully considered all of that input in developing this final rule. We agree that patient and clinician perspectives are essential inputs into our policy development. Regarding the commenter who recommended that we explore with the wider patient community and subject matter experts the degree to which application of an MFP on a qualifying single source drug that includes a fixed combination drug constitutes a deterrent for investment and research into novel indications, we appreciate this recommendation. As discussed elsewhere in this final rule, we do not anticipate that proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) will meaningfully affect investment in innovation given the narrow scope of products that it covers and that, as previously discussed, researchers have found no association between drug prices and R&D investment levels. We will continue to seek input from patients, clinicians, and other stakeholders as the Negotiation Program is implemented and as we consider future rulemaking.
Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the general fixed combination drug policy, as well as the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that

are new formulations, with technical modifications to improve organizational clarity. Specifically, we are finalizing the general fixed combination drug policy—which we proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)—at § 429.125(b)(4)(i), and we are finalizing the specific fixed combination drug policy for new formulations—which we proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i)—at new § 429.125(b)(4)(ii). We also are adding a paragraph header containing the word “General” to finalized § 429.125(b)(4)(i). Finally, in finalized § 429.125(b)(4)(i), we are replacing the reference to “paragraph (b)(4)(i)” with a reference to “paragraph (b)(4)(ii)”. These technical modifications do not substantively change the proposed policy, and the language finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii) is identical to the language proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i). CMS will monitor the implementation of the policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations and will consider potential modifications after gaining experience with the policy.
(2) Alternatives Considered
We considered expressly limiting the proposed modification of the application of the general fixed combination drug policy to biological products (other than vaccines for infectious disease(s) identified at proposed § 429.125(b)(3)), as currently such biological products licensed in BLAs pose the program integrity risks of which we are currently aware. However, in line with our aim to apply the statutory requirements at sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act equally to all new formulations of a drug, whether the new formulation is approved in an NDA or licensed in a BLA, and to account for the possibility that the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) could apply to drugs in the future, we did not propose to limit the proposed modification to these biological products. This approach would ensure that we are treating new formulations equally, whether that new formulation is a drug or biological product.
We also considered proposing an alternative modification to the general fixed combination drug policy that would target the program integrity risk as described in the Negotiation Program Guidance wherein CMS identification of potential qualifying single source drugs under the fixed combination drug policy would not take into account an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that is not biologically active against the disease state(s) the drug is indicated for and thus does not result in a clinically meaningful difference from other drug or biological products that otherwise have the same active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s). However, we instead proposed to focus on products that differ in active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s) due to the inclusion of an active moiety/active ingredient/antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies)/active ingredient(s)/antigen component(s). As noted in section II.B.6.a.1. of this final rule, we believe the proposed approach narrowly addresses the program integrity risks with the general fixed combination policy and the specific elements of the policy that are in tension with section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act, which directs CMS to aggregate across dosage forms and strengths, including new formulations of the drug, and section 1196(a)(2) of the Act, which directs CMS to apply the MFP across different strengths and dosage forms of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulations or package size or package type of such drug.
We considered maintaining the policy established for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, wherein, for a fixed combination drug with two or more active moieties/active ingredients/antigen components, we would treat the distinct combination of active moieties/active ingredients/antigen components as one active moiety/active ingredient/antigen component. However, for the reasons described in section II.B.6.a.1. of this final rule, we believe that this policy poses program integrity risks and is in tension with sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act.
Finally, we considered proposing a policy to address program integrity risks posed by co-packaged drugs. In the Negotiation Program Guidance, we stated that the general fixed combination drug policy would apply to a co-packaged drug, in which two active moieties/active ingredients are not co-formulated but rather co-packaged and sold in a single package, but that we may address co-packaged drugs in rulemaking for initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years. That is, for purposes of the Negotiation Program in initial price applicability year 2028, if a drug (including a co-packaged drug) contained two or more active moieties/active ingredients/antigen components, the distinct combination of active moieties/active ingredients/antigen components would be considered as one active moiety/active ingredient/antigen component for the purpose of identifying potential qualifying single source drugs, whether such drug was co-formulated or co-packaged. After further consideration, and based on our assessment that at this time co-packaged drugs do not appear to pose substantive program integrity risks to the Negotiation Program because manufacturers are not adopting co-packaging practices that undermine current program policies, we proposed that the general fixed combination drug policy at proposed § 429.125(b)(4) continue to apply to co-packaged drugs. We are monitoring this approach and potential gaming of co-packaged drugs and may consider revisiting this policy in the future.
We solicited comments on our proposal and these alternatives.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that CMS' proposal inadvertently creates a loophole for co-packaged products, stating that, in their view, the evidentiary requirements for co-packaging are generally significantly lower than those for reformulating an alternative route of administration, making this pathway both accessible and commercially attractive, and requested that CMS close this potential loophole before it is exploited. These commenters also noted that the proposal creates a distinction between fixed-combination products and co-packaged products that is not grounded in clinical differences and that CMS should clarify whether co-packaged products would be treated the same as fixed combination products under the final rule.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback. We are not finalizing a change to the treatment of co-packaged drugs in this final rule. Under our existing policy, co-packaged products continue to be treated in the same manner as fixed combination drugs for purposes of identifying qualifying single source drugs under the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4). The policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) applies only to fixed combination products that differ from the original drug because of an added active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration. It does not extend to co-packaged products as a category. We recognize that commenters raised concerns about the potential for manufacturers to use co-packaging as a means of achieving the same route-of-administration change while avoiding the policy at proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i). We take these concerns seriously. Consistent with our
(
printed page 72228)
response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we will continue to monitor the use of co-packaged products in the context of the Negotiation Program. Commenters did not identify specific documented instances of manufacturers using co-packaging to circumvent the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and the underlying statutory provisions. Should our monitoring indicate that co-packaged products present program integrity risks similar to those addressed by proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), we will consider whether additional rulemaking is warranted. We will consider these comments in our policy development for this issue in future rulemaking. Regarding commenters' concerns that the policy creates a distinction between fixed combination products and co-packaged products that is not grounded in clinical differences, the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) addresses a discrete and well-defined category of products. We do not agree that extending that policy to all co-packaged products is warranted at this time.

After consideration of public comments, we are not finalizing any of the alternatives considered in section II.B.6.a.2. of the Negotiation Program proposed rule.
b. Time Since Approval or Licensure (§ 429.125(c))
In accordance with section 1192(e)(1) of the Act and consistent with policies for implementation as described in Negotiation Program Guidance, and accounting for the treatment of certain former orphan drugs in accordance with section 1192(e)(4) of the Act as addressed in proposed § 429.125(c)(3), we proposed at § 429.125(c)(1) and (c)(2) that at least 7 years (for drugs) or 11 years (for biological products) must have elapsed between the FDA date of approval or licensure of the potential qualifying single source drug identified at proposed § 429.125(b) and the selected drug publication date with respect to an initial price applicability year. To determine the date of approval for a potential qualifying single source drug that is a drug with more than one FDA application number, we would use the initial date of approval associated with the earliest-approved FDA application belonging to the NDA holder and containing the active moiety (or in the case of a potential qualifying single source drug identified under the general fixed combination drug policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4), for the distinct combination of active moieties). For a potential qualifying single source drug identified under proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) that is a drug, we would use the initial date of approval associated with the earliest-approved FDA application belonging to the NDA holder and containing the shared active moiety(ies) used to identify the potential qualifying single source drug. To determine the date of licensure for a potential qualifying single source drug that is a biological product (except in the case of a vaccine for infectious disease(s), for which we would determine the date of licensure as described later in this section) with more than one FDA application number, we would use the initial date of licensure associated with the earliest-approved FDA application belonging to the BLA holder and containing the active ingredient (or in the case of a potential qualifying single source drug identified under the general fixed combination drug policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4), for the distinct combination of active ingredients). For a potential qualifying single source drug identified under proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i) that is a biological product, we would use the initial date of licensure associated with the earliest-approved licensure of the FDA application belonging to the BLA holder and containing the shared active ingredient(s) used to identify the potential qualifying single source drug.

Comment:
Many commenters supported CMS' proposed approach at § 429.125(e)(1). Many commenters specifically appreciated the criteria to broaden the scope of the orphan drug exclusion to include drugs with multiple orphan drug designations. A few commenters urged CMS to finalize an approach that supports the innovation and development of orphan drugs for rare diseases. A few commenters opposed CMS' proposed approach to broaden the scope of the orphan drug exclusion to include drugs with multiple orphan designations. A couple of commenters urged CMS to apply the exclusion as narrowly as the law permits. A commenter stated that the expansion of the orphan drug exclusion prevents negotiation for high-cost drugs, forcing patients to wait longer for lower prices. In response to the commenter's recommendation to retroactively apply the revised orphan drug exclusion to include drugs selected for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027, CMS disagrees with the commenter's recommendation and interpretation of statute. Section 71203(a) of the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation amended section 1192(e)(3)(A) of the Act and added section 1192(e)(4) to the Act, and section 71203(b) of the “Working Families Tax Cut” legislation specifies that these amendments shall apply with respect to initial price applicability years (as defined in section 1191(b) of the Act) beginning on or after January 1, 2028. We believe our interpretation is more consistent with a plain reading of these provisions, under which the reference to “qualifying single source drug” in section 1191(b)(2) of the Act denotes that the price applicability period, as defined in section 1191(b)(2) of the Act, is specific to each product that CMS determined was a “qualifying single source drug” at the time of selection with respect to a given initial price applicability period and which, for a period of time described in sections 1191(b)(2) and 1192(c) of the Act, is considered a “selected drug” within its “price applicability period.” We believe that this interpretation gives effect to all relevant provisions and is in accord with the structure of the statute which does not otherwise contemplate a continued requirement that selected drugs remain qualifying single source drugs as defined under section 1192(c) after they are selected.

d. Bona Fide Marketing of an Approved Generic Drug or Licensed Biosimilar and Deselection of a Selected Drug (§ 429.125(d), § 429.130, and § 429.135)
Key provisions of the Negotiation Program statute govern CMS' evaluation of generic and biosimilar competitors to potential qualifying single source drugs and CMS' further consideration of such products in the deselection of selected drugs. First, section 1192(e)(1)(A)(iii) of the Act states that, to be considered a qualifying single source drug, a drug cannot be the listed drug for any drug approved and marketed under an ANDA under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act. For a biological product, section 1192(e)(1)(B)(iii) of the Act states that the biological product cannot be the reference product for any biological product that is licensed and marketed under section 351(k) of the PHS Act (that is, a biosimilar). Second, section 1192(c)(1) specifies a selected drug that is included on the list of selected drugs for an initial price applicability year will remain a selected drug for that year and each subsequent year beginning before the first year that begins at least nine months after the date on which CMS determines: (1) the FDA has approved a generic drug under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act that identifies as its reference-listed drug a product that is included in the selected drug, or FDA has licensed a biosimilar under section 351(k) of the PHS Act that identifies as its reference product a product that is included in the selected drug; and (2) the generic drug or biosimilar, as applicable, is marketed pursuant to such approval or licensure.
Based on the authorities described previously, CMS conducts the following inquiry to determine whether a drug or biological product can be considered a qualifying single source drug. First, using FDA reference sources including the Orange Book and Purple Book, CMS would evaluate whether at least one generic drug is approved under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act using any dosage form or strength of the potential qualifying single source drug as the listed drug or at least one biosimilar is licensed under section 351(k) of the PHS Act using any dosage form or strength of the potential qualifying single source drug as the reference product, consistent with proposed § 429.125(d)(1). This approach is consistent with the approach of aggregating different dosage forms and strengths as a single potential qualifying single source drug as required under section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act (stating that a qualifying single source drug is inclusive of all strengths and dosage forms, which is described in further detail in section II.B.6.a. of this final rule). In other words, consistent with proposed in § 429.125(d), if CMS determines there is a generic drug or biosimilar that is approved or licensed, as applicable, for any dosage form or strength of a drug or biological product, and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing, then that drug or biological product would not meet the statutory criteria in section 1192(e)(1)(A)(iii) or section 1192(e)(1)(B)(iii) of the Act to be a qualifying single source drug. We proposed that the determination of whether a potential qualifying single source drug includes the listed drug or reference product for an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar, respectively, would be made irrespective of whether the indication(s) approved for the listed drug or reference product were or are covered under Part D, payable under Part B, or both.
We note that because section 1192(e)(2)(A) of the Act provides that an “authorized generic” drug “shall be treated as the same qualifying single source drug,” we will not consider an authorized generic drug to be a generic drug or biosimilar for the purposes of identifying whether there is an
(
printed page 72235)
approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar for any strength or dosage form of a potential qualifying single source drug. An authorized generic drug is defined in section 1192(e)(2)(B) of the Act as: (1) in the case of a drug, an authorized generic drug (as such term is defined in section 505(t)(3) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act); and (2) in the case of a biological product, a product that has been licensed under section 351(a) of such Act
[
70
]
and is marketed, sold, or distributed directly or indirectly to retail class of trade under a different labeling, packaging (other than repackaging as the reference product in blister packs, unit doses, or similar packaging for use in institutions), product code, labeler code, trade name, or trade mark than the reference product.
Second, consistent with the policies for implementation of section 30.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we would conduct a holistic inquiry based on the totality of the circumstances when evaluating whether any approved generic drug(s) or licensed biosimilar(s) is or are subject to Bona Fide Marketing as defined at proposed § 429.20 and described in proposed § 429.130. CMS must evaluate, as part of the determination described in section 1192(e) of the Act, whether a generic drug or biosimilar “is. . .marketed” and whether the potential qualifying single source drug is a listed drug “for any drug that is approved and marketed under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act” or a reference product “for any biological product that is licensed and marketed under section 351(k) of the PHS Act.” The terminology specified in sections 1192(e) of the Act for purposes of the Negotiation Program is distinct from the terminology specified elsewhere in the Act for purposes of the Medicare Part B Drug Inflation Rebate Program (section 1847A(i) of the Act) and the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program (section 1860D-14B of the Act), also established through the IRA. For Medicare inflation rebates, the statute refers to the date that a drug is “first marketed”. The absence of the term “first marketed” in section 1192 of the Act indicates that, for purposes of the Negotiation Program, a generic drug or biosimilar must have a continuing presence on the market in order to affect the status of a listed drug/reference product. Consistent with the statutory purpose of lowering drug prices through the mechanisms described in Title I, Subtitle B, Part 1 of the Inflation Reduction Act, and as CMS has explained in response to comment on the Negotiation Program Guidance, CMS will consider whether meaningful competition exists on an ongoing basis between any dosage form or strength of a potential qualifying single source drug that includes the listed drug or reference product and any one or more generic drug(s) or biosimilar(s). Therefore, as reflected in proposed § 429.130(a)(1) and (2), we understand that whether a product “is marketed” requires more than solely token or de minimis availability. We appreciate that, while sales and utilization data provide important indicators of market competition, they are not the only sources of information that may illustrate whether such competition exists between a listed drug or reference product and a generic drug or biosimilar. For example, we are also aware there may be situations in which a manufacturer of a brand name drug or biological product has entered into a market-limiting agreement with a manufacturer of a generic drug or biosimilar, where the generic drug or biosimilar manufacturer agrees to limit production or distribution of the generic drug or biosimilar, such that only a nominal quantity of product is allowed to enter the market. The result is a lack of meaningful price competition, and in that circumstance the generic drug or biosimilar is not “marketed” within the meaning of that term as it is used in section 1192 of the Act (for example, specifically within the context of marketed at section 1192(e) of the Act). Therefore, as proposed in § 429.130(b), whether such competition exists between a listed drug or reference product and an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar would depend on a holistic inquiry based on the totality of circumstances in existence at the time that CMS evaluates whether an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing and not on the presence, or absence, of any single factor.
Specifically, in accordance with sections 1192(e) of the Act, to consider whether there are ongoing sales and/or utilization of a generic drug or biosimilar in the market, we proposed at § 429.130(a)(1)(i) through (iii) to review the following data sources: PDE data, AMP data, and ASP data. Additionally, as part of CMS' holistic consideration of whether one or more manufacturers of a generic drug or biosimilar are engaging in Bona Fide Marketing of the approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar, we proposed at § 429.130(a)(1)(iv) that CMS may also review sales and/or utilization data from additional data sources, including, but not limited to, Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data, and data from nationally representative and commercially available databases. Further, to consider whether there is meaningful competition, CMS may also consider other factors proposed at § 429.130(a)(2) and (3) that include whether the approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar is regularly and consistently available for purchase through the pharmaceutical supply chain, whether any licenses or other agreements between a Primary Manufacturer and a generic drug or biosimilar manufacturer limit the availability or distribution of the generic drug or biosimilar, and other available data and informational sources on market share and relative market competition of the approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar that CMS may identify.
If any dosage form or strength of a potential qualifying single source drug is the listed drug or reference product for one or more generic drugs or biosimilars that CMS determines are approved or licensed and subject to Bona Fide Marketing based on the information as described in proposed § 429.130(a), the potential qualifying single source drug would not be considered a qualifying single source drug for the applicable initial price applicability year (as described in proposed § 429.125(d)). As set forth in proposed § 429.125(d) and in accordance with § 429.130(c)(1), we would review the information set forth in proposed § 429.130(a) for any potential qualifying single source drug for initial price applicability year 2029 and any initial price applicability year thereafter in January prior to the selected drug publication date (proposed at § 429.20 and described in section II.A.2. of this final rule). For example, for initial price applicability year 2029, CMS would review this information for any potential qualifying single source drugs in January 2027, prior to the February 1, 2027 selected drug publication date.
Consistent with section 1192(c)(1) of the Act, a drug selected for negotiation for an initial price applicability year would remain a selected drug for that initial price applicability year and each subsequent year beginning before the first year that begins at least nine months after the date as of which CMS determines at least one generic drug is approved under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act using the selected drug as the
(
printed page 72236)
listed drug or at least one biosimilar is licensed under section 351(k) of the PHS Act using the selected drug as the reference product, and such generic drug or biosimilar is marketed pursuant to such approval or licensure, as applicable. As discussed previously in this section, we understand that whether a product “is marketed” requires more than solely token or de minimis availability. Therefore, when evaluating whether a generic drug or biosimilar for a selected drug is subject to Bona Fide Marketing for the purposes of determining if a selected drug ceases to be a selected drug consistent with section 1192(c) of the Act and proposed § 429.135(a), we would implement the same approach that we proposed for evaluating whether a generic drug or biosimilar for a potential qualifying single source drug is subject to Bona Fide Marketing.
If CMS determines that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed for the selected drug, and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing (as set forth in proposed § 429.130(a)) on a date during the period beginning on the selected drug publication date (as defined in proposed § 429.20) and ending on November 1 of the year that begins 2 years prior to the initial price applicability year for which the drug is selected for negotiation, consistent with section 1192(c)(2) of the Act and proposed § 429.135(b)(1)(i), the selected drug is no longer subject to the negotiation process—including, for example, any applicable negotiation meeting(s) or offer and counteroffer exchanges—for such initial price applicability year. Similarly, consistent with section 1194(f)(5)(B) of the Act and proposed § 429.135(b)(2), if CMS determines that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed for a selected drug and that such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing (as set forth in proposed § 429.130(a)) on a date during the period beginning on the selected drug publication date (as defined in proposed § 429.20) and ending on November 1 of the year that begins 2 years prior to the initial price applicability year for which the drug is selected for renegotiation, then the selected drug is no longer subject to the renegotiation process. Therefore, for drugs selected for negotiation and renegotiation (if any) for an initial price applicability year, we proposed we would review the information set forth in proposed § 429.130(a) on a monthly basis starting in March of the calendar year of the negotiation period (or renegotiation period, as applicable) until November 1 of the year that begins 2 years prior to the initial price applicability year for which the drug was selected for negotiation (or renegotiation, as applicable) (see proposed § 429.130(c)(4) and (c)(5).
Pursuant to section 1192(c)(1) of the Act, once the negotiation period concludes, a selected drug would cease to be a selected drug if CMS determines that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing based on the information considered in proposed § 429.130(a). We proposed that we would review the information set forth in proposed § 429.130(a), biannually in March and October, starting in October of the calendar year after CMS and the Primary Manufacturer reached an agreement on an MFP for the initial price applicability year for which the drug was selected originally for negotiation and until CMS determines that a selected drug meets the requirements at proposed § 429.135(a) to cease being a selected drug.
Section 1194(f)(5) of the Act clarifies that a renegotiation-eligible drug for which CMS determines there is a generic drug that is approved or biosimilar that is licensed, and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing before or during the renegotiation period shall not be subject to the renegotiation process. Thus, for any renegotiation-eligible drug, we would review the information set forth in proposed § 429.130(a), in January, prior to the selected drug publication date (defined at § 429.20 and described in section II.A.2. of this final rule) as proposed in § 429.130(c)(3).
Finally, after determining that a generic drug is approved or biosimilar is licensed and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing, we would monitor that the approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar continues to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing. We would review the information set forth in proposed § 429.130(a) to monitor whether such generic drug(s) or biosimilar(s) continues to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing consistent with the schedule proposed at § 429.130(c)(2) and (7), which includes, but is not limited to January of each calendar year.
For each of these points in time CMS reviews the applicable data to determine whether a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing (which includes prior to selection for negotiation or renegotiation of selected drugs, after selection of drugs for negotiation or renegotiation, or after a selected drug ceases to be a selected drug), beginning with drug selection for negotiation and renegotiation for initial price applicability year 2029 and initial price applicability years thereafter, we proposed a schedule for reviewing the data at proposed § 429.130(c) that varies from the policies in the applicable guidance for drugs that were potentially eligible for selection or have been selected for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028. We have observed across the administration of the Negotiation Program to date that there are certain points in time across a calendar year that are key to the drug selection process of the Negotiation Program and/or have an impact on CMS and manufacturer operations related to plan year coverage contracts and related determinations. For example, it is necessary for CMS to review whether any applicable generic drugs and biosimilars are subject to Bona Fide Marketing as part of the review steps CMS undertakes to identify qualifying single source drugs for purposes of drug selection for negotiation (proposed at § 429.130(c)(1)) and to identify selected drugs ineligible to be selected for renegotiation (proposed at § 429.130(c)(3)) prior to the selected drug publication date. Once a drug is selected, but prior to the agreement of an MFP or the end of the negotiation period during the negotiation process, CMS must regularly review if any applicable generic drugs and biosimilars are subject to Bona Fide Marketing as an essential part of determining if a selected drug remains subject to the negotiation process. Therefore, consistent with the policies for implementation as described in Negotiation Program Guidance, CMS would maintain monthly reviews of data during this period as proposed at § 429.130(c)(4) for drugs selected for negotiation and as proposed at § 429.130(c)(5) for drugs selected for renegotiation (if any) for initial price applicability years 2029 and thereafter. However, after the negotiation period ends, we believe that less frequent reviews are sufficient and would provide manufacturers, Part D plan sponsors, and other interested parties with notice regarding the specific points in time across a calendar year at which CMS would review the specified data and provide public notice of any selected drugs that are deselected (consistent with proposed § 429.135(a) and (d)) because CMS determined that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed for the selected
(

drug and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. For example, we understand that manufacturers, plan sponsors, and other relevant parties may begin negotiations for Part D plan bids more than a year prior to the plan year and CMS' deadline for Part D sponsor bids (see § 423.265(b)). Therefore, we believe that one key date includes October to ensure manufacturers and Part D plan sponsors are aware prior to the subsequent June due date for Part D plan sponsors to provide CMS with any required plan bids for the next Medicare plan contract year (as indicated in § 423.265(b)(1)) of any selected drugs that may be deselected. For example, if we determine in October 2028 that a generic drug or biosimilar is approved or licensed, as applicable, for a selected drug for initial price applicability year 2029 and that generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing, that selected drug ceases to be a selected drug on January 1, 2030 and the MFP would not be applicable for that year. Manufacturers and plan sponsors would then be aware in November 2028 that the selected drug would cease to be a selected drug in contract year 2030, bids for which are due in June 2029. Finally, as described in proposed § 429.130(c)(2) and (7), we would periodically monitor, including at least annually in January prior to each selected drug publication date, the marketing of any applicable generics and biosimilars in the following circumstances: (1) if a potential qualifying single source drug was determined by CMS not to qualify as a qualifying single source drug for any prior initial price applicability year because CMS determined that at least one generic drug was approved using the potential qualifying single source drug as the listed drug or at least one biosimilar was licensed using the potential qualifying source drug as the reference product, and such generic drug or biosimilar was subject to Bona Fide Marketing, and (2) if a selected drug ceases to be a selected drug in accordance with proposed § 429.135(a) (in other words, because CMS determined that a generic drug is approved or a biosimilar is licensed for the selected drug and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing).

Specifically, for PDE data, consistent with proposed § 429.130(a)(1)(i) and using the example of CMS' review in October, this means that CMS would review PDE data reported from October of the prior calendar year through September of the current calendar year. Submission deadlines for the data source would determine the data available to CMS at the time of review. CMS would pull such data in the month specified for CMS' review, and the specific date on which CMS may pull the data would vary year to year and may be impacted, for example, by the date of Federal holidays. To provide further clarity to manufacturers and interested parties in this final rule, we provide the following example. If, in accordance with proposed § 429.130(c)(4), CMS conducts a review in March 2027 to consider whether an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing for a selected drug selected for negotiation for initial price applicability year 2029, this means CMS may pull the relevant data on any day on or between March 1, 2027 and March 31, 2027. However, as specified in proposed § 429.130(a), the information reviewed is the information “available to” CMS when CMS pulls the data. Due to lags in data reporting for various sources, this means the data reviewed may cover a period that ends days, weeks, or months prior to the date of the data pull. For example, if CMS pulled AMP data on March 31, 2027, CMS would review the most recent 12 months of AMP data available as of March 31, 2027. Due to lags in the availability of AMP data, this means CMS would review AMP data covering the period from February 2026 through January 2027.
Further, to continue the previous example, CMS' review of the information pulled on or between March 1, 2027 and March 31, 2027 may extend into the following month to ensure a fulsome consideration of the data available as of the date the information was pulled and may lead CMS to determine as of March 2027 that the drug selected for initial price applicability year 2029 has an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar, and such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. Consistent with the policies for implementation as described in Negotiation Program Guidance, we provide the following examples of potential factors considered in CMS' review of whether an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. While the circumstances illustrated in these examples weigh in favor of, or against, considering a generic drug or biosimilar to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing, CMS' inquiry for any particular drug would be based on the totality of the circumstances and not on the presence, or absence, of any single factor. First, as an example, if a potential qualifying single source drug has at least one approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar that has high and consistent PDE utilization, AMP sales, and/or ASP sales, we would consider the generic(s) or biosimilar(s) of the potential qualifying single source drug to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing. As a second example, a potential qualifying single source drug might have a newly or recently approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar and the product has relatively low PDE utilization, AMP sales, and/or ASP sales. In this example, if CMS finds in additional review of public information that the generic drug or biosimilar manufacturer has successfully launched their product, and there is no evidence of agreements limiting distribution of the generic drug or biosimilar, then we may consider the generic drug or biosimilar of the potential qualifying single source drug to be subject to Bona Fide Marketing. As a third example, a potential qualifying single source drug might have an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar product with no PDE utilization, AMP sales, and/or ASP sales. In this example, if CMS finds in additional review of public information that there are ongoing patent disputes and no generic drug or biosimilar manufacturer has successfully launched their product, then we may consider the

Section 1192(c)(1) of the Act specifies that each negotiation-eligible drug included on the list of drugs published for an initial price applicability year consistent with section 1192(a) of the Act will be a “selected drug” with respect to that year and each subsequent year beginning before the first year that begins at least 9 months after the date on which the Secretary determines at least one drug is approved under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act using the selected drug as the listed drug or at least one biological product is licensed under section 351(k) of the PHS Act using the selected drug as the reference product, and that such drug or biological product is marketed pursuant to such approval or licensure. Additionally, section 1192(c)(2) of the Act states that a negotiation-eligible drug shall not be subject to the negotiation process under section 1194 of the Act for the applicable negotiation period but shall continue to be considered a selected drug for purposes of the number of negotiation-eligible drugs published on the list with respect to such initial price applicability year if the Secretary determines that the criteria in section 1192(c)(1) of the Act are met before or during the negotiation period for that initial price applicability year. Therefore, in accordance with sections 1192(c)(1) and (2) of the Act, we proposed in § 429.135 to codify provisions related to deselection of a selected drug subject to the timeline and situations proposed in § 429.135(b).
Specifically in proposed § 429.135(a), each drug selected for negotiation for an initial price applicability year would remain a selected drug, with respect to such initial price applicability year and each subsequent year beginning before the first year that begins at least 9 months after the date on which CMS determines that at least one generic drug is approved under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act using any dosage form or strength of the selected drug as the listed drug or at least one biosimilar is licensed under section 351(k) of the PHS Act using any dosage form or strength of the selected drug as the reference product, and that such generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing.
