We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters shared their perspectives about the interplay of the definition of a qualifying single source drug and Bona Fide Marketing. Specifically, a commenter suggested that a manufacturer might manipulate the policies by focusing marketing on new formulations and permitting biosimilar competition on the older formulation. The commenter suggested that CMS consider the formulations without a generic drug or biosimilar when considering spending for selection and after selection retain formulations that lack marketing. A couple of commenters expressed concern that generic entry for a minimally utilized dosage form and strength would mean the MFP no longer applies to highly utilized dosage forms and strengths that may not face generic competition and recommended CMS consider the share of utilization when evaluating whether Bona Fide Marketing is occurring. Another commenter suggested measuring utilization across the aggregated dosage forms and strengths may prolong the period the product is subjected to the negotiation process. Another commenter noted their support for CMS' approach to identifying qualifying single source drugs and the interplay with Bona Fide Marketing.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance and the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, and with respect to a commenter's concern that competition on older formulations or specific dosage forms and strengths could result in a qualifying single source drug avoiding selection or being deselected, we acknowledge this, but for consistency, will continue to mirror the approach to aggregation across dosage forms and strengths of a drug for selection pursuant to section 1192(d)(3)(B) of the Act.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that CMS lacks statutory authority to review Bona Fide Marketing to implement the statutory requirement of determining if a generic or biosimilar is “approved and marketed” or “licensed and marketed” under sections 1192(c) and (e) of the Act. Many commenters stated that “marketing” is already a term defined in the pharmaceutical industry, including by FDA and CMS. In addition, these commenters stated that any review of “marketing” for purposes of drug selection under section 1192(e) of the Act or deselection under section 1192(c) of the Act must be based on the first “market date,” consistent with the plain meaning of “to market.” One of these commenters noted this is consistent with the best meaning of the statute. Additionally, a commenter recommended CMS have manufacturers certify that the generic or biosimilar is marketed consistent with such definition. Some commenters recommended CMS withdraw proposed § 429.130. Many commenters recommended CMS utilize an alternative approach when evaluating Bona Fide Marketing, such as distinguishing between market entry
(
printed page 72240)
and patient access, and emphasized the importance of transparent and predictable standards. A couple of commenters stated that the FTC would regulate any areas of marketing concern. A few commenters raised concerns about the impact of CMS' review of Bona Fide Marketing on the biosimilar (including a request for a biosimilar delay) and generics markets. Additionally, some commenters suggested that CMS lacks statutory authority to monitor marketing after a drug/biological is determined ineligible for selection or is deselected. A commenter supported the approach, including the ongoing monitoring of selected drugs removed from selection.
Response:
Consistent with our response to similar comments in Negotiation Program Guidance, the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, and proposed §§ 429.125(d), 429.130 and 429.135, section 1192 of the Act requires CMS to make a determination whether a generic drug or biosimilar “is marketed” in order to determine whether a listed drug/reference product should be selected as a qualifying single source drug or whether a selected drug should be deselected. The statute uses different terminology in section 1192 of the Act than in section 1860D-14B of the Act, which established the new Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program. In the latter provision, the statute referred to the date that a drug is “first marketed.” The absence of similar terminology in section 1192 of the Act demonstrates that, for purposes of the Negotiation Program, a generic drug or biosimilar would have a continuing presence on the market in order to affect the status of a listed drug/reference product. Consistent with the purpose of the statute to lower prices for Medicare through negotiation or price competition, the statute contemplates that, in making this determination, we would consider whether meaningful competition exists on an ongoing basis between a listed drug or reference product and a generic drug or biosimilar. This determination requires more than solely token or de minimis availability of the products. For example, we are aware of situations in which a manufacturer of a brand name drug or biological product has entered into a market-limiting agreement with a manufacturer of a generic drug or biosimilar. In the event only a nominal quantity of the generic drug or biosimilar enters the market, the generic drug or biosimilar would not be “marketed” within the meaning of that term as it is used in section 1192 of the Act. Given the Negotiation Program is targeted at single source drugs and biological products that have been on the market for some time, for which no generic drug or biosimilar competition currently exists, the statutory directive would not be met if a qualifying single source drug were to avoid selection or be removed from the selected drug list where generic drug or biosimilar availability is limited by the Primary Manufacturer. It is consistent with the purpose of the statute to avoid selection or remove a qualifying single source drug from the selected drug list only when there is evidence that the selected drug is subject to meaningful competition. For example, section 1192(e)(2)(A) of the Act provides that an “authorized generic” drug or biosimilar product “shall be treated as the same qualifying single source drug.” Although an authorized generic may appear to be competing with the reference drug, authorized generics are marketed by the brand name drug company or another company under the brand company's NDA, meaning that the relationship between the brand drug and its authorized generic is not meaningful competition. Whether such competition exists between a listed drug or reference product and a generic drug or biosimilar will depend on the totality of circumstances in existence at the time that we perform the function of evaluating whether a generic drug or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing.
Comment:
Some commenters raised concerns with using a “totality of the circumstances” approach to review Bona Fide Marketing as a vague standard that may vary by case, while a commenter shared support for the review of Bona Fide Marketing, and another commenter appreciated additional transparency. A commenter stated that CMS' previously stated concern that a manufacturer might “launch into the market a token or de minimis amount of a generic drug or biosimilar for the selected drug and the manufacturer of that selected drug could claim that the MFP should no longer apply” is not a scenario they are aware of ever happening with a biosimilar and a reference product.
Response:
We thank commenters for sharing their specific observations of the market and feedback on potential scenarios for review. Consistent with our response to similar comments in Negotiation Program Guidance and the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and as described at § 429.130(b), we reiterate that the determination whether an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing on an ongoing basis is a totality-of-the circumstances inquiry that will not necessarily turn on any one source of data. Further, it is consistent with the purpose of the statute to avoid selection or remove a qualifying single source drug only when there is evidence that the selected drug is subject to meaningful competition and not just when there are “any” sales of the generic drug or biosimilar as suggested by a commenter. We are aware of situations in which a manufacturer of a brand name drug or biological product has entered into a market-limiting agreement with a manufacturer of a generic drug or biosimilar. In the event only a nominal quantity of the generic drug or biosimilar enters the market, the generic drug or biosimilar would not be “marketed” within the meaning of that term as it is used in section 1192 of the Act (for example, specifically within the context of marketed at section 1192(e) of the Act). We note that such a situation has not materialized to date because, in accordance with the statute and CMS' policies established in previous program guidance, such availability would not allow for a manufacturer to claim that the drug should be deselected and no longer subject to an MFP.

A few commenters shared feedback on the examples provided of when CMS may or may not consider Bona Fide Marketing to be occurring. A commenter stated that the modification to the second example to state CMS “may” consider Bona Fide Marketing to be occurring rather than “will” introduces additional uncertainty to the example. A couple of commenters raised concerns that the examples do not provide sufficient predictability to manufacturers of the Bona Fide Marketing standard. A commenter disagreed with the third example and recommended it be deleted—according to this comment, this example would result in the wrong outcome where a particular biosimilar has recently launched, for example, at risk or based on a settlement without any patent litigation proceedings as to its biosimilar (notwithstanding the existence of other patent disputes as to biosimilars of the same reference product), but PDE, AMP, and ASP sales do not yet reflect the launch.

Response:
We thank commenters for their suggestions related to additional data sources with timely utilization data for drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D. We may consider additional data sources to review utilization as available. We clarify in this response to comments that additional data sources may include, for example, MA encounter data (subject to data use and release limitations in
42 CFR 422.310(f)
) or OM Part B claims. Consideration of Bona Fide Marketing is based on a review of the totality of the circumstances. Therefore, an uptick in the data alone is not determinative of whether Bona Fide Marketing is occurring. We direct commenters to the additional relevant factors specified in § 429.130, which include, for example, whether the approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar is regularly and consistently available for purchase through the pharmaceutical supply chain and whether any licenses or other agreements between a Primary Manufacturer and an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar manufacturer limit the availability or distribution of the approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar.
We appreciate the commenter's concern about data lags that may not reflect the recent launch of a product. We recognize that the timing for CMS to pull data and compile materials for review may include data covering an earlier time period for lagged data sources. We are finalizing our policy as proposed at § 429.130(a) with modifications at § 429.130(a)(1)(i) through (iii) to clarify the information considered in CMS' review of Bona Fide Marketing, specifically that CMS evaluates the most recent 12 months of PDE data, 12 months of AMP data and 4 quarters of ASP data, as applicable, available to the agency when CMS conducts its review and that the period of such data to be reviewed need not end with the last “full month” or “full quarter” of data available. Additionally, we clarify in § 429.130(a)(1)(iv) that CMS may evaluate sales and utilization data for the generic drug or biosimilar for the most recent 12 months, 4 quarters, or 52 weeks of a data source, if available and as applicable to such data source, other than those data sources listed in paragraph (a)(1)(i) through (iii) of this section including, but not limited to, Medicaid State Drug Utilization Data and data from nationally representative and commercially available databases, available to CMS at the time CMS reviews such data consistent with paragraph (c) of § 429.130. This modification provides CMS with the flexibility to include data from sources that are updated on a weekly basis so as to not artificially limit the agency's consideration of sales and utilization data that are updated at an interval not included in the proposed rule.
We appreciate commenter feedback on the timing of review. We proposed in § 429.130(c)(6) that we would conduct our review biannually in March and October, starting in October of the calendar year after CMS and the Primary Manufacturer reached an agreement on an MFP for the initial price applicability year for which the drug was selected originally for negotiation and until CMS determines that a selected drug meets the requirements at § 429.135(a) to cease being a selected drug. The review in March enables us to determine any selected drugs that must be deselected by the following January. Additionally, we understand that manufacturers, plan sponsors, and other relevant parties may begin negotiations for Part D plan bids more than a year prior to the plan year and CMS' deadline for Part D sponsor bids (see § 423.265(b)). Therefore, we proposed to review in October to ensure manufacturers and Part D plan sponsors are aware prior to the subsequent June due date for Part D plan sponsors to provide CMS with any required plan bids for the next Medicare plan contract year (as indicated in § 423.265(b)(1)) of any selected drugs that may be deselected. We proposed in § 429.130(c)(4) and (5) to conduct monthly reviews during the negotiation and renegotiation period, respectively, because monthly reviews during these periods enable us to promptly determine any selected drugs that are no longer subject to the negotiation or renegotiation process, as applicable. We proposed in § 429.130(c)(1) and (3) to review annually in January to identify potential qualifying single source drugs and any selected drugs ineligible for renegotiation, respectively, prior to the selected drug publication date. After any determination in which CMS finds a generic drug was approved or a biosimilar was licensed and such generic or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing, CMS engages in periodic reviews to monitor that meaningful competition exists on an ongoing basis between a listed drug or reference product and a generic drug or biosimilar as contemplated by the statute. We believe the timing of the review articulated here allows the agency to consider the most recent available information for considering whether an approved generic or licensed biosimilar is subject to Bona
(

Fide Marketing in accordance with key dates for the Negotiation Program or the submission of Part D plan bids, and thus we decline to alter or conduct more frequent reviews. We believe conducting more frequent reviews would be administratively infeasible at this time and altering the timing of the review to announce decisions earlier would result in less information being available for determining whether a generic drug was approved or a biosimilar was licensed and such generic or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing by the key dates previously articulated.

Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing §§ 429.125(d) and 429.135 as proposed, and we are finalizing the policy as proposed at § 429.130 with certain modifications as described later in this section. We also are clarifying as described in section II.B.6 of the proposed rule (

C. Negotiation Program Agreement (§§ 429.200 Through 429.210)
1. Entrance Into an Agreement With CMS (§ 429.200)
Section 1193(a) of the Act directs CMS to enter into agreements with manufacturers of selected drugs with respect to a price applicability period, by not later than February 28 following the selected drug publication date and provides for certain requirements of such agreements. With respect to initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, we implemented these requirements through guidance, including, for example, section 40.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028.
In section 1191(c)(1) of the Act, the Negotiation Program statute adopts the definition of “manufacturer” established in section 1847A(c)(6)(A) of the Act. Section 1193(a)(1) of the Act establishes that CMS will negotiate, or renegotiate, as applicable, an MFP with “the manufacturer” of the selected drug. To the extent that more than one entity meets the definition of manufacturer for a selected drug for purposes of initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, we would designate the entity that holds the NDA(s)/BLA(s) for the selected drug to be “the manufacturer” of the selected drug, hereinafter referred to as the “Primary Manufacturer” (as defined in proposed § 429.20). We would refer to any other entity that meets the statutory definition of manufacturer for a drug product included in the selected drug and that either: (1) is listed as a manufacturer in an NDA or BLA for the selected drug; or (2) markets the selected drug pursuant to an agreement with the Primary Manufacturer but is not listed on the NDA or BLA, as a Secondary Manufacturer (as defined in proposed § 429.20). Consistent with sections 1193(a)(4) and 1193(a)(5) of the Act, and as described in part 429, the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug that enters into a Negotiation Program Agreement must collect and report all necessary information applicable to the selected drug, inclusive of NDC-11s of the selected drug manufactured, marketed, controlled, or sold by a Secondary Manufacturer. Likewise, as the entity that is party to the Negotiation Program Agreement, the Primary Manufacturer will be solely responsible for compliance with all provisions of the Negotiation Program Agreement and will be accountable for ensuring compliance with respect to units of the selected drug manufactured, marketed, controlled, or sold by a Secondary Manufacturer.
With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 40.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, proposed § 429.200 establishes the Negotiation Program Agreement and the requirements of which a willing Primary Manufacturer is subject to upon executing a Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS. We would not enter into a Negotiation Program Agreement with any Secondary Manufacturer of a selected drug with respect to that selected drug. In accordance with section 1193(a) of the Act, as proposed in § 429.200(a)(1), the deadline for a Primary Manufacturer to enter into a Negotiation Program Agreement is 11:59 p.m. Pacific Standard Time (PST) on February 28 following the selected drug publication date with respect to the initial price applicability year for which the selected drug was selected for negotiation. We proposed at § 429.200(a)(2) that the negotiation period would begin on the earlier of two dates: (1) February 28 of the year of the selected drug publication date with respect to the initial price applicability year for which the selected drug was selected for negotiation; or, (2) the date that the Negotiation Program Agreement is fully executed by 11:59 p.m. PST. The Negotiation Program Agreement would be executed on the day that the last party to sign the Negotiation Program Agreement signs the Negotiation Program Agreement and would be in effect until terminated in accordance with proposed § 429.205(a).
We have established a model Negotiation Program Agreement in accordance with section 1193(a) of the Act. A Primary Manufacturer's obligation to make the MFP available applies during the entirety of the selected drug's price applicability period for which the manufacturer has a Negotiation Program Agreement in place. At proposed § 429.200(b), consistent with the provisions of such model Negotiation Program Agreement, we proposed to codify requirements that a willing Primary Manufacturer will agree to comply with upon execution of the Negotiation Program Agreement, namely: (1) to comply with all applicable requirements and conditions set forth in sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act and all applicable guidance and regulations, including in part 429, implementing those provisions and any changes to the Act that affect the Negotiation Program; We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed the requirement for Primary Manufacturers to report data of Secondary Manufacturers, such as NDCs, and expressed concerns regarding the distinction between Primary and Secondary Manufacturers as it relates to the Negotiation Program Agreement. One of these commenters stated the use of “manufactured, marketed, controlled, or sold” adds ambiguity to the scope of information to be reported. Another commenter recommended CMS allow the Primary Manufacturer or Secondary Manufacturer to determine which should enter into an agreement with CMS. A couple commenters recommended CMS clarify that Primary Manufacturers not be held accountable for noncompliance with the Negotiation Program Agreement based on third party actions outside the manufacturer's control.
Response:
As discussed in CMS' response in Negotiation Program Guidance and in the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, given that section 1193(a)(1) of the Act instructs CMS to negotiate with “the manufacturer” to arrive at the MFP for a given selected drug to which “the manufacturer” would provide access in accordance with the statute, and given that the term “the manufacturer” appears repeatedly throughout the statutory provisions establishing the Negotiation Program, the best statutory interpretation is to interpret the term “manufacturer” as a single entity for the negotiation process, responsible for negotiation of a single MFP for a given selected drug. Thus, in accordance with section 1193(a)(1) of the Act and other statutory references to “the manufacturer,” CMS will enter into a Negotiation Program Agreement with “the manufacturer” of a selected drug, where “the manufacturer” is the NDA/BLA holder. CMS has adopted the designations of “Primary Manufacturer” and “Secondary Manufacturer,” respectively, to establish a process to negotiate the maximum fair price with “the manufacturer” to align with the meaning of the statutory language and establish responsibilities and requirements of the Primary Manufacturer related to data collection and submission and MFP availability for the selected drug sold by the Secondary Manufacturer(s).
Consistent with sections 1193(a)(3) through 1193(a)(5) of the Act, and as described in part 429, the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug that enters into a Negotiation Program Agreement must collect and report all necessary information applicable to the selected drug, and must provide access to the MFP for the selected drug, inclusive of NDC-11s of the selected drug manufactured, marketed, controlled, or sold by a Secondary Manufacturer. The use of the “manufactured, marketed, controlled, or sold by a Secondary Manufacturer” language is intended to clarify and standardize the scope of the selected drug for which the Primary Manufacturer is responsible for data collection and submission and MFP availability.
Therefore, as the entity that is party to the Negotiation Program Agreement, in accordance with section 1193(a) of the Act, the Primary Manufacturer will be solely responsible for compliance with all provisions of the Negotiation Program Agreement and will be accountable for ensuring compliance with respect to units of the selected drug, inclusive of NDC-11s of the selected drug manufactured, marketed, controlled, or sold by a Secondary Manufacturer.
Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing § 429.200 as proposed, but with a clarifying change to § 429.200(c) to add “as defined in § 429.20” after Authorized Representative of the Primary Manufacturer.

With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, consistent with policies for implementation as described in section 40.7 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed at § 429.210(a) to codify that if any provision of the Negotiation Program Agreement is found to be invalid by a court of law with competent jurisdiction, the Negotiation Program Agreement would be construed in all respects as if any invalid or unenforceable provision(s) were eliminated, and without any effect on any other provision. In accordance with section 1193(a)(5) of the Act, consistent with policies for implementation as described in section 40.7 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed at § 429.210(c) to codify that if, after entering in a Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS, the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug transfers ownership of one or more NDAs or BLAs, as applicable, of a selected drug to another entity, the Primary Manufacturer remains responsible for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement associated with the transferred NDA(s) or BLA(s), including the requirement to provide access to the MFP as described in proposed subpart I, unless and until the Primary Manufacturer transfers all the NDAs or BLAs of the selected drug that it holds to an entity and such acquiring entity assumes responsibility as the new Primary Manufacturer. CMS proposed in § 429.210(c)(1)(ii) that the acquiring entity's assumption of responsibility as the new Primary Manufacturer must be evidenced by a novation to the transferring Primary Manufacturer's original Negotiation Program Agreement, which, as discussed later in this section, must be provided to CMS for review and approval at least 30 calendar days before the intended effective date of the transfer. In proposed § 429.210(c)(1)(ii), CMS also requires that the novation be signed by the transferring Primary Manufacturer and the acquiring entity and must include, at minimum, the legal name of the acquiring entity (which would be the new Primary Manufacturer), the effective date of the transfer of ownership of all transferred NDAs or BLAs of the selected drug that the transferring Primary Manufacturer holds and of the transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to the acquiring entity, a list of all transferring NDAs or BLAs of the selected drug, and agreement that the acquiring entity assumes all obligations and liabilities under the transferring Primary Manufacturer's Negotiation Program Agreement as the successor in interest.
We proposed at § 429.210(c)(2), that if the transferring Primary Manufacturer submits a novation agreement that meets the requirements proposed at § 429.210(c)(1)(ii), and is approved by CMS, the acquiring entity becomes the successor in interest to the transferring Primary Manufacturer's Negotiation Program Agreement and the Primary Manufacturer of the applicable selected drug as of the novation's effective date of the transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement.
We proposed at § 429.210(c)(1)(ii), that the transferring Primary Manufacturer must provide CMS with documentation of the intended transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to the acquiring entity, in the form of a novation, at least 30 calendar days before the intended effective date of any such transfer, for CMS review and approval. We encourage Primary Manufacturers to consult with CMS regarding their potential novation before submission of the novation to CMS at least 30 calendar days before the intended effective date of any such transfer.
We proposed at § 429.210(c)(3) that the transferring Primary Manufacturer remains responsible for any outstanding Negotiation Program rebate liabilities related to the Biosimilar Delay under section 1192(f) of the Act unless, and until, such liabilities are transferred to the acquiring entity as the new Primary Manufacturer.
If the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug transfers all NDAs or BLAs of the selected drug, and the acquiring entity assumes responsibility as the new Primary Manufacturer of the selected drug for purposes of the Negotiation Program, we recognize that this transfer of ownership could enable the original Primary Manufacturer to avoid potential excise tax liability for future sales, as well as render unnecessary the efforts by the original Primary Manufacturer to comply with the statutory suspension of the excise tax and the termination process for a Primary Manufacturer seeking to invoke the statutory suspension of the excise tax. We recognize that whether this transfer of ownership would have these impacts may depend on whether the transfer of the NDA(s) or BLA(s) was made to an entity that is not a related party and complied with relevant principles of tax law.

We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A couple commenters shared appreciation for the proposed novation agreement provision. A few commenters emphasized the importance of clarity regarding which entity is responsible for making the MFP available. A couple of these commenters recommended CMS implement specific safeguards to ensure continuity during a transfer in ownership. Some commenters expressed concern that the novation agreement may interfere with commercial transactions, goes beyond what is required by statute, and lacks specific standards, such as defined timelines and an appeals process. One of these commenters recommended new requirements be prospective only and not impact novation agreements for drugs selected for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback. We agree that promoting continuity during a transfer of ownership and ensuring clarity as to which entity is the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug responsible for compliance with program requirements are important for successful implementation of the Negotiation Program. Consistent with these goals, the novation agreement provision at § 429.210(c) is intended to ensure that all parties to the Negotiation Program Agreement as well as interested parties know who is the Primary Manufacturer and on which date all of the obligations and liabilities under the Negotiation Program Agreement transfer to an acquiring entity as the successor in interest, including the obligation to provide access to the MFP. Consistent with the Negotiation Program Guidance and as described in § 429.210(c), the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug remains responsible for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement associated with transferred NDA(s) or BLA(s) of the selected drug, including the requirement to provide access to the MFP, unless and until the Primary Manufacturer transfers all NDA(s) or BLA(s) of the selected drug that it holds to an entity and such acquiring entity assumes responsibility as the new Primary Manufacturer in accordance with § 429.210(c). If the requirements of § 429.210(c)(1) are met and, as set forth in § 429.210(c)(2), if the transferring Primary Manufacturer submits a novation agreement that meets the requirements proposed at § 429.210(c)(1)(ii), and is approved by CMS, the acquiring entity becomes the successor in interest to the transferring Primary Manufacturer's Negotiation Program Agreement and the Primary Manufacturer of the applicable selected drug as of the novation's effective date of the transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement.
A novation is a standard instrument by which the parties to an agreement may agree to update a party to such agreement to reflect an original signatory's successor in interest and memorialize the effective date on which the liabilities and obligations under the agreement transfer to the successor in interest. Accordingly, we disagree with commenters that § 429.210(c), which is consistent with the Negotiation Program Guidance and is intended to provide additional details related to the process by which such a novation would be effectuated, interferes with commercial transactions or goes beyond the statute. Section 1193(a) of the Act requires CMS to enter into an agreement with “the manufacturer” of a selected drug. If such Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug would like to transfer its NDA(s) or BLA(s) of the selected drug and its Negotiation Program Agreement, including the liabilities and obligations thereunder, to another entity, then § 429.210(c) provides the Primary Manufacturer with a process to do so in a manner that offers clarity and continuity, while ensuring there remains an agreement between CMS and “the manufacturer” in accordance with section 1193(a) of the Act.
Additionally, we have specified the requirements for such a novation agreement in § 429.210(c) and do not believe additional details are necessary. As discussed in the proposed rule, CMS encourages Primary Manufacturers to consult with CMS regarding their potential novation before submission to ensure that it meets the requirements of § 429.210(c), including specifying the effective date of such transfer and ensuring that the acquiring entity assumes all obligations and liabilities as the successor in interest. Consistent with the Negotiation Program Guidance, § 429.210(c)(1)(ii) requires at least 30 days' notice to ensure sufficient time for CMS, as the counterparty to the Negotiation Program Agreement, to review and, if approved, for all interested parties to prepare for the transfer of responsibilities, including the transferring and acquiring manufacturers, dispensing entities, Part B providers, and the MTF.
With respect to the commenter's recommendation regarding timing, we reiterate that these regulations are applicable to the Negotiation Program beginning with respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and will apply starting in 2029 with respect to the drugs selected for initial price applicability years of 2026, 2027, or 2028. Requirements for novation of the Negotiation Program Agreement for drugs selected for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 are currently set forth in guidance. As previously discussed, consistent with the Negotiation Program Guidance, § 429.210(c) is intended to provide additional details related to the process for transferring responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to an acquiring entity. Prior to 2029, we still encourage Primary Manufacturers to consult with CMS regarding a potential novation before the required submission of the novation to CMS at least 30 calendar days before the intended effective date of any such transfer to ensure that all requirements are met.
Comment:
A commenter recommended CMS require notice-and-comment rulemaking for substantive changes to the Negotiation Program Agreement, that such changes operate prospectively, that manufacturers receive at least 90-day notice, and that CMS identify whether future changes are binding, contractual, or non-binding.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's feedback. As described in § 429.210(b), CMS retains the authority to amend the Negotiation Program Agreement to reflect changes in law, regulations, or guidance as applicable. This provision is consistent with the existing Negotiation Program Agreement and is intended to ensure that the Negotiation Program Agreement remains up-to-date in the event of any future changes to law, regulation, or guidance, as applicable. Without such a provision, Negotiation Program Agreements between CMS and Primary Manufacturers would be at risk of including provisions that become out-of-date and inapplicable in the event of, for example, changes to the Negotiation Program statute. As stated in section IV(b) of the Negotiation Program Agreement, when possible, CMS will give the Primary Manufacturer at least 60 days' notice of any change to the Negotiation Program Agreement. We believe this timing is sufficient to provide the Primary Manufacturer with advance notice, but acknowledge that CMS may not be able to provide such notice in cases where changes in law, regulation, or guidance necessitate a more expeditious amendment to the Negotiation Program Agreement to ensure that the Negotiation Program Agreement accurately reflects the law.

We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters requested CMS share additional information regarding the procedures used for protecting confidential information and proprietary information included in the information submitted by Primary Manufacturers. A few commenters suggested CMS develop and publish data privacy and security protection protocols and safeguards for storage and limited access by personnel and, for example, a notification process to Primary Manufacturers of use or disclosure of confidential information outside of the Negotiation Program. A couple of these commenters recommended CMS continue to allow manufacturers to indicate which information submitted they deem to be confidential or proprietary. One of these commenters recommended that CMS indicate that other non-public information related to research and development, such as FDA applications and approvals.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comments on safeguarding data submitted by manufacturers. Consistent with our response to similar comments in Negotiation Program Guidance, we reaffirm our commitment to protect sensitive and confidential data submitted by Primary Manufacturers and continue to acknowledge the importance of data security. Upon establishment of the Negotiation Program, starting with procedures and data related to initial price applicability year 2026, we implemented internal controls to ensure the safeguarding of these data and to provide select CMS staff with access that appropriately aligns with their role and duties. We include later in this section the information previously provided in response to similar comments received for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028, and we believe this information is both adequate to detail the protocols and safeguards used in handling manufacturer-submitted data and, as discussed in further detail later in this section, is consistent with other CMS programs suggested by the commenters because of agency-wide CMS requirements. Over the course of the negotiation process, Primary Manufacturers will submit information to CMS via the CMS HPMS or, in some instances, an authorized secure platform such as Box. Box provides a secure way to share content and improve collaboration both within CMS and with outside entities. Box has been authorized as a High Federal Information and Security Modernization Act (FISMA) categorization, which means it can support the storage of all CMS data types, inclusive of PII, PHI, and agency sensitive information. Inviting collaborators through named email addresses of authorized individuals is the preferred method for this collaboration to help ensure the confidentiality and integrity of the content being shared. The CMS HPMS adheres to all applicable policies, procedures, controls, and standards required by HHS and CMS information security and privacy programs to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of manufacturer information and government information systems. The CMS HPMS system is the primary CMS system for exchange of information between CMS and Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Plans, and as such is designed to receive and keep confidential proprietary and commercially sensitive information. As required by CMS, the CMS HPMS integrates security into every aspect of the system development life cycle. The CMS HPMS is subject to the agency's Security Assessment and Authorization (SA&A) process, a rigorous methodology during which the system must demonstrate a sound and comprehensive information security posture. To achieve and maintain an Authority to Operate (ATO), the CMS HPMS routinely undergoes system penetration testing as well as a Security Control Assessment (SCA), where independent auditors perform a detailed assessment to ensure that the system's security controls meet the CMS Acceptable Risk Safeguards (ARS). An individual must apply for and obtain a CMS-issued user account and password to access the CMS HPMS. In addition to the CMS issued user ID and password, internal CMS staff must use an HHS identification badge (referred to as a “PIV card”) when accessing the website on the CMS network, while all users accessing the system from outside of the CMS network must use multi-factor authentication. The CMS HPMS further employs role-based access, ensuring that each user is granted access only to those functions required by their position. The CMS HPMS is hosted at a CMS approved cloud service provider. The

system is protected by a suite of firewall and intrusion detection services, including Akamai Content Delivery Network (CDN), which serves as an additional web application firewall that offers robust distributed denial of services protection and access control. The CMS HPMS utilizes a multizone architecture comprised of a presentation zone, an application zone, and a data zone, designed to provide further defense against security attacks. CMS will employ encryption at rest in the database for sensitive manufacturer data (for example, proprietary information, including trade secrets and confidential commercial or financial information) in addition to encryption in transit. The CMS HPMS adheres to the CMS Information Security Incident Handling Procedures, which are supplemented by the CMS HPMS Security Incident Handling Procedures. These documents outline the procedures for managing known or suspected security or privacy incidents, including, but not limited to, roles and responsibilities, escalation procedures, and guidelines for notifying impacted individuals or organizations. 4. Calculation of the 30-Day Equivalent Supply (§ 429.415)
Consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 60.2.1.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed at § 429.415 a methodology for determining the 30-day equivalent supply for a selected drug and therapeutic alternative(s), as applicable. The price per 30-day equivalent supply methodology facilitates the determination of a single ceiling price, and the negotiation of a single MFP, across dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug where units (for example, milligrams versus milliliters) and treatment regimens (for example, daily consumption of tablets versus monthly injections of solutions) differ. The proposed 30-day equivalent supply methodology also provides a standardized methodology to calculate a price for a standardized treatment duration for all dosage forms and strengths of selected drugs and its therapeutic alternative(s), if any; gives a more complete picture of beneficiary utilization when compared to a unit-based approach; and allows for comparison across the selected drug and the respective therapeutic alternative(s), if any.
We considered several alternatives, including those submitted through public comment for the Negotiation Program Guidance. The alternatives that we considered included a per-unit approach; price per course of treatment; consulting with the Primary Manufacturer of each selected drug to determine a methodology; and a flexible methodology to accommodate the clinical disease state and treatment landscape. We do not believe these alternatives provide for the standardization needed across different formulations, dosage forms, and strengths of a selected drug and its therapeutic alternative(s), if any, necessary to consider the selected drug as described in section 1194(e) of the Act and apply a single ceiling and a single MFP across dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug as required in section 1191(c)(3) of the Act. In addition, using a different methodology for selected drugs that are covered under Part D from selected drugs that are payable under Part B or for selected drugs that are both covered under Part D and payable under Part B could lead to inconsistencies and issues with comparing the selected drug to therapeutic alternative(s), if any.
Using a per-unit price approach, particularly for drugs payable under Part B, would not provide the standardization necessary to compare a selected drug with a therapeutic alternative nor to apply a single ceiling and a single MFP for a selected drug. This is because for drugs payable under Part B, unit type may differ both across HCPCS codes within a selected drug and across therapeutic alternatives payable under Part B, especially if a drug is both payable under Part B and covered under Part D. Using a price-per-course of treatment approach to creating a 30-day equivalent supply is time and resource intensive because treatment duration and dosing may be specific to individual patients and can also differ due to factors such as individual adherence, delays due to adverse events, or expected gaps due to adjuvant therapy or procedures. The option wherein we would work with the Primary Manufacturer on an individual methodology for each selected drug would be time and resource intensive and potentially not lead to a standardized approach and methodology that could be used for selected drugs and its therapeutic alternative(s), if any. This approach would also create inconsistency across selected drugs. We also believe that a 30-day equivalent supply methodology to accommodate the clinical disease state and treatment landscape, wherein we would use FDA labeling and treatment guidelines to tailor the methodology, would not capture patient-specific dosing regimens whereas the proposed approach using days between services approach would capture such patient-specific variation.
After considering these alternatives, we proposed at § 429.415(a)(1), that for selected drugs that are covered under Part D, we would use the methodology as described at
42 CFR 423.104(d)(2)(iv)(A)(2)
which relies on the “days' supply” field in PDE records to calculate the 30-day equivalent supply for each PDE record associated with the selected drug.
Consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 60.2.1.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed at § 429.415(a)(2) that CMS will use a different methodology to calculate the 30-day equivalent supply for selected drugs payable under Part B because Part B data does not contain a “days' supply” field like the PDE records for selected drugs that are covered under Part D. The methodology we proposed to use for calculating the 30-day equivalent supply for drugs payable under Part B involves calculating a “days between services” amount for each instance of Part B data associated with the selected drug. As an example of the approach proposed at § 429.415(a)(2)(ii), consider if the date of service for the first instance of Part B data is January 12, 2025, and the immediately subsequent instance of Part B data with the same active moiety/active ingredient has a date of service of March 12, 2025, then the first claim or record's “days between services” amount would be calculated as 59 days. If the beneficiary's third instance of Part B data was August 1, 2025, the number of “days between services” amount, for days between March 12, 2025, and August 1, 2025, would be calculated as 142 days for the second claim or record. The resulting “days between services” amounts in this example would be the same amount if the subsequent claim was a PDE record rather than an instance of Part B data. We proposed at § 429.415(a)(2)(i)(B) that the subsequent instance of Part B data or any PDE record be for a drug or biological product with the same active moiety/active ingredient identified as set forth at § 429.125(b), as the selected drug.

We discuss our proposed approach for drugs typically administered one time later in this section.
We understand that drugs payable under Part B often have recurrent administrations and variable dosing depending on body weight, indication, treatment phase, or response to treatment. The proposed “days between services” methodology addresses these concerns by using observed data from individual patients, which can potentially capture if providers are using patient-specific dosing regimens which can cause the variations. The “days between services” methodology would reduce the possibility of undervaluing the costs of drugs payable under Part B when attempting to determine the cost per 30-day equivalent supply.
Part B data is billed at the HCPCS code level, and some calculations using the 30-day equivalent supply of the selected drug require NDC-level 30-day equivalent supply amounts, so we proposed at § 429.415(a)(2)(iv) to allocate a portion of the 30-day equivalent supply calculated at the level of each HCPCS code to each NDC within the HCPCS code that includes a selected drug to calculate a 30-day equivalent supply at the NDC level. We proposed at § 429.415(a)(2)(v) steps to determine the total Part B 30-day equivalent supply at the NDC level.

to assign a value of “12” for the 30-day equivalent supply for drugs that are typically administered one time (for example, some vaccines and cancer therapies), by identifying HCPCS codes that generally have a median of one claim per calendar year. This value would apply to any selected drug and therapeutic alternative(s) of the selected drug, if any, for purposes of determining the initial offer as described in § 429.510, that are typically administered one time and payable under Part B. However, unlike for claims described in § 429.415(a)(2)(ii)(B), the reason for a lack of a second claim for these drugs is because these drugs are typically administered once for the lifetime of a patient. A “days between services” amount would therefore generally not be calculated for any claim associated with such drugs under the proposed methodology at § 429.415(a)(2)(ii) without this second claim. To calculate a single amount for the ceiling and for offers and counteroffers for the MFP under the methodologies proposed under this subpart E, a value for the 30-day equivalent supply needs to be assigned for these drugs in order to be included in the calculation. We proposed that assigning a value of “12” as a 30-day equivalent supply facilitates the necessary calculations in a manner that reasonably and accurately reflects such drugs usage. This approach is also consistent with our policy of developing a standardized methodology to calculate a price for all dosage forms and strengths of selected drugs and its therapeutic alternative(s).
We considered an alternative approach to the proposed 30-day equivalent supply methodology for drugs typically administered one time described previously, wherein we would use a price-per-administration or price per HCPCS billing unit for such drugs. Under this alternative approach, instead of calculating a 30-day equivalent supply and price per 30-day equivalent supply, we would instead calculate a price-per-administration or price-per-HCPCS billing unit for a selected drug. However, if such selected drug includes multiple HCPCS codes, calculating a single price per administration across HCPCS codes may not be appropriate (for example, if the existing price-per-administration differs significantly across HCPCS codes due to different treatment patterns). Calculating a price-per-administration would also not account for different volumes of the drug used in different instances of administration, which would conflict with our typical use of a payment limit per HCPCS billing unit for payment under Part B.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters suggested for CMS to use a unit of measure approach, rather than a 30-day equivalent supply, for calculation of a single ceiling price and MFP of a selected drug. One of these commenters suggested this approach only for selected drugs payable under Part B. A commenter suggested CMS adopt a lower unit of measure approach for drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D to promote accuracy, transparency, and operational feasibility. A commenter supported CMS' proposed 30-day equivalent supply methodology for calculating the ceiling and MFP because it uses a consistent and uniform approach. A commenter stated they appreciate CMS' proposed methodology and stated that it will be appropriate for many medications and they support the methodology in those cases, but they continue to have concerns if applied to all selected drugs. A commenter stated that a unit-based approach anchored to the price of the product would promote accuracy, transparency, and operational feasibility. Many commenters opposed or expressed concern with CMS' approach of using a 30-day equivalent supply to apply MFP across dosage forms and strengths, particularly with drugs with dosing variation across indications or dosing that involves titration, loading, weight-based, or severity-based variation. A few commenters recommended that CMS calculate the 30-day equivalent supply based on the dosing schedule provided in the prescribing information approved by the FDA (label-based) for selected drugs where dose quantity and schedule do not vary based on patient characteristics. Some commenters suggested CMS work with Primary Manufacturers of a selected drug and to come to an agreement with the Primary Manufacturer on the best approach to use for that selected drug in order to calculate the ceiling and negotiate a single MFP. Some commenters opposed the use of a 30-day equivalent supply, especially applying to drugs payable under Part B and using a “days between supply” methodology. A few commenters stated that Part B and Part D claims are fundamentally different and that comparing a 30-day equivalent supply across them produces unequal, untenable, distorted, and invalid comparisons. A commenter stated that nothing in statute requires CMS to calculate the MFP as a price per 30-day equivalent supply, but that statute specifically refers to a “unit” with respect to each drug or biologic and that this reference supports the use of a per-unit basis for when determining the MFP.
Response:
We appreciate these commenters for their feedback and suggestions. We appreciate the support
(
printed page 72257)
from the commenters regarding the 30-day equivalent supply methodology. Section 1196(a)(2) of the Act directs CMS to establish procedures to compute and apply agreed-upon MFPs across different dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of such drug. Section 1194(a)(1) of the Act directs CMS to develop and use a consistent methodology and process for negotiations that aim to achieve the lowest MFP for each selected drug. Consistent with these statutory directives, in the Negotiation Program proposed rule, and consistent with the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed to use a 30-day equivalent supply methodology as it allows CMS to calculate a price for a standardized treatment duration for all dosage forms and strengths of a given drug, and it allows comparison of such standardized prices across drugs. Using the price per 30-day equivalent supply to calculate this amount facilitates aggregation across dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug where units (for example, mg versus mL) and treatment regimens (for example, daily consumption of tablets versus monthly injections of solutions) differ. We believe that the 30-day equivalent supply methodology provides accurate and consistent calculations that can be used for most selected drugs and therapeutic alternative(s) and therefore supports CMS' ability to carry out sections 1194(a)(1) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. A 30-day equivalent supply methodology is the most transparent and operationally feasible approach.
We disagree with commenters advocating a unit-based methodology. We believe a 30-day equivalent supply creates a more direct comparison for drugs that have different dosage forms, strengths, and treatment regimens than a unit-based approach. We believe that a 30-day equivalent supply methodology also gives a more complete picture of beneficiary utilization. A unit-based approach is less preferable given that unit types may differ across HCPCS codes to which a selected drug payable under Part B is assigned and across therapeutic alternative(s) for a selected drug. We do not believe that a methodology based on the unit of measure assigned to the HCPCS code would work as well as the 30-day equivalent supply methodology because unit types can vary across HCPCS codes to which a selected drug is assigned, and across therapeutic alternatives, especially if the selected drug and/or a therapeutic alternative has both Part B and Part D utilization. Although Part B and Part D claims may differ from one another, a 30-day equivalent supply methodology allows a consistent methodology for comparison of a selected drug and therapeutic alternative(s) that have Part B only, Part D only, or both Part B and Part D utilization. A unit-based approach lacks the benefits of a 30-day equivalent supply methodology that are previously described.
In response to the commenters concerned with CMS' 30-day equivalent supply methodology being used for drugs with dosing variation across indications or dosing that involves titration, loading, weight-based, or severity-based variation and the commenters' recommendation that CMS calculate the 30-day equivalent supply based on dosing schedule provided in the prescribing information approved by the FDA (label-based) for selected drugs where dose quantity and schedule do not vary based on patient characteristics, using an approach to reference the FDA label rather than using actual real-world utilization data, we note that dosing schedules may vary individually for patients (both for patients taking Part B drugs as well as Part D drugs) and statute requires us to have a consistent process and methodology, and the 30-day equivalent supply approach is the most consistent methodology which can be used across selected drugs and which best reflects real-life patterns of use of the drugs among Medicare beneficiaries.
In response to the commenters' suggestion for CMS to work with Primary Manufacturers of a selected drug and to come to an agreement with the Primary Manufacturer on the best approach to use for that selected drug in order to calculate the ceiling and negotiate a single MFP, working with each Primary Manufacturer on an individual methodology for each selected drug would be time and resource intensive and potentially not lead to a standardized approach and methodology that could be used for other selected drugs and its therapeutic alternative(s), if any.
In response to the commenters opposed to the use of a 30-day equivalent supply applying to drugs payable under Part B and CMS using a “days between supply” methodology, we understand that drugs payable under Part B often have recurrent administrations and variable dosing depending on body weight, indication, treatment phase, or response to treatment. The proposed “days between services” methodology addresses these concerns by using observed data from individual patients, which can potentially capture if providers are using patient-specific dosing regimens which can cause the variations. The “days between services” methodology would reduce the possibility of undervaluing the costs of drugs payable under Part B when attempting to determine the cost per 30-day equivalent supply.
In response to the commenter referencing “unit” in statute, the meaning is defined at section 1191(c)(6) of the Act, which states that the term “unit” means, with respect to a drug or biological product, the lowest identifiable amount (such as a capsule or tablet, milligram of molecules or grams) of the drug or biological product that is dispensed or furnished, we disagree that this definition requires the use of a unit based approach to determining offers and counteroffers for selected drugs. For example, there is no reference to “unit” in section 1194(c) of the Act, which describes the determination of the ceiling for MFP. The only reference to “unit” within section 1194 of the Act, which describes the process for negotiation and renegotiating MFPs for selected drugs, is the requirement in section 1194(e)(1)(B) of the Act that we consider the “current unit costs of production and distribution” for a selected drug in determining offers and counteroffers. We do not believe this spare reference is best interpreted as requiring a unit-based approach, particularly when, as previously described, such an approach would be in tension with the statutory directives in sections 1194(a)(1) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act. Therefore, we disagree with the commenter's interpretation of having to use a unit-based methodology versus a 30-day equivalent supply methodology as proposed and finalized in § 429.415. As stated previously in this section, we believe that the 30-day equivalent supply methodology for selected drugs provides accurate and consistent calculations that can be used for most selected drugs and therapeutic alternative(s) and therefore supports our ability to carry out sections 1194(a)(1) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act.
Comment:
Many commenters provided feedback on CMS' plans to assign a value of “12” for the 30-day equivalent supply for drugs typically administered one time (for example, some vaccines and cancer therapies), whereby CMS would identify HCPCS codes that generally have a median of one claim per calendar year. Many commenters opposed CMS assigning a value of “12” for the 30-day equivalent supply for drugs typically administered
(
printed page 72258)
one time. Some commenters recommended for CMS to establish a more tailored and flexible methodology for these selected drugs. A commenter recommended that CMS create an “outlier policy” for selected drugs. A commenter encouraged CMS to continue to assess feedback from stakeholders on an adequate approach to use. A couple of commenters stated that they appreciate or understand CMS' goal of standardization but cautioned that this convention does not resolve the underlying problem in that it systematically misvalues therapies whose clinical benefit is decoupled from a monthly dosing and that the proposed methodology is unlikely to produce accurate results for many selected drugs. A commenter stated that regardless of the methodology, it is critically important that CMS use consistent inputs across all phases of the ceiling calculation, MFP determination, and application process.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their feedback. Assigning a value of “12” as a 30-day equivalent supply for drugs typically administered one time facilitates the necessary ceiling calculations in a manner that is reasonable and accurately reflects the drug's usage because when we look for utilization data, we look within a year's timeframe, so the value of “12” represents the maximum value possible in the calculation. Thus, the value of “12” for drugs typically administered one time accurately captures and covers a full year and allows comparison to drugs that may be administered multiple times within a year's timeframe. As a commenter suggested, this approach uses consistent inputs that allows for accurate and consistent ceiling calculations, negotiation of a single MFP, and application of the MFP.
As stated in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36277
), this approach is also consistent with our policy of developing a standardized methodology to calculate a price for all dosage forms and strengths of selected drugs and its therapeutic alternative(s). We considered an alternative approach to the proposed 30-day equivalent supply methodology for drugs typically administered one time described previously, wherein we would use a price-per-administration or price per HCPCS billing unit for such drugs. Under this alternative approach, instead of calculating a 30-day equivalent supply and price per 30-day equivalent supply, we would instead calculate a price-per-administration or price-per-HCPCS billing unit for a selected drug. However, if such selected drug includes multiple HCPCS codes, calculating a single price per administration across HCPCS codes may not be appropriate (for example, if the existing price-per-administration differs significantly across HCPCS codes due to different treatment patterns). Using this approach could preclude us from comparison with therapeutic alternatives, including those not payable under Part B or those that may be taken daily. Calculating a price-per-administration would also not account for different volumes of the drug used in different instances of administration, which would conflict with our typical use of a payment limit per HCPCS billing unit for payment under Part B.
We appreciate the commenters' suggestion to establish a more tailored methodology, the commenter's recommendation to assess feedback from stakeholders on an adequate approach to use, and the commenter's suggestion to create an “outlier policy.” We are still considering an outlier policy for future rulemaking and encourages stakeholder input, suggestions, and feedback.
Final Decision:

5. Determination of the Sum of the Plan-Specific Enrollment Weighted Amounts (§ 429.420)
Section 1194(c)(2) of the Act describes the calculation for the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amount for prescription drug plan or an MA-PD plan with respect to a covered Part D drug for purposes of section 1194(c)(1)(B)(i) of the Act. Consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 60.2.2.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed at § 429.420(b) to use a 30-day equivalent supply methodology to calculate the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts.
Plan sponsors report Part D PDE data to CMS at the NDC-11 level and report direct and indirect remuneration data to CMS at the NDC-11 level in the annual Detailed Direct and Indirect Remuneration (DIR) Report. As directed by statute, and proposed at § 429.420(a) and (b)(1), we proposed to use plan sponsors' reported Part D PDE data and DIR data for the year that is 4 years prior to the initial price applicability year of the selected drug, which would be the most recent year for which data would be available, for purposes of determining the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts for selected drugs that are covered under Part D. As proposed at § 429.420(a), we would include all Part D plans found in the PDE data that meet the inclusion criteria described in the definition of “total expenditures under Part D” at proposed § 429.20. We intend to identify Part D plans based on the combination of the Part D contract identifier and the plan benefit package identifier.
We proposed at § 429.420(a)(1) to use the list of NDC-11s of the selected drug (as determined in proposed § 429.100(c) and discussed in section II.B.1. of this final rule), to determine which NDC-11s of the selected drug are included in this ceiling calculation.
We note that because we would not have PDE data for Part D plans in the following circumstances, such Part D plans would, by definition, be excluded from the calculation proposed at § 429.420(b):
Plans that have no utilization of the selected drug; and
Plans that have no enrollment for the year that is 4 years prior to the initial price applicability year of the selected drug.

We proposed at § 429.420(b)(1) to use the most recent year for which all data is available, which is generally the year that is 4 years prior to the initial price applicability year with respect to which the selected drug was selected for negotiation. To determine which month(s) of enrollment to include in our analysis, we conducted an analysis of monthly Part D plan enrollment changes during 2022 and determined that monthly enrollment changes were the lowest from November to December, so we proposed at § 429.420(b)(5) that December would be the most stable

Comment:

A commenter recommended that when rebate and direct and indirect remuneration data are used as inputs to the MFP that CMS should neutralize the percentage-of-price component so that the calculated MFP reflects the actual net acquisition cost and not a figure inflated by compensation that rises with the gross price. A commenter recommended for CMS to explain, with specificity, the data that manufacturers may request to validate the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts, what confidentiality protections would apply to any such disclosure, and what recourse exists if a manufacturer identifies a discrepancy that it cannot fully substantiate without access to the plan level data.

6. Determination of the Payment Amount Under Section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act (§ 429.425)
Section 1194(c)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act provides for the use of an amount equal to the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) for a selected drug that is payable under Part B for the year prior to the year of the selected drug publication date with respect to the initial price applicability year for the selected drug. Consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 60.2.2.2 of the Negotiation Program Guidance and in accordance with section 1194(c)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act, CMS proposed at § 429.425 to calculate for a selected drug payable under Part B and paid under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act, an amount equal to the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act for the year prior to the year of the selected drug publication date with respect to the initial price applicability year for that drug or biological product (that is, 3 years prior to the initial price applicability year of the selected drug). We interpret “payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4)” under section 1194(c)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act to refer to an amount calculated for such year calculated using the methodology specified in section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act which is, for single source drugs and biological products, separately calculating the annual ASP and WAC described at proposed § 429.425(a)(2)(i) and taking the lesser of, as proposed at § 429.425(a)(2)(ii). When calculating this amount, we proposed at § 429.425(a)(1) to use the list of NDC-11s of the selected drug (as determined in proposed § 429.100(c) and discussed in section II.B.1. of this final rule).
Additionally, as directed by statute, we proposed to calculate the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act by using the quarterly reported ASP and WAC data for the calendar year 3 years prior to the initial price applicability year of the selected drug, for the purpose of determining the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act. This calculated amount proposed in § 429.425(a)(2) would apply for only selected drugs that are payable under Part B and paid according to section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act. When calculating the payment amount under 1847A of the Act for each HCPCS code we would use NDC-level data from the ASP Data Collection System (that is, the ASP portal). ASP data are required to be submitted to the ASP portal within 30 days after the close of each calendar quarter, and CMS uses that data to calculate payment amounts under section 1847A of the Act for the subsequent quarter, which results in a two-quarter lag between the quarter of ASP data used and when the Part B payment limits apply. We would apply this two-quarter lag when conducting all relevant calculations of the ceiling and application of MFP that rely on data from the ASP portal. For example, when calculating the annual ASP to determine the “payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4)” of the Act for calendar year 2028, CMS would use ASP portal data reported for the third quarter of 2027 through the second quarter of 2028.

We proposed at § 429.425(a)(2)(i) to convert the quarterly ASP and WAC reported by the manufacturer for the year as set forth in § 429.425(a) for each NDC-11 for a selected drug that is associated with a HCPCS code to an annual calendar year ASP or WAC amount for each HCPCS code. We proposed to do so by taking an average of the reported ASP or WAC amounts for the HCPCS code across all four quarters of such calendar year, weighted by the total number of billing units in the Part B data within that HCPCS code each quarter.
We proposed at § 429.425(a)(2)(i)(A), that if the total number of billing units in the Part B data within the HCPCS code are zero for a given quarter, we would assign that quarter the lowest positive total units from among the other quarters in the same calendar year for that HCPCS code.
We proposed at § 429.425(a)(2)(i)(B), that for each of the separate ASP and WAC calculations, if the reported price is negative, zero, or missing for all applicable NDC-11s assigned to the HCPCS code in a given quarter for the calendar year as set forth in § 429.405(a), we would exclude that quarter from the applicable calculation.
We proposed at § 429.425(a)(2)(i)(C), that if the WAC reported to the ASP portal is negative, zero, or missing for all applicable NDC-11s assigned to the HCPCS code for all four quarters for the calendar year as set forth in § 429.405(a), then we would use the WAC reported by the Primary Manufacturer of the selected drug to CMS under section 1194(e)(1) of the Act as described in § 429.505(b)(2)(v).

Therefore, we believe the exclusion of self-administered drugs from the determination of the payment amount for selected drugs under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act is appropriate since self-administered drugs are not factored into payment amounts under section 1847A(b)(4) for drugs that are not selected for negotiation.

We proposed at § 429.425(b), that the sequestration payment adjustment is not applied to the amount described under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act. 7. Determination of the Combined Part B and Part D Amount (§ 429.430)
Section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act provides for the calculation of “an amount,” in the singular, under such subparagraph for each selected drug. Section 1194(c)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act then specifies the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act as an amount to be used under section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act for selected drugs that are payable under Part B and paid under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act and separately specifies at section 1194(c)(1)(B)(i) of the Act the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts as an amount to be used for under section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act for selected drugs covered under Part D. It does not specify that we should select only one of these two different amounts when calculating the amount for under section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act for a selected drug is both covered under Part D and payable under Part B.
For such selected drugs, we interpret section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act, which states “. . . an amount equal to . . .” when referring to calculating a single amount under such subparagraph for each selected drug, to mean that we should calculate an amount that captures both the payment amount under section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act and the sum of the plan-specific enrollment weighted amounts, where both amounts are available for such drug (that is, where such drug is payable under Part B and is paid according to section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act). Our proposed interpretation gives effect to the entirety of section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act for such drugs when both amounts described thereunder are applicable. In contrast, we do not believe section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act is best read as permitting the selection and use of just one of the two applicable amounts under such subparagraph. Such subparagraph offers no criteria by which CMS would choose which of the amounts described thereunder to apply for selected for which both amounts are applicable. Moreover, we do not believe section 1194(c)(1) of the Act is best read as permitting CMS to use only the amount described in section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act for such drugs, because both amounts described under section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act are applicable to such drugs and CMS can calculate a single amount that accounts for both such amounts.

Section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii) of the Act requires that for initial price applicability year 2027 and subsequent years, that the lower of the average non-FAMP amounts described in sections 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) and 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act is used as the average non-FAMP amount. Section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act describes the second amount as the average non-FAMP for such drug for the year prior to the selected drug publication date with respect to such initial price applicability year. Consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 60.2.3 of the Negotiation Program Guidance and in accordance with section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii) of the Act, we proposed at § 429.435(a) to use the methodology and comparison described to determine the lower of the two applicable non-FAMP amounts and apply the applicable percent described in section 1194(c)(3) of the Act.

Consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 60.2.3 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed at § 429.435(a)(2)(ii) to use the same methodology for calculating the average non-FAMP for the calendar year 3 years prior to the initial price applicability year of the selected drug as used for the calculation proposed at § 429.435(a)(1)(ii) through (iv) for calendar year 2021, noting that the set of NDCs used to calculate the annual average non-FAMP calculation for each may differ.
