9. Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs (§ 429.440)
a. Definitions
In proposed § 429.440, we proposed to codify the following definitions applicable to § 429.440 based on policies detailed in this final rule.
(1) “Part B 2021 Manufacturer”
We proposed to define “Part B 2021 Manufacturer” to mean the NDA holder or the BLA holder for the qualifying single source drug on December 31, 2021.
(2) “Part D 2021 Manufacturer”
We proposed to define “Part D 2021 Manufacturer” as the entity that either (1) had a Medicare Coverage Gap Discount Program (CGDP) Agreement under section 1860D-14A of the Act in effect for the qualifying single source drug on December 31, 2021, or (2) had an arrangement whereby the manufacturer's labeler codes were listed on another manufacturer's Medicare CGDP Agreement, consistent with section 1860D-14A of the Act, in effect on December 31, 2021.
(3) “Part B 2021 Manufacturer and Its Controlled Group”
We proposed to define “Part B 2021 Manufacturer and its controlled group” as comprising all persons that, as of December 31, 2021, were treated as a single employer under subsection (a) or (b) of section 52 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 with the Part B 2021 Manufacturer.
(4) “Part D 2021 Manufacturer and its controlled group”.
We proposed to define “Part D 2021 Manufacturer and its controlled group” as comprising all persons that, as of December 31, 2021, were treated as a single employer under subsection (a) or (b) of section 52 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 with the Part D 2021 Manufacturer and had a CGDP Agreement in effect on December 31, 2021.
Final Decision:
We did not receive public comments on these definitions, and therefore, we are finalizing § 429.440(a) as proposed.
b. Implementation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs
Section 1192(d)(2) of the Act established the Small Biotech Exception (SBE), which states that a negotiation eligible drug shall not include, with respect to initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028, a qualifying single source drug that meets either the criteria at section 1192(d)(2)(A)(i) or section 1192(d)(2)(A)(ii) of the Act. With respect to initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, CMS implemented the requirements set forth in section 1192(d)(2) of the Act for a qualifying single source drug to be determined a Small Biotech Drug and therefore eligible for the SBE through guidance, including for example, section 30.2.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028.
Section 1194(d) of the Act requires that for a selected drug that is a qualifying single source drug that meets the requirements set forth in section 1192(d)(2) of the Act to be determined a Small Biotech Drug, and with respect to which the first initial price applicability year of the price applicability period with respect to such drug is 2029 or 2030, CMS will not offer or agree to a counteroffer for an MFP that is lower than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. To fulfill the statutory obligation at section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the Act, which states that reference to the first initial price applicability year of the price applicability period with respect to such drug shall be treated as the first initial price applicability year of such period for which the maximum fair price established pursuant to renegotiation applies, drugs selected for renegotiation also would be eligible to be considered for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs described in section 1194(d). Section 1194(d) of the Act states that the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs shall be equal to 66 percent of the average non-FAMP for such drug for 2021 (or, in the case that there is not an average non-FAMP available for such drug for 2021, for the first full year following the market entry for such drug), increased by the percentage increase in the CPI-U from September 2021 (or December of such first full year following the market entry), as applicable, to September of the year prior to the year of the selected drug publication date with respect to such initial price applicability year.

We would first determine if an adjusted ceiling is needed by calculating the unadjusted ceiling as described at proposed § 429.410(b) or the renegotiated unadjusted ceiling as described in § 429.620(b) (as applicable), as well as the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech drugs as described at proposed § 429.440(b)(3), and then would determine if the unadjusted ceiling is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. If the unadjusted ceiling is greater than or equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, then this ceiling would apply, and we would not offer or accept a counteroffer for an MFP that is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs or greater than the ceiling for the selected drug. If, however, such ceiling is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, we would calculate an adjusted ceiling, as described in proposed § 429.440(b)(4)(i) or (ii), as applicable. To calculate an adjusted ceiling, we proposed in § 429.440(b)(4)(i) that, for purposes of determining the potential ceiling amount described under section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act, rather than selecting the lower of the average non-FAMP available for such drug in 2021 (or the first full year following market entry for such drug if there is not a non-FAMP for such drug or an average non-FAMP cannot be calculated), as described in section 1194(c)(1)(C)(i) or section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act and proposed § 429.435(a)(1) or § 429.620(b) (as applicable), or the average non-FAMP for such drug for the year prior to the selected drug publication date, as described in section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act and proposed § 429.435(a)(2) or § 429.620(b) (as applicable), to calculate the lower amount of the applicable percent of the average non-FAMP, as described in proposed § 429.410(b) (or § 429.620(b) for both non-FAMPs as applicable), we would only consider the average non-FAMP for such drug for the prior year to the selected drug publication date (that is, the amount described in section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act). Therefore, the adjusted ceiling proposed in § 429.440(b)(4)(i) would determine the ceiling as described in § 429.410(b) (or § 429.620(b) as applicable) except that the lower amount of the applicable percent of the average non-FAMP, as proposed in § 429.435 (or § 429.620(b) as applicable), would consider only the average non-FAMP for such drug for the prior year to the selected drug publication date, as described in § 429.435(a)(2) (or § 429.620(b), as applicable). We believe that removing the average non-FAMP available for such drug in 2021 from the calculation of the lower amount of the applicable percent of the average non-FAMP allows for the implementation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs while preserving the ceiling calculation, giving effect to both provisions, and is the most appropriate and narrowly tailored way to reconcile cases where the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs exceeds the ceiling for a selected drug, as the average non-FAMP available for such drug in 2021 may be in direct tension when calculating the ceiling and the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, due to the applicable percent being applied in contradictory ways in the ceiling and the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. If this adjusted ceiling is greater than or equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, then such adjusted ceiling would be used as the ceiling for the negotiation
(
printed page 72267)
between CMS and the Primary Manufacturer, and we would not offer or agree to a counteroffer for an MFP that is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs or greater than this adjusted ceiling for the selected drug.
If this adjusted ceiling is still below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, then, as described in proposed § 429.440(b)(4)(ii), we would raise the ceiling to be equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. We believe that raising the ceiling to be equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs appropriately balances the statutory requirements to establish a ceiling for a selected drug while ensuring the negotiation process also gives full effect to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs provision at section 1194(d) of the Act. We note that the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs provision applies only with respect to negotiations and renegotiations that occur for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030 for eligible drugs, and it would not apply to any subsequent renegotiations of drugs selected for renegotiation with respect to an initial price applicability year after initial price applicability year 2030. We considered disregarding the ceiling entirely, but we do not believe this approach would align with the statutory requirements for both a ceiling and a Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. We also considered using the amount calculated in section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act (as proposed in § 429.410(b)(1) or § 429.620(b)) as the sole amount for the ceiling, however we do not believe this approach would align with the statutory requirements to apply an applicable percent in section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act, and would result in a ceiling that would not distinguish between a short-monopoly drug, a long-monopoly drug, and an extended-monopoly drug (beginning in initial price applicability year 2030). In accordance with section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act, because the ceiling and the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for a selected drug would equal the same price, we would only offer or agree to a counteroffer for an MFP that is equal to such price. We believe that this stepwise approach addresses circumstances in which the ceiling is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs while maintaining the integrity of the negotiation process and implementing the statutory responsibility to not offer or accept a counteroffer of an MFP that is above the ceiling or below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs.
As proposed in § 429.440(b)(5), if a Primary Manufacturer submits an application for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, we would provide a notice in writing to the Primary Manufacturer, alongside the calculation information provided as set forth in § 429.445(a), which would include: a determination of whether the selected drug is a Small Biotech Drug; and, if the selected drug is eligible for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, the calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs as proposed in § 429.440(b)(3) (or adjusted ceiling, if applicable, as proposed in § 429.440(b)(4)). We proposed in § 429.440(b)(6) to allow a Primary Manufacturer that believes in good faith that CMS has made an error in calculations pertaining to the calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, as proposed in § 429.440(b)(3), or the adjusted ceiling, if applicable, calculated for a drug that receives the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, as proposed in § 429.440(b)(4), to submit a Suggestion of Error as proposed in § 429.445(c).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters offered feedback on our proposal for a stepwise approach to determining an adjusted ceiling in circumstances in which we determine that the statutory ceiling for a selected drug that qualifies for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. While these commenters acknowledged the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs provision can conflict with provisions governing the ceiling, these commenters expressed differing views over how we should resolve this conflict. Many commenters proposed eliminating the ceiling in cases where the ceiling determined under proposed § 429.410(b) (negotiation) or § 429.620(b) (renegotiation) is lower than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Some commenters rationalized that Congress did not intend for any statutory ceiling to apply to long-monopoly and extended-monopoly drugs that qualify for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs because, for such drugs, it is mathematically impossible to calculate a ceiling that exceeds the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Other commenters maintained that the proposal for a stepwise approach in these circumstances is arbitrary and capricious because they contended that the “adjusted” ceiling has no basis in statute. A couple of commenters stated that the use of “or” in section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act's prohibition against offering or agreeing to a counteroffer for any MFP that exceeds the ceiling
or
is less than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for the selected drug allows for CMS to apply either the ceiling, or as applicable, the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, effectively allowing these provisions to operate as “separate constraints.” Further, a few commenters stated that the proposed adjusted ceiling calculation undermines the negotiation process for Small Biotech Drugs. Specifically, these commenters contended that in instances in which the adjusted ceiling would be equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, small biotech manufacturers would be obligated to submit data based on factors described under section 1194(e) of the Act and comply with the Negotiation Program Agreement, which would impose substantial and unnecessary burden on both manufacturers and CMS, even though CMS would have “no need” to consider data submitted because there would only be one possible MFP available for consideration.
On the other hand, a couple of commenters suggested that for circumstances in which the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs is above the statutory ceiling for a Small Biotech Drug, CMS should instead raise the ceiling to be equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, which the commenters contended gives effect to the provision described under section 1194(b)(1) of the Act (“aim to achieve the lowest maximum fair price”). Finally, another commenter suggested CMS revise its proposal for a stepwise approach under which it would disregard all non-FAMP-based amounts under section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act and instead use the specified amount under section 1194(c)(1)(B) of the Act, as applicable, as the ceiling.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback, including suggestions for alternative approaches to implementation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. We proposed the stepwise approach described in proposed § 429.440(b)(4) for selected drugs that qualify for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to address the limited, although possible, scenario in which the ceiling determined under proposed § 429.410(b) (negotiation) or § 429.620(b) (renegotiation) is lower than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. For example, in cases where a long-monopoly drug is selected for negotiation in IPAY 2029 and is determined to be a Small Biotech Drug, the ceiling amount determined under
(
printed page 72268)
section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act equals 40 percent of the drug's non-FAMP in 2021, which would be less than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs (66 percent of the drug's non-FAMP in 2021). Our proposed stepwise approach would only be triggered in these (and similar) circumstances (that is, where the unadjusted ceiling calculation as described in proposed § 429.410(b) (negotiation) or § 429.620(b) (renegotiation) is less than that of the Temporary Floor calculated under proposed § 429.440(b)(3) for such Small Biotech Drug). Our proposed stepwise approach would not apply for a selected drug that qualifies for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs in initial price applicability years 2029 or 2030 for which these conditions are not met, nor for a selected drug that does not qualify for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs in initial price applicability years 2029 or 2030.
We disagree that the proposed stepwise approach exceeds the agency's authority or is otherwise inconsistent with statute. Instead, our proposal reflected our intention to give effect to all the relevant statutory provisions governing the determination of offers and counteroffers and negotiation of an MFP for a selected drug. Section 1194(b)(1) of the Act requires the development and use of a consistent methodology and process, in accordance with the requirements set forth in section 1194(b)(2) of the Act, for negotiation that “aims to achieve the lowest maximum fair price.” Section 1194(b)(2) of the Act provides for a process that requires an initial offer for the MFP to the manufacturer and allows for an exchange of subsequent offers and counteroffers. Moreover, section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act directs that CMS shall not offer (or agree to a counteroffer for) an MFP for a selected drug that exceeds the ceiling determined under section 1194(c) of the Act for the selected drug and year; or, as applicable, is less than the floor determined under section 1194(d) of the Act. In turn, section 1194(c) of the Act requires that an MFP negotiated under section 1194 of the Act for a selected drug, with respect to the first initial price applicability year of the price applicability period with respect to such drug, shall not exceed the lower of the amounts under section 1194(c)(1)(B) or section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act. Section 1194(d) of the Act expressly directs that for certain qualifying selected drugs, and with respect to initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030, the MFP for such drugs shall not be below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs as provided under that subsection.
Our stepwise approach, as finalized in this rule, reflects our interpretation that section 1194(d) of the Act, which provides for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, is not best read as eliminating the rest of the statutory requirements in section 1194 of the Act, as described previously. Instead, our policy reflects our interpretation that the possibility of a direct conflict, with respect to certain drugs as previously described, between the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, determined under section 1194(d) of the Act, and the potential ceiling amount is best resolved by removing all non-FAMP (as identified under sections 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) and 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II)) per our updated stepwise approach, as described in more detail later in this section.
Similarly, we believe that the alternative recommended by commenters that would eliminate the ceiling altogether for Small Biotech Drugs would fail to give effect to all statutory provisions and is inconsistent with the IRA's text, structure, and purpose. We disagree with commenters suggesting that the use of “or” in section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act's prohibition against offering or agreeing to a counteroffer for any maximum fair price that exceeds the ceiling
or
is less than the floor for the selected drug is best read as requiring CMS to ignore the statutory ceiling provisions for Small Biotech Drugs. We believe that the statutory directive that the MFP cannot be greater than the ceiling
or
less than the floor is more naturally and best read as accounting for the simple proposition that because a ceiling cannot be below a floor, a single offer or counteroffer cannot both “exceed the ceiling”
and
be “less than the floor.” Accordingly, we believe section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act's use of “or” is best read as effectuating two distinct prohibitions on offer amounts. Moreover, the commenters' suggestion to read section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act as to eliminate the ceiling provisions with respect to Small Biotech Drugs would also fail to give effect to the separate prohibition in section 1194(c) of the Act against an MFP exceeding the amount determined under such subsection; there is nothing in section 1194(d) of the Act to suggest that the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs should be applied in place of that prohibition. Accordingly, when read in light of the overall structure and purpose of the Negotiation Program statute, including the establishment of a ceiling for MFP negotiations and renegotiations to establish a maximum price above which an MFP cannot be agreed to, we disagree that section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act is best read as implicitly nullifying the applicability of the ceiling for Small Biotech Drugs.
For the same reasons, we also disagree that section 1194(b)(2)(F) of the Act can be read as removing the ceiling for selected drugs that qualify for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs and whose floor is greater than the applicable ceiling, but not for others that qualify for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Under such a reading, certain Small Biotech Drugs that have longer periods since the date of approval or licensure would be more likely to qualify for an otherwise unique and unstated exception where their negotiations would have no limitations on the maximum MFP that can be agreed upon. Such a reading conflicts with the ordinary operation of the ceiling provisions, particularly the ceiling amounts determined under section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act, which provide for lower ceiling amounts for selected drugs with longer periods since the date of approval or licensure. We do not believe there is any indicia in the statute that in circumstances where the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs applies, the statute is best read as operating otherwise.
With respect to the comments that the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs provision is designed to be mathematically impossible to calculate the ceiling for long-monopoly and extended-monopoly drugs at a numerical value that exceeds the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, we agree that in limited circumstances with respect to certain selected drugs qualifying for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, the potential ceiling amount determined under section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act would not exceed the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs determined under section 1194(d) of the Act. However, we disagree that this possibility for a limited set of potential selected drugs is best read as evidence that the statute was drafted to implicitly eliminate the ceiling for such drugs. We believe it would be more likely that such a requirement, which would rewrite much of section 1194 of the Act with respect to a limited and specific set of selected drugs, including eliminating section 1194(c) of the Act for such drugs, would be made explicit. As previously discussed, we believe that the interpretation suggested by the commenters that the statute intends for long-monopoly and extended-monopoly
(
printed page 72269)
selected drugs to be negotiated without a ceiling would be contrary to the statute's typical treatment of long-monopoly and extended-monopoly drugs, which are generally subject to lower ceilings.
For the reasons provided previously and in the proposed rule, we disagree with commenters' suggestions not to apply the ceiling otherwise determined under § 429.410(b) or § 429.620(b) when it is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. However, we agree with the commenter's suggestion regarding the treatment of the other non-FAMP amount described in section 1194(c)(1)(C) of the Act in the adjusted ceiling calculations. We believe that in the event that removing from consideration the potential ceiling amount described in section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act (that is, the non-FAMP for 2021 or first year after market entry) does not result in a ceiling that exceeds the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, it is appropriate to include a subsequent step that removes the potential ceiling amount described in section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act (that is, the non-FAMP for the year prior to the selected drug publication date). While our proposal was narrowly tailored to the amount described in section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act, as that amount is determined using the same non-FAMP amount as the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, we note that the potential ceiling amount described under section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act may create a similar conflict. Accordingly, we believe we can better resolve such potential conflicts for more Small Biotech Drugs, while preserving a negotiation process subject to a ceiling as described in section 1194(c) of the Act, by incorporating into our stepwise approach an additional step that addresses the potential ceiling amount described in section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act. We believe this revision is consistent with the intent of our proposed stepwise approach, in that it aims to address the direct conflict between the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs and the ceiling determined under § 429.410(b), while still both providing the Small Biotech Drug the benefit of the floor under section 1194(d) of the Act and preserving a negotiation process subject to a ceiling as described in section 1194(c) of the Act.
In particular, we will consider the treatment of non-FAMP in two distinct stages before determining whether to exclude it from the ceiling calculation. At § 429.440(b)(4)(i), we will exclude the average non-FAMP in 2021 identified under section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(I) of the Act from the ceiling determination made under § 429.410(b) or § 429.620(b), as applicable, with respect to such selected drug. Under new § 429.440(b)(4)(i), if the resulting amount is equal to or above the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, then we will apply that amount as the adjusted ceiling, notwithstanding § 429.410(b) or § 429.620(b). However, under new § 429.440(b)(4)(ii), if the resulting amount determined under § 429.440(b)(4)(i) is lower than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, we will then, notwithstanding § 429.410(b) or § 429.620(b), exclude the average non-FAMP for the year preceding the selected drug publication with respect to the first initial price applicability period for which the drug is being negotiated, or, as applicable, the most recent year prior for which data is available, as set forth in § 429.435(a)(2), identified under section 1194(c)(1)(C)(ii)(II) of the Act, from the ceiling determination made under § 429.410(b) or § 429.620(b), as applicable. Under new § 429.440(b)(4)(ii), if the resulting amount as determined under paragraph § 429.440(b)(4)(ii) is equal to or above the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs established in § 429.440(b)(3), we will apply that amount, as applicable, as the adjusted ceiling. Lastly, in § 429.440(b)(4)(iii) (previously § 429.440(b)(4)(ii) in the proposed rule), we stated that the adjusted ceiling will equal the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs established in § 429.440(b)(3), notwithstanding § 429.410(b) or § 429.620(b), if the resulting amount determined under § 429.440(b)(4)(ii) is still below the Temporary Floor.
Finally, we also disagree with the proposed alternative to raise the ceiling as otherwise determined under § 429.410(b) or § 429.620(b) to be equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech drugs in lieu of a stepwise approach. We believe our stepwise approach—as revised based on public comments received—is consistent with the text, structure, and purpose of the statute in that it provides a methodology for calculating the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for negotiations, allows CMS and the Primary Manufacturer to conduct negotiations subject to a ceiling as described in section 1194(c) of the Act, and provides for the limitations on an offer or counteroffer amount in accordance with sections 1194(b)(2)(F) and 1194(c) of the Act. The approach recommended by the commenters would effectively limit the offers which CMS could consider or make to an amount equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs in every instance in which the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs exceeded the amount determined to be the ceiling under section 1194(c) of the Act. Consistent with our response to commenters suggesting that CMS eliminate the ceiling for selected drugs that qualify for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs when the ceiling is lower than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, we disagree that the statute is best read as requiring CMS to so limit the negotiation process provided under section 1194 of the Act in every instance because, in limited circumstances, there may be conflict between the ceiling provisions and the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Rather, we believe our stepwise approach, as revised, would give effect to as much of section 1194 of the Act as possible. Under our stepwise approach, the applicable ceiling would be raised to equal the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs only in instances in which the conflict between the amounts provided under sections 1194(c)(1)(C) and 1194(d) of the Act cannot be resolved; in instances where the conflict can be resolved, the resulting ceiling would be higher than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Finally, we note our stepwise approach, consistent with section 1194(d) of the Act, would be limited to initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern about CMS' formula for calculating total expenditures for the purposes of determining eligibility for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. This commenter stated that CMS should limit the Total Expenditure calculation of the 80 percent threshold to the manufacturer's qualifying single source drugs and should exclude non-innovator and multi-source drugs. They note that including such drugs in the denominator used for the Total Expenditure calculation may distort the result and potentially disqualify a small biotech manufacturer from being eligible for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Additionally, this commenter recommended CMS consider a full year of sales to more fully capture a manufacturer's total Medicare expenditures for drugs launched during calendar year 2021.
Response:
We thank the commenter for its concern. We note that section 1192(d)(2) of the Act expressly sets forth the denominator and time period to be used for calculating total expenditures
(
printed page 72270)
for the purposes of determining whether a drug is a Small Biotech Drug. Sections 1192(d)(2)(A)(i)(II) and 1192(d)(2)(A)(ii)(II) of the Act require that the 80 percent threshold be calculated with respect to all qualifying single source drugs of the manufacturer for which payment may be made under Part B during such year (for calculations involving drugs payable under Part B) or with respect to all drugs covered under Part D for which the manufacturer of the drug has an agreement in effect under section 1860D-14A of the Act during such year (for drugs covered under Part D). With regards to the recommendation to consider a full year of sales for drugs launched in 2021, we similarly note that section 1192(d)(2) of the Act limits us in determining eligibility for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to consider only total expenditures under Part D and Part B “during 2021.”
Comment:
Some commenters supported CMS' proposals related to the implementation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs because it helps protect small biotech manufacturers that may have small business portfolios and less ability to absorb financial risk. One of these commenters also supported CMS' treatment of manufacturers under common control. Another of these commenters suggested CMS explain how corporate relationships, acquisitions, and ownership changes affect a selected drug's eligibility for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs or CMS' calculation of the temporary floor amount. Lastly, a commenter recommended CMS should clarify that licensing, co-marketing, and distribution arrangements that in essence function as a transfer of control should render a drug ineligible for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs.
Response:
We appreciate the support of these commenters. With respect to the commenter's question regarding how corporate relationships, acquisitions, and ownership changes affect eligibility, the policies discussed in section § 429.440 as finalized regarding eligibility for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs explain the relevant statutory criteria for eligibility for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Section 1192(d)(2)(B)(i) of the Act precludes a selected drug from being a Small Biotech Drug if the Primary Manufacturer of the selected drug is acquired after 2021 by another manufacturer that does not meet the definition of a specified manufacturer under section 1860D-14C(g)(4)(B)(ii) of the Act, effective at the beginning of the plan year immediately following such acquisition or, in the case of an acquisition before 2025, effective January 1, 2025. With respect to the recommendation that CMS extend ineligibility for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs based on licensing, co-marketing, and distribution arrangements, our proposal reflects the statutory criteria specified in section 1192(d)(2) of the Act.
Comment:
Some commenters suggested various refinements to the proposal to further protect small biotech manufacturers, including revising eligibility standards and extending the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs provisions beyond initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030. One of these commenters suggested CMS and the Administration work with Congress to preserve and extend the Small Biotech Exception and the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Another commenter suggested that CMS start evaluating whether a temporary floor limited to initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030 is sufficient to protect small biotech manufacturers and to determine if an extension is warranted.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' suggestions. The statute provides specific eligibility criteria for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs and provides that it applies only for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030. We do not have the authority to amend the statute to provide additional eligibility standards or extend the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs.
Comment:
A commenter recommended CMS report whether a selected drug was deemed eligible for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs in its explanation of the MFP, noting that doing so would not raise confidentiality concerns since CMS has already made the determination and because providing this information could help demonstrate effectiveness of the negotiation process. Additionally, this commenter stated that CMS should publish the drugs excluded under the Small Biotech Exception for previous initial price applicability years to allow stakeholders to understand how the provision affected drug selection. Another commenter suggested that CMS track and publicly report on whether the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs sufficiently protects small biotech manufacturer innovation.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their suggestions to provide public reporting on the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, including adding specific information in MFP explanations. Consistent with § 429.705(b), the MFP explanation will include a narrative explanation of the negotiation process that occurred with that Primary Manufacturer and redacted information regarding the section 1194(e) data received, exchange of offers and counteroffers, and the negotiation meetings, if applicable. If a selected drug qualifies for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs in initial price applicability years 2029 or 2030, we will consider whether to disclose such status in the MFP explanation consistent with our approach to redact confidential information and proprietary information, as well as with our policies finalized at § 429.300. Consistent with our approach to initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 to date, we decline to publish the drugs that qualified for the Small Biotech Exception in previous initial price applicability years. The comment to track and report on whether the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs sufficiently protects small biotech manufacturer innovation is outside the scope of this final rule.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS should reconsider its proposal to extend the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to renegotiation based on section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the Act and instead exercise discretion by adopting a narrower interpretation under section 1194(d) of the Act that the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs applies only when negotiating the initial MFP for drugs selected for negotiation. This commenter suggested that applying the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to drugs selected for renegotiation may limit CMS' ability to fully account for the circumstances that warranted selection for renegotiation or other landscape changes for the pharmaceutical market and constrain the renegotiation process.
Response:
We decline to adopt the commenter's suggestion to adopt a narrower interpretation such that drugs selected for renegotiation for initial price applicability years 2029 or 2030 would not be eligible to be considered for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs described in section 1194(d) of the Act. Section 1194(f)(4)(B) of the Act describes the statutory requirements that aspects of the renegotiation process be consistent with the negotiation process and states that for purposes of applying section 1194(d) of the Act (that is, the section that establishes the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs), reference to the first initial price applicability year of the price applicability period with respect to such drug shall be treated as
(
printed page 72271)
the first initial price applicability year of such period for which the maximum fair price established pursuant to renegotiation applies. This reference indicates that the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs applies with respect to renegotiation under section 1194(f) of the Act. Because of this statutory directive, drugs selected for renegotiation also will be eligible to be considered for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs described in section 1194(d) of the Act and § 429.440 as finalized and we do not have the discretion to otherwise limit such eligibility.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that in therapeutic classes with only two drugs, if CMS applies the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to an eligible selected drug and not its competitor in cases where the competitor is also a selected drug, this could distort the market and hurt the manufacturer selling a drug at a lower WAC. To address this concern, this commenter recommended that CMS first request information from the applicant for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs regarding the number of competing manufacturers in a class and then grant the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to the drug of the other manufacturer, if selected for negotiation.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter raising this concern and recommending an approach. We decline to adopt the commenter's suggestion to automatically apply the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to both the selected drug and the competing selected drug of another manufacturer in cases when there are only two drugs in a therapeutic class. Section 1194(d) of the Act states that the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs is only applicable in the case of a selected drug that meets the Small Biotech Exception criteria under section 1192(d)(2) of the Act. As a result, we do not have the authority to extend the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to other selected drugs in a therapeutic class when such drugs do not meet the criteria in section 1192(d)(2) of the Act to qualify for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs section.
Comment:
A commenter recommended CMS apply the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to the small biotech company instead of the selected drug to support innovation for certain drugs and help protect small biotech companies that are acquired by another manufacturer. The commenter recognized the statute sets forth limits for drugs being acquired by another manufacturer, but suggested CMS use its rulemaking discretion to apply the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs to a company and signal this issue for Congress.
Response:
We recognize the commenter's interest in having the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs apply to the small biotech company instead of the selected drug. However, the statute is clear at sections 1192(d) and 1194(d) of the Act that the Small Biotech Exception and the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, respectively, apply to the drug specifically that meets the eligibility criteria, not the “small biotech company” generally. Furthermore, consistent with section 1192(d)(2)(B)(ii) of the Act, a selected drug is precluded from being eligible for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs if the Primary Manufacturer of such drug is acquired after 2021 by another manufacturer that does not meet the definition of a specified manufacturer under section 1860D-14C(g)(4)(B)(ii) of the Act, effective at the beginning of the plan year immediately following such acquisition or, in the case of an acquisition before 2025, effective January 1, 2025. We do not have the authority to change these statutory requirements via rulemaking.
Comment:

10. Calculation Information and Suggestion of Error (§ 429.445)
In implementing the statutory provisions of the Negotiation Program, CMS is required to execute a number of multi-step calculations. Section 1194(b)(2)(F)(i) of the Act requires that, in negotiating the MFP of a selected drug, including during renegotiation, CMS would not make an offer or agree to a counteroffer for an MFP that exceeds the ceiling specified in section 1194(c) of the Act. Section 1196(a) of the Act describes certain of CMS' administrative duties, including section 1196(a)(2) of the Act, which requires CMS to establish procedures to compute and apply the MFP across dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of such drug. Section 1194(d) of the Act requires that for a selected drug that is a qualifying single source drug that meets the requirements set forth in section 1192(d)(2) of the Act to be determined a Small Biotech Drug, and with respect to which the first initial price applicability year of the price applicability period with respect to such drug is 2029 or 2030, CMS will not offer or agree to a counteroffer for an MFP that is lower than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. With respect to initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, we implemented a suggestion of error process for Primary Manufacturers if they believe in good faith that CMS has made an error in calculating the ceiling or in applying the MFP across dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug, including, for example, in section 40.5 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028. With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 40.5 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, as revised based on the proposed modifications discussed in this section, we proposed in § 429.445 to provide a Primary Manufacturer the opportunity to submit a suggestion of error if they believe in good faith that CMS has made an error in the calculation of the ceiling or the computation of how CMS intends to apply a single MFP across dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug.
We proposed at § 429.445(a) to provide a Primary Manufacturer with the following information, as applicable: information on CMS' calculation of the ceiling, as described in §§ 429.410 through 429.435; the computation of how we will apply a single MFP across dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug, as described in § 429.700(b) and (c); and information on CMS' calculations of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs (and adjusted ceiling, as applicable), as described in § 429.440(b)(3) and (b)(4). The information on CMS' calculations of the ceiling would include each intermediate step in the calculation of the section 1847A(b)(4) of the Act payment amount as described in § 429.425, and the non-FAMP amounts as described in § 429.435. The plan-specific enrollment weighted amount as described in § 429.420 would also be included in the information on CMS' calculations of the ceiling but the intermediate steps that make up the plan-specific weighted amount would not, as the plan sponsor's reported Part D PDE data is proprietary data of the plan sponsors and is protected from disclosure, as described in the confidentiality policy proposed in § 429.300(b). The computation of how we will apply a single MFP across dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug would include each intermediate step in our calculation for all applicable NDCs associated with a selected drug, as described in § 429.700 to demonstrate how we will apply a single MFP across dosage forms and strengths. If a selected drug is eligible for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, the information on the calculations of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs would include each intermediate step in the calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs as described in § 429.440(b)(3). We would also include the information on CMS' calculation of the ceiling, as described previously, and information on CMS' calculation of the adjusted ceiling, if applicable. The information on CMS' calculations of the alternative ceiling will include a modified version of the ceiling calculations, based on whether the selected drug's adjusted ceiling is calculated using proposed § 429.440(b)(4)(i), (ii), or (iii).

Further, we proposed in § 429.445(c) that Primary Manufacturers would have 10 days to submit a suggestion of error with respect to these calculations if they believe that CMS has made a calculation error. A calculation error is any error related to the mathematical equations that make up the calculation of the ceiling, the computation of how CMS will apply a single MFP across dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug, or the calculations of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs (and adjusted ceiling, if applicable) for a selected drug eligible for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. This includes errors in the sums, products, and quotients of values in the mathematical equations. In contrast, objections to policies and methodologies for implementing the relevant calculations would not be considered a relevant suggestion of error.
Under the applicable guidance for initial price applicability years 2027 and 2028, Primary Manufacturers have 21 days to submit a suggestion of error. We proposed to change the length of time that a Primary Manufacturer has to submit a suggestion of error with respect to the information provided under proposed § 429.445(a)(1) and (a)(3) in order to ensure we can meet deadlines for the negotiation process established in statute. As described in section II.C.1. of this final rule, in accordance with section 1194(b)(2)(A) of the Act, the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug must submit, no later than March 1 of the year of the selected drug publication date, with respect to the selected drug, certain information, including non-FAMP data and other information required to carry out the negotiation process, including the information specified at section 1194(e)(1) of the Act. In accordance with section 1194(b)(2)(B) of the Act, and as proposed at § 429.520(a), CMS would provide the Primary Manufacturer with the written initial offer no later than June 1 following the selected drug publication date. Therefore, CMS has only 3 months to process and analyze Primary Manufacturer data that the agency must consider when preparing the written initial offer. Our experience implementing the Negotiation Program to date has demonstrated that a suggestion of error period of 21 days (or more) impedes our ability to perform the analysis necessary to meet the June 1st statutory deadline. In particular, we have found that additional time is needed beyond March 1st to engage with Primary Manufacturers regarding their required data submissions to ensure that they have submitted the data necessary for us to perform the required calculations and that such information is presented with sufficient clarity for us to be able to use it, in accordance with their obligations under the Negotiation Program Agreement. We cannot provide the ceiling calculation information described in proposed § 429.410 through § 429.435, until we have engaged in this process. Reducing the time for Primary Manufacturers to submit a suggestion of error to 10 days will allow for a timely review of Primary Manufacturer submissions of the section 1194(e)(1) factors, the opportunity for Primary Manufacturers to supplement and clarify submissions in accordance with agency requests in accordance with proposed § 429.900(b), and allow for the delivery of the information to the Primary Manufacturer and the suggestion of error window to be complete prior to the June 1st statutory deadline for written initial offers.
Additionally, we proposed to change the length of time that a Primary Manufacturer has to submit a suggestion of error with respect to the information provided under proposed § 429.445(a)(2) in order to incorporate Primary Manufacturer feedback to the extent practicable and as appropriate, into MFP application calculations prior to the MFP going into effect. As described in section II.B.1. of this final rule, a Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug has an ongoing obligation to report, at least 30 calendar days prior to the change taking effect, any changes to the list of NDC-11s provided in proposed § 429.100(d) to ensure the list of NDC-11s of the selected drug remains complete and accurate. Our experience implementing the Negotiation Program to date has demonstrated that a suggestion of error period of 21 days does not leave the agency sufficient time to consider Primary Manufacturer feedback prior to implementation of revised MFPs and MFPs for new NDCs. Reducing the time for Primary Manufacturers to submit a suggestion of error to 10 days will allow for CMS to consider, and incorporate, to the extent practicable and as appropriate, Primary Manufacturer feedback prior to implementation of revised MFPs and MFPs for new NDCs.
As further specified in proposed § 429.445(c), the suggestion of error process would not affect a Primary Manufacturer's obligation to comply with Negotiation Program requirements and would not alter or change any timelines or requirements of the Negotiation Program.
A Primary Manufacturer must submit any suggestion of error on the calculation of the ceiling, the computation of how CMS would apply a single MFP across dosage forms and strengths, and information on CMS' calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs (and adjusted ceiling, as applicable) of the selected drug in a form and manner specified by CMS, as proposed in § 429.445(d).

Comment:
A few commenters opposed the reduction of the Suggestion of Error review window from 21 days to 10 days. They stated the calculations are complex multiple-step computations that can include hundreds of NDC-11s and multiple data sources and stated that the proposal would significantly reduce their review time. A couple of commenters suggested that CMS streamline internal processes instead of shortening the review window for manufacturers. Another commenter
(
printed page 72274)
suggested that CMS disclose any analysis or workpapers that support the conclusion that a suggestion of error period of 10 days is adequate for manufacturers.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their feedback. As recognized by the commenters, CMS proposed this change in the suggestion of error period for CMS' calculation of the ceiling and for CMS' calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs (and adjusted ceiling, as applicable), as applicable, to ensure that CMS meets the statutory deadlines for the Negotiation Program, where in accordance with section 1194(b)(2)(A) of the Act, the Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug must submit requested information regarding the selected drug not later than March 1 following the selected drug publication date, and, in accordance with section 1194(b)(2)(B) of the Act, CMS must provide the Primary Manufacturer with a written initial offer no later than June 1 following the selected drug publication date. This change in the suggestion of error period provides more time for CMS to engage with Primary Manufacturers regarding their data submissions, provide Primary Manufacturers with the opportunity to supplement or clarify their submissions, and consider their feedback prior to providing the initial offer to the Primary Manufacturer. The proposed review window is based on our experience implementing the Negotiation Program. Given the limited scope of the suggestion of error process as described in § 429.445, CMS expects that the 10-day period will be sufficient for manufacturers to perform their reviews.
Comment:
A commenter opposed the identification of the calculations for which a suggestion of error can be made in response to the comment solicitation on whether the regulatory text should expressly identify each of the calculations for which this suggestion of error process would be available. Given the array of potential circumstances that may arise, the commenter encouraged CMS to maintain flexibility to work with manufacturers on suggestions of error. Another commenter supported the clarity provided by the identification of topics in-scope for the suggestion of error process in regulatory text and urged CMS to reconsider the exclusion of objections to policies and methodologies from suggestions of error.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their feedback. As described in § 429.445(c), the suggestion of error process is intended to provide Primary Manufacturers with the opportunity to identify potential errors in CMS' calculation of the ceiling, the application of the single MFP across dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug, and CMS' calculation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, as specified in paragraphs (a)(1), (a)(2), or (a)(3) of § 429.445. Furthermore, the sections referenced in § 429.445(a)(1) through (a)(3) (that is, §§ 429.410 through 429.435, § 429.700(b) and (c), and § 429.440(b)(3) and (4)) specify the provisions describing calculations that may be subject to the suggestion of error process (see § 429.410(c) (specifying the calculation in § 429.410(b) is subject to the suggestion of error process), § 429.415(b) (specifying the calculation in section § 429.415(a) is subject to the suggestion of error process), § 429.420(c) (specifying the calculation in § 429.420(b) is subject to the suggestion of error process), § 429.425(c) (specifying the calculations in § 429.425(a)(2) and (a)(4) are subject to the suggestion of error process), § 429.430(b) (specifying the calculation in § 429.430(a) is subject to the suggestion of error process), § 429.435(b) (specifying the calculations at § 429.435(a) are subject to the suggestion of error process), § 429.440(b)(6) (specifying the calculations in § 429.440(b)(3) and (4) are subject to the suggestion of error process), and § 429.700(d) (specifying the calculations in § 429.700(b) and (c) are subject to the suggestion of error process)). Therefore, we believe it is not necessary to further specify in regulatory text the calculations for which the suggestion of error process will be available. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance, submissions related to statutorily required criteria or the policies adopted in Negotiation Program guidance or in this final rule are outside the scope of the suggestion of error process.

F. Negotiation Process (§§ 429.500 through 429.535)
1. General Rule (§ 429.500)
Section 1194 of the Act describes the process that CMS must follow when conducting negotiation and renegotiation. Specifically, section 1194(b)(2) of the Act directs CMS to use a consistent methodology and process for negotiation that aims to achieve the lowest MFP for each selected drug. Further, section 1194(e) of the Act requires CMS to consider section 1194(e)(1) factors and section 1194(e)(2) factors as the basis for determining offers and counteroffers. CMS proposed to codify these provisions at § 429.500(a). We also proposed in § 429.500(b) that to formalize an agreed-upon MFP, CMS and the Primary Manufacturer must sign an Addendum to the Negotiation Program Agreement, as described in proposed § 429.200(e) and discussed in section II.C.1. of this final rule.
With respect to initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, we implemented these requirements through guidance, including, for example, sections 60.3 and 60.4 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028. With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, we proposed in §§ 429.500 through 429.535 to codify the negotiation process consistent with the requirements of the IRA and such prior guidance, with proposed revisions noted in these sections.
Final Decision:
We did not receive public comments on this provision, and therefore, we are finalizing § 429.500 as proposed.

These factors include data submitted by the Primary Manufacturer, as specified in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act and evidence about alternative treatments, as specified in section 1194(e)(2) of the Act. With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, consistent with the policies for implementation as described in section 50 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, proposed § 429.505, as described more fully in the next section, codifies our collection of data related to the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act, the process for such data collection, the timing of such data collection, and requirements for the Primary Manufacturer to update submitted data. This section also discusses how we proposed to consider evidence from
