as well as any updates that may be issued by FDA in the future, when determining the extent to which a selected drug addresses an unmet medical need for a condition.
(b) Analysis for Conditions of Selected Drugs Without Therapeutic Alternatives
For conditions of selected drugs without therapeutic alternatives, we would consider the information regarding the four factors outlined in section 1194(e)(2) of the Act collectively. We proposed at § 429.510(e)(4)(ii) certain parameters for our review of conditions of selected drugs where we need to account for the lack of therapeutic alternatives for such conditions. Specifically, we proposed at § 429.510(e)(4)(ii)(A) that for each condition for which a selected drug is used but does not have a therapeutic alternative, we would consider the totality of available information relevant to the section 1194(e)(2) factors as detailed previously and in proposed § 429.510(e)(1), including information received from Primary Manufacturers and the public as described in proposed § 429.505(d), and evidence identified through a CMS-led literature review. We also proposed at § 429.510(e)(4)(ii)(B) to consider the selected drug and any existing treatment options, which may include pharmacologic or non-pharmacologic treatments, to determine the extent to which the selected drug addresses an unmet medical need (as defined in § 429.20) at the condition level. For purposes of the Negotiation Program, anytime CMS considers an unmet medical need, CMS would consider the extent to which the selected drug addresses an unmet medical need at the time of consideration based on all available information at such time of consideration. We would consider unmet medical need in the same manner as discussed in section II.F.3.a. of this final rule. At proposed § 429.20, we proposed to define unmet medical need as a circumstance in which the relevant condition is one for which no treatment options exist, or existing treatments do not adequately address the condition. As noted previously, we may consider the nonbinding recommendations in the FDA “Guidance for Industry Expedited Programs for Serious Conditions—Drugs and Biologics,” as well as any updates that may be issued by FDA in the future, when considering the extent to which a selected drug addresses an unmet medical need for the purpose of the Negotiation Program.
Finally, as described at proposed § 429.510(e)(4)(ii)(C), we proposed to examine improvements in outcomes, such as the magnitude of differences in outcomes of interest conferred by the selected drug, for a condition wherein CMS has not identified a therapeutic alternative to determine the extent to which a selected drug represents a therapeutic advance. For purposes of the Negotiation Program, anytime CMS considers therapeutic advance, CMS would consider the extent to which the selected drug represents a therapeutic advance at the time of consideration based on all available information at such time of consideration
(c) Preliminary Price
As noted in section II.F.3.d.1.a. of this final rule, we proposed to take a qualitative approach to adjusting the starting point based on the unique characteristics of the drug and its therapeutic alternative(s), if any, as well as the patient population(s) taking the selected drug. For each selected drug, we proposed to adjust the applicable starting point (as determined in proposed § 429.510(d)) upward or downward or to not adjust (as described in proposed § 429.510(e)(5)) based on the totality of the relevant information and evidence submitted and gathered through our analysis based on section 1194(e)(2) factors. We may adjust the starting point based on how the section 1194(e)(2) factors apply with respect to individual condition(s) in cases where there are notable differences relative to the therapeutic alternative(s).
After the starting point is adjusted, if applicable, as described in proposed § 429.510(e)(4), as appropriate, based on section 1194(e)(2) factors, evaluated using data submitted by the Primary Manufacturer and the public through the Drug Price Negotiation ICR and gathered through our analyses and literature review, the resulting price is referred to as “the preliminary price” (defined in proposed § 429.20).
We proposed to adjust the preliminary price, as appropriate, based on data submitted by the Primary Manufacturer in accordance with section 1194(e)(1) of the Act, as described in detail in section II.F.3.d.(2). of this final rule and proposed at § 429.510(f).
(2) Adjusting the Preliminary Price Based on Consideration of Section 1194(e)(1) Factors
Section 1194(e)(1) of the Act directs CMS to consider certain factors, which must be reported by each Primary Manufacturer, when determining offers and counteroffers. To fulfill this requirement, we proposed at § 429.510(f) to adjust the preliminary price based on the factors listed at section 1194(e)(1) of the Act. The preliminary price may be adjusted upward, adjusted downward, or not adjusted to account for these manufacturer-specific data elements. In accordance with section 1194(b)(1) of the Act, this process would be conducted with the aim of achieving the lowest MFP for each selected drug. The section 1194(e)(1) factors are listed at proposed § 429.505(b)(2) and include: (1) R&D costs of the manufacturer for the drug and the extent to which the manufacturer has recouped R&D costs; (2) current unit costs of production and distribution of the drug; (3) prior Federal financial support for novel therapeutic discovery and development with respect to the drug; (4) data on pending and approved patent applications or exclusivities recognized by the FDA, and applications and approvals under section 505(c) of the FD&C Act or section 351(a) of the PHS Act for the drug; and (5) market data and revenue and sales volume data for the drug in the United States.
We proposed to consider the five factors outlined in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act in totality at proposed § 429.510(f)(1) and apply an upward adjustment, downward adjustment, or no adjustment to the preliminary price as described at proposed § 429.510(f)(2). We provide illustrative examples of how we might adjust, or not adjust, the preliminary price based on evaluation of a manufacturer-specific data element
(
printed page 72284)
later in this section. However, the overall adjustment, inclusive of all five elements taken together, may differ from the example adjustment for any single element viewed in isolation.
Section 1194(e)(1)(A) of the Act requires CMS to consider the extent to which the Primary Manufacturer has recouped its R&D costs. As an example of how we could approach this consideration, CMS could compare the R&D costs with the global and U.S. net revenue for the selected drug reported by the Primary Manufacturer to determine the extent to which the Primary Manufacturer has recouped its R&D costs. For example, if a Primary Manufacturer has not recouped its R&D costs, we may consider adjusting the preliminary price upward. Conversely, if a Primary Manufacturer has recouped its R&D costs, we may consider adjusting the preliminary price downward or apply no adjustment. We may use the R&D costs reported by the Primary Manufacturer and the calculated recouped costs, including the assumptions and calculations in the accompanying narrative text, and/or other factors as described in proposed § 429.505(b)(2) to adjust the preliminary price.
As an example for how we may consider the relationship between the preliminary price and the unit costs of production and distribution (the factor listed at section 1194(e)(1)(B) of the Act), we may consider adjusting the preliminary price downward if the unit costs of production and distribution are lower than the preliminary price, or upward if the unit costs of production and distribution are greater than the preliminary price. Again, we may consider the assumptions and calculations in the accompanying narrative text submitted by the Primary Manufacturer of the selected drug as described in proposed § 429.505(b) to determine if an adjustment is appropriate.
As an example of how we may consider the extent to which the Primary Manufacturer benefited from Federal financial support with respect to the selected drug (the factor listed at section 1194(e)(1)(C) of the Act), we may consider adjusting the preliminary price downward if funding for the discovery and development of the drug was received from Federal sources.
We would also review the patents and exclusivities reported as we develop our initial offer, consistent with section 1194(e)(1)(D) of the Act. We believe that this information would support CMS' consideration of the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act and in proposed § 429.505(b)(2) and (d)(3). For instance, patents and exclusivities may inform our understanding of therapeutic alternatives and other available therapy for the purposes of adjusting for clinical benefit, including consideration of the extent to which the selected drug represents a therapeutic advance or the extent to which the selected drug addresses an unmet medical need. More specifically, in light of exclusivities, there may be no other available therapy aside from the selected drug that adequately addresses treatment or diagnosis of a disease or condition, and consideration of such information would be relevant to our consideration of the extent to which the selected drug addresses an unmet medical need for that disease or condition.
Finally, we would consider how the market data and revenue and sales volume data compare to the preliminary price in accordance with section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act. For example, if the average commercial net price is lower than the preliminary price, we may consider adjusting the preliminary price downward. If the average commercial net price is greater than the preliminary price, we may consider adjusting the preliminary price upward.
We proposed in § 429.510(f)(3) that after any adjustments to the preliminary price are made as described in paragraphs (f)(1) and (f)(2), the result is the initial offer unless paragraph (f)(3)(i) applies. As proposed in § 429.510(f)(3)(i), if the resulting amount is above the ceiling (as determined in § 429.410), then the initial offer will be equal to the ceiling, and if the amount is below the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs (as determined in proposed § 429.440), if applicable, then the initial offer will be equal to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that while they support clinical practice guidelines as a component of the evidence that CMS considers during the negotiation process, they indicated that guidelines offer the standards of care for a disease based on the information available at the time of publication and may not reflect the current evidence base or advancements in treatments; that is, clinically accepted uses can emerge before guidelines and compendia are updated and CMS should consider guidelines alongside other evidence.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their input and agree that clinical practice guidelines, like other forms of evidence, may have limitations and biases. We believe clinical practice guidelines, when available, are an important component of understanding how a drug contributes to the course of care for a condition. As we stated in section II.F.3.d.1. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36292
), we will use a qualitative approach to broadly evaluate the body of available evidence, which includes clinical guidelines and other forms of evidence including information received from the public and the Primary Manufacturer, evidence identified through a CMS-led literature review, Medicare claims or other datasets, potentially including evidence related to health care resource utilization and usage patterns of the selected drug versus its therapeutic alternative(s), clinical data, or other information relevant to the selected drug and its therapeutic alternative(s). We also proposed at § 429.510(e)(2) that we may consult with clinicians, patients or patient organizations, researchers, FDA, or some combination thereof. We also note that the Primary Manufacturer can provide additional context or information on clinical guidelines, including whether there may be a change in clinical approach, throughout the negotiation period. We believe the combined approach of discussions with the Primary Manufacturer, reviewing the most recent guidelines, and consulting with clinicians, patients or patient organizations, researchers, FDA, or some combination thereof, as needed, provides CMS with a robust and up-to-date understanding of clinical guidelines and where recommendations may evolve.
Comment:
A few commenters stated CMS should provide more transparency in how the section 1194(e)(1) factors are used and weighted during development of the initial offer and counteroffers. A commenter suggested that CMS should adjust the initial offer downward if R&D costs have been recouped for the selected drug. A commenter recommended that CMS place minimal weight on R&D recoupment. A commenter cautioned that CMS should not use prior Federal financial support, the factor listed at section 1194(e)(1)(C) of the Act, to adjust the preliminary price downward because it may discourage future innovation. A few commenters suggested that CMS should provide an upward adjustment for the factor listed at section 1194(e)(1)(D) of the Act (particularly, data on pending and approved patents and exclusivities) to indicate CMS' recognition of the innovation of the selected drug. A few
(
printed page 72285)
commenters stated that CMS should review patents and exclusivities for a selected drug to determine if such patents and exclusivities are indicative of innovation or if they indicate efforts to extend monopolies without associated clinical benefit. As a component of the factor listed at section 1194(e)(1)(A) of the Act, a commenter suggested that CMS increase the weighting of post-approval research that results in new indications or addresses an unmet medical need and also increase the weighting for active development of an additional indication. A commenter stated CMS should “pay for the marginal cost of production and distribution” for drugs used by Medicare beneficiaries. A commenter requested that CMS state how it considers the gross-to-net relationship of the price of a selected drug when developing the preliminary price. A commenter stated that CMS has not affirmed that section 1194(e)(1) factors may result in an upward adjustment to the preliminary price. A commenter supported the proposal to consider section 1194(e)(1) factors in totality.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their input. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and the Negotiation Program Guidance, we believe it is important to maintain flexibility when considering how each negotiation factor contributes to the initial offer and subsequent offers and counteroffers, as applicable, which may be impacted by the unique characteristics of each selected drug, the populations each selected drug is intended to treat, and information that may emerge from meaningful discussions with manufacturers, patients, and patient representatives. Therefore, we decline to adopt the commenters' suggestions to apply specific positive or negative adjustments to specific section 1194(e)(1) or (e)(2) factors. With regard to suggestions that CMS provide more information on how a factor is weighted when developing the initial offer, we note that, as proposed at § 429.505(e), we consider all factors listed in section 1194(e) of the Act in the development of the initial offer. All applicable negotiation factors will be considered in totality for each selected drug, as proposed at § 429.510(f)(1). We also note that as proposed at § 429.510(f)(2), the preliminary price may be adjusted upward, downward, or not adjusted based on CMS' consideration of the section 1194(e)(1) factors.
Comment:
A couple of commenters provided input on how CMS should consider clinical benefit for a selected drug that includes a fixed combination drug subject to the proposed policy described in section II.B.6.a.1. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36260
) and at proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i). One of these commenters recommended that CMS keep separate approaches for identification of potential qualifying single source drugs at proposed § 429.125(b) and valuation of selected drugs during negotiation at proposed § 429.510(e), stating that CMS may properly aggregate two products into the same qualifying single source drug to circumvent program integrity concerns while still recognizing during the negotiation process that each product provides distinct value. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS clarify in the final rule that when a selected drug subject to the negotiation process includes a fixed combination drug in accordance with proposed § 429.125(b)(4)(i), CMS will still consider formulation-specific clinical evidence under § 429.510(e) during the negotiation process.
Response:
We appreciate the input from these commenters. As we stated in the Negotiation Program proposed rule at section II.B.6.a.1. (
91 FR 36260
) and as proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i), we clarified how CMS would comply with sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act for fixed combination drugs that include an active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component that creates a new formulation and enables an alternative route of administration for the co-administered active moiety(ies), active ingredient(s), or antigen component(s), when identifying qualifying single source drugs for purposes of drug selection. We agree with the commenter that the process for identification of potential qualifying single source drugs is separate from our review of the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act, which we will consider as the basis for developing offers and counteroffers. We will follow the process described at § 429.510, including considering clinical and other evidence, for all drugs selected for negotiation for which the Primary Manufacturer has signed a Negotiation Program Agreement.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS provide more detailed information on the framework used to develop the initial offer to promote transparency and consistency. Specifically, many commenters recommended that CMS assign greater weight to section 1194(e)(2) factors because these factors reflect the benefit a selected drug provides to patients, caregivers, society, and the health care system; some commenters also suggested that CMS should place less weight on section 1194(e)(1) factors as placing too much weight on such factors might undervalue innovation and overemphasize manufacturer costs and other manufacturer-submitted data. Some commenters requested that CMS consider factors not mentioned in the proposed rule, including the impact of a selected drug on the health system, costs to the patient, the societal value of a selected drug, cost offsets (such as avoiding ineffective or harmful treatment options and reducing downstream costs to the health care system), adherence, the value of multi-indication drugs, the value of companion diagnostics, and the mental and social wellbeing of patients and caregivers. A few commenters encouraged CMS to consider the full range of patient outcomes including but not limited to patient preferences, caregiver burden, and quality of life. A few commenters recommended applying greater weight to unmet medical need when adjusting for section 1194(e)(2) factors. A commenter suggested that when considering whether a selected drug represents a therapeutic advance, CMS should consider cost and outcomes metrics including patient and caregiver perspectives, reduced treatment burden, reduced hospitalizations, decreased reliance on adjunct therapies, and improved care coordination. A commenter suggested that the safety profile of a drug should be weighted when considering section 1194(e)(2) factors. A commenter recommended that CMS adopt an approach like the one used in Germany by the Institute for Quality and Efficiency in Health Care (IQWiG) to categorize therapeutic benefit. Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback on the adjustments related to the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act. As we stated in the Negotiation Program Guidance, section 1196(a)(4) of the Act provides the Secretary with the authority to establish a negotiation and renegotiation process in accordance with section 1194 of the Act. This section directs the Secretary to establish a consistent methodology and process for negotiation (section 1194(b)(1) of the Act) and to consider the section 1194(e) factors as the basis for determining the offers and counteroffers (section 1194(e) of the Act) but does not dictate the manner in which those factors must be considered. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance and the previously provided response related specifically to section 1194(e)(1) factors, we believe that flexibility in determining which section 1194(e) factors to emphasize over others will depend on the unique considerations related to each selected drug, the populations each selected drug is intended to treat, and information that may emerge from meaningful discussions with manufacturers, patients, and patient representatives. Considerations for how evidence will be prioritized are proposed at § 429.505(d) and (e) and section II.D.1. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36292
); these considerations are also applicable to renegotiation as proposed at § 429.620(d) and section II.G.5.c. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36308
). All applicable negotiation factors will be considered in totality for each selected drug.
We appreciate the suggestion to use the ESMO-MCBS to assess section 1194(e)(2) factors and the approach used by IQWiG to categorize therapeutic benefit. As noted in our response to similar suggestions in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we consider whether the general approaches used in these frameworks may be informative for evaluating evidence in the context of the Negotiation Program and whether their use would be consistent with statutory requirements. We also note that the ESMO-MCBS is a tool specifically developed to assess cancer therapies and is not broadly applicable to all selected drugs. In situations where an interested party provides an ESMO-MCBS score for a particular selected drug or therapeutic alternative, we may consider such information in the context of the section 1194(e)(2) factors.
Comment:
A few commenters supported CMS' approach described in section II.F.3.d. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36292
) to consider source, rigor, and risk of bias, among other factors, when evaluating evidence. A commenter stated that CMS has not articulated an evidence review protocol. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS prioritize high quality, robust real-world evidence (RWE) while a commenter requested additional guidance on how CMS assesses RWE. A commenter suggested prioritizing evidence provided by clinicians and manufacturers given their expertise in the selected drug; a commenter suggested prioritizing evidence submitted by patients and clinicians. A commenter stated the CMS should recognize that while rigorous evidence is important, conventional evidence standards may not be appropriate to apply to rare diseases, small clinical populations, heterogenous conditions, or underrepresented patient populations. A couple of commenters stated that CMS should leverage claims and other datasets to understand utilization and usage patterns for a selected drug and its therapeutic alternative(s), if any.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support and their feedback regarding how we will consider evidence and how we will prioritize such evidence. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance and as described in section II.F.3.d. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36292
), when reviewing the data submissions from the public and manufacturer (including the previous examples of data) as well as literature from CMS' review, we intend to consider the source, rigor of the study methodology, current relevance to the selected drug and its therapeutic alternative(s), whether the study has been through peer review, study limitations, degree of certainty of conclusions, risk of bias, study time horizons, generalizability, study population, and relevance to the negotiation factors listed in section 1194(e)(2) of the Act to ensure the integrity of the contributing data within the negotiation process. We will prioritize research, including both observational research and research based on randomized samples, that is methodologically rigorous, appropriately powered (that is, has sufficient sample size) to answer the primary question of the research, and structured to avoid potential false positive findings due to multiple subgroup analyses. We believe this approach will ensure the integrity of data within the negotiation process.
Comment:
Some commenters urged CMS to provide more information on how the information provided by the public, particularly patients, is used in the development of the initial offer. Suggestions included publication of a plain language summary of the major patient and caregiver themes received for each selected drug and an explanation of how those themes informed the negotiation process, publishing decisions throughout the negotiation process, and leveraging the National Health Council Patient-Centered Value Assessment Rubric and Rubric to Capture the Patient Voice to create a public framework for how evidence is considered and included in the negotiation process. A commenter suggested leveraging FDA Voice of the Patient Reports when available for selected drugs. A couple of commenters indicated express support for inclusion of patient and caregiver perspectives in the negotiation process, including related data such as patient-centered outcomes and patient experience data.
Response:
We thank commenters for their suggestions. Consistent with the response provided to similar comments in the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027 and the Negotiation Program Guidance, we agree that considerations related to the patient and caregiver experience are important and relevant for consideration of the section 1194(e)(2) factors. We direct commenters to the provision proposed at § 429.510 and responses to comments about this section, which concern how we will use the section 1194(e) data, including patient and caregiver perspectives and experiences (such as through FDA Voice of the Patient Reports, as applicable), in developing an initial offer and, if any, counteroffers. We also believe the information provided in the explanation of the MFP as described in II.H.2. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36311
), which we will make available to the public per the provision proposed at § 429.705(b), serves to provide sufficient information regarding use of the section 1194(e)(2) factors submitted and redacted copies of the section 1194(e)(2) factors submitted by interested parties that we considered during the negotiation process.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS should share with the Primary Manufacturer whether CMS used the standard or alternative 30-day equivalent supply methodology described at § 429.510(d)(2)(iv) prior to or within the concise justification for
(
printed page 72287)
the initial offer. A commenter suggested that CMS should weight therapeutic alternative utilization such that utilization reflects the populations and uses for which the selected drug is prescribed in cases where aggregate utilization does not reflect the populations and uses for which the selected drug is prescribed. A commenter requested that CMS commit to a process that assesses and weights therapeutic alternatives by utilization across conditions, to avoid devaluing products that have shown benefit across multiple indications. A commenter requested that CMS clarify how it weights net prices across multiple indications and therapeutic alternatives. A commenter recommended that CMS calculate indication-level therapeutic alternative starting points and weight those starting points based on the Medicare utilization of the therapeutic alternatives relative to the selected drug in the same population.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their suggestions. Although we do not include a detailed methodology of therapeutic alternative calculations in the concise justification for an initial offer, we welcome specific methodology questions related to how we calculated the starting point using the prices of therapeutic alternatives from the Primary Manufacturer during the optional negotiation meetings. We believe this approach appropriately balances transparency with the Primary Manufacturer while protecting proprietary information related to a therapeutic alternative.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed CMS' consideration of off-label use for the purpose of determining indications and therapeutic alternatives to the selected drug stating that this conflicts with section 1194(e)(2)(B) of the Act. A commenter requested clarity on the “threshold for inclusion” of an off-label use and a commenter stated CMS should apply the same evidentiary rigor when reviewing off-label use as is applied to review of FDA-approved indications. A commenter suggested that CMS only consider off-label use for negotiation if it is voluntarily submitted by the Primary Manufacturer by adopting the provision for renegotiation eligibility as was proposed at § 429.605(c)(1)(ii). A commenter stated that Primary Manufacturers should not be responsible for submitting information on off-label use. A commenter stated that CMS should ensure that therapeutic alternatives are grounded in clinically appropriate FDA-approved indications and distinguish between approved uses and other off-label uses.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback on consideration of off-label use of the selected drug when determining conditions for which the selected drug is used (as proposed at § 429.510(a)(2)) and therapeutic alternatives for the selected drug (as proposed at § 429.510(c)(2)(i)). Regarding the comments indicating that section 1194(e)(2)(B) of the Act directs CMS to consider prescribing information approved by FDA for such drug and therapeutic alternatives as the basis for determining offers and counteroffers, we affirm that we consider such information as described at § 429.510(e)(1) in the adjustment to the starting point based on section 1194(e)(2) factors. We also clarified in this final rule that we consider FDA prescribing information when determining therapeutic alternatives, if any, by revising proposed § 429.510(c)(2) to include a new paragraph (ii) indicating that CMS will consider prescribing information as approved by FDA. As other commenters have noted, particularly for rare diseases or small subpopulations or in situations where clinical evidence is not yet published, off-label use is an important component of patient care. Further, the Medicare program recognizes the importance of evidence-based off-label use of certain drugs by making such drugs payable under Part B, covered under Part D, or both for such uses. It is for this reason we define “off-label use” as described at § 429.20 as the use of a drug that is “included in evidence-based clinical practice guidelines and is a medically accepted indication payable under Part B or covered under Part D or both, taking into consideration major drug compendia, authoritative medical literature, and accepted standards of medical practice, or some combination thereof.” Under this definition, not all off-label uses are considered.
For these reasons, we believe that consideration of off-label use for the purposes of identifying conditions for which the selected drug is used and identifying therapeutic alternatives for those conditions, as applicable, is appropriately grounded in evidence and statute. We also believe that it is not necessary to solely consider off-label use if voluntarily submitted by a Primary Manufacturer for the purposes of identifying conditions for which the selected drug is used and identifying therapeutic alternatives for those conditions. When we are undergoing these processes, a drug has already been selected for negotiation or renegotiation and we are fulfilling our statutory directive to achieve the lowest MFP for the selected drug under section 1194(b)(1) of the Act. These are fundamentally different processes from determining renegotiation eligibility. We also note that neither in negotiation nor renegotiation is a Primary Manufacturer required to submit information on off-label use; in both cases submission of such information is optional.
Comment:
A couple of commenters stated that CMS should not use generics, biosimilars and reference products as therapeutic alternatives in the development of the initial offer, as reliance on these products as therapeutic alternatives is not authorized by the statute. A few commenters stated that CMS should select therapeutic alternatives based on clinical appropriateness and solicit input from relevant stakeholders, including clinicians, patients, caregivers, and manufacturers, when evaluating clinical appropriateness. A few commenters suggested that CMS seek input from clinicians with expertise in treating the indications of the selected drug when selecting therapeutic alternatives, as well as seek input from patients, caregivers, manufacturers, and other stakeholders. A commenter stated that therapeutic alternatives should be based on clinical appropriateness and not based on least costly alternatives. A commenter stated that CMS should not rely on off-label use when comparing costs of therapeutic alternatives, absent robust evidence for the relevant condition. A commenter recommended that CMS account for variation in site-of-care practices and explain data and assumptions for determining that use of a drug occurs solely outside of Part B and Part D.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback regarding the identification of a therapeutic alternative(s) for the selected drug. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance and final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, we will identify the therapeutic alternative(s) for the indications of a selected drug by using data submitted by the Primary Manufacturer and the public, prescribing information approved by the FDA, drug classification systems commonly used in the public and private sector for formulary development, major drug compendia, widely accepted clinical guidelines, evidence identified through the CMS-led literature review, published drug or drug class reviews, peer-reviewed studies, and Medicare claims or other data sets. We believe the framework
(
printed page 72288)
described in the proposed rule allows us to select appropriate therapeutic alternatives for the indications of current and future selected drugs, if such alternatives exist. We disagree with the commenters that state the statute does not authorize CMS to consider generics, biosimilars, or reference products as therapeutic alternatives in the development of the initial offer. Section 1194(e)(2) of the Act directs CMS to consider various evidence regarding therapeutic alternatives of the selected drug and does not limit the scope of therapeutic alternatives to exclude such products. However, if a Primary Manufacturer disagrees with CMS' identification of appropriate therapeutic alternatives to the selected drug, including any biosimilars or generic drugs, the Primary Manufacturer will have multiple opportunities to share that feedback with CMS, as described in § 429.515 and section II.F.4.a. of this final rule.
We agree with commenters that robust public input can provide important information on the selected drug and its therapeutic alternatives. As described at § 429.510(c), we may consult with FDA to obtain information regarding other therapies with FDA-approved indications for the same condition. We may also consult with clinicians, patients or patient organizations, and/or researchers, to ensure that appropriate therapeutic alternatives are identified. As such, we encourage members of the public, including manufacturers, Medicare beneficiaries, researchers, clinicians, caregivers, and other interested parties, to provide information about the selected drug and its therapeutic alternative(s), if any, through the Drug Price Negotiation ICR. We will consider information submitted through the Drug Price Negotiation ICR when developing the initial offer and throughout the negotiation process.
Regarding consideration of off-label use for therapeutic alternatives and their associated costs, we note that our policy includes the criteria that must be met for CMS to consider an off-label use of a selected drug as described at § 429.20. That is, we may consider off-label use when identifying indications if such use is included in evidence-based clinical practice guidelines and the off-label use is a medically accepted indication payable under Part B or covered under Part D, taking into consideration the major drug compendia, authoritative medical literature, accepted standards of medical practice, or some combination thereof. In addition to consideration of public input and consultation when considering therapeutic alternatives, we also note that consistent with the policies in the Negotiation Program Guidance, the negotiation process policies described at § 429.515 include an opportunity for the Primary Manufacturer to meet with CMS regarding the data submission for the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act prior to CMS sending the initial offer. This initial meeting, as well as the negotiation process, including offer and counteroffer exchanges and negotiation meetings, provide additional opportunities for the Primary Manufacturer to discuss off-label use(s) and therapeutic alternatives with CMS.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS not treat within-class drugs as necessarily interchangeable therapeutic alternatives. A commenter suggested CMS limit selection of therapeutic alternatives to products in the same category and class that share a common clinical use. A commenter recommended that CMS limit therapeutic alternatives to pharmaceutical products that share the same mechanism of action as the selected drug, an overlapping indication, and occupy a comparable position in the treatment pathway for the same population. A commenter recommended that CMS identify therapeutic alternatives separately by each indication or line of therapy, or role of the drug in a multi-agent regimen. A commenter recommended that CMS not identify products as therapeutic alternatives that fail a clinical study for use in a condition in which a selected drug is approved. A commenter recommended CMS consider how FDA defines indicated populations and treatment settings, clinical guidelines, how clinician input addresses sequencing, contraindications, and Medicare utilization when considering therapeutic alternatives.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback regarding the identification of a therapeutic alternative(s) for the selected drug. Consistent with the response provided to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance and the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, as well as the previous comment response, we will identify the therapeutic alternative(s) for the indications of a selected drug by using data submitted by the Primary Manufacturer and the public, prescribing information approved by the FDA, drug classification systems commonly used in the public and private sector for formulary development, major drug compendia, widely accepted clinical guidelines, evidence identified through the CMS-led literature review, published drug or drug class reviews, peer-reviewed studies, and Medicare claims or other data sets. We believe the framework provided at § 429.510(b) allows us to select appropriate therapeutic alternatives for the indications of current and future selected drugs, if such alternatives exist. As described at § 429.510(c)(1) we may consult with FDA to obtain information regarding other therapies with FDA-approved indications for the same condition and may also consult with clinicians, patients or patient organizations, researchers, or some combination thereof to ensure that appropriate therapeutic alternatives are identified.
Comment:
A commenter recommended CMS leverage several resources when reviewing evidence related to therapeutic alternatives, including the National Pharmaceutical Council's Guiding Practices for Patient-Centered Value Assessment; The Myth of Average: Why Individual Patient Differences Matter, published by the National Pharmaceutical Council; ISPOR—The Professional Society for Health Economics and Outcomes Research and the International Society for Pharmacoepidemiology (ISPE) practices for real-world data studies of comparative effectiveness; and National Health Council (NHC) resources on patient-centeredness in value assessment. A commenter suggested that CMS adopt best practices from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's (AHRQ) Effective Health Care Program guidance for therapeutic alternative selection.
Response:
Consistent with our response in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we appreciate the suggested resources for best practices in observational comparative effectiveness research, real-world data studies of comparative effectiveness, and patient-centeredness in value assessments. We believe the methods and approach to therapeutic alternative selection and review of evidence related to therapeutic alternatives appropriately include similar elements and is aligned with the requirements of section 1194(e)(2) of the Act.
Comment:
Some commenters recommended that CMS provide clarity on and adopt a consistent, transparent process for evaluation and selection of therapeutic alternatives. A commenter requested that CMS clarify how appropriate comparators are identified. A few commenters suggested that CMS provide detail on the data sources used to inform identification of therapeutic alternatives. A few commenters suggested that CMS provide
(
printed page 72289)
justifications for selections of therapeutic alternatives. A few commenters recommended that CMS disclose to the Primary Manufacturer the list of drugs it considers to be therapeutic alternatives and supporting evidence for those determinations early in the negotiation process. A few commenters recommended that CMS provide more transparency on how CMS distinguishes between clinically meaningful differences in therapeutic alternatives and how the agency selects therapeutic alternatives. A commenter recommended that CMS allow the Primary Manufacturer to object to the determination of a therapeutic alternative and for CMS to consider such objection before making a final determination. A commenter recommended offering Primary Manufacturers the opportunity to submit comparative effectiveness evidence after CMS has identified indications and therapeutic alternatives and seek input from manufacturers and other stakeholders on these alternatives, then using the prioritized alternatives for comparative effectiveness analysis.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their input. As discussed in previous responses in this final rule, as well as consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we believe the framework provided at § 429.510 allows us to select appropriate therapeutic alternatives for the indications of current and future selected drugs, if such alternatives exist. We also note that the Primary Manufacturer is provided with information about the therapeutic alternative(s) selected per this process, if any, in the concise justification accompanying the initial offer proposed at § 429.520(b). In addition to consideration of public input and consultation when considering therapeutic alternatives, we also noted in a previous response that, consistent with the policies in the Negotiation Program Guidance, the negotiation process policies at § 429.515 include an opportunity for the Primary Manufacturer to meet with CMS regarding the data submission related to the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act prior to provision of the initial offer. This initial meeting, as well as the negotiation process, including offer and counteroffer exchanges and negotiation meetings, provide additional opportunities for the Primary Manufacturer to discuss therapeutic alternatives with CMS, including the opportunity to provide additional information or context, as suggested by a commenter. We believe this provides sufficient opportunity for discussions with the Primary Manufacturer while also adhering to the statutory timeline provided in section 1194(b)(2) of the Act.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS publish the list of potential therapeutic alternatives when selected drugs are announced and allow for stakeholder comment, while also allowing the Primary Manufacturer to see the list of therapeutic alternatives before submitting data.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback. Currently, the selected drug list is published no later than the selected drug publication date as defined in § 429.20 with respect to such initial price applicability year per § 429.100(b). We do not believe it is feasible to review drugs for selection for negotiation and renegotiation by the selected drug publication date and also determine potential therapeutic alternatives, if any, for such drugs. Further, such a process would preclude CMS' ability to review the information submitted by the Primary Manufacturer and interested parties under § 429.505 to inform selection of therapeutic alternatives, including engagement opportunities described at § 429.515(b). We also reiterate that the negotiation process policies at § 429.515 include an opportunity for the Primary Manufacturer to meet with CMS regarding the data submission related to the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act prior to provision of the initial offer and that we provide information about therapeutic alternatives in the concise justification accompanying the initial offer proposed at § 429.520(b).
Comment:
A commenter supported CMS' approach for adjusting the starting point of the initial offer but stated that the prices of therapeutic alternatives should not be used as the starting point, as this approach would entrench high prices into the negotiation process. A few commenters opposed CMS' proposals for developing a starting point. A commenter stated that the starting point is extra-statutory. A couple of commenters stated that CMS should anchor its initial offer to the statutory ceiling and evaluate section 1194(e) factors independently from that ceiling. A commenter stated that CMS should not use not-yet-effective MFPs of therapeutic alternatives as the basis for setting a starting point, as the not-yet-effective MFP is not a price that presently exists in the marketplace. A commenter stated that CMS should not build the starting point for a drug in one monopoly status on the price of a drug in a different monopoly status. A commenter stated that CMS should not consider starting points based on reference prices, costs of production or distribution, or other factors that do not provide clinical value to Medicare beneficiaries. A commenter recommended that CMS base an initial offer on risk-adjusted research and development costs; the extent to which those costs have been recouped by the manufacturer; federal investment; and section 1194(e)(2) factors. The commenter also recommended that once an initial offer is determined, CMS should compare the price of the selected drug to therapeutic alternatives and offer an MFP that is no higher than the lowest price of a therapeutic alternative that has a comparable safety and efficacy profile.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback on determining a starting point for developing the initial offer. We disagree that the approach to determining a starting point for development of the initial offer is not grounded in statute. As described earlier, section 1194(e)(2)(A) of the Act directs CMS to consider both the extent to which a selected drug represents a therapeutic advance compared to its therapeutic alternative(s) and the cost of such existing therapeutic alternative(s). We previously considered several alternative options for what price should be used as the starting point for developing the initial offer, including the unit cost of production and distribution for the selected drug, the ceiling, a domestic reference price (for example, the FSS price), or a “fair profit” price based on whether R&D costs have been recouped, and margin on unit cost of production and distribution. We determined using Net Part D Plan Payment and Beneficiary Liability, ASP, WAC, or MFP of therapeutic alternatives is consistent with the Act and provides a point at which to start developing the initial offer within the context of the cost and clinical benefit of one or more drugs that treat the same disease or condition, if available, and then make adjustments based on the factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act. The other options considered do not provide a starting point that reflects the cost of therapeutic alternatives in the current market, which is an important factor when considering the overall benefit that a treatment brings to Medicare beneficiaries relative to the other drug(s) available to treat the patient's disease or condition.
Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we believe the negotiation process described in subpart
(
printed page 72290)
F, and the renegotiation process described in subpart G, results in an MFP for a selected drug that reflects each selected drug's circumstances and is based on the factors outlined in section 1194(e) of the Act, which we are required to consider. We believe this includes situations where the starting point is another selected drug's MFP (in cases where there is one therapeutic alternative) or includes an MFP (in cases where there are multiple therapeutic alternatives and only one or some of the therapeutic alternatives are selected drugs). Consistent with the Negotiation Program Guidance, the policy to use the MFP as the starting point in cases where the therapeutic alternative was itself a selected drug and the MFP is lower than the Net Part D Payment and Beneficiary Liability is aligned with the statutory directive in section 1194(e)(2)(A) of the Act to consider the costs of therapeutic alternatives, which may include selected drugs with an agreed-upon MFP, including situations where there is an agreed-upon MFP but such MFP has not taken effect. And, consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance, offering the ceiling without a more thorough review of section 1194(e)(1) factors, including manufacturer-submitted data, may not achieve that objective and is inconsistent with the statutory directive at section 1194(e) of the Act. Regarding the comment that once an initial offer is determined, CMS should compare the price of the selected drug to therapeutic alternatives and offer an MFP that is no higher than the lowest price of a therapeutic alternative that has a comparable safety and efficacy profile if the initial offer is not already below such price, we believe such an approach might overweight the factors listed at section 1194(e)(2)(A) and (C) (and further overweight a single therapeutic alternative, if multiple therapeutic alternatives are identified), as those would be the only factors reflected in an initial offer when such an offer was made, in contrast to the proposed approach in which all factors listed at section 1194(e) of the Act may impact the development of the initial offer. Upon consideration of these comments, we decline to adopt these alternative approaches to establishing a starting point for developing the initial offer to preserve agency flexibility in making adjustments to the price based on section 1194(e) factors.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended CMS develop and implement a clear, consistent and transparent methodology for developing a starting point for the initial offer. A commenter offered support for CMS' proposed approach to consider patient-centered outcomes, patient experience data, and patient and caregiver preferences in the framework for evaluation of the initial offer. The commenter also suggested CMS consider whether negotiated prices could correspond with measurable, real-world outcomes, such as medication persistence and reduction in treatment interruptions, while ensuring that these outcomes are examined across patient populations. A commenter stated that CMS does not provide a transparent methodology or information on how factors in CMS' valuation framework are applied and recommended that CMS provide an explanation to manufacturers on how it applies its valuation methodology to each selected drug. A commenter stated that CMS does not articulate how it operationalizes definitions of unmet medical need and therapeutic alternatives, and that Primary Manufacturers are unaware of how such data is weighted, or if a selected drug satisfies either definition. The commenter recommended that CMS specify reference points governing in-scope evidence and describe the process by which such evidence is evaluated. A commenter recommended CMS apply a transparent two-stage qualitative framework that assesses the relevance and credibility of appropriate analyses and then synthesizes the body of work writ large to determine relevance across comparative direction, economic materiality, certainty and Medicare applicability. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS provide transparency on the types of evidence used to evaluate therapeutic advance, unmet need, and effects of the selected drug on specific populations. A commenter requested that CMS disclose the methodology and assumptions used when calculating prices for therapeutic alternatives. A commenter requested that CMS commit to a holistic review of evidence when developing the initial offer, including real world evidence, benefits to subpopulations, patient preferences and treatment of conditions with limited alternatives. A commenter requested CMS specify how it will value unmet medical need when a selected drug is used in combination with a therapeutic alternative. The commenter also requested CMS clarify how the cost of a therapeutic alternative will impact the assessment of a therapeutic advance. A commenter recommended that CMS pursue the lowest MFP permitted by law and give substantial weight to evidence demonstrative what constitutes a reasonable price. A commenter stated that the proposed value assessment framework does not effectively account for viral suppression, adherence outcomes or public health costs of averted HIV transmissions. The commenter recommended that injectable forms of long-acting HIV therapies receive appropriate consideration as therapeutic alternatives, as well as off-label utilization.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback and recognize the importance of balancing transparency and confidentiality in the negotiation process. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance and the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, we reiterate that we believe it is important to maintain flexibility when considering how each negotiation factor contributes to the initial offer and subsequent offers and counteroffers, as applicable, which may be impacted by the unique characteristics of each selected drug, the populations each selected drug is intended to treat, and information that may emerge from meaningful discussions with manufacturers, patients, and patient representatives.
Section II.D.1. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36292
) describes how CMS will prioritize evidence related to the section 1194(e) factors; these considerations are also applicable to renegotiation as discussed at section II.G.5.c. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36308
). All applicable negotiation factors will be considered in totality for each selected drug.
Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we will evaluate the extent to which a selected drug addresses an unmet medical need or represents a therapeutic advance at the time of consideration based on all available information at such time of consideration.
Regarding the commenter's suggestion that we pursue the lowest MFP permitted by law, we refer the commenter to section II.D. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36292
) where we introduce our methodology and process as developed in accordance with section 1194(b) of the Act, which requires CMS to aim to achieve the lowest MFP possible. We believe the framework outlined in the proposed rule and adopted by this final rule achieves this statutory directive and decline to adopt commenters' recommendations.

Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing § 429.510(a), (b), and (f) as proposed.
We are finalizing § 429.510(c) as proposed but with a modification to § 429.510(c)(2) to include a new paragraph (ii) indicating that we consider FDA approved prescribing information when determining therapeutic alternatives, if any. We also are adding “all of the following” to § 429.510(c)(2) and are deleting “and” in the re-numbered § 429.510(c)(2)(iv).
We are finalizing § 429.510(d) as proposed but with the following technical changes: we are adding “the following” to § 429.510(d)(1)(i); we are deleting “or” in § 429.510(d)(1)(i)(B); we are adding “the following” to § 429.510(d)(1)(ii); we are deleting “or” in § 429.510(d)(1)(ii)(B); we are adding “the following” to § 429.510(d)(3)(i); and we are deleting “or” in § 429.510(d)(3)(i)(B).
We are finalizing § 429.510(e) as proposed but with the following technical changes: we are adding “all of the following” to § 429.510(e)(3)(i); we are deleting “and” at § 429.510(e)(3)(i)(C); we are adding “both of the following” to § 429.510(e)(3)(ii); we are deleting “and” at § 429.510(e)(3)(ii)(A); we are adding “both of the following” to § 429.510(e)(4)(i); we are deleting “and” at § 429.510(e)(4)(i)(A); we are adding “all of the following” to § 429.510(e)(4)(ii); and we are deleting “and” at § 429.510(e)(4)(ii)(B).
4. Engagement With Primary Manufacturers and Interested Parties (§ 429.515)
a. Engagement With Primary Manufacturers
Consistent with policies for implementation as described in section 60.4 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed in § 429.515 to hold up to four, optional meetings in a form and manner specified by CMS with Primary Manufacturers of selected drugs that have submitted the information set forth in proposed § 429.505. As proposed in § 429.515(a)(1), the first meeting that we would offer Primary Manufacturers to attend would be intended for the Primary Manufacturer to provide additional context on their data submission of the section 1194(e)(1) factors and section 1194(e)(2) factors described in proposed § 429.505(b)(2) and (d)(3), respectively, as we begin evaluating the data submission and developing an initial offer as described in proposed § 429.510. We would also offer Primary Manufacturers the opportunity to attend up to three optional meetings that would focus on the section 1194(e)(1) factors and section 1194(e)(2) factors, and other topics aimed at working toward an agreement on an MFP. During these meetings, discussion of disputes and program policies regarding the negotiation process would be considered out of scope. As proposed in § 429.515(a)(2), meetings would be attended solely by representatives of the Primary Manufacturer and of CMS. The number of attendees would be limited as specified by CMS via future communications with the Primary Manufacturer specific to each initial price applicability year. For example, as described in section 60.4.4 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, CMS and the Primary Manufacturer were permitted to bring up to eight meeting attendees and both parties would share their participant lists ahead of each meeting. We determined this meeting attendee number after considering the roles from each party that would be critical to the conversation while ensuring that the meeting is sized appropriately to encourage active discussion. Given these considerations, we proposed at § 429.515(a)(2) to continue to limit the number of meeting attendees.
We proposed at § 429.515(a)(3)(i) that Primary Manufacturers may share new information on section 1194(e)(2) factors during meetings. We also proposed that the Primary Manufacturer may bring materials to facilitate discussion which must comply with limits on the amount and format of such materials as specified by CMS, and we may request that the Primary Manufacturer provide copies of any presented or discussed materials after the meeting in which they are presented or discussed, as proposed in § 429.515(a)(3)(ii). For example, for initial price applicability year 2028, if a Primary Manufacturer is interested in sharing materials at a negotiation meeting, such materials are limited to 15 pages (or a combination of pages, slides, and/or charts and graphs totaling 15 pages) and no more than 30 citations, to focus the discussion on issues that can reasonably be discussed within the scope of the meeting. We would specify the limits on the amount and format of materials specific to each initial price applicability year via future communications with the Primary Manufacturer. We proposed at § 429.515(a)(1)(ii) that new data related to section 1194(e)(1) factors, as described in proposed § 429.505(b), would not be considered. Rather, we proposed that any information shared during these meetings and materials shared afterwards should only contextualize the Primary Manufacturer's submission of data related to section 1194(e)(1) factors specified in proposed § 429.505(b).
We proposed at § 429.515(a)(4) for the first optional meeting that CMS would offer to Primary Manufacturers to attend would occur, at a time to be specified by CMS, after the data submission deadline specified in section II.F.2. of this final rule and in proposed § 429.505(b)(1) and (d)(2) and before the provision of CMS' initial offer, as set forth in proposed § 429.520. We would offer up to three additional optional meetings to occur after the provision of CMS' initial offer. If accepted by the Primary Manufacturer, such meeting(s) would occur, at a time to be specified by CMS, after the provision of CMS' initial offer as set forth in proposed § 429.520 and before the provision of CMS' final offer, if applicable, as specified in proposed § 429.535. A written record of these meetings would be developed and retained by CMS in compliance with applicable Federal laws, including the Federal Managers' Financial Integrity Act and the Federal Records Act, and would be subject to the confidentiality policy described in section II.D.1. of this final rule and in proposed § 429.300. As described in section II.D.1. of this final rule regarding proposed § 429.300, we would not publicly discuss ongoing negotiations with a Primary Manufacturer, including details of the negotiation meetings. b. Engagement With Interested Parties
At proposed § 429.515(b), we proposed to codify the policy as described in section 60.4.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance to hold events in a form and manner and at times to be specified by CMS with interested parties to seek input from patients and other interested parties about selected drugs and therapeutic alternatives. These public engagement events are intended to bring together patient-focused interested parties to share feedback with us on patient experiences with the conditions or diseases treated by the selected drug, as well as with the selected drugs and therapeutic alternatives to the selected drugs, and other information as we review data related to section 1194(e)(2) factors and develop an initial offer for each selected drug. These public engagement events allow us to hear from patients and other stakeholders close to the patient experience—directly and in their own words—about patients' personal experiences and perspectives on their condition(s) and about the drug(s) used to treat those conditions. This type of information helps inform CMS' understanding of what matters to patients. We would use the information shared during these patient-focused events to better understand patients' experiences with the conditions and diseases treated by the selected drug and their experiences with the selected drugs themselves, as well as to inform CMS' identification of therapeutic alternatives, key outcomes, and adjustment of the starting point to develop the initial offer. These events would be held annually in the Spring.
Public engagement events for each initial price applicability year may include, for example, patient-focused roundtable events that would be open to patients, patient advocacy organizations, and caregivers and would allow for discussion among speakers. These patient-focused roundtable events may focus on one selected drug or group selected drugs by condition when appropriate as determined by CMS.
The public engagement events also may include one town hall meeting for all selected drugs that would be focused on the clinical considerations related to the selected drugs and would be open to practicing clinicians and researchers, as well as other interested parties. This town hall meeting may be divided into multiple sessions and may be held across multiple days. We may have the opportunity to ask follow-up questions of participants at the town hall meeting.
Lastly, we may incorporate drugs selected for renegotiation into the public engagement events for drugs selected for negotiation or we may hold separate events specifically for drugs selected for renegotiation.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed appreciation for CMS codifying public engagement events in regulation and supported CMS' continued efforts to engage patients and interested parties in the negotiation process. However, some commenters noted their disappointment that CMS did not establish minimum requirements and standards around public engagement events through rulemaking, such as committing to multiple public meetings for each selected drug. They encouraged CMS to do so. A few of these commenters acknowledged CMS' preference to preserve flexibility but they expressed concern that without clear requirements, CMS falls short of supporting meaningful stakeholder engagement.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' input. By codifying public engagement events in regulation, we are establishing a minimum requirement—that is, we are committing to holding these events for future initial price applicability years. We believe it is important to maintain flexibility when holding these events because of the potential for an increase in the number of selected drugs covered under Part D and/or payable under Part B in future cycles of negotiations. We disagree that maintaining flexibility indicates that these events inadequately support meaningful stakeholder engagement. As stated in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36296
), the public engagement events allow us to hear from patients and other stakeholders—directly and in their own words—about patient's personal experiences and perspectives on their condition(s) and about the drug(s) used to treat those conditions.
Comment:
Many commenters provided feedback on and recommendations for CMS to improve upon public engagement events held for initial price applicability year 2028. Recommendations included: simplifying the event registration process; publishing CMS' speaker selection criteria; providing a list of discussion questions in advance of the events; providing more time for participants to prepare for the events; broadening the information asked of patients to more holistically address how they value medications and treatment; expanding outreach efforts; expanding the public engagement events to include more participants; providing more accessibility accommodation such as translated materials and interpretation services; expanding conflict of interest disclosure and reporting by CMS; publishing thematic event summaries in addition to event transcripts; providing greater transparency in explaining how information gathered via public engagement events is used in negotiations.
Response:
We appreciate commenters providing specific feedback about the public engagement events held for initial price applicability year 2028 and offering recommendations for improvement and refinement. We will consider these recommendations as we plan the events for future negotiation cycles.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS expand the methods for patients and other interested parties to provide information to CMS beyond participating in public engagement events, including offering opportunities for ongoing input. Examples cited include asynchronous input such as written comments, audio submissions, or recorded video statements.
Response:
We appreciate these suggestions about increasing the ways interested parties share information with us. We recognize the importance of patients having access to multiple methods for sharing information about their experiences. We hosted such events in a non-livestreamed venue that included only patients, patient advocacy organizations, and caregivers for initial price applicability years 2027 and 2028. Additionally, patients, patient advocacy organizations, caregivers, and others such as clinicians, researchers, and the public at large, may submit written comments via the Drug Price Negotiation ICR. We intend to submit this final ICR for OMB approval upon publication of the final rule. Once approved, patients and others will have the opportunity to submit their information in early 2027 for initial price applicability year 2029. At this time, we are unable to accept recorded comments or audio submissions for the Negotiation Program. However, we broadly welcome input from interested parties and the public by email at:
IRARebateandNegotiation@cms.hhs.gov
.
We review and respond to inquiries received via the IRA mailbox.

5. Provision of CMS' Initial Offer and Concise Justification (§ 429.520)
Section 1194(b)(2)(B) of the Act requires that, not later than June 1 following the selected drug publication date with respect to the initial price applicability year, CMS shall provide the Primary Manufacturer of the selected drug with a written initial offer that contains the proposal for the MFP of the drug and a concise justification based on the factors described in section 1194(e) that were used in developing such offer. With respect to initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, we implemented this requirement through guidance, including, for example, section 60.4 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028.
With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, and consistent with policies for implementation as described in section 60.4 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed in § 429.520(a) that the written initial offer from CMS would be provided to the Primary Manufacturer no later than June 1 following the selected drug publication date as defined in proposed § 429.20. We proposed at § 429.520(a)(1) that this written initial offer would be accompanied by an Addendum to the Negotiation Program Agreement populated with the proposal for the MFP for CMS and the Primary Manufacturer to formalize agreement upon the MFP if such agreement is reached at this stage. Consistent with proposed § 429.410(a), no written initial offer can exceed the statutorily determined ceiling as defined in section 1194(c) of the Act and described in section II.E.3. of this final rule and in proposed § 429.410(b). Consistent with proposed § 429.440(b), no written initial offer can be less than the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, if final, as defined in section 1194(d) of the Act and described in section II.E.9. of this final rule.
With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, we proposed in § 429.520(b) that CMS would include a concise justification for the written initial offer based on the data set forth in proposed § 429.505. Consistent with proposed § 429.505(a), CMS considers the Primary Manufacturer-required data specified in § 429.505(b)(2) and evidence about the selected drug and therapeutic alternatives specified in § 429.505(d)(3), as applicable to the drug, as the basis for determining the offers and counteroffers for the selected drug. As proposed in § 429.520(b)(1), the concise justification would include a qualitative description of the factors from section 1194(e) of the Act as proposed in § 429.505(b) and (d) and a description of the methodology that CMS used to develop the written initial offer as described in section II.F.3. of this final rule and under proposed subpart F. As proposed in § 429.520(b)(2), the information contained in the concise justification would provide the Primary Manufacturer with information on the range of evidence and other information considered under section 1194(e) of the Act that CMS found compelling during the development of the written initial offer and may include information obtained through events with interested parties as proposed in § 429.520(b)(3). We believe the information in the concise justification would provide the Primary Manufacturer with information to build a statutory written counteroffer if the Primary Manufacturer decides to reject the written initial offer.
The written initial offer and concise justification would not include information that we determine to be third-party proprietary pricing information, information that could lead to the calculation of a third-party's proprietary pricing information, PHI/PII, other information that is protected from disclosure under other applicable law in accordance with the confidentiality policies described in section II.D.1. of this final rule and in proposed § 429.300, or the starting point.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses. Given that commenters combined feedback on these proposals regarding the initial offer and concise justification with feedback on the proposal for counteroffers at § 429.525, we include the comments received on counteroffers and proposed § 429.525 in this section.
Comment:
A commenter recommended CMS provide a meaningful justification for the initial offer and provide manufacturers with the opportunity to comment on CMS' response to any counteroffers. Another commenter stated that without a meaningful justification from CMS in the initial offer, manufacturers cannot provide a meaningful justification in a statutory written counteroffer. A few commenters suggested that the concise justification and CMS' response to any counteroffer should detail specific information, such as the sources CMS referenced, evidence considered, section 1194(e) data considered and how they were weighted, therapeutic alternatives considered, interested parties consulted, and benefits and impacts of the drugs considered. Another commenter recommended CMS' concise justification should have a consistent documented structure containing certain elements relevant to the proposal for the MFP.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their feedback. Consistent with our response to similar comments in Negotiation Program Guidance and the final guidance for initial price applicability year 2027, section 1194(b)(2)(B) of the Act directs CMS to provide a concise justification to the Primary Manufacturer when the initial offer is made. CMS implements the requirement to provide an initial offer and concise justification to a Primary Manufacturer in a consistent manner across all Primary Manufacturers, as required by section 1194(b)(1) of the Act. We will include information regarding the range of evidence and other information submitted pursuant to section 1194(e) of the Act that CMS found compelling in developing its initial offer, which includes the identification of therapeutic alternatives. Because this information will be shared with the Primary Manufacturer, we believe the concise justification will be meaningful and will provide the Primary Manufacturer with information to build a statutory written counteroffer if the Primary Manufacturer decides to reject the initial offer. While any statutory written counteroffer should respond to the justification provided in CMS' written initial offer, a Primary Manufacturer is not limited by the information provided in CMS' written initial offer when developing a statutory written counteroffer. As described in § 429.515(a)(1), the first meeting that we will offer Primary Manufacturers to attend will be intended for the Primary Manufacturer to provide additional context on their data submission of the section 1194(e)(1) factors and section 1194(e)(2) factors described in § 429.505(b)(2) and (d)(3), respectively, as we begin evaluating the data submission and developing an initial offer as described in § 429.510. We will also offer Primary Manufacturers the opportunity to attend up to three optional meetings that would focus on the section 1194(e)(1) factors and section 1194(e)(2) factors, and other topics aimed at working toward an agreement on an MFP. These meetings also provide a Primary Manufacturer with an opportunity to comment on CMS' response to any counteroffer.

Additionally, as described in § 429.530, the additional price exchange opportunities enable CMS and Primary Manufacturers to initiate additional written offers and counteroffers via the CMS HPMS, and this functionality includes an optional text field to enable the offering or counteroffering party to include additional contextual information for the offer or counteroffer.
Final Decision:
