I. Manufacturer Compliance and Oversight (§ 429.900)
Section 1196(b) of the Act requires that CMS monitor compliance by a Primary Manufacturer with the terms of the Negotiation Program Agreement and establish a mechanism through which violations of such terms shall be reported. With respect to initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, we implemented these requirements through guidance, including, for example, section 90.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028. With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, we proposed to codify our policies for effectuating the compliance monitoring required by section 1196(b) of the Act, consistent with those policies described in section 90.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, in proposed subpart J. Section 429.900 codifies sections 90 through 90.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance.
1. Monitoring Manufacturer Compliance (§ 429.900)
Proposed § 429.900 establishes CMS' approach to monitoring and assessment of Primary Manufacturer compliance with the terms of the Negotiation Program Agreement as described in proposed § 429.200, the Primary Manufacturer's obligation to cooperate with CMS' compliance monitoring activities, and actions CMS may take to address Primary Manufacturer noncompliance.
In accordance with section 1193(a)(5) of the Act, section 429.900(a) proposed that CMS may monitor and assess Primary Manufacturer compliance with the Negotiation Program Agreement, including compliance with all applicable requirements and conditions set forth in sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act and all applicable guidance and regulations, including part 429, implementing those provisions and any changes to the Act that affect the Negotiation Program. We will closely monitor the Primary Manufacturer's compliance with the terms of the Negotiation Program Agreement, including the requirements for Primary Manufacturers of selected drugs as described in part 429. Following the publication of selected drugs for negotiation and renegotiation for each initial price applicability year, as described in proposed § 429.100, we may provide information about the negotiation or renegotiation process, as applicable, to the Primary Manufacturer of each selected drug. We anticipate this information would include operational and statutory timelines, procedural requirements, systems instructions, IRA resources, and contact information. During the negotiation and renegotiation periods and in accordance with proposed § 429.900(a), we would track and monitor progress during all steps of the process. CMS compliance monitoring will continue beyond the negotiation period and extend to all aspects of Primary Manufacturer participation in the Negotiation Program. For example, during the negotiation period and after it has closed, we may require additional information from the Primary Manufacturer to administer or monitor compliance with the Negotiation Program in accordance with section 1193(a)(5) of the Act and as proposed in § 429.900(b). This may include requiring recurring reporting (for example, providing evidence that the MFP is being made available), or making specific ad hoc requests to the Primary Manufacturer for information related to targeted monitoring, auditing, or investigation efforts. Methods CMS may use to monitor and assess compliance, during the negotiation and renegotiation periods or otherwise, include but are not limited to: evaluation of complaints made by individuals and entities to CMS; CMS' engagement in direct communications with the Primary Manufacturer; and CMS audits and comprehensive reviews.
As described in proposed § 429.900(b), Primary Manufacturers must cooperate with CMS compliance monitoring activities. This includes providing complete, accurate, and relevant responses to CMS requests for clarifications, corrections, and additional information and complying fully with requests for corrective action during the compliance monitoring process and when noncompliance is identified. For example, we proposed that Primary Manufacturers must submit complete, accurate, and relevant responses, in the form and manner and on the timeline specified by CMS, in response to written requests CMS provides to the Primary Manufacturer in the course of our compliance monitoring activities when we deem appropriate. We are committed to providing Primary Manufacturers with reasonable timeframes to accommodate these information requests; Primary Manufacturers have the burden of establishing why an extension of any deadline to submit information should be considered by CMS. As stated in the proposed rule, if a Primary Manufacturer articulates a reasonable basis for seeking an extension for a reasonable duration of time, and the request is submitted at a reasonable point in time before the deadline (for example, 3 calendar days prior to the initial deadline), then CMS may grant an extension of a limited duration to the extent consistent with statutory
(
printed page 72319)
timelines and other operational considerations.
Likewise, we proposed in § 429.900(b) that a Primary Manufacturer must comply fully with corrective action requests that we provide to the Primary Manufacturer when we deem it appropriate; for example, including but not limited to, in the event that a Primary Manufacturer fails to submit data as described in proposed §§ 429.100 and 429.505 of this final rule. We recognize the substantial role that manufacturer-submitted information will play in the negotiation and renegotiation processes and the need for complete and accurate information. Should CMS determine that a submission is incomplete or contains inaccurate information, CMS may provide a written request to the Primary Manufacturer to clarify the submission, correct the inaccuracy, or provide the necessary information, with a deadline by which the Primary Manufacturer must respond. The written corrective action request would outline the needed action and establish a deadline for the Primary Manufacturer to correct the submission and/or provide additional information to validate the accuracy and completeness of the original submission. We intend to be available to engage with the Primary Manufacturer about the specifics of a corrective action request and to answer questions and provide clarification.
The information outlined in the proposed rule is necessary for CMS to administer and monitor the Negotiation Program in accordance with section 1193(a)(5) of the Act. As such, as proposed at § 429.900(b), failure to provide complete and accurate information, initially or in response to CMS' initial questions or corrective action requests, may result in the Primary Manufacturer being subject to a CMP as authorized under section 1197(c) of the Act and as described in proposed § 429.1005.
In proposed § 429.900(c), we proposed to establish the actions CMS may take if we conclude that a Primary Manufacturer is noncompliant with one or more requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement, including all applicable requirements and conditions set forth in sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act and all applicable guidance and regulations, including part 429, implementing those provisions and any changes to the Act that affect the Negotiation Program. Upon identifying a violation, CMS may take one or more of the following actions: (1) CMS may provide a written notice to the Primary Manufacturer of the violation; (2) CMS may request the Primary Manufacturer to take specific corrective action to address the noncompliance; or (3) CMS may impose a CMP on the Primary Manufacturer as set forth in subpart K. In instances in which CMS provides a written notice to the Primary Manufacturer of the violation and/or requests specific corrective action, the agency may offer the Primary Manufacturer the opportunity, by a specified deadline, to provide information regarding the circumstances of violation, evidence seeking to refute the finding of violation, proof of mitigation of noncompliance, and other factors for CMS' consideration. CMS proposed to consider such information if timely submitted when determining whether to pursue further enforcement action such as imposition of CMPs.
We received public comments on the proposed provisions to establish the actions CMS may take if the agency concludes that a Primary Manufacturer is noncompliant with one or more requirements and conditions set forth in sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act and all applicable guidance and regulations, including part 429, implementing those provisions and any changes to the Act that affect the Negotiation Program. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter requested protection from enforcement in instances where 340B covered entities refuse to share data needed for 340B claim deduplication.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback provided by this commenter. First, as this comment addresses a process related to MFP effectuation, it is considered outside the scope of this final rule. However, broadly, in the final rule, we decline to designate any specific compliance safe harbors under the Negotiation Program, including related to instances where 340B covered entities refuse to share data related to the 340B eligibility of a claim. CMS reiterates the policy established in Negotiation Program Guidance describing a Primary Manufacturer's obligation to transmit payment of an amount that provides access to the MFP of a selected drug to the dispensing entity within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window and applicability of section 1193(d)(1) of the Act only if: (1) the claim for the selected drug is a 340B-eligible claim; and (2) the 340B ceiling price is lower than the MFP for the selected drug. As described in sections 40.4.3.1 and 40.4.4.2 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, in cases where a Primary Manufacturer receives claim-level data elements for a selected drug that it reasonably believes is subject to the exception under section 1193(d)(1) of the Act, the Primary Manufacturer would indicate so when reporting claim-level payment elements to the MTF and declining to transmit payment in an amount that provides access to the MFP within the 14-day prompt MFP payment window. In this scenario, the Primary Manufacturer would be required to provide documentation demonstrating the claim was 340B-eligible and the 340B ceiling price was lower than the MFP upon request from CMS as described in section 90.2 of the Negotiation Program Guidance.
In the course of its monitoring and oversight functions, CMS may investigate Primary Manufacturer compliance with MFP effectuation requirements, including to assess whether an MFP refund was owed rather than the exception in section 1193(d)(1) of the Act applying. As part of such investigations, CMS will review the extent to which the Primary Manufacturer reasonably believed that the exception in section 1193(d)(1) of the Act applied and the role that any operational barriers played in the Primary Manufacturer being able to take timely action to meet its statutory obligation to make MFP available, as applicable, with respect to these claims. Consistent with enforcement policies described later in this section, in instances where CMS finds noncompliance with Negotiation Program requirements, CMS intends to exercise the authority to impose CMPs for instances of noncompliance that substantively obstruct Negotiation Program processes and/or availability of the MFP.
Comment:
A few commenters raised concerns that Primary Manufacturers may be subject to enforcement actions despite acting in good faith to fulfill their compliance obligations under the Negotiation Program. A couple of commenters mentioned that a Primary Manufacturer may reasonably misinterpret an information request for which CMS may deem a response to be incomplete or inaccurate. When addressing noncompliance and imposing CMPs, a commenter felt that CMS was departing from HHS' general practices by penalizing Primary Manufacturers without assessing good faith effort. Another commenter mentioned that there are a number of ways that a Primary Manufacturer could unintentionally omit reporting data when responding to CMS. Another commenter remarked that the proposed changes deviate from principles of good faith and timely resolution of issues related to data integrity. A commenter
(
printed page 72320)
suggested that CMS define what constitutes as a good faith compliance effort.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their feedback. As discussed in section II.J.1. of this final rule, CMS intends to exercise the authority to impose CMPs in instances of noncompliance that substantively obstruct administration of the Negotiation Program. We are establishing a structure for enforcement actions that, among other things, is not punitive in response to immaterial noncompliance or other instances of noncompliance that are not substantive. Consistent with policy established in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we provide in § 429.900(b) that Primary Manufacturers must cooperate with CMS compliance monitoring and evaluation activities, including providing complete and accurate responses to CMS requests for clarifications, corrections, and additional information, and complying fully with all requests for corrective action. These monitoring efforts reflect CMS' intent to continue to engage in Negotiation Program compliance monitoring and oversight activities in accordance with HHS' established practices for managing noncompliance by offering, when warranted and at CMS' discretion, opportunities for correction, including clarification. The determination of whether to exercise enforcement discretion with respect to identified noncompliance is based on the facts, circumstances, and totality of evidence available to CMS for each specific case. Primary Manufacturers are expected to make good faith efforts to resolve compliance issues and maintain open communication with CMS. CMS recommends that Primary Manufacturers maintain documentation evidencing their good faith efforts to comply with Negotiation Program obligations. CMS may request or consider such documentation when considering whether to impose CMPs with respect to identified noncompliance. We intend to offer opportunities for Primary Manufacturers to undertake corrective action when appropriate and at CMS' discretion. Regarding the request for CMS to define what constitutes a “good faith compliance effort”, we emphasize that every instance of noncompliance is assessed on a case-by-case basis. In all instances, we encourage communication, cooperation, and timely attempts to rectify compliance issues. Where a Primary Manufacturer can demonstrate that it has made reasonable, good faith efforts to fulfill its obligations, or that compliance was impeded by circumstances outside its control, this will be considered in our assessment of whether to impose CMPs.
Comment:
A few commenters requested more specificity in proposed § 429.900(c) where CMS outlines the enforcement actions the agency may take in response to Primary Manufacturer noncompliance. To address noncompliance, the proposed language states that CMS may take one or more of the following actions: provide notice of violation, request corrective action, and/or impose a CMP. These commenters expressed that the language is too vague and open-ended. These commenters recommended that CMS provide clarity on the applicable guidance and requirements for the respective enforcement actions. Particularly, commenters are unclear as to which requirements would trigger a CMP response.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their feedback regarding enforcement actions CMS may take if we conclude a Primary Manufacturer is noncompliant with one or more of the requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement, including all applicable requirements and conditions set forth in sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act and all applicable guidance and regulations. Our primary goal is to successfully administer all aspects of the Negotiation Program; we intend to exercise the authority to impose CMPs in instances of noncompliance that substantively obstruct Negotiation Program processes. In evaluating whether to impose CMPs in instances of identified noncompliance, we will consider the circumstances of each case, taking into account the severity and frequency of noncompliance. As described in section II.J.1. of this final rule, instances of noncompliance that may warrant the imposition of CMPs include, but are not limited to, egregious or knowing violations of Negotiation Program requirements or repeated violations of the Negotiation Program Agreement or other Negotiation Program requirements. Examples of substantive violations for which CMPs may be appropriate can be found in Table 4—Examples of Substantive Violations of this final rule. Note that the examples in Table 4 are not an exhaustive list of violations that may warrant CMPs. As appropriate and upon determination of an instance of noncompliance, we may issue a written notice to the Primary Manufacturer of the violation(s), request the Primary Manufacturer to take specific corrective action to address the noncompliance, and/or impose a CMP. If we make a determination to assess a CMP, we will follow the procedures outlined in section II.J.4. of this final rule.
Comment:
A few commenters encouraged CMS to have robust mechanisms in place for compliance oversight to ensure manufacturers fulfill program obligations. A commenter stressed the need for increased enforcement. Another commenter supported CMS' proposed compliance and enforcement efforts, including broad monitoring authority.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback provided by commenters regarding the monitoring and enforcement efforts related to Primary Manufacturer compliance with the Negotiation Program Agreement. We recognize the importance of effective oversight mechanisms to ensure that Primary Manufacturers meet their obligations under the Negotiation Program Agreement. Our approach is to maintain a robust monitoring and oversight program intended to foster transparency, accountability, and adherence to established guidelines throughout the operation of the Negotiation Program.
Comment:
A commenter encouraged CMS to be cognizant of the administrative burden on downstream entities as the agency continues to develop policies related to compliance monitoring and other procedures. The commenter expressed concern that providing flexibility for manufacturers adopting manufacturer-specific approaches to MFP effectuation could result in inconsistency across different products and markets, resulting in heightened administrative burden in navigating the program for downstream entities.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback provided by this commenter. We remain committed to considering stakeholder burden across Negotiation Program operations, including program monitoring, oversight, and enforcement activities; we routinely aim to minimize burden on manufacturers, dispensing entities, and other downstream entities related to compliance activities while balancing the need to operate robust monitoring and oversight as we implement the Negotiation Program. For example, we conduct extensive monitoring and oversight exercises internally at CMS, such as conducting ongoing analysis using program and industry data. With respect to the comment regarding “manufacturer-specific” approaches to MFP effectuation, we note that MFP effectuation policies are outside the scope of this final rule. However, we note generally that public input is
(
printed page 72321)
considered when designing operational processes, including agency compliance monitoring and oversight processes. CMS works to gather such input both through informal channels (for example, monthly stakeholder technical meetings) and formal channels (for example, public comment periods on program policy and various Information Collection Requests). These collective efforts allow stakeholders to provide insight into real-world perspectives, stakeholder data, and emerging issues to inform agency decision-making to support our goal of streamlining operations and reducing burden. Importantly, we have designed compliance and oversight processes that are applied consistently across manufacturers and intend to continue to operate in a consistent manner.
Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing § 429.900 as proposed.
J. Civil Monetary Penalties (§§ 429.1005 Through 429.1020)
1. Civil Monetary Penalties
Section 1197 of the Act provides for the imposition of CMPs on manufacturers for: (1) failure to provide access to a price that is less than or equal to the maximum fair price for a drug; (2) failure to pay the rebate amount for a biological product inclusion of which on the selected drug list was delayed but has since undergone negotiation, as described in section 1192(f)(4) of the Act; (3) violation of certain terms of the Negotiation Program Agreement; and (4) the provision of false information as described in section 1197(d) of the Act.
With respect to initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, we implemented these requirements through guidance, including, for example, section 100 of the Negotiation Program Guidance with respect to initial price applicability year 2028. With respect to initial price applicability year 2029 and subsequent years, with the exception of our authority pursuant to section 1197(a) of the Act as described later in this section, we proposed to codify our policies for implementation of our CMP authorities as set forth in section 1197 of the Act, consistent with those policies described in section 100 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, in proposed subpart K.
In future rulemaking, we will codify our policies for implementation of section 1197(a) of the Act, under which manufacturers may be subject to a CMP for failure to provide access to a price less than or equal to the MFP, for 2029 and subsequent years. Consistent with the statutory directive to use program instruction or other forms of program guidance to implement sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act for 2026, 2027, and 2028, a Primary Manufacturer's compliance obligations with respect to its obligation to provide access to a price less than or equal to the MFP for 2026, 2027, and 2028 are established in the applicable program guidance, and we are reserving codifying the CMP associated with violation of this obligation, including the process, calculation, and substantive compliance obligations, for 2029 and subsequent years, for future rulemaking.
In proposed § 429.1005, we address potential imposition of CMPs for a Primary Manufacturer's violation of a requirement determined by CMS to be necessary for the purposes of administering and monitoring compliance with the Negotiation Program, including without limitation, the requirement to submit information pursuant to section 1193(a)(4) of the Act, in accordance with section 1197(c) of the Act. In proposed § 429.1010, we address potential imposition of CMPs for provision of false information for use in applying the eligibility rules at sections 1192(d)(2)(B) and (f)(1)(C) of the Act, in accordance with section 1197(d) of the Act. In proposed § 429.1015, we address potential imposition of CMP for failure to pay a rebate as required by section 1192(f)(4) of the Act, in accordance with section 1197(b) of the Act. In proposed § 429.1020, we address details about the process for imposition of CMPs. Separate from CMS imposition of CMPs, per
26 U.S.C. 5000D
, failure of a Primary Manufacturer to comply with certain Negotiation Program deadlines and other requirements of the Negotiation Program may result in potential excise tax liability.
Our primary goal is to successfully administer all aspects of the Negotiation Program; we intend to exercise the authority to impose CMPs in instances of noncompliance that substantively obstruct Negotiation Program processes. Such instances may include, but are not limited to, the examples shown in Table II.F3, such as failure to provide timely, complete, and accurate information that is necessary to execute the negotiation process or other administrative or monitoring functions of the Negotiation Program; repeated violations of the Negotiation Program Agreement or other Negotiation Program requirements determined by CMS to be necessary for the purposes of administering and monitoring compliance with the Negotiation Program; or egregious or knowing violations of Negotiation Program requirements. Note that these examples are not an exhaustive list of violations that could warrant CMPs. We reserve the authority to issue CMPs for other violations as required to effectively administer and monitor the Negotiation Program.
(
printed page 72322)
Broadly, we proposed to establish a structure for enforcement actions that: (1) is within CMS' statutory authority; (2) is not punitive in response to immaterial noncompliance, or other instances of noncompliance that are not substantive; (3) can be applied consistently across applicable instances of Primary Manufacturer noncompliance; and (4) facilitates the ability to successfully engage in all components of the negotiation process within the established timeframes.
2. Violations of the Negotiation Program Agreement (§ 429.1005)
In accordance with section 1197(c) of the Act, any Primary Manufacturer of a selected drug that has entered into a Negotiation Program Agreement with CMS as set forth in proposed § 429.200 that fails to comply with requirements determined by CMS to be necessary for the purposes of administering the Negotiation Program and monitoring compliance with the Negotiation Program, including failure to provide information required under section 1193(a)(4) of the Act, including information required to be submitted under proposed § 429.405(a) and (b), may be subject to statutorily-specified CMPs for each day of such violation. The statutorily specified amount of $1,000,000 a day is updated yearly per the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustments Improvements Act of 2015. In applying CMPs for Primary Manufacturer violations of the Negotiation Program Agreement, we intend to use discretion such that CMPs are reserved for instances of substantive noncompliance.
Effective oversight of the Negotiation Program requires that CMS receive complete and accurate data from Primary Manufacturers. We view the authority to impose CMPs as established in section 1197(c) of the Act as a tool to ensure that a Primary Manufacturer is participating in the Negotiation Program consistent with its signed Negotiation Program Agreement, including, but not limited to, providing complete and accurate information CMS deems necessary for administering and monitoring compliance with the Negotiation Program and promptly responding to any communications from CMS regarding the Negotiation Program, including requests for clarification, correction, additional information, or specific corrective actions.
In the proposed rule, we proposed to consolidate and clarify our approach to monitoring and enforcement in the context of data reporting. Specifically, we did not propose to codify the policies previously stated in section 40.2.3 of the Negotiation Program Guidance but rather we proposed to pursue a consolidated approach to monitoring and enforcement that is consistent with the policies regarding data reporting obligations stated in sections 90 and 100 of the Negotiation Program Guidance. For example, we may impose a CMP for violation of a requirement of the Negotiation Program Agreement if a Primary Manufacturer fails to provide data required under the Drug Price Negotiation ICR Forms, such as information on non-FAMP for each applicable quarter, as described in proposed § 429.405 of this final rule, for each NDC-11 of the selected drug for the applicable period, by the deadline established at proposed § 429.505(b)(1). In this scenario, upon identifying the missing data, we may take a variety of actions. For one, in accordance with proposed § 429.900(c), we may send the Primary Manufacturer a request for corrective action to address the noncompliance, such as a request that
(
printed page 72323)
the Primary Manufacturer provide a complete and accurate production of the outstanding non-FAMP data by a specified date. If the Primary Manufacturer complies with the request for corrective action by timely providing complete and accurate non-FAMP data, we may exercise discretion and determine not to impose a CMP for the Primary Manufacturer's initial failure to provide complete and accurate non-FAMP data by the specified deadline. Or, depending on the circumstances, in accordance with enforcement priorities, we may determine that, even if a Primary Manufacturer complies with a request for corrective action, it remains appropriate to issue a violation notice and impose a CMP for the initial violation. Alternatively, in accordance with proposed § 429.900(c), we may not issue a request for corrective action and instead send a notice of violation to the Primary Manufacturer and impose a CMP in accordance with subpart K. Finally, if we send the Primary Manufacturer a request for corrective action and the Primary Manufacturer does not comply with such request, in accordance with proposed § 429.900(c), we may issue a violation notice and impose a CMP for the failure to comply with CMS' corrective action request, which would be separate from any violation notice and CMP imposition addressing the violation that arose from the Primary Manufacturer's initial failure to provide complete and accurate non-FAMP data by the specified deadline.
In a case where a CMP is pursued, we stated that we intended to send a written CMP notification, as described in proposed § 429.1005(d), that reflects the start date of the penalty accrual, the end date of the penalty accrual, and the total amount of the penalty assessed, as described in proposed § 429.1020(a). As described at proposed § 429.1005(c), the state date of the penalty accrual is the first day of the violation as set forth in proposed § 429.1005(a). In the earlier example, the start date of the penalty accrual would be the day after the applicable submission deadline. As described at proposed § 429.1005(c), the CMP shall accrue until the Primary Manufacturer has provided the necessary information or otherwise taken any corrective action determined by CMS to be necessary to address the violation, including, as applicable, providing documentation to evidence that the Primary Manufacturer has provided all past due information, or the Negotiation Program Agreement is terminated. In the earlier example, in the event the Primary Manufacturer never provides the required information, the daily CMP would continue to accrue until the Negotiation Program Agreement was terminated as described in proposed § 429.205. We plan to adopt the same approach to enforcement in a circumstance where a Primary Manufacturer failed to provide data for a drug selected for renegotiation, with a violation accruing each day after the deadline established for provision of the data in proposed § 429.615 until the Primary Manufacturer provided the data. In the event the Primary Manufacturer never provides the required data, the CMP will continue to accrue until the Negotiation Program Agreement is terminated as described in proposed § 429.205. The imposition of a CMP related to failure to provide required data for the renegotiation process does not negate the Primary Manufacturer's ongoing obligation to provide access to the previously negotiated MFP. Primary Manufacturers continue to have the obligation to make the previously negotiated MFP available.
Another example of when CMS may impose a CMP for violation of the Negotiation Program Agreement is if the Primary Manufacturer submits information that is required under the Negotiation Program Agreement and CMS determines the information is false. In this example, the Primary Manufacturer would be determined to be noncompliant with the requirement to submit information and may be subject to a CMP. In instances of a Primary Manufacturer submitting false information that is required under the Negotiation Program Agreement, in accordance with proposed § 429.1005, a CMP would begin to accrue on the day after the established deadline for submission of information under the Negotiation Program Agreement and would continue to accrue until the Primary Manufacturer provides a complete and accurate submission of the required information to CMS or the Negotiation Program Agreement is terminated as described in § 429.205. The start and end date of CMP accrual as well as the total amount accrued will be noted on the CMP notification sent by CMS, following the process established in proposed § 429.1020.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters opposed the policy proposed at § 429.1005 because they stated it bypasses the opportunity for corrective action in certain instances of identified noncompliance. These commenters noted that section 40.2.3 of the Negotiation Program guidance governing initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 explicitly afforded a 5-business day window to respond to corrective action requests and provided the opportunity to rectify any issues related to submission of information required under section 1193(a)(4) of the Act and that this 5-day window was not included in the proposed rule. A few commenters advocated for CMPs to be imposed only for repeated and severe violations. A commenter stated that the proposed rule is a “more aggressive approach to enforcement,” and advocated for warning notices to be issued prior to potential applicability of excise taxes. A few commenters stated that CMS did not provide an explanation as to why the proposed rule no longer includes a 5-day window for rectifying issues regarding noncompliance related to submission of information required under section 1193(a)(4) of the Act and stated that the Supreme Court has held that agencies must provide a reasoned explanation when making new policy changes. A commenter requested that CMS maintain the current oversight and enforcement methods and reserve any process changes for future rulemaking opportunities. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS establish a corrective action process as a mandatory step prior to CMP issuance, rather than limiting corrective action opportunities specifically to circumstances in which CMS determines such opportunities are warranted.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their input. In implementing § 429.1005, we reiterate that we intend to exercise the authority to impose CMPs in instances of noncompliance that substantively obstruct the processes of the Negotiation Program. We remain committed to providing opportunities for corrective action in situations where we deem it appropriate and intend to maintain our operational approach of providing Primary Manufacturers reasonable time periods to fulfill requests for information and/or corrective action and considering requests for extensions as warranted. For example, if we determine that a submission from a Primary Manufacturer is incomplete or contains inaccurate information, we may issue a written request to the Primary Manufacturer to clarify the submission, correct the inaccuracy, or provide the missing information. This written request will specify a deadline by which the Primary Manufacturer must respond. If the Primary Manufacturer
(
printed page 72324)
complies with the request for corrective action by timely providing complete and accurate information, we may exercise enforcement discretion and determine not to impose a CMP for the Primary Manufacturer's initial failure to provide complete and accurate information by the specified deadline. Alternatively, in accordance with§ 429.900(c), we may not issue a request for corrective action and instead send a notice of violation to the Primary Manufacturer and impose a CMP in accordance with subpart K. In evaluating whether to impose CMPs in instances of identified noncompliance, we will consider the circumstances of each case, including but not limited to taking into account the severity and frequency of noncompliance. The enforcement framework outlined in the final rule is designed to ensure that penalties are not imposed in a punitive manner for immaterial or non-substantive instances of noncompliance. In section II.J.2. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36314
through
15
), we outlined scenarios demonstrating how outcomes may vary, including situations where corrective action may or may not be pursued.
We intend to be available to engage with Primary Manufacturers about the specifics of a corrective action request and to answer questions and provide clarifications. Additionally, we intend to provide Primary Manufacturers with reasonable deadlines to respond to requests for information requests and/or corrective action. This approach is designed to facilitate timely and effective resolution of compliance issues.
In response to requests for further explanation regarding the absence of the specified 5-day response time to corrective action requests in response to noncompliance related to submission of information required under section 1193(a)(4) of the Act, we note that the policy in the proposed rule, which we are finalizing herein, is not a significant change to the approach previously described in section 40.2.3 of the Negotiation Program Guidance. By consolidating and clarifying the policies described in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we seek to ensure that stakeholders understand the agency's enforcement processes and how they will be applied within the Negotiation Program. The monitoring and enforcement policies adopted in this final rule aim to provide the guidance and support necessary to facilitate consistent, good faith compliance. Operationally, CMS intends to continue to provide Primary Manufacturers with opportunities to correct information submissions or to provide additional information with reasonable timeframes to respond to such actions or both. However, offering these opportunities is not a required precursor to potential enforcement actions for any failure to meet these obligations.
We decline to explicitly establish that a corrective action process will be required as the initial step prior to CMP issuance in every instance under the final rule. We may choose to pursue corrective action, impose a CMP, or both depending on the nature of the violation and its potential effects on program operations. Regarding the comment on potential applicability of excise taxes, we refer this commenter to
26 U.S.C. 5000D
for additional information. We note that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) is responsible for administering and enforcing the excise tax, not CMS.
Comment:
Commenters recommended that CMS add to § 429.200(b), which specifies requirements and conditions to which a Primary Manufacturer agrees when executing a Negotiation Program Agreement, a specific reference to a Primary Manufacturer's obligation to timely report updates to the NDC-11 information of the selected drug as described in § 429.100(e), to more explicitly warn manufacturers of a potential CMP for failure to report NDC updates as provided in § 429.100(e) and to further support adherence to program compliance.
Response:
We thank these commenters for their feedback. Consistent with the policy described at § 429.1005, failure of a Primary Manufacturer that has entered into a Negotiation Program Agreement to comply with certain Negotiation Program deadlines and other requirements of the Negotiation Program, including failure to provide updated NDC-11 information to CMS as described in the proposed rule under § 429.100(e), which we are finalizing herein, may result in CMPs. The specific regulatory sections identified in § 429.200(b) are illustrative and not exhaustive of the Negotiation Program requirements for which a violation may give rise to the imposition of CMPs. As mentioned in previous responses, we intend to use our authority to impose CMPs for substantive noncompliance that obstructs Negotiation Program processes, while remaining committed to offering corrective action opportunities when appropriate. We will provide Primary Manufacturers reasonable timeframes to meet requests for information or corrective action and will consider extension requests as warranted.
Comment:
A few commenters raised concerns about the potential for CMS to impose concurrent CMPs for a Primary Manufacturer's failure to provide complete and accurate information. For example, a CMP could be imposed for the initial failure to provide complete and accurate information followed by an additional CMP due to failure to comply with a CMS corrective action request. A few commenters indicated that because of the complexity and extent of the information collection requests for the negotiation process Primary Manufacturers may inadvertently provide inaccurate or incomplete information. A few commenters requested that CMS clarify its intent and recommended the elimination of duplicative CMPs stemming from the same underlying violation.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback provided by commenters regarding enforcement actions for program violations. We emphasize that CMS retains the authority to address separate and distinct violations of the Negotiation Program even where such violations may be related or run concurrently. However, CMS is not establishing a policy that more than one CMP would be issued for the same underlying violation. Enforcement actions may be applied separately to each applicable case of noncompliance, ensuring that the response aligns with the specific nature and impact of the violation.
We are establishing an enforcement framework that operates within our statutory authority and provides clear and consistent procedures for addressing noncompliance within the Negotiation Program. Further, we reiterate that the enforcement framework is designed to ensure that penalties are not imposed in a punitive manner for immaterial or non-substantive instances of noncompliance.
Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing § 429.1005 as proposed.

In accordance with section 1197(d) of the Act, we proposed at § 429.1010 two circumstances where CMS may impose a CMP due to provision of false information: (1) CMS proposed we may impose a statutorily specified CMP on a Biosimilar Manufacturer for each item of false information the Biosimilar Manufacturer knowingly provides to CMS for use in applying the aggregation rule described at proposed § 429.110(b)(1)(iv)(A); and (2) CMS
(

Section 1197(d) of the Act provides for imposition of a CMP in the amount of $100,000,000 per item of false information. This amount will be updated yearly per the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Improvements Act of 2015.
CMS proposed to adopt a standard for “knowingly” that conforms with the Office of Inspector General definition at § 1003.110 in the application of CMPs. 5. Notice and Appeal Procedures (§ 429.1020)
Under section 1197(e) of the Act, CMPs imposed in accordance with sections 1197(a) through (d) of the Act are subject to the provisions of section 1128A of the Act (other than subsections (a) and (b)). Accordingly, when CMS makes a determination to assess a CMP, we intend to provide a written CMP notification that the manufacturer has engaged in one or more violations as described at proposed §§ 429.1005 through 429.1015 and is subject to a CMP. We proposed at § 429.1020(a) that the CMP notification would include the following:
A description of the basis for the determination.
The basis for the penalty,
The start date of the penalty (if applicable).
The end date of the penalty (if applicable).
The total amount of the penalty assessed.
The date the penalty is due.
The manufacturer's right to a hearing.
Information about where to file the request for a hearing.
In the case of violations associated with CMPs with daily accruals as described in proposed § 429.1005, we intend to send the CMP notification after the accrual has ended to reflect both the start date, end date, and total amount of penalty assessed within the notice. We have considered an alternative policy in which CMP notification letters would be issued during the period that the daily penalty amounts are still actively accruing. Such an approach would result in assessment of interim CMPs on Primary Manufacturers, each for the dollar amount that had accrued as of the date we issue each applicable interim CMP notice. We would issue such interim notices at set time intervals (for example, every 14 days) throughout the period in which the penalty continues to accrue as described in proposed § 429.1005. CMS solicited comment on this alternative option.
Per section 1128A of the Act, CMPs are due 60 calendar days after the receipt of the CMP notification, unless the manufacturer chooses to initiate an appeal. At the conclusion of any appeal process initiated by the manufacturer, where there is still a CMP amount owed, the civil monetary penalty is due within 60 calendar days of the appeal decision.
To operationalize the CMP appeal process in the Negotiation Program, we proposed adopting the existing procedures as codified in
42 CFR part 423 subpart T
: Appeal Procedures for Civil Money Penalties (see
42 CFR 423.1000
through
423.1094
) that currently apply to Part D sponsors and to manufacturers under the Manufacturer Discount Program. In accordance with this appeals process, the manufacturer would have 60 calendar days after receipt of the CMP notification to request a hearing (
42 CFR 423.1020
). If the manufacturer requests a hearing, the procedures outlined in section 1128A of the Act and operationalized by part 423, subpart T would apply. As set forth in section 1128A(f) of the Act, if the manufacturer does not pay the CMP timely, the CMP amount may be deducted from any sum then or later owing by the United States. CMP funds would be deposited in accordance with section 1128A(f) of the Act.
As described in proposed § 429.1020(e), in the event that a manufacturer declares bankruptcy, as described in title 11 of the United States Code and fails to pay either the full rebate amount of a Biosimilar Delay rebate owed or the total sum of CMPs imposed, the government reserves the right to file a proof of claim with the bankruptcy court to recover the unpaid rebate amount and/or CMPs owed by the manufacturer. Filing a proof of claim does not waive any other rights of the United States to recover such amounts or to assert priority status as permitted under applicable law. CMS may exercise its offset authority under section 1128A(f) of the Act independently of, and in addition to, other available collection remedies permitted under Federal law.

III. Implementation of Inflation Reduction Act Provisions for the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program
A. Part D Formulary Inclusion of Selected Drugs
1. Background
Sections 11001 and 11002 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (
Pub. L. 117-169
) created Part E under Title XI of the Act (sections 1191 through 1198) which established the Negotiation Program to negotiate maximum fair prices (MFPs) for certain high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products.
Section 11001(b) of the IRA added section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of Act, which requires that, starting in 2026 and for each subsequent year, Part D plan sponsors include on their formularies each covered Part D drug that is a selected drug under section 1192 of the Act for which an MFP (as defined in section 1191(c)(3) of the Act) is in effect with respect to the year. Section 11001(b) of the IRA also added section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act, which clarifies that nothing in clause (i) shall be construed as prohibiting Part D plan sponsors from removing from their formularies such a selected drug if such removal would be permitted under § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) or any successor regulation.
Section 11001(c) of the IRA directed the Secretary to implement the provisions in section 11001 of the IRA, including amendments made by such section, for 2026, 2027, and 2028, by program instruction or other forms of program guidance. In accordance with the law, CMS has issued several guidance documents for implementing the Negotiation Program, including the requirement that Part D plan sponsors include on their formularies selected drugs for which an MFP is in effect, starting in 2026.
CMS issued revised or final guidance on June 30, 2023, October 2, 2024, and September 30, 2025 for implementation of the Negotiation Program for initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028, respectively.
