2. Part D Formulary Inclusion of Selected Drugs (§ 423.120)
Section 11001(b) of the IRA added section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act to require that for 2026 and each subsequent year, Part D plans include each covered Part D drug that is a selected drug under section 1192 of the Act on Part D formularies if an MFP is in effect for that drug with respect to that year. For 2026, 2027, and 2028, we have implemented this requirement through guidance.
[
96
]
With the expiration of the IRA program instruction requirement for the Negotiation Program at the end of 2028, we proposed to codify this requirement at new § 423.120(b)(2)(vii) with respect to selected drugs for which an MFP is in effect in 2029 and subsequent years.
While section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act specifies that Part D plans must include on their Part D formularies covered Part D drugs that are selected drugs for which an MFP is in effect with respect to the year, it does not otherwise specify formulary requirements for tier placement or utilization management. CMS received comments
[
97
]
expressing concerns that plans may hinder beneficiary access to selected drugs (for example, by applying utilization management requirements that are not based on medical appropriateness or placing selected drugs on less favorable tiers compared to non-selected drugs). In response to these comments, we stated
[
98
]
that CMS agrees on the importance of ensuring meaningful beneficiary access to selected drugs and their MFPs and ensuring that plans do not engage in behavior that hinders access to selected drugs or non-selected drugs when medically appropriate. However, CMS also understands that not all selected drugs and drug classes will present Part D plan sponsors and their Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committees with the same formulary considerations, and the same formulary placement might not be warranted in all situations. In order to ensure meaningful beneficiary access to selected drugs and their MFPs, CMS would continue to use its comprehensive formulary review process to assess any practices that may undermine beneficiary access to selected drugs and ensure that Part D plan sponsors comply with existing statutory and regulatory restrictions on formulary design.
Sections 1860D-2(b)(2)(B) and 1860D-4(c)(1)(A) of the Act permit Part D plan sponsors to use formularies and tiered cost sharing in their benefit design, subject to certain limitations, and require them to have a cost-effective drug utilization management program that includes incentives to reduce costs when medically appropriate. Under section 1860D-11(e)(2)(D)(i) of the Act, CMS may approve a prescription drug plan only if the agency does not find that the design of the plan and its benefits (including any formulary and tiered formulary structure) are likely to substantially discourage enrollment by certain Part D eligible individuals under the plan. In addition, § 423.272(b)(2)(i) requires that CMS not approve a bid if it finds that the design of the plan and its benefits (including any formulary and tiered formulary structure) or its utilization management program are likely to substantially discourage enrollment by certain Part D eligible individuals under the plan. Further, § 423.120(b)(2)(iii) requires each Part D plan formulary to “include adequate coverage of the types of drugs most commonly needed by Part D enrollees, as recognized in national treatment guidelines”. Finally, § 423.120(b)(1)(v) requires that in making decisions about formulary design, the entity designing the formulary must “base clinical decisions on the strength of scientific evidence and standards of practice”. CMS maintains a robust clinical formulary review process to ensure that all Medicare Part D plans meet these and other applicable requirements. CMS reviews all formularies annually to ensure that each formulary meets the agency's clinical review criteria, which include comprehensive evaluation of tier placement and all utilization management restrictions and criteria.
Consistent with section 110 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, given CMS' statutory obligation to monitor Medicare Part D plans' compliance with all applicable formulary requirements, we would continue to use our formulary review process to assess: (1) any instances where Part D plan sponsors place selected drugs on non-preferred tiers; (2) any instances where a selected drug is placed on a higher cost-sharing tier than non-selected brand drugs in the same class; (3) any instances where Part D plan sponsors require utilization of an alternative non-selected brand drug prior to a selected drug (that is, step therapy); or (4) any instances where
(
printed page 72328)
Part D plan sponsors impose more restrictive utilization management (for example, step therapy and prior authorization) for a selected drug compared to a non-selected brand drug in the same class.
For this review, we would consider, consistent with section 110 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, class to mean the FDA Established Pharmacologic Class or other source that groups like drugs with similar mechanisms of action and similar indications. Specifically, CMS would expect Part D plan sponsors to provide a reasonable justification to support their submitted plan benefit design and formulary design that includes any of the practices noted previously during the annual bid review process. This justification should address applicable clinical factors, such as clinical superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence of the selected and non-selected drugs, as well as the plan design's compliance with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements (for example, the requirement to have a cost-effective drug utilization management program that bases decisions on the strength of the clinical evidence and standards of practice). CMS would evaluate these justifications for compliance with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements and would approve a Part D plan bid submitted by a Part D plan sponsor only if the plan benefit design and formulary design complies with those requirements.
As discussed in the Negotiation Program Guidance, CMS also is aware that there are concerns that Part D plan sponsors could broadly shift access with respect to a drug selected for negotiation after the drug has been announced as a selected drug, that is, in the contract year prior to the selected drug's MFP taking effect. To address these concerns, CMS would continue to monitor trends in formulary placement for selected drugs beginning after drugs are selected for an initial price applicability year. We believe this approach would continue to provide Part D plan sponsors with the flexibility to continue to manage costs through utilization management in a clinically appropriate manner, while allowing us to monitor practices that may undermine beneficiary access to selected drugs and potentially inform new requirements for future contract years.
Finally, because a selected drug includes all dosage forms and strengths to which the MFP applies, section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act requires that formularies include all such dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug that constitute a covered Part D drug and for which the MFP is in effect. Thus, consistent with section 110 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed that Part D plan sponsors would continue to be required to include all such dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug that constitute a Part D drug and for which the MFP is in effect on their formularies.
In summary, in alignment with section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act, as added by section 11001(b) of the IRA, we proposed to codify at new § 423.120(b)(2)(vii) the requirement that, for 2026 and each subsequent year, Part D plan sponsors include each Part D drug that is a selected drug under section 1192 of the Act for which a maximum fair price (as defined in section 1191(c)(3) of the Act) is in effect with respect to the year.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposal to codify the requirement that Part D plan sponsors include each Part D drug that is a selected drug on their formularies if an MFP is in effect with respect to that year.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
Many commenters who supported codifying the selected drug formulary inclusion requirement also argued that formulary inclusion alone does not ensure meaningful, timely, or affordable beneficiary access to selected drugs. Several commenters stated that a selected drug may technically remain on a formulary while being placed on an unfavorable tier, subjected to prior authorization or step therapy, or restricted through a narrow pharmacy network, and that these practices can undermine the practical value of an MFP and can result in delayed treatment, treatment switching, or interruption of established therapy or lead beneficiaries to abandon treatment altogether. A commenter argued that the MFPs under the Negotiation Program alter the underlying economics for selected drugs, for example, by replacing existing rebate arrangements and creating altered incentives that favor cost management strategies over clinically appropriate access decisions. Other commenters raised a related concern that, because Part D plans have historically preferred higher-priced drugs that generate larger rebates, the lower point-of-sale prices resulting from MFPs may lead plan sponsors and their PBMs to favor higher-cost competing therapies in the same class, including non-selected drug alternatives that carry a higher net cost to Medicare and beneficiaries, in order to capture greater rebate revenue, and to steer patients toward those products through less favorable tier placement or utilization management requirements on selected drugs.
Several commenters urged CMS to go beyond formulary inclusion and establish stronger protections, including requiring that selected drugs be placed on a tier no less favorable than coverage for competing therapies and that utilization management for selected drugs be clinically grounded and no more restrictive than what is applied to therapeutic alternatives in the same class. A few commenters urged CMS to prohibit step therapy that is not supported by scientific and clinical evidence, and to implement continuity-of-care protections so that patients already stabilized on a selected drug are not subjected to new utilization management requirements, less favorable cost sharing, or non-medical switching driven by MFP implementation rather than clinical need.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support of our proposal to codify the formulary inclusion requirement. We are committed to ensuring that beneficiaries can meaningfully access selected drugs.
We appreciate commenters' concerns. However, as we explained in section III.A.2 of the proposed rule (
91 FR 36318
), section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act requires that Part D plan sponsors include on their formularies each covered Part D drug that is a selected drug for which an MFP is in effect. We do not believe additional regulatory requirements beyond the formulary inclusion requirement that we are finalizing in this rule are needed at this time. We do not believe it is necessary to impose tier placement or utilization management requirements specific to selected drugs because Part D regulations already require oversight of tier placement and utilization management. Our existing requirements for Part D plan sponsor Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committees require that these determinations be grounded in clinical evidence. Under § 423.120(b)(1), a Part D plan sponsor's formulary must be developed and reviewed by a Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee and this committee must, among other requirements, base clinical decisions on the strength of scientific evidence and standards of practice, consider whether the inclusion of a particular Part D drug in a formulary or formulary tier has any therapeutic advantages in terms of safety and efficacy, review policies that
(
printed page 72329)
guide exceptions and other utilization management processes, and review and approve all clinical prior authorization criteria, step therapy protocols, and quantity limit restrictions applied to each covered Part D drug. Therefore, the additional requirements the commenters recommend would duplicate requirements that already apply to Part D formulary and utilization management decisions, including those affecting selected drugs.
We are committed to using our existing authorities to monitor and address plan practices that may undermine meaningful beneficiary access to selected drugs and the respective MFPs. As stated in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36318
), and consistent with section 110 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we will continue to use our formulary review process to assess: (1) any instances where Part D plan sponsors place selected drugs on non-preferred tiers; (2) any instances where a selected drug is placed on a higher cost-sharing tier than non-selected brand drugs in the same class; (3) any instances where Part D plan sponsors require utilization of an alternative non-selected brand drug prior to a selected drug (that is, step therapy); or (4) any instances where Part D plan sponsors impose more restrictive utilization management (for example, step therapy and prior authorization) for a selected drug compared to a non-selected brand drug in the same class. We will expect Part D plan sponsors to provide a reasonable clinical justification to support any such formulary design during the annual bid review process, and we will evaluate those justifications for compliance with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements. We will approve a Part D plan bid only if the plan benefit design and formulary design comply with those requirements.
Comment:
Several commenters noted that selected drug status is a pricing designation under the Negotiation Program and not a determination of clinical superiority. However, not all these commenters drew the same conclusions from that shared premise. A few commenters recommended that CMS should clearly state that selection of a drug for negotiation or the establishment of an MFP does not, standing alone, provide a clinical rationale for plans to impose more restrictive utilization management requirements on selected drugs. Other commenters argued that selected drug status should not be treated as a presumption of clinical appropriateness that limits a plan's ability to apply otherwise permissible formulary and utilization management requirements on the selected drug.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. As described in section 1192 of the Act and proposed and finalized at §§ 429.105 through 429.125, CMS selects a negotiation-eligible drug based on certain statutory eligibility criteria and total expenditures under Part B and Part D. A selected drug, as defined at § 429.20, is, in part, a qualifying single source drug that ranks among the highest in total expenditures under Part B and Part D and is selected from the ranked list of negotiation-eligible drugs. Selection therefore reflects a drug's total expenditures and eligibility profile under those statutory criteria and is not a determination that the drug is clinically superior or inferior to therapeutic alternatives.
Further, as proposed and finalized at § 423.120(b)(1)(v), a Part D plan sponsor's Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee must base clinical decisions on the strength of scientific evidence and standards of practice, including assessing peer-reviewed medical literature, pharmacoeconomic studies, outcomes research data, and other such information as it determines appropriate. As described in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36318
), we also expect Part D plan sponsors to provide a reasonable justification to support their submitted plan benefit design and formulary design that includes any of the practices identified in that section of the final rule during the annual bid review process. This justification should address applicable clinical factors, such as clinical superiority, non-inferiority, or equivalence of the selected and non-selected drugs, as well as the plan design's compliance with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements (for example, the requirement to have a cost-effective drug utilization management program that bases decisions on the strength of the clinical evidence and standards of practice). We evaluate these justifications for compliance with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements and will approve a Part D plan bid submitted by a Part D plan sponsor only if the plan benefit design and formulary design complies with those requirements.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns specifically about access to selected drugs within the six protected classes. A commenter urged CMS to ensure beneficiary access to selected drugs within the six protected classes is not restricted compared to non-selected drugs within the protected classes. This commenter noted that this is particularly crucial, arguing that there have been widespread and significant reductions in beneficiary access since the passage of the IRA. A commenter urged CMS to confirm that nothing in this rule creates a loophole around existing protections for protected class drugs.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their input. Consistent with section 1860D-4(b)(3)(G) of the Act and § 423.120(b)(2)(v), Part D plan sponsors are required to include in their formularies all covered Part D drugs in the classes and categories of clinical concern identified by the Secretary, with limited exceptions, as described in § 423.120(b)(2)(vi) and Chapter 6, Section 30.2.5, of the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Manual.
[
99
]
Part D plan sponsors remain subject to all applicable requirements with respect to protected class drugs, including selected drugs that fall within a protected class, and this final rule does not change that. Our formulary review process will continue to assess compliance with those existing requirements. With respect to the commenter's assertion that there have been reductions in beneficiary access to protected class drugs since the passage of the IRA, based on our review of available data, we have not seen evidence to support this claim.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns that the Negotiation Program alters the incentive structure for Part D plan sponsors in a way that may affect beneficiary access not only to selected drugs but also to non-selected drugs in the same therapeutic class. A few commenters noted that when prices for selected drugs decrease to reflect the MFP, plans and their PBMs may have financial incentives to favor non-selected drugs in the same class that continue to generate higher rebates and administrative fees. A few commenters also stated that plans may place selected drugs on less favorable tiers or impose more burdensome utilization management requirements than non-selected drugs to encourage patients to prefer higher-cost non-selected alternatives.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters sharing their concerns about the potential effects of the Negotiation Program on beneficiary access to selected drugs and non-selected drugs in the same therapeutic class. We recognize that by significantly altering the Part D benefit design and implementing the Medicare Drug Price
(
printed page 72330)
Negotiation Program, the IRA changed the structure of liabilities for Part D plan sponsors and may create incentives for plans to alter their formulary and utilization management decisions not only with respect to selected drugs but also with respect to non-selected drugs in the same class. As discussed in our response above, our formulary review process assesses whether Part D plan sponsors place selected drugs on higher cost-sharing tiers than non-selected brand drugs in the same class and whether plans impose more restrictive utilization management for a selected drug compared to non-selected brand drugs in the same class. We will continue to monitor formulary and utilization management trends at the class level and will use our existing authorities to address plan practices that are inconsistent with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements.
Comment:
Several commenters who supported codification of the selected drug formulary inclusion requirement also noted that they oppose the imposition of additional tier placement, utilization management, or other special formulary requirements for selected drugs. Most of these commenters argued that the statute does not require preferred formulary placement for selected drugs, exemption from utilization management, or treatment that is more favorable than other covered Part D drugs and that the IRA established a formulary inclusion requirement, not a formulary preference requirement for selected drugs. A commenter emphasized that Part D plan sponsors and their P&T Committees must retain the ability to evaluate selected drugs alongside therapeutic alternatives based on clinical evidence, safety, effectiveness, utilization, and net cost, with a couple of other commenters noting that many selected drugs may be older while newer, non-selected drugs may represent the preferred standard of care for new patient initiation. A commenter urged CMS to maintain its existing case-by-case formulary review process for assessing formulary management decisions involving selected drugs. A couple of other commenters urged CMS to review selected drugs under the same formulary standards applied to non-selected drugs, rather than subjecting selected drugs to a higher standard of review.
Several commenters also noted that if CMS were to create additional formulary requirements, they would have concerns about the downstream effects on plan leverage and drug costs, arguing that mandatory preferred placement would significantly diminish the effectiveness of formularies as a key tool to promote competition, inhibit plans' ability to negotiate price concessions on therapeutically similar non-selected products, and could unduly impact formulary, rebate, and other negotiations for non-selected drugs.
A few commenters urged CMS to confirm that its monitoring is intended to assess compliance with the statutory inclusion requirement and existing Part D requirements, rather than establish an implicit expectation regarding tier placement, cost sharing, or utilization-management design, and to avoid using formulary placement trends as a basis for imposing additional requirements not established by statute or regulation. A couple of commenters expressed concern that CMS has begun applying selected drug formulary expectations before the year in which an MFP is in effect and recommended that CMS clarify that such expectations apply only in years an MFP is in effect.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support of our proposal. At this time, we are not imposing tier placement, utilization management, or other special formulary requirements for selected drugs. As discussed in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36318
), we believe our current approach provides Part D plan sponsors with the flexibility to continue to manage costs through utilization management in a clinically appropriate manner, while allowing us to monitor practices that may undermine beneficiary access to selected drugs and potentially inform new requirements for future contract years.
Our monitoring of formulary placement for selected drugs is intended to assess compliance with the statutory inclusion requirement and existing Part D requirements, while safeguarding beneficiary access at a time when the Part D benefit has undergone significant change. We will continue to use our existing formulary review process to evaluate plan formulary designs consistent with the standards described in this final rule and applicable statutory and regulatory requirements.
With respect to the commenters' concerns about the application of formulary review standards prior to MFP effectuation for a selected drug, we clarify that our formulary review process, as discussed in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36319
), only applies in years for which an MFP is in effect for a selected drug. As discussed in this same section of this final rule, we will separately continue to monitor trends in formulary placement for selected drugs beginning after drugs are selected for an initial price applicability year, and we clarify that our monitoring during this period is intended to identify practices that may undermine beneficiary access.
Comment:
Several commenters opposed additional formulary requirements for selected drugs and urged CMS to provide greater clarity and predictability in its formulary review process. A commenter stated that plan sponsors have had limited success obtaining CMS approval for non-preferred placement or utilization management of selected drugs, even when supported by clinical evidence, and urged CMS to establish clear standards identifying the formulary placement and utilization management approaches plans may apply to selected drugs.
A commenter requested that CMS provide clear reasoning and citations when a formulary placement or utilization management choice is rejected and create more windows for plans to update utilization management criteria during the plan year, noting that the current process can lack transparency and result in last-minute formulary changes that increase plan and program costs. Another commenter urged CMS to ensure that its policies encourage preferred formulary placement of lower-cost generics and biosimilars over selected drugs when appropriate and noted that current review practices discourage plans from preferring lower-cost alternatives. A commenter requested that CMS confirm in the final rule that a Part D plan sponsor can provide a reasonable justification for placing a selected drug on a less preferred tier when the plan demonstrates that a more cost-effective, clinically appropriate alternative is available.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. With respect to commenters' requests for clearer standards and more specific reasoning when formulary placements or utilization management choices are rejected, we note that the standards governing our formulary review of selected drugs are described in detail in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36319
). In response to the commenter's request to create more windows for plans to update utilization management criteria during the plan year, we note that existing regulations and guidance already provide Part D plan sponsors with meaningful opportunities to make maintenance and non-maintenance formulary changes during the plan year, consistent with § 423.120(e) and Chapter 6, Section 30.3 of the Medicare Prescription Drug
(
printed page 72331)
Benefit Manual. We believe our current approach appropriately balances Part D plan sponsors' need for flexibility with the importance of formulary stability for beneficiaries.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that CMS' proposed approach to rely on its existing formulary review process and on monitoring formulary trends is inadequate to guarantee that beneficiaries can access their prescribed medications and urged CMS to attach enforcement consequences to its review. Many commenters expressed concern that, without consequences, plans could impose utilization management that limits beneficiary access to selected drugs, undermining the Negotiation Program's intent. A few commenters noted that because plans are facing increased financial liability under the Part D redesign, they have strong incentives to manage utilization of selected drugs through prior authorization, step therapy, and non-preferred tiering. A few commenters stated that CMS is relying too heavily on existing processes and noted that the proposed rule largely defers to the existing formulary review process. A commenter urged CMS to preemptively modernize and strengthen its formulary review standards for a post-IRA era, and another commenter urged CMS to commit additional resources to formulary reviews.
A commenter stated that annual formulary review at the bid submission stage does not constrain plan behavior during the plan year. This commenter also argued that if CMS is only considering restrictive formulary designs individually, there is a risk that broader market-wide trends of restricting access to specific selected drugs may be missed. A couple of commenters urged CMS to attach concrete consequences, such as bid disapproval under § 423.272(b)(2)(i) or a required corrective action plan, to its monitoring so that monitoring results in enforcement, not just observation.
Several commenters recommended year-round monitoring with expedited corrective action, a clearly identified process through which beneficiaries, prescribers, and patient organizations may report emerging access barriers, and routine audits of plan coverage practices for selected drugs. A commenter recommended that CMS treat a plan's use of an identified restrictive practice as presumptive evidence that a plan is impeding meaningful access and also recommended that, in these instances, CMS should require the plan to provide a drug-specific clinical justification supported by scientific evidence and accepted standards of care, noting that a generalized assertion of cost management would be insufficient to meet that standard.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters sharing their concerns about CMS' formulary review process and enforcement recommendations. We are committed to ensuring that beneficiaries can meaningfully access selected drugs.
As described in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36318
), we conduct a robust review of each Part D plan's formularies and expect Part D plan sponsors to provide a reasonable clinical justification for any formulary design that: (1) places a selected drug on a non-preferred tier; (2) places a selected drug on a higher cost-sharing tier than non-selected brand drugs in the same class; (3) requires utilization of an alternative non-selected brand drug prior to a selected drug (that is, step therapy); or (4) imposes more restrictive utilization management (for example, step therapy and prior authorization) for a selected drug compared to a non-selected brand drug in the same class. We will approve a Part D plan bid only if the plan benefit design and formulary comply with applicable requirements, and we may disapprove a bid under § 423.272(b) when a plan's formulary design does not meet those requirements. For this review, we consider, class to mean the FDA Established Pharmacologic Class or other source that groups like drugs with similar mechanisms of action and similar indications.
As stated in Chapter 6, Section 30.3.3 of the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Manual, both industry best practices and the best interests of Medicare beneficiaries call for limited formulary changes during the contract year. We believe that formulary stability is extremely important so that beneficiaries maintain access to the benefit they chose during enrollment as represented to them by the Part D plan sponsor. We note that Part D plan sponsors are subject to limitations on mid-year formulary changes under § 423.120(e). Except in limited circumstances, such as immediate substitutions under § 423.120(e)(2)(i) and market withdrawals under § 423.120(e)(2)(ii), Part D plan sponsors must submit a negative formulary change request to CMS prior to implementing any negative formulary change, and non-maintenance changes, as defined at § 423.100, may not be implemented until CMS provides approval of the change. These limitations provide an important safeguard against mid-year access disruptions for beneficiaries.
We will continue to monitor formulary and utilization management trends for selected drugs and will use the information gathered through that monitoring to inform our formulary review standards and guidance in future years and to identify any systemic trends that may warrant further action.
Finally, we note that beneficiaries may report any issues or concerns regarding access to their prescribed medications, including selected drugs, to their plan first, and also to CMS by utilizing the public-facing online portal
[
100
]
for the Negotiation Program, supported by the MTF platform, or by contacting 1-800-MEDICARE.
Comment:
Many commenters urged CMS to expand the scope of its monitoring of selected drugs beyond formulary inclusion and recommended that monitoring assess not only whether a selected drug appears on the formulary but also how it is treated relative to comparable alternatives, including its formulary placement and utilization management. A commenter specifically recommended that monitoring assess whether a selected drug's placement or utilization management materially disadvantages it relative to clinically comparable non-negotiated alternatives without a sufficient clinical justification. Several commenters recommended that CMS monitor formulary tier placement and cost sharing, prior authorization, step therapy, and quantity limit requirements, approval, denial, appeal, reversal, and decision-time measures, and treatment switching and prescription abandonment. A few commenters urged CMS to evaluate the actual out-of-pocket financial impact of plan cost-sharing designs, including shifts from copayment to coinsurance, rather than relying solely on tier placement. A commenter also urged CMS to monitor the average number of medicines covered per class and ensure the number does not decrease.
Several commenters also urged CMS to evaluate access longitudinally by comparing formulary placement and utilization management before selection, after selection, and after the MFP takes effect to identify changes associated with the Negotiation Program, with a commenter noting that plans may alter formulary placement or utilization management in anticipation of future MFP implementation. A commenter urged CMS to monitor changes in comparator medications and clinical alternatives to selected drugs, noting
(
printed page 72332)
that comparators should be defined broadly, not just by pharmacologic class, as clinical substitution can occur across classes. Another commenter recommended that CMS monitor and publish pharmacy-level access measures for selected drugs, including dispensing and reversal rates, dispensing delays, inventory-related complaints, and geographic availability, to identify access problems arising specifically from MFP effectuation at the pharmacy counter.
A commenter expressed concern about the impact on beneficiaries in long-term care and nursing facility settings and recommended that monitoring specifically account for continuity of care disruptions in those populations. A couple of commenters also noted that patients with rare diseases and cancer typically have a limited set of effective therapeutic options and that monitoring should account for rare-disease subtypes, patient-specific characteristics, and the lack of clinically interchangeable alternatives in these populations. Another commenter recommended that CMS collect plan-level data on treatment continuity within specific disease areas, such as antiretroviral therapy stability for people living with HIV.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' detailed recommendations regarding the scope of our monitoring of selected drugs and the importance of a comprehensive monitoring framework that captures a range of plan practices that may affect beneficiary access to selected drugs. As described in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36319
), our formulary review process already assesses a range of formulary and utilization management practices for selected drugs. We will continue to use that framework as a foundation for our ongoing monitoring of selected drug access. We appreciate the commenters' recommendations and will take these recommendations into account as we continue to refine our monitoring framework in future years. We also note that public use files are available on
CMS.gov
for external researchers.

These files include formulary inclusion, tier placement, utilization management edits such as prior authorization, step therapy and quantity limits, as well as plan-level cost sharing and pricing data available for each contract year.

Many commenters urged CMS to publicly report the data it collects through monitoring activities, arguing that the current process remains largely opaque to beneficiaries and the patient organizations that advocate on their behalf. Several commenters urged CMS to publish the information it already collects and reviews as part of its bid review, formulary review, and Negotiation Program oversight activities so that researchers, beneficiary advocates, and policymakers can identify potential access concerns before they become widespread. A commenter noted that existing Part D reporting is aggregated and does not provide the drug- and plan-level transparency needed.
Several commenters recommended that CMS publish drug and plan-level data at the product, therapeutic area, and disease level, including formulary tier placement and cost sharing, prior authorization, step therapy, and quantity limit requirements, and approval, denial, appeal, reversal, and decision-time measures. A couple of commenters also requested CMS to publish a plain-language account of its formulary review criteria and oversight process and to provide sufficient information regarding the basis and disposition of individual formulary reviews to provide meaningful public accountability. Another commenter noted that formulary submissions and written criteria do not show how those policies operate in practice and urged CMS to publish operational measures rather than relying solely on plan-submitted formulary information.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations regarding public reporting on formulary placement, utilization management, and access outcomes for selected drugs. We will take these recommendations into consideration. We note that public use files are available on
CMS.gov
for external researchers.

These files include formulary inclusion, tier placement, utilization management edits such as prior authorization, step therapy and quantity limits, as well as plan-level cost sharing and pricing data available for each contract year. We further note that CMS does not publish the results of its formulary reviews or the clinical justifications submitted by Part D plan sponsors or publicly share such clinical justifications with any external stakeholders, including manufacturers.
Comment:
Many commenters urged CMS to strengthen and streamline the appeals, exceptions, and coverage determination processes for selected drugs, arguing that the existing processes are insufficient to provide timely beneficiary relief when formulary changes or utilization management requirements interfere with access. A few commenters stated that exceptions and appeals must be clear, accessible, and timely, with expedited review available when a preferred alternative is unsuitable and urged CMS to ensure that beneficiaries and prescribers have clear, timely information concerning coverage requirements and the ability to seek an exception when a preferred alternative is not appropriate.
A few commenters recommended that CMS create a more robust step therapy exceptions process for selected drugs, requiring plans to respond within 24 to 72 hours, and a commenter recommended allowing exceptions in specified clinical circumstances, including where the patient has already tried and failed the required drug, where delayed treatment will cause irreversible consequences, where the required drug will cause harm to the patient, or where the patient is stable on their current medication. A few commenters recommended that CMS establish an expedited process through which beneficiaries, prescribers, and patient organizations can report access barriers associated with selected drugs directly to CMS. A commenter requested that CMS' monitoring include the availability of expedited review and whether beneficiaries experience interruptions while an exception or appeal is pending. Another commenter also recommended that CMS actively monitor appeals, grievances, and exception requests that beneficiaries file with their plans in order to maintain a near real-time view of emerging access issues for selected drugs and improve the underlying appeals and grievance processes.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations regarding the coverage determination, exceptions, and appeals processes for selected drugs. We note that existing Part D requirements under subpart M of part 423 (§§ 423.558 through 423.638) already provide robust due process for enrollees seeking access to selected
(
printed page 72333)
drugs, and this process applies to selected drugs in the same manner as other covered Part D drugs. With regard to the commenters' recommendations on timing, we note that § 423.568(b) already requires that when a party makes a standard request for a drug benefit, the Part D plan sponsor must notify the enrollee (and the prescribing physician or other prescriber involved, as appropriate) of its determination as expeditiously as the enrollee's health condition requires, but no later than 72 hours after receipt of the request. For an exceptions request, the Part D plan sponsor must notify the enrollee (and the prescribing physician or other prescriber involved, as appropriate) of its determination as expeditiously as the enrollee's health condition requires, but no later than 72 hours after receipt of the physician's or other prescriber's supporting statement. Consistent with §§ 423.570 and 423.572, an enrollee or an enrollee's prescribing physician or other prescriber may also request that a Part D plan sponsor expedite a coverage determination or exceptions request, which requires that a Part D plan sponsor make a determination no later than 24 hours after receiving the request or the physician's or other prescriber's supporting statement.
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations that CMS establish a process through which beneficiaries, prescribers, and patient organizations can report access barriers associated with selected drugs directly to CMS. Beneficiaries may report any issues or concerns regarding access to their prescribed medications, including selected drugs, to their plan first, and also to CMS by utilizing the public-facing online portal

for the Negotiation Program, supported by the Medicare Transaction Facilitator (MTF) platform, or by contacting 1-800-MEDICARE. Complaints are recorded in the CTM and assigned to the appropriate plan and, as required under the contract provisions established at §§  422.504(a)(15) and 423.505(b)(22), plans are required to address and resolve the complaints received by CMS against them in the CTM. Comment:
A few commenters requested that CMS amend the proposed regulatory text at § 423.120 to reflect the language CMS states in preamble, that: “because a selected drug includes all dosage forms and strengths to which the MFP applies, section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act requires that formularies include all such dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug that constitute a covered Part D drug and for which the MFP is in effect.” Therefore, the commenters requested that the language “include each Part D drug” in proposed § 423.120(b)(2)(vii) be replaced with “include all dosage forms and strengths of each Part D drug”. A commenter stated that this will clarify Part D plan sponsors' legal obligations and ensure that the regulation aligns with CMS' stated policy in the preamble.
Response:
Under our proposed regulation, because a selected drug includes all dosage forms and strengths to which the MFP applies, the formulary inclusion requirement applies to all dosage forms and strengths of a selected drug for which an MFP is in effect. Our regulation at § 429.700(a), which we are finalizing in this rule, states that the MFP is computed and applied across different dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug, as defined at § 429.20. Additionally, the Part D regulations already define “selected drug” at § 423.100 as having the meaning given such term in section 1192(c) of the Act and any applicable regulations and guidance, which will include our regulations at part 429. As such, we do not believe it is necessary to revise our proposed regulation at § 423.120(b)(2)(vii) and are finalizing § 423.120(b)(2)(vii) as proposed.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS to adopt new actuarial equivalence tests to more accurately and quantitatively track whether plan sponsors are offering what the commenter described as sufficient coverage of drugs selected for negotiation. The commenter argued that existing formulary review processes do not provide a sufficiently rigorous or quantitative basis for assessing whether a plan's overall treatment of selected drugs—across tier placement, cost sharing, and utilization management—is equivalent to its treatment of comparable non-selected drugs, and recommended that CMS develop and apply actuarial equivalence standards as part of its formulary oversight framework for selected drugs.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their feedback. As discussed in the Negotiation Program proposed rule (
91 FR 36319
), section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act requires that Part D plan sponsors include on their formularies each covered Part D drug that is a selected drug for which an MFP is in effect. Sections 1860D-2(b)(2)(B) and 1860D-4(c)(1)(A) of the Act continue to permit Part D plan sponsors to use formularies, tiered cost sharing, and cost-effective drug utilization management programs, subject to applicable statutory and regulatory requirements. We do not believe it is necessary at this time to implement requirements that Part D plan sponsors treat selected drugs in a manner that is equivalent to their treatment of non-selected drugs through an actuarial equivalence standard.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS to clearly distinguish authorized generics on the Formulary Reference File (FRF) so Part D sponsors can ensure inclusion of authorized generics that are selected drugs on their formularies when their MFP takes effect and can separately administer formulary status for authorized generics and
(
printed page 72334)
ANDA generics. The commenter states that the FRF does not always distinguish authorized generics from ANDA generics through separate RXCUIs, such as when the products share the same drug name. The commenter states that as a result, Part D plans may either inadvertently fail to include an authorized generic on formulary when required or be unable to assign different formulary treatment to authorized generics and ANDA generics, including different tier placement or utilization management requirements, or to submit an immediate substitution change.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concern regarding the ability of Part D plan sponsors to distinguish between ANDA generic products and NDA authorized generic products when NDCs for those products are associated with the same RxCUI. RxNorm generally associates NDCs for ANDA generic products and authorized generic products with the same RxCUI when the products share the same RxNorm concept. CMS relies on the RxCUI assignments established in RxNorm and therefore cannot independently assign separate RxCUIs to distinguish these products on the FRF.
We recognize that a shared RxCUI may affect Part D plan sponsors' ability to separately administer formulary status for an authorized generic and an ANDA generic associated with that RxCUI. Accordingly, we will continue to provide submission guidance to Part D plan sponsors when an ANDA generic product (of a selected drug) becomes available on the market and is assigned the same RxCUI as the authorized generic product. We provided such technical guidance to all Part D plan sponsors when ANDA dapagliflozin NDCs became available and were associated with the same RxCUI as authorized generic dapagliflozin NDCs marketed under an NDA. This guidance is intended to assist Part D plan sponsors in complying with applicable formulary requirements for selected drugs and, where applicable, appropriately reflect separate formulary treatment for ANDA generic products and authorized generic products that share the same RxCUI.
Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing § 423.120(b)(2) as proposed.
3. Successor Regulation Exception Permitting Formulary Substitutions of Selected Drugs
Section 11001(b) of the IRA added section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act, which states that nothing in section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act shall be construed as prohibiting a Part D plan sponsors from removing a selected drug from a formulary if such removal would be permitted under § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) or any successor regulation.
At the time the IRA was enacted, then-current § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) permitted a plan to immediately substitute on the formulary a newly available generic drug for its brand name drug if certain notice and timing requirements were met. However, due to changes made to the regulations in the Contract Year 2025 Parts C/D Final Rule (
89 FR 30448
), there is no longer a § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) in the current Part D regulations. Under the current Part D regulations, the approval requirements for immediate substitutions, which were revised to provide for the substitution of additional types of products, are now codified at § 423.120(e)(2)(i), and the corresponding notice requirements for such formulary changes are now codified at § 423.120(f)(2) through (4).
Because there was no longer a § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) in the Part D regulations, CMS had to identify the successor regulation to § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) for the purposes of the exception to the formulary inclusion requirement for selected drugs in section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act. a. Exception Permitting Formulary Substitutions of Selected Drugs
As discussed in the previous section, we proposed to codify our identification of § 423.120(e)(2)(i), (f)(2), (3), and (4) as the successor regulation for purposes of implementing section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act. Under § 423.120(e)(2)(i), a Part D plan sponsor is permitted to make negative formulary changes to a brand name drug, a reference product, or a brand name biological product within 30 days of adding a corresponding drug to its formulary on the same or lower cost sharing tier and with the same or less restrictive formulary prior authorization (PA), step therapy (ST), or quantity limit (QL) requirements, so long as the Part D sponsor previously could not have included such corresponding drug on its formulary when it submitted its initial formulary for CMS approval . . . because such drug was not yet available on the market, and the Part D sponsor has provided advance general notice as specified in paragraph (f)(2) of [§ 423.120].
Under § 423.120(f)(2), (3), and (4), a Part D plan sponsor making an immediate substitution under § 423.120(e)(2)(i) is required to provide advance general notice and retrospective notice to enrollees, among others, and to ensure that written notices include specified content. The required retrospective notice must be provided to affected enrollees as soon as possible, but no later than by the end of the month following any month in which the change takes effect. We disagree with the commenter's assertion that our proposed codification of the successor regulation exception is extra-statutory. The statute does not explicitly limit the exception to § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) at the time of enactment. We believe it is significant that the statute did not establish a static exception (for example, by indicating that the exception was limited to § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) at the time of enactment), but rather expressly indicated that the exception would include “any successor regulation.” The statute could have limited the meaning or scope of “any successor regulation” to apply only to the scope of § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) at the time of enactment (that is, brand name drugs and their therapeutically equivalent generic drugs), but it did not do so. Other provisions of the Part D statute make clear that when the statute limits a provision that cross-references an existing regulation to the terms of such regulation at a particular point of time, the statute expressly states that this is the case. For example, section 1860D-14A(g)(6) of the Act defines “negotiated price” to have “the meaning given such term in [
42 CFR 423.100

as in effect on March 23, 2010

42 CFR 423.120(b)(5)(iv)
as codified at a specific time, but instead expressly includes the words “or any successor regulation,” leaving it to CMS to identify any such successor regulation as necessary.
Furthermore, the statute does not explicitly limit the exception to brand name drugs and their therapeutically equivalent generic drugs. When CMS codified § 423.120(b)(5)(iv), there were no Part D drugs that were interchangeable biological products. At the time the IRA was enacted, there were no codified requirements for immediate substitutions with interchangeable biological products, nor were there codified requirements for maintenance changes with interchangeable biological products or biosimilar biological products other than interchangeable biological products. As a result, at the time of enactment, it would not have been possible for the statute to point to specific regulations permitting formulary changes other than those related to therapeutically equivalent generic drugs. Therefore, the inclusion of interchangeable biological products reflects the evolution of the Part D regulations since the IRA was enacted and is consistent with our statutory authority to identify a successor regulation.
With respect to the commenter's concerns about patient access, we note that the immediate substitution framework includes notice and timing requirements designed to protect beneficiaries during formulary transitions, and that existing coverage determination and exception processes remain available to beneficiaries with a documented medical need to remain on a particular product.

b. Corresponding Drugs Do Not Include Selected Drugs
Consistent with CMS' proposed codification of the current identification of § 423.120(e)(2)(i), (f)(2), (3), and (4) as the successor regulation for the purposes of section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act, a Part D plan sponsor may remove a selected drug from its formulary if, in accordance with § 423.120(e)(2)(i) and the notice requirements of § 423.120(f)(2) through (4), the Part D plan sponsor adds to its formulary on the same or lower cost sharing tier and with the same or less restrictive PA, ST, or QL requirements a newly available corresponding drug with respect to such selected drug.
Section 423.100 currently defines “corresponding drug” as “respectively, a generic or authorized generic of a brand name drug, an interchangeable biological product of a reference product, or an unbranded biological product marketed under the same biologics license application (BLA) as a brand name biological product.” As discussed in section 90 of the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions, when read in isolation, the current definition might incorrectly appear to suggest that a Part D plan sponsor could remove a selected drug under section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act, if the Part D plan sponsor adds an authorized generic of the brand name drug or an unbranded biological product marketed under the same BLA as the brand name biological product.
However, such a removal would be inconsistent with the Part D plan sponsor's obligation under section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act, and proposed § 423.120(b)(2)(vii), to include on its formulary each covered Part D drug that is a selected drug under section 1192 of the Act for which an MFP is in effect with respect to the year.
As stated in section 1192(e)(2)(A) of the Act (as added by section 11001 of the IRA), and as discussed in section II.B.6 of this final rule, an authorized generic drug and the qualifying single source drug that is the listed drug or reference product of that authorized generic drug shall be treated as the same qualifying single source drug and, thus, the same selected drug. For the purposes of the Negotiation Program, an “authorized generic drug” is defined in section 1192(e)(2)(B) of the Act and in proposed § 429.20 as—:
In the case of a drug product, an authorized generic drug (as such term is defined in section 505(t)(3) of the FD&C Act); and
In the case of a biological product, a product that has been licensed under section 351(a) of the PHS Act and is marketed, sold, or distributed directly or indirectly to the retail class of trade under a different labeling, packaging (other than repackaging as the reference product in blister packs, unit doses, or similar packaging for institutions), product code, labeler code, trade name, or trademark than the reference product.
As discussed in section II.B.6.a of this final rule, authorized generics of a brand name drug that is a selected drug and unbranded biological products marketed under the same license as a brand name biological product that is a selected drug are treated as the same selected drug as the respective listed drug or reference product.
For example, section II.B.6.a. of this final rule states that, for drug products, CMS proposed at § 429.125(b)(1) to identify a potential qualifying single source drug using all dosage forms and strengths of the drug with the same active moiety and the same holder of a New Drug Application (NDA), inclusive of products that are marketed under different NDAs. The potential qualifying single source drug also includes all dosage forms and strengths of the drug with the same active moiety and marketed under the same NDA(s) that are authorized generic drugs (defined in section 1192(e)(2)(B)(i) of the Act and at proposed § 429.20) that are marketed under such NDA(s). Likewise, section II.B.6.a. of the final rule states that, for biological products, CMS proposed at § 429.125(b)(2) to identify a potential qualifying single source drug using all dosage forms and strengths of the biological product with the same active ingredient and the same holder of a Biologics License Application (BLA), inclusive of products that are marketed under different BLAs. The potential qualifying single source drug also includes all dosage forms and strengths of the biological product with the same active ingredient and marketed under the same BLA(s) that are authorized generic drugs, the definition of which at section 1192(e)(2)(B)(ii) of the Act and proposed § 429.20 includes unbranded biological products that are marketed under such BLA(s).
Because an authorized generic of a brand name drug that is a selected drug or an unbranded biological product marketed under the same BLA as a brand name biological product that is a selected drug also qualifies as the selected drug, section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act, and proposed § 423.120(b)(2)(vii), requires the Part D plan sponsor to include each such authorized generic or unbranded biological product that is a covered Part D drug for which an MFP is in effect on its formulary.
Consequently, the statute does not permit a Part D plan sponsor to remove a selected drug that is a brand name drug or brand name biological product on the basis of adding an authorized generic of the brand name drug or an unbranded biological product marketed under the same BLA as the brand name biological product.
In situations where a selected drug includes both a brand name biological product and an unbranded biological product marketed under the same BLA as the brand name biological product, a Part D plan sponsor may remove both the brand name biological product and the unbranded biological product from its formulary when making an immediate substitution under § 423.120(e)(2)(i) by adding a single interchangeable biological product to its formulary. The interchangeable biological product that is the corresponding drug for the selected drug may replace both the reference product and the unbranded biological product provided that the requirements specified in the proposed successor regulation at § 423.120(e)(2)(i), (f)(2) through (4) are met.
To ensure consistency with the IRA's formulary inclusion requirement, which we proposed to codify at § 423.120(b)(2)(vii), and avoid any potential confusion related to the identification of § 423.120(e)(2)(i) as part of the successor regulation to § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) for the purposes of section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act, we amended the definition of “corresponding drug” in section 90 of the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions, consistent with the statutory directive to implement section 11001 of the IRA, including amendments made by such section, by program instruction or other forms of program guidance. Specifically, section 90 of such program instructions defined “corresponding drug” for 2026 to “mean, respectively, a generic or authorized generic of a brand name drug, an interchangeable biological product of a reference product, or an unbranded biological product marketed under the same biologics license application (BLA) as a brand name biological product. A corresponding drug does not include a selected drug as defined in section 1192(c) of the Act.” Section 110.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance incorporated section
