c. Timing of Immediate Substitutions
Section 423.120(e)(2)(i), (f)(2), (3), and (4), which we proposed to codify as the successor regulation consistent with current guidance, permit a Part D plan sponsor, provided it has met the notice requirements, to remove a selected drug that is a brand name drug or reference product from its formulary and replace it with a generic of the brand name drug or an interchangeable biological product of the reference product “so long as the Part D sponsor previously could not have included such corresponding drug on its formulary
when it submitted its initial formulary
for CMS approval consistent with paragraph (b)(2) of this section because such drug was
not yet available on the market”
[emphasis added]. As such, under these regulations, for Part D plan sponsors that have a selected drug for initial price applicability year 2029 on their 2028 formulary, if a generic drug or interchangeable biological product of a selected drug becomes available on the market in 2028 after the Part D plan sponsor submitted its initial 2029 formulary for CMS approval, consistent with our longstanding policy on immediate substitutions, a Part D plan sponsor could add such generic drug or interchangeable biological product and remove the selected drug from its formulary as an immediate substitution for 2028, as well as for 2029. In other words, where the Part D plan sponsor could not have included the generic drug or interchangeable biological product on either its 2028 initial formulary submission or its 2029 initial formulary submission, and such Part D plan sponsor removes the selected drug as an immediate substitution, the Part D plan sponsor can apply the removal to both the current year formulary as well as the already-submitted formulary for the following year.
A Part D plan sponsor that does not have the selected drug on its 2028 formulary, but has submitted a formulary for 2029 that includes the selected drug, in accordance with section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act, could remove the selected drug as part of an immediate substitution only with respect to its 2029 formulary. That is, if a generic drug of a brand name drug that is a selected drug or an interchangeable biological product of a reference product that is a selected drug was first available on the market after the initial submission of the 2029 formulary, the Part D plan sponsor could, in the latter part of 2028, remove that selected drug from its 2029 formulary.
This application of the immediate substitutions policy to both the 2028 and 2029 formularies with respect to a generic drug or interchangeable biological product that becomes available on the market after the Part D plan sponsor has already submitted its initial formulary to CMS is consistent with section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I) of the Act. As discussed previously, the formulary inclusion requirement in section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I) of the Act applies with respect to selected drugs starting in initial price applicability year 2026 and the only permitted exception to the requirement is the “removal” of “such selected drug.” The plain text of the statute contemplates that a selected drug will need to be included on the plan's formulary for the first initial price applicability year in which the MFP for the selected drug is in effect, regardless of whether the plan ever previously included the drug. Moreover, the only statutory exception to the formulary inclusion obligation is the “removal” of “such a selected drug” in accordance with § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) or its successor regulation, which we proposed to codify as § 423.120(e)(2)(i), (f)(2) through (4). The references to “removal” and “such selected drug” indicate that the selected drug must first be included on the formulary for the initial price applicability year under section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act and only then can be removed under section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act.
Accordingly, as discussed previously, a Part D plan sponsor that includes a selected drug with an initial price applicability year of 2029 on its initial formulary submission for 2029 could remove the selected drug as part of an immediate substitution prior to the start of 2029 if a generic drug or interchangeable biological product of the selected drug becomes available on the market in 2028 after the initial formulary submission. In such cases, the Part D plan sponsor will have included the selected drug on the formulary with respect to the initial price applicability year in which the MFP is in effect (that is, 2029), as required by section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act, and subsequently removed the selected drug, as permitted by section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act.
Further, we note that there may be scenarios in which a generic drug or interchangeable biological product of, for example, a selected drug with an initial price applicability year of 2029 becomes available on the market in 2028 (after the Part D plan sponsor has submitted its initial 2028 formulary in 2027) but before the Part D plan sponsor submits its 2029 initial formulary for CMS approval in 2028. Under such a scenario, a Part D plan sponsor would be permitted, assuming all requirements are met, to remove the selected drug with an initial price applicability year of 2029 (prior to its MFP taking effect) from its 2028 formulary under § 423.120(e)(2)(i), but would be required under section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act to include the selected drug with an initial price applicability year of 2029 on its 2029 formulary when the MFP takes effect.
Consistent with section 90 of the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions, if there is a generic drug or interchangeable biological product for a selected drug with an initial price applicability year of 2029 and such generic drug or interchangeable biological product is available on the market before a Part D plan sponsor's 2029 initial formulary submission, such Part D plan sponsor would still need to include the selected drug on its 2029 formulary submission, regardless of whether the Part D plan sponsor had removed such selected drug from its 2028 formulary via an immediate substitution in 2028, to comply with the formulary inclusion requirement in section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act. Moreover, the Part D plan sponsor would not be permitted to remove the selected drug from the formulary for 2029 as an immediate substitution and replace it with the generic drug or interchangeable biological product that became available on the market prior to the initial formulary submission for 2029 because section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act permits removal only in accordance with § 423.120(b)(5)(iv) or its successor regulation. As discussed previously, the successor regulation, which we proposed to codify for 2029 and subsequent years, includes § 423.120(e)(2)(i), which, like
(
printed page 72339)
§ 423.120(b)(5)(iv) at the time of enactment, permits an immediate substitution only if the Part D plan sponsor previously could not have included such corresponding drug on its formulary when it submitted its initial formulary for CMS approval. In this scenario, because the Part D plan sponsor could have included the generic drug or interchangeable biological product in its initial formulary submission for 2029, an immediate substitution would not be available.
Further, consistent with section 90 of the Final CY 2026 Part D Redesign Program Instructions, the regulatory language at § 423.120(e)(2)(i), that a Part D plan sponsor previously could not have included the corresponding drug on its formulary when it submitted its initial formulary for CMS approval, would continue to mean, in practice, that the corresponding drug is not included on the final formulary reference file (FRF) update that CMS releases before the bid submission deadline. Consistent with our longstanding practice, the determination of whether a new generic drug or interchangeable biological product is included on the final FRF update that CMS releases before the bid submission deadline will be based on the presence of a RxNorm Concept Unique Identifier (RxCUI) on that FRF update that represents the generic drug or interchangeable biological product.
Finally, consistent with section 110.1 of the Negotiation Program Guidance, we proposed that removals under the statutory formulary inclusion exception, which we proposed to codify at new § 423.120(b)(2)(viii), cannot be carried over to subsequent years within the price applicability period simply because a selected drug was removed in a preceding year during the price applicability period. Instead, any removal must independently meet the immediate substitution requirements for each plan year because, consistent with CMS' longstanding policy, CMS considers each plan year's formulary to be separate and distinct from the prior year. Therefore, a removal could only apply to multiple plan years in a price applicability period if it independently meets the immediate substitution requirements for each applicable plan year.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters requested that CMS allow immediate substitutions for selected drugs in one year to carry over to subsequent years in order to prevent situations where a selected drug may need to be re-added to a formulary after it has been removed under an immediate substitution. The commenters recommended that CMS allow for the removal of selected drugs from a formulary as soon as a competitor generic or interchangeable biological products becomes available on the market, regardless of whether this is before or after the initial formulary submission. A commenter argued that Congress likely intended for the exception to the formulary inclusion requirement to consistently apply once generic or biosimilar competition exists for a selected drug to promote greater competition and affordability. Another commenter expressed concern that the requirement to re-add drugs to a formulary could artificially limit effective member migration from the selected drug to its generic or biosimilar equivalent. An additional commenter stated that requiring a selected drug that has lower cost alternatives to be re-added to a formulary can reduce incentives for competition, impede the adoption of generic and biosimilar alternatives, and prevent plans from realizing the full benefits of generic and biosimilar entry.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations to allow immediate substitutions to carry over to subsequent plan years. However, we decline to adopt this recommendation as our approach is consistent with CMS' longstanding policy to consider each plan year's formulary to be separate and distinct from the prior year. In this final rule, we are maintaining that a removal could only apply to multiple plan years in a price applicability period if it independently meets the immediate substitution requirements for each applicable plan year.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS require Part D plan sponsors to retain on formulary any selected drug for which an MFP remains in effect, regardless of whether a generic or biosimilar has entered the market. The commenter stated that this protection should apply equally to small molecule drugs and biological reference products and would help ensure that the IRA's pricing provisions continue to function in a manner that meaningfully benefits patients. The commenter shared an example of a plan using immediate substitution to remove an innovator drug as soon as an interchangeable biological product is approved, but before that interchangeable biological product is stocked and available at local pharmacies, which would leave patients without access to their prescribed therapy. The commenter also requested that CMS implement “grandfathering” requirements to protect patients currently stabilized on a selected drug from abrupt access disruptions when plans utilize immediate substitution, particularly when a newly approved substituting product is not yet widely available at pharmacies.
Response:
We disagree with the commenter's recommendation that Part D plan sponsors be required to retain on formulary any selected drug for which an MFP remains in effect regardless of whether a corresponding generic or biosimilar has entered the market. As described in section III.A.3.a. of this final rule, section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(ii) of the Act expressly provides that nothing in the formulary inclusion requirement shall be construed as prohibiting a Part D plan sponsor from removing a selected drug from a formulary if such removal would be permitted under the successor regulation. The immediate substitution framework at § 423.120(e)(2)(i) and (f)(2) through (4) includes notice and timing requirements designed to protect beneficiaries during formulary transitions, and existing coverage determination and exception processes remain available to beneficiaries.
Comment:
A commenter raised concerns about the operational impact of mid-year immediate substitutions in long-term care (LTC) settings and recommended that CMS establish LTC-specific safeguards for immediate substitutions, including advance notice to the dispensing LTC pharmacy, a reasonable transition period that aligns with LTC dispensing and unit-dose packaging cycles, and protections to ensure continuity of care for stabilized residents during any mid-year product transition.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's recommendations regarding LTC-specific safeguards for immediate substitutions and recognize the operational complexities that mid-year formulary changes can present in LTC settings. However, we decline to establish LTC-specific requirements for immediate substitutions. The immediate substitution framework at § 423.120(e)(2)(i) and the notice requirements at § 423.120(f)(2) through (4) apply uniformly to Part D plan sponsors and already include beneficiary protections relevant to the commenter's concerns, including the requirement that a corresponding drug be added on the same or a lower cost-sharing tier and with the same or less restrictive formulary prior authorization, step therapy, or quantity limit requirements, and advance general and retrospective notice requirements. In addition, for beneficiaries who have
(
printed page 72340)
a medically necessary reason to remain on a selected drug that has been removed from the formulary, they may seek continued coverage through the coverage determination and exception processes under subpart M of part 423.
Comment:
A commenter supported CMS' proposal to apply the immediate substitution regulation consistently to generic and interchangeable biological products. They urged CMS to provide clear operational guidance—including when a sponsor may implement a substitution, what notice is required, and how the change should be reflected in the applicable formulary and beneficiary materials—for circumstances in which such products become available during or after the formulary development and bid submission cycles. The commenter requested that CMS ensure that the timing of these requirements does not unnecessarily delay adoption of clinically appropriate lower-cost alternatives.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support for our proposal and agree on the importance of clear operational guidance to support Part D plan sponsors in implementing the immediate substitution framework. As discussed in section III.A.3.a. of this final rule, we are codifying § 423.120(e)(2)(i) and (f)(2) through (4) as the successor regulation for purposes of new § 423.120(b)(2)(viii). Part D plan sponsors should refer to those regulations and the preamble discussion in this final rule for guidance on when an immediate substitution may be implemented, what notice is required, and how the change should be reflected in applicable formulary and beneficiary materials.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS clarify that plans may begin a contract year with a qualifying corresponding biosimilar on formulary in place of a selected drug when the biosimilar is already available on the market at the time of bid submission. The commenter stated that plans have reported operational challenges when attempting to do so and the practical result is that beneficiaries may face a full plan year of higher cost-sharing on a reference product before substitution can occur, even when a lower-cost biosimilar was available on the market before the plan year began.
Response:
We thank the commenter for this recommendation. We interpret this comment as a request that CMS permit a Part D plan sponsor to begin a contract year with a biosimilar on its formulary in place of a selected drug that is a reference product, where the biosimilar was available on the market at the time the sponsor submitted its bid and initial formulary. As explained below, the successor regulation does not permit removal of the selected drug in that circumstance, and we decline to adopt the recommendation.
Under the successor regulation we are finalizing, § 423.120(e)(2)(i) and the notice requirements at § 423.120(f)(2) through (4), a Part D plan sponsor may remove a selected drug that is a reference product from its formulary via an immediate substitution and replace it with an interchangeable biological product only if the Part D plan sponsor previously could not have included the drug on its formulary when it submitted its initial formulary for CMS approval because such drug was not yet available on the market. In the circumstance the commenter describes where the biosimilar is already available at the time of bid and initial formulary submission, the Part D plan sponsor could have included that product on its initial formulary, and therefore the immediate substitution exception is not permitted.
In addition, we note that only an interchangeable biological product qualifies as a corresponding drug for the purpose of the successor regulation exception. Accordingly, a Part D plan sponsor must include the selected drug that is a reference product on its formulary for the year in which the MFP is in effect, consistent with section 1860D-4(b)(3)(I)(i) of the Act and new § 423.120(b)(2)(vii).
We also note that including the selected drug on its formulary does not prevent a Part D plan sponsor from also covering an available biosimilar. A Part D plan sponsor may add a biosimilar biological product to its formulary at any time during the plan year, while retaining the reference product that is a selected drug on the formulary.
Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing § 423.120(b)(2)(vii) and (viii) as proposed.
B. Negotiated Price for Selected Drugs
Section 1860D-2(d)(1) of the Act requires Part D sponsors to provide beneficiaries with access to negotiated prices for covered Part D drugs. Section 1860D-2(d)(1)(A) of the Act requires Part D sponsors to “provide enrollees with access to negotiated prices used for payment for covered Part D drugs.” Subparagraph (B) further clarifies that negotiated prices, subject to subparagraph (D), “shall take into account negotiated price concessions, such as discounts, direct or indirect subsidies, rebates, and direct or indirect remunerations, for covered Part D drugs, and include any dispensing fees for such drugs.”
The negotiated price is the price paid to the network pharmacy or other network dispensing provider for a covered Part D drug dispensed to a plan enrollee and reported to CMS at the point of sale by the Part D sponsor. This point-of-sale price is used to calculate beneficiary cost sharing. The negotiated price also serves as the primary basis for adjudicating the Part D benefit because it is used to determine plan, beneficiary, manufacturer, and government liability during the payment year, subject to final reconciliation after the coverage year ends.
Section 11001(b) of the IRA amended section 1860D-2(d)(1) of the Act by adding subparagraph (D). That provision requires that, in the case of a covered Part D drug that is a selected drug, with respect to a price applicability period, the negotiated price “used for payment (as described in this subsection) shall be no greater than the [maximum fair price] for such drug . . . plus any dispensing fees for such drug.” Section 11001(b) of the IRA also added “subject to subparagraph (D)” to section 1860D-2(d)(1)(B) of the Act.
Section 11001(c) of the IRA directed CMS to implement section 11001 of the IRA, including the amendments made by such section, by program instruction or other forms of program guidance for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028. Accordingly, we applied the statutory negotiated price requirements for selected drugs through the applicable Negotiation Program guidance for 2026, 2027, and 2028. Specifically, we stated that under section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, the negotiated price for selected drugs “must not exceed the applicable [maximum fair price (MFP)] plus any dispensing fees for such drug.” We also stated that the statute requires manufacturers to provide access to the MFP for selected drugs to pharmacies, mail order services, and other dispensing entities with respect to MFP-eligible individuals who are dispensed such drugs.
With the expiration of the IRA program instruction requirement for the Negotiation Program at the end of 2028, we proposed to codify the statutory amendments to the definition of negotiated price for selected drugs in the definition of “negotiated price” at § 423.100 for 2029 and subsequent years. We proposed to revise paragraph (2) of the definition to state that the required elements of the negotiated price are subject to a new paragraph (4) and add a new paragraph (4) to the definition to require that, for a covered
(
printed page 72341)
Part D drug that is a selected drug, and for each year of a price applicability period with respect to such selected drug, the negotiated price used for payment, as described in paragraphs (1) through (3) of the negotiated price definition, must not exceed the MFP for such drug, plus any applicable dispensing fees.
In addition, to better align the definition of “negotiated price” at § 423.100 with our historical interpretation of this definition, we proposed to revise the required elements of the negotiated price in subparagraph (2) to add sales tax and vaccine administration fees to the definition of “negotiated price” without altering any existing elements of that definition. Specifically, we proposed deleting the word “and;” from the end of paragraph (2)(ii), redesignating paragraph (2)(iii) as 2(v), and adding new paragraph (2)(iii) to require the inclusion of sales tax and new paragraph (2)(iv) to require the inclusion of vaccine administration fees.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters supported the proposal to codify section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act to require that the negotiated price paid to dispensing entities for a selected drug not exceed the MFP plus applicable dispensing fees. A commenter requested that CMS confirm Part D sponsors or pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) have the ability to negotiate rates for selected drugs that are lower than the MFP, and that the ceiling does not alter the ability of Part D sponsors or PBMs to negotiate permissible pharmacy reimbursement arrangements or other contractual terms, provided that the resulting negotiated price used for payment complies with the statutory ceiling.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and note that under section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, as amended by section 11001(b) of the IRA, the negotiated prices used in payment by each Part D plan sponsor for each selected drug must not exceed the MFP plus any dispensing fees for such drug. This does not prohibit plans from negotiating rates for selected drugs that are lower than the MFP. We encourage plan sponsors to work with pharmacies to ensure adequate and fair compensation for dispensing selected drugs.
Comment:
A commenter supported CMS' inclusion of sales tax and applicable vaccine administration fees in the definition of negotiated price.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their support.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns regarding pharmacy reimbursement for selected drugs. A commenter recommended that CMS revise the program such that Part D plans and PBMs must pay pharmacies no less than the MFP plus a commensurate dispensing fee when providing selected drugs with an agreed-upon MFP, and that Part D plans and PBMs must not assess Direct and Indirect Renumeration (DIR) fees on selected drugs with an agreed-upon MFP. A couple of commenters urged CMS to ensure that dispensing fees adequately compensate pharmacies and provided recommendations, such as requiring dispensing fees and any service fees be stated as flat, service-based amounts rather than as a percentage of the MFP, requiring the provision of a minimum dispensing fee, and affirming that dispensing fees for selected drugs must reflect the actual cost of dispensing selected drugs for long-term care (LTC) pharmacies.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their input. We expect plans and PBMs to engage in sustainable and fair reimbursement practices with all pharmacies to ensure access to selected drugs, consistent with their statutory obligations, for individuals with Part D. As noted in our response to a similar comment in the Negotiation Program Guidance, under section 1860D-2(d)(1)(D) of the Act, as amended by section 11001(b) of the IRA, the negotiated prices used in payment by each Part D plan sponsor for each selected drug must not exceed the applicable MFP plus any dispensing fees for a selected drug with an agreed-upon MFP. We are not establishing requirements for dispensing fees for selected drugs but will continue to closely monitor plan reimbursement for selected drugs, including pharmacy price concessions and dispensing fees.
Final Decision:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing § 423.100 as proposed.

Comment:
A commenter suggested that the burden estimate should include tasks other than submission of data that are involved with the production of the requested data, including internal review, legal analysis, data extraction, documentation, certification, and correction processes.
Response:
CMS thanks this commenter for their feedback. As noted in the description of the roles involved with responses to information collections, the burden estimates already include the tasks related to the preparation of submissions. For example, the burden estimate for each Primary Manufacturer to submit negotiation data elements for drugs selected for negotiation includes 200 hours for business operation specialists to gather cost data and compile required information, 600 hours for economists to perform economic analyses, 50 hours for a financial manager to review the analysis results and cost estimates, 4 hours for a lawyer to review the data submission, 142 hours for a cost estimator to compile and report the data to CMS and 4 hours for a chief executive to review the data submission and certify the submission.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS' interpretation that CMS can only consider section 1194(e)(1) factors submitted by manufacturers is incorrect. The commenter stated that the phrase could instead be providing clarification that CMS is able to require manufacturers to submit data on the 1194(e)(1) factors but not necessarily requiring CMS to exclude publicly available information. Similarly, a couple of commenters stated that CMS should not require manufacturer submission of data that is otherwise accessible to the Agency. A commenter
(
printed page 72342)
requested CMS extend the timeframe for manufacturers to submit required data. A few commenters asked that CMS decrease the burden imposed by the data collection requirement at § 429.505(b)(1), and among these commenters, a few suggested options to streamline the collection of information on section 1194(e)(1) factors. A commenter stated that aligning manufacturer requirements more closely with section 1194(e)(1) of the Act would minimize manufacturer burden and, as such, stated that CMS should not expand on the factors as provided in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act—for example by requesting information on anticipated loss of exclusivity, litigation updates, payer mix by indication, or other commercial data. A commenter suggested that CMS allow manufacturers to submit information that they believe is most relevant to the section 1194(e)(1) factors and provide a justification for the submission. A few commenters suggested that CMS should allow a single response from manufacturers to attest as to whether they have recouped research and development costs as required by section 1194(e)(1)(A) of the Act. A commenter suggested that CMS invest in the CMS HPMS submission portal to support standardized formatting and streamlined document upload, which could improve the accuracy and completeness of the information CMS relies upon during negotiation, and in any dispute or during the suggestion-of-error process.
Response:
We appreciate these comments and acknowledge the burden on manufacturers as described in the Drug Price Negotiation ICR and the Drug Selection ICR. We endeavor to continue to refine these ICRs to minimize burden on Primary Manufacturers and the public. Consistent with our response to similar comments in the Negotiation Program Guidance, we respectfully disagree that we can obtain the information related to the factors listed at section 1194(e)(1) of the Act from sources other than the manufacturer of a selected drug. Section 1194(e)(1) of the Act specifically refers to the list of section 1194(e)(1) factors as, “. . . the following data, with respect to such selected drug, as submitted by the manufacturer.” We believe this indicates that the information for section 1194(e)(1) factors must come from the manufacturer of the selected drug. Additionally, consistent with our response to similar comments received in relation to the collection of section 1194(e)(1) data for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027, we maintain that although some of the information may be available through other sources, we may not be able to ensure that such data are complete or up to date, and, ultimately, we believe that the Primary Manufacturer is best positioned to provide the requested data.
With regards to the comments on data collected on section 1194(e)(1) factors, including more closely aligning with section 1194(e)(1) of the Act and allowing manufacturers to determine what information is most relevant to submit, based on experience thus far, we determined that the information to be collected informs our consideration of the factors listed in section 1194(e)(1) of the Act and is needed to ensure a holistic evaluation of the selected drug. For example, payer mix is core to understanding a selected drug's market data in the United States consistent with section 1194(e)(1)(E) of the Act, which requires CMS to consider “market data and revenue and sales volume data for the drug in the United States”. We believe this additional information is a low burden for manufacturers as this information is estimated in the ordinary course of business.
With regards to the comment on allowing an attestation for recoupment of research and development costs, at this time we believe that the full information sent and received is consistent with the statutory intent to collect “research and development costs of the manufacturer for the drug” as specified in section 1194(e)(1)(A) of the Act and supports a holistic evaluation of the selected drug. Based on experience to date, we do not believe that allowing solely an attestation in lieu of collecting this information would be sufficient.
With regards to the comment regarding the CMS HPMS submission portal, we continue to identify opportunities to apply lessons learned and to improve this process, including by considering respondent feedback and suggestions. We appreciate the suggestions brought forward by this commenter on potential submission options. However, in order to continue to meet statutory timing requirements, we will not adopt these suggestions at this time. We remind interested parties that we provide technical assistance throughout the ICR submission process if a Primary Manufacturer has questions about the CMS HPMS.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed concern with CMS' data collection and notification processes for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. A commenter requested greater transparency around the deadlines for the application, notice of determination, and calculation as it relates to the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs. Some commenters suggested CMS determine eligibility for the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs using information CMS possesses.

We thank commenters for raising these concerns. The Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs ICR Form may be submitted to CMS no later than March 1, 2027 for initial price applicability year 2029. CMS does not have information to determine whether manufacturers of drugs and biological products payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D were treated as a single employer with other entities under subsection (a) or (b) of section 52 of the IRC as of December 31, 2021. V. Regulatory Impact Analysis
A. Statement of Need
This rule finalizes and codifies, with limited modification, policies related to the implementation of certain provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (
Pub. L. 117-169
, August 16, 2022), which were established in the final guidance for the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (hereinafter the “Negotiation Program”). The primary driver for this rulemaking is the statutory mandate to codify changes made by the IRA. Without regulatory implementation of the Negotiation Program, the Medicare program cannot comply with Federal law, reduce prescription drug costs for beneficiaries, or achieve cost savings provided under statute.
This rulemaking finalizes and codifies policies for the Negotiation Program at part 429 consistent with sections 1191 through 1198 of the Social Security Act (hereinafter “the Act”) and to codify policies for the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program at part 423 consistent with section 11001(b) of the IRA, which made certain amendments to the Act, including with respect to Medicare Part D. Our policies in this rulemaking specifically address: general provisions; identification of selected drugs; Negotiation Program Agreement; program administration; establishment of a single maximum fair price (MFP) and determination of the ceiling; negotiation process; renegotiation of an MFP; implementation of the MFP; manufacturer compliance and oversight; civil monetary penalties; and requirements related to qualified prescription drug coverage. In addition, we finalized new policies for the Negotiation Program as follows: a policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations; clarification for drugs that formerly qualified for the orphan drug exclusion; revisions regarding the process and schedule of CMS review of information in making determinations with respect to Bona Fide Marketing; additional details related to the Primary Manufacturer transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to an acquiring entity; calculation of the 30-day equivalent supply for a selected drug that is typically administered one time; implementation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030; and clarification of off-label use in consideration for renegotiation eligibility and selection. The policies reflect CMS' stewardship of the Medicare program and overarching policy objectives for lower prices for Medicare through negotiation or price competition by lowering drug prices and making Medicare prescription drugs more affordable for beneficiaries.
The absence of regulatory action would result in statutory non-compliance regarding IRA implementation and missed opportunities for program improvement and innovation. Therefore, this rulemaking is necessary to ensure the Negotiation Program operates effectively, efficiently, and in compliance with Federal law while serving the best interests of Medicare beneficiaries.

C. Detailed Economic Analysis
The CMS Office of the Actuary estimated the impacts of the drug provisions of the IRA using the 2024 President's Budget as a baseline early in calendar year 2023. These estimates were made prior to many policy decisions to implement the law, and independently from other components of CMS. Since the majority of these provisions have already been implemented through program instruction, including Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program guidance with respect to initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028 (as discussed in further detail in section I.A.2. of this final rule), this estimate should be taken only in its historical context, not as a reflection on the experience since its effectuation. We will highlight certain components of this estimate where recent experience has diverged from our initial assumptions. The IRA has a range of Medicare provisions, including restraining price growth and negotiating drug prices for certain drugs payable under Part B and covered under Part D, as well as redesigning the Part D benefit structure to decrease beneficiary out-of-pocket costs. The provisions of the IRA take effect over several years, resulting in very different effects by year. Much of the Part D benefit redesign became effective in 2025, for example, before the Negotiation Program provisions can have any offsetting effects.
To model the negotiation provisions of the IRA, we first determined which drugs would be selected for negotiation in accordance with sections 11001 and 11002 of the IRA. Using 2022 experience for Part B and Part D claims, we ranked drugs by Part B and Part D expenditures and then applied the eligibility criteria specified in the IRA—verifying, in particular, that the ranked drugs had been on the market long enough to qualify for negotiation. From this list, we generated the potential list of drugs to be negotiated in each year for Part B and Part D.
To estimate the impact of negotiation and to measure the differences between the current prices and the ceiling price and other pricing parameters laid out in the IRA, we used 2021 data from a variety of sources, including PDE records, Medicaid AMP data, and Part B ASP data. We assumed, after comparing the Medicare prices to the ceiling prices in each projection year, that Medicare would be able to negotiate slightly below the ceiling price in Part D. We then adjusted for generic and biosimilar launches that, should they happen after the selection process, would potentially limit the impact of the MFP. Lastly, we adjusted for changes in the percentage of spending that the selected drugs would represent over time. The discounts relative to total 2021 Part D allowed cost, prior to manufacturer rebates and total Part B allowed cost, are shown in Table V.C1.
For Part D, the benefit is considerably enriched under the IRA, and the most impactful changes took effect in 2025. To estimate these effects inclusive of the Negotiation Program impacts, we incorporated the negotiated price at the drug level into a beneficiary- and claim-level detailed model. Then, we recalculated the new benefit on the negotiated prices to determine the combined result under the defined standard benefit design by year. To protect beneficiaries from large premium increases, the IRA limits the premium change in years 2024 through 2029 before ultimately readjusting the base beneficiary premium percentage to a minimum of 20 percent in 2030 and later years. The major benefit changes and beneficiary premium protections by year are shown in Table V.C2.
(
printed page 72350)
To complete the modeling of the Negotiation Program, prescription drug inflation rebates, and benefit provisions, we applied the results from the Part D claim-level detailed simulation to our total Part D benefit model. This model also incorporated changes to the per capita cost trends to reflect: (i) the impact of most existing brand-name drugs moving to a CPI-level increase; (ii) the expected growth in new drug costs; and (iii) the expected induced utilization due to the enriched benefit. We assumed that drugs with a significant amount of spending in Part D would temper their price increases rather than pay the inflation rebates required by the IRA. Additionally, we reduced our estimate of manufacturer rebates to compensate for the lower negotiated prices and lower price growth on existing drugs.
For drugs payable under Part B, we applied the negotiated price discounts to the OM spending for separately payable Part B drugs. We further adjusted these results to account for the impact to private health plan expenditures to obtain a total impact. While there are also inflation rebates required for certain drugs payable under Part B under the IRA, price increases on existing drugs payable under Part B historically have been close to the CPI in aggregate, and therefore we did not project an effect for this provision in the drugs payable under Part B. We also incorporated other, less significant changes from the IRA, such as the lower cost sharing for insulins furnished under durable medical equipment and the temporary payment increase for qualifying biosimilar products.
Our assumptions on the impacts of the IRA differed from those used in other public estimates in a few critical ways. Most importantly, we assumed that the inflation rebates required by the IRA would result in manufacturers owing relatively small inflation rebate amounts for drugs covered under Part D and nothing for drugs payable under Part B. We assumed that manufacturers would prefer to have lower price trends that would incentivize greater use than pay publicly reported fees for price increases that exceed inflation. Under this assumption, the effects of the inflation rebate provisions of the IRA are changed because the difference in price is shared across the benefit rather than accruing directly to the government. In other words, lower list price trends will reduce prices paid at the pharmacy relative to the baseline, which results in lower beneficiary cost-sharing and lower state clawback payments, thereby increasing the Federal cost for the Part D benefit. To compensate for the loss of price increases, we expected manufacturers to reduce rebates offered to plan sponsors.
Additionally, we expected that the initial pool of drugs covered under Part D selected for negotiation would have a large proportion of heavily rebated drugs. In these cases, we expected that the price net of rebate will be substantially lower than the other ceiling prices described in the IRA. We further estimated that the effect of negotiation in the early years would be similar to the impact of shifting rebates to the point of sale. This shift reduces beneficiary cost sharing as the price at the point of sale is lower but increases bid amounts and increases Federal expenditures.
In summary, the total effects were to reduce government expenditures for Part B, to increase expenditures for Part D through 2030, and to decrease Part D expenditures beginning in 2031. Part B savings were primarily due to: (i) the substantial lowering of payments, relative to current payment, as a result of MFPs; and (ii) small impacts from other provisions. Part D ultimately generated cost savings at the end of the budget window, but many of the gains from MFPs and lower trends were initially spent on increased benefits and the loss of manufacturer rebates. The impact on benefits and premiums and the impact in total are shown in Table V.C3 using the 2024 President's Budget as a basis.

Since we produced these estimates, both the Part B and Part D programs have had large increases in drug expenditures. Part D trends have accelerated dramatically, with the per capita gross drug cost increasing more than 18 percent in 2025 over 2024, driven by higher glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and specialty drug usage. Meanwhile, Part B drug trends have also increased, although the primary driver was skin substitutes that were payable as biological products for the purposes of Medicare payment. There are a variety of other causes contributing to observed changes in expenditures for both programs.
The Part D trends in per capita gross costs are shown in Figure V.C1. Much of the IRA Part D benefit redesign took effect in 2025, including limiting annual out of pocket expenditures to $2,000 per enrollee for 2025 (to be annually increased by the annual percentage increase, as described in section 1860D-2(b)(6) of the Act). While this new feature could have induced spending beyond the assumption we included in our initial estimate, it is worth noting that the 2024 benefit structure under the IRA also eliminated cost-sharing in the catastrophic phase of the benefit, effectively implementing an out-of-pocket maximum without a pronounced increase in costs. Additionally, some of the increase may be attributable to manufacturers reducing spending on patient assistance programs, which would cause more claims to run through the Part D program. Expanded indications for cancer drugs also contributed to the increase.

1. Analysis of New Policies
In addition, we finalized new policies for the Negotiation Program as follows: a policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations; clarification related to drugs that formerly qualified for the orphan drug exclusion; revisions regarding process and schedule of CMS review of information in making determinations for Bona Fide Marketing; additional details related to the Primary Manufacturer transfer of responsibility for all requirements of the Negotiation Program Agreement to an acquiring entity; calculation of the 30-day equivalent supply for a selected drug that is typically administered one time; how CMS would implement the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030; and clarification of off-label use in consideration for renegotiation eligibility and selection. Of these finalized provisions, only the policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations would potentially have an impact as the other provisions are technical changes that would not result in additional costs or savings to the Negotiation Program.
The fixed combination drug provision involves costs and savings that extend outside the budget window for this regulatory impact analysis. For purposes of this discussion, consider Product A, which contains the active ingredient X; and consider a later-developed Product B, which contains active ingredient X plus another active ingredient Y, and which meets the criteria finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii). The final policy would aggregate Product A and Product B into the same potential qualifying single source drug and, if such potential qualifying single source drug were ultimately selected, result in Product A and Product B being part of the same selected drug. This would result in any agreed-upon MFP being applied earlier, with respect to the later-developed Product B, than under the current general fixed combination drug policy in which Product A and Product B would be treated as separate potential qualifying single source drugs. This may result in savings in the short term. This policy would also expand the number of products aggregated under a selected drug that would become deselected once a generic or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing for any dosage form or strength of the selected drug, resulting in Product B potentially having an agreed-upon MFP applied earlier, but for a shorter period of time, than if it had been identified as a separate qualifying single source drug that was selected and negotiated separately, thus resulting in potential lost savings in the long term. Therefore, potential savings generated by aggregating more products into a qualifying single source drug to which, if selected, the agreed-upon MFP would apply could be limited due to corresponding potential savings lost by the larger number of products that would be deselected once a generic or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing, though changes in price after the drug is deselected may be contained (and thus savings preserved) by the Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program for drugs payable under Part B.

In addition, a policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations that would aggregate Product A and Product B into the same potential qualifying single source drug could result in a scenario where Product A has a generic or biosimilar that is subject to Bona Fide Marketing before that qualifying single source drug's eligibility for selection, which could result in both Product A and Product B being ineligible for selection for negotiation, meaning that an MFP could not be negotiated for either product.
As an illustrative example, consider a biological product that has a new formulation that is a fixed combination drug containing hyaluronidase. Under the finalized policy, for drug selection with respect to initial price applicability year 2029, the formulations of that biological product both with and without hyaluronidase would be considered the same potential qualifying single source drug, and potentially selected drug, if the criteria in finalized § 429.125(b)(4)(ii) were met. In this case and with respect to this biological product if it were selected, the MFP, if one is agreed to by CMS and the Primary Manufacturer, would apply to all dosage forms and strengths of the selected drug, including the new formulation containing hyaluronidase, in initial price applicability year 2029 and each subsequent year until CMS makes a determination in accordance with § 429.135(a) that such drug ceases to be a selected drug because a manufacturer for a biosimilar for, most likely, the earlier-formulated non-hyaluronidase product has been licensed and is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. Alternatively, if we had not finalized the proposal, the new formulation containing hyaluronidase would not be considered the same potential qualifying single source drug as the original biological product, and so might be separately selected for negotiation in 2039 (an illustrative year to represent the earliest date when the 11-year timing criterion set forth in proposed § 429.125(c)(2) for a biological product has been reached). These effects would be outside the budget window, and we do not have a credible, drug-level forecast for that time period. Such a forecast would be required to estimate this provision, as the impacted set of drugs is small and the effects will depend on the level of utilization of this subset of drugs far in the future. Additionally, we are unable to accurately estimate the impact of finalizing the policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations within the budget window since the budgetary effects of the counterfactual (that is, not finalizing such proposal) are outside the budget window, and we do not have baseline estimates for that time horizon. We welcomed comments on methodologies to estimate these effects.

Comment:
A few commenters raised concerns that the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations could reduce savings under the Negotiation Program because, once a generic or biosimilar emerges for the original product, both the original formulation and the new formulation will be deselected from the Negotiation Program, even though the reformulated products themselves may not yet face generic or biosimilar competition. One of these commenters stated that manufacturers could exploit this dynamic by shifting utilization to the reformulated version, leaving consumers and Medicare to pay monopoly prices on a product to which the MFP no longer applies. To address this concern, the commenter recommended that CMS monitor prescribing and pricing patterns for reformulated products after deselection, use the material-change and renegotiation authorities in §  429.605(d) to bring reformulated products back into the program when warranted, and work with Congress so that a reformulation without genuine generic or biosimilar competition cannot evade the MFP. A commenter noted CMS' statement in the Regulatory Impact Analysis that the relevant costs and savings of the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations extend outside the budget window for the analysis. The commenter stated that CMS' inability to quantify the proposal does not establish that its effects are negligible but rather demonstrates that CMS lacks an adequate basis to conclude that the proposal will improve the Negotiation Program without producing material unintended consequences. A few commenters requested that CMS analyze changes in research programs, clinical development, and regulatory applications to attempt to quantify the foregone innovation and regulatory cost if the proposal is finalized.
Response:
We appreciate the input and reiterate our statement in the proposed rule (
91 FR 36333
) that the proposed policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations involves costs and savings that extend outside the budget window for the rule's regulatory impact analysis. There, we acknowledged that potential savings generated by aggregating more products into a qualifying single source drug to which, if selected, the agreed-upon MFP would apply could be limited due to corresponding potential savings lost by the larger number of products that would be deselected once a generic or biosimilar is subject to Bona Fide Marketing. However, we also noted that changes in price after the drug is deselected may be contained (and thus savings preserved) by the Inflation Rebate Program for drugs payable under Part B.
[
114
]
While we are unable to produce a quantitative estimate of the financial impacts on the Negotiation Program, we do not treat this uncertainty as evidence that such costs are negligible. We disagree that our inability to quantify these effects means CMS lacks an adequate basis for this policy and have carefully considered the costs qualitatively. We weighed the statutory requirement to aggregate new formulations under sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act, the program integrity risks of not doing so, and the narrow scope of drugs affected, against the acknowledged but unquantifiable potential foregone savings in the long term were a new formulation to have an agreed-upon MFP applied earlier but for a shorter period of time due to an approved generic drug or licensed biosimilar for a product included in the qualifying single source drug engaging in Bona Fide Marketing, as compared to potential foregone savings in the short term if it had been identified as a separate qualifying single source drug. We weighed the potential responses to this policy against the risk that, absent this policy, manufacturers could use the development of new formulations that enable an alternative route of administration to avoid or delay MFP applicability, an outcome that would undermine the statutory purpose of sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) and create the program integrity risk the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) is designed to address. On balance, we believe the qualitative benefit of closing this gap and the potential short-term savings generated outweigh the uncertain and likely limited foregone long-term savings under the Negotiation Program given that the policy applies only to a narrow set of new formulations meeting specific criteria proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii).
Regarding the recommendation that CMS monitor prescribing and pricing patterns for reformulated products following deselection, we intend to monitor utilization and pricing trends for such products as part of our ongoing
(

program oversight. Regarding the recommendation that CMS work with Congress to address reformulations that lack genuine generic or biosimilar competition, we appreciate the suggestion. However, statutory changes are outside the scope of this final rule. Regarding the request that CMS use the material-change and renegotiation authorities in §  429.605(d) to bring reformulated products back into the Negotiation Program when warranted, we understand this comment as a request that CMS use our renegotiation authorities under section 1194(f) of the Act to select for renegotiation a drug that has been deselected due to the approval or licensure and engagement in Bona Fide Marketing of a generic drug or biosimilar for a product included in the selected drug. We decline this request because section 1194(f)(2) of the Act limits renegotiation-eligible drugs to selected drugs.
Final Decision:
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our regulatory impact analysis as proposed.
D. Alternatives Considered
In this section, CMS includes discussions of alternatives considered.
1. Fixed Combination Products (§ 429.105(b)(4))
The first alternative we considered would have further narrowed the scope of the policy for specific fixed combination drugs that are new formulations proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii) to biological products only. As compared to the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii), this alternative may not meaningfully impact which products would be aggregated under a qualifying single source drug.
The second alternative we considered was an articulation of the policy as aggregating drugs for which one of the active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components contained is not biologically active against the disease state(s) the drug is indicated for and thus does not result in a clinically meaningful difference. We believe the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii), provides a clearer and more administrable standard for CMS and manufacturers to apply consistently, which is why we did not pursue this alternative.
The third alternative we considered would have maintained the policy established for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, wherein, for a fixed combination drug with two or more active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components, we would treat the distinct combination of active moieties, active ingredients, or antigen components as one active moiety, active ingredient, or antigen component. We did not adopt this alternative because we believe our proposed policy better applies, in a predictable and administrable way, our interpretation of the directives in sections 1192(d)(3)(B) and 1196(a)(2) of the Act, which require the aggregation of data across dosage forms and strengths of the drug, including new formulations of the drug, and not based on the specific formulation or package size or package type of such drug. As compared to the policy proposed at § 429.125(b)(4)(i) and finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii), this alternative may reduce the number of products that would be aggregated under a qualifying single source drug. If we maintained the policy established for initial price applicability years 2026 through 2028, selection and negotiation for a new formulation of a qualifying single source drug, which would otherwise be aggregated with and subject to the MFP under the finalized policy at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii), could instead be delayed, which might reduce total savings under the Negotiation Program.
Because these alternatives considered involve financial impacts outside the 10-year budget window, and we do not have credible drug-level forecast that far out, quantifying longer-term effects would be speculative, and only considering impacts within the window would not adequately explain the full results of these alternatives.
Further discussion of the policy finalized at § 429.125(b)(4)(ii) is included in section II.B.6.a. of this final rule.

F. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)
The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief for small entities. For purposes of the RFA, small entities include small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions. Individuals and states are not included in the definition of a small entity. The RFA requires that CMS analyze regulatory options for small businesses and other entities unless CMS certifies that a rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. The analysis must include a justification concerning the reason action is being taken, the kinds and number of small entities the final rule effects, and an explanation of any meaningful options that achieve the objectives with less significant adverse economic impact on the small entities.
(
printed page 72357)
HHS considers a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities to be one with a 3 percent revenue effect on 5 percent of small entities.
115
CMS would consider a “significant impact” to be 3 percent or more of the affected entities' costs or revenues, and a “substantial number” to mean 5 percent or more of affected small entities within the total number of the small businesses in that North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) industry description. As discussed in section II. of this final rule, the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program requires the Secretary to negotiate and renegotiate, for applicable periods, Medicare prices for certain high expenditure, single source drugs and biological products. Our analysis shows that this final rule may directly impact one category of small entities, Primary Manufacturers. Given the uncertainty on negotiation outcomes and available data, CMS concludes that this final rule may have an economic impact on small entities. This analysis as well as other sections in this final rule, serves as the Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis, as required by the RFA. As its measure of significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, HHS uses a change in revenue of more than 3 to 5 percent. We have determined that this threshold will not be reached by the requirements in this final rule. The resources needed to produce and distribute a drug with expenditures that exceed the low-spend Medicare drug exclusion described in section II.B.6.c.2. of this final rule is expected to require a workforce larger than the small entity threshold; thus, we expect that no Primary Manufacturer would qualify as a small entity. Therefore, the Secretary has certified that this final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
1. Description and Number of Affected Small Entities
We use the NAICS to identify the industry potentially affected by this final rule. We also use the Small Business Administration (SBA) size standards in “number of employees” and “millions of dollars” to identify small entities.
[

]
The SBA considers any “Pharmaceutical Preparation Manufacturing” firm (NAICS code 325412) with fewer than 1,300 employees as a small business. As defined in section 1192(e)(3)(B)(i) of the Act, a selected drug must have total expenditures of $200 million or more during the defined measurement period, between June 1, 2022 and May 31, 2023, for initial price applicability year 2026, adjusted by inflation in subsequent years (hereinafter the “low-spend Medicare drug exclusion”).
For purposes of this final analysis, we are unable to determine the actual employee size or revenue of all manufacturers that may ever have a selected drug in the Negotiation Program. Assuming the low-spend Medicare drug exclusion described previously, we estimate that no Primary Manufacturer would be considered to be a small entity because we expect that the resources needed to produce and distribute a drug with Medicare expenditures that meet this threshold would require a workforce larger than the small entity threshold of 1,300 employees. As Table V.F1 demonstrates, none of the drugs that were selected for negotiation, as set forth in § 429.105 of this final rule, were manufactured by small entities during the first 3 years of the Negotiation Program.
2. Description of the Potential Impacts on Small Entities
With the expiration of the Small Biotech Exception, which applies to initial price applicability years 2026, 2027, and 2028, and the implementation of the Temporary Floor for Small Biotech Drugs, which becomes effective for initial price applicability years 2029 and 2030, manufacturers of small biotech drugs could have a selected drug for initial price applicability year 2029 or a future year. It is possible that a manufacturer of a small biotech drug could have 1,300 or fewer employees, but CMS does not have credible information to forecast if or when such manufacturers would have a selected drug.

Specifically, the estimates are based on the current status of drug negotiations, employment and revenue information using 2024 or other available data as of the publication of this final rule. Despite this uncertainty, CMS certifies that the final rule will not have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entity Primary Manufacturers because the resources needed to produce and distribute a drug with expenditures that meet the low-spend Medicare drug exclusion is expected to require a workforce larger than the small entity threshold, therefore, we expect that no Primary Manufacturer would qualify as a small entity. The vast majority of the policies discussed in this final rule, including timing for reporting and publications and effective dates of rates, are required by sections 1191 through 1198 of the Act. In addition, section 1102(b) of the Act requires us to prepare a regulatory impact analysis if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 604 of the RFA. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a metropolitan statistical area and has fewer than 100 beds. This final rule will not have a significant impact on small rural hospitals because our analysis shows that this final rule may directly impact one category of entities, Primary Manufacturers, and small rural hospitals are not entities involved in the Negotiation Program. Therefore, the Secretary has certified that this final rule will not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals.
G. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
Section 202 of UMRA also requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold is approximately $193 million. This final rule is not anticipated to have an unfunded effect on State, local, or tribal governments, in the aggregate, or on the private sector of $193 million or more. The analysis of impacts on this final rule does not report an estimate of any unfunded effect on State, local, or tribal governments, in the aggregate, or on the private sector that exceeds the $193 million threshold. However, this final rule will result in additional impacts associated with changes in behavior; these are not quantified. Therefore, the Secretary has concluded that the requirements of section 202 of the UMRA have been met for this final rule. We requested comments, including on the potential magnitude of this impact. We did not receive public comments on this URMA conclusion, and therefore, we are finalizing as proposed.
