C. What is the statutory authority for this action?
CAA section 112, as amended, provides the statutory authority for this action.
[
4
]
CAA section 112 establishes a multi-stage regulatory process to develop standards for emissions of HAP from stationary sources. Generally, the first stage involves establishing technology-based standards that reflect application of the maximum achievable control technology (MACT) or appropriate alternative.
[
5
]
The second stage involves evaluating those standards within 8 years under CAA section 112(f)(2) to determine whether the EPA needs to promulgate standards to address any remaining risk associated with HAP emissions.
[
6
]
This second stage is commonly referred to as the “residual risk review.” In addition to conducting the residual risk review, pursuant to CAA section 112(d)(6), the EPA must review the standards every 8 years and to “revise [them] as necessary,” taking into account any “developments in practices, processes, and control technologies.”
[
7
]
This review is commonly referred to as the “technology review.”
In the first stage of the CAA section 112 standard-setting process, the EPA promulgates technology-based standards under CAA section 112(d) for categories of sources identified as emitting one or more of the HAP listed in CAA section 112(b). The CAA refers to sources of HAP emissions as either major sources or area sources. “Major sources” are those that emit or have the potential to emit 10 tons per year (tpy) or more of a single HAP or 25 tpy or more of any combination of HAP.
[
8
]
All other sources are “area sources.” CAA section 112 establishes different requirements for major source standards and area source standards. For major sources, CAA section 112(d)(2) provides that the technology-based NESHAP must reflect the maximum degree of reduction in emissions of HAP achievable (after considering cost, energy requirements, and non-air quality health and environmental impacts). These standards are commonly referred to as MACT standards. In developing MACT standards, CAA section 112(d)(2) directs the EPA to consider the application of measures, processes, methods, systems, or techniques, including, but not limited to, those that reduce the volume of or eliminate HAP emissions through process changes, substitution of materials, or other modifications; enclose systems or processes to eliminate emissions; collect, capture, or treat HAP when released from a process, stack, storage, or fugitive emissions point; are design, equipment, work practice, or operational standards; or any combination of the above.
CAA section 112(d)(3) establishes a minimum control level for MACT standards, known as the MACT “floor,” based on emission controls achieved in practice by the best performing sources. For new sources, the MACT floor cannot be less stringent than the emission control achieved in practice by the best-controlled similar source. For existing sources, the MACT standards can be less stringent than floors for new sources, but the standards cannot be less stringent than the average emission limitation achieved by the best-performing 12 percent of existing sources in the category or subcategory (or the best-performing five sources for categories or subcategories with fewer
(
printed page 70798)
than 30 sources).
[
9
]
In certain instances, as provided in CAA section 112(h), the EPA may set work practice standards in lieu of numerical emission standards. The EPA must also consider control options that are more stringent than the floor, often referred to as “beyond-the-floor” standards, and may establish standards more stringent than the floor taking into consideration the cost of achieving the emission reductions, and any non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements.
[
10
]
In the second stage of the regulatory process, for categories of major sources and any area source categories subject to MACT standards, CAA section 112 requires the EPA to identify and address any remaining (
i.e.,
“residual”) risk within 8 years pursuant to CAA section 112(f)(2) and to conduct a technology review pursuant to CAA section 112(d)(6). This latter provision requires the EPA to review the technology-based standards and revise them “as necessary (taking into account developments in practices, processes, and control technologies)” no less frequently than every 8 years. In conducting the technology review, the EPA is not required to recalculate the MACT floors that the Agency established in earlier rulemakings.
[
11
]
The EPA may consider cost in deciding whether to revise the standards pursuant to CAA section 112(d)(6).
[
12
]
Finally, the EPA reviews available data to determine if there are certain unregulated emissions of HAP within the major source category and evaluates these data for use in developing new emission standards.
[
13
]
For the residual risk review required by CAA section 112(f), within 8 years of promulgating the technology-based standards for a source category, the EPA must evaluate the risk to public health remaining after the application of the technology-based standards and revise the standards, if necessary, to provide an ample margin of safety to protect public health or to prevent an adverse environmental effect, taking into consideration costs, energy, safety, and other relevant factors. For categories of area sources subject to generally available control technologies or management practices (GACT) standards, the CAA does not require the EPA to address residual risk. However, CAA section 112(d)(6) requires the EPA to conduct a technology review for all standards established under CAA section 112(d), including GACT standards that apply to area sources. For categories of area sources subject to GACT standards, CAA section 112(d)(5) and (f)(5) provide that the EPA is not required to conduct a residual risk review under CAA section 112(f)(2).
The EPA first set MACT standards for the PVC and Copolymer Production major source category in 2002 (“2002 Final Rule”).
[
14
]
Upon vacatur and remand by the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit (“D.C. Circuit”),
[
15
]
the EPA promulgated new MACT standards for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category for major sources and revised the area source NESHAP in the 2012 Final Rule.
[
16
]
After receiving petitions for reconsideration of the 2012 Final Rule, the EPA proposed reconsideration of several aspects of that rule in the 2020 Proposal.
[
17
]
This final action addresses only the proposed reconsideration of the new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit. The EPA intends to address the remaining issues presented in the 2020 Proposal in a separate action.
D. Where can I get a copy of this document and other related information?
In addition to placing this action in the docket, the EPA provides an electronic copy on the internet. Following signature by the EPA Administrator, the Agency will post a copy of this action at
https://www.epa.gov/​stationary-sources-air-pollution/​polyvinyl-chloride-and-copolymers-production-national-emission
.
Following publication in the
Federal Register
(FR), the EPA will post the
Federal Register
version of the final rule and key technical documents at this same website. The EPA has placed in the docket a memorandum showing the “track changes” version of the regulatory language that incorporates the changes in this action.
[
18
]
E. Judicial Review and Administrative Reconsideration
Under CAA section 307(b)(1), a party may obtain judicial review of this action only by filing a petition for review in the D.C. Circuit by January 8, 2027. CAA section 307(b)(2) prohibits a party from separately challenging this final rule in any civil or criminal enforcement proceedings that the EPA brings.
CAA section 307(d)(7)(B) provides that, during judicial review, a party may raise only an objection to a rule or procedure that the party raised with reasonable specificity during the period for public comment (including any public hearing). This section also requires the EPA to reconsider the rule if the person raising an objection demonstrates to the Administrator that either it was impracticable to raise the objection during the period for public comment or that the grounds for the objection arose after the period for public comment (but within the time specified for judicial review) and if the objection is of central relevance to the outcome of the rule. Any person seeking to make such a demonstration should submit a petition for reconsideration to the Office of the Administrator, U.S. EPA, Room 3000, WJC South Building, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460. The person should also send a copy to both the person(s) listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this preamble, and the Associate General Counsel for the Air and Radiation Law Office, Office of General Counsel (Mail Code 2344A), U.S. EPA, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460.
II. Background
A. What is the PVC and Copolymer Production source category, and how does the NESHAP regulate HAP emissions from the source category?
The EPA first promulgated the PVC and Copolymer Production source category NESHAP with the 2002 Final Rule and codified the NESHAP at
40 CFR part 63, subpart J
.
[
19
]
Following judicial review, the D.C. Circuit vacated and remanded the 2002 Final Rule to the EPA after determining that the Agency failed to adequately explain the basis for the decision to use vinyl chloride as a surrogate for other HAP.
[
20
]
The EPA separately promulgated an area source NESHAP for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category on January 23, 2007, and codified it at
40 CFR part 63, subpart DDDDDD
.
[
21
]
With the 2012 Final Rule, the EPA promulgated new major source standards for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category at
40 CFR part 63, subpart HHHHHHH
and aligned
(
printed page 70799)
the major and area source NESHAP by revising
40 CFR part 63, subpart DDDDDD
.
The EPA received multiple petitions for reconsideration of the 2012 Final Rule.
[
22
]
To better assess the issues raised for reconsideration, the EPA issued CAA section 114 information collection requests (ICRs) to gather additional information on PVC and copolymer production process vents and wastewater. Additionally, industry stakeholders identified that the EPA used data from outside the PVC and Copolymer Production source category to establish the major and area source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits. The EPA agreed with industry stakeholders and promulgated the 2015 Final Rule to rescind the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits for new and existing area sources.
[
23
]
In addition, the D.C. Circuit resolved certain contested issues via
Mexichem Specialty Resins, Inc.
v.
EPA
[
24
]
and
U.S. Sugar Corporation
v.
EPA,
[
25
]
thus mooting the need for the EPA to act on requests to reconsider those aspects of the rule. To further address the remaining reconsideration issues and other technical and editorial corrections, the EPA issued the 2020 Proposal to reconsider certain aspects of the major source PVC NESHAP, including the major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits.
[
26
]
This final action addresses the proposed reconsideration of the new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit. The EPA intends to address the remaining issues presented in the 2020 Proposal in a separate action.
The 2012 Final Rule regulates HAP emissions from PVC and copolymer production process units (PVCPU) that produce PVC and copolymers as their primary product(s). A PVCPU is the collection of process components assembled and connected by hard-piping or duct work used to process raw materials to manufacture PVC and/or PVC copolymers and includes, but is not limited to, polymerization reactors, resin stripping operations, resin blend tanks, resin centrifuges, resin dryers, resin product separators, recovery devices, reactant and raw material charge vessels and tanks, holding tanks, mixing and weighing tanks; finished resin product storage tanks or storage silos; finished resin product loading operations; and connected duct and piping. A PVCPU also includes pumps, compressors, agitators, PRDs, sampling connection systems, open-ended valves or lines, valves and connectors, and instrumentation systems.
PVC is the third most widely produced synthetic polymer in the world and comes in a variety of rigid and flexible forms depending on the application. Vinyl chloride monomer is the primary raw material in PVC and copolymer production, and manufacturers add other components to the polymerization reaction as necessary to modify the properties of the resulting resin to meet product specifications. As such, there are a wide variety of PVC and copolymer resin recipes, and each recipe will result in different HAP present in the PVCPU. There are multiple ways to produce PVC and copolymer resins including bulk polymerization, dispersion polymerization, and suspension polymerization.
[
27
]
The HAP emission sources at PVC and copolymer production facilities include process vents, storage vessels, equipment leaks, heat exchange systems, wastewater, and stripped resin. While all PVC and copolymer production sources emit vinyl chloride, a PVCPU may also emit other HAP such as benzene, formaldehyde, and toluene depending on the specific resin recipes. The PVC NESHAP includes numeric emission limits for process vents, stripped resin, and wastewater; a mixture of numeric emission limits and work practices for storage vessels depending on the volume and pressure; and work practices for equipment leaks and heat exchange systems.
The EPA identified that this action may affect one potential new major source upon construction and startup. However, this potential new source has not yet commenced construction. While existing sources may reconstruct their PVCPU(s) and become subject to the new source standards, the EPA is unaware of any ongoing reconstruction efforts. As such, the EPA does not anticipate that this action will have any immediate cost or emissions impacts (see section IV of this preamble for additional details).
B. What changes did we propose for the PVC and Copolymer Production source category in our 2020 Proposal?
In 2020, the EPA proposed reconsideration of several aspects of the 2012 Final Rule to resolve reconsideration issues that the D.C. Circuit had not addressed.
[
28
]

demonstrate that steam stripping reduces emissions of the majority of organic HAP in PVC and copolymer production to levels similar to or below that of vinyl chloride. However, it is not necessary to reduce the ethylene glycol concentration below that of vinyl chloride for vinyl chloride to be a valid surrogate, as the EPA explains later in this comment response.
Responding to the commenter's arguments regarding the lawfulness and validity of the proposed (and final) surrogacy, the EPA disagrees that it is unlawful for the Agency to use vinyl chloride as a surrogate for non-vinyl chloride organic HAP in PVC and copolymer production process wastewater.
When considering the surrogacy relationship between particulate matter (PM) and metal HAP, the D.C. Circuit applied three general criteria that clearly demonstrate that a surrogate is reasonable: (1) “HAP metals are invariably present in . . . PM;” (2) “PM control technology indiscriminately captures HAP metals along with other particulates;” and (3) “PM control is the only means by which facilities `achieve' reductions in HAP metal emissions.”

In that situation, PM is the surrogate for metal HAP. Applying these criteria to PVC and copolymer production process wastewater, the EPA interprets similar criteria to be: (1) both non-vinyl chloride organic HAP and vinyl chloride must be present in the wastewater streams; (2) the vinyl chloride control technology must indiscriminately capture both non-vinyl chloride organic HAP and vinyl chloride; and (3) steam stripping is the only means by which affected sources achieve reductions in non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emissions. The EPA notes that other commenters who expressed support for the proposed (and final) surrogacy identified the same criteria.
With respect to the first criterion, the EPA explained in the 2020 Proposal that both vinyl chloride and non-vinyl chloride HAP are invariably present in PVC and copolymer production process wastewater streams.
[

e.g.,
methanol, chloroform, benzene, hexane) are not.

As other commenters noted, vinyl chloride monomer is the primary feedstock for PVC and copolymer resin manufacturing, and the resin recipes dictate the presence of other non-vinyl chloride organic HAP in the resulting process wastewater. When a source does not identify the presence of a particular organic HAP in a wastewater stream, it does not necessarily indicate that the source achieved complete control of the given organic HAP. Instead, it more likely indicates that the resin recipe did not call for that specific HAP, and it was never present in the process. This is particularly relevant considering that steam stripping will remove a similar fraction of HAP from the wastewater for 26 of the 33 HAP identified in table 1 of the wastewater analysis, as the EPA explains later in this comment response.

Using vinyl chloride as a surrogate will address those concerns by allowing facilities to monitor for a single representative HAP to demonstrate adequate control.
The EPA also notes that it is common for chemical sector rulemakings to have more general standards for streams potentially containing a wide variety of HAP (

A similar situation applies for the PVC NESHAP; however, vinyl chloride is the primary feedstock common to all PVC and copolymer production operations, and all process wastewater streams contain vinyl chloride. Thus, while the presence of other organic HAP may vary between sources, measuring control via vinyl chloride provides the best indication of the level of control despite the potential differences in HAP composition between sources.

4. What is the rationale for our final approach and final decisions for the new source wastewater emission limits?
The EPA is finalizing the revisions to the approach to regulating new major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emissions without change. Specifically, the EPA is finalizing the removal of the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit for new major PVC and copolymer production sources; the associated testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and
(
printed page 70804)
reporting requirements; and that vinyl chloride can serve as a surrogate for non-vinyl chloride organic HAP in PVC and copolymer production process wastewater, without change.
This action focuses on the removal of a regulatory barrier for new major source PVC and copolymer production manufacturers. The EPA is not taking final action on the proposed removal of the existing major source total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit at this time. Although the EPA believes that the current new major source vinyl chloride wastewater emission limit ensures sufficient control of non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emissions, the current existing major source vinyl chloride emission limit for PVC and copolymer production process wastewater is 24 times larger than the equivalent emission limit for new major sources (6.8 ppmw vinyl chloride for existing major sources versus 0.28 ppmw vinyl chloride for new major sources). With vinyl chloride acting as a surrogate, this corresponds to potentially 24 times more non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emissions from existing major sources than from new major sources. Although the total existing source non-vinyl chloride organic HAP concentration in the process wastewater must remain below 110 ppmw, the non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emission limit is 16 times greater than the vinyl chloride emission limit. Given that steam stripping removes a similar fraction of HAP for 26 of the 33 non-vinyl chloride organic HAP in PVC process wastewater, if sources are controlling vinyl chloride to just below the existing source emission limit (
i.e.,
6.8 ppmw), and there are similar amounts of vinyl chloride as other organic HAP in the process wastewater, then wastewater streams at existing major sources could contain 16 organic HAP with concentrations up to 24 times greater than equivalent wastewater streams at new major sources. As such, it is appropriate for existing major sources to continue to test, monitor, and report total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP concentrations in process wastewater and to comply with the associated emission limit at this time. The EPA notes that existing sources have complied with the current existing source vinyl chloride and total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits for over a decade.
Similarly, the EPA is not taking final action on removing the non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater monitoring requirements for area source PVC and copolymer production manufacturers. The area source vinyl chloride process wastewater emission limits are 7.5 times greater than the new major source vinyl chloride process wastewater emission limit (2.1 ppmw vinyl chloride for new and existing area sources versus 0.28 ppmw for a new major source). This corresponds to potentially 7.5 times more emissions per HAP from area source process wastewater as compared to similar streams at a new major source. In addition, although the EPA rescinded the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limits with the 2015 Final Rule, the NESHAP has required area sources to monitor and report total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP concentrations in process wastewater for more than a decade.
[
62
]
As sources have continued the monitoring without major adverse effect, the EPA anticipates continuing to test, monitor, and report total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP concentrations will not be burdensome. Therefore, the EPA believes it is appropriate for area PVC and copolymer production sources to continue monitoring and reporting total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP concentrations at this time.
The EPA is also not taking final action on the proposed revisions to the major source vinyl chloride process wastewater emission limits at this time. The EPA continues to evaluate the comments on the 2020 Proposal and the Agency's identification of the best performing sources with respect to process wastewater. The EPA intends to make final determinations on whether it is appropriate to remove the total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP process wastewater emission limit for existing major sources, revise the vinyl chloride emission limits for new and existing major sources, and remove the associated total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP testing and monitoring requirements in addressing the other aspects of the proposed reconsideration at a later date.
C. What are the effective and compliance dates of the standards?
CAA section 112(i) and 5 United States Code (U.S.C.) 801(3) provide that for the finalized requirements, all new affected sources that commenced construction after May 20, 2011, must comply with all requirements under CAA section 112(d)(2), (3), (6), and 112(h) by November 9, 2026, or upon startup, whichever is later.
IV. Summary of Environmental and Economic Impacts
A. What are the affected sources?
While no new PVC sources have become operational since the 2012 Final Rule, the EPA is aware that an industry stakeholder has expressed interest in potentially developing, constructing, and operating a new PVC manufacturing facility within the next decade. If constructed, this final rule could impact such a new facility. The EPA approximated the impacts of reducing the testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements in the rule to provide a conservative estimate of this action's cost-savings on a per facility basis (see section IV.C of this preamble for additional details).
B. What are the air quality impacts?
The EPA does not expect any air quality impacts as a result of this rule, as there will be no change to the total emissions from the PVC and Copolymer Production source category. This action does not affect existing major PVC and copolymer production sources, and so there will be no emission changes from currently operating facilities. While this action will affect new major sources (
i.e.,
sources that commenced construction after May 20, 2011), vinyl chloride will act as a surrogate for non-vinyl chloride organic HAP, and the EPA is not revising the new major source vinyl chloride emission limit. In addition, the EPA is unaware of any new sources currently subject to the rule. As such, there will be no changes to the potential vinyl chloride and non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emissions if a new source becomes operational.
The EPA notes that if stakeholders construct a new PVC and copolymer production facility and it becomes operational, the sector's HAP emissions will increase. However, the EPA cannot speculate on the potential impacts of emissions that may never occur. As such, the EPA does not anticipate any immediate impacts to human health as a consequence of this final rule. If stakeholders construct a new facility and it becomes operational, the EPA will consider the associated emissions when conducting future rulemakings.
C. What are the costs?
The EPA does not anticipate any operational changes for existing PVC and copolymer manufacturing facilities to accommodate the revisions in this final action. As such, existing sources will incur no costs as a result of this final action. In addition, as the EPA is unaware of any new sources currently subject to the rule, new sources will also
(
printed page 70805)
incur no cost as a result of this final action. Thus, this action will have no immediate cost impacts.
However, if a new PVC and copolymer production facility becomes operational, the EPA estimates owners and operators would save approximately $2,900 in initial capital/startup costs as well as an estimated $30,000 in annual costs (both in 2025 dollars) compared to the facility's costs if it became operational after May 20, 2011, but prior to this final action due to the reductions in the non-vinyl chloride organic HAP testing, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements the Agency is finalizing with this action.
The EPA calculated these cost savings using information from the ICR supporting statement, assuming one respondent (see section V.C of this preamble for additional details).
[
63
]
The EPA estimates that the costs for initial total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP testing for stripped wastewater and uncontrolled wastewater are $820 and $2,100, respectively. A new major source subject to the requirements in this final rule would no longer incur those costs. In addition, a new major source would no longer need to conduct monthly total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP monitoring for treated wastewater streams (resulting in $9,800 saved annually) or annual monitoring for untreated wastewater streams ($2,100 saved annually).
Also, new major sources subject to the requirements in this final rule would save on labor costs. The EPA estimated that sampling would require approximately 4 hours per sample and two samples per wastewater stream. Using labor rates from the United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics and inflating them by 110 percent to account for varying industry wage rates and the additional overhead business costs, the EPA estimated that new major sources would save approximately $18,000 in labor costs per year while incurring a one-time cost of $2,000 to read and understand this final action.
[
64
]
Finally, the EPA estimated that new major sources would save approximately $1,900 per year in recordkeeping costs due to no longer having to keep, retain, or report total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP concentrations in process wastewater.
D. What are the benefits?
This action removes a regulatory barrier affecting the potential construction of new major source PVC and copolymer production manufacturing facilities. By removing this barrier, the EPA is addressing feasibility concerns and reducing overall regulatory burden by simplifying the NESHAP without increasing the potential total non-vinyl chloride organic HAP emissions from process wastewater from a newly constructed PVC and copolymer production plant.
E. What are the economic impacts?
The EPA anticipates no emission or air quality impacts and no qualitative or quantitative changes in health benefits. Therefore, there are no estimated monetized health or emissions impacts, and the potential costs detailed in section IV.C of this preamble are the only potential economic impacts of this final action.

Abstract of Proposed Collection
The DS-2031 form is necessary to document imports of shrimp and products from shrimp pursuant to the State Department's implementation of Section 609 of Public Law 101-162, which prohibits the entry into the United States of shrimp harvested in ways which are harmful to sea turtles. Respondents are exporters of shrimp and products from shrimp and government officials in countries that export shrimp and products from shrimp to the United States. The importer is required to present the DS-2031 form at the port of entry into the United States, to retain the DS-2031 form for a period of three years subsequent to entry, and during that time to make the DS-2031 form available to U.S. Customs and Border Protection or the Department of State upon request.
Methodology
The DS-2031 form is completed by the exporter, the importer, and under certain conditions a government official of the harvesting country. The DS-2031 form accompanies shipments of shrimp and shrimp product to the United States and must be made available to U.S. Customs and Border Protection at the time of entry and for three years after entry.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is superseding Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-17-10, which applied to Lycoming Engines (Lycoming) Model O-235, O-540, and IO-540 engines with a certain piston pin installed. AD 2026-17-10 required replacement of the affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation and, for certain engines, oil change and visual inspection of the engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen for metal particulates. AD 2026-17-10 also prohibited the installation of an affected piston pin on any engine. Since the FAA issued AD 2026-17-10, the manufacturer has identified additional Lycoming Model engines that are subject to the unsafe condition, and the FAA determined the need to clarify the definition for an “affected piston pin,” and include corrective action for engine models that were not listed in the manufacturer's service material. This AD requires replacement of the affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation and, for certain engines, oil change and visual inspection of the engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen for metal particulates. This AD also prohibits the installation of an affected piston pin on any engine. This AD also expands the applicability to include additional affected engines with a certain piston pin installed. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective November 24, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written data, views, or arguments about this final rule. Send your comments using a method listed under the
ADDRESSES
section. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13797; Project Identifier AD-2026-01052-E” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the final rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this final rule because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov
, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this final rule.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this AD contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this AD, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this AD. Submissions containing CBI
(
printed page 70782)
should be sent to Ramanpreet Singh, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1701 Columbia Avenue, College Park, GA 30337. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2026-17-10, Amendment 39-23454 (
91 FR 55451
, August 28, 2026) (AD 2026-17-10), for Lycoming Model O-235, O-540, and IO-540 engines with a certain piston pin installed. AD 2026-17-10 required replacement of the affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation and, for certain engines, oil change and visual inspection of the engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen for metal particulates. AD 2026-17-10 was prompted by several reports of piston pin failure that resulted in metal particulate contamination in the engine oil and engine failure. The FAA issued AD 2026-17-10 to prevent failure of the piston pin.
Actions Since AD 2026-17-10 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2026-17-10, the manufacturer has identified additional Lycoming Model engines that are subject to the unsafe condition and identified Lycoming Model engines that were included in the applicability of AD 2026-17-10 that are not subject to the unsafe condition. Additionally, the FAA determined the need to clarify the applicability, the definition for an “affected piston pin,” and corrective actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
FAA's Determination
The FAA is issuing this AD because the agency determined the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR part 51
The FAA reviewed Lycoming Service Instruction No. 1009BF, dated July 20, 2026, which identifies the compliance times between overhauls for certain Lycoming Model engines.
This AD also requires the following material, which the Director of the Federal Register approved for incorporation by reference as of September 14, 2026 (
91 FR 55451
, August 28, 2026).
Lycoming Mandatory Service Bulletin No. (MSB) 667A, dated March 12, 2026 (Lycoming MSB 667A).
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
AD Requirements
This AD requires replacement of the affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation and, for certain engines, oil change and visual inspection of the engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen for metal particulates. This AD also prohibits the installation of an affected piston pin on any engine. This AD also expands the applicability to include additional affected engines with a certain piston pin installed.
Differences Between This AD and the Referenced Material
This AD requires oil change and visual inspection of the engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen for metal particulates within 5 hours time-in-service (TIS), while Lycoming MSB 667A does not have this requirement.
Justification for Immediate Adoption and Determination of the Effective Date
Section 553(b) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.
) authorizes agencies to dispense with notice and comment procedures for rules when the agency, for “good cause,” finds that those procedures are “impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Under this section, an agency, upon finding good cause, may issue a final rule without providing notice and seeking comment prior to issuance. Further, section 553(d) of the APA authorizes agencies to make rules effective in less than thirty days, upon a finding of good cause.
An unsafe condition exists that requires the immediate adoption of this AD without providing an opportunity for public comments prior to adoption. The FAA has found that the risk to the flying public justifies forgoing notice and comment prior to adoption of this rule because piston pin microcracks and inclusions are difficult to detect prior to failure, and can result in internal damage to the engine, in-flight shutdown, and loss of control of the airplane. The FAA has determined that affected engines will need to be inspected and have affected piston pins replaced within 25 hours TIS or earlier after the effective date of this AD depending on the engine model. Additionally, the compliance time in this AD is shorter than the time necessary for the public to comment and for publication of the final rule. Accordingly, notice and opportunity for prior public comment are impracticable and contrary to the public interest pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
.
In addition, the FAA finds that good cause exists pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
for making this amendment effective in less than 30 days, for the same reasons the FAA found good cause to forgo notice and comment.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The requirements of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) do not apply when an agency finds good cause pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
to adopt a rule without prior notice and comment. Because FAA has determined that it has good cause to adopt this rule without prior notice and comment, RFA analysis is not required.
Costs of Compliance
The FAA estimates that this AD affects 957 engines installed on airplanes of U.S. registry.
The FAA estimates the following costs to comply with this AD:

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue
(
printed page 70783)
rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
This AD will not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This AD will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify that this AD:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
, and
(2) Will not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska.

(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective November 24, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
This AD replaces AD 2026-17-10, Amendment 39-23454 (
91 FR 55451
, August 28, 2026).
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to Lycoming Engines (Lycoming) Model engines identified in table 1 to paragraph (c) of this AD with an installed piston pin having part number (P/N) LW-13445 that was manufactured between January 7, 2021 to December 15, 2025. If the date of manufacture for the piston pin cannot be determined, this AD is applicable. If the current piston pins (P/N LW-13445) were installed prior to January 7, 2021, this AD is not applicable.

(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by reports from Lycoming of metal particulates found in the engine oil during oil change and two non-detectable engine failures. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent failure of the piston pin. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in engine failure, loss of thrust control, in-flight shutdown, damage to the airplane, and loss of control of the airplane.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Definitions
(1) For the purpose of this AD, a “part eligible for installation” is one of the following:
(i) A piston pin that does not have P/N LW-13445.
(ii) A piston pin having P/N LW-13445 that was not manufactured between January 7, 2021 to December 15, 2025.
(2) For the purpose of this AD, an “affected piston pin” is a piston pin having P/N LW-13445 and one of the following:
(i) A date of manufacture between January 7, 2021 to December 15, 2025.
(ii) A date of manufacture that is unknown.
(3) For the purpose of this AD, Group 1 engines are all affected engines, except engines with an installed piston pin having P/N LW-13445 with a manufacture date between March 23, 2023 to December 15, 2025, or an installed piston pin having P/N LW-13445 with a manufacture date that is unknown.
(4) For the purpose of this AD, Group 2 engines are engines with an installed piston pin having P/N LW-13445 with a manufacture date between March 23, 2023 to December 15, 2025, or an installed piston pin having P/N LW-13445 with a manufacture date that is unknown.
(h) Required Actions
(1) For Group 1 and Group 2 engines, except for Group 2 engines with greater than or equal to 150 hours time in service (TIS)
(
printed page 70784)
as of the effective date of this AD, within 5 hours TIS after the effective date of this AD, perform an oil change and visual inspection of the engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen for metal particulates.
Note 1 to paragraph (h)(1):
Guidance for engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen inspection instructions and identification of metallic solids may be found in Lycoming Mandatory Service Bulletin No. (MSB) No. 480F, dated May 25, 2017.
(2) If any metal particulates are found during the oil change and inspection required by paragraph (h)(1) of this AD, before further flight, replace any affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation in accordance with the Required Action of Lycoming MSB 667A, dated March 12, 2026 (Lycoming MSB 667A), as applicable to engine model.
(3) For Group 1 engines with an installed piston pin with a manufacture date between January 07, 2021, to March 22, 2023, where metal particulates were not found during the oil change and inspection required by paragraph (h)(1) of this AD, at the next maintenance event requiring the removal of a cylinder assembly with an affected piston pin, or at the next engine overhaul not to exceed the time between overhaul specified in Lycoming Service Instruction No. 1009BF, dated July 20, 2026, whichever occurs first after the effective date of this AD, replace any affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation in accordance with the Required Action of Lycoming MSB 667A, as applicable to engine model.
(4) For Group 2 engines with greater than or equal to 150 hours TIS as of the effective date of this AD, before further flight, replace any affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation in accordance with the Required Action of Lycoming MSB 667A, as applicable to engine model.
(5) For Group 2 engines with less than 150 hours TIS as of the effective date of this AD, within 25 hours TIS after the effective date of this AD but before or upon reaching 150 total hours TIS since installation of the affected piston pins, whichever comes first after the effective date of this AD, replace any affected piston pin with a part eligible for installation in accordance with the Required Action of Lycoming MSB 667A, as applicable to engine model.
(i) Installation Prohibition
After the effective date of this AD, do not install an affected piston pin as defined in paragraph (g)(2) of this AD on any engine.
(j) No Return of Parts
Although the service material specifies returning certain parts to the manufacturer, this AD does not include those requirements.
(k) Special Flight Permits
(1) Special flight permits may be issued in accordance with
14 CFR 21.197
and
21.199199
for the replacement requirements of this AD provided no metal particulates are found during the inspection required by this AD. For Group 2 engines that are not affected by paragraph (h)(1) of this AD, an oil change showing that no metal particulates are present would be required prior to issuing a special flight permit.
(2) Special flight permits, as described in
14 CFR 21.197
and
21.199
, are not allowed for the visual inspection of the engine oil filter, oil pressure screen, and oil suction screen for metal particulates requirement of this AD.
(l) Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs)
The Manager, East Certification Branch, FAA, has the authority to approve AMOCs for this AD, if requested using the procedures found in
14 CFR 39.19
. In accordance with
14 CFR 39.19

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry licensing regulations to streamline the licensing process and reduce regulatory burden for license applicants. Specifically, FAA proposes to allow a launch and reentry vehicle operator to protect against high consequence events during an uncontrolled atmospheric return by showing that there would be sufficient breakup of the vehicle to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties.
DATES:
Send comments on or before December 9, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Send comments identified by docket number FAA-2026-9942 using any of the following methods:
(
printed page 70814)

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Overview
In accordance with Executive Order (E.O.) 14335 “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry regulations at
14 CFR part 450
to further streamline the commercial licensing process. Specifically, FAA proposes to add an option by which applicants may comply with the high consequence event protection requirements in § 450.101(c). The proposed rule would allow an applicant to meet the requirement for an uncontrolled atmospheric return (UAR), commonly called a “random reentry,” by showing that the UAR would result in sufficient breakup of the vehicle, including all vehicle components and undeployed payloads, to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties.
II. Authority for This Rulemaking
The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at
51 U.S.C. 50901-50924
, authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the United States (U.S.) or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. As codified in
49 CFR 1.83(b)
, the Secretary has delegated authority to the FAA Administrator to carry out these functions.
III. Background
FAAhasestablishedcommercial space regulations governing licensing of launch and reentry in
14 CFR chapter III
. On December 10, 2020, FAA issued a final ruleconsolidatingall substantive launch and reentry licensing regulations into a new part 450 (
85 FR 79566
) that went into effect on March 10, 2021.
On August 13, 2025,the President issued
E.O. 14335
, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” requiring the Secretary of Transportation to “reevaluate, amend, or rescind” the part 450 regulations for the purpose of further streamlining the commercial licensing process. This proposed rule is being published in furtherance of this executive order.
In accordance with current FAA guidance, high consequence events include incidents that could involve multiple casualties, massive toxic exposures, extensive property or environmental damage, or events that jeopardize the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.
[
1
]
The term “high consequence events” does not generally include incidents that result in only one casualty. The potential for any casualties remains covered by the individual and collective risk criteria in § 450.101(a) and (b). The objective of high consequence protection is to provide additional constraints beyond the individual and collective risk criteria.
Currently, in accordance with § 450.101(c), an operator must protect against a high consequence event by one of three methods: flight abort, ensuring that conditional expected casualties (CE
C
) would fall below a specified threshold, or demonstrated reliability. However, these three methods are not well-attuned for protection against high consequence events during a UAR. A UAR, commonly called a “random reentry,” occurs when a vehicle makes an uncontrolled descent from orbit as a result of natural orbital decay, rather than as a result of action by the operator.
Currently, no UARs are close to attaining the demonstrated reliability necessary to protect against high consequence events, which makes compliance with § 450.101(c)(3) improbable at this time. Likewise, any vehicle flight that could be aborted in accordance with § 450.101(c)(1) is not a UAR because the operator is able to accomplish a controlled end to the flight; a UAR is always an uncontrolled end to flight. Thus, operators currently must comply with the CE
C
requirement in § 450.101(c)(2), which can be a labor-intensive calculation.
IV. Discussion of the Proposal
The proposed rule would amend § 450.101(c)(2) to allow an operator to demonstrate protection against a high consequence event resulting from a UAR by showing that the UAR would result in sufficient breakup of the vehicle, including all vehicle components and payloads, to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties. The proposed method of demonstrating compliance to high consequence events for UARs provides an equivalent level of safety to the current requirements.
An uncontrolled atmospheric return is fundamentally a return in which the operator has no control over the eventual impact site of the vehicle. Accordingly, the proposal would define “uncontrolled atmospheric return” in § 401.7 to include two characteristics that limit the definition to cover only those returns over which the operator exercises no control. The first proposed defining characteristic of a UAR would be that only natural forces cause the orbit of an object to decay and eventually impact the Earth or burn up in the atmosphere. Natural forces that cause orbital decay include aerodynamic drag, gravitational variations, solar radiation, and third-body gravitational effects. A perigee of
(
printed page 70815)
70 nautical miles (nm) or greater is considered the threshold of being in orbit (see definition of “Deorbit” in § 401.7). Thus, a scenario in which propulsion (which is not a natural force) reduces the perigee below the 70 nm threshold would not be considered a UAR. However, a propulsion system that fails before the perigee reaches the threshold could result in a UAR. The second proposed defining characteristic of a UAR would be that the operator lacks control over the trajectory. Thus, a flight that uses orientation to control aerodynamic forces to reduce the perigee below the 70 nm threshold would not be considered a UAR. Likewise, a vehicle that falls out of orbit due to natural forces, but which an operator may abort or otherwise guide, would not be considered a UAR.
The proposed method of demonstrating compliance to high consequence events at proposed § 450.101(c)(2)(ii) would only be available for UARs (as opposed to controlled returns) because UARs have unique properties. First, the impact probability distributions from a UAR, which are the subject of § 450.123(b), are extremely large. It is most likely that debris would impact in areas with relatively low population density because high-density populations are concentrated in small areas. In addition, when multiple fragments survive deorbit during a UAR, they are generally dispersed over a large geographical area, so it is unlikely that separate fragments would injure multiple people from the same UAR as long as the collective risk safety criterion in § 450.101(a) or (b) is satisfied.
The proposed requirement for operators to demonstrate sufficient breakup of the vehicle acts as an added layer of protection against multiple casualty events. Typically, deorbit produces extreme aerothermal and inertial forces that cause extensive breakup of vehicles that were not designed to survive substantially intact. However, extensive break-up is not always a guaranteed outcome. Therefore, an operator would be required to demonstrate that each piece of resulting debris from a UAR has a small enough effective casualty area to make multiple casualties an unlikely outcome. This demonstration would use the information already required by the debris analysis in accordance with § 450.121 and consequence analysis in § 450.135(b), so no additional analysis or application requirements would be needed.
V. Regulatory Notices and Analyses
A. Regulatory Impact Analysis
E.O. 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”) and
E.O. 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) require agencies to regulate in the “most cost-effective manner,” to make a “reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify its costs,” and to develop regulations that “impose the least burden on society.” The Office of Management and Budget has determined this proposed rule is not a significant regulatory action as defined in Section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
. FAA is seeking comments on the following analysis.
Currently, most applicants meet the requirement in § 450.101(c) to protect against high consequence events by ensuring that the consequence of any reasonably foreseeable failure mode, in any significant period of flight, is no greater than 1 x 10
−3
CE
C
. The proposed rule would allow an applicant to forgo this demonstration for a UAR if the applicant shows that there is sufficient breakup of the launch or reentry vehicle, including all vehicle components and undeployed payloads.
The applicant would make the showing using the information already required by the debris analysis in accordance with § 450.121 and consequence analysis in § 450.135(b). Consequently, no additional analysis or application requirements would be needed.
FAA estimates that forgoing the CE
C
demonstration for a UAR would save each applicant around 60 hours of labor. An aerospace engineer would complete this work. The base 2024 wage rate of a private industry worker working full-time as an aerospace engineer is $67.88 per hour.
[
2
]
When including benefits, the total compensation for an aerospace engineer
[
3
]
is $96.28 per hour. Therefore, the total cost savings for industry would be $5,777 per application.
For FAA, an aerospace engineer would take about 30 hours to provide guidance and review the data. The aerospace engineer is on the FAA Core Compensation Plan at a J band
[
4
]
with a base hourly rate of $95.33. FAA uses a factor of 1.3625 for benefits
[
5
]
which results in a total loaded hourly wage of $129.88. This results in total cost savings of $3,897 per application for FAA. Therefore, the total cost savings between FAA and an applicant would be $9,674 per application. Any cost savings would only impact new applicants, and FAA expects about 40 new applications in the next 5 years. However, not all applicants would apply to conduct operations where UARs are possible. Therefore, the total number of applications impacted would be less than 40.
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act
Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
), agencies must prepare and make available for public comment a regulatory flexibility analysis that describes the effect of the rulemaking on small entities (
i.e.,
small businesses, small organizations, and small government jurisdictions). No regulatory flexibility analysis is required, however, if the head of an agency certifies that the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. FAA has concluded and hereby certifies that this proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities; therefore, an analysis is not included.
C. International Trade Impact Assessment
The Trade Agreements Act of 1979 (Pub. L. 96-39), as amended by the Uruguay Round Agreements Act (Pub. L. 103-465), prohibits Federal agencies from establishing standards or engaging in related activities that create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States. Pursuant to these Acts, the establishment of standards is not considered an unnecessary obstacle to the foreign commerce of the United States, so long as the standard has a legitimate domestic objective, such as
(
printed page 70816)
the protection of safety, and does not operate in a manner that excludes imports that meet this objective. The statute also requires consideration of international standards and, where appropriate, they be the basis for U.S. standards.
FAA has assessed the potential effect of this proposed rule and determined that it would not create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States.
D. Unfunded Mandates Assessment
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
) governs the issuance of Federal regulations that require unfunded mandates. An unfunded mandate is a regulation that requires a State, local, or Tribal government or the private sector to incur direct costs without the Federal Government having first provided the funds to pay those costs. FAA determined the proposed rule would not result in the expenditure of $193,000,000 or more ($100,000,000 adjusted for inflation using the most current Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product) by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or the private sector, in any one year.
E. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3507(d)
) requires FAA consider the impact of paperwork and other information collection burdens imposed on the public. FAA has determined there would be no new requirement for information collection associated with this proposed rule.
F. International Compatibility
In keeping with U.S. obligations under the Convention on International Civil Aviation, it is FAA policy to conform to International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices to the maximum extent practicable. FAA has determined there are no ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices that correspond to these proposed regulations.
G. Environmental Analysis
The Department has analyzed the environmental impacts of this notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) (
42 U.S.C. 4321
,
et seq.
). FAA has determined this proposed rule is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G. Categorical exclusions are categories of actions FAA has determined normally do not significantly affect the quality of the human environment and therefore do not require either an environmental assessment (EA) or environmental impact statement (EIS). In analyzing the applicability of a categorical exclusion, FAA must also consider whether extraordinary circumstances are present that would warrant the preparation of an EA or EIS. This rulemaking, which would allow a launch and reentry vehicle operator to protect against high consequence events during an uncontrolled atmospheric return by showing that there would be sufficient breakup of the vehicle to ensure protection against a single event expected to produce multiple casualties, is categorically excluded pursuant to FAA Order 1050.1G, Appendix B, Paragraph B-2.6(f), which categorically excludes issuance of regulatory documents. FAA does not anticipate any environmental impacts, and there are no extraordinary circumstances present in connection with this rulemaking.
VI. E.O. Determinations
A.
E.O. 13132
, Federalism
FAA has analyzed this proposed rule under the principles and criteria of
E.O. 13132
, Federalism. FAA has determined this action would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, or the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government, and, therefore, would not have federalism implications.
B.
E.O. 13175
, Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
Consistent with
E.O. 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments,
[
6
]
and FAA Order 1210.20, American Indian and Alaska Native Tribal Consultation Policy and Procedures,
[
7
]
FAA ensures Federally Recognized Tribes (Tribes) are given the opportunity to provide meaningful and timely input regarding proposed Federal actions that have the potential to affect uniquely or significantly their respective Tribes. At this point, FAA has not identified any unique or significant effects, environmental or otherwise, on Tribes resulting from this proposed rule.
C.
E.O. 13211
, Regulations That Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use
FAA analyzed this proposed rule under
E.O. 13211
, Actions Concerning Regulations that Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use (May 18, 2001). FAA has determined it would not be a “significant energy action” under the E.O. and would not be likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution, or use of energy.
D.
E.O. 13609
, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation
E.O. 13609
, Promoting International Regulatory Cooperation, promotes international regulatory cooperation to (1) meet shared challenges involving health, safety, labor, security, environmental, and other issues and to reduce, eliminate, or (2) prevent unnecessary differences in regulatory requirements. FAA has analyzed this action under the policies and agency responsibilities of
E.O. 13609
and has determined this action would have no effect on international regulatory cooperation.
E.
E.O. 14192
, Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
This proposed rule, if finalized as proposed, is expected to be an
E.O. 14192
deregulatory action because it has total costs less than zero as it streamlines the licensing process and reduces regulatory burden for license applicants.
VII. Additional Information
A. Comments Invited
FAA invites interested persons to participate in this rulemaking by submitting written comments, data, or views. FAA also invites comments relating to the economic, environmental, or federalism impacts that might result from adopting the proposals in this document. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. To ensure the docket does not contain duplicate comments, commenters should submit only one time if comments are filed electronically, or commenters should send only one copy of written comments if comments are filed in writing.
FAA will file in the docket all comments it receives, as well as a report summarizing each substantive public contact with FAA personnel concerning this proposed rule. Before acting on this proposal, FAA will consider all
(
printed page 70817)
comments it receives on or before the closing date for comments. FAA will consider comments filed after the comment period has closed if it is possible to do so without incurring expense or delay. FAA may change this proposal in light of the comments it receives.
B. Confidential Business Information
Confidential Business Information (CBI) is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to the person in the

section of this document. Any commentary FAA receives that is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.

All documents FAA considered in developing this proposed rule, including economic analyses and technical reports, may be accessed in the electronic docket for this rulemaking.
D. Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act

Safety criteria.

High consequence event protection.
An operator must protect against a high consequence event in uncontrolled areas for each phase of flight by:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Overview
In accordance with Executive Order (E.O.) 14335, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” FAA proposes to amend its commercial space launch and reentry regulations at
14 CFR part 450
to further streamline the commercial licensing process. The regulations at
14 CFR 450.108(c)
require a vehicle operator to determine flight safety limits that define when the operator must initiate flight abort. To address applicant confusion about the meaning of
14 CFR 450.108(c)(4)
, FAA proposes to reword the paragraph to clarify which inputs are necessary for establishing flight safety limits to prevent high consequence events.
II. Authority for This Rulemaking
The Commercial Space Launch Act of 1984, as amended and codified at
51 U.S.C. 50901-50924
, authorizes the Secretary of Transportation to oversee, license, and regulate commercial launch and reentry activities, and the operation of launch and reentry sites within the United States or as carried out by U.S. citizens. Section 50905 directs the Secretary to exercise this responsibility consistent with public health and safety, safety of property, and the national security and foreign policy interests of the United States. In addition, section 50903 requires the Secretary to encourage, facilitate, and promote commercial space launches and reentries by the private sector. As codified in
49 CFR 1.83(b)
, the Secretary has delegated authority to the FAA Administrator to carry out these functions.
III. Background
FAA has established commercial space regulations governing licensing of launch and reentry in
14 CFR chapter III
. On December 10, 2020, FAA issued a final rule consolidating all substantive launch and reentry licensing regulations into a new part 450 (
85 FR 79566
) that went into effect on March 10, 2021.
On August 13, 2025, the President issued
E.O. 14335
, “Enabling Competition in the Commercial Space Industry,” requiring the Secretary of Transportation to “reevaluate, amend, or rescind” the part 450 regulations for the purpose of further streamlining the commercial licensing process. This proposed rule is being published in furtherance of this E.O.
Section 450.101(c) provides that an operator may use flight abort as a hazard control strategy to protect against a high consequence event in uncontrolled areas.
[
1
]
Flight abort accomplishes a controlled ending to vehicle flight, such as through explosive destruct. Section 450.108 provides requirements for flight abort, including requirements for flight safety limits. Flight safety limits, in this context, define the criteria under which a vehicle operator must initiate flight abort.
One of the requirements for flight abort, located at § 450.108(c)(4), provides that an operator must determine and use flight safety limits defining when the operator must initiate flight abort “to prevent conditional expected casualties (CE
C
) greater than 1 × 10
−2
in uncontrolled areas due to flight abort or due to flight outside the limits of a useful mission from any reasonably foreseeable off-trajectory failure mode in any significant period of flight . . . .” The purpose of § 450.108(c)(4) is to ensure that, when an operator cannot develop flight safety limits that prevent hazards from affecting uncontrolled areas, the flight safety limits nonetheless protect against
(
printed page 70822)
high consequence events in uncontrolled areas. The paragraph asks operators to compute the CE
C
in each significant period of flight
[
2
]
where flight abort or flight outside the limits of a useful mission
[
3
]
may be an outcome for each reasonably foreseeable off-trajectory failure mode.
[
4
]
If the maximum CE
C
developed through this method is not greater than 1 × 10
−2
, an operator can demonstrate high consequence event protection. If this analysis does not demonstrate compliance with high consequence event protection, an operator may modify the limits of a useful mission or flight safety limits, and an operator should update the flight safety limits analysis accordingly until compliance with § 450.108(c)(4) can be demonstrated.
However, the phrasing of paragraph (c)(4) has led some applicants to misinterpret the paragraph as requiring two separate CE
C
calculations: one for outcomes resulting in flight abort and one for outcomes that result in flight outside the limits of a useful mission. Meanwhile, other applicants have interpreted the paragraph to mean that an applicant may select only one of these two outcomes and ignore the other in CE
C
calculations. In AC 450.108-1,
Flight Abort Rule Development,
FAA attempted to clarify the requirement, writing that “[t]he CE
C
results from various end states, such as break-up due to aerodynamic loads or FSS activation, from flight abort and flight outside the limits of a useful mission should be averaged together to compute the mean CE
C
for each significant period of flight.” However, misinterpretations of the rule have persisted and led to repeated exchanges with the applicants, requiring additional time and effort to develop an acceptable application.
IV. Discussion of the Proposal
The proposed rule would reword § 450.108(c)(4) to reduce confusion among applicants regarding how to comply with the requirement. The proposed rule would clarify that the CE
C
should be calculated as an average that accounts for both breakup states due to flight abort and any outcomes involving flight outside the limits of a useful mission—but not breakups within the limits of a useful mission—and evaluated against the threshold for each failure mode within each significant period of flight. This clarification would ensure that both outcomes are combined and accounted for as a single CE
C
for each failure mode within each significant period of flight.
V. Regulatory Notices and Analyses
A. Regulatory Impact Analysis
E.O. 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”) and
E.O. 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) require agencies to regulate in the “most cost-effective manner,” to make a “reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify its costs,” and to develop regulations that “impose the least burden on society.” The Office of Management and Budget has determined this proposed rule is not a significant regulatory action as defined in Section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
. FAA is seeking comments on the following analysis.
Currently,
14 CFR 450.108(c)
requires a vehicle operator to determine flight safety limits that define when the operator must initiate flight abort. The proposed rule would reword
14 CFR 450.108(c)(4)
to clarify which inputs are necessary for establishing flight safety limits to prevent high consequence events. The current wording has caused confusion among vehicle operators, which has prompted operators to seek guidance from FAA.
The analysis first provides an estimate of the cost savings per operator. This is a one-time cost savings per operator because they would only seek this guidance once. FAA estimates the labor time, per operator, to provide this guidance is eight hours for FAA and operators each. For FAA, an analyst at a G-Band would complete this work at an hourly wage with benefits of $72.80.
[
5
]
This amounts to $582 per operator. For an operator, an aerospace engineer would seek this guidance from FAA. At an hourly wage rate
[
6
]
with benefits
[
7
]
of $96.28, the aerospace engineer cost is $770 per applicant.
[
8
]
Thus, the cost savings per operator would be $1,347.
The cost savings would be minimal because FAA expects there to be 40 new license applications over the next 5 years. Assuming eight applications per year, the total undiscounted cost savings would be $53,880. At a seven percent discount rate, the total cost savings would be $50,355, and $48,888 at a three percent discount rate.

L. 103-465), prohibits Federal agencies from establishing standards or engaging in related activities that create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States. FAA has assessed the potential effect of this proposed rule and determined that it would not create unnecessary obstacles to the foreign commerce of the United States.
D. Unfunded Mandates Assessment
The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
) governs the issuance of Federal regulations that require unfunded mandates. An unfunded mandate is a regulation that requires a State, local, or Tribal government or the private sector to incur direct costs without the Federal Government having first provided the funds to pay those costs. FAA determined the proposed rule would not result in the expenditure of $193,000,000 or more ($100,000,000 adjusted for inflation using the most current Implicit Price Deflator for the Gross Domestic Product) by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or the private sector, in any one year.

G. Environmental Analysis
