However, many raised significant concerns regarding the disincentives created by current quality measurement and reimbursement frameworks that may penalize HHAs for serving patients who primarily require palliative care services. Specifically, commenters stated outcome measures tied to hospitalization and functional improvement in mobility and self-care may systematically disadvantage HHAs that appropriately prioritize comfort and quality of life over curative or rehabilitative goals. Commenters emphasized that for palliative care patients, a decline in these areas is often expected due to the natural progression of advanced disease and should not be interpreted as poor quality of care. Commenters expressed concern that as a result, HHAs that appropriately accept and manage these patients may receive lower performance scores and lower Star Ratings despite delivering high-quality, patient-centered care. Some commenters suggested CMS consider excluding palliative care patients from outcome measures that are based on functional improvement, discharge to community, and potentially preventable hospitalizations, or alternatively, implementing additional risk adjustment methodologies that account for the expected decline associated with serious progressive illness. Other commenters suggested a palliative track within the Home Health Quality Reporting Program, updating quality measures to distinguish between traditional home health patients and those receiving palliative care services.
Other commenters expressed concern regarding audit denials without specific, clinically realistic sub-regulatory guidance. Commenters consistently urged CMS to act quickly to update chapter seven of the BPM with concrete palliative care examples to avoid a scenario where policy encouragement exists in theory but is undermined in practice by audit risk, payment penalties, or lack of interdisciplinary infrastructure. Some commenters asked CMS to clarify how the homebound requirement applies to seriously ill patients who leave home for palliative-intent outpatient treatment (for example, palliative radiation or infusions), where leaving the home requires a considerable and taxing effort. These commenters also encouraged CMS to ensure Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) medical review aligns with new guidance.
Several commenters raised regulatory concerns that the homebound requirement is a barrier to earlier palliative intervention and suggested a potential non-homebound pathway to home-based palliative care; the need for nurse and nurse practitioner (NP) reimbursement integration within the home health interdisciplinary team; distinct Part B payment pathways for a community-based palliative care benefit, including the possibility of an add-on payment or development of specific CPT codes; and revising the regulations to explicitly include palliative care among covered home health services. Additionally, we received some comments indicating confusion regarding whether this discussion on palliative care was indicative of a new benefit or distinct service model under Medicare. Other commenters emphasized that CMS should avoid establishing separate palliative care eligibility criteria, duplicative assessments, or additional documentation standards that could discourage providers from furnishing these services. Additionally, a commenter asked whether the clarification of the provision of palliative care services under the home health benefit would require other providers or suppliers to enroll or be certified as an HHA in order to furnish palliative care.
One commenter cautioned that expanding palliative care without competency standards risks diluting specialty palliative care and further delays appropriate hospice referrals. A commenter specifically noted that HHAs do not have the resources to furnish these services at scale to beneficiaries with such complex and serious illness; that these patients require much more comprehensive, longitudinal, and coordinated care than can be provided by HHAs. This commenter pointed to the Home-Based Primary Care (HBPC) model as the standard for which palliative care should be provided in the community and stated that CMS discussing palliative care provision under the home health benefit understates the complex nature of palliative care and the importance of home-based primary care clinicians as the primary coordinators of palliative care services in the home. Several commenters urged CMS to maintain a clear boundary between the home health and hospice benefits, recognizing that the home health benefit is not a substitute for hospice, but may be a bridge for those seriously ill beneficiaries who are not ready to elect hospice. These commenters stressed that home health does not support the same intensity of interdisciplinary care that the hospice benefit provides.
And finally, some commenters requested that CMS clarify that palliative care can be provided across all disciplines and all PDGM clinical groups and is not only limited to the MMTA clinical group, and that we study the resource use of palliative and
(
printed page 72077)
maintenance periods of care and pay commensurately.
Response:
CMS thanks all commenters for their thoughtful and detailed input on the provision of community-based palliative care under the Medicare home health benefit. The breadth and quality of these comments reflect the deep commitment of clinicians, advocates, caregivers, and health systems to improving care for seriously ill beneficiaries, and CMS acknowledges the broad commenter support for its goal of expanding access to community-based palliative care by acknowledging its provision under the existing home health benefit. We agree that seriously ill beneficiaries stand to benefit significantly from improved pain and symptom management, caregiver support, and enhanced quality of life when palliative care principles are integrated into home health services. CMS remains committed to advancing this goal in a manner that is clinically sound, operationally feasible, and equitable across the beneficiary population.
We recognize concerns regarding current quality measures including improvement standards, which are less likely to occur in palliative care patients. We agree this would not indicate poor quality of care but rather could be expected in this population as a result of the natural progression of serious illness. With current discussions about opportunities for potential alignment between the expanded Home Health Value-Based Purchasing (HHVBP) Model and the Home Health Quality Reporting Program (HH QRP), the home health measure sets used for both the HH QRP and the expanded HHVBP Model will emphasize measures that address expected functional outcomes instead of an emphasis on functional improvement. For example, the Discharge Function measure used in the HH QRP and the expanded HHVBP Model assesses each patient's expected functional status at discharge based on the patient's clinical profile and then evaluates management of functional status based on whether the patient is expected to improve, maintain or decline in function. Over time, the functional status measures used in the expanded HHVBP Model and HH QRP measure sets will focus more on a patient's expected outcome and not simply assess functional improvement.
CMS recognizes commenter concerns that palliative requires specialized clinical skills, including advanced symptom assessment, goals-of-care communication, and interdisciplinary coordination; however, we believe that HHAs are well-positioned to provide these services given their existing infrastructure for interdisciplinary care planning, skilled nursing and therapy, and coordination with physicians, as part of comprehensive, home-based care. CMS will explore the development of minimum competency expectations for HHA staff providing palliative care services, in consultation with relevant clinical and professional organizations. Any future guidance will seek to preserve the integrity of specialized clinical skills in palliative care while enabling broader access to these services at the community level. Further, CMS recognizes the critical role NPs play in expanding access to care, particularly in underserved communities, and we note that “allowed practitioners” include NPs, physician assistants (PAs), and clinical nurse specialists (CNSs). These types of providers are allowed to certify patients for Medicare home health services and establish the plan of care, affording them the ability to participate in and manage community-based palliative care delivery under the home health benefit. CMS disagrees, however, that supporting home-based primary care and strengthening HHAs palliative care capacity are competing strategies. The regulatory framework already governing Medicare-certified HHAs makes them a well-suited, and readily scalable, environment for furnishing palliative care, consistent with the goals underlying this rule. The Conditions of Participation (CoPs) at CFR 42 part 484 require HHAs to conduct a comprehensive patient assessment, develop an individualized plan of care, and deliver services through an interdisciplinary group encompassing skilled nursing, therapy, medical social services, and aide support. These same requirements, symptom management, psychosocial and caregiver support, and coordinated interdisciplinary planning are the operational building blocks of palliative care.
CMS is not proposing a new service delivery model or a new benefit in this rule; rather, this clarification is intended to confirm that HHAs may furnish palliative care as a component of a skilled service already covered under the home health benefit, such as skilled nursing visits for pain and symptom management, patient and caregiver education, or care planning. It does not create a new, distinct benefit category or service type, and it does not modify the existing HH PPS payment methodology. Accordingly, CMS is not establishing a separate payment, add-on payment, or billing code specific to palliative care furnished under the home health benefit. HHAs should continue to bill for these services consistent with existing home health billing and coverage requirements, and any palliative care activities performed by home health staff must fit within the scope of a covered skilled service and be included in the individualized plan of care.
Additionally, this rule does not modify the eligibility requirements for the home health benefit or require any provider or supplier to enroll or be certified as an HHA in order to furnish palliative care. All home health eligibility requirements (homebound status, a qualifying skilled need, an allowed-practitioner order, a plan of care, and a face-to-face encounter) all still apply to palliative care patients. Regarding homebound status, the same criteria exist for determining whether a patient is confined to the home, meaning a patient can still be considered homebound if absences from the home are infrequent or for periods of relatively short duration, or are attributable to the need to receive health care treatment. Additionally, nothing in this rule alters the requirement that home health services be furnished under a physician or allowed practitioner established plan of care. These clinicians, often the patient's primary care provider, retain full authority over diagnosis, treatment planning, and goals-of-care decisions. Enhancing HHAs' palliative care role would extend that plan of care into more frequent, hands-on interdisciplinary contact, complementing, not substituting for, the clinician relationship present in the HBPC model. Further, while we stated in the proposed rule that MMTA would likely be the most appropriate grouping for palliative care services, we recognize that these services can be applied across all home health disciplines and as outlined in the care plan.
Regarding concerns that CMS may be indicating these services are substitutes for hospice care, we agree that the home health and hospice benefits, while complementary, serve distinct purposes and beneficiary populations. We recognized in the proposed rule that the home health benefit can be an important step in the care continuum when a patient needs palliative care, either during episodes of serious illness or near end of life, before choosing hospice care. However, we do not intend for this clarification to blur the distinction between home health and hospice care, and we will continue to monitor program data and beneficiary experience to ensure that beneficiaries are directed to the benefit that best matches their care needs.

And finally, CMS agrees that consistent review and implementation across MACs is essential to the success of any palliative care policy initiative. CMS will work with MACs to ensure that medical review criteria, documentation expectations, and coverage determinations reflect updated guidance. We will issue specific MAC instructions and education materials in conjunction with BPM updates to promote national consistency and reduce audit-related and claims denial deterrents to palliative care delivery. We also thank commenters for submitting suggested examples for the BPM and will update this sub-regulatory guidance promptly to represent the various palliative care services we believe HHAs can provide under the home health benefit.
G. Request for Information on the Construction of a Home Health Specific Wage Index
For CY 2027, we are finalizing our proposal to continue to use the concurrent pre-floor, pre-reclassified IPPS hospital wage index as the basis for the HH PPS wage index. We continue to believe that this is the best available Medicare data to estimate costs per day, in accordance with our longstanding wage index policy at § 412.424(a)(2). The purpose of this comment solicitation was to gain information from the public regarding the appropriateness of alternative data sources consistent with our statutory authority and regulatory requirements. We noted that other payment systems have explored and are exploring alternative wage index methodologies under their specific programmatic and statutory circumstances. For example, CMS finalized changes to the ESRD PPS wage index using Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) occupation-level wage data in the CY 2025 ESRD PPS final rule (
89 FR 89116
). We noted that while this approach was developed under the specific programmatic and statutory circumstances of the ESRD PPS and may not be directly transferable to the HH PPS, CMS is interested in exploring whether similar methodologies using publicly available wage data could be used to better reflect the geographic variation in labor costs for HHAs. In addition, we noted that we are also considering the potential use of alternative data sources in other payment systems, including with respect to hospices (
91 FR 17361
through
17363
), the Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities PPS (
91 FR 17206
and
17207
), and the Skilled Nursing Facilities PPS (
91 FR 17692
).
Furthermore, in its 2023 Report to the Congress,
[
9
]
MedPAC discussed various conceptual approaches to Medicare wage indexes, including the use of county-level wage data from BLS with an occupational mix to construct wage indexes that are more specific to the payment setting. MedPAC has previously written about using all-employer, occupation-level wage data to establish different weights for setting-specific occupational labor mixes as one approach to geographic adjustments.
We solicited public comments on whether we should consider using alternative data sources to construct an HHA specific wage index for potential use in future years. CMS sought feedback to understand the potential advantages and limitations of using alternative data sources, such as BLS data and home health Medicare cost reports, as well as other methodologies that stakeholders believe could appropriately reflect the geographic variation in labor costs for HHAs. We also sought feedback on the unique considerations applicable to HHAs that should inform how CMS considers the potential use of alternative data sources.
The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Overall, commenters expressed support for an approach that would more closely represent the geographic variation of wages related to occupations used in home health. Commenters requested that CMS provide more information on the potential methodology to calculate a home health specific wage index using alternate data sources and home health specific occupational mix, and recommended CMS convene a Technical Expert Panel to seek broader input based on presented analysis. Many commenters stated that any occupational mix must extend beyond RNs and therapists to include home health aides, medical social workers, LPNs, and community health workers. Commenters were split on data sources: many favored BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics as independent and more current, while others raised concerns that BLS data is not home-health-specific, excludes benefits, dilutes the labor pool with non-Medicare providers, and relies on unverifiable survey samples. Some commenters stated that home health cost reports have serious data-quality problems, such as inconsistent contract-labor reporting, lack of audits, and distortion from what they describe as high-fraud cohorts such as Los Angeles County. All commenters supported publishing a detailed prototype/RFI with methodology, occupational weights, and provider/county-level impact files before implementation; convening a Technical Expert Panel; multi-year phase-in with continuation of the 5 percent cap on decreases; and robust stakeholder/industry engagement.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback. While we will not be responding to specific comments submitted in response to this RFI in this final rule, we intend to use this information to inform future development of a home health specific wage index and for potential future rulemaking as appropriate.
III. Home Health Quality Reporting Program (HH QRP)
A. Background and Statutory Authority
The HH QRP is authorized by section 1895(b)(3)(B)(v) of the Act. Section 1895(b)(3)(B)(v)(II) of the Act requires that, for 2007 and subsequent years, each home health agency (HHA) submit to the Secretary in a form and manner, and at a time, specified by the Secretary, such data that the Secretary determines are appropriate for the measurement of health care quality. To the extent that an HHA does not submit data in accordance with this clause, the Secretary shall reduce the home health market basket percentage increase applicable to the HHA for such year by 2 percentage points pursuant to section 1895(b)(3)(B)(v)(I) of the Act. As provided at section 1895(b)(3)(B)(vi) of the Act, depending on the market basket percentage increase applicable for a particular year, as further reduced by the productivity adjustment (except in 2018 and 2020) described in section 1886(b)(3)(B)(xi)(II) of the Act, the reduction of that increase by 2 percentage points for failure to comply with the requirements of the HH QRP may result in the home health market basket percentage increase being less than 0.0 percent for a year, and may result in payment rates under the HH PPS for a year being less than payment rates for the preceding year. Section 1890A of the Act requires that the Secretary establish and follow a pre-rulemaking process, in coordination with the consensus-based entity (CBE) with a contract under section 1890 of the Act, to solicit input from certain groups regarding the selection of quality and efficiency measures for the HH QRP. D. Opportunities for Potential Alignment Between the HH QRP and the Expanded HHVBP Model
As discussed in the proposed rule, CMS has identified substantial opportunities to better align the HH QRP and the expanded HHVBP Model. While the HH QRP and expanded HHVBP Model share similar goals and measures, differences in measure sets, reporting periods, and performance assessment processes may create unnecessary complexity and administrative burden for HHAs. For example, misalignment between HH QRP APU reporting periods and the expanded HHVBP Model's annual performance period may contribute to confusion. Greater alignment would support more consistent evaluation of HHA quality performance and advance CMS quality priorities. Greater alignment is also consistent with CMS's priority of reducing provider burden and creating efficiencies across CMS programs. Opportunities for potential alignment between the HH QRP and expanded HHVBP Model include the following:
Increasing alignment in expanded HHVBP Model and HH QRP Quality of Patient Care (QoPC) Star Ratings measure sets.
Aligning HH QRP and expanded HHVBP Model measure reporting periods.
Aligning HH QRP APU and expanded HHVBP Model annual payment reporting periods.
Aligning expanded HHVBP Model Interim Performance and HH QRP QoPC Star Rating Reports.
Aligning timeframe of appeals/suppression review processes for the expanded HHVBP Model and HH QRP.
Updating scoring methodology to incorporate HH QRP APU penalties in expanded HHVBP Model payment adjustments and factoring HH QRP Quality Assessments Only (QAO) values into QoPC Star Ratings scoring.

E. Form, Manner, and Timing of Data Submission Under the HH QRP
1. Revise HH QRP Data Submission Deadlines Beginning With the CY 2027 HH QRP
a. Background
Section 1899B(f)(1) of the Act also requires the Secretary to provide confidential feedback reports to PAC providers on the performance of such PAC providers for quality, resource use, and other measures required under sections 1899B(c)(1) and (d)(1) of the Act beginning 1 year after the applicable specified application date. Further, section 1899B(g) of the Act requires the Secretary to establish procedures for making available to the public information regarding the performance
(
printed page 72081)
of individual PAC providers for quality, resource use, and other measures required under sections 1899B(c)(1) and (d)(1) of the Act beginning not later than 2 years after the applicable specified application date. The procedures must ensure, including through a process consistent with the process applied under section 1886(b)(3)(B)(viii)(VII) of the Act for similar purposes, that each PAC provider has the opportunity to review and submit corrections to the data and information that are to be made public for the PAC provider prior to such data being made public.
Although assessment data submission, quarterly performance reports, and public reporting are required by statute, timing of data submission under the HH QRP was not initially specified. Thus, in the CY 2017 HHS PPS final rule (
81 FR 76784
) we finalized our proposal to comply with the requirements of section 1899B(g) of the Act, that HHAs would have approximately 4.5 months after the reporting quarter to correct any errors of their assessment-based data to calculate the measures. During the time of data submission for a given quarterly reporting period and up until the quarterly submission deadline, HHAs could review and perform corrections to errors in the assessment data used to calculate the measures.
Public reporting of data collected under our quality reporting programs, such as the HH QRP, is designed to provide consumers and their families with the most current information to empower them to make quality-informed decisions about where to receive their care. We have identified that the time between when data on measures is submitted to us and when those data are publicly reported (approximately nine months) may be too long to provide the most accurate and up to date information for the public. We have received feedback from the provider community and TEPs that the aged data used in publicly reported quality measures diminishes their value to consumers. Furthermore, we have heard from HHAs that the HH QRP measure results they receive prior to public reporting are less useful for their quality improvement efforts due to the aged data and the delay in when they receive these reports.
Currently, the largest contributing factor to the 9-month lag between the end of the data collection period and when measures are publicly reported is the 4.5-month timeframe for data submission. Reducing the data submission timeframe from 4.5 months to the 15th day of the second month after the end of the calendar quarter could reduce this lag by up to 3 months, resulting in more timely public reporting of data for consumers and increasing the value of publicly reported data. Additionally, this timeframe provides HHAs with more recent data in support of their quality improvement activities.
In the CY 2026 HH PPS proposed rule, we included a request for information (RFI) on reducing the OASIS assessment data submission deadline from 4.5 months to 45 days (
90 FR 29182
). We refer readers to the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule (
90 FR 55429
and
55430
) for a full summary of the public comments received.
b. Revise the HH QRP Assessment Data Submission Deadline
Beginning with the CY 2027 HH QRP, we proposed that HHAs be required to complete their data submissions and make corrections to their OASIS assessment data where necessary no later than the 15th day of the second month after the end of the calendar quarter. However, if the 15th day of the second month fell on a Friday, weekend, or Federal holiday, the date would be delayed until 11:59 p.m. EST on the next business day. We proposed that HHAs follow the deadlines presented in Table 19 for the CY 2027 HH QRP. We also proposed that similar calendar year data submission deadlines apply to future years' payment determinations.
We believe that requiring HHAs to submit OASIS assessment data by the 15th day of the second month after the end of the calendar quarter is reasonable. We conducted an analysis on the potential impact of reducing the timeframe by determining how many assessments are currently being submitted by this deadline, which is approximately within 45 days of the end of the quarter. Using 2024 data, we determined that 99.27 percent of all OASIS assessments were submitted to CMS within a 45-day timeframe. Of the remaining 0.73 percent submitted beyond 45 days, 0.24 percent of the total (that is, about one third of the post-45 day timeframe) were submitted after the current 4.5-month data submission deadline and would not be further impacted by a change in the data submission deadline. Therefore, only 0.49 percent of OASIS assessments will be impacted by changing the data submission deadline from 4.5 months to require data submission by the 15th day of the second month after the end of the calendar quarter.
We received public comments on the proposal to require that HHAs complete their data submissions and make corrections to their OASIS assessment data where necessary no later than the 15th day of the second month after the end of the calendar quarter beginning with the CY 2027 HH QRP. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A majority of commenters supported CMS' proposal to revise the OASIS data submission deadline, stating that more timely reporting of
(
printed page 72082)
HHQRP data could help HHAs implement quality improvement initiatives and beneficiaries and their caregivers make better-informed decisions when selecting HHAs. Several commenters supported the proposal based on data showing that most HHAs are already meeting the 45-day submission requirement. Many commenters who supported the proposal urged CMS to ensure clear guidance and training is in place to support the implementation of this proposal.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that this proposal would give patients and consumers more timely access to quality data and give HHAs better data for quality improvement. Clear guidance around the new submission deadline will be available through the range of communication channels used to reach HHAs.
Comment:
Some commenters supported the proposal and the goal of improving the timeliness of publicly reported data, but had concerns about operational and staffing challenges, administrative burden, and data validation, especially for small or rural HHAs that may struggle with staffing challenges and operational issues. A few commenters expressed concerns that providers continue to experience staffing shortages and turnover of HH staff. Some commenters that supported the proposal noted the current clinical and administrative burden around implementing OASIS all-payer submissions and changing payment requirements. Several commenters encouraged CMS to establish a phased implementation or grace period to meet submission requirements, to provide flexibility for the first several data submission cycles. A few other commenters cited recent implementation of the HOPE tool to stress the benefits of a phased implementation.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns about operational and staffing challenges, especially for small or rural HHAs. However, we do not believe that the proposal adds burden for HHA staff by changing the data submission deadline; rather, it shifts the existing workflow from 4.5 months after each quarterly data collection period to the 15th day of the second month after the end of the calendar quarter. Since workflows are in place for the necessary processes, we do not believe a phased implementation approach is necessary. As previously stated in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule, our internal analysis showed that 99.27 percent of all OASIS assessments are already being submitted within a 45-day timeframe, which suggests that data submission within this timeframe is the current practice for most HHAs. Further, we believe a phased implementation approach would add operational complexity, as providers would have to update workflows and modify staffing numerous times over the implementation period. We will continue to monitor data submission compliance rates as part of already implemented program monitoring.
Comment:
Some commenters were concerned that the proposed timeline may not provide adequate time for agencies to validate data to identify and correct errors, particularly for new admissions near the end of a reporting quarter. They raised concerns that review processes are critical to ensuring high-quality data but may no longer be feasible within a 45-day submission window.
Response:
We believe that we are providing HHAs sufficient time to adjust staffing and workflow operations that will allow them to validate data and make any corrections needed by the new deadline. In general, we believe data validation and quality checks to be complete with the initial data submission, with better proximity to the patient. We would also like to note that this proposal will benefit HHAs by allowing them to have access to more timely data for quality improvement efforts.
Comment:
A few commenters supported the proposal but recommended allowing HHAs to request an extension if there are circumstances out of the HHA's control impacted the HHA's ability to submit data in a timely manner.
Response:
Currently, in the event they were unable to submit quality data due to extraordinary circumstances beyond their control, we provide HHAs with the opportunity to request an exception or extension from the program's reporting requirements. HHAs affected by a natural or man-made disaster or other extraordinary circumstances may request an exception or extension using instructions provided on the HH QRP website:
https://www.cms.gov/​medicare/​quality/​home-health/​home-health-quality-reporting-reconsideration-and-exception-extension
.
Comment:
Some commenters recommended that CMS provide enhanced technical assistance and support as part of the transition to the new reporting timeframe. Several commenters suggested updated training resources and outreach to HHAs to ensure providers have sufficient support to implement this proposal. A few commenters requested the ability for vendors to have a test period for submissions.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' input and recommendations for implementation of this proposal. We would like to note that we currently conduct national outreach (such as email communications) about upcoming data submission deadlines. We also provide guidance and technical manuals, data submission deadline documents, and training resources. We intend to make updates to our outreach processes, manuals, data submission deadline documents and training resources related to this change. Regarding technical assistance and support, we list resources and on our website:
https://www.cms.gov/​medicare/​quality/​home-health/​home-health-quality-reporting-training
.
We do not anticipate that the new submission timeframe will require data processing since the submission processes have not been changed with this proposal.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed to require that HHAs submit their OASIS assessments and make corrections to their OASIS assessment data where necessary no later than the 15th day of the second month after the end of the calendar quarter beginning with the CY 2027 HHQRP.

Comment:

We will also work to ensure training materials related to the HHQRP APU addresses OASIS all-payer data submission. After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed to revise the OASIS APU reporting timeframe to a calendar year period effective January 1, 2027. We are also finalizing the transition period in which the six months of data collected from July 1, 2026 through December 31, 2026 would serve as the OASIS APU data reporting timeframe to determine the HHQRP 2028 APU. We are finalizing the 2029 OASIS APU data reporting timeframe would be the first iteration in which the OASIS APU data reporting timeframe would be for a calendar year, from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2027.
3. Revise the HHCAHPS Annual Payment Update Reporting Timeframe
a. Background
HHAs are required to submit quality data in a timely manner as outlined under section 1895(b)(3)(B)(v) of the Act. Failure to submit HHCAHPS data in a timely manner with respect to a HH QRP year could result in the reduction of the annual home health market basket percentage increase otherwise applicable to an HHA for the corresponding calendar year by 2 percentage points. HHCAHPS data
(
printed page 72084)
inclusion in the HH QRP was finalized with the CY 2010 HH PPS Final Rule (FR 74 58098 through 58104). Adding a HHCAHPS annual payment update (APU) to the current HH QRP requirements was also finalized with the CY 2010 HH PPS Final Rule where CMS finalized the policy that HHCAHPS will be included in the APU reporting for the CY 2012 APU based on 6 months of data from October 2010 to March 2011 (FR 74 58103). In the CY 2011 HH PPS final rule, CMS finalized a policy that HHCAHPS APU calculations would require four quarters of data collection from April 1, 2011 to March 31, 2012 for the CY 2013 HHCAHPS APU (FR 75 70406). The proposed revision of the HHCAHPS APU data reporting to a calendar year timeframe would require a transition year in which the current reporting timeframe was moved to the new proposed reporting timeframe. We also proposed that the 2029 HHCAHPS APU data reporting timeframe would be the first iteration in which the HHCAHPS APU data reporting timeframe would be for a calendar year, from January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2027. We would continue this new pattern for each subsequent HHCAHPS APU with effective dates for data reporting of January 1 through December 31. HHA OASIS assessments would be considered complete if they complied with the HH CoPs and Conditions for Payment that apply to the applicable year. Please see Table 21 that outlines the HHCAHPS current APU data reporting timeframe, the proposed transition reporting timeframe, and the revised APU timeframe used for the CY 2029 APU and later.

F. HH QRP Measure Concepts Under Consideration for Future Years—Request for Information (RFI)
In the CY 2024 HH PPS proposed rule (
88 FR 43738
through
43740
), we included an RFI on a set of principles for selecting and prioritizing HH QRP measures, identifying measurement gaps, and suitable measures for filling these gaps. We refer readers to the CY 2024 HH PPS final rule (
88 FR 77773
through
77774
) for a summary of the public comments received in response to the RFI.
We sought input on the importance, relevance, appropriateness, and applicability of the quality measure concepts related to advance care planning (ACP). Advance care planning is a continuous process that supports people in understanding and communicating their goals, values, and preferences regarding future medical decisions.
[
10
]
The Patient Self Determination Act of 1990
[
11
]
supports this process by requiring healthcare facilities to inform patients of their rights regarding medical decisions, including advance directives and end of life care.
[
12
]
In post-acute care (PAC) settings, where patients recover from acute illness, injury, or major procedures, their needs and goals may evolve as their condition changes. Factors such as clinical stability, functional status, therapy tolerance, cognition function, prognosis, and
(
printed page 72086)
personal preferences can all shift during recovery. Regular reassessment and transparent communication are essential to maintaining person-centered care, while advance care planning facilitates shared decision-making by documenting patient preferences and ensuring goal-concordant care throughout care transitions.
[
13
]
As we review new measure concepts, we will prioritize evidence-based outcome measures that promote person-centered care practices. We sought input on the relevant aspects of advance care planning and measures appropriate for the HH setting. We received public comments on this request for information, and the following is a summary of the comments we received.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed support for CMS's exploration of an ACP quality measure within the HH QRP while emphasizing the need for a patient-centered, practical, and clinically meaningful approach. Most commenters agreed that ACP is an important component of quality home health care, particularly for individuals with serious illness, chronic conditions, cognitive impairment, or complex care needs. Commenters who supported an ACP measure emphasized that home health clinicians are uniquely positioned to facilitate discussions about goals of care because they work directly with patients and families in the home environment and often develop trusted relationships that provide insight into patient preferences, caregiver capacity, safety concerns, and evolving care needs.
Some commenters who supported the ACP concept for HH shared that ACP should be understood as an ongoing process rather than a one-time documentation exercise. They cautioned CMS against creating a measure that simply rewards the presence of an advance directive or other legal document. Instead, commenters recommended focusing on meaningful conversations, shared decision-making, identification of patient goals and values, and documentation that reflects patient preferences over time. Several commenters stressed that success should be measured by whether care is aligned with patient wishes rather than whether a specific form has been completed. They also suggested that patients must retain the right to decline ACP discussions or defer decisions without providers being penalized.
Some commenters who support an ACP QM linked ACP closely with palliative care and serious illness management. Organizations representing patients, providers, and palliative care advocates noted that ACP plays a critical role in helping individuals understand treatment options, manage symptoms, plan for future care needs, and make informed decisions throughout the course of illness. Commenters highlighted that home health agencies increasingly serve older, frail, and medically complex beneficiaries whose primary goals may include symptom management, quality of life maintenance, caregiver support, avoiding hospitalizations, and remaining at home.
Several commenters argued that current home health quality measures primarily reward functional improvement, which may not accurately reflect quality care for patients with progressive or terminal illnesses. They encouraged CMS to develop measures that recognize goal-concordant care, symptom management, stabilization, caregiver preparedness, and successful transitions to hospice when appropriate.
Other commenters linked the palliative care RFI in a separate section of the proposed rule with the ACP RFI. These commenters generally supported CMS's efforts to expand awareness and accessibility of palliative care and appreciate clarification that beneficiaries do not need to be terminally ill or forgo curative treatment to receive these services. They suggested that increased access to palliative care can improve symptom management, pain control, patient and caregiver support, care coordination, and overall quality of life. They also noted that earlier integration of palliative care may help patients better understand their treatment options and align care with individual goals and preferences.
Some commenters who expressed support for measuring ACP warned against creating additional documentation requirements that duplicate existing OASIS assessments, care planning processes, or regulatory obligations. Commenters recommended leveraging existing workflows and data whenever possible and ensuring that any new measure is operationally feasible for agencies of all sizes. Several organizations also noted that home health agencies currently lack reimbursement mechanisms akin to those available to physicians for conducting ACP conversations. They argued that meaningful ACP discussions require significant clinician time, training, and interdisciplinary collaboration and that CMS should consider payment pathways that support these activities in HH.
Several commenters emphasized that ACP information is most valuable when it can travel with patients across settings, including hospitals, rehabilitation facilities, home health agencies, palliative care programs, and hospice. Commenters urged CMS to align future ACP measures with national interoperability standards and structured electronic data exchange rather than relying solely on OASIS items or scanned documents. They argued that standardized, machine-readable ACP information would improve care transitions and increase the likelihood that patient preferences are known and honored across the continuum of care.
Despite this support, several commenters requested additional guidance regarding how palliative care should be operationalized within home health settings. Commenters sought clearer distinctions between palliative care and hospice services, more detailed eligibility criteria, clarification regarding documentation and reporting requirements, and practical examples illustrating when palliative care interventions would be appropriate. Concerns were also raised about potential confusion among providers, patients, and caregivers if definitions and expectations are not clearly communicated.
Several commenters also highlighted the importance of health equity, communication access, and caregiver engagement. Recommendations included accommodating individuals with communication disorders, cognitive impairment, limited English proficiency, low health literacy, cultural differences, and varying levels of caregiver support. Commenters stressed that family caregivers often play an essential role in decision-making, care coordination, and implementation of patient preferences and should be included in future quality measurement efforts. Some commenters recommended risk adjustment, stratification, and appropriate exclusions to ensure providers caring for complex or vulnerable populations are not unfairly disadvantaged. Commenters also consistently encouraged comprehensive testing, technical expert review, and ongoing collaboration before implementing any ACP measure in the HH QRP.
Commenters that supported ACP measure concept for HH also shared concerns regarding accountability and quality measurement. Commenters
(
printed page 72087)
caution against measures that hold home health agencies' responsibility for outcomes outside their control, such as whether a patient completes an advanced care directive or changes previously established preferences. Commenters recommend that CMS develop measures that assess whether agencies offered information, facilitated discussions, and appropriately documented patient choices. Such an approach would more accurately reflect the quality of care provided while protecting patient choice and reducing unnecessary administrative burden.
Commenters who did not support an ACP concept in HH contend that home health agencies (HHAs) are not the most appropriate setting or provider type to lead ACP discussions. They also argue that home health services are typically short-term and intermittent, agency staff often lack the long-term relationship, clinical authority, and comprehensive knowledge of a patient's medical history needed to guide complex decisions regarding prognosis, treatment options, and end-of-life preferences. Commenters suggest that primary care physicians and other long-term care providers are better positioned to lead these conversations.
Commenters who do not support an ACP QM expressed concerns about proposed ACP measures that would require documentation of an advance care directive or a completed decision. They argued that such measures could create inappropriate pressure on vulnerable patients, raise privacy concerns, duplicate existing documentation requirements, and unfairly hold agencies accountable for outcomes beyond their control. Many recommend that CMS instead measure whether a goals-of-care discussion was offered, documented, and conducted, regardless of whether a formal directive or final decision resulted.
Several commenters emphasized the importance of correct reimbursement, training, and quality measurement infrastructure that does not exist in HH for an ACP QM. They note that meaningful ACP and palliative care require significant clinician time, expertise, and care coordination. They urge CMS to first develop appropriate payment and reporting mechanisms that appropriately recognize these activities before looking to develop a measure.
Response:
We thank all the commenters for responding to this RFI. While we are not responding to specific comments in response to the RFI in this final rule, we will take this feedback into consideration for our future measure development efforts for the HH QRP.

CMS publishes two types of routine performance feedback reports that provide HHAs with information on their measure performance:
The first report type is the Interim Performance Report (IPR), which is issued quarterly. The information in the IPR reflects calculation of the TPS based on rolling data periods that are updated each quarter. CMS issues two versions of the IPR—a preliminary version and a final version that reflects any changes made as a result of the recalculation request process. The IPRs provide interim performance scores, achievement and improvement points, and TPS.
The second report is the Annual Performance Report (APR). The APR provides HHAs with information on their measure performance using data from the prior calendar year. Like the IPR, the APR provides feedback to HHAs about performance relative to quality measure achievement thresholds, benchmarks, and improvement thresholds. Additionally, the APR includes the HHA's payment adjustment percentage for the upcoming CY, an explanation of when the adjustment will apply, and how CMS determined the adjustment.

V. Durable Medical Equipment and Provider Enrollment Provisions
A. Overview
In this section of the final rule, we proposed changes and sought comment on the following DME and provider enrollment provisions:
In section V.B. of the final rule, we will clarify the application of the DMEPOS face-to-face encounter requirements and the related documentation necessary to support the replacement of DMEPOS items.
In section V.C. of the final rule, we proposed a number of Medicare provider enrollment provisions to strengthen and clarify certain aspects of the provider enrollment process.
In section V.D. of the final rule, we proposed to make changes to the Medicare Part B definition of DME regulations in accordance with the statutory changes implemented via section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026.
In section V.E. of the final rule, we discussed requesting revisions to the information collection requirements that will require DMEPOS CBP contract suppliers to report the country of origin for the lead items furnished during the contract's period of performance.
B. DMEPOS Encounter Requirements for Identical Replacement Items
1. Background
Section 1834(a)(11)(B)(ii) of the Social Security Act, as amended by section 504 of MACRA and codified in the Code of Federal Regulation (CFR) at
42 CFR 410.38
, outlines a condition of payment for certain items of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS). Specifically, it requires a physician, physician assistant (PA), nurse practitioner (NP), or clinical nurse specialist (CNS) (as these four terms are defined in section 1861 of the Act) to write an order that is communicated to the supplier prior to delivery and document that the physician, PA, practitioner, or specialist has had a face-to-face encounter (including through use of telehealth under section 1834(m) of the Act) with the individual involved, during the 6-month period preceding such written order.
On November 8, 2019 (
84 FR 60648
), we published a process whereby items identified as potential vulnerabilities to the Trust Fund may be placed on the
Master List of DMEPOS Items Potentially Subject to Face-to-Face Encounter and Written Orders Prior to Delivery and/or Prior Authorization Requirements
(“Master List”). We analyze the Master List and select items from the Master List to be placed on the
Required Face-to-Face Encounter and Written Orders Prior to Delivery List
(“Required F2F/WOPD List”) via
Federal Register
notice. The face-to-face encounter requirements outlined in
42 CFR 410.38
are only applicable to items that are selected and placed on the Required F2F/WOPD List via
Federal Register
notice.
For the identified items, the treating practitioner must document and communicate to the DMEPOS supplier that the treating practitioner has had a face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary within the 6 months preceding the date of the written order/prescription. The regulation requires supporting documentation to include the subjective and objective beneficiary specific information used for diagnosing, treating, or managing a clinical condition for which the DMEPOS is ordered.
Separately, in our Medicare Benefit Policy Manual (100-02) (Chapter 15, Section 110.2—Repairs, Maintenance, Replacement, and Delivery) we define replacement as the provision of an identical or nearly identical item. Replacements may occur as a result of loss, theft, or irreparable damage, which may be due to a specific incident or event, or irreparable wear, in consideration of the reasonable useful lifetime of the equipment.
Section 414.210(f) discusses payment for replacement of equipment. As specified at
42 CFR 414.210(f)(1)
, the reasonable useful lifetime of durable medical equipment is generally determined through program instructions, or in the absence of program instructions, may be determined by the Medicare Administrative Contractors and be no less than 5 years. If the item of equipment has been in continuous use by the beneficiary for the equipment's useful lifetime or if the contractor determines that the item is lost, stolen, or irreparably damaged, the beneficiary may elect to obtain a new piece of equipment. Replacement may be paid when the practitioner reaffirms the medical necessity of the item through a new order.
2. Provisions of the Regulation and Responses to Public Comments
CMS proposed to clarify that while an order would continue to be required for replacement DMEPOS items, a new face-to-face encounter would not need to occur to support payment for these DMEPOS items. We further proposed to clarify that, for purposes of
42 CFR 410.38(d)(2)(iii)
, a “replacement” refers to the provision of an item that replaces an item falling under the same Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System (HCPCS) code; it does not include those situations involving the provision of a different item, for example, because of a change in medical condition. In other words, for paragraph(d) the replacement would be the same type of item (that is, the same HCPCS code as that originally ordered and rendered) with no change to the type of item ordered and rendered. When an order is written to replace an item falling under the same HCPCS code, requiring a new face-to-face examination to document subjective and objective beneficiary specific information regarding how the DMEPOS item will continue to be used in relation to the beneficiary's clinical condition seems burdensome and redundant. If
(
printed page 72089)
the item is not a replacement item identified by the same HCPCS code, then a new face-to-face encounter would continue to be required, as described in existing
42 CFR 410.38
. This clarification does not eliminate the need for a new order, nor does it supersede or eliminate any other coverage instruction-including those iterated in national or local coverage determinations. In addition, we note that such claims may nonetheless be subject to medical review to ensure the appropriateness of claims billed for payment; particularly when there is concern for aberrant billing behaviors or potential fraud.
We received public comments on these proposals. In addition to the comments outlined below, CMS received some comments outside the scope of this regulation which will not be addressed. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters supported and encouraged finalization of CMS' proposal that a new face-to-face encounter would not need to occur to support payment for replacement DMEPOS items. Commenters acknowledged that the updates would prevent potential delays in the provision of replacement items, avoid unnecessary burdens and protect beneficiary access.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their review and support of the proposed clarification.
Comment:
A commenter suggested that CMS should consider establishing a reasonable timeframe after which a new face-to-face encounter would again be required to support continued use of the item. For example, if a replacement occurs many years after the original order, they shared their belief that a new clinical assessment may be appropriate to confirm that the beneficiary's condition, functional needs, and prescribed equipment remain consistent with current medical necessity requirements.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their suggestion. We note that this clarification does not remove the need for the practitioner order, nor the need for the initial assessment to be provided, upon request, to support compliance with coverage requirements. We believe that these program integrity protections, coupled with regular clinical practice, will help ensure ongoing practitioner oversight of our beneficiary population.
Comment:
Commenters requested that CMS look outside of the face-to-face requirements for evidence to support the item was initially medically necessary when such documentation is unavailable due to the lapse in time or other third-party documentation constraints.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's suggestion. We are finalizing the clarification that a face-to-face encounter does not need to be repeated for the sole purpose of ordering replacement items. However, we note that the regulation at
42 CFR 410.38
requires a face-to-face encounter for certain DMEPOS items. As such, documentation to support that the face-to-face encounter occurred when the item was initially furnished continues to be required.
Comment:
A commenter requested CMS provide claim examples that define ‘identical replacement’ by HCPCS code, explain what documentation suppliers and treating practitioners should retain, and confirm that payment will not be denied solely because no new encounter occurred when the original encounter documentation remains valid and available.
Response:
We do not believe that providing claim examples is necessary. The definition of `identical replacement' is defined in this regulation as the same HCPCS code. In this regulation we clarify that when an identical DMEPOS item is being replaced, such claim will not be denied because a new encounter did not occur. However, we also clarify that the provider is expected to retain documentation to support that the original encounter occurred, as appropriate, when the item is initially furnished and that such documentation demonstrates compliance with our coverage requirements.
Comment:
Commenters asked CMS to clarify that updated technologies, successor products, and newer device generations remain eligible for the replacement-item framework when they fall within the same HCPCS code and serve the same medical purpose.
Response:
We agree. As stated in our proposal, it is our intent that this clarification would apply to the provision of an item that replaces an item falling under the same HCPCS code; it does not include those situations involving the provision of a different item, for example, because of a change in medical condition.
Comment:
Commenters asked that CMS expand our current definition of an identical item as being the same HCPCS code to include any transitions within the same clinical product family, such as a beneficiary moving from a standard intermittent catheter to a hydrophilic-coated intermittent catheter. C. Provider Enrollment
1. Background and Applicability
a. Enrollment Process
Section 1866(j)(1)(A) of the Act requires the Secretary to establish a process for the enrollment of providers and suppliers into the Medicare program. The overarching purpose of the enrollment process is to help confirm that providers and suppliers (hereafter collectively “providers” unless otherwise noted) seeking to bill Medicare for services and items furnished to Medicare beneficiaries meet all applicable Federal and State requirements to do so. The process is, to an extent, a “gatekeeper” that prevents unqualified and potentially fraudulent individuals and entities from entering and inappropriately billing Medicare. Since 2006, we have undertaken rulemaking efforts to outline our enrollment procedures. These regulations are generally codified in
42 CFR part 424, subpart P
(currently §§ 424.500 through 424.575 and hereafter occasionally referenced as subpart P). They address, among other things, requirements that providers must meet to obtain and maintain Medicare billing privileges.
As outlined in § 424.510, one such requirement is that the provider must complete, sign, and submit to its assigned Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) the appropriate enrollment form, typically the Form CMS-855 (OMB Control No.: 0938-0685). The Form CMS-855, which can be submitted via paper or electronically through the internet-based Provider Enrollment, Chain, and Ownership System (PECOS) process (SORN: 09-70-0532, PECOS), collects important information about the provider. Such data include, but are not limited to, general identifying information (for example, legal business name), licensure and certification data, and practice locations. The application is used for a variety of provider enrollment transactions, including the following:
Initial enrollment—The provider is—(1) enrolling in Medicare for the first time; (2) enrolling in another Medicare contractor's jurisdiction; or (3) seeking to enroll in Medicare after having previously been enrolled.
Change of ownership—The provider is reporting a change in its ownership.
Revalidation—The provider is revalidating its Medicare enrollment information in accordance with § 424.515. (Suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) must revalidate their enrollment every 3 years; all other providers and suppliers must do so every 5 years.)
Reactivation—The provider is seeking to reactivate its Medicare billing privileges after it was deactivated in accordance with § 424.540.
Change of information—The provider is reporting a change in its existing enrollment information in accordance with § 424.516.
After receiving the provider's initial enrollment application, CMS or the MAC reviews and confirms the information thereon and determines whether the provider meets all applicable Medicare requirements. We believe this screening process has greatly assisted CMS in executing its responsibility to prevent Medicare fraud, waste, and abuse.
As previously mentioned, over the years we have issued various final rules pertaining to provider enrollment. These rules were intended not only to clarify or strengthen certain components of the enrollment process but also to enable us to take further action against providers: (1) engaging (or potentially engaging) in fraudulent or abusive behavior; (2) presenting a risk of harm to Medicare beneficiaries or the Medicare Trust Funds; or (3) that are otherwise unqualified to furnish Medicare services or items. Consistent therewith, and as we discuss in this section V.C. of this final rule, we proposed several changes to our existing Medicare provider enrollment regulations.
b. Legal Authorities
There are two principal categories of legal authorities for our proposed Medicare provider enrollment provisions:
Section 1866(j) of the Act furnishes specific authority regarding the enrollment process for providers and suppliers; and
Sections 1102 and 1871 of the Act provide general authority for the Secretary to prescribe regulations for the efficient administration of the Medicare program.
c. Applicable Provider and Supplier Types
The provisions in section V.C. of this final rule apply to all Medicare provider and supplier types except as specifically indicated otherwise. The most prominent proposed provisions that would apply only to certain types of providers or suppliers include the following:
New § 424.530(a)(20), which would permit denial of a hospice's enrollment application for the reasons specified therein.
New §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25), which would allow denial or revocation of a hospice's, home health agency's, or DMEPOS supplier's enrollment for failing to comply with the change in majority ownership provisions in §§ 424.550(b) or 424.551.
Revised § 424.540(b)(3)(i), which would require reactivating hospices to undergo a State survey or accreditation prior to reactivation.
Revisions to our DMEPOS accreditation requirements in § 424.58.
d. Comment Solicitation
We solicited and welcomed comments on all of the proposed provider enrollment provisions that follow. We received approximately 375 sets of comments from stakeholders. We thoroughly and carefully read, reviewed, and considered all of them in full. Most comments will be addressed within the subject-matter section to which the comment pertained. More general comments, as well as comments that seemingly pertained to multiple topics, will be addressed at the end of this section (V.C.) (For instance, sets of comments that expressed the same concerns across several provisions.) This will reduce repetition and facilitate both clarity and brevity.
We also note that in some cases, it was difficult to determine whether the stakeholder's comment referenced a particular enrollment proposal or our current enrollment process as a whole; for example, some commenters were unclear as to whether they were requesting changes to: (1) a proposed enrollment revocation reason; (2) how providers are currently revoked; or (3) both. We interpreted these comments as best we could based on their plain language.
2. Revocations and Denials of Enrollment
Under § 424.535(a), CMS may revoke a Medicare provider's enrollment for any of the reasons specified in that paragraph. These reasons include, for example, the provider's: (1) failure to adhere to Medicare enrollment requirements; (2) exclusion by the HHS Office of Inspector General (OIG); (3) felony conviction within the previous 10 years; (4) pattern of improper or abusive billing; and (5) termination by another Federal health care program. A revocation helps safeguard the Medicare program, the Trust Funds, and beneficiaries by removing from (and preventing payment to) Medicare providers that have engaged in
(
printed page 72091)
problematic or otherwise non-compliant behavior. When a provider is revoked, it is generally barred from reenrolling in Medicare for a period of 1 to 10 years.
CMS also has numerous reasons in § 424.530(a) for which it can deny a provider's enrollment application, some of which duplicate our revocation grounds in § 424.535(a) (for instance, OIG exclusion). The general rationale for a denial is akin to that for a revocation: to protect the Medicare program and its beneficiaries from potentially fraudulent or abusive activity.
We have previously finalized a number of regulations adding or revising revocation and denial reasons in subpart P to address particular program integrity vulnerabilities and types of provider conduct. We have also used rulemaking to refine other revocation and denial policies, such as the effective dates of revocations. With our continuing obligation to establish strong payment safeguards, we proposed several changes to our revocation and denial policies in subpart P.
a. Modifications of Current Revocation Provisions
(1) Abuse of Billing Privileges (§ 424.535(a)(8)(ii))
Section 424.535(a)(8) permits revocation based on the provider's abuse of billing privileges. Per § 424.535(a)(8)(ii), this includes situations where CMS determines that the provider has a pattern or practice of submitting claims that fail to meet Medicare requirements. In making this determination, CMS considers, as appropriate or applicable, the following factors (outlined in § 424.535(a)(8)(ii)(A) through (D)):
The percentage of submitted claims that were denied during the period under consideration (paragraph (a)(8)(ii)(A)).
Whether the provider or supplier has any history of final adverse actions and the nature of any such actions (paragraph (a)(8)(ii)(B)).
The type of billing non-compliance and the specific facts surrounding said non-compliance (to the extent this can be determined) (paragraph (a)(8)(ii)(C)).
Any other information regarding the provider or supplier's specific circumstances that CMS deems relevant to its determination (paragraph (a)(8)(ii)(D)).
As we stated in the December 5, 2014, final rule that promulgated § 424.535(a)(8)(ii), a provider “should be responsible for submitting valid claims at all times and that the provider or supplier's repeated failure to do so poses a risk to the Medicare Trust Funds.”
[
15
]
We proposed the following two revisions to § 424.535(a)(8)(ii):
Removing all the factors in § 424.535(a)(8)(ii)(A) through (D).
Removing the second sentence of § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) that reads “In making this determination, CMS considers, as appropriate or applicable, the following”.
We have seen a wide variety of potential § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) cases over the years. However, our existing factors often constrain our ability to effectively address all these factual scenarios. We noted the following in the proposed rule:
Final Adverse Actions—Most aberrant billing we have seen is done by providers with no history of adverse actions (for example, Medicare revocations or OIG exclusions). Yet the adverse action factor in § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) essentially requires us to weigh against a finding of improper billing for such providers. That is, this factor assists non-compliant providers so long as the provider lacks an adverse history, which it often will; this hinders our efforts to invoke § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) against the provider.
Percentage of Claims Denied—This factor, too, is problematic. Non-compliant billing often occurs notwithstanding a low percentage of denied claims, especially with providers that submit many claims. Similar to the adverse history factor, the claim denial criterion thus makes it more difficult to use § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) even if a pattern of abusive billing exists. Moreover, the factor is limited to claim denials and does not consider other types of non-compliant claims (such as rejected claims). In our view, it is the lack of compliance itself, rather than the type of claim involved, that is pertinent.
In sum—and given our responsibility to protect the Trust Funds and taxpayers from improper billing—we must have the ability to address all possible § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) scenarios without the rigid constraints of our existing factors. Even with the “as appropriate or applicable” qualifier in the opening paragraph of § 424.535(a)(8)(ii), there could still be an implication that we must consider all the factors in our determinations, which, as indicated, hampers the usefulness of § 424.535(a)(8)(ii).
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed our removal of factors from § 424.535(a)(8)(ii). They stated that clear criteria and thresholds (such as a minimum number of claims needed to constitute a “pattern or practice”) are needed to foster transparency and certainty for providers. Some commenters stated that CMS should not only retain the current factors but also include new ones such as (though not limited to): (1) the statistical validity and representativeness of any claim sample that CMS reviews; (2) the dollar amount, frequency, nature, severity, and materiality of the alleged errors; (3) whether the provider knew or reasonably should have known of the noncompliance; (4) whether CMS or the MAC previously notified or educated the provider; (5) whether the provider promptly refunded overpayments and implemented corrective action; (6) the provider's compliance history and prompt rectification of errors; (7) the presence or absence of fraud, waste, abuse, or beneficiary harm; and (8) whether the pattern or practice involved final adjudicated claims rather than initial denials.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns and suggestions. Yet as previously explained, specifically delineated and mandatory factors have inhibited our ability to effectively utilize § 424.535(a)(8)(ii). This said, we emphasize strongly that CMS will take into account the facts and circumstances of every evaluation under § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) and, as we currently do, will only revoke under this ground when genuinely warranted and not as a matter of course. Moreover, stakeholders should not assume that our removal of § 424.535(a)(8)(ii)'s factors means that we will never again consider matters such as the percentage of claims denied or the type of billing non-compliance in our § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) determinations. Our change to § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) simply reflects the program integrity need to move away from explicit factors and towards a broader, more flexible “facts and circumstances” approach. This is also partly why we have not established a fixed, regulatory definition of “pattern or practice” with numerical and time thresholds.
We stress that up through 2014, none of CMS' denial or revocation grounds contained enumerated, mandatory factors—and even today, a number of our grounds do not. Both then and now, a lack of factors does not mean providers will be treated unfairly. We have for decades reviewed every case with the utmost care and consideration, recognized the heavy consequences of a

(2) False or Misleading Information (§ 424.535(a)(4))
Section 424.535(a)(4) permits revocation if the provider or supplier certified as “true” misleading or false information on the enrollment application to be enrolled or maintain enrollment in the Medicare program. This would include but not be limited to: (1) enrollment-related forms created by and/or submitted to CMS contractors; (2) false or misleading documentation furnished as part of the completion or submission of the CMS or Medicare enrollment-related form; (3) the Form CMS-588 (Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) Authorization Agreement; OMB Control Number 0938-0626), which must be submitted with the enrollment application; (4) documents required to demonstrate compliance with HHA capitalization requirements in § 489.28; (5) opt-out affidavits under

We stated that providers and suppliers must always submit truthful enrollment and enrollment-related information to CMS and its contractors regardless of the form or document involved. Any false or misleading information could lead to serious doubts about the provider's veracity, a non-compliant provider being inadvertently enrolled in Medicare, or improper
(

The submission need not be intended to gain or maintain Medicare enrollment. For § 424.535(a)(4) purposes, the ultimate aim of the submission—be it to enroll, revalidate enrollment, reactivate enrollment, voluntarily terminate enrollment, report changed EFT data, etc.—is not as crucial as the truthfulness of the submission. If we continued to limit § 424.535(a)(4) to “gain or maintain enrollment” situations, providers might believe they can submit false information on other enrollment-related documents without concern about possible revocation.

The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses. Note that some of these comments and responses also pertain to proposed revised § 424.530(a)(4), which would permit denial based on the same grounds identified in proposed § 424.535(a)(4). Our final decision regarding § 424.530(a)(4) will be addressed later.
Comment:
Numerous commenters stated that our proposed expansion of §§ 424.530(a)(4) and 424.535(a)(4) could result in denials and revocations based on inadvertent or immaterial administrative errors. They stated that CMS should distinguish between intentional fraud and technical or minor mistakes that are promptly corrected. They added that CMS should: (1) include a materiality-based standard—like “knowing and material misrepresentation”—and other factors in §§ 424.530(a)(4) and 424.535(a)(4) (for example, whether the information is relevant to program integrity); (2) permit providers to cure any unintentional or clerical errors before revocation (such as a 30-day correction timeframe); and (3) always consider mitigating circumstances in its paragraph (a)(4) determinations.

We appreciate these comments and address them as follows.
First, our proposal was not intended to change the standard we always apply when reviewing potential §§ 424.530(a)(4) and 424.535(a)(4) situations. We will continue to carefully consider the facts and circumstances of each case and only deny or revoke when truly justified.
Second, we respectfully decline to establish knowledge, materiality, or other regulatorily specified criteria or thresholds. Sections 424.530(a)(4) and 424.535(a)(4) have never had a knowledge or intent standard or required the data to be material, and we did not propose in this rule to establish such requirements. If we required knowledge or intent, providers might submit false data believing they could later simply disavow awareness thereof to avoid denial or revocation. A materiality threshold, meanwhile, would enable providers to, knowingly or unknowingly, submit incorrect information without fear of consequences so long as it is not deemed material. As for establishing new factors, we reiterate our previously noted concerns about required criteria that constrain our ability to take denial or revocation action when necessary. We also stress that it has long been CMS policy that the enrolling or enrolled provider bears ultimate legal responsibility for the accuracy and thoroughness of all submitted data, a point we reiterated in the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule.
Third, and consistent with our aforementioned quoted statement from the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule, we believe that permitting a pre-revocation correction period and/or quasi-appeals process could disincentivize providers to submit correct and truthful information in their initial submission.
