(4) Expansion and Reorganization of Retroactive Revocation Grounds (§ 424.535(g))
Section 424.535(g) addresses revocation effective dates. Current paragraph (g)(1) states that except as described in paragraphs (g)(2) and (g)(3), a revocation becomes effective 30 days after CMS or the CMS contractor mails notice of its determination to the provider; the revocation is thus prospective. Existing paragraphs (g)(2)(i) through (xv) list situations where the revocation effective date is retroactive. This generally means that the revocation's effective date is retroactive back to the date on which the provider's non-adherence to Medicare requirements commenced.
The purpose of paragraph (g)(2) is to prevent payments to a provider while it is out of compliance. Using an example we included in the proposed rule, assume a provider's medical license is revoked by the State on March 1. CMS learns of this and sends a revocation notice to the provider on March 15. If we applied the prospective “30 days after mailing” timeframe in paragraph (g)(1), the provider could bill and be paid for services furnished between March 1 and April 15 while unlicensed, resulting in potentially thousands of dollars in improper Medicare payments. Preventing improper payments is a cornerstone of provider enrollment, and retroactive revocation effective dates are vital mechanisms for ensuring that taxpayer monies are paid only to compliant providers. As § 424.500 makes clear: “Providers and suppliers must meet and maintain [part 424, subpart P's] enrollment requirements to bill either the Medicare program or its beneficiaries for Medicare-covered services or supplies.” This means, by extension, that if said requirements are not met, the provider cannot bill—or, in turn, receive payment—for Medicare services or supplies.
Our concerns about paying non-adherent providers are why we have increased the number of retroactive revocation grounds over the years. In the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule, we finalized numerous revisions to § 424.535(g) such that many of our existing revocation reasons are now retroactive.
[
18
]
So critical is it to make payments only to qualified providers and to be consistent with §§ 424.500 and 424.505 that we proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS final rule to make the remainder of current prospective revocation grounds retroactive. We also believe that the prospect of a retroactive revocation no matter the § 424.535(a) reason could help spur providers to ensure constant compliance with Medicare requirements.
We proposed two sets of changes to § 424.535(g). First, we would add new retroactive revocation bases. Second, we proposed to restructure § 424.535(g) to remove current § 424.535(g)(1) (which addresses prospective revocations) and realign the existing retroactive grounds to correspond to the numerical order of our § 424.535(a) revocation reasons. The following summarizes our proposed provisions in revised § 424.535(g)(1).
(a) General Non-Compliance, Licensure, and Provider Agreements
CMS may revoke a provider under § 424.535(a)(1) if the provider is not in compliance with the enrollment requirements in Title 42 of the Act or in the enrollment application applicable to its provider type. We proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(i)(A) that said revocation would be effective on the date the non-compliance began (per CMS' or the CMS contractor's determination). This comports with several other current retroactive grounds for which the commencement of non-compliance is the effective date; for said current grounds—as well as proposed § 424.535(g)(1)(i)(A)—the rationale is that payments should not be made to non-adherent providers.
State licensure revocations, suspensions, and surrenders (in lieu of further disciplinary action) are also grounds for revocation. As stated in existing § 424.535(g)(2)(iii) and (v), these revocation effective dates are the dates of the revocation, suspension, or surrender. We proposed to consolidate paragraphs (g)(2)(iii) and (v) within new § 424.535(g)(1)(i)(B), retaining their current effective dates.
Current § 424.535(g)(2)(vii) addresses effective dates for revocations based on a provider agreement termination under part 489. We proposed to retain these dates and incorporate them into new § 424.535(g)(1)(i)(C).
(b) Exclusions/Debarments, Felony Convictions, False Information, and Non-Operational Status
These revocation grounds are addressed in § 424.535(a)(2), (3), (4), and (5)(i), with their concomitant effective dates outlined in existing § 424.535(g)(2)(i), (ii), (ix), and (iv), respectively. Per § 424.535(g)'s proposed reorganization, § 424.535(g)(2)(i), (ii), (ix), and (iv) would become new § 424.535(g)(1)(ii), (iii), (iv), and (v)(A), respectively.
(Due to our aforementioned expansion of § 424.535(a)(4), we proposed that new § 424.535(g)(1)(iv) would include an additional effective date for paragraph (a)(4) revocations based on the submission of false or misleading data not involving the signature of a provider enrollment application certification statement. For these other false/misleading communications, the revocation effective date would be the date the false/misleading information was submitted.)
(c) Failure To Satisfy Enrollment Requirements
Section 424.535(a)(5)(ii) permits revocation if the provider fails to satisfy any Medicare enrollment requirement. We proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(v)(B) that a § 424.535(a)(5)(ii) revocation becomes effective on the date the Medicare enrollment requirement was not satisfied.
(d) Application Fee Payment
CMS can revoke a provider's enrollment under § 424.535(a)(6) in various situations concerning the required payment of a provider application fee under § 424.514. We proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(vi) that a § 424.535(a)(6) revocation is effective on the date on which CMS or its contractor determines that the provider or supplier should be revoked under this paragraph.
(e) Misuse of Billing Number
CMS may revoke a provider's enrollment under § 424.535(a)(7) if the provider knowingly sells to or allows another individual or entity to use its billing number. (This excludes providers who enter into a valid reassignment of benefits under § 424.80 or a § 489.18 change of ownership.) Given the seriousness of this conduct—with its significant potential for fraud—we proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(vii) that the revocation effective date should be the date on which the conduct resulting in the revocation occurred.
(f) Abuse of Billing Privileges
The effective dates for revocations under § 424.535(a)(8)(i) and (ii) are addressed in § 424.535(a)(8)(iii). So that all revocation effective dates can be located in one paragraph, we proposed to move and redesignate § 424.535(a)(8)(iii) as new § 424.535(g)(1)(viii). Paragraph (iii) would be deleted from § 424.535(a)(8).

(g) Reporting Enrollment Data Changes
Section 424.535(a)(9) permits revocation if the provider failed to comply with the change of information reporting requirements in §§ 424.516(d) or (e), 410.33(g)(2), or 424.57(c)(2). These four paragraphs collectively address all Medicare provider and supplier types (except Medicare Diabetes Prevention Programs (MDPPs), which are dealt with in § 424.205)) and all types of enrollment data changes. Current § 424.535(g)(2)(x) partially addresses the effective date of a § 424.535(a)(9) revocation. For revocations based on the provider's failure to timely report a change of ownership or adverse legal action (or a change, addition, or deletion of a practice location), the effective date under § 424.535(g)(2)(x) is the day following the date by which the provider was required to report the change, addition, or deletion. All other changes are prospective under current § 424.535(g)(1).
We proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(ix) to make all § 424.535(a)(9) revocations retroactive to the day following the due date for reporting the change. While ownership, adverse legal action, and practice location changes are important (hence their inclusion in existing § 424.535(g)(2)(x)), other data changes are as well. A failure to timely report a new managing employee or corporate officer, for example, could result in CMS unknowingly paying a provider with a high-level official who poses a program integrity risk based on past or current conduct. If we do not timely learn of a provider's new bank, billing agency, or correspondence address, CMS risks sending funds or information to—or receiving claims from—the wrong entity or individual; this could lead to incorrect payments or the inadvertent release of confidential data. As we emphasized in the proposed rule: (1) outdated or erroneous enrollment information of any type—not simply ownership, adverse action, or location data—can threaten the Trust Funds; and (2) any failure to timely report such changes means the provider is non-compliant with enrollment requirements. For these reasons—and because the prospect of a retroactive revocation could encourage providers to timely report all enrollment changes—we believed that § 424.535(g)(1)(ix) is warranted.
Although the provider is ultimately responsible for ensuring that its enrollment data is timely updated and always accurate, we solicited stakeholder comment on any administrative difficulties in reporting changes in enrollment information and how they could be addressed.
(h) Failure To Document or Furnish Documentation
CMS can revoke a provider under § 424.535(a)(10) if the provider fails to comply with the documentation or CMS access requirements in § 424.516(f). In general, § 424.516(f) requires providers (including physicians and eligible professionals) to: (1) retain for 7 years all documents regarding written orders, certifications, referrals, prescriptions and requests for payments for Part A or B services, items, or drugs; and (2) furnish access to that documentation upon CMS or CMS contractor request.
We proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(x)(A) and (B) that a § 424.535(a)(10) effective date is as follows:
For revocations based on a failure to retain documentation, the date on which CMS or the CMS contractor determines that the provider has not complied with this retention requirement.
For revocations based on a failure to provide access to that documentation, the day after the date by which the provider was required to give access.
We believed that proposed § 424.535(g)(1)(x)(A) and (B) balance the need for retroactivity—due to, for instance, the provider's non-compliance and our inability to make payment to non-adherent providers—and the need for a clear effective date. To illustrate, suppose CMS discovered several years after a particular service was ordered or certified that the provider lacks documentation thereof. CMS would have no means of knowing whether the documentation was never kept, discarded after 2 years or 4 years, etc. Therefore, it is difficult to establish an effective date in this scenario, hence the need to use the proposed—and much more precise—§ 424.535(g)(1)(x)(A) date. Regarding § 424.535(g)(1)(x)(B), the provider's failure to provide the documentation constitutes non-compliance, similar to a provider's failure to timely report changes of information. Thus, we believe that the day after the due date for furnishing access is an appropriate effective date.
(i) Initial Reserve Operating Funds (IROF)
Under
42 CFR 489.28
, HHAs must demonstrate that they have sufficient available funds upon application submission and for the 3-month period following the conveyance of Medicare billing privileges to operate the HHA for this 3-month timeframe. CMS can revoke the HHA under § 424.535(a)(11) if, within 30 days of a CMS or Medicare contractor request, the HHA cannot furnish supporting documentation verifying that it meets the IROF requirement. For the same reasons behind proposed § 424.535(g)(1)(x)(B)—specifically, the provider's non-compliance with § 489.28 based on its failure to demonstrate adequate funds—we proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(xi) that the § 424.535(a)(11) revocation effective date is the day after the date by which the HHA was required to submit the requested documentation.
(j) Other Program Termination
CMS under § 424.535(a)(12) may revoke a provider's Medicare enrollment if the provider is terminated, revoked, or otherwise barred from participation in a State Medicaid program or any other Federal health care program. The effective date of a § 424.535(a)(12) revocation is, consistent with existing § 424.535(g)(2)(vi), the date of the termination, revocation, or bar (from the other program). As part of our restructuring of § 424.535(g), we proposed to redesignate § 424.535(g)(2)(vi) as new § 424.535(g)(1)(xii); however, we would include the terms “revocation” and “bar” within the latter to correspond to § 424.535(a)(12). (Current § 424.535(g)(1)(vi) only references terminations.)
(k) Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Certificates
Section 424.535(a)(13)(i) and (ii) permit revocation if—
A physician or other eligible professional's DEA Certificate of Registration to dispense a controlled substance is currently suspended or revoked or is surrendered in response to a show cause order; or
The applicable licensing or administrative body for any State in which the physician or eligible professional practices suspends or revokes the individual's ability to prescribe one or more drugs.
Existing § 424.535(g)(2)(xi) permits retroactive revocation based on the surrender of the provider's DEA certificate of registration in response to a show cause order. (The revocation effective date is the date the certificate was surrendered.) We proposed to include DEA certificate revocations and suspensions within this paragraph, with the date of the revocation or suspension as the effective date. It is the permanent or temporary loss of the certificate itself—rather than the form of loss (for example, revocation or surrender)—that is important for program integrity

purposes; it would be illogical for certificate surrenders to be part of paragraph (g)(2)(xi) but not revocations or suspensions. As we stated in the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule that promulgated paragraph (g)(2)(xi), meeting all applicable Federal and State requirements is necessary for enrollment.

If a provider is prescribing or dispensing drugs while non-compliant, we believe the risk this presents to beneficiaries after the certificate loss warrants a revocation back to the date said loss occurred.
Per current § 424.535(g)(2)(xii), the effective date of a revocation based on a State's suspension or revocation of the physician's or practitioner's ability to prescribe one or more drugs is the date of the suspension or revocation. We proposed to redesignate this paragraph without change as new paragraph (g)(1)(xiii)(B), with existing (g)(2)(xi) redesignated as new paragraph (g)(1)(xiii)(A).
(l) Improper Prescribing Practices
Section 424.535(a)(14) permits revocation if the physician or practitioner has a pattern or practice of prescribing Medicare-covered drugs that is abusive, represents a threat to the health and safety of Medicare beneficiaries, or fails to meet Medicare requirements. We proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(xiv) that the effective date of a § 424.535(a)(14) revocation would be the last date of the prescription(s) in question. (This approach mirrors that for § 424.535(a)(8)(ii)'s revocation effective date, which, as noted, is the last date of service on the claims in question.) Applying a prospective effective date to a § 424.535(a)(14) would essentially allow the individual to continue prescribing for at least another 30 days, during which time additional beneficiaries might be placed as risk.
(m) False Claims Act (FCA)
Revocation is permissible under § 424.535(a)(15) if the provider (or owner, managing employee or organization, officer, or director thereof) has had an FCA civil judgment against them within the previous 10 years. We proposed in new paragraph (g)(1)(xv) a retroactive revocation effective date back to the date of the judgment.
(Proposed new § 424.535(g)(1)(xvi) is addressed later in this section V.C. of this final rule.)
(n) Debts Referred to Treasury
Section 424.535(a)(17) permits revocation if the provider failed to repay a debt that CMS appropriately referred to the United States Department of Treasury. (Paragraph (a)(17) does not apply if: (1) the debt has been discharged by a bankruptcy court; or (2) the administrative appeals process regarding the debt has not been exhausted or the timeframe for filing the appeal (at the appropriate appeal level) has not expired.)
All providers are responsible for satisfying their financial obligations to Medicare. Consistent with our rationale for the original promulgation of § 424.535(a)(17), we believe that referral to the Department of Treasury may indicate the provider's unwillingness to repay a debt, which raises doubts regarding whether the provider is a reliable participant in the Medicare program.
With the need to protect the Medicare program's financial integrity, we proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(xvii) that the effective date of a § 424.535(a)(17) revocation would be retroactive back to the date on which CMS referred the debt to Treasury. As we explained in the proposed rule, a prospective effective date would give the provider more time to incur additional debts that it also might not repay, placing the taxpayers at considerable financial risk. We also believe that the prospect of a retroactive revocation under § 424.535(g)(1)(xvii) could spur providers to ensure that they repay all debts before the latter are sent to Treasury.
(o) Revoked Under Different Name or Identity
CMS under § 424.535(a)(18) may revoke a provider that is currently revoked under a different name, numerical identifier, or business identity, and the applicable reenrollment bar period under § 424.535(c) has not expired. The objective is to prevent situations where a revoked provider changes its identity in order to re-enter Medicare and thus circumvent its existing bar on reenrollment. In light of such improper conduct, we proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(xviii) that a § 424.535(a)(18) revocation effective date would be the same as the effective date of the provider's current enrollment.
(p) Undue Risk
Per § 424.535(a)(19), CMS may revoke a provider or supplier that has or has had an affiliation under § 424.519 that poses an undue risk of fraud, waste, or abuse to the Medicare program. Due to the many different scenarios that could fall within § 424.535(a)(19)'s purview, we proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(xix) that a revocation under § 424.535(a)(19) is effective on the date on which CMS or its contractor determines that the provider or supplier should be revoked under this paragraph.
(q) Billing From Non-Compliant Location
CMS may revoke enrollment under § 424.535(a)(20) if the provider billed for services performed at or items furnished from a location that it knew or should have known did not comply with Medicare enrollment requirements. Given the importance of maintaining constant compliance with enrollment requirements, we proposed that a § 424.535(a)(20) revocation's effective date would be the earliest date on the claims for the non-compliant location that are triggering the revocation.
(r) Abusive Ordering, Certifying, Referring, or Prescribing
Section 424.535(a)(21) permits revocation if the physician or eligible professional has a pattern or practice of ordering, certifying, referring, or prescribing Part A or B services, items, or drugs that is abusive, represents a threat to the health and safety of Medicare beneficiaries, or otherwise fails to meet Medicare requirements. As with proposed § 424.535(g)(1)(xiv) regarding § 424.535(a)(14), the seriousness of the conduct described in § 424.535(a)(21) and the threats it can present to Medicare patients and the Trust Funds (for instance, ordering unnecessary tests) warrants a retroactive effective date. This date under proposed § 424.535(g)(1)(xxi) would be the date of the last order, certification, referral, or prescription in the applicable pattern or practice, akin to the proposed § 424.535(a)(14) effective date.
(s) Patient Harm
Revocation under § 424.535(a)(22) is permissible if the physician or other eligible professional has been subject to prior action from a State oversight board, Federal or State health care program, Independent Review Organization (IRO) determination(s), or any other equivalent governmental body or program that oversees, regulates, or administers the provision of health care with underlying facts reflecting improper conduct that led to patient harm. Considering the need to protect Medicare beneficiaries from potential harm, we proposed that this effective date per new § 424.535(g)(1)(xxii) would be the date of the prior action that resulted in the revocation.

The following is a summary of the comments we received on our retroactive revocation proposals and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed CMS' proposal to extend its retroactive revocation authority to all revocations and recommended that it not be finalized. They stated that retroactive revocations can impose severe and disproportionate financial consequences on otherwise legitimate providers and suppliers.
Response:
We appreciate and understand the concerns expressed. We respond as follows.
First, and as previously noted, in past years we have gradually expanded the reasons for which we may retroactively revoke providers. In last year's CY 2026 HH PPS final rule, we added roughly 10 new retroactive grounds. Accordingly, retroactive revocations are not a novel concept but have been used to a considerable degree for some time. Our retroactive revocation proposals in this year's rule are consistent with current practice.
Second, we explained to commenters in last year's CY 2026 HH PPS final rule that retroactive revocations are intended to recoup payments to which the provider is not entitled due to its non-compliance. Generally, once the provider is non-adherent to Medicare enrollment requirements, it cannot receive payment for services furnished beginning on or after the point the non-compliance began. We especially emphasized in that rule that: (1) our allowance of prospective dates for certain revocation grounds has resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in payments to non-compliant providers; and (2) we have an obligation to the American taxpayers to halt this.
[
20
]
We maintain this position in the present final rule; taxpayer monies must be protected against improper payments.
Third, retroactive liability under § 424.535(g) does not occur without a revocation. This may seem obvious, but it is critical for stakeholders to understand that revocations are actually quite rare when weighed against the universe of well over 2 million Medicare providers and suppliers. In fact, only about 3 percent of providers are ever revoked. It is never a step we wish to take—partly because, like the commenters, we fully recognize its consequences and the potential retroactive financial liability—and in many cases we instead apply more modest actions such as deactivations under § 424.540 and stays of enrollment under § 424.541; indeed, we promulgated the latter action in the CY 2024 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (
88 FR 78818
)
[
21
]
to give us greater flexibility to address certain instances of comparatively minor non-compliance without having to pursue revocation.
In sum, despite our recognition of the commenters' concerns, we are unable to make payment to providers that are not compliant with Medicare enrollment requirements. This is consistent with the requirements of §§ 424.500 and 424.505 and underlies the need for our proposed expansion of retroactive revocation grounds. Yet because we recognize the consequences of a retroactive revocation, we seek to assure providers that revocations are not only infrequent but also are only imposed when genuinely warranted. This will not change under revised § 424.535(g).
(
printed page 72098)
Comment:
Several commenters stated that retroactive revocations can impair or interrupt beneficiary access to care.
Response:
Our expansion of retroactive revocation grounds in past years has not, to our knowledge, resulted in the material prevention or disruption of beneficiary care. Thus, we have no reason to believe said hindrances will occur with our revisions to § 424.535(g); this is especially true given, again, the infrequency of revocations. Nonetheless, we will, as we always have, remain watchful for any access to care issues.
Comment:
Numerous commenters expressed concern that CMS' proposal would, in essence, unfairly convert technical or minor provider errors into a finding that every covered service during the period in question is unpayable. They stated that such deficiencies should not trigger a retroactive revocation, the current prospective dates for these reasons should remain (for example, reporting a change of information), and retroactive revocations should be reserved for serious misconduct, such as, but not limited to: (1) criminal activity; (2) intentional or systemic provider fraud, waste, or abuse; (3) material non-compliance; or (4) patient harm.
Response:
While we appreciate these comments, they appear to presume that every minor error does or will automatically result in a revocation. This has never been the case. As explained earlier, we frequently use other actions (for example, stays) to address such situations. On the other hand, we reiterate that non-compliance with enrollment requirements—even if the provider believes it is a mere technical or inconsequential violation—should result in non-payment. The current prospective effective date in § 424.535(g) for certain revocations is directly antithetical to this, which is why: (1) a retroactive date is needed if we believe the non-compliance warrants a revocation; and (2) we cannot restrict retroactive revocations to matters such as criminal or fraudulent behavior or beneficiary harm. Non-compliance at any level and to any degree remains non-compliance.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that CMS' retroactive revocation proposals lack clear, explicit congressional authorization and fail the independent statutory interpretation standard.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. We previously stated that sections 1102 and 1871 of the Act give the Secretary discretion to promulgate regulations that are necessary for the efficient administration of the Medicare program; section 1866(j), meanwhile, states in paragraph (1) that the Secretary shall establish by regulation a process for the enrollment of providers of services and suppliers under this title. In our view, establishing revocation effective dates and ensuring that Medicare payments are made correctly and only to compliant providers and suppliers—which is the central purpose of retroactive revocations—clearly falls within the scopes of sections 1102, 1871, and 1866(j) of the Act. Hence, we believe—as we have with our prior regulatory expansions of retroactive revocations—that sections 1102, 1871, and 1866(j) of the Act furnish sufficient authority for our § 424.535(g) proposal.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS' proposed expansion of § 424.535(g) is inconsistent with certain aspects of section 1866(b)(2) of the Act. Under section 1866(b)(2)(i) and (ii), CMS may refuse to enter into a provider agreement or—upon such reasonable notice to the provider and the public—may refuse to renew or may terminate such an agreement if CMS determines that the provider fails to: (1) comply substantially with the provisions of the agreement, with the provisions of Title XVIII and regulations thereunder, or with a corrective action required under section 1886(f)(2)(B); or (2) substantially meet the applicable provisions of section 1861 of the Act. The commenters appeared to contend that a provider that is retroactively revoked has not been given “reasonable notice” of its non-compliance because, in effect, the provider: (1) might not have realized it is non-compliant; (2) had thus been furnishing legitimate services in good-faith; (3) only belatedly learned of its non-adherence; and (4) is now responsible for repaying Medicare. Accordingly, they concluded that the revocation's retroactive nature violates section 1866(b)(2) of the Act. Another contention seemingly was that so long as the provider “substantially” (as that term is used in section 1866(b)(2) of the Act) complies with enrollment requirements, a retroactive revocation is impermissible.
Other commenters stated that section 1866(b)(2) would be violated if CMS applied one of its proposed retroactive revocation grounds to a time period prior to January 1, 2027. This is because, the commenters contended, the section 1866(b)(2) of the Act requirement of “reasonable notice” to the provider will not have been met—particularly if the revocation effective date goes back several years.
Response:
Provider enrollment and provider agreements are different concepts operating under different authorities and requirements. In general, Medicare provider enrollment is the process by which providers and suppliers seek to obtain and maintain Medicare billing privileges; it is largely governed by section 1866(j) of the Act and
42 CFR 424.500
through
424.575
. A provider agreement, as defined in
42 CFR 489.3
, is an agreement between CMS and a provider identified in § 489.2(b) to furnish services to Medicare beneficiaries and to comply with the requirements of section 1866 of the Act. Subparts A and B of part 489 address provider agreements. The provisions and parameters of section 1866(b)(2) of the Act, in short, do not apply to provider enrollment, and we emphasize that complete compliance with enrollment provisions—rather than merely “substantial” compliance—is required to obtain and maintain billing privileges.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that retroactive revocations under § 424.535(a)(8)(ii) and any associated recoupment could violate section 1879(a)(2) of the Act whereby, the commenters contended, a provider need not reimburse any overpayment if it “did not know, and could not reasonably have been expected to know, that payment would not be made.”
Response:
We respectfully disagree with this comment. Section 1879(a)(2) of the Act is only one of two requirements needed for section 1879(a) of the Act to apply. The other, section 1879(a)(1) of the Act, requires a CMS determination that—based on section 1862(a)(1) or (9) of the Act or by reason of a coverage denial described in section 1862(g) of the Act—Part A or Part B payment may not be made for any expenses incurred for items or services furnished by a provider of services or by another person pursuant to an assignment under section 1842(b)(3)(B)(ii) of the Act. Section 1879(a)(1) of the Act does not apply to retroactive revocations because, among other things, the specific denial reasons listed in that section are not applicable to the overpayment determination.
Comment:
A commenter stated that retroactive revocations could disincentivize providers from self-disclosure and prompt remediation of non-compliance out of concern that CMS will revoke the provider based on said non-adherence.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. We saw no evidence of this following previous expansions of retroactive revocation grounds. In fact, we believe it will encourage providers to be more vigilant in their reporting responsibilities.
(
printed page 72099)
Comment:
A few commenters maintained that our retroactive revocation provisions would violate section 1866(b)(3) of the Act. Section 1866(b)(3) of the Act states that the effective date of a termination or refusal to renew a provider agreement shall become effective on the same date and in the same manner as an exclusion from participation under section 1128(c) of the Act. Section 1128(c)(1) of the Act conditions such an exclusion on “reasonable notice,” and section 1128(c)(2)(A) of the Act limits this exclusion to services furnished to an individual on or after the effective date. Moreover, section 1128(c)(2)(B)(ii) of the Act provides that—absent a health and safety determination—an exclusion does not apply to payment for home health services and hospice care furnished to an individual under a plan of care established before the date of the exclusion. It follows, the commenters concluded, that: (1) under these statutes, a provider must first receive adequate notice prior to the effective date of any such termination action, including revocation; and (2) proposed § 424.535(g) would violate this requirement because the termination effective date would precede notice and apply retroactively to services already provided.
Response:
We respectfully disagree with these contentions for two reasons. First, section 1866(b)(3) of the Act, like section 1866(b)(2) of the Act, is inapplicable to provider enrollment. As discussed earlier, provider enrollment and provider agreements are different concepts operating under different authorities and requirements, and termination of a provider agreement is distinct from a denial or revocation of enrollment in Medicare. Second, section 1128(c) does not apply to Medicare denials and revocations but only to OIG exclusions. Consequently, these retroactive revocation provisions do not violate section 1866(b)(3) of the Act.
Comment:
Commenters recommended that in its retroactive revocation determinations, CMS should consider whether: (1) the provider reasonably believed it was compliant with enrollment requirements when it provided the services; and (2) the services were medically necessary, documented, and otherwise covered (including whether CMS or its contractor possessed the relevant information while continuing to process claims).
Response:
We appreciate these suggestions but decline to commit to them. As we stated in the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule and have noted in other provider enrollment rules, it is ultimately the provider's responsibility to ensure constant adherence to Medicare enrollment requirements.
[
22
]
While we say this most respectfully, simply having a reasonable or good-faith belief that is it compliant with these requirements does not exempt the provider from the obligation to actually be compliant. Payments to a non-adherent provider are inappropriate irrespective of: (1) the provider's belief in its compliance; or (2) whether the furnished services were otherwise proper.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS should limit recoupment to claims causally related to the identified noncompliance. Another commenter requested that accredited Complex Rehabilitation Technology suppliers be exempt from retroactive revocation effective dates.
Response:
We respectfully refer these commenters to our previous response. The issue is the submission of claims for services furnished while the provider is non-compliant, irrespective of whether the claim is related to the non-compliance or to the type of provider or supplier involved; it is partly for this latter reason that we cannot exempt certain provider or supplier types from retroactive revocation application.
Comment:
A commenter supported our retroactive revocation proposals. The commenter stated that prospective revocations create a window during which noncompliant providers can continue billing Medicare after the basis for revocation has been identified; retroactive revocations close this gap. The commenter also recommended that CMS supplement this provision with standardized documentation requirements that establish what evidence must be collected and maintained before a retroactive revocation decision is made.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support and entirely concur with the concerns expressed about prospective revocation effective dates. However, we respectfully decline the commenter's documentation recommendation because we must retain the operational flexibility to address all types of potential retroactive revocations; given the very different facts of each case, a fixed, required form of documentation might not fit all scenarios.

(5) Claim Submissions After Revocation (§ 424.535(h))
Under § 424.535(h)(1)(i) (and excluding HHAs), a revoked provider must—within 60 calendar days after the revocation's effective date—submit all claims for items and services furnished before the date of the revocation letter. For revoked HHAs, § 424.535(h)(1)(ii) states that claims must be submitted within 60 days after the later of the following: (1) the revocation effective date; and (2) the date that the HHA's last payable episode ends.
Prior to 2009, the post-revocation claim submittal period was up to 27 months. It was changed to 60 days for certain provider and supplier types in the CY 2009 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (
73 FR 69726
).
[

It was later made applicable to all provider and supplier types in a December 5, 2014, final rule (
79 FR 72500
).
[
28

In both rules, we explained that the reduction to 60 days was necessary because the prior 27-month period posed significant risk to the Medicare program; it gave problematic providers over 2 years to potentially continue their conduct via the submission of inappropriate claims.
Although the current 60-day period is far less than the prior 27-month timeframe, we have long remained concerned about possible fraudulent, improper, or other non-compliant activity by revoked providers. If a provider engaged in such conduct before the revocation, it may continue it afterwards—and 2 months is still an extensive timeframe in which to do so. Indeed, a revoked provider could submit hundreds of improper claims for hundreds of thousands of dollars during this period. If other providers did the same after their revocations, many millions of Trust Fund dollars would be threatened. With the need to protect taxpayer monies from such parties, we believe that further reducing the submission timeframe could correspondingly lessen the program integrity risk, for providers would have less time to engage in inappropriate billing. For these reasons, we proposed to change the 60-day timeframe referenced in § 424.535(h) to 15 days. While we recognized in the proposed rule that this would be a substantial time reduction, we believed the risk warrants it.
We proposed an additional change to § 424.535(h). We previously explained our proposal to make the remainder of our prospective revocation reasons retrospective. Under existing § 424.535(h), though, if a provider had 60 days from the revocation effective date to submit its claims but the effective date was more than 60 days retroactive, the submission period might well have expired before the provider even received the revocation letter. To ensure that the provider actually has an opportunity to submit its claims, we proposed to change:
Section 424.535(h)(1)(i) to state that a revoked provider must—within 15 calendar days of the date of the revocation letter—submit all claims for items and services furnished before the revocation effective date.
Section 424.535(h)(1)(ii) to state that a revoked HHA must—within 15 calendar days of the date of the revocation letter—submit all claims for items and services furnished before the later of the following:
(We did not propose to change §§ 424.535(h)(1)(i)(A) and (B) or (h)(2) (which references the timely filing requirements of § 424.44).)

(6) New Revocation Reasons
We also proposed to add several new grounds for revocation in § 424.535(a).
(a) High-Risk Enrollments (§ 424.535(a)(24))
As explained in the proposed rule, we have seen an alarming increase in situations where an unusually and disproportionately large number of providers and suppliers—sometimes of the same type—are simultaneously operating within a very small geographic area (for instance, a multi-block sector), the same complex or building, or even the same suite. Examples include: (1) several dozen hospices within a four-block area of Los Angeles County; (2) 18 HHAs within the same building in Columbus, Ohio; (3) at least nine cases in Ohio where at least five HHAs have the same practice location address, with four of these nine situations involving at least nine HHAs in one location; and (4) similar situations with several certified providers of the same type operating out of one building in Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, and Texas. Per CMS data, the number of HHAs in Los Angeles County between 2019 and 2023 rose over 45 percent, and at least 1,400 new HHAs have enrolled in the county since 2019. There was no medical need for such an enormous rise, which was entirely out of proportion with any increase in the county's beneficiary population and can be a strong indicator of widespread fraud. Others share our concerns about this, including the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission,
[
30
]
members of Congress,
[
31
]
and even several national HHA and hospice organizations.
[
32
]
We recognize that many medical facilities, complexes, and geographic areas have large numbers of providers and suppliers located therein. To illustrate, a medical building on a hospital campus may have seven physician practices with different specialties, two laboratories, etc. Also, some areas may have several types of providers and suppliers within a particular neighborhood. The vast preponderance of these situations do not, in and of themselves, necessarily mean that fraud, waste, and abuse exists or that program integrity risks are otherwise present. Yet we believe those cases mentioned in the previous paragraph—as well as other situations—can and do. Fraud schemes can indeed involve problematic (or potentially problematic) providers operating in same general vicinity, as shown in the Los Angeles County and Columbus situations. Although having, for example, four organizational providers/suppliers of the same type (such as ambulance companies) in a seven-block area does not automatically signify fraud, waste, and abuse, it does—based on our experience—raise questions as to whether there is a patient need for all these providers or whether other considerations, such as fraud, are involved.
With tens of millions of Medicare dollars at risk in any fraud scheme, our role in safeguarding the Trust Funds requires the ability to take revocation action—if circumstances warrant—to address such situations. This is especially important because we currently lack authority under § 424.535(a) to revoke providers/suppliers based on program integrity threats stemming from an excessive number of enrolled providers/suppliers within a particular area. We accordingly proposed in new § 424.535(a)(24) that CMS may revoke a provider's or supplier's enrollment if it deems the enrollment as presenting a high risk of fraud, waste, or abuse due to the provider's or supplier's location within a limited geographic area that has an excessive number of providers and suppliers. We noted the following regarding § 424.535(a)(24) in the proposed rule.
First, the term “high risk” for purposes of § 424.535(a)(24) does not mean the provider must be in: (1) the “high” screening level under § 424.518(c); or (2) a region that has traditionally posed a high risk of fraud, waste, and abuse, such as south Florida. To be sure, § 424.518(c) providers—as well as providers in known program integrity hotspots—pose elevated risks, a matter we may consider in § 424.535(a)(24) determinations. Yet other provider types in other areas can present threats as well. The risk that a particular provider poses based on its proximity to other providers—somewhat more so than the provider type and historic geographic risk—is the main consideration under proposed § 424.535(a)(24).
(
printed page 72103)
Second, a potential fraud scheme can involve multiple provider and supplier types; for example, several HHAs, hospices, DMEPOS suppliers, physicians, etc., might be participating in a single operation. A § 424.535(a)(24) revocation therefore would not require the provider in question and the other providers/suppliers in the area to be of the same type.
Third, the terms “limited geographic area” or “excessive number” in the context of § 424.535(a)(24) will have their ordinary, plain-language meanings. This is due to the many factual situations that could arise and our need to address them—something that thresholds such as minimum/maximum distance or numbers of providers would obstruct. Moreover, such thresholds would alert potentially problematic providers as to how to circumvent a § 424.535(a)(24) revocation. If, to illustrate, we stated that § 424.535(a)(24) only applies if there are at least X number of providers within a radius of Y miles, providers seeking to engage in fraud might enroll immediately outside said radius and/or within an area with fewer providers. This would defeat the purpose of § 424.535(a)(24). That said, our primary focus is on providers in smaller areas—common buildings and complexes, city and town blocks, neighborhoods, etc. Although we reserve the right to apply § 424.535(a)(24) to providers in larger areas (especially if there is an abnormally high number of providers therein), § 424.535(a)(24)'s application would typically be relatively narrow in scope.
Fourth, an actual finding of fraud, waste, or abuse by the provider or another provider in the area would not be required for a § 424.535(a)(24) revocation. This is akin to section 1866(j)(5) of the Act (codified in § 424.519), which permits denial or revocation if (1) the provider has or has had a certain type of affiliation with another provider or supplier, and (2) the affiliation poses an undue risk of fraud, waste, or abuse; no determination of actual fraud, waste, or abuse is needed. Section 424.535(a)(24) revocations would be based on the assessed risk and not whether the provider or nearby providers have actually engaged in fraudulent conduct.
Fifth, while several existing revocation reasons in § 424.535(a) require CMS to consider specified factors in its revocation decisions, we are not proposing the same for § 424.535(a)(24). Consistent with our prior discussion regarding § 424.535(a)(8)(ii), we must be able to address all potential § 424.535(a)(24) scenarios without the rigid restrictions of required criteria and based solely on the unique facts and circumstances of each case.
Sixth, some interested parties may detect certain similarities between § 424.535(a)(24) and our authority under section 1866(j)(7) of the Act (codified in § 424.570) to impose a temporary enrollment moratorium. Although we address temporary moratoria in greater detail later in section V.C.1.f.(2).(b). of this final rule, we state here that a moratorium differs from § 424.535(a)(24) in many ways. The latter, for instance: (1) is a revocation reason rather a prohibition on new enrollments; and (2) takes into account the provider's proximity to other providers of all types, not simply the number of (or risk posed by) providers of the same type.
As much as anything else, though, we emphasized that proposed § 424.535(a)(24) was not principally designed to revoke good-faith providers who otherwise present no apparent risks even though they might, for example, be in an area with numerous other providers. Providers should not at all assume they would be revoked under § 424.535(a)(24) merely because they operate near other providers. Indeed, the overwhelming preponderance would not be. Section 424.535(a)(24) would only be applied in exceptional instances where, based on the facts and circumstances, the risk genuinely justifies it.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed our proposal. They noted that providers—urban and rural, large and small—are frequently located near other providers for reasons such as: (1) administrative and financial efficiency (for example, sharing a building to reduce costs); and (2) the facilitation of patient care as part of multi-provider, comprehensive treatment. A provider's mere presence among other providers, they contended, does not by itself indicate program integrity risk. While, in certain instances, they stated that proximity might be a basis for closer CMS review or investigation, it should never be grounds for revocation. They urged CMS to withdraw proposed § 424.535(a)(24) and instead use other means of addressing geographic concentration, such as enhanced screening and oversight.
Response:
We appreciate these comments and respond as follows.
First, and as we have stated, we acknowledge that hospitals, medical complexes, office buildings, densely populated communities, etc., frequently have numerous providers and provider types operating within and around them. Many of these situations by themselves do not involve fraud, waste, or abuse, or risks thereof, and we do not believe the proposed rule stated otherwise. Our principal focus is instead on isolated cases we have seen where, for instance, there are obvious, extremely heavy, and highly aberrant clusters of providers—frequently of the same provider type—operating within a very small area similar to that we saw in our aforementioned Los Angeles and Columbus examples. Established health care systems, hospital campuses, medical complexes, etc., are not the targets of § 424.535(a)(24). We fully understand the concerns that commenters expressed about § 424.535(a)(24). We wish to again reassure providers and suppliers that, by and large, we are not seeking to target legitimate, common, and standard concentrations of providers in places such as hospital medical centers and health system complexes that would normally have a greater number of providers and suppliers therein. It is the unusual situations that we seek to address—and even in some of these cases, revocation might not occur.
Second, and on the other hand, we disagree that concentration must never be a reason for revocation. Such a position, in our view, disregards the crucial concept of risk. While, as stated, concentration does not automatically mean that a program integrity risk exists—it very frequently will not—this does not mean that said risk can never exist. Consider the Columbus situation, where, inexplicably, there were 18 HHAs operating within one building and the program integrity risk was accordingly very high. If we took the stance that no action could be taken because concentration never means risk, we effectively must wait until we learn that fraud has actually occurred before taking measures—by which point millions of dollars in taxpayer monies may have been lost. This would reflect the pay-and-chase formula that has proven far less effective in halting fraud, waste, and abuse than the approach of stopping fraud before it begins. We believe that our duty to the American people to protect the Trust Funds and beneficiaries requires us be preventive and proactive—not reactive—in response to program integrity risks, hence the need for § 424.535(a)(24). Hence we respectfully decline to withdraw our proposal and maintain that it would be the most effective way—more so than other potential
(
printed page 72104)
program integrity mechanisms—to address this particular vulnerability.
Comment:
Commenters requested that CMS establish regulatory factors or standards that CMS must consider in determining risk and, in turn, whether to revoke a provider under § 424.535(a)(24). Criteria and parameters that commenters suggested included (but were not limited to): (1) the provider's ownership, billing patterns, adverse legal history, compliance history, history of timely responses to CMS inquiries, operational status, physical capacity, and specific conduct; (2) whether the provider furnished services inconsistent with beneficiary diagnoses; (3) the provider's relationships (if any) with other providers within the concentrated area; (4) beneficiary complaints against the provider; (5) beneficiary demand and market access needs; (6) whether the provider engaged in patient harm; (7) numerical thresholds for a revocation to occur—such as a certain number of providers of a particular type within a regulatorily specified geographic area (for instance, within X number of square miles or neighborhood blocks; X square feet of a building or medical center size; (8) defining “limited area” and “excessive number” (potentially after consulting with the applicable State agency regarding provider need and market saturation); (9) referral sources and beneficiary overlap; and (10) the degree of concentration, including sub-factors CMS should consider in determining this. The commenters stated that having required factors will ensure objectivity and transparency and, a commenter contended, facilitate a “totality of the circumstances” approach.
Response:
We appreciate these recommendations and reiterate that we will consider the facts and circumstances of every potential § 424.535(a)(24) case. This could, if warranted, include some of the data the commenters recommended. Yet as previously explained, we must have flexibility in potential denial and revocation determinations under §§ 424.530 424.535 in light of the wide range of factual situations that can and do arise. Having explicit, inflexible factors and numerical thresholds that we must consider in every case significantly hinders this ability. It can also, as already noted, alert dishonest providers as to what CMS contemplates in its denial and revocation decisions, hence enabling them to adjust their behavior to circumvent these criteria and thresholds; to illustrate, if we defined “excessive number” as meaning the particular cluster must have at least X number of providers within less than X square miles for § 424.535(a)(24) to apply, providers in a fraud scheme could position their locations so as to avoid this threshold. For all these reasons, § 424.535(a)(24) will not contain regulatorily-specified factors, parameters, or definitions.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that CMS clarify a number of operational considerations regarding § 424.535(a)(24). These included, but were not limited to: (1) the data CMS will use in its determination and whether the provider may review it; (2) whether CMS' methodology and the criteria CMS used will be made public; (3) the frequency with which CMS will re-review and, if needed, update said determination; and (4) whether a provider that is revoked under § 424.535(a)(24) based strictly on saturation may enroll in a different but non-saturated area.
Response:
We will explain the basis for each revocation in our revocation letter to the provider. However, consistent with our decades-long revocation processes, we do not plan to disclose to the public the specific facts, data, and methodology used in each case. Furthermore, except as specified in the appeal process described in
42 CFR part 498
, CMS also will not re-review § 424.535(a)(24) revocations. As for the fourth issue, we respectfully cannot pre-determine a particular situation based on hypothetical facts.
Comment:
Commenters stated that § 424.535(a)(24) raises due process concerns because an otherwise compliant and legitimate provider could be revoked simply because of its location. They stated that in any § 424.535(a)(24) case, CMS should: (1) require clear evidence and an individualized finding of the provider's specific conduct (rather than mere location within a certain area), with several commenters requesting a formal finding of fraud, waste, or abuse; and (2) allow the provider to challenge and submit evidence to rebut CMS' decision—and to cure any deficiencies—before the revocation occurs.
We appreciate these comments, understand the concerns expressed, and state as follows.
First, we respectfully disagree with the apparent assertion that a § 424.535(a)(24) revocation is based entirely on the provider's location per se. The basis, rather, is the fraud, waste, and abuse risk the enrollment poses within the context of the area in question. Explained otherwise, risk, not location, is the central issue. This distinction is important. For purposes of § 424.535(a)(24), a provider and its physical location—standing alone—typically do not raise concerns. When viewed in conjunction with other providers' nearby locations, though, a program integrity risk can arise, and this risk is what triggers the revocation. As noted, this situation is not considerably different from that addressed in section 1866(j)(5) of the Act and § 424.519, whereby denial or revocation can occur if the provider has or has had a certain type of affiliation that poses an undue risk of fraud, waste, or abuse. In both cases, the provider in question need not have engaged in fraud, waste, abuse, or other misconduct. The focus instead is the risk that either the affiliation or, with § 424.535(a)(24), the enrollment (based on proximity and concentration) poses. Likewise, we disagree that an actual fraud, waste, or abuse finding should be required since this would involve reverting to a “pay-and-chase” formula. We must take measures when risk arises instead of only doing so after the improper conduct occurs.
Second, in considering the facts and circumstances in a § 424.535(a)(24) situation, the provider's conduct may, if CMS deems it warranted, be a consideration in its decision. Yet because the issue is risk and because we are not establishing mandatory factors, we respectfully decline to require an assessment or individualized finding of the provider's behavior. Our finding will involve determining the risk described in § 424.535(a)(24).
Third, we are unable to establish the requested pre-revocation appeals process or cure opportunity for reasons previously stated. We believe that our current appeals process under
42 CFR part 489
affords providers adequate due process for revocations and denials.
Comment:
Several commenters maintained that in any § 424.535(a)(24) revocation, CMS should: (1) furnish specific written findings (including, for example, (i) methodology, (ii) the legal basis for the action, (iii) the reasons why CMS believes a high risk exists, and (iv) the time period, comparator group, provider density, claims, locations, individuals, ownership relationships, etc. on which CMS relies); (2) give the provider access to the supporting evidence; (3) grant expedited review if the action threatens beneficiary access; (4) ensure that any review is performed by a CMS official who did not make the original decision; (5) stay any revocation and recoupment during a timely administrative appeal; and (6) explain, if applicable, the recoupment and repayment period and schedule.
Response:
CMS in every revocation sends a letter to the provider explaining,
(
printed page 72105)
among other things, the basis for revocation (including the legal basis) and the provider's appeal rights; the latter includes a statement that the appeals/reconsideration review is performed by a CMS official who did not make the original decision. We also separately inform providers of the process and timing of recoupment.
We previously explained why we do not postpone revocations or recoupment pending the completion of appeals. In addition, the appeals process in
42 CFR part 498
does not provide for expedited provider enrollment appeals for certain types of providers or situations. To do so, we believe, would be unfair to those without expedited appeal rights. All providers and suppliers are, and should be, subject to the same appeals procedures and timeframes.
Comment:
Commenters recommended that CMS establish a safe harbor or rebuttable presumption of “no high risk” under § 424.535(a)(24) for legitimate providers that, for example, maintain bona fide locations, appropriate personnel, no problematic ownership relationships, etc. Some commenters went further and stated that providers with a passed site visit, an active State license and accreditation, and no adverse history should be explicitly excluded from (a)(24)'s purview. Other commenters urged CMS to explicitly state in the rule (including in the regulatory text) that: (1) provider concentration can be an investigative factor but cannot alone be grounds for revocation; and (2) § 424.535(a)(24) requires documented and individualized evidence that the provider presents a material and specific risk of fraud, waste, abuse, or beneficiary harm.
Response:
We thank the commenters for these recommendations but must respectfully decline them. Formally establishing the requested presumption in the rule would hamstring our efforts to address the Los Angeles and Columbus-type situations heretofore mentioned. We would be stating at the outset of any potential § 424.535(a)(24) situation that the provider very likely presents no risk if the criteria the commenters reference (for example, operational locations) are met. We cannot make such pre-judgments before the facts and circumstances are reviewed, and we again remind commenters that the central question is not the risk the individual provider actually presents but the risk posed by the scenario in § 424.535(a)(24). Merely because we earlier recognized that provider proximity often does not present material program integrity concerns does not mean we must or should create an official presumption in this rule that this is so. Furthermore, we have seen instances where a licensed or accredited provider's location, ownership, management, services, background, etc., appeared legitimate, but the provider later engaged in fraud, waste, or abuse as part of a larger scheme. In brief, we are unable to establish formal carve-outs or suppositions with respect to § 424.535(a)(24) since every situation will be different and will require an objective analysis of the facts and circumstances without preexisting assumptions.
Concerning the last comment regarding individualized findings, we refer the commenters to our earlier statements on this topic.
Comment:
Several commenters believed that CMS' reference in the proposed rule to section 1866(j)(5) of the Act when explaining proposed § 424.535(a)(24) is erroneous. They contended that: (1) under section 1866(j)(5) of the act, the provider has an affiliation with an entity that had previously been suspended or excluded, whereas § 424.535(a)(24) permits revocation absent an affiliation or a prior adverse finding; and (2) neither section 1866(j)(5) nor any other statute allows the action that § 424.535(a)(24) contemplates.
Response:
We stated in the proposed rule that a § 424.535(a)(24) situation “is not considerably different from” that addressed in section 1866(j)(5) of the Act and § 424.519. This is correct, for in both cases, the provider in question need not have engaged in fraud, waste, abuse, or other misconduct. The focus instead is the risk that either the affiliation or, with § 424.535(a)(24), the enrollment (based on proximity and concentration) poses.”
[
33
]
The quoted statement merely aimed to show that § 424.535(a)(24)'s concept of revocation based on risk is not new. Respectfully, it neither stated nor implied that we were relying upon section 1866(j)(5) as authority for § 424.535(a)(24); the relevant authorities for this provision are sections 1102, 1871, and 1866(j) of the Act.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that § 424.535(a)(24) could: (1) restrict beneficiaries' access to care and limit their choice of providers; (2) discourage providers from locating in certain areas or associating with other providers; and (3) make it more difficult for smaller, independent providers to compete with larger health care organizations that have greater resources, thus leading the former to be acquired by the latter.
Response:
We respectfully disagree with these contentions. We reiterate that we always carefully examine the facts of the case before undertaking revocation action, and that § 424.535(a)(24) revocations would largely be limited to exceptional situations. Accordingly, we do not believe patient care or choice will be impacted. Second, we have over the years increased the number and scopes of our revocation reasons; this included expanding the types of provider relationships and affiliations that could result in revocations. To our knowledge, none of these regulatory revisions led to the second and third events the commenters cited, and there is no evidence to suggest they will with respect to § 424.535(a)(24).
Comment:
A few commenters questioned how § 424.535(a)(24) would apply to fixed-site institutional providers, with other commenters requesting that they be formally exempted from § 424.535(a)(24).
Response:
The provision will apply to all providers in the same manner irrespective of provider size and type, and for reasons already noted we cannot establish carve-outs or exceptions to § 424.535(a)(24).
Comment:
Some commenters contended that § 424.535(a)(24) inappropriately amounts to: (1) a certificate of need program (whereby, within some States and territories, certain new or expanding providers must demonstrate a need for their services); (2) a § 424.570-type temporary moratorium on the enrollment of specific new provider types within a particular area; and (3) a CMS-enforced limit on the number of providers an area may have, with revocations of all providers that exceed that threshold.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. Section 424.535(a)(24) does not prohibit enrollment, require a demonstration of need, or impose strict numerical limits. It is solely limited to the isolated and very individualized situations previously described involving a provider excess in a limited area leading to a high risk of fraud, waste, or abuse.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that the scenario described in § 424.535(a)(24) is not among the grounds in section 1866(b)(2) of the Act for provider agreements terminations. Hence, § 424.535(a)(24) violates this statutory provision.
Response:
We disagree because, as previously explained, section 1866(b)(2) of the Act pertains to provider agreements. It does not apply to provider enrollment.
After considering the comments received, we are finalizing § 424.535(a)(24) without modification.

(b) Certain Misdemeanor Convictions (§ 424.535(a)(16))
In the CY 2024 PFS proposed rule (
88 FR 52262
), we proposed in new §§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16) to deny or revoke enrollment if the provider—or any owner, managing employee or organization, officer, or director thereof—was convicted of a Federal or State misdemeanor within the past 10 years that CMS deems detrimental to the best interests of the Medicare program and its beneficiaries. We stated that offenses would include (but not be limited in scope or severity) to the following:
Fraud or other criminal misconduct involving the provider's participation in a Federal or State health care program or the delivery of services or items thereunder.
Assault, battery, neglect, or abuse of a patient (including sexual offenses).
Any other misdemeanor that places the Medicare program or its beneficiaries at immediate risk, such as a malpractice suit that results in a conviction of criminal neglect or misconduct.
[
34
]
We outlined in that CY 2024 proposed rule our increasing concern about providers convicted of misdemeanors for conduct that could endanger the Trust Funds and beneficiaries. We stated that our oversight of the Medicare program requires that we be able to take protective action in such instances.
We also noted that while some States may designate a particular crime as a misdemeanor while others deem it a felony, this does not lessen the risk that the former can pose to Medicare and its beneficiaries.
[
35
]
It is the conduct itself, not its classification under State law, that concerns us. This is particularly true since restricting our revocation authority for criminal convictions to felonies could leave us unable to address situations where a felony charge results in a misdemeanor plea.
We did not finalize this proposal in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 78818
).
[
36
]
However, we emphasized in that final rule that: (1) we would continue to monitor cases of misdemeanor convictions involving significant misconduct; (2) we might pursue future rulemaking to address them; and (3) many misdemeanors—especially those involving assault, battery, neglect, or abuse of a patient (including sexual offenses)—can involve disturbing activity.
[
37
]
As explained in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule, two particularly disconcerting categories of misdemeanor convictions we have recently seen involve sexual assault and financial misconduct. The former can endanger Medicare beneficiaries while the latter can threaten the Trust Funds—both of which we must safeguard. In line with our aforementioned willingness to pursue future rulemaking if warranted, we proposed in § 424.535(a)(16) (currently designated as “Reserved”) to revoke enrollment if the provider or supplier—or any owner, managing employee or organization, officer, or director thereof—was convicted of a Federal or State misdemeanor related to sexual assault or financial misconduct within the past 10 years that CMS deems detrimental to the best interests of the Medicare program and its beneficiaries.
While parts of this proposal duplicate those in the CY 2024 proposed rule (for example, the 10-year period, the applicability to owners, directors, etc.), there is one critical difference: it is much narrower in scope. Whereas the CY 2024 proposal was rather open-ended in terms of potential misdemeanors, the present one is limited to sexual assault and financial misconduct. We believe this would reduce stakeholders' possible concerns that proposed § 424.535(a)(16) is too broad. In addition, we stress that: (1) terms such as “financial misconduct” would be based on their plain meanings; and (2) the misdemeanor convictions described in this paragraph must be detrimental to Medicare's (and Medicare beneficiaries') best interests, meaning that not every such conviction would result in revocation.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses. Some of these comments and responses also reference proposed revised § 424.530(a)(16), which would permit denial based on the same grounds identified in proposed § 424.535(a)(16). Our final decision regarding § 424.530(a)(16) will be addressed later.
Comment:
Commenters requested guidance on how CMS will determine whether a misdemeanor: (1) is detrimental to the best interests of the Medicare program; and (2) constitutes “financial misconduct.” The commenters also requested that CMS define this latter term (as well as “sexual assault”) and outline all offenses that could fall within either category.
Response:
As we do with the same “detrimental to the best interests standard” in §§ 424.530(a) and 424.535(a) for felony convictions, CMS considers the facts and circumstances of the case. Also, and as previously indicated, “financial misconduct” and “sexual assault” will have their plain meanings. Considering that the scope of offenses that fit within these two categories can vary by state, we are unable to list all of them.
Comment:
Commenters requested that CMS establish regulatory factors and criteria it must consider in every potential §§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16) case. Among commenters' suggested standards were: (1) whether any evidence of rehabilitation exists; (2) whether there is a connection between the provider and the behavior leading to the revocation; (3) whether a nexus exists between the criminal conviction on the one hand and either the Trust Funds or the provider's health care operations on the other; (4) how long ago the conviction occurred; (5) the nature of the offense; (6) the convicted party's current role within the organization; and (7) whether the underlying conduct leading to the misdemeanor has already been reviewed by the applicable State licensing or regulatory authority.
Response:
We appreciate this request but reiterate our previously explained concerns about the restraints that factors pose. These concerns apply to §§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16), too. Thus, we respectfully decline to include specific criteria in these two regulatory provisions.
Comment:
Several commenters supported this proposed revocation and denial reason.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS confirm that the actions of an unpaid board member would not invoke §§ 424.530(a)(16) or 424.535(a)(16).
Response:
Although it is somewhat unclear, we believe the commenter is referencing “directors” as that term is defined in § 424.502. A person can qualify as a director regardless of whether they are paid or unpaid. Sexual assault and financial misconduct misdemeanors by unpaid board
(
printed page 72107)
members consequently fall within the scope of §§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16).
Comment:
Some commenters stated that CMS should: (1) explain how providers are expected to identify potentially qualifying convictions; (2) identify the safeguards that would apply before an individual's conduct results in the organization's revocation; (3) establish reasonable due diligence expectations, provider notification procedures, and clear responsibilities when a potentially qualifying conviction becomes known but CMS has not yet determined whether it is detrimental to Medicare; and (4) explain what a provider must do upon discovering a potentially disqualifying misdemeanor conviction.
Response:
We were unclear as to certain aspects of these comments. Based on our best reading, we address them as follows. First, this provision (like §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3)) does not require providers to review their personnel for potential convictions as part of the provider enrollment process. Whether they choose to do so is the provider's internal, independent business decision. Second, the principal safeguard is that CMS will, as always, consider the facts and circumstances of the case before taking action. (We are uncertain as to which other “safeguards” the commenters were referencing or seeking.) Third, if, as we suspect, the commenters are asking how much research they must perform regarding their employees' backgrounds, we refer them to our response to the first comment. Fourth, providers are notified by letter of any denial or revocation (regardless of the specific denial or revocation reason). Fifth, we believe the commenters are asking whether the provider must take certain action if CMS is reviewing a potential §§ 424.530(a)(16) or 424.535(a)(16) situation. If so, the answer is no—assuming the question's context is limited to the mere fact that the case is under CMS review. Sixth, CMS cannot direct providers on a particular course of action in the scenario described in the fourth comment. That, too, is an internal provider decision. We can only state that CMS would have the ability to utilize §§ 424.530(a)(16) or 424.535(a)(16) as circumstances warrant.
We wish to expound upon our responses to the first and third comments because, as discussed later, additional commenters raised similar issues concerning other provider enrollment proposals. Although the provider is not required under subpart P of part 424 to conduct these personnel reviews, this does not absolve the provider of ultimate responsibility if one of its owners, managing employees, etc., engages in conduct that could generate a revocation or denial. In addition, CMS cannot establish a “due diligence” standard that prohibits CMS from denying or revoking the provider so long as the provider conducted a certain degree of review and did not find any prior adverse history, but CMS later found that the owner, director, etc., has such history. This has for decades been CMS' position for every denial or revocation reason that involves conduct by an owning or managing party. Applying a due diligence standard would mean that a provider could always avoid denial or revocation by simply stating that it examined the owner's or manager's background but found nothing. This would leave the Medicare program, the Trust Funds, and beneficiaries at tremendous risk; under this scenario, program integrity would be based strictly on the provider's actual or purported review of its affiliated parties rather than actual or potential threats to the program and its patients. Put otherwise, while we understand commenters' concerns about unknown adverse actions, we cannot predicate our payment safeguard efforts on the extent of providers' internal investigative activities (should they wish to perform them).
Comment:
Some commenters requested that the proposed 10-year lookback period be reduced to, for example, 5 years.
Response:
We believe the proposed 10-year period is appropriate. It achieves consistency the 10-year period in §§ 424.530(a)(3) or 424.535(a)(3), and convictions from as long as 10 years ago can still raise program integrity concerns.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that “financial misconduct” misdemeanors should be limited to those involving the delivery of a health care item or service as described in section 1128 of the Act.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. Considering our need to protect the Trust Funds against fraud, waste, and abuse, it is the conviction itself—and the financial misconduct behind it—that must take precedence over the precise forum in which the behavior occurred.
Comment:
Several commenters questioned whether §§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16) will be applied prospectively or retroactively in terms of when the conviction occurred.
Response:
The interpretation of the terms “within the preceding 10 years” will generally be similar to the identical language appearing in §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3)(i). CMS, as appropriate, may issue public guidance on this issue.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that CMS in proposed §§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16) is effectively requiring providers to research their organizations for parties with financial misconduct and sexual assault misdemeanor convictions without providing a mechanism for providers to obtain this data.
Response:
Consistent with our earlier statements—as well as with prior rulemaking efforts where we expanded the scope of various denial and revocation reasons to include additional parties—§§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16) do not require providers to perform the research the commenters indicate.
Comment:
Several commenters supported proposed §§ 424.530(a)(16) and 424.535(a)(16).
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support.
After considering the comments received, we are finalizing §§ 424.5355(a)(16) without modification.

Consistent with our proposed retroactive effective dates for all revocation reasons, we proposed the following effective dates for proposed § 424.535(a)(16) and (24). The § 424.535(a)(16) effective date would be the date of the conviction; this date would be referenced in new § 424.535(g)(1)(xvi). For § 424.535(a)(24), we proposed in new § 424.535(g)(1)(xxiv) an effective date that is the date on which CMS or its contractor determines that the provider should be revoked under § 424.535(a)(24); this is due to the difficulty in establishing a concrete date as to when the risk addressed in § 424.535(g)(1)(xxiv) commenced.

Numerous commenters opposed these proposed retroactive effective dates. They maintained that a misdemeanor conviction occurring some time ago should not require the provider to repay potentially years of Medicare payments. Regarding § 424.535(a)(24), they believed it would be unfair to recoup payments simply because the provider's location is near other providers. The commenters, in short, believed these retroactive dates could financially harm providers and cause beneficiary access issues.
(
