Response:
We appreciate this feedback. Concerning § 424.535(a)(16), the proposed effective date is the same as that for felony convictions § 424.535(a)(3). In both cases, the conviction presents a risk regardless of when it occurred. Hence, we believe it is appropriate to use the date it occurred as the revocation effective date. With respect to § 424.535(a)(24), we reiterate that: (1) as with § 424.535(a)(19), the issue is the risk presented and not the provider's location per se; and (2) § 424.535(a)(24) will only be used in exceptional situations. We add that even if the risk under § 424.535(a)(24) began years ago, the revocation effective date only goes back to the date on which CMS determines that the provider should be revoked. (7) Revised and New Denial Reasons (§ 424.530(a))
We also proposed a number of revised and new denial reasons in § 424.530(a).
(a) Changes to Existing Denial Reasons
Some of the following proposed denial reasons would be expanded to include actions by managing employees and managing organizations. We received comments from stakeholders: (1) regarding the meaning of “managing employee” in the context of these denial reasons; and (2) expressing concern that a broad interpretation of “managing employee” could result in an increased number of denials. These comments will be addressed in our later discussion of our proposed revision to § 424.502's “managing employee” definition.
(i) Debt (§ 424.530(a)(6))
Current § 424.530(a)(6)(i) and (ii) permit denial if the enrolling provider or owner (as defined in § 424.502) thereof—
Has an existing Medicare debt; or
Was previously the owner of a provider that had a Medicare debt when the latter provider's enrollment was voluntarily terminated, involuntarily terminated, or revoked (and additional criteria in § 424.530(a)(6)(ii)(A) through (C) are met).
We proposed to include within the scope of § 424.530(a)(6) the provider's managing employees, managing organizations, and individuals and entities with any other form of business or financial relationship with the provider.
As noted in prior rulemaking efforts, managing employees and managing organizations (as defined in § 424.502) often have as much or more influence over a provider's day-to-day operations as an owner. Yet § 424.530(a)(6) only references the provider itself and its owners. Section 424.530(a)(6) thus cannot prevent enrollment if, for instance, a managing employee or organization of the prior provider ran its daily operations, was responsible for its accumulation of large debts, and now seeks to re-enter Medicare through their ownership of the new provider. Too, we have seen instances where parties other than owners and managing employees and organizations were involved with the former provider in some capacity. Therefore, the central issue is not the precise form or label of the relationship with the former provider—that is, whether it was ownership, financial, etc. It is instead the relationship itself and the party's effort to enroll new locations or reenter Medicare through the new provider.
We received a number of comments on our proposal.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that before denying a provider under § 424.530(a)(6)(i) or (ii) based on the debt of another party (for instance, managing employee), CMS should add required factors to both paragraphs. Other commenters maintained that CMS's proposed § 424.530(a)(6) expansion could deny enrollment to providers based on financial obligations of parties that might only be minimally involved with the provider.
Response:
After reviewing the comments received, we are not finalizing our proposed revisions to § 424.530(a)(6).
(ii) Payment Suspension (§ 424.530(a)(7))
Denial is permitted under § 424.530(a)(7) if the provider, or any owning or managing employee or organization of the provider, is currently under a Medicare or Medicaid payment suspension (as defined in §§ 405.370 through 405.372 or in § 455.23). We proposed to expand § 424.530(a)(7) to include individuals and entities with any other form of business or financial relationship with the provider. We explained that because a payment suspension is a serious matter, relationships other than those involving ownership and management should be considered under § 424.530(a)(7).
As with proposed § 424.530(a)(6), commenters expressed concern that the “any other form of business or financial relationship” category is unclear and potentially very wide in applicability. After reviewing these and other comments, we have decided not to finalize our proposed revisions to § 424.530(a)(7).
(iii) Program Terminations/Suspensions (§ 424.530(a)(14))
CMS may deny enrollment under current § 424.530(a)(14)(i) if—
The provider is currently terminated or suspended (or otherwise barred) from participation in a State Medicaid program or any other Federal health care program; or
The provider's license is currently revoked or suspended in a State other than that in which the provider is enrolling.
We proposed two changes to § 424.530(a)(14)(i). One would include the provider's owners, managing employees, and managing organizations within its scope. This aligns with several other denial reasons—such as existing § 424.530(a)(3) and, as noted, (a)(7)—that include actions against owners and managing employees/organizations. Similar to these other denial grounds, revised § 424.530(a)(14)(i) would help prevent situations where the owning/managing party's conduct that led to the licensure action or the other program termination/suspension could be repeated with the prospective Medicare provider, especially considering the influence such parties typically have over a provider's operations. Furthermore, it could keep such parties from entering Medicare via a new provider, hoping to shield themselves from § 424.530(a)(14)(i)'s application due to the provision's current limitation to providers.
The other change would expand licenses to include those voluntarily surrendered in lieu of further disciplinary action. We have provisions in §§ 424.530 and 424.535 whose purview includes voluntary surrenders, and we believe the same approach for § 424.530(a)(14)(i) is needed because our overriding concern is the loss of the license rather than the type of loss. Voluntary surrenders in lieu of further disciplinary action, in our view, are as much a threat to the Trust Funds and beneficiaries as revocations and suspensions, since they all involve problematic conduct.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
(

Comment:
Commenters questioned how CMS would apply § 424.530(a)(14)(i) in light of our proposed expansion of § 424.502's “managing employee” definition. Others stated that the proposed expansion of § 424.530(a)(14)(i) is too broad and should not be finalized.

We also disagree that revised § 424.530(a)(14)(i) would be too broad. The addition of managing employee and organizations to its scope is consistent with other denial and revocation grounds pertaining to such parties.

(b) New Denial Reasons
(i) Misdemeanor Convictions (§ 424.530(a)(16))
(A) New § 424.530(a)(16)
As previously noted, w proposed to duplicate proposed § 424.535(a)(16) in § 424.530(a)(16) (also presently designated as “Reserved”) as a new denial ground. The same rationale is involved: the need to protect beneficiaries and the Trust Funds against parties convicted of sexual assault or financial misconduct misdemeanors.
The comments we received on this proposal mirrored those concerning § 424.535(a)(16), discussed earlier. Our responses are also the same. Thus, we are finalizing proposed § 424.530(a)(16) without modification.
(B) “Final Adverse Action” Definition
Section 424.502 defines “final adverse action” as any of the following: (1) Medicare revocation; (2) State health care license suspension or revocation; (3) revocation or suspension by an accreditation organization; (4) felony conviction; or (5) exclusion or debarment. Given our proposed denial and revocation reasons based on a misdemeanor conviction for sexual assault or financial misconduct, we proposed to add such misdemeanors as new paragraph (6) in the “final adverse action” definition. (As with felony convictions in paragraph (4), the 10-year period would be that preceding enrollment, revalidation, or reenrollment.)
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS should delay this change (suggesting 2 years of non-enforcement) to enable providers to evaluate applicable individuals, obtain updated disclosures, and take corrective action where necessary.
Response:
We respectfully are unable to delay the implementation or enforcement of this or any of our finalized provisions considering the important program safeguard issues they address.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS explain the practical implications of our revision to the “final adverse action” definition.
Response:
The principal implication is that under § 424.518(c)(3)(ii)(E), providers with a final adverse action within the past 10 years are screened at the “high” level. We believe providers with the misdemeanors in question would warrant this elevated screening.
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing our proposed revision to the “final adverse action” definition without modification.
(ii) Same Suite (§ 424.530(a)(19))
We proposed a new denial ground in § 424.530(a)(19) based on the provider having its practice location in the same suite or office as another provider whose Medicare enrollment has been revoked or denied. Sharing a suite or office with a provider who has been deemed non-compliant with Medicare requirements could spur concerns about the newly enrolling provider's own willingness to retain compliance if enrolled. This is particularly true when—in situations we have seen—several providers in the same suite engage (or seek to engage) in a fraud scheme, have their Medicare enrollments revoked or denied, and another provider aims to enroll in that same office. Considering the risks posed by the revoked or denied provider, we believe we must be able to prevent the new enrollment if circumstances justify it.
We explained in the proposed rule that § 424.530(a)(19) would differ from proposed § 424.535(a)(24). The latter is a revocation reason and not a denial ground; it is also partly based on the
(
printed page 72110)
number of nearby providers, whereas § 424.530(a)(19) is based on shared suites and offices. Sections 424.530(a)(19) and 424.535(a)(24) therefore complement but do not duplicate each other.
We recognize that, for example, physicians that are part of a group frequently share the same suite. If 10 physicians are in the group and one (Dr. X) has their enrollment revoked, this does not automatically mean that a prospective (and Medicare enrolling) 11th group member will be denied enrollment based on Dr X's revocation. Every situation is different, and CMS will only invoke § 424.530(a)(19) when proper.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Numerous commenters opposed our proposal. They stated that space and office sharing is extremely common—especially for purposes of cost-savings and strengthening of patient care—and not indicative of fraud, waste, or abuse. It would be improper, they added, to deny a provider on this ground, especially when the provider may have no knowledge of, connection to, or control over a neighboring provider's enrollment status.
Response:
We appreciate and understand this feedback. As stated, we acknowledge that space-sharing (particularly involving physician practices) is very common and does not by itself raise serious program integrity concerns. Yet we reiterate that there have been situations where providers in a shared office or suite have engaged—or, based on the facts and circumstances of the case, may engage in—improper activity. The need to protect Medicare beneficiaries and the Trust Funds requires that we have the ability to address these situations. We believe that § 424.530(a)(19) could assist in this by enabling denial of an enrollment that might exacerbate the problem.
Comment:
Commenters stated that CMS should establish regulatory factors, criteria, standards, and thresholds for potential § 424.530(a)(19) cases. These should include, for example, requiring: (1) a clear connection between the enrolling provider and the other provider's denied or revoked enrollment (and the conduct behind (or basis for) that other denial or revocation); (2) the enrolling provider's knowledge of the other denial or revocation; (3) common ownership, control, or coordination between the two providers; and (4) a lookback period, whereby § 424.530(a)(19) would not apply if the other provider's revocation or denial occurred more than a certain number of years ago.
Response:
For reasons mentioned previously, we respectfully decline to add said criteria and thresholds to § 424.530(a)(19). As mentioned, though, CMS will only invoke § 424.530(a)(19) when warranted by the facts and circumstances of the case.
Comment:
Commenters stated that instead of § 424.530(a)(19), CMS should concentrate on the individual behavior of each provider rather than tie the latter to a co-tenant's improper conduct. Additional commenters recommended that any § 424.530(a)(19) denial require a documented, individualized finding connecting the enrolling provider to fraud, waste, or abuse.
Response:
While we appreciate the commenters' feedback, we have explained in this rule, the proposed rule, and prior rules that certain relationships and affiliations—whether organizational, managerial, business-based, geographic, etc.—can present significant risks to Medicare. This by no stretch means that all (or even most) of them do, but some can in certain circumstances. If we simply disregarded all potentially problematic relationships and arrangements and only took action after an individual provider engaged in fraud or misconduct, this would—as previously noted with respect to § 424.535(a)(24)—revert to a “pay-and-chase” model. In other words, we must: (1) proactively prevent improper activity before it happens; (2) treat the risk of misconduct as seriously as we do actual misconduct; and (3) deter possible wrongdoing involving relationships, multiple providers, and multiples parties as much as that involving a single provider. This is the basic reason for § 424.530(a)(19), § 424.535(a)(24), and certain other provisions promulgated in this and past rules. Even if the enrolling provider was not directly involved in its co-tenant's activities, we must have to ability to take action as needed to protect the Medicare program against potential threats.
Comment:
Commenters stated that CMS should establish a safe harbor for providers that can demonstrate a legitimate, documented clinical or business rationale for co-location.
Response:
While we appreciate this recommendation, the issue is not the need or rationale for the co-location; many such arrangements are for entirely legitimate purposes. Rather, it is the risk associated with the co-location due to the other provider's denial or revocation, which is why we must respectfully decline the commenters' safe-harbor request.
Comment:
A commenter stated that because existing § 424.57(c)(29) prohibits DMEPOS suppliers from co-locating with another provider or supplier, § 424.530(a)(19) is unnecessary and duplicative.
Response:
We respectfully disagree because the two provisions address different situations. Section 424.57(c)(29) is restricted to DMEPOS suppliers and prohibits co-location. Proposed § 424.530(a)(19) is not provider-type specific, does not itself bar space-sharing, and involves sharing an office or suite with a denied or revoked provider.
Comment:
A few commenters contended that § 424.530(a)(19) should not apply if the enrolling provider has no ownership, management, financial, or operational relationship with the revoked or denied provider.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. As stated elsewhere in this final rule section V.C., we cannot regulatorily exclude potential scenarios from our proposed denial and revocation provisions, for the facts of each case will vary. Indeed, such exemptions could impair program integrity if, to illustrate, the circumstances of a particular exempted situation warranted denial or revocation but the exception prohibited action on our part.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that § 424.530(a)(19) could discourage physicians and practitioners from joining and co-locating with group practices out of concern that their enrollments may be denied if the group has a denied or revoked provider.
Response:
We respectfully disagree for two reasons. First, denials on this ground will be the exception, not the norm. They will only occur when genuinely justified. Second, we have added and expanded numerous denial and revocation grounds over the past two decades to include certain relationships and affiliations. We are unaware of large numbers of providers and other parties avoiding such arrangements as a result. We believe this will hold true with § 424.530(a)(19), too.
Comment:
A few commenters urged CMS to state in the regulatory text that § 424.530(a)(19) would not apply to situations where a physician is: (1) joining an established group practice; or (2) otherwise enrolling at a location where the revoked or denied provider is no longer present.
Response:
For reasons already stated, we cannot exempt certain arrangements from § 424.530(a)(19)'s scope. Regarding the second comment, CMS will issue guidance on this matter.

Comment:

Response:
We respectfully believe that this phrase's meaning is plain on its face.
Comment:
Noting our earlier scenario of a 10-physician group, a commenter—seemingly believing this constituted an exception to § 424.530(a)(19)—requested that it be included in the regulatory text.
Response:
While we appreciate this request, our scenario was not an exemption. (iii) Hospice Medical Directors and Administrators (§ 424.530(a)(20))
We explained at length in the proposed rule the serious program integrity issues involving hospices. CMS in recent years has taken numerous steps to address them, including, for example:
Under § 424.518(c), requiring persons who directly or indirectly own 5 percent or more of a newly enrolling hospice (or a hospice undergoing any ownership change) to submit fingerprints for a criminal background check.
Requiring hospice medical directors who certify a patient's terminal illness under § 418.22(c) to be enrolled in or opted out of Medicare, which enables CMS to screen the medical director.
Clarifying that hospice medical directors and administrators are “managing employees” (as that term is defined in § 424.502) and thus must be reported on the hospice's Form CMS-855A enrollment application (OMB Control No. 0938-0685). This helps ensure that CMS knows the identities of these parties and can vet them for potential issues.
In light of medical directors' and administrators' managing control over hospices, we believed that closer oversight of these individuals was necessary—particularly considering: (1) the criminal and False Claims Act cases we have seen involving hospice operators;
[
38
]
and (2) reports of physicians falsely certifying patients' terminal statuses.
[
39
]
Despite the aforementioned steps, we continue to have program integrity concerns about hospice operators. We still see instances of false physician certifications, kickbacks to certifying physicians, criminal cases involving administrators, hospices billing Medicare while non-compliant with enrollment requirements, etc. On a more specific level, we outlined in the proposed rule three particularly problematic issues.
First, there are individuals who serve as medical director or administrator of numerous hospices. Ensuring—(1) quality care to hospice patients; (2) the efficiency of the hospice's operations; (3) compliance with Medicare requirements; and (4) hospice program integrity requires the full attention and oversight of the medical director and administrator. We believe that having these roles at numerous facilities limits the time the individual can spend on each facility's operations and raises questions about the person's commitment to oversight. This places hospice beneficiaries and program integrity at risk.
Second, we have seen cases where the medical director or administrator is very far from the physical hospice facility; several instances, in fact, involved the hospice and medical director being on opposite sides of the country (for instance, the medical director is in New York, and the hospice is in California). This, too, generates significant concerns about the individual's oversight of the hospice.
Third, certain hospices have been using medical directors with inactive licenses. Section 418.22(c), as noted, requires the medical director who initially certifies the beneficiary's terminal status to be enrolled in or opted-out of Medicare. However, if the medical director is not certifying Medicare beneficiaries' terminal status—and said physician is neither billing Medicare nor ordering/certifying the services/items outlined in § 424.507—enrollment is not required. Therefore, CMS might not know whether the medical director's license is active and only learn of the inactive status later. Since the medical director Conditions of Participation (CoPs) at § 418.102 and personnel requirements for physicians at § 418.114(b)(1) require hospice medical directors to be physicians (and thus licensed), hospices that have medical directors with inactive licenses are not compliant with the CoP Medicare requirements.
To further address hospice medial director and administrator program integrity issues and to protect beneficiaries, we proposed new § 424.530(a)(20). This would permit denial of a hospice's enrollment application if any of the following apply:
The enrolling hospice's medical director is—
++ The medical director of multiple other hospices, or
++ Practices at such a distance (for example, in a different state) from the enrolling hospice that the medical director cannot realistically perform all medical director functions required under
42 CFR part 418
.
The enrolling hospice's administrator is—
++ The administrator of multiple other hospices; or
++ Located at such a distance from the enrolling hospice that the administrator cannot realistically perform all administrator functions required under
42 CFR part 418
.
The hospice's medical director does not have an active physician medical license in the State in which they are practicing.
Section 424.530(a)(20) would not: (1) formally prohibit medical directors and administrators from serving at more than one hospice; or (2) change hospice CoPs or other hospice policies in
42 CFR part 418
. It would simply help us address situations where the hospice's prospective enrollment raises the program integrity concerns outlined in this section V.C. of this final rule.

Commenters opposed the multiple hospice and distance provisions in § 424.530(a)(20). They believed our proposal could harm the ability of these hospices (particularly rural ones) to attract such officials. A
(

It is instead aimed at isolated but highly disconcerting situations we have seen that involve, for instance, potential program integrity or beneficiary safety issues. We seek to assure hospices that—as with other denial and revocation grounds—we would only apply § 424.530(a)(20) in limited instances and after a careful review of the facts and circumstances involved. (8) Reapplication Bar (§ 424.530(f))
Under § 424.530(f), CMS may prohibit a prospective provider from enrolling in Medicare for up to 10 years if its enrollment application is denied because the provider submitted false or misleading information on or with (or omitted information from) its application to gain enrollment in Medicare. The goal is to prevent dishonest providers from submitting false information on their initial application and, after being denied enrollment on this ground under § 424.530(a)(4), simply submitting a new application with correct data.
We believe that restricting § 424.530(f) to instances involving false information limits its potential effectiveness, for there are other § 424.530(a) denial reasons that could involve similarly inappropriate provider behavior. Assume a prospective provider's enrollment is denied because the provider is: (1) unlicensed; (2) OIG excluded or has a recent felony conviction; (3) using a false storefront as its practice location; (4) under a current Medicare and Medicaid payment suspension based on a credible allegation of fraud; (5) terminated from another Federal health care program; or (6) revoked from Medicare and attempting to enroll under a different identity. This casts serious doubt as to the provider's honesty and trustworthiness, since the provider likely knows it cannot enroll but is nonetheless hoping to somehow “sneak into” the program; indeed, without a reapplication bar in these and similar situations, the provider might routinely submit more such applications with this nefarious objective in mind.
Accordingly, and to safeguard the Medicare program, we proposed to revise the introductory text of § 424.530(f) to allow CMS to impose a reapplication bar for up to 10 years based on any § 424.530(a) denial reason (not merely § 424.530(a)(4)). We also proposed to delete factors at § 424.530(f)(2) that CMS currently must consider in determining whether to impose a reapplication bar (and the length thereof) for a § 424.530(a)(4) denial. There are two related reasons for this latter proposal. First, the current § 424.530(a)(4) factors pertain strictly to false or misleading data situations and would thus be inapplicable to other denial grounds. Second, proposing different § 424.530(a)(4) criteria would essentially present the same problem mentioned in the previous sentence—specifically, a single set of § 424.530(f) factors could not possibly apply to all § 424.530(a) denial reasons considering the varying facts of each.
Unlike reenrollment bars under § 424.535(c), reapplication bars are discretionary. CMS need not impose them, and we are not proposing to change this. We recognize that less serious denial situations—such as, but not limited to, failure to pay an application fee—might not warrant a reapplication bar. Our focus is mostly on providers whose conduct raises significant program integrity concerns.
We would retain current § 424.530(f)(1) and (f)(3), which address, respectively, the bar's: (1) applicability to the provider's other names, identities, etc.; and (2) impact on the ordering, referral, certification, or prescription of services, items, or drugs. Paragraph (f)(3), though, would be re-designated as revised paragraph (f)(2).

Only if a 10-year bar is truly necessary will it be imposed, and we will carefully consider the facts and circumstances in every reapplication bar case.

(9) Changes in Majority Ownership (CIMOs)
We previously mentioned § 424.550(b) and § 424.551, the former pertaining to HHAs and hospices and the latter to DMEPOS suppliers (hereafter collectively “providers”). Under these provisions, if the provider undergoes a CIMO within 36 months of its initial enrollment—or within 36 months of its most recent CIMO—and no exception applies, the provider's enrollment is terminated. (For HHAs and hospices, the provider agreement is also terminated and does not transfer to the new owner.) The provider under its new majority ownership must enroll as a new provider and undergo a State survey or accreditation. (DMEPOS suppliers must obtain a new accreditation.)
There are two main purposes of this “36-month rule”. First, it enables CMS to perform a complete screening and vetting of the provider under its new ownership. This is vital for ensuring that the provider is compliant with all Medicare enrollment requirements. Second, it helps prevent “flipping”. This involves a party enrolling a provider for the sole purpose of quickly selling it to another party without the latter having to newly enroll or undergo a survey/accreditation. The seller's exclusive objective is profit and not patient care, which places beneficiaries and the Trust Funds at risk.
While the 36-month rule has helped to stem flipping and facilitate closer scrutiny of new owners, we have seen provider efforts to circumvent or ignore it. These include, but are not limited to:
Failing to notify CMS of the ownership change—meaning the sale occurs and the buyer assumes ownership under the existing enrollment without enrolling the entity as a new provider with a new survey/accreditation. Only later does CMS learn of the sale.
Using a management (or similar) agreement in lieu of a formal sales agreement. Here, the management agreement states that: (1) managerial (and effectively all other) authority over the provider is transferred to Party X; and (2) X intends to later purchase the provider. Once the 36-month period expires, the sale occurs. In essence, Party X is purchasing the provider within the 36-month period but under the guise of a “management agreement”.
Such inappropriate attempts to avoid the 36-month rule undercut the rule's overriding objective of protecting beneficiaries and the Trust Funds from unvetted and potentially problematic entities. To deter these efforts, we proposed in new §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25) that we may deny or revoke enrollment if CMS determines that the HHA, hospice, or DMEPOS supplier failed to comply with the provisions and requirements of, as applicable, §§ 424.550(b) or 424.551. The § 424.535(a)(25) revocation effective date under new § 424.535(g)(1)(xxv) would be the date on which CMS or its contractor determined that the provider should be revoked.

address various types of factual situations.
