Several commenters expressed concern that our proposals appear to prohibit management agreements in CIMO situations. They stated that such arrangements are common and legitimate.
Response:
Sections 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25) do not prohibit such agreements
per se.
However, and depending on the situation's circumstances, they can involve improper efforts to sidestep the 36-month rule and its important protections—hence our citing it as an example of §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25)'s potential applicability.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS identify which types of ownership arrangements it deems “abusive” under the 36-month rule.
Response:
We respectfully decline the commenter's request because: (1) neither §§ 424.530(a)(22) nor 424.535(a)(25) use the term “abusive”, nor did we do so in the proposed rule's preamble discussion of these two provisions; and (2) we cannot deem certain transactions as abusive or not abusive without assessing the case's specific and unique facts.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS to: (1) remove the reference to § 424.550(b) in § 424.535(a)(25); and (2) state that revocation is permissible if an HHA or hospice failed to report material ownership-related information within 30 days as required in § 424.516(e)(1). While it was somewhat unclear, the commenter appeared to contend that so long as the provider reported material data about the CIMO within 30 days, this should satisfy CMS' concerns about CIMO compliance.
Response:
We respectfully disagree for two reasons. First, neither § 424.516(e)(1) nor § 424.550(b) contains a materiality standard. Required data must be reported regardless of its materiality. Second, and as explained in the proposed rule, our concerns go beyond the mere timely reporting of the change to include, for instance, non-compliance with other requirements as well as circumvention.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that CMS should: (1) furnish additional guidance on what constitutes a CIMO and outline the facts that demonstrate a compliant CIMO; and (2) allow providers to obtain formal, pre-sale determinations directly from CMS or the MAC regarding whether their transaction (or potential transaction) triggers the 36-month rule's requirements.
Response:
We appreciate the comments but believe they are outside the scope of this final rule.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS establish a risk-based “Trusted Provider” CIMO voluntary registration and recognition mechanism. Under this approach, vetted, good-faith HHAs and hospices—such as, the commenter believed, those with no adverse history or that are currently accredited—may complete a CIMO via expedited screening, with the provider agreement and billing privileges remaining intact; no new enrollment and survey would be required. The commenter maintained that this would be consistent with CMS' existing risk-based screening process under § 424.518.
Response:
We appreciate this suggestion but believe it is outside the scope of this final rule.
Comment:
A commenter opposed proposed § 424.535(g)(1)(xxv)'s revocation effective date of “the date on which CMS or its contractor determined that the provider should be revoked.” The commenter believed this: (1) is inconsistent with the more fixed effective dates in § 424.535(g); and (2) would give CMS complete discretion to make the effective date retroactive to the provider's initial enrollment date. The commenter stated that the effective date should instead be that of the management agreement or other event that triggered the § 424.550(b) violation.
Response:
Most respectfully, we believe the commenter may be misinterpreting this effective date. The § 424.535(g)(1)(xxv) date is the date of CMS's decision to revoke, not any random date back to which CMS believes the revocation should be made retroactive. The decision date is, in fact, a fixed date—and as previously explained, it is necessary due to (1) the variety of situations that can arise under § 424.535(a)(25); and(2) the consequent difficulty of assigning a single effective date to cover all of them.
Comment:
A commenter stated that a DMEPOS supplier should not be required to enroll as a new supplier and obtain a new accreditation after a CIMO.
Response:
While we appreciate this comment, it appeared to relate to the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule wherein we finalized §§ 424.551. Hence, we believe it is outside the scope of the present final rule.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that the following parties and situations should be exempt from §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25): (1) management or operating arrangements in connection with a bona fide joint venture—regardless of which joint venture participant holds the provider agreement or State license during the transition; (2) within-window providers as part of a bona fide package transaction not involving circumvention of § 424.550(b); and (3) management arrangements used to bridge CHOW processing for such packages.
Response:
While we appreciate these requests, we are unable to formally exempt these and other transactions from the purview of §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25) because: (1) such situations can still involve §§ 424.550(b) and 424.551 non-compliance; and (2) doing so would involve CMS making determinations before reviewing the facts of a particular case.
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing proposed §§ 424.530(a)(22) and 424.535(a)(25) without modification.
3. Preclusion List (
42 CFR 422.2
and
423.100
)
Addressed primarily in
42 CFR 422.222
and
423.120
, the preclusion list is a compilation of providers and prescribers who are prohibited from receiving payment for furnished, ordered, or prescribed MA items/services and Part D drugs. The list's objective is to effectively bar from the MA and Part D programs various entities and persons that pose program integrity risks. Per the definition of “preclusion list” in §§ 422.2 and 423.100, a party may be placed on said list if they fall into any of the following three categories:
Currently revoked under Medicare for a reason other than that in § 424.535(a)(3) (which addresses felony convictions), the reenrollment bar has not expired, and CMS determines that the underlying conduct that led to the revocation is detrimental to the Medicare program's best interests.
Engaged in behavior, other than that described in § 424.535(a)(3): (1) for which CMS could have revoked the provider/prescriber to the extent applicable had they been enrolled in Medicare; and (2) that CMS determines is detrimental to the Medicare program's best interests.
Regardless of whether the provider/prescriber is or was enrolled in Medicare, has been convicted of a felony under Federal or State law within the previous 10 years that CMS deems detrimental to the Medicare program's best interests.
We proposed to expand this third category to include felony convictions against the provider/prescriber's owner, managing employee, managing organization, corporate director, or corporate officer. As already stated,
(
printed page 72116)
these parties typically exercise considerable influence over a provider/prescriber's operations, and a felony conviction against said party greatly concerns us; indeed, this is precisely why §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3) permit denial or revocation based on felony convictions against owners, managing employees/organizations, and corporate officers/directors. Our proposed change would not only ensure greater consistency with §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3) but also help protect the MA and Part D programs from program integrity risks.
The specific regulatory revisions would be to paragraph (3) of the “preclusion list” definitions in §§ 422.2 and 423.100. The language therein stating that the prescriber/provider, “regardless of whether they are or were enrolled in Medicare, has been convicted of a felony. . . ” would be changed to the prescriber/provider, “regardless of whether they are or were enrolled in Medicare—or an owner, managing employee, managing organization, director, or officer (as those terms are defined in § 424.502) thereof—has been convicted of a felony . . .”.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters disagreed with our proposed preclusion list expansion. They stated that providers could have difficulty identifying and verifying information regarding individuals associated with the provider. They requested that CMS: (1) establish reasonable due diligence expectations; and (2) ensure that providers are not penalized for information they could not reasonably have known or verified. Commenters further recommended that CMS promulgate factors for determining whether the provider should be added to the preclusion list. Recommended criteria included (but were not limited to) a nexus between the provider and the owning or managing party's action, the nature of the conviction, the risk posed to Medicare, when the conviction occurred, and the convicted party's role within the provider organization.
Response:
Consistent with §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3)'s application to felony convictions of parties other than the provider, the primary consideration must always be the party's felony conviction itself and not: (1) the provider's efforts in screening personnel or associated parties; or (2) whether the provider knew of (or was involved in) the conduct. Similar to our earlier statements, we cannot base preclusion decisions under revised paragraph (3) on a knowledge or due diligence standard. If we did, providers could consistently avoid denial or revocation by simply asserting that they knew nothing of the conduct; this obviously would hamper our program integrity efforts, harm the Trust Funds, and potentially endanger beneficiaries. Hence, we respectfully decline to establish the requested knowledge or diligence standard.
Insofar as promulgating factors, we maintain our position that regulatorily-specified criteria hamstring our efforts to take required action against problematic providers. Therefore, we must decline to establish them with respect to revised paragraph (3) of the “preclusion list” definition.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that it would be unfair to place a provider on the preclusion list based on a felony conviction of a party who may not have close, constant involvement with the provider's operations. They believed that CMS should not finalize its proposed expansion or, at a minimum, remove managing employees and organizations from the proposal.
Response:
We disagree. Felony convictions are very serious matters, and the parties we propose to include within the preclusion list definition are sufficiently linked to the provider to—if warranted under the facts and circumstances—trigger the preclusion list's application.
Comment:
A few commenters questioned whether a provider whose managing employee has a felony conviction would be added to or removed (as applicable) from the preclusion list if the provider terminated the person's employment. They requested that CMS allow providers to avoid the preclusion list by severing such relationships upon CMS notice of the issue.
Response:
Section 424.535(e), in certain instances, affords a revoked provider a 15-day opportunity to remove from their organization the entity or individual whose action (for example, a managing employee's felony conviction) generated the provider's revocation. While there is no concomitant provision in our preclusion list regulations, we will consider this issue for future rulemaking.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS explain why: (1) this preclusion list expansion is necessary; and (2) the problem cannot be addressed via existing means such as screening, denial, or revocation. The commenter added that a provider should only be included on the preclusion list per our proposal if a clear and ongoing program integrity risk exists.
Response:
As we explained in the proposed rule, in this final rule, and when we promulgated (and later expanded) §§ 424.530(a)(3) and 424.535(a)(3), providers with owners and managing employees that have felony convictions have always generated serious and justifiable program integrity concerns. This is partly, but by no means exclusively, due to the possibility that the person's conduct may be replicated in the provider setting. Since there are no other statutory or regulatory means of addressing this vulnerability with respect to Medicare programs other than Parts A and B, our proposal is necessary.
Regarding the commenter's last statement, CMS: (1) reviews the facts and circumstances of every potential preclusion list case under current paragraph (3) of the “preclusion list” definition; (2) will do the same with our proposed change; and (3) takes action only when justified.
Comment:
A comment stated that in light of the “preclusion list” definition expansion, CMS should—
Explain how qualifying convictions will be identified and verified;
Clarify how and when providers, prescribers, and MA and Part D plans will be notified;
Identify when preclusion list updates and associated payment consequences will take effect;
Identify w responsibilities plans will have before payment is affected;
Ensure that affected providers receive timely notice and a meaningful opportunity to—
++ Correct erroneous information;
++ Demonstrate that the provision does not apply; or
++ Otherwise challenge the proposed placement on the preclusion; and
Clarify how MA and Part D plans should proceed while a determination is disputed or under review so that payment is not improperly disrupted based on unresolved information.
Response:
Our proposed expansion does not change any procedures regarding the six issues the commenter raised, though we note there is no pre-preclusion quasi-appeals system. Should the commenter have questions regarding the preclusion list process, we respectfully recommend visiting CMS' preclusion list website at
https://www.cms.gov/​medicare/​enrollment-renewal/​providers-suppliers/​chain-ownership-system-pecos/​preclusion-list
.
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing our proposed changes to the preclusion list
(
printed page 72117)
definitions in §§ 422.2 and 423.100 without modification.
4. Temporary Moratoria (§ 424.570)
Pursuant to section 1866(j)(7) of the Act and § 424.570, we imposed several temporary enrollment moratoria between 2013 and 2019, and—as of May 13, 2026—there are national moratoria on the enrollment of new HHAs and hospices.
[
40
]
All moratoria (including a moratorium extension) are announced via a notice published in the
Federal Register
. Under §  424.570(a)(1)(iii)(A) through (C), a temporary moratorium does not apply to any of the following:
Changes in practice location (except if the location is changing from a location outside the moratorium area to a location inside the moratorium area).
Changes in provider or supplier information, such as phone numbers.
Changes in ownership (except changes in ownership of HHAs that would require an initial enrollment).
Since restarting the moratorium process in 2026 after more than 6 years, we have seen several issues that we believe must be addressed in regulation.
a. Effective Date
Per §  424.570(a)(1)(iv), a temporary moratorium does not apply to any enrollment application received by the Medicare contractor prior to the date the moratorium is imposed. We proposed to revise §  424.570(a)(1)(iv) as follows:
Existing §  424.570(a)(1)(iv) would be redesignated as new §  424.570(a)(1)(iv)(A).
New §  424.570(a)(1)(iv)(B) would state that the date the moratorium is imposed is the moratorium's effective date, which is the date on which the moratorium notice was filed for public inspection at the Office of the Federal Register (OFR).
There are often gaps between when a document (such as a proposed rule) is filed for OFR public inspection and when it is published in the
Federal Register
. If we used the latter as the moratorium's imposition/effective date, the affected providers/suppliers might have several days to submit their initial applications in order to “beat the deadline.” This would partly obstruct the moratorium's goal of halting all new enrollments and could lead to a rush of new applicants during this gap, some of whom may present program integrity threats. Using the OFR filing date would prevent this scenario, for the moratorium's imposition would be immediate.
b. Ownership Changes
We proposed to change the aforementioned parenthetical in §  424.570(a)(1)(iii)(C) from “(except changes in ownership of home health agencies that would require an initial enrollment)” to “(except changes in ownership that require an initial enrollment, such as, but not limited to, an HHA, hospice, or DMEPOS supplier change in majority ownership under §§ 424.550(b) or 424.551)”. This update would codify existing CMS policy that—like HHAs—hospices and DMEPOS suppliers that undergo a non-exempt CIMO under §§ 424.550(b) or 424.551 must enroll as a new provider/supplier and are thus subject to the moratorium.
c. Other Applicability
Section 424.570(a)(1)(i) states that CMS may impose a moratorium on the enrollment of new Medicare providers and suppliers of a particular type or the establishment of new practice locations of a particular type in a particular geographic area. To clarify what qualifies as a “new” provider/supplier or practice location under the moratorium, we proposed to outline in new § 424.570(a)(1)(i)(A) through (E) the application types that—solely for purposes of § 424.570(a)—are considered “new” and to which a moratorium applies:
Initial enrollment applications.
Change of ownership applications that require an initial enrollment per § 424.570(a)(1)(iii)(C).
Enrollment applications from revoked providers/suppliers whose reenrollment bars under § 424.535(c) have expired and are seeking to enroll again in the Medicare program.
Reactivation applications.
Enrollment applications from voluntarily terminated providers/suppliers seeking to enroll again in the Medicare program.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters opposed making the moratorium effective date the date of filing at the OFR instead of the publication date. They stated that providers may not receive adequate notice of the moratorium when the notice is placed on display. They also disagreed with our statement that providers could quickly submit applications between the display and publication dates to get ahead of an effective date based on publication. They believed that using the latter date would be fairer and would give providers more time to prepare.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their thoughts. Commenters can access the
Federal Register
website for newly displayed documents no less than for newly published ones; in both cases, the information is public and retrievable. Regarding application submission, providers can indeed attempt to send in applications before the notice is published—even if the application might be incomplete due to the abbreviated timeframe to prepare and submit it. Given the important program integrity aspects of a moratorium and the consequent need for immediate implementation, we cannot afford to assume that no providers will be able to submit applications during this period. We believe the OFR filing date is appropriate notwithstanding commenters' concerns about reasonable advance notice.
Comment:
Commenters disagreed with including reactivations within § 424.570's purview. They maintained that deactivations can sometimes occur for what commenters stated were minor reasons—such as a failure to timely report certain information or 6 consecutive months of Medicare non-billing—or on grounds unrelated to fraud, waste, abuse, or other misconduct. They believed it would be unfair to prevent these providers from reactivating their enrollment based on the moratorium. In addition, they contended that reactivations do not involve the enrollment of a “new” provider because: (1) the provider remains enrolled during the deactivation period; and (2) the reactivation process is less onerous than initial enrollment. Another commenter stated that including reactivations within § 424.570 violates section 1866(j)(7) of the Act.
Response:
We thank stakeholders for these comments. We addressed the reactivation matter in the proposed rule and restate our position here.
Deactivation means the provider's billing privileges are stopped but can be restored (or “reactivated”) upon the submission of information required under § 424.540. While a deactivated provider is not revoked from Medicare, the provider's: (1) ability to bill Medicare is halted pending its reactivation; (2) enrollment is effectively shut down; and (3) participation in
(
printed page 72118)
Medicare is blocked in a manner akin to a revocation. The only material differences between a revoked and a deactivated provider are that the former: (1) is subject to a reenrollment bar and a potentially more exhaustive reentry process (for instance, undergoing a State survey or accreditation); and (2) involves appeal rights under
42 CFR part 498
whereas the latter triggers rebuttal rights. Also, the bases for both revocations and deactivations typically involve concerning provider behavior, such as non-compliance with enrollment requirements or a non-operational practice location. Even if the deactivation was based on non-billing with no nefarious conduct, said conduct could have ensued if, for example, an unscrupulous party attempted to access the provider's billing number during the non-billing period. We continue to believe that the significant similarities between deactivations and revocations warrant including reactivations within § 424.570(a)(1)(i).
We further maintain that: (1) we indeed have the legal authority to define in regulation the scope of the term “new” as used in section 1866(j)(7); and (2) we do not foresee beneficiary access issues arising from revised § 424.570 based on our past experience with moratoria.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CIMOs that (1) adhere to §§ 424.550(b) or 424.551, (2) involve compliant providers, or (3) pose no program integrity risk should be exempt from a moratorium.
Response:
We respectfully disagree because non-exempt CIMOs under §§ 424.550(b) and 424.551 are—and have always been—considered new enrollments. This is because the provider must initially enroll and undergo a State survey or accreditation to bill Medicare under its new ownership. In addition, exempting certain CIMOs based on risk would require a CMS examination of said risk for each CIMO scenario and potentially result in case-by-case moratorium exceptions, which section 1866(j)(7) does not permit.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS' moratorium authority is too broad because a moratorium can impact bona fide providers as much as problematic ones. They recommended that CMS use more targeted means of addressing fraud, waste, and abuse that would not negatively impact honest providers and their patients.
Response:
While we appreciate these comments, we believe they focused on our use of moratoria as a whole rather than our specific proposed revisions. Accordingly, we believe they are outside the scope of this final rule.
As an aside, we emphasize to stakeholders that moratoria under § 424.570(a)(1)(i) are actually very infrequent and typically limited. While our present hospice and HHA moratoria—as well as our 6-month long and now expired DMEPOS medical supply company moratorium—are nationwide—these three are the only national enrollment moratoria we have ever implemented going all the way back to 2011. Our moratoria from 2013 to 2019 were restricted to only a few provider and supplier types in certain regions. All this means that the overwhelming majority of providers and provider types—even newly enrolling ones—have not been impacted by § 424.570 to the extent it might appear to some.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that including reactivating providers within § 424.570 could lead to access to care issues without improving program integrity.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. Again, moratoria are, generally speaking, quite limited, meaning that comparatively few reactivating providers would be impacted and, consequently, patient care should not be affected. We also restate our position regarding the program integrity need for adding reactivations to § 424.570.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS should exempt from § 424.570: (1) service-line and other provider expansions involving legitimate providers; and (2) reenrollments.
Response:
We are respectfully unclear as to the specific exemptions the commenter seeks. If, by “service-line expansions”, the commenter is referencing practice location additions, these have previously been included in our moratoria because—depending in part on the provider or supplier type involved—they involve the establishment of a new site. Insofar as reenrollments, we believe the commenter is referencing situations where a provider has either voluntarily or involuntary departed the Medicare program and seeks to enroll in Medicare again. These have always been treated as initial enrollments and thus subject to our moratoria.
Comment:
A commenter supported our proposed changes to § 424.570.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS should complement any imposed temporary moratorium with the following: (1) issuing sub-regulatory guidance clarifying appropriate billing requirements for G0390 (a HCPCS code used to report trauma response team activation), including activation criteria and documentation expectations; (2) conducting targeted program integrity reviews focused on outlier billing patterns, rather than applying broad-based restrictions that may affect compliant providers; (3) increasing transparency regarding how CMS identifies and monitors high-risk utilization patterns; and (4) considering a revised reimbursement model for trauma services aligned with developing a national military and civilian system. The commenter also stated that CMS should impose a temporary moratorium on the enrollment of new trauma centers in geographic areas experiencing oversaturation.
Response:
We appreciate these suggestions but believe they are outside the scope of this final rule.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS establish a process by which reactivating providers can request an exemption from a moratorium's applicability based on administrative deactivation, contractor error, or deactivations under appeal.
Response:
While we appreciate this request, we reiterate that section 1866(j)(7) of the Act does not permit individual, case-by-case exceptions to a moratorium.
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing our proposed changes to § 424.570 without modification.
5. Hospice Reactivations (§ 424.540(b)(3))
We mentioned earlier that hospices (like HHAs) that undergo a non-exempt CIMO within 36 months of their initial enrollment (or within 36 months of their previous CIMO) must initially enroll as a new hospice and have a State survey or accreditation. A new enrollment and survey/accreditation help confirm that the hospice under its new ownership is properly vetted, is committed to furnishing quality care, meets all enrollment requirements and CoPs, and does not pose program integrity risks. The program integrity and quality of care benefits of a State survey/accreditation are why in 2009 we promulgated § 424.540(b)(3)(i), which requires a deactivated HHA to obtain an initial survey/accreditation before it can be reactivated.
We believe the payment safeguard and patient care protections afforded by § 424.540(b)(3) should be extended to hospices. The previously noted hospice problems we have seen require, in our view, much closer scrutiny of reactivating hospices—particularly
(
printed page 72119)
since, deactivated hospices are essentially blocked from Medicare. We must ensure that the reentering hospice is compliant with all Medicare requirements. Thus, we proposed to revise § 424.540(b)(3)(i) to include hospices.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported our proposed change.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support.
Comment:
A commenter stated regarding our proposal that CMS has not demonstrated that: (1) current reactivation processes are inadequate; or (2) providers deactivated for administrative reasons pose a heightened quality or program integrity risk warranting additional survey requirements. Several other commenters contended that the hospice reactivation survey requirement should exclude hospices that were deactivated for reasons other than fraud, abuse, or patient harm.
Response:
We respectfully disagree with these comments. In our view, the existing reactivation process for hospices is not entirely adequate because it lacks the protection that surveys provide. While we are uncertain as to which “administrative” reasons the commenter had in mind, all deactivated providers present a degree of risk based on the deactivation itself. This is especially the case with deactivated hospices in light of—as explained in the proposed rule—the high risk that hospices as a provider category present. Given all this, we must ensure that a reactivating hospice (that, as explained, is effectively seeking to reenter Medicare) meets the hospice CoPs via a new survey or accreditation. This protects both beneficiaries and the Trust Funds.
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing our proposed change to § 424.540(b)(3)(i) without modification.
6. Opt-Out (
42 CFR Part 405, Subpart D
)
Section 1802(b)(1) of the Act permits certain physicians and practitioners to opt-out of Medicare. Under opt-out, neither the physician/practitioner nor the beneficiary submits a bill to Medicare for services performed. Instead, the beneficiary pays the physician/practitioner out-of-pocket and neither party is reimbursed by Medicare. A private contract is signed between the physician/practitioner and the beneficiary that states, in essence, that neither can receive payment from Medicare for the services performed. The physician/practitioner must also submit an affidavit to Medicare expressing a decision to opt-out of the program and confirming, as further described in § 405.420, compliance with opt-out requirements. Opt-out periods are for 2 years.
Provisions in
42 CFR part 405, subpart D
, govern Medicare opt-out. We proposed the following two regulatory clarifications, both of which reflect current policy.
First, opt-out periods are automatically renewed pursuant to section 1802(b)(3) of the Act unless the physician/practitioner—consistent with § 405.445(a)—notifies the appropriate MAC not later than 30 days before the end of the 2-year period indicating that they do not want to extend the affidavit's extension for a subsequent 2-year period. In outlining the types of CMS opt-out determinations that are considered “initial” under § 498.3(b) (and thus appealable under
42 CFR part 498
), § 405.450(a) includes the individual's failure to “timely renew opt-out”. Since opt-out is automatically extended absent the occurrence in § 405.445(a), we proposed to change the quoted language in § 405.450(a) to “timely cancel automatic renewal”; a similar change would be made to § 498.3(b)(19), which lists various initial opt-out-related determinations.
Second, § 405.400 defines “opt-out period” as meaning, in part—with respect to an affidavit that meets the requirements of § 405.420—a 2-year period beginning on the date the affidavit is signed (as specified by § 405.410(c)(1) or (2)). There are instances where the MAC, in reviewing and processing the physician/practitioner's submitted affidavit, needs and requests additional information or clarification from the physician/practitioner. Interested parties have asked whether—if a new affidavit must be submitted per the MAC's request and it is subsequently approved—the opt-out period begins on the signature date of the second or the first submitted affidavit. To address this, we proposed in § 405.400 to change the “opt-out period” definition that states “the date the affidavit is signed” to “the date the first submitted affidavit is signed.” This reflects our existing policy on this issue.
The comments we received on these proposed changes were supportive. No opposition was expressed. Hence, we are finalizing them without modification.
7. Affiliations
Consistent with section 1866(j)(5) of the Act, § 424.519 states that upon a CMS request, an initially enrolling or revalidating provider or supplier (hereafter collectively “provider” unless otherwise noted) must disclose any and all affiliations that it or any of its owning or managing employees or organizations (per § 424.502's definitions of “owner” and “managing employee”) has or, within the previous 5 years, had with a currently or formerly enrolled Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP provider that has a disclosable event (as defined in § 424.502). If CMS determines that the affiliation poses an undue risk of fraud, waste, or abuse, CMS may deny or revoke the provider's enrollment under § 424.530(a)(13) or § 424.535(a)(19), respectively.
Section 424.502 defines a “disclosable event” as any of the following: (1) a current uncollected debt to Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP; (2) a payment suspension under a Federal health care program; (3) an OIG exclusion; or (4) a denial, revocation or termination of a Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP enrollment.
For purposes of § 424.519, an “affiliation” under § 424.502 includes any of the following (outlined in paragraphs (1) through (5) of the “affiliation” definition):
A 5 percent or greater direct or indirect ownership interest that an individual or entity has in another organization.
A general or limited partnership interest (regardless of the percentage) that an individual or entity has in another organization.
An interest in which an individual or entity exercises operational or managerial control over, or directly or indirectly conducts, the day-to-day operations of another organization (including sole proprietorships)—either under contract or through some other arrangement, regardless of whether or not the managing individual or entity is a W-2 employee of the organization.
An interest in which an individual is acting as an officer or director of a corporation.
Any reassignment relationship under § 424.80.
These provisions were established in a final rule published in the
Federal Register
on September 10, 2019 (
84 FR 47794
).
[
41
]
Since establishing these affiliation regulations, CMS has emphasized identifying current and past relationships between and among different providers and suppliers and, if an undue risk exists, denying or revoking the applicable provider(s).
(
printed page 72120)
This helps protect the Trust Funds and beneficiaries from threats that certain provider associations can pose. Nevertheless, we have found three issues in § 424.519 that we believe hinder the provision's effectiveness.
One involves the 5-year lookback period. Situations have arisen where a relationship from more than 5 years ago still presents an undue risk of fraud, waste, abuse. In excluding consideration of these affiliations—and, in turn, being unable to deny or revoke enrollment under §§ 424.530(a)(13) or 424.535(a)(19)—we are effectively permitting a potentially significant fraud, waste, or abuse risk to remain. This is antithetical to our duty to protect the Medicare program.
The second pertains to the “affiliation” definition in § 424.502. While it covers several types of associations, there are other conceivably problematic relationships we have encountered in our program integrity efforts. We cited the following hypotheticals in the proposed rule:
An individual or entity operates a small building with over 30 HHAs and hospices that list the building address as their practice location. Considering our earlier discussion of the high payment safeguard risk in such situations, the building operator might be involved with these providers in some type of fraud scheme.
A provider had a relationship with a financial services company that had several high-level officials convicted of fraudulent activity.
A provider hired Marketing Firm X. X had solicited beneficiaries for four DMEPOS suppliers, all of which were later revoked with a 10-year reenrollment bar.
These and other scenarios demonstrate that associations beyond those listed in the “affiliation” definition can endanger the Medicare program, for nefarious parties of all types constantly seek new means of perpetuating Medicare fraud.
The third issue also involves the “affiliation” definition, though on a narrower level—specifically, an aspect of paragraph (3) thereof warranting additional clarification. As noted, paragraph (3) addresses relationships where an individual or entity has operational or managerial control over (or directly or indirectly conducts) the day-to-day operations of another organization. (This mirrors our current definitions of “managing employee” and “managing organization in § 424.502.) As explained in the proposed rule, a recent situation arose where an individual was a medical director (Dr. A) of two providers—B and C. C was revoked from Medicare. Since a medical director is a managing employee under § 424.502, B was revoked under § 424.535(a)(19) consistent with paragraph (3) of the affiliation definition; that is, Dr. X was an individual with operational or managerial control over another entity—Providers B and C. This established the affiliation between B and C, with Dr. X as the clear link—a view that aligns not only with our longstanding interpretation of paragraph (3) but also with section 1866(j)(5) of the Act. Furthermore, we believe our position helps ensure section 1866(j)(5)'s usefulness. A provider generally acts through its owners, managers, and other personnel. If we applied paragraph (3) only to situations where a provider operates or manages another provider, we would be unable to address other cases where the real fraud, waste, and abuse risk is posed by parties affiliated with both providers. In other words, we need the ability to go within the provider organization to the operators and managers to address threats they present.
With all three issues, we believe the fraud, waste, and abuse risk itself is much more important than when the relationship triggering the risk occurred, whether the provider entity poses the risk or, instead, the managing employee, etc. Hence, we proposed the following revisions to our affiliation provisions in part 424, subpart P:
Removing the 5-year period from § 424.519(b).
Adding new paragraph (6) to the “affiliation” definition. This paragraph would include any marketing, business, fulfillment, financial, managerial, or beneficiary relationship. (The “managerial” relationships in paragraph (6) would be those not otherwise falling within paragraph (3) of the “affiliation” definition.)
Adding in paragraph (3) of the “affiliation” definition the following language between “individual or entity,” and “exercises operational”: “or any of its owning or managing employees or organizations,”.
In §§ 424.530(a)(13) and § 424.535(a)(19), insert the following language between “provider or supplier” and “has or has had”: “or any of its owning or managing employees or organizations,”.
The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed our changes to the affiliation provisions. They believed it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to detect various affiliations: (1) from more than 5 years ago; and (2) involving the provider's owners, managers, and other affiliated parties. It could also be challenging to obtain data from more distant parties. They stated that these revisions would impose a massive reporting burden and should either be significantly delayed or not finalized.
Response:
We appreciate these comments. While we understand the concerns expressed, we emphasize that affiliation data need only be reported upon a CMS request—and CMS has, to date, never requested that a provider to do so; this is because we recognize the burden this could present to providers. In utilizing §§ 424.530(a)(13) and § 424.535(a)(19), CMS has instead relied upon its authority under §§ 424.519(i) to apply these two provisions even if the provider has not yet reported (or is not required at that time to report) the affiliation to CMS. To the maximum extent possible, we will continue this approach so as not to impose these disclosure obligations and the associated burden on providers.
Comment:
Commenters maintained that regardless of whether our expanded affiliation data must be reported, there will be a substantial burden on providers because they must now research and constantly monitor all parties with whom they have or ever had an affiliation. A commenter stated that CMS in the aforementioned September 10, 2019, final rule with comment period estimated the annual cost of this activity to be $937,500—an amount that will be greatly increased if our proposed affiliation provisions are finalized.
Response:
We disagree with these comments. Providers are under no obligation to perform this monitoring. If they choose to do so, that is an independent business decision. In addition, the cited $937,500 cost was for the compilation and reporting of affiliation information pursuant to a CMS request. It was unrelated to any internal monitoring that a provider wishes to undertake on its own volition.
Although discussed in more detail in the ICR and RIA sections of this final rule, we maintain our stance that our affiliation revisions would impose no burden on providers. This is because: (1) we do not at this time anticipate making requests for disclosures; and (2) providers are not required to undertake any form of regular research or tracking of actual or potential affiliations.
Comment:
Commenters stated that if CMS finalizes its proposed affiliation changes, it should ensure that providers under §§ 424.530(c) and 424.535(e) can demonstrate termination of affiliations, managing employee relationships, or
(
printed page 72121)
business relationships—not simply for sanctions, exclusions, debts, or felonies of associated parties.
Response:
We appreciate this comment and will consider clarifying this issue in post-final rule guidance.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern that the addition of parties and relationships to § 424.535(a)(19) and § 424.502's “affiliation” definition (and the resulting potential linkages to many different providers) could result in unwarranted revocations. A commenter stated that such downstream revocations should be prohibited under § 424.535(a)(19).
Response:
We wish to assure providers that CMS reviews each potential § 424.535(a)(19) case individually, based on its own particular circumstances. This will remain so under revised § 424.535(a)(19). For this same reason, though, we cannot automatically bar these downstream revocations; if a particular case, judged on its own facts, warrants a § 424.535(a)(19) revocation, we must be able to take action regardless of whether it is downstream.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern about the meaning of “any marketing, business, fulfillment, financial, manag-erial or beneficiary relationship” and that CMS did not define these terms. They stated that this could include virtually any party with which the provider has any dealings, no matter how slight. They maintained that legitimate providers should not be penalized for very tenuous associations or held responsible for the actions of distant parties over which the provider has no control.
Response:
We note several things. First, we believe that with respect to the affiliation definition, the six types of relationships in the previously quoted language have their plain meanings. Second, our addition of paragraph (6) to the affiliation definition does not mean that every such relationship will lead to the provider's denial or revocation if a disclosable event exists. We acknowledge that many of these affiliations do not involve an undue risk of fraud, waste, and abuse. As previously mentioned, though, we have seen instances where they do, and for this reason we believe our affiliation expansions are warranted. Third, and in a similar context, the main issue is not: (1) whether the provider could control or even knew of the actions of the other party; or (2) the organizational distance (or tenuousness or materiality of the relationship) between the provider and the affiliate. It is instead the risk the affiliation poses to the Medicare program. This is the main test for whether §§ 424.530(a)(13) and 424.535(a)(19) should apply in a particular situation and is consistent with the language in section 1866(j)(5) of the Act.
All this said, we agree with commenters' concerns about including beneficiary relationships within new paragraph (6) of the “affiliation” definition. We are therefore not finalizing said inclusion.
Comment:
Commenters stated that CMS should: (1) limit the definition of “affiliation” to relationships that either have a meaningful nexus to Medicare program integrity or involve a material connection between the provider on the one hand and the other party and their disclosable event on the other; (2) define the scope of reportable affiliations; (3) require an individualized determination that the affiliation presents a current and undue risk; (4) establish reasonable due diligence expectations that reflect what providers can realistically know and verify through ordinary business practices; and (5) promulgate required factors and thresholds (such as common ownership and control). Some commenters requested that CMS explicitly exclude from reporting (and from potential denial or revocation) all routine commercial, patient care, referral, and vendor relationships. Other associations that commenters stated should be exempted included, but were not limited to, manufacturer, wholesaler, insurance, banking, accreditation, and other ordinary-course dealings. Additional commenters stated that the “affiliation” definition, the associated reporting requirements, and CMS' overall oversight of potentially problematic relationships should be restricted to more proximate associations involving, for example, ownership interests, governance authority, operational control, financial control, coordinated conduct, and program integrity threats. Without such parameters, they maintained, legitimate and routine business transactions could become reportable affiliations.
Response:
While we appreciate these comments, we cannot exempt certain categories of affiliations beforehand simply because they might on the surface appear to lack a “meaningful nexus” or other significant connection, or do not meet a materiality (or similar) threshold. There are many types of affiliations—both involving close relationships and those more distant—that can present a program integrity threat. Our obligation to protect the Medicare program consequently requires that we broaden our affiliation definition to include more relationships. Indeed, if we restricted this definition in the manner the commenters requested (for example, ownership, close nexus, financial control, etc.) the hypothetical scenarios previously outlined would remain unaddressed, conceivably harming the Trust Funds and beneficiaries.
We address the scope of the affiliations within the definition of that term. If the commenters are referencing the scope of the “any marketing, business . . .”, language, we restate that the categories of relationships within this term will—for purposes of §§ 424.530(a)(13) and 424.535(a)(19)—have their plain meaning.
While we are somewhat unclear as to the commenters' reference to “individualized determinations”, we emphasize that—as with all §§ 424.530(a)(13) and 424.535(a)(19) decisions—CMS will carefully and thoroughly consider the facts of each case and only take action when justified under the circumstances.
We respectfully decline to establish a “due diligence” threshold for applying §§ 424.530(a)(13) and 424.535(a)(19) because, again, we do not at this time anticipate making disclosure requests, and providers are not required to conduct internal research of possible affiliations.
Regarding factors and thresholds, we repeat our earlier concerns about the restraints that fixed, inflexible criteria impose on our ability to assess each case based its own unique circumstances.
Comment:
Numerous commenters opposed the removal of the 5-year lookback period. They stated, in general, that this would increase the burden and complexity of reporting without helping to identify fraud or promote program integrity.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. We refer the commenters to our prior statements concerning disclosure requests, and we stress that affiliations older than 5 years can still present a current risk of fraud, waste, or abuse.
Comment:
Commenters stated that before denial or revocation occurs, providers should be able to correct or add affiliation data that was inadvertently erroneous or missing in their disclosure submission.
Response:
We refer the commenters to our prior statements regarding data disclosure.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that CMS should be able to identify affiliations and disclosable events via internal systems without requiring providers to report this information. They noted that providers often will not have access to (or be able to obtain from associated parties) certain affiliation
(
printed page 72122)
data. Accordingly, provider disclosure of this data should not be necessary.
Response:
While CMS may request submission of provider affiliation data at any time, we agree with the commenters' general position and will, to the extent feasible, utilize existing data when making §§ 424.530(a)(13) and 424.535(a)(19) determinations.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS should request affiliation disclosures involving specified disclosable events and then evaluate whether an affiliation poses an undue risk (akin to the processes CMS outlined in the aforementioned September 10, 2019, final rule). The commenter believed that a revocation process where CMS assumes affiliations pose undue risk without some reasonable fact-finding in which CMS solicits information from the provider with the affiliation is punitive and unnecessary.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's feedback but note several things. First, and as stated, although we retain the right to do so under § 424.519, we do not anticipate requesting affiliation data due to the provider burden. Second, CMS does not revoke providers under § 424.535(a)(19) without having information on file—the overwhelming majority of which is already on file with CMS based on the provider's various Form CMS-855 submissions and is linked in PECOS to other providers' submissions (for instance, shared managing employees)—demonstrating an undue fraud, waste, and abuse risk. Third, we believe that whether the data is reported via a specific request under § 424.519(b) or is currently on file based on prior submissions or other information is less important than our need to alleviate provider burden.
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing our proposed revised affiliation provisions with two modifications, both of which involve proposed paragraph (6) of the “affiliation” definition. The first, as mentioned, is the removal of beneficiary relationshipstherefrom. The second involves adding the following language at the end of said paragraph: “whether direct or indirect (including, for example, common use of the same organization to perform these services.” In our view, this additional language—which we do not believe is different in intended scope from what we proposed and is primarily a clarification—will help stakeholders more clearly understand the concepts and examples outlined in the proposed and final rules. Such transparency is critical given: (1) the concerns that commenters expressed; and (2) what we perceived to be some provider confusion as to the meaning and scope of certain aspects of our proposal.
In closing, we do not believe that the non-finalization of our proposed changes to §§ 424.530(a)(6), 424.530(a)(7), and 424.535(i) is inconsistent with our finalization of revisions to some of our affiliation provisions. This is because they can address somewhat different factual situations; for example, proposed §§ 424.535(i) referenced a denied provider potentially having its other enrollment applications revoked, whereas our affiliation changes focused more on the wider question of undue risk of fraud, waste, and abuse involving certain relationships.

9. Managing Employees (§ 424.502)
The term “managing employee” is defined in § 424.502. It means, in part, a general manager, business manager, administrator, director, or other individual who exercises operational or managerial control over, or who directly or indirectly conducts, the day-to-day operation of the provider. Managing employees have long been required to be disclosed on the provider's Medicare enrollment application. Since managing employees sometimes have as much or more influence over a provider's daily operations as an owner, we must know whether such persons present risks to the Trust Funds.
Yet the risks are not strictly financial. We have repeatedly noted over the years our role in protecting the health and safety of Medicare beneficiaries. From a provider enrollment perspective, part of this involves our current collecting of information on certain medical professionals within a provider organization. This includes, for example: (1) IDTF supervising physicians, interpreting physicians, and technicians; (2) ordering OTP personnel; and (3) hospice and SNF medical directors. The purpose is to ensure that such persons not only pose no payment safeguard threats but also are qualified for their roles (such as meeting State licensure requirements). Unqualified or unvetted medical personnel can harm Medicare patients.
So great is our concern about this matter that we believe additional clinical parties should be disclosed on the provider enrollment application. Hence, we proposed to expand upon our aforementioned inclusion of hospice and SNF medical directors within the “managing employee” definition. The following persons would be added:
Medical directors (not merely those at SNFs and hospices)
Clinical directors
Departmental heads (for example, a hospital's chief of cardiology)
Supervising physicians (not simply those at IDTFs)
Nursing directors
Alternate administrators
All other clinical personnel that meet the “managing employee” definition.
We noted four things in the proposed rule. First, these categories apply to all provider and supplier types, including SNFs and hospices. Second, we believe the persons in these categories already qualify as “managing employees” and should have always been reported. They clearly have direct or indirect control of the provider's day-to-day operations, and the fact that they are clinical personnel (rather than administrative) is irrelevant for purposes of determining whether a person is a managing employee. Our inclusion of them within the “managing employee” definition is, in large part, a reminder to stakeholders that clinical staff must be disclosed if the definition is met. Third, these seven new bulleted categories do not establish any minimum threshold for disclosure; for example, even if an individual has less influence than a departmental head, the person must still be reported as long as the managing employee definition is met. Fourth, and on the other hand, this does not mean that every clinical employee regardless of influence must be reported. Disclosure is only required if the person is a managing employee.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed our proposed revision on several grounds. First, they did not believe these persons qualify as managing employees simply because of their title—with some commenters maintaining that they did not qualify at all because they do not fall within the generally understood meaning of “managing employee”; they seemingly contended that the definition is restricted to administrative and non-clinical officials with very high-level leadership and supervisory authority over the provider's entire operation. Second, they stated that the burden of reporting these individuals as managing employees would be enormous, especially for larger providers with many clinical employees. Third, and in a similar vein, they disagreed with our assertions that (i) these individuals should always have been reported as managing employees and (ii) there would thus be no additional reporting burden (as we stated in the ICR and RIA sections of the proposed rule). Fourth, they maintained that our use of phrases such as “additional clinical parties” and “expand upon” when describing our change in the proposed rule was not only a contradiction but also a
de facto
CMS admission that: (i) these persons never qualified as managing employees; (ii) our revision constitutes a new reporting requirement; and (iii) CMS must calculate the reporting burden accordingly.
Response:
We respectfully disagree with all these comments. We believe the clinical parties listed in our proposed revised definition clearly are managing employees. Even if one assumed that a person's title is not absolutely and conclusively dispositive as to whether they meet the “managing employee” definition, we have always viewed it as by far the strongest indicator of such. More importantly, we have long interpreted this definition much more broadly than the commenters apparently have. It has never been limited to the highest administrative officers in the organization, it has never excluded officials who oversee only certain parts or offices of a provider, and we have never indicated that clinical personnel
(
printed page 72125)
do not fall within its scope. Indeed, the definition encompasses not only those who exercise “operational or managerial control over” the provider's day-to-day operations but also persons “who directly or indirectly conduct” said operations. This covers—and has long covered—a wide range of parties; as an illustration, a clinical department head at a local hospital, in our view, unquestionably participates in conducting the provider's day-to-day operations. Given all this, we retain our stance that these individuals should always have been disclosed.
The phrases “additional clinical parties” and “expand upon” were merely references to our listing of more officials within the definition as a reminder that they qualify as managing employees. It was neither a contradiction nor an indication that they never before qualified, for we expressly stated in several places in the proposed rule that they already did. In short, it was an addition of language, not an addition or expansion of scope—two very different things, especially since the actual definition itself is not changing but only the listing of parties for clarity purposes. It was no different than our 2023 revision of this definition to list SNF and hospice medical directors and administrators;
[
52
]
this, too, was not an expansion and, we note, generated no public comments during the rulemaking process claiming an additional burden.
We refer commenters to the ICR section of this final rule for a discussion of burden.
Comment:
Commenters stated that CMS should apply a due diligence standard to the reporting of clinical and other managing employees. So long as the provider made a reasonable effort to obtain all managing employee data, they believed this should be sufficient for CMS—and that CMS should take no denial, revocation, deactivation, or other measure against the provider. Several commenters believed this approach would comport with CMS' sub-regulatory guidance regarding the reporting of SNF additional disclosable party (ADP) information—whereby, the commenters maintained, SNFs can outline for MACs its “maximum feasible” but unsuccessful efforts to obtain ADP data.
[
53
]
Response:
We disagree with these comments. While we understand it can occasionally be challenging to secure certain managing employee data, CMS has never had a “best efforts” or similar allowance for this information. It must be reported, and CMS can take action if it is not.

Several commenters stated that clinical directors, nursing leaders, department heads, and other clinicians may supervise patient care but do not necessarily exercise ownership-level or financial control and may have limited managerial authority over the provider.

For reasons already stated, we believe the clinical parties identified in our proposed definition revision clearly qualify as managing employees. We add that one need not exercise ownership-level or financial control or wide-ranging, high-level managerial authority to fall within the very broad “managing employee” definition.

Commenters stated that the proposed “managing employee” definition should be significantly narrowed while containing a clear, minimum threshold for disclosure. We believe both the existing and proposed versions of the definition are plain on their face as to who must be reported. If the individual falls within the definition, they must be disclosed.

Commenters stated that a person's authority—not their title—should determine who is or is not a managing employee. As stated previously, we believe titles are an extremely heavy indicator of one's authority, and, accordingly, that the clinical personnel in question are indeed managing employees; hence, we cannot make the unequivocal statement the commenters request. Moreover, if we deferred the reporting of managing employees entirely to the provider's judgment and prohibited ourselves from even questioning whether all the provider's managing employees were disclosed, providers would have every incentive to avoid reporting certain individuals.

Response:
We respectfully disagree. Our inclusion of SNF and hospice medical directors: (1) was merely a reminder that these persons are managing employees; and (2) never implied that these were only clinical personnel who needed to be disclosed.

A commenter stated that if CMS finalizes its proposed revised definition, it should increase the timeframe for reporting managing employee changes.

We respectfully disagree. Such changes have long been required to be disclosed within 30 days given this data's vital importance to program integrity.

Several commenters stated that if CMS finalizes its proposal, it should: (1) provide clear examples of individuals who would and would not qualify as managing employees within different provider types and organizational structures; (2) establish an appropriate implementation timeframe and grace period before initiating enforcement actions, including giving providers time to review and update their enrollment records; and (3) hold providers harmless for failing to report individuals who—under what they believe is CMS' revised interpretation—would now be considered managing employees but were not previously understood to fall within the regulatory definition. Other commenters questioned whether all providers must submit enrollment applications to report clinical managing employees who were not previously disclosed.

CMS will, if appropriate, issue guidance regarding the commenters' first request and the last question. (This is also why we disagree with the commenters' assertion that our proposal constitutes a “revised interpretation” of the definition.)

10. Definition of “Operational” (§ 424.502)
a. Background and Provisions
Per § 424.510(d)(6), a provider must be “operational” to obtain Medicare billing privileges. “Operational” is defined in § 424.502 as meaning the provider meets all of the following:
Has a qualified physical practice location
Is open to the public for the purpose of providing health care related services
Is prepared to submit valid Medicare claims
Is properly staffed, equipped, and stocked (as applicable, based on the type of facility or organization, provider or supplier specialty, or the services or items being rendered) to furnish these items or services.
The “operational” definition's core purpose is to help confirm that the provider is bona fide. Unfortunately, we have discovered instances where a provider appears to meet the definition but turns out to be a fraudulent operation. We believe stronger, broader, and clearer components of the definition would better ensure the provider's operational status and legitimacy and assist us in preventing sham providers from entering Medicare. Therefore, we proposed the following changes to our definition.
First, we proposed an opening sentence to the definition that would read “
Operational
means (as applicable, based on the type of facility or organization, provider or supplier specialty, or the services or items being rendered) the provider or supplier meets all of the following:”. The parenthetical—which is in the current definition—would elucidate for stakeholders that: (1) certain components of our revised definition may not apply to all provider types; and (2) CMS would account for this in applying the definition.
Second, the previously referenced four bulleted components of the existing definition would be designated as new paragraphs (1) through (4) therein. This would improve the definition's readability. (We did not propose changes to the first requirement concerning a qualified physical practice location.)
Third, proposed paragraph (2) would explain that the requirement that the provider “[i]s open to the public for the purpose of providing health care related services” includes, but is not limited to, all of the following:
The provider's location is fully accessible to all patients and lacks safety hazards.
The provider's hours of business are sufficient to regularly serve patients.
Medicare beneficiaries can contact and locate the provider's location based on publicly available information (for example, the internet).
We believe these three requirements would help verify the provider's compliance with paragraph (2). In our view, a provider whose location threatens patient safety, is inaccessible to beneficiaries, or cannot be found via public means raises doubts as to whether the location is truly “open.”
For purposes of the “operational” definition, we proposed to define “accessible” as meaning both of the following:
The provider is located in an area and a building that patients can enter with reasonable ease.
The location is compliant with all Federal Americans with Disabilities Act regulations and all applicable and equivalent State and local laws.
These requirements would make clear that providers must—from an accessibility standpoint—accommodate beneficiaries with disabilities and those without. We noted in the proposed rule that the phrase “located in an area” does not mean the provider's location must be, for instance, within a short drive or a mere 5-mile radius of the beneficiary's home. “Area” in this context would mean the location's immediate vicinity, such as the parking lot or a larger, multi-building complex in which the provider has its office. Also, nothing in the first bullet would prevent the provider from having security locks or security personnel between its office(s) and the building entrance. It instead references the beneficiary's ability to enter the building once access is granted (for instance, security staff signs in the beneficiary and directs the beneficiary to the provider's office).
Third, we proposed in new paragraph (3) to change “prepared” to “prepared and able”. If the provider lacks the administrative or logistical ability to submit valid claims—even if it may be “prepared” to do so—we do not believe the provider can be considered operational for purposes of Medicare enrollment.
Fourth, and similar to proposed paragraph (2), proposed paragraph (4) would include the following additional requirements concerning the “properly staffed, properly equipped . . . .” criterion:
Provider staff must be qualified (such as licensed or certified if required under State law) to perform their health care-related functions.
Equipment must be functional, appropriate for the services and items the provider intends to furnish, and in sufficient quantity to provide these items and services.
Appropriate medications for the services and items the provider intends to furnish and in sufficient quantity to provide these items and services.
We also believe that operationality should require more than proposed paragraphs (1) through (4), particularly with respect to administration, safety, and patient care. Hence, we proposed in new paragraph (5) that operationality requires the provider to have adequate written policies and records regarding its operations, such as, but not limited to, procedures for patient care, patient safety, medical and patient recordkeeping, and general administration.
(
printed page 72127)
We further stated in the proposed rule that the wide variety of provider types and scenarios might at times require us to consider information not addressed in our revised definition in order to determine the provider's operationality. Suppose a case arises where most of the definition's requirements are inapplicable to the provider, but this leaves insufficient remaining criteria for us to determine operational status. We believe we must have the ability to contemplate other information in this and other cases. We hence proposed an additional (though un-numerated) paragraph at the end of our revised definition stating that CMS may consider any information in determining whether the provider is operational.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters sought CMS confirmation that certain provider types, such as HHAs, would not be required to meet all the “operational” criteria due to those providers' particular characteristics. Another commenter requested that CMS not: (1) interpret “open to the public” to require a home health administrative office to operate as a patient-facing clinical site; (2) require an HHA to stock medications or equipment that it does not lawfully dispense, own, or routinely furnish; or (3) rely on an unlimited “catch-all” category (referenced previously) allowing CMS to consider “any information” without explaining how that data relates to “operational” regulatory requirements.
Response:
Although we are unable in this rule to formally exclude specific provider types from various requirements in the “operational” definition, we recognize that certain provisions may not apply in all instances to all providers and suppliers—hence our “as applicable” reference in the proposed revised definition. We will keep this in mind—as we do with the current “operational” definition—when enforcing our revised definition. Regarding the “catch-all” category, this is necessary to account for situations not explicitly addressed within the “operational” definition.
Comment:
Several commenters supported our proposed revised definition of “operational.” A commenter in particular agreed that providers should have adequate written policies and records regarding their operations, including patient care and patient safety.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support.
Commen
t: Some commenters requested CMS to: (1) exempt State surveyed and accredited providers and suppliers from the “operational” requirement; or (2) rely on State survey or accreditation findings when determining operationality so as to avoid duplicity and inconsistent requirements. If CMS does neither, a few commenters stated that CMS should explain how: (1) the expanded definition will apply to institutional providers already subject to Federal and State oversight; and (2) overlapping State survey and operationality requirements will be reconciled before a denial or revocation occurs.
Response:
We respectfully decline the commenters' first two requests. Again, provider enrollment requirements—such as § 424.510(d)(6)—are separate from State survey and accreditation requirements. The former must be met even if the provider is surveyed or accredited; this has been the case for decades. Insofar as the final two comments, we are respectfully unclear as to the guidance the commenter seeks. We can only reiterate that State survey, accreditation, and other State and Federal oversight requirements are separate from our consideration of whether a provider is operational.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that CMS issue guidance and examples regarding what does and does not constitute “operational” status under our revised definition.
Response:
To the extent we deem necessary, we will release guidance on its expanded definition of “operational.”
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing our proposed revised “operational” definition without modification. We are making one technical correction to our regulatory text, though. We mentioned previously that we are retaining the requirement that the provider have a “qualified physical practice location.” This has been a requirement for decades. Yet paragraph (1) of the proposed revised definition did not include the word “physical”, even though it was intended. We are including it in paragraph (1) in our final regulatory text.
11. Signage (§ 424.510(f))
Sections 424.57(c)(7)(i)(D) and 410.33(g)(14)(ii) require DMEPOS suppliers and IDTFs, respectively, to maintain a permanent visible sign in plain view posting their normal hours of operation. The former adds that if the supplier's place of business is located within a building complex, the sign must be visible at the main entrance of the building (or the hours can be posted at the entrance of the supplier). We proposed in new § 424.510(f) to expand this requirement to include all providers and suppliers; § 424.510(f) would mirror the current language of § 424.57(c)(7)(i)(D). This would assist beneficiaries and site visit personnel in locating the provider's business, something that has occasionally proven difficult because the location contains no signage. To ensure consistency, we would also revise § 410.33(g)(14)(ii) to duplicate the language in proposed § 424.510(f).
Consistent with our proposed revisions to the definition of “operational”, however, § 424.510(f) is not intended to supersede any other Medicare requirements regarding signage. Section 424.510(f) is strictly an enrollment requirement. In addition, we recognize that our proposed signage requirement may not be practicable in all circumstances. This could be due to, for instance, the type of provider involved, its particular business circumstances, etc. Thus, we proposed the following exceptions to the signage requirement:
The provider shares office space with another provider (for example, physicians in a group practice sharing a common suite, though the group itself must have signage).
The provider treats patients in the patients' homes.
The provider treats patients in the provider's home and only uses the provider's address for administrative purposes.
The provider performs telehealth services from home.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.
Comment:
A number of commenters opposed our proposed requirement, believing it would, in some cases, be burdensome and operationally infeasible for certain provider and supplier types; for example, providers located in large office buildings may be unable to maintain signage due to space limitations, building policies, etc. The commenters accordingly recommended several modifications to our proposal. These included but were not limited to: (1) treating the signage requirement as met if the provider is identifiable via publicly available means, such as a building directory or website; (2) permitting shared or centralized signage for providers in multi-tenant buildings, health system campuses, or similar facilities; (3) clarifying that a periodic signage lapse due to matters outside the provider's control (such as construction or natural disaster)—or minor signage
(
printed page 72128)
violations per a materiality standard—will not result in an adverse CMS finding; (4) limiting CMS enforcement to corrective action by allowing the provider time to remedy the issue (after CMS notification) before denying, revoking, or deactivating the provider; (5) exempting field-based and privacy-sensitive behavioral health sites from the signage requirement; and (6) adding more regulatory exceptions to the signage requirement, perhaps based on provider type and potentially including hospitals, HHAs, telehealth providers, and providers that furnish services in beneficiaries' homes.
Response:
We appreciate these comments and respond as follows:
We respectfully disagree with the commenters' first and second recommendations. We do not believe a public directory or shared signage is an adequate substitute for individual, provider-specific signage; indeed, the former would completely undercut the need for the latter. We also must decline the commenters' third and fourth requests based on our earlier explanations that: (1) any degree of non-compliance still involves non-compliance; and (2) a mandatory pre-appeals cure period could reduce providers' willingness to maintain constant compliance, knowing that they can always correct the problem later. Regarding the fifth and sixth, we are unable to grant additional provider type exceptions in this final rule without further review of the issue. Nonetheless, we will monitor the implementation of § 424.510(f) and, if need be, consider future rulemaking to address.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS should deem § 424.510(f) as satisfied if the provider's signage complies with State survey, licensure, local, and other requirements.
Response:
We respectfully disagree because Medicare enrollment requirements are—and have always been—separate and distinct from State and local requirements. Compliance with the latter does not mean automatic compliance with the former.
Comment:
A few commenters questioned (1) how § 424.510(f) applies to institutional providers that are part of campuses or large medical complexes; (2) what type of signage is acceptable in such cases; and(3) what constitutes “normal business hours” and “visible business signage”.
Response:
CMS will, as applicable, issue public guidance on these topics as well as others concerning the signage requirement.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that when enforcing § 424.510(f), CMS should account for situations such as (but not limited to) landlord restrictions, building types, local ordinances, or others than might prevent full compliance through no fault of the provider. A commenter requested that CMS explicitly state in the regulatory text that § 424.510(f) may not apply in all situations.
