We respectfully decline to add the final commenter's requested statement, for it could give the impression that CMS will grant exceptions in every case where the provider claims it cannot meet § 424.510(f) due to factors outside its control. This said, we recognize that atypical situations involving signage compliance may occur based on the facts involved. CMS will keep this in mind when applying§ 424.510(f)'s requirements.
Comment:
A commenter supported our proposed exceptions to the signage requirement.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support.
After reviewing the comments received, we are finalizing our proposed signage requirements without modification.
12. Retention and Furnishing of Documentation (§ 424.516)
We explained previously that under § 424.516(f)(1), providers and suppliers that furnish covered ordered, certified, referred, or prescribed Part A or B services, items or drugs must:
Maintain the documentation described in § 424.516(f)(1)(ii) for 7 years from the date of service; and
Upon CMS' or a Medicare contractor's request, provide access to that documentation.
The documentation described in § 424.516(f)(1)(ii) includes written and electronic documents (including the NPI of the physician or, when permitted, other eligible professional who ordered, certified, referred, or prescribed the Part A or B service, item, or drug) relating to written orders, certifications, referrals, prescriptions, and requests for payments for Part A or B services, items or drugs.
Section 424.516(f)(2) contains a similar documentation retention and submission requirement for physicians (or, when permitted, eligible professionals) who order, certify, refer, or prescribe Part A or B services, items or drugs. Section 424.516(a)(10), meanwhile, permits revocation if the provider or supplier fails to comply with the documentation and CMS access requirements in § 424.516(f).
In general, § 424.516(f) helps CMS determine, for instance, whether the service was reasonable and necessary, whether fraud, waste, or abuse is involved, and whether the provider is compliant with Medicare requirements.
We proposed to add new § 424.516(f)(3) clarifying that all documentation required to be retained and furnished under § 424.516(f) must be accurate, complete, and compliant with all CMS requirements. In our documentation reviews, we have seen: (1) patient charts missing medical director signatures; (2) hospice certifications signed before the face-to-face encounter; (3) certification end dates preceding the certification start dates; and (4) other types of inaccurate records. This makes it difficult for CMS and its contractors to verify the provider's compliance and the service's necessity; the program integrity benefits of § 424.516(f) are reduced if the documentation is inaccurate or non-adherent. We accordingly believe § 424.516(f)(3) is necessary.
We emphasize that our proposal is not intended to establish any new condition of payment. It would be restricted to the scope of documents addressed in § 424.516(f).
The following is a summary of the comments we received on this proposal and our responses.

A commenter supported our proposal but suggested that CMS—in potential § 424.535(a)(10) revocation cases—take into account situations where claims documentation has been lost due to natural disasters or other similar events. Another commenter requested that CMS: (1) confirm that records under § 424.516(f) may be retained and produced electronically; (2) specify accepted electronic formats and a secure transmission channel; and (3) provide a reasonable and defined production before utilizing § 424.535(a)(10).
Response:
While we appreciate the commenters' support, recommendations, and requests, our proposal was limited to the need for documentation to be accurate and complete, rather than whether and how it could or should be furnished in the situations the commenters describe. Consequently, we respectfully believe these comments are outside the scope of this final rule.

A few commenters requested that CMS clarify that a provider will not be revoked under § 424.535(a)(10) for § 424.516(f)(3) documentation deficiencies that are immaterial (for example, the commenter stated, the error does not materially affect the ability to validate a claim), technical, or inadvertent.
Response:
While we cannot make the blanket statement the commenters request, we acknowledge that not all

documentation errors are the same. As with all revocations, CMS will carefully evaluate the facts and circumstances of the case.

A commenter stated that when enforcing § 424.516(f)(3), CMS should recognize that some provider and supplier types, such as HHAs and hospices, furnish services in patients' homes.
Response:
While we appreciate this comment, we again state that our proposal only referenced the need for the documentation to be accurate, complete, and compliant—a requirement that we respectfully do not believe should depend on the provider type involved or where or how services are furnished.

12. Corrective Action Plans (CAPs), Rebuttals, and Appeals
In certain situations, a provider or supplier may have an opportunity to correct a deficiency or contest a CMS finding regarding its enrollment by submitting, as applicable: (1) a CAP in response to a §§ 424.530(a)(1) or 424.535(a)(1) denial or revocation, respectively; (2) a rebuttal to a stay or deactivation of enrollment under §§ 424.541 or 424.546, respectively; or (3) an appeal of an initial determination under
42 CFR 498.3
. We proposed several revisions to these processes.
a. CAPs (§ 405.809)
Sections 424.530(a)(1) and 424.535(a)(1) permit CMS to deny or revoke enrollment, respectively, if the provider is not compliant with the enrollment requirements in Title 42 or in the enrollment application applicable for its provider type. The provider may submit a CAP in response to this denial or revocation, which allows the provider to remedy the deficiency or deficiencies in question and achieve compliance. As has long been CMS practice, though, §§ 424.530(a)(1) and 424.535(a)(1) are the only denial or revocation reasons under §§ 424.530 and 424.535 for which the provider may submit a CAP. While § 405.809(a)(1) makes this clear with respect to § 424.535(a)(1), it is silent as to § 424.530(a)(1). To incorporate this CAP policy into regulation, we proposed to add § 424.530(a)(1) denials to § 405.809's purview. This would involve the following revisions:
Section 405.809's title would change from “Reinstatement of provider or supplier billing privileges following corrective action” to “Granting or reinstatement of provider or supplier billing privileges following corrective action.”
In paragraph (a)(1), the language “revocation for noncompliance under § 424.530(a)(1)” would change to “denial or revocation for non-compliance under § 424.530(a)(1) or § 424.535(a)(1)”.
In paragraph (a)(2), “revocation” would change to “denial or revocation”.
In paragraph (b)(1), “Reinstates” would change to “Approves or reinstates”.
Paragraph (b)(1)(i) would be redesignated as paragraph (b)(1)(i)(B).
Under new paragraph (b)(1)(i)(A), the effective date of the approval is based on the applicable timeframes described in §§ 424.520 and 424.521. This is consistent with existing practice.
In paragraph (b)(1)(ii), “reinstatement” would change to “approval or reinstatement”.
In paragraph (b)(2), “reinstate” would change to “approve or reinstate”.
b. Notification of Determinations
Section 498.3(b) lists several CMS or MAC provider enrollment decisions that are considered “initial determinations”. These include, for example, enrollment denials, enrollment revocations, and inclusion of a provider on the preclusion list. The affected provider under § 498.5 may request a reconsideration of the initial determination, for which CMS or, if applicable, the MAC issues a reconsideration determination. Under §§ 498.20(a)(1) and 498.25(a)(1), CMS mails notice of the initial determination or reconsidered determination, respectively, to the provider. Furthermore, § 405.800 requires that denial and revocation notices (as well as notice regarding the addition of years to a reenrollment bar) be sent by certified mail. We proposed to revise §§ 405.800(a), (b)(1), and (c)(1), 498.20(a)(1) and 498.25(a)(1) to include email as an acceptable form of notice. We believe this would facilitate faster notice to the provider without the expense of paper mailing.
c. Appeals of Reactivation Effective Dates
Along with listing types of initial determinations, paragraph (d) of § 498.3 outlines administrative actions that are not initial determinations and thus not appealable under part 498. One type of provider enrollment finding that is not mentioned in either § 498.3(b) or (d) is the effective date of a reactivation under § 424.540(b). Under § 424.540(d)(2), a reactivation effective date is the date on which the Medicare contractor received the provider's reactivation submission that the Medicare contractor processed to approval. Due to lack of clarity among some stakeholders as to whether an assigned reactivation effective date may be appealed or rebutted, we proposed several regulatory changes.
First, we proposed to add new paragraph (3) to § 424.540(d) stating that a provider or supplier may rebut their assigned reactivation effective date via the general deactivation rebuttal procedures in § 424.546. As deactivations are not considered initial determinations—and to ensure consistent approaches—we do not believe reactivation effective dates should, either. Yet we also believe the provider should have an opportunity to be heard on the matter, and a rebuttal would provide that.
To accommodate reactivation effective date rebuttals within § 424.546,

Change the title from “Deactivation rebuttals” to “Rebuttals of deactivations and of reactivation effective dates”.
In paragraph (a)(1), insert the following between “under § 424.540,” and “the provider or supplier has 15 calendar days”: “or is assigned a reactivation effective date by CMS or its contractor under § 424.540(d)(2),”.
In paragraph (b)(2), insert the following between “effective date,” and “and the reasons”: “(or with the assigned reactivation effective date)”.

14. DMEPOS Accreditation (§ 424.58)
Consistent with §§ 424.57(c)(22) and 424.58, DMEPOS suppliers must be accredited by a CMS-approved accrediting organization (AO) to enroll and remained enrolled in Medicare. Section 424.58 details the general procedures and policies associated with DMEPOS accreditation. Many of these were added to § 424.58 in the CY 2026 HH PPS final rule (
90 FR 55342
) in an effort to strengthen CMS' oversight of the DMEPOS accreditation program in general and the DMEPOS AOs in particular. This included requirements regarding information and agreements that AOs must submit to CMS as part of their application/reapplication process. Three of these requirements are as follows:
Per § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(D), agreeing to notify CMS in writing of any decision to terminate, revoke, withdraw, or amend the accreditation status of a specific DMEPOS supplier within 3 business days of the date the AO took action.
Per § 424.58(c)(1)(xxii), describing the AO's processes for—
++ Detecting and addressing DMEPOS supplier fraud, waste, and abuse (including identifying the AO's definitions of fraud, waste, and abuse); and
++ Reporting this activity to CMS and, as applicable, law enforcement.
Per § 424.58(c)(1)(vii)(D), outlining the AO's policies and procedures for avoiding conflicts of interest and the appearance thereof involving individuals who conduct surveys or participate in accreditation decisions.
Upon further reflection since these three provisions were promulgated, we proposed the following changes thereto.
One revision would change the 3-business day period in § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(D) to 5 calendar days. This would better align with § 424.58(e)(5)(i), which requires approved AOs to report the same information to CMS within 5 calendar days.
In addition, there currently is no timeframe in § 424.58 for reporting the fraud, waste, and abuse described § 424.58(c)(1)(xxii). We proposed in new § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(N) that the AO must agree to notify CMS in writing (and, if applicable, law enforcement) of suspected fraud, waste, and abuse—consistent with the AO's CMS-approved definitions of those terms—within 3 calendar days of the date on which the AO determines that fraud, waste, or abuse may have occurred. (Current § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(N) would be redesigned as new § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(O)).
Notwithstanding the provisions of § 424.58(c)(1)(vii)(D) regarding conflicts of interest, none of them actually require the AO to report in its application/reapplication whether it has such conflicts. To help ensure that CMS makes fully informed AO approval decisions, we proposed to revise § 424.58(c)(1)(vii)(D)(
4
) to require the AO to also disclose to CMS all conflicts of interest (as described in § 424.58(c)(1)(vii)(D)(
3
) and (5)) it currently has and explain how and when it will terminate them.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on these proposals and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS should: (1) identify the types of conflicts of interest that must be reported to CMS and the vehicle for doing so; (2) specify the phrase “suspected fraud, waste, and abuse” and the reporting requirements associated therewith; and (3) explain how the AOs should contact law enforcement.
Response:
CMS will issue separate guidance to the AOs on this matter.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that to account for holidays and weekends, CMS should change its: (1) proposed 3 calendar-day period in § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(N) to, for example, 3 business days or 7 business days; and (2) proposed 5 calendar-day timeframe in § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(D) to 5 business days.
Response:
While we appreciate these suggestions, we believe the time periods we proposed are necessary given: (1) the risk that fraud, waste, and abuse can pose to the Trust Funds and beneficiaries; and (2) the importance of us receiving critical information from the AOs as soon as possible.
Comment:
A commenter stated that proposed § 424.58(c)(1)(xxiii)(N) risks overwhelming the AOs and CMS with unsubstantiated fraud reports, hence diverting resources from the prevention of actual fraud. The commenter urged CMS to either to raise the reporting threshold or provide guardrails or guidance to avoid this.
Response:
We respectfully disagree with the commenters' concern. We do not anticipate a mass of unsubstantiated reports arising from our proposal. Beyond this, we have an obligation to the American people to treat all potential fraud, waste, and abuse (even if it is only suspected and is awaiting investigation) with the utmost seriousness. Waiting to learn from the AO about DMEPOS fraud, waste, and abuse until after it happens reflects the aforementioned, insufficient “pay and chase” model. Immediately learning
(
printed page 72132)
when fraud, waste, and abuse is suspected will better enable us to be proactive in our program integrity activities.

A commenter requested that DMEPOS AOs have direct access to CMS enrollment data.

We appreciate this request but believe it is outside the scope of this final rule.

15. Miscellaneous Comments
We received additional comments on our proposals. In general, these pertained to either our proposed enrollment provisions as a whole, multiple provisions regarding a single topic (such as revocations), or our existing provider enrollment process.
Comment:
Several commenters supported our proposals to strengthen provider enrollment requirements and combat fraud. A commenter stated that these protections are especially important for vulnerable home health beneficiaries who may have limited ability to identify and report fraudulent or substandard care. The commenter suggested that CMS also consider whether HHAs should be required to document staff training as part of enrollment and ongoing compliance requirements.
Response:
We thank the commenters' for their support. While we also appreciate the commenter's recommendation regarding documentation, we believe it is outside the scope of this final rule.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed our enrollment proposals overall. They stated that the provisions could: (1) reduce and discourage provider participation; and (2) limit beneficiary health care access, especially in underserved areas. They recommended that CMS implement operational safeguards to avoid abrupt loss of access to care when a provider is revoked, denied, deactivated, etc. Some stated that CMS should clearly distinguish between fraudulent, intentional, or material noncompliance (as well as material risk) on the one hand, and technical, administrative, inadvertent, or promptly corrected noncompliance on the other—and to limit revocation and denial to the former. (An example commenters cited was failing to timely report changes in enrollment information (such as managing employees), which commenters did not believe should result in revocation.) Other commenters maintained that our proposals, taken together, would make Medicare enrollment substantially less predictable and reliable for providers acting in good faith. They stated that providers make significant investments in their facilities/practices, personnel, compliance, and patient care in the expectation that they will remain Medicare-enrolled absent clear evidence of fraud or intentional misconduct. Additional commenters maintained that the lack of factors, definitions, etc., in some of our new denial and revocation grounds make the latter arbitrary and capricious because they would give CMS unfettered revocation and denial discretion.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns expressed. We do not expect provider participation or beneficiary access to be reduced given: (1) the limited number of revocations that traditionally occur; and (2) that previous promulgations of provider enrollment regulations (including those that added new denial and revocation grounds) did not lead to said reductions. Nonetheless, we constantly monitor potential access to care issues and will do with our new enrollment provisions.
As noted earlier, CMS carefully considers each potential denial and revocation situation and often utilizes measures such as deactivations and stays in lieu of revocations. Yet we cannot apply a materiality threshold to revocations or denials because: (1) non-compliance remains non-compliance regardless of the degree thereof; and (2) providers would have little incentive to remain consistently adherent to Medicare enrollment requirements if they knew that CMS only takes action if the non-compliance is material. Indeed, and most respectfully, providers should not assume that their mere avoidance of fraud and intentional misconduct exempts them from remaining compliant with all enrollment requirements.
We do not believe our new revocation and denial grounds would be arbitrary and capricious because, again, CMS will only take action when warranted and as specified in our regulations after a thorough and fair examination of the facts and circumstances of the case.
Comment:
Commenters stated that Medicare enrollment enforcement (as well as our proposed enrollment provisions) must be targeted, evidence-based, and accompanied by meaningful procedural protections. Additional commenters stated that CMS should ensure that the consequence is proportionate to the conduct.
Response:
We have always ensured that every potential denial or revocation case is meticulously assessed, and we only take action when justified. We do not routinely revoke providers and, as stated, often apply deactivations and stays to avoid the more significant consequences of a revocation and to ensure that the action is proportionate. Too, denied and revoked providers have robust due process rights under
42 CFR part 489
, and denial and revocation letters explain the facts and legal basis behind the action.
Comment:
Commenters stated that CMS's: (1) proposed denial and revocation reasons should be limited to provider and supplier types for which evidence exists of a program integrity problem; and (2) program integrity efforts should target higher-risk providers rather than burdening lower-risk ones.
Response:
Several of our proposed grounds (for example, § 424.530(a)(20) and 424.535(a)(25)) are indeed limited to higher-risk provider and supplier types. The others address provider enrollment issues we have seen that are not limited to a few types of providers. While we appreciate the commenters' feedback, CMS cannot restrict its program integrity activities to higher-risk providers, for provider enrollment non-compliance—as well as fraud, waste, and abuse—can occur with any provider or supplier type.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern that our enrollment provisions were proposed in the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule instead of a stand-alone enrollment rule. They stated that some provider and supplier types do not regularly review home health rules, believing that its provisions would not apply to them. Since many of our proposals apply to all providers and suppliers, they might not have seen important provisions. Hence, the commenters contended, CMS did not give adequate notice of its enrollment proposals, should withdraw them from the HH PPS proposed rule, and re-propose them in separate enrollment rule. Several commenters noted that CMS previously used stand-alone enrollment rulemaking (such as in 2003 and 2016)
[
54
]
to propose requirements applicable to all providers and suppliers. Other commenters stated that CMS should have at least proposed its provisions in the CY 2027 Physician
(
printed page 72133)
Fee Schedule
[
55
]
(
91 FR 43842
) proposed rule to ensure a wider audience.
Response:
We respectfully disagree with the commenters for a number of reasons.
First, the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule's title explicitly listed “Provider Enrollment” as one of its topics. Thus, the proposed rule was a provider enrollment rule as well and not merely a proposed regarding home health or hospice payment. This “Provider Enrollment” reference, moreover, was not prefaced by “Hospice” or “Home Health”. That is, it was broadly “Provider Enrollment” and not “Home Health and Hospice Provider Enrollment”, making clear that the enrollment provisions were not limited to certain provider types.

86 FR 62240
,
88 FR 77676
, and
90 FR 55342

These included, for instance: (1) adding roughly 10 new retroactive revocation reasons; (2) expanding the maximum reapplication bar period from 3 years to 10 years; (3) adding in regulation new reasons for which we can return or reject an enrollment application or deactivate a provider's enrollment; (4) reducing the period of non-billing for which we can deactivate a provider from 12 consecutive months to 6 consecutive months; and (5) documentation request requirements. No commenters in those proposed rules indicated concern about a lack of adequate notice or requested that our provisions be removed and reproposed in an enrollment-only rule.
Third, the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule was especially appropriate for our provisions given: (1) the need to remedy as quickly as possible the serious program integrity issues the proposals address; and (2) the hospice-specific proposals in the rule.

As explained previously: (1) we do not anticipate requesting affiliation data; (2) managing employees must be reported, and there has never been a “due diligence” standard for this requirement; and (3) for denial or revocation reasons based on the conduct of an owner, managing employee, managing organization, etc., we respectfully cannot base our decision on whether the provider knew of or could have controlled said conduct.

Response:
Our finalized enrollment provisions are effective on January 1, 2027, and we will be able to timely implement them. In addition, and except for our preclusion list revision, our changes do not apply to PACE providers that are not otherwise enrolled in Medicare.

A few commenters stated that enrollment actions against individual providers can affect an entire coordinated-care network, including physician-led Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs). While we appreciate these comments, we are respectfully unclear as to: (1) the transition process, alternative capacity arrangements, penalties, and network disruptions the commenters are referencing; and (2) whether the stakeholders' comments pertain strictly to our proposals or to our larger provider enrollment process. If the commenters are requesting, in effect, a postponement in revocation enforcement until appeal rights are exhausted, we refer the commenters to our earlier statements regarding our inability to do so. We can reiterate, though, that: (1) CMS takes revocation action only when truly warranted and, for this reason, we do not expect our proposals to materially affect ACOs or other provider networks; and (2) providers are notified of any revocation or denial action.
Comment:
Commenters stated that our proposed revocation reasons are overreaching. They maintained that CMS' program integrity efforts—both proposed and current—should instead be directed towards demonstrably fraudulent parties, high-risk providers, and intentional misconduct, not good-faith and historically compliant providers. Another commenter stated that Complex Rehab Technology suppliers should be exempt from our proposed denial and revocation reasons.
Response:
We respectfully disagree with these comments. Rather than being overreaching, our proposed revocation reasons are principally targeted towards specific scenarios we have seen and are not intended to be widely utilized. Too, we again note the matter of non-compliance with enrollment requirements. Merely because a provider is not, for example, (1) screened at the “high” level under § 424.518, (2) in a traditionally high-risk geographic area, or (3) engaged in intentional misconduct does not mean we should ignore any non-compliance on that provider's part. We must ensure that all providers are compliant irrespective of their relative risk level or provider or supplier type.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS should not finalize any of its expanded denial and revocation reasons until it publishes data regarding Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) reversal rates for enrollment denials and revocations—in particular, §§ 424.535(a)(1) and 424.535(a)(8)(ii) revocations. The commenter maintained, in essence, that denial and revocation reasons should not be added or broadened until CMS can ensure correct denial and revocation decisions as evidenced by low reversal rates for current grounds.
Response:
We respectfully disagree. CMS must take quick action to address
(
printed page 72134)

We respectfully direct the commenters to our previous statements regarding pre-denial and pre-revocation appeals processes.

The commenter suggested, for instance, revalidation of providers in the risk area, pre-claim review, and examining extreme utilization patterns and patient recertification rates.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate these recommendations and note that CMS has indeed taken targeted steps to address Los Angeles County-type situations. However, program integrity is a national issue and, as earlier mentioned, we must be proactive in addressing enrollment non-compliance and potential payment safeguard risks—irrespective of the particular geographic location or the provider or supplier type involved. We cannot wait until misconduct occurs in a certain location before taking action.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern that a provider error on an enrollment application or in enrollment data reporting could keep them out of business for 10 years. Response:
We reaffirm that providers are not revoked or denied as a matter of practice but only when genuinely justified under the case's facts and circumstances and based on the applicable data; we consider this to be a “targeted” approach. Further, and to reiterate, CMS frequently applies deactivations and stays instead of revocations given our acknowledgement of the significance of a revocation.
CMS addresses payment safeguard threats via numerous vehicles. Yet this does not mean that CMS must forgo all others. Program integrity requires a comprehensive approach, and the provider enrollment process—including establishing new denial and revocation grounds directed at specific vulnerabilities—is a critical component thereof.

D. DME Benefit Expansion for Infusion Pumps and Drugs
1. Background
a. Home Infusion Therapy Benefit
In section 5012 of the 21st Century Cures Act (
Pub. L. 114-255
), Congress amended section 1861(s)(2) of the Act and added sections 1834(u) and 1861(iii) of the Act to establish a new Medicare home infusion therapy benefit effective January 1, 2021. This benefit covers certain professional services associated with the provision of home infusion therapy to a beneficiary who is under the care of a physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant. Home infusion therapy involves the intravenous or subcutaneous administration of drugs or biologicals to an individual at home through an external infusion pump. As indicated in a final rule we published in the
Federal Register
on November 8, 2019, titled “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; CY 2020 Home Health Prospective Payment System Rate Update; Home Health Value-Based Purchasing Model; Home Health Quality Reporting Requirements; and Home Infusion Therapy Requirements,” the external infusion pump and other supplies, including home infusion drugs necessary for the effective use of the pump, are covered under the Part B DME benefit rather than the home infusion therapy benefit (
84 FR 60612
). Pursuant to section 1861(iii) of the Act, we published a final rule in the
Federal Register
on November 13, 2018, titled “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; CY 2019 Home Health Prospective Payment System Rate Update and CY 2020 Case-Mix Adjustment Methodology Refinements; Home Health Value-Based Purchasing Model; Home Health Quality Reporting Requirements; Home Infusion Therapy Requirements; and Training Requirements for Surveyors of National Accrediting Organizations” (
83 FR 56406
) to define the scope of “home infusion therapy,” “home,” “qualified home infusion therapy supplier,” and “home infusion drug” at
42 CFR 486 Subpart I
.
Section 486.525(a) implements the definition of “home infusion therapy” set forth at section 1861(iii)(1) of the Act, defining the term to include professional services, including nursing services, furnished in accordance with the plan of care described under
42 CFR 486.520
, patient training and education (not otherwise paid for as DME), remote monitoring and monitoring services for the provision of home infusion therapy services and home infusion drugs furnished by a qualified home infusion therapy supplier in the individual's home. Section 486.505 implements the definition of “home” set forth at section 1861(iii)(3)(B) of the Act, defining the term as a place of residence used as the home of an individual, including an institution that is used as a home. An institution that is used as a home may not be a hospital, critical access hospital (CAH), or skilled nursing facility (SNF) as defined in section 1861(e)(1), 1861(mm)(1), or 1819(a)(1) of the Act, respectively.
Section 486.505 implements the definition of “qualified home infusion therapy supplier” set forth at section 1861(iii)(3)(D)(i) of the Act, defining the term to mean a supplier of home infusion therapy that meets all of the following criteria which are set forth at section 1861(iii)(3)(D)(i) of the Act: (1) furnishes infusion therapy to individuals with acute or chronic conditions requiring administration of home infusion drugs; (2) ensures the
(
printed page 72140)
safe and effective provision and administration of home infusion therapy on a 7-day-a-week, 24-hour-a-day basis; (3) is accredited by an organization designated by the Secretary in accordance with section 1834(u)(5) of the Act; and (4) meets such other requirements as the Secretary determines appropriate. A qualified home infusion therapy supplier may subcontract with a pharmacy, physician, provider of services, or supplier to meet these requirements.
Section 486.505 implements the definition of “home infusion drug” set forth at section 1861(iii)(3)(C) of the Act, currently defining the term as a parenteral drug or biological administered intravenously, or subcutaneously for an administration period of 15 minutes or more, in the home of an individual through a pump that is an item of DME, excluding insulin pump systems and self-administered drugs or biologicals on a self-administered drug exclusion list.
b. Durable Medical Equipment Benefit
Under the Medicare Part B benefit for DME, a limited number of home infusion drugs (as defined under
42 CFR 486.505
) are covered if it is determined that it is medically necessary to use an external infusion pump classified as DME for administration of the home infusion drug, and the home infusion drug being used with the pump is, itself, reasonable and necessary for the treatment of an illness or injury (
84 FR 60612
).
For an external infusion pump and associated supplies to be covered under the Part B DME benefit, the pump must, among other statutory and regulatory requirements, be “appropriate for use in the home” (see
42 CFR 414.202
). This requirement means that the equipment must be capable of being safely and effectively used by the beneficiary or caregiver in the home without the assistance of a health care professional (
84 FR 60628
). As noted previously, section 1861(iii)(3)(C) of the Act limits the home infusion therapy benefit to drugs administered in the patient's home through a pump covered under the DME benefit as defined under section 1861(n) of the Act. Therefore, historically, external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs that do not meet the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement have not been eligible for coverage under the DME benefit and services associated with administering the home infusion have not been covered under the Part B home infusion therapy benefit.
2. Current Issues
Section 6222(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (CAA, 2026) (
Pub. L. 119-75
) amended section 1861(n) of the Act to expand the scope of the Medicare Part B benefit for DME to include certain external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs (as defined in section 1861(iii)(3)(C) of the Act) or other associated supplies that would not otherwise qualify as DME because the use of such an item would not meet the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement applied to the DME definition at
42 CFR 414.202
. As stated in section V.D.1. of this final rule, CMS has historically interpreted the requirement that DMEPOS must be “appropriate for use in the home” to mean that the equipment must be capable of being safely and effectively used by the beneficiary or caregiver in the home without the assistance of a health care professional.
Effective for items furnished on or after April 1, 2027, section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026, states an external infusion pump and associated home infusion drug (as defined in section 1861 (iii)(3)(C) of the Act) or other associated supplies that do not meet the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement applied to the definition of DME under
42 CFR 414.202
(or any successor to such regulation) must be treated as meeting such requirement if each of the following criteria is satisfied:
The prescribing information approved by the FDA for the home infusion drug associated with the pump instructs that the drug should be administered by or under the supervision of a health care professional;
A qualified home infusion therapy supplier, as defined in section 1861(iii)(3)(D) of the Act, administers or supervises the administration of the drug or biological in a safe and effective manner in the patient's home, as defined in section 1861(iii)(3)(B) of the Act; and
The FDA-approved prescribing information instructs that the home infusion drug be infused at least 12 times per year:
++ Intravenously or subcutaneously; or
++ At infusion rates that the Secretary determines would require the use of an external infusion pump.
Section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026 does not define the term “health care professional.” In the proposed rule titled “Calendar Year 2027 Home Health Prospective Payment System (HH PPS) Rate Update; Requirements for the HH Quality Reporting Program and the Expanded HH Value-Based Purchasing Model; Medicare Provider Enrollment, Durable Medical Equipment (DME), and DME, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies (DMEPOS) Policies,” which we published in the
Federal Register
on July 6, 2026, we proposed that the term “health care professional” would refer to any of the following clinicians, provided that such clinician is permitted to administer or supervise the administration of a home infusion drug in accordance with Federal and State law: physician (as defined in section 1861(r) of the Act); a clinical nurse specialist, nurse practitioner, or a physician assistant (as such terms are defined in section 1861(aa)(5) of the Act and regulations at
42 CFR 410.74
through
410.76
); or a registered nurse otherwise licensed to practice nursing in the State in which the home infusion drug is administered (
91 FR 41305
). To ensure consistency across the Medicare program, we proposed to define physician, clinical nurse specialist, nurse practitioner, and physician assistant as such terms are defined under the Medicare home health benefit. Given that sections 1861(r) and (aa)(5) of the Act (as codified at
42 CFR 410.74
through
410.76
) do not define “registered nurse,” we proposed to define “registered nurse” as a clinician licensed to practice nursing in the State in which the home infusion drug is administered (
91 FR 41305
).
Because of the risks associated with administering certain home infusion drugs in the home under the expanded DME benefit, we proposed limiting the definition of “health care professional” to these practitioners (
91 FR 41305
). We stated that we are aware of at least one drug, patisiran, that presents heightened safety risks and that may meet the new criteria and definition of home infusion drug under the revised definition of DME at section 1861(n) of the Act (
91 FR 41305
). In accordance with the prescribing information for the drug patisiran, adverse reactions during clinical trials included upper respiratory tract infections as well as infusion-related reaction symptoms including dizziness, headaches, chest pain, and other symptoms. Four serious adverse reactions of atrioventricular (AV) heart block (2.7 percent) occurred in patients treated with patisiran, including three cases of complete AV block. Warnings and precautions regarding infusion-related reactions under the highlights of prescribing information include the need to monitor for signs and symptoms of reactions during infusion, slow or interrupt the
(
printed page 72141)
infusion if clinically indicated, and discontinue the infusion if a serious or life-threatening infusion-related reaction occurs. Infusion-related reactions for other home infusion drugs that may be covered under the expansion of the DME benefit could be even more serious and require emergency medical assistance in certain situations. Based on our review, we stated that we believe that such safety concerns may be adequately monitored and mitigated if either a physician, clinical nurse specialist, nurse practitioner, physician assistant, or registered nurse administers or supervises the administration of the home infusion drug (
91 FR 41305
). We stated that we believe any of these clinicians, if available on hand, could address any emergency medical events that occur during the course of the infusion of the drug (
91 FR 41305
). We solicited comments on the proposal, including whether there are other clinicians that may be equally qualified to administer or supervise the infusions of the drugs in the home and also address any emergency medical events that occur during the course of the infusion of the drug (
91 FR 41305
).
We note that we did not propose that the term “health care professional” be defined to include a licensed practical nurse (LPN) or licensed vocational nurse (LVN) under the supervision of a registered nurse or physician (
91 FR 41305
). State law varies in terms of whether an LPN or LVN can perform certain emergency services such as delivering emergency medications. Thus, we stated that it is not clear that addressing the adverse effects associated with the administration of certain home infusion drugs would consistently fall under an LPN's or LVN's scope of practice (
91 FR 41305
). Additionally, as LPNs and LVNs practice under supervision without the same level of independent clinical authority as the professionals identified previously, we stated that we believe they are less suited to serve as a health care professional for administering complex home infusion drugs under the expanded Medicare DME benefit. In addition, we stated that we do not believe that supervising the administration of the drug in the home should be done remotely as this could violate state laws and compromise the safety of the home infusion therapy as a health care professional would not be present to perform any necessary emergency services (
91 FR 41305
). In order to be present and able to perform emergency services in the home setting if necessary for the safety and health of the beneficiary, we proposed that the health care professional be on site at the home to administer or directly supervise the administration of a home infusion drug covered under the expanded DME benefit (
91 FR 41305
). We solicited comments on the proposal (
91 FR 41305
).
As stated previously, section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026 expands the DME benefit category to include external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs that the prescribing information instructs should be infused at least 12 times per year: (1) intravenously or subcutaneously (section 1861(n)(3)(A) of the Act); or (2) infused at infusion rates that the Secretary determines would require the use of an external infusion pump (section 1861(n)(3)(B) of the Act). Based on our review, we stated that there do not currently appear to be any home infusion drugs that must be infused at rates that would require the use of an external infusion pump that do not otherwise already fall under the criterion set forth under section 1861(n)(3)(A) of the Act (
91 FR 41305
). Therefore, we did not propose to include additional drugs under the scope of this DME benefit category expansion that do not already meet the criterion set forth under section 1861(n)(3)(A) of the Act (
91 FR 41306
). The criterion specified in section 1861(n)(3) of the Act is that the drug must be infused at least 12 times per year. Because of the way dosing information is typically framed in the prescribing information, we proposed that to meet this requirement, the drug must be infused at least once per month (
91 FR 41306
). We stated that we believe such clarification would be appropriate given that it is aligned with how home infusion drugs are typically framed in the prescribing information. Therefore, we proposed that home infusion drugs covered under this expanded DME benefit must be infused at least once a month (
91 FR 41306
). We solicited comments on the proposal (
91 FR 41306
).
We note that we did not propose a minimum or maximum number of times a drug must be infused to qualify as a “home infusion drug” (
91 FR 41306
). The duration of treatment is not always clear and is often patient-dependent. Prescribing information for infusion drugs will often call for infusions to continue indefinitely, until toxicity, or until adverse reactions preclude further treatment.
Finally, section 6222(b) of the CAA, 2026 requires the Secretary to ensure that patients are notified of the cost sharing for electing home infusion therapy compared to other applicable settings of care for the furnishing of infusion drugs under the Medicare program. We stated that we plan to implement this provision through subregulatory guidance (
91 FR 41306
).
3. Provisions of the Regulation
We proposed to revise the definition of DME under
42 CFR 414.202
to incorporate the amendments to section 1861(n) of the Act for implementation of section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026, effective April 1, 2027 (
91 FR 41306
). Specifically, we proposed to provide that certain external infusion pumps, associated home infusion drugs, and related supplies will be treated as meeting the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement when the following three criteria under paragraphs (1) through (3) of section 1861(n) of the Act are satisfied (
91 FR 41306
):
The prescribing information approved by the FDA for the home infusion drug (as defined in § 486.505) associated with the pump instructs that the drug should be administered by or under the supervision of a health care professional. The health care professional must be a clinical nurse specialist (as defined in § 410.76), nurse practitioner (as defined in § 410.75), physician assistant (as defined in § 410.74), physician as defined in section 1861(r) of the Act, or a registered nurse otherwise licensed to practice nursing in the State in which the home infusion drug is administered. The health care professional must be on site at the home to administer or supervise the administration of the home infusion drug.
A qualified home infusion therapy supplier (as defined in § 486.505) administers or supervises the administration of the home infusion drug in a safe and effective manner in the patient's home (as defined in § 486.505).
The prescribing information instructs that the home infusion drug be infused at least 12 times per year (at least once a month), either intravenously or subcutaneously
,
or at infusion rates that the Secretary determines would require the use of an external infusion pump. We solicited comments on the proposal. We received comments on the proposed DME benefit expansion for infusion pumps and drugs from a range of stakeholders, including home infusion and specialty pharmacy organizations, health care providers and health systems, patient advocacy organizations, pharmaceutical manufacturers, DME suppliers, clinician organizations, device and technology stakeholders, and other health care
(
printed page 72142)
organizations. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters generally supported expanding Medicare coverage for certain external infusion pumps, associated home infusion drugs, and related supplies that would not otherwise meet the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement. Commenters stated that the expansion could improve access to home infusion and allow beneficiaries to receive clinically appropriate therapies in the home. Several commenters also expressed concern that the statutory expansion remains limited and may not substantially address the broader difference between home infusion coverage available to Medicare beneficiaries and individuals with commercial insurance.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support for expanding the DME benefit for certain external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs and supplies. Section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026 amended section 1861(n) of the Act to provide that certain external infusion pumps and associated home infusion drugs or other associated supplies that would not otherwise meet the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement are treated as meeting that requirement when the statutory criteria are satisfied. We are finalizing the expansion consistent with section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026 and as proposed. To the extent comments requested expansion beyond the therapies that satisfy the statutory criteria, those requests are beyond the scope of this rulemaking and, where they would require modification of the statutory criteria, would require legislative action.
Comment:
The majority of commenters supported the proposed requirement that the health care professional be physically present in the home to administer or supervise administration of the home infusion drug, emphasizing patient safety and the need for clinical support when administering therapies that may result in serious infusion reactions or require emergency intervention. A commenter recommended that CMS permit supervision through real-time audio and video technology when clinically appropriate and consistent with FDA approved prescribing information, rather than requiring physical presence in every circumstance.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comments. We continue to believe that requiring the health care professional to be physically present in the home is appropriate for the therapies covered under this expanded DME benefit. As discussed in the proposed rule, certain drugs that may qualify under this provision may present safety risks that require the health care professional to be available in the home to address an adverse event or provide emergency services. Accordingly, we are finalizing the physical presence requirement as proposed. Administration or supervision for purposes of this provision may not be furnished remotely.
Comment:
Several commenters supported CMS's proposal to limit the health care professionals who may administer or supervise the administration of home infusion drugs to physicians, clinical nurse specialists, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and registered nurses, stating that the designated health care professionals have the appropriate clinical training and authority to administer or supervise home infusion drugs. Some commenters also supported excluding licensed practical nurses and licensed vocational nurses because their scope of practice and authority may vary by State.
Several other commenters recommended that CMS not limit the definition to the specific professional categories identified in the proposed rule. Concerns were raised that a fixed list of professional types could restrict access to home infusion, particularly in rural and underserved areas. These commenters recommended allowing appropriately licensed health care professionals to administer or supervise administration when authorized under applicable State scope of practice and licensure requirements. The commenters also emphasized competency, appropriate training, and authority under State law rather than professional title alone.
A commenter recommended that CMS not categorically exclude pharmacists where State law authorizes them to administer parenteral medications and to recognize the role pharmacists may play in infusion therapy. A commenter also requested that CMS clarify that home infusion drugs are administered by health care professionals, while qualified home infusion therapy suppliers remain the entities authorized to furnish and bill for home infusion therapy services.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comments regarding the definition of health care professional. In the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule (
91 FR 41305
), we proposed, that to be covered under the expanded DME benefit, the prescribing information approved by the FDA for the home infusion drug (as defined in § 486.505) associated with the pump must instruct that the drug should be administered by or under the supervision of one of the following health care professionals: a clinical nurse specialist (as defined in § 410.76), nurse practitioner (as defined § 410.75), physician assistant (as defined in § 410.74), physician as defined in section 1861(r) of the Act, or a registered nurse otherwise licensed to practice nursing in the State in which the home infusion drug is administered because of the risks associated with administering certain home infusion drugs in the home. We excluded LPNs and LVNs from this definition for two related reasons: (1) State law varies as to whether LPNs and LVNs may independently perform certain tasks associated with home infusion drug administration, such as responding to adverse drug events; and (2) because LPNs and LVNs typically practice under supervision rather than with independent clinical authority, we were concerned that they would be less suited, as a category, to administer complex home infusion drugs.
After further review and consideration of the public comments, we continue to believe that it is important for a health care professional administering or supervising the administration of a home infusion drug to have the clinical authority necessary to safely administer or supervise the administration of the drug and respond to adverse events or other medical events that may occur during the infusion.
However, both concerns are more accurately and more precisely addressed by the independent clinical authority that a State has conferred on a given professional to administer or supervise the administration of the home infusion drug, rather than by a categorical exclusion based on license title. State scope-of-practice determinations already reflect a judgment about which activities a licensed professional—including an LPN or LVN—may perform independently versus only under supervision and categorical exclusions may not adequately account for differences in these state rules and regulations. We also agree with commenters concerned about beneficiary access to the expanded benefit in areas where there may be a shortage of registered nurses and other specific types of health care professionals named in the proposed rule, especially in rural areas, and believe that not limiting the definition of health care professional to the specific categories identified in the proposed rule may prevent certain
(
printed page 72143)
situations where patients in rural or underserved areas cannot access home infusion therapy simply because their available clinician does not fall within a specifically named profession type. We believe this approach appropriately addresses the safety concerns identified in the proposed rule while also addressing potential beneficiary access concerns.
After consideration of the public comments, we are not finalizing the proposed limitations on the definition of a health care professional and are revising
42 CFR 414.202(2)(i)(A)
to state that the administration or supervision of the home infusion drug must be within the scope of the health care professional's practice as specified by applicable Federal and State laws, regulations, and licensure requirements. This would enable any health care professional to provide these services if it is within their scope of practice, in order to more accurately reflect the clinical authority States have already conferred and to address potential access problems in rural areas. Regarding the comment requesting that we clarify that home infusion drugs are administered by a health care professional, we note that the proposed
42 CFR 414.202(2)(i)
, consistent with section 6222(a)(1) of the CAA, 2026, requires that the FDA-approved prescribing information for the home infusion drug instruct that the drug be administered by or under the supervision of a health care professional. Separately,
42 CFR 414.202 (2)(ii)
, consistent with section 6222(a)(2) of the CAA, 2026, requires that a qualified home infusion therapy supplier administer or supervise the administration of the home infusion drug in a safe and effective manner in the patient's home. These requirements address different aspects of the provision. Paragraph (2)(i) addresses the health care professional who may administer or supervise the administration of the drug, while paragraph (2)(ii) addresses the role of the qualified home infusion therapy supplier in furnishing home infusion therapy services.
We also believe that the qualified home infusion therapy supplier will employ, contract with, or coordinate with the health care professional who administers or supervises the administration of the home infusion drug. Section 1861(iii)(3)(D)(i) of the Act permits a qualified home infusion therapy supplier to subcontract with a pharmacy, physician, provider of services, or supplier to meet the applicable qualified home infusion therapy supplier requirements. The qualified home infusion therapy supplier remains responsible for furnishing and billing for the home infusion therapy services in accordance with the applicable requirements. For these reasons, and due to the scope-of-practice standard in
42 CFR 414.202(2)(i)(A)
, we believe we have appropriately addressed the commenter's concerns.
Comment:
Commenters expressed differing views regarding CMS's proposal to interpret the statutory requirement that the prescribing information instruct that the home infusion drug be infused at least 12 times per year to mean at least once per month. Several commenters supported the proposed interpretation, stating that it would provide a reasonable and administratively workable standard for applying the statutory frequency criterion. Some commenters also supported not establishing a separate minimum or maximum number of infusions.
Several other commenters recommended that CMS apply the statutory language of at least 12 times per year without specifying an infusion during every calendar month. These comments stated that annual and monthly frequency requirements are not necessarily equivalent because dosing schedules may vary based on the drug, treatment phase, clinical response, and other clinical circumstances. A comment provided an example of a therapy administered through treatment cycles that result in more than 12 infusions annually without an infusion occurring during every calendar month. Comments also stated that the “at least once a month” criterion is not what is provided in the statute and that CMS has arbitrarily read additional requirements into the statute that Congress did not include.
Several commenters also raised concerns regarding loading periods, temporary treatment interruptions, illness, travel, scheduling issues, provider shortages, and individualized dosing adjustments. The comments requested flexibility so that these circumstances would not unnecessarily affect access to the benefit.
Other comments sought broader relief from the annual frequency criterion of 12 infusions, stating that the statutory frequency threshold limits the range of therapies that may qualify for the expanded benefit.
Response:
We thank the commenters for expressing their thoughts and concerns regarding the frequency criterion. Section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026 amended section 1861(n) of the Act to require, among other applicable criteria, that the prescribing information instruct that the home infusion drug be infused at least 12 times per year. In the proposed rule, we proposed to interpret this statutory requirement to mean that the drug must be infused at least once per month based on how dosing information for home infusion drugs is typically described in prescribing information.
We agree that the statutory requirement of at least 12 infusions per year does not necessarily require an infusion during every calendar month. A dosing schedule may provide for 12 or more infusions per year while also including treatment cycles or periods during which an infusion does not occur.
After consideration of the public comments expressing concern about our deviation from the statutory language, we are not finalizing our proposed interpretation that at least 12 times per year means at least once per month. We are not including the parenthetical “at least once a month” in paragraph (2)(iii) of the definition of DME in
42 CFR 414.202
, and we are finalizing the regulatory text consistent with the statutory requirement of “at least 12 times per year.”
We clarify that this criterion is not based on how often an individual beneficiary receives an infusion, but rather what the applicable prescribing information instructs regarding the frequency of infusion. However, we disagree with comments requesting that CMS waive, reduce, or establish exceptions to the requirement that the prescribing information instruct that the drug be infused at least 12 times per year. Congress expressly established the 12 times per year criterion in section 1861(n)(3) of the Act. We do not have authority through this rulemaking to eliminate or modify that statutory requirement. A change to that requirement would require a change in the statute.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern that Medicare beneficiaries may face higher cost sharing when receiving infusion therapy in the home and recommend that beneficiaries receive clear information regarding expected costs before electing home infusion.
Response:
Section 6222(b) of the CAA, 2026 requires the Secretary to ensure that beneficiaries are notified of the cost sharing for electing home infusion therapy compared with other applicable settings of care. We agree that beneficiaries should be appropriately notified of cost sharing implications, and CMS plans to implement this statutory requirement through subregulatory guidance.
(
printed page 72144)
Comment:
Commenters from home infusion and specialty pharmacy organizations, health care providers, pharmaceutical manufacturers, patient advocacy organizations, DME suppliers, and device and technology stakeholders provided feedback regarding implementation of the expanded DME benefit. Several commenters addressed reasonable and necessary determinations for external infusion pumps, drugs, and associated supplies, pump necessity including a comment that specifically mentioned, titration and dose ramp up periods, and infusion monitoring technology. Several commenters also addressed implementation of the Medicare home infusion therapy services benefit, including payment categories, HCPCS coding, Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) coordination, supplier enrollment and billing, subcontracting and supplier arrangements, claims processing, operational guidance, and implementation timing.
Response:
The provisions of this rule address the scope of the DME benefit under section1861(n) of the Act, as amended by section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026. Reasonable and necessary determinations under section 1862(a)(1)(A) of the Act and issues concerning home infusion therapy payment, coding, supplier arrangements, billing, claims processing, and other operational matters are outside the scope of these provisions. Reasonable and necessary determinations for pumps, drugs, and supplies will be addressed by the DME MACs through the applicable coverage process. CMS is also working to address other implementation issues following publication of this final rule and in advance of the effective date, as appropriate. Additionally, we encourage suppliers to provide beneficiaries with a voluntary advance notice (for example, a voluntary Advance Beneficiary Notice of Non-coverage) when the mode of administration of a drug changes from an external infusion pump to another mode (for example, IV drip) and the requirements set forth under section 1861(n)(3) of the Act are not met, so that beneficiaries understand the potential impact of such a change on Medicare coverage and payment. We believe this notice will support beneficiary understanding about their financial responsibility and informed decision-making.
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing modifications to the definition of DME under
42 CFR 414.202
to incorporate the amendments to section 1861(n) of the Act by section 6222(a) of the CAA, 2026, effective April 1, 2027. Specifically, we are finalizing that certain external infusion pumps, associated home infusion drugs, and related supplies will be treated as meeting the “appropriate for use in the home” requirement when the following criteria under paragraphs (1) through (3) of section 1861(n) of the Act are satisfied:
The prescribing information approved by the FDA for the home infusion drug (as defined in § 486.505) associated with the pump instructs that the drug should be administered by or under the supervision of a health care professional. The health care professional must be on site at the home to administer or supervise the administration of the home infusion drug, and the administration or supervision must be within the health care professional's scope of practice as specified by applicable Federal and State laws, regulations, and licensure requirements.
A qualified home infusion therapy supplier (as defined in § 486.505) administers or supervises the administration of the home infusion drug in a safe and effective manner in the patient's home (as defined in § 486.505).
The prescribing information instructs that the home infusion drug be infused at least 12 times per year either intravenously or subcutaneously, or at infusion rates that the Secretary determines would require the use of an external infusion pump.
E. DMEPOS Competitive Bidding Program—Country of Origin
In the CY 2027 HH PPS proposed rule, CMS discussed requiring Durable Medical Equipment, Prosthetics, Orthotics, and Supplies (DMEPOS) Competitive Bidding Program (CBP) contract suppliers to report the country of origin for the lead items furnished during the DMEPOS CBP contract's period of performance. Under section 1847(b)(3)(A) of the Act and
42 CFR 414.422(a)
, CMS specifies the terms and conditions of DMEPOS CBP contracts.
During an active round of the DMEPOS CBP, contract suppliers are required, as a term of their contracts, to use a reporting form, known as Form C, to provide product information (manufacturer name, model name, and model number) for the lead item they furnish. The information provided in the form is included in the Medicare Supplier Directory on the
Medicare.gov
website with the products the supplier plans to provide during the next 6-month period. Contract suppliers are also required to maintain the accuracy of their product information for the lead item they furnish using Form C. Form C includes an attestation that all the reported information is accurate and up to date. This attestation needs to be completed to fulfill a Form C submission requirement.
We will request that the information collection be revised to include the country of origin for each lead item they report on a new “country of origin” field on Form C. As done historically with the other product information reported on Form C by a contract supplier, the reported country of origin information would also be populated on the Medicare Supplier Directory for the contract supplier during the contract period of performance. This information would allow beneficiaries and interested parties to have access to the information on the country from which the DMEPOS item originated, if interested.
Contract suppliers would identify the country of origin based on the markings on the product for the lead item, or where an exemption to marking applies, obtain documentation from the manufacturer or distributor. Under U.S. Customs and Border Protections rules (
19 CFR 134.11
,
134.46
), imported goods must be properly marked to indicate the country of origin (for example): “Made in [Country]”), unless an exemption applies (for example, an item that is incapable of being marked, like a catheter), as explained at
19 CFR 134.32
.
To correctly identify the country of origin for a product in the absence of a marking or to verify a marking, contract suppliers may need to obtain documentation from the manufacturer or distributor indicating the country of origin for its product, which could include one or a combination of the following: manufacturer certifications, bills of materials, manufacturing process descriptions, commercial invoices, U.S. Customs and Border Protection entry documentation, or a Harmonized Tariff Schedule classification.
The details for this update to Form C will be included under OMB Control Number 0938-1408 (CMS-10744).
We received public comments on these revisions. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the increased transparency that the discussed change would provide to beneficiaries, stating that transparency regarding product sourcing helps beneficiaries make informed decisions.
Response:
CMS appreciates commenters' support and agrees that transparency regarding a product's
(
printed page 72145)
country of origin helps beneficiaries make informed decisions about their DMEPOS suppliers and the DMEPOS they purchase. CMS views this requirement as a complement to the manufacturer and model information that contract suppliers have historically provided and is available in the Medicare Supplier Directory during an active round of the DMEPOS CBP.
Comments:
Several commenters opposed the proposal. Commenters discussed that the country of origin offers limited value to beneficiaries because suppliers already report the manufacturer and model information beneficiaries actually care about; that manual entry of information via Form C will create unnecessary burden for contract suppliers; that responsibility for verifying manufacturer information should not shift to home health agencies; and that it is questionable whether beneficiaries would actually inquire about the country of origin.
Response:
Manufacturer and model information does not indicate where a product is made, so country of origin remains a distinct, complementary data point that supports beneficiaries who wish to consider the country of origin when selecting a supplier and the DMEPOS they want to purchase. CMS acknowledges concerns about the burden of manual Form C entry and will explore options, including a bulk data entry method, to streamline reporting. CMS did not intend, and does not intend, to shift verification responsibility to home health agencies as the reporting obligation applies to contract suppliers, which are best positioned to confirm country of origin information. Finally, even if not all beneficiaries actively seek country of origin information, making it available increases transparency and supports informed decision-making for those who do.
Comments:
Commenters raised several concerns: some stated that the discussed change does not explain how country of origin information will be used and asked for clarification on whether it will inform future policy or enforcement actions; some noted that the discussed change does not identify enforcement actions, and another commenter expressed concern that country of origin reporting alone would not be enough to address concerns related to ownership structures, supply chain security, or other policy objectives. Commenters also discussed that the competitive bidding program's cost-driven structure could let unvetted foreign manufacturers supply substandard or non-compliant products, risking beneficiary safety. Commenters expressed concern that reporting only on the lead item would give beneficiaries an incomplete understanding of the country of origin, since non-lead items can fall under the same HCPCS code as a lead item yet may have a different country of origin; beneficiaries unfamiliar with country of origin distinctions may incorrectly assume all products under a HCPCS code share the lead item's origin.
Response:
CMS clarifies that the primary purpose of this discussed change is to increase beneficiary-facing transparency about a product's country of origin, not to establish a new enforcement mechanism. CMS may use aggregate country of origin data to inform future policy considerations, such as identifying whether reliance on limited number of countries for certain DMEPOS items creates supplier chain vulnerabilities, in later rulemaking. CMS acknowledges that country of origin reporting alone will not fully address broader ownership structure or supply chain security objectives and will continue to explore complementary policy approaches. Regarding beneficiary safety, existing supplier standards and product quality standards remain in effect regardless of a product's country of origin, and this discussed change does not change the bid evaluation or supplier qualification criteria that bidders must meet to be awarded a DMEPOS CBP contract. CMS acknowledges that beneficiaries may assume all items under a HCPCS code share the lead item's country of origin and, therefore, intends to provide education clarifying that the lead item's country of origin does not necessarily apply to non-lead items furnished under the same HCPCS code. Regarding the availability and reliability of country of origin data, CMS notes that under U.S. Customs and Border Protection rules, imported goods must generally be marked “Made in [Country]” unless an exemption applies as provided at
19 CFR 134.32
. Where a marking is absent or requires verification, contract suppliers may need to obtain documentation from the manufacturer or distributor identifying the product's country of origin, which could include manufacturer certifications, bills of materials, manufacturing process descriptions, commercial invoices, U.S. Customs and Border Protection entry documentation, or a Harmonized Tariff Schedule classification, individually or in combination.
Comments:
Commenters offered several recommendations. Commenters suggested that CMS should include more than just the lead item's country of origin, with several recommending that the Medicare Supplier Directory display the country of origin for all products, not only the lead item. Additionally, commenters recommended CMS specify a clear definition of the “country of origin” field, use uniform definitions and reliable documentation standards, and permit suppliers to rely on documentation provided by manufacturers or distributors. Commenters also recommended that CMS require prospective reporting of country of origin, displayed in advance and updated promptly whenever products change, with a couple of these commenters also recommending a correction or audit process for information changes. Furthermore, commenters recommended educational materials. These recommendations included beneficiary education explaining what country of origin information means and the distinction between lead and non-lead items, as well as providing educational materials before the bidding window opens. Another commenter requested that CMS display manufacturer, model, and interoperability information alongside country of origin. A commenter suggested CMS allow bulk data entry to reduce burden associated with the discussed changes. Finally, a commenter recommended that, rather than country of origin reporting, CMS focus on stronger supplier vetting, manufacturer quality standards, and product approval safeguards.
Response:
We appreciate these recommendations. The Medicare Supplier Directory will display the country of origin information, but CMS believes requiring contract suppliers to report on both lead items and non-lead items is too burdensome. However, we can expand the policy later, if needed. CMS agrees that a clear, uniform definition of “country of origin” and reliable documentation standards will improve consistent reporting. CMS believes the proposed rule provided guidance to contract suppliers on identifying country of origin and the types of documentation that may be used, as follows: “Contract suppliers would identify the country of origin based on the markings on the product for the lead item, or where an exemption to marking applies, obtain documentation from the manufacturer or distributor.” Under U.S. Customs and Border Protection's rules (
19 CFR 134.11
and
134.46
), imported goods must be properly marked with: “Made in [Country],” unless an exemption applies (for example, an item that is incapable of being marked, like a catheter), as
(
printed page 72146)
explained at
19 CFR 134.32
. To correctly identify the country of origin for a product in the absence of a marking or to verify a marking, contract suppliers may need to obtain documentation from the manufacturer or distributor indicating the country of origin for its product, which could include one or a combination of the following: manufacturer certifications, bills of materials, manufacturing process descriptions, commercial invoices, U.S. Customs and Border Protection entry documentation, or a Harmonized Tariff Schedule classification. CMS agrees that timely, prospective reporting improves usefulness for beneficiaries and will provide guidance on the expected timeframe for updates following a product change, and will consider establishing a correction process suppliers can use to promptly amend inaccurate entries. CMS agrees that education supports successful implementation and plans to provide materials explaining country of origin information and the lead/non-lead item distinction in advance of the next competitive bidding contract period of performance, which is expected to start no sooner than January 1, 2028. CMS will display manufacturer, model, and country of origin information on the Medicare Supplier Directory to give beneficiaries a more complete product view. CMS notes that the comments about interoperability information are out of scope. Finally, CMS agrees that supplier vetting and product quality standards are important complements to transparency measures, and country of origin reporting is not intended to replace, but instead strengthen, existing vetting and quality requirements under the DMEPOS CBP.
After considering all comments, we will proceed with the information collection revision through the standard PRA process.
