Comment:
Commenters were generally not in support of our proposed values for Implantation of Extra-articular Shock Absorber—Medial Knee. Commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVU which was lower than the survey 25th percentile. Many commenters argued that the proposed work RVU did not account for the time and intensity needed to perform the service along with the cognitive load, demanding precision, and lack of margin for error with placement of the device under fluoroscopy. Several commenters noted that the RUC survey did not include other codes for joint replacements or neutral comparators such as knee arthroplasty or medial compartment orthopedic procedures. Several commenters noted that if the joint-sparing option is valued below the joint-replacing option, practitioners may not offer the procedure to beneficiaries which would decrease access to this less invasive option.
Response:
We continue to believe that the proposed work RVU of 13.16 for CPT code 27494, based on the RUC recommendation, is the most accurate valuation for this service. In our review of this code, we compared CPT code 27494 to other similar 90-day global codes with 90 minutes of intraservice time and found that the RUC's recommended work RVU of 13.16 matched other codes with similar time values. The RUC looked at two key reference codes and compared the surveyed code to the top key reference code, CPT code 29916 (
Arthroscopy, hip, surgical; with labral repair)
which has a work RVU of 14.63 and intraservice time of 90 minutes, and CPT code 29888 (
Arthroscopically aided anterior cruciate ligament repair/augmentation or reconstruction)
which has a work RVU of 13.94 and intraservice time of 98 minutes. The RUC noted that both services typically involve the same amount or slightly higher intraservice time as compared with CPT code 27494. Ninety percent of the survey respondents indicated the surveyed CPT code 27494 was more intense and complex to perform than these key references, making them relative to one another. We do not believe that other codes for joint replacements or neutral comparators such as knee arthroplasty procedures would necessarily be appropriate comparator codes solely based on clinical similarity, or that it would maintain relativity for CPT code 27494 to be valued significantly higher than every other 90-day global code in this range of time values. We continue to believe that the PFS is a relative value based system and we do not base valuation only on things that are clinically related but rather on time and intensity.
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing the work RVU and direct PE inputs for CPT code 27494 as proposed.

(15) Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Implant, Edge-to-Edge Repair (CPT Codes 33469, 33466, and 33467)
In September 2025, the CPT Editorial Panel approved the addition of CPT codes 33469
(Transcatheter tricuspid valve implantation (TTVI)/replacement with prosthetic valve, percutaneous approach, including right heart catheterization, temporary pacemaker insertion, and selective right ventricular or right atrial angiography, when performed),
CPT code 33466
(Transcatheter tricuspid valve edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER), percutaneous approach; initial clip),
and CPT code 33467
(Transcatheter tricuspid valve edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER), percutaneous approach; each additional clip during same session).
These codes were surveyed for the January 2026 RUC meeting.
The RUC recommended the inclusion of an inpatient hospital visit (CPT code 99233) within the global period of CPT codes 33469 and 33466, despite the fact that both codes were recommended with 0 day global periods. We disagree that this inpatient hospital visit should be included within the valuation of these services, as 0 day global periods are specifically defined to include only postoperative care that takes place on the day of the procedure itself without incorporating any postoperative days. We therefore proposed to remove the inpatient hospital visit (CPT code 99233) from both CPT codes 33469 and 33466, including the removal of 55 minutes of associated work time from each procedure.
We disagree with the RUC-recommended work RVU of 24.38 for CPT code 33469 and we instead proposed a work RVU of 17.52 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 95391
(Percutaneous transcatheter closure of paravalvular leak; initial occlusion device, aortic valve).
Our review of CPT code 33469 found that the RUC's recommended work RVU of 24.38 placed it far higher than any other 0-day global code with similar time values on the PFS, especially after accounting for the removal of the work time associated with the inpatient hospital visit
(
printed page 71046)
described earlier in this section. Most codes with 120 minutes of intraservice time and approximately 220 minutes of total time were valued around a work RVU of 13.00-15.00 and there were zero codes valued higher than a work RVU of 17.52. While we concur that CPT code 33469 is a difficult and intensive procedure to perform, we do not believe it is accurately valued at 7 RVUs higher than any other code with comparable time values. We instead proposed a work RVU of 17.52 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 95391, the highest 0-day global valuation with comparable work times, as this will avoid distorting relativity with other services on the PFS. We also note that CPT code 33469 has comparable intensity at our proposed work RVU to the top reference code from the survey, CPT code 33477, which we believe better serves relativity than the RUC's recommended work RVU. The RUC's recommended work RVU of 24.38 would result in an intensity for CPT code 33469 nearly 50 percent higher than the already complex and difficult transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation procedure described in the reference code, which we do not believe would be typical.
For CPT code 33466, we disagree with the RUC's recommended work RVU of 23.92 and we instead proposed a work RVU of 17.06. Although we disagree with the RUC-recommended work RVU for CPT 33466, we concurred that the relative difference in work between CPT codes 33469 and 33466 is equivalent to the recommended interval of 0.46 RVUs. Therefore, we proposed a work RVU of 17.06 for CPT code 33466, based on the recommended interval of 0.46 below our proposed work RVU of 17.52 for CPT code 33469.
For CPT code 33467, we disagree with the RUC-recommended work RVU of 8.00 and we instead proposed a work RVU of 6.34 based on a crosswalk to CPT 22552
(Arthrodesis, anterior interbody, including disc space preparation, discectomy, osteophytectomy and decompression of spinal cord and/or nerve roots; cervical below C2, each additional interspace (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure).
Our review of CPT code 33467 found that the RUC's recommended work RVU of 8.00 placed it far higher than almost any other add-on code with similar time values on the PFS, with the sole exception of CPT code 61642 (Balloon dilatation of intracranial vasospasm, percutaneous; each additional vessel in different vascular territory) which is an outlier valuation at a work RVU of 8.66. Most add-on codes with approximately 50 minutes of total time were valued around a work RVU of 3.00-5.00 and there was only a single code valued higher than a work RVU of 6.34. While we concur that CPT code 33467 is a difficult and intensive procedure to perform, we do not believe it is accurately valued at nearly two RVUs higher than other codes with comparable time values. We instead proposed a work RVU of 6.34 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 22522, the highest non-outlier add-on code valuation with comparable work times, as this will avoid distorting relativity with other services on the PFS. We note that this valuation will also maintain relative intensity between CPT code 33467 and the first two codes in the family at our proposed work RVUs.
The RUC did not recommend and we did not propose any direct PE inputs for the three codes in this family.
Comment:
The majority of commenters disagreed with our proposal to exclude the inpatient hospital visit (CPT code 99233) from both CPT codes 33469 and 33466, including the removal of 55 minutes of associated work time from each procedure. These commenters believe the inpatient hospital visit should be included based on a survey for TTVR and T-TEER where the specialty societies requested, and the Research Subcommittee approved, use of the 000-day Global with visit survey template for the 000-day codes. Commenters also mentioned the TTVR codes are similar to the TAVR codes, which include a same-day post-operative visit. For CPT code 33469 many commenters disagreed with our crosswalk to CPT 95391 and recommended CMS to retain the RUC-recommended value. For CPT code 33466, many commenters disagreed with our proposal to adjust the relative difference through the usage of a recommended interval of 0.46 RVUs. These commenters stated that while they support a slightly higher value for this code, they do not believe any formulaic approach should be used as the primary methodology and rather CMS should rely on clinical inputs and specialty society committees to value services. Lastly, for CPT code 33467, many commenters disagree with our valuation based on the crosswalk to CPT code 22522 stating that it falls below the survey 25th percentile and is less intense than the surveyed code. A commenter also stated that CPT code 61642 is not an outlier, explaining that its high intensity as an add-on code reflects the significant inherent risk throughout the procedure.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. We wish to clarify that our proposal to exclude an inpatient hospital visit (CPT code 99233) from both CPT codes 33469 and 33466 does not suggest that TTVR or T-TEER patients do not require inpatient postoperative care but rather, because 33469 and 33466 have 0-day global periods, we determined that a subsequent-day hospital visit (99233) and its associated 55 minutes should not be incorporated into the procedural work RVU. Accordingly, the exclusion of the inpatient visit is accounting for whether that subsequent-day visit represents physician work intrinsic to the typical tricuspid procedure, rather than considering whether TAVR codes historically included such a visit.
Additionally, for CPT code 33466, we stated in our proposal that we established the recommended interval of 0.46 based on the difference in work values between CPT codes 33469 and 33466. We believe the use of an incremental difference between codes is a valid methodology for setting values, especially in valuing services within a family of revised codes where it is important to maintain appropriate intra-family relativity. Historically, we have frequently utilized an incremental methodology in which we value a code based upon its incremental difference between another code or another family of codes. For example, in the CY 2025 PFS Final Rule, CMS concurred that the relative difference in work between CPT codes 66682 and 66683 is equivalent to the recommended interval of 1.93 RVUs (
89 FR 97710
). We note that the RUC has also used the same incremental methodology on occasion when it was unable to produce valid survey data for a service. Lastly, regarding CPT code 33467, we recognized in our proposal that CPT code 33467 is a difficult and intensive procedure to perform. As a result, we finalized a crosswalk to the highest add-on codes with comparable work times, CPT code 22522, the highest non-outlier add-on code to have a similar level of valuation.
After consideration of public comments, CMS will finalize as proposed (1) removal of the inpatient hospital visit (CPT code 99233) from both CPT codes 33469 and 33466, including the removal of 55 minutes of associated work time from each procedure; (2) a work RVU of 17.52 for CPT code 33469; (3) a work RVU of 17.06 for CPT code 33466; and (4) a work RVU of 6.34 for CPT code 33467. We are also finalizing no direct PE inputs for the three codes in this family as proposed.

(16) Percutaneous Transcatheter Closure (CPT Code 33340)
In April 2025, the RAW identified CPT code 33340 (
Percutaneous transcatheter closure of the left atrial appendage with endocardial implant, including fluoroscopy, transseptal puncture, catheter placement(s), left atrial angiography, left atrial appendage angiography, when performed, and radiological supervision and interpretation)
as a code that has Medicare utilization of 10,000 or more that has increased by at least 100 percent from 2018 through 2023. The specialty societies indicated and the RUC agreed that CPT code 33340 be surveyed for the January 2026 RUC meeting.
We disagree with the RUC's recommendation of the current work RVU of 9.99 for CPT code 33340 and we instead proposed a work RVU of 9.00 based on crosswalk to CPT code 37271
(Revascularization, endovascular, open or percutaneous, femoral and popliteal vascular territory, with transluminal atherectomy, including transluminal angioplasty when performed, including all maneuvers necessary for accessing and selectively catheterizing the artery and crossing the lesion, including all imaging guidance and radiological supervision and interpretation necessary to perform the atherectomy and angioplasty when performed, within the same artery, unilateral; straightforward lesion, initial vessel).
The RUC survey indicated that the typical time needed to perform CPT code 33340 has decreased, with the intraservice time decreasing from 70 minutes to 62 minutes and the total time decreasing from 165 minutes to 154 minutes. While we do not believe that the decrease in time as reflected in survey values should always equate to a one-to-one or linear decrease in newly valued work RVUs we do believe that, since the two components of work are time and intensity, absent an obvious or explicitly stated rationale for why the relative intensity of a given procedure has increased, significant decreases in time should be reflected in decreases to work RVUs although not necessarily in a linear manner. The RUC's recommendation to maintain the current work RVU of 9.99 for CPT code 33340 can only be justified if the intensity to perform the service has increased over time. However, there has been no change to the code descriptor for CPT code 33340 and no apparent change in clinical practice which would warrant the roughly 15 percent increase in intensity as recommended by the RUC. Since we do not believe that there is evidence indicating that CPT code 33340 has typically become more intense to perform, we therefore proposed a work RVU of 9.00 which maintains the current intensity of the service. This valuation is based on a crosswalk to CPT code 37271, a recently reviewed service from CY 2026 that has a higher intraservice time and nearly identical total time.
We proposed the direct PE inputs for CPT code 33340 as recommended by the RUC without refinement.
Comment:
The majority of commenters disagreed with our proposal due to what they stated was an underestimation of intensity for CPT 33340, significant cuts in the overall payment for CPT code 33340 in preceding years, and the belief that the proposed crosswalk does not reflect the clinical procedure and complications that can arise with CPT 33340. These commenters requested CMS to maintain the current value of the work RVU of 9.99 for this code.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback. We continue to believe our proposed work RVU of 9.00 for CPT code 33340 is the most accurate valuation for this service based on a crosswalk to CPT 37271, which maintains the current intensity. Differences in clinical procedures alone do not establish that the crosswalk is inappropriate or that a different valuation is warranted. Additionally, as mentioned in our proposal, the recommendation to maintain the current work RVU of 9.99 for CPT code 33340 can only be justified if the intensity to perform the service has increased over time. However, there was no evidence to suggest the intensity has increased. Furthermore, CPT code 33340 was surveyed and because physician work reflects both the time and intensity required to furnish a service, a decrease in intensity supports a corresponding decrease in the work RVU.
In consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the work RVU and direct PE inputs for CPT code 33340 as proposed.

Injection procedure during cardiac catheterization including imaging supervision, interpretation, and report; for selective right ventricular or right atrial angiography (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
) is valued at a work RVU of 0.49 with an intraservice time of 10 minutes and CPT code 64484 (
Injection(s), anesthetic agent(s) and/or steroid; transforaminal epidural, with imaging guidance (fluoroscopy or CT), lumbar or sacral, each additional level (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)

Comment:

Response:
We appreciate the support for our proposed valuations from the commenters.
Comment:
Some commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVU of 0.68 for CPT code 55716. Commenters requested the RUC's recommended work RVU of 0.80 for the add-on CPT code 55716
rather than the proposed work RVU of 0.68. Commenters stated that the proposed valuation for CPT code 55716 understates the work involved and a work RVU of 0.68 would create a rank order anomaly with CPT code 76872. Commenters argued that the proposed crosswalk code for CPT code 55716 (CPT code 93567) does not accurately reflect the physician work or the intensity of this service being performed. Commenters stated that CPT code 55716 needs to be valued higher than CPT code 76872 because the former code has imaging and biopsy work while the later code is only an imaging code. Commenters felt the proposed work RVU of 0.80 would not maintain relativity within the family. Commenters felt the proposed work valuation of 0.68 would also be compounded by the effect of the conversion factor.

We continue to believe CPT code 55716 is less intense compared to the predecessor CPT code 55715 which has a work RVU of 1.05 and included imaging in the code's valuation. Additionally, a work RVU of 0.80 would be vastly higher than any other comparable add on code in this range of time values. We also disagree with commenters that a work RVU of 0.68 would create a work order anomaly within the code family as compared with the imaging code CPT code 76872. However, CPT code 76872 is significantly longer than CPT code 55716, nearly quadruple the time with a total time of 23 minutes as compared to 6 minutes in duration for CPT code 55716. We agree with commenters that CPT code 55716 is significantly more intense but disagree that it is inappropriate for these codes to be valued similarly given the large discrepancy in their work times. We disagree with commenters that a work RVU of 0.68 would pose a rank order anomaly in this family as the greater intensity of CPT code 55716 is offset by the far greater time of CPT code 76872.

(27) Maternity Care Services (CPT codes 59320, 59325, 59412, 59871, 59080, 59081, 59082, 59083, 59030, 59051, 59431, 59432, 59414, 59300, 59502, 59503, 59504, 59623, 59433, 59434, and 59160)
a. Background and Update
At the January 2026 AMA RUC meeting, the maternity global codes were revised to delete 17 legacy CPT codes, create 12 new CPT codes, and revise 9 CPT codes describing maternity care services. See Table A-D2 for a summary of the codes and their long descriptors. These codes were restructured from the maternity (MMM) global period to individual codes to reflect changes in practice. The previous MMM global period included 12 prenatal E/M visits bundled into CPT codes 59400, 59510, 59610, and 59618. In May 2025, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published new clinical guidelines, recommending that obstetrician-gynecologists and other maternity care professionals tailor the visit frequency and monitoring schedule to the needs of the pregnant woman. These new clinical guidelines provide a sample schedule for prenatal care services and visit frequency, which describes 8 visits for average-risk pregnant women without medical or pregnancy complications, and 13 visits for pregnant women with greater-than-average risk. This sample schedule specifies that additional services may be offered as needed throughout the pregnancy.
When the RUC reviewed these codes, they included 12 prenatal E/M visits (two level 2 established patient office
(
printed page 71052)
visits, eight level 3 established patient office visits, and two level 4 established patient office visits) in the calculations to make these changes budget-neutral despite the revisions to the clinical guidelines suggesting that 12 visits would no longer be typical. As the clinical guidelines have changed to reflect a revised assumption about the typical number of visits, estimating work neutrality based on the assumption that all 12 prenatal E/M visits in the base year would be reported in the predictive year overestimates the total utilization and as a result, undervalues the work RVUs as recommended by the RUC. To improve payment accuracy of the new codes, we proposed to refine the RUC's recommended utilization crosswalk to remove four E/M visits (two level 2 established patient office visits and two level 4 established patient office visits) from the utilization estimate calculation and reallocate those RVUs within the code family to the new labor and delivery codes. This would mean reallocating 11,810 additional work RVUs to the new labor and delivery codes (CPT codes 59080-594503). Since the RUC provided a utilization estimate of 12,791 for CPT codes 59080-594503, this would result in a 15 percent increase in work RVUs for each labor and delivery code. We would like to emphasize that we are not endorsing a reduced number of prenatal visits for pregnant women. Our recalculation of the utilization estimates in the valuation of these services should not be used to determine the appropriate number of visits to provide reasonable and necessary care to beneficiaries. As with all PFS services, maternity services should be furnished when medically reasonable and necessary.
There are no RUC-recommended direct PE inputs for these CPT codes. Table A-D2 also shows the RUC-recommended and CMS proposed work RVUs for the 21 CPT codes.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported our proposals to adopt CPT codes 59320, 59325, 59412, 59871,
(
printed page 71053)
59080, 59081, 59082, 59083, 59030, 59051, 59431, 59432, 59414, 59300, 594502, 594503, 59504, 59623, 59X1159433, 59434, and 59160. Commenters stated that these revised codes would create a uniform system between payors, as many other payors and payment systems such as the OPPS, have already adopted or proposed to adopt the revised coding structure. Additionally, commenters discussed that these codes would increase the transparency of antepartum and postpartum visits performed. Commenters also believed that the updated codes better reflect modern, personalized maternity care. Many commenters supported our proposed work RVU increases to the labor and delivery codes, as these services have become increasingly complex and require significant clinical decision-making, care coordination, and clinician work. A few commenters did not support our proposed increases to the labor and delivery codes, and requested us to finalize the RUC recommendations, because they believed that the RUC's recommendations account for the number of E/M visits increasing for some patients and decreasing for others. Some commenters believed that we should increase the work RVUs for all of the CPT codes, since in some clinical scenarios, the new codes could pay less than the current maternity codes. We also received several questions seeking coding guidance for the new maternity CPT codes.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters for this information and will consider additional refinements in future rulemaking. Although we are not specifying a maximum number of antepartum or postpartum visits that can be billed, we expect that ACOG's guidelines will be followed, and that, as with all services paid under the PFS, all services furnished must be reasonable and necessary. We will also continue to consider methods of bundling under the PFS, including information on the range of antepartum or postpartum visits as stakeholders develop more familiarity with the new code set. We defer to CPT and/or the billing practitioner's MAC for clarification on coding guidance for the new maternity CPT codes.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed.
b. Comment Solicitation on Maintaining Current Coding Through Creation of HCPCS G-Codes
We were interested in thinking about different approaches to how maternity care codes are valued and paid under the PFS. Although the RUC asserts that these proposed coding changes discussed previously reflect clinical consensus, we had concerns that our adoption of the new codes would be disruptive based on how the longstanding existing code structure is currently accounted for in clinical practice patterns. We sought comment on whether CMS should create HCPCS G-codes that would maintain the current coding and payment for maternity services to ameliorate this concern, while we continue to consider the potential impact that changes in the maternity care code family have on clinical outcomes for maternal care. These codes would be used in lieu of adoption of the new CPT codes for purposes of Medicare payment. We were specifically interested in additional information to support or oppose this concern, as well as additional information to support or oppose the use of the creation of HCPCS G-codes in lieu of adoption of the new CPT codes.
Specifically, for payment for maternity care services under the PFS, we were considering, and sought comment on, the creation of 15 new HCPCS G-Codes for CY 2027 that reflect the previous MMM global code structure, with the code descriptors and work RVUs detailed in Table A-D3, as an alternative to the revaluation of the codes as discussed in section (a), of the proposed rule (
91 FR 43842
through
44557
). We sought public comment on these HCPCS G-codes and, after consideration of public comment, could finalize payment for these codes. We sought comment on these HCPCS G-codes and also sought comment on any other HCPCS G-codes that may be needed to reflect the necessary service elements for this code family. These HCPCS G-codes would adopt all current conditions of payment for the MMM global codes, as well as maintain the MMM global period, if finalized.
(
printed page 71054)
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Almost all commenters were opposed to maintaining current coding through the creation of HCPCS G-codes. Commenters stated that the creation of these codes for Medicare would increase administrative burden and market confusion, as well as not representing some of the services described in the proposed CPT codes (including tamponade and 3rd and 4th degree laceration repair). Many commenters believed that the structure of these codes no longer reflect health care delivery, and the proposed CPT codes allow information gathering about the services performed and encourage patient-centered care that these HCPCS G-codes do not. Some commenters did not support finalizing these codes since we did not publish the Practice Expense (PE) and Malpractice RVUs associated with these HCPCS G-codes.
A few commenters supported the creation of these HCPCS G-codes. These commenters expressed concerns about potential cost-sharing, claims denials, more complex billing, and the additional resources needed to adopt the new CPT codes. Some commenters supported a set payment that the HCPCS G codes would provide, and not having payments that vary patient to patient when services are performed with the CPT codes. A few commenters stated that E/M coding does not specifically describe antepartum or postpartum care.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters for this information. We disagree with commenters that any change in maternity coding discussed in this rule, whether the new CPT codes or the proposed HCPCS G-codes, would change any policies impacting cost-sharing or claims denials. While we understand that additional resources may be needed for the higher overall number of codes being billed, we believe that this provides valuable utilization information that cannot be obtained with the continued use of bundled codes. Although E/M coding does not specifically describe antepartum or postpartum care, these codes are used by many specialties to describe professional services that may not explicitly be stated in the E/M code descriptor.
Comment:
Most commenters who requested the adoption of the HCPCS G-codes requested that we adopt both the CPT codes and the HCPCS G-codes for CY 2027. Some commenters requested adopting both codes, but having a defined sunset date and limiting the use of both code sets to Medicare. One of the primary reasons why commenters requested both code sets for CY 2027 was due to concerns about billing guidance for pregnancies that begin in CY 2026 and continue into CY 2027.
Response:
We defer to AMA and ACOG guidance on the correct billing structure for pregnancies that begin in CY 2026 and continue into CY 2027.We also understand that there may be cases in which the prior CPT codes may be needed when billing and paying for episodes of care with service start dates in 2026. CMS published an enforcement discretion under
45 CFR 162.1101
allowing HIPAA covered entities to temporarily use CPT 2026 Maternity Care Services codes for billing and
(
printed page 71055)
payment purposes after January 1, 2027. Payers and health plans may issue business rules in advance of January 1, 2027 instructing providers, clearinghouses and other trading partners regarding CPT code use when billing for Maternal Care Service episodes of care in which services begin in 2026 and end in 2027. Questions can be sent to
AdministrativeSimplification@cms.hhs.gov
with the subject line: Enforcement Discretion.
After consideration of public comments, we are not finalizing the creation of these HCPCS G-codes, although we may consider the creation of bundled codes describing maternity care services in future rulemaking using the information on the billing patterns associated with the unbundled visit codes.

We believe that the RUC's recommended work RVU of 7.06 is an overestimation based on a comparison to other codes with similar time values, particularly the key reference code CPT code 22869 (

). There was a decrease in the surveyed work times, such as the intraservice time decreasing from 60 minutes to 37 minutes, which was not fully accounted for in the RUC's recommended work RVU of 7.06. We also note that the procedure does not seem to have become more intense, as the code descriptor did not change.
In the interest of maintaining relativity with similarly timed codes, we instead proposed a work RVU of 6.23 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 46707.
This code has an almost identical intraservice time and similar total time. The proposed work RVU accounts for the decrease in both intraservice time and total time and is well bracketed by CPT code 67912
(Correction of lagophthalmos, with implantation of upper eyelid lid load (e.g., gold weight)),
valued at a work RVU of 6.20 with an intraservice time of 40 minutes, and CPT code 24358

Comment:
Commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVU of 6.23 for CPT 62287 stating that the complexity of the surveyed code's physician work was not adequately represented and was below the surveyed 25th percentile. Commenters also stated that the crosswalk does not maintain relativity within the code family and is not clinically related to the proposed code. Commenters stated that the proposed valuation does not adequately account for the technical precision, imaging interpretation, anatomical localization, clinical judgment, mental effort, procedural intensity, and risks associated with percutaneous lumbar decompression. Commenters disagreed that a time reduction alone deserves a lower value when the work is unchanged and that the valuation methodology should account for this shift in complexity rather than treat the reduced time alone as justification for a proportionally reduced work RVU.
Commenters stated that the RUC-recommended work RVU of 7.06 would be more appropriate for CPT code 62287 and cited CPT codes 62330 (
Decompression, percutaneous, with partial removal of the ligamentum flavum, including laminotomy for access, epidurography, and imaging guidance (i.e., CT or fluoroscopy), bilateral; one interspace, lumbar
) and 62331 (
Decompression, percutaneous, with partial removal of the ligamentum flavum, including laminotomy for access, epidurography, and imaging guidance (i.e., CT or fluoroscopy), bilateral; additional interspace(s), lumbar (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
) as relevant comparators within the lumbar decompression family. A commenter
(
printed page 71056)
identified CPT code 22869 (
Insertion of interlaminar/interspinous process stabilization/distraction device, without open decompression or fusion, including image guidance when performed, lumbar; single level
), the RUC's key reference service, as an appropriate crosswalk because it similarly involves invasive lumbar spine intervention, image guidance, spatial judgment, and spinal procedural risk.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. We are not compelled by the arguments that a work RVU of 6.23 would not maintain relativity in the family. CPT code 62330 has a higher intraservice time and total time which accounts for why it has a higher work RVU as compared with our proposed valuation of CPT code 62287. We also note that CPT code 62330 has historically had a higher intensity than CPT code 62287, which would be reversed by the RUC's recommended work RVU of 7.06; we do not believe that this reversal of their relative intensities would be the case given that there was agreement from the commenters that the clinical practice of CPT code 62287 had not changed. We also do not believe that the work RVUs of CPT codes 62287 and 62331 are directly comparable since the latter code is an add-on procedure with only 43 minutes of total time. We disagree with the comment that identified CPT code 22869 as an appropriate crosswalk because it similarly involves invasive lumbar spine intervention, image guidance, spatial judgment, and spinal procedural risk. We want to reiterate that the PFS is a relative value-based system and not all reference codes are necessarily clinically related.
We continue to believe that since there was a decrease in the surveyed work times which was not fully accounted for in the RUC's recommended work RVU of 7.06, the work RVU should decrease correspondingly since valuation is based on time and intensity. We also continue to disagree that there has been a significant increase in intensity for this code which would warrant the work RVU recommended by the RUC. Intensity of work under the Physician Fee Schedule reflects skill, expertise, effort, stress, and other factors that influence the assessed relative value of time spent. We disagree with the commenters that performing the same work in less time inherently means that the intensity of a procedure has increased; changes in practice patterns, improvements in technology, or greater efficiencies in the delivery of care can all account for shorter procedure times without a corresponding increase in intensity. Commenters agreed that CPT code 62287 had undergone no significant change in the procedure's performance as reflected by its unaltered code descriptor. Under our methodology for work valuation, if the surveyed work times are decreasing and there is general agreement that the procedure itself has remained unchanged, this supports a decrease in the work RVU, not a conclusion that the intensity of the procedure has increased to match the decrease in surveyed work time. We believe that the agreement from the commenters that there has been no significant change in the clinical performance of CPT code 62287 supports our proposed work RVU of 6.23, not undermines it.
After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing the work RVU and direct PE inputs for CPT code 62287 as proposed.

(34) Radiation Oncology Treatment Delivery (CPT Codes 77402, 77407, and 77412)
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49379
through
49383
), we finalized our proposal to utilize the relationship
(
printed page 71058)
between the Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) Ambulatory Payment Classifications (APC) relative weights for APCs 5621, 5622, and 5623 to inform the valuation of PE-only CPT codes 77402 (
Radiation treatment delivery; Level 1 (e.g., single-electron field, multiple-electron fields, or 2D photons), including imaging guidance, when performed
), 77407 (
Radiation treatment delivery; Level 2, single-isocenter (e.g., 3D or IMRT), photons, including imaging guidance, when performed
), and 77412 (
Radiation treatment delivery; Level 3, multiple isocenters with photon therapy (e.g., 2D, 3D, or IMRT) or a single-isocenter photon therapy (e.g., 3D or IMRT) with active motion management, or total skin electrons, or mixed-electron/photon field(s), including imaging guidance, when performed
) when paid under the PFS. We also stated that we calculated the RVUs for these codes so that the overall PE and MP RVUs for these services represent the same share of total PE and MP RVUs in CY 2025 and CY 2026. To accomplish this, we developed PE and MP RVUs using the assumed distribution of services indicated in the utilization crosswalk.
We proposed to utilize the RUC-recommended crosswalk for these services, which assumed that 45 percent of the billed charges would be reported with CPT code 77412. Some commenters stated that CPT code 77412 would represent only 15 percent of the volume for these services. We stated in the CY 2026 PFS final rule that it is difficult to ascertain how services furnished in the past would be most accurately reported using a future code set (
90 FR 49385
). In response to comments and considering the disparate information we received, we finalized a modified crosswalk that adjusted downward the estimated portion that CPT code 77412 would be reported compared to CPT code 77407 based on commenters who represent those who provide care in the non-facility setting. Specifically, we modified the utilization crosswalk to crosswalk 35 percent of the utilization to CPT code 77412 and 55 percent of the utilization to CPT code 77407. Since the publication of the CY 2026 PFS final rule, interested parties have reported that the 35 percent utilization assumption for CPT code 77412 was still overstated despite our downward adjustment in the CY 2026 PFS final rule, and that the actual utilization for CPT code 77412 is approximately 18 percent. Given the importance of the assumed distribution of services in ensuring that we achieved our target of maintaining the same share of total PE and MP RVUs, we reviewed the claims data to evaluate the actual distribution of utilization among CPT codes 77402, 77407, and 77412. We noted that during the first 3 months of 2026, CPT code 77412 comprised approximately 18 of the total volume of these services.
Given that we valued these services by utilizing the relative relationship between the OPPS APC relative weights rather than our standard PE methodology, shifts in utilization over time are not automatically incorporated into the annual development of PE RVUs for these services over time. Consequently, we proposed to refine the relativity within this family of codes for CY 2027 based on available claim data that corroborates the information submitted to us by outside parties. We did not propose to change the assumptions about the total number of services, but rather, to revalue the PE RVUs using the observed distribution of services, such that the PE and MP RVUs for these services represent the same share of total PE and MP RVUs as they did in CY 2025.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters generally supported recalibrating this family of codes but urged CMS to use both Q1 and Q2 CY 2026 claims data, not Q1 alone, for a more reliable utilization basis before finalizing CY 2027 values. One specialty society called the correction necessary, noting that OPPS-derived APC weights import hospital rate-setting anomalies into the PFS and that the restructured code set selects codes by clinical complexity, treatment area, target number, and dose rather than technique. This commenter said correcting the utilization assumption frees existing radiation oncology PE-pool RVUs to recalibrate CPT code 77407 without affecting overall PFS budget neutrality.
Other commenters cautioned that fixing the internal distribution within a fixed payment pool does not confirm the pool itself is adequate. Commenters reported a 23-30 percent decline in average radiation oncology payment from 2025 to 2026 that the proposed correction would not offset, and asked CMS to use existing authority to provide retrospective CY 2026 relief. This commenter stated that these payment reductions occurred with no corresponding drop in staffing, equipment, safety, or facility costs, calling current operations financially unsustainable. A freestanding practice cited a third-party financial model projecting only a 0.61 percent net increase in freestanding global revenue from 2026 to 2027, versus an estimated 14.21 percent increase under the OPPS methodology, with hospital outpatient departments paid about 34 percent more for the same three delivery levels. A commenter said the CY 2027 recalculation, though reasonable, preserves the same aggregate PE/malpractice pool without testing whether payment for a full treatment course is adequate.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support for updating the utilization assumptions and its impact on recalibrating the valuation for CPT code 77407. We agree that aligning the utilization assumption with the restructured code set's selection criteria improves accuracy. Regarding the commenters who described declines in revenue of 23-30 percent from 2025 to 2026, we note that these figures are inconsistent with our estimates for Medicare payments. Regarding the commenter who stated that the proposed CY 2027 rate only yields a 0.61 percent net increase, we note that the proposed RVUs for CPT codes 77402, 77407, and 77412 increased significantly more than that: for instance, the total RVU for 77407 is approximately 12% higher than the CY 2026 total RVU.
With respect to the request to incorporate Q2 claims data for a more reliable utilization basis, we note that including these claims did not significantly alter the PE RVUs for these services. With respect to comments about payment adequacy, as we stated in the CY 2026 final rule, we calculated the proposed RVUs so that the aggregate PE and MP RVUs for this family of codes—weighted by each code's utilization volume—would remain consistent with CY 2025 levels. In other words, our goal was to preserve the overall RVU share represented by this code family, not to hold each individual code's RVUs constant. For CY 2027, we proposed to improve the precision of our calculation using actual utilization data. If interested parties believe other codes as part of the course of treatment are inadequately valued or should be closer to the OPPS values, we refer them to the potentially misvalued code process for consideration in future rulemaking. Under the PFS we use the best information available to calculate RVUs for a given year. We do not have statutory authority to provide retrospective 2026 payment adjustments.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS reassign CPT code 77407 to APC 5623 (Level 3
(
printed page 71059)
Radiation Therapy), reiterating a recommendation made in its CY 2026 comment letter. The commenter stated that the legacy IMRT codes (CPT codes 77385 and 77386) consolidated into the revised code family were previously assigned to APC 5623, and that keeping CPT code 77407 in APC 5622 undervalues a service now accounting for a substantial share of external-beam delivery volume. The same commenter recommended that CMS refine the transitional crosswalk mapping legacy CPT codes 77385/77386 and 77412 claims to the revised codes, noting that some services historically billed under legacy 77386 may more appropriately correspond to revised CPT code 77407 rather than CPT code 77412.
Response:
We consider comments regarding APC assignments to be outside the scope of this final rule.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern regarding proposed reductions to core physician-work-based services, including radiation treatment planning (CPT code 77263), IMRT planning (CPT code 77301), conventional treatment management (CPT code 77427), and stereotactic treatment management (CPT codes 77432 and 77435). Commenters also expressed concern about reductions to other related services resulting from the efficiency adjustment. Commenters also expressed concerns about reduction resulting from the conversion factor reduction.
Response:
We refer commenters to sections X.X and X.X of this final rule where we respond to comments about the efficiency adjustment and the reduction to the conversion factor.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that because the CY 2026 code descriptors represent materially different, bundled services (including image guidance) but reuse legacy CPT numbers, many commercial payers have carried forward prior rates, edits, and authorization rules associated with the deleted codes, producing underpayment, downcoding, denials, and costly renegotiations outside traditional Medicare. Commenters requested that CMS recognize the redesigned codes as new services for payment purposes and work with the AMA CPT Editorial Panel and specialty societies to establish new, distinct CPT identifiers; pending such action, commenters recommended that CMS implement temporary HCPCS codes or another mechanisms to distinguish the redesigned services from prior code definitions and values.
Response:
We acknowledge commenters' concerns about coding issues related to commercial payers. However, we consider these comments to be outside the scope of this final rule. We refer commenters to the CPT Editorial Panel to address issues related to CPT identifiers.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS not to treat the observed 18 percent Level 3 utilization rate as a quota or audit benchmark, arguing that early 2026 claims data were generated during a documented period of coding uncertainty, and that a longer, more mature claims period together with clear national coding/documentation guidance are needed before such a rate is relied upon. Commenters recommended that CMS formally clarify that the ~18 percent CPT code 77412 utilization figure is not intended to function as a fixed quota or audit trigger.
Response:
The adjustment that we proposed to recalibrate the PE RVUs based on early claims history was intended to improve the accuracy of the PE RVUs. We did not intend to establish a benchmark for the percentage of claims billed with Level 3.
Comment:
Commenters recommended that CMS evaluate the PFS and OPPS payment changes together, including their combined effects on practice closures, consolidation, Medicare spending, and rural access, and provide immediate transition protection for freestanding and rural centers while a fuller episode-level revaluation is completed. A commenter recommended that CMS support development of a longer-term, non-annually-volatile payment reform for radiation oncology, including the Radiation Oncology Case Rate (ROCR) Act, as a structural remedy to the volatility in payment.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' concerns and may consider these issues in future rulemaking.
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to revalue the PE RVUs using the observed distribution of services, such that the PE and MP RVUs for these services represent the same share of total PE and MP RVUs as they did in CY 2025.
(35) Proton Beam Treatment Delivery (CPT Codes 77520, 77522, 77523, and 77525)
Payment amounts for proton beam treatment delivery services described by CPT codes 77520 (
Proton treatment delivery; simple, without compensation
), 77522 (
Proton treatment delivery; simple, with compensation
), 77523 (
Proton treatment delivery; intermediate
), and 77525 (
Proton treatment delivery; complex
) are currently determined by local Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs). We have not previously established RVUs for these services due to the unique nature of the equipment costs associated with these services compared to other capital costs addressed by our usual PE methodology. In the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule, we sought comment on establishing national payment rates for proton beam treatment delivery services. In the CY 2026 final rule (
90 FR 49390
), we indicated our intent to establish national pricing for proton beam treatment delivery services in future rulemaking.
Interested parties have raised concerns about wide geographic payment disparities with the current contractor pricing that are unrelated to the cost of providing care and have requested that CMS nationally price proton beam treatment delivery services. For example, 2024 claims data for CPT code 77525, which has the second highest utilization of the code family, reflects allowed charges that ranged from $122.15 to $1,374.26. Interested parties recommended that CMS establish identical payment rates for PFS and OPPS, calculating a weighted average of the payment rates to maintain budget neutrality across the PFS and OPPS. Other interested parties expressed concern about reliance on OPPS cost data to value proton beam treatment delivery services, as the substantial capital outlays required by freestanding centers could be greater than those faced by hospital systems and the freestanding centers lack the purchasing power or amortization flexibility that hospitals may have.
After considering the comments we received in response to the CY 2026 PFS rule regarding establishing national payment rates for proton beam treatment, similar to the policy we finalized for CY 2026 for radiation treatment delivery services, we proposed to calculate the PE RVUs for these services as follows:
Use the total allowed charges paid by the MACs for CPT codes 77520, 77522, 77523, and 77525 to establish the pool of PE RVUs to allocate to the services in this code family.
Allocate PE RVUs to the individual services using the relationship between the APC relative weights for APCs 5625 (to which CPT codes 77522, 77523, and 77525 are assigned) and APC 5623 (to which CPT code 77520 is assigned) under the OPPS. We believe our proposal appropriately balances interested parties' requests to establish national payment rates with the difficulties we have faced when considering the capital-intensive and
(
printed page 71060)
specialized resources for services like proton beam therapy services.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters broadly agreed that replacing inconsistent, non-transparent MAC-based pricing with a national methodology is a reasonable long-term goal. However, most commenters stated that the specific inputs, data sources, and allocation methodology proposed for CY 2027 are flawed, insufficiently disclosed, and would produce underpayment. Some commenters supported the general direction while requesting technical fixes. Another commenter supported proceeding with national pricing on the proposed CY 2027 timeline.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for establishing a national payment rate for proton beam treatment delivery.
We did not use direct PE inputs to calculate the PE RVUs for these services, as we would under our standard PE methodology. Instead, we used the following two-step approach:
First, we calculated a pool of PE RVUs equal to the amount implied by the rates that MACs currently pay for these services. In other words, we started from current MAC payment levels, converted to RVU terms, rather than building the rate up from individual PE inputs (equipment, supplies, labor time, etc.).
Second, we allocated that pool of RVUs across the individual codes based on the relative relationship between the applicable Ambulatory Payment Classifications (APCs). For example, CPT 77520 is assigned to APC 5623, while CPT codes 77522, 77523, and 77525 are each assigned to APC 5625. At the time of the development of the proposed rule, the relative payment ratio of APC 5625 to APC 5623 was approximately 2.24. We therefore allocated the pool such that the PE RVU for each of CPT codes 77522, 77523, and 77525 was approximately 2.24 times the PE RVU for CPT 77520.
We note that the public use files accompanying the proposed rule inadvertently included a different set of inputs—specifically, inputs from previous RUC recommendations and an equipment utilization assumption. These had not previously appeared in the files because the files are only populated with direct PE inputs for services we price nationally. We confirm that we did not use these inputs—the previous RUC recommendations or the equipment utilization assumption—in calculating the PE RVUs. Our calculation relied solely on the MAC-rate-derived pool and the APC-relationship allocation described previously.
We disagree with commenters who stated that we insufficiently disclosed our methodology. We used this same two-step approach—(1) maintaining the pool of RVUs implied by current rates and (2) allocating that pool based on the relative relationship between applicable APCs—to establish payment rates for radiation oncology treatment delivery and surface radiation treatment codes in the CY 2026 final rule (
90 FR 49379
).
Comment:
Some commenters criticized the proposed 90% equipment utilization assumption as inappropriate and understated for proton beam treatment delivery equipment. Commenters noted this rate is typically reserved for diagnostic imaging equipment, while other radiation oncology equipment generally assumes 60-70% utilization. Sensitivity analyses cited by commenters indicated that adopting a 70% utilization assumption would raise the proposed per-treatment payment from approximately $1,029 to over $1,300.
Response:
As we stated earlier in this section, we did not use the direct PE inputs in the PUF to calculate the PE RVUs for these services. The equipment utilization assumption is therefore irrelevant to this calculation.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that CMS published materially different, inconsistent proposed rate figures for the same codes within a single rulemaking cycle without explaining why the methodology changed. Commenters stated this rollout undermines confidence that the methodology is ready for finalization and makes it harder for stakeholders to evaluate or comment meaningfully on the proposal.
Response:
We acknowledge that the PE RVUs we initially published did not match our proposed methodology, due to a separate technical error. After interested parties raised this issue, we posted corrected PE RVUs. There was no underlying change in methodology. We corrected this technical error 1 week after we published the proposed rule, and stakeholders confirmed they were aware of the correction. We therefore do not believe this limited stakeholders' ability to comment meaningfully.
Comment:
Several commenters noted that the CY 2026 elimination of separately payable image guidance (CPT code 77014, replaced by the professional-only CPT code 77387) removed reimbursement for a technical resource that should now be reflected in the bundled proton beam treatment delivery rates, particularly given that over 92% of patients receive daily image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT). Commenters argued that the proposed methodology does not adequately account for this shift in cost.
Response:
We reviewed claims data from CY 2025 and CY 2026 in response to this concern. We found that MAC payment rates increased significantly in 2026, reflecting the bundling of image guidance. We are therefore calculating the pool of current RVUs using the first two quarters of CY 2026 claims, which increases the PE RVUs for these services.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that using OPPS relative weights—derived from hospital outpatient cost structures—to allocate payments among freestanding, MPFS-paid centers does not adequately capture these facilities' capital and operating costs. Commenters calculated that the proposed freestanding rate (approximately $1,029) sits approximately 28-30 percent below the comparable OPPS hospital rate (approximately $1,434), despite similar underlying equipment and staffing costs. One provider organization noted that only 14 of the 50 operating proton beam treatment delivery facilities nationally are freestanding, community-based centers paid under the MPFS. This organization stated that these centers lack other service lines to offset losses from underpayment. A commenter supported proceeding with national pricing but proposed a specific compromise: adopt a fixed 70 percent equipment utilization rate, discontinue CPT codes 77520 and 77522 as separately payable, and set a single rate of approximately $1,280 for CPT codes 77523 and 77525. The commenter positioned this proposal as a middle path between the proposed MPFS rate and the OPPS benchmark rate.
Response:
We proposed to use the relationship between the APCs to which these CPT codes are assigned to allocate the pool of PE RVUs. We believe the relative relationship between the resources required to furnish each of these services under the PFS are likely to be similar to the relative relationship of the resources required under the OPPS. We acknowledge commenters' concerns about the considerable difference between the freestanding rate and the comparable OPPS rate. The current payment structure already reflects this difference, and we proposed to maintain the current pool of PE RVUs based on that structure. We may consider these comments in future rulemaking. We appreciate the commenter's alternative proposal: to establish a single payment rate of approximately $1,280 for CPT codes
(
printed page 71061)
77523 and 77525, to adopt a fixed 70 percent equipment utilization rate, and to discontinue separate payment for CPT codes 77520 and 77522. The CPT Editorial Panel, not CMS, is responsible for coding changes to CPT codes. As we explained earlier in this section, the equipment utilization assumption is irrelevant to calculating PE RVUs for these services. We are not adopting a rate of approximately $1,280. We believe our proposed approach—using the total pool of PE RVUs implied by the existing MAC-priced claims, updated with the first two quarters of CY 2026 claims data as described previously in response to comments on image guidance bundling—produces a more accurate rate. Consistent with the commenter's recommendation, our approach also results in a single payment rate for CPT codes 77523 and 77525.
Comment:
Some commenters noted that MACs used materially different, non-transparent methodologies to generate the historical allowed charges being pooled. They noted that CPT 77525/77522 payment ratios ranged from 1.159x to 1.382x across MACs, even within the same locality. Commenters also noted that utilization-weighting the pooled data gives two to three MACs outsized combined influence—approximately 78%—over the resulting national rates. Other commenters recommended that CMS refine the methodology using validated practice-expense data specific to freestanding centers that furnish proton beam treatment delivery, rather than hospital-based cost data. Another commenter offered to supply facility-level data to assist.
Response:
Commenters supported nationally pricing these services in part because of these non-transparent contractor payment methodologies, as we summarized earlier in this section. We believe that, generally speaking, national pricing for individual services is preferrable to contractor pricing since it better maintains relativity across the PFS and minimizes regional variations that can create barriers to care access. Although contractor pricing is appropriate for some services, most often used for new and emerging technologies, we believe that CPT codes 77520, 77522, 77523, and 77525 will be more accurately valued using our proposed national pricing.
We agree that weighting the data by utilization means, by definition, that rates where MACs more frequently furnish these services have greater influence on the average. We believe weighting by utilization is reasonable here. When practitioners continue to furnish a service at a given rate over time, that provides at least some evidence the rate has sufficiently sustained provider participation. We believe this approach achieves our goal of maintaining the pool of total PE RVUs implied by the rates that MACs currently pay for these services. We acknowledge commenters' recommendation to use a validated cost study specific to proton beam treatment delivery. However, our approach is intended to move away from direct PE inputs and instead use the relative relationship between the APCs to which these CPT codes are assigned.
Comment:
A commenter stated that this approach may not satisfy the Social Security Act's resource-based valuation requirements. Commenters requested that we defer national pricing until at least January 1, 2028, and establish a defined period to validate the methodology.
Response:
Section 1848(c)(2)(N) of the Act authorizes us to establish or adjust PE RVUs using cost, charge, or other data. Our approach—using the relative APC relationships to allocate the PE RVUs implied by the claims data—is resource-based because the APC relationships reflect differences in resource costs. We do not believe that deferring national pricing to CY 2028 and adding a period to validate the methodology would produce a more accurate payment rate than the methodology we are finalizing. We believe the total pool of PE RVUs implied by the current MAC-priced claims should serve as the source for calculating PE RVUs. Because we would use this same source regardless, changing the methodology further would not materially change the resulting PE RVUs.
Comment:
Commenters raised a range of access-related concerns, including potential impacts on pediatric, rural, and other vulnerable patient populations; the risk of facility closures, particularly among freestanding centers with limited ability to offset losses; the effect of reimbursement policy on hospital-versus-freestanding market dynamics; and high rates of commercial prior-authorization denials for proton beam treatment delivery. Numerous individual patients and a joint patient advocacy letter also described proton beam treatment delivery as critical to their care and urged CMS not to finalize a methodology that could lead to treatment center closures.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns commenters raised about patient access, including impacts on pediatric and rural populations, the risk of facility closures among freestanding centers, and the effect of payment policy on the hospital-versus-freestanding market. As we discussed previously in response to comments on the proposed methodology, our approach maintains the total pool of PE RVUs currently implied by MAC-priced claims. We updated this pool to reflect the first two quarters of CY 2026 claims data to account for the bundling of image guidance. This is not a reduction in overall payment for proton beam treatment delivery; rather, our approach redistributes the existing pool across codes using a transparent, national methodology instead of inconsistent contractor-specific rates.
We believe this approach mitigates the closure risk commenters raised, because it does not cut payment relative to current levels for the pool of services as a whole. We recognize that a national rate may still shift payment for some codes or facilities relative to what a single MAC previously paid. We will monitor claims and utilization data after implementation to assess whether this affects access, including for freestanding centers and vulnerable populations.
Commercial prior-authorization denials involve non-Medicare payer practices and fall outside the scope of Medicare's practice expense methodology. We encourage stakeholders to raise this issue through the appropriate commercial payer or regulatory channels. We thank the individual patients and advocacy organizations who shared their experiences, and we will continue to consider patient access as we monitor this policy's impact in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Multiple commenters cited the same third-party Medicare claims analysis (2019-2022) to argue that proton beam treatment delivery produces downstream systemic savings that justify adequate reimbursement. Cited findings included the lowest 90-day mortality (approximately 2%), the lowest inpatient admission rate (10-11% versus 14% or more for other modalities), the longest time to emergency-room visit, and the lowest emergency-room visit costs among comparable modalities.
Response:
We appreciate the data commenters provided on mortality, admission, and emergency-department outcomes for proton beam treatment delivery. These findings speak to its clinical value relative to other modalities, but they do not bear on how we set practice expense rates. The resource-based PE methodology sets RVUs according to the relative cost of furnishing a service—equipment, supplies, and staff time—not according
(
printed page 71062)
to a service's downstream clinical or cost outcomes. Section 1848(c)(2) directs us to value services based on the resources used to furnish them; it does not authorize us to adjust PE RVUs based on comparative efficacy or systemic savings.
After consideration of the comments received, we are finalizing our proposal, with the modification of using the claims data from the first two quarters of 2026 to establish the total pool of RVUs implied by the MAC-paid claims.

(37) Intracoronary Drug Delivery Balloon Services (CPT Codes 92922 and 92976)
In May 2025, the CPT Editorial Panel created two new codes, CPT code 92922 (
Percutaneous transcatheter therapeutic drug delivery by intracoronary drug-delivery balloon (e.g., drug-coated, drug-eluting), including mechanical dilation by nondrug-delivery balloon angioplasty, single major coronary artery and/or its branch(es)
) and CPT code 92976 (
Percutaneous transcatheter therapeutic drug-delivery by intracoronary drug-delivery balloon (e.g., drug-coated, drug-eluting), single major artery and/or its branches (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
) to describe percutaneous transcatheter therapeutic drug delivery by intracoronary drug-delivery balloons. The RUC reviewed these two new CPT codes at the September 2025 RUC meeting.
We reviewed the RUC's recommended work valuations and found the RUC's recommended work RVU of 10.00 for CPT code 92922 to be high, based on a search of 000 global day codes with between 45 and 75 minutes of intraservice time and between 109 and 149 minutes of total time in the RUC database. For CY 2027 we proposed a work RVU of 8.05, based on the RUC survey 25th percentile, for CPT code 92922. We proposed the RUC-recommended work RVU of 4.38 for CPT code 92976. The RUC did not recommend, and we did not propose any direct PE inputs for these codes.
Comment:
We received a small number of comments. Nearly all commenters argued that CPT 92922
(Percutaneous transcatheter therapeutic drug delivery by intracoronary drug-delivery balloon (e.g., drug-coated, drug-eluting))
contains all of the work of CPT code 92920 (
Percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty, single major coronary artery and/or its branch(es)
) plus some additional resource costs. Some commenters also described the additional physician work involving lesion assessment, vessel preparation, drug coated balloon (DCB) selection and sizing, evaluation of the angioplasty result, and determination of whether a stent-free result is safe and durable. As such, the CMS proposed work RVU results in a work RVU anomaly. A couple commenters asserted that this additional work makes the work of the entire procedure similar to the work of placing a stent and that a crosswalk to CPT code 92928 (
Percutaneous transcatheter placement of intracoronary stent(s), with coronary angioplasty when performed; single major coronary artery or branch).
Response:
After consideration of the comments, we have increased the work RVU because we were persuaded by commenters that we were creating a work RVU anomaly with our proposed valuation of 8.05. However, we find the RUC's recommended work RVU of 10.00 (60 minutes intraservice time and 129 minutes total time) for CPT code 92922 to be too high relative to other CPT codes with similar time values. We do not agree the additional work described by commenters raises the intensity of the procedure to warrant a crosswalk to CPT code 92928.
