(a) Pediatric G-Code for Speech-Language Pathology Services
We have heard from interested parties of the need to preserve CPT code 92507 (
Treatment of speech, language, voice, communication, and/or auditory processing disorder; individual
) specifically related to the pediatric population. Interested parties stated that the 10 new CPT codes do not accurately capture the time and intensity of work as it relates to pediatric patients. To be responsive to interested parties, we proposed to create and pay separately for a new HCPCS code, HCPCS code G0903, to accurately reflect the time and resources spent in providing these services to pediatric patients.
We proposed the following code descriptor: HCPCS code G0903 (
Treatment of speech, language, voice, communication, and/or auditory processing disorder; individual; for the pediatric population up to age 21
). We proposed that HCPCS code G0903 would be reported by a speech-language pathologist performing these services specific to the pediatric population.
We proposed that this code could be billed only once per patient per day. We proposed to assign a XXX global period payment indicator for HCPCS code G0903. The XXX global period payment indicator would indicate that the global period does not apply to this service.
As previously discussed in this section, we proposed to designate HCPCS code G0903 as an always therapy service and add it to the list of codes that are subject to the MPPR for therapy services.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters were in support of the pediatric G-code, while many commenters were mixed. Many commenters were not in support of the G-code for multiple reasons, citing duplication, inadequate clinical specificity, unclear pediatric age parameters, uncertain treatment time requirements, outdated valuation assumptions for CPT code 92507, and departure from the CPT process. Some commenters noted that replacing untimed CPT code 92507 with ten disorder-specific timed codes does not fit how pediatric therapy is delivered. Commenters questioned the time requirements and requested clarification regarding the proposed “60-minute work time” requiring 60 minutes of time for the service. Commenters specifically asked if the proposed 60-minute work time represented the valuation methodology only (similar to CPT code 92507), or if CMS is intending to require a minimum 60-minute treatment session in order to report the new G-code. Commenters noted concerns that the time requirement of 60 minutes is not clinically appropriate and may reduce the effectiveness of therapy due to fatigue, decreased attention, and diminished participation. A time of 60 minutes would also reduce the number of patients they could see and would as a result decrease access to care. Commenters also noted that face-to-face time alone cannot solely measure time for services.
Many commenters noted that if the new G-code was finalized, the code should be untimed as pediatric patients often cannot tolerate longer sessions. Commenters asked about the midpoint of time or if there was or was not a minimum of time required in order to bill the code. Other commenters asked if time referred to face-to-face time or total time of the encounter. Others asked if pre and post time were included. A few commenters requested the G-code to be timed. Other commenters shared concerns that inconsistent adoption of the new G-code across payors could create coding confusion, claim denials, and additional administrative burden.
Response:
We note that the proposed new pediatric G-code was meant to maintain the current billing mechanism and valuation for CPT code 92507, which had a work RVU of 1.30. We believe that this value accurately captures the time and intensity of the work for providing these services. We understand from commenters the pre and post service work involved in furnishing these services and how the work for pediatric patients differs from that of an adult since there are many other components of care, caregivers who need training, follow ups, and school involvement. We did not propose for the G-code to be a timed code and did not include or propose a time in the code descriptor or a minimum session length. The midpoint of time would only apply to a code that is timed and as such, since we did not propose and are not finalizing the G-code to be a timed code, there would not be a minimum time required, of face-to-face time or total time, in order to bill for the service nor would there be a time threshold required for billing.
Comment:
Many commenters asked for clarification and were unsure who in the pediatric population was eligible to bill the new G-code as the code descriptor was noted to be different and had separate references of “up to 21” and references of “up to age 18 to 21” in the telehealth section of the proposed rule. Commenters also asked CMS to obtain pediatric-specific data on time, intensity and cost before finalizing the valuation.
Response:
We understand the confusion with regard to age that stemmed from different code descriptors in the proposed rule. We wish to clarify that the G-code may be billed for patients age 21 and under to be inclusive of as many pediatric patients as possible. In other words, the G-code may be billed for patients through age 21 years and 364 days, and after the patient's 22nd birthday, the 10 new CPT codes would be used.
Comment:
Commenters requested clarification as to whether pediatric providers could bill using the 10 CPT codes or have to use HCPCS code G0903. Commenters asked CMS to allow clinicians to select HCPCS code G0903 or the timed treatment codes based on the service furnished, with the two pathways mutually exclusive on the same date of service. Commenters agreed that a mutually exclusive coding structure would prevent duplicate reporting while allowing for clinical need. Many commenters recommend using the differentiated CPT family for pediatric services while others suggested that CMS create HCPCS G-codes that mirrored all 10 new CPT codes but specific to the pediatric population. Commenters stated that the new proposed G-code does not distinguish between disorders.
Response:
We thank commenters for their suggestion of creating 10 additional G-codes that would parallel
(
printed page 71067)
the 10 new CPT codes for speech-language services in the pediatric population. We wish to clarify that we did not preclude practitioners from utilizing the 10 new CPT codes for the pediatric population. We were persuaded by stakeholders that the new CPT codes may not work for all pediatric patients and that some practice workflows would work best with a specific G-code for billing pediatric patients. To provide the most flexibility to practitioners, we are allowing practitioners to select the codes, either the G-code or the 10 new CPT codes, that most appropriately encompass the services being provided. However, practitioners cannot use both codes (that is, the G-code and one of the 10 new CPT codes) concurrently as this would be double billing for services. We wish to clarify that CMS is permitting clinicians to report the new timed treatment codes for beneficiaries age 21 and under when those codes more accurately describe the clinical encounter. The G-code and the 10 new CPT codes would be mutually exclusive.
Comment:
Many commenters asked CMS questions regarding the 10 new CPT codes and whether they can bill two of the CPT codes concurrently if two therapies were provided, for example if language and swallowing services are both provided concurrently. Many commenters submitted detailed lists of billing questions asking CMS to address in the final rule and prior to implementation for January 1st. Commenters asked CMS to provide clear guidance before implementation including reimbursement rates, authorization requirements, documentation standards, and billing rules.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comments. As stated previously, we will not preclude practitioners from using the 10 new CPT code for the pediatric population and we understand that there are different modalities in terms of treatment of speech-language disorders. We are providing flexibility to practitioners regarding the choice of coding they wish to use in their practice. We want to reiterate that billing the 10 new CPT code or the new G-code shall be mutually exclusive and practitioners cannot bill both at the same time. We are allowing clinicians to report the new timed treatment codes for beneficiaries age 21 and under when those codes more accurately describe the clinical services provided and it is possible for multiple CPT codes to be billed during a single encounter. We thank commenters for the billing and implementation questions asked and we will take into consideration for subregulatory guidance, MLNs, and other resources as needed. We wish to reiterate that we created the pediatric G-code, HCPCS G0903, in order to maintain the flexibility of the predecessor code, CPT code 92507. Therefore, all associated billing rules would apply to the new G-code.
We are finalizing the code descriptor for HCPCS code G0903 to read as follows:
Treatment of speech, language, voice, communication, and/or auditory processing disorder; individual; for the pediatric population age 21 and under.
We note that `age 21 and under' would include patients up to 21 years and 364 days old.
Comment:
Many commenters also requested that CMS specifically propose adding several new HCPCS G-codes to the telehealth list, including the new pediatric G-code HCPCS code G0903, to allow payment for the G-code when services are provided via telehealth and all necessary conditions are met. Commenters noted that the 10 new disorder-specific speech-language pathology treatment codes were not identified for addition to the telehealth list. Commenters noted that, given that CPT code 92507 has historically supported access to speech-language pathology services delivered through telehealth, CMS should ensure that replacing CPT code 92507 did not unintentionally disrupt beneficiary access to clinically appropriate telehealth services.
Response:
We appreciate the comments related to telehealth and the Speech-Language Pathology Services and we refer to section II.D of this final rule for that discussion. The new G-code is being added to the telehealth list for CY 2027.
After a review of the comments, we are finalizing the designation of HCPCS code G0903 as an always therapy service and are adding it to the list of separately payable always therapy codes that are subject to the therapy MPPR.
(b) Valuation for HCPCS Code G0903
We note that the proposed valuation of HCPCS code G0903 is meant to reflect the time and resource costs, for speech-language pathology services inherent to the pediatric population. Therefore, we believe that CPT code 92507 serves as an appropriate reference for the purpose of valuing HCPCS code G0903. We believe there will be relatively the same work involved for HCPCS code G0903 when compared to the work of CPT code 92507 as it relates to pediatric patients, considering the amount of time needed to furnish the elements discussed earlier in this section. Therefore, we proposed a work RVU of 1.30, which represents the assigned work for 60 minutes of CPT code 92507. Additionally, we proposed a work time of 60 minutes established for CPT code 92507, personally performed by the billing practitioner.
We proposed the same direct PE inputs for HCPCS code G0903 as CPT code 92507, as we believe that the relative resource costs for this service will remain the same. To help inform whether our proposed valuation reflects the typical service for the pediatric population, we sought comment on the typical time and intensity practitioners spend furnishing these services.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.

Commenters questioned whether the proposed valuations adequately account for the clinician work and practice expenses involved in providing speech-language pathology services. We mirrored the valuation of the new proposed G-code after the predecessor code CPT code 92507. It was our intention to maintain the existing billing mechanism for the pediatric population. We continue to believe that the same work is involved for HCPCS code G0903 when compared to the work of CPT code 92507 as it relates to pediatric patients, considering the amount of time needed to furnish the elements discussed earlier in this section.

(41) Endoluminal Coronary Intravascular Ultrasound (IVUS) (CPT Codes 92978 and 92979)
In April 2025, the RAW identified CPT code 92978 (
Endoluminal imaging of coronary vessel or graft using intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) or optical coherence tomography (OCT) during diagnostic evaluation and/or therapeutic intervention including imaging supervision, interpretation and report; initial vessel (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
) as a code that has Medicare utilization of 10,000 or more that has increased by at least 100 percent from 2018 through 2023. CPT codes 92978 and 92979 (
Endoluminal imaging of coronary vessel or graft using intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) or optical coherence tomography (OCT) during diagnostic evaluation and/or therapeutic intervention including imaging supervision, interpretation and report; each additional vessel (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
) were surveyed for the January 2026 RUC meeting.
We disagree with the RUC-recommended work RVUs for these codes and instead we proposed work RVUs of 1.40 for CPT code 92978 and 1.04 for CPT code 92979 to account for the significant decreases in physician intraservice time for both codes. The RUC's recommendation to maintain current work RVUs for these codes does not appear to fully account for these intraservice time decreases. While we do not believe that the decrease in time as reflected in survey values should always equate to a one-to-one or linear decrease in newly valued work RVUs we do believe that, since the two components of work are time and intensity, absent an obvious or explicitly stated rationale for why the relative intensity of a given procedure has increased, significant decreases in time should be reflected in decreases to work RVUs although not necessarily in a linear manner, and we do not believe it is appropriate to decrease physician time while maintaining the current work RVUs.
We reviewed the RUC recommendations and found them to be high, relative to other codes with the same or similar work times. Based on a search of similarly timed codes in the RUC database, the RUC-recommended work RVU of 1.76 for CPT code 92978 is higher than 44 of 47 add-on codes with 15 minutes of physician intraservice time. Similarly, the RUC-recommended work RVU of 1.40 for CPT code 92979 would be the second highest work RVU for add-on codes with 12 to 14 minutes of physician intraservice time. Therefore, we disagree with the RUC recommended work RVU of 1.76 for CPT code 92978 and we are instead proposing a work RVU of 1.40 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 93572 (
Intravascular Doppler velocity and/or pressure derived coronary flow reserve measurement (coronary vessel or graft) during coronary angiography including pharmacologically induced stress, when performed; each additional vessel (List separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
). This proposed work RVU is higher than the reverse building block work RVU of 1.06 and results in a higher intensity for the code than its current work RVU and physician time. The resulting increase in intensity more accurately accounts for the RUC's assertion that the intensity and complexity has increased with the evolution of these services because a higher proportion of the skin-to-skin time is now dedicated to more intense activities and interventions.
We also disagree with the RUC recommendation to maintain the current work RVU of 1.40 for CPT code 92979 and proposed a work RVU of 1.04 based on the RUC-recommended increment of 0.36 work RVUs between CPT codes 92978 and 92979. Similarly, this represents an increase in intensity compared to the code's current work RVU and work time to account for the increased intensity that has occurred with the evolution of these services. The RUC did not recommend and we did not propose any direct PE inputs for CPT codes 92978 and 92979.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVUs for CPT codes 92978 and 92979 and stated that CMS should finalize the RUC-recommended work RVUs instead. Commenters stated that CMS had not adequately accounted for the intensity of physician work for these services and that the RUC recommendations preserved relativity within the code family and recognized their greater intensity. Commenters stated that a service should not lose a fifth of its value based on a survey time decrease.
Response:
We continue to believe that changes in work time should be reflected in changes to the work RVU. We note that using the intraservice time ratio, the total time ratio, and the
(
printed page 71069)
reverse building block method for CPT codes 92978 and 92979 all would have resulted in even lower work RVUs of 1.06 and 0.73 respectively. The RVUs that we proposed resulted in a higher intensity for these codes than the current work RVUs and physician time.
Comment:
A couple of commenters disagree with CMS making any valuation for CPT code 92979 based on an incremental difference.
Response:
We continue to believe the use of an incremental work RVU difference of 0.36 between CPT codes 92978 and 92979 is a valid methodology for setting values, especially in valuing services within a family of revised codes where it is important to maintain appropriate intra-family relativity. Historically, we have frequently utilized an incremental methodology in which we value a code based upon its incremental difference between another code or another family of codes. We note that the RUC has also used the same incremental methodology on occasion when it was unable to produce valid survey data for a service.
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing the work RVUs for CPT codes 92978 and 92979 for the Endoluminal Coronary Intravascular Ultrasound (IVUS) code family as proposed. We did not propose and we are not finalizing any direct PE inputs for CPT codes 92978 and 92979.

In February 2025, the CPT Editorial Panel created six new codes to report autonomic function testing with the use of a tilt table, sudomotor tests, and combined procedures to address an earlier RUC referral: CPT code 95944 (T
esting of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; use of tilt table
), CPT code 95945 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; sudomotor, thermoregulatory sweat test
), CPT code 95946 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; sudomotor, assessing the sympathetic skin response (SSR) potential
), CPT code 95947 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; combined parasympathetic and sudomotor testing, quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (QSART) or silastic sweat imprint
), CPT code 95948 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; combined sympathetic adrenergic with at least 5 minutes of passive tilt (ie, tilt table) and sudomotor testing, quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (QSART) or silastic sweat imprint
), and CPT code 95949 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; combined parasympathetic, sympathetic adrenergic function with at least 5 minutes of passive tilt (ie, tilt table), and sudomotor testing, quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (QSART) or silastic sweat imprint
). The CPT Editorial Panel also revised four existing codes to include interpretation and report and clarification on tilt table use: CPT code 95921 (T
esting of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; cardiovagal innervation (parasympathetic function), including 2 or more of the following: heart rate response to deep breathing with recorded R-R interval, Valsalva ratio, and 30:15 ratio
), CPT code 95922 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; vasomotor adrenergic innervation (sympathetic adrenergic function), including beat-to-beat blood pressure and R-R interval changes during Valsalva maneuver and at least 5 minutes of passive tilt (i.e., tilt table)
), CPT code 95923 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; sudomotor, quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test (QSART) or silastic sweat imprint
), and CPT code 95924 (
Testing of autonomic nervous system function, with interpretation and report; combined parasympathetic and sympathetic adrenergic function testing with at least 5 minutes of passive tilt (i.e., tilt table)
). This code family was surveyed for the April 2025 RUC meeting. We proposed the RUC-recommended work RVU for seven of the ten codes in this family. We proposed a work RVU of 0.34 for CPT code 95944, a work RVU of 0.96 for CPT code 95922, a work RVU of 0.88 for CPT code 95923, a work RVU of 1.00 for CPT code 95945, a work RVU of 0.50 for CPT code 95946, a work RVU of 1.50 for CPT code 95924, and a work RVU of 1.17 for CPT code 95947. We note that several of these work RVUs were affected by the efficiency adjustment which was applied at the start of CY 2026, as the RUC recommendations were based on pre-adjustment work valuations.
We disagree with the RUC-recommended work RVU of 0.88 for CPT code 95921 and we are instead proposing a work RVU of 0.74 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 97813 (
Acupuncture, 1 or more needles; with electrical stimulation, initial 15 minutes of personal one-on-one contact with the patient
). When reviewing this code family, we noticed that CPT code 95921 had one of the highest intensities in the family at the RUC-recommended work RVU of 0.88 despite having some of the shortest surveyed work times and describing one of the seemingly least intensive procedures. The revised code descriptor for CPT code 95921 describes a single test for cardiovagal innervation, and we do not agree that this service should be valued with a higher intensity than some of the other codes in this family that contain multiple kinds of autonomic function testing. The RUC's recommended work RVU would also value CPT code 95921 at the same 0.88 as CPT code 95923 despite the latter code having significantly more total work time (32 minutes as compared to 25 minutes). We are aware that these codes share the same current work RVU, however the new surveyed work times indicate that CPT code 95921 typically takes less time to perform than CPT code 95923, and, since the two components of work are time and intensity, we believe that CPT code 95921 should be valued at a lower rate. Therefore we proposed a work RVU of 0.74 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 97813, an acupuncture procedure with the identical intraservice and total work time as CPT code 95921. We also note that this valuation of CPT code 95921 maintains the current intensity of the procedure, as well as better maintaining relativity with the other codes in the family.
We disagree with the RUC-recommended work RVU of 1.75 for CPT code 95948 and we are instead proposing a work RVU of 1.56 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 77047 (
Magnetic resonance imaging, breast, without contrast material; bilateral
). We disagree with the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.75, based on the survey median result, as it represents a significant increase in work valuation and intensity over the other codes in this family. For example, the RUC recommended a work RVU of 1.50 for CPT code 95924 in comparison to 1.75 for this code, despite CPT code 95948 having only 5 minutes of additional intraservice time and 3 minutes of additional total time (50 minutes as compared with 47 minutes). CPT code 95948 would require an anomalously high intensity relative to the rest of the family to justify the recommended work valuation of 1.75, which we do not agree would be warranted here given that this code is performing the same autonomic function tests that take place in CPT code 95922 and 95923. Therefore we proposed a work RVU of 1.56 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 77047, a breast
(
printed page 71070)
MRI procedure with the identical intraservice time and similar total work time as CPT code 95948. We believe that this valuation of CPT code 95948 better maintains relativity with the other codes in the family instead of requiring an anomalously high intensity as was the case at the RUC's recommended work RVU.
We disagree with the RUC-recommended work RVU of 1.91 for CPT code 95949 and we are instead proposing a work RVU of 1.77 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 78831 (
Radiopharmaceutical localization of tumor, inflammatory process or distribution of radiopharmaceutical agent(s) (includes vascular flow and blood pool imaging, when performed); tomographic (SPECT), minimum 2 areas (eg, pelvis and knees, chest and abdomen) or separate acquisitions (eg, lung ventilation and perfusion), single day imaging, or single area or acquisition over 2 or more days
). As was the case with CPT code 95948, we believe that the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.91 for CPT code 95949, based on the survey 25th percentile result, represents a significant increase in work valuation and intensity over the other codes in this family. While we do agree with the RUC that CPT code 95949 includes the most autonomic function tests and should have the highest intensity within the code family, we disagree that CPT code 95949 should be valued at a work RVU that results in an intensity approximately 50 percent higher than the rest of this family. To use the same example again, the RUC recommended a work RVU of 1.50 for CPT code 95924 in comparison to 1.91 for this code, despite CPT code 95949 having only 5 minutes of additional intraservice time and 7 minutes of additional total time (52 minutes as compared with 47 minutes). We believe that the work valuation and intensity are simply too high at the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.91 as this does not maintain relativity with the other codes in this family, given that the same tests are being performed. Therefore, we proposed a work RVU of 1.77 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 78831, a radiopharmaceutical procedure with the identical intraservice time and similar total work time as CPT code 95949. We note that this work valuation still assigns the highest intensity in the family to CPT code 95949, while bringing it more in accordance with its peer codes. We believe that this valuation of CPT code 95949 better maintains relativity with the other codes in the family instead of requiring an anomalously high intensity as was the case at the RUC's recommended work RVU.
We proposed the RUC-recommended direct PE inputs for CPT codes 95921, 95944, 95922, 95923, 95945, 95946, 95924, 95947, 95948, and 95949 without refinement.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that they supported CMS' proposal the RUC recommended work RVU for seven of the ten codes in this family.
Response:
We appreciate the support for our proposed values from the commenters.
Comment:
Several commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVU of 0.74 for CPT code 95921. Commenters stated that CPT code 95921 is “slightly more intense” than the rest of the codes in this family due to the short duration of the procedure and the number of tests performed, including heart rate response to deep breathing with recorded R-R interval, Valsalva ratio, and 30:15 ratio tests. Commenters stated that CPT code 95921 required the same practitioner work as CPT code 95923 and the same intraservice time of 15 minutes. Commenters stated that the only variation was the difference in preservice and postservice time of seven minutes; commenters stated that this difference in time was minimal and it was appropriate that these services be valued at the same work RVU of 0.88.
Response:
We disagree with the commenters and continue to believe that CPT code 95921 is more accurately valued at the proposed work RVU of 0.74. The RUC's recommended work RVU of 0.88 would have assigned an intensity to CPT code 95921 roughly 50-70% higher than the other single test procedures in this family, such as CPT codes 95922, 95923, and 95945, as well as increasing its intensity by roughly 35 percent above the current intensity of the code. This valuation would not be “slightly more intense” in comparison to the rest of the family. Our proposed work RVU of 0.74 maintains the current intensity of CPT code 95921, which is modestly higher than the other single test procedures and matches the request of the commenters for a slight increase in intensity relative to the other single test procedures.
We also disagree with the commenters that CPT codes 95921 and 95923 should have the same work RVU. As we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43887
), we are aware that these codes share the same current work RVU, however the new surveyed work times indicate that CPT code 95921 typically takes less time to perform than CPT code 95923, and, since the two components of work are time and intensity, we believe that CPT code 95921 should be valued at a lower rate. While it is true that the difference in work time between these codes occurs in the preservice and postservice periods, we disagree with the commenters that this difference is minimal: CPT code 95921 has 25 minutes of total work time as compared against 32 minutes for CPT code 92923. This is a difference of roughly 25% in total procedure time which we continue to believe should be reflected in a lower work RVU for CPT code 95921.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that the crosswalk code CMS used for valuation (CPT code 97813) was marked by the RUC with “Do Not Use to Validate Physician Work.” Commenters stated that CPT code 97813 met the RUC's survey response threshold, over 30, however, it will be reviewed in April 2029 since related CPT code 97814 did not meet the survey response threshold with 29 responses. Commenters stated that therefore CMS should not use CPT code 97813 as a crosswalk for valuing CPT code 95921. A separate commenter stated that the structure and valuation of CPT code 97813 did not adequately represent the full work, malpractice, and practice expense associated with the patient's entire treatment period, including time during which the patient remains under the practitioner's responsibility but is not receiving continuous one-on-one contact.
Response:
We remind the commenters that the RUC's “Do Not Use to Validate Physician Work” indicator is an internal RUC identification that has not been proposed or finalized by CMS. We continue to believe that the nature of the PFS relative value system is such that all services are appropriately subject to comparisons to one another. Although codes that describe clinically similar services are sometimes stronger comparator codes, we do not agree that codes must share the same site of service, patient population, or utilization level to serve as an appropriate crosswalk. In the case of CPT code 97813, we believe that it is a strong crosswalk choice for valuation since it is a recently reviewed service with exactly the same surveyed work time values as CPT code 95921.
Comment:
Several commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVU of 1.56 for CPT code 95948. Commenters stated that the intensity in the RUC recommended work RVU of 1.75 and work time of 30 minutes for CPT code 95948 falls in line with the other services in this family, and that the intraservice work per unit of time calculation was not useful when comparing XXX global period services
(
printed page 71071)
with relatively short intraservice times. Commenters stated that CPT code 95948 would not be anomalous with the other services in this family if valued at the RUC recommended work RVU 1.75; since CPT code 95948 is reported when both sympathetic and sudomotor function are tested (and requires the use of a tilt table), commenters stated that the combined tests are more complex due to the necessity of integrating more data points into a cohesive interpretation. Commenters stated that CPT code 95948 requires more total work time and should be valued higher than CMS crosswalk code 77047, and urged CMS to finalize the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.75.
Response:
We disagree with the commenters and continue to believe that CPT code 95948 is more accurately valued at the proposed work RVU of 1.56. We do not agree that the intensity for CPT code 95948 falls in line with other services in the family at the RUC's recommended work RVU; as we stated in the proposed rule, CPT code 95948 would require an anomalously high intensity relative to the rest of the family (roughly 20-50% higher depending on the code) to justify the recommended work valuation of 1.75. We do not agree that this valuation would be warranted given that this code is performing the same autonomic function tests that take place in CPT code 95922 and 95923. We do concur with the commenters that performing the two autonomic tests taking place in CPT code 95948 is more complex than performing them separately, which is why our proposed work RVU still assigns a higher intensity to this procedure than the intensities of CPT codes 95922 and 95923. We also note that our proposed work RVU of 1.56 assigns a higher intensity to CPT code 95948 than the historic codes that previously described autonomic function testing in recognition of this complexity. However, we continue to believe that the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.75 is excessive since it accounts for almost no overlap at all in performing the two tests. CPT codes 95922 and 95923 would have a work RVU of 1.84 if simply added together and the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.75 represents a decrease of only 5 percent. Since the sum of the work times of CPT codes 95922 and 95923 is 68 minutes while CPT code 95948 by itself was surveyed at 50 minutes, a decrease of more than 30 percent, there are clearly significant time savings taking place from combining the two tests which we believe supports the proposed work RVU of 1.56.
We also disagree with the commenters that intensity is not useful for comparing XXX global services given that the statute specifically tasks CMS with valuing services based on time and intensity. Although intensity is not a “one size fits all” tool and needs to be employed with care, the codes in this family cannot be valued properly without incorporating both time and intensity into the analysis.
Comment:
Several commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVU of 1.77 for CPT code 95949. Commenters stated that because the survey 25th percentile is already a conservative measure of work, CMS' proposal to assign a work RVU below that level would result in an excessive and inappropriate reduction. Commenters stated that this approach failed to recognize that CPT code 95949 includes parasympathetic, sympathetic adrenergic, and sudomotor testing, making it the most comprehensive and complex service in the family. Commenters stated that valuing the service below the 25th percentile would not accurately reflect the intensity, clinical judgment, and total physician work involved and urged CMS to finalize the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.91.
Response:
We disagree with the commenters and continue to believe that CMS code 95949 is more accurately valued at the proposed work RVU of 1.77. As we stated in the proposed rule, we agreed that CPT code 95949 includes the most autonomic function tests and therefore our proposed work valuation still assigned it the highest work RVU and highest intensity in the family. However, we disagreed that CPT code 95949 should be valued at a work RVU that resulted in an intensity approximately 50 percent higher than the rest of this family; commenters did not provide an adequate rationale which would support a valuation that high. We continue to believe that this valuation of CPT code 95949 better maintains relativity with the other codes in the family instead of requiring an anomalously high intensity as was the case at the RUC's recommended work RVU. We also note that the RUC itself recommended the work RVU for multiple codes within this same code family below the survey 25th percentile, including CPT codes 95944 and 95923.
After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing the work RVUs and direct PE inputs for the codes in the Autonomic Function Testing family as proposed.
