For CY 2027, the RUC recommended a work RVU of 0.81 for CPT code 95847, a work RVU of 1.05 for CPT code 95848, and a work RVU of 1.60 for CPT code 95849. These codes are professional component only services and have no direct PE inputs; we also note that the RUC recommendations for CPT codes 95847 and 95848 were affected by the efficiency adjustment which was applied at the start of CY 2026, as the RUC recommendations were based on pre-adjustment work valuations. For CPT code 95847, we proposed the RUC's recommended work RVU of 0.81 and for CPT code 95848, we proposed the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.05.
However, we disagree with the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.60 for CPT code 95849 and we instead proposed a work RVU of 1.42 based on a crosswalk to CPT code 92014 (
Ophthalmological services: medical examination and evaluation, with initiation or continuation of diagnostic and treatment program; comprehensive, established patient, 1 or more visits
), which has 24 minutes of intraservice time and 37 minutes of total time. CPT code 95849 is a similarly timed code with 20 minutes of intraservice time and 39 minutes of total time. We are aware that the RUC's recommended work RVU is lower than the survey 25th percentile work RVU and further understand that the increase in intensity from moderate complexity of 5 to 10 channels that generate at least 6 to 8 parameter categories to complexity of 11 or more channels that generate at least 9 parameter categories may not be linear. The additional parameters could be more complex, which could result in higher intensity and may not be fully captured in the previous two codes. We agree that the intensity for CPT code 95849 should be higher; however, we do not believe that the intensity associated with the RUC recommended RVU of 1.60 is typical for this service since it would be nearly double the intensity of CPT codes 95847 and 95848. Therefore, we believe that CPT code 92014 is an appropriate crosswalk compared to the RUC's recommended crosswalk to CPT code 99203 (
Office or other outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of a new patient, which requires a medically appropriate history and/or examination and low level of medical decision making. When using total time on the date of the encounter for code selection, 30 minutes must be met or exceeded.
). We believe that our proposed valuation of 1.42, based on the crosswalk from 92014, more accurately values CPT code 95849 since it does not result in the sizable increase in intensity as recommended by the RUC. In addition, we have maintained relativity between the codes in this family with similarly timed codes.
For CPT codes 95843, 95844, and 95846, which are Practice Expense (PE) only codes, we proposed the RUC-recommended direct PE inputs. However, we noted concerns regarding two direct PE inputs: CA021 (Perform procedure/service—NOT directly related to physician work time) and CA042 (Perform procedure/service in post-service period—NOT directly related to physician work time). For CPT codes 95843 and 95844, the RUC recommended 15 minutes for the CA021 activity, and 25 minutes for CPT code 95846. The rationale for this increase from 15 minutes for CPT codes 95843 and 95844 to 25 minutes for CPT code 95846 was not clearly stated in the PE Summary of Recommendations although this is an increase of 66.7 percent. Similarly, for the CA042 activity, the RUC recommended 40 minutes for CPT code 95843, 50 minutes for CPT code 95844, and 70 minutes for CPT code 95846. We noted that there is a 10-minute increase from CPT code 95843 to CPT code 95844, and a 20-minute increase from CPT code 95844 to CPT code 95846. The rationale for these 10-minute and 20-minute increases was also not clearly stated. We appreciate that explanations for the direct PE inputs were provided in the PE Summary of Recommendations, given that this is a non-standard clinical labor activity. However, as CPT code 95843 describes a low-complexity study, CPT code 95844 describes a moderate-complexity study, and CPT code 95846 describes a high-complexity study, we welcomed public comments providing additional information, particularly regarding the increases in time for these direct PE inputs across these three CPT codes.
Also, for CPT codes 95843, 95844, and 95846, the RUC recommended use of the “other” formula for three new equipment items and based the time assumption of 960 minutes (that is, 16 hours). We are soliciting comments on whether it would be typical for the equipment in question to be worn for the full 16 hours. According to the PE Summary of Recommendations, patients typically arrive later in the day (for example, around 4 p.m.) for an appointment to perform a test run with the equipment, then take the equipment home and return it the following morning (typically around 9 a.m.). Therefore, the RUC recommended a 16-hour period, representing two nights, as this duration currently exists in the RUC database and is generally consistent with clinical practice. However, we sought public comments on whether two nights of use are required and typical for home sleep testing, as the reported equipment time may represent the total period the patient has the device outside the office rather than the time it is actually in use.
Lastly, we received invoices for a new supply item and three new equipment items for CPT codes 95843, 95844, and 95846. The new supply item is SA143 (Nox A1 Sensor Kit adult), and the new equipment items are EQ417 (Nox A1s System with SpO2, US), EQ418 (Apnea Link Air), and EQ419 (Apnea Trak Legacy). However, a single invoice for each supply or piece of equipment may not be reflective of typical costs, we encouraged interested parties to submit invoices to improve the accuracy of pricing for these items in the direct PE database.
We proposed the RUC-recommended direct PE inputs for CPT codes 95843, 95844, and 95846 without refinement.
Comment:
Commenters overwhelmingly opposed our proposed work RVU of 1.42 for CPT code 95849, which we crosswalked to CPT code 92014 (
Ophthalmological services: medical examination and evaluation, with initiation or continuation of diagnostic and treatment program; comprehensive, established patient, 1 or more visits
).
The RUC disagreed with CMS's proposed work RVU of 1.42 for CPT code 95849 and urged CMS to finalize its original recommendation of 1.60 instead. The RUC stated that CPT code 95849 involves interpreting at least 11 channels and 9 or more parameter categories, representing roughly twice the complexity of the lowest-tier code in this family. The RUC identified the following reference comparator codes, which it noted have similar time values but higher work RVUs than CMS's proposed value: CPT code 74176 (
Computed tomography, abdomen and pelvis; without contrast material
); CPT code 78452 (
Myocardial perfusion imaging, tomographic (SPECT) (including attenuation correction, qualitative or quantitative wall motion, ejection fraction by first pass or gated technique, additional quantification, when performed); multiple studies, at rest and/or stress (exercise or pharmacologic) and/or redistribution
(
printed page 71073)
and/or rest reinjection
); and CPT code 93351 (
Echocardiography, transthoracic, real-time with image documentation (2D), includes M-mode recording, when performed, during rest and cardiovascular stress test using treadmill, bicycle exercise and/or pharmacologically induced stress, with interpretation and report; including performance of continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, with supervision by a physician or other qualified health care professional
). Based on this comparison, the RUC urged CMS to finalize a work RVU of 1.60 for CPT code 95849.
Many commenters urged CMS to finalize the RUC-recommended work RVU of 1.60 for CPT code 95849, noting that the RUC's recommended value of 1.60 falls below the survey's 25th percentile value of 1.75. According to the commenters, CPT code 95849 requires interpreting 11+ channels and 9+ parameter categories (roughly double the complexity of CPT codes 95847/95848), and the proposed crosswalk to CPT code 92014 did not reflect that intensity. Commenters stated that the RUC's recommended work RVU of 1.60 was already a conservative valuation relative to survey data. A commenter suggested a work RVU of 2.44, the value assigned to CPT code 95810 (
Polysomnography; age 6 years or older, sleep staging with 4 or more additional parameters of sleep, attended by a technologist
), arguing that interpretation of unattended studies can require greater physician effort. Another commenter proposed a compromise work RVU of 1.52.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters for their feedback. We disagree that CPT code 99203 is an appropriate crosswalk, as its intraservice time exceeds that of CPT code 95849 by approximately 20 percent. We also do not find sufficient support for the claim that CPT code 95849 is twice as complex as CPT code 95848, given that unattended sleep studies of the highest complexity typically record no more than 10 to 12 parameters.
However, we were persuaded by the commenters that the proposed work RVU of 1.42 did not fully capture the clinical work and intensity described by CPT code 95849. We believe that CPT code 64567 (
Percutaneous electrical nerve field stimulation, cranial nerves, without implantation
) serves as a better crosswalk in light of the additional information provided by commenters, sharing identical intraservice and total time with CPT code 95849 at a work RVU of 1.50. We further find that a work RVU of 1.50 preserves more consistent intervals across the CPT code 95847, 95848, and 95849 family than the RUC-recommended 1.60, which would create a disproportionately large gap relative to CPT code 95848. Thus, we are finalizing a work RVU of 1.50 for CPT code 95849, based on a crosswalk to CPT code 64567. We believe this valuation reflects the identical time components shared between CPT codes 95849 and 64567, addresses commenters' concerns regarding the proposed rule's valuation, and results in a more appropriate distribution of relative values across the CPT code 95847, 95848, and 95849 family than either the proposed work RVU of 1.42 or the RUC-recommended work RVU of 1.60.
Comments:
A commenter submitted results from an independent survey of sleep testing providers who subscribe to Sleep Review Magazine; this study shows that WatchPAT devices, not ApneaTrak Legacy, are the typical device for moderate-complexity sleep testing. Based on this data, the commenter asked CMS to replace equipment code EQ419 with supply code SD362 for CPT code 95844.
Response:
We thank the commenter for the survey results. We note that the survey population consists of 60 subscribers to Sleep Review Magazine—a convenience sample of magazine subscribers, not a random or claims-based sample of Medicare-billing providers. Thus, these study results may not be representative of sleep medicine practitioners, patients, or providers broadly, and we believe that the study findings cannot be generalized beyond that limited group. We seek more generalizable study results.
Comments:
Commenters raised concerns about the practice expense supply and equipment inputs for the new technical-component codes, with the greatest volume of comments addressing CPT code 95844. Commenters raised significant concerns about the direct practice expense inputs that CMS proposed for CPT code 95844 and suggested to weigh all supplemental invoices submitted.
Commenters stated that our proposed equipment input, based on equipment code EQ419 (ApneaTrak Legacy), does not reflect current clinical practice. Some commenters recommended to delete equipment code EQ419 from the direct PE inputs for 95844, and add supply code SD362 (WatchPAT ONE) as the replacement direct PE input by stating that one invoice for the new supply/equipment items may not reflect typical costs. Commenters further stated that EQ419 reflects approximately $20 in direct costs, compared with approximately $100 for SD362. Commenters recommended that CMS substitute SD362 for EQ419 in the direct PE inputs for this code.
Commenters submitted approximately 800 invoices to support an update in the pricing of the SD362 supply. Another commenter recommended adding a supply item for code CPT code 95844 priced between $73.32 and $105.97 per test and submitted 49 invoices for their own SANSA sensor kit.
Response:
We thank the commenters for submitting invoices. We will update the price of supply code SD362 accordingly; based on the very large quantity of submitted invoices associated with this item and the wide range of prices varying from $45 to $243, we are finalizing the median price of $100.35 rather than attempting to calculate an average to avoid the effects of outliers. However, we were not persuaded by the commenters that the use of a disposable device would be more typical than the reusable equipment recommended by the RUC for CPT code 95844. Commenters described a wide variety of different devices that used different pricing structures, making it difficult to determine if any one of these would represent the typical case. Given this conflicting information, we are finalizing the direct PE inputs as proposed and not adding this new supply item to CPT code 95844, as it may not reflect typical cost.
Comments:
Commenters were divided on the proposed equipment time of 960 minutes (16 hours) for the unattended sleep testing device used across this code family. Some commenters supported the proposed 960-minute input. These commenters, including the RUC, supported the proposed value, stating that it appropriately reflects the period the device is dedicated to one patient and unavailable for reuse, consistent with our existing PE methodology. Other commenters stated that 960 minutes understates real-world equipment time, particularly for mail-based distribution and repeat-night testing, both of which extend the period a unit is unavailable for reuse well beyond a single overnight cycle. These commenters recommended higher equipment time values, with several converging on approximately 64 hours as a conservative minimum.
Response:
After consideration of the public comments, we believe that the time assumption of 960 minutes accurately reflects the typical equipment time. Although commenters provided examples of cases where patients could require more than two nights of use for the equipment, we remind interested parties that direct PE
(
printed page 71074)
inputs for the PFS are valued based on typical usage, not unusual or outlier cases.
Comments:
Commenters including the RUC supported the RUC-recommended clinical labor time inputs CA021 and CA042 for CPT codes 95843 through 95846, stating that the incremental increases in staff setup, demonstration, and post-service data processing time appropriately reflect the added complexity of each code in the family. A commenter stated that if CMS revised the equipment input for these codes to reflect disposable rather than reusable devices, the post-service time in CA042 should be reduced accordingly, since disposable devices would eliminate the retrieval, cleaning, and refurbishment work currently reflected in that time.
Response:
We thank the RUC and commenters for providing additional explanation regarding practice expense inputs for 95843-95846. We are finalizing the RUC recommended CA021 and CA042 clinical labor time inputs for CPT codes 95843 through 95846 as proposed.
Comments:
Commenters also suggested that CMS define these terms clearly, tie them to FDA clearance, and align CPT coding with coverage policy. They stated that without clear and shared definitions, providers, manufacturers, and Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) could classify functionally similar devices into different complexity tiers, or count channels differently (for example, counting derived measurements or multiple EEG derivations as separate channels).
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback and for the additional information provided.
Comment:
Several commenters, including the RUC, stated that they would like to offer a technical correction to the utilization crosswalk from several 2026 deleted codes to new 2027 codes. The commenters stated that CPT codes 95843 and 95847 should crosswalk from CPT code 95800, while CPT codes 95844 and 95848 should crosswalk from CPT code 95806; the prior crosswalk used in the proposed rule was an unintended technical error submitted to CMS.
Response:
After reviewing the information provided by the commenters, we agree with this technical correction. We are finalizing an update to the utilization crosswalk as described previously for CY 2027; the full utilization crosswalk table is available in the file titled “CY 2027 PFS Final Rule 2025 Utilization Data Crosswalked to 2027” on the CMS website under downloads for the CY 2027 PFS final rule at
https://www.cms.gov/​medicare/​payment/​fee-schedules/​physician/​federal-regulation-notices
.
After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing the work RVUs and direct PE inputs for the codes in the Unattended Sleep Testing family as proposed, with the exception of finalizing a work RVU of 1.50 for CPT code 95849 as detailed previously.
(44) Laser Treatment for Inflammatory Skin Diseases (CPT Codes 96920, 96921, and 96922)
In May 2025, the CPT Editorial Panel revised three codes to reflect the intended use for inflammatory or auto-immune skin diseases (
e.g.,
psoriasis): CPT codes 96920
(Laser treatment, 308-312 nanometer wavelengths, for inflammatory or auto-immune skin diseases (e.g., psoriasis); total area less than 250 sq cm),
96921
(Laser treatment, 308-312 nanometer wavelengths, for inflammatory or auto-immune skin diseases (e.g., psoriasis); 250 sq cm to 500 sq cm),
and 96922
(Laser treatment, 308-312 nanometer wavelengths, for inflammatory or auto-immune skin diseases (e.g., psoriasis); over 500 sq cm).
These codes were last discussed in the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 97797
through
97801
) and CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49303
through
49306
). These revisions were based on flaws in the prior valuation process and a change in the patient population. The specialty society surveyed the code family for the September 2025 RUC meeting.
For CY 2027, we proposed the RUC-recommended work RVUs of 1.00 for CPT code 96920, 1.24 for CPT code 96921, and 1.50 for CPT code 96922. We proposed the RUC-recommended direct PE inputs for CPT codes 96920, 96921, and 96922 without refinement.
Comment:
Commenters generally supported our proposal of the RUC recommended work RVUs and direct PE inputs for CPT code 96920, 96921, and 96922. A commenter requested refinements to various practice expense inputs, including the equipment utilization rate, maintenance costs, and recurring consumables that the commenter stated are required to operate the device for CPT codes 96920-96922. The commenter also requested that CMS treat excimer laser systems as a supply-based item.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support of our proposals. For the practice expense refinements, we would like to acknowledge that the RUC's PE Subcommittee reconsidered direct PE inputs, which were developed based on typical clinical practice and current AMA RUC/PE guidelines, at the September 2025 RUC meeting, where no modifications were made. As stated in section II.B. of this final rule, we currently use an equipment utilization rate assumption of 50 percent for most equipment, with the exception of expensive diagnostic imaging equipment, for which we use a 90 percent assumption as required by section 1848(b)(4)(C) of the Act. We do not agree with the commenter that it would be appropriate to drastically reduce the utilization rate based on the limited data provided, as the utilization rate assumption of 50 percent is used for most equipment.
Additionally, as discussed in section II.B. of this final rule, we finalized a 5 percent factor for annual maintenance in the CY 1998 PFS final rule with comment period (
62 FR 33164
). As we previously stated in the CY 2016 PFS final rule with comment period (
80 FR 70897
), we do not believe the annual maintenance factor for all equipment is precisely 5 percent, and we stated that this estimate likely understates the true cost of maintaining some equipment. We also noted that we believe it likely overstates the maintenance costs for other equipment. When we solicited comments regarding data sources containing equipment maintenance rates, commenters could not identify an auditable, robust data source that CMS could use on a wide scale. As a result, in the absence of publicly available datasets regarding equipment maintenance costs or another systematic data collection methodology for determining a different maintenance factor, a variable maintenance factor for equipment cost per minute pricing was not proposed as we did not believe that we had sufficient information at that present time. Therefore, we reminded readers that we did not believe voluntary submissions regarding the maintenance costs of individual equipment items would be an appropriate methodology for determining costs.
As previously discussed in the CY 2025 PFS Final Rule (
89 FR 97798
), CMS currently does not include the costs of consumable gas (code EQ154) and the optical delivery system (code EQ155) in the direct practice expense cost for these services. The commenter requested the inclusion of EQ154 and EQ155 in our PE calculations for these services; however, the commenter's letter characterizes EQ154 and EQ155 as replacement/maintenance items, not equipment items that are used for each service. In response to the commenter's request that CMS treat excimer laser systems as a supply-based item, we
(
printed page 71075)
continue to believe, as was previously discussed in the CY 2025 PFS Final Rule (
89 FR 97798
), that the equipment item EQ161 (excimer laser), which the specialty society confirmed remains the typical equipment used for this code set, is available for purchase and is already accounted for under our equipment methodology. We previously did not propose the May 2023 RUC recommendation to change the business model for excimer lasers to a pay-per-use subscription-based model, as rental and licensing fees are typically considered forms of indirect PE under our methodology. We continue to believe that CPT codes 96920 through 96922 should not be valued based on a significantly more expensive pay-per-use rental version of the excimer laser when the same treatment is cheaper and available as a purchasable form of equipment.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing CPT codes 96920, 96921, and 96922 as proposed.
(45) Real-Time Fluorescence Wound Imaging (CPT Code 97611)
In September 2025, the CPT Editorial Panel created a new code to report real-time florescence wound imaging, CPT code 97611 (
Real-time fluorescence wound imaging with clinical darkness to identify presence, location, load of bacteria and measure wound size, per day
). The specialty society did not conduct a survey for CPT code 97611 because they determined it would be unable to conduct a successful survey that met the RUC's minimum survey threshold, and therefore, the RUC recommended contractor pricing for CY 2027.
Due to persistent payment variability for the predecessor CPT codes 0598T and 0599T, and limited geographical uptake of the technology, the device manufacturer requested that CMS actively price CPT code 97611 and provided work RVU and direct PE input recommendations. After consideration of the manufacturer's recommendations, we proposed a work RVU of 0.80 and physician pre-evaluation time of 6 minutes, intraservice time of 15 minutes, and immediate post service time of 5 minutes, totaling 26 minutes of physician time. For direct PE in the non-facility, we proposed a direct crosswalk of clinical labor activities and time from CPT code 97610 (
Low frequency, non-contact, non-thermal ultrasound, including topical application(s), when performed, wound assessment, and instruction(s) for ongoing care, per day
), with the addition of 10 minutes for CA026 Clean surgical instrument package for CPT code 97611, for a total of 42 minutes of clinical labor time. Additionally, we proposed the following supply items and quantities in the non-facility for CPT code 97611.
Additionally, we proposed the following equipment items and equipment minutes in the non-facility to correspond with the 30 and 36 minutes of clinical labor time included in the default and instrument pack equipment formulas, respectively, for CPT code 97611. The real-time fluorescence wound imaging system (ER131) was added to the direct PE database for inclusion in CPT code 97611 assuming a 5-year useful life and purchase price of $21,500 based on the provided invoices. We did not propose to include the carrying case for the real-time fluorescence wound imaging system in the equipment costs for CPT code 97611 as recommended by the device manufacturer. We have a longstanding policy that medical equipment must be at least $500 and all equipment inputs under $500 are considered indirect expense. We welcomed public comment on the appropriateness of our proposed work RVU and the typicality of our proposed physician work times and direct PE inputs.
(
printed page 71076)
We sought comments on whether this service will typically be billed alongside wound debridement codes (that is, greater than 50 percent of the time), and if so, which of the proposed direct PE inputs may be duplicative of those already included in the wound debridement codes, such as CPT codes 11042 (
Debridement, subcutaneous tissue (includes epidermis and dermis, if performed); first 20 sq cm or less)
and 97597 (
Debridement (e.g., high pressure waterjet with/without suction, sharp selective debridement with scissors, scalpel and forceps), open wound, (e.g., fibrin, devitalized epidermis and/or dermis, exudate, debris, biofilm), including topical application(s), wound assessment, use of a whirlpool, when performed and instruction(s) for ongoing care, per session, total wound(s) surface area; first 20 sq cm or less)
). We noted in the proposed rule that CPT code 97611's predecessor codes, CPT codes 0598T and 0599T, were billed with wound debridement codes 35.1 percent and 46.6 percent of the time, respectively. However, we understand that such concurrent billing with wound debridement may become more common as adoption of this technology increases. For example, we sought comments on whether the following proposed supply items are duplicative of debridement codes if it is anticipated that these codes will be typically billed together: SB007, SB019, SB044, SC056, SF007, SG018, SG035, SG051, SG052, SG079, SH069 and SJ046. We also sought comments on whether these wound care supply items are typical for CPT code 97611, given that the code descriptor specifies wound imaging but does not include any wound care elements. Finally, we noted in the proposed rule that the direct PE crosswalk code, CPT code 97610, is billed alone 64.4 percent of the time and with debridement CPT code 11042 only 4.3 percent of the time. Therefore, we sought comments on the appropriateness of this code as a direct PE crosswalk considering the different billing patterns of CPT code 97610 and 97611 based on its predecessor codes.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
The majority of commenters supported the proposed valuation for CPT code 97611 and stated that it accurately represented the work and practice expense involved in providing a typical real-time wound imaging procedure.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
A couple of commenters did not support the proposed RVU of 0.80 and recommended contractor pricing for CPT code 97611 instead.
Response:
We continue to believe that the proposed valuation for CPT code 97611 is appropriate and accurately represents the work and practice expense involved in performing this procedure. We believe that, generally speaking, national pricing for individual services is preferrable to contractor pricing since it better maintains relativity across the PFS and minimizes regional variations that can creates barriers to care access. Although contractor pricing is appropriate for some services, it is most often used for new and emerging technologies, and we believe that CPT code 97611 will be more accurately valued using our proposed national pricing.
Comment:
A couple of commenters requested that the name of the new ER131 equipment item should be changed from the proposed “MolecuLight DX System” to “real-time fluorescence wound imaging system.” The commenters stated that direct PE item descriptions should accommodate qualifying technologies from multiple manufacturers and requested that CMS clarify that a product name in the PE database does not restrict payment to that manufacturer.
Response:
We agree with the commenters that direct PE item descriptions should typically use generic descriptions rather than product names from specific manufacturers. We are therefore finalizing this change in the name of the ER131 equipment to the requested “real-time fluorescence wound imaging system” and clarifying that the equipment is not restricted to a single manufacturer. Also, all references to ER131 have been updated with the generic description.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended removing supply items SF007 (blade, surgical (Bard-Parker)) and SJ046 (silver nitrate applicator) from the direct PE inputs for CPT code 97611 because neither of these items are used in performing fluorescence wound imaging. Commenters stated that a surgical blade is a debridement instrument and silver nitrate a hemostatic agent.
Response:
We agree with the commenters and we are finalizing the removal of supply items SF007 and SJ046 from the direct PE inputs for CPT code 97611.
Comment:
For new supply item SB061 (MolecuLight DX Eco Dark Drapes), a commenter wanted CMS to clarify that clinical darkness is an imaging condition achieved consistent with the real-time fluorescence wound imaging device's labeling, and that supply item SB061 may not always be required each time this service is performed, depending on the lighting conditions.
Response:
We determine the direct PE for a specific service by adding the costs of the direct resources (that is, the clinical staff, medical supplies, and medical equipment) typically involved with furnishing that service. A supply item that is used more than 50 percent of the time when performing a service would be considered typical for that service. We were not persuaded by the commenter that the SB061 drape would be used less than 50 percent of the time given the need for clinical darkness in this procedure. We also note that we received several comments in support of the direct PE inputs proposed for CPT code 97611, including the SB061 drape.
Comment:
Many commenters requested that CPT code 97611 not be considered a therapy service and remain on the Skilled Nursing Facility
(
printed page 71077)
Consolidated (SNF) Billing Exclusion list.
Response:
We agree with the commenters and will not designate CPT code 97611 as a sometimes therapy service, which will allow it to remain on the list of services excluded from SNF consolidated billing.
Comment:
A commenter stated that in hospital outpatient department (HOPD) wound care settings, the proposed facility PE RVU of 1.05 for 97611 should be evaluated against actual equipment, clinical labor, and supply costs. The commenter requested that CMS engage with HOPD wound care programs with real-time fluorescence imaging experience to validate whether the proposed PE inputs adequately reflect HOPD-specific cost structures.
Response:
We did not propose any direct PE inputs in the Facility setting for CPT code 97611, following our standard PE methodology, as these costs would be borne by the institution under non-PFS payment systems. The PFS payment for this service in the facility setting only covers practitioner work, malpractice, and indirect PE costs; for hospital outpatient expenses, these would be accounted for under the OPPS.
Comment:
A commenter noticed a typo for supply item SG018 (bandage, Kling, non-sterile 3in) as it was inadvertently listed as SF018 when we sought comments on whether the proposed supply items for 97611 are duplicative of those used for debridement codes. The description for SF018 is: cautery, monopolar, electrode, needle.
Response:
We thank the commenter for pointing this out and agree that SF018 as it appeared in the text was a typo. We also note that SG018 was correctly listed in Table A-D4 for the supply items for CPT code 97611 and elsewhere.
Comment:
We sought comments on whether CPT code 97611 would typically be billed with wound debridement codes (that is, greater than 50 percent of the time), and asked which of the proposed direct PE inputs may be duplicative of those already included in the wound debridement codes. Many commenters stated that CPT code 97611 would not typically be billed with debridement codes and that CMS should maintain separate, unbundled reimbursement for these PE inputs when imaging is furnished during the same encounter as wound debridement. Commenters stated that real-time fluorescence wound imaging informs clinical decision-making rather than performing tissue removal and that the imaging and the debridement are not interchangeable steps. Therefore, commenters stated that the direct PE inputs for 97611, including specialized imaging equipment and supplies, were separate and non-duplicative of those used in debridement procedures. A commenter's personal experience was that a debridement procedure was performed with real-time fluorescence wound imaging 42 percent of the time. Several other commenters said that it was reasonable to expect CPT code 97611 to be billed in a similar pattern as predecessor CPT codes 0598T and 0599T, which were only billed with wound debridement codes 35.1 percent and 46.6 percent of the time, respectively. Another commenter stated that CPT code 97611 would be separate from cellular, acellular, and matrix-like products (CAMP) application and debridement procedures (not a component of the procedural encounter).
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the work RVU and direct PE inputs for CPT code 97611 as proposed, with the exception of the removal of supply items SF007 and SJ046 as detailed previously.
(46) Lactation Care Services (CPT Codes 98963 and 98964)
At the May 2025 CPT Editorial Panel meeting, two new CPT codes were created for reporting lactation care directed by a physician or qualified health care professional (QHP): CPT codes 98963 (
Lactation care directed by a physician or other qualified health care professional, including history, assessment, training, and report; first 30 minutes
) and 98964 (
Lactation care directed by a physician or other qualified health care professional, including history, assessment, training, and report; each additional 15 minutes
). These new CPT codes were surveyed at the September 2025 AMA RUC Meeting.
For CY 2027, we proposed the RUC-recommended work RVU of 0.18 for CPT code 98963. The RUC did not recommend, and we did not propose a work RVU for CPT code 98964, which has been designed as a PE only service.
We proposed the RUC-recommended direct PE inputs for CPT codes 98963 and 98964, including the creation of a new clinical staff type for Lactation Consultant (L076A) and a new EF052 equipment item (scale, infant, digital, fine gradation). We adopted CPT language and requirements for the Lactation Consultant: “The qualifications of the lactation consultant/counselor must be recognized by a physician society, nonphysician health care professional society/association, or other appropriate source.” We proposed to value this new clinical staff type at the same 0.76 rate per minute currently used by the RN (L051A) clinical staff type as recommended by the RUC; we sought comment regarding this new clinical staff type and whether there may be a more appropriate crosswalk than the RN clinical staff type. We proposed the RUC-recommendation of the RN clinical staff type as a proxy for pricing purposes, but sought comment on whether Lactation Consultants are typically RNs with additional credentialing/certification to be qualified to serve as a lactation consultant.
Comment:
We received a large volume of public comments regarding the Lactation Care Services codes. Many commenters provided additional information concerning the clinical benefits of the care provided by lactation consultants. Commenters stated that lactation consultants obtain and evaluate maternal and infant histories, assess milk production and feeding effectiveness, observe feeds, evaluate milk transfer, identify maternal and infant risk factors, develop individualized care plans, provide counseling and education, document clinical findings, reassess response to interventions, and determine when referral or coordination with another healthcare professional is necessary. Commenters stated that families frequently present with multiple, overlapping concerns including pain while feeding, low milk production, pumping challenges, supplementation, bottle refusal, or concerns about the infant's ability to feed effectively which cannot always be addressed through a standardized approach. Many commenters provided personal accounts detailing the importance of the care that they received from lactation care services.
Response:
We appreciate the additional details provided by the commenters regarding the clinical benefits of these services. We agree with the commenters regarding the importance of these lactation care services which have now been recognized with formal CPT coding.
Comment:
Many commenters responded to the comment solicitation in the proposed rule regarding whether lactation consultants are typically RNs with additional credentialing/certification. Many commenters stated that lactation consultants are not necessarily RNs with additional credentialing; this included personal accounts from many lactation
(
printed page 71078)
consultants who clarified that they had significant training but were not certified as RNs. Commenters stated that holding both credentials reflects meeting two separate sets of requirements, rather than one credential containing the other, and cited other groups (such as registered dietitians, occupational therapists, and speech-language pathologists) who all practice in hospital settings without being expected to hold RN licensure. Commenters stated that an RN prerequisite for lactation consultants would add years of unrelated education and cost, restrict access to skilled lactation care, and could shrink a workforce that's already stretched thin. Many commenters cited International Board Certified Lactation Consultants (IBCLCs), an independent, lactation-specific credential with established education, clinical training, and certification requirements separate from RNs. Commenters requested CMS clarify that lactation consultants, including IBCLCs, are not required to be registered nurses.
Response:
We appreciate the detailed feedback from the commenters regarding our lactation consultant comment solicitation. We can clarify for the commenters that our solicitation was intended for informational purposes and that we are not finalizing a requirement that lactation consultants must also be certified as RNs. Our proposed use of the RN was a proxy for the pricing of the lactation consultant clinical labor type, not intended as a new certification requirement.
Comment:
Commenters stated that the code descriptors for CPT codes 98963 and 98964 were unclear whether these codes are intended to recognize the IBCLC as the professional furnishing and reporting the service, or whether they assume a model in which the IBCLC functions as clinical staff beneath another independently billing practitioner. Many commenters requested that CMS expressly recognize IBCLCs as qualified practitioners who may directly bill for the lactation services they provide. Commenters stated that lactation challenges most often emerge in the days and weeks after hospital discharge so a direct-supervision standard requiring the billing practitioner to be immediately available on-site would make these codes unusable in the postpartum setting where they are needed most.
Response:
As we stated in the proposed rule, we adopted CPT language and requirements for the Lactation Consultant: “The qualifications of the lactation consultant/counselor must be recognized by a physician society, nonphysician health care professional society/association, or other appropriate source.” These licensing requirements are outside the scope of the code valuation for CPT codes 98963 and 98964 discussed in this portion of the rule; we did not propose and we are not finalizing IBCLCs or other lactation consultants as qualified practitioners who may directly bill for the lactation services they provide.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that CMS add CPT codes 98963 and 98964 to the Medicare Telehealth Services List so that lactation support could reach patients in the home.
Response:
We did not propose and we are not finalizing the addition of these codes to the Medicare Telehealth Services List. Although we understand that these lactation care services are sometimes provided in a home setting, the CPT codes as designed by the CPT Editorial Panel were not intended to be provided via telehealth.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that comprehensive lactation care frequently involves two patients: the lactating parent and infant. Commenters stated that separate billing for the mother and infant when both receive distinct, medically necessary services is imperative to accurately value lactation healthcare. Commenters stated that separate billing should not be considered duplicate billing when the mother and infant are separate patients and each receives separately identifiable, medically necessary services supported by documentation.
Response:
The coding instructions for CPT code 98963 specifically state that it is used to report lactation care services ordered by a physician or other QHP and provided by a lactation consultant/counselor in the office or other outpatient setting for a mother/baby dyad. Separate billing that requires additional medically necessary services would therefore not be typical for these codes.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that lactation care services lasted significantly longer than the 30 minute duration described by CPT code 98963. Commenters stated that lactation care does not stop requiring professional judgment after the first 30 minutes and stated that the clinician continues to assess the parent-baby dyad, interpret findings, modify the care plan, evaluate response to interventions, and provide counseling for a much longer span of time. Different commenters stated that 60 minutes, 90 minutes, or 120 minutes constituted a typical amount of time for lactation care services and disagreed with the 30 minutes of time associated with CPT code 98963 as both insufficient to provide care and not typical of their patient encounters.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback from the commenters regarding the typical duration of patient encounters for lactation care services. We note that the new CPT codes do not mandate 30 minute patient encounters, as CPT code 98963 can be billed for the first 30 minutes followed by CPT code 98964 for each additional 15 minutes. We believe that this remains the most appropriate time structure for the coding based on the current data available to CMS. However, given the volume of comments regarding how the proposed times for these codes did not match the experience of lactation care services providers, this is a subject that may warrant revisiting by CMS, the RUC, or the CPT Editorial Panel at a later date.
Comment:
Many commenters disagreed with the proposed work RVU of 0.18 for CPT code 98963 and the lack of a proposed work RVU of CPT code 98964. Commenters stated that lactation care does not stop requiring professional judgment after the first 30 minutes. Commenters stated that the proposed work valuations undervalue the complex work involved in providing comprehensive lactation care, as lactation consultations are a clinical assessment that considers the needs of both the parent and the infant. Several commenters stated that CPT code 98963 should be valued comparably to CPT code 99213 at a work RVU of 1.30. Commenters requested that CMS assign an appropriate work RVU to add-on CPT code 98964 to compensate clinicians for direct, prolonged face-to-face care.
Response:
We continue to believe that the proposed work RVU of 0.18 for CPT code 98963 as recommended by the RUC is the most accurate current valuation for this service. We agree with the RUC that CPT code 99211 is the most direct analog for CPT code 98963, as it describes an office or other outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of an established patient that may not require the presence of a physician or other qualified health care professional. Similarly, we continue to believe that CPT code 98964 was accurately valued as a PE-only code with no work RVU since it only contains clinical staff time for the lactation consultant. Based on the information that we have at present, we believe that these are the appropriate work valuations for CPT code 98963 and 98964. However, we do note that there was a flawed survey used by the RUC for these codes, due to a potential
(
printed page 71079)
misunderstanding by survey respondents regarding who was performing the service. As we stated previously in regard to the work times of these codes, given the volume of comments regarding how the proposed work RVUs for these codes did not match the experience of lactation care services providers, this is a subject that may warrant revisiting by CMS, the RUC, or the CPT Editorial Panel at a later date.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that they supported the proposed direct PE inputs for CPT codes 98963 and 98964, including the proposed RN crosswalk as a reasonable minimum proxy for the time, skill, and clinical intensity of the lactation consultant. Other commenters disagreed and stated that the proposed 0.76 rate for the L076A clinical labor type did not represent the amount paid to an IBCLC, nor did it capture the complete cost of operating an accessible, compliant lactation care service. A commenter requested valuing the L076A clinical labor type at 0.90 per minute based on a study published in the Journal of Human Lactation in 2013
[
8
]
along with current benchmarked salary data for the lactation consultant profession.
Response:
We appreciate the additional data provided by the commenters regarding the typical salary of a lactation consultant. Based on this additional data, we are finalizing an increase in the pricing of the L076A lactation consultant clinical labor type, from the proposed 0.76 to 0.90 as provided by the commenters.
Comment:
A commenter stated that the direct practice expense file also appeared to use the L076A clinical labor type for CPT code 98963 but the RN (L051A) clinical labor type for the add-on CPT code 98964. The commenter stated that CMS should correct or explain this inconsistency and use the lactation consultant staff type consistently when lactation care is performed by an appropriately qualified lactation consultant.
Response:
We appreciate the assistance from the commenter in identifying this unintended technical error. We are correcting this error for the final rule; both CPT code 98963 and 98964 were intended to use the L076A lactation consultant for their clinical labor.
After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing the work RVUs and direct PE inputs for CPT code 98963 and 98964 as proposed, with the update to the pricing of the L076A clinical labor type and technical correction to the clinical labor used in CPT code 98964 detailed previously.

), 97159 (
