The RUC HCPAC Review Board reviewed the 14 codes in the revised code family at the January 2026 RUC HCPAC.
The RUC is recommending contractor pricing for all fourteen codes in the family. The existing CPT codes 97151 through 97158 are currently contractor priced. We proposed to contractor price the six new codes and make no change to the status indicator for the eight revised existing codes that are already contractor priced.
Comments:
We received many comments on our proposal to adopt and contractor price the six new adaptive behavior services, CPT codes 97148, 97149, 97159, 97160, 97173 and 97180, and make no change to the status indicator for the eight revised CPT codes 97151, 97152, 97153, 97154, 97155, 97156, 97157, and 97158 that are already contractor priced. Nearly all commenters expressed support for the proposals. Many commenters asked CMS to add the new CPT codes to the telehealth list. Many commenters focused on the benefit of two new codes, CPT code 97159 and CPT code 97160, billing two technicians simultaneously.
A few commenters did not support CMS adoption of the new CPT codes. A commenter recommended the adoption of a bundled Adaptive Behavior Services coding framework of 3 comprehensive service categories: Assessment, Treatment, and Caregiver Training instead of adopting the six new codes into the existing code family. Another expressed concern that the adoption of CPT codes 97148, 97149, 97159, 97160, 97173 and 97180, particularly CPT code 97180 for non-face-to-face services, created heightened risks of insufficient documentation, upcoding, and duplicative or concurrent billing, potentially increasing spending without clear evidence of additional clinical value. Another commenter similarly recommended monitoring of utilization patterns to better understand how services are being furnished across settings and provider types and to assess whether beneficiaries are receiving evidence-based and clinically appropriate care. Another commenter advocated national pricing for CPT codes 97173 and 97180 but did not offer an opinion on what that pricing should be.
Response:
We thank all the commenters and appreciate the support for our proposals. We believe that the coding framework developed by the CPT Editorial Panel will help specify appropriate times, define terms, address reporting gaps, and clarify reporting for face-to-face and non-face-to-face adaptive behavior services. We believe that the new coding better defines these services and provides a more comprehensive framework than the prior, more patchwork methods of reporting. With regards to national pricing, we agree with the HCPAC that since these services are currently contractor priced and the existing payment models and practice patterns are varied, the newly revised codes should also remain contractor priced at this time.
After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing contractor pricing for all fourteen codes in the family as proposed. Finally, we are adding CPT codes 97148, 97149, 97159, 97160, and 97173 to the Medicare Telehealth Services list. We are not adding CPT code 97180 as the service is a non-face-to-face service.
(48) Remote Monitoring (CPT Codes 98975, 98976, 98977, 98978, 98980, 98981, 98984, 98985, 98986, 98979, 99091, 99453, 99454, 99457, 99458, 99473, 99474, 99445, and 99470)
(a) Background and Overview
In recent years, we have established payment for two code families that describe certain remote monitoring services: remote physiologic monitoring (RPM) and remote therapy monitoring (RTM). In the CY 2018 PFS final rule, we summarized feedback from a comment solicitation aimed at informing new payment policies that would allow for separate payment for remote monitoring services (
82 FR 53014
). In the CY 2019 PFS final rule (
83 FR 59574
through
59576
), we established valuations and payment policy for the RPM code family. In the CY 2020 PFS final rule (
84 FR 62697
through
62698
), we explained that the RPM code family describes chronic care RPM services that involve the collection, analysis, and interpretation of digitally collected physiologic data, followed by the development of a treatment plan and the managing of a patient under the treatment plan (
84 FR 62697
). In the CY 2020 PFS final rule, we finalized that CPT codes 99457 and 99458 would be included as designated care management services, allowing RPM services to be furnished under the general supervision of the physician or other qualified health care professional (who is qualified by education, training, licensure/regulation and facility privileging) (
84 FR 62698
). In the CY 2023 PFS final rule, in response to comments, we clarified that RTM or RPM services could be billed concurrently with Chronic Care Management (CCM), Transitional Care Management (TCM), Principal Care Management (PCM), Chronic Pain Management (CPM), or Behavioral Health Integration (BHI) (
86 FR 69528
through
69539
).
In September 2024, the Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) Editorial Panel added one code and made code revisions to report RPM device supply for 2 to 15 days and 16 to 30 days within a 30-day period; created one new code and code revisions to report RPM treatment management services for the first 10 minutes, first 20 minutes, and each additional 20 minutes thereafter; added three RTM device supply codes to report respiratory, musculoskeletal and cognitive behavioral therapy for 2 to 15 days and 16 to 30 days within a 30-day period; created one new code and made code revisions to report RTM treatment management services for the first 10 minutes, first 20 minutes, and each additional 20 minutes thereafter; and revised remote monitoring guidelines. We reviewed the RUC recommendations for these services in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49394
through
49404
). In response to recent reports and recommendations from the Office of the Inspector General (Additional Oversight of Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare Is Needed
[
9
]
and Billing for Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare
[
10
]
), for CY 2027, we proposed refinements to the policies surrounding remote physiologic and remote therapeutic monitoring, as detailed later in this section.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters agreed with CMS' concern for protecting against fraud, waste, abuse, and fragmented care, such as programs that
(
printed page 71081)
solicit beneficiaries for services they do not need and care models in which the billing practitioner lacks meaningful oversight. However, many commenters provided information about remote monitoring programs that deliver quality care and improve outcomes in a deflationary manner. Some commenters felt that requirements that could limit the adoption of RPM and RTM services were not in alignment with other stated CMS goals on advancing rural health and the adoption of innovative health technology, or with specific programs, including the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) and the CMS Innovation Center's Advancing Chronic Care with Effective, Scalable Solutions (ACCESS) model.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support. We agree that there are many remote monitoring programs that provide reasonable and necessary care, and we agree with commenters that identified potential fraud, waste, and abuse as concerns. We do not believe that these requirements would limit CMS goals on advancing rural health, or the adoption of innovative health technology, and CMS remains committed to expanding beneficiary and clinician access to high-value, technology-supported care, as evidenced by the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) and the CMS Innovation Center's ACCESS model. Rather, the requirements would minimize factors that may contribute to potential fraud, waste, abuse, and fragmented care in remote monitoring services paid under the PFS.
Comment:
Some commenters raised questions about the relationship between the ACCESS model and the proposed RPM and RTM policies, noting differences in their scope and payment approaches.
Response:
We thank commenters for these comments. The ACCESS model is a separate CMS Innovation Center model testing outcome-aligned payments for technology-supported chronic care in Original Medicare, with payment primarily tied to beneficiary outcomes rather than specific activities. RPM and RTM services are PFS services that pay for the furnishing of specified remote monitoring services and related activities. The policies finalized in this final rule are intended to preserve access to appropriate RPM and RTM services while strengthening safeguards to maintain beneficiary and clinician access to technology-supported care and minimizing factors that may contribute to potential fraud, waste, abuse, and fragmented care for remote monitoring services paid under the PFS.
Comment:
The AMA informed CMS that in response to our concerns over a lack of data to inform accurate valuation of these services, all 19 RPM and RTM codes will have their practice expense reviewed at the January 2027 RUC meeting.
Response:
We thank the AMA for this information and look forward to reviewing any forthcoming recommendations from the RUC regarding the practice expense for these services.
Comment:
Some commenters did not support the use of OIG reports to refine the policies surrounding RPM and RTM, including expressing concern that CMS was proposing to implement requirements not explicitly called for in the relevant OIG reports on RPM and RTM services. Some commenters stated that OIG's findings identified only a small number of practices as being of particular concern.
Response:
We would like to clarify that the recommendations specified in the OIG reports are not the only measures that CMS is limited to in order to ensure that remote monitoring services paid under the PFS are not subject to potential fraud, waste, and abuse. Although we cited OIG's concerns around RPM in the proposed rule, CMS has also observed troubling trends that may indicate potential fraud, waste, abuse, and fragmented care. These trends align with, but also sometimes go beyond, what OIG has cited.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that the OIG reports used data collected during the public health emergency (PHE), when observed growth in remote monitoring was part of a larger digital health transformation.
Response:
The OIG report, Additional Oversight of Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare Is Needed
[
11
]
, used claims and encounter records with dates of service from January 1, 2019, through December 31, 2022. The OIG report, Billing for Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare,
[
12
]
used claims and encounter records with dates of service from January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. Both OIG reports analyze claims and encounter data from before and after the COVID-19 PHE, which began on January 31, 2020 (retroactive to January 27, 2020) and ended on May 11, 2023. We agree with commenters that some of the growth in remote monitoring services during this time may have been in response to the PHE, but we have continued to see high growth of these services in the years since the end of the PHE that may indicate potential fraud, waste, abuse, and fragmented care.
Comment:
Several commenters wrote that findings in published OIG reports were only applicable to RPM and not to RTM. Commenters stated that RPM and RTM are unique services, and that there is not sufficient published evidence to support applying uniform policies to both. These commenters believe that RTM should not raise the same program integrity concerns that may exist for RPM since RTM furnished by therapists has existing incident to, plan of care, and recertification requirements. Commenters also cited that RTM has not experienced recent high growth like RPM. Commenters also believed that RTM valuation was accurate and did not need to be refined, as RTM has gone through the RUC process twice in the past four years.
Response:
We thank commenters for this information. While we agree with commenters that the OIG report was focused on RPM, we continue to believe that the concerns specified in the OIG reports and in this rule also apply to RTM. The RTM codes are newer and have not been subject to audits, as RPM has. We note that RTM services were not payable under the PFS until January 1, 2022. The OIG report, Additional Oversight of Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare Is Needed,
[
13
]
used claims and encounter records with dates of service from January 1, 2019, through December 31, 2022. The OIG report, Billing for Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare,
[
14
]
used claims and encounter records with dates of service from January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. At the time of these analyses, RTM was not payable for the entirety of the claims and encounter data review or was a new service with limited claims and encounter data. Although we agree with commenters that RTM has not experienced as large an increase in utilization as compared to RPM, we have observed an increase in utilization since these services have become payable under the PFS and since the OIG reports reviewed claims and encounter records. The program integrity concerns expressed in the proposed rule apply to both RPM and RTM services. We reiterate our concerns that RTM, like RPM, services may be
(
printed page 71082)
susceptible to fraud, waste, abuse, and fragmented care.
(b) Established Patient Requirements
In the CY 2021 PFS final rule (
85 FR 84542
through
84546
), we established that, when the PHE for COVID-19 ended, we again required that RPM services be furnished only to an established patient. Patients who received initial remote monitoring services during PHE were considered established patients for purposes of the new patient requirements that were effective after the last day of the PHE for COVID-19.
For CY 2027, we proposed to require that RTM services also be furnished only to established patients. We proposed this condition of payment because we believe that a practitioner with an established relationship with a patient would likely have had the opportunity to collect relevant patient history and conduct a physical exam, as appropriate. As a result, the practitioner would possess information needed to understand the current medical status and needs of the patient prior to ordering RTM services to collect and analyze the patient's data and would be able to use the results of remote therapeutic monitoring to manage the patient under a specific treatment plan or therapy plan of care.
This proposal would also assist in resolving OIG's findings that some practices did not have a prior relationship with patients for whom they billed remote monitoring services for (Billing for Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare
15
).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed support for the requirement that RTM services be furnished only to established patients, as these changes would create symmetry between requirements for RTM and RPM services. We also received comments supporting both the established patient requirement and the initiating visit requirement as reasonable program integrity measures. Some commenters did not support our proposed requirement for RTM, and a few commenters requested that we no longer require that RPM have an established patient requirement. Some commenters expressed concern that requiring that patients be established before RTM services can be furnished adds unnecessary cost and administrative burden to practices and could delay the onset of monitoring for some patients.
Response:
We thank commenters for their comments on our proposal. At this time, we continue to believe that an established patient requirement ensures that the practitioner would possess information needed to understand the current medical status and needs of the patient prior to ordering RTM services. This requirement also ensures that the practitioner collects and analyzes the patient's data and uses the results of remote therapeutic monitoring to manage the patient under a specific treatment plan or therapy plan of care.
Comment:
Commenters requested CMS publish a precise definition of “established patient” for purposes of remote monitoring services.
Response:
We are adopting the definition of “established patient” used elsewhere in the PFS. An established patient is one who has received any professional services from the physician or other qualified health care professional or another physician or other qualified health care professional of the same specialty who belongs to the same group practice within the past three years (see Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 12, section 30.6.7). Although, we note that for certain healthcare professionals, such as physical therapists, occupational therapists, and speech-language pathologists, an established patient is one who is receiving services furnished under a therapy plan of care that may extend throughout the length of that episode of care (see (
86 FR 65116
) and (
87 FR 69643
and
69647
)).
Comment:
Many commenters requested that a beneficiary be considered an established patient after they have received an initiating visit. Commenters expressed that this would be important in scenarios where early intervention is important (post-discharge, post-injury, etc.).
Response:
For the purposes of this policy, we would like to clarify that a beneficiary may be considered an established patient after they have met the initiating visit requirements for remote monitoring services detailed later in this section.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the requirement that RTM services be furnished only to established patients.
(c) Initiating Visit Requirements
For CY 2027, we proposed that practitioners reporting RPM or RTM services must furnish a separately reportable initiating visit in association with the onset of RPM or RTM services, since these services require a level of care coordination that cannot be effective without appropriate evaluation of the patient's needs. The initiating visit would also ensure the billing practitioner assesses the beneficiary to determine clinical appropriateness of RPM or RTM and provide an opportunity to obtain the required beneficiary consent to receive RPM or RTM services. We proposed that RPM or RTM services must be initiated by the billing practitioner during a face-to-face (in-person or telehealth) visit. CPT codes that do not involve a face-to-face visit by the billing practitioner or are not separately payable under Medicare cannot be used as the visit for RPM or RTM initiation. If RPM or RTM is not discussed with the patient at that visit, that visit cannot count as the initiating visit for RPM or RTM. The RPM or RTM initiating visit can be separately billed.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters supported the overall objective of ensuring that patient monitoring begin from a clinical decision by a practitioner who has evaluated the patient.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support of this proposal.
Comment:
We received many comments suggesting additional clarification and requirements for our initiating visit proposal. Some commenters recommended CMS create a standard for documentation on how RTM/RPM data will be incorporated into the patient's treatment plans, as a condition of payment. A few commenters commented that such requirements could include information about the ordering provider, the type of health information being monitored, and the suspected/target health condition being monitored.
Response:
We thank commenters for their suggestions and may consider this for future rulemaking. We are not finalizing any additional documentation requirements at this time, as we believe additional documentation requirements may create unnecessary administrative burden.
Comment:
We received several comments seeking clarification and offering suggestions on which specific visit types and which specific practitioners would satisfy the requirements for an initiating visit. Many commenters recommended that a separate initiating visit only be required for certain beneficiaries or clinical scenarios, including exempting beneficiaries aligned to an Accountable Care Organization (ACO). Commenters suggested CMS adopt the same initiating visit requirements for RPM and RTM as are required for Chronic Care
(
printed page 71083)
Management (CCM) and Advanced Primary Care Management (APCM) services.
Response:
We would like to clarify that while RPM or RTM services must be initiated by the billing practitioner during a face-to-face (in-person or telehealth) visit, the initiating visit does not have to be for the sole purpose of discussing remote monitoring services. CPT codes that do not involve a face-to-face visit by the billing practitioner or are not separately payable under Medicare cannot be used as the visit for RPM or RTM initiation. If RPM or RTM is not discussed with the patient at that visit, that visit cannot count as the initiating visit for RPM or RTM. At this time, we are not finalizing any exemptions to initiating visit requirements, including for patients aligned to ACOs, as these services require a level of care coordination that cannot be effective without appropriate evaluation of the patient's needs. We continue to believe that an initiating visit is the best way to ensure this evaluation is occurring.
Comment:
Commenters additionally sought clarification on the definition of “onset” of RPM or RTM services. Commenters asked CMS to define the permissible amount of time between the initiating visit and the activation of monitoring. A number of commenters expressed concern that requiring a separate face-to-face initiating visit with the billing practitioner for patients already established with RTM services via discharge from a hospital or other facility would be duplicative and may lack a meaningful clinical benefit. Some commenters expressed concern that requiring practitioners reporting RPM or RTM services to furnish a separately reportable initiating visit in association with the onset of RPM or RTM services adds unnecessary cost and administrative burden to practices, could disadvantage some patients, and could delay the onset of monitoring for others. Some also expressed concern that some patients may be unduly burdened if required to travel solely for purposes of attending an initiating visit.
Response:
We thank commenters for this information. At this time, we continue to believe that these services require a level of care coordination that cannot be effective without appropriate evaluation of the patient's needs and that an initiating visit before RPM or RTM services can begin is the best way to ensure this evaluation is occurring. For the purposes of this policy, the onset of RPM or RTM services refers to the onset of these services at the billing provider level. Billing for RPM or RTM services may not begin until the initiating visit has been furnished. We are not finalizing a restriction on the amount of time between the initiating visit and the activation of monitoring, as long as RPM or RTM is discussed with the patient at that visit. To minimize beneficiary burden associated with this initiating visit requirement, we are allowing initiating visits to be furnished via telehealth when furnished in accordance with the requirements in section 1834(m) of the Act. In addition, for the purposes of this policy, a beneficiary may be considered an established patient after they have met the initiating visit requirements. We are not establishing a definition of “onset” for RPM and RTM in this rule, however, we welcome ongoing feedback on this policy and may consider this additional information for future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters requested clarification on whether the initiating visit must be performed by the billing practitioner, or if it can be furnished by practitioners within the same practice.
Response:
Like other services paid under the PFS, physicians in the same group practice who are in the same specialty must bill and be paid as though they were a single physician. We note that this is consistent with the Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 12, § 30.6.5—Physicians in Group Practice (Rev. 1, 10-01-03), where, “Physicians in the same group practice who are in the same specialty must bill and be paid as though they were a single physician; physicians in the same group practice but in different specialties may bill and be paid without regard to common group membership.”
Comment:
Commenters sought confirmation as to whether an initiating visit can be held over telehealth. We received several comments seeking clarification on how the telehealth pathway for the initiating visit will operate if the statutory telehealth flexibilities lapse.
Response:
As discussed in the proposed rule, the initiating visit must be face-to-face, which may be an in-person or telehealth visit. CMS does not have statutory authority to further extend telehealth flexibilities. After December 31, 2027, absent further legislation, the use of telehealth services for purposes of the initiating visit for remote monitoring services will be limited by the requirements of section 1834(m) of the Act that remain in effect.
Comment:
Some comments requested clarification on the documentation requirements needed to substantiate the initiating visit.
Response:
We are not finalizing the requirement of any additional documentation requirements at this time outside of the documentation requirements for all services paid under the Physician Fee Schedule.
Comment:
Several commenters sought clarification on whether the discussion of RPM and RTM needed to be the sole purpose of the visit, for it to qualify as an initiating visit.
Response:
We would like to clarify that the initiating visit does not have to be for the sole purpose of discussing remote monitoring services. RPM or RTM must be discussed with the patient at that visit, but does not have to be the sole purpose of the visit or sole topic discussed.
Comment:
We received multiple comments seeking clarification on what is meant by “separately billable” for purposes of an initiating visit. Commenters asked whether service could be initiated as part of a discharge service or global surgical service.
Response:
We would like to clarify that the initiating visit can be separately billable, but does not have to be in all scenarios. We refer readers to the CY 2024 PFS Final Rule (
88 FR 78883
through
78884
) for additional discussion of RPM or RTM services during a global period.
Comment:
Some commenters asked for clarification on how the new initiating visit requirement applies under the Community Health Center (CHC) or Federally Qualified Health Center (FQHC) Prospective Payment System (PPS), specifically whether a same-day qualifying visit requirement applies, and how the “separately billable” standards operate under encounter-based CHC billing versus the Physician Fee Schedule fee-for-service billing.
Response:
Effective January 1, 2025, Rural Health Clinics (RHCs) and FQHCs are required to bill the individual CPT/HCPCS base codes and add-on codes for each of the care coordination services to receive payment separate from the Rural Health Clinic All-Inclusive Rate (RHC AIR) or FQHC PPS. RHCs and FQHCs may bill care coordination services either alone or with other payable services. If the care coordination service is furnished on the same day as a qualifying visit, the RHC or FQHC will receive two separate payments. Care coordination services are paid at the national non-facility PFS payment rates. Since RHCs and FQHCs report the individual care coordination codes, they must follow the requirements established under the PFS for each code.
Comment:
Commenters asked whether each new episode of monitoring requires its own initiating visit. Commenters requested
(
printed page 71084)
clarification on whether a new initiating visit would be required when oversight of a patient is passed from an established billing practitioner to a new billing practitioner located within the same practice. Some commenters requested clarification on whether a new initiating visit would be required when a new or upgraded monitoring device is acquired by or for the patient. Commenters requested clarification on whether a new initiating visit would be required for patients after a clinical change, a temporary hold status has ended, or after a re-enrollment into an active monitoring program.
Response:
We would like to clarify that an initiating visit would only be required before the onset of remote monitoring services for that beneficiary. A separate visit is not required for routine clinical changes, which could include, but are not limited to a change of device, clinical change, or change of billing practitioner within the same practice.
Comment:
In situations where monitoring is initiated during a visit that also includes a higher-valued global-period procedure, a commenter recommended CMS not reduce the separately reportable E/M visit per the modifier 25 proposal.
Response:
We refer readers to section XX of this final rule for additional details discussing modifier 25. As discussed in that section, we are not finalizing service level exceptions at this time. We believe that there are overlapping resource costs for procedures, including an initiating visit for remote monitoring.
Comment:
We received several comments requesting that beneficiaries already established in a remote monitoring program be considered “grandfathered” for purposes of the initiating visit requirement.
Response:
We agree with commenters that requiring beneficiaries who are already receiving remote monitoring services to have an initiating visit would be particularly burdensome. We would like to clarify that beneficiaries who are already receiving remote monitoring services before this policy becomes effective on January 1, 2027, would not need to have an initiating visit to continue remote monitoring services, so long as all other requirements for these services are met. CMS discourages any misuse of enrolling beneficiaries in remote monitoring services between the publication of this rule and January 1, 2027. As with all services paid under the PFS, all remote monitoring services furnished must be reasonable and necessary.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed.
(d) Supervision Requirements
Currently, RPM or RTM services may be outsourced to third-party companies that provide services via telephone and online contact only, using staff who have little to no established relationship with the beneficiary or other members of the care team and have little to no interaction with the office staff and billing practitioner. After reviewing the findings discussed in recent OIG reports, such as companies “cold calling” beneficiaries to solicit them for remote monitoring services they may not need (Additional Oversight of Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare Is Needed
[
16
]
) and working to improve the transparency of “incident to” services, we believe outsourcing RPM/RTM services to a third party can fragment care, lead to insufficient involvement and oversight of the billing practitioner, or result in services that do not actually represent or facilitate all required aspects of RPM or RTM services. Provision of these services by entities having only a loose association with the treating practitioner can detract from longitudinal, patient-centered care. We do not believe that RPM or RTM services provided by clinical staff contracted by a third party can ensure the billing practitioner has adequate oversight, management, or collaboration to bill RPM or RTM services. If there is little oversight by the billing practitioner or a lack of clinical integration between a third-party providing RPM/RTM and the billing practitioner, we do not believe that the full scope of service elements required to bill these codes are being met.
We proposed to only allow payment for RPM or RTM services when furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice. To count the time spent by clinical staff providing aspects of RPM or RTM services, the clinical staff must be a direct employee of the practitioner or the practitioner's practice. This would have meant that for the purposes of billing Medicare, beginning January 1, 2027, the RPM and RTM codes could not be billed in cases where the service is not performed by clinical staff of the billing practitioner and will not allow contracting out to third-party companies. This does not mean the clinical staff must necessarily always be physically located within the practice, nor does it require that the beneficiary be on-site for the provision of remote monitoring services. Under our proposed revised policy, the time spent by clinical staff providing RPM or RTM services can be counted, provided that the clinical staff are under the general supervision of the billing practitioner, all other requirements of the “incident to” regulations at §  410.26 are met, and the clinical staff is a direct employee of the practitioner or the practitioner's practice. We sought comment on this proposal, specifically on how often third-party billing currently occurs and how this policy, if finalized, could impact access to remote monitoring services.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed support for CMS' proposal to only allow payment for RPM or RTM services when furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice. Some commented that it would better ensure that clinicians are made aware of relevant data collected, would support fraud prevention, and support quality outcomes.
Response:
We thank commenters for supporting our proposal.
Comment:
Several commenters suggested other program integrity-related requirements CMS could pursue in the future instead of this policy. Several commenters suggested CMS consider establishing stricter credentialing requirements for clinicians and vendors delivering RPM and RTM services. A few commenters suggested CMS consider limiting payment to conditions or disease states that have robust data demonstrating the value of remote monitoring services.
Response:
We thank commenters for the additional information and may consider this for future rulemaking.
Comment:
Many commenters requested that CMS clarify how this proposal relates to the technology used for remote monitoring services. For example, commenters requested that working with outside companies to license software platforms, purchase devices, and resolve technical issues not be prohibited.
Response:
We would like to clarify that a practitioner or practice's use of a third-party technology platform does not affect the requirement that clinical staff must be a direct employee of the practitioner or the practitioner's practice. This policy would not prohibit working with vendors who do not supply third-party staff time, but supply software, devices, technical support, etc. The intent of this policy was not to
(
printed page 71085)
require billing practitioners to develop proprietary monitoring platforms or devices. Practices may obtain devices, software, connectivity, data hosting, cybersecurity, implementation support, technical assistance, and interoperability services from outside companies.
Comment:
Commenters requested clarification regarding CMS' reasoning that remote monitoring services should be held to a higher standard than other services paid under the PFS that are assigned general supervision, as detailed in “incident to” regulations at
42 CFR 410.26
. Commenters specified that the regulation text under § 410.26 defines employee, leased employee, and independent contractors, and permits these clinical staff types.
Response:
We note that these services are assigned general supervision and we are not finalizing any changes to supervision requirements or to the regulation text under § 410.26, as it pertains to remote monitoring services.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that allowing payment for RPM or RTM services only when they are furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice would unintentionally limit the types of practices that can offer these services and limit access to care for patients. Several commenters cited the example of academic health systems that employ clinical staff and faculty staff under different entities. Several commenters also cited hospitals utilizing clinical staff who are not direct employees as an example of an entity that would no longer be able to provide RPM or RTM services. A number of commenters expressed concerns that patients receiving RPM or RTM services would experience limited access to clinical staff and cited specific examples such as access becoming limited to only regular business hours instead of the 24/7/365 service that may be available via third parties. Some commenters stated that a reduction in the number of practices offering RPM or RTM services could increase overall costs to the healthcare system by driving patients towards in-person care and utilization of urgent care and emergency services.
Response:
We thank commenters for their comments on our proposal. At this time, we continue to believe that allowing payment only when RPM or RTM services are furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice is the best way to ensure care is integrated, there is sufficient oversight and involvement of the billing practitioner and that services provided represent all required aspects of RPM or RTM services.
Comment:
Commenters, whether they did or did not support our proposal, cited the increased cost of employing clinical staff in-house as opposed to using a third-party contractor. Many commenters expressed concern that small and independent practices lack the financial resources to fully manage remote monitoring programs with only staff under their direct employment. Some expressed concern this would disproportionally impact patients living in rural and underserved communities, those with multiple chronic conditions, and those with specialized needs. Many commenters expressed concerns that limiting payments to only RPM or RTM services furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice will exacerbate workforce shortages. Some stated that practices would be unable to hire adequate staff due to geographic limitations and other concerns. Some commenters noted that contracting with third parties afforded practices flexibility during periods in which they may be short-staffed or need access to clinical expertise not otherwise available in their own practice. Commenters also expressed concern that not allowing practices to contract out to third-party companies would limit their ability to develop partnerships with community providers not directly employed by the practitioner or the practitioner's practice, such as EMS agencies, paramedicine providers, and pharmacists.
Response:
We thank commenters for this information. At this time, we continue to believe that allowing payment only when RPM or RTM services are furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice is the best way to ensure care is integrated, there is sufficient oversight and involvement of the billing practitioner and that services provided represent all required aspects of RPM or RTM services.
Comment:
A few commenters noted that findings published by the OIG regarding the cold-calling and solicitation of beneficiaries could be properly addressed by requirements related to an initiating visit. Some suggested CMS pursue oversight and credentialing of third parties before implementing supervision requirements. Many commenters stated that requiring direct employment is not a reliable indication that staff are integrated into workflows and contributing to quality outcomes. Some suggested CMS should implement guidelines more closely connected to quality outcomes and audit to ensure compliance.
Response:
We thank commenters for their comments on our proposal. At this time, we continue to believe that allowing payment only when RPM or RTM services are furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice is the best way to ensure care is integrated, there is sufficient oversight and involvement of the billing practitioner and that services provided represent all required aspects of RPM or RTM services.
Comment:
Many commenters requested clarity on what “employed by the practice” means for purposes of payment for RPM or RTM services. Many cited examples of specific employment and contracting arrangements and asked for clarification on whether they would be acceptable under the proposed policy. Many also requested CMS consider exemptions for specific arrangements. Some commenters requested CMS define “direct employee of the practitioner or the practitioner's practice” for purposes of providing RPM or RTM services. Many commenters requested CMS delay any new requirements related to supervision requirements until at least January 1, 2028. Several provided specific examples of challenges that would be encountered if the proposed policy were to take effect on January 1, 2027. Some commenters expressed concerns that health systems relying on contracted staff for some portion of their RPM or RTM services would be unable to alter or discontinue their existing contracts prior to a January 1, 2027 effective date. Commenters stated that practices would need beyond January 1, 2027 to hire and train sufficient staff and establish appropriate workflows and processes. Many commenters requested CMS delay any new requirements related to supervision of staff until at least January 1, 2028. A few commenters expressed concern that not allowing adequate time for implementation could cause providers to be less willing to make substantial, multi-year investments in technology and infrastructure in the future.
Response:
We thank commenters for this information. We disagree that the proposed policy would discourage future investment by practices in technology and infrastructure. However, we agree that it is appropriate to delay implementation of the proposed policy to allow sufficient time for implementation. We also agree with commenters that there may be a need for additional time for CMS to specify additional clinical staff arrangements that may be appropriate for remote monitoring services. Due to the additional information provided by
(
printed page 71086)
commenters, we are finalizing this proposal with modifications. Specifically, we are providing a 2-year delay in implementation to allow for practices to hire and train staff for “in-house” workflows for remote monitoring services. We would like to emphasize that, although we will continue to allow contracting out to third-party companies until December 31, 2028, all of the existing “incident to” and other rules for billing remote monitoring services under the PFS must be met. If there is little oversight by the billing practitioner or a lack of clinical integration between a third party and the billing practitioner, we do not believe the criteria for billing remote monitoring services are actually being met and therefore, the practitioner should not bill for remote monitoring services in those instances. As such, the billing practitioner must retain a certain level of involvement in remote monitoring services. The codes for reporting clinical staff time are valued to include a certain amount of ongoing work and supervision by the billing practitioner consistent with the included service elements that may not be delegated to any other parties. After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing that for the purposes of billing Medicare, beginning January 1, 2029, the RPM and RTM codes cannot be billed in cases where the service is not performed by clinical staff that is a direct employee of the practitioner or the practitioner's practice and contracting out to third-party companies will not be allowed after that time. Prior to this date, CMS will be publishing sub-regulatory guidance further clarifying clinical staff arrangements that may be appropriate for remote monitoring services.
(e) Valuation
Remote physiologic monitoring (RPM) represents the remote monitoring of parameters such as weight, blood pressure, and pulse oximetry to monitor a patient's condition and inform their management. The remote physiologic monitoring code set currently includes CPT codes 99091, 99445, 99453, 99454, 99457, 99458, 99470, 99473, and 99474 (code descriptors in Table A-D6). Remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM) represents the monitoring of adherence to at-home therapeutic interventions. For RTM, there are distinct device supply codes for three types of therapeutic monitoring: respiratory system, cognitive behavioral therapy, and musculoskeletal system monitoring. The remote therapeutic monitoring code set currently includes CPT codes 98975, 98976, 98977, 98978, 98979, 98980, 98981, 98984, and 98985 (code descriptors in Table A-D6). There are three components of RPM and RTM services: education and setup, device supply, and treatment management.
(
printed page 71087)
For CPT codes 99453 and 98975, which are PE-only codes describing RPM and RTM initial set-up and patient education on use of equipment, respectively, we proposed to crosswalk the direct PE inputs from CPT code 99473 (
Self-measured blood pressure using a device validated for clinical accuracy; patient education/training and device calibration
), as we believe the existing valuation of CPT codes 99453 and 98975 may not accurately reflect the resource costs involved in those services. Specifically, we are concerned that, due to lack of information regarding the typical device used to perform these procedures, these services are overvalued. We believe that the typical device used for these procedures in the physician office setting may not be accurately captured in the data previously used for valuation, as we have received very little invoice or pricing information from interested parties for the specific devices used in RTM and RPM services. We believe that a crosswalk to the direct PE inputs associated with CPT code 99473 may more accurately capture the resource costs associated with a typical device set-up and patient education on use of equipment. We sought comment on this proposal, specifically information regarding the typical clinical workflow for the initial set-up and patient education on use of equipment services used in furnishing RPM or RTM and their associated costs.
For CPT codes 99445 and 99454, which are PE-only codes describing RPM device(s) supply with daily recording(s) or programmed alert(s) transmission, we proposed to crosswalk the direct PE inputs from CPT code 99474 (
Self-measured blood pressure using a device validated for clinical accuracy; separate self-measurements of two readings one minute apart, twice daily over a 30-day period (minimum of 12 readings), collection of data reported by the patient and/or caregiver to the physician or other qualified health care professional, with report of average systolic and diastolic pressures and subsequent communication of a treatment plan to the patient
). For CPT codes 98976, 98977, 98978, 98984, 98985, and 98986, which are PE-only
(
printed page 71088)
codes describing RTM device(s) supply for data access or data transmissions, we proposed to crosswalk the direct PE inputs from CPT code 93270 (
External patient and, when performed, auto activated electrocardiographic rhythm derived event recording with symptom-related memory loop with remote download capability up to 30 days, 24-hour attended monitoring; recording (includes connection, recording, and disconnection)).
We believe the existing valuation of CPT codes 99445, 99454, 98976, 98977, 98978, 98984, 98985, and 98986 may not accurately reflect the resource costs involved in these services, especially since we continue to lack data surrounding the typical RPM and RTM devices and the costs associated with them. Specifically, we are concerned that, due to lack of information regarding the typical device used to perform these procedures, these services are overvalued. We believe that the typical device used for these procedures in the physician office setting may not be accurately captured in the data previously used for valuation, as we have received very little invoice or pricing information from interested parties for the specific devices used in RTM and RPM services. We believe that the crosswalk to the direct PE inputs associated with the proposed codes discussed earlier may more accurately capture the resource costs associated with a typical device. We solicited comments on this proposal, specifically information regarding the typical devices used in furnishing RPM or RTM, not just their associated costs and invoices, but robust evidence detailing what providers are actually paying for these devices, including discounts or other typical pricing details. We sought other types of pricing data and information for RPM or RTM devices, including if the costs include software, hardware, or both, as well as more information about the typical devices. For CPT codes 99470, 99457, 99458, 98979, 98980, and 98981, which describe the physician/QHP work associated with treatment management, we proposed to eliminate PE inputs for these codes, as we believe resource costs for these services are accurately captured in the work RVUs, and we do not believe the typical clinical workflow for these services would involve clinical staff time. We proposed that the current work RVUs and current work times for these codes be maintained. We welcomed information regarding the typical clinical workflow for these services.
We solicited comments on these proposals, as well as requested general feedback from the public that may be useful in further development of our payment policies for remote monitoring services that are currently separately payable under the PFS.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed support for the revaluation of RPM and RTM codes as RPM payment in its current form incentivizes a focus on generating billable encounters, regardless of whether those interactions provide meaningful clinical value. We also received a comment expressing concern regarding incentive systems that rewarded intervention rather than clinical restraint. A few other commenters agreed with CMS that remote monitoring device costs have declined since the codes were first valued and requested CMS pair the revaluation with a published methodology and a transparent, periodically updated device cost benchmark.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support of our proposals.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern that CMS lacked adequate information on costs to properly revalue codes and requested CMS gather more information related to true costs of RPM and RTM services from stakeholders, including the RUC, before finalizing any revaluation of codes. Some recommended confidential submissions on cost data be accepted. Many commenters did not believe the services used in the crosswalks were analogous to the services described in the remote monitoring code set, including that the remote monitoring services are more comprehensive in the crosswalk codes. Commenters were concerned that the lower valuations may reduce incentives for thorough set up, education, and treatment management services. Some commenters stated that devices represented in the crosswalk were not analogous to the universe of devices used in RPM and RTM services. Commenters stated that some devices include enhanced features such as built-in internet connectivity, automatic data transmission capabilities, the generation of clinically actionable alerts, and connectivity capabilities in otherwise connectivity-limited areas. Commenters believed such devices were undervalued in the proposed crosswalk. A few commenters commented that RPM programs would be incentivized to adopt hardware based solely on price rather than devices selected for clinical benefit and recommended CMS base reimbursement on the capability of the device. Some commenters requested CMS disclose the data used to inform the final valuation of codes. Many commenters expressed concern that the proposed crosswalk of codes did not take into account fixed costs practices incur to support RPM and RTM programs, including infrastructure upkeep and connectivity costs, and costs related to accessing device-specific platforms and data generated from devices. Some commenters recommended CMS carry the current values forward while the revaluation is completed or phase-in any revaluation codes over a period of multiple years.
Response:
We thank commenters for this additional information. The AMA informed CMS that in response to our concerns over a lack of data to inform accurate valuation of these services, all 19 RPM and RTM codes will have their practice expense reviewed at the January 2027 RUC meeting. We look forward to reviewing the information from the RUC, as well as any additional information that interested parties provide regarding the costs of these services for future rulemaking. We would also like to clarify that, for many of these remote monitoring CPT codes, the phase-in of significant RVU reductions and its associated adjustment will be applied (cite PE step 19). Section 1848(c)(8) of the Act requires CMS to phase-in decreases in total RVUs for a service that is not a new or revised code over two years if the RVUs would otherwise be decreased by an estimated amount equal to or greater than 20 percent. Since a 19 percent reduction is the maximum 1-year reduction for any service not described by a new or revised code, many of these changes will be phased in over multiple calendar years.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the work and direct PE inputs as proposed for CPT codes 99445, 99453, 99454, 98975, 98976, 98977, 98984, and 98985.
Comment:
A few commenters requested that CMS clarify the status and valuation of CPT codes 98978 and 98986.
Response:
As discussed in the proposed rule, CPT codes 98978 and 98986 will be actively priced beginning in CY 2027. Since these codes were formerly contractor priced, they are considered to be “new or revised” codes and therefore the phase-in transition does not apply like it does to the other remote monitoring codes (for additional information regarding the phase-in of significant RVU reductions, we direct readers to the CY 2016 PFS final rule (
80 FR 70927
through
70929
)). In the
(
printed page 71089)
proposed rule, the valuation of CPT codes 98978 and 98986 was lower than the RTM device supply codes for other conditions. Due to being assigned different indirect PE allocations in the NPRM, CPT codes 98978 and 98986 had different valuations. We agree with commenters data that these codes do not have drastically different resource costs than RTM device supply codes for other conditions and that CPT codes 98978 and 98986 should be treated like other device supply codes. As discussed in the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we continue to believe that since the device is supplied to the beneficiary for the full 30-day period, regardless of the number of days that data is transmitted, these codes should be assigned the same valuation.
After consideration of public comments, for CY 2027, we are finalizing that CPT codes 98978 and 98986 be crosswalked to CPT code 98977 to ensure that all three codes share the same PE RVU.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concern that the proposed reimbursement valuation changes do not adequately recognize the clinical resources required to furnish clinically meaningful RPM and RTM services. Several commenters suggested that the proposals to eliminate expenses associated with clinical labor based on an assumption that a typical clinical workflow for some services would not involve clinical staff time, were inherently in tension with other proposals to only allow payment for RPM or RTM services when furnished by clinical staff employed by the practice. Many commenters also identified that clinical staff time is specified in the code descriptors for these services.
Response:
We thank commenters for the additional information regarding the typical clinical workflow for these services. After reviewing this information, we agree with commenters that clinical staff are often used when furnishing treatment management services for remote physiologic and remote therapeutic monitoring.
After consideration of public comments, we are not finalizing as proposed to eliminate direct PE inputs for CPT codes 99470, 99457, 99458, 98979, 98980, and 98981.
(f) Comment Solicitation in the Proposed Rule
We have concerns about the administrative burden of the numerous remote monitoring codes and proliferation of this code family. We also continue to work to implement recommendations from the recent OIG reports that we are concerned cannot be fully resolved with the current coding structure of the remote monitoring code family, such as ensuring that beneficiaries receive all components of the remote monitoring service. For example, the OIG report found that, “About 43 percent of enrollees who received remote patient monitoring did not receive all 3 components of it, raising questions about whether the monitoring is being used as intended.” (Additional Oversight of Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare Is Needed
[
17
]
).
We also considered, and sought comment on, bundling CPT codes 99453, 99445, 99454, 99091, 99470, 99457, 99458, 98975, 98984, 98976, 98985, 98977, 98986, 98978, 98979, 98980, and 98981 through the creation of new codes that describe initial set up and monthly monitoring/management for RPM and RTM, respectively. For payment for remote monitoring services under the PFS, we also considered, and sought comment on, the creation of four new HCPCS G-Codes:
GRPM1: RPM initial set-up and patient education.
GRPM2: Remote monitoring of physiologic parameter(s) (
e.g.,
weight, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, respiratory flow rate), per calendar month, including:
++ Device(s) supply with daily recording(s) or programmed alert(s) transmission.
++ 2 or more days of data transmission.
++ Treatment management services, requiring at least one real-time interactive communication with the patient/caregiver; time totaling at least 20 minutes.
GRTM1: RTM initial set-up and patient education.
GRTM2: Remote monitoring of therapeutic parameter(s) (e.g., therapy adherence, therapy response, digital therapeutic intervention), per calendar month, including:
++ Device(s) supply for data access or data transmissions.
++ 2 or more days of data transmission.
++ Treatment management services, requiring at least one real-time interactive communication with the patient or caregiver; time totaling at least 20 minutes.
We sought comment on these HCPCS G-codes and also sought comment on any other revisions needed to the code descriptors to reflect the necessary service elements for this code family. These HCPCS G-codes would adopt all current conditions of payment for the remote therapeutic and remote physiologic codes finalized in prior rulemaking, as well as the proposed established patient, initiating visit, or supervision or both requirements outlined earlier in this section, if finalized. As drafted, all service elements outlined in the G-code descriptors would be required each calendar month. We sought public comment on these HCPCS G-codes.
The creation of these G-codes could alleviate administrative burden, as this would reduce the number of remote monitoring codes from 17 to four. These HCPCS G-codes would also ensure that beneficiaries receive treatment management services when receiving remote monitoring services. According to the OIG Reports, billing for Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare
[
18
]
and Additional Oversight of Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare Is Needed,
[
19
]
some beneficiaries do not regularly receive treatment management services. The OIG Report, Additional Oversight of Remote Patient Monitoring in Medicare Is Needed,
[
20
]
also stated that 43 percent of enrollees who received remote patient monitoring did not receive at least one of the three components (patient education and set-up, device supply, and treatment management). Although we have not required that providers bill for all three components, this data from the OIG Report raises questions about how these services are being used. By incorporating device supply, data transmission, and treatment management into one code, we could ensure that those service elements are always provided.

88 FR 79071
through

89 FR 97998

We received public comments on this comment solicitation. We appreciate the commenters for their comments. After consideration of public comments, we will take the comments into consideration for possible future rulemaking.
(49) National Payment for Non-Sheet Form Skin Substitutes
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49500
), we finalized contractor pricing for non-sheet form skin substitutes. We stated that these products have the potential to be payable as skin substitutes; but that the units, as expressed in a product's coding, are difficult to standardize for payment purposes. Therefore, we finalized that we would maintain the current coding mechanism for these products and would direct the Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) to determine appropriate payment, which is generally consistent with how these products are currently paid. We stated that we would continue to evaluate payments for these products to determine if an alternative payment methodology may be better suited to non-sheet products.
Based on ongoing analysis and feedback from internal and external interested parties, we have come to believe that, on the balance, the resource costs per cm
2
for non-sheet form skin substitutes is consistent with the resource costs associated with sheet form skin substitutes. For non-sheet skin substitute products, cm
2
reflects the wound surface area treated rather than the physical dimensions of the product. Therefore, for CY 2027, we proposed to nationally price the non-sheet form skin substitutes consistent with the payment rates associated with the sheet form skin substitutes. For a list of the non-sheet form skin substitutes, please refer to the skin substitutes section located on the CMS website (
https://www.cms.gov/​medicare/​payment/​fee-schedules/​physician-fee-schedule/​skin-substitutes
).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters raised concerns with our previously finalized skin substitute policy in the CY 2026 PFS Final Rule. These commenters stated specific concerns with the decision to weigh the national payment rate for sheet form skin substitutes of $127.14 per cm
2
for CY 2026 using product-specific hospital outpatient data as they believe it is not indicative of true costs across both settings of care. Commenters also mentioned they believe the $127.14 per cm
2
payment rate is too low. Additionally, commenters noted that CMS should not update the skin substitute payment rate using ASP data and instead use an inflationary update to ensure increases in manufacturer costs are appropriately captured in the payment rate. Lastly, some commenters also suggested CMS should remove the geographic adjustments to skin substitute products serviced in office settings due to patient access issues.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback expressed by commenters regarding their concerns about our overall approach to payment for skin substitute products. However, we note that we did not propose any changes to the payment rate itself nor any changes to how the payment rate is calculated or updated. Instead, we proposed in the CY 2027 PFS Proposed Rule to establish the same national payment rate for non-sheet skin substitutes that is consistent with the payment rate established for the sheet form skin substitutes.
Comment:
A few commenters requested CMS to clarify what payment amount will be used for the non-sheet form skin substitute products.
Response:
The same rate established for the sheet-form skin substitutes of $127.14 per cm
2
will apply for the non-sheet form skin substitute products.
Comment:
Many commenters raised concerns that measuring non-sheet form skin substitute products per cm
2
does not fully account for three-dimensional wound characteristics, including depth and volume. Additionally, a few commenters suggested that CMS recognize the concepts of Internal Surface Area (ISA) and Therapeutic Treatment Area (TTA) as described in the recently published wound-care consensus recommendations as an alternative unit of measure.
Response:
We acknowledge commenters' concerns that non-sheet skin substitute products may be used to treat wounds of varying depth and volume. However, we do not believe that these factors prevent the use of a per cm
2
payment methodology as a per cm
2
payment rate accounts for differences in wound surface area that can be used to estimate volume. We therefore do not believe that differences in product form, or variations in wound depth and volume alone, necessarily warrant a separate payment methodology for non-sheet products.
Comment:
A few commenters questioned that the per cm
2
approach for non-sheet form skin substitute does not align with the products' code descriptors because they contain various forms of measurement such as, “per mL,” “per cc,” or “per mg.” These commenters requested CMS to clarify how the proposed nationally priced payment approach of per cm
2
for non-sheet skin substitute products would correspond with the variety of measurements displayed in the current code descriptors.
Response:
We acknowledged in the CY 2026 PFS final rule that non-sheet skin substitute products may be described and supplied using units other than square centimeters, including milliliters, cubic centimeters, milligrams, or other units (
90 FR 49500
). Similar to how non-sheet form skin substitute products are currently being paid under MAC pricing with no modifications to the code descriptors, we believe it is appropriate to maintain existing HCPCS descriptors that
(
printed page 71091)
accurately reflect the form and quantity of the product. Our proposal to establish a per cm
2
payment for non-sheet form skin substitute products based on wound surface area does not require that the product itself be packaged or marketed in a per cm
2
unit.
Comment:
Many commenters brought to our attention the proposed rule provides limited instruction regarding the interaction between the new HCPCS application codes (G0681-G0684) and the corresponding non-sheet form skin substitute product HCPCS codes. Some of these commenters urged CMS to create national payment rates for G0681-G0684, with the same RVUs as the current administration codes for sheet form skin substitutes described under CPT codes 15271-15278.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback and clarify that HCPCS application codes G0681-G0684 are only to be used for non-sheet form skin substitute products. CMS stated in the CY 2027 PFS Proposed Rule that we would align the same payment rate for sheet form skin substitute products as we would for the non-sheet form skin substitute products. We maintain this consistency is relevant for the application codes for non-sheet form skin substitutes described under HCPCS G0681-G0684. Therefore, CMS will establish a national payment rate for the non-sheet form skin substitute application codes G0681-G0684 similar to how CPT codes 15271-15278 are currently paid.
Comment:
Some commenters requested CMS provide additional analysis, including HCPCS-defined billing units, price basis, cost data, conversion assumptions, and sensitivity analyses used to reach its resource-equivalence conclusion. These commenters stated our proposal is unsupported and additional information on analyses is required to understand how CMS came to the approach that non-sheet form skin substitutes can be treated on a per cm
2
basis.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback. However, we disagree that our proposal to standardize payment for non-sheet form skin substitute products reflects an unsupported assumption of resource equivalence. In the CY 2026 rulemaking, we specifically sought comment on how non-sheet form skin substitute products furnished in units such as milliliters, cubic centimeters, and milligrams could be incorporated into a standardized payment methodology. After taking into consideration the comments received from the CY 2026 PFS Proposed Rule, we determined that additional evaluation was warranted and finalized contractor pricing for CY 2026 while we continued to assess an appropriate methodology. Our CY 2027 proposal reflects that continued evaluation and feedback from interested parties. We therefore believe our proposal effectively demonstrates the progression of our consideration of non-sheet form skin substitute products.
Comment:
Many commenters were in support of our proposal to nationally price non-sheet form skin substitutes consistent with the payment rate associated with sheet form skin substitutes. These commenters agreed with CMS's assessment that the resource costs per cm
2
for non-sheet form skin substitutes is consistent with the resource costs associated with sheet form skin substitutes. Additionally, commenters noted our proposal would protect beneficiaries and ensure good value for the Medicare program and thus taxpayers. Lastly, commenters also stated they believe our proposal will continue to address unsustainable spending growth and clinical inconsistency in the skin substitute product space.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and reiterate our commitment to protecting beneficiaries, promoting appropriate use of Medicare resources, and safeguarding taxpayer dollars while further preventing fraud, waste, and abuse.
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to nationally price the non-sheet form skin substitutes on a per cm
2
basis, consistent with the payment rates associated with the sheet form skin substitutes.
(50) Smoking and Tobacco Use Cessation (CPT Codes 99406, 99407) and Structured Assessment, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment (SBIRT) (HCPCS Codes G2011, G0396, G0397)
The Trump Administration Executive Order, “Establishing the President's Make America Health Again Commission”
[
21
]
is a top priority for CMS, as such we continue to focus on the prevention and management of chronic disease. Chronic disease remains a significant public health concern, with three in four American adults having at least one chronic condition, and more than half having two or more chronic conditions. Many preventable chronic diseases are caused by a short list of risk behaviors, including smoking, poor nutrition, physical inactivity, and excessive alcohol use.
[
22
]
These patterns reinforce the need for accessible behavioral health services that can help individuals reduce these risk behaviors.
In the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79006
through
79010
), we finalized an increase in the valuation for timed behavioral health services under the PFS by applying an upward adjustment of 19.1 percent to the work RVUs for time-based psychotherapy codes payable under the PFS. This increase is being implemented over a 4-year transition period.
We believe similar adjustments are warranted for smoking and tobacco use cessation, CPT codes 99406 (
Smoking and tobacco use cessation counseling visit; intermediate, greater than 3 minutes up to 10 minutes
) and 99407 (
Smoking and tobacco use cessation counseling visit; intensive, greater than 10 minutes
) and screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment (SBIRT) services, HCPCS codes G2011 (
Alcohol and/or substance (other than tobacco) misuse structured assessment (e.g., audit, dast), and brief intervention, 5-14 minutes
), G0396 (
Alcohol and/or substance (other than tobacco) misuse structured assessment (e.g., audit, dast), and brief intervention 15 to 30 minutes
), and G0397(
Alcohol and/or substance (other than tobacco) misuse structured assessment (e.g., audit, dast), and intervention, greater than 30 minutes
).
Smoking and tobacco cessation and SBIRT services are evidence supported behavioral health interventions. Quitting smoking provides immediate health improvements including lowering the likelihood of developing lung cancer and other smoking-related cancers, and reduces the risks of coronary heart disease, stroke, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Evidence based smoking and tobacco cessation treatments are effective, including the combination of behavioral counseling and medication therapy.
[
23
]
SBIRT effectively addresses substance use. In primary care and other clinical settings, SBIRT has been shown to help decrease unhealthy substance use and misuse.
[
24
]
The smoking and tobacco cessation services (CPT codes 99406 and 99407) and SBIRT services HCPCS codes G0396 and G0397 were last valued in 2008, and the SBIRT service HCPCS code G2011 was created and last valued in
(
printed page 71092)
2019. Given the evidence supported role these services play in preventing and managing chronic disease and behavioral health conditions including alcohol and/or substance misuse, we believe that valuation should more accurately reflect the clinical intensity and work associated with these time-based services.
Therefore, we proposed applying the same upward adjustment of 19.1 percent to the work RVUs for these time-based services aligning with the adjustments made to the time-based psychotherapy codes, in conjunction with the fourth and final year of the phase-in for time-based psychotherapy codes that we finalized in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79006
through
79010
). Although the upward adjustment of 19.1 percent for the time-based psychotherapy codes has been implemented over a 4-year period, with CY 2027 being the fourth year, we proposed to apply the full 19.1 percent to smoking and tobacco use cessation services and SBIRT services in this final year of the transition. This approach ensures that these services are brought into alignment with the psychotherapy codes at the completion of the 4-year phase-in timeline, rather than initiating a new multiyear phase-in period. We proposed to refine the work RVU of smoking and tobacco use cessation services codes as follows: for CPT code 99406 by increasing the work RVU to 0.29 from the current 0.24, and CPT code 99407 by increasing the work RVU to 0.60 from the current 0.50; and for the SBIRT services codes, we proposed to refine the work RVU as follows, for HCPCS code G2011 by increasing the work RVU to 0.39 from the current 0.33, for HCPCS code G0396 by increasing the work RVU to 0.77 from the current 0.65, and for HCPCS code G0397 by increasing the work RVU to 1.55 from the current 1.30.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters were overwhelmingly in support of the proposed upward adjustment of 19.1 percent to the work RVUs for Smoking and Tobacco Use Cessation (CPT codes 99406, 99407) and SBIRT (HCPCS codes G2011, G0396, G0397) services. Commenters indicated that these services are important for prevention, chronic disease management, behavioral health integration, and improved patient outcomes.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support. Additionally, we are clarifying that although the proposed rule described SBIRT as
screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment,
for purposes of PFS payment, SBIRT, specifically HCPCS codes G2011, G0396, and G0397, are defined as
structured assessment, brief intervention, and referral to treatment for substance use disorders.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that similar upward valuation adjustments should also be applied to other time-based behavioral health codes, including neurobehavioral status exam, developmental test administration, psychological testing evaluation, neuropsychological testing evaluation, and test administration and scoring services. Some of the commenters indicated that these codes describe time-based behavioral health services and are intended to inform diagnosis and care recommendations for a wide range of medical and psychological issues. The commenters continued to state that lagging values for these services impacts patient access and discourages workforce development in these areas.
Response:
We thank commenters for this feedback. After consideration of the comments, we continue to believe, as stated in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79009
), that the codes referenced by the commenters are describing psychological and neuropsychological testing services, which are distinct from the psychotherapy services with regard to the nature of the work, such that, these codes describing psychological and neuropsychological testing services are not necessarily timed services that are provided without assistance from clinical staff. Therefore, these services do not fit the same criteria as the services addressed in the CY 2024 PFS final rule, which formed the basis for increasing the valuation of smoking and tobacco cessation and SBIRT services. However, we may consider updates to the valuation of these services for future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters supported applying the full upward adjustment of 19.1 percent to the work RVUs without an additional phase-in period. However, a couple of commenters recommended a phase-in approach in the work RVU increase, similar to how the psychotherapy codes were phased in over a four-year transition period.
Response:
We thank commenters for this feedback. After consideration of the comments, we will apply the full 19.1 percent to the work RVUs to smoking and tobacco use cessation services and SBIRT services in this final year of the of the phase of these updates.
Comment:

Initiation of medication for the treatment of opioid use disorder in the emergency department setting, including assessment, referral to ongoing care, and arranging access to supportive services (list separately in addition to code for primary procedure)
) for consistency with SBIRT codes since CMS originally established the valuation of G2213 using a direct crosswalk to HCPCS code G10397, one of the SBIRT codes. A commenter recommended for CMS to apply the same work RVU adjustment to HCPCS codes G0442 (
Annual alcohol misuse screening, 5 to 15 minutes

Brief face-to-face behavioral counseling for alcohol misuse, 15 minutes
