Response:
We thank commenters for this feedback; we may consider updates to the valuation of these services in future rulemaking.
Comment:
A commenter recommended replacing HCPCS G0396 and G0397 with CPT codes 99408 and 99409, to assist with reducing administrative burden due to recognition of different codes by different payers.
Response:
We thank the commenter for this feedback. As explained in the CY 2008 PFS final rule (
72 FR 66371
) and CY 2013 PFS final rule (
77 FR 68955
), the code descriptions for CPT codes 99408 (
Alcohol and/or substance (other than tobacco) abuse structured screening (e.g., AUDIT, DAST), and brief intervention (SBI) services; 15 to 30 minutes
) and 99409 (
Alcohol and/or substance (other than tobacco) abuse structured screening (e.g., AUDIT, DAST), and brief intervention (SBI) services; greater than 30 minutes

Commenters are welcome to submit codes by February 10th of the coming year for consideration as potentially misvalued services in the CY 2028 PFS proposed rule. See the discussion regarding Potentially Misvalued Services Under the PFS in this final rule for more information on how to submit a nomination for a potentially misvalued code.
(
printed page 71093)
Comment:
A few commenters supported the proposal to increase the work RVUs for Smoking and Tobacco Use Cessation and SBIRT and requested CMS ensure that the change does not disrupt existing community health center (CHC) prospective payment system (PPS) reimbursement. After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to apply the same upward adjustment of 19.1 percent to the work RVUs for these time-based services, Smoking and Tobacco Use Cessation (CPT codes 99406, 99407) and SBIRT (HCPCS codes G2011, G0396, G0397), aligning with the adjustments made to the time-based psychotherapy codes, in conjunction with the fourth and final year of the phase-in for time-based psychotherapy codes that we finalized in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (

Specifically we are finalizing a work RVU of 3.25 for CPT code 99492, a work RVU of 2.56 for CPT code 99493, work RVU of 1.28 for CPT code 99494 and HCPCS code G2214, a work RVU of 3.25 for HCPCS code G0568, and a work RVU of 2.56 for HCPCS code G0569.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended increasing the valuation of the general behavioral health integration (BHI) codes (CPT code 99484 and HCPCS code G0323), alongside the CoCM codes. Some of the commenters stated that the general BHI codes should remain model-agnostic to support diverse evidence-based care models and support diverse workforce participation. Some commenters also recommended related increases in the valuation of HCPCS G0570, and office-based treatment for opioid use disorder service HCPCS code G2086, G20876 and G2088.
Response:
We thank commenters for their input and welcome additional feedback on the valuation of general BHI services and office-based treatment for opioid use disorder services. We may consider valuation updates for these services in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Commenters were overwhelmingly in support of increasing the Behavioral Health Care Manager (L057B) clinical labor rate from $0.57 to $0.70 per minute using the CORF social worker/psychologist crosswalk. Commenters indicated that this adjustment more accurately reflects the qualifications, training, and responsibilities of behavioral health care managers.
Response:
We appreciate the support for this proposal.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended removing unnecessary requirements that limit who can provide and/or bill for integrated care, such that psychologists, social workers, nurses, and other behavioral health professionals would be able to bill and get reimbursed directly for the integrated care services they provided. A commenter requested clarification that the management of alcohol use disorder (AUD) constitutes a qualifying behavioral health integration (BHI) activity under the Advanced Primary Care Management (APCM) behavioral add-on codes (G0568, G0569, and G0570).
Response:
As discussed in CY 2017 Final Rule (
81 FR 80231
), we believe that the CoCM services would be reported by the treating physician or other qualified health care professional and include the services of the treating physician or other qualified health professional, the behavioral health care manager who would furnish the services incident to services of the treating physician or other qualified health care professional, and the psychiatric consultant whose consultative service would be furnished incident to services of the treating physician or other qualified health care professional. The management of alcohol use disorder (AUD) may qualify as behavioral health integration (BHI) under the APCM behavioral health add-on code. Beneficiaries can receive BHI services if they have an eligible condition, such as SUD, including AUD. Therefore, when all applicable billing and service requirements are met, management of AUD may be furnished as part of BHI services under the APCM behavioral health add-on code.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS should ensure that remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM) for cognitive behavioral therapy and the collaborative care model are treated as complementary rather than competing pathways, because a beneficiary receiving collaborative care may also benefit from an FDA-authorized digital therapeutic, and Medicare policy should not force a choice between them
Response:
CoCM and RTM may be billed concurrently when reasonable and necessary. The minutes counted for the CoCM services cannot also be counted towards other services.
Comment:
A commenter encouraged CMS to explicitly recognize appropriately structured, evidence-based group intervention as permissible behavioral health care manager activities within CoCM.
Response:
Please refer to the Shared Medical Appointments (SMA) section for a more detailed discussion. If the billing practitioner determines a shared medical appointment is the appropriate route for providing CoCM services for a patient, and the patient consents to the SMA, assuming all SMA criteria are met, the billing practitioner may bill the service using the SMA procedure code. We would also note that services provided under an SMA cannot be billed separately because the minutes of the service counted toward the SMA service code cannot also be counted for any other billed service.
After consideration of the public comments, we find many of the commenters' suggestions persuasive and are finalizing as proposed with a
(
printed page 71096)
modification to base the valuation for the CoCM codes and APCM add-on codes on a level 4 E/M visit. We are also finalizing revaluing the rate of the Behavioral Health Care Manager (L057B) clinical labor type with a per minute rate of $0.70.
(52) Tympanostomy (HCPCS Code G0561)
In January 2026, the Practice Expense (PE) Subcommittee reviewed the following practice expense only add-on HCPCS code G0561 (
Tympanostomy with local or topical anesthesia and insertion of a ventilating tube when performed with tympanostomy tube delivery device, unilateral)
on the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule which is currently contractor priced.
The RUC recommended one direct PE input for a new supply item, an Automated PE tube delivery device (SD395), and submitted invoices to price the supply at $497.50. We proposed the RUC-recommended direct PE input for HCPCS code G0561 without refinement.
The RUC did not recommend, and we did not propose a work RVU for HCPCS code G0561, which has been designed as a PE only service.
We received public comments on our proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter explained that because a bilateral procedure requires two separate, single-use tympanostomy tube delivery devices—one for each ear—application of the standard 150-percent bilateral adjustment would recognize only half the cost of the second device. The commenter noted that if the 150-percent bilateral payment methodology were applied to HCPCS code G0561, it would recognize only 50 percent of the practice expense (PE) value of the second device, despite the fact that the second device is purchased and consumed at 100 percent of its cost. The commenter requested that CMS establish a payment and claims-processing methodology for HCPCS code G0561 that recognizes 100 percent of the PE value associated with each separately utilized single-use device in a bilateral procedure, along with clear guidance on billing units and modifiers.
An additional commenter recommended addressing this issue through unit-based reporting rather than a modifier, explaining that the automated tube delivery device described by HCPCS add-on code G0561 is supplied, purchased, and billed as a discrete unit, meaning that modifier 50 would not be appropriate to use when reporting a bilateral case. This commenter stated that when the primary tympanostomy procedure (CPT code 69433) is performed bilaterally, HCPCS code G0561 should be reported with two units to reflect the utilization of two automated tube deployment devices, rather than by appending modifier 50.
Another commenter, while supporting the proposed valuation, requested that CMS ensure that the G code is paid in full for both ears so that the provider is not unintentionally disadvantaged by application of a multiple procedure payment reduction policy, reasoning that in cases where the G code is reported twice for bilateral procedures, two devices are used, so the G code should be reimbursed in full, once for each ear, when performed bilaterally.
Response:
We appreciate commenters bringing this issue to our attention and agree that the standard bilateral payment adjustment methodology does not appropriately reflect the resource costs associated with HCPCS code G0561 when the underlying tympanostomy procedure is performed bilaterally. As commenters explained, HCPCS code G0561 describes the use of a discrete, single-use automated tympanostomy tube delivery device. When the primary procedure (CPT code 69433) is performed on both ears, two separate devices are purchased and consumed in their entirety—one for each ear. The standard bilateral adjustment under indicator “1,” which pays 100 percent for the first side and 50 percent for the second, is designed for procedures in which the bilateral performance generates efficiencies relative to a single-sided procedure (for example, shared setup, positioning, or overhead). That rationale does not apply to HCPCS code G0561, because the device used for the second ear represents a full, independent, non-reusable cost rather than an incremental or duplicative one.
We agree with commenters that reporting via modifier 50 is not well suited to this code. Because G0561 is defined and billed as a discrete per-device unit rather than as a procedure capable of being performed on paired anatomic structures in the same operative pass, we are finalizing an approach under which HCPCS code G0561 is reported with two units—rather than modifier 50 or modifiers RT/LT—when the primary procedure is performed bilaterally, consistent with the recommendation of the commenter who addressed this issue. This unit-based approach more accurately reflects that two distinct devices were supplied and used.
Consistent with this unit-based reporting methodology, we are also revising the bilateral surgery indicator assigned to HCPCS code G0561 from “1” to “3.” A bilateral indicator of “3” signifies that the standard bilateral payment adjustment does not apply to the code; rather, each reported unit is paid at 100 percent of the fee schedule amount, subject to any other generally applicable payment adjustments. This change ensures that both devices used in a bilateral procedure are reimbursed at their full PE value, addressing the concern raised by the first commenter that a 150-percent bilateral adjustment would otherwise recognize only 50 percent of the value of the second device.
We also agree with the commenter who requested that HCPCS code G0561 be paid in full for both ears without reduction under multiple procedure payment policies. Because each unit of HCPCS code G0561 reflects the full, independent cost of a separately purchased and consumed device rather than a duplicate or overlapping service, we do not believe it is appropriate to apply a multiple procedure payment reduction across the two reported units of this add-on code.
Comment:
A commenter appreciated CMS's proposal to add supply code SD395 to the direct PE inputs for HCPCS code G0561 but stated that there are additional direct PE inputs for equipment, supplies, and labor that must be included for HCPCS code G0561. The commenter noted that when CMS originally adopted HCPCS code G0561, CMS explicitly acknowledged that the purpose of the code was to describe the additional resource costs related to higher expected intraservice work, plus the cost of the tympanostomy tube delivery device used during the tympanostomy procedure. The commenter therefore argued that it is not sufficient to adopt national pricing reflecting only the device supply cost. The commenter further stated that while it does not disagree with the establishment of supply code SD395 with an associated cost of $497.50, it strongly disagrees that the national average Medicare payment amount for HCPCS code G0561 should be less than $497.50. The commenter recommended that, if CMS requires additional time to determine appropriate additional inputs, CMS maintain contractor pricing for CY 2027 rather than finalize SD395 as the sole input.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support for the addition of supply code SD395 to the direct PE inputs for HCPCS code G0561, and we
(
printed page 71097)
have considered the commenter's concerns regarding the sufficiency of this input and the recommendation to continue contractor pricing.
We disagree that contractor pricing should be maintained for HCPCS code G0561 for CY 2027. Having obtained the additional information we previously indicated was necessary (
90 FR 49348
), we no longer believe it is appropriate to delay the assignment of national pricing for this code. Contractor pricing is intended to serve as an interim payment mechanism while adequate information is developed to support accurate, nationally applicable direct PE inputs; it is not intended to persist indefinitely once that information becomes available.
With respect to the commenter's assertion that additional direct PE inputs for equipment, supplies, and labor beyond SD395 are necessary to fully capture the resource costs associated with HCPCS code G0561, we note that the same specialty society's RUC Advisors, who are positioned to evaluate the full scope of resources involved in furnishing this service, concluded that HCPCS code G0561 reflects additional practice expense only and specifically identified no additional physician work associated with the code. We are not aware of additional evidence in the record identifying specific equipment, supply, or labor inputs beyond those reflected in SD395 that the commenter believes should be included. To the extent the commenter possesses specific information regarding additional direct PE inputs it believes are necessary to accurately value HCPCS code G0561 or CPT code 69433, we direct the commenter to the established process for nominating a code as potentially misvalued. Under our regulations at § 414.22(b)(3), interested parties may submit a request, together with supporting evidence, that we examine a code believed to be potentially misvalued through the annual potentially misvalued code nomination process. We believe this process is the appropriate vehicle through which the commenter may submit the specific additional input information it believes supports a higher valuation, rather than through continued contractor pricing of HCPCS code G0561.
Comment:
A commenter stated that they supported the RUC's recommendation to establish national pricing for HCPCS code G0561 based on direct invoice costs. The commenter submitted an invoice for $525.00 reflecting the acquisition cost of the Automated PE tube delivery device (SD395) supply and requested that CMS use this invoice to support HCPCS code G0561's pricing, rather than the proposed $497.50 supply cost.
Response:
We appreciate the submission of this additional invoice associated with the SD395 supply. Rather than disregarding the earlier invoices used to establish the proposed $497.50 supply cost, however, we are instead averaging the two invoice prices together and finalizing a price of $511.25 for the SD395 supply.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to adopt a new direct PE input under supply code SD395 and modify our proposed supply cost of $497.50 to $511.25. We are also finalizing our proposals to apply national pricing to HCPCS code G0561, retain it as a PE-only service, and provide payment at 100 percent of the applicable fee schedule amount for each unit when HCPCS code G0561 is reported with two units in connection with a bilateral tympanostomy procedure described by CPT code 69433.
(53) Evaluation and Management (E/M) Visit Complexity Add-On (HCPCS Code G2211)
(a) Background
In the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 78970
through
78982
), we finalized separate payment for the O/O E/M visit complexity add-on code, HCPCS code G2211 (
Visit complexity inherent to evaluation and management associated with medical care services that serve as the continuing focal point for all needed health care services and/or with medical care services that are part of ongoing care related to a patient's single, serious condition or a complex condition. (Add-on code, list separately in addition to office/outpatient evaluation and management visit, new or established)
). This policy was originally proposed in CY 2019, as part of a proposed overhaul to the E/M code set (
83 FR 59628
) where we proposed two codes, one for primary care and one for non-procedure specialty care. We learned that the CPT Editorial Panel and AMA RUC were planning to review and refine the O/O E/M code set, so we did not finalize this proposal or the other proposed changes to the E/M code set. The CPT Editorial Panel and AMA RUC reviewed and refined the O/O E/M code set, which were finalized by CMS in the CY 2021 PFS final rule (
84 FR 62844
through
62856
). We combined the two proposed complexity add-on codes into one, and we finalized separate coding and payment for HCPCS code add-on code GPC1X in the CY 2020 PFS final rule (
84 FR 62854
through
62856
). This became HCPCS code G2211 in the CY 2021 final rule (
85 FR 84569
). However, implementation of G2211 was delayed by Congress (section 113 of Division CC of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (
Pub. L. 116-260
, December 27, 2020) (CAA, 2021)), and we began actively paying for HCPCS code G2211 in CY 2024.
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49462
through
49464
), we finalized our proposal to allow HCPCS code G2211 to be billed as an add-on code with the home or residence E/M visits code family (CPT codes 99341, 99342, 99344, 99345, 99347, 99348, 99349, 99350). We finalized refinements to the code descriptor of HCPCS code G2211
(Visit complexity inherent to evaluation and management associated with medical care services that serve as the continuing focal point for all needed health care services and/or with medical care services that are part of ongoing care related to a patient's single, serious condition or a complex condition. (Add-on code, list separately in addition to home or residence or office/outpatient evaluation and management service, new or established)
to reflect this change.
This service is intended to recognize the longitudinal relationship between the patient and the practitioner, which differentiates the E/M visit from visits that are not longitudinal in nature. As discussed in section II.E. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 43842
through
44557
), we are continuing to examine primary care in the PFS, and how we can appropriately recognize the resource costs of longitudinal and especially primary care, given the generality of E/M coding.
(b) Changes to the Billing Mechanism for Inherent Complexity
(i) Modifier MOD1
Since we began actively paying for HCPCS code G2211 in CY 2024, we have come to believe that the resource costs of furnishing longitudinal care for beneficiaries is not best characterized as a separate service requiring a separate code. Rather, we believe that since this work is an inherent part of the visit, it would be more accurately valued as a modifier to the base E/M code. We also believe that transitioning HCPCS code G2211 from an add-on code to a modifier will be more streamlined from an operational perspective. This should also reduce operational burden, as it will not require the submission of a separate claim line, because the modifier will be placed on the claim line for the associated E/M code. We therefore proposed to replace HCPCS
(
printed page 71098)
code G2211 with a modifier, which we referred to in the proposed rule as MOD1, which was a placeholder to be replaced with a two-digit HCPCS modifier. We are finalizing modifier B1 as the modifier to replace placeholder MOD1. Later in this section, we will discuss placeholder MOD2, which we are finalizing as modifier B2.
We proposed that modifier MOD1 will be billed under the same circumstances that HCPCS code G2211 is billed now. We discussed in the CY 2024 final rule (
88 FR 78973
) that HCPCS code G2211 was intended to characterize the associated E/M code as a service with a practitioner who serves as the continuing focal point for all needed health care services, or with medical care that is part of ongoing care related to a patient's single, serious, or complex condition. HCPCS code G2211 was meant to describe the inherent complexity of these visits that would otherwise be unaccounted for. The application of the add-on code is not based on the characteristics of particular patients (even though the rationale for valuing the code is based on recognizing the typical complexity of patient needs), but rather the relationship between the patient and the practitioner.
We proposed to match the code descriptor for HCPCS code G2211 to MOD1, with some technical changes. The new proposed modifier descriptor is:
Visit complexity inherent to new or established office/outpatient or home or residence evaluation and management service, associated with medical care services that serve as the continuing focal point for all needed health care services and/or with medical care services that are part of ongoing care related to a patient's single, serious condition or a complex condition.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposed change, stating that the transition to a modifier eliminates duplicative documentation while preserving recognition of longitudinal, post-acute, and transitional care. Other commenters who supported the shift to a modifier stated that the modifiers will increase payer standardization and reduce confusion, denials, and EHR errors. Some commenters expressed concerns with the introduction of a new modifier, citing tracking and payer-adherence difficulties. Additionally, we received comments that noted that most EHR systems limit claims to four billing modifiers per code, and providers may already use all four slots in certain situations, leaving no room to add a fifth modifier.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for the proposal and agree with commenters that the introduction of a modifier will simplify billing by reducing duplicative documentation and promoting consistency across payers. We also acknowledge the concerns regarding the administrative burden of transitioning from a standalone HCPCS code to a modifier.
Regarding the four-modifier limit some EHR systems impose, we note that the claim form itself is not limited to four modifiers. The Medicare Claims Processing Manual (CMS Internet-Only Manual, Pub. 100-04, Ch. 26) explains that the claim form has the ability to capture up to four modifiers, and if more than four modifiers are needed, providers should use modifier -99 (overflow) as the fourth modifier and enter the additional modifiers in the narrative field of the claim. We believe this overflow mechanism addresses the EHR slot limitation described by commenters, and we encourage providers and EHR vendors to configure billing systems to support modifier -99 and the narrative field where necessary to accommodate modifiers B1 and B2 alongside other required modifiers.
Comment:
Commenters requested that we confirm whether the modifiers can be associated with virtual or telehealth visits.
Response:
We thank commenters for requesting clarification regarding the applicability of the modifier when the service is furnished via telehealth. Since both HCPCS code G2211 and the O/O and home or residence E/M visits are currently on the Medicare telehealth services list, we are clarifying that Modifiers B1 and B2 can be used when an O/O or home/residence E/M visit is furnished via telehealth, provided all other requirements are met.
Comment:
Commenters raised concerns that eliminating HCPCS code G2211 as a standalone code and replacing it with a modifier that carries no independent work RVU value would impact productivity-based compensation for physicians. Commenters asked that we publish a crosswalk file to map modifier values to comparable RVUs at each E/M level so practices and health systems can accurately account for physician compensation. Others requested that CMS publish its resource-based rationale, utilization assumptions, and specialty-level budget-neutrality effects before finalizing the differential, and asked CMS to revise its utilization estimates with additional evidence that the modifier payment scales proportionally with the E/M service.
Response:
We acknowledge that this represents a shift in direct-RVU calculated income for this service. Although productivity-based models are a common compensation structure, there are other compensation strategies that could account for this modifier. Furthermore, modifiers B1 and B2 are only two of many modifiers that affect a HCPCS or CPT code's reimbursement amount, and for this reason we believe this change is consistent with other instances in which the PFS has adjusted payment mechanisms. We are sympathetic to the operational concerns that may arise from the switch from HCPCS code G2211 to modifiers B1 and B2. In response, we are publishing a public use file (PUF) with this final rule that maps modifier B1 and modifier B2 values to comparable RVUs at each E/M level. This file will be available on the CMS website under downloads for the CY 2027 PFS final rule at
https://www.cms.gov/​medicare/​payment/​fee-schedules/​physician/​federal-regulation-notices
. Regarding specific data surrounding this policy such as utilization assumptions and specialty-level budget neutrality calculations, we are often asked for specific information regarding the impacts of a policy, however, we have historically only published the cumulative specialty-level impacts of all policies.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the creation of modifier B1 as proposed. We note that modifier MOD1 was a placeholder code in the proposed rule. The finalized modifier descriptor for modifier B1 is: (
Visit complexity inherent to new or established office/outpatient or home or residence evaluation and management service, associated with medical care services that serve as the continuing focal point for all needed health care services and/or with medical care services that are part of ongoing care related to a patient's single, serious condition or a complex condition).
(ii) Modifier MOD1 Valuation
When HCPCS code G2211 was finalized in the CY 2020 PFS final rule (
84 FR 82854
through
82855
), we crosswalked it to 100 percent of the valuation of CPT code 90785
(Interactive complexity (List separately in addition to the code for primary procedure)),
which was created to capture additional work that occurs with certain psychiatric and psychotherapy codes. We believed that this service was analogous to the additional work involved in maintaining a longitudinal relationship
(
printed page 71099)
with patients as described by CPT code 90785. CPT code 90785 has a work RVU of 0.33 and a physician time of 11 minutes. In reexamining this policy after a few years of utilization, we have come to believe that a flat rate as described by HCPCS code G2211 does not reflect the variation in work of the various E/M visit levels.
Table A-D7 illustrates that the addition of HCPCS code G2211 as an add-on to the associated E/M visit represents a higher increase in total value for base codes with lower total non-facility RVUs than it does for more intense services. For example, HCPCS code G2211 has a total RVU of 0.52 in the non-facility (NF) setting. CPT code 99212 (
Office or other outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of an established patient, which requires a medically appropriate history and/or examination and straightforward medical decision making. When using total time on the date of the encounter for code selection, 10 minutes must be met or exceeded.
) has a total NF RVU of 1.78. So, when HCPCS code G2211 is appended to CPT code 99212, the overall value of the service is increased by 29 percent. However, when HCPCS code G2211 is appended to CPT code 99215 (
Office or other outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of an established patient, which requires a medically appropriate history and/or examination and high level of medical decision making. When using total time on the date of the encounter for code selection, 40 minutes must be met or exceeded.
) with a NF total RVU of 5.76, it only represents a 9 percent increase in the total value of the service. We believe that HCPCS code G2211 should reflect an increase to the base code that is proportional across all types of E/M visits. Therefore, we proposed a modifier to replace HCPCS code G2211 with the valuation of 16 percent of the base E/M code. We established this percentage using a weighted average of the percentage increase that G2211 comprised relative to the O/O E/M code, weighted by HCPCS code G2211 utilization and adjusted to achieve budget neutrality.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the underlying concept of scaling the complexity payment to the level of the base E/M service, specifically endorsing the 16 percent valuation rather than applying a flat amount. Several commenters noted that replacing HCPCS code G2211 with MOD1 more appropriately pays for complexity reflected in medical decision-making and physician work across E/M levels. Some commenters requested that CMS retain a flat rate valuation for the modifier rather than scaling it to the E/M level. A commenter supported this with a quantitative analysis showing that a percentage-based modifier would shift value away from the HCPCS codes 99213/99214 visits that make up most primary care. This commenter recommended retaining HCPCS code G2211's flat rate value and setting a floor so no E/M level receives less than 0.33 work RVUs.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for the proposed valuation of modifier B1 and scaling the complexity payment to the level of the base E/M service and agree that this approach more accurately accounts for the complexity reflected in medical decision-making and physician work across E/M levels. We appreciate the concern that this valuation structure may shift value away from primary care; our intention is to more accurately pay for the intensity of longitudinal care by aligning it to a percentage of the base code. As illustrated in Table A-D7, a flat rate add-on produces a disproportionate benefit for lower-intensity visits and a comparatively smaller benefit for higher-intensity visits, and we understand that there are trade-offs in any system. We believe this approach is the correct one, but we appreciate commenters bringing this to our attention, and we may re-examine this in future rulemaking.
(c) G2211 in Medicare Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs)
(i) Background
The Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program) established under section 1899 of the Act, offers doctors, hospitals, and other health care providers an opportunity to create an Accountable Care Organization (ACO). Shared Savings Program ACOs are groups of doctors, hospitals, and other health care professionals that work together to give patients high—quality, coordinated service and health care, improve health outcomes, and manage costs.
[
27
]
In Original Medicare, physicians are reimbursed for reasonable and necessary services necessary for diagnosis or treatment of illness or injury. In an ACO, the doctor-patient relationship in Original Medicare is expanded such that the doctors, hospitals and other health care professionals are not just providing services under the reasonable and necessary standard, but there is additional work conducted to manage the beneficiaries' overall health, considering their personal health goals and values. This is how CMS defines an “accountable care relationship,” and this relationship may lead patients to be less likely to get repeated medical tests or unnecessary services, since clinicians consider a patient's entire health history when developing a treatment plan, and the doctors and other health professionals communicate and collaborate to improve the patient's long-term health.
[
28
]
CMS believes accountable care supports the professional ethos of health professionals to take responsibility for their patients in a way that beneficiaries expect. When these accountable care relationships succeed and the ACO succeeds in delivering high-quality care and reducing expenditures, the ACO may be eligible to share in the savings. For more information on the Shared
(
printed page 71100)
Savings Program and policies directly relating to Shared Savings Program, see section III.G. of the proposed rule (
91 FR 43842
through
44557
).
The CMS Innovation Center recently announced the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model which will launch on January 1, 2027. LEAD builds upon previous accountable care work and was designed to attract health care providers that have previously had limited participation in ACOs. It also aims to encourage health care providers to deliver preventive care, empower beneficiaries to be more actively involved in their care, and support health care providers who serve high needs and dually eligible beneficiaries to improve care and reduce costs.
(ii) Modifier MOD2
In the PFS, we have established a complexity add-code (HCPCS code G2211) that we proposed to change to a modifier (MOD1) that supports care relationships which may approximate but are not accountable care. This modifier is meant to recognize the additional complexity of services associated with providing ongoing, longitudinal care to a beneficiary. We proposed that the complexity of care established in that longitudinal relationship fundamentally differs in Original Medicare where physicians are providing all reasonable and necessary care for diagnosis and treatment of a clinical condition versus when they are in an accountable care relationship. As previously discussed, we proposed applying the complexity add-on (we proposed to change this to a modifier) to reflect the ongoing resource costs associated with being the focal point for all needed health care services performed under this reasonable and necessary standard.
We believe this standard is distinct from care provided in an ACO, where in addition to being responsible for all needed health care services that are part of ongoing care, clinicians are also responsible for managing the accountable care relationship, which involves managing a beneficiary's overall health, personal goals, values, and coordinating care with responsibility for both quality and cost. We consider the complexity associated with serving as the focal point of care for all necessary services within an accountable care relationship, responsibility for the entire patient, and responsibility for quality and cost of care, to be inherently more complex than serving in this role outside of an accountable care relationship. We are therefore proposing two levels for this modifier to reflect the additional resource costs associated with accountable care.
For example, the most common condition for which HCPCS code G2211 was billed in 2024 in Original Medicare was hypertension.
[
29
]
Outside of an accountable care relationship, the complexity add-on (proposing in this rule to change to a modifier) would be billed by clinicians for E/M visits managing a beneficiary's hypertension over time. The additional time and resource costs for serving as this focal point in care may address a patient's reservations about initiating pharmacologic treatment for hypertension (for example, perhaps the beneficiary wishes to trial complementary or alternative medicine approaches, so the clinician and patient engage in shared decision-making to understand the risks and benefits of this approach preceding pharmacologic intervention).
[
30
]
They may also discuss risk factor reduction (for example, smoking cessation) and lifestyle changes (for example, following the dietary approaches to stop hypertension or `DASH' diet and meeting physical activity recommendations), or perhaps engage in motivational interviewing to facilitate behavior change. While the current HCPCS code G2211 is meant to take into account the additional time and resource intensity for these services, we expect even more from clinicians participating in an ACO.
For example, a beneficiary has general anxiety disorder and hypertension and monitors their blood pressure at home. They have an instance in which their blood pressure exceeds 140/90mmHg, and they also feel panic or a sense of impending doom or chest pain. They decide to go to the emergency room, but the slightly elevated blood pressure may or may not be the physiologic trigger of their symptoms. This patient may continue to seek care at the emergency room for similar episodes indefinitely unless their practitioner identifies this trend on their own and provides education to the patient on distinguishing the symptoms of anxiety from hypertension, and when it may be appropriate to go to the emergency room. If this same patient was in an ACO, that ACO might have already established admission discharge transfer (ADT) notifications which would alert the team (near-real time) for the admission. This would allow for earlier intervention to ensure that both the patient's anxiety and blood pressure were being managed in the correct setting, and that the patient had the best information to understand their intersecting conditions.
The additional time and resources associated with coordinating care for this complex patient considering both quality and cost are distinct. We proposed differentiating the resource costs associated with HCPCS code G2211 outside of and within an accountable care environment to account for the additional resource costs associated with serving as the focal point of care for the entire beneficiary within an accountable care relationship. We are clarifying that we do not believe every encounter a patient has within an ACO qualifies as longitudinal. For example, if instead of presenting to the ED, the patient calls the clinic and is able to see another ACO participant, ACO professional, ACO provider/supplier (as each is defined at § 425.20, for the Shared Savings Program), or LEAD Participant Provider who is available the same day, this encounter would not necessarily meet the criteria of inherent complexity, if that practitioner is not supporting the beneficiary's longitudinal care, and if this visit is not more inherently complex. Simply providing an E/M visit while being part of an ACO does not necessarily meet the threshold of inherent complexity.
We believe that MOD2 aligns with the goals of the Shared Savings Program and LEAD, which involve groups of health care providers working together to enhance beneficiary health through high quality, longitudinal primary and preventative care. One of the features of Shared Savings Program and LEAD ACOs is that beneficiaries benefit from ACO participants balancing goals of having total cost of care accountability and improving quality of care, while avoiding unnecessary services and medical errors. While the specifics vary between the Shared Savings Program and the LEAD model, in general, participating ACOs are required to report quality measures that align with these objectives, and they are measured against their past performance, and the performance of similar ACOs.

For example, health care providers may join ACOs to help defray the costs of large capital investments such as electronic medical records.

Visit complexity inherent to new or established office/outpatient or home or residence evaluation and management service, associated with medical care services furnished by a participant or practitioner participating in a Medicare accountable care organization. Services must serve as the continuing focal point for all needed health care services and/or be part of ongoing care related to a patient's single, serious condition or complex condition.
(ii) Modifier Valuation for Medicare ACO Participants
With these goals in mind, we proposed that, in place of reporting G2211, ACOs would have the option to report a modifier on a claim (referred to in this proposed rule as placeholder MOD2, which if finalized would be replaced with a two-digit HCPCS modifier), which will be valued at 32 percent of the associated E/M visit when performed by Shared Savings Program ACO participants, ACO professionals, and ACO providers/suppliers (as each is defined at § 425.20), as well as Participant Providers in the LEAD Model. We proposed that MOD2 would pay twice the rate of MOD1 to better account for the inherent complexity of some visits in the ACO context, specifically applying to Shared Savings Program and LEAD ACOs in situations that require increased time and intensity. This increased valuation is meant to reflect the cognitive work of providing longitudinal care, follow-up discussions through an assigned care coordinator with the beneficiary or other providers, and expanded access to educational resources, care options, and provider communication methods. The value-based care provided through a Shared Savings Program or LEAD ACO puts greater emphasis on integrated care, meaning health care providers work together to address a person's physical, mental, behavioral and social needs. In this way, providers treat an individual as a whole person, rather than focusing on a specific health issue or disease.

We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
We received comments in support of the higher rate for modifier B2 noting that it would serve as an appropriate incentive for accountable care participation. Many commenters supported the differential as recognition of accountable care investments that are inherent to ACO participants. According to commenters, these investments include care coordination, data analytics, and population health management, none of which are reflected in standard fee-for-service payment. Commenters also noted that the differential accounts for the work of addressing social and behavioral factors that influence health outcomes. Additionally, they explained that improving quality while responsibly managing total cost of care requires infrastructure and interdisciplinary care teams and that the higher rate recognizes this investment. Commenters also stated that the higher payment rate creates a meaningful financial incentive for clinicians to participate in an accountable care relationship. A commenter suggested that CMS provide specific guidance to providers that beneficiaries assigned to an ACO are automatically eligible for the utilization of modifier B2 by ACO participants or automatically apply the modifier, when applicable. In addition to support modifier B2, we received comments opposed to paying the higher rate (32 percent) only to ACO-participating clinicians while limiting other clinicians to billing modifier B1 (16 percent) for what they characterized as identical clinical work. Some commenters supported the general shift from HCPCS code G2211 to a modifier but explicitly opposed the 32 percent ACO-specific tier. Commenters expressed concern that we have not provided empirical evidence for the differential, that MOD2 could be billed for beneficiaries not attributed to the ACO, that it would increase aggregate beneficiary cost-sharing, and that it could reduce net Medicare savings under ACO models by rewarding billing volume over shared-savings performance. Other commenters, including MedPAC, raised concerns that because the modifier increases payment as a percentage of the underlying E/M
(
printed page 71102)
service, beneficiaries receiving higher-level E/M visits would face correspondingly higher cost-sharing obligations, regardless of whether that beneficiary is assigned to an ACO. MedPAC additionally noted that this proposal could impact a Medicare ACO's ability to generate net savings for Medicare by maximizing payments through the delivery of services eligible for the MOD2 modifier.
Several commenters argued that the clinical resources of longitudinal care do not depend on ACO participation and that reserving the higher payment for ACO participants risks separating payment from the resources required to furnish care, explaining that independent practices also coordinate complex care and maintain ongoing relationships with patients.
Response:
We acknowledge the concerns raised by many commenters who opposed paying modifier B2 at 32 percent only to ACO-participating clinicians while limiting other clinicians to the 16 percent modifier B1 rate for what they viewed as identical clinical work. We acknowledge the comments that increasing the value of the modifier when billed by ACO participants increases the cost sharing for beneficiaries and that it could impact an ACO's expenditures and shared savings. The use of the higher rate modifier is optional for ACO participants and ACOs can take the factors raised by commenters into consideration when choosing whether to bill the higher rate modifier. We also note that in Section III.G.6.2 of this final rule, we are finalizing a Part B cost sharing support policy under which eligible ACOs could offer cost sharing support for all Part B items and services except durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, supplies and prescription drugs for eligible beneficiaries under the Shared Savings Program. Under the Part B cost sharing support, an approved ACO could choose to offer cost sharing reductions for these services for their assigned beneficiaries which could, in some cases, mitigate for the higher cost sharing associated with the modifier.
We agree with commenters that clinicians in ACOs make investments in care coordination, data infrastructure, population health management, quality improvement, and patient engagement that extend beyond an individual billable encounter and that the PFS can better align fee-for-service payment with the infrastructure and support required to deliver accountable care. We agree with commenters that the proposal creates a direct financial incentive for clinicians to join and remain in ACOs and note that the higher modifier B2 rate serves as an appropriate recognition of the relative resource costs in this setting, including additional investments ACOs make, and that it continues CMS's recognition of the value of longitudinal care for beneficiaries with complex needs.
We acknowledge the comment suggesting that CMS consider providing guidance to practitioners that could increase the utilization of modifier B2 by ACO participants and will consider this for the future. We reiterate that we expect that not all E/M services provided by ACO participants would meet the definition of longitudinal care, and we remind practitioners that each code or modifier that is billed must be medically reasonable and necessary, which we feel would be a difficult standard to maintain in any automatic processes. We additionally explained in the proposed rule's Regulatory Impact Analysis (
91 FR 44248
) that the proposal to pay for services furnished in an ACO using a modifier (B2) that pays 32 percent of the total RVUs for the E/M service on the claim is expected to increase payment for practitioners that furnish a higher percentage of their services in ACOs.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing modifier B2 as proposed. We note that modifier MOD2 was a placeholder code in the proposed rule. The finalized modifier descriptor is B2 (
Visit complexity inherent to new or established office/outpatient or home or residence evaluation and management service, associated with medical care services furnished by a participant or practitioner participating in a Medicare accountable care organization. Services must serve as the continuing focal point for all needed health care services and/or be part of ongoing care related to a patient's single, serious condition or complex condition.).
(iii) Use of MOD2 Modifier by ACOs
Modifier MOD2 would be exclusively available for ACO participants, ACO professionals, and ACO providers/suppliers (as each is defined at § 425.20, for the Shared Savings Program), as well as LEAD Participant Providers, when the visit complexity is met, provided the individual is a medical professional who can bill office and outpatient E/M visits or home visit services, regardless of specialty. Utilization and claims of either modifier will be included in ACOs' expenditure calculations for benchmarking and performance year expenditures and used in the determination of total cost of care.
As described earlier in this section, we proposed a differential payment for MOD2 that is meant to provide a meaningful increase in the way we pay for primary care provided by ACO participants, ACO professionals, and ACO providers/suppliers (as each is defined at § 425.20, for the Shared Savings Program), as well as LEAD Participant Providers who often provide additional care coordination to beneficiaries in their care as demonstrated by their participation in an ACO, as described in the examples provided earlier in this section. We are further proposing that the use of this modifier be voluntary; and ACO participants, ACO professionals, ACO providers/suppliers (as each is defined at § 425.20, for the Shared Savings Program), and LEAD Participant Providers would determine if this modifier is necessary based on visit complexity and would append MOD1, MOD2, or no modifier, as appropriate. Additionally, we proposed that ACO participants, ACO professionals, and ACO provider/suppliers (as each is defined at § 425.20, for the Shared Savings Program), as well as LEAD Participant Providers may bill this modifier for all beneficiaries to whom they provide care, regardless of whether that beneficiary is assigned, aligned, or attributed to an ACO, to encourage similar care to be provided to all beneficiaries served by health care providers who participate in ACOs. Given that ACO Primary Care Flex (ACO PC Flex) Model participation is predicated on participation in the Shared Savings Program, we proposed that ACO PC Flex Model ACOs may also utilize the MOD2 modifier. Finally, we proposed that LEAD Participant Providers billing under a Participant TIN that is in a LEAD ACO may bill modifier MOD2. Refer to the discussion later in this section for additional information on the use of modifier MOD2 on alignment in the LEAD model.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters expressed support for the enhanced ACO payment as a lever to grow accountable care participation and improve care coordination, requesting that it apply to Advanced APMs as well as Shared Savings Program ACOs. Commenters supported allowing ACO participants to bill MOD2 for all beneficiaries they treat, not only those assigned to the ACO, viewing this as recognition of the broader care-management infrastructure ACOs maintain and use for all
(
printed page 71103)
beneficiaries. Commenters also asked CMS to extend MOD2 eligibility to CMS Innovation Center models Kidney Care Choices and Enhancing Oncology. Additionally, we received comments asking how the higher MOD2 payment interacts with ACO expenditure benchmarking, so the incentive does not partially cancel itself.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree with commenters that the enhanced ACO payment is a mechanism to grow accountable care participation and strengthen care coordination.
Regarding the comments mentioning that this incentive extends to Advanced APMs as well as Shared Savings Program ACOs, we clarify that the utilization of modifier B2 is specific to ACO participants in the Shared Savings Program ACOs, the LEAD model, and ACO PC Flex. While certain tracks within these or other CMS Innovation Center models may represent Advanced APMs, this policy does not extend to all Advanced APMs or to other CMS Innovation Center models. We may consider such an expansion for future rulemaking. In response to inquiries concerning ACO expenditure benchmarking, we clarify that claims including modifier B1 or B2 will not be carved out of Shared Savings Program, LEAD, or ACO PC Flex financial calculations, including benchmark determination, financial reconciliation, or assignment plurality determinations. Modifier B2 is meant to reflect the additional resources associated with longitudinal care provided by ACO participants; however, ACOs remain accountable for the total cost of care for their beneficiaries and carving out these expenditures would be counter to that goal.
Comment:
Several commenters urged CMS to finalize the changes as proposed and, notably, to require Medicare Advantage plans to adopt the 32 percent modifier on the same timeline as traditional Medicare without added MA-specific documentation or prior authorization requirements.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' interest in payment parity and in limiting administrative burden for practitioners who participate in both traditional Medicare and MA, however, we note that this rule is issued under our authority to establish payment policy for services furnished to beneficiaries under the traditional Medicare fee-for-service program under Part B. It does not directly govern the methodologies MA organizations use to pay contracted providers under Part C.
Comment:
Some commenters requested that CMS broaden MOD1 and MOD2 eligibility across several settings and code sets. Commenters stated that the beneficiaries most in need of longitudinal care are also in settings such as nursing facilities, Rural Health Clinics (RHCs), Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), and Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs). Others asked for the use of MOD1 and MOD2 in conjunction with codes beyond E/M codes, such as collaborative care management services, the shared medical appointment codes proposed earlier in this section, and medical nutrition therapy.

We thank commenters for their thoughtful feedback and interest in ensuring that beneficiaries get the longitudinal care they need. We note that many of the settings commenters recommended are paid under different payment structures or systems, and so extending this policy to those structures would need to be examined in separate rulemaking. We have received similar comments regarding the extension of HCPCS code G2211 (now modifiers B1 and B2) to other settings in several rulemaking cycles, and we addressed these concerns most recently in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49462
through

We are clarifying that modifiers B1 and B2 may only be used in conjunction with E/M visits performed in the O/O or home or residence setting and may not be performed in conjunction with E/M visits in other settings, such as SNF, RHC, FQHC, CAH, or other places of service. The limit on place of service for use of these modifiers is tied to the location and type of the E/M visit, rather than the modifier. We may consider changes to this policy in future rulemaking, and we welcome continued engagement with practitioners in these settings.
We also thank the commenters for their ideas on other types of services that may be more inherently complex when the practitioner has a longitudinal relationship with the patient, such as collaborative care management services. However, we disagree that E/M services provided in other settings do not adequately recognize the increased complexity of this relationship in the valuation of those services. HCPCS code G2211 (now modifiers B1 and B2) was originally designed to capture the differences in complexity between different types of E/M visits provided in an office/outpatient or home/residence settings, which is not the case for E/M visits provided in other settings or services captured within a prospective payment system.

(B) Impacts on Assignment of Beneficiaries to LEAD ACOs
In LEAD, if this proposal is finalized, we will handle the deletion of HCPCS code G2211 and the transition to the modifiers similarly to the Shared Savings Program. As indicated in Appendix C of the LEAD Request for Applications, the HCPCS code G2211 code is one of the Primary Care Qualified Evaluation and Management (PQEM) services that CMS uses to align beneficiaries to LEAD ACOs via claims-based alignment. We will continue to use HCPCS code G2211 allowable charges to conduct claims-based alignment in LEAD when HCPCS code G2211 was an allowable service in the requisite claims look back period. For example, when conducting initial claims-based alignment in Performance Year (PY) 2027, we will reference claims from October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026. HCPCS code G2211 allowable charges will be included in the claims-based alignment run since it is an allowable service during this period.
When aligning beneficiaries to LEAD ACOs, CMS looks first for an existing primary care relationship within the claims lookback period. If 10 percent or more of a beneficiary's PQEM allowable charges (measured by dollar amount) were billed by physicians or non-physician health care providers with a primary-care specialty (family medicine, internal medicine, geriatrics, general practice, nurse practitioner, physician assistant, and clinical nurse specialist), alignment is based solely on these primary care providers. If less than 10 percent of a beneficiary's PQEM allowable charges were billed by primary-care specialties, alignment considers certain non-primary care providers that manage chronic or complex conditions (for example, cardiology, nephrology, endocrinology, psychiatry, etc.). The beneficiary is aligned to a LEAD ACO if the Participant TIN that furnished the largest share of allowable charges incurred for PQEM services during the lookback period is participating in a LEAD ACO.
Once the claims-based alignment look back period rolls forward to include 2027 (and future years) the LEAD alignment methodology will include the allowed charges associated with modifier MOD1 and MOD2 when conducting claims-based alignment (the underlying O/O or home or residence E/M service that will be modified by MOD1 and MOD2 are already LEAD PQEM services). LEAD ACOs will be accountable for expenditures incurred by using either modifier MOD1 or MOD2. More information on the impact to claims processing, capitated payments, and LEAD benchmarks will be shared with ACOs that were selected for participation in LEAD in PY 2027.

(54) Shared Medical Appointment (HCPCS Codes G0686 and G0687)
In accordance with President Trump's Executive Order, “Establishing the President's Make America Healthy Again Commission,”
[
42

the Administration is directing agency focus towards understanding and drastically lowering chronic disease rates. As part of this commitment, we remain focused on the prevention and management of chronic disease, including through approaches that address underlying behavioral and lifestyle drivers of health.
In CY 2026, we solicited feedback on how CMS could further support the prevention and management of chronic diseases. In response to our request for information on chronic disease prevention and management, commenters indicated that many services that help prevent and manage chronic disease, such as lifestyle modification support, health education, and peer support, require time, coordination and multidisciplinary engagement that is not adequately supported under the current PFS. Additionally, many commenters indicated that social isolation and loneliness is a persistent barrier to
(
printed page 71105)
effective care for Medicare beneficiaries. The commenters indicated that although health care providers are already implementing interventions to identify and address social isolation, these efforts are resource intensive and not adequately supported under the current PFS.
Based on this feedback, we recognize the importance of health care delivery approaches that enable multidisciplinary support, foster beneficiary engagement, and encourage sustainable lifestyle and behavioral changes. Shared medical appointments (SMAs) are one such approach to offer a group-based environment in which beneficiaries can receive clinical guidance while also engaging with peers facing similar health challenges. SMAs may also help address social isolation and loneliness for some beneficiaries.
SMAs, also known as shared medical visits or group visits, are voluntary group-based sessions where multiple patients with a common chronic condition, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus, receive medical care together. In general, SMAs involve more than one healthcare provider, such as a person trained or skilled in delivering patient education or facilitating patient interaction and a prescribing practitioner to make and initiate a comprehensive care plan. SMAs generally last from 60 to 120 minutes and incorporate time for social integration, interactive education, and adjustments to the patient's care plan.
[
43
]
Compared with group education alone, SMAs allow patients to participate in clinical care activities that are tailored to the needs of both the group and the individual participants.
[
44
]
During the SMA session, a practitioner may meet with a patient individually in a private or semi—private manner or conduct the visit in a group setting where other patients are able to listen and, in some cases, contribute to the discussion.
[
45
]
Reported advantages of shared medical appointments include providing patients more time with their health care provider, creating opportunities for patients to learn from and share self-management strategies with one another, improving access to care, incorporating nonpharmacologic treatment approaches, enhancing the overall quality of care, and helping reduce emergency department visits.
[
46
]
Currently there is no CPT or HCPCS code specifically designated for SMAs. However, practitioners typically bill SMAs using existing Evaluation and Management (E/M) codes, CPT codes 99212-99215, based on medical decision-making criteria; and if another billable clinician such as a registered dietician assists with the SMA, the registered dietician may also bill for their portion of the SMA separately (for example, CPT code 97804 (
Medical nutrition therapy; group (2 or more individual(s)), each 30 minutes)
). Therefore, we proposed to create coding and valuation specifically for SMAs.
We proposed that SMAs be limited to beneficiaries who have received a professional service from the billing physician or other qualified health professional or another physician or other qualified health care professional of the exact same specialty and subspecialty who belongs to the same group practice within the previous 12 months. We believe this requirement is necessary to ensure beneficiaries have an existing clinical relationship with the practitioner before the beneficiary is integrated into a group-based medical care setting.
We proposed requiring beneficiaries to consent to SMA participation, since they may elect to receive individual medical appointments instead. Additionally, we proposed that beneficiaries must consent to confidentiality terms because personal health information would be discussed in the group setting.
SMA sessions generally last 60 to 120 minutes and may include up to 25 patients, however SMAs most commonly consist of 6 to 10 patients.
[
47
]
We proposed establishing SMAs as 60-minute sessions with a maximum of 10 beneficiaries per session.
The expansion of telehealth services has increased opportunities for SMAs to improve access for individuals in geographically remote areas, and those with transportation challenges. We proposed that SMA sessions can be held either in-person or via telehealth, and we proposed to add the SMA service to the Medicare Telehealth list accordingly.
We proposed that each shared SMA session be documented in each participating beneficiary's medical record. Each beneficiary receives individualized clinical care, and the medical record must reflect the specific services that the individual beneficiary received during the SMA session. The need for individualized care may depend on the intervention and surrounding evidence. Therefore, if a beneficiary requires a level of individualized care that extends beyond what can appropriately be provided within the group-based session of a SMA, that individualized care should be provided in a separate individual medical appointment. The services provided to the group as a whole at each session would also need to be captured in the medical record. We seek comments on additional guardrails to consider in preventing fraud, waste and abuse when billing SMAs, such as following an evidence-based protocol for delivery of the intervention, conducting fidelity checks to ensure it is being delivered as intended, identifying key outcomes and goals that are established in shared decision making, and ensuring that the interventionist is trained in the intervention as appropriate.
SMAs are an approach in managing chronic conditions, especially among motivated patients.

Therefore, we proposed to establish coding and payment for SMAs provided for medical conditions that are modifiable with lifestyle change. We seek comment on how to determine when SMAs would be appropriate, including identifying which medical conditions would be considered modifiable with lifestyle change, and suggest we would typically consider those conditions with medical guidelines that include lifestyle change as part of prevention and treatment of the condition in this category, such as evidence-based interventions that support lifestyle change.

CMS acknowledges the substantial changes in patients' lives associated with coping with chronic illness, the behavioral modifications inherent in managing serious and unexpected illnesses, however we would reserve SMA provision for just those conditions which may be treated or prevented with lifestyle changes.
SMAs typically involve multiple healthcare providers, usually two to four. The sessions are generally led by a physician, physician assistant (PA), or an advanced practice registered nurse (APRN), and may have ancillary staff help when the provider is meeting with patients individually.

that service is considered part of the SMA and should not be billed separately, in addition to the physician or qualified nonphysician practitioner billing for the SMA.
We proposed requiring each SMA session to include the following components:
Evaluation and Management (E/M) elements, consistent with the complexity of the beneficiary's condition. Individualized clinical care with medical documentation in the medical record that reflects the specific services that the individual beneficiary received during the SMA session.
Education, based upon evidence-based content, and discussions related to self—care, wellness, and disease management.
Discussion of positive lifestyle changes, focusing on behavior modification. Medication management, as clinically appropriate and applicable.
In the event it is medically necessary for a beneficiary to receive an E/M visit on the same day as a SMA by the same physician or other qualified health professional or another physician or other qualified health care professional of the exact same specialty and subspecialty who belongs to the same group practice, we proposed that any time and effort cannot be counted more than once. We proposed not to consider and treat this as two E/M same-day visits and seek public comment on this proposal. Additionally, we seek comments on what components must be required for each SMA session.
We proposed the following descriptor for SMAs:
HCPCS code G0686:
Voluntary, group-based medical session involving multiple patients with common medical condition(s), receiving medical care in a group setting; billed and led by a physician or qualified nonphysician practitioner and may include services provided by other qualified healthcare professionals, clinical staff, or auxiliary personnel under the direction of the supervising physician or other practitioner. Session integrates group education, counseling, and peer support with individualized patient clinical assessment and care, 2-10 patients, billed once per patient, per session.
Because SMA sessions would integrate group education, counseling, and peer support with individualized patient clinical assessment and care, in developing the valuation for the SMA HCPCS code, we proposed to use a building block methodology that sums up the values associated with two reference codes. For the overall E/M elements of the SMA service, we are incorporating the work RVUs, work time and direct PE inputs associated with a level 3 O/O visit for an established patient, CPT code 99213 (
Office or other outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of an established patient, which requires a medically appropriate history and/or examination and low level of medical decision making. When using total time on the date of the encounter for code selection, 20 minutes must be met or exceeded.),
which has a work RVU of 1.30, and a total work time of 30 minutes, which is based on a pre-service evaluation time of 5 minutes, an intraservice time of 20 minutes, and a post service time of 5 minutes. E/M visit level selection does not need to be based on time; practitioners may select the visit level based on the level of medical decision making (MDM). Additionally, as we discussed earlier in this section, we proposed that SMAs be limited to beneficiaries who have received a professional service from the billing physician or other qualified health professional or another physician or other qualified health care professional of the exact same specialty and subspecialty who belongs to the same group practice within the previous 12 months. Given this pre-existing clinical relationship and the anticipated clinical profile of beneficiaries that would participate in an SMA, we believe that the level 3 O/O visit for an established patient represents the most typical level of service for the individualized patient clinical assessment component of the SMA.
For the group education, counseling, and peer support elements of the SMA service, we are incorporating CPT code 96202 (
Multiple-family group behavior management/modification training for parent(s)/guardian(s)/caregiver(s) of patients with a mental or physical health diagnosis, administered by physician or other qualified health care professional (without the patient present), face-to-face with multiple sets of parent(s)/guardian(s)/caregiver(s); initial 60 minutes
), which has a work RVU of 0.43 and a total work time of 15 minutes, which is based on a pre-service evaluation time of 2 minutes, an intraservice time of 10 minutes, and a post service time of 3 minutes.
While a SMA may include up to 10 beneficiaries in a 60—minute session, the individualized care for a participating beneficiary may vary, such that some beneficiaries may receive more or less individualized care than others; nonetheless, documentation in the medical record must reflect the specific services that the individual beneficiary received during the SMA session. As we price services under the PFS based on a typical case, the proposed valuation for HCPCS code G0686 reflects a typical SMA session and is not intended to represent the
(
printed page 71107)
exact time distribution for every beneficiary in every SMA. We note that the total work time proposed is for the purposes of valuation and not meant as a requirement for billing. We believe this reflects a typical amount of time for both the individualized patient clinical assessment and the beneficiary's proportionate share of group education, counseling, and peer support that occurs concurrently across all participating beneficiaries during a SMA session.
Considering the aforementioned building block methodology for SMA valuation, we proposed a work RVU of 1.73 and a total work time of 45 minutes, which is based on a pre-service evaluation time of 7 minutes, an intraservice time of 30 minutes, and a post service time of 8 minutes.
In addition to seeking comments on establishing the proposed HCPCS code G0686, we also seek comment on the proposed work RVUs, work times, and direct PE inputs.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed strong support for CMS's proposal to establish a dedicated code and payment pathway for SMAs and stated that SMAs are an effective approach for managing chronic conditions. Many stakeholders highlighted evidence for SMAs, noting improved patient outcomes, reduced emergency and inpatient utilization, enhanced engagement, and greater efficiency in chronic disease management. Several commenters emphasized that SMAs are particularly valuable for populations with multiple chronic conditions, behavioral health needs, and those facing social isolation or barriers to care. A few commenters recommended that CMS treat the creation of the SMA code as an iterative first step, with ongoing refinement based on utilization and outcomes data. A few commenters opposed the establishment of a dedicated code and payment for SMAs under the Medicare PFS, suggesting instead that CMS test these concepts through limited demonstration or alternative payment models (APM) first.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback received from commenters regarding creating coding and payment for SMAs. As we recognize the value that SMAs may bring to managing chronic disease, we are finalizing coding and payment for SMAs.
Comment:
Several commenters supported SMAs as an appropriate approach for conditions modifiable with lifestyle change. Commenters supported the creation of coding for SMAs and some recommended eligibility of specific conditions including but not limited to tobacco use disorder, alcohol use disorder, other substance use disorders, obesity, behavioral health conditions, fibromyalgia and central sensitization syndromes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and infertility-associated metabolic and hormonal conditions. Another commenter stated CMS should avoid establishing an exhaustive list of eligible diagnoses and instead recommended that eligibility be available when authoritative clinical guidelines or sufficient evidence base recognize lifestyle modification.
Many commenters supported broadening the eligible conditions for SMAs beyond the proposed “lifestyle-modifiable” criteria. Several commenters recommended not restricting SMAs to conditions deemed “lifestyle-modifiable,” citing reviews and/or experience demonstrating benefits across hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, obesity, COPD, osteoporosis, migraine, chronic pain, depression, cancer survivorship, Parkinson's disease, rheumatoid arthritis, neuromuscular disease, and prenatal care. Several commenters noted that most Medicare beneficiaries participating in SMAs have multiple chronic conditions, making diagnosis-specific or lifestyle-only restrictions impractical and inconsistent with real-world clinical care.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback, including the commenters supporting SMAs as an appropriate approach for conditions modifiable with lifestyle change, and commenters that recommended specific conditions for SMA services. After consideration of the comments, we are not creating an exhaustive list of eligible diagnoses and conditions, and we continue to believe that SMAs are an appropriate approach for conditions that are modifiable with lifestyle change. To the extent that conditions, including those that commenters recommended for inclusion, are modifiable with lifestyle change, they would not be precluded from the SMA service.
Comment:
Several commenters raised the importance of patient choice, privacy, and voluntary participation as considerations for SMA designs. A commenter stated that participation in SMAs should remain voluntary since HIPAA protects patient health information and many commenters may feel uncomfortable discussing sensitive medical concerns in front of others. The commenter cautioned that paying for SMAs could unintentionally encourage practices to rely more heavily on group visits for efficiency rather than patient preference, and SMAs should not replace the option of one-on-one appointments for patients who prefer them. A commenter recommended clarification on confidentiality terms including prohibition on beneficiaries posting information about other participants on social media. Commenters recommended that CMS require clear documentation of consent and confidentiality terms, with a couple comments specifically suggesting that consent be documented in the medical record.
Response:
We thank the commenters for feedback regarding voluntary participation in SMAs and continue to believe that SMAs must be voluntary. We have updated the code descriptor to emphasize this point. We also continue to believe that beneficiaries need to consent to SMA participation and must consent to confidentiality terms. These requirements are intended to ensure that participation in SMAs is based on informed patient choice, and that privacy is protected. We agree that SMAs should not replace the option of one-on-one appointments for patients who prefer them and that clear documentation of consent and confidentiality, including prohibitions on sharing information about other participants are needed safeguards.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended greater flexibility in the session duration for SMAs, rather than the proposed 60-minute limit. Many commenters recommended that CMS allow sessions to extend to 90 or 120 minutes, citing evidence and operational experience that longer sessions are often necessary to accommodate comprehensive education, peer discussion, individualized clinical care, and skills-based learning. Several commenters suggested either establishing add-on codes for longer sessions or permitting sessions to exceed 60 minutes, stating this would better reflect real-world practice and improve the effectiveness of SMAs.
