A few commenters noted that patient surveys and operational realities identify group discussion and shared learning as beneficial components of participation, and that additional time is needed to support these elements. Some commenters noted that rigid time limits could reduce access and limit the value of SMAs for patients with complex needs.
However, a few commenters supported the proposed 60-minute duration as a reasonable safeguard. A commenter expressed support for the 60-minute session requirement, noting it
(
printed page 71108)
provides a safeguard for quality and clinical appropriateness, but also encouraged CMS to evaluate future increases in session duration based on outcomes data and operational experience.
Response:
We thank commenters for their input regarding SMA session duration. After consideration of comments received, we were persuaded by commenters that the SMA service code should allow for a longer session duration than the originally proposed 60-minutes. We are finalizing an add-on code (HCPCS code G0687) that will permit up to two units in 30-minute increments, providing greater flexibility for practitioners to accommodate group education, counseling, peer support, individualized clinical assessment and care. Practitioners may bill up to two additional 30-minute units when medically necessary, allowing an SMA to last up to 120 minutes in total. A 120- minute SMA session would have a combined work RVU of 3.47.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended increasing the proposed group size limit of 10 beneficiaries per session, with many suggesting allowing up to 15 beneficiaries per session, and a few advocating for larger groups, such as up to 20 participants. Several commenters recommended increasing the group size to better reflect operational realities, peer-reviewed evidence, and the need to accommodate attrition and no-shows. Several commenters stated that group sizes of 12-15 are common in SMA models, and that a cap of 10 beneficiaries would result in smaller groups due to cancellations, thereby undermining peer dynamics. A few commenters recommended setting a minimum group size (such as five patients) to ensure operational flexibility for smaller or rural practices that may struggle to reach higher numbers. Some commenters suggested that CMS allow practitioners to use their judgment in determining the appropriate group size based on patient needs, session duration, and care team composition. One comment referenced peer reviewed literature supporting effective SMAs with groups of 8-20 patients and recommend allowing SMA billing for groups of up to 20 patients. A few commenters supported the proposed cap of 10 beneficiaries per session. One of the commenters stated that the cap sessions at 10 participants provide reasonable safeguards for quality and clinical appropriateness. Another commenter support that no more than 10 beneficiaries may participate in a SMA per session, as this is the maximum number of participants who can benefit from a session and whom practitioners can serve at a time. A couple of commenters support a limit of 2 to 10 patients per session as the requirement would provide reasonable safeguards while preserving flexibility for them to design group visits to meet their patients' needs.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback regarding the proposed group size for SMAs. After consideration of comments, we continue to believe that we should limit SMAs to a maximum of 10 beneficiaries per session. This approach is intended to provide patients with more individualized time with the practitioner when needed, ensuring that each beneficiary participating in the SMA receives adequate attention and support. We understand that a larger SMA group size may boost operational efficiency and help accommodate attrition or no-shows, however we have concerns that increasing the group size further could dilute the quality of clinician-patient interaction and potentially undermine the peer dynamics that are central to successful SMA models.
Comment:
A majority of commenters strongly supported the inclusion of multidisciplinary teams in SMAs, emphasizing that effective group visits depend on the participation of multiple clinicians, including physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, dietitians, behavioral health specialists, pharmacists, physical therapists, health coaches, acupuncturists, and other allied health professionals. Several commenters highlighted the importance of team-based care for addressing the complex medical, behavioral, and lifestyle needs of Medicare beneficiaries. Many commenters urged CMS to ensure that the SMA payment structure adequately supports the work of the full interdisciplinary team, warning that insufficient valuation could push practices toward a bare-minimum version of the benefit rather than the comprehensive model intended.
Several commenters requested preserving separate billing for distinct, nonduplicative services furnished by qualified professionals during SMAs, such as group medical nutrition therapy (MNT), diabetes self-management training (DSMT), physical activity interventions, and behavioral health services. A few commenters recommended allowing registered dietitians and other specialists to bill for their services separately when appropriate, rather than bundling all work into a single SMA payment. A few commenters supported the proposed requirements for physician or qualified nonphysician practitioner leadership, describing them as reasonable safeguards for quality and clinical appropriateness. However, most commenters requested greater flexibility, including allowing auxiliary personnel and allied health professionals to furnish components of SMAs under appropriate supervision.
Response:
We thank commenters for supporting and providing feedback regarding the inclusion of multidisciplinary teams in SMAs. We agree that team-based care is important for addressing the complex medical, behavioral, and lifestyle needs of Medicare beneficiaries. Services provided under an SMA cannot be billed separately because the minutes of the service counted toward the SMA service code cannot also be counted for any other billed service. This ensures that the SMA payment structure remains consistent and avoids duplication of billing for overlapping services.
Comment:
A few commenters supported the proposed valuation for SMA as a reasonable starting point. A commenter expressed general support for the building block methodology and encouraged CMS to monitor outcomes and revisit the valuation as needed. Several commenters addressed the proposed valuation for SMAs, and several commenters expressed concerns that the building block methodology may undervalue the complexity and resources required for effective group visits. Many commenters stated the combination of CPT 99213 and 96202 (resulting in 1.73 work RVUs) may not adequately reflect the work involved in moderate or high-complexity SMAs, especially those serving patients with multiple chronic conditions and requiring multidisciplinary team input. A few commenters suggested a crosswalk to group health behavior intervention codes (CPT codes 96164 and 96165) instead of CPT code 96202 for the group education, counseling, and peer support elements, arguing that these codes better capture the service delivery and intensity of SMAs. Several commenters recommended tiered complexity codes (analogous to CPT codes 99213 and 99214), the addition of the complexity add-on code (HCPCS code G2211), or time-based payment options to ensure that the valuation matches the clinical work and team-based care required. A couple of commenters stated that the proposed valuation underestimates clinician time and administrative complexity, and recommended increases to the work RVU to incentivize the use of SMAs and
(
printed page 71109)
support sustainable delivery. A commenter raised concerns about the utilization estimate for SMAs. The commenter noted that CMS's addenda tables project 410,100 unadjusted allowed services for 2027 and stated the assumptions underlying this estimate were not clearly explained. The commenter cautioned that the projected number may be too high and could result in resources being removed from the fee schedule. The commenter requested CMS to clarify its methodology for estimating utilization to ensure that resource allocation is appropriate and sustainable.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback regarding the valuation of SMAs. We appreciate the support for the proposed methodology and the encouragement to monitor outcomes and revisit the valuation as needed. As previously discussed, after consideration of comments, we are finalizing the addition of a new add-on code for SMAs (HCPCS code G0687) to account for additional time spent during the session, in 30-minute increments up to two units. The new add-on code will be valued at half the work RVU of the base code, resulting in a finalized work RVU of 0.87. With this additional coding and the option to add time as needed for the duration of the SMA, we believe that the valuation of the add on code and valuation of the base SMA code with a work RVU of 1.73 work is appropriate for SMAs.
Additionally, in response to the commenter who provided input on the SMA utilization estimate for 2027, we note that the estimate was based on approximately 3 percent of the utilization of CPT code 99213 specifically billed by primary care specialties, including family practice, general practice, and internal medicine; this translated into approximately 0.6 percent of all billings of CPT code 99213. Our understanding is that practitioners are currently billing for shared medical appointments using CPT code 99213, and the projected utilization for HCPCS code G0686 would replace some of this utilization. We derived the 3 percent estimate from a published survey,
[
52
]
in which 3 out of the 107 survey respondents were actively involved in group visits at the time of survey, which indicated that less than 3 percent of primary care clinicians were actively involved in furnishing group visits. We will continue to monitor utilization and outcomes, and welcome ongoing feedback as we may refine the valuation in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters provided feedback regarding same-day billing for E/M visits and SMAs, with a majority expressing support for allowing separate billing when both services are medically necessary and distinctly documented. Many commenters recommended clarification to permit same-day billing for E/M visits and SMAs, provided that the time and work for each service are not double-counted and that documentation clearly supports the distinct nature of each encounter. Several commenters emphasized that prohibiting same-day billing could create barriers to comprehensive patient care, delay necessary evaluation and treatment, and increase administrative burden for both patients and providers. A couple of commenters requested clarification that the limitation on counting same-day SMA and E/M services separately would not preclude separate payment for distinct, medically necessary services that require privacy and cannot appropriately be furnished in a group setting. Other commenters recommended explicit billing guidance to ensure that practitioners can address acute issues that arise during SMA sessions without being penalized.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback regarding same-day billing for E/M visits and SMAs. We agree with the majority of commenters and will finalize our proposal such that in the event it is medically necessary for a beneficiary to receive an E/M visit on the same day as an SMA by the same physician or more than one physician in the same specialty in the same group, we are finalizing that any time and effort cannot be counted more than once. Accordingly, we will not consider or treat this as two separate E/M same-day visits. This approach is intended to ensure that time and work are not double counted, maintaining the integrity of documentation and billing while supporting comprehensive patient care.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed strong support for permitting SMAs to be delivered via telehealth, emphasizing that this flexibility would expand access for rural, mobility-limited, and underserved populations. Several commenters recommended finalizing the proposal to add SMAs to the Medicare Telehealth Services List. Many commenters highlighted that telehealth delivery is essential for overcoming transportation barriers, supporting continuity of care, and enabling participation for beneficiaries with functional limitations. A few commenters requested clarification in the final rule that SMAs may be furnished in hybrid formats, with some participants attending in person and others joining via telehealth, and that the SMA service should be billable for each beneficiary present regardless of modality.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters and are finalizing that SMA sessions can be held either in-person or via telehealth and clarifying that SMAs may be furnished in hybrid formats, with some participants attending in person and others joining via telehealth.
Comment:
Many commenters opposed the proposed 12-month existing clinical relationship with the practitioner requirement, arguing that it would unnecessarily restrict access to SMAs and delay care for patients who could benefit from group visits. Several commenters recommended removing or relaxing the 12-month existing clinical relationship with the practitioner requirement. Many commenters suggested that eligibility should be determined by medical necessity and practitioner judgment, rather than the timing of a prior visit. Several commenters requested to allow referrals from any treating clinician within a health system, not just the same specialty or group practice, to preserve continuity of care and expand timely access. A couple of commenters stated that conditioning SMA access on a documented prior encounter introduces avoidable delays, especially for patients newly diagnosed or identified as needing intervention. Some commenters stated that the 12-month existing clinical relationship with the practitioner requirement could exclude complex beneficiaries and create administrative burdens for small or rural practices.
A few commenters supported the proposed 12-month existing clinical relationship with the practitioner requirement and expressed support for the 12-month prior-visit requirement, describing it as a reasonable safeguard for quality and clinical appropriateness.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback regarding the proposed 12-month existing clinical relationship with the practitioner requirement for SMAs. After consideration of comments, we continue to believe that a 12-month existing clinical relationship between the practitioner and patient is appropriate. This relationship is important for determining whether SMAs would be suitable and beneficial for the patient. By maintaining this requirement, we aim to safeguard clinical appropriateness and quality of
(
printed page 71110)
care, while supporting continuity between the practitioner and patient.
Comment:
Several commenters described the operational frequency and cadence of SMAs based on their experience and other evidence. A commenter referenced evidence-based cadences from literature, referencing intensive weekly series of 6 to 16 weeks followed by monthly or quarterly maintenance. A couple of commenters reported that their programs commonly operate SMAs once weekly for several weeks or once monthly for ongoing support, reflecting the need for flexibility to accommodate patient needs and program goals. Many commenters recommended allowing operational flexibility and avoid imposing rigid frequency limits, noting that the optimal cadence may vary depending on the condition, patient population, and care model. A few commenters suggested that if CMS establishes a per-beneficiary limit, it should be set at not fewer than 36 sessions per calendar year to accommodate intensive and maintenance schedules documented in the literature.
Response:
We thank commenters for providing valuable information regarding the operational frequency and cadence of SMAs. After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing a frequency limit of not more than one SMA session per week per beneficiary.
Comment:
Many commenters provided detailed recommendations for program integrity and safeguards, reflecting broad consensus that robust protection is essential for SMAs. Several commenters emphasized the importance of individualized documentation for each participant, attendance verification (such as sign-in sheets or platform logs), documented consent and confidentiality terms, and staff training in group facilitation and SMA protocols. A couple of commenters recommended routine claims audits and periodic outcomes review as part of the integrity framework. Several commenters suggested establishing a reasonable annual encounter limit (for example, at least 36 sessions per beneficiary per year) to prevent runaway volume while supporting intensive and maintenance schedules.
A few commenters cautioned against rigid structural limits (such as diagnosis, duration, or group size) as primary safeguards, arguing that individualized documentation and compliance audits are more effective and less burdensome. Some commenters requested balanced safeguards against administrative burden, ensuring that legitimate SMAs remain practical for small, rural, and community practices.
Response:
We thank the commenters for providing detailed recommendations regarding program integrity and safeguards for SMAs. After consideration of commenter's input, we are finalizing the requirement that each SMA session be documented in each participating beneficiary's medical record. This documentation ensures individualized care and accountability, and we will continue to monitor this process and welcome ongoing feedback. We note that it may be beneficial for practitioners to retain attendance verification for the SMAs (such as sign-in sheets or platform logs) as this may be helpful in the event of a routine claims audit. We would appreciate additional information on recommended staff training requirements for SMAs and may address this along with additional safeguards in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Commenters stated that the proposed rule did not clearly address whether RHCs and FQHCs may furnish and bill for SMAs and requested that CMS explicitly extend G0686 eligibility to these settings. Commenters cited the high chronic disease burden and access barriers (rural geography, transportation, limited specialty care) faced by beneficiaries served by RHCs and FQHCs. Another commenter also requested that, if RHCs and FQHCs are permitted to furnish SMAs, CMS allow separate payment for a same-day individual E/M visit when a beneficiary requires individualized attention for an acute issue arising during a group session.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comments. A billable RHC or FQHC visit requires a medically necessary, face-to-face, one-on-one encounter between a beneficiary and an RHC or FQHC practitioner (§ 405.2463). SMAs, by design, involve concurrent group participation and do not meet this definitional requirement.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns about cost sharing and out-of-pocket costs for beneficiaries participating in SMAs. A commenter recommended that CMS address beneficiary cost sharing in the final rule, urging that copayments for SMAs should not exceed those charged for individual appointments. A couple of commenters emphasized the importance of reducing cost-sharing barriers to ensure equitable participation, especially for underserved and vulnerable populations. Many commenters highlighted that minimizing out-of-pocket costs would help maximize access to SMAs and support health equity.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. In response to the comments regarding elimination of beneficiary cost sharing for SMA services, most services covered under Medicare Part B carry cost sharing obligations (deductible and co-payment) unless the statute specifies that they do not apply. SMA services would be subject to applicable deductible and co-payment requirements as we do not have statutory authority that would allow us to remove or waive applicable cost sharing for SMA services.
Comment:
Several commenters provided feedback on how HCPCS code G0686 should be described and coded. Many commenters recommended that the descriptor should clearly identify SMAs as voluntary, group-based medical sessions that integrate individualized clinical assessment and care with group education, counseling, and peer support. Several commenters requested that the code language explicitly require individualized documentation for each participant, consent and confidentiality terms, and allow for multidisciplinary team participation under appropriate supervision. Many commenters urged preserving flexibility in the descriptor language, allowing practitioners to determine session length, group size, and team composition based on clinical need and operational realities. Several commenters emphasized that SMAs should not be characterized as group visit, as this understates the SMA service, and they recommend adopting terminology that includes the term “medical.”
A few commenters raised concerns about the use of the term “peer support” in the SMA descriptor as this may be confused with peer support services provided by peer support specialists. They recommended removing or avoiding the term in the SMA code description. Conversely, a few commenters appreciate explicitly identifying education and peer support in the code description.
Response:
We thank commenters for providing feedback regarding the SMA descriptors. After considering comments, we are modifying the code descriptor with technical refinements and changes. Although the code descriptor already included the term “voluntary”, we modified the code descriptor to emphasize the voluntary nature of SMAs. We also acknowledge commenters' emphasis that SMAs should be described by including the term “medical” and are finalizing the descriptor to begin with the terms
(
printed page 71111)
“Group-based medical session.” The inclusion of the term “peer support” in the descriptor is intended to reflect the supportive interaction among patients within SMAs. The long descriptors for SMAs will be finalized as follows:
HCPCS code G0686:
Group-based medical session involving multiple patients with common medical condition(s) and receiving medical care in a group setting. The voluntary session is billed and led by a physician or other qualified healthcare professional (QHP) and may include services provided by other QHPs, clinical staff, or auxiliary personnel under the direction of the supervising physician or QHP. The voluntary session integrates group education, counseling, and peer support with individualized patient clinical assessment and care, includes 2-10 patients, billed once per patient, first 60 minutes.
HCPCS code G0687:
Group-based medical session involving multiple patients with common medical condition(s) and receiving medical care in a group setting. The voluntary session is billed and led by a physician or other qualified healthcare professional (QHP) and may include services provided by other QHPs, clinical staff, or auxiliary personnel under the direction of the supervising physician or QHP. The voluntary session integrates group education, counseling, and peer support with individualized patient clinical assessment and care, includes 2-10 patients, billed per patient, each additional 30 minutes (list separately in addition to code for primary service).
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to create coding and separate payment for shared medical appointments with modifications. We are finalizing an add on code (HCPCS code G0687) with a work RVU of 0.87. Practitioners may bill up to two additional 30-minute units when medically necessary, allowing an SMA to last up to 120-minutes, and resulting in a combined work RVU of 3.47 for the SMA session. We are finalizing the HCPCS G0686 valuation as proposed. We are finalizing a frequency limit of not more than one SMA session per week per beneficiary. Additionally, we are finalizing a modified long descriptor for HCPCS G0686. However, we continue to welcome additional information and continued engagement on SMAs and may consider refinements through future rulemaking.
(55) Vaccine Adverse Effects Management (HCPCS Code G0576)
Vaccines prevent serious illnesses and even death in persons who receive them and serve a public health benefit. Vaccines are intended to produce active immunity to specific antigens. An adverse reaction is an undesirable side effect that occurs after a vaccination. Vaccine adverse reactions are classified as (1) local; (2) systemic; or (3) allergic. Local reactions (for example, redness) are usually the least severe and most frequent. Systemic reactions (for example, fever) occur less frequently than local reactions, and severe allergic reactions (for example, anaphylaxis) are the least frequent reactions.
[
53
]
Licensed vaccines are safe and effective; however, adverse events have been reported after administration of each type of available vaccine.
[
54
]
Vaccine providers should be familiar with identifying immediate-type allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, and be competent in treating these events at the time of vaccine administration. Providers, including practitioners, should also have a plan in place to contact emergency medical services immediately in the event of a severe acute vaccine reaction.
[
55
]
Before a vaccine is licensed, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) takes steps to make sure the vaccine is safe. FDA requires that a vaccine goes through extensive safety testing. Even though careful studies are done before a vaccine is licensed, rare adverse effects may not be found until a vaccine is given to millions of people with different backgrounds and medical histories.
[
56
]
According to clinical trial data, most vaccine‐associated adverse events are mild; however, severe adverse reactions such as anaphylaxis, myocarditis, thrombotic events, and pneumonitis have been reported.
[
57
]
After a vaccine is licensed, the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) is one of the mechanisms used to monitor for any problems, or “adverse events,” that happen after vaccination.
[
58
]
We believe that the CPT evaluation and management code set may capture the work and clinical decision making involved in the evaluation and management of most vaccine adverse reactions. However, we believe that physician and nonphysician practitioners' work may not be accurately reflected under the CPT medical decision-making framework relating to the evaluation and management of rare and severe vaccine adverse reactions. E/M visits, like other services under the PFS, are valued based on an assumption of a typical case. We believe that these are additional resource costs that don't fit under a typical E/M. Therefore, we proposed an add-on code and payment for diagnosis and management of a suspected vaccine adverse reaction for services going above and beyond those captured in an evaluation and management (E/M) visit. These services entail listening to patient concerns, answering questions, and building trust; selecting diagnosis strategies and conveying information in a manner specific to each patient's concerns, cultural and religious beliefs, and literacy level; providing patients with appropriate resources; and planning with patients the treatment of symptoms of vaccine adverse effects. We proposed that this add-on code, HCPCS code G0576 (
Office or other outpatient evaluation and management service(s) for the diagnosis and treatment of vaccine adverse effects, new or established patient; each 15 minutes personally performed by the physician or qualified healthcare professional (list separately in addition to CPT codes 99202, 99203, 99204, 99205, 99211, 99212, 99213, 99214, 99215, 99341, 99342, 99344, 99345, 99347, 99348, 99349, 99350)
), would be payable when a physician or nonphysician practitioner (NPP): (1) establishes and documents a temporal relationship to vaccination, and (2) performs a medically appropriate assessment to rule out alternative causes.
For the purposes of valuation, we proposed a direct crosswalk for HCPCS code G0576 to HCPCS code G2212 (
Prolonged office or other outpatient evaluation and management service(s) beyond the maximum required time of the primary procedure which has been selected using total time on the date of the primary service; each additional 15 minutes by the physician or qualified healthcare professional, with or without direct patient contact (List separately in addition to CPT codes 99205, 99215, 99483 for office or other outpatient evaluation and management services) (do not report G2212 on the same date of service as 99358, 99359, 99415, 99416) (do not report G2212 for any time unit less than 15 minutes)
) for 0.61 work RVUs and for direct PE inputs.
(
printed page 71112)
We welcomed comments on whether a second HCPCS code for 15 minutes of physician or NPP work time should be finalized and structured as a stand-alone code to more accurately capture the work entailed in cases where a patient is being evaluated for only a vaccine related complaint, outside the context of an E/M visit being furnished for a separate complaint. We also welcomed comments on whether in finalizing such a stand-alone HCPCS code we should crosswalk its work RVU and PE inputs to HCPCS code G2212.
We received many public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comments:
The majority of comments expressed were identical, anonymous comments expressing support for the new vaccine adverse effects HCPCS add-on code G0576. These commenters requested that this and other immunization administration codes be removed from National Correct Coding (NCC) bundling when billed with E/M codes on the same date of service, as bundling defeats the purpose of encouraging screening/preventive services. A few other commenters expressed unqualified support and a few others expressed support but asked CMS to monitor utilization for potential misuse of the code that would result in duplicative billing or unnecessary testing or services that are not supported by the patient's presentation. A couple of commenters requested consideration of policies beyond the scope of this rulemaking.
Finally, many commenters opposed the creation of the HCPCS code G0576 because they felt that the new coding is clinically unnecessary given existing coding mechanisms and furthermore the new coding risks generating misleading data that could be used to overstate vaccine-related harm and undermine public confidence in immunization. Some felt that the separate payment could create incentives to misattribute nonspecific symptoms to vaccination without clear clinical evidence. Nearly all of those that were opposed asked that CMS articulate a clearer distinction between the proposed HCPCS code G0576 service and work that is already reportable through established E/M coding and diagnosis reporting mechanisms. A commenter suggested that G0576 is fundamentally counseling services and should be explicitly described as such in the code descriptor and accompanying guidance. Another commenter asked that CMS issue clear guidance so that practitioners and billing staff can reliably determine when HCPCS code G0576 applies instead of a base code E/M or prolonged E/M service. Commenters generally requested clear guidance regarding the documentation necessary to establish the required temporal relationship and medically appropriate assessment of alternative causes stating that requirements should reflect reasonable clinical documentation and should not become rigid technical conditions that generate denials despite the furnishing of medically necessary care. Another commenter also felt that HCPCS code G0576 was more of a counseling service that should be taking place before a vaccination is given rather than after the vaccination has already taken place and bemoaned that CMS coding does not allow clinicians to report vaccine counseling time when a vaccine is not administered. Finally, a commenter stated that the apparent frequency of suspected vaccine adverse reactions could reflect differences in provider coding behavior, reimbursement incentives, documentation practices, and patient attribution—not differences in the underlying incidence or severity of adverse events.
Response:
We thank commenters for their comments. We believe that physician and nonphysician practitioners' work may not be accurately reflected under the CPT medical decision-making framework relating to the evaluation and management of rare and severe vaccine adverse reactions. E/M visits, like other services under the PFS, are valued based on an assumption of a typical case. We believe that these services involve additional resource costs that do not fit under a typical E/M service code. These services entail listening to patient concerns, answering questions, and building trust; selecting diagnosis strategies and conveying information in a manner specific to each patient's concerns, cultural and religious beliefs, and literacy level; providing patients with appropriate resources; and planning with patients the treatment of symptoms of suspected vaccine adverse effects.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing coding and payment for HCPCS add-on code G0576 (
Office or other outpatient evaluation and management service(s) for the diagnosis and treatment of vaccine adverse effects, new or established patient; each 15 minutes personally performed by the physician or qualified healthcare professional (list separately in addition to CPT codes 99202, 99203, 99204, 99205, 99211, 99212, 99213, 99214, 99215, 99341, 99342, 99344, 99345, 99347, 99348, 99349, 99350)
) as proposed for the diagnosis and management of a suspected vaccine adverse reaction. We expect practitioners to support reporting of HCPCS code G0576 with sufficient evidence in the medical record for services going above and beyond those captured in an E/M visit. We are finalizing adding HCPCS code G0576 to the Medicare Telehealth List.
(56) Health Coaching (CPT Codes 0591T, 0592T, and 0593T)
Per the Trump Administration's Executive Order, “Establishing the President's Make America Healthy Again Commission,”
[
59
]
the Administration is directing agency focus towards understanding and drastically lowering chronic disease rates, through thinking on nutrition, physical activity, healthy lifestyles, over-reliance on medication and treatments, the effects of new technological habits, environmental impacts, and food and drug quality and safety. Furthermore, the Executive Order directs that agencies shall ensure the availability of expanded treatment options and the flexibility for health insurance coverage to provide benefits to support beneficial lifestyle changes and disease prevention.
As such, in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule, we sought comment on a wide range of possible rulemaking topics to promote prevention and management of chronic disease, and in particular, asked more detailed questions surrounding health coaching and motivational interviewing. More specifically, we asked whether we should consider coding and payment for health coaching and motivational interviewing beyond the current contractor-priced CPT codes describing health coaching, as an incident-to service performed under general supervision of a billing practitioner, what an appropriate description would be, what types of clinical staff perform motivational interviewing, how long a session lasts, the overlap between motivational interviewing and health coaching, training requirements for motivational interviewing and health coaches, the types of clinical circumstances where motivational interviewing and health coaching are performed, relevance for audiovisual or audio-only telecommunication, the experience of payers and providers using the CPT Category III CPT codes, and relevance for Evidence-Based Programs that effectively manage or prevent chronic disease. Commenters
(
printed page 71113)
responded, stating that health coaching could support CMS' goal of preventing or managing chronic disease. Many health coaches wrote about their personal experience working with patients with chronic diseases, assisting them in making behavioral and lifestyle changes to self-manage their conditions, and noted that health coaching is a low-cost and highly effective strategy that empowers patients to manage their health. Many commenters requested paying separately for health coaching via the creation of HCPCS G-codes or another payment mechanism that would allow providers to reliably schedule and bill for health coaching services. Commenters also emphasized the importance of requiring that these services be provided by health coaches with appropriate training and certification.
To ensure we adequately capture the time and resources for health coaching, we proposed conditions of payment and valuation for 0591T (
Health and well-being coaching face-to-face; individual, initial assessment, 60-90 minutes
), 0592T (
Individual, follow-up session, at least 30 minutes),
and 0593T (
Health and well-being coaching, group [2 or more individuals], at least 30 minutes
). CPT code 0593T would be billed once per beneficiary in the group.
We also proposed to adopt the CPT prefatory language for 0591T, 0592T, and 0593T: “Health and well-being coaching is a patient-centered approach wherein patients determine their goals, use self-discovery or active learning processes together with content education to work toward their goals, and self-monitor behaviors to increase accountability, all within the context of an interpersonal relationship with a coach. The health and well-being coach is qualified to perform health and well-being coaching by education, training, national examination and, when applicable, licensure/regulation, and has completed a training program in health and well-being coaching whose content meets standards established by an applicable national credentialing organization. The training includes behavioral change theory, motivational strategies, communication techniques, health education and promotion theories, which are used to assist patients to develop intrinsic motivation and obtain skills to create sustainable change for improved health and well-being.”
We proposed that CPT codes 0591T, 0592T, and 0593T may be performed under direct supervision of the billing practitioner, as defined by § 410.26(a)(3). We also proposed that when the service is performed under direct supervision by auxiliary personnel, the auxiliary personnel must have received appropriate certification to perform the services, which includes, but is not limited to, fulfilling the National Board for Health and Wellness Coaching National Standards, the National Commission for Health Education Credentialing eligibility for Certified Health Education Specialists, or the American Holistic Nurses Credentialing national standards for Certified Nurse Coaches. In response to the Request for Information (RFI) in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule (
90 FR 49479
through
49480
), we received comments from interested parties pointing us towards these standards. We also proposed that appropriate certification for auxiliary personnel to perform the services can also be fulfilled by receiving training from the evidence-based health promotion and disease prevention programs funded under the Older Americans Act and overseen by the Administration for Community Living (ACL). These programs undergo review, meet significant evidence thresholds, and have training requirements built into the program requirements. We solicited comments on these certification standards for auxiliary personnel performing these services.
Furthermore, we understand that occasionally, community-based organizations (CBOs) are the entities that employ health coaches. As noted in the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69790
) and explained in the CY 2023 PFS proposed rule (
87 FR 46102
), when we refer to CBOs, we mean public or private not-for-profit entities that provide specific services to the community or targeted populations in the community to address the health needs of those populations. They may include community care hubs, community-action agencies, housing agencies, area agencies on aging, centers for independent living, aging and disability resource centers or other non-profits that apply for grants or contract with healthcare entities to perform social services. They may receive grants from other agencies in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, including Federal grants administered by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Administration for Community Living (ACL), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), or State-funded grants to provide social services. Generally, we believe such organizations know the populations and communities they serve and may have the infrastructure or systems in place to assist practitioners to provide these services. We noted that individuals employed by CBOs may operate under general supervision of the billing practitioner, as long as the training and certification guidelines outlined earlier in this section are met.
Finally, we proposed national payment for CPT codes 0591T, 0592T, and 0593T. We proposed to crosswalk work and direct PE inputs for 0591T and 0592T to CPT codes 99490 (Chronic care management) and 99439 (Chronic care management, each additional 20 minutes), respectively, since, like Chronic Care Management (CCM), these visit-based services are performed under general supervision. For 0593T, since it is a group visit billed in 30-minute increments, we proposed to crosswalk the work and PE inputs to CPT code G0109 (Group diabetes self-management training). Therefore, we proposed a work RVU of 1.00 for CPT code 0591T, 0.70 for CPT code 0592T, and 0.23 for CPT code 0593T. Since multiple sessions in the same calendar month may be needed, we did not propose frequency limitations for these codes, as long as they are reasonable and necessary. We will monitor utilization and may re-evaluate these policies in future rulemaking. These services were added to the Medicare Telehealth Services List in the CY 2024 PFS Final Rule (
88 FR 78859
through
78860
).
We solicited comments on the valuation of these services and the conditions of payment. We also solicited comments on whether we should consider creating HCPCS G-codes to describe these services for CY 2027, rather than actively pricing these Category III CPT codes that describe health coaching services, including what the potential benefits of G-codes would be compared to using the existing codes.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
The majority of commenters were in support of finalizing national payment for health and well-being services, emphasizing their value in chronic disease prevention, patient engagement, adherence and bridging the gap between clinical advice and sustainable behavior change. A few commenters do not recommend establishing coding or payment for these services under the PFS and suggested testing these concepts through a limited
(
printed page 71114)
demonstration or an alternative payment model (APM) first.
Response:
We appreciate all input received from commenters regarding national payment for health and well-being services. After consideration of the comments submitted in response to the CY 2026 Request for Information (RFI) on health coaching and comments received on this proposed rule, we are finalizing national pricing for health and well-being coaching, as we recognize the value these services bring to chronic disease prevention. While a few commenters suggested further testing through limited demonstration or APMs, we do not believe this is necessary. These codes have been in effect since January 1, 2020, and are already recognized and used by practitioners. We believe that establishing national pricing at this time best supports the advancement and accessibility of health and well-being coaching services.
Comment:
Many commenters were in support of national payment for health and well-being services but raised concerns regarding the proposed valuation for the codes. The commenters indicated that the proposed valuation undervalues the time and professional contribution required for effective health coaching for CPT codes 0591T and 0592T, which would lead to non-utilization of the codes. Commenters noted that the chronic care management codes may provide a reasonable conceptual reference point citing similarities in longitudinal care and general supervision. Several commenters stated that the proposed valuation for the health coaching codes are undervalued because the time used to value the codes are significantly less than what is required. A few commenters, indicated that the proposed crosswalk for the 60-minute initial assessment, CPT code 0591T to CPT code 99490, and the 30-minute follow-up session, CPT code 0592T to CPT code 99439, uses only the first 20-minute increment of the Chronic Care Management (CCM) codes, resulting in both codes being allotted approximately 25 minutes of clinical labor time, such that a 60-minute session and a 30-minute session are valued nearly identically, and both at a fraction of their actual time, leading to payment rates that do not reflect the duration and effort required for these services. A few commenters recommended prorating the CCM crosswalk practice-expense RVUs to reflect the actual time the coaching service requires. Another commenter recommended work RVUs of approximately 3.15, 1.10, and 0.30 for the health coaching services respectively, and if CMS did not adopt this refinement, they recommend at a minimum adopting another commenter's recommended work RVU values of 3.00, 1.05, and 0.29 respectively. Some commenters recommended finalizing national payment as proposed.
Response:
We thank the commenters for communicating their concerns, indicating that the time duration of the proposed crosswalk codes would undervalue the health coaching services. Several commenters expressed concerns that our proposed crosswalks for CPT codes 0591T and 0592T did not adequately account for the time required to furnish these services. We agree that the proposed crosswalks do not sufficiently reflect the time associated with furnishing these services. Therefore, in consideration of the comments received, we are valuing the work RVU of CPT code 0591T at 1.81 and CPT code 0592T at 1.00, based on a crosswalk to CPT codes 99487 and 99489. We are crosswalking the work RVUs, work times, and direct PE inputs directly to these complex care management codes that account for more time, specifically, 60 minutes of clinical staff time and each additional 30 minutes, which more closely aligns with the health coaching service CPT codes 0591T and 0592T respectively. We continue to believe crosswalking the work RVU of CPT code 0593T to G0109 is appropriate and were not persuaded that CPT code 0593T required additional time and work valuation. Therefore, we are finalizing it as proposed.
Comment:
Many commenters provided feedback on the supervision requirements for health and well-being coaching services (CPT codes 0591T, 0592T, 0593T). The majority of commenters expressed strong support for general supervision, based on operational feasibility, and stated that CMS's proposal was inconsistent because CMS crosswalked the valuation of CPT codes 0591T and 0592T to Chronic Care Management (CCM) codes (CPT codes 99490 and 99439) which are furnished under general supervision, while proposing direct supervision for health coaching itself, and would separately allow health coaches employed by community-based organizations to work under general supervision. Many commenters indicated that direct supervision for health coaching would create unnecessary barriers and would impede access for populations most in need. Some commenters requested adding language that would provide health coaching under general supervision by updating the codes to the designated care management services provision at § 410.26(b)(5), enabling general supervision for health coaching. Nurse organizations and credentialed nurse coaches specifically requested exemption from supervision requirements for licensed professionals, advocating for deference to state scope-of-practice laws and direct billing pathways. A few commenters supported direct supervision. Some commenters recommended that virtual or on-call supervision (real-time audio-video availability) could satisfy the requirements of direct supervision, consistent with recent CMS policy for incident-to services.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback regarding the supervision requirements for health coaching. Based on comments received, we now agree that health and well-being coaching should be performed under general supervision of the billing practitioner instead of as proposed with direct supervision. We believe this position is supported by several factors, including that chronic care management services can be delivered under general supervision which offers flexibility for auxiliary personnel to provide services without the billing practitioner being physically present. Additionally, 24/7 access is not necessary for health coaching and is not a required element for similar services such as Community Health Integration (CHI) and Principal Illness Navigation (PIN), which also operate under general supervision. We also want to note that direct supervision is typically reserved for highly clinical services where immediate oversight is needed to reduce potential harm, whereas health coaching is not as directly clinical and aligns more closely with services CMS historically allows under general supervision. As many commenters noted, CMS proposed health coaching codes valuation using a crosswalk to chronic care management codes which permit general supervision, and behavioral health services with similar goals also allow general supervision. We believe that requiring direct supervision would be inconsistent with other chronic care management services and could limit the operability and uptake of health coaching, especially among community-based organizations employing health coaches. Therefore, we are finalizing that health coaching may be furnished under general supervision, ensuring greater workforce capacity, improved patient access, and alignment with CMS's established practices. Additionally, we are making updates to
(
printed page 71115)
§ 410.26(b)(5) to specify general supervision for health coaching services accordingly.
Comment:
Many commenters provided feedback on qualification and credentialing pathways for health and well-being coaching. Many commenters supported the credentialing pathway of the National Board for Health & Wellness Coaching (NBHWC), citing the rigor of its nationally standardized examination and training process as a quality safeguard. In addition, some commenters advocated for explicit retention of the National Commission for Health Education Credentialing (NCHEC) pathways, including Certified Health Education Specialist (CHES) and Master Certified Health Education Specialist (MCHES), as qualifying credentials for health coaching auxiliary personnel. Some commenters requested for American Holistic Nurses Credentialing Corporation (AHNCC) board-certified Nurse Coaches (NC-BC, HWNC-BC) be explicitly recognized among qualified personnel. Some commenters supported CMS's proposal to recognize training completed through evidence-based health promotion and disease-prevention programs funded under the Older Americans Act and overseen by the Administration for Community Living (ACL), and some commenters recommended aligning the Older Americans Act to HCPCS codes G0108 and G0109 rather than health coaching codes. Several commenters recommended allowing professionals such as occupational therapists, exercise professionals, registered dietitians, pharmacists, community health workers, and social workers to be included as eligible health coaches. They recommended that qualification standards be based on demonstrated skills and competency in evidence-based behavior change principles, allowing these professionals to serve as health coaches, if they can show they have the appropriate education, training and competency to deliver health and well-being coaching services. Several commenters recommended that occupational therapists be recognized as qualified health coach providers without requiring additional certification. Some commenters indicated that credentialing standards should be flexible, avoiding an exhaustive list that could inadvertently exclude qualified professionals as the workforce evolves.
Response:
We note that as previously discussed, we are finalizing that CPT codes 0591T, 0592T, and 0593T may be performed under general supervision, as defined by § 410.26(a)(3). In addition, we continue to believe that auxiliary personnel must have received appropriate certification to perform the services, which includes, but is not limited to, fulfilling the National Board for Health and Wellness Coaching National Standards, the National Commission for Health Education Credentialing eligibility for Certified Health Education Specialists, or the American Holistic Nurses Credentialing national standards for Certified Nurse Coaches. In addition, we agree with the comments submitted in response to the RFI in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule (
90 FR 49479
through
49480
) that appropriate certification for auxiliary personnel to perform the services can be fulfilled by receiving training from the evidence-based health promotion and disease prevention programs funded under the Older Americans Act and overseen by the Administration for Community Living (ACL) because these programs undergo review, meet significant evidence thresholds, and have training requirements built into the program requirements. Accordingly, we are finalizing as proposed. As such, auxiliary personnel who have received appropriate certification to perform the services, which includes, but is not limited to, fulfilling the National Board for Health and Wellness Coaching National Standards, the National Commission for Health Education Credentialing eligibility for Certified Health Education Specialists, or the American Holistic Nurses Credentialing national standards for Certified Nurse Coaches, and/or have received training from the evidence-based health promotion and disease prevention programs funded under the Older Americans Act and overseen by the Administration for Community Living (ACL) may provide health coaching services under general supervision of a physician or non-physician practitioner. The applicable list of the evidence-based health promotion and disease prevention programs funded under the Older Americans Act and overseen by the Administration for Community Living (ACL) can be found on the
ACL.gov
website (
https://acl.gov/​programs/​health-wellness/​disease-prevention
).
Comment:
Many commenters recognized the essential role of community-based organizations (CBOs) in delivering health and well-being coaching services, emphasizing their unique ability to engage local populations and address social drivers of health. Many commenters noted that CBOs are trusted entities within their communities. Credentialed health education specialists, such as CHES and MCHES professionals, frequently work in CBOs and bring expertise in health education, behavior change, communication, and program implementation. Commenters recommended CMS explicitly allow CBOs to employ and furnish health coaching services under general supervision, highlighting that CBOs may lack on-site practitioners but can still provide high-quality, evidence-based coaching through trained personnel.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. CBOs often employ health coaches, and individuals employed by CBOs may operate under general supervision of the billing practitioner as long as the training and certification guidelines outlined earlier in this section are met. Accordingly, auxiliary personnel employed by a CBO, or otherwise affiliated with a CBO that employs health coaches, who have received appropriate training and certification to perform health coaching services, may provide health coaching services under general supervision of a physician or non-physician practitioner.
Comment:
Commenters overwhelmingly supported the inclusion of telehealth as an allowable delivery option for health and well-being coaching services, emphasizing its critical role in expanding access for Medicare beneficiaries who face geographic, transportation, mobility, or caregiving barriers. Commenters also recommended flexible delivery as essential for accommodating evening and weekend sessions, and for matching beneficiaries with specialized coaches, such as those fluent in American Sign Language or with expertise in particular health conditions. Several commenters requested CMS to clarify that audio-only telehealth encounters should be permitted when video is not feasible, ensuring accessibility for individuals with sensory, cognitive, or technological limitations.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support. These services were added to the Medicare Telehealth Services List in the CY 2024 PFS Final Rule (
88 FR 78859
through
78860
). Section 6209(e) of the CAA, 2026 extends the flexibilities to allow audio-only Medicare telehealth services from January 30, 2026 to the extended date of January 1, 2028. Please refer to section II.C. Payment for Medicare Telehealth Services of this final rule for additional information.
Comment:
Several commenters supported CMS's proposal to not propose frequency limitations on health and well-being coaching services. The commenters noted that the frequency and duration of coaching sessions
(
printed page 71116)
should be determined by clinical need and beneficiary-specific goals, rather than arbitrary caps. Several commenters highlighted that higher-frequency coaching is often necessary during the early period of a new patient relationship.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support in not establishing frequency limits for health and well-being services. Since multiple sessions in the same calendar month may be needed, we are not finalizing frequency limitations for these codes, as long as they are reasonable and necessary. We will monitor utilization and may re-evaluate these policies in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters provided feedback regarding adopting the CPT prefatory language for 0591T, 0592T and 0593T. Commenters expressed the importance of maintaining clear, inclusive, and precise descriptors as established by the AMA CPT Editorial Panel. Several commenters recommended preserving the existing CPT language, which defines the scope, session duration, and credentialing standards for health coaching. Some commenters suggested that CMS revise the CPT code descriptors to clarify minimum session times, such as specifying “at least 60 minutes” for the initial assessment (CPT code 0591T), “at least 30 minutes” for follow-up (CPT code 0592T), and “each 30 minutes” for group coaching (CPT code 0593T), to help ensure consistent billing and proper reimbursement, especially for sessions that may require accommodations or longer durations. Some commenters recommended adopting language that would allow multiple units of CPT code 0593T to be billed for longer group sessions.
Many commenters advocated transitioning from temporary Category III CPT codes to permanent HCPCS G-codes for health and well-being coaching. The commenters stressed the need for payment stability and billing clarity. Conversely, several commenters supported retaining the Category III CPT codes, stating that the existing Category III codes are already recognized nationally, and retaining them would ease dual Medicare-commercial billing, reduce administrative complexity, and provide a clear path for eventual conversion to permanent Category I CPT status. The commenters stated creating new G codes could introduce confusion, duplicative coding, and especially for practices and payers already set up to use the existing CPT codes.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback on the adoption of CPT prefatory language for codes 0591T, 0592T, and 0593T. After consideration of comments, we will finalize adopting the CPT prefatory language for these codes and retain the Category III CPT codes, 0591T, 0592T, and 0593T. We agree with commenters that maintaining the established CPT prefatory language and CPT codes, which are recognized nationally, will help ensure clarity and consistency. We believe this approach will help avoid unnecessary confusion and administrative complexity, especially for practices and payers already set up to use the existing CPT codes.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended not limiting health coaching services solely to medical conditions, emphasizing the importance of including behavioral health needs within the scope of reimbursable coaching. The commenters stated that health and well-being coaching can play an important role in supporting beneficiaries with stress management, sleep improvement, treatment engagement, and broader health behavior change. The commenters stated that behavioral health and medical health are deeply interconnected, and that coaching interventions often address factors such as motivation, adherence, self-management, and lifestyle modification, which are relevant for both physical and behavioral health outcomes.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback regarding including behavioral health needs within the scope of reimbursable health coaching services. Behavioral health needs should not be precluded from being addressed by health coaches when medically necessary.
Comment:
Commenters requested that CMS expand recognized delivery settings for the coaching codes (CPT 0591T, 0592T, 0593T) to explicitly include RHCs and FQHCs. A commenter stated the proposed “employing entity” provision is limited to community-based organizations and asked CMS to confirm RHCs and FQHCs may report the codes on a fee-for-service basis. Another commenter stated that RHC exclusion under the proposed policy is inconsistent with CMS's goal of aligning payment across settings, and noted that RHCs already employ certified health coaches; this commenter urged CMS to permit RHC billing for coaching services.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comments. Health and well-being coaching services furnished under the general supervision of an RHC or FQHC practitioner, do not constitute a billable RHC or FQHC visit (§ 405.2463).
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing our proposal with modifications. Specifically, we are finalizing the valuation for health and well—being coaching, CPT codes 0591T and 0592T based on a crosswalk to CPT codes 99487 and 99489, with work RVUs of 1.81 and 1.00 and finalizing the valuation of CPT code 0593T as proposed. We are also finalizing that health coaching may be furnished under general supervision and updating § 410.26(b)(5) accordingly.
(57) Vascular Embolization or Occlusion Procedure With Use of a Pressure-Generating Catheter (HCPCS Code G0577)
HCPCS code C9797 (
Vascular embolization or occlusion procedure with use of a pressure-generating catheter (e.g., one-way valve, intermittently occluding), inclusive of all radiological supervision and interpretation, intraprocedural roadmapping, and imaging guidance necessary to complete the intervention; for tumors, organ ischemia, or infarction
) was created for the April, 2025 Quarterly Release for the OPPS and Ambulatory Surgical System (ASC) to describe use of a pressure-generating catheter inclusive of imaging guidance for vascular embolization. Subsequently, we also created HCPCS code C8004 (
Simulation angiogram with use of a pressure-generating catheter (e.g., one-way valve, intermittently occluding), inclusive of all radiological supervision and interpretation, intraprocedural road mapping, and imaging guidance necessary to complete the angiogram, for subsequent therapeutic radioembolization of tumors
) to describe the simulation angiogram associated with the use of the pressure-generating catheter described by HCPCS code C9797 for the April, 2025 OPPS Quarterly Release. For CY 2026, HCPCS code C9797 is assigned to APC 5194 with a payment rate of around $18,729 while HCPCS code C8004 is assigned to APC 5193 with a payment rate of around $11,874. Currently both HCPCS codes C9797 and C8004 are only payable in the OPPS and ASC settings, as there is currently no coding for the physician office setting describing use of this technology. Under the PFS, vascular embolization procedures are reported using CPT code 37243 (
Vascular embolization or occlusion, inclusive of all radiological supervision and interpretation, intraprocedural roadmapping, and imaging guidance necessary to complete the intervention; for tumors, organ
(
printed page 71117)
ischemia, or infarction
) regardless of the technology used to perform the service.
Interested parties have indicated that use of this technology has expanded beyond the OPPS and ASC settings and into the physician office setting; however, the resource costs associated with CPT code 37243 do not accurately account for the use of innovative catheter technology. While this technology may not yet be typical and as such is appropriately absent from the valuation of CPT code 37342, we are concerned that the lack of appropriate coding and payment for the use of innovative catheter technology may negatively impact access in the non-facility setting.
Beginning July 1, 2026, we began making separate payment for vascular embolization or occlusion procedure with the use of a pressure-generating catheter through the contractor priced HCPCS code G0577 (
Vascular embolization or occlusion procedure with use of a pressure-generating catheter (e.g., one-way valve, intermittently occluding), inclusive of all radiological supervision and interpretation, intraprocedural roadmapping, and imaging guidance necessary to complete the intervention; for tumors, organ ischemia, or infarction performed in the non-facility setting)
and proposed to nationally price this service for CY 2027. We sought comment on whether there is a need for creation of a HCPCS G-code to mirror HCPCS code C8004 as currently there are no claims for this service in the HOPD setting.
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized use of the relationship between the OPPS APC relative weights to inform the PE RVUs for those services under the PFS. We believe a similar policy is necessary here to establish the initial valuation for vascular embolization using a pressure generating catheter given the lack of pricing information in the non-facility setting. Therefore, we proposed to use the relative relationship between the approximate APC payment amounts between CPT code 37243 and HCPCS code C9797 to value the PE portion of HCPCS code G0577 and a direct crosswalk to the work and MP RVUs associated with CPT code 37243 as well as the physician time. We sought comments on these values. We also noted in the proposed rule that this valuation is preliminary and we will consider updates for future rulemaking if use of this technology becomes more widespread in the non-facility setting.
Comment:
We received comments requesting clarification on the methodology used to value the PE RVUs for HCPCS code G0577, noting that the reference to approximate APC payment amounts could not be independently replicated. Another comment separately raised a concern that the published PE RVU and total non-facility RVU for G0577 in the proposed rule addenda did not appear consistent with applying the adjustment ratio to the PE RVU alone before adding work and malpractice RVUs and requested that we review the calculation.
Response:
We are revising our methodology for the final rule. Rather than relying on a single OPPS-based ratio, we compared the relative payment relationship between CPT code 37243 and HCPCS code C9797 under two measures of OPPS payment: the ratio of the OPPS APC payment amounts for the two codes, and the ratio of the OPPS geometric mean costs for the two codes. We then averaged the resulting ratios to produce a single adjustment factor. We are applying this adjustment factor to the existing non-facility PE RVUs for CPT code 37243 to derive the non-facility PE RVUs for HCPCS code G0577.
