(58) Accounting for E/M Resource Overlap Between Stand-Alone Visits and Global Periods
(a) Background
Surgical procedures with a global surgery period include all the necessary services normally provided by the practitioner before, during, and after a procedure. The global surgery payment includes things like pre-operative visits, typical intra-operative services for that procedure, post-operative follow-up visits, supplies, and other services such as dressing changes, and removal of items used during or after surgery like sutures, staples, splints, or casts.
[
60
]
The payment and coding structure of global surgery periods includes the same foundational pieces as other codes in the PFS: work RVUs, practice expense RVUs, and malpractice RVUs. The work RVUs include time crosswalked from E/M codes to reflect the valuation of things such as pre-operative and post-operative visits. Given that global surgical packages already account for the resource costs associated with visits, standalone E/M codes are not billable on the same day as a procedure code unless they are significant and separately identifiable from the procedure. These visits are identified through appending of modifier -25 to the claim. This proposal is meant to address the likely overlap and duplication of payment between the E/M services already paid for during the global surgical package, and any additional E/M services billed for through the use of modifier -25 as significant and separately identifiable.
The PFS has other existing policies where we reduce payments if multiple procedures are furnished on the same day for the same patient, the multiple procedure payment reduction (MPPR) policies. MPPR is a longstanding Medicare policy to reduce payment by 50 percent for the second and subsequent surgical procedures furnished on the same day to the same patient, largely based on the efficiencies in PE and pre- and post-surgical physician work. Since the implementation of the PFS, MPPR policies were also established on nuclear medicine diagnostic procedures, the professional and technical component of diagnostic imaging, the technical component of diagnostic cardiovascular and ophthalmology procedures, and always-therapy services. In the 2019 PFS proposed rule (
83 FR 35840
through
35841
), as part of a suite of proposals designed to modify the payment structure of E/M visits, we proposed to reduce payment by 50 percent for the least expensive 0-day global procedure or visit that the same physician (or a physician in the same group practice) furnishes on the same day as a separately identifiable E/M visit, currently identified on the claim by an appended modifier -25.
In the 2019 PFS final rule (
83 FR 59638
through
59640
), many commenters opposed this proposal, stating that current billing rules allow these services to be billed only when modifier -25 is used, which makes it clear that the visits are significant and separately identifiable. Other commenters described that the RUC review process includes adjustments to account for any costs that the RUC considers duplicative, which means that CMS is making an unnecessary second adjustment. Commenters also stated that CMS provided insufficient rationale for a 50 percent payment reduction instead of other potential adjustments. Some physician organizations and patient advocacy groups also stated concerns that physicians might respond to financial incentives to bring patients back for necessary visits on a different day to avoid triggering the payment reduction. MedPAC, among others, were supportive of the proposal, stating that when a standalone E/M visit occurs on the same day as a procedure, there are efficiencies such as pre- service and post-service clinician work and practice expense, that are not currently accounted for in the system. Other commenters suggested alternative reductions, such as a 5 percent or 25 percent reduction.
In our response to commenters in the CY 2019 final rule (
83 FR 59638
through
59640
), we stated that we continued to have concerns about 0- and 10-day global periods on the same day as E/M visits. We appreciated the efforts of the RUC to address overlaps when they recognize that a code is often reported with a same day E/M visit, but we also noted that the RUC tends to recommend only minor adjustments to physician time and direct PE inputs to account for overlap. We also discussed that there are several thousand codes with global periods, and while we routinely prioritize review of high-volume services, we believe code-level reviews are not a practical solution to ensuring the accuracy of accounting for these types of efficiencies. We also stated that if practitioners begin deliberately scheduling visits on separate days to avoid the payment adjustment, this could create undue burden and create potential medical risk for beneficiaries.
We did not finalize this proposal in CY 2019 for a few reasons. First, we had concerns related to balancing the appropriate valuation of these codes with potential disruption to patient care. We reiterated that we find the possible practice of scheduling medical services to maximize payment highly problematic, and we invited interested party feedback regarding how to address these challenges. Second, we did not finalize any of the suite of proposals related to the valuation of the E/M code set in CY 2019, as the AMA and the CPT Editorial Panel stated plans to revisit coding for O/O E/M, and we delayed further action to allow that process to play out (
83 FR 59638
).
(b) Proposed Changes to Payments Using Modifier -25
As we stated in the CY 2019 final rule (
83 FR 59638
through
59640
), we continue to believe that there are efficiencies when the same physician (or a physician in the same group practice) provides an E/M service for the same patient in conjunction with a procedure with a global period, and that we are likely duplicating payment under the current payment methodology. We proposed to reduce payment, as described later in this section, when a separately identifiable O/O E/M visit is furnished by the same physician (or a physician in the same group practice) on the same day as a 0-, 10-, and 90-day global procedure. Under this proposal, the most expensive service (either surgical or E/M visit) would be paid at 100 percent, and all other surgical procedure(s) or E/M visit(s) would be paid at 50 percent. For example, a patient receives an O/O E/M visit using CPT code 99212 (
Office or other outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of an established patient, which requires a medically appropriate history and/or examination and straightforward medical decision making. When using total time on the date of the encounter for code section, 10 minutes must be met or exceeded
) at a dermatologist's office, and then has two skin lesions removed, one using CPT code 11300 (
Shaving of epidermal or dermal lesion, single lesion, trunk, arms, or legs; lesion diameter 0.5 cm or less
) and one using CPT code 11301 (
Shaving of epidermal or dermal lesion, single lesion, trunk, arms or legs; lesion diameter 0.6 to 1.0 cm).
Using 2026 RVU values, the total non-facility (NF) RVU of CPT code 99212 is 1.78, the total NF RVU of CPT code 11300 is 2.89, and the total NF RVU of CPT code 11301 is 3.48. Since CPT code 11301 is the highest paid service, CPT code 11301 will be paid at 100 percent (total RVU
(
printed page 71119)
of 3.48), and CPT code 11300 and the payment for CPT code 99212 will both be reduced by 50 percent, CPT code 11300 down to 1.445 RVUs and CPT code 99212 down to 0.89 RVUs.
The 50 percent value aligns with our previous proposal from CY 2019 PFS proposed rule (
83 FR 35840
through
35841
) and matches the longstanding surgical MPPR discussed previously in this section. We welcomed comments on the value of this adjustment, including whether it would be more appropriate to match a different MPPR value, such as 25 percent.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters noted that we proposed but did not finalize this policy for CY 2019. Commenters asked us to explain why we re-proposed this policy for CY 2027, seeking to understand what had changed between 2019 and now. Other commenters had a more general objection, stating that this was the “wrong policy in 2019” and “remains the wrong policy now.”
Many commenters also disagreed with our view that there are existing efficiencies that are currently unaccounted for when an O/O E/M is furnished on the same day as a 0-, 10-, or 90-day global procedure. Many commenters disagreed that we had proven the existence of this overlap, and we received several comments requesting more information on the empiric data CMS used to make this claim. Commenters also stated that the RUC process already takes any overlap into account through the existing process of screening procedures that are furnished with an E/M visit on the same day more than 50 percent of the time. These commenters felt that the RUC process was sufficient and questioned our assertion that it was inadequate. The RUC responded to our claim that the corresponding edits they make to account for overlap are insufficient by asserting that the overlap is small, therefore, the adjustments are accordingly small. Other commenters stated that this proposal was too broad and recommended that we take a more granular code-level approach. Commenters also recommended that we work with the RUC to identify and account for overlap or use other existing processes such as the Potentially Misvalued Code (PMVC) process.
Several commenters supported our proposal. MedPAC noted that they supported this proposal in 2019, and they continue to believe there are efficiencies in providing these services on the same day to the same patient, such as in pre-service and post-service clinician work and practice expense that are not accounted for in the current payment system. They also noted that this policy would have redistributive effects within the PFS, increasing payment rates for many types of services such as primary care and behavioral health services. A few other commenters supported our proposal, with a commenter stating that we struck an appropriate balance between reducing duplicative payment for overlapping services and preserving reimbursement for separately identifiable E/M services that involve additional clinical work beyond what is captured in the procedural payment.
AHIP (America's Health Insurance Plans) provided detailed comments in support of our proposal, citing 2024 Original Medicare claims data which showed that approximately 50 million of the 220 million O/O E/M visits in 2024 were billed with modifier -25, representing approximately $5.7 billion in total Medicare allowed charges. AHIP hypothesized that if one quarter of the resource costs fully overlap with the same resources included in surgical procedures, that would be approximately $1.5 billion in annual Original Medicare PFS payments that are redundant and inappropriate. They went on to emphasize that the potential for redundancy not only extends to physician work and clinical resources, but to indirect practice expense and overhead, which they stated represents approximately 75 percent of the indirect practice expense costs per hour for surgical services. AHIP went on to say that when an E/M visit is performed with a procedure, there is only one professional claim filed, making coding, billing, and revenue cycle management much more efficient, as well as front office staff work and use of the waiting room, exam room, electronic health record, IT equipment, and other administrative costs.
AHIP also discussed that the current methodology that is applied by CMS and the RUC to account for overlap is applied only on a case-by-case basis. The analysis done by AHIP using publicly available RUC documents and the Medicare Carrier 5% standard analytic file dataset indicates that overlap adjustments appear to have only been incorporated into physician time and/or valuation for fewer than 100 global surgical procedures. However, AHIP stated that Medicare claims data indicate that more than 800 procedures are reported with modifier -25 and a same day O/O E/M visit. They went on to state that since this process relies on Original Medicare claims data and a 5% sample of Medicare beneficiaries, this may under-identify overlap associated with newer services, lower-volume procedures, or procedures primarily furnished to non-Medicare populations, and added that this process likely recognizes only a small subset of services impacted and is likely applied inconsistently across the PFS. AHIP also provided a few examples of codes with unaddressed overlap. The first code they cited is CPT code 52000
(Cystourethroscopy (separate procedure)),
which had over 700,000 Original Medicare claims in 2024 and is reported with an E/M service almost half the time. This code was last reviewed by CMS and RUC in the CY 2018 rulemaking cycle, but no overlap was accounted for in physician work time, medical staff and indirect practice expense resources. AHIP also cited CPT code 17261
(Destruction, malignant lesion (eg, laser surgery, electrosurgery, cryosurgery, chemosurgery, surgical curettement), trunk, arms, or legs; lesion diameter 0.6 to 1.0 cm),
which had approximately 130,000 Original Medicare claims in 2024 and occurs with a same-day E/M more than 40 percent of the time. In this code, roughly 30 percent of the procedure's total physician time is pre-service and immediate post-service work, and yet the valuation reflects no overlap adjustment. AHIP also stated that since O/O E/M services are now selected based on either medical decision-making or total practitioner time, it may not always be straightforward for clinicians to distinguish between work attributable to the separately reported E/M service and the work that is already reflected in the procedure's pre-service, intraservice, or post-service valuation, which further supports the need for a systematic approach to overlap adjustments.
AHIP also noted that our proposal would likely improve relativity across services since the current methodology undertaken by the RUC to account for these efficiencies is inconsistent and is not flexible enough to handle individual patient encounters. AHIP also pointed out that for procedures where overlap has already been incorporated into the RVU valuation, providers who furnish the procedure without an associated E/M visit are not receiving payment that reflects the full resources required to perform the service. AHIP agrees with CMS that the code-by-code approach does not fully address the large number of surgical procedures and widespread use of modifier -25.
Response:
We thank all the commenters for their comments. Regarding the presence of overlap
(
printed page 71120)
between O/O E/M visits and global periods, as we stated in the CY 2019 final rule (
83 FR 59640
), “We continue to have significant concerns about the appropriate payment when codes with global periods, especially 0- and 10-day global periods, are billed on the same day as an E/M visit. Generally, we understand that the global codes are valued to include the typical amount of evaluation and management furnished to patients as part of the service.”
We went on to state (
83 FR 59640
), “Although many commenters suggested that the overlapping resource costs between global codes and E/M visits billed on the same day have already been accounted for, we are not persuaded by the statements that the RUC process has achieved this goal, and we agree with MedPAC's assessment of the significant problem with valuation of codes that describe global services. We acknowledge and appreciate the efforts of the RUC to address overlaps when they recognize that a code is usually reported with a same day E/M visit. However, as observers to the RUC process, we have noted a general tendency for the RUC to recommend only minor adjustments in physician time and direct PE inputs to account for overlap. We also often make adjustments to the RUC-recommended valuation in cases where the agency believes there is overlap between services frequently billed together that has not been adequately addressed through the RUC process. More importantly, even if the RUC valuation process better accounted for the overlapping resource costs, those adjustments would be made to national valuation of particular codes based on snapshot, national claims data for a given year, and would apply to all physicians reporting the services regardless of whether or not these particular physicians were achieving the efficiencies that occur when visits are reported on the same day as codes with global periods.”
We believe that these concerns have not been adequately addressed in the intervening years. We note that while the RUC continues to assert that this overlap is accounted for, we did not receive a list of codes from the RUC outlining all codes where the RUC has already accounted for overlap. We have also found no other process to validate which specific codes out of the thousands of global procedures for which overlap has been accounted, beyond individually searching through RUC meeting materials. Regarding the comments asking us for a more empiric analysis or data, we welcome additional information from the public to help inform a process for addressing overlapping resources in the future. Additionally, we welcome feedback from the RUC and others regarding particular codes that may be misvalued for consideration through future rulemaking.
We thank MedPAC for their continued support of this policy, and we agree with MedPAC's assertion that there is still overlap that is unaccounted for, such as in pre- and post-service clinician work and practice expense. We also thank the commenters who noted this policy is meant to strike a balance between allowing these services to occur on the same day while recognizing that there are efficiencies that are not currently recognized.
We appreciate the work and data analysis done by AHIP, and we believe that this analysis further supports our point. We note that the current RUC process to account for overlap is only used when the global code is billed more than 50 percent of the time with an O/O E/M visit with modifier -25 appended. Both of the codes provided by AHIP support this assertion, and we note that both codes are frequently billed with O/O E/M visits, but do not meet the 50 percent threshold. We also note that one of those codes, CPT code 17261, was last reviewed by the RUC in 2010, furthering our point that this piecemeal approach to accounting for overlap code by code relies on a RUC process that is not an accurate representation of the current reality, since it represents decades-old data. In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49335
), we reiterated similar concerns surrounding the delay and piecemeal approach to RUC data when we finalized the efficiency adjustment. We noted that while there is significant variability in how often codes are reviewed by the RUC, we estimated that there is an average of 17.69 years since the last review of a code. This delay also has an impact on accounting for the overlap of O/O E/M services and global procedures, since any overlap that the RUC takes into account only happens when codes are reviewed.
Comment:
We received several comments discussing our proposed application of this policy to services provided by the same physician (or a physician in the same group practice). Commenters representing large multi-specialty group practices and academic medical centers noted that beneficiaries may schedule several appointments the same day with physicians of different specialties, especially if they have to travel for these appointments. Commenters recommended we modify our language to say, “same physician (or a physician in the same specialty in the same group practice).” Another commenter recommended that we limit it only to the services provided by the same physician.
Response:
We thank the commenters for pointing this out, and we agree with them that our intention was not to target services furnished the same day by practitioners of different specialties. We are amending our application of this policy to services furnished by, “the same physician (or a physician in the same specialty in the same group practice).” We note that this is consistent with the Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 12, § 30.6.5—Physicians in Group Practice (Rev. 1, 10-01-03), where, “Physicians in the same group practice who are in the same specialty must bill and be paid as though they were a single physician; physicians in the same group practice but in different specialties may bill and be paid without regard to common group membership.”
Comment:
We received many comments that discussed the potential impact of our proposed 50 percent reduction in reimbursement, describing diminishing operational margins, staffing cuts, and inability to take on more Medicare patients if we finalize a 50 percent payment reduction. Other commenters stated that this policy would have a compounding impact with other reductions in payment such as the CY 2026 PFS final rule efficiency adjustment, declining Medicare conversion factors over the years, and the impact of inflation on costs such as staffing and supplies. We received comments from across the health care industry, including practitioners, health systems, private practices, and clinical and non-clinical support staff describing the potential impacts of this policy. These commenters reported that the impacts of this policy would directly impact their operational capacity to see Medicare patients and reiterated that this policy would have devastating impacts on the beneficiaries that they serve.
Most commenters stated that there was no payment reduction that would be appropriate. A few commenters stated that if a payment reduction was necessary, 25 percent would be an acceptable alternative. Another commenter stated that 50 percent seemed too steep, but that a 20 percent reduction would be more reasonable. A few other commenters stated that if we proceeded with a payment reduction, it should be below 50 percent. While AHIP supported a 50 percent payment reduction, they recommended that we phase in the policy, with a 25 percent
(
printed page 71121)
reduction for CY 2027 and CY 2028, with a 50 percent reduction going into effect for CY 2029 to minimize disruption. Another commenter recommended that we go forward with a 50 percent payment reduction but requested that we create a clear and objective exception process to account for the “limited” circumstances in which a beneficiary requires a separate clinical assessment involving distinct decision-making, evaluation, counseling, or examination that goes beyond the work accounted for in the global procedure. A few commenters including the RUC and the AMA also noted that our 2019 proposal only included 0-day global periods, and they questioned our inclusion of 10- and 90-day global procedures in our proposal this year.
Response:
We are sensitive to the overwhelming response we received from commenters. We are also sensitive to the potential compounding impacts of many different policies across the healthcare system. Our intention with this proposal was to more accurately pay for the relative resource costs involved in furnishing an O/O E/M visit on the same day as a global procedure. We also appreciate the commenters who put forth suggestions for other percentages, such as 25 percent or 20 percent as alternatives, or those who stated it should be below 50 percent. While we acknowledge that the RUC takes overlap into account in some instances, we continue to believe that the RUC's approach is piecemeal and both underestimates the amount of overlap and does not recognize cases in which overlap exists when both codes are billed in conjunction less than 50 percent of the time.
In response to comments, and in acknowledgement of the overlap that has already been accounted for through the limited current RUC process, we are finalizing a 20 percent reduction in payment to all services except the highest value service when an O/O E/M visit is performed on the same day with the same practitioner (or a practitioner of the same specialty in the same group practice) as a service with a 0-day global period. We believe that a 20 percent reduction in payment is both responsive to commenters and strikes a balance between paying more accurately for services performed on the same day and the real-world impact of this policy. We reiterate that our original proposed reduction of 50 percent was based on long-standing MPPR payment reductions for surgical services. However, there are other MPPRs of 25 percent for the Technical Component (TC) of diagnostic cardiovascular services, as well as a 20 percent reduction to the TC for diagnostic ophthalmology, and a 5 percent reduction for the Professional component (PC) of diagnostic imaging. We reiterate that we welcome feedback and collaboration with the RUC and through the existing PMVC process.
Regarding an exception process, we invite feedback through PMVC nominations, and we welcome code specific recommendations from the RUC. Regarding the inclusion of 10- and 90-day global periods in this proposal, commenters are correct that we did not include these periods in the CY 2019 proposal. As we stated in the proposed rule (
91 FR 43908
), we believe overlap exists between any global period and an O/O E/M service performed on the same day for the same patient. We agree with commenters that the resources involved in furnishing a 10- or 90-day global service occur throughout the global period, making the overlap that occurs on just one day of a 10- or 90-day global period more difficult to quantify. We are therefore finalizing this policy to apply only to O/O E/M visits billed on the same day as 0-day global procedures. While we proposed to apply this policy only to O/O E/M visits, we sought comments on whether it should also apply to other E/M visits, such as inpatient E/M visits.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
We received several comments about applying this policy to only O/O E/M visits. A few commenters sought clarification on whether this policy applies to other E/M codes, such as emergency room or critical care codes. Several other commenters asked us not to expand this policy to any other E/M visits, including inpatient E/M visits. A commenter encouraged us to expand this policy to inpatient E/M visits, stating that the overlap that they believe exists in O/O E/M visits also exists in inpatient settings.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback. We reiterate that we are finalizing that this policy only applies when an office/outpatient E/M visit is performed on the same day as a 0-day global procedure.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the application of this policy to O/O E/M codes (CPT codes 99202, 99203, 99204, 99025, 99211, 99212, 99213, 99214, and 99215).
We also reiterate that we do not find it appropriate to schedule medical services for patients to maximize payment, which would create undue burden and potential medical risk for beneficiaries. We have a number of data analysis tools to monitor for potentially problematic utilization patterns which may be useful in the future, if necessary, for monitoring for this practice, including distinct claims editing to identify problematic utilization patterns, comparative billing reports to identify to providers their outlier status, and medical review capabilities to determine if the patterns are problematic and indicative of waste or abuse. We also sought comment on whether or not it is necessary to revise the conditions of payment to mitigate such payment abuses.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
We received many comments stating that this proposal would “require” patients to come back for a second, separately billed visit, as physicians respond to the reduced payment by scheduling the evaluation and the procedure on separate days. A few commenters expressed concern that practices or health systems may put processes in place that prevent practitioners from performing an O/O E/M visit on the same day as a global procedure. Other commenters stated that we were “forcing” practitioners to “choose between our patients and our own financial viability.” We received several comments from beneficiaries that included a copy of a letter or outreach they received from their practitioner or practitioner's office. Others included pictures of letters posted in their doctors' offices. These letters either implied or stated directly that Medicare would no longer pay for same day procedures and that beneficiaries would be forced by Medicare to come back another day.
Many commenters requested that CMS monitor utilization to ensure that beneficiaries were not being brought back to maximize payment. Many commenters stated that requiring beneficiaries to come back another day for a surgical procedure would impose a direct burden on beneficiaries through a second copayment, additional transportation and time away from work, have disproportionate impact on rural and underserved beneficiaries, and added difficulty for those who rely on caregiver support.
However, a supportive commenter refuted the claim of higher cost-sharing, noting that beneficiary cost-sharing would decrease under this proposal since beneficiaries are generally responsible for 20 percent coinsurance, and when overlapping expenses are
(
printed page 71122)
paid separately for the procedure and the E/M visit, beneficiaries incur additional cost even though those services were effectively only used once during the single encounter. This commenter also noted that this policy would support payment accuracy, program integrity, and the prudent stewardship of Medicare resources.
Response:
We would like to clarify that this policy does not prohibit same-day procedures from occurring with an office visit. We see comments received and patient letters that imply a limit on same-day procedures as highly concerning, as we feel that practitioners who are directly misleading their patients are not operating in good faith of the doctor-patient relationship. We would also like to reiterate that we find the possible practice of scheduling medical services to maximize payment problematic. As noted in the proposed rule, we have a number of data analysis tools to monitor for potentially problematic utilization patterns which CMS plans to use to monitor for this practice. These tools include distinct claims editing to identify problematic utilization patterns, comparative billing reports to identify to providers their outlier status, and medical review capabilities to determine if the patterns are problematic and indicative of waste or abuse.
We agree with the commenters who noted that cost-sharing burden would decrease under this policy, and we would like to reiterate that if practitioners bring patients back another day for their procedure, this would actually increase beneficiary cost-sharing.
(c) Intravitreal Eye Injections
We also sought comment on how this policy might apply to an E/M visit reported on the same day as intravitreal eye injection, such as CPT code 67028, a high volume 000-day global code. In recent years, since new injected medications were developed to treat retinal diseases, there has been new focus from auditors (such as the OIG), MACs, professional eye associations and the AMA, to better understand the standard of care for patients receiving these treatments, in terms of when same-day eye examinations are clinically indicated and separately identifiable from the injection procedure, for the injected eye or the fellow eye. We have heard that patients with retinal diseases require examination every one to three months based on their treatment response, and importantly, both eyes are examined at each visit because of the high incidence of bilateral (though often asynchronous) involvement. The associations have written to CMS outside of the rulemaking process, indicating that around 50 percent of the time, a separately reported E/M visit on the same day to examine the eye(s) may be prompted or required by the symptom or condition for which the injection is being provided. The fellow eye could require examination if the patient reports symptoms in that eye when they present for an injection, and same-day exams determine if the type of medication is appropriate and the length of time between injections can be extended.
To help us ensure accurate payment and address questions raised in the most recent OIG audit, we sought to better understand the clinical circumstances involved, and any overlap with resources already accounted for in valuation of the global procedure, such as for (1) established patients without symptoms in the fellow eye; (2) established patients with symptoms in the fellow eye, whether prior or newly reported upon presenting for their injection; (3) new patients; (4) does it vary according to diagnosis and exam findings; (5) are injections in the fellow eye always deferred to another day; and (6) how CMS might be able to confirm or ensure that the visit being reported is significant and separately identifiable absent medical record review, for example, should we expect to see a new or different diagnosis code on the claim. See
https://oig.hhs.gov/​reports/​all/​2025/​medicare-payments-for-evaluation-and-management-services-provided-on-the-same-day-as-eye-injections-were-at-risk-for-noncompliance-with-medicare-requirements/​
.
We also sought to better understand whether the E/M work associated with new patients is typically included in valuation of the minor procedures, or whether there is extra work for new patients that is significant and separately identifiable enough to always warrant separate payment.
Comments:
We received many comments from specialty societies, providers, practitioners and other stakeholders describing the standard of care for patients receiving intravitreal injections, any overlap with resources already accounted for in valuation of the global procedure, and how our proposal to apply an MPPR to same-day visits reported with Modifier 25 on the same day as global procedures might apply to an E/M visit reported on the same day as intravitreal eye injection.
Response:
We appreciate all of the detailed information provided by comments and will consider this information for future rulemaking.
(59) Revisions to Teaching Physician Policy Related to the Primary Care Exception
(a) Background
As a general matter, E/M visit codes under the PFS can only be reported when the care is personally provided by a qualified practitioner. Currently, under the primary care exception described at § 415.174, in the case of certain visit codes of lower and mid-level complexity, Medicare contractors may be able to make PFS payment for a service provided by a resident without the presence of a teaching physician, but in specific outpatient primary care centers and when certain conditions must be met. For example, the teaching physician must direct the care from such proximity as to constitute immediate availability (that is, to effectively provide direct supervision).
During the Public Health Emergency (PHE) for the 2019 Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, CMS allowed through an interim final rule (
85 FR 19230
through
19292
) that all levels of an O/O E/M service provided in specified primary care centers may be provided under supervision of the teaching physician by interactive telecommunications technology (
85 FR 19259
). At the conclusion of the PHE this flexibility expired, such that only lower and mid-level complexity visits (as specified by CMS in program instructions) could be provided without the presence of a teaching physician under the terms specified in § 415.174.
Additionally, in the CY 2020 PFS final rule (
84 FR 62851
through
62854
), E/M visits were revised to allow visits to be based on time and medical decision making. According to our claims data, we note that the most commonly billed O/O E/M visit level is now a moderate level visit (level 4), whereas in the past, a mid-level (level 3) visit was most common.
(b) Revisions to Current Policy
We have received multiple requests from interested parties requesting us to allow residents to perform moderate and high (level 4 and 5) E/M visits under the supervision of the teaching physician and to defer to the clinical judgment of that graduate medical education (GME) program as to whether or not these high level visits may be performed without the presence of the teaching physician.
After consideration and evaluation of interested parties' requests, we proposed that all levels of an O/O E/M service provided in primary care centers, and meeting the requirements in § 415.174, may be provided under direct supervision of the teaching
(
printed page 71123)
physician in such cases where the teaching physician believes such care is clinically appropriate and without the presence of a teaching physician. Specifically, we proposed modifications to the requirements at § 415.174 Exception: Evaluation and management services furnished in certain centers, to expand coverage of services for teaching physicians as part of a graduate medical education (GME) program. We proposed to modify the requirements for certain E/M codes to allow physician fee schedule payment for a service furnished by a resident provided under direct supervision. We proposed to modify paragraph (a) to state that certain evaluation and management codes (as specified by CMS in program instructions), may be paid by the physician fee schedule and are thus proposing to remove the language “of lower and mid-level complexity” to potentially allow for certain moderate and higher-level evaluation and management codes to be billed if the visit meets all the criteria in § 415.174. We proposed § 415.174 (a) to read as follows: “In the case of certain evaluation and management codes (as specified by CMS in program instructions), Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) may make physician fee schedule payment for a service furnished by a resident without the presence of a teaching physician. For the exception to apply, all of the following conditions must be met.”
We believe this proposal would provide some autonomy to residents as well as the teaching physician if the specific GME program would support it. We considered that some visits may take more time in the beginning since residents are still learning and we will continue to monitor the visit levels over time. We welcomed comments on this proposal.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters were overall in support of our proposal that all levels of an office/outpatient E/M service provided in primary care centers, and meeting the requirements in § 415.174, may be provided under direct supervision of the teaching physician in such cases where the teaching physician believes such care is clinically appropriate and without the presence of a teaching physician. Commenters noted this will improve resident training and allow the program to prepare senior residents to practice autonomously. Other commenters noted this policy would discourage inadvertent downcoding driven by billing constraints and would allow teaching physicians to focus their supervision on residents who need the most guidance. Other commenters noted that residents must develop experience caring for patients across the full spectrum and this policy would support that.
Several commenters noted that expanded resident autonomy should be accompanied by maintaining the current safeguards and appropriate oversight and accountability. The commenters stated that teaching physicians must retain ultimate responsibility for patient care and clinical decision-making, and documentation should continue to demonstrate compliance with supervision requirements and continue to clearly identify the respective roles of the resident and teaching physician. Additionally, commenters supported our proposed regulation text change to 42 CFR § 415.174.
We received many comments asking CMS to make other changes to the primary care exception (PCE) to include adding preventive and whole-person services to the PCE, as well as requests to add specific psychotherapy services when billed with specific E/M visits, to update the language that restricts the PCE to services furnished in centers where the residents are being claimed for GME payments by a hospital, and to update the “teaching setting” definition to include Federally Qualified Health Centers. These comments were out of scope for this year's proposal.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support and feedback. We are finalizing as proposed that all levels of an O/O E/M service provided in primary care centers, and meeting the requirements in § 415.174, may be provided under direct supervision of the teaching physician in such cases where the teaching physician believes such care is clinically appropriate and without the presence of a teaching physician. We are also finalizing the proposed changes to 42 CFR § 415.174. We express appreciation for the feedback from commenters on other policies related to the primary care exception and will take the comments into consideration for possible future rulemaking.

(61) Software as a Medical Service (SaMS) Laboratory Analyses
In recent years, there have been rapid developments in the use of software-based technologies with novel functionalities to support clinical decision-making in the outpatient and physician office settings. New clinical software, which includes clinical decision support software, clinical risk modeling, and computer aided detection (CAD), is becoming increasingly available to practitioners. These technologies often perform data analysis of diagnostic images from patients, relying on complex algorithms or statistical predictive modeling to aid in the diagnosis or treatment planning of a patient's condition. In previous rulemaking, we have referred to these algorithm-driven services that assist practitioners in making clinical assessments or diagnoses as Software as a Service (SaaS). Unlike prescription digital therapeutics (PDTs), for example PDTs that provide cognitive behavioral therapy to treat substance disorders or chronic insomnia, SaaS technologies do not currently treat illnesses or patient injuries. SaaS is also separate from remote patient monitoring (RPM) and remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM), which are digital healthcare tools for tracking patient data outside traditional office settings (
90 FR 49394
). For CY 2027, we proposed a change in terminology (
91 FR 43910
). We noted that we now understand that, in other industries, the existing SaaS terminology is used for general cloud-based computing service models outside of a health care context, which may cause confusion as we are using it to describe specific services that provide a medical function for purposes of PFS Medicare payment policy. To dispel any ambiguity and clarify that distinction, we proposed to change our terminology from SaaS to Software as a Medical Service (SaMS) to refer to software-based technologies that support clinical decision making through algorithmic analysis, including those that provide clinical or diagnostic functionality. We welcomed public comments on the proposed change in terminology.
For further discussion of this terminology and other OPPS SaMS proposals, please see the CY 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Final Rule.
We received public comments on our proposed terminology change from SaaS to SaMS. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposed terminology change from SaaS to SaMS. A commenter explained that the proposed terminology would clarify the distinction between clinical algorithms and generic cloud tooling. A commenter requested that we clarify whether the transition to SaMS is intended solely as a naming convention or whether it reflects broader distinctions regarding the scope, classification, valuation or payment treatment of these technologies.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support. The terminology change from SaaS to SaMS seeks to clarify, as a commenter explained, the distinction between clinical algorithms used to furnish these services and generic cloud tooling.
Comment:
Some commenters did not support our proposed terminology change, stating that our proposed definition is too broad, and we should limit SaMS to stand-alone software services that analyze previously generated diagnostic information, excluding services that examine a patient specimen and make a new clinical measurement, or should distinguish between a stand-alone software analysis and software that is an integrated component of a laboratory, imaging, or other diagnostic service. Some commenters requested additional clarifications regarding inclusion and exclusion criteria and how our terminology relates to FDA's Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) or CPT's AI terminology.
Response:
We thank commenters for the additional information. At this time, our aim is to limit our definition of SaMS to refer to software-based technologies that support clinical decision making through algorithmic analysis, including those that provide clinical or diagnostic functionality. This also aligns with the definition and terminology discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS final rule. We note that we will consider these comments as we continue to refine this definition and terminology.
Based on the comments received, for CY 2027, we are finalizing our proposal to change the terminology for these algorithm-based software services that are paid under Medicare from “SaaS” to “SaMS.”
In recent years, we have seen an increase in laboratory tests that combine laboratory analyses, such as genomic sequencing or immunoassays, with computer algorithms to produce a clinical test result. The AMA CPT Editorial Panel created a category called Multi-Analyte Assays with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA's), to categorize test codes that combined laboratory analyses with computer algorithms to generate clinical information. More recently, however, we are seeing the development of distinct algorithmic analyses alone with distinct CPT codes.
For example, when the genomic sequencing of an individual is performed, this sequencing will likely only need to be performed once by a laboratory. However, once the genomic sequence has been generated, the subsequent algorithmic analyses of that sequence data can be performed an infinite number of times to produce a wide range of results and/or diagnostic or risk-related information. These secondary analyses of original genomic sequences can be proprietary and unique to a single laboratory, but could also be conducted at a range of settings. For purposes of this final rule, we are referring to subsequent stand-alone algorithmic analyses as “SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests”.
As discussed in the proposed rule, currently, certain SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are treated as clinical diagnostic laboratory tests (CDLTs) and paid under the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) (
91 FR 43911
). Section 1861(s) of the Act specifies items and services included as “medical and other health services” under Part B, including diagnostic X-ray tests, diagnostic laboratory tests, and other diagnostic tests as described in section 1861(s)(3) of the Act. Sections 1833(h) and 1834A of the Act and the implementing regulations at
42 CFR part 414, subpart G
,
set
forth the CLFS rate setting methodologies for CDLTs. We stated in the proposed rule that we do not believe it is appropriate to consider these secondary algorithmic analyses, when performed alone, to be CDLTs or establish CLFS payment rates for these analyses because we believe these secondary algorithmic analyses may not
(
printed page 71125)
currently require laboratory services or entities, to perform them.
Our position, as stated in the proposed rule, is that the secondary analyses, which have distinct CPT codes,
[
61
]
are “other diagnostic tests” under section 1861(s)(3) of the Act as opposed to “diagnostic laboratory tests.” As noted previously, Medicare will not pay for CDLTs on the CLFS unless they are furnished by laboratories that meet applicable certification requirements. Tests that examine materials derived from the human body are assigned to and paid under the CLFS only when furnished by such certified laboratories, in accordance with
42 CFR 410.32(d)
. Because SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are downstream evaluations of the data generated by a prior laboratory test, which are described by distinct CPT codes, an entity that performs only algorithmic analyses of previously sequenced data may not meet the definition of a “laboratory” under
42 CFR 493.2
or qualify for payment under CLFS. We believe SaMS that evaluate data generated by a prior laboratory test should not be treated as CDLTs for Medicare payment purposes.
As discussed in the proposed rule, we are also concerned that paying for these analyses based on existing CLFS payment methodologies may create significant vulnerabilities for the Medicare program, due to the lack of data transparency and CDLTs not being subject to beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality. Section 414.508 outlines the rate setting methodologies CMS uses to set payment rates for new tests on the CLFS. Under § 414.508(b), CMS determines the payment amount based on either crosswalking or gapfilling methodologies until applicable information is available to establish a payment amount under the methodology described in § 414.507(b). Crosswalking is used if it is determined that a new CDLT is comparable to an existing test, multiple existing test codes, or a portion of an existing test code. Gapfilling is used when no comparable existing CDLT is available. Public consultation for payment for new CDLTs is required in determining payment amounts, receiving public comments and recommendations (and data on which the recommendations are based) as well as recommendations from the Medicare Advisory Panel on CDLTs per 42 CFR § 414.506. A significant challenge to the rate setting process for CMS is in receiving transparent data from laboratories outlining resource costs of a test, particularly for the algorithmic portions of tests that are combined with other analytes. In the past, laboratories have explained to CMS that the algorithmic components of laboratory tests are highly proprietary and details cannot be shared. Thus, CMS has worked with the limited information available on the details of methods or resources for the algorithmic portions of tests or analyses and has thus far relied on the other laboratory methods provided in the CPT descriptor (that is, NGS sequencing, RT-PCR, or DNA methylation analysis). As we have gathered more information on SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, we now believe that since these analyses are entirely computer-based, comparison based on laboratory methodologies is not appropriate. We believe that these analyses are substantially similar to other SaMS already paid under the PFS. Additionally, in contrast to the PFS, the CLFS generally does not include beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality adjustments, which limits transparency regarding pricing and creates challenges for ensuring appropriate valuation of these services.
CMS has an interest in ensuring that services that are fundamentally similar are paid for and treated in the same way, regardless of the setting of care in which the service is furnished. Since we believe SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests perform algorithmic analyses on previously generated data, we believe SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are substantively similar to other SaMS technologies that are currently paid under the PFS. Accordingly, we believe that whether the SaMS performs algorithmic analyses of an imaging test (for example, CT scan) or whether it performs an algorithmic analysis on data generated from a laboratory test, all algorithmic analyses should be treated consistently from a payment perspective. We believe that this approach for SaMS technologies would promote stability and predictability in payment for similar services.
Finally, we note that CMS and CDC issued a Request for Information (RFI) on July 16, 2026, regarding CLIA regulations, the results of which may be used to help inform the agencies as to what types of action, if any, should be taken to update the existing CLIA regulations through future notice and comment and rulemaking (
91 FR 43586
). The RFI closed for comments on September 15, 2026. CMS may refine SaMS payment and policies based on RFI responses and make changes in future rulemaking.
For CY 2027, we proposed to contractor price ten HCPCS codes describing various SaMS analysis performed on laboratory tests under the PFS (
91 FR 43911
). We note that SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests would not require FDA marketing authorization in order to receive payment under the PFS. SaMS payment and policies may be refined in future rulemaking. Table A-D8 in the proposed rule (
91 FR 43912
) shows the list of currently payable SaMS analysis performed on laboratory tests under the CLFS that we proposed to contractor price under the PFS. These ten HCPCS codes were identified by the CPT descriptor for the code. We noted in the proposed rule that, if there were no laboratory methods included in the code descriptor, and only an algorithmic analysis was described, we identified the code as a SaMS laboratory analysis. We referred to the 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Proposed Rule (
91 FR 41918
) for discussion of payment for these services under the OPPS, where we proposed to assign the same SaMS analysis performed on laboratory tests to new technology APCs.
We invited public comment on this proposed list and any other similar analyses that should be removed from the CLFS and contractor priced under the PFS. We sought comment more broadly on other approaches to payment for these services, including, but not limited to, a direct crosswalk to the proposed OPPS new technology APC dollar amounts for all proposed analyses, a subset of these analyses, or specific analyses as opposed to contractor pricing.
In addition, for CY 2027 and subsequent years, we proposed to assign any new codes that describe SaMS analysis performed on a laboratory test to contractor pricing for payment under the PFS. We requested public comment on these proposals, including the list of ten HCPCS codes that we identified as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, as well as any additional HCPCS codes that we should designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and pay under the PFS rather than the CLFS. We stated in the proposed rule that CMS may finalize a policy that includes such payment for additional HCPCS codes in the PFS final rule based on public comment.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
(

Comment:
Some commenters, including large cancer treatment centers, supported our proposal to establish a payment methodology for software-based analyses performed on laboratory tests distinct from the underlying laboratory test. These commenters supported migrating software-based analyses performed on laboratory tests from payment under the CLFS to payment under the PFS and agreed that such analyses are better characterized as “other diagnostic tests.” Commenters added that this policy correctly recognizes algorithmic re-analysis of previously obtained data as a separately payable clinical service. In addition, commenters expressed support for establishing a consistent, cross-setting payment framework for algorithmic analyses, citing that this policy seeks to adapt and evolve with changing healthcare environments. The commenters noted that it is especially critical that this payment policy evolve to reflect the value and resource costs of these technologies.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support and note that we will consider these comments as we continue to refine this payment policy.
Comment:
Some commenters, including independent laboratories, supported our proposal but requested that CMS develop the payment methodology transparently, and ensure the payment for algorithm-driven services rests on evidence of clinical benefit. Commenters requested that CMS establish a payment mechanism for these services when the patient is seen in a place of service not paid under the PFS, noting that as proposed, the framework would leave no payment mechanism for a substantial share of medically necessary testing. Commenters requested CMS establish a defined, confidential process through which laboratories may submit cost and clinical outcomes data to support valuation as CMS develops a more comprehensive payment methodology. One commenter supported the proposal but requested that CMS defer changes to CLFS payment for algorithm-only laboratory analyses until the necessary coding, regulatory, and operational infrastructure has been established.
Response:
CMS appreciates the suggestion to be transparent and thoughtful in the implementation of this policy. We believe that publicly proposing this policy in the proposed rule, inviting comments, and addressing those comments in this rule has made this process transparent. We also appreciate the recommendation to evaluate the clinical benefit of a given SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We remind readers that our goal in this rulemaking cycle is to establish the category of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and the general payment mechanism for those services under the PFS. Regarding a request to establish a separate confidential process through which laboratories may submit cost and clinical data, we remind commenters that we are available to meet with interested parties where information may be shared with CMS. However, because payment rates are finalized through the notice-and-comment rulemaking process, which requires providing the underlying reasoning for our proposals and final policy, establishing a separate confidential process would not be compatible with the existing rulemaking process. Further, finalizing this policy would not eliminate Medicare payment for these services, or prohibit certain facilities from billing Medicare, but rather, it would define how these services would be paid under the PFS. We do not believe that it is appropriate to delay the movement of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests from the CLFS to the PFS, given the speed at which SaMS technologies are developing and the goal of having a consistent policy across payment systems for similar services. These similar algorithm-based services will be billed and paid for under the same payment system, depending on the hospital or physician setting (that is, OPPS or PFS).
Comment:
A few commenters, specifically large laboratory associations, requested that we not finalize the policy as proposed. Commenters generally believed that CMS should engage with the laboratory community more closely prior to finalizing payment changes for SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. Commenters specifically expressed concerns that the proposed policy could inadvertently create duplicate or inconsistent payment pathways and fragment integrated laboratory services by separating algorithmic analyses from the laboratory responsible for validation, quality, clinical interpretation, and reporting. Several commenters expressed concerns regarding the implications of introducing beneficiary cost sharing for services that generally are not subject to cost sharing under the CLFS if this policy were to be finalized. Some commenters explained that, if CMS is concerned about unregulated software vendors billing Medicare, CMS should condition Medicare payment for designated SaMS laboratory services on performance by a CLIA-certified, appropriately accredited laboratory.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' concerns and we will continue to consider them while we implement the policy. Regarding cost sharing, we acknowledge that while cost sharing shifts some costs to beneficiaries, it also encourages greater efficiency by health care providers and more economical delivery of medically necessary items and services, which would contain unnecessary growth in Medicare spending long-term to the benefit of both Medicare and beneficiaries.
We disagree with concerns that this final policy would fragment integrated laboratory services, as this policy would apply to HCPCS codes that already recognize a distinct SaMS analysis component. To ensure that this policy only impacts HCPCS codes describing the secondary analyses, we requested public comment on the list of HCPCS codes we proposed to designate as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. As discussed further in this section, based on public comments received, PFS payment for HCPCS codes describing integrated services, meaning those codes that describe both the wet lab and SaMS secondary analyses, is not being finalized under this policy for CY 2027. These HCPCS codes would continue to be paid under the CLFS.
Concerns about billing and regulations regarding vendors of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are outside of the scope of this final rule.
While we understand the commenters' concerns, we believe that the proposed policy provides a uniform payment pathway for SaMS that should be implemented for CY 2027. We continue to maintain that paying for SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests under the CLFS may create significant vulnerabilities for the Medicare program, due to the challenges in receiving transparent data regarding the algorithms themselves and CDLTs on the CLFS generally not being subject to beneficiary cost-sharing or budget neutrality. As mentioned previously, we believe SaMS technologies generally should be treated and paid for consistently across the Medicare program because these algorithm-based services are functionally equivalent, despite differences in the type of clinical service or data. For example, both SaMS currently paid under the OPPS and the SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests that we proposed to pay for under PFS perform algorithm-based analyses on existing data. We anticipate that resource costs may be
(
printed page 71127)
similar between these kinds of services. For SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests, paying for these services under the PFS means similar algorithm-based services will be billed and paid for under the same payment system. We will continue to engage the broader laboratory community in further dialogue as we consider potential refinements to this policy in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Some commenters, especially large laboratory associations, asked CMS to not finalize its proposal to reassign SaMS analyses performed on prior laboratory tests to the PFS and to continue paying for these services as CDLTs on the CLFS. A few commenters urged CMS to exempt current and future software-based laboratory tests from this proposed policy and only designate the proposed tests as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests.
Response:
CMS appreciates these comments but believes it is important for SaMS-based technologies to be treated consistently across the Medicare program, rather than establishing distinct payment policies for similar SaMS, depending on whether the analysis is performed on an imaging service or on a laboratory test.
Comment:
Commenters generally expressed concern that the proposed framework to distinguish SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests from other laboratory tests would be challenging to apply in practice. Commenters stated that these services have generally been classified and paid as CDLTs under the CLFS, reflecting longstanding treatment from CMS, the AMA CPT process, and the FDA. Commenters expressed concern regarding using CPT code descriptors to determine which HCPCS codes should be designated as a SaMS analyses performed on a laboratory test since descriptors do not always indicate whether activities, such as slide preparation or immunostaining, are included in the reported service. Commenters explained that although SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests are defined as being both separate from specimen examination and entirely computer-based, several of the examples CMS identified appear to involve wet lab components, creating uncertainty regarding how the criteria would be operationalized, and that as a result, interested parties may face difficulty determining whether a given service qualifies as a purely algorithmic analysis or should continue to be treated as a laboratory test incorporating wet lab processes. Commenters requested that CMS provide additional guidance and examples to support consistent classification and payment for these services.
Response:
Medicare utilizes the description of services as provided by the HCPCS code descriptors in determining appropriate payment.- For the proposed policy, we identified services listed on the CLFS that indicated algorithmic analysis in the CPT long descriptor and in the description of intraservice work (as provided by AMA in its valuation of CPT codes) and proposed to treat those services as SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. Specifically, we considered code descriptors that included phrases such as “augmentative algorithmic analysis” or “previously established sequence,” as we believed that these indicated that the code described SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests. We requested public comments on the proposed list of codes, understanding that we may have inadvertently omitted certain codes or included codes that do not solely describe subsequent, computer-based analyses as intended.
We appreciate the comments regarding the proposed list of codes. In this final rule, we have removed a few HCPCS codes from the proposed list, based on an additional understanding of the code descriptors and public comments received, but we retained the HCPCS codes that contained phrases such as “augmentative algorithmic analysis” or “previously established sequence”, which we discuss in further detail later in this section. We believe that the finalized list of HCPCS codes being reassigned from the CLFS to the PFS is limited to those that are entirely computer-based secondary analyses and do not include specimen examination performed as part of the wet lab component.
Comment:
Commenters requested that CMS incorporate additional specificity into the SaMS definition to ensure that technologies and services with meaningful differences, such as algorithm-only laboratory-developed tests, laboratory Software as a Medical Device, and imaging Software as a Medical Device, are not treated as equivalent for payment purposes. A commenter proposed that CMS limit the services included in this policy to algorithmic reanalysis of a prior laboratory test's reported results, and exclude any service that examines a patient's specimen, physical or digitized, or that measures a defined analyte from that specimen.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' input. We remind readers that our goal in this rulemaking cycle is to establish the category of SaMS analyses performed on laboratory tests and the general payment mechanism for those services under the PFS, noting that payment alignment is a priority for these technologies. We will take the definitional concerns raised by the commenters, including incorporating additional specificity regarding differences in SaMS service for purposes of Medicare payment, into consideration for future rulemaking. We welcome public engagement from interested parties on these issues, including whether there are additional services that should be designated as SaMS in the future.
Comment:
Some commenters, particularly large laboratory associations, disagreed with the premise underlying our proposal, explaining that the diagnostic testing process as a whole, not the physical location where the final computational step occurs, is what defines a CDLT. These commenters did not agree that the absence of a new wet-lab step converts a patient-specific computational analysis of laboratory-derived data into something other than laboratory testing and argued that treating the final analytical step as severable from the laboratory service that produced the underlying data misconstrues how these tests are developed, validated, and clinically interpreted. Relatedly, these commenters requested that CMS confirm in the final rule that a test incorporating a laboratory assay measuring an analyte from the specimen remains a CDLT paid under the CLFS, and that specimen preparation, staining, and digitization are not the “prior laboratory test” on which SaMS designation depends.
Response:
We disagree with these commenters that the location of the final analytical step is immaterial to the payment classification of these services. While we recognize that the underlying specimen collection, sequencing, or other data-generating steps may require laboratory services, the algorithmic analysis at issue here is a separate step that is performed on data that has already been generated, and may not necessarily require access to the specimen or laboratory equipment. The fact that a service has historically been billed and paid as a single, integrated CDLT on the CLFS does not mean that each component of that service must continue to be paid as such, particularly where the analytical component is distinguishable from the data-generating component as provided by the HCPCS code descriptor, both in the resources required to perform it and in the manner in which its costs are incurred. Accordingly, we are finalizing our
(
printed page 71128)
proposal to treat the algorithmic analysis as an “other diagnostic test” under section 1861(s)(3) of the Act distinct from the underlying laboratory test for purposes of PFS payment. We will take the definitional concerns regarding SaMS into consideration for future rulemaking.

Commenters noted that the proposal could be read to create ambiguity on this point, and requested that CMS include the following clarifying statement in the final rule: that algorithmic interpretation of specimen-derived pathology data, performed within or under arrangement with a CLIA-certified laboratory, remains subject to CLIA.
Response:
This policy does not seek to make changes to the requirements governing CLIA-certified laboratories. We consider these algorithmic analyses as “other diagnostic tests” that are performed on an underlying laboratory test. This policy seeks to provide consistency in paying for all SaMS algorithmic analyses in the PFS. Comment:
While we proposed contractor pricing in the proposed rule, many commenters did not support the proposal to contractor price these services, as they stated they did not believe these services have different costs in different Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) geographic jurisdictions and that this proposal would place additional burden on MACs. Other commenters asserted that contractor pricing these services would lead to less payment predictability than when they were paid for as CDLTs under the CLFS. Some commenters requested that we crosswalk the PFS payment for these services to the OPPS payment rates, as the OPPS payment rates are using current CLFS payment rates to inform their pricing, in order to encourage site-neutral pricing between payment systems. A few commenters requested that, if contractor pricing is finalized, we communicate with MACs to encourage a published uniform national methodology, so that beneficiary access does not depend on jurisdiction. Some commenters did not agree with our proposal to assign any new codes that describe SaMS analysis performed on a laboratory test to contractor pricing for payment under the PFS in subsequent years.
Response:
We thank commenters for the additional information. As discussed in the CY 2027 OPPS Final Rule, this is a first step towards a more comprehensive payment policy. We agree with commenters that contractor pricing these services could lead to less payment predictability than when they were paid for as CDLTs under the CLFS, as contractor priced services could vary between MACs. We agree with commenters that a more predictable payment methodology would be crosswalking OPPS payment rates for these services, as they are using CY 2026 CLFS payment rates to inform their pricing. This payment methodology would also encourage site-neutral pricing between payment systems, which could encourage providers to choose the most clinically appropriate setting based on patient needs rather than financial incentives. Therefore, we are finalizing national pricing for these services under the PFS for CY 2027, based on a crosswalk to the OPPS payment rates.
