4. Potentially Misvalued Services Under the PFS
a. Background
Section 1848(c)(2)(B) of the Act directs the Secretary to conduct a periodic review, not less often than every 5 years, of the relative value units (RVUs) established under the PFS. Section 1848(c)(2)(K) of the Act requires the Secretary to periodically identify potentially misvalued services using certain criteria and to review and make appropriate adjustments to the relative values for those services. Section 1848(c)(2)(L) of the Act also requires the Secretary to develop a process to validate the RVUs of certain potentially misvalued codes (PMVC) under the PFS, using the same criteria used to identify PMVC, and to make appropriate adjustments.
As outlined in section II.D. of this final rule, under Valuation of Specific Codes, each year we develop appropriate adjustments to the RVUs taking into account recommendations provided by the American Medical Association (AMA)/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale (RVS) Update Committee (referred to as the RUC), MedPAC, and other interested parties. For many years, the RUC has provided us with recommendations on the appropriate relative values for new, revised, and potentially misvalued PFS services. We review these recommendations on a code-by-code basis and consider these recommendations in conjunction with analyses of other data, such as claims data, to inform the decision-making process as authorized by statute. We may also consider analyses of work time, work RVUs, or direct practice expense (PE) inputs using other data sources, such as the Veterans Health Administration (VHA), National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP), the Society for Thoracic Surgeons (STS), and the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) data. In addition to considering the most recent available data, we assessed the results of physician surveys and specialty recommendations submitted to us by the RUC for our review. We also consider information provided by other interested parties such as from the general medical-related community and the public. We conduct a review to assess the appropriate RVUs in the context of contemporary medical practice. We noted in the proposed rule that section 1848(c)(2)(A)(ii) of the Act authorizes the use of extrapolation and other techniques to determine the RVUs for physicians' services for which specific data are not available and requires us to take into account the results of consultations with organizations representing physicians who provide the services. In accordance with section 1848(c) of the Act, we determine and make appropriate adjustments to the RVUs.
In its March 2006 Report to the Congress (
https://www.medpac.gov/​document/​report-to-the-congress-2006-medicare-payment-policy/​
), MedPAC discussed the importance of appropriately valuing physicians' services, stating that misvalued services can distort the market for physicians' services, as well as for other health care services that physicians order, such as hospital services. In that same report, MedPAC postulated that physicians' services under the PFS can become misvalued over time. MedPAC stated, “When a new service is added to the physician fee schedule, it may be assigned a relatively high value because of the time, technical skill, and psychological stress that are often required to furnish that service. Over time, the work required for certain services would be expected to decline as physicians become more familiar with the service and more efficient in furnishing it.” We believe services can also become overvalued when PE costs decline. This can happen when the costs of equipment and supplies fall, or when equipment is used more frequently than is estimated in the PE methodology, reducing its cost per use. Likewise, services can become undervalued when physician work increases, or PE costs rise.
As MedPAC noted in its March 2009 Report to Congress (
https://www.medpac.gov/​docs/​default-source/​reports/​march-2009-report-to-congress-medicare-payment-policy.pdf
), in the intervening years since MedPAC made the initial recommendations, CMS and the RUC have taken several steps to improve the review process. Also, section 1848(c)(2)(K)(ii) of the Act augments our efforts by directing the Secretary to specifically examine, as determined appropriate, potentially misvalued services in the following categories:
Codes that have experienced the fastest growth.
Codes that have experienced substantial changes in PE.
Codes that describe new technologies or services within an appropriate time-period (such as 3 years) after the relative values are initially established for such codes.
Codes which are multiple codes that are frequently billed in conjunction with furnishing a single service.
Codes with low relative values, particularly those that are often billed multiple times for a single treatment.
Codes that have not been subject to review since implementation of the fee schedule.
Codes that account for the majority of spending under the PFS.
Codes for services that have experienced a substantial change in the hospital length of stay or procedure time.
Codes for which there may be a change in the typical site of service since the code was last valued.
Codes for which there is a significant difference in payment for the same service between different sites of service.
Codes for which there may be anomalies in relative values within a family of codes.
Codes for services where there may be efficiencies when a service is furnished at the same time as other services.
Codes with high intraservice work per unit of time.
Codes with high PE RVUs.
Codes with high-cost supplies.
Codes as determined appropriate by the Secretary.
Section 1848(c)(2)(K)(iii) of the Act also specifies that the Secretary may use existing processes to receive recommendations on the review and appropriate adjustment of potentially misvalued services. In addition, the Secretary may conduct surveys, other data collection activities, studies, or other analyses, as the Secretary determines to be appropriate, to facilitate the review and appropriate adjustment of potentially misvalued services. This section also authorizes the use of analytic contractors to identify and analyze potentially misvalued codes, conduct surveys or collect data, and make recommendations on the review and appropriate adjustment of potentially misvalued services. Additionally, this section provides that the Secretary may coordinate the review and adjustment of any RVU with the periodic review described in section 1848(c)(2)(B) of the Act. Section 1848(c)(2)(K)(iii)(V) of the Act specifies that the Secretary may make appropriate coding revisions (including using current processes for consideration of coding changes), which may involve consolidating individual services into bundled codes for payment under the PFS.

Analyses of work time, work RVU, or direct PE inputs using other data sources (for example, VA, NSQIP, the STS National Database, and the MIPS data).
National surveys of work time and intensity from professional and management societies and organizations, such as hospital associations.
We evaluate the supporting documentation submitted with the nominated codes and assess whether the nominated codes appear to be PMVC appropriate for review under the annual process. (7) Hyperbaric Oxygen Under Pressure (HCPCS Code G0277)
The RUC has requested the deletion of HCPCS code G0277
(Hyperbaric oxygen under pressure, full body chamber, per 30-minute interval),
and recommended that CPT code 99183 be revised to be time-based as well to appropriately describe the treatment delivery, attendance and supervision. The RUC concluded that maintaining a separate G-code creates unnecessary coding complexity without adding clinical or administrative value and that one clear and consistent coding structure should exist for this service.
In 2015, CMS created HCPCS code G0277 to describe direct practice expense inputs associated with CPT code 99183
(Physician or other qualified health care professional attendance and supervision of hyperbaric oxygen therapy, per session).
We noted that under the Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS), the treatment used to be reported using separate treatment code C1300
(Hyperbaric oxygen under pressure, full body chamber, per 30-minute interval.)
Therefore, we created HCPCS code G0277 to report the treatment delivery and to maintain consistency with the OPPS coding and PFS payment systems.
HCPCS code G0277 was identified as a high-volume growth code that has Medicare utilization of 10,000 or more. High utilization of this magnitude reflects that the code has been broadly adopted across multiple care settings and underscores its operational importance within the Medicare program. Deleting or replacing a high-volume code without an equivalent can disrupt billing practices, create reporting gaps, and impose unnecessary administrative burden on providers who have integrated it into their standard practice. As such, we believe there is a reason to continue to maintain the use of the G-code for hyperbaric oxygen therapy since HCPCS code G0277 is utilized in multiple Medicare payment systems to report the time the patient uses the hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Accordingly, we proposed to maintain HCPCS code G0277.
Comment:
Several commenters opposed the AMA RUC's recommendation to crosswalk HCPCS code G0277's direct practice expense (PE) inputs into CPT code 99183 (multiplied by a factor of 4) and delete G0277. These commenters supported CMS's proposal to retain HCPCS code G0277 as a distinct code and preserve separate reporting of CPT code 99183 and HCPCS code G0277. Commenters stated that the two-code structure accurately reflects physician work and treatment-delivery costs as separate resources.
Commenters stated that CPT code 99183 and HCPCS code G0277 describe clinically and operationally distinct services. They explained that CPT code 99183 describes physician attendance and supervision during hyperbaric oxygen therapy, while HCPCS code G0277 describes the resources required to deliver the treatment itself, including the hyperbaric chamber, oxygen-delivery and monitoring systems, trained ancillary staff, and associated safety and maintenance requirements. A commenter stated that physicians who report HCPCS code G0277 understand the existing distinction between HCPCS code G0277 and CPT code 99183, and that deleting HCPCS code G0277 and revising CPT code 99183 would introduce confusion into an area of billing that functions appropriately under the current structure.
Commenters further stated that because HCPCS code G0277 is a HCPCS code rather than a CPT code, the RUC referred CPT code 99183 to the CPT Editorial Panel for possible revision. Commenters explained that the RUC's current recommendation to convert CPT code 99183 into a time-based code incorporating delivery, attendance, and supervision would require either incorporating multiple 30-minute PE segments into CPT code 99183 or substantially redefining the code, neither of which has been adopted through the CPT process. Commenters stated that this approach would also increase administrative burden for small, office-based practices.
Several commenters stated that similar coding changes have previously caused Medicare and commercial payment disruption, citing extended Medicare prepayment review and delayed commercial payer adoption following implementation of HCPCS code G0277 in 2015. Commenters stated
(
printed page 71164)
that consolidating HCPCS code G0277 into CPT code 99183 could result in comparable disruption.
Many commenters recommended that CMS retain HCPCS code G0277 as a distinct code, preserve separate reporting of CPT code 99183 and HCPCS code G0277, reject the RUC's recommended crosswalk and deletion of HCPCS code G0277, continue to evaluate physician work and treatment-delivery resources independently, and evaluate the effects of any future restructuring across all applicable sites of service.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback and support of retaining CPT code 99183 and HCPCS code G0277 as two distinct codes. We agree that the two codes reflect distinct components of care.
Comment:
The RUC stated that the CY 2026 proposed rule did not adopt the RUC's earlier recommendation to establish direct practice expense (PE) inputs for CPT code 99183 or to delete HCPCS code G0277. The RUC reiterated its recommendation that CMS crosswalk the January 2023 direct PE inputs for HCPCS code G0277 to CPT code 99183, multiplied by a factor of four to reflect a full two-hour treatment session, and that CMS delete HCPCS code G0277 on the basis that CPT code 99183, once revalued, could appropriately account for the service.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their feedback. However, we continue to believe that two codes represent separate components of care. We also note that HCPCS code G0277 has high utilization and broad adoption across care settings. Deleting such a high-volume code without an appropriate equivalent can disrupt billing practices, creating reporting gaps and imposing an unnecessary administrative burden on providers.
Comment:
A commenter took no position on CMS's proposal to retain HCPCS code G0277 or the RUC's recommendation to delete it and revise CPT code 99183. The commenter instead urged CMS to continue collaborating with the RUC and affected specialty societies to develop a coding structure that accurately reflects the service while avoiding duplication and administrative complexity.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback.
After consideration of the public comments, we continue to believe the existing coding structure, which distinguishes professional attendance and supervision (CPT code 99183) from treatment-delivery resources (HCPCS code G0277), remains appropriate and should be maintained. Therefore, for CY 2027, we are finalizing the proposal to maintain HCPCS code G0277 as a distinct code and to preserve separate reporting of CPT code 99183 and HCPCS code G0277.
(8) Image-Guided Robotic Linear Accelerator Stereotactic Radiosurgery (HCPCS Codes G0339 and G0340)
Image-guided robotic linear accelerator-based stereotactic radiosurgery services are currently reported by and paid for using HCPCS G-codes established the in CY 2007 PFS final rule HCPCS codes G0339
(Image-guided robotic linear accelerator-based stereotactic radiosurgery, complete course of therapy in one session or first session of fractionated treatment)
and G0340
(Image-guided robotic linear accelerator-based stereotactic radiosurgery, delivery including collimator changes and custom plugging, fractionated treatment, all lesions, per session, second through fifth sessions, maximum five sessions per course of treatment)
. In April 2025, the RAW identified HCPCS code G0340 with 2023 Medicare utilization over 10,000 and Medicare status of “C” contractor priced. The Workgroup requested an action plan for G0340 for September 2025. In September 2025, the Workgroup reviewed the action plan and recommended that the RUC request that CMS delete G0339 and G0340 having identified a CPT code 77373 (
Stereotactic body radiation therapy, treatment delivery, per fraction to 1 or more lesions, including image guidance, entire course not to exceed 5 fractions)
that is available to report in lieu of G0339 and G0340.
A review of Medicare claims data shows that HCPCS codes G0339 and G0340 are billed frequently. HCPCS code G0339 was billed approximately 3,000 times and HCPCS code G0340 12,000 times in 2024 respectively. As such, we believe there is a reason to maintain the G codes for image-guided robotic linear accelerator-based stereotactic radiosurgery services since both sets of codes are billed so frequently, and we do not want to cause disruption in billing practice. Since the RUC planned on reviewing these codes during its September 2026 meeting if the codes are not deleted for CY 2027, we welcomed the RUC's additional information regarding appropriate coding and payment for these services.
Comment:
The RUC recommended that CMS delete HCPCS codes G0339 and G0340 for CY 2027 rather than maintain them. The commenter stated that only 17 centers in 11 states currently offer robotic radiosurgery, and that of 234 physicians who reported these codes in 2023, 68 no longer offer the service and 20 have retired. The RUC further noted that CMS's own provider-and-service data show only 68 practice locations billed HCPCS code G0339 and only 96 billed HCPCS code G0340 in 2024, notwithstanding the higher claims-line counts cited in the proposed rule. The commenter argued this indicates the affected provider population is small and identifiable, such that requiring these practices to report existing CPT code 77373 in lieu of the G-codes would not impose material burden, and would promote uniform payment across all stereotactic body radiation therapy modalities. The commenter indicated the RAW would review action plans for both codes again at its September 2026 meeting to further support deletion.
Other commenters, including a specialty society representing radiation oncology professionals, supported continued use of the G-codes in the near term but urged CMS to treat the coding question as secondary to a broader valuation concern. These commenters stated that stereotactic radiosurgery and stereotactic body radiation therapy share capital-intensive and infrastructure-dependent characteristics with other radiation treatment delivery services for which we have already adopted OPPS-informed practice expense methodologies (for example, CPT codes 77402, 77407, and 77412, and proposed proton beam delivery codes). These commenters recommended that, rather than resolving valuation through the G-code deletion question alone, CMS link SRS/SBRT services to OPPS data beginning January 1, 2028, consistent with the stated rationale for adopting alternative PE methodologies for other radiation oncology services that do not fit the standard non-facility PE framework.
An individual commenter, a practicing radiation oncologist, did not comment specifically on the coding treatment of HCPCS codes G0339 and G0340, but urged CMS broadly to avoid payment reductions affecting stereotactic body radiation therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery services. The commenter stated that these modalities allow patients, including those in rural areas, to complete treatment in as few as five sessions rather than a longer conventional course, and that reduced payment for the planning, physics, and management services supporting these modalities could jeopardize access to this care.
Response:
We acknowledge the RUC's data showing that utilization of HCPCS codes G0339 and G0340 is concentrated among a limited number of practice
(
printed page 71165)
locations (68 and 96, respectively, in 2024). However, we continue to place significant weight on the high overall claims volume associated with these codes—approximately 3,000 claims for HCPCS code G0339 and over 12,000 claims for HCPCS code G0340 in 2024—which indicates that these services remain a frequently furnished and clinically significant component of radiation oncology care for Medicare beneficiaries, even though they are billed by a comparatively small number of sites. We are concerned that deleting high-volume codes without a transition period could disrupt billing practices, create reporting gaps, and impose administrative burden on the providers who have integrated them into standard practice, regardless of how many distinct locations are affected. We are therefore not finalizing deletion of HCPCS codes G0339 and G0340 for CY 2027.
Comment:
A commenter was concerned about the broader importance of maintaining adequate payment for the planning, physics, and management services that support stereotactic body radiation therapy and stereotactic radiosurgery, including the role these modalities play in enabling shorter courses of treatment for patients in rural and underserved areas.
Response:
While this comment did not address the coding treatment of HCPCS codes G0339 and G0340 specifically, we considered it alongside the broader comments regarding valuation methodology for these services. We will consider any future recommendations, together with the high utilization of these codes and the comments on OPPS-informed valuation methodology for SRS/SBRT services, in future rulemaking.

The nominator provided evidence that current physician work time values in the PFS do not accurately reflect real-world clinical practice for 13 CPT codes across five code families. Their methodology focused on codes involving large discrepancies between empirically derived intraservice estimates and intraservice times assigned in the PFS. The nominator did not assert that their research provided confirmatory evidence for every intraservice time discrepancy, which is why their analysis focused on coding families related to the 13 CPT codes listed previously (Table A-D14). They provided additional details on their findings related to the 13 CPT codes and other codes included in their coding families in this section.
Using the 2023 Maryland All-Payer Claims Database (MD-APCD), the nominator's analysis indicates that some of these codes are likely to be overvalued. In their nomination, their analysis reveals that the 88305 (Level IV Tissue Exam by Pathologist) code had the highest number of provider days with intraservice time exceeding an 8-hour workday, with more than 1,763 days, which was significantly higher than the other 12 CPT codes. For these 1,763 days, when they added up the total time spent on services (including other codes billed in a day, and pre-services times as well), the average time that services were billed for during these days was 2,217 minutes (approximately 37 hours). In the proposal rule, we stated that we appreciated the detailed information provided to us by external interested parties and welcomed comments from the public regarding any potential actions for CY 2027 or for future rulemaking. We acknowledged the limitations associated with NSQIP data in terms of its applicability to other settings, as it is representative of the hospital setting, however we believe this empirical data may be a better input than limited survey data. Comment:
The RUC and many commenters requested that CMS not rely on data from the Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC). The RUC noted that 5 of the 13 codes do not warrant further action: CPT codes 37227 and 37229 were deleted for CY 2026, and CPT codes 23472, 27130, and 27447 were resurveyed for CY 2027 with RUC-recommended decreases to physician time, work RVUs, and post-operative visits, as reflected elsewhere in this final rule. The RUC raised concerns about the reliability of the MHCC methodology, including limited sample size, failure to account for specialty-specific billing patterns, and use of claims data that may not reflect actual physician work time. Commenters requested that CMS not rely on this data and, if CMS proceeds with review, that we defer action on the remaining 8 codes to the CY 2028 PFS rulemaking cycle.
Many commenters urged CMS not to revalue these codes based on data from the MHCC, and instead to refer any valuation question to the RUC process. First, they stated that MHCC's methodology was flawed (for example, it mistakenly assumes the billed date equals the date the physician actually performed the work). Second, they stated that only about 2.9% of CPT code 88305 provider-days exceeded MHCC's 8-hour threshold, which is not typical. Also, multiple commenters stated that the 2016 Urban Institute pilot study's 2-minute time estimate for CPT code 88305 (versus the current 25-minute PFS value) relied on a convenience sample. Many commenters noted that a pure time-based claims analysis misses the real intensity of the pathology work.
A couple of commenters supported the use of empirical, claims-based data to revalue potentially misvalued codes. A commenter stated that such data are more reliable than survey data submitted through the RUC process, and recommended that CMS collect such data on an ongoing basis rather than through isolated or one-time efforts. Another commenter recommended that CMS adopt empirically derived operative times from the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (NSQIP) in place of current PFS time estimates when valuing potentially misvalued codes, noting that NSQIP data, while skewed toward complex cases at academic medical centers, offer a more reliable empirical basis and a more gradual transition than other data sources. This commenter further recommended that CMS evaluate and revalue entire families of related codes, rather than individual codes in isolation, to avoid rank-order anomalies and unintended distortions in clinical practice. Finally, the commenter re-examined Maryland's all-payer claims database and found that the discrepancy
(
printed page 71167)
persisted, confirming its statement that CPT code 88305 is overvalued. Given this result, the commenter reiterated its recommendation that CMS adopt the Urban Institute's empirically derived intraservice time of 2 minutes.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback, and we appreciate the commenter's follow-up analysis regarding CPT code 88305. The majority of commenters opposed this approach to revaluing the potentially misvalued codes using empirical data and recommended referring any valuation questions to the RUC process. We must also note a range of concerns about using empirical data for revaluation, including the representativeness of the underlying data sources, the methodology used to translate empirical data into revised time and work values, and the potential effects of the proposed changes on affected specialties and on beneficiary access to care.
After considering public comments, we are neither revaluing the cited codes based on the empirical data provided nor finalizing any changes to these codes. However, we may take these comments into consideration in future rulemaking and welcome additional studies and data submissions on this topic.
(10) Request for Reassessment of Assigned RVUs for “Harvard-Valued” Codes (CPT Codes 24515, 22216, 22210, 64721, 29824, 20610, and 20680)
We received notification from concerned interested parties about the “Harvard-valued” codes from 1992 that have not undergone a reassessment of assigned RVUs for over 20 years in some cases (see Table A-D15). We share their concerns about whether the current values for the CPT codes accurately reflect the resource inputs associated with furnishing the services. Because the CPT codes have not been recently reviewed and potentially significant technological changes have occurred during this time, we proposed these CPT codes as potentially misvalued and requested that the RUC and other interested parties review these services in terms of appropriate work RVUs, work time assumptions and direct PE inputs.
Comment:
The majority of commenters, including the RUC and several specialty societies, disputed the factual basis for including these codes on the list of potentially misvalued services. Commenters stated that seven of the eight identified codes have, in fact, been surveyed and revalued by the RUC subsequent to the original 1992 Harvard valuation, in some instances as recently as the January 2026 RUC meeting, and provided documentation of survey dates and corresponding rule cycles for each code. A commenter noted that CPT code 29824 was created in 2002, a decade after implementation of the Harvard-based RBRVS and therefore cannot reflect an unrevised Harvard value. Commenters stated they were unable to identify a rationale supporting the nomination because the nomination letter was not included in the public use files accompanying the proposed rule. Commenters requested that we remove these codes from consideration as potentially misvalued.
Another commenter representing urologic surgeons did not dispute that certain services within this category may warrant review, but expressed concern regarding the methodology by which any resulting revaluation would occur. The commenter stated that changes in surgical technique, particularly the adoption of minimally invasive approaches, have altered physician work in more than one direction simultaneously, reducing intraoperative time in some cases while increasing equipment complexity, intraoperative decision-making, and preoperative optimization associated with treating an older and more medically complex patient population. The commenter recommended that CMS rely on specialty society input and published survey data before proposing any revised values, rather than assuming that a reduction in operative time corresponds to a proportional reduction in physician work. An additional commenter supported the inclusion of long-unreviewed 1992-era codes for reassessment and recommended that CMS extend the same reasoning to legacy gynecologic surgical codes of comparable age, which the commenter stated reflect a documented and sustained valuation disparity relative to comparably complex procedures.
Response:
We acknowledge commenters' documentation that seven of the eight codes have undergone subsequent RUC survey and revaluation since 1992, and that CPT code 29824 was established in 2002. However, our proposal was not premised on these codes retaining unrevised 1992 Harvard values; rather, our concern is whether the currently assigned work RVUs, time assumptions, and direct PE inputs still
(
printed page 71168)
accurately reflect the resources involved in furnishing these services in light of technological and practice changes. A prior RUC survey does not foreclose the need for further review where subsequent changes in technique or technology may warrant it, and we do not believe the revaluation history identified by commenters is sufficient basis to remove these codes from consideration.
We recognize commenters' concerns regarding the absence of nomination documentation in the public use files and will consider whether additional transparency is appropriate in future rulemaking.
Regarding the methodology concern, we agree that changes in surgical technique may affect physician work in more than one direction and that revaluation should not assume operative time and physician work decline proportionally. We will take this into account, in coordination with the RUC, as these codes proceed through review.
We note, however, that section 1848 of the Social Security Act assigns CMS the responsibility for establishing relative values for physicians' services. We are not in a position to commit to adopting specialty society recommendations in every instance or to treat survey data as dispositive; there are cases in which claims data, internal consistency across the fee schedule, or other evidence leads us to propose a value that differs from the RUC-recommended value. We believe this approach is consistent with our statutory obligation to ensure that relative values reasonably reflect the relative resources involved in furnishing a service.
We will continue to consider specialty society input and published survey data as important components of our valuation process in this and future rulemaking cycles, and we encourage continued engagement from specialty societies and other stakeholders in this process.
With respect to legacy gynecologic surgical codes, we did not propose such codes as potentially misvalued in this cycle and are not identifying them as such in this final rule. Interested parties may nominate potentially misvalued services, including these, through our established annual nomination process.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the identification of CPT codes 20610, 20680, 22210, 22216, 24515, 29824, 29848, and 64721 as potentially misvalued, as proposed.
(11) Allergy Immunotherapy (CPT Code 95165)
In the CY 2001 PFS final rule (
65 FR 65393
), we discussed the direct PE inputs for CPT code 95165
(Professional services for the supervision of preparation and provision of antigens for allergen immunotherapy; single or multiple antigens (specify number of doses)).
As in the case of venoms, some non-venom antigens cannot be mixed together, that is, they must be prepared in separate vials. An example of this is mold and pollen. Therefore, some patients will be injected at one time from one vial—containing in one mixture all of the appropriate antigens—while other patients will be injected at one time from more than one vial. We extensively discussed how the practice expense component for mixing a multidose vial of antigens was computed, and how we observed that the most common practice at the time was to prepare a 10 cc vial; we also observed that the most common use was to remove aliquots with a volume of 1 cc. Therefore, a physician's removing 10 1cc aliquot doses captured the entire PE component for the service.
Recently we have received interested parties' communication from relevant specialties on the definition of a dose as it pertains to an allergy immunotherapy. They are concerned that clinical practice is not using this method of dosage to treat patients and the definition that Medicare is using is causing general confusion. They note that Medicare's 1 cc aliquot dose is now creating reimbursement-driven changes to medical practice, rather than changes that align with clinical practice and is increasingly adopted by commercial payers and Medicaid plans, thereby negatively impacting the delivery of medically necessary and cost-effective patient care to Medicare beneficiaries. According to the specialty societies, when this Medicare policy was implemented, few Medicare beneficiaries received allergy immunotherapy—most practices report that less than 5 percent of patients receiving treatment at that time were Medicare beneficiaries. Today, specialty societies report, Medicare beneficiaries often comprise more than 20 percent of an individual practice's allergy immunotherapy patients.
We invited comment from the wider medical community, including analyses or studies, regarding CPT code 95165 and the definition of an allergy immunotherapy dose. In particular, we stated in the proposed rule, we are interested in how these concepts are interpreted and implemented within clinical practice.
Additionally, Medicare utilizes a medically unlikely edit (MUE) of 30 doses per claim to flag potential overutilization. Specialty societies claim a more appropriate policy should use common clinical practice, by having an annual limit on doses of medically necessary treatment. For example, the annual limit of up to 160 doses per year during the first year of therapy would be higher to account for the build-up phase, then reduced to 130 or fewer doses per year thereafter when the beneficiary is receiving maintenance doses.
We welcomed comments, including research or opinions from the medical community, on appropriate annual dose limits billed for CPT code 95165 based on clinical practice.
Comment:
Commenters were nearly unanimous in urging CMS to rescind the current definition of a dose for CPT code 95165 as a 1 cc aliquot and instead align with the definition used for the companion CPT codes 95115 and 95117, under which a dose is a single injection from a multidose vial. They argued the 1 cc standard, unchanged since 2000, does not reflect current practice, since maintenance doses are typically prepared at approximately 0.5 cc—meaning the existing definition effectively pays for only about half of clinically prepared doses. Building on this, commenters noted that certain allergens, such as molds, cockroach antigen, and pollens, cannot be safely combined due to proteolytic activity and cross-reactivity, requiring multiple separately prepared vials that the current definition does not account for. A commenter added historical context, citing a 2002 HHS OIG report that found the original 1 cc definition was based on inaccurate dosing data at the time of adoption, a finding never addressed through subsequent rulemaking.
Commenters further argued that the stakes of this definition have grown over time, since Medicare beneficiaries now make up a much larger share of immunotherapy patients than when the policy was adopted—reportedly over 20 percent today compared to under 5 percent historically—and Medicaid programs and commercial payers increasingly mirror Medicare's definition, extending its effects well beyond the Medicare population.
Closely related to the dose definition, commenters addressed the 30-unit per-claim MUE applied to CPT code 95165, asking CMS to eliminate it in favor of an annual, per-beneficiary parameter that reflects higher utilization during the buildup phase and lower utilization
(
printed page 71169)
during maintenance, paired with an exception process for documented medical necessity. Recommended annual limits varied: two national societies proposed up to 150 doses in the first year and 120 during maintenance; a multistate alliance and a regional society recommended up to 160 doses in the first year and 130 during maintenance, consistent with figures referenced in the proposed rule; and one individual commenter recommended a higher limit of 200 doses, citing patients on accelerated buildup protocols requiring four or more separately prepared vials.
Several commenters extended these concerns into related payment methodology requests, recommending that CMS recognize preparation of dilution vials during the buildup phase as a separately payable component, recalculate the direct practice expense input for antigen supply costs using a representative mix of invoice data across vial sizes rather than the largest available vial, and exclude any resulting valuation correction from the proposed 5 percent practice expense stabilization limit, or alternatively allow accelerated implementation of such a correction.
To illustrate the practical scope of these issues, several commenters offered supporting data. A commenter representing a large practice reported thousands of patients actively receiving immunotherapy, drawn from a Medicare-related population exceeding 8,000 individuals over an18-month period, and stated that its standard preparation methodology uses 2 cc per unit—twice the volume recognized under the current definition. Other commenters, particularly those in rural and medically underserved areas, reported that Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries make up a disproportionate share of their immunotherapy patients, in some cases exceeding 60 percent, and expressed concern that inadequate reimbursement could lead to discontinuation of immunotherapy services where few or no alternative providers exist.
Commenters also tied these access concerns to patient safety, stating that maintaining separate dosing conventions for Medicare and non-Medicare patients introduces variability into dosing and labeling that may increase the risk of medical error, and that MUE-driven delays in preparing multiple vials on separate dates could compound this risk, particularly for patients with severe allergic disease, including venom hypersensitivity.
Finally, commenters situated these recommendations within the broader clinical and economic significance of allergen immunotherapy, noting that it remains one of the few disease-modifying treatments available for allergic rhinitis, allergic asthma, and related conditions, and that reduced access could increase downstream use of medications, emergency care, and other services. A commenter cited a published cost-effectiveness analysis suggesting that reimbursement reductions causing access reductions beyond a modeled threshold would not be cost-effective from either a societal or health-system perspective.
Response:
We agree that the current volume-based definition, unchanged since 2000, no longer reflects contemporary clinical practice, under which maintenance doses are routinely prepared in volumes smaller than 1 cc. We further agree that this discrepancy has had the practical effect of valuing only a fraction of the doses actually prepared and administered. We also recognize that certain allergen combinations cannot safely be consolidated into a single vial due to proteolytic activity and cross-reactivity, and that the revised definition better accommodates the use of multiple, separately prepared vials in these clinical circumstances. With respect to the 2002 HHS OIG findings regarding the data underlying the original 1 cc standard, we acknowledge that this definitional change addresses a long-standing inconsistency between Medicare policy and current clinical practice.
The recommendation to eliminate the 30-unit per-claim MUE for CPT code 95165 in favor of an annual, per-beneficiary utilization parameter—including the specific thresholds proposed for buildup and maintenance phases and the associated medical necessity exception process—is outside the scope of this rulemaking. MUE values are established and maintained through a subregulatory process administered separately from the annual PFS rulemaking cycle. We will refer this recommendation to the appropriate subregulatory process for further consideration.
The recommendations regarding payment methodology, including separate payment for dilution vial preparation, recalculation of the direct practice expense input for antigen supply costs based on a representative mix of vial-size invoice data, and an exclusion or accelerated correction relative to the proposed 5 percent practice expense stabilization limit, raise substantive questions about current valuation inputs that merit further review beyond the scope of this rule. We intend to consider these recommendations, along with the supporting utilization and practice-cost data submitted, in future rulemaking.
We appreciate the data provided regarding the growing share of Medicare beneficiaries within the immunotherapy patient population and the extension of Medicare's dose definition into Medicaid and commercial coverage policies. We also appreciate the concerns raised regarding access in rural and medically underserved areas, and the patient safety considerations associated with maintaining divergent dosing conventions across payers. We recognize the clinical and economic significance of allergen immunotherapy as a disease-modifying treatment and will take the broader cost-effectiveness and access considerations raised into account as we evaluate the remaining payment methodology questions in future rulemaking.
After consideration of the public comments received, we are finalizing our proposal to revise the definition of a dose for CPT code 95165 from a 1 cc aliquot to a single injection from a multidose vial, consistent with the definition used for CPT codes 95115 and 95117. The recommendation to adopt an annual, per-beneficiary utilization parameter in place of the current MUE will be referred to the appropriate subregulatory process for further consideration.
(12) Ultrasonic Wound Assessment (CPT Code 97610)
An interested party nominated CPT code 97610 (
Low frequency, non-contact, non-thermal ultrasound, including topical application(s), when performed, wound assessment, and instruction(s) for ongoing care, per day
) as potentially misvalued due to an inflated supply costs direct PE input. The nominator stated that this inflation causes a site of service disparity where CMS pays significantly more for the non-facility practice expense compared to the hospital outpatient (OPPS) payment rate. The CY 2026 non-facility PE RVU of 11.51 for CPT code 97610 results in a payment of $384, compared to an OPPS payment rate of $205, representing a payment differential of $179. The nominator stated that this disparity is primarily driven by the $320 direct PE input, SA119 (kit, low frequency ultrasound wound therapy (MIST)). The nominator provided a hyperlink to the UltraMIST® system manufacturer's Investor Presentation
[
70
]
from December 2025 which states that “consumable costs = ~$100/procedure (list price).” On slide 13 of the
(
printed page 71170)
presentation, it states that the single use applicators are $100 and that the pricing reflects manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP). The nominator also estimated an implied sales price of $86 per disposable kit on average using publicly available manufacturer disclosures and Medicare claims data. The nominator stated that the manufacturer reported $21.0 million in U.S. consumable and parts net revenue for CY 2024. The nominator was able to estimate the total volume of kits sold by the manufacturer by assuming each of the 745 unique billing NPIs in Medicare claims have approximately one of the ~1,000 UltraMist® systems in the field, such that the 181,851 Medicare claim lines account for 74.5 percent of total volume ($21.0 million/[181,851/{745/1,000}] = $86), noting that actual sales price would vary due to volume-based or other supplier discounts, commercial utilization, and other factors.
We agree with the nominator and proposed CPT code 97610 as potentially misvalued. Additionally, we proposed to change the cost of supply code SA119 to $100 in the direct PE database. We sought comment on this proposal and invited interested parties to submit paid invoices for supply code SA119 (kit, low frequency ultrasound wound therapy (MIST)). We also noted that physician time may be currently overstated for CPT code 97610, as the December 2025 Investor Presentation asserts that the procedure takes about 3 to 20 minutes, with an average of 6 minutes. The current total physician time is nearly 26 minutes, with a work RVU of 0.39. Because the current intraservice time is over double the time asserted by the supply manufacturer in the Investor Presentation, we sought comment on whether the typical physician time to perform this service is closer to the manufacturer's assertion of 6 minutes or the current intraservice time of nearly 15 minutes.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that an input price of $100 for supply code SA119 does not reflect the wide range of costs across different device manufacturers and technologies used to furnish CPT code 97610 (such as Vaporox, Sanuwave, and Arobella). Commenters reported supply costs ranging from $20 to $250 in some geographic areas, and specifically requested that CMS evaluate costs across all technologies rather than relying on data from a single manufacturer's investor presentation. The most common cost for SA119 that commenters referenced was $125, particularly among small practices and individual providers. Most commenters requested that CMS rely on paid invoice data rather than pricing derived from an investors presentation. Several commenters stated they would provide invoices for the device and applicator upon request, though a couple of commenters submitted an invoice to substantiate alternative costs for SA119. The commenters submitted invoices for a per-use device fee ranging from $60 to $125 discussed later in this section, and a disposable treatment kit specific to Vaporox ranging from $35 to $50.
Response:
We note that commenters gave us a range of costs for SA119, but no commenters asserted that they pay the current $320.18 for SA119. We appreciate commenters' input regarding the range of costs across different technologies used to furnish CPT code 97610. We appreciate the commentators' submission of invoices and note in response to commentors who stated they would submit invoices upon request, that we specifically requested invoice submission in the proposed rule. However, consistent with our standard ratesetting methodology, we establish direct PE inputs and their values to reflect the typical cost of furnishing a service, not the costs associated with any one product, manufacturer, or business arrangement.
Comment:
The AMA RUC indicated that they intend to review an action plan at their September 2026 meeting to determine whether this code should be re-reviewed. The RUC and several other commenters requested that CMS delay finalization of changes to CPT code 97610 pending this RUC review process. Other commenters raised coding concerns, noting the code lacks depth, size, wound quantity, or anatomic-site distinctions, and same-day billing restrictions with other wound care codes, and requested referral back to the RUC on these grounds as well.
Response:
While we recognize that the RUC may consider resurveying and revaluation for a future rulemaking cycle, we do not believe it is appropriate to delay finalization on the individual supply cost concern identified through our misvalued code initiative, considering no commenters asserted that they pay the current $320.18 for SA119 and we believe it is significantly overvalued. In the event that there is a new RUC review of this service, we would look forward to receiving any additional information, invoices, or new data about the broader coding structure, specifically regarding depth, size, wound quantity, or anatomic-site distinctions, and same-day billing restrictions.
Comment:
A commenter stated that they pay $97 for the single use UltraMIST applicator but requested that CMS maintain the current $320.18 price for the kit because it carried the cost of other consumables (such as saline, dressings, PPE, and clinician travel between homes) and created a margin for practices to recover the $27,500 device cost.
Several commenters stated that CMS conflated the cost of the single-use applicator with the cost of the SA119 kit. A commenter stated that the kit includes the applicator and tubing, plus saline and dressings purchased separately. The commenter also stated that their members report kit pricing above and below our proposed $100 depending on purchase volume. Several commenters requested that CMS include saline in CPT code 97610's supplies, with a commenter specifically requesting the inclusion of SH069 (sodium chloride 0.9% irrigation (500-1000ml uou)).
Response:
We can clarify that the proposed $100 price for supply code SA119 is intended to reflect the cost of the kit, consistent with the cited manufacturer's investor presentation describing $100 in consumable costs. Supply code SA119 is separate and distinct from the other direct PE supplies included in CPT code 97610 which are not affected by our proposal. We note that the valuation of CPT code 97610 already accounts for multiple different bandages, dressings, gauzes, and PPE. We encourage commenters to review the direct PE input public use files, available on the CMS website, which detail all supply, equipment, and clinical labor direct PE inputs. We note that a couple of commenters provided invoices and they indicated the single-use disposable treatment kit specific to Vaporox ranges from $35 to $50. We do not believe that this range is representative of the typical kit cost across all technologies and devices. Additionally, we agree with the commenters that saline should be a supply input for CPT code 97610 and we are therefore adding 1 quantity of supply code SH069 to CPT code 97610 in the non-facility setting for the final rule.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that they did not agree with the proposed $100 for SA119 because they use the Vaporox system and pay a per-treatment operating or rental charge for the device, in addition to a separate $50 device-specific disposable kit cost. Commenters stated that this per-treatment cost of $160 in total, rather than the $100 figure derived from a competing manufacturer's disclosed consumable price, should be used to value supply code SA119 because they made no capital equipment investment
(
printed page 71171)
and pay per use instead. A couple of commenters provided invoices, but they corroborated the commenters' prices. Another commenter stated that some of their members use an alternative system with higher capital acquisition cost but reusable applicators that are autoclaved between patients rather than discarded. The commenter stated that those practices have significantly lower supply costs, while capital acquisition, equipment, and clinical labor costs are higher. A few commenters stated that the MIST Therapy system acquisition cost is significantly higher than cost indicated in the investors presentation, but did not provide invoices to substantiate their figures for consideration in updating the device cost in the direct PE database.
Response:
We do not agree that a pay-per-use operating charge should be used to set the direct PE supply input for SA119. As we have stated in rulemaking as recent as CY 2025 (
89 FR 97798
), while we understand that there may be alternative business models, we do not believe a rental, subscription, or per-use fee of an equipment item that is still available to be purchased and is already accounted for with our equipment methodology is appropriate. Similarly, while we appreciate the submissions of per-use invoices for the Vaporox device, we believe that the typical cost of the device is appropriately and adequately accounted for in the equipment formulas for EQ372 (MIST Therapy System) and EQ368 (MIST Therapy Cart) (based on our standardized formula which accounts for years of useful life, utilization rate, purchase price, and minutes per year of use, outlined in detail in section II.B. of this final rule, Determination of PE RVUs). We do not believe that CPT code 97610 should be valued based on a significantly more expensive pay-per-use business model when the same treatment is cheaper and available as a purchasable form of equipment.
Comment:
Some commenters requested that, if CMS must finalize a price of $100 for SA119, it should phase in the reduction over time.
Response:
As discussed in section II.B. of this final rule, we note that the proposed changes to the supply code SA119's price decreased CPT code 97610's PE RVU. Because this reduction was the result of revaluation of the code's supply input, CPT code 97610 is exempt from the proposed PE stabilization adjustment, but the statutory phase-in of significant total RVU decreases will apply because its total RVU decrease is greater than 19 percent. Therefore, we agree with commenters and note that the reduction in total RVUs that resulted from the updated price for SA119 will be phased in, not due to a staggered implementation of the SA119 supply price, but rather due to the preexisting phase-in transition policy (see the CY 2016 PFS final rule
80 FR 70927
through
70929
for additional details).
Comment:
Many commenters provided feedback in response to our comment solicitation about physician time, mostly stating that our current physician time is not overstated or, in some cases, possibly understated. A few commenters stated that service is performed primarily by clinical staff under supervision, and that physician time may be overstated for the wound assessment and documentation portions of the service that are performed by a physician. Some commenters provided detailed clinical labor activities and times, some indicating undervaluation. A commenter highlighted possible clinical labor anomalies and stated they planned to survey its membership for corrected clinical labor inputs prior to the PFS final rule. Another commenter provided empirical times: a single wound takes 24.9 minutes of physician time and 4.1 minutes of clinical staff time, and each additional wound adds 12 minutes of physician time and 3 minutes of clinical staff time. The commenter stated that treating 2 wounds per encounter is typical. Another commenter provided aggregated data over 41 months and 110,237 recorded treatments that showed machine-recorded active device runtimes averaged 43.4 minutes, with a median of 42 minutes and a range of 14 to 56 minutes.
Response:
We thank the commenters for the detailed feedback. We reiterate that we did not propose any changes to physician time, work RVU, or clinical labor time but appreciate the commenters feedback that the current physician and clinical labor times are not overstated.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the addition of 1 quantity of SH069 to CPT code 97610 in the non-facility setting, and a supply cost of $125 for SA119. We note that we are finalizing $125 despite the lack of an invoice to substantiate that price because we believe the current price of $320.18 is significantly overpriced based on commenters' feedback, and $125 was the most common price commenters referenced for SA119. We believe this strikes a balance between the few invoices we received for the single-use disposable treatment kit specific to Vaporox that ranges from $35 to $50, the lack of consensus and clarity about what is included in the SA119 kit, the range of technologies used to furnish CPT code 97610, and the absence of any support or indication from commenters that the current price of $320.18 for SA119 is accurate. We continue to invite interested parties to submit paid invoices reflecting actual costs for supply code SA119 and information about what is included in the kit for consideration in future rulemaking.

We received a request from a nominator to review HCPCS code G0465
(Autologous platelet rich plasma (PRP) or other blood-derived product for diabetic chronic wounds/ulcers, using an FDA-cleared device for this indication, (includes as applicable administration, dressings, phlebotomy, centrifugation or mixing, and all other preparatory procedures, per treatment)
as potentially misvalued. Application of skin substitute graft to face, scalp, eyelids, mouth, neck, ears, orbits, genitalia, hands, feet, and/or multiple digits, total wound surface area up to 100 sq cm; first 25 sq cm or less wound surface area
), however, the nominator believes this is not an appropriate crosswalk for G0465.

However, we note the sample size of the survey shows only 34 respondents and so we have concerns as to whether this is a representative sample size of practitioners furnishing this service. Additionally, we continue to believe that the MPPR payment adjustment is applicable to multiple units of this service billed to the same beneficiary on the same day due to overlapping resource costs.
