Comment:
A commenter requested CMS reconsider the policy discussed in the CY 2024 PFS final rule that weight-based doses, BSA-based doses, loading doses, escalation, or titration doses, tapering doses, and dose adjustments for toxicity are not unique circumstances. The commenter stated that discarded amounts may be unavoidable when continuously variable, patient-specific doses must be prepared from a discrete set of available vial sizes and compared such loss to the loss associated with required filtration described in section 1847A(h)(8)(B)(ii) of the Act. The commenter stated that vial-size optimization has not adequately reduced discarded amounts for BSA-dosed products and recommended that, if CMS maintains its current policy, that CMS should publish data on discarded amounts for BSA-dosed Part B oncology drugs with a high volume of claims to provide greater transparency into that policy. The commenter also requested that CMS ensure the discarded drug refund policy does not influence clinicians to select doses or products based on vial economics rather than clinical considerations, while recognizing dose rounding within clinically validated parameters.
Response:
We thank the commenter for describing the challenges associated with matching patient-specific and variable dosing regimens, including weight-based doses, BSA-based doses, loading doses, escalation, or titration doses, tapering doses, and toxicity-related dose adjustments, to available vial or container sizes. These comments are out of scope for this final rule, as we did not make proposals or discuss these topics in the proposed rule.
We previously discussed similar dosing circumstances in the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69715
). For example, we explained that when an induction or loading dose is administered, a larger amount of drug may subsequently be left in the single-dose container compared with the amount of drug left in the container if a typical dose had been administered. Nevertheless, we explained that amounts left in the vial were considered unused and discarded because they were not part of the dose intended to produce a therapeutic effect.
With respect to vial-size optimization that has not adequately reduced discarded amounts for BSA-dosed products, we continue to believe that manufacturers can use vial-size optimization studies to identify a set of container sizes for which less than 10 percent of the labeled amount, while recognizing that introducing or modifying vial sizes may present operational and economic challenges for manufacturers and may impose additional burdens on providers that must stock and administer those vial sizes, as discussed in the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69713
). Notwithstanding these operational considerations, section 1847A(h) of the Act requires manufacturers to pay refunds calculated under the statutory formula when the amount of discarded units exceeds the applicable percentage of estimated total allowed charges. Consistent with the 2020 data discussed in the CY 2023 PFS final rule, data collected since implementation of the program indicate that Medicare Part B spending on discarded amounts remains concentrated among a relatively small number of products. We note that § 414.940(e) provides a process through which a manufacturer may request an increased applicable percentage for a refundable drug with product-specific unique circumstances and supporting information.
With respect to the request that CMS publish data on discarded amounts for BSA-dosed Part B oncology drugs, CMS issues annual discarded drug refund reports through the Manufacturer Payment Portal. These reports include quarterly information on discarded billing units and the refund amount for a manufacturer's refundable drugs, including those dosed based on BSA. Oncology drugs account for about half of all refundable drugs that owed a refund in the first two program years. Manufacturers of refundable drugs for which no refund is due also receive reports reflecting a zero-refund amount. Separately, CMS publishes prior program-year refund information and quarterly Part B spending by drug on its website.
Finally, the discarded drug refund policy does not require clinicians to change a clinically appropriate dose, select a different product, or round a dose based on a manufacturer's refund liability. The refund requirement applies to manufacturers after Medicare claims are processed and does not affect Medicare's payment to providers for administered and discarded amounts. Consistent with CMS policy, discarded amounts are identified using the JW modifier; the JZ modifier is required on claims when there are no discarded amounts.

printed page 71200)

Several commenters provided feedback regarding the interaction between the discarded drug refund policy and the Maximum Fair Price (MFP) for selected drugs payable under Part B. We appreciate the commenter's recommendations and concerns. The proposed rule did not address the methodology for calculating estimated total allowed charges for selected drugs subject to MFP, and we did not propose or solicit comments on these issues. However, we note that the statutory framework governing the discarded drug refund requirement, including the definition of a refundable drug, the exclusions specified in section 1847A(h)(8)(B) of the Act, and the refund calculation methodology under section 1847A(h)(3)(A) of the Act, is set forth in statute and discussed later in this section.
Section 1847A(h)(8)(A) of the Act defines a refundable drug and section 1847A(h)(8)(B) of the Act specifies the categories excluded from that definition. In the CY 2023 PFS final rule, we implemented section 1847A(h) of the Act and finalized at § 414.902 the definition of a refundable single-dose container or single-use package drug, including the statutory exclusions for radiopharmaceuticals and imaging agents, certain drugs requiring filtration during preparation, and certain drugs approved or licensed on or after November 15, 2021, for which payment has been made under Part B for fewer than 18 months (
87 FR 69710
through
69724
). In the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 97973
through
97974

We are not establishing additional exclusions in this final rule.
Section 1847A(h)(3)(A) of the Act and § 414.940 provide that the refund amount is an amount equal to the estimated amount (if any) by which the product of the number of discarded units and the amount of payment determined under either section 1847A(b)(1)(B) of the Act in the case of a single source drug or biological product or section 1847A(b)(1)(C) of the Act in the case of a biosimilar biological product, as applicable, exceeds an amount equal to the applicable percentage of the estimated total allowed charges for such drug during the calendar quarter. Section 1847A(b)(1)(B) specifies that in the case of a single source drug or biological product that is a selected drug (as referred to in section 1192(c) of the Act), with respect to a price applicability period (as defined in section 1191(b)(2) of the Act), the amount of payment determined under such section is 106 percent of the MFP for such drug and year during such period.
Comment:
A commenter expressed support for the discarded drug refund policy as a means of reducing payment for excessive discarded amounts. The commenter stated that the current modifier-based approach to identifying discarded amounts, including use of the JW and JZ modifiers, imposes administrative burden and does not directly address incentives associated with vial size. The commenter recommended that Medicare instead base payment on the quantity of drug actually administered, using electronic medication administration record data or claims reconciliation where feasible, rather than relying on manual modifier reporting. The commenter also stated that manufacturers should bear the cost of discarded amounts attributable to product packaging beyond clinically unavoidable levels.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's support for the discarded drug refund policy, including the commenter's concern that incentives associated with vial size can contribute to excessive discarded amounts. The discarded drug refund policy addresses that concern directly, by requiring manufacturers to provide refunds for discarded amounts of refundable single-dose container or single-use package drugs for which payment is made under Part B exceeding an applicable percentage of the estimated total allowed charges for such a drug (less the amount paid for packaged drugs) during the quarter.
Section 1847A(h) of the Act establishes the manufacturer refund at issue for certain discarded amounts and does not alter Medicare's longstanding payment policy. When a provider or supplier must discard an unused portion of a separately payable drug from a single-dose container or single-use package after administering a dose to a Medicare beneficiary, Medicare provides payment for both the administered amount and the appropriately discarded amount, up to the amount indicated on the product labeling. Section 1847A(h) of the Act further provides for determining discarded amounts using a mechanism such as the JW modifier (or any successor modifier that includes the same data) and under the JW and JZ modifier policy finalized in the CY 2023 PFS final rule, the JZ modifier is required when there are no discarded amounts from single-dose containers or single-use packages payable under Part B (
87 FR 69718
through
69719
). This claims-based reporting of administered and discarded amounts is the mechanism CMS uses to identify discarded amounts for purposes of
(
printed page 71201)
calculating refunds under section 1847A(h) of the Act. The commenter's recommendations to limit Medicare payment to the quantity administered and to replace the JW and JZ modifier requirements with an electronic medication administration record-based or other claims-reconciliation mechanism would involve changes to existing Medicare Part B payment and claims reporting policies and are out of scope for this final rule.
As explained in the CY 2023 PFS final rule regarding provider burden (
87 FR 69716
), we continue to believe providers are the only party that can obtain complete and accurate information on used and discarded amounts of variably dosed drugs. While we acknowledge that, in some situations, it may be difficult to quantify discarded quantities of drugs and associate the specific amount with a single beneficiary, we believe that, in most situations, there are no practical impediments that would prevent billing providers or other staff, such as nurses or pharmacists, from incorporating the measurement of discard amounts into the process of preparing and administering the drug. We also believe that the observation and recording of no discard amounts using the JZ modifier does not add additional burden beyond the existing requirement of measuring discarded amounts by use of the JW modifier. If a provider is already required to determine whether there are discarded amounts from single-dose packages, then they are already assessing and documenting what is needed for the JZ modifier.
Regarding the commenter's recommendation to shift to manufacturers the cost of amounts attributable to product packaging beyond clinically unavoidable levels, this recommendation is also out of scope for this final rule. Section 1847A(h) of the Act requires manufacturers to provide a refund to CMS for certain discarded amounts from a refundable drug. The refund is based on the amount of discarded drug that exceeds an applicable percentage, which is required to be at least 10 percent of total charges for the drug in a given calendar quarter. Accordingly, to the extent the commenter's recommendation that manufacturers be responsible for discarded amounts beyond clinically unavoidable levels would result in an applicable percentage below 10 percent, that recommendation would not be consistent with the statutory requirement that the applicable percentage be at least 10 percent under section 1847A(h) of the Act. Section 1847A(h)(3)(B)(ii) of the Act permits the Secretary, through notice-and-comment rulemaking, to increase the applicable percentage for a refundable drug with qualifying unique circumstances.

We appreciate the commenter's concerns regarding access to biologicals and infusion-based therapies, including the concerns raised regarding women veterans. B. Rural Health Clinics (RHCs) and Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs)
1. Background on RHC and FQHC Payment Methodologies
As provided in
42 CFR part 405, subpart X
of our regulations, RHC and FQHC visits generally are defined as face-to-face encounters between a patient and one or more RHC or FQHC practitioners during which one or more RHC or FQHC qualifying services are furnished. RHC and FQHC practitioners are physicians, nurse practitioners (NPs), physician assistants (PAs), Certified Nurse Midwives (CNMs), clinical psychologists (CPs), licensed marriage and family therapists, mental health counselors, and clinical social workers, and, subject to certain conditions, a registered nurse or licensed practical nurse that is furnishing care to a homebound RHC or FQHC patient in an area verified as having shortage of home health agencies. Transitional Care Management (TCM) services can also be paid by Medicare as an RHC or FQHC visit. In addition, Diabetes Self-Management Training (DSMT) or Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT) services furnished by a certified DSMT or MNT program may also be considered FQHC visits for Medicare payment purposes. Only medically necessary medical, mental health, or qualified preventive health services that require the skill level of an RHC or FQHC practitioner are RHC or FQHC billable visits. Services furnished by auxiliary personnel acting under the supervision of the RHC or FQHC practitioner, are considered incident to the visit and are included in the per-visit payment.
RHCs generally are paid an all-inclusive rate (AIR) for all medically necessary medical and mental health services and qualified preventive health services furnished on the same day (with some exceptions). The AIR is subject to a payment limit, meaning that an RHC will not receive any payment beyond the specified limit amount per visit. As of April 1, 2021, all RHCs are subject to statutory upper payment limits determined in accordance with section 1833(f) of the Act, as amended by section 130 of Division CC of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (Pub. L. 116—260).
FQHCs were paid under the same AIR methodology until October 1, 2014. Beginning on that date, in accordance with section 1834(o) of the Act (as added by section 10501(i)(3) of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (
Pub. L. 111-148
, March 23, 2010)), FQHCs began to transition to the FQHC
(
printed page 71202)
PPS system, in which they are paid based on the lesser of the FQHC PPS rate or their actual charges. The FQHC PPS rate is adjusted for geographic differences in the cost of services by the FQHC PPS geographic adjustment factor (GAF). The rate is increased by 34 percent when an FQHC furnishes care to a patient that is new to the FQHC, or to a beneficiary receiving an initial preventive physical examination (IPPE) or has an annual wellness visit (AWV). Section 1834(o)(2)(B)(ii) of the Act requires the FQHC PPS base rate be updated annually by the percentage increase in a market basket of Federally qualified health center goods and services as promulgated through regulations, or if such an index is not available, by the percentage increase in the Medicare Economic Index (MEI) (as defined in section 1842(i)(3) of the Act) for the year involved. See section III.B.4 of this final rule, for the final CY 2027 updates.
Under the general authority of section 1834(o) of the Act, CMS codified at §§ 405.2462 and 405.2464 to pay historically excepted tribal FQHCs using the Medicare outpatient per visit rate established annually by IHS, rather than the FQHC PPS rate (
80 FR 71089
). These rates are set by IHS under sections 321(a) and 322(b) of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act based on prior-year cost reports. The outpatient per visit rate applies only to provider-based IHS or tribal facilities (see § 413.65(m)) and historically excepted tribal FQHCs. For CY 2026, the outpatient per visit rate is $733 per visit in the lower 48 States.
Both the RHC AIR and FQHC PPS payment rates were initially designed to reflect the cost of all services and supplies that an RHC or FQHC furnished to a patient in a single day. These nearly all-inclusive rates are not adjusted at the individual level for the complexity of individual patient health care needs, the length of an individual visit, or the number or type of practitioners involved in the patient's care. Instead, for RHCs, all costs for the facility over the course of the year are aggregated, and an AIR is derived from these aggregate expenditures. For FQHCs, the FQHC PPS base rate is updated annually by the percentage increase in a market basket of Federally qualified health center goods and services as discussed in section III.B.4 of this final rule.
RHCs and FQHCs are also paid for non-face-to-face care management work involved in coordinating care outside of the RHC AIR and FQHC PPS (§ 405.2464(c)). That is, payment is based on the PFS national non-facility payment rate and is made in addition to the otherwise billable visit for patients utilizing chronic care management (CCM), principal care management (PCM), general behavior health integration (BHI), chronic pain management (CPM), remote physiologic monitoring (RPM), remote therapeutic monitoring (RTM), community health integration (CHI), principal illness navigation (PIN), PIN-peer support services, advanced primary care management (APCM), and psychiatric collaborative care model (CoCM). In addition, payment is based on the PFS national non-facility payment rate and is made in addition to the otherwise billable visit for communication technology-based services (CTBS) and remote evaluation services (§ 405.2464(e)).
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49556
through
49558
), we finalized a policy that effective January 1, 2026, services that are established and paid under the PFS and designated as care management services would be considered “care coordination services” for purposes of separate payment for RHCs and FQHCs. The care coordination codes can be found in the PFS table entitled “Designated Care Management Services”, which is published annually with the PFS Final Rule Addenda on the CMS website.
2. Payment for Certain Preventive Services
a. Background
Medicare Part B covers a comprehensive set of preventive services aimed at promoting early detection and reducing the risk of chronic disease.
[
163
]
These services include wellness visits (such as the IPPE and AWV), evidence-based screenings for cancer and chronic conditions, behavioral health and risk factor screenings, certain vaccinations, and preventive counseling interventions. Coverage for many of these services was expanded under sections 4103 and 4104 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (
Pub. L. 111-148
); the services are covered without beneficiary cost-sharing when furnished according to Medicare requirements. Collectively, they are designed to support proactive, patient-centered care and improve long-term health outcomes, particularly when delivered in primary care settings. CMS has implemented these statutory provisions through regulations at
42 CFR part 410
, which define, among other things, the coverage, eligibility, and frequency requirements for preventive services.
CMS also establishes and updates coverage of preventive services through the National Coverage Determination (NCD) process, if such services are recommended with a grade of A or B by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF). These processes specify the conditions under which preventive services are considered reasonable and necessary for Medicare beneficiaries.
Payment for preventive services is made in accordance with applicable Medicare payment systems, for example, the PFS under
42 CFR part 414
. CMS provides additional operational guidance through subregulatory instructions, including manuals and program transmittals, to ensure consistent implementation of coverage and payment policies. Beneficiary copayment and deductible (where applicable) is waived by the Affordable Care Act for the IPPE and AWV, and for Medicare-covered preventive services recommended by the USPSTF with a grade of A or B.
When statutorily permissible, we pay for covered preventive services under Medicare Part B to RHCs and FQHCs pursuant to such facilities' encounter-based payment methodologies, rather than as PFS separately billable services, except where the statute specifies otherwise.
RHCs are paid under the AIR methodology for a limited number of qualified preventive health services furnished by an RHC practitioner. FQHCs are paid under the FQHC PPS for qualified preventive health services and preventive primary health services required under section 330 of the PHS Act.
[
164
]
A qualified preventive health service refers to a Medicare-covered preventive service that also meets the requirements for a billable RHC or FQHC visit, including a face-to-face encounter with a RHC or FQHC practitioner (that is, the service is at a level that requires the expertise of a RHC or FQHC practitioner).
(
printed page 71203)
Specifically, RHCs and FQHCs are paid for the professional component of allowable preventive services when the program requirements are met and frequency limits (where applicable) have not been exceeded.
[
165
]
In this context, professional component refers to the practitioner's clinical service associated with a preventive service, as opposed to the technical or ancillary elements of the service. Preventive services furnished in other settings, for example, physician offices, are generally paid on a service-by-service basis. However, preventive services that do not constitute a separate billable RHC or FQHC visit must be furnished as part of a qualified RHC or FQHC visit (for example, an evaluation and management (E/M) visit) to be billable to Medicare. If a preventive service that is not part of a billable RHC or FQHC visit is furnished to a beneficiary, it may not be payable under Medicare.
b. Federal Initiatives To Improve Health Outcomes and Access to Care
(1) The Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Commission
On February 13, 2025, the President signed an Executive Order establishing the MAHA Commission within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
[
166
]
The Commission is chaired by the Secretary of HHS and includes representatives from multiple Federal agencies. The Commission was directed to assess contributing factors to chronic disease and to develop a coordinated Federal strategy to improve population health outcomes, with an initial focus on pediatric populations.
In 2025, the Commission released an assessment identifying a range of factors associated with chronic disease, including dietary patterns, environmental exposures, physical inactivity, and other behavioral and upstream drivers of health. The Commission subsequently issued a strategy outlining potential Federal actions to address these factors through cross-agency coordination, research, and programmatic initiatives.
[
167
]
Although the Commission's initial focus is on childhood health, its findings are relevant to Federal health programs serving other populations, including Medicare beneficiaries. Chronic conditions associated with the factors identified by the Commission are prevalent among Medicare beneficiaries and are significant drivers of program expenditures.
(2) The Rural Health Transformation (RHT) Program
The RHT Program was authorized by section 71401 of
Public Law 119-21
(July 4, 2025), which CMS refers to as the Working Families Tax Cut (WFTC) legislation, and empowers States to strengthen rural communities across America by improving healthcare access, quality, and outcomes by transforming the healthcare delivery ecosystem. The RHT Program represents a $50 billion Federal investment over five Federal fiscal years (FY 2026 to FY 2030), with $10 billion available annually, intended to strengthen health care infrastructure, expand access to care, and improve health outcomes in rural communities across the United States.
The program has five strategic goals, grounded in the permissible uses of funds under the statute: Make Rural America Healthy Again—Support rural health innovations and new access points to promote preventive health and address the root causes of disease; Sustainable Access—Improve the efficiency and long-term sustainability of rural health care providers as enduring access points for care; Workforce Development—Strengthen recruitment and retention of qualified health care professionals in rural communities; Innovative Care—Advance innovative care models that improve health outcomes, coordinate care, and promote flexible care arrangements; and Technology Innovation—Foster the adoption of innovative technologies that promote efficient care delivery, data security, and access to digital health tools for rural facilities, providers, and patients.

c. Increasing Access to Diabetes Self-Management Training (DSMT) and Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT) Services in RHCs
Section 4105 of the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 (
Pub. L. 105-33
) added section 1861(qq) of the Act to permit Medicare coverage of outpatient DSMT services when these services are furnished by a certified provider who meets certain quality standards. This program is intended to educate beneficiaries in the successful self-management of diabetes. The program includes instructions in self-monitoring of blood glucose; education about diet and exercise; an insulin treatment plan developed specifically for the patient who is insulin dependent; and motivation for patients to use the skills for self-management. DSMT services may be covered by Medicare only if the treating physician or treating qualified non—physician practitioner who is managing the beneficiary's diabetic condition certifies that such services are needed. The referring physician or qualified non-physician practitioner must maintain the plan of care in the beneficiary's medical record and documentation substantiating the need for training on an individual basis when group training is typically covered, if so ordered. A designated certified provider bills for DSMT provided by an accredited DSMT program. Certified providers must submit a copy of their accreditation certificate to the contractor. The statute states that a “certified provider” is a physician or other individual or entity designated by the Secretary that, in addition to providing outpatient self-management training services, provides other items and services for which payment may be made under title XVIII of the Act, and meets certain quality standards.
We designated all providers and suppliers that bill Medicare for other individual services such as hospital outpatient departments, renal dialysis facilities, physicians and durable medical equipment suppliers, as eligible to be certified providers. All suppliers/providers who may bill for other Medicare services or items and who represent a DSMT program that is accredited as meeting quality standards can bill and receive payment for the entire DSMT program.
Registered dietitians are eligible to bill on behalf of an entire DSMT program on or after January 1, 2002, if the provider employing or contracting with the dietitian has obtained a Medicare provider number. A dietitian may not be the sole practitioner of the DSMT service.
[
169
]
Under our regulations at § 410.144(a)(4)(ii), there is an exception for dietitians working in rural areas. In a rural area, an individual who is qualified as a registered dietitian and as a certified diabetic educator who is currently certified by an organization approved by us may furnish training and is deemed to meet the multidisciplinary team requirement. DSMT requirements for coverage, beneficiary eligibility, services and frequency of services and provider certification and accreditation are

codified in
42 CFR 410 subpart H
and
the

Section 1861(s)(2)(V) of the Act authorizes Medicare Part B coverage of MNT for certain beneficiaries who have diabetes or a renal disease. Regulations for MNT were established effective January 1, 2002, at
42 CFR 410 subpart G
(
66 FR 55246
and
55331
). The NCD 180.1 establishes the duration and frequency limits for the MNT benefit and coordinates MNT and DSMT.
[
171
]
MNT services are defined in section 1861(vv) of the Act as nutritional diagnostic, therapy, and counseling services provided by a registered dietitian or nutrition professional for the purpose of disease management under a referral by a physician. The provider qualifications for registered dieticians and nutrition professionals are defined in § 410.134.
Effective January 1, 2022, coverage of MNT, for the first year a beneficiary receives MNT, with either a diagnosis of renal disease or diabetes as defined at
42 CFR 410.130
, is 3 hours of administration. Coverage in subsequent years for renal disease or diabetes is 2 hours. The dietitian/nutritionist may choose how many units are administered per day as long as all of the other requirements of the NCD and §§ 410.130 through 410.134 are met. Under the exception at § 410.132(b)(5), additional hours are considered to be medically necessary and covered if the physician determines that there is a change in medical condition, diagnosis, or treatment regimen related to diabetes or renal disease that requires a change in MNT and orders additional hours during that episode of care. If the physician determines that receipt of both MNT and DSMT is medically necessary in the same episode of care, Medicare will cover both DSMT and MNT initial and subsequent years without decreasing either benefit as long as DSMT and MNT are not provided on the same date of service.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43958
) we stated that section 5114 of the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 amended section 1861(aa)(3) of the Act to add DSMT and MNT services as covered and paid under the FQHC benefit, effective January 1, 2006. Then the Affordable Care Act further expanded the scope of FQHC services to include preventive services defined under section 1861(ddd)(3) of the Act; however, RHCs were not similarly addressed. Under this statutory authority, DSMT and MNT services furnished by certified providers are stand-alone billable visits in FQHCs when all of the requirements are met. If DSMT or MNT services are provided on the same day as another qualified visit, the FQHC is paid for one visit, and the charges associated with DSMT or MNT are waived from coinsurance obligations (
79 FR 25447
). We noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, group DSMT is not payable in FQHCs because Medicare payment is limited to individual, face-to-face encounters under the FQHC PPS, and group training does not meet the definition of a billable visit.
We explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, for RHCs, DSMT services and MNT services rendered by registered dietitians or nutrition professionals are included under the RHC benefit, if all relevant program requirements are met. Separate payment under Part B to RHCs for these services provided by these practitioners is precluded as set forth in regulations at §§ 414.63 and 414.64. However, RHCs are permitted to become certified providers of DSMT and MNT services and bundle the cost of such services into their clinic payment rates. The provision of these services would not generate an RHC visit, though their costs may be included in the cost report and used for determining the AIR.
[
172
]
Consequently, RHCs are not paid for encounters where only DSMT or MNT services are provided.
We also explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that interested parties have expressed concern about access to DSMT and MNT services in RHCs for several years (
91 FR 43958
). Those commenters stated that, because these are preventive services, not treating these services as a separate encounter is impacting access to care for rural beneficiaries. They stated that there are additional concerns regarding the payment for DSMT and MNT services between RHCs and FQHCs and rural interested parties have requested aligning payment for these services. They believe that we should recognize DSMT and MNT services as a qualified visit for RHCs when these services are provided by a certified provider and all the requirements are met. They believe that the utilization rate is low for beneficiaries receiving care in RHCs and explained that if we allow RHCs to receive payment for furnishing DSMT and MNT services, then this rate may increase.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43959
) we discussed recent studies that highlight a continued need for DSMT and MNT services in rural areas, driven by rising diabetes prevalence and significant access disparities. Some of the barriers identified for people living in rural communities, especially for getting access to diabetes education and prevention programs, include limited number of providers, longer distance to medical facilities, higher costs, outdated cultural beliefs, lack of transportation, and limited community resources. More efforts to reduce these barriers may help reduce the overall high burden of diabetes in the rural US.
[
173
]
We explained that the necessity of DSMT and MNT in rural areas is supported by findings such that, they are clinically essential, diabetes control is improved, complications are reduced, lower costs, rural populations have equal or greater need, there are higher diabetes burden (widely established in rural health literature), access is systematically worse in rural areas, there are fewer providers, geographic maldistribution, and lower utilization despite need. Therefore, we opined that expanding DSMT and MNT in rural areas is not just beneficial, it is necessary to address documented health differences in access and outcomes.
[
174
]
In addition, we stated that we have observed low utilization for these services in rural settings. That is, we provided an analysis of Medicare claims data from 2024 that indicated that utilization of DSMT and MNT in RHC settings is substantially lower than in comparable care settings. In CY 2024, DSMT services were furnished to approximately 125 RHC beneficiaries, representing 0.005 percent of the total RHC beneficiary population of approximately 2.3 million. MNT services were furnished to approximately 439 RHC beneficiaries, representing 0.019 percent of the total RHC beneficiary population. On a claims basis, DSMT accounted for 0.002 percent and MNT for 0.007 percent of total RHC claims in CY 2024. By comparison, FQHCs showed DSMT utilization rates approximately 22 times higher and MNT utilization rates
(
printed page 71205)
approximately 28 times higher than RHCs on a per-beneficiary basis. On a claim basis, FQHC utilization of DSMT and MNT exceeded RHC utilization by approximately 31 times and 32 times, respectively. Rural physician offices, whose patients share the geographic and demographic characteristics of RHC patient populations, showed DSMT and MNT utilization rates approximately 17 times and 7 times higher than RHCs, respectively, on a per-beneficiary basis. We observed that the analysis further demonstrated that within the PFS setting, where DSMT and MNT are most readily identifiable in claims data, these services represent a very small share of total Medicare spending less than 0.01 percent and 0.02 percent of total PFS line item payments, respectively, in CY 2024. We stated that these findings could suggest that beneficiaries receiving care in RHCs may have disproportionately lower participation due to potential provider shortages and structural payment barriers when compared to other settings of care.
As such, we explained that we believed we should attempt to align access and payment for RHCs and FQHCs to the extent possible, given the statutory differences in benefit design between the two settings of care. Because DSMT and MNT are affirmatively covered Medicare Part B benefits under sections 1861(s)(2)(S) and 1861(s)(2)(V) of the Act, respectively, and are defined under sections 1861(qq) and 1861(vv) of the Act, we stated there is a compelling basis for ensuring these clinically essential services are payable under the RHC benefit. We stated that continuing to exclude these services from RHC payment limits access for rural Medicare beneficiaries and would be inconsistent with both the statutory coverage framework and the foundational purpose of the RHC program (
91 FR 43959
). We explained that reducing differences between RHCs and other settings in which DSMT and MNT are furnished and paid, such as in FQHCs and physician office, may help expand access to care for Medicare beneficiaries in rural areas. We also stated that this policy would strengthen access to services that address chronic conditions prevalent among Medicare beneficiaries which are significant drivers of program expenditures.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43959
), we stated that since DSMT and MNT services may be furnished by certified providers other than RHC practitioners as defined in §§ 410.141 and 410.134, respectively, these services could be furnished by certified providers under the direct supervision of an RHC practitioner. Direct supervision does not require the physician (or other supervising practitioner) to be present in the same room. However, the physician (or other supervising practitioner) must be present in the RHC or FQHC and immediately available to provide assistance and direction throughout the time the incident to service or supply is being furnished. See definitions at § 405.2401(b) “Direct Supervision.”
For the reasons discussed previously, we proposed to recognize DSMT and MNT services as qualified preventive services that are covered and paid the AIR as stand-alone billable visits under the RHC benefit (
91 FR 43959
). We proposed that to constitute as a billable RHC visit, these services would need to be furnished by a certified provider under the direct supervision of RHC professional staff. We stated that we believe aligning payment policies in RHCs with other settings, for example FQHCs and physician offices, would help expand access to care for Medicare beneficiaries in rural areas while supporting Federal initiatives to strengthen rural healthcare. As such, we proposed to revise § 405.2463(a) and (b)(2) to allow DSMT and MNT services to be stand—alone billable visits in RHCs. We proposed that, similar to FQHCs, when DSMT or MNT is furnished on the same day as another qualified visit, the RHC would be paid one AIR for that encounter. We explained that we considered these policies to align an incongruency between FQHC and RHC access to preventive services and that we did not expect in future rulemaking to propose additional preventive services beyond those which are currently paid for in FQHCs and physician offices. We invited public comments on these proposals.
We received approximately 130 comments on this proposal from a broad range of commenters, including national physician and nurse practitioner associations, registered dietitian and nutrition professional organizations, disease-specific advocacy organizations, rural health clinic and health center representation organizations, individual RHCs and health systems, state and regional primary care associations, medical device and pharmaceutical industry commenters, and individual clinicians, dietitians, nurses, and students practicing in rural and underserved communities. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
The majority of the commenters were supportive of the proposal to recognize DSMT and MNT services as qualified visits for RHCs when these services are provided by a registered dietician or nutritional professional. Commenters stated that they believe providing separate reimbursement for DSMT and MNT encounters furnished in RHCs will strengthen the ability of rural practices to offer comprehensive, patient-centered care and improve access to services that are essential for the prevention and management of chronic disease. Most commenters framed the proposal as correcting a long-standing inconsistency: DSMT and MNT have been separately billable in FQHCs since the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005, and in physician offices for even longer, but RHCs have been able only to absorb these costs into their cost report and have not been able to generate a separately payable visit. Commenters characterized this as an unnecessary inconsistency or a structural payment barrier that CMS is now proposing to close, and specifically credited CMS's own stated rationale—that aligning RHC policy with FQHCs and physician offices would expand rural access.
A large subset of commenters went further than general endorsement and cited CMS's claims data from the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43959
) directly as evidence the current structure suppresses utilization rather than reflects a lack of need. Several of these commenters explicitly argued that this gap cannot be explained by differences in clinical need, since rural Medicare beneficiaries carry a disproportionate burden of diabetes and chronic kidney disease—the very conditions MNT is intended to treat.
Many commenters pointed to structural barriers specific to rural beneficiaries, that is, longer travel distances, clinician and registered dietitian nutritionist (RDN) workforce shortages, and limited specialty access—arguing that bundling DSMT/MNT into another visit compounds rather than accommodates these constraints. A smaller number of commenters supplied concrete, clinic-level accounts as indication that the barrier is payment structure, not clinical capability or willingness. One commenter reported it had previously offered DSMT and MNT at its RHCs but could not sustain clinician coverage once the services proved unpayable as stand-alone visits and stated it would restore and expand both services if separate payment were finalized. Another commenter cited a member poll finding that 23.5% of responding RHCs already furnish DSMT/MNT today but are unable to generate payment for doing so under current rules.
(
printed page 71206)
Response:
We thank commenters for their support of this proposal to recognize DSMT and MNT services as qualified visits for Rural Health Clinics (RHCs) when furnished by a registered dietitian or nutrition professional. We appreciate the clinic-level experience commenters shared illustrating the practical effect of the current payment structure, including accounts of discontinued services and of RHCs that currently furnish DSMT and MNT without generating separate payment. We believe this information supports our expectation that this policy would enable RHCs to sustain and, in some cases, restore or expand access to these services for their patients. We believe that the commenter feedback received underscores the importance of aligning payment policies across care settings to expand access and address longstanding inconsistencies.
Comment:
One commenter did not dispute the clinical value of DSMT and MNT but opposed making them stand-alone billable visits, cautioning that per-visit billing risks recreating an encounter-counting dynamic. The commenter recommended incorporating DSMT/MNT into a Primary Care Month or diabetes episode-based payment, with incentives tied to clinical outcomes rather than visit volume.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their suggestion and appreciate the commenter's support for the clinical value of DSMT and MNT and their broader concern about avoiding payment structures that incentivize volume over outcomes. However, RHCs are paid on the basis of an all-inclusive rate and subject to a payment limit per visit (§ 405.2462(a)). Our proposal to recognize DSMT and MNT as stand-alone, qualified visits under the RHC AIR payment methodology is consistent with how these services are already recognized and paid in other settings, such as physician offices and FQHCs. Under current policy, RHCs cannot bill for DSMT and MNT when it is the only service furnished in a day, which we believe may have limited beneficiary access to these services. We believe that making DSMT and MNT stand-alone, qualified visits removes this access barrier and aligns payment incentives with furnishing medically necessary diabetes education and nutrition counseling.
We recognize the commenter's broader point about episode-based or population-based payment models that tie payment to clinical outcomes rather than visit counts. We agree that such models may hold promise for chronic disease management, including diabetes care, and note that Medicare has several programs that tie payment to diabetes-related care and clinical outcomes. RHCs can participate in Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) under the Medicare Shared Saving Program, a value-based care initiative which allows ACOs that reduce healthcare costs while meeting quality benchmarks, including diabetes management metrics, to earn a share of the savings they generate. However, the RHC benefit as structured under current statute and regulations does not provide for incentives tied to clinical outcomes.
Comment:
Several commenters asked CMS to confirm that DSMT and MNT may be furnished in a group or shared format. One commenter recommended that CMS remove its general limitation on group visits in RHCs, or at minimum establish a DSMT/MNT-specific exemption similar to the exemption previously adopted for intensive outpatient services furnished in RHCs, noting that DSMT in particular is often delivered in a group education format.
Response:
We recognize that the Medicare DSMT and MNT benefit permits training to be furnished in both individual and group settings under the requirements applicable to that benefit. However, whether a service is covered under the Medicare DSMT or MNT benefit is distinct from whether the service constitutes a payable visit under the RHC or FQHC payment methodology. The RHC and FQHC payment methodologies are generally based on a qualifying visit between an individual beneficiary and a qualified practitioner. Consistent with this longstanding framework, group services generally do not constitute payable RHC or FQHC visits, as detailed in § 405.2463.
We also do not agree that the payment policies for intensive outpatient program services provide a basis for establishing a comparable exception for DSMT or MNT. Effective January 1, 2024, Medicare coverage and payment for IOP services furnished by RHCs and FQHCs were established pursuant to section 4124 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (
Pub. L. 117-328
). The payment policies applicable to group therapy furnished as part of an IOP implement that distinct statutory benefit and payment framework. Accordingly, the availability of payment for qualifying group therapy under the IOP benefit does not alter the requirements that otherwise apply in determining whether a service constitutes a payable RHC or FQHC visit.
Comment:
Several commenters would like CMS to remove the direct supervision requirement. They noted that requiring direct supervision which they understood to mean that the supervising physician or practitioner would have to be physically present in the RHC and immediately available throughout the entire DSMT or MNT encounter—is inconsistent with how these services are furnished in every other Medicare setting. These commenters noted that FQHCs and physician offices require only a physician referral and provider certification, with no supervision requirement and RDNs bill independently under their own provider number once a referral is made. Commenters stated that importing a direct-supervision standard for RHCs alone runs counter to CMS's own stated objective of reducing payment and operational differences between RHCs and other settings, and that it would recreate, in a different form, the access barrier the proposal is intended to resolve: in rural clinics where the supervising physician or NP is typically fully scheduled, requiring that practitioner to remain immediately available for the full duration of a DSMT or MNT encounter would mean the service either displaces physician visit time or does not occur. Two commenters submitted specific proposed regulatory text, recommending that CMS collapse proposed § 405.2463(a)(2) into paragraph (a)(1) and list qualified MNT and DSMT providers, as defined under
42 CFR part 410, subparts G
and
H
, directly among the practitioners whose face-to-face encounters constitute a billable RHC visit—without a separate supervision clause. One commenter recommended a different resolution: transitioning DSMT and MNT from direct to general supervision, which they believe would allow RHCs to contract with external or telehealth-based RDN networks rather than requiring an on-site supervising practitioner, an approach they stated is particularly important for small, resource-constrained rural clinics that cannot staff a full-time RDN.
Other commenters, generally representing physician and nursing professional associations, supported the direct supervision requirement as an appropriate mechanism for team-based care and practitioner oversight. One commenter supported the requirement and specifically noted that it appropriately includes nurses among the RHC professional staff who may provide supervision. Another commenter characterized the requirement as appropriately recognizing the value of team-based care while allowing RHCs to leverage the
(
printed page 71207)
expertise of qualified health professionals such as registered dietitians under practitioner oversight. A third commenter supported the proposal's approach of supervision by RHC professional staff, such as a nurse practitioner.
Response:
With respect to the supportive comments, we agree that this policy would recognize team-based care models. Allowing RHCs to bill for DSMT and MNT encounters furnished by a registered dietitian or nutrition professional, under practitioner oversight, reflects the role these professionals already play in furnishing these services in other settings and allows RHCs to make full use of this expertise without requiring a billing practitioner to furnish the service directly.
We also acknowledge the other commenters' concerns regarding workforce limitations and access barriers associated with direct supervision in rural clinics, and their observation that MNT and DSMT are furnished and paid without a comparable supervision requirement in FQHCs and physician offices under §§ 410.130 through 134 and 410.140 through 146. However, as discussed above, DSMT and MNT are separately identified Part B benefits, with payment available under the physician fee schedule when applicable requirements are met. Congress also specifically expanded the FQHC benefit to include these services, and we recognize DSMT and MNT encounters as billable FQHC visits. The RHC benefit was not similarly amended. Under existing RHC policy, DSMT and MNT services may be included in clinic costs, but they do not independently generate an RHC visit payment. To receive payment for an encounter in an RHC, the service furnished must be at the skill level of an RHC practitioner. To be in compliance with the regulation at § 405.2463, we required direct supervision for DSMT and MNT services furnished by certified providers in RHCs
We have, however, considered commenters' concerns about the operational burden of requiring the supervising practitioner's continuous, on-site presence for the full duration of the encounter and offer clarification. Under § 405.2401(b), direct supervision means that the physician (or other supervising practitioner) must be present in the RHC or FQHC and immediately available to furnish assistance and direction throughout the performance of the service. It does not, however, mean that the physician (or other supervising practitioner) must be present in the room when the service is performed. We clarify that, consistent with § 405.2401(b), the presence of the physician (or other practitioner) includes virtual presence through audio/video real-time communications technology (excluding audio-only). We believe this clarification addresses much of the concern about scheduling conflict commenters described, without requiring a change to the underlying practitioner scope of service requirement.
For the recommendation to adopt general, rather than direct, supervision for DSMT and MNT services in RHCs, we decline to make this change in this final rule. We continue to believe direct supervision, as clarified above to include virtual presence, is necessary to maintain the connection to RHC practitioner services required under § 405.2463. We recognize the appeal of a general supervision model for enabling RHCs to contract with external or telehealth-based RDN networks, particularly for clinics unable to staff a full-time RDN, and we will continue to evaluate this feedback in consideration of statutory authority for potential policy refinements.
We clarify one point raised by a commenter who supported the direct supervision requirement on the understanding that it includes nurses among the RHC professional staff who may provide the required supervision. The direct supervision requirement for DSMT and MNT services is satisfied only by an RHC practitioner. Registered nurses and other RHC professional staff who do not meet the skill level of an RHC practitioner may not serve as the supervising individual for purposes of this requirement.
Comment:
A recurring concern across several supportive comments was that the proposal, while expanding access to DSMT and MNT, did not clearly define or protect the role of the RDNs who are the specialists trained to deliver these services. One commenter supported the proposal but asked that the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics be included as an interested party in implementation discussions and separately opposed any accompanying restrictions on physicians that might come at RDNs' expense.
Other commenters focused less on payment parity and more on whether RHCs will have access to qualified nutrition professionals. One commenter noted that many rural clinics lack in-house dietitians, and that the proposal does not clearly specify that an RDN (in person or virtual) must be the one furnishing the service. Similarly, the commenter asked CMS to be explicit about the RDN clinical role providing clear guidance on staffing, referral, documentation, and care coordination arguing that nutrition policy too often names the intervention but leaves the clinician vague, which risks leaving the workforce question unaddressed even if the payment pathway is finalized.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support for expanding access to DSMT and MNT services in RHCs. We recognize the important clinical role of RDNs and agree that recognizing these services as billable visits should not obscure the qualifications of the professionals who furnish them. This proposal addresses payment for qualifying DSMT and MNT encounters under the RHC benefit; it does not replace the service-specific requirements governing who may furnish these services. For MNT, provider qualifications for RDNs and nutrition professionals continue to be governed by § 410.134. For DSMT, instructor and multidisciplinary team qualifications, including the existing rural exception permitting a dually qualified registered dietitian and certified diabetes educator to satisfy the multidisciplinary team requirement in rural areas, continue to be governed by § 410.144(a)(4). This proposal does not alter, narrow, or supersede those qualification standards in RHCs. We also did not propose any restriction on physician billing for other services as a condition of, or offset to, this proposal.
We acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding the availability of qualified nutrition professionals in rural communities. We believe that recognizing DSMT and MNT services as stand-alone billable visits under the RHC benefit will help address a payment barrier and support RHCs in making these services more readily available, creating greater opportunities for rural Medicare beneficiaries to benefit from the expertise of RDNs and other qualified professionals.
We appreciate the recommendation to include the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics in implementation discussions and welcome input from the Academy, RDNs, RHCs, and other interested parties. Our objective is to improve access to these covered services while maintaining the professional qualifications and program requirements applicable to their delivery.
Comment:
Several commenters requested CMS permit separate payment when DSMT or MNT is furnished on the same day as another qualifying RHC visit. They cited continuity of care, the complementary nature of these services, and the burden rural beneficiaries face when required to make multiple trips.
(
printed page 71208)
One commenter specifically recommended extending the FQHC same-day multiple-visit exception in § 405.2463(c)(3) to RHCs.
Other commenters stated that the one-AIR-per-day limit could eliminate the financial incentive to furnish DSMT or MNT during the same visit as medical care, particularly when patients cannot return on another day. They recommended separate, stackable AIR payments or a carve-out similar to existing RPM and RTM payment policies. A commenter relatedly requested a supplemental payment mechanism in the FQHC PPS context.
Some commenters sought only implementation guidance, asking CMS to clarify payment when DSMT or MNT is furnished on the same day as another qualified RHC visit. Another commenter asked CMS to confirm whether RHCs would follow the same one-visit-per-day treatment currently applicable to FQHCs.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback regarding same day billing for DSMT and MNT services furnished in RHCs. One commenter's recommendation relied on § 405.2463(c)(3) as a provision currently permitting FQHCs paid under the reasonable cost system to receive payment for more than one visit per day when DSMT or MNT is furnished alongside another visit. We note that FQHCs no longer bill Medicare under the reasonable cost system for most services; all FQHCs bill under the FQHC PPS. Under the FQHC PPS, DSMT or MNT furnished on the same day as another qualified visit results in payment for one visit, unless the exception under § 405.2463(c)(4) is applicable.
Consistent with the RHC AIR payment methodology's existing treatment of multiple same-day services (§ 405.2463(c)(1)), and with the comparable FQHC treatment under the FQHC PPS described above, when DSMT or MNT is furnished on the same day as another qualified RHC visit, the RHC will be paid one AIR for that encounter, rather than separate, stackable AIR payments for each service. This approach maintains consistency between RHC and FQHC treatment of same-day visits, which has been the general organizing principle of encounter-based payment under both the RHC AIR and FQHC PPS methodologies. That is, encounters with more than one RHC or FQHC practitioner on the same day, or multiple encounters with the same RHC or FQHC practitioner on the same day, constitute a single RHC or FQHC visit and are payable as one visit. This policy applies regardless of the length or complexity of the visit, the number or type of practitioners seen, whether the second visit is a scheduled or unscheduled appointment, or whether the first visit is related or unrelated to the subsequent visit. This would include situations where an RHC or FQHC patient has a medically necessary face-to-face visit with an RHC or FQHC practitioner and is then seen by another RHC or FQHC practitioner, including a specialist, for further evaluation of the same condition on the same day, or is then seen by another RHC or FQHC practitioner, including a specialist, for evaluation of a different condition on the same day.
We understand commenters' concern that this approach may limit the near-term financial incentive for RHCs to furnish DSMT or MNT alongside an existing medical visit, particularly given that rural beneficiaries may consolidate care into a single visit for reasons of distance, cost, and transportation. We did not propose a stackable or supplemental payment mechanism, or a carve-out of DSMT or MNT from the AIR, however, as such a change would be a substantial departure from the per-diem, encounter-based structure of the AIR methodology generally and was outside the scope of this proposal as presented in the proposed rule.
Comment:
One commenter requested CMS to clarify whether the stand-alone DSMT/MNT billing treatment would extend to “historically excepted Tribal FQHCs”, which are paid under a separate methodology—the IHS outpatient per-visit rate under §§ 405.2462(f) and 405.2464(d)—rather than the standard FQHC PPS rate the proposed rule's discussion references. The commenter asked whether a DSMT or MNT encounter would count as a qualifying visit at these centers on the same terms as RHCs and FQHCs. The commenter supported the request by noting that AI/AN adults have the highest diagnosed diabetes prevalence of any tracked group, concentrated in the same rural areas this proposal targets.
Response:
We thank the commenter for this clarifying question. Historically excepted Tribal FQHCs are paid at the lesser of the Medicare outpatient per-visit rate as set annually by the IHS, or the actual charge for the service, under §§ 405.2462(g)(1)(ii) and 405.2464(d). The proposal does not change that payment methodology, and historically excepted Tribal FQHCs are paid this way for all covered services, including DSMT and MNT. We note, as finalized in the CY 2016 PFS final rule, historically excepted Tribal FQHCs are paid for services included in the FQHC benefit (
80 FR 71089
through
71096
). Under this authority, DSMT and MNT services furnished by certified providers are stand-alone billable visits in FQHCs when all of the requirements are met, without a supervision requirement.
For whether a DSMT or MNT encounter constitutes a qualifying visit, we confirm that DSMT (G0108 Diabetes outpatient self-management training services, individual, per 30 minutes) is a qualifying visit for both FQHC payment codes G0466 (FQHC visit, new patient) and G0467 (FQHC visit, established patient). We also confirm that MNT (97802 Medical nutrition therapy; initial assessment and intervention, individual, face-to-face with the patient, each 15 minutes) is a qualifying visit for both FQHC payment codes G0466 (FQHC visit, new patient) and G0467 (FQHC visit, established patient). Also, MNT (97803 Medical nutrition therapy; re-assessment and intervention, individual, face-to-face with the patient, each 15 minutes) and (G0270 Medical nutrition therapy; reassessment and subsequent intervention(s) following second referral in same year for change in diagnosis, medical condition or treatment regimen (including additional hours needed for renal disease), individual, face to face with the patient, each 15 minutes) are each a qualifying visit for FQHC payment code G0467 (FQHC visit, established patient).

]
We acknowledge the commenter's observation that American Indian and Alaska Native adults have the highest rate of diagnosed diabetes of any racial or ethnic group tracked by CDC, underscoring the importance of ensuring clarity on this point for historically excepted Tribal FQHCs and confirm that, when Tribal FQHCs provide DSMT or MNT services, these services qualify as an FQHC visit.
Comment:
Several commenters requested CMS clarify whether DSMT and MNT may be furnished through telecommunication technology, including in group or shared formats, by all personnel otherwise qualified under the existing benefits. They emphasized that virtual access is particularly important for rural beneficiaries who may have limited access to RDNs and diabetes educators.
Other commenters recommended making telehealth payment permanent, eliminating geographic and originating-site restrictions, paying RHC telehealth services at the full AIR rather than the
(
printed page 71209)
lower physician fee schedule rate, and using CMMI or other demonstration authority to test accredited virtual or asynchronous DSMT models in RHCs and FQHCs.
Commenters also noted that, while in-person DSMT and MNT would qualify for the full stand-alone AIR, virtually delivered services would be paid at a lower and declining physician fee schedule rate. They stated that this disparity could discourage virtual care in rural clinics with limited on-site staffing and undermine access for beneficiaries least able to travel. One commenter therefore recommended extending the in-person-visit waiver under section 6209(c) of the CAA, 2026 to DSMT and MNT, allowing virtually delivered services to receive the same stand-alone AIR through at least 12/31/2027.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for expanding access to DSMT and MNT services for beneficiaries receiving care in RHCs and FQHCs, including through the use of telecommunications technology. As discussed in section III.B.3. of this final rule, the Congress has extended through December 31, 2027, the authority for RHCs and FQHCs to furnish certain non-behavioral health services as Medicare telehealth services. As HCPCS codes 97802 and G0108 are listed in the Medicare telehealth services list, they are eligible for payment under the payment policy for non-behavioral services when furnished via telecommunications technology in RHCs and FQHCs. Under the current framework, non-behavioral health services furnished by an RHC or FQHC using telecommunications technology are paid under the methodology set forth in § 405.2464(g), rather than the RHC AIR or FQHC PPS. This methodology bases payment on the national average payment rates of the list of services available as Medicare telehealth services under the Physician Fee Schedule. DSMT and MNT services furnished through telecommunications technology remain subject to the applicable RHC and FQHC telehealth requirements and payment methodology and do not qualify for AIR payment solely because the same service would be payable as a stand-alone visit if furnished in person.
We also acknowledge commenters' concerns that differences between payment for in-person and telehealth services may affect RHCs' ability to invest in or expand virtual care arrangements. Similar concerns were raised in response to our broader proposals concerning RHC and FQHC telehealth policy, including requests to pay for non-behavioral health telehealth services at the RHC AIR or FQHC PPS rate. As explained in section III.B.3. of this final rule, revisions to the payment methodology for non-behavioral telehealth services are outside the scope of the conforming changes finalized in this rulemaking. We will consider commenters' views, as appropriate, in the context of future rulemaking addressing RHC and FQHC telehealth payment policy.
For requests concerning expansion or permanent extension of telehealth flexibilities, elimination of geographic or originating-site requirements, and use of Innovation Center or other demonstration authority to test virtual or asynchronous models, these recommendations concern broader Medicare telehealth, benefit, payment, or demonstration policies that are outside the scope of this rulemaking. We therefore are not addressing those recommendations substantively in this final rule but may take them into consideration in future policy development.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to recognize DSMT and MNT services as qualified preventive services that are covered and paid the AIR as stand-alone billable visits under the RHC benefit. To constitute as a billable RHC visit, these services would need to be furnished by a certified provider under the direct supervision of an RHC practitioner. As we clarified above, consistent with the definition of “direct supervision” in § 405.2401(b), the presence of the physician (or other supervising practitioner) includes virtual presence through audio/video real-time communications technology (excluding audio-only). We believe this clarification mitigates the burden of workforce limitations that may exist in RHCs since it offers a virtual direct supervision option. We believe aligning payment policies in RHCs with other settings, for example FQHCs and physician offices, would help expand access to care for Medicare beneficiaries in rural areas while supporting Federal initiatives to strengthen rural healthcare. We are also finalizing our proposal to revise § 405.2463(a) and (b)(2) to allow DSMT and MNT services to be stand—alone billable visits in RHCs, as proposed. Similar to FQHCs, when DSMT or MNT is furnished on the same day as another qualified visit, the RHC would be paid one AIR for that encounter.
Comment:
In addition to the comments addressed previously, several commenters offered recommendations that, while related to DSMT and MNT generally, go beyond the specific scope of this proposal. We summarize these comments below but do not address them substantively in this final rule, as they concern separate statutory or regulatory provisions, or policy changes not proposed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule.

One commenter requested CMS amend § 410.132(c) to permit MNT referral by nonphysician practitioners (NPs and PAs) authorized to refer for DSMT, noting that most RHCs are staffed predominantly by mid-level practitioners who currently cannot generate a qualifying MNT referral.
A small number of additional recommendations fell outside the scope of this proposal: removing the one-year expiration on the initial 10 hours of DSMT; reconsidering CMS's general valuation methodology for low-intensity preventive services; requiring state Medicaid programs to recognize RDNs as eligible MNT providers, and revisiting the 85 percent-of-PFS payment cap for RDN-furnished MNT; encouraging referral pathways from DSMT/MNT to medically tailored meal programs; and addressing the effect of the proposed CY 2027 conversion factor reduction on PFS-billed MNT codes.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's feedback however these comments are outside the scope of this proposal.
3. Services Furnished Using Telecommunication Technology
a. Background
Section 3704 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act) (
Pub. L. 116-136
, March 27, 2020) directed the Secretary to establish payment for RHC and FQHC services that are provided as Medicare telehealth services by RHCs and FQHCs
(
printed page 71210)
serving as a distant site (that is, where the practitioner is located) during the PHE for COVID-19. Specifically, section 1834(m)(8)(B) of the Act, as added by section 3704 of the CARES Act, required that, for the duration of the PHE for COVID-19, the Secretary develop and implement payment methods for FQHCs and RHCs that serve as a distant site. The payment methodology outlined in the CARES Act requires that rates be based on rates that are similar to the national average payment rates for comparable telehealth services under the Medicare PFS. Accordingly, we established payment rates for these services furnished by RHCs and FQHCs based on the average PFS payment amount for all Medicare telehealth services, weighted by volume in a Special Edition Medicare Learning Network Article (SE20016). Congress has extended this payment flexibility beyond the PHE for COVID-19 through a series of statutory amendments, most recently under section 6209(c) of the CAA, 2026, which extended this payment flexibility through December 31, 2027.
We codified this payment policy at
42 CFR 405.2464(g)
. As amended in the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98554
), § 405.2464(g) states that for an encounter furnished using interactive, real-time, audio/visual telecommunications technology or for certain audio-only interactions in cases where the patient is not capable of, or does not consent to, the use of video technology services that are not described in § 405.2463(b)(3), payment to RHCs and FQHCs are subject to the national average payment rates for comparable services under the PFS and costs associated with these services shall not be used in determining payments under the RHC all-inclusive rate or the FQHC prospective payment system.
In the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65210
and
65211
), we revised payment for mental health visits in RHCs and FQHCs furnished via interactive, real-time, audio/visual or audio-only telecommunications technology. Instead of paying for these services under the national average payment rates for comparable services under the PFS, as is done for non-behavioral health services, we amended the regulation at § 405.2463 to permit mental health visits in RHCs and FQHCs furnished via audio/visual or audio-only telecommunication to be paid under the RHC AIR and FQHC PPS rates. In addition, to align with the Medicare telehealth statutory requirements for mental health services, we finalized at §§  405.2463(b)(3) and 405.2469(d) that there must be an in-person mental health service furnished within 6 months prior to the furnishing of the telecommunications service and that an in-person mental health service (without the use of telecommunications technology) must be provided at least every 12 months while the beneficiary is receiving services furnished via telecommunications technology for diagnosis, evaluation, or treatment of mental health disorders, unless, for a particular 12-month period, the physician or practitioner and patient agree that the risks and burdens outweigh the benefits associated with furnishing the in-person item or service, and the practitioner documents the reasons for this decision in the patient's medical record.
However, beginning with section 304 of Division P of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022 (CAA, 2022) (
Pub. L. 117-103
, March 15, 2022), the in—person visit requirements for mental health visits were delayed. These requirements were further delayed through various laws that included extension of the telehealth flexibilities. Following the publication of the CY 2026 PFS final rule, section 6208 of the Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026 (
Pub. L. 119-37
, November 12, 2025) extended the delay until January 30, 2026. Most recently, section 6209(d) of the CAA, 2026 extended the abeyance of the RHC/FQHC mental health in-person requirements through December 31, 2027.
b. Conforming Regulatory Text Changes
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43960
), we explained that because section 6209(c) of the CAA, 2026 extended authority for CMS to pay for FQHC and RHC non-behavioral health telecommunication technology services as Medicare telehealth services, we did not propose any modifications for this provision to § 405.2464(g).
We also explained that because section 6209(d) of the CAA, 2026 extended the abeyance of the RHC and FQHC mental health in-person requirements through December 31, 2027, we proposed to make conforming regulatory text changes at §§ 405.2463(b)(3) and 405.2469(d). We stated that this provision, as proposed, would require that the in-person visit requirements not apply to any services furnished through December 31, 2027.
We received public comments on our proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters supported our proposal to make regulatory changes to conform to statutory requirements. Commenters stated that telehealth-related flexibilities in general improve access to behavioral health and other services for beneficiaries in rural and underserved areas, where provider shortages, transportation barriers, mobility limitations, and long travel distances may make in-person care difficult to obtain. A commenter noted that these flexibilities may facilitate access to substance use disorder treatment, including the initiation and continuation of treatment through telehealth. Another commenter described the importance of telehealth for individuals with significant mobility, respiratory, communication, and other functional limitations and encouraged CMS to preserve flexible access to telehealth, including audio-only services when clinically appropriate.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for our proposed conforming changes. The regulatory revisions proposed in this rulemaking are conforming changes intended to reflect statutory requirements.
Comment:
Several commenters also urged that the telehealth flexibilities be made permanent rather than extended for limited periods. These commenters stated that successive temporary extensions create uncertainty for RHCs and FQHCs and may discourage investment in telehealth infrastructure, staffing, and other resources necessary to sustain telehealth services over the long term.
Response:
We acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding the effects of temporary extensions on RHCs' and FQHCs' ability to plan for and invest in telehealth services. The amendments addressed in this section are conforming changes intended to reflect current statutory requirements, including the statutory extension through December 31, 2027, of the delay of the in-person visit requirements for RHC and FQHC mental health services furnished using telecommunications technology. Because the duration of that extension is established by statute, making the extension permanent is beyond the scope of these conforming amendments.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed concerns regarding payment for non-behavioral health services furnished by RHCs using telecommunications technology. Commenters asserted that payment under HCPCS code G2025 is lower than the payment RHCs would receive under the RHC AIR for an in-person visit and,
(
printed page 71211)
in some cases, lower than Medicare Physician Fee Schedule payment for comparable services. Commenters stated that this payment methodology may create a financial disincentive for RHCs to furnish or expand telehealth services and requested that CMS reconsider the payment methodology, establish payment parity, or align payment for RHC telehealth services with the RHC AIR. A commenter described the use of RHC telehealth to furnish specialty services, including pulmonology, gastroenterology, and neurology services, and stated that higher payment would support expansion of specialty care in rural communities.

We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the potential effects of the current payment methodology on RHCs' and FQHCs' ability to furnish or expand telehealth services, including specialty care. The proposed changes concerning payment for non-behavioral health services furnished using telecommunications technology were limited to conforming and technical changes to reflect current statutory authority. Accordingly, broader revisions to the payment methodology, including requests to establish payment parity or align payment for these services with the RHC AIR or FQHC PPS, are outside the scope of this rulemaking. We may consider commenters' views, as appropriate, in the context of future rulemaking addressing RHC and FQHC telehealth payment policy.
