) whereby CMS would change the definition of an RHC or FQHC medical visit to include visits furnished using telecommunications technology so that such services would be paid under the RHC AIR or FQHC PPS, similar to how we previously revised the regulations for mental health visits. The commenter stated that the current payment differential between in-person and medical telehealth visits limits RHCs' ability to invest in telehealth technology and incorporate telehealth into their care delivery models. The commenter acknowledged that the special payment rule for RHC and FQHC telehealth services was established by statute but urged CMS to further consider whether it has authority to adopt an alternative approach or work with Congress to address the payment differential. The commenter also requested that CMS further explain statements made in prior rulemaking regarding potential unintended consequences, program integrity concerns, and administrative burden associated with the alternative payment approach discussed in the CY PFS 2026 final rule. The commenter questioned whether such concerns would arise in practice and suggested that CMS could address potential program integrity concerns through claims modifiers or other safeguards rather than maintaining the current payment methodology.
Response:
The regulatory revisions proposed in this rulemaking are conforming changes intended to reflect statutory requirements, and revisions to the payment methodology for non-behavioral services furnished using telecommunications technology are out of scope for purposes of this rulemaking. We note that our proposed changes concerning payment for non-behavioral health services furnished using telecommunications technology were limited to conforming and technical changes to reflect current statutory authority. We may consider commenters' views, as appropriate, in the context of any future rulemaking addressing RHC and FQHC telehealth payment policy.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed conforming amendments to §§ 405.2463(b)(3) and 405.2469(d). 4. CY 2027 FQHC PPS Market Basket Update
Section 1834(o)(2)(B)(ii) of the Act requires the FQHC PPS base rate be updated annually by the percentage increase in a market basket of Federally qualified health center goods and services as issued through regulations, or if such an index is not available, by the percentage increase in the MEI (as defined in section 1842(i)(3) of the Act) for the year involved. For CY 2027 (that is, January 1, 2027, through December 31, 2027), we proposed to use an estimate of the percentage increase in the 2022-based FQHC market basket to update payments to FQHCs based on the best available data (
91 FR 43960
). Additionally, as finalized in the CY 2025 final rule (
89 FR 98032
), a productivity adjustment is included in the 2022-based FQHC market basket.
For CY 2027, we proposed to update the CY 2026 FQHC PPS base rate by the historical percentage increase through the second quarter of 2026 of the productivity-adjusted FQHC market basket (which we refer to as the FQHC market basket update). For CY 2027, the proposed FQHC market basket update was estimated to be 2.5 percent and was based on the expected historical percentage increase of the FQHC market basket update. Multiplying the CY 2026 FQHC PPS base rate amount of $207.72 by the proposed CY 2027 FQHC market basket update of 2.5 percent ($207.72 × 1.025) resulted in a proposed CY 2027 FQHC PPS base rate amount of $212.91. In the CY 2027 proposed rule, we proposed that the CY 2027 market basket update and the productivity adjustment would be updated to reflect historical data through the 2nd quarter of 2026 (
91 FR 43960
).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters noted appreciation for the proposed CY 2027 market basket update for Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), also referred to as community health centers (CHCs). These commenters stated that while the proposed 2.5 percent increase is appreciated, it does not resolve their underlying concern that Medicare payments have not kept pace with the actual cost of furnishing comprehensive care in FQHCs.
Commenters stated that the CY 2027 update relies on the 2022-based FQHC market basket, which reflects a cost structure several years removed from CY 2027, and noted that general inflation has grown at a faster rate than the FQHC market basket updates between 2022 and 2026. Commenters also described concurrent cost pressures facing CHCs, including workforce recruitment and retention costs, health information technology and cybersecurity investments, administrative and compliance requirements, anticipated Medicaid coverage losses, and instability affecting the 340B Drug Pricing Program.
Commenters stated that annual market basket adjustments alone cannot correct an underlying prospective payment system (PPS) methodology that was established more than a decade ago and may no longer adequately capture the cost and complexity of contemporary care provided by these facilities. These commenters requested CMS undertake a comprehensive evaluation of the FQHC PPS using current Medicare cost report data and identify opportunities to simplify Medicare cost reporting while preserving the information needed to accurately assess FQHC costs.
(
printed page 71212)
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concern regarding inflationary pressure facing FQHCs/CHCs and the proposed CY 2027 market basket update.
The 2022-based FQHC market basket is a fixed-weight, Laspeyres-type index that measures price changes over time. A Laspeyres-type price index measures the change in price, over time, of the same mix of goods and services purchased in the base period. Any changes in the quantity or mix of goods and services (that is, intensity) purchased over time are not measured.
Since the inception of the FQHC PPS, the FQHC payment rates (with the exception of statutorily-mandated updates) have been updated by the FQHC market basket percentage increase.
Additionally, the market basket updates appropriately differ from other payment updates (such as increases in the Consumer Price Index) that are not consistent in concept with the statutory requirement for the index to reflect the relative costs associated with furnishing FQHC visits.
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the adequacy of the FQHC PPS methodology and the suggestion that we undertake a comprehensive evaluation of the system using current Medicare cost report data. We recognize that FQHCs continue to face evolving operational and financial pressures, and we value the ongoing feedback we receive through the rulemaking process on how well the FQHC PPS reflects current costs of care.
We agree that the annual market basket update described in this rule is required by section 1834(o)(2)(B)(ii) of the Act and is intended to adjust the FQHC PPS base rate for input price inflation; however, it is not intended to serve as a mechanism for broader structural revisions to the payment methodology itself. A comprehensive reevaluation of the FQHC PPS, including the underlying cost reporting requirements and payment structure, would require a more extensive process involving consideration of statutory authority, detailed analysis of current Medicare cost report data, and opportunity for additional interested parties input beyond the scope of this annual update. Regarding the monitoring of trends in FQHC costs and operations, including the impact of the factors commenters raised, we may take these concerns into account as we consider future policy development.
Final Rule Action:
As is our general practice, we proposed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that if more recent data became available, we would use such data, if appropriate, to derive the final CY 2027 FQHC market basket update for the final rule. Therefore, for this final rule, based on historical data through the second quarter 2026, the final 2022-based FQHC market basket update for CY 2027 is 2.6 percent, which is 0.1 percentage point higher than the projected CY 2027 market basket update in the proposed rule. Multiplying the CY 2026 FQHC PPS base rate amount of $207.72 by the final CY 2027 FQHC market basket update of 2.6 percent ($207.72 × 1.026) results in a final CY 2027 FQHC PPS base rate amount of $213.12.

C. Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS): Consolidated Appropriations Act (CAA), 2026
1. Background on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule
Prior to January 1, 2018, Medicare paid for clinical diagnostic laboratory tests (CDLTs) on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) under section 1833(a), (b), and (h) of the Act. Under the previous payment system, CDLTs were paid based on the lesser of: (1) the amount billed; (2) the local fee schedule amount established by the Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC); or (3) a national limitation amount (NLA), which is a percentage of the median of all the local fee schedule amounts (or 100 percent of the median for new tests furnished on or after January 1, 2001). In practice, most tests were paid at the NLA. Under the previous payment system, the CLFS amounts were updated for inflation based on the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), and reduced by a productivity adjustment and other statutory adjustments, but were not otherwise updated or changed. Coinsurance and deductibles generally do not apply to CDLTs paid under the CLFS.
Section 1834A of the Act, as established by section 216(a) of the Protecting Access to Medicare Act of 2014 (PAMA), required significant changes to how Medicare pays for CDLTs under the CLFS. In a final rule that appeared in the June 23, 2016
Federal Register
(
81 FR 41036
), entitled Medicare Clinical Diagnostic Laboratory Tests Payment System (hereinafter referred to as the CLFS final rule), we established requirements to implement section 1834A of the Act at
42 CFR part 414, subpart G
.
Under the CLFS final rule, “reporting entities” must report to CMS during a “data reporting period” “applicable information” collected during a “data collection period” for their component “applicable laboratories.” The first data collection period occurred from January 1, 2016, through June 30, 2016. The first data reporting period occurred from January 1, 2017, through March 31, 2017. On March 30, 2017, we announced a 60-day period of enforcement discretion for the application of the Secretary's potential assessment of civil monetary penalties for failure to report applicable information with respect to the initial data reporting period.

2. Payment Requirements for Clinical Diagnostic Laboratory Tests
In general, under section 1834A of the Act, the payment amount for each CDLT on the CLFS furnished beginning January 1, 2018, is based on the applicable information collected during the data collection period and reported to CMS during the data reporting period and is equal to the weighted median of the private payor rates for the test. The weighted median is calculated by arraying the distribution of all private payor rates, weighted by the volume for each payor and each laboratory. The payment amounts established under the CLFS are not subject to any other adjustment, such as geographic, budget neutrality, or annual update, as required by section 1834A(b)(4)(B) of the Act. Additionally, section 1834A(b)(3) of the Act, implemented at § 414.507(d), provides for a phase-in of payment reductions, limiting the amounts the CLFS rates for each CDLT (that is not a new advanced diagnostic laboratory test (ADLT) or new CDLT) can be reduced
(
printed page 71214)
as compared to the payment rates for the preceding year. Under the original provisions enacted by section 216(a) of PAMA, for the first 3 years after implementation (CY 2018 through CY 2020), the reduction could not be more than 10 percent per year. For the next 3 years after implementation (CY 2021 through CY 2023), section 216(a) of PAMA stated that the reduction could not be more than 15 percent per year. Under sections 1834A(a)(1) and (b) of the Act, as enacted by PAMA, for CDLTs that are not ADLTs, the data collection period, data reporting period, and payment rate update were to occur every 3 years. As such, the second data collection period for CDLTs that are not ADLTs was originally scheduled to take place from January 1, 2019, through June 30, 2019, and the next data reporting period was originally scheduled to take place from January 1, 2020, through March 31, 2020, with the next update to the Medicare payment rates for those tests based on that reported applicable information scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2021.
Section 216(a) of PAMA established a new subcategory of CDLTs known as ADLTs, with separate reporting and payment requirements under section 1834A of the Act. The definition of an ADLT is set forth in section 1834A(d)(5) of the Act and implemented at § 414.502. Generally, under section 1834A(d) of the Act, the Medicare payment rate for a new ADLT is equal to its actual list charge during an initial period of 3 calendar quarters. After the new ADLT initial period, ADLTs are paid using the same methodology based on the weighted median of private payor rates as other CDLTs. However, under section 1834A(d)(3) of the Act, updates to the Medicare payment rates for ADLTs occur annually instead of every 3 years.

Comment:
Commenters supported our proposal to make regulatory changes to conform to the statutory requirements pursuant to section 6226 of the CAA, 2026. Several commenters, however, expressed concerns about the private payor rate-based CLFS methodology and the potential effects of future payment reductions. Commenters stated that reported private payor rates may not fully reflect the costs or market value of laboratory services or adequately represent the range of laboratories furnishing services to Medicare beneficiaries, including physician-office, hospital outreach, rural, community-based, and oncology laboratories. Commenters cited inflationary pressures, labor and supply costs, limited negotiating leverage with commercial insurers, and increasing regulatory requirements, and expressed concern that additional payment reductions under the CLFS could affect laboratory sustainability, beneficiary access, diagnostic innovation, and practice consolidation. Similarly, another commenter expressed concern that upcoming CLFS rates could result in substantial payment reductions beginning in 2027 and continuing through 2029. The commenter stated that such reductions could make it difficult to invest in new or expanded laboratory services and could threaten access to care, particularly in rural areas.
Commenters urged CMS to monitor the completeness and representativeness of reported private payor data and the effects of resulting CLFS payment rates, limit or defer payment reductions where possible, and consider broader changes to CLFS data collection and rate setting. Another commenter recommended that CMS evaluate whether the applicable laboratory methodology and low-expenditure threshold result in sufficiently representative data and examine whether increasing Medicare Advantage penetration affects which laboratories satisfy the applicable laboratory criteria.
A commenter also urged Congress and CMS to further delay CLFS payment reductions while evaluating alternative approaches to data collection and rate setting and recommended that future payment updates rely on transparent and representative market data that account for laboratory services furnished across diverse provider settings.
Response:
We appreciate the support of commenters for our proposed conforming regulatory changes and we appreciate their concerns regarding the completeness and representativeness of private-payor data, the composition of the reporting population, and the potential effects of CLFS payment changes. As the regulatory revisions proposed in this rulemaking are conforming changes intended to reflect statutory requirements, revisions to the statutory private payor rate-based methodology and timing of payment reductions are out of scope for purposes of this rulemaking. We note that the recommended changes to the statutory timing of payment reductions, the private payor rate-based methodology, or to other requirements established by section 1834A of the Act would require further Congressional action. We note that section 1834A(b)(3) of the Act limits the amount by which the payment amount for an existing test may be reduced, compared with the payment amount for the preceding year, as a result of implementing updated CLFS rates based on applicable information. Accordingly, the actual payment reduction for a particular test will depend on the applicable weighted median private payor rate and may be less than 15%, or may not result in a reduction, while the statutory phase-in provision prevents an annual payment reduction from exceeding 15 percent for CYs 2027 through 2029.
We will take the commenters' other recommendations, such as suggestions to review the regulatory low expenditure threshold, under advisement.
Comment:

6. Technical Correction (§ 414.523(a)(1))
a. Background
Section 1833(h)(3)(A) of the Act generally requires the Secretary to provide for and establish a nominal fee to cover the appropriate costs in collecting the sample on which a CDLT was performed and for which Medicare payment is made, in addition to the amounts provided under the Medicare CLFS. In addition, section 1834A(b)(5) of the Act requires that, when the sample is collected from an individual in a skilled nursing facility (SNF) or by a laboratory on behalf of a home health agency (HHA), the otherwise applicable nominal specimen collection fee be increased by $2.00.
In the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69744
through
69760
), we finalized a policy to codify specimen collection fee provisions at § 414.523(a)(1), including updating the base specimen collection fee amount and establishing an annual CPI-U update. In that rulemaking, we also stated that the statutory $2.00 increase for specimens collected from a Medicare beneficiary in a SNF or by a laboratory on behalf of an HHA would continue to apply, consistent with section 1834A(b)(5) of the Act. However, due to a drafting or codification error, the operative regulatory text implementing this increase in the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 70225
through
70226
) was not fully included in § 414.523(a)(1), and only a partial introductory clause remains in paragraph (a)(1)(v). Specifically, the introductory text to § 414.523(a)(1) states that payment is made “[e]xcept as provided in paragraph (a)(1)(v),” but § 414.523(a)(1)(v), as codified, consists only of the fragment: “For a specimen collected from a Medicare beneficiary.” This text is incomplete and does not contain operative language establishing an exception or alternative payment methodology. In addition, other provisions within § 414.523(a)(1), including paragraph (a)(1)(ii), already specify that the specimen must be collected from a Medicare beneficiary, creating an apparent internal inconsistency when read together with the introductory exception clause.

In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (

We noted that we do not believe that this proposal reflects a substantive policy change. In the CY 2023 PFS proposed rule (

(
printed page 71217)

through
69760

(2) Background
ASM will test whether holding physician specialists accountable for the quality and cost of care associated with the longitudinal management of specific chronic conditions, heart failure and low back pain, can reduce Medicare expenditures while preserving or enhancing quality of care for Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) beneficiaries. Clinical decisions made by specialists in ambulatory settings can meaningfully influence disease progression as well as downstream utilization and spending. ASM's design, in its goal to reduce Medicare expenditures while preserving or enhancing the quality of care, aims to: (1) improve the management of chronic disease and slow disease progression through more effective risk assessment; (2) increase active collaboration between specialists and primary care providers, and (3) reduce avoidable hospitalizations and low-value procedures (that is, procedures that provide little clinical benefit or the risk of harm outweighs its potential benefit).
In developing ASM, we considered specialist-managed conditions that often require ongoing outpatient management, diagnostic evaluation, medication management, coordination by specialists with other clinicians across different care settings, and, in some cases, procedural or surgical intervention (
90 FR 49562
through
49564
). Based on these factors, ASM selects individual specialists who manage one of two ASM targeted chronic conditions, heart failure or low back pain. As we designed ASM's participation criteria and performance evaluation framework to cover multiple conditions and associated specialists, we continue to explore whether including additional conditions and specialists would be appropriate.
Our goal with the model test is to select specialists who have a meaningful level of engagement in the care of Medicare FFS beneficiaries with ASM targeted chronic conditions as ASM participants. Under the provisions finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49571
through
49596
), we select ASM participants by a combination of a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) and a National Provider Identifier (NPI). ASM participants are clinicians who meet four ASM participant eligibility criteria: (1) bill claims under the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule, (2) have a selected physician specialty type relevant to an ASM targeted chronic condition, (3) meet a historical volume threshold of condition-specific episode-based cost measure (EBCM) episodes, and (4) have a service location in a selected mandatory geographic area (that is, selected Core-Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs) and metropolitan divisions). ASM heart failure participants include cardiologists, and ASM low back pain participants include physicians with specialty types of anesthesiology, interventional pain management, neurosurgery, orthopedic surgery, pain management, and physical medicine and rehabilitation.
ASM evaluates ASM participants across four ASM performance categories: quality, cost, improvement activities, and Promoting Interoperability. The evaluation of ASM participant performance leverages the MIPS Value Pathways (MVP) framework, which utilizes a cohesive set of measures and activities focused on performance in furnishing care for a particular specialty or clinical condition. ASM participants must meet each ASM performance category's requirements and report required data. We use data reported by ASM participants and other administrative data, such as inputs gathered from claims, to evaluate each ASM participant's performance on an annual basis. We determine a composite final score for each ASM participant based on performance across the four ASM performance categories and adjust final scores to account for beneficiary medical and social complexity as well as practice size.
Based on performance relative to other specialists treating the same ASM targeted chronic condition in an ASM cohort, ASM participants will receive a positive, neutral, or negative payment adjustment on all Medicare Part B claims for covered professional services during the CY 2 years following the applicable ASM performance year (for example, performance during the 2027 ASM performance year results in the application of ASM payment adjustments during the 2029 ASM payment year). Payment adjustments will range from negative 9 percent to positive 9 percent in the first 2 ASM payment years, gradually increasing to 12 percent in the final ASM payment year.

b. Participation
(1) Background
As discussed in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49571
through
49596
), we designed ASM with a focus on clinicians who commonly treat Medicare FFS beneficiaries in an ambulatory setting, develop longitudinal relationships with patients, and co-manage beneficiaries with primary care providers (PCP). In addition, we believe clinicians who treat ASM targeted chronic conditions are well-positioned to benefit from improved integration between specialty and primary care, creating greater opportunities to incentivize high-value care and tertiary prevention.
We determined the model would assess quality of care provided at the individual clinician level, as identified by a combination of TIN and NPI, rather than at the level of a group practice or facility, with limited exceptions, to align accountability with individual clinical decision-making and to better capture variation in individual clinical practice patterns among clinicians within the same organization (
90 FR 49574
). As a result, each ASM participant is individually responsible for meeting model requirements and is evaluated independently for the purposes of ASM performance category scoring, final scoring, and determining an ASM payment adjustment factor and corresponding ASM payment multiplier.

(4) ASM Participant Exceptions
We recognize that there may be limited circumstances in which an ASM participant selected for participation for an ASM performance year should be excepted from certain ASM requirements for that ASM performance year and consequently excepted from the application of an ASM payment multiplier to the ASM participant's Medicare Part B payments for covered professional services during the corresponding ASM payment year. Accordingly, we finalized a narrow set of ASM participant “exclusions,” or situations in which an ASM participant is excepted from specified ASM requirements in the CY 2026 PFS final rule to balance operational feasibility with the need for robust evaluation and generalizable findings (
90 FR 49582
through
49583
). As finalized at § 512.710(c), an ASM participant who stops reassigning billing rights to the TIN we used to select the ASM participant and begins reassigning billing rights to a new TIN during an ASM performance year is not subject to certain ASM requirements—specifically the requirements for performance assessment described at § 512.715, data submission described at § 512.720, final scoring described at § 512.745, and payment adjustment described at § 512.750—and is no longer eligible for Medicare program waivers provided under the model described at § 512.775 for the applicable ASM performance year. An exception from specified ASM requirements for one ASM performance year does not apply for the entire ASM test period because we consider clinicians who meet ASM participant eligibility criteria for at least one ASM performance year to be an ASM participant for the remainder of the ASM test period. This means that an ASM participant will receive payment adjustments during a corresponding ASM payment year based on performance from an ASM performance year for which they were required to meet these specified ASM requirements (
90 FR 49571
through
49574
). In other words, if an ASM participant meets the ASM participant eligibility criteria for the 2027 and 2028 ASM performance years, but not the 2029 and 2030 ASM performance years, by continuing to remain an ASM participant, the ASM payment multipliers calculated based on the ASM participant's performance during the 2027 and 2028 ASM performance years would be applied to the ASM participant's Medicare Part B payments for covered professional services during the corresponding ASM payment years (that is, CY 2029 and CY 2030 respectively).
After internal review, we believed it would be more precise to refer to the situations in which an ASM participant is not required to meet specified ASM requirements for applicable ASM performance year(s) as “exceptions” to ASM requirements rather than ASM participant “exclusions.” We believed this revision to the terminology would better capture the intended policy to not require an ASM participant to meet certain ASM requirements for an ASM performance year under certain circumstances. Accordingly, we proposed revisions to existing regulatory text to clarify the current circumstances under which an ASM participant may be excepted from certain ASM requirements and proposed new provisions to include additional circumstances under which an exception would apply.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43968
), we proposed, in addition to the current exception due to a change in the reassignment of billing rights (that is, change in TIN), to recognize a new exception. Specifically, we proposed that ASM heart failure participants who meet certain specialty type redesignation requirements may be excepted from specified model requirements. For each exception, we discussed proposals around the requirements and process for notifying us of a change that may warrant an exception. Finally, in accordance with the revisions to § 512.710(a)(2) discussed earlier in this section of this final rule, we made proposals at § 512.710(c) to describe the effect and duration of an exception due to a change in TIN or redesignation of primary specialty type.

We proposed to revise § 512.710(c)(1) to describe how we may determine an exception applies. Specifically, we proposed that an ASM participant who demonstrates the circumstances described by an exception apply (that is, change in TIN or approved primary specialty type redesignation) would be excepted from specified ASM requirements, subject to CMS determination for the duration specified for each exception. We believed this provision provided additional clarity on how the notification processes proposed at §§ 512.710(c)(1)(i)(A) and 512.710(c)(1)(i)(B) could lead to an exception.
Third, we proposed new provisions related to ASM participant TIN changes that occur before the start of an ASM performance year. At § 512.710(c)(1)(i)(A), we proposed that an ASM participant who stops reassigning billing rights to the TIN that we used to select them as an ASM participant before the applicable ASM performance year must notify us in writing no later than 60 days after the start of the applicable ASM performance year; after receiving such notice, we may determine an exception to specified ASM requirements applies for the ASM performance year. We recognized that ASM participants may change organizational affiliations between the time we select ASM participants and the start of an ASM performance year. Based on our previously finalized provisions related to the TIN change exception in the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we believed that the same challenge of having consistent claims history and EBCM data to evaluate ASM participant eligibility criteria under the new TIN would apply in this circumstance and thus an exception would be appropriate. We believe that requiring the ASM participant to notify us in writing no later than 60 days after the start of the ASM performance year would provide an adequate window to provide us with notice of such change after we release the list of ASM participants for a given ASM performance year.
Finally, we proposed at § 512.710(c)(1)(i)(B) that an ASM participant who stops reassigning their billing rights to the TIN we used to select them for participation in ASM during an ASM performance year would not be required to reassign billing rights to a new TIN during the same ASM performance year to be potentially eligible for an exception from specified ASM requirements. We believed the proposed modification would capture additional organizational affiliation changes, such as retirements, that merit an exception from specified ASM requirements. We further believed this proposal was consistent with the original intent of the TIN change exception policy we finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule. We also proposed that an ASM participant who changes their TIN during an ASM performance year would need to provide written notice of the change in a form and manner determined by us within 30 days of stopping reassignment to that TIN. We believe that adding this additional detail on the form of the notification and required timing would clarify the notification process for ASM participants.
We sought comment on our proposal at § 512.710(c)(1) describing the notice and determination process for an exception from specified model requirements. We also sought comment on our proposal at § 512.710(c)(1)(i) to describe the requirements for an exception from specified model requirements for an ASM participant who stops reassigning billing rights to the TIN we used to select them as an ASM participant. We also sought comment on: (1) our proposed notification process for TIN changes that occur before the start of an ASM performance year described at § 512.710(c)(1)(i)(A); (2) our proposal to remove the requirement that an ASM participant who no longer reassigns their billing rights to the TIN we used to select them as an ASM participant during an ASM performance year must begin reassigning billing rights to a new TIN to be eligible for exception as described at § 512.710(c)(1)(i)(B); and (3) our proposal that an ASM participant must provide written notice of the change in TIN within 30 days of stopping reassignment of billing rights to the ASM participant's TIN as described at § 512.710(c)(1)(i)(B).

(b) Exceptions Due to Heart Failure-Related Specialty Type Redesignations
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we did not propose or consider an exception based on redesignations of specialty type made through Medicare enrollment before or during an ASM performance year.
Since publication of the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we received interested parties' feedback that we should consider adjustments to ASM participant eligibility determinations based on more recent Medicare enrollment information related to specialty type, which is used to derive the Medicare Part B claims-based specialty type that we use to evaluate ASM participant eligibility criteria.
We believe that using historical data to evaluate ASM participant eligibility criteria for each ASM performance year is still appropriate. In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49583
through
49585
), we explained that determining a clinician's specialty type based on historical data from 2 CYs before an ASM performance year provides an objective and consistent approach because it allows us to use historical claims data to evaluate clinician specialty type, as well as the EBCM episode threshold, as part of the ASM participant eligibility criteria. This approach also supports operational feasibility because it enables us to provide advance notification for ASM participants to prepare for the start of an ASM performance year.
However, we recognize that clinicians may not have had sufficient time to formally update an out-of-date specialty type before the end of CY 2025 because ASM was not finalized until November 2025. For example, specialty type redesignations made in CY 2026 would not be reflected in the CY 2025 data used to select final ASM participants for the 2027 ASM performance year. Setting an appropriate scope of ASM participant exceptions is important in a mandatory model such as ASM to preserve the integrity of the model design and evaluation, and to ensure a representative ASM participant population. While allowing unrestricted ASM participant exceptions due to specialty type redesignations could introduce selection bias and undermine the model test, we believe that certain limited and clinically appropriate redesignations may warrant consideration based on the timing of ASM's announcement and selection of ASM participants.
Accordingly, we proposed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43968
) that ASM heart failure participants who officially redesignate their primary specialty type through an approved Medicare enrollment application (either PECOS or CMS-855 form paper application) to a limited set of specialty types and demonstrate proof of board certification would be excepted from specified ASM requirements and ineligible for Medicare program waivers and the safe harbor provisions available in the model for the applicable ASM performance year and for all remaining ASM performance years in the ASM test period.
Specifically, we proposed at § 512.710(c)(1)(ii) that we may approve an exception from specified model requirements for an ASM heart failure participant upon receipt of written notification of updated Medicare enrollment to the following redesignated primary specialty types described at § 512.710(c)(1)(ii)(A): cardiac electrophysiology, cardiac surgery, interventional cardiology, advanced heart failure and transplant cardiology, and adult congenital heart disease. We proposed at § 512.710(c)(1)(ii)(B) that an ASM heart failure participant who redesignated their primary specialty type through an approved Medicare enrollment application (either PECOS or CMS-855 form paper application) would need to provide us written notification of the approved redesignation, along with verification of board certification in the newly designated primary specialty type described under § 512.710(c)(1)(ii)(A) within 30 days of the effective date of the approved redesignation.
We believed that recognizing an exception for ASM heart failure participants who redesignate their specialty type to one of the proposed specialty types would be appropriate because these specialty types reflect highly specialized or procedure-focused practice areas that are distinct from the broader management of cardiovascular disease and heart failure captured under
(
printed page 71226)
the cardiology specialty. Excepting cardiac electrophysiology, cardiac surgery, and interventional cardiology would be appropriate because these specialties are predominantly procedure—focused and are generally organized around the performance of invasive or technical interventions rather than the longitudinal medical management of cardiovascular disease. Cardiac electrophysiology primarily involves the diagnosis and treatment of cardiac arrhythmias through procedures such as ablation and device implantation; interventional cardiology centers on catheter—based interventions (for example, percutaneous coronary intervention). Cardiac surgery involves operative treatment for cardiac conditions. Advanced heart failure and transplant cardiology specialists primarily manage patients with end-stage heart failure, mechanical circulatory support, or transplant-related care, while adult congenital heart disease specialists treat individuals with complex congenital conditions that persist into adulthood. Because the specialty types proposed for exception represent narrower scopes of practice than general heart failure management, their exception from specified requirements would help ensure that ASM remains focused on specialists who manage heart failure in a comprehensive and ongoing manner, thereby improving the specificity and consistency of the ASM heart failure cohort.
To be excepted from the specified ASM requirements under this proposal, we proposed that the ASM participant must (1) officially redesignate their primary specialty type to one of the specialty types described earlier through an approved Medicare enrollment application and (2) provide evidence of board certification in the redesignated specialty to ensure that an exception to specified ASM requirements is valid and appropriate. While Medicare enrollment requirements stipulate a clinician must supply documentation supporting eligibility for Medicare enrollment under § 424.510(d), these enrollment regulations do not specify a mechanism for substantiating specialty type. Initial enrollment, revalidation, and any interim changes to an existing enrollment require a physician to select a primary specialty and attest that they meet all State or Federal requirements for their selected primary specialty. Physicians must meet the same requirements for any secondary specialty selected. They must also provide information on the active certification relating to their selected primary specialty type, specifically certification number, effective date, certifying entity, and State where issued. If no certification is associated with the selected primary specialty, then the physician must report the certification relevant to the secondary specialty.

MACs have operational authority to validate reported information, including requesting supporting documentation, if needed. In addition to requiring the redesignation through a Medicare enrollment application, we believed that requiring an ASM participant to report additional proof of board certification in one of the proposed specialty types eligible for exception would promote a more accurate approach to the exception process while avoiding unrestricted or unverified exceptions that could introduce selection bias into the model test. Further, all of the proposed specialty types for exception have a certifying entity that provides evidence of board certification. The American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) provides board certification for cardiac electrophysiology, interventional cardiology, advanced heart failure and transplant cardiology, and adult congenital heart disease specialty types. The American Board of Thoracic Surgery provides board certification for the cardiac surgery specialty type. Therefore, we believed that an ASM heart failure participant seeking an exception would be able to produce evidence of board certification for all specialty types proposed for exception.
We considered an alternative proposal whereby we would only recognize specific specialty type redesignation-based exceptions that occur during 2027 and 2028 ASM performance years to limit the number of ASM participants potentially excepted. Based on the announcement of ASM in the CY 2026 PFS final rule in November 2025, we believed that potential ASM participants may not have had adequate time to officially redesignate their primary specialty type such that it is reflected in the Medicare Part B claims used to select ASM participants for these ASM performance years. For example, a 2027 ASM participant who redesignated their primary specialty type in CY 2026 would not have that change reflected in the CY 2025 claims data used to evaluate their eligibility. A similar timing challenge could occur for the 2028 ASM performance year because we will use CY 2026 data to select ASM participants for the 2028 ASM performance year. We believe that finalization of ASM in the CY 2026 PFS final rule provided potential ASM participants advanced notice to redesignate their specialty type, if appropriate, for CY 2027, which is the year of data that we will use to select ASM participants for the 2029 ASM performance year. However, we recognized that appropriate specialty type redesignations could occur after the 2028 ASM performance year and that allowing the potential for an exception based on specific specialty type redesignations for a longer period would retain consistency in the application of the proposed exception for specified ASM requirements.
We considered but did not propose exceptions based on specialty type redesignations for ASM low back pain participants. Unlike cardiac specialties, the specialty types included in the ASM low back pain cohort typically do not have Medicare specialty types that reflect further specialization that would be appropriate for excepting ASM low back pain participants. We also believed that the larger number of specialty types in the ASM low back pain cohort would naturally capture common changes in specialty type by ASM low back pain participants over time. For example, we would capture an anesthesiologist ASM low back pain participant who redesignates their primary specialty type to pain management or interventional pain management over the course of the ASM test period through our existing use of historical Medicare Part B claims to identify specialty type. Our rationale for recognizing exceptions based on specialty type redesignation was to ensure each ASM cohort represents specialists who can be appropriately held accountable for longitudinal management of heart failure or low back pain. Accordingly, we believed that the existing ASM low back pain participant specialty type criteria, together with the minimum episode attribution volume for the low back pain EBCM, accomplishes this objective and allowing unrestricted exceptions based on specialty type redesignations in the ASM low back pain cohort could introduce selection bias into the model test.

(c) Effect and Duration of Exceptions to Specific ASM Performance Requirements
We proposed at § 512.710(c)(2) to define the effect of an approved exception for an ASM participant. Specifically, we proposed that an ASM participant with an approved exception would: (1) not be subject to performance assessment described at § 512.715, data submission described at § 512.720, and final scoring described at § 512.745 for the applicable ASM performance year; (2) not be subject to payment adjustments described at § 512.750 for the corresponding ASM payment year; (3) not be eligible for Medicare program waivers available under the model described at § 512.775 for the applicable ASM performance year, and (4) not be eligible for the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor described at § 512.765 for the period for which we determine an exception applies. We believed that the proposed effect of an exception retains the intent of the finalized provisions related to ASM participant exclusions due to TIN changes in the CY 2026 PFS final rule while adding new elements that strengthen program integrity. This proposal was also similar to the effect of an ASM participant not meeting the ASM participant eligibility criteria for an ASM performance year discussed in more detail in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43965
).
We proposed at § 512.710(c)(3)(i) that an exception related to a TIN change would be effective on the CMS-determined date and would only apply for the applicable ASM performance year. We believed that limiting an exception to a single ASM performance year would allow us to select the ASM participant with the exception (that is, the same TIN/NPI combination) for a future ASM performance year should the NPI again reassign billing rights to that same original TIN and meet ASM participant eligibility criteria under that original TIN.
We considered whether to extend an exception related to a TIN change for the remainder of the ASM test period. However, we believed that this approach could lead to unnecessary exceptions for later ASM performance years, particularly in the case that an excepted ASM participant begins reassigning billing rights to the same original TIN under which we previously selected them as an ASM participant, and excepted them, for a previous ASM performance year.
We proposed at § 512.710(c)(3)(ii) that an exception related to specialty type redesignation would be effective on the CMS-determined date and would apply for the applicable ASM performance year and remain effective for all ASM performance years in the remainder of the ASM test period. We believed that excepting ASM participants for specified specialty type redesignations for the remainder of the ASM test period would be appropriate since these ASM participants do not represent the target specialty type of an ASM cohort, and would, therefore, improve the specificity and consistency of the ASM cohort for the purposes of performance comparison.
We considered effectuating the exception related to specialty type redesignation type on the CMS-determined date and only having it apply for the applicable ASM performance year. However, we believed that effectuating the exception for the remainder of the ASM test period would be preferrable since we believe an ASM participant would be unlikely to revert to their previous primary specialty type redesignation during the remainder of the ASM test period.
We sought comment on the proposed effect of an exception from specified ASM requirements at § 512.710(c)(2). We did not receive specific comments on the proposed effect of an exception as proposed at § 512.710(c)(2).
We also sought comment on the proposed duration of an exception related to TIN changes as proposed at § 512.710(c)(3)(i), as well as the alternative we considered of setting the duration of a TIN change-related exception as the remainder of the ASM test period. We also sought comment on the proposal at § 512.710(c)(3)(ii) that an exception related to specialty type redesignation would apply for the ASM performance year for which we provide notice that the exception applies and for the remainder of the ASM test period. Finally, we sought comment on the alternative we considered to effectuate an exception related to specialty type redesignation for the applicable ASM performance year only.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters requested clarification regarding the duration of exceptions related to TIN changes or recommended avoiding repeated notification requirements when the circumstances supporting an exception have not changed. A commenter highlighted that under the duration-relation proposal, an ASM participant would need to notify CMS of the same organizational change every ASM performance year to continue the exception. A few commenters recommended that the exception should continue in each subsequent ASM performance year unless the NPI reassigns billing rights to the same TIN under which they were selected as an ASM participant later in the ASM test period.
(
printed page 71230)
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' feedback on the duration of an exception related to a TIN change. Based on our use of historical information to select ASM participants and determine for which ASM performance years ASM participants must meet specified requirements, we acknowledge that the duration of a TIN change-based exception, as proposed, could require repeated notifications from an ASM participant. Consider an ASM participant who must meet the 2027 ASM performance year requirements but stops reassigning billing rights to TIN A (that is, the original TIN) and begins reassigning billing rights to TIN B during the 2027 ASM performance year. Given our use of historical data to select ASM participants and determine which ASM performance years they must meet specified requirements, we may still identify EBCM episodes attributed to the ASM participant under TIN A during CY 2026 and CY 2027. Accordingly, this ASM participant could be required to meet specified ASM requirements under TIN A for the 2028 and 2029 ASM performance years. Under the proposed notification requirement and duration of the TIN change-based exception, this example ASM participant would be required to notify us multiple times of this TIN change for the 2028 and 2029 ASM performance years. As discussed earlier in this section of this final rule, we are not finalizing the ASM participant notification requirements. Accordingly, we acknowledge that proposed duration of the TIN change-based exception would be potentially confusing to ASM participants if not effectuated for the ASM test period for which they remain unaffiliated with the TIN under which we originally selected them as an ASM participant. We intentionally designed ASM's participation provisions to account for movements across organizations and to select new ASM participants across the ASM test period, meaning that the same NPI under a different TIN could be selected as an ASM participant if they meet all ASM participant eligibility criteria later in the ASM test period. Accordingly, should an ASM participant decide to again reassign billing rights to their original TIN under which we selected them as an ASM participant (for example, TIN A in the earlier scenario) after an exception applies, but later in the ASM test period, we would not want to prevent that ASM participant from actively participating in ASM under this original TIN again. Therefore, we believe it would be appropriate to modify the duration of a TIN change-based exception to begin in the CMS-specified ASM performance year and last for the remainder of the ASM test period unless the ASM participant begins reassigning billing rights to that original TIN under which we selected the NPI as an ASM participant when they otherwise meet the ASM participant eligibility criteria under that original TIN for a future ASM performance year. Because we select an ASM participant using a unique TIN and NPI combination, we note that an NPI who we excepted under their original TIN could be selected as an ASM participant under a new TIN for a future ASM performance year should they meet the ASM participant eligibility criteria under that new TIN.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that an exception related to a TIN change should take effect automatically and be retroactive to the beginning of the ASM performance year in which the change occurs.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their feedback. We would like to clarify that we proposed that a TIN change-based exception would apply for a specific ASM performance year and would be effective as of the CMS-specified date in the notice we provide to the ASM participant.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal that an exception related to a specialty type redesignation would apply for the remainder of the ASM test period.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support of this proposal.
Comment:
A commenter suggested that CMS should clarify the effect on exceptions resulting from moving away from an ASM mandatory geographic area, retirement, and death.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their recommendations. We believe that an ASM participant no longer furnishing services in one of ASM's mandatory geographic areas would be covered by exceptions related to TIN changes. Additionally, as we discussed earlier in this final rule, we believe that the revisions to the exceptions based on TIN changes (that is, no longer reassigning billing rights to a TIN) will also capture retirements. Under the finalized ASM participant termination provisions discussed later in this section of this final rule, we will terminate a deceased ASM participant from participation in the model.
After consideration of public comments, including specific recommendations from commenters to remove notification requirements related to ASM participant exceptions, we are finalizing the proposed effect of an exception from specified ASM requirements at § 512.710(c)(2) with a modification. Specifically, to further clarify our intent in the proposed rule, we are finalizing that an exception is effective as of the date we specify in the notice to an ASM participant that the exception applies. We finalize this change to conform with the removal of the proposed requirement that an ASM participant provide notice to us regarding exceptions. We have also finalized regulatory text at § 512.710(c)(2)(i) through (iv) to add clarifications regarding effective dates. As noted throughout this section of this final rule, an ASM participant may voluntarily notify us if they believe they meet the criteria for an exception in a form and manner specified by CMS, but emphasize that such notice is not required to receive an exception.
We are finalizing the duration of exceptions described at § 512.710(c)(3) with modifications. For the duration of an exception related to TIN changes described at § 512.710(c)(3)(i), we are finalizing that a TIN-based exception will continue for the remainder of the ASM test period unless the ASM participant: (1) begins reassigning billing rights to the TIN under which they receive an exception later in the ASM test period and (2) meets ASM participant eligibility criteria under that TIN for a future ASM performance year. We are finalizing the proposed duration of an exception related to a specialty type redesignation at § 512.710(c)(3)(ii) as proposed but with modifications to clarify and align the regulatory text.
We provide several illustrative examples of how an exception related to a TIN change will work in practice, including the effect of such exceptions on the application of payment adjustments under ASM. In our first example, ASM participant Dr. A (TIN A/NPI A) receives a final score and an ASM payment multiplier for their performance at TIN A in the 2027 ASM performance year. Dr. A receives an exception applicable for the 2028 ASM performance year based on termination of billing rights to TIN A and reassignment of billing rights to TIN B. Under TIN B, Dr. A remains located in the same mandatory geographic area as they were located under TIN A. Dr. A is not required to meet the specified ASM requirements under TIN A or TIN B for the 2028 ASM performance year and for the rest of the ASM test period unless they begin reassigning billing rights to TIN A or TIN B and meet the ASM participant eligibility under either TIN for a future ASM performance year. However, because Dr. A began reassigning billing rights to TIN B after
(
printed page 71231)
the end of the 2027 ASM performance year but before the end of the 2029 ASM payment year, we will apply the ASM payment multiplier determined for the 2027 ASM performance year to payments for Medicare Part B covered professional service claims submitted by Dr. A under TIN B during the 2029 ASM payment year. We refer readers to section III.D.2.g. of this final rule and § 512.750(f) for additional information on payment adjustment provisions related to TIN changes that occur after an ASM performance year but before the end of the corresponding ASM payment year. We also note that Dr. A in this example could be selected as an ASM participant under TIN B for the 2030 ASM performance year if they meet ASM participant eligibility criteria under TIN B based on CY 2028 data. In this situation, Dr. A would be included in the list of ASM participants for the 2030 ASM performance year.
We also provide an example of how an exception due to TIN changes will work for an NPI who is selected as an ASM participant under multiple TIN/NPI combinations. As discussed in the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we believe that it would be rare, but possible, for the same NPI to be selected as an ASM participant under multiple TINs for the same ASM performance year (
90 FR 49602
). An exception based on a TIN change for one TIN/NPI combination does not affect the ASM participant's obligation to meet specified ASM requirements under any other TIN/NPI combination for which we selected the NPI as an ASM participant. For example, Dr. B (NPI B) is selected as an ASM participant under TIN C and TIN D for the 2028 ASM performance year. If Dr. B stops reassigning billing rights to TIN C during the 2028 ASM performance year and receives an exception applicable for the 2028 ASM performance year and the remainder of the ASM test period, then Dr. B is excepted from the specified ASM requirements under TIN C but must continue to meet ASM's requirements under TIN D for the 2028 ASM performance year and any future ASM performance years for which Dr. B meets the ASM participant eligibility criteria under TIN D.
We also provide several illustrative examples of how the exception related to specialty type redesignations will work in practice, including the effect of such exception on the application of payment adjustments under ASM. For example, consider ASM heart failure participant Dr. C (TIN E/NPI C) who receives a final score and an ASM payment multiplier for their performance under TIN E for the 2027 ASM performance year. Dr. C is notified of an exception during the 2028 ASM performance year because they redesignated their primary specialty type to cardiac electrophysiology as part of their Medicare enrollment. Dr. C will be excepted from the specified ASM requirements for the 2028 ASM performance year and the remainder of the ASM test period under TIN E. However, they will continue to receive payment adjustments on their Medicare Part B covered professional service claims submitted under TIN E during the 2029 ASM payment year based on the ASM payment multiplier determined for their performance during the 2027 ASM performance year. As we emphasized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49696
through
49699
), our goal is to maintain accountability for an ASM participant's performance for a given ASM performance year through performance-based payment adjustments during the corresponding ASM payment year.
A specialty type redesignation-based exception will apply to all TIN/NPI combinations for which we select the NPI as an ASM participant. For example, Dr. D (NPI D) is considered an ASM heart failure participant under TIN F and TIN G for the 2028 ASM performance year. Dr. D redesignates their primary specialty type to interventional cardiology as part of their Medicare enrollment during the 2028 ASM performance year. After our identification of the specialty type redesignation and providing notification, Dr. D will be excepted from specified ASM requirements for the 2028 ASM performance year and the remainder of the ASM test period under both TIN F and TIN G.
(5) ASM Participant Terminations
In the 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized application of the Standard Provisions for Mandatory Innovation Center Models (
42 CFR part 512, subpart A
) to ASM (
90 FR 49720
). These provisions describe actions that we may take to remediate actions associated with risks to program integrity.
As discussed in the proposed rule, these standard provisions are not intended to encompass all terms and conditions that apply to each Innovation Center model, because each model has unique design features and implementation plans that may require additional, more tailored provisions (
91 FR 43971
).
We proposed to include an additional remedial action for purposes of ASM starting in 2027 whereby we could terminate an ASM participant from participation in the model upon our determination that one or more grounds for remedial action described in § 512.160(a) has taken place. In addition, we proposed that we could terminate an ASM participant if we determine that continued participation would be inconsistent with the purposes of ASM or applicable law (
91 FR 43971
). Under this proposal, any termination of an ASM participant's participation would occur only upon a determination by CMS. For the avoidance of doubt, our proposal did not establish a right for an ASM participant to terminate their own participation.
We proposed to codify this provision at § 512.710(h) and to include a corresponding reference to termination in § 512.710(a)(1), which addresses the duration of participation under ASM.
We sought comment on this proposal at § 512.710(h).
In this section of this final rule, we summarize and respond to the public comments we received on these proposals.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that termination of an ASM participant from the model could have significant consequences for ongoing remuneration and for model-related safe harbor and waiver protections, including potential retroactive liability for conduct undertaken in reliance on those protections.
Response:
We appreciate concerns raised by commenters and provide clarifications as to our intent. We proposed § 512.710(h) to allow us to terminate an ASM participant only if we determine that (1) one or more grounds for remedial action described at § 512.160(a) have occurred, or (2) the ASM participant's continued participation would be inconsistent with the purposes of ASM, ASM's regulations, or applicable law. As discussed in the proposed rule, the grounds for remedial action at § 512.160(a) include failure to comply with Innovation Center model or Medicare program requirements, actions that threaten patient health or safety, submission of false data or representations, and changes in control that present a program integrity risk. The proposed regulatory text connects termination to these existing grounds for remedial action, adding termination as a supplemental action that we could take when appropriate. We believe the grounds for remedial action are sufficiently specified at § 512.160(a).
With respect to our proposal at § 512.710(h)(1)(ii) addressing termination when continued participation would be inconsistent with the purposes of ASM, the
(
printed page 71232)
requirements of ASM under its regulations, or applicable law, we do not intend for this provision to establish an open-ended basis for termination. Instead, our intent is to provide the ability for CMS to address situations where continued participation no longer makes sense due to changes in circumstances concerning the ASM participant in consideration of the model's structure and purpose. Examples of termination under this provision that we envision may include but are not limited to when an ASM participant is deceased.
We also appreciate the commenter's request for clarification on how termination affects the availability of the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor. We refer readers to section III.D.2.h of this final rule for discussion of safe harbor policies.
Comment:
A commenter stated concern with the termination proposal, noting that it is unbounded by any specified notice requirement from CMS.
Response:
We appreciate this commenter's remarks and agree that our regulations should describe a notice requirement in the event we terminate an ASM participant from the model. Accordingly, we are finalizing a modification to § 512.710(h) to add new paragraph § 512.710(h)(2 ) stipulating that, if we terminate an ASM participant from the model, we will provide notification to that ASM participant and specify the effective date of such termination in that notice. This approach preserves our ability to respond to circumstances arising during the model test period while informing an ASM participant of the basis for the termination.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that CMS' proposal would terminate Medicare billing rights without adequate process. The commenter recommended that CMS establish a formal notice-and-cure process that includes written notice of the specific grounds for termination, at least a 30-day cure period for remediable violations, and an administrative appeal before an independent decision-maker prior to termination.
Response:
We disagree that termination under proposed § 512.710(h) would affect a clinician's Medicare billing rights. The termination authority at § 512.710(h) applies only to a clinician's participation in ASM; it does not terminate, suspend, revoke, or otherwise directly affect a clinician's Medicare enrollment or billing privileges. These matters are outside the scope of ASM, its regulations, and this rulemaking. Termination, as the term is used under § 512.710(h), refers solely to termination from ASM.
As stated above, we nevertheless recognize that termination from ASM has consequences for model-related obligations and protections and are modifying our final policy to address concerns around notification of termination.
As described, we are finalizing § 512.710(h)(2) to state that we will provide notice of termination to an ASM participant identifying the grounds for termination and the effective date of a termination. We refer the commenter to the standard provisions at part 512, subpart A for information regarding administrative appeals processes.
We believe the modification we are finalizing to provide notice to ASM participants of termination, together with the existing framework under part 512, subpart A, appropriately balances transparency with our ability to respond to circumstances where termination is warranted.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing with modification our proposal at § 512.710(h) to terminate an ASM participant on grounds of remedial action or when participation is inconsistent with the model, its regulations, or applicable law. We are finalizing paragraphs §§ 512.710(h)(1), 512.710(h)(1)(i), and 512.710(h)(1)(ii) as proposed. We are finalizing the addition of new paragraph § 512.710(h)(2) to specify that, in the event an ASM participant is terminated from ASM, we will provide notice to the ASM participant specifying the grounds for termination and the effective date of such termination. We believe these modifications made in final regulation address commenters' requests for clarification and concerns.
c. Data Submission
(1) Background
We finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule that an ASM participant must meet established data submission requirements across the quality, improvement activities, and Promoting Interoperability ASM performance categories, consistent with §§ 512.725, 512.735, and 512.740, respectively (
90 FR 49596
through
49605
). We did not establish data submission requirements for the cost ASM performance category or for administrative claims-based quality measures as we will calculate performance on these measures using administrative claims data.
For the quality ASM performance category, we require the submission of numerator and denominator data for at least one required quality measure that satisfies the data completeness criteria (that is, data is submitted on at least 75 percent of the ASM participant's patients that meet a quality measure's denominator criteria). ASM participants in small practices (that is, a TIN with 15 or fewer clinicians) may submit quality data at the group (that is, TIN) level, while ASM participants in non-small practices must submit quality measure data at the individual (that is, TIN/NPI) level. Data submission for the improvement activities ASM performance category requires an ASM participant to attest at the group (that is, TIN) level. Finally, ASM participants must report the Promoting Interoperability ASM performance category at the group (that is, TIN) level. Regardless of the data submission level for each ASM performance category, each ASM participant receives an individual-level final score and corresponding ASM payment adjustment factor and ASM payment multiplier, which is used to adjust payments for each ASM participant's Medicare Part B covered professional service claims.
(2) Quality ASM Performance Category Data Submission for ASM Participants in Small Practices
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized policies at § 512.720(a) describing data submission for the quality ASM performance category, including the requirement that quality measure data be submitted at the individual (that is, TIN/NPI) level. We also finalized at § 512.720(f) that ASM participants in small practices may report quality ASM performance category data at the group (that is, TIN) level.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43971
), we proposed to reorganize § 512.720(a)(1)(i) and make technical, clarifying edits to the organization and text of our regulations to bring greater clarity to our provisions and better reflect our policy intent. We proposed to relocate where we describe small practice quality measure reporting from § 512.720(f) to new § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(C). Section 512.720(a)(1)(i)(C) would provide that an ASM participant in a small practice has the option to submit ASM quality measure data at either the group (that is, TIN) level or the individual (that is, TIN/NPI) level, consistent with our policy intent to provide ASM participants in small practices with flexibility in reporting ASM quality measure data.
We also proposed to make technical modifications at § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(A) to
(
printed page 71233)
correct a minor typographical error and at § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(B) to cross-reference new § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(C).
We solicited public comment on these proposals. The following is a summary of the public comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters supported CMS addressing typographical errors and the proposal to consolidate and clarify the regulatory text regarding quality data submissions, noting reorganized text improves readability and clarity.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support and agree that the reorganized text improves readability.
Comment:
Several commenters broadly supported allowing ASM participants in small practices to submit quality measure data at either the group level or the individual level and appreciated clarifications included in the proposed rule. Commenters stated that this flexibility recognizes the operational realities and varying administrative capacities of small practices while preserving meaningful quality measurement and accountability.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for our proposed clarification regarding small practice quality ASM performance category data submissions.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposals at § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(A) to correct a minor typographical error, clarify the small practice reporting flexibility for the quality ASM performance category at § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(C), and update at § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(B) to cross-reference new § 512.720(a)(1)(i)(C).
(3) Improvement Activities ASM Performance Category Data Submission
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized that ASM participants submit improvement activity ASM performance category data by attesting to the completion of required improvement activities at the group (that is, TIN) level (
90 FR 49599
through
49602
). We believed that group-level data submission would be appropriately reflective of the team-based care and coordination envisioned by the improvement activities (
90 FR 49601
). We also believed that group-level data submission for the improvement activities ASM performance category would reduce administrative burden (
90 FR 49601
).
Since the publication of the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we received feedback from interested parties that group-level data submission for improvement activities may have unintentional consequences for certain ASM participants. In response to this feedback, we proposed at § 512.720(a)(1)(ii)(B) to allow an ASM participant to submit data for the improvement activities ASM performance category at either the group (that is, TIN) level or the individual (that is, TIN/NPI) level (
91 FR 43972
). We noted in the proposed rule that such policy would not affect how an ASM participant or its affiliated TIN may choose to structure a CCA required under improvement activity (IA)-2.
We sought comment on our proposal at § 512.720(a)(1)(ii)(B) to allow ASM participants to attest to completing ASM's improvement activities at either the group (that is, TIN) level or the individual (that is, TIN/NPI) level.
We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported CMS' proposal to allow ASM participants to submit improvement activity ASM performance category data at either the individual (that is, TIN/NPI) level or the group (that is, TIN) level. A commenter described how this policy would reduce the risk of subjecting ASM participants within a TIN to scoring penalties if certain ASM participants within the same TIN do not perform the required activities. Several commenters stated such flexibility reduces administrative burden for physicians practicing within larger organizations, including integrated delivery systems. A commenter that supported individual-level reporting noted this better aligns individual accountability frameworks with individual clinical decision-making, consistent with ASM's stated design principles.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support for our policy. We agree that this flexibility can reduce the risk of unintended scoring consequences while allowing practices to use group-level reporting where it aligns with their existing workflows. We appreciate the comment that individual level reporting supports the model's broader individual accountability framework.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended further flexibilities beyond those proposed, including that CMS recognize subgroups for purposes of ASM improvement activity data submissions. A commenter stated that the proposed approach to allow for group or individual level reporting would increase the burden on a subgroup of physicians who meet the requirements for ASM improvement activities.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' recommendations. However, we are not adopting additional reporting levels, such as subgroups. Introducing subgroup or other reporting configurations would add complexity to data submission, validation, and scoring and could make the reporting framework more difficult for ASM participants to understand and implement. We believe permitting reporting at either the individual or group level provides meaningful flexibility while maintaining a clear and administratively workable reporting structure. Further, we disagree that our proposal would create additional burden for subgroups of ASM participants. A TIN that includes multiple ASM participants may attest to completing the improvement activities ASM performance category data at the TIN level if all ASM participants within that TIN perform the required activities. If that group also includes non-ASM participants, that group could still attest “yes” to ASM improvement activities so long as all ASM participants in the group met the activity's requirements. If only some ASM participants within that group perform the required improvement activities, then individual level reporting would be available for those ASM participants who performed the required activities, and those ASM participants that did not perform required activities would not be able to submit an affirmative attestation. Thus, we do not agree there would be added benefit from subgroup reporting that would overcome the complexity it would introduce.
We also received comments on the improvement activities ASM performance category that were out of scope from the proposed rule, which are not addressed in this rule. However, we thank commenters for providing input on these matters.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal at § 512.720(a)(1)(ii)(B) to allow ASM participants to attest to completing ASM improvement activities at either the group (that is, TIN) level or the individual (that is, TIN/NPI) level.
(4) Treatment of Multiple Data Submissions for the Quality, Improvement Activities, and Promoting Interoperability ASM Performance Categories
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized policies addressing the treatment of multiple data submissions for the quality, improvement activities, and Promoting Interoperability ASM performance categories at § 512.720(e) (
90 FR 49604
through
49606
). For the
(

We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters supported CMS' reorganization of the multiple data submission provisions of regulations. A commenter stated that such revisions bring greater clarity to the treatment of multiple submissions and scoring methodologies and help to reduce administrative complexity while supporting consistent and transparent performance assessment.
Response:
