We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposed 5-point rural scoring adjustment, stating that it would recognize the unique infrastructure, technology, staffing, workforce, and access challenges faced by ASM participants serving rural communities. Commenters supported allowing eligible rural ASM participants to receive the rural scoring adjustment in addition to the small practice or solo practitioner and complex patient scoring adjustments. Commenters requested clarifications regarding how the rural adjustment would interact with the small practice and solo practitioner scoring adjustments and whether the adjustments would be cumulative.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support of the rural scoring adjustment policy and application. We refer readers to the CY 2027 proposed rule (
91 FR 43990
), where we propose that ASM participants who are eligible for the rural scoring adjustment are also eligible for the complex patient scoring adjustment and/or small practice scoring adjustment provided that they meet the requirements as specified in sections § 512.745(a)(3) and § 512.745(a)(4) respectively.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposed rural scoring adjustment but recommended modifications or additional safeguards. A commenter recommended limiting the rural adjustment to ASM participants who are not eligible for the small practice scoring adjustment, stating that receiving both adjustments could reduce incentives for performance improvement. Another commenter recommended an additional adjustment for physicians caring for disproportionately high numbers of low-income or socially complex beneficiaries.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' feedback and acknowledge the commenters' recommendation to limit awarding the rural scoring adjustment to ASM participants who are not eligible for the small practice scoring adjustment. However, we disagree and stress that each scoring adjustment targets the unique challenges faced in different practice types. The small practice scoring adjustment is focused on correcting issues such as CEHRT implementation, and staff training costs (
90 FR 49674
). While the rural adjustment addresses workforce shortages, and thinner operating margins (
91 FR 43990
). We believe that an ASM participant in a rural area and small practice may experience both sets of challenges; thereby necessitating the need for the scoring adjustments to be additive.
We also stress that as stated earlier in this section of the final rule, preliminary ASM participant data for the 2027 ASM performance year found that ASM participants in rural areas are typically part of larger practices. Awarding both the small and rural scoring adjustments to a smaller percentage of ASM participants who meet both scoring adjustment requirements recognizes the significant challenges these ASM participants may face while not substantially changing scoring and payment incentives.
Additionally, we do not believe that the 5-point rural adjustment significantly diminishes the incentive for ASM participants receiving this scoring adjustment to improve. Because ASM's payment methodology remains tied to an ASM participant's performance relative to their ASM cohort, and not a pre-set performance threshold, an ASM participant who might receive both adjustments would still have an incentive to improve their performance components that factors into the final score. If an ASM participant's performance improves more than others in their ASM cohort, the ASM scoring and payment framework rewards the ASM participant with an increase in their payment adjustment factor regardless of their small or rural scoring adjustments.
Lastly, we note that the CY 2026 final rule finalized at § 512.745(a)(3) the ASM complex patient scoring adjustment. The complex patient scoring adjustment accounts for the HCC risk scores and the proportion of dually eligible beneficiaries of an ASM participant. We refer readers to the CY 2026 final rule where we document the link between dual eligible status and income level (
90 FR 49674
).
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS consider similar adjustments to the rural scoring adjustment be awarded to non-rural clinicians and practices facing comparable resource or operational constraints, including small independent specialty practices, hospital-based or ambulatory surgical center (ASC) clinicians, and non-patient-facing clinicians.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their recommendation. We emphasize that the ASM complex patient scoring adjustment as finalized at § 512.745(a)(3) accounts for social and medical risk factors faced by ASM participants regardless of size or geography. We did not consider awarding an additional scoring adjustment to ASM participants in hospitals or ambulatory surgical centers because we believe that the complex patient scoring adjustment adequately accounts for the challenges ASM participants serving in those practices face. We also stress that to receive a final score, an ASM participant must be attributed 20 EBCM episodes for the ASM performance year. If ASM participants do not meet the minimum 20 case threshold they would receive an automatic neutral payment adjustment (
90 FR 49669
). Furthermore, as part of the EBCM methodology, to qualify as an ASM participant a specialist would need to have billed at least 30 percent of triggering or confirming codes on Part B Physician/Supplier claim lines related to the ASM condition for the beneficiary (
90 FR 49579
). We therefore disagree with the commenter that a positive adjustment should be made to the final scores of non-patient-facing ASM participants. We expect that the EBCM minimum threshold and billing requirements will award ASM final scores primarily to patient-facing clinicians.
Comment:
A commenter recommended comparing an ASM participant's performance with their peers in similar practice environments, patient populations, shared resource constraints, and geographic characteristics rather than relying solely on additional scoring adjustments like the rural scoring adjustment.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their creative approach to scoring; however, we disagree and believe that a rural scoring adjustment adequately supports ASM participants in rural
(
printed page 71261)
areas facing targeted challenges. As discussed in the CY 2026 final rule (
90 FR 49684
) we finalized our proposal to calculate incentive pools and payment adjustment factors separately for each ASM cohort. We believe that calculating payment adjustments separately by ASM cohort supports meaningful comparisons among ASM participants treating the same targeted chronic condition. Further stratifying ASM participants based on practice environment, patient population, resource constraints, or geographic characteristics would result in smaller comparison groups. Thereby creating a situation in which small differences in an ASM participant's final score could lead to vastly different payment adjustment factors, an outcome not aligned with the model's stated goal of creating meaningful payment incentives (
90 FR 49684
).
Comment:
A commenter requested that to account for specialists practicing at multiple sites who predominantly serve rural communities, CMS determine rural status based on the plurality of ASM beneficiaries served during the ASM performance year rather than solely on the specialist's primary PECOS enrollment address.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their proposal to determine rural status based on the location of the plurality of ASM beneficiaries served during the ASM performance year. As discussed earlier in this section of this final rule, we believe that calculating the ASM rural scoring adjustment using the same definition and determinations of a “rural area” as defined, interpreted, and updated at § 414.1305 under MIPS will significantly reduce confusion and burden. We will provide specifications regarding the identification of the ASM participant's ZIP Code for use in the rural scoring adjustment determination through sub-regulatory technical documentation.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed the proposed rural scoring adjustment, while acknowledging that some rural practices face additional challenges. Commenters stated that rural status alone may not reliably identify ASM participants facing greater barriers to ASM performance because some non-rural practices may experience comparable or greater socioeconomic, access, infrastructure, or patient-population challenges, while some rural practices may not experience any such challenges. A few commenters recommended addressing differences in practice circumstances through attribution, risk adjustment, benchmarks, measure specifications, and other relevant factors rather than adding points to ASM participants' final scores. Commenters also expressed concern that, because ASM performance is scored relative to other ASM participants, increasing the final scores of ASM participants in rural areas would affect the relative standing and payment adjustments of ASM participants in non-rural areas.
Response:
We acknowledge commenters' concerns that some ASM participants in non-rural areas may experience similar or comparable challenges. However, the rural scoring adjustment is not intended to address all differences in ASM participant or patient circumstances. ASM includes other methodological features that account for relevant differences in performance. For example, the cost ASM performance category incorporates risk adjustment, as described in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49638
), and MIPS Q492 in the quality measure set for the ASM heart failure cohort includes a risk-adjustment model incorporating demographic, clinical, and social risk factors. We believe these methodologies, together with the rural scoring adjustment and other applicable ASM scoring adjustments, appropriately account for differences in ASM participant and patient circumstances.
We also acknowledge that the ASM payment adjustment factors are determined relative to the performance of other ASM participants in the ASM cohort. We do not believe however that this effect provides a basis for excluding circumstances associated with ASM participants in rural areas. As discussed earlier in this section of the final rule the ASM rural adjustment is meant to correct for unmeasured disadvantages, rather than simply giving an arbitrary advantage to ASM participants in rural areas.
Comment:
A commenter stated that its analysis of historical MIPS performance among likely ASM participants showed similar average performance for rural and non-rural physicians, while showing larger differences between small and large practices. The commenter therefore recommended that CMS not establish a rural scoring adjustment and instead waive interoperability requirements for ASM participants in rural areas and for ASM participants in non-rural areas when community conditions create a hardship.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's analysis of historical MIPS performance data among likely ASM participants. However, we stress that ASM's requirements differ in important respects from MIPS, including the improvement activities ASM performance category. Consequently, we do not believe that historical MIPS performance data provides an appropriate basis for determining whether a rural scoring adjustment is warranted under ASM.
As finalized in the CY 2026 final rule at § 512.735(c)(2) IA-2 requires established communication and collaborations with primary care using a CCA. As discussed earlier in this section of this final rule, ASM participants in rural areas may face challenges forming partnerships with primary care practices due to limited primary care availability. Therefore, we believe that historical MIPS performance may not fully reflect the circumstances and challenges ASM participants in rural areas experience when they move from MIPS to ASM.
We also considered but ultimately did not propose waiving IA-2 for ASM participants in rural areas in the CY 2027 proposed rule (
91 FR 43990
). A central goal of the ASM is to incentivize ASM participants to ensure that their patients have a regular source of primary care (
90 FR 49563
). We therefore believe that removing IA-2 entirely for ASM participants in rural areas would not provide sufficient incentive for improved care coordination.
Comment:
A commenter supported the proposed 5-point rural scoring adjustment but stated that it would be insufficient to address the structural and financial challenges facing rural specialists in Kentucky and Indiana. The commenter cited rural hospital closure risks, Medicaid payment shortfalls, low rural hospital operating margins, and physician shortages in both States and expressed concern that the potential negative ASM payment adjustment could further threaten the financial viability of rural specialty care. The commenter also stated that many rural ASM participants may not qualify for the small practice scoring adjustment because CMS's analysis indicated that rural ASM participants tend to be in larger practices. The commenter recommended that CMS exempt Kentucky and Indiana from mandatory ASM participation or establish differential penalty structures for ASM participants in rural areas until additional geographic adjustments, infrastructure supports, and rural-specific quality measures are in place.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' feedback and support. We do though believe that the rural scoring adjustment appropriately addresses the structural concerns the commenter highlighted facing practices in Kentucky and Indiana. We also note that the rural scoring adjustment does not operate in
(
printed page 71262)
isolation. Eligible ASM participants, including those in Kentucky and Indiana, may also receive the complex patient scoring adjustment as described in § 512.745(a)(3). Elsewhere in the ASM performance category scoring methodology, the cost ASM performance category incorporates risk adjustment into the EBCM used to calculate the cost ASM performance category score as described in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49638
); and the Risk-Standardized Acute Unplanned Cardiovascular-Related Admission Rates for Patients with Heart Failure measure (MIPS Q492) incorporates risk adjustment on demographic, clinical, and social risk factors (
90 FR 49607
).
We acknowledge that the rural scoring adjustment does not eliminate ASM's peer-relative scoring or guarantee avoidance of a negative payment adjustment. However, we believe the adjustment appropriately recognizes rural circumstances while preserving ASM's underlying goal of comparing ASM participants to their peers within an ASM cohort. We do not believe a separate payment adjustment structure for ASM participants in rural areas is appropriate as that would decrease the size of the ASM cohort and thereby create an inappropriate payment approach as discussed earlier in this section of this final rule. We refer readers to the CY 2026 final rule for a complete discussion regarding mandatory participation and its importance in ensuring a valid and robust model evaluation (
90 FR 49589
).
Comment:
A commenter stated that it lacked sufficient information and comparative data to assess the proposed rural scoring adjustment and recommended that CMS examine anticipated differences in ASM scores between ASM participants in rural areas and ASM participants in non-rural areas before implementing the adjustment.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's recommendation; however, we believe that we have sufficient information to implement this adjustment as proposed. As discussed earlier in this section of this final rule, ASM participants in rural areas face specific interoperability and primary care coordination challenges. We believe that these circumstances could make success difficult for ASM participants in rural areas and therefore a rural scoring adjustment is warranted. We will closely monitor the results of the ASM rural scoring adjustment, and any modification will be made in future notice-and-comment rulemaking.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposed corresponding adjustments to the final score formula at § 512.745(a)(6), our proposal to revise § 512.745(a) to cross-reference the final score formula now described at § 512.745(a)(6), our proposed definition of rural area at § 512.705, our proposal at § 512.745(a)(5) to add 5 points to the final score of an ASM participant who is in a rural area and meets the requirements to receive a final score greater than zero, and our corresponding proposal at § 512.745(a)(6) to incorporate the rural scoring adjustment into the final score formula.

g. Payment Approach
(1) Background
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized the overall payment approach for ASM (
90 FR 49679
through
49699
). We will apply performance-based payment adjustments to all payments for Medicare Part B covered professional service claims from ASM participants during an ASM payment year based on their performance during the corresponding prior ASM performance year. We explained that this approach will create meaningful financial incentives tied to performance in the model, while maintaining administrative feasibility and transparency (
90 FR 49679
through
49680
). To determine these payment adjustments, we finalized a methodology to compare ASM participant performance within each ASM cohort using final scores, which reflect ASM participants' performance across the four ASM performance categories (
90 FR 49681
through
49683
). We also finalized a methodology to calculate ASM payment adjustment factors and ASM payment multipliers used to apply the payment adjustments from the distribution of final scores (
90 FR 49685
through
49696
). We also finalized the level of two-sided risk (that is, the maximum and minimum payment adjustment), including the gradual increase in the two-sided ASM risk level from 9 percent in the 2027 and 2028 ASM performance years to 12 percent in the 2031 ASM performance year. We explained that this methodology supports strong incentives for performance improvement while maintaining ASM risk levels similar to MIPS during early model years. We will apply the ASM payment multiplier to all payments for Medicare Part B for covered professional services, not only those services related to each ASM cohort's ASM targeted chronic condition, during an ASM payment year (
90 FR 49696
through
49699
).
(2) Application of ASM Payment Adjustments With Changes in TIN Affiliations
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized that Medicare Part B professional service claims submitted by an NPI who is an ASM participant for an ASM performance year but under a TIN (1) that we did not select the NPI as an ASM participant for the applicable ASM performance year and (2) to which the NPI began assigning billing rights after the ASM performance year but before the end of the corresponding ASM payment year would be adjusted using the ASM payment multiplier calculated for the ASM participant. In the limited instances where a single NPI is selected as an ASM participant under multiple TINs for an ASM performance year, we finalized that we would apply the highest of any ASM payment multipliers to all Medicare Part B covered professional service claims submitted under a new TIN during the applicable ASM payment year (
90 FR 49696
). We refer readers to Table B-D10 in the CY 2026 PFS final rule for additional information on how ASM payment adjustments will be applied under multiple scenarios (
90 FR 49697
). The goal of these policies is to maintain accountability for the ASM participant's performance through the application of their performance-based payment adjustments. By doing so, we track accountability to the ASM participant regardless of their specific TIN affiliation at the time we make payment adjustments.
While we did not propose substantive changes to these policies in the proposed rule, we noted that there are inconsistencies in the regulatory text describing how we will adjust payment in situations where the ASM participant begins reassigning billing rights to a new TIN during an ASM payment year.

h. Applicability of CMS-Sponsored Model Safe Harbor at 42 CFR 1001.952(ii)
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we determined that the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor at § 1001.952(ii) is available to ASM participants that comply with applicable requirements (
90 FR 49709
). We codified the availability of the safe harbor for ASM at § 512.765 with respect to remuneration associated with beneficiary incentives and remuneration exchanged under CCAs.
Once a clinician is selected as an ASM participant for any ASM performance year during the ASM test period, that clinician remains an ASM participant for the duration of the ASM test period. However, in limited circumstances, an ASM participant may not be required to meet specified model requirements for an ASM performance year. Specifically, if we determine that an ASM participant does not satisfy the ASM participant eligibility criteria as specified under § 512.710(a)(2) or is determined to meet an exception under § 512.710(c), the ASM participant is not: (1) subject to ASM performance assessment under § 512.715, (2) required to submit data under § 512.720, (3) subject to final scoring under § 512.745, and (4) eligible for the waivers available under the model described at § 512.775 (
90 FR 49572
,
90 FR 49583
).
When we finalized these policies in the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we did not address how a period of ineligibility or excepted status affects the availability of the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentive safe harbor (§ 1001.952(ii)), as made available for ASM under § 512.765.
We proposed that the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor would be available only for remuneration attributable to periods during which an ASM participant is performing under the model. Conversely, the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor would not be available for remuneration attributable to a period during which an ASM participant is not performing under the model due to not meeting ASM participant eligibility criteria as described at § 512.710(a)(2) or a determination that an exception applies under § 512.710(c)
We proposed to add § 512.765(c) to provide that the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor is available only with respect to remuneration attributable to a period during which the ASM participant is performing under the model. We further proposed to specify that the safe harbor is not available with respect to remuneration attributable to any period of the ASM test period during which the ASM participant does not meet the ASM participant eligibility criteria as specified in § 512.710(a)(2) or is excepted from specified ASM requirements under § 512.710(c).
We sought comment on this proposal.
Comment:
Several commenters requested clarification regarding the applicability of the fraud and abuse safe harbors when ASM participants become ineligible for, are excepted from specified ASM requirements, or exit the model.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' requests for clarification. The CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor, as applied to ASM under § 512.765, is available only with respect to remuneration attributable to a period during which an ASM participant is performing under the model.
Eligibility under § 512.710(a)(2) is determined on an annual ASM performance year basis. Therefore, if CMS determines that an ASM participant does not meet the eligibility criteria for a particular ASM performance year, the safe harbor would not be available to protect remuneration attributable to that ASM performance year.
An exception under § 512.710(c), by contrast, may become effective during an ASM performance year. Under § 512.710(c), we determine whether an exception applies, provide notice to the ASM participant, and specify the effective date of the exception in the notice. In response to requests for clarification, we are finalizing § 512.765(c) with modification to more precisely describe the period for which the safe harbor is unavailable and to align this provision with the exception provisions at § 512.710(c). Specifically, we are clarifying the safe harbor is unavailable for remuneration attributable to the period beginning on the date specified in the exception notice, which is described in § 512.710(c)(2)(iv). This modification retains our original intent that the safe harbor would not be available during the period an exception applies but provides greater certainty around when that period begins by tying that date to the date specified in an exception notice. An exception does not affect the availability of the safe harbor for remuneration attributable to a period before the date specified in an exception notice, provided all requirements for the safe harbor are met.
“Remuneration attributable to” refers to the period in which the underlying model activities occurred, rather than the date on which remuneration is exchanged. As we explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 43992
), remuneration related to model performance in one period may be exchanged in a subsequent period. Any such exchange must still satisfy all applicable safe harbor conditions.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended alternatives to our proposal regarding the periods during which the safe harbor would be available under ASM. For example, commenters recommended establishing a “wind-down period” or making the
(
printed page 71265)
safe harbor available for the duration of the ASM test period regardless of whether an ASM participant remains eligible for, or subject to the requirements of, the model. One commenter stated that conditioning safe harbor availability on an ASM participant's eligibility is inconsistent with ASM's goal of improving care for patients with chronic conditions and could adversely affect patients and physicians. Specifically, the commenter expressed concern that annual fluctuations in attributed patient counts around the 20-patient threshold could cause ASM participants to lose safe harbor protection and discontinue in-kind patient engagement incentives or arrangements supporting primary care practices, even when they continue treating the same patients. The commenter stated that an ASM participant who furnished an item or service to a beneficiary during an ASM performance year in which the ASM participant met the eligibility criteria could be required to withdraw the item or service in a later year if the ASM participant subsequently became ineligible.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' feedback. We disagree that the safe harbor should remain available for the duration of the ASM test period regardless of whether an ASM participant remains eligible for the model or is subject to an exception from specified ASM requirements. We continue to believe that limiting the safe harbor under § 512.765 to remuneration attributable to periods during which an ASM participant is performing under the model appropriately balances program integrity and beneficiary protections with the need to provide ASM participants flexibility to furnish or exchange remuneration that supports beneficiary and primary care engagement consistent with the purposes and requirements of the model.
We also disagree with the characterization that our proposal would require an ASM participant to retrieve an item or service already furnished to an ASM beneficiary as a patient incentive under § 512.770 solely because the ASM participant subsequently becomes ineligible for the model or is subject to an exception under § 512.710(c). Neither § 512.765 nor § 512.770 requires an ASM participant to retrieve an item or service that was furnished in accordance with § 512.770 solely because of a subsequent change in the ASM participant's eligibility or exception status.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that termination of an ASM participant from the model could have significant consequences for ongoing remuneration and for model-related safe harbor and waiver protections, including potential retroactive liability for conduct undertaken in reliance on those protections.
Response:
The CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor would not be available to a clinician who is terminated from ASM because that clinician is no longer an ASM participant after they are terminated. Under § 512.765, the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor is available only for remuneration furnished in accordance with the collaborative care arrangements that meet all safe harbor requirements set forth in §§ 1001.952(ii) and 512.771 or in the form of ASM beneficiary engagement incentives that meet all safe harbor requirements set forth in §§ 1001.952(ii) and 512.770. Termination does not, by itself, retroactively remove safe harbor protection for remuneration exchanged or furnished before the effective date of termination that otherwise satisfies all applicable requirements.
We are finalizing our proposal at § 512.765(c) with modification. Under our final policy, the safe harbor at § 512.765 will not be available with respect to remuneration attributable to: (1) any ASM performance year for which we determine that the ASM participant does not meet the ASM participant eligibility criteria under § 512.710(a)(2); or (2) in the case of an exception under § 512.710(c)(1), to the period described in § 512.710(c)(2)(iv).
i. Collaborative Care Arrangements (CCAs)
(1) Background
The improvement activities ASM performance category is intended to advance core goals of ASM to drive better outcomes through improved care coordination, increased collaboration between specialists and primary care practices, and interventions that address upstream drivers of health.
We finalized two improvement activities for ASM in the CY 2026 PFS final rule at § 512.735 that we believe best support these aims:
Improvement Activity 1 (IA-1): Connecting to Primary Care and Ensuring Completion of Health-Related Social Needs Screening; and
Improvement Activity 2 (IA-2): Establishing Communication and Collaboration Expectations with Primary Care using CCAs (
90 FR 49648
through
49655
).
To receive the maximum score available for the improvement activities ASM performance category, an ASM participant must attest “yes” to both improvement activities.
IA-2 specifications require an ASM participant to enter into at least one collaborative care arrangement (CCA) with a primary care practice with which the ASM participant shares a patient who is an ASM beneficiary. IA-2 also requires that a CCA address at least three of the five elements specified at § 512.735(c)(2)(ii): data sharing, co-management, transitions in care planning, closed-loop communication, and care coordination integration.
In addition to IA-2 specifications at § 512.735(c)(2)(ii), we outline requirements for CCAs at § 512.771. The function of the CCA is to memorialize the coordination activities central to ASM and described in IA-2.
We proposed certain updates to the CCA provisions at § 512.771 to improve implementation by ASM participants and primary care practices and to more closely align CCA conditions with IA-2 by revising § 512.771(a) and adding new paragraph § 512.771(d). In summary, proposed changes to § 512.771 included:
Permitting one or more ASM participants to enter into a CCA with the same primary care practice, provided each ASM participant reassigns billing rights through the same entity's TIN and are named as parties to the CCA;
Clarifying the requirement that an ASM participant and a primary care practice share a patient who is an ASM beneficiary and how this requirement applies in the context of the limitation on considering the volume or value of referrals;
Streamlining the provision containing an illustrative list of authorities with which parties to a CCA must comply to simplify it, improve clarity, and reduce ambiguity;
Updating the provisions that currently reference any elective exchange of payments between CCA parties to instead refer to the elective exchange of remuneration, to reflect a broader scope of value that may be exchanged under a CCA;
Reorganizing regulatory requirements under § 512.771(a) that are associated only with the exchange of any elective remuneration under a CCA such that they appear together under a new paragraph at § 512.771(d) to bring greater clarity and to distinguish between those requirements that apply to all CCAs and those that apply only to CCAs that electively include the exchange remuneration;

Revising the payment limitation that caps the exchange of remuneration based on an ASM participant's performance adjustment such that it can be more readily calculated in a timely manner and requiring that parties that elect to exchange remuneration before the limitation can be calculated reconcile any amounts that exceed the limitation following reconciliation;
Clarifying that current requirements relating to traceability will continue to apply to monetary remuneration;
Updating the contemporaneous documentation requirements to reflect any remuneration exchanged and adding requirements to bring transparency into the methodologies used to determine the value of such remuneration; and
Relocating the conditions associated with remuneration at current §§ 512.771(a)(7) and 512.771(a)(8) to new paragraphs §§ 512.771(d)(2) and 512.771(d)(3), respectively, in accordance with our proposal to address requirements associated with CCAs that include an exchange of remuneration together under one paragraph. To conform with this relocation, we would redesignate existing sections §§ 512.771(a)(9) through 512.771(a)(13) to §§ 512.771(a)(7) through 512.771(a)(11). We would revise newly redesignated § 512.771(a)(7) (former § 512.771(a)(9)) to reference “[a]ll parties” rather than “[b]oth parties” and revise newly redesignated § 512.771(a)(9) (former § 512.771(a)(11)) to update documentation requirements as described, but otherwise would not revise text at newly redesignated § 512.771(a)(8) (former § 512.771(a)(10)), § 512.771(a)(10) (former § 512.771(a)(12)), or § 512.771(a)(11) (former § 512.771(a)(13)).
(2) Parties to a CCA
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized at § 512.771(a)(1) a requirement that a CCA be in writing, signed by both parties, and contain the effective date of the arrangement. We also finalized at § 512.771(a)(2) a requirement that a CCA be exclusively between an ASM participant and a primary care practice with which the ASM participant shares at least one established patient who is an ASM beneficiary. At that time, we considered, but declined to permit, multiple ASM participants reassigning billing rights through the same TIN to be parties to a single CCA with a primary care practice party, citing concerns around the ability of ASM participants to accurately track any remuneration exchanged under a multi-ASM participant arrangement (
90 FR 49712
).
Following publication of the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we received interested party feedback anticipating significant burden associated with establishing separate CCAs for each individual ASM participant when more than one ASM participant is in the same group practice and such ASM participants wish to collaborate with the same primary care practice. As an example, 20 ASM participants operate within a single health system and reassign their billing rights to that system's TIN. Even if such ASM participants coordinate care regularly with the same primary care practice and wish to establish a CCA with the same primary care practice, the current regulation would require negotiation, execution, documentation, and tracking of 20 separate CCAs.
We believe that requiring a separate CCA for each ASM participant could impose administrative burden without a corresponding programmatic benefit. We now believe that concerns related to tracking remuneration under CCAs involving multiple ASM participants could be addressed through more targeted safeguards that apply to CCAs that elect to include remuneration, rather than a broader restriction applicable to all CCAs, including those that do not involve any exchange of remuneration.
Accordingly, we proposed to amend §§ 512.771(a)(1) and 512.771(a)(2) to permit one or more ASM participants to be parties to the same CCA, provided that each ASM participant be named as a party to the CCA and all ASM participants reassign billing rights to the same TIN. We would maintain the existing requirements at § 512.771(a)(1) that the CCA be in writing and specify an effective date; we would also maintain the requirement that a CCA be signed by the parties but proposed to amend regulatory text to stipulate CCA execution would be required for “all” parties rather than “both” parties.
We believed restricting a multi-ASM participant CCA to ASM participants within the same TIN is appropriate as clinicians who practice under the same group practice are more likely to be supported by shared operations, such as shared EHR systems, clinical support staff, and standardized administrative workflows. Accordingly, we believe terms of a CCA could be standardized across ASM participants within the same organization (that is, TIN) without compromising the level of detail needed to support meaningful care coordination. In contrast, ASM participants from separate, unaffiliated TINs may have distinct infrastructure, care coordination needs, support structures, and operational workflows. It is therefore unclear how a single arrangement could establish cohesive terms regarding shared responsibilities with a primary care partner in a manner consistent with the intent of CCAs. We are concerned that attempting to encompass these different capabilities and variable workflows within a single agreement could result in vague, overly broad, or highly fragmented contractual terms, which could undermine the intent of the CCA.
Our proposal to permit one or more ASM participants billing under the same TIN to join the same CCA with a primary care practice does not alter ASM's fundamental accountability framework. As noted, we proposed to clarify that any ASM participant seeking to join and rely on one CCA be expressly named as a party to the arrangement. We believe such requirement maintains individual ASM participant accountability, while reducing administrative burden. We did not propose to permit a group practice or TIN to serve as a sole contracting party on behalf of unnamed ASM participants, as this could obfuscate individual ASM participant accountability and introduce operational complexity, particularly when an ASM participant departs a group practice during an ASM performance year. Requiring each ASM participant to be named as a party would mitigate such concerns while still reducing contracting burden.
We clarified in the proposed rule that we did not intend to establish and did not propose prescriptive requirements around the meaning of a “primary care practice” that must be a party to a CCA. Our intent is that a CCA reflects coordination between the ASM participant and their ASM beneficiary's source of primary care services. We refer readers to discussion in response to interested party questions in the CY 2026 PFS final rule for further information (
90 FR 49653
).
Our proposal intended to reduce burden for ASM participants who practice within the same group and coordinate care with the same primary care practice. It does not intend to discourage individual CCAs. ASM participants who belong to the same group may continue to enter into separate CCAs and should consider a separate arrangement when doing so better reflects individual clinical relationships, sources of primary care for their individual ASM beneficiary panel, and care coordination needs.
We sought comment on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
(

Comment:
Many commenters supported CMS' proposal to permit one or more ASM participants reassigning billing rights through the same TIN to be parties to the same CCA with a primary care practice. Commenters stated that requiring separate CCAs for each ASM participant would impose unnecessary administrative burden on both ASM participants and primary care practices. Commenters representing integrated health systems stated that a single CCA would better reflect practice operations where clinicians share EHR systems, clinical support staff, and administrative infrastructure. A commenter stated that requiring a primary care practice to sign multiple duplicative agreements could make such practices less willing to assent to further agreements.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' support. We agree that permitting ASM participants who reassign billing rights through the same TIN to enter into a single CCA with the same primary care practice would help reduce duplicative negotiation, execution, documentation, and tracking and better reflect shared operations. At the same time, requiring each ASM participant to be expressly named as a party to the CCA preserves individual accountability for satisfying applicable ASM requirements. We believe this approach appropriately balances administrative flexibility with the accountability and oversight objectives of the CCA requirements.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that CMS not limit multi-participant CCAs to ASM participants under one TIN. A commenter stated that such limitation would prevent solo practitioners or small practices from entering into a common CCA with a primary care practice. A commenter described that a single agreement could facilitate collaboration and reduce contracting burden and noted that independent practices may already contract collectively through arrangements such as independent practice associations. A commenter stated that ASM participants may practice within the same health system but reassign billing rights through different affiliated TINs and recommended that CMS permit such ASM participants to enter into a common CCA where they can demonstrate shared EHR infrastructure, unified workflows, and consolidated data governance.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' consideration of varying organizational structures, including solo practitioners and small practices and integrated systems with multiple TINs but shared systems. We continue to believe that the TIN establishes the most appropriate boundary for a multi-participant CCA.
As we stated in the proposed rule, ASM participants practicing under the same TIN are more likely to share operational infrastructure, including EHR systems, clinical support staff, and standardized administrative workflows, such that a common set of CCA terms can meaningfully apply to each ASM participant. We recognize that some integrated delivery systems operating across multiple TINs may have comparable levels of operational integration. However, the degree and nature of integration across such systems may vary, and the existence of shared clinical or administrative systems across TINs would not, by itself, provide a similarly clear and readily administrable basis for determining which ASM participants should be permitted to participate under a common CCA.
We also distinguish such integrated delivery systems from independent practice associations and other joint-contracting arrangements. The existence of a contractual mechanism through which otherwise independent practices negotiate or contract collectively does not necessarily demonstrate that ASM participants share the operational infrastructure, workflows, or care-coordination processes necessary to support a common CCA. Accordingly, we do not believe that participation in an independent practice association or other joint-contracting arrangement, by itself, provides a sufficient basis to extend the multi-participant CCA policy across TINs. We may address ways to alleviate burden associated with CCAs for solo practitioners or small practices as appropriate based on experiences under the model, such as through additional resources or in future rulemaking.
Comment:
A few commenters observed that CMS proposed to permit multi-participant CCAs while enforcing strict remuneration limits and restricting safe harbor applicability during exception periods. A commenter recommended that CMS tailor safe harbors for integrated delivery networks to allow alignment between employed primary care, hospital facilities, and specialists.
Response:
We note that, as revised, the limitation on remuneration under a CCA is structured to account for and scale with the number of ASM participants joining a CCA. We proposed such revision to account for the proposed change allowing multi-participant CCAs.
We clarify that the applicability of the CMS-sponsored model arrangements and patient incentives safe harbor to ASM as described at § 512.765 is tailored to ASM since it was made available for purposes of ASM, rather than specifically to an integrated delivery system.
Comment:
Commenters suggested that ASM participants or primary care practices may already participate in accountable care models, such as accountable care organizations (ACOs) and that such existing collaborations or shared infrastructures should count toward meeting CCA requirements. A commenter noted that the requirement for a formal contractual arrangement between ASM participants and primary care providers may impose burden without clear evidence of care improvement. Another commenter noted that requiring a new written arrangement where effective collaboration is already documented and operating adds paperwork without a demonstrated clinical gain. The commenter further asked CMS to publish model arrangement templates and operational guidance well in advance of the model start date, so that participants have time to evaluate requirements, build the workflows, execute the arrangements and train staff before performance is measured.
Response:
We continue to believe that CCAs will drive meaningful collaboration by facilitating conversation and agreement among primary care and specialists on responsibilities for managing shared patient's care. Organizations that have existing pathways between ASM participants and primary care practices that facilitate those activities envisioned by IA-2 and CCAs can leverage those existing structures when meeting ASM requirements.
We appreciate requests for resources to assist with preparations for ASM, including CCAs, and note that we have published resources on our website to assist ASM participants with preparing for improvement activity requirements, including CCAs. We will continue to engage with ASM participants to learn what additional resources and information is needed to support them.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that authorized leadership within a practice be permitted to execute a CCA on behalf of the respective parties, for example, cardiology leadership and primary care leadership—rather than requiring each individual ASM participant's signature. The commenter stated this flexibility would be particularly beneficial for large practices and organizations with 100 or more participating providers.
(
printed page 71268)
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concern regarding the burden associated with executing a CCA that includes multiple ASM participants. The purpose of the signature and party requirements under § 512.771 is to ensure that each ASM participant relying on the CCA is expressly identified as a party, is bound by the arrangement, and remains accountable for the applicable requirements thereunder. We do not intend to prescribe the internal process by which a party determines who has authority to execute an agreement on its behalf, provided the CCA is executed in accordance with applicable law and each ASM participant relying on the CCA is expressly named as a party and bound by its terms.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that CMS eliminate ASM improvement activities, eliminate CCAs, or continue to substantially simplify CCAs to reduce compliance and documentation burden. Commenters expressed concern that requiring a formal contractual arrangement between ASM participants and primary care providers could discourage collaboration, particularly where care coordination structures are already in place. Several commenters recommended CMS minimize overlapping requirements, such as for practices that already participate in programs such as the Medicare Shared Savings Program, in an integrated health system, or in an advanced APM by excepting from IA-2 requirements any ASM participants who demonstrate that they have existing coordination structures with primary care. A commenter suggested it is impractical to have detailed formal arrangements with multiple practices when as few as one patient is shared between each practice. The commenter further expressed that there is no requirement on primary care practices to join a CCA and anticipated this would create difficulty for specialists to convince primary care partners to engage in a CCA, recommending that CMS eliminate the CCA requirement and allow specialists to determine the best way to engage with primary care practices in the communities they serve.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns and recognize that some ASM participants may already have established mechanisms to coordinate with primary care practices. Where an ASM participant and a primary care practice have established care coordination infrastructure, those efforts may support meeting the requirements of the CCA. However, the existence of an affiliation or an informal collaboration would not, by itself, satisfy ASM performance requirements. As specified in § 512.771, a CCA must meet certain conditions, including that it be in writing, identify the parties, involve at least one shared patient who is an ASM beneficiary, and address at least three of the five collaborative elements specified at § 512.735(c)(2)(ii). We do not believe it would be appropriate to except an ASM participant from IA-2 or the associated CCA requirement based solely on affiliation status or on participation in another program or model. We continue to believe that requiring a CCA provides an important opportunity for specialists and primary care practices to formalize expectations regarding co-management, care coordination, data sharing, transitions in care planning, and infrastructure support for shared patients.
We emphasize that, although we encourage ASM participants to enter into multiple CCAs where doing so would support care coordination for a broader population of ASM beneficiaries, IA-2 requires only one CCA. An ASM participant therefore is not required to establish a CCA with every primary care practice with which they share a patient. Accordingly, we do not agree with the commenter's characterization that IA-2 necessarily requires detailed formal arrangements with every such practice.
We also appreciate the concern that primary care practices are not independently required to enter into a CCA. ASM is designed to include specialists as ASM participants, not primary care practices. We believe that primary care practices will be interested in efforts to address gaps in care for their patients and in collaborating with specialists for this purpose.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS establish a 90-day grace period from January 1, 2027 through March 31, 2027, during which an ASM participant would not receive a reduction to the improvement activities ASM performance category score for not having a CCA in place. The commenter stated that such a period would provide additional time to establish a CCA with primary care, EHR workflows, and data-sharing infrastructure.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's consideration of the steps that may be necessary to operationalize a CCA. However, we do not believe a separate 90-day grace period is necessary. Under § 512.735(a), the performance period for the improvement activities ASM performance category is a minimum of 90 continuous days within the applicable calendar year. Thus, an ASM participant is not required to have a CCA in place by January 1, 2027, or even by March 31, 2027. Rather, the ASM participant may use time during CY 2027 to establish the necessary workflows, data-sharing processes, and written CCA and still complete the required continuous 90-day performance period for improvement activities for the 2027 ASM performance year.
Comment:
Several commenters supported CMS' refinements to CCA regulations at § 512.771 ahead of the model launch, stating that expanded CCA flexibilities would help make the model more administrable.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support and agree that revisions will improve operationalizing CCAs.
After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing our policy at § 512.771(a)(1) and § 512.771(a)(2) to permit more than one ASM participant billing under the same TIN to join a common CCA, provided each ASM participant is named as a party to the CCA, with minor modifications to the regulatory text. We make a textual modifications to § 512.771(a)(1) from the proposed regulatory text to specify that the CCA must be exclusively between an ASM participant, or one or more ASM participants who reassign billing rights through the same TIN, and a primary care practice. We are modifying the final regulatory text at § 512.771(a)(2) to state that a primary care practice party must share one or more patients who are ASM beneficiaries with at least one ASM participant party to the collaborative care arrangement. This retains the substance of the proposal while making clear a CCA may be with one ASM participant regardless of whether that clinician reassigns billing rights.
(3) Requirement That CCA Parties Share a Patient Who Is an ASM Beneficiary
Sections 512.735(c)(2)(i) and 512.771(a)(2) require that parties to a CCA share a patient who is an ASM beneficiary. In the proposed rule, we proposed to retain the requirement at § 512.771(a)(2) that an ASM participant party or parties and the primary care practice party share at least one patient who is an ASM beneficiary. Under the proposal, this requirement would be satisfied if at least one that an ASM participant party or ASM participant parties and the primary care practice share a patient who is an ASM beneficiary would be satisfied so long as at least one shared patient who is ASM
(
printed page 71269)
beneficiary exists between any one ASM participant party to the CCA and the primary care practice party, regardless of the total number of ASM participants who are parties to that CCA.
The purpose of requiring the parties to share “one or more” patients who are ASM beneficiaries is to ensure a clear nexus exists between the CCA and coordination activities undertaken on behalf of shared ASM beneficiaries. In the absence of any shared ASM beneficiaries, there would be no common patient population with respect to which the parties could coordinate care consistent with the purpose of the CCA.
We also proposed to remove the term “established” from § 512.771(a)(2). Current § 512.771(a)(2) provides that, for purposes of satisfying the shared ASM beneficiary requirement, the ASM beneficiary must be an “established” patient. By contrast, the IA-2 specifications at § 512.735(c)(2)(i) do not include an “established” patient requirement. Upon further review, we concluded that the “established” qualifier is unnecessary and creates an inconsistency between § 512.771(a)(2) and the IA-2 specifications. We therefore proposed to remove the term “established” from § 512.771(a)(2) to align the CCA requirement with § 512.735(c)(2)(i).
Comment:
A commenter supported the proposal to require the ASM participant or ASM participants and the primary care practice who are parties to the CCA share at least one patient who is an ASM beneficiary, agreeing that shared patients encourage collaboration and should be an expectation of the CCA. The commenter also agreed with the proposal to remove the term “established.”
Response:
We appreciate the support and agree that a shared patient relationship is fundamental to the purpose of a CCA.
We are finalizing our proposal at § 512.771(a)(2) that the primary care practice party share at least one patient who is an ASM beneficiary with at least one ASM participant party to the CCA, and finalizing the removal of the term “established” from § 512.771(a)(2) to conform with the IA-2 specifications at § 512.735(c)(2)(i).
