31 U.S.C. 3729
et seq.
); the anti-kickback statute (
42 U.S.C 1320a-7b(b)
); the civil monetary penalties law (
42 U.S.C. 1320a-7a
); and the physician self-referral law (
42 U.S.C. 1395nn
).
We proposed to remove the illustrative list of legal authorities from § 512.771(a)(5) while retaining the requirement that parties to a CCA comply with all applicable statutes, regulations, and guidance (
91 FR 43994
). We invited comment on this proposal.
We did not receive public comments on this provision and therefore are finalizing without modification our changes to § 512.771(a)(5), which remove the illustrative list of legal authorities while retaining the requirement that all parties comply with applicable statutes, regulations, and guidance, and replacing “[b]oth” with “[a]ll” parties, as proposed.
(5) Restriction on Conditioning Remuneration on Referrals
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we established that neither the opportunity to enter a CCA nor the amount of any payment under a CCA may be conditioned, directly or indirectly, on the volume or value of past or anticipated referrals or business generated by, between, or among the parties to the arrangement or any other person (
90 FR 49711
). Separately, § 512.771(a)(2) requires that an ASM participant and a primary care practice party to a CCA share at least one patient who is an ASM beneficiary.
After review of our regulations, we became concerned that the current language at § 512.771(a)(6), when read together with the shared-beneficiary requirement at § 512.771(a)(2), could be interpreted to unnecessarily constrain the formation of the CCAs. The existence of shared ASM beneficiaries may reflect existing care relationships between ASM participants and primary care practices. As a result, § 512.771(a)(6) could be read to preclude prospective CCA parties from considering the existence of the very beneficiary-sharing relationship required under § 512.771(a)(2). We did not intend for this prohibition on conditioning entry into a CCA on referrals or business generated to prevent parties from considering whether they satisfy the shared-beneficiary requirement that is itself a requirement to CCAs.
Accordingly, we proposed to revise § 512.771(a)(6) to clarify that an ASM participant may consider, as a criterion for entering into a CCA, whether the ASM participant and a primary care practice share at least one patient who is an ASM beneficiary, provided that consideration of the shared-beneficiary relationship is for purposes of furthering the care coordination objectives of the CCA. Under the proposed revision, consideration of the existence of such a shared-beneficiary relationship would not, by itself, constitute conditioning the opportunity to enter into a CCA on the volume or value of referrals or other business generated.
We sought comment on this proposal and targeted revision intending to permit parties to consider whether they share one or more ASM beneficiaries for purposes of satisfying the shared-beneficiary requirement at §  512.771(a)(2) and furthering the purpose of the CCA. We also invited comment on whether our proposed approach is sufficiently clear and appropriately accommodates the operational realities of how practices contemplate establishing CCAs.
We received public comment on this proposal. The following is a summary of comments received and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter agreed with the proposal that potential remuneration under a CCA should not be dependent on referral patterns or the generation of business based on referrals.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's agreement with our proposal.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing our proposed changes to § 512.771(a)(6) as proposed, which permits prospective parties to consider whether they share at least one patient who is an ASM beneficiary for purposes of furthering the care-coordination objectives of the CCA, while preserving the prohibition on conditioning participation or remuneration on the volume or value of past or anticipated referrals or other business generated.
(6) CCAs That Include the Exchange of Remuneration
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we stated our intent to allow ASM participants and their primary care partners to negotiate arrangements that are best suited to their practices (
90 FR 49712
). We also recognized that parties to a CCA may wish to include model-related incentives under a CCA to support shared accountability for the outcomes of ASM beneficiaries and to support coordination activities that benefit shared patients (
90 FR 49713
). Accordingly, we made the CMS-sponsored model arrangements safe harbor at § 1001.952(ii)(1) available under ASM at § 512.765 to protect remuneration exchanged under a CCA, provided that all requirements of the safe harbor at § 1001.952(ii)(1) and CCA
(
printed page 71270)
regulations at § 512.771 are met (
90 FR 49713
).
As stated in the proposed rule, we believe that provisions of § 512.771 that refer to payments exchanged under a CCA should be revised to apply more broadly to remuneration exchanged under a CCA to the extent applicable. Applying these provisions to remuneration would better align § 512.771 with § 512.765 and the CMS-sponsored model arrangements safe harbor at § 1001.952(ii)(1), both of which address remuneration. It would also more accurately reflect the full range of value that parties may exchange under a CCA, including monetary payments and in-kind items or services that support care coordination and other model-related activities.
Accordingly, we proposed to revise § 512.771 such that applicable provisions referencing payment instead reflect and apply more broadly to remuneration exchanged under a CCA. We believed this proposed modification would clarify that safe harbor protections, as well as requirements, apply to both monetary and in-kind remuneration exchanged under a CCA. We emphasized in the proposed rule that remuneration is not a required element of a CCA. Rather, parties to a CCAs may elect to include monetary or in-kind incentives that promote improvement activities or the goals of the model, provided that all applicable requirements are met (
90 FR 49654
). In-kind remuneration, such as shared data analytics platforms, care managers, or technology infrastructure could support the type of care coordination envisioned by ASM.
We also proposed to add new paragraph § 512.771(d) to introduce the additional requirements that apply when parties to a CCA elect to exchange remuneration. We would relocate conditions applicable to CCAs that elect to include remuneration such that they appear together under new paragraph § 512.771(d). We believe this construction would more clearly distinguish the regulatory requirements that apply to all CCAs from the additional conditions that apply when remuneration is exchanged under a CCA.
We received public comments on these proposals.
Comment:
A few commenters stated that CMS appeared to be expanding application of the requirements under § 512.771 to include the broader category of remuneration, rather than just payment and expressed concern specifically in regard to application of the limitation described at § 512.771(d)(2) to in-kind remuneration, rather than just payment.
Response:
We appreciate these comments and address these concerns in the section discussing § 512.771(d)(2), given that the expressed concerns are more closely associated with that specific provision rather than with the proposed change to expand the scope of the protections under the safe harbor more broadly.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing without modification the proposed changes to § 512.771, which revise references from “payment” to instead apply to “remuneration” as applicable. We are also finalizing our proposal to reorganize § 512.771 such that provisions applying to all CCAs are addressed together, and provisions that apply only to remunerative CCAs are addressed under § 512.771(d).
(a) Requirement for Remuneration To Reasonably Relate To CCA Purpose
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized at § 512.771(a)(3) that a CCA must be entered into for the purpose of either furthering the ASM participant's performance in the improvement activities ASM performance category or furthering the clinical goals of the model as described by § 512.771(b) (
90 FR 49712
through
49714
).
We proposed to require at new § 512.771(d)(1) that any remuneration exchanged by the parties to a CCA be reasonably related to the purpose of the CCA, as defined in § 512.771(a)(3). We believed that aligning the purpose of any exchange of remuneration with the purpose of the CCA would support bona fide care coordination incentives while protecting program integrity.
We sought comment on our proposal at § 512.771(d)(1) to require that any remuneration exchanged under a CCA be reasonably related to the purpose of the arrangement, consistent with § 512.771(a)(3).
We did not receive public comment on the proposal at § 512.771(d)(1) to require that any remuneration exchanged under a CCA be reasonably related to the purpose of the arrangement as defined in § 512.771(a)(3) and therefore are finalizing it as proposed.
(b) Limitation on Remuneration
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49712
through
49714
), we finalized a limitation to the amount of any payments exchanged under a CCA at § 512.771(a)(7). Specifically, we finalized a requirement that any payment exchanged under a CCA must not exceed the sum total of the payment adjustments made to an ASM participant's claims for a given ASM payment year, which would be calculated based on the of application of the ASM payment adjustment factor to the ASM participant's payments for Medicare Part B covered professional services during the corresponding ASM payment year.
Our intent was to ensure that any financial or in-kind exchanges between CCA parties remain appropriately tied to patient outcomes and ASM's clinical goals (
90 FR 49712
).
We stated in the proposed rule our belief that the methodology finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule may be difficult for parties to operationalize and warrants revision. ASM payment adjustments are applied 2 CYs after the applicable ASM performance year. As a result, the information needed to determine the maximum amount permitted to be exchanged may not be available until well after the close of the applicable ASM performance year. This could create operational difficulty for parties that wish to exchange remuneration during or near the ASM performance year when care coordination activities are occurring.
Accordingly, we proposed updates to modify the temporal period used to calculate this limitation and provide for a reconciliation and repayment process to support compliance with the limitation. Consistent with our organizational update to § 512.771, we proposed to include the revised limitation on remuneration in new § 512.771(d)(2).
We proposed to tie the limitation on remuneration to performance-based payment adjustments made to an ASM participant's payments for Medicare Part B covered professional services using the ASM participant's ASM payment adjustment factor for the applicable ASM performance year, multiplied by the amount otherwise paid to the ASM participant by CMS under Medicare Part B for covered professional services during that ASM performance year. Stated another way, the proposed revision would change the temporal period used to calculate the limitation amount from the ASM payment year to the ASM performance year. Under both the current and proposed methodologies, the operative component is the ASM payment adjustment factor based on performance for the ASM performance year; the proposed revision changes only the temporal period used to calculate the limitation amount.
In accordance with our proposal permitting more than one ASM participant to join the same CCA, we
(
printed page 71271)
proposed to clarify that the remuneration limitation under proposed § 512.771(d)(2) would be calculated separately for each ASM participant that is a party to a CCA.
We also proposed additional safeguards to support consistent implementation of this limitation. Specifically, under proposed § 512.771(d)(2)(i), the CCA would be required to specify a methodology for identifying and calculating the total value of remuneration exchanged under the arrangement for the ASM performance year and determine whether the total value exceeds the applicable limitation. To the extent that remuneration is in-kind, we proposed at § 512.771(d)(2)(ii) that the valuation of such remuneration would be based on the offeror's costs using any reasonable accounting methodology, or the fair market value of the in-kind item or service. We believed this would support ASM participants that elect to exchange in-kind remuneration in ensuring such exchange complies with our regulations. Under proposed § 512.771(d)(2)(iii), the arrangement would be required to provide for reconciliation, if applicable, after the limitation is determined. Under proposed § 512.771(d)(2)(iv), if the total value of remuneration exchanged under the arrangement for the ASM performance year exceeds the limitation, the party that received the excess amount would be required to repay that excess amount to the other party within a reasonable time. We believed these provisions would promote consistent administration, clarify compliance requirements, and facilitate CMS oversight. We anticipated that these revisions to the remuneration limitation would establish a more viable pathway for parties to exchange remuneration during or close to the applicable ASM performance year by offering greater regulatory certainty that, should those exchanges exceed the final limitation, there would be a defined mechanism to reconcile the difference later.
We also recognized the inherent complexity with a limitation based on a mathematical formula as described in proposed § 512.771(d)(2) in the context of in-kind remuneration. Valuing in-kind remuneration to ensure it does not exceed the calculated threshold, and 'repaying' excess in-kind value during the reconciliation process, may present operational difficulties that could impede good faith exchanges of in-kind items or services intended to support the purpose of the CCA. We considered but did not propose an alternative where the limitation in proposed § 512.771(d)(2) would apply only to monetary payments (or cash equivalents) exchanged under a CCA. Under such alternative, we would establish a separate limitation for in-kind remuneration, such as requiring that any in-kind items or services exchanged meet a fair market value and commercial reasonableness standard rather than a limitation based on a dollar amount. While a separate safeguard tailored to in-kind remuneration could ease operational burden for ASM participants and their primary care partners, we believe that having one mathematical formula for valuing any remuneration exchanged under a CCA would be simpler for parties to CCAs to implement and therefore did not propose this approach.
We sought comment on these proposals.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed applying the existing payment limitation more broadly to all remuneration exchanged under a CCA. A commenter stated that extending the limitation to in-kind support could make arrangements involving resources such as care managers difficult to operationalize, particularly where an ASM participant receives a negative payment adjustment and could effectively require a primary care practice to compensate an ASM participant for the value of in-kind support, noting that it appeared CMS was expanding the scope of the limitation in the proposed rule. Furthermore, another commenter expressed concern that this limitation would require practices to value and document in-kind arrangements that may lack published market-pricing benchmarks, making valuation complex and potentially contentious. Lastly, commenters recommended that CMS issue sub-regulatory guidance describing acceptable methodologies for valuing in-kind CCA remuneration, eliminate the limitation all together, or establish a fixed dollar threshold
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns and questions regarding this proposal. We did not intend to create additional burden or limit bona fide in-kind remuneration exchanged to advance a clinical goal of ASM in a manner that makes the provision of in-kind support impractical. We did not propose to establish a fixed dollar threshold however we may consider this suggestion in the future.
We are finalizing § 512.771(d)(2) as proposed. This provision describes the upper limit of remuneration exchanged under a CCA and describes a reconciliation process if the amount exchanged exceeds the limitation once it can be calculated.
With experience implementing ASM, we may modify the limitation on remunerative CCAs described through future rulemaking if we determine codified limitations present unnecessary and unintended barriers.
(c) Other Requirements for Remuneration Exchanged Under a CCA
We finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule that any payment exchanged under a CCA must be solely between the parties and be made by check, electronic funds transfer, or another traceable cash transaction (§ 512.771(a)(8)) (
90 FR 49712
through
49714
). Consistent with our organizational update to § 512.771, we proposed to include this requirement, with revisions to address remuneration more broadly, in new § 512.771(d)(3).
Specifically, we would require that any remuneration exchanged under a CCA be solely between the parties and that, to the extent the exchange is a monetary payment, payment must be made by check, electronic funds transfer, or other traceable transaction at § 512.771(d)(3).
We sought comment on these proposals.
We did not receive public comments on the proposal to relocate and revise the traceability requirement at new § 512.771(d)(3) and therefore are finalizing changes as proposed.
(d) Documentation Requirements
We finalized a requirement that ASM participants maintain contemporaneous documentation regarding all CCAs, including the relevant agreement and date and amount of payment at § 512.771(a)(11).
We proposed to update documentation requirements to better support ASM participants and their primary care partners in their compliance with applicable regulations and to update references to conform with other changes proposed under § 512.771, including that we proposed to redesignate existing §§ 512.771(a)(11) to 512.771(a)(9).
Specifically, we proposed to revise the documentation requirement at proposed revised § 512.771(a)(9) such that an ASM participant would be required to maintain contemporaneous documentation, in accordance with § 512.135, regarding all CCAs entered into, records of all remuneration exchanged for each ASM participant under a CCA, a description of the
(
printed page 71272)
remuneration, the value of the remuneration, the methodology for determining the value of any in-kind remuneration, and the date on which the remuneration was exchanged.
We also proposed to require documentation of the identity of each ASM participant that would be a party to the CCA. We proposed this change to conform with our proposal that a CCA may include more than one ASM participant to promote appropriate recordkeeping regarding the identity of each ASM participant covered by a CCA.
Together, we believed these proposed changes would clarify the minimum documentation that must be maintained by an ASM participant, better support compliance, and reduce ambiguity regarding documentation when a CCA includes multiple ASM participants as parties. These proposed changes would be reflected in proposed revised § 512.771(a)(9), if finalized.
We considered requiring that ASM participants maintain documentation supporting that all ASM participants who join the same CCA reassign their billing rights through the same TIN as a safeguard supporting compliance with our proposal that, if more than one ASM participant joins as a party to a CCA, such ASM participants must all reassign billing rights to the same TIN. We did not propose this approach as we believe we would be able to verify this information based on data already available to us.
We sought comment on these proposed changes.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended CMS keep documentation requirements as simple as possible, particularly for arrangements involving multiple ASM participants. One commenter encouraged CMS to recognize existing care-coordination infrastructure and to further simplify documentation and record-retention requirements so that ASM participants can focus resources on clinical collaboration rather than administrative activities of limited incremental value to beneficiaries.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' interest in keeping documentation requirements simple. The requirements at revised § 512.771(a)(9) specify the minimum documentation an ASM participant must maintain—contemporaneous documentation of relevant written agreements. This is the primary documentation requirement unless the CCA elects to include remuneration. Where remuneration is exchanged, we proposed to require a record and description of the remuneration, its value, the methodology for valuing any in-kind remuneration, and the date exchanged. We believe these requirements reflect the minimum necessary to support compliance and oversight, particularly where multiple ASM participants are parties to a single CCA. We do not believe these provisions establish overly burdensome documentation requirements and that such records are necessary to support compliance.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS craft regulations regarding remuneration and documentation requirements with technology-enabled coordination in mind, noting that much of the coordination these arrangements contemplate occurs asynchronously through shared care plans, event notifications, electronic consultation, and shared access to monitoring data. The commenter recommended that documentation expectations be satisfiable through the electronic record rather than through a parallel paper trail.
Response:
We appreciate the suggestion and agree with the commenter on the importance of technology-enabled coordination. The documentation requirements at revised § 512.771(a)(9) require an ASM participant to maintain contemporaneous documentation of all CCAs, including the written agreement and specified information regarding remuneration, if included under a CCA. Our regulations do not prescribe the medium in which the documentation must be maintained. ASM participants may satisfy these requirements through appropriate electronic means, including existing electronic health record and data systems, rather than a separate paper record.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our policies at § 512.771(a)(9) as proposed, which make updates to the documentation requirements for remunerative CCAs to include additional elements describing any remuneration, its value, the methodology for valuing any in-kind remuneration, and the date exchanged.
j. Medicare Program Waivers
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we finalized at § 512.775 a waiver of MIPS reporting obligations for an ASM participant in each ASM performance year in which the ASM participant meets ASM eligibility criteria at § 512.710(b), except as specified in § 512.710(a)(2). Section 512.710(a)(2) addresses circumstances in which an ASM participant does not meet eligibility requirements for mandatory participation for a given ASM performance year.
We proposed to update § 512.775 to reflect our policy that when an ASM participant is excepted from specified ASM requirements pursuant to § 512.710(c), the MIPS waiver would similarly not apply in ASM performance years in which an exception applies. Specifically, we proposed to update § 512.775(a) to replace the reference to “§ 512.710(a)(2)” with “§ 512.710(a)(2) or § 512.710(c)”. We sought comment on this proposal.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter supported CMS' efforts to align ASM regulations with CMS' stated policy. The commenter requested clarification how the MIPS waiver will apply as traditional MIPS sunsets and MVP reporting becomes required in CY 2029, including whether any ASM reporting waiver would extend to MVP reporting obligations.
Response:
We appreciate this comment. We do not intend the transition to MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs) to impact the waiver of MIPS performance and associated payment adjustments for purposes of ASM under § 512.775. The transition to MVPs envisions moving MIPS eligible clinicians to MVPs, and thus we do not believe at this time that revisions to our regulatory text are necessary to account for this transition. However, we may revisit the regulatory text in the future if it would add clarification that the waiver's scope applies to MVP reporting, once the transition occurs.
After consideration of the comments, we are finalizing § 512.775 as proposed.

E. Limiting Medicare Coverage of Certain Individuals
1. Background
On July 4, 2025,
Public Law 119-21
, which we refer to as the “Working Families Tax Cut” (WFTC) legislation, was enacted. Section 71201 of the WFTC legislation amended title XVIII of the Social Security Act (the Act) to add a new section 1899C, which provides that, subject to subsection 1899C(b) of the Act, an individual may be entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare benefits only if the individual is in one of the following four groups: (1) a citizen or national of the United States; (2) an alien who is lawfully admitted for permanent residence under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (lawful permanent resident or LPR); (3) an alien who has been granted the status of Cuban and Haitian entrant (CHE);
[
207
]
or (4) an individual who lawfully resides in the United States
[
208
]
in accordance with a Compact of Free Association (COFA migrant).
Prior to enactment of the WFTC legislation, benefits payable under the Medicare program for noncitizens generally depended on whether the individual was “lawfully present.” Section 401 of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA) (
Pub. L. 104-193
, August 22, 1996), codified at
8 U.S.C. 1611
, generally provides that, subject to certain exceptions, only “qualified aliens” are eligible for Federal public benefits. However, section 401(b)(3) of PRWORA provides that Medicare benefits under title XVIII of the Act are not limited solely to “qualified aliens,” but instead may be available to individuals who are lawfully present in the United States. Section 401(b)(2) of PRWORA similarly provides that noncitizens who are lawfully present in the United States may be eligible for benefits payable under title II, such as Social Security retirement or disability insurance benefits. Historically, before paying Medicare or title II benefits, the Social Security Administration (SSA) used a common process to verify an individual's lawful presence status by determining whether the applicant was a U.S. citizen or was otherwise lawfully present in the United States and whether the individual resided in the United States. The SSA maintains a large set of policy and operational guidance, called Program Operations
(
printed page 71274)
Manual System (POMS), that CMS and the SSA update as needed. The SSA's procedures for verifying lawful presence before payment of title II and Medicare benefits are delineated in POMS. Prior to the statutory changes to Medicare eligibility made by the WFTC legislation, a noncitizen could qualify for payment of Medicare benefits if they met all other eligibility criteria and the individual was in an immigration status or category considered lawfully present under
8 CFR 1.3(a)
, which encompasses a broad range of immigration classifications. These “lawfully present” categories included, but were not limited to, the following:
An alien who is an LPR.
[
209
]
An alien who is granted asylum.
[
210
]
An alien admitted to the United States as a refugee.
[
211
]
An alien who is paroled into the United States for a period of at least 1 year.
[
212
]
An alien who is a Cuban and Haitian entrant.
[
213
]
An individual who lawfully resides in the United States under a Compact of Free Association (COFA).
[
214
]
The WFTC legislation did not modify the requirements for payment of title II benefits under sections 202(y) and 223 of the Act. As such, noncitizens who are lawfully present in the United States, as defined by
8 CFR 1.3(a)
, may remain eligible for payment of title II benefits. As a result, eligibility for payment of title II benefits is no longer coextensive with eligibility for payment of Medicare benefits under title XVIII of the Act for certain noncitizens. Because continued reliance on the lawful presence verification framework used to determine noncitizen eligibility for payment of title II benefits would conflict with section 1899C of the Act when applied to Medicare, we proposed to establish Medicare-specific definitions and related enrollment and termination criteria concerning citizenship, nationality, and immigration status.
2. Limiting Coverage Under Medicare Part A and Part B to Certain Individuals
a. Amending the Eligibility Criteria for Part A and Part B
Sections 226 and 226A of the Act establish the conditions under which individuals are entitled to Medicare Part A benefits based on attainment of age 65, disability, or end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Individuals entitled to Medicare Part A under these provisions are not required to pay premiums for such coverage (known herein as premium-free Medicare Part A) and may elect to enroll in Medicare Part B. In general, individuals entitled to title II retirement benefits prior to attaining age 65 or entitled to title II disability benefits, upon attainment of age 65 or after satisfying any applicable waiting period, respectively, are automatically enrolled in premium-free Medicare Part A and will be enrolled automatically in Medicare Part B unless they decline Medicare Part B enrollment.
[
215
]
There are no statutory requirements for citizenship, nationality, immigration status, or residency in sections 226 and 226A of the Act. Eligibility determinations, including citizenship and lawful presence verification, for premium-free Medicare Part A have historically been made through the title II lawful presence verification framework administered by the SSA.
Section 1818 of the Act establishes the conditions under which certain individuals who are not entitled to premium-free Medicare Part A may enroll in the hospital insurance program by paying a monthly premium (herein referred to as premium Medicare Part A). Under section 1818 of the Act, an individual who has attained age 65, enrolled in Medicare Part B, and is not otherwise entitled to premium-free Medicare Part A may enroll if the individual is a resident of the United States and is either a citizen of the United States or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence who has resided continuously in the United States for the 5 years immediately preceding the month in which the individual applies for enrollment.
Section 1836 of the Act establishes eligibility requirements for Medicare Part B (also known as supplementary medical insurance). Under section 1836 of the Act, an individual may enroll in Medicare Part B if the individual is entitled to Medicare Part A or, alternatively, has attained age 65, is a resident of the United States and is either a citizen of the United States or an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence who has resided continuously in the United States for the 5 years immediately preceding the month in which the individual applies for enrollment. The WFTC legislation did not eliminate the 5-year continuous residency requirement for LPRs in sections 1818(a)(3) and 1836(a)(2) of the Act and, as a result, we did not propose to alter this requirement. In other words, LPRs who meet the 5-year continuous residency requirement and other applicable Medicare requirements would maintain their Medicare benefit.
Similar to premium-free Medicare Part A, enrollment in Medicare Part B under section 1836(a)(1) of the Act has historically been administered in coordination with the SSA's lawful presence verification framework for confirming citizenship, nationality, lawful presence, and residency status for payment of title II benefits. However, section 1899C of the Act establishes specific statutory categories of individuals who may be entitled to, or enrolled in, Medicare under title XVIII of the Act. As a result, title II's lawful presence requirements no longer fully align with the Medicare Part B eligibility framework established by section 1899C of the Act.
To align Medicare eligibility regulations with section 1899C of the Act, we proposed to add a new definition of “eligible noncitizen” at
42 CFR 400.200
that includes the categories of noncitizens eligible for Medicare under sections 1899C(a)(2) through (4) of the Act. Specifically, the proposed definition would state that an “eligible noncitizen” is an individual who is (1) an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence under the INA; (2) an alien who has been granted the status of CHE, as defined in section 501(e) of the Refugee Education Assistance Act of 1980 (Pub. L. 96-422); or (3) an individual who lawfully resides in the United States in accordance with a COFA referred to in
8 U.S.C. 1612(b)(2)(G)
.
The proposed definition of “eligible noncitizen” was not intended to apply to noncitizen U.S. nationals who are expressly eligible for Medicare under section 1899C(a)(1) of the Act. The proposed definition of “eligible noncitizen” applicable to Medicare eligibility would be distinguishable from the immigration status or category criteria in
8 CFR 1.3
applicable to noncitizen eligibility for title II benefits, which continues to be based on the “lawfully present” framework in section 401(b)(2) of PRWORA.

42 CFR part 407

We noted in the proposed rule that the WFTC legislation also has implications for the Medicare Part B Immunosuppressive Drug benefit (Part B-ID) under section 1836(b) of the Act. Part B-ID is a limited Part B benefit that provides coverage only for immunosuppressive drugs for certain individuals whose entitlement to Medicare based solely on end-stage renal disease (ESRD) ended 36 months after a successful kidney transplant and who do not have other disqualifying health coverage. Although eligibility for Part B-ID is governed by the specific criteria set forth in § 407.55, individuals seeking to enroll in, or remain enrolled in, Part B-ID must also satisfy the citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category requirements in section 1899C(a) of the Act. Accordingly, we proposed to revise § 407.55 (Eligibility to Enroll) to add new paragraphs (a)(1) and (2) to clarify that eligibility for Part B-ID is also subject to the limitations established by section 1899C(a) of the Act.
We received a number of comments that were outside the scope of the policies discussed in the proposed rule (for example, general immigration policies, general opposition or support of the WFTC, effects on safety-net providers, eligibility requirements for other HHS programs, the broader health care system, and employers). We will not be addressing those comments in this rulemaking.
We also received a number of comments on the changes to the eligibility criteria as well as general comments on CMS and the SSA's implementation of these statutory changes. The following is a summary of the general comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Multiple commenters expressed general opposition to, or concern regarding, implementation of section 71201 of the WFTC legislation and the mandated changes to the eligibility criteria for all parts of the Medicare program. Some commenters, while noting CMS's obligation to implement the statute, urged CMS to use its available administrative authority to minimize harm with the implementation of these provisions and take into consideration the disproportionate impact on certain populations that have greater communication barriers, resources, and physical and mental health care needs and the potential harm to broader community health, such as preventable hospitalizations and communicable disease outbreaks.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' feedback. The WFTC legislation established section 1899C of the Act, which requires that, in order to be enrolled or entitled to Medicare, an individual must be a U.S. citizen or national, a lawful permanent resident, an alien who is a CHE, or a COFA migrant, and these new eligibility requirements apply to all parts of Medicare. As noted by the commenters, CMS is obligated to implement the new Medicare eligibility requirements as established by section 1899C of the Act.
To help beneficiaries impacted by the statutory changes prepare for implementation of these changes, CMS, along with the SSA, plans to conduct an outreach effort for impacted individuals, caregivers, and relevant interested parties including healthcare providers, taking into account the needs of the impacted population, such as using existing resources to address language barriers. In addition, we are finalizing policies in this final rule to notify those
(
printed page 71276)
who will be terminated from coverage due to not meeting requirements in section 1899C of the Act and to provide information regarding how individuals can regain Medicare should they become eligible again. Finally, we appreciate commenters' concerns regarding potential broader community health effects, including preventable hospitalizations and communicable disease outbreaks. However, these potential downstream effects are beyond the scope of this rulemaking.
Comment:
Multiple commenters noted that implementation of these new Medicare requirements are being implemented at the same time similar changes are occurring with Medicaid and eligibility for premium tax credits (PTCs) as enacted in sections 71109 and 71301 of the WFTC legislation, respectively. Commenters also expressed concern that the cumulative effect of these coverage changes could increase administrative burdens on healthcare providers and disproportionally impact dual-eligible populations. A commenter also suggested that CMS coordinate implementation and information provided regarding the Medicaid and Medicare eligibility changes to limit disruption on dual-eligible enrollees.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' concerns. Implementation of changes to Medicaid and changes to eligibility for PTCs in the WFTC legislation and the potential impact due to loss of coverage from those two programs are outside of scope of this final rule. We note that the related statutory provisions have different applicability dates: section 71109 applies beginning October 1, 2026; section 71302 applies for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025; and section 71301 applies for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. These differing statutory timelines limit the extent to which implementation of the Medicare, Medicaid, and Marketplace changes can be aligned. We acknowledge that the cumulative changes could impact health care providers and dual-eligible enrollees disproportionately. CMS plans to conduct outreach to impacted individuals, caregivers, providers, plans, and other interested parties on the changes to Medicare eligibility. We plan to include states and those serving dual-eligible enrollees who are losing eligibility for both Medicare and Medicaid in our outreach efforts.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS and HHS urge Congress to grandfather individuals who were already Medicare beneficiaries when the law was enacted and who had Medicare taxes withheld for many years. The commenter also requested clarification on the treatment of individuals pursuing lawful permanent residence status and if Medicare coverage could continue without interruption while status is pending. Another commenter requested clarification on whether individuals who were granted asylum and are currently enrolled in Medicare would be impacted.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns. The new eligibility criteria in section 1899C of the Act does not provide the authority to grandfather individuals enrolled into Medicare prior to enactment. The commenter's request that CMS and HHS advocate for such a legislative change is outside the scope of this rulemaking, which implements section 1899C as enacted. Further, the new eligibility criteria require that an individual be either a U.S. citizen or national or an eligible non-citizen in order to be enrolled or entitled to Medicare, and once this rule goes into effect, coverage must be terminated in accordance with this final rule if an individual does not meet that requirement. Further, noncitizens who do not meet the new eligibility requirements set forth in section 1899C of the Act will no longer be eligible to be entitled to or enrolled in Medicare, including individuals granted asylum, unless the individual also has an immigration status or category that meets the requirements of section 1899C(a). Further, the fact that an individual has applied for an immigration status or category that, if approved, would meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) does not, in itself, confer eligibility. In other words, a pending application for a particular immigration status or category is not sufficient. An individual's application for an immigration status or category that meets the requirements of section 1899C(a) must have been granted.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that the title and abstract of the proposed rule did not specifically identify the provisions addressing Medicare eligibility based on citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category and that beneficiaries, immigrant rights organizations, and other interested parties primarily focused on Medicare eligibility could therefore have difficulty identifying or locating these provisions.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenter's concern. Including this provision, “Limiting Medicare Coverage of Certain Individuals,” in the Physician Fee Schedule proposed rule provided CMS with the opportunity to reach a broad audience of interested parties and ensure timely implementation of the new statutory requirements, especially in regard to the grace period population outlined in Section 1899C(b)(2)(A) and (B). In addition to being included in the broader proposed rule, this provision was highlighted in fact sheets and outreach materials on the proposed rule. Based on the comprehensive feedback we received from a variety of stakeholders on the proposed rule, we are confident that interested parties were able to locate these provisions and provide thoughtful feedback.
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that CMS and the SSA conduct robust outreach and interested parties' engagement before implementing section 1899C of the Act. Commenters' recommendations include training, educational materials, frequently asked questions (FAQs), phone scripts, provider education, and other resources to organizations that will assist affected individuals, including State Health Insurance Assistance Programs (SHIPs), Aging and Disability Resource Centers (ADRCs), Area Agencies on Aging, legal services organizations, immigrant-serving organizations, disability and aging organizations, community health centers, religious organizations, Medicare providers, Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, Part D sponsors, Medicaid managed care organizations, and Programs of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) organizations.
Response:
We plan to conduct a robust outreach and education effort that is accessible, multimodal, and broad in reach. CMS and the SSA have been working to develop a comprehensive communications plan to support implementation of section 1899C of the Act and to provide timely and understandable information to affected individuals and the organizations that assist them. We also plan to use existing communication and education channels, including the Medicare Learning Network (MLN), to provide information and educational resources to Medicare providers and other interested parties. We have also notified the SHIPs of the changes in eligibility and are planning additional communications to the provider community. CMS will continue to coordinate with the SSA and other partners, as appropriate, to refine materials and outreach activities.
Comment:
Several commenters noted the impact on providers needing to verify Medicare eligibility and to provide guidance to their patients who lose Medicare due to not meeting the requirements in section 1899C of the
(
printed page 71277)
Act. Commenters requested guidance for providers and other interested parties that includes information on the implementation timing, guidance on eligibility file updates, and on processes related to the new enrollment periods.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' request for guidance. As mentioned above, CMS and the SSA plan to conduct a robust outreach and education effort that includes using MLN to share relevant information with providers regarding the implementation of the new eligibility criteria, including information on timing and enrollment periods. CMS will take the feedback provided by the commenters into account when developing future communications. Regarding eligibility verification, there are no changes proposed to the HIPAA Eligibility Transaction System (HETS) associated with the implementation of section 1899C of the Act and providers should continue to use this system to verify Medicare eligibility using existing procedures.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS work with the SSA to establish new POMS processes and procedures for implementing section 1899C of the Act and protecting individuals affected by the new Medicare eligibility restrictions. The commenter also requested that the new POMS provisions be made available to the public for comment before implementation.
Response:
CMS recognizes that implementation of section 1899C of the Act will require coordination with the SSA and clear operational instructions for the review, notice, termination, correction, and enrollment processes. CMS will coordinate with the SSA, as appropriate, regarding updates to operational guidance, including POMS instructions, needed to support implementation of section 1899C of the Act. As POMS represent internal agency guidance and technician instructions, POMS are not made available to the public prior to publication.
CMS will continue to coordinate with the SSA, as appropriate, to support accurate implementation of section 1899C of the Act and to provide information needed by affected individuals, the SSA staff, and other partners.
Comment:
Multiple commenters recommended that CMS engage in ongoing data analysis and monitoring of the implementation of section 1899C of the Act. Commenters recommend tracking the number of notices sent, eligibility determinations corrected prior to termination and actual terminations due to ineligibility based on the criteria in section 1899C(a) of the Act. A commenter also recommended that CMS track related appeals, challenges, complaints, requests for language access, use of the newly established SEP, and track the dates between attaining qualifying eligibility status for Medicare and reinstating coverage, which should be considered a core implementation outcome. This commenter recommended that where legally permissible and statistically reliable, these outcomes should be examined by State, language, disability status, race and ethnicity, and other relevant characteristics.
Commenters also recommended monitoring impacts to individuals after Medicare coverage is terminated including tracking gaps in coverage, uncompensated care due to loss of Medicare, ability to acquire alternative health coverage, emergency health care use, and interruptions in care.
Multiple commenters suggested that CMS make the number of individuals who lose or regain Medicare eligibility due to the implementation of section 1899C of the Act publicly available. In addition, several commenters also recommended that CMS report on a variety of measures publicly, including terminations, corrections, reenrollment, coverage gaps, language assistance, complaints, and the impact of uncompensated care particularly on safety-net providers, and unnecessary use of acute care due to loss of Medicare. A commenter recommended using CY 2026 as a baseline for these measurements and reporting annually on these measures compared against the baseline year.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their suggestions on monitoring and oversight of the implementation of section 1899C of the Act and the recommendation to report data and analysis publicly. CMS and the SSA track a number of internal measures to monitor enrollment and eligibility in Medicare and will utilize existing resources to monitor the number of individuals who receive notice of termination, if terminations become effective, and those who regain eligibility. CMS and the SSA also monitor enrollment periods used and will continue to monitor the use of all SEPs, including the newly established SEP. CMS does track the amount of uncompensated care reported to us by hospitals for purposes of Medicare Uncompensated Care Payments and we will monitor this data to help assess the impact of section 1899C to the extent that the changes are significant enough to fall outside the expected variability range. We will take the commenters' suggestions on additional measures to monitor implementation into consideration in our oversight and monitoring of the implementation of section 1899C of the Act. We do not track and analyze the healthcare experience of individuals who are no longer enrolled in Medicare.
Finally, we do not publicize granular data on Medicare terminations or enrollments. Currently, we publish enrollment reports that provide summarized information on total Medicare enrollees, Original Medicare enrollees, Medicare Advantage and other health plan enrollees, newly enrolled beneficiaries, deaths, Medicare-Medicaid enrollees, and Medicare Part D enrollees by yearly trend, demographic characteristics, and geography. We will take the recommendations for making additional data and analysis publicly available into consideration.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS establish a formal mechanism through which SHIPs, community health centers, civil-rights organizations, aging organizations, disability groups, legal-service providers, and other community-based organizations could report implementation issues for section 1899C of the Act.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's recommendation. We have regular communication with interested parties, including SHIPs, States, providers, and community-based organizations and appreciate feedback provided during those communications on our programs, especially newly implemented policies. We will take this recommendation into consideration on whether additional communication channels are warranted to monitor the implementation of section 1899C of the Act.

b. Termination of Entitlement for Individuals Who Were Entitled to, or Enrolled for, Medicare as of July 4, 2025, in Accordance With Section 71201 of the WFTC Legislation (“Grace Period” Population)
Due to the statutory changes to Medicare eligibility made by section 71201 of the WFTC legislation, individuals who are not U.S. citizens or U.S. nationals and who have an immigration status or category other than LPR, CHE, or COFA migrant, and who were entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare as of July 4, 2025, will no longer be eligible for Medicare on the date that is 18 months after July 4, 2025. As shorthand, we are referring to this 18-month time period as the “grace period” and the applicable individuals identified and notified during the grace period as the “grace period population.” Section 1899C(b)(2)(A) of the Act directs the SSA to complete a review of all individuals entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare as of July 4, 2025, and identify those beneficiaries entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare as of July 4, 2025, who do not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. Section 1899C(b)(2)(A) of the Act provides the SSA with 1 year to complete this task for the grace period population. Section 1899C(b)(2)(B) of the Act directs the SSA to provide notice to such beneficiaries as soon as practicable after identifying such beneficiaries that their entitlement to, or enrollment in, Medicare will be terminated as of the date that is 18 months after July 4, 2025.
As stated in the proposed rule, the notice will inform them that the SSA records indicate that they do not meet one of the eligibility criteria in section 1899C(a) of the Act, and their Medicare entitlement and enrollment will be terminated if they cannot provide evidence proving eligibility. The proposed rule also stated that individuals would be instructed to contact the SSA if they believe the information is incorrect and to provide updated evidence of eligibility before their entitlement and enrollment is terminated. In addition, the proposed rule also stated that, if applicable, the notice would state that a formal initial determination of ineligibility will be sent prior to their termination date if the individual takes no action to update their records or if the individual confirms that they do not meet the eligibility criteria in section 1899C(a) of the Act. As proposed, the SSA would provide a termination notice towards the end of December 2026 to all identified individuals determined to be ineligible based on data available to the SSA. The termination notice would explain that the identified individuals do not satisfy the requirements in section 1899C(a) of the Act and therefore are not entitled to, and may not be enrolled for, Medicare. As explained in the proposed rule, the notice would state that termination of enrollment will be effective February 1, 2027. The notice would inform individuals of their appeal rights under existing appeals regulations for initial determinations delineated in
42 CFR
, part 405, subpart I, specifically
42 CFR 405.900(b)(1)
, which establishes that appeals of initial determinations for entitlement to benefits under Part A or Part B of Medicare are administered in accordance with the SSA's regulations governing reconsiderations of these initial determinations at
20 CFR
, part 404, subpart J.

c. Termination Process for Certain Noncitizens Entitled to, or Enrolled for, Medicare Who Were Not Identified and Notified by the SSA Per Section 1899C(b)(2) of the Act (Outside of the “Grace Period” Population)
We turn now to the proposed termination processes that would be used for all other individuals whose eligibility for Medicare, including both initial eligibility and continued eligibility, is impacted by the statutory changes to Medicare eligibility made by section 71201 of the WFTC legislation and whose entitlement and enrollment was not terminated by the SSA under the processes implementing section 1899C(b) of the Act. The proposed termination processes for this population provides the framework to terminate enrollment in Medicare if they are not eligible to be entitled or enrolled per section 1899C of the Act while ensuring all impacted individuals are notified of termination and retain their appeal rights. Under this proposal, all terminations made under section 1899C of the Act would be prospective.
We proposed that entitlement and enrollment for those not identified during the grace period and found not to meet the citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category requirements in section 1899C(a) of the Act would end according to the termination processes in the following proposals: § 406.14(c) and (d) for those with premium-free Part A, § 406.28(g)(2) and (3) for those with premium Part A, and § 407.27(e)(2) and (3) for those with Part B benefits. The proposed termination processes in §§ 406.14(d), 406.28(g)(3) and 407.27(e)(3) included providing notice to such individuals that their entitlement and enrollment for Medicare will be terminated if they do not meet section 1899C(a) of the Act, and for terminating entitlement or enrollment where the SSA determines that the individual either does not or no longer meets the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act.
As stated, this proposed termination process would apply to anyone enrolled in Medicare whom the SSA determines does not meet eligibility requirements under section 1899C(a) of the Act and was not part of the grace period population per section 1899C(b)(2)(B) of the Act. The proposed rule acknowledged that there would be a period of time between enactment of the WFTC legislation on July 4, 2025, and the SSA starting to screen individuals for new Medicare enrollment under the criteria in section 1899C(a) of the Act, which we noted in the proposed rule is expected to begin in 2026. Individuals enrolled after enactment of the WFTC legislation but before screening procedures are implemented do not fall into the grace period population because they were not enrolled as of the date of enactment. Thus, the proposed rule noted that individuals enrolled during the previously discussed time period who do not meet the eligibility requirements in section 1899C(a) of the Act would be terminated according to proposed §§ 406.14(d), 406.28(g)(3) or 407.27(e)(3), as appropriate.
Additionally, the proposed termination process would apply to anyone enrolled in Medicare whom the SSA determines does not meet the eligibility requirements in section 1899C(a) of the Act and was not notified as part of the grace period population per section 1899C(b)(2)(B) of the Act. This would include individuals whose status changed prior to the finalization of this rule, such as an individual who was enrolled in Medicare in October 2024 and met the eligibility requirements under section 1899C(a) of the Act based on their conditional LPR status when the SSA identified and notified the grace period population. Therefore, they were not included in the grace period population per section 1899C(b)(2)(B) of the Act. However, if the SSA's records indicate that their conditional LPR status is scheduled to expire in December 2026, and the status is not extended and is terminated accordingly, this proposed termination process would apply upon termination of their conditional LPR status and would provide the framework for this individual's Medicare enrollment to be terminated as they would no longer satisfy the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. We emphasized that the same process would also apply to individuals enrolled after this proposed rule is implemented, if finalized as proposed. As an example, consider the case of an individual enrolled in Medicare with conditional LPR status whose enrollment began in April 2028. In February 2030, the SSA records indicate that the individual's conditional LPR status expires in April 2030, and the status is not extended. Upon termination of the individual's status following expiration of their conditional LPR status in April 2030, the individual would no longer satisfy the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, and the SSA would send notice to the individual that they no longer meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. As a result, under the proposed process for termination of enrollment, the individual's Medicare enrollment would be terminated at the end of the month following the month in which the notice is dated.
There are several circumstances in which individuals are identified as no longer meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act outside the grace period. We proposed the same termination process for individuals in these circumstances in proposed §§ 406.14(d), 406.28(g)(3) or 407.27(e)(3), as appropriate.
For these individuals outside the grace period, we proposed that a termination notice from the SSA would be sent to each individual identified as ineligible. We proposed the notice would explain that, per data available to the SSA, the individual does not satisfy the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. Under the proposed termination process, an individual would not lose Medicare entitlement or enrollment during the month in which the SSA determines that the individual does not or no longer meets the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. Rather, Medicare entitlement or enrollment would terminate at the end of the month following the month in which the notice is dated. For example, if the date of the termination notice is in March 2027, termination would be effective at the end of April 2027. This proposed termination timeline would be explained in the notice. We emphasized that the SSA will not terminate anyone's entitlement or enrollment prior to notification. Further, no termination of Medicare would occur for any individual entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare for failure to meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act prior to the effective date of this rule, if finalized as proposed. We proposed an effective date of January 1, 2027.

Therefore, to implement the proposed termination framework, we proposed adding and revising the following sections:
Premium-Free Medicare Part A:

We received public comments on the proposed termination process. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Multiple commenters recommended that the preliminary notice be sent to the grace period population as early as possible and well in advance of their termination date. Commenters requested multiple notices, with several commenters specifying at least three notices and several recommending that preliminary notices be sent at least 90 days before termination. A commenter suggested color coded notices and another recommended patient navigators and providing notices through a variety of methods, such as phone calls, text messages, e-mails, and letters.
Response:
We acknowledge the comments regarding the timing and frequency of notices to the grace period population. We stated in the proposed rule that, in accordance with section 1899C(b)(2)(B) of the Act, the SSA would send, as soon as practicable, notice to individuals identified as not meeting or potentially not meeting one of the eligibility criteria in section 1899C(a). Accordingly, the SSA plans to send to these individuals a preliminary notice in November 2026. As such, preliminary notices will be sent almost 90 days before a termination would take effect. The preliminary notice will instruct the individual to contact the SSA and provide updated evidence of eligibility and inform them that they could potentially lose entitlement to Part A and/or enrollment in Part B. Individuals who do not establish continued eligibility will subsequently
(
printed page 71281)
receive a formal termination notice in December 2026 before their Medicare entitlement and/or enrollment terminates.
Additionally, CMS plans to send a notice in December 2026 to those affected following the SSA's preliminary notice. CMS's notice will emphasize the importance of reviewing SSA's preliminary notice and encourage individuals to call 1-800-MEDICARE or reach out to the SSA for any needed assistance. CMS will include in the notice taglines in 14 different languages for those with limited English proficiency. CMS also plans to send emails to beneficiaries who have a
Medicare.gov
account and are receiving a disenrollment notice from the SSA. CMS's and the SSA's call centers are prepared for calls from beneficiaries. CMS has also notified the SHIPs of the changes in eligibility and is planning communications to the provider community.
At this point, color-coded notices are not feasible. We will take into consideration other mechanisms of communication, such as outbound telephone calls and text messages, as those avenues become available. We believe the SSA preliminary notice, the CMS notice, and the SSA termination notice, as well as emails to those with a
Medicare.gov
account, provide several opportunities for affected and potentially affected individuals to be informed in advance of proposed termination dates.
Comment:
Multiple commenters recommended that notices explain the basis for the determination of ineligibility (including the specific immigration status of the individual), the effective date of termination, the information or records relied upon, the documentation the individual may submit to establish continued eligibility or correct the determination, applicable appeal or review rights, the availability of good-cause extensions of appeal deadlines, and where the individual may obtain free assistance. Another commenter suggested that CMS make notices to impacted individuals available for comment and review before distribution.
Response:
CMS appreciates the commenters' recommendations regarding the content of notices. The preliminary notice will explain that based on the information that the SSA has, the individual does not or potentially does not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act and will instruct the individual to contact the SSA and provide updated evidence if they believe the determination is incorrect. The notices will also explain how to obtain a copy of and correct their immigration record with the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). The preliminary notice will provide contact information for the SSA, including the website, customer service number, and a telephone number for contacting their local office.
If the individual fails to provide updated or sufficient evidence of eligibility and the SSA subsequently determines that the individual does not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, the termination notice will explain the determination, state the effective date of termination, and provide information regarding the individual's appeal rights. The termination notice will also inform the individual that an appeal filed after the deadline may be accepted if the individual shows good cause for the late filing. For assistance, the notice provides the SSA customer service number, website, and telephone number for contacting their local SSA office.
CMS and SSA have an existing process for developing notices and communications to Medicare enrollees and will follow the current process for issuance of these new notices consistent with applicable statutory and regulatory requirements and we will not be issuing these notices for public comment prior to release.
Creating individualized notices delineating the sources relied upon, the immigration status of each individual, and the specific documentation needed to maintain eligibility is not operationally feasible at this time. The notices are similar in content to what was previously used for individuals who were not lawfully present. However, the SSA will ensure that guidance for evidentiary requirements for Medicare entitlement and enrollment is clear for both employees and the public. Finally, CMS and the SSA will take these suggestions regarding including individualized information in the preliminary notice into consideration for future updates.
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that notices clearly explain that a determination under section 1899C of the Act concerns Medicare entitlement or enrollment and does not, by itself, terminate an individual's Social Security title II benefits.
Response:
We thank commenters for the recommendation. The SSA will be issuing notices based on whether the individual is receiving Medicare only or both title II and Medicare benefits. That is, if the individual is only receiving Medicare coverage, the notice will only refer to Medicare benefits, whereas individuals that are entitled to title II benefits, but not entitled to Medicare, will receive a notice stating that they will continue to receive title II benefits and their Medicare entitlement and enrollment will be terminated.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS require that notices sent out by the SSA and any other entity contain an explanation of the Cuban and Haitian Entrant (CHE) classification, how to prove the classification, and community resources to assist individuals in determining whether they qualify as a CHE.
Response:
We thank the commenter for this recommendation. The preliminary and termination notices from the SSA will state the citizenship and immigration categories that qualify for Medicare entitlement and enrollment under section 1899C of the Act. In addition, the notices will direct individuals to the USCIS to get a copy of their immigration record to determine their status and how to correct the records, if necessary. The USCIS also provides information on the types of documentation that may be presented to demonstrate CHE status.
