216
]
Finally, as noted above, CMS and the SSA plan outreach to community resources, such as organizations that assist affected individuals, including SHIPs and other community-based and immigrant-serving organizations, to help connect individuals with additional information and assistance regarding the new Medicare eligibility requirements.
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that notices comply with the language-access requirements of section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act and other Medicare language access requirements; be written in plain language and at an accessible reading level; be translated into commonly spoken languages; and be accessible to individuals with disabilities and limited English proficiency.
Response:
We thank commenters for these recommendations. The SSA will develop and issue these notices consistent with current applicable Federal plain-language, language-access, and accessibility requirements.
The SSA has existing procedures for providing notices in accessible formats to certain individuals who are blind or visually impaired through its Special Notice Option program. Under these procedures, available notice options include Braille, large print, audio CD, a Microsoft Word file on CD, certified mail, or first-class mail accompanied by a follow-up telephone call, as
(
printed page 71282)
applicable. The SSA's POMS GN 00211.001, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973: Standard and Non-Standard Accommodations, also provides procedures for requests for other notice accommodations. These existing accessibility processes will continue to apply, as appropriate, to individuals receiving the SSA's communications.
The SSA also provides language assistance to individuals who prefer to conduct business in a language other than English. The SSA provides free interpreter services by telephone and in Social Security offices, where interpreters are available in more than 200 languages. The SSA translates most Social Security notices into Spanish; notices not available in Spanish include a Spanish-language cover letter offering translation assistance through a local Social Security office. The SSA also makes public information materials available in multiple languages through its Multilanguage Gateway.
Finally, CMS plans to send a courtesy notice to the grace period population and to those individuals outside the grace period following the SSA's notice. CMS's notice will include taglines in 14 different languages for those with limited English proficiency and contains a statement informing individuals that they can request accommodations.
Comment:
A couple of commenters recommended that Medicare termination notices include information to help affected individuals maintain access to health care after their Medicare entitlement or enrollment ends. Commenters requested that CMS and the SSA provide information regarding continuity-of-care considerations and resources that may assist individuals in identifying other health coverage options for which they may be eligible. Some commenters also recommended that CMS and the SSA facilitate handoffs to alternate coverage options or providers to help individuals transition from Medicare coverage.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns regarding continuity of care and access to other health coverage following termination of Medicare. As availability of other coverage options will be dependent on an individual's circumstances, it will not be feasible to include information on other health care options in individual notices or facilitate handoffs to alternative coverage options. CMS and the SSA plan to implement a robust outreach and education effort with the implementation of section 1899C of the Act and will include relevant information on other health coverage options available, whenever possible.
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that CMS and the SSA provide individuals outside the grace period population with earlier and more robust notice before terminating Medicare entitlement or enrollment under section 1899C of the Act. Commenters recommended that individuals outside the grace period population receive a preliminary notice at least 90 days before termination. Commenters also recommended that preliminary notices be provided on an ongoing basis for individuals identified after the initial implementation period.
Response:
We thank commenters for their recommendations regarding advance notice for individuals outside the grace period population. The SSA plans to send a preliminary notice in November 2026 to all individuals it has identified as not meeting or potentially not meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, regardless of whether the individual is within the grace period population. As such, preliminary notices will be sent almost 90 days before a termination would take effect. The preliminary notice will inform individuals that the SSA's records indicate that they may not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, instruct them to contact the SSA and provide updated evidence of eligibility, and inform them that they could potentially lose entitlement to Part A and/or enrollment in Part B. Similar to the grace period population, individuals who receive the preliminary notice who do not establish continued eligibility will subsequently receive a formal termination notice in December 2026 before their Medicare entitlement and/or enrollment terminates. As discussed previously, termination for those individuals outside of or not notified as part of the grace period population will be effective at the end of the month following the month in which the termination notice is dated. Therefore, for these individuals, this final rule provides that, based on a December 2026 termination notice date, the earliest that Medicare entitlement/enrollment termination will occur is at the end of January 2027. In practical terms for Medicare beneficiaries, this means that they will not have Medicare coverage beginning February 1, 2027.
To note, the SSA and CMS currently plan to send preliminary notices only to Medicare enrolled individuals that the SSA is able to identify before November 2026 as not meeting or potentially not meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. The preliminary notice is an additional implementation measure intended to provide affected individuals with an opportunity to update their records during the initial transition to the new Medicare eligibility requirements established by section 1899C of the Act. Because this rule implements new statutory eligibility requirements and establishes a new termination framework, we believed that additional advance communication was appropriate during this transitional period. However, once the new requirements have been fully implemented, notices will be sent consistent with the process described in this final rule.
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that CMS explicitly hold harmless individuals who became entitled to, or enrolled in, Medicare after July 4, 2025, before the SSA implemented screening procedures for the new eligibility requirements under section 1899C of the Act, and who are subsequently determined not to meet the new eligibility requirements. A commenter requested that terminations not apply retroactively to physician payments and that guidance be provided regarding services rendered prior to an individual's termination date.
Response:
We thank commenters for these recommendations. Individuals who were enrolled in Medicare after July 4, 2025, but before the SSA implemented screening for the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, and who are subsequently determined not to meet those requirements, will have their Medicare entitlement or enrollment terminated prospectively under the termination process described previously. Their Medicare entitlement or enrollment will not be retroactively terminated for the months in which they were enrolled.
Accordingly, CMS will take no action to recover any Medicare payments for services rendered before the individual's prospective termination due to not meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. Claims for services rendered prior to a termination of entitlement and enrollment will be processed according to existing procedures. Because the termination framework does not retroactively terminate the individual's Medicare entitlement or enrollment for those months, a separate hold-harmless policy is not necessary.
Comment:
Multiple commenters were concerned with the high likelihood of erroneous terminations and requested that CMS and the SSA delay implementation to establish stronger pre-termination review procedures and safeguards for all individuals whose
(
printed page 71283)
Medicare entitlement or enrollment may be terminated under section 1899C of the Act. A commenter also recommended that CMS extend the 18-month grace period, which would in effect delay implementation of terminations for individuals in the grace period population.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations. The SSA used and is using the most current information and verification tools available to it to make accurate determinations under section 1899C of the Act, including information or documentation provided by individuals. Individuals identified as potentially not meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, including those individuals in the 18-month grace period population, will receive a preliminary notice and have an opportunity to provide updated evidence to the SSA before a formal determination of ineligibility is made. We believe that sufficient safeguards have been established to identify ineligible individuals and to provide them with opportunities to furnish updated evidence of eligibility and appeal determinations that individuals believe are erroneous. Further, section 1899C(b)(1) of the Act specifies that individuals entitled to, or enrolled for Medicare benefits as of July 4, 2025, who no longer meet the requirements under section 1899C(a) of the Act, will have their Medicare entitlement and enrollment terminated beginning on the date that is 18 months after July 4, 2025. No provision in section 1899C of the Act permits extension of the grace period.
Comment:
Multiple commenters stated that, regardless of when or how an individual is identified as potentially ineligible, the individual should have a meaningful opportunity to correct inaccurate, incomplete, outdated, or inconsistent citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category information before coverage ends or to promptly restore coverage.
Response:
We thank commenters for these recommendations. As noted previously, individuals identified as not meeting or potentially not meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act prior to November 2026 will be sent preliminary notices from the SSA instructing them to contact the SSA and provide updated evidence if they believe they meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) before a formal notice of termination of entitlement and enrollment is sent. Further, any individual identified as not meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act will receive a termination notice stating that their enrollment will be terminated at the end of the month following the month in which the notice is dated and will have the opportunity for successive levels of appeals, including a reconsideration, a hearing before an administrative law judge, a hearing before the Appeals Council, and filing a complaint with a Federal district court, subject to any applicable requirements for each level of appeal.
Comment:
Multiple commenters also requested that CMS clarify what happens when an individual submits documentation before the scheduled termination date but agency review remains pending. Commenters urged CMS and the SSA to delay Medicare terminations when an individual has timely submitted documentation or other information to establish continued eligibility under section 1899C of the Act but agency review remains pending, and not to terminate coverage solely on the basis of an automated data match or incomplete administrative record..
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' request for clarification and recommendation that Medicare termination be delayed while an eligibility review or correction request is pending. Except as provided in section 1899C(b)(1) of the Act, an individual may not remain entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare unless the individual meets the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. CMS therefore does not have authority to establish a continued-coverage exception based solely on the pending status of an eligibility review or correction request. In some cases, an individual may submit documentation before termination, but the SSA may not complete its review until after the termination has taken effect. If the SSA subsequently determines that the individual met the applicable Medicare eligibility requirements at the time of termination, existing procedures allow the prior determination to be corrected and Medicare entitlement or enrollment to be reinstated retroactively, as appropriate. For premium Part A or Part B, the individual may be responsible for applicable premiums for any retroactive period. Once entitlement or enrollment is restored retroactively, Medicare claims for covered services furnished during the restored period may be processed, consistent with applicable Medicare claims rules.
Individuals have the right to file an appeal, or a request for reconsideration, within 60 days of receiving notice of the SSA's determination. The 60-day timeframe for filing a request for reconsideration may be extended for good cause. Finally, in making a determination under section 1899C(a), the SSA will consider available information from its records and any updated information or documentation provided by the individual. As available to SSA and appropriate, SSA will also consider information available from records from other agencies.
Comment:
Multiple commenters requested that termination notices clearly explain applicable reconsideration, appeal, and judicial review rights, including how to challenge an erroneous determination. Further, multiple commenters requested that Medicare coverage continue during a timely appeal process.
Response:
We appreciate these comments and note that termination notices sent by the SSA to individuals that do not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act will provide information regarding the individual's appeal rights and how to request the first level of appeal, which is a request for reconsideration. Appeals of Medicare Part A and Part B entitlement determinations are administered under
20 CFR part 404, subpart J
. This process provides for reconsideration, a hearing before an administrative law judge, Appeals Council review, and judicial review, as applicable. However, section 1899C of the Act does not provide CMS with authority to extend Medicare coverage during an appeal.
Comment:
Multiple commenters also requested that notices explain how individuals may request good-cause extensions of appeal deadlines when they need additional time to gather documentation, are receiving medical treatment, or otherwise cannot file within the standard timeframe.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' request. As noted previously, appeals of initial determinations, or a request for reconsideration, regarding Medicare Part A or Part B entitlement and enrollment are governed by existing SSA appeals procedures. Under those procedures, a request for reconsideration generally must be filed within 60 days after the individual receives notice of the initial determination. An individual who misses the filing deadline can request an extension based on good cause, including where the individual did not timely receive the notice. Termination notices will state that individuals can file beyond the 60-day reconsideration deadline if they have a good reason.
Comment:
Several commenters requested expedited appeal or pre-termination review procedures for individuals who are terminated or denied enrollment in order to challenge
(
printed page 71284)
determinations that the individuals believe are erroneous. A commenter suggested that reconsideration decisions be issued within a set timeframe. Additionally, a commenter recommended that the appeal timeframe be changed to run from the time the person first became aware that they are not covered, for example, when they learn at a medical appointment that they no longer have Medicare, rather than from the notice date.
Response:
We thank commenters for these recommendations. As noted previously, appeals of initial determinations regarding Medicare Part A or Part B entitlement are governed by existing SSA reconsideration procedures. Under the existing process, a request for reconsideration generally must be filed within 60 days after the individual receives notice of the initial determination, rather than 60 days from the date of the notice. This ensures that the time required for delivery of the notice does not reduce the individual's 60-day period to request reconsideration. SSA generally presumes that an individual receives the notice five days after it is mailed, unless the individual shows otherwise. If an individual does not timely receive the notice or otherwise has good cause for missing the filing deadline, the individual may request an extension for good cause under existing SSA procedures, which may include situations in which an individual demonstrates that they did not receive notices. If an individual timely requests reconsideration, and the SSA determines that the individual meets the requirements of section 1899C(a) and that their Medicare entitlement and enrollment should not have been terminated, the SSA will reinstate Medicare entitlement and enrollment, as appropriate. The SSA's existing appeals procedures have been used for decades to adjudicate questions of Medicare entitlement and enrollment, and we believe these procedures are well suited to address eligibility issues under section 1899C(a) of the Act. Therefore, we are not adopting a separate appeals process or timelines for individuals who are terminated for failure to meet the eligibility criteria under section 1899C(a) of the Act.
Comment:
Multiple commenters expressed concern that individuals may be incorrectly identified as ineligible and therefore denied or terminated for Medicare under section 1899C of the Act because citizenship, nationality, or immigration-status information maintained across Federal systems may be incomplete, outdated, delayed, or inconsistent. Commenters stated that the SSA may need to coordinate with CMS, DHS, USCIS, and other Federal agencies to ensure that noncitizen status is accurately and timely established and that individuals who remain eligible are not swept into termination processes because of data-sharing delays, database mismatches, name or identifying-information discrepancies, pending document renewals, or other record errors.
Response:
We thank commenters for their comments regarding the accuracy of citizenship, nationality, and immigration status or category information used to implement section 1899C of the Act. To reduce the risk of erroneous determinations resulting from incomplete, outdated, or inconsistent records, the SSA will only use data that has been determined appropriately accurate to assure fairness in its determinations. The SSA will also consider updated information or documentation provided by the individual. When available information indicates that an individual may not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, individuals will have an opportunity to contact the SSA and provide updated evidence if they believe the information is incorrect or has changed.
CMS will continue to coordinate with the SSA and other Federal agencies, as appropriate, regarding implementation of these verification processes and explore opportunities to enhance coordination and ensuring up-to-date information.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS address potential confusion among mixed-status families, or families that have members with different Federal health insurance program enrollments when issuing immigration-related Medicare notices. The commenter stated that notices should clearly identify whose Medicare eligibility is changing, whose eligibility is not changing, and where families can obtain reliable assistance. The commenter also requested that CMS state plainly that a Medicare eligibility change affecting one household member does not, by itself, alter another eligible family member's Medicare, Medicaid, or other health-program eligibility. Another commenter stated that confusion about eligibility or administrative complexity may deter individuals and families from seeking needed healthcare services.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' concerns regarding communications to mixed-status families. Eligibility determinations under section 1899C of the Act are made with respect to the individual whose Medicare entitlement or enrollment is being reviewed. A change in one individual's Medicare eligibility under section 1899C of the Act does not, by itself, change another family member's eligibility for Medicare, Medicaid, or another health program; eligibility for other household members continues to be determined under the requirements applicable to each program. CMS and the SSA will address these issues, as appropriate, through beneficiary notices, educational materials, and subregulatory guidance.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that the SSA may not have sufficient staffing, resources, systems, or call-center capacity to implement section 1899C of the Act accurately and timely and recommended that CMS and the SSA prepare the SSA field offices and call centers, develop standardized scripts and multilingual materials, and ensure staff are trained to respond to questions from affected individuals and organizations assisting them.
Response:
We thank commenters for their comments regarding the SSA staffing and operational capacity. CMS and the SSA are coordinating to ensure a robust outreach effort, including call center scripts, updated educational and translated materials, and training of the SSA field office technicians. The SSA is working to ensure sufficient customer service in addressing interested parties' questions and the processing of documentation.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing, as proposed, the provisions pertaining to termination processes for certain noncitizens entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare—both the grace period population, as well as those that fall outside of the grace period.
3. Enrollment Pathway for Individuals Who Gain or Regain Eligibility
Section 1899C of the Act limits eligibility for Medicare to specified categories of individuals based on citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category. As a result, except as provided in section 1899C(b) of the Act, no individual may be entitled to, or enrolled for, Medicare if the individual does not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. Conversely, individuals may later become eligible if their citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category changes, such that they satisfy section 1899C(a) of the Act, as well as applicable Medicare eligibility requirements.
To address circumstances in which individuals who initially did not meet the eligibility requirements of section
(
printed page 71285)
1899C(a) of the Act at the time they met all other Medicare eligibility requirements but, subsequently, do meet the section 1899C(a) of the Act requirements, we proposed to establish a special enrollment period (SEP) under §§ 406.27(f) and 407.23(f). The SEP would also apply to those individuals whose Medicare entitlement or enrollment is terminated because they do not or no longer meet the requirements in section 1899C(a) of the Act, but who subsequently experience a change such that they meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. Establishing an SEP for these scenarios is within the Secretary's authority under sections 1837(m) and 1838(g) of the Act, which provide for the establishment of SEPs for exceptional conditions. In the proposed rule, we stated that we consider the enactment of the WFTC legislation and addition of section 1899C of the Act to constitute an exceptional condition because it created a new and narrower class of noncitizens who may be eligible for Medicare than are eligible for title II benefits, despite the close associations between title II entitlement and Medicare entitlement, as discussed in section III.F.1. of the proposed rule, and despite the fact that lawful presence has been the standard for noncitizen eligibility for both title II and Medicare benefits for decades. In addition, the statutory changes made by the WFTC legislation fundamentally altered the consequences of changes in immigration status. We noted in the proposed rule that prior to enactment of the WFTC legislation, noncitizens enrolled in Medicare who had a loss of lawful presence status would have remained enrolled in Medicare, but payment for benefits would have been suspended. Now, in accordance with section 1899C of the Act, an individual who no longer meets the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act must have their entitlement and enrollment terminated. If such an individual later meets the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, it may be at a time that does not clearly fall within an established enrollment period. In addition, individuals who otherwise meet the eligibility requirements for Medicare but for the eligibility requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act may gain eligibility at a time that does not clearly fall within an established enrollment period. For this proposed SEP, we also proposed that the general rule in §§ 406.27(a) and 407.23(a) that an individual must have missed an enrollment period due to the exceptional condition would not apply. We believe this is necessary because, for example, as explained below, the 7-month initial enrollment period under sections 1818(c)(1) and 1837(d) of the Act does not align well with the unpredictable nature as to when an individual may experience a change in citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category, such that they would meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. As another example, an individual may lose and subsequently regain eligibility under section 1899C(a) of the Act during a period that does not overlap with an otherwise available enrollment period, such that no enrollment period is actually missed. Accordingly, this SEP would be available to individuals who later meet, or again meet, the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, regardless of whether an enrollment period was missed.
We proposed that the SEP would begin in the month in which the individual, upon contacting the SSA, provides sufficient documentation to establish eligibility, and the proposed SEP would end 6 months later. The duration of this proposed SEP would be the same time frame afforded to individuals granted an SEP for exceptional conditions under §§ 406.27 and 407.23. We proposed that entitlement and enrollment would be prospective for premium Part A and Part B, beginning with the first day of the month following the month of enrollment. We believed a prospective effective date is appropriate and consistent with the Secretary's authority under section 1818(c)(8) of the Act for premium Part A and section 1838(g) of the Act for Part B to establish the date on which coverage begins for individuals enrolling during an SEP, in a manner consistent, to the extent practicable, with protecting continuity of health benefit coverage. Although an individual may in some cases be able to demonstrate an earlier date on which the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act were met, we proposed a uniform prospective effective date for premium Part A and Part B because citizenship data in the SSA records is gathered and verified at a point in time and does not provide a reliable or administrable basis for consistently establishing earlier eligibility dates for enrollment purposes. In addition, a retroactive effective date for premium Part A and Part B could require the assessment of back-due premiums for months of coverage that the individual had not yet affirmatively elected, which would add operational complexity and could create unexpected financial obligations for beneficiaries. We believed a prospective-only approach is therefore the most practicable and administrable method for implementing this SEP for premium Part A and Part B.
We considered an alternative pathway which consisted of establishing an initial enrollment period for premium Part A and Part B for eligible noncitizens who would have been eligible for Medicare based on entitlement to benefits under title II of the Act and attainment of age 65 or completion of the 24-month waiting period for disability benefits, as applicable, but whose entitlement was never effectuated because they did not meet the citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category requirements specified in section 1899C(a) of the Act. However, we note that the 7-month initial enrollment period articulated in sections 1818(c)(1) and 1837(d) of the Act is largely tied to the attainment of age 65 or completion of the 24-month waiting period for disability benefits and begins on the first day of the third month before the month in which an individual meets the eligibility requirements for premium Part A and Part B. Traditionally, this 3-month pre-eligibility period provides an opportunity for individuals to explore coverage options (for example, original Medicare or MA) and enroll in Part A and Part B. This 3-month period helps individuals avoid delays and gaps in coverage. As a practical matter, such an initial enrollment period could not be applied in an analogous manner to changes that would make an individual eligible for Medicare by virtue of meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act because an individual may not be enrolled for Medicare benefits unless and until they meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. As a result, establishing an initial enrollment period under sections 1818(c)(2) and 1837(d) of the Act or these individuals would effectively shorten the enrollment period by 3 months because such individuals could not be enrolled in Medicare until the section 1899C(a) of the Act requirements are met, which would conflict with the requirements of the Act. Instead, we opted for a proposed approach of establishing a SEP for individuals enrolling in Medicare for the first time, as well as individuals who lost and regained Medicare, due to changes in citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category because it comports with the requirements of the Act.
For premium-free Medicare Part A, we proposed that entitlement may be retroactive for up to 6 months, but not

If the earliest month of eligibility cannot be established based on acceptable documentary evidence, entitlement would instead begin on the first day of the month in which the SSA verifies that the individual satisfies § 406.5(a)(2).

We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Multiple commenters expressed support for CMS's proposal of an SEP but urged CMS to extend the proposed 6-month SEP, with some recommending either an 8-month, 12-month, or an indefinite SEP, because affected individuals may need additional time to obtain immigration or citizenship documentation, secure appointments with the SSA, update Federal records, and complete verification.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' suggestions and concur with extending the duration of the SEP. We recognize the unique challenges that individuals may face and the additional time that may be required to obtain documentation from their countries of origin, navigating through immigration processes, updating documentation, and providing pertinent documentation to the SSA. Therefore, we are modifying the proposed SEP from 6 months to 12 months to account for the additional time that may be required and to provide flexibility to individuals establishing Medicare eligibility. The SEP will begin on the first day of the month in which the individual contacts the SSA and provides sufficient information to establish that the applicable eligibility requirements are met, and ends the last day of the 12th month after the month in which the individual provides sufficient evidence of eligibility.
Comment:
Multiple commenters also requested that individuals enrolling under the SEP be permitted to elect prospective or retroactive premium Part A and Part B coverage. Several commenters suggested allowing individuals to select the retroactive coverage start month.
Response:
We concur with commenters' suggestions to allow the choice of prospective or retroactive coverage for premium Part A and Part B enrollment. The option to select retroactive coverage is intended to provide time for individuals who become eligible for Medicare following a change in citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category to gather relevant paperwork and contact the SSA, while preventing extended gaps in coverage. As noted above, in the proposed rule, prospective-only entitlement and enrollment for premium Part A and Part B was proposed due to the fact that citizenship and immigration status data in the SSA records is gathered and verified at a point in time, which we were concerned would not provide a reliable or administrable basis for establishing earlier, retroactive eligibility dates for enrollment purposes. We were also concerned that retroactive eligibility for premium Part A and Part B could result in back-due premiums, which would add operational complexity and could create unexpected financial obligations for beneficiaries. However, upon
(
printed page 71287)
reviewing comments on the proposed rule and after further consideration, we are finalizing providing beneficiaries the option of prospective or retroactive coverage for premium Part A and Part B enrollment. We recognize that it is feasible to provide evidence of and to verify retroactive eligibility for Medicare, especially as verification procedures and informational databases improve in the future. Allowing for retroactive coverage will minimize gaps in coverage and provide flexibility for individuals to obtain documentation and make a choice that best fits their circumstances. The choice of retroactive coverage will also allow individuals to determine whether they can pay retroactive premiums. The limit of retroactive coverage to six months serves as a guardrail by limiting the amount of retroactive premiums owed and mitigating potential abuse of individuals delaying enrollment and using the SEP to avoid late enrollment penalties.
We are modifying the proposed effective date for premium Part A and Part B to state that the default will be for a prospective enrollment date, that is, the first day of the month following the month of enrollment, but individuals will have the option to elect retroactive coverage. When individuals use the SEP, they will be presented with the option of retroactive coverage through enrollment forms and prompts, which the SSA will then process. The individual will need to provide the SSA with sufficient evidence of retroactive eligibility. If an individual chooses retroactive coverage, the effective coverage date is 6 months before the month of enrollment, but not before the month in which the individual meets all of the Medicare eligibility requirements. The individual must provide sufficient documentation for which the SSA can verify their eligibility for any months of retroactive coverage. The individual would not be allowed the option to pick the number of retroactive months, which is consistent with other SEPs that allow retroactive enrollment. In addition, the individual would be required to pay all applicable premiums if they choose a retroactive enrollment date. To illustrate, if a 70-year old individual who was previously ineligible for Medicare goes to an SSA office in July of 2029, applies for and uses a Medicare special enrollment period, and presents evidence of becoming a lawful permanent resident three months earlier, that individual could select the option of retroactive coverage. The individual would be responsible for paying three months of retroactive premiums since only three months of retroactive Medicare eligibility has been established and verified. If the individual cannot pay retroactive premiums as a one-time payment, the individual could request an installment plan, per the SSA's existing procedures.
[
217
]
In the event of retroactive coverage, the individual would inform their providers of their retroactive entitlement/enrollment status and the provider could submit claims to the Medicare Administrative Contractor for payment and reimburse previously paid claim amounts to the individual or other payor.
We are adopting a 6-month retroactive coverage period, which aligns the treatment of premium Part A and Part B under this SEP with the retroactive coverage period applicable to premium-free Part A. This SEP is not intended to replace or limit the Secretary's authority under section 1837(h) of the Act and 42 C.F.R. §§ 406.38 and 407.32 to provide appropriate relief where the statutory requirements are satisfied.
Comment:
Multiple commenters further urged CMS to ensure that individuals whose Medicare coverage is interrupted because they no longer meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, and who later regain eligibility, are not subject to late enrollment penalties, or other disadvantages attributable solely to the statutory termination or processing delays. Commenters stated that these individuals should not be treated as having voluntarily declined or delayed Medicare enrollment and requested protections to facilitate prompt reenrollment and minimize gaps in coverage and care.
Response:
We appreciate these comments regarding late enrollment penalties and other enrollment consequences. Individuals who enroll in premium Part A or Part B using the SEP will not be assessed a late enrollment penalty in connection with the enrollment, consistent with the treatment of SEPs for exceptional conditions under sections 1818(c) and 1839(b) of the Act. The SEP provides individuals with the opportunity to enroll once eligibility is established minimizing gaps in coverage and care and avoiding any late enrollment penalties.
Comment:
A few commenters requested that CMS and the SSA maintain accessible nondigital pathways, such as telephone, mail, and in-person appointments, for individuals to correct citizenship, nationality, or immigration status information and to enroll or reenroll in Medicare after meeting the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comments. The SSA has a national customer service number, as well as a telephone number and address for individuals to contact their local social security office, which often have in-person appointments available. In addition, individuals can create an individualized social security account on ssa.gov. CMS and the SSA will maintain the existing pathways and consider additional pathways as they become available to allow individuals to update their documentation and verify eligibility.
Comment:
A couple commenters requested that CMS clarify how Medicare enrollment rules apply to individuals who first become eligible for Medicare because they newly meet the citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category requirements in section 1899C(a) of the Act. The commenters stated that individuals who qualify for Medicare for the first time based on a change to an eligible immigration status or citizenship should be entitled to the same initial enrollment period as other new Medicare enrollees.
Response:
We acknowledge the comments regarding initial enrollment periods (IEP) for individuals who first meet the citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category requirements under section 1899C(a) of the Act. We considered establishing an IEP for individuals who would otherwise initially meet the age- or disability-based Medicare requirements, but whose Medicare entitlement or enrollment was not effectuated because they did not meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act. However, as discussed in the proposed rule, the IEPs in sections 1818(c) and 1837(d) of the Act are tied to an individual's attainment of age 65 or completion of the 24-month disability waiting period. Those IEPs include a period before the individual first becomes eligible for Medicare, which allows the individual to enroll before eligibility begins and avoid delays in coverage.
That predictable timeframe and structure does not apply in the context of when an individual may attain eligible non-citizen status for Medicare. In this circumstance, eligibility to enroll or be entitled to Medicare is predicated on a future change in citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category, and the timing of any such change is likely unpredictable. Therefore, an IEP beginning three
(
printed page 71288)
months before the month in which the individual first meets section 1899C(a) of the Act proves infeasible. More pointedly, applying the IEP provisions in sections 1818(c) and 1837(d) of the Act in the cases of individuals who meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) later than when they meet, for example, the age or disability criteria for Medicare eligibility would be unfair to those individuals, as they would functionally lose out on several months of an enrollment period that they would have been eligible for during an IEP based on age or disability.
Sections 1818(c) and 1837(m) of the Act authorize the Secretary to, in his discretion, establish the SEP for individuals who first meet the requirements of section 1899C(a) of the Act, or who lose and later regain Medicare eligibility due to a change in citizenship, nationality, or immigration status or category. In exercising this discretion, the Secretary is establishing an enrollment period timeframe that provides an analogous enrollment opportunity that they would have during an initial IEP. Further, the extension of the SEP to 12 months, along with the option of up to 6 months of retroactive coverage provides a greater opportunity for enrollment and minimizes gaps in coverage.
Comment:
A commenter also requested clarification on whether a protective filing date for an SEP would be established when a person contacts the SSA in person.
Response:
The SSA's rules on protective filing dates for disability applications are not relevant for purposes of the timing or duration of the SEP. We are finalizing, as proposed, that the SEP begins on the first day of the month in which the individual contacts the SSA and provides the SSA with sufficient information to demonstrate that the Medicare eligibility requirements have been met. This policy will apply regardless of how the individual contacts the SSA or whether the individual provides the information (necessary to prove U.S. citizenship or nationality or eligible noncitizen status) in person, by mail, or electronically (such as through an individual's ssa.gov account), which will then require verification by the SSA. The individual will have 12 months from the month in which the individual contacts the SSA and provides the SSA with sufficient information to demonstrate that the Medicare eligibility requirements have been met to enroll prospectively using the SEP. As noted previously, an individual enrolling during the SEP may elect retroactive coverage of up to 6 months, but not before the month in which the individual first met all of the Medicare eligibility requirements. The requirements for retroactive coverage for premium Part A and Part B are at §§ 406.27(f)(3)(ii) and 407.23(f)(3)(ii).
The effective date rules in this SEP do not govern coverage established under a State buy-in agreement under sections 1843 and 1818(g) of the Act; the beginning of coverage under a buy-in agreement continues to be governed by §§ 406.26(b) and 407.47.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the changes to §§ 406.27 and 407.23 as proposed, with the following modifications:
Sections 406.27(f)(2) and 407.23(f)(2) would be revised to reflect that the SEP duration is 12 months; and
In §§ 406.27 and 407.23, paragraph (f)(3) would be revised to reflect that individuals enrolling during the SEP will have prospective coverage (that is, the first day of the month following the month of enrollment) unless they elect retroactive coverage (up to 6 months).
4. Limiting Coverage Under Medicare Part C, Medicare Part D, and Cost Plans to Certain Individuals
Under section 1851(a)(3) of the Act, MA is available only to individuals who are entitled to Medicare Part A and are enrolled in Medicare Part B. Medicare Part D (the Medicare prescription drug benefit) is available to individuals who are entitled to Medicare Part A or are enrolled in Medicare Part B, as specified in section 1860D—1(a)(3) of the Act. Section 1876(a)(1)(A) of the Act outlines eligibility requirements to enroll in Medicare cost plans and provides that individuals may enroll in cost plans if they are entitled to Medicare Part A and are enrolled in Part B or are enrolled in Part B only. Eligibility for enrollment in an MA plan, Part D plan, or cost plan is therefore dependent on an individual's underlying entitlement to and/or enrollment in Medicare Part A and/or Part B, as applicable. Prior to the enactment of section 1899C of the Act, individuals who satisfied the statutory conditions for Medicare Part A entitlement and/or Medicare Part B enrollment, as applicable, were likewise eligible to enroll in MA plans, Part D plans, or cost plans, provided they met applicable enrollment requirements. The eligibility requirements in section 1899C of the Act apply to all parts of Medicare. Individuals who do not meet the eligibility requirements of section 1899C of the Act are not eligible for Medicare Part A or Part B and may not enroll or remain enrolled in MA plans, Part D plans, or cost plans.
Individuals enrolled in MA plans, Part D plans, or cost plans who do not meet the eligibility requirements of section 1899C of the Act must be disenrolled from those plans. Under
42 CFR 417.460(b)(2)(iii)
,
422.74(b)(2)(ii)
, and
423.44(b)(2)(ii)
, individuals who lose eligibility for enrollment are involuntarily disenrolled from the plan. Such disenrollments will be prospective and effective the first day of the calendar month following the month in which the plan receives a notice from CMS of the individual's loss of entitlement to Part A or Part B as specified under
42 CFR 417.460(h)
,
422.74(d)(5)
, and
423.44(d)(3)
.
Plans do not process these disenrollments. CMS processes these automatically through the MARx system when the SSA provides updated eligibility and entitlement records and CMS will notify the plan of the disenrollment due to loss of entitlement, through MARx transaction reply codes. Plans have the option, but are not required, to provide a notice of disenrollment due to loss of entitlement. Since the SSA provides a loss of entitlement notice for Part A and Part B, there is no need to require plans to provide additional notification.

(

Comment:

If an appeal results in a determination that the individual met the applicable Medicare eligibility requirements at the time of termination, including section 1899C(a) of the Act, the SSA will correct the prior determination and restore Medicare entitlement or enrollment retroactively, as appropriate, consistent with existing procedures. Related plan reinstatement would be addressed based on the corrected period of entitlement or enrollment, in line with current procedures.

F. Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program
1. Background
a. Overview of the Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program
Sections 11101 and 11102 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (Pub. L. 117—169, enacted August 16, 2022) established requirements under which drug manufacturers must pay inflation rebates if they raise their prices for certain drugs payable under Part B and/or covered under Part D faster than the rate of inflation. Specifically, section 11101 of the IRA amended section 1847A of the Act by adding new subsection (i) which establishes a requirement for drug manufacturers to pay rebates into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund for Part B rebatable drugs if the specified amount, as determined under section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act, exceeds the inflation—adjusted payment amount, which is calculated as set forth in section 1847A(i)(3)(C) of the Act. The IRA, under section 1847A(i)(5) of the Act, also provides for an adjustment to the beneficiary coinsurance amount in cases where the price of a Part B rebatable drug increases faster than the rate of inflation such that the beneficiary coinsurance is calculated based on the lower inflation—adjusted payment amount instead of the applicable payment amount. Section 1847A(i)(2) of the Act defines a “Part B rebatable drug,” as a single source drug or biological product (as defined in section 1847A(c)(6)(D) of the Act), including a biosimilar biological product (as defined in section 1847A(c)(6)(H) of the Act), but excluding a qualifying biosimilar biological product (as defined in section 1847A(b)(8)(B)(iii) of the Act) for which payment is made under Part B, except such term also does not include a drug or biological described in clause (i) and (ii) of such section 1847A(i)(2)(A) of the Act.
Section 11102 of the IRA added section 1860D-14B of the Act, which requires drug manufacturers to pay rebates into the Medicare Prescription Drug Account in the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund for each 12-month applicable period, starting with the applicable period that began on October 1, 2022, for Part D rebatable drugs if the annual manufacturer price (AnMP) of such drug, which is calculated as set forth in section 1860D-14B(b)(2) of the Act, exceeds the inflation-adjusted payment amount, which is calculated as set forth in section 1860D-14B(b)(3) of the Act. Section 1860D-14B(g)(1)(A) of the Act defines a “Part D rebatable drug,” as a drug or biological described at section 1860D-14B(g)(1)(C) of the Act that is a “covered Part D drug” as that term is defined in section 1860D-2(e) of the Act, and excludes drugs and biologicals described in subparagraph (B) of such section 1860D-14B(g)(1) of the Act. The definition of a Part D rebatable drug includes drugs approved under a new drug application under section 505(c) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act, drugs approved under an abbreviated new drug application under section 505(j) of the FD&C Act that meet certain sole source criteria described at sections 1860D-14B(g)(1)(C)(ii)(I) through (IV) of the Act, and biologicals licensed under section 351 of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act, including biosimilars.
The IRA sets forth different parameters for determining rebates under the Medicare Part B Drug Inflation Rebate Program and the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program. In regard to the rebates owed, for each calendar quarter beginning on or after January 1, 2023, the manufacturer of a Part B rebatable drug is required, for such drug, not later than 30 days after the date of receipt of the Rebate Report from us, to pay a rebate into the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund if the amount specified in section 1847A(i)(3)(A)(ii)(I) of the Act exceeds the inflation-adjusted payment amount (calculated as set forth in section 1847A(i)(3)(C) of the Act) for an applicable calendar quarter. In contrast, for each 12-month applicable period beginning on or after October 1, 2022, the manufacturer of a Part D rebatable drug is required, for such drug, not later than 30 days after the date of receipt of the Rebate Report from us, to pay a rebate into the Medicare Prescription Drug Account in the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund if the amount of the AnMP (calculated as set forth in section 1860D-14B(b)(2) of the Act) exceeds the inflation-adjusted payment amount (calculated as set forth in section 1860D-14B(b)(3) of the Act). In regard to invoicing manufacturers for the rebate amount owed, under section 1847A(i)(1) of the Act, we must report
(
printed page 71292)
rebate amounts to each manufacturer of a Part B rebatable drug no later than 6 months after the end of each calendar quarter, except that for calendar quarters beginning in 2023 and 2024, section 1847A(i)(1)(C) of the Act provides that we had until September 30, 2025, to invoice manufacturers for rebates. In contrast, under section 1860D-14B(a) of the Act, we must report rebate amounts to each manufacturer of a Part D rebatable drug no later than 9 months after the end of each applicable period, except that for the first two applicable periods (that is, October 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, and October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2024), section 1860D-14B(a)(3) of the Act provides that we had until December 31, 2025, to invoice manufacturers for Part D inflation rebates. Additionally, there are statutory differences in the inputs (that is, data sources) used to calculate the rebate amounts for Part B and Part D.
In the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98228
through
98313
), to implement sections 11101 and 11102 of the IRA, we codified these requirements and established other policies at parts 427 and 428 under title 42, chapter IV of the Code of Federal Regulations for Part B and Part D, respectively.
b. Summary of Policies for the Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program
We proposed new policies for the Medicare Part B Drug Inflation Rebate Program as follows:
Section 427.20 will clarify the definition of “first marketed date” to clarify the data sources we will use to identify the first marketed date when relevant Average Sales Price (ASP) data is not available.
Section 427.101(b)(5) will modify the skin substitutes excluded product category for Part B rebatable drugs so that the exclusion applies only to certain skin substitute products.
Section 427.302(e)(6) and (f)(1) will clarify what Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) data will be used to determine the benchmark period CPI-U in place of the month for which CPI-U data are unavailable.
We also proposed new policies for the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program as follows:
Section 428.20 will clarify the definition of “applicable period CPI-U” when the CPI-U data for the first month of the applicable period are not available.
Section 428.202(e)(6) will clarify what CPI-U data would be used to determine the benchmark period CPI-U in place of the month for which CPI-U data are unavailable.
Section 428.203(c) will require providers and suppliers that are covered entities as defined at § 10.3 to submit Part D 340B data to the 340B repository beginning with claims with a date of service on or after January 1, 2027.

2. Medicare Part B Drug Rebates for Single Source Drugs and Biological Products With Prices That Increase Faster Than the Rate of Inflation
a. Definitions (§ 427.20)
In the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98579
), we codified at § 427.20 the definition of “first marketed date” to mean the earliest date of first sale of any NDC-11 within a billing and payment code among all products and package sizes under the same FDA application. In that definition, we specify that the first marketed date will be identified using ASP data reported by NDC-11 to CMS by a manufacturer as required under sections 1927(b)(3)(A)(iii)(I) and 1847A(f)(2) of the Act, if available. We noted in the proposed rule that we use “date of first sale” as reported in the ASP Data Collection System for the first marketed date as specified at § 427.20. There may be scenarios where a drug is being marketed but the first marketed date is not available in the ASP data such as when a manufacturer is not subject to sections 1927(b)(3)(A)(iii)(I) or
(
printed page 71293)
1847A(f)(2) of the Act and is not required to report ASP data. In this example, ASP units sold also would be unavailable in the ASP Data Collection System. Currently we generally use the NDC Directory to identify the first marketed date when it is not available in the ASP Data Collection System. In the proposed rule, to improve transparency of operations to address instances when first marketed date is missing from ASP data, we proposed to amend § 427.20 for the definition of the term “first marketed date” to clarify the data sources we would use to identify the first marketed date when ASP data are not available. Specifically, when the first marketed date is missing from ASP data for any NDC-11 associated with any FDA application number ever associated with the billing and payment code, we proposed to identify the first marketed date from an alternative public source, such as from the NDC Directory. For example, when the first marketed date is missing from ASP data for a given NDC, we would identify the first marketed date for the NDC-11 from the NDC Directory; and if the first marketed date also is missing from the NDC Directory for a given NDC, we would default to using the FDA approval date as listed in the Orange Book or Purple Book. We noted in the proposed rule that we believe data in the NDC Directory are accurate, reliable, and up to date. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) updates the NDC Directory daily with information submitted to FDA by labelers. A labeler may be a manufacturer, including a repackager or relabeler, or the entity named on the product label that is required to list their products with FDA under
21 CFR part 207
. The FDA also requires that labelers update their drug product listing data twice a year or certify that there were no changes to such data.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended CMS use alternative data sources to the ones CMS proposed to use to identify “first marketed date” when the first marketed date is missing from ASP data for any NDC-11 associated with any FDA application number ever associated with the billing and payment code. A couple of commenters recommended CMS use the “market date” from the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program (MDRP); a commenter suggested using the “market date” from MDRP in place of the NDC Directory in instances when “first marketed date” is missing from the ASP Data Collection System and another commenter suggested using the “market date” from MDRP in place of the Orange Book and Purple Book in instances when “first marketed date” is missing from the NDC Directory. Both commenters noted that MDRP's “market date” is an established benchmark for determining rebate liability in Medicaid and that using this date would promote consistency across Federal drug pricing programs. Additionally, a commenter recommended that CMS rely on manufacturers to provide the “first marketed date” via an attestation of the date the drug was first made commercially available. This commenter expressed concern that CMS' described hierarchy of data sources to determine first marketed date may not always provide an accurate or sufficiently precise indication of when a drug or biological product was first marketed. In particular, the commenter raised that the Orange Book and Purple Book do not include the first marketed date and instead include the marketing status as “Prescription” or “Discontinued,” adding that a marketing status of “Prescription” does not necessarily indicate that commercial sales have occurred. The commenter also noted that the Orange Book and Purple Book are not comprehensive and are not updated daily. Lastly, the commenter stated that if CMS finalizes its definition as proposed, CMS should provide additional guidance regarding the specific data sources, documentation, and procedures that will govern first marketed date determinations, including any potential disputes that manufacturers may have with CMS' determinations, noting that doing so would promote transparency, consistency, and accuracy.
Response:
We appreciate commenters recommending alternative data sources to the sources that CMS proposed. With regards to the Orange Book and Purple Book not being accurate or sufficiently precise and up to date, we note that as stated in the proposed rule we generally use the NDC Directory to identify the first marketed date when it is not available in the ASP Data Collection System and that we would use the FDA approval date as listed in the Orange Book or Purple Book only in instances when the first marketed date for a given NDC also is missing from the NDC Directory. Although such instances are infrequent, they do occur and so we proposed to use the FDA approval date in the Orange Book and Purple Book and not the marketing status field, which we do not believe is sufficiently precise, as the commenter noted. The monthly updates that occur for the Orange Book and the Purple Book provide up-to-date information for CMS to calculate quarterly rebate calculations for Part B rebatable drugs. We do not use MDRP data for any other variables in the Part B inflation rebate calculation. Using such data in the infrequent instances when first marketed date is not available in the ASP Data Collection System would be operationally inconsistent with how we have implemented section 1847A(i) of the Act. In contrast, we already use the listed FDA sources for these Part B inflation rebate calculations. Specifically, we use the first marketed date from the NDC Directory to determine whether a drug is sold or marketed during the applicable calendar quarter, and we use the Orange Book to determine if a Part B rebatable drug has become a multiple source drug by reviewing for therapeutic equivalence. Therefore, we decline to use “market date” from the MDRP for the calculation of Part B inflation rebates. Further, based on our analysis, the NDC Directory appears to be a more comprehensive resource, compared to MDRP, for determinations of first marketed date when such date is not available in the ASP Data Collection System, such as scenarios when a manufacturer is not subject to sections 1927(b)(3)(A)(iii)(I) or 1847A(f)(2) of the Act and is not required to report ASP data. In this circumstance, such drug or biological may not appear in the MDRP, and then we would need to rely on another source to identify the marketed date. In contrast, we are required by statute to use MDRP data for certain inputs in the Part D inflation rebate calculation. Additionally, establishing an operational process requiring manufacturers to provide and attest to their first marketed date would create administrative burden and demand additional resources for both CMS and manufacturers. Therefore, we decline to implement the commenter's suggestion at this time. Lastly, with regards to the suggestion that CMS provide additional guidance on the specific data sources, documentation, and procedures that will govern first marketed date determinations, we do not believe this is necessary because we will follow the process described in § 427.302(c). That is, we will use the earliest first marketed date (as defined at § 427.20) of any NDC ever marketed under any FDA application under which any NDCs that have ever been assigned to the billing and payment code as of the applicable calendar quarter have been marketed.

Section 1847A(i)(3)(C) of the Act provides that, for each Part B rebatable drug by billing and payment code, CMS will calculate the inflation-adjusted payment amount for each quarter using the benchmark period CPI-U and the rebate period CPI-U, among other inputs, as described at § 427.302(g). For each Part B rebatable drug, we identify the applicable benchmark period CPI-U as described at §§ 427.302(e)(1) and (2), and subject to paragraphs (e)(3) through (5). Specifically, under section 1847A(i)(3)(E) of the Act and as described at § 427.302(e)(1), for a Part B rebatable drug first approved or licensed
(

Additionally, under section 1847A(i)(4)(A) of the Act and as described at § 427.302(e)(2), for a Part B rebatable drug that is a subsequently approved drug, the benchmark period CPI-U is the CPI-U for the first month of the first full calendar quarter after a drug's first marketed date. For the rebate period CPI-U, we will identify and use the greater of the benchmark period CPI-U index level or the CPI-U index level for the first month of the calendar quarter that is 2 calendar quarters before the applicable calendar quarter in which the Part B rebatable drug is furnished, under section 1847A(i)(3)(F) of the Act and as described at § 427.302(f).

Comment:
A few commenters stated CMS' proposed approach to use the CPI-U data for the first month for which CPI-U data are available following the month for which CPI-U data are unavailable does not recognize seasonal fluctuations in the U.S. economy. Specifically, the commenters stated that prolonged government shutdowns are more likely to occur in October because the Federal fiscal year ends on September 30, which would increase the likelihood that the October CPI-U may be unpublished. The commenters noted that the November CPI-U, which is the CPI-U that likely would be used in rebate calculations, is often lower than the October CPI-U due to seasonal fluctuations in inflation common in November (for example, holiday discounts and decreasing gasoline prices). A few commenters stated that our proposed approach could have adverse financial consequences for manufacturers by decreasing their ability to predict the financial impact of inflation rebates, impacting future rebate liability when BLS CPI-U data are not available, or systematically underestimating inflation.
(
printed page 71296)
Response:
Section 1847A(i)(3)(F) of the Act specifies that with respect to a calendar quarter, the rebate period CPI-U is the greater of the benchmark period CPI-U and the CPI-U for the first month of the calendar quarter that is two calendar quarters prior to such described calendar quarter. Section 1847A(i)(3)(E) of the Act defines the benchmark period CPI-U as the CPI-U for January 2021. However, section 1847A(i)(4)(A) of the Act provides that for Part B rebatable drugs approved or licensed after December 1, 2020, the benchmark period CPI-U is defined as the CPI-U for the first month of the first full calendar quarter after the day on which the drug was first marketed. The statute does not specify other factors to consider when determining the rebate period or benchmark period CPI-U values to use in rebate calculations, including how such values are impacted by seasonality or how such value impacts rebate liability. Therefore, we believe it is consistent with statute to determine the rebate period and benchmark period CPI-U values using data from within the same calendar quarter as soon as there is CPI-U data available from a month within that specified calendar quarter.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that we consider the CPI-U values for the month prior to and the month following the month(s) with unavailable CPI-U data and then use the higher CPI-U value. Among these commenters, a few also stated that if CMS declines to adopt this recommendation, then CMS should use the average of the CPI-U values for the month prior to and the month following the month(s) with unavailable CPI-U data. A few commenters suggested that CMS adopt the contingency method used by Treasury instead of BLS' CPI-U values for the month following the month in which such data is unavailable. These commenters stated that while statute does not require CMS to use a specific source for determining the CPI-U, the statute does require CMS to apply the CPI-U in a specific month for Part B inflation rebate calculations. Additionally, a commenter stated that CMS did not meaningfully evaluate reasonable alternatives such as options to estimate the CPI-U for the month for which the CPI-U is needed to calculate a Part B inflation rebate, did not consider seasonality of inflation values, did not evaluate relative effects of the proposed approach on payment amounts, coinsurance, and rebate liability, and did not sufficiently explain why the proposed approach is more consistent with statute than using CPI-U from the month prior to the month in which CPI-U is missing. Another commenter stated that CMS' proposed approach raises concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) because CMS did not adequately address predictable seasonality, financial consequences, uncertainty, and alternative approaches. A few commenters stated that the proposed approach exceeds CMS' statutory authority because the statute requires CMS to use the CPI-U for a specific month but does not specify the source from which the CPI-U value must originate.
Response:
As discussed in section III.F.2.c. of this final rule, we considered alternative approaches and why we believe those alternatives are not feasible or appropriate. As noted in that section, we considered an approach in which we would use the previous month for which CPI-U data are available but believe this approach is less consistent with statute than using CPI-U values that are within the same calendar quarter as the month for which CPI-U data is missing. Section 1847A(i) of the Act describes the identification of CPI-U values after a specified time period has elapsed, and using data from a month that is before that time period is inconsistent with statute. For this same reason, we do not believe alternatives to use the average of or the higher of the month prior and the month subsequent to the month for which CPI-U values are missing are supported by statute and we therefore decline to adopt these approaches. We also considered using Treasury's index number according to the index contingency provisions for Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities; however, as we stated, this alternative approach does not align with statute (specifically section 1847A(i)(3)(F) of the Act), which directs CMS to use the CPI-U value from the first month of the relevant period and makes no reference to an alternate calculated value. As such, we decline to adopt the suggestion to use Treasury's contingency method. Lastly, regarding the comment that CMS did not consider options to estimate the CPI-U for the month for which the CPI-U is missing, we considered calculating our own inflation factor rather than using the BLS reported CPI-U data; however, we determined that it is impracticable for us to administer a CPI-U survey and calculate an alternate CPI-U index. Similarly, we determined that was inconsistent with statute to estimate an alternate CPI-U value because statute directs CMS to use the CPI-U for a specific month.

e. Enforcement of Manufacturer Payment of Rebate Amounts (§ 427.600)
In accordance with section 1847A(i)(1)(B) of the Act, the manufacturer of a Part B rebatable drug is required to provide a rebate equal to the rebate amount specified in section 1847A(i)(3) of the Act for the rebatable drug for the calendar quarter not later than 30 days after receipt of the rebate amount from CMS. Section 1847A(i)(7) of the Act gives us the authority to impose a civil money penalty (CMP) equal to at least 125 percent of the rebate amount for each drug for each applicable calendar quarter on a manufacturer that fails to pay the rebate amount for each rebatable Part B drug. Subpart G implements this section of the Act and establishes the procedures for determining and collecting a CMP.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44008
), we clarified that the imposition of CMPs under section 1847A(i)(7) of the Act, in accordance with § 427.600, is not the exclusive remedy for a manufacturer's failure to comply with its rebate payment obligations described in § 427.505(a), nor the exclusive remedy for other conduct that may impact obligations, such as rebate amounts owed, under the Medicare Part B Drug Inflation Rebate Program. For example, whether imposing CMPs under section 1847A(i)(7) of the Act or not, when warranted, we may refer manufacturers to the Department of Justice, the Department of the Treasury, and/or the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General for further review and investigation.
