As part of this reevaluation, we revisited comments we received on the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule. In particular, we revisited comments that explained the unique nature of ADAPs compared to other covered entity types, and the limitations in the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology's ability to identify PDE records for ADAP clients as 340B-eligible. As a commenter explained, the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology may under-identify 340B-eligible PDE records for ADAP clients for two reasons. First, PDE records for ADAP clients would typically not meet the first criterion of the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology (that is, that the prescriber with the NPI listed on the PDE record provides care at a covered entity). ADAPs are not providers or suppliers as defined under § 400.202, and a patient enrolled in an ADAP is typically prescribed medications by a provider not affiliated with the ADAP. Therefore, for a PDE record for an ADAP client, the prescriber NPI on the PDE record will not be affiliated with the covered entity that claimed the 340B price for such dispense (that is, the ADAP). Second, the majority of ADAPs access 340B pricing via a rebate model.
[
231
]
These ADAPs allow their clients to fill medications at a broad network of pharmacies that may not be registered in the OPAIS database as contract pharmacies. A PDE record for an ADAP client will thus not meet the second criterion of the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology (that is, that the pharmacy NPI on the PDE record is a contract pharmacy for the same covered entity that the prescriber NPI is affiliated with).
After further review of the additional evidence as discussed previously and revisiting comments we received on the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule, we conducted a more comprehensive analysis to assess whether the existing Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology adequately identifies 340B-eligible drugs obtained through ADAPs for Medicare Part D enrollees. The analysis was conducted in two parts. The first reexamined the preliminary analyses described in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49747
) assessing whether the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology systematically under-identifies drugs used in the treatment of HIV as 340B-eligible relative to all other drugs, and it built upon this analysis by examining whether the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology under-identifies drugs used in the treatment of HIV as 340B-eligible for ADAP clients specifically. We identified ADAP clients using the Coordination of Benefits (COB)-Other Health Insurance (OHI) file—specifically the COB-OHI Supplemental Record file—using a Supplemental Type Code that flags enrollees that have supplemental ADAP coverage.
[
232
]
This analysis reaffirmed our preliminary findings that the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology identifies drugs used in the treatment of HIV at a percentage close to the overall Part D average for all drug classes. However, when the analysis was isolated to ADAP clients only, we found that the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology identified drugs used in the treatment of HIV as 340B-eligible at a significantly lower percentage than was identified for Part D beneficiaries overall. This finding is contrary to expectations given that ADAPs are eligible to be enrolled with the 340B Program as covered entities, and that HRSA has affirmed that any individual registered in an ADAP will be considered to meet the 340B patient definition (as described earlier in this section). Further, this under-identification of 340B units for ADAP clients could impact the completeness and accuracy of data used for Part D inflation rebate calculations for certain drug classes such as antiretrovirals, if not sufficiently addressed.
The second part of the analysis examined how a modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology would identify drugs used in the treatment of HIV as 340B-eligible compared to the existing Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology. We analyzed the impact on the overall percentage of identified Part D 340B units for both antiretrovirals and all other drug classes if CMS were to consider all Part D units for ADAP clients as 340B-eligible. This analysis of the modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology to treat all ADAP units as 340B-eligible determined that: (1) for certain drug
(
printed page 71301)
classes, specifically antiretroviral medications used in the treatment of HIV, a modification to account for ADAP clients would result in a meaningful increase in the number of rebatable units identified as 340B-eligible, and (2) for all other drug classes, the modification would not have a substantial impact on the percentage of Part D units identified as 340B-eligible. Based on the additional evidence reviewed and subsequent analyses demonstrating the extent to which relevant PDE records for ADAP clients would be under-identified as 340B-eligible, we now concur with comments on the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule that we revisited. We agree with the commenters' assertion that a modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology is needed to fully account for 340B-eligible units for ADAP clients. Where the ADAP acts as a payor of the Part D medication, we would consider all Part D units for ADAP clients as 340B-eligible. Such units would be removed from the total number of units and total rebate amount for a Part D rebatable drug as described in the Preliminary Rebate Report and Rebate Report detailed at § 428.401(b) and (c), respectively.
Specifically, we proposed the following modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology: CMS would identify PDE records for beneficiaries who have ADAP supplemental coverage as listed in the COB-OHI Supplemental Record file using the Supplemental Type Code that flags enrollees that have supplemental ADAP coverage. CMS would then exclude all units associated with those PDE records from Part D inflation rebate calculations.
If a beneficiary included in the COB-OHI Supplemental Record file is identified as having supplemental insurance from an ADAP at the time a Part D drug was dispensed to such beneficiary during the applicable period, we would designate the units as 340B-eligible and remove the associated units from the inflation rebate calculation. Because State ADAP formularies can vary, and because we will not have State-specific insight regarding an ADAP's formulary coverage for a specific beneficiary's claims dispensed in a specific State, we would treat all PDE records dispensed for a beneficiary identified as having ADAP supplemental insurance on the COB-OHI file as 340B-eligible and remove the units associated with these PDE records. Since some of the ADAP clients identified in the proposed modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology may already have Part D units identified as 340B-eligible using the existing Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology, counting all ADAP clients' units identified under the proposed modification as 340B-eligible could potentially double-count 340B-eligible units. To avoid double-counting, we would identify units that were already flagged as 340B-eligible using the existing Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology and exclude those from the count of ADAP 340B-eligible units identified under the proposed modification.
CMS acknowledges that this approach may result in an overestimation of 340B-eligible units for ADAP clients. Notwithstanding this limitation, CMS has determined that treating all Part D drugs dispensed to ADAP clients as 340B-eligible is appropriate for the following reasons: (1) the manner in which 340B discounts are realized for 340B-eligible ADAP units varies among State ADAP programs, and (2) variability in drug coverage across State-specific drug formularies presents significant challenges in developing a single, uniformly applicable methodology capable of accurately identifying 340B eligibility on a drug-by-drug or program-by-program basis. Further, in CMS' analysis of the proposed modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology, and the corresponding treatment of all ADAP client units as 340B-eligible, CMS determined that: (1) for certain drug classes, specifically antiretroviral medications used in the treatment of HIV, the proposed modification would result in a meaningful increase in the percentage of Part D rebatable units identified as 340B-eligible, and (2) for all other drug classes, the proposed modification would not have a substantial impact on the percentage of units identified as 340B-eligible if all ADAP client units were treated as 340B-eligible. In other words, CMS' analysis indicates, for the majority of drug classes with exception of antiretroviral medications used in the treatment of HIV, treating all ADAP client units as 340B-eligible is expected to have minimal or no impact on the identification of 340B-eligible units from the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology. These findings demonstrate that the modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology is narrowly and appropriately targeted towards antiretroviral medications used in the treatment of HIV, which aligns with the evidence described earlier in this section suggesting that the percentage of 340B units identified for antiretrovirals may be higher than the average percentage of 340B units identified overall. In light of these considerations, CMS has determined that a broad, programmatic approach to identifying 340B-eligible ADAP units is preferable to a more granular methodology that may yield inconsistent or inaccurate results. If adopted, the modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology included in the proposed rule would be effective for Rebate Reports issued for the applicable period that begins October 1, 2025, and subsequent applicable periods.

Comment:
Many commenters supported CMS' proposal to modify the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology to exclude Part D units dispensed to beneficiaries with ADAP supplemental coverage, as identified through the COB-OHI file, from Part D inflation rebate calculations.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support.
Comment:
A couple of commenters stated that the existing Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology undercounts ADAP-associated 340B units because ADAPs function as payors rather than prescribers and often access 340B pricing through rebates from drug manufacturers rather than access the 340B discount upfront through registered contract pharmacies and stated that a beneficiary-level identification approach is more workable than a claim-level one because claim-level identification depends on linking a prescriber NPI to a covered entity and matching a dispensing pharmacy to that entity's registered OPAIS contract pharmacy, and it cannot capture ADAP-associated 340B units since ADAPs have neither element. A couple of commenters identified a specific mechanism, distinct from the general overestimation CMS acknowledged, that would further inflate estimates of rebatable claims: ADAP rebate model claims are triggered only when an actual cost-sharing payment occurs, and most ADAP clients reach the Part D out-of-pocket cap early in the plan year, but the proposed methodology would treat all ADAP-associated units as 340B-eligible. One of these commenters recommended that CMS acknowledge this dynamic explicitly in the final rule and also confirm that the COB-OHI file reliably and promptly reflects new ADAP enrollments and disenrollments. Another commenter separately stated
(
printed page 71302)
there are over- and under-counting risks in the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology generally, stating that in-house dispensing pharmacies and unreported Medicare Provider Numbers to the OPAIS database can cause 340B units to be missed. A commenter stated their concern that the proposed methodological enhancement to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology could reduce 340B savings available to RW clinics and other safety-net providers, with downstream effects on wrap-around services, pharmacy participation, and continuity of HIV treatment. Another commenter recommended that CMS consider an all-payer rebate model as a longer-term solution, stating that following every State's ADAP formulary in real time to identify covered drugs is not feasible under the current Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology, and that an all-payer model could improve the precision of CMS' Part D inflation rebate calculations without replacing the existing ADAP rebate model.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback and suggestions for further improvement to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology to mitigate potential for over- or under-counting ADAP units as 340B-eligible. We acknowledge the broader over- and under-counting risks commenters raised regarding in-house dispensing pharmacies and unreported Medicare Provider Numbers. As finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we addressed the unreported Medicare Provider Number concern through an augmented prescriber NPI mapping methodology, and we addressed the in-house pharmacy concern by incorporating covered entities' OPAIS-listed “Shipping Addresses” as additional dispensing locations. These enhancements do not, however, address the distinct circumstance of ADAP clients. The proposed modification is intended to close that remaining gap. We agree with commenters that the proposal may result in overestimation of 340B-eligible units for ADAP clients. We have determined that treating all Part D claims for ADAP clients as 340B-eligible is nonetheless appropriate for two reasons: (1) the manner in which 340B discounts are realized for ADAP-associated units varies among State ADAPs, and (2) variability across State-specific drug formularies presents significant challenges to developing a single, claim-level methodology capable of accurately identifying 340B eligibility on a drug-by-drug basis. Our analysis of the modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology to treat all ADAP units as 340B-eligible determined that: (1) for certain drug classes, specifically antiretroviral medications used in the treatment of HIV, a modification to account for ADAP clients would result in a meaningful increase in the number of rebatable units identified as 340B-eligible, and (2) for all other drug classes, the modification would not have a substantial impact on the percentage of Part D units identified as 340B-eligible. Therefore, a broad, programmatic approach is preferable to a more granular methodology that could yield inconsistent results. Additionally, we are taking steps to minimize overestimation; for example, to avoid double counting 340B units, we will identify units already flagged as 340B-eligible under the existing Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology and exclude those units from the count of ADAP-associated 340B-eligible units identified under this modification. We also confirm that the COB-OHI Supplemental Type Code is updated monthly to reflect new ADAP enrollments and disenrollments, and we will continue to monitor the reliability of this data source as we implement the methodology. In response to concern that the proposed modification to the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology could affect 340B savings available to RW clinics and other safety-net providers, we note that the methodology is designed to account for and exclude 340B units associated with ADAP clients from the Part D inflation rebate calculation and does not alter the underlying 340B Program discounts available to covered entities. Comments recommending that we adopt an all-payer rebate model are out of scope for this final rule. These comments address a broader payment methodology beyond the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program policies addressed in this rule.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the policy as proposed to identify PDE records for beneficiaries who have ADAP supplemental coverage as listed in the COB-OHI Supplemental Record file. If a beneficiary included in the COB-OHI Supplemental Record file is identified as having supplemental insurance from an ADAP at the time a Part D drug was dispensed to such beneficiary during the applicable period, we will designate the units as 340B-eligible and remove the associated units from the inflation rebate calculation.

(a) Background: Requirement for Physicians, Other Suppliers, and Providers To Maintain and Provide Access to Documentation
Section 1866(j)(1)(A) of the Act requires the Secretary to establish a process for the enrollment of providers and suppliers into the Medicare program. The overarching purpose of the enrollment process is to help confirm that providers seeking to bill Medicare for services and items furnished to Medicare beneficiaries meet all applicable Federal and State requirements to do so. The process is, to an extent, a “gatekeeper” that prevents unqualified and potentially fraudulent individuals and entities from entering and inappropriately billing Medicare. Since 2006, we have undertaken rulemaking efforts to implement enrollment procedures. These regulations are generally codified in
42 CFR part 424, subpart P
. They address, among other things, requirements that providers must meet to obtain and maintain Medicare billing privileges.
Section 6406(a) of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA) amended section 1842(h) of the Act by adding a new paragraph which establishes that the Secretary may revoke enrollment, for a period of not more than one year for each act, for a physician or supplier if such physician or supplier fails to maintain and, upon request of the Secretary, provide access to documentation relating to written orders or requests for payment for durable medical equipment, certifications for home health services, or referrals for other items or services written or ordered by such physician or supplier under Title XVIII of the Act, as specified by the Secretary.
In addition, section 6406(b)(3) of the ACA amended section 1866(a)(1) of the Act to require that providers maintain and, upon request of the Secretary, provide access to documentation relating to written orders or requests for payment for durable medical equipment, certifications for home health services, or referrals for other items or services written or ordered by the provider, as specified by the Secretary.
To implement section 6406 of the ACA, on May 5, 2010, CMS published an interim final rule titled “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Changes in Provider and Supplier Enrollment, Ordering and Referring, and Documentation Requirements; and Changes in Provider Agreements,” (
75 FR 24437
) which amended §  424.516(f) to specify requirements for, among other things, documentation and access to documentation related to certain orders and referrals. We clarified in that rulemaking that the documentation includes both written and electronic documentation. CMS also amended §  424.535(a)(10) to establish that CMS may revoke enrollment, for a period of not more than one year for each act of noncompliance, for a provider or a supplier if such provider or supplier fails to meet the requirements of §  424.516(f). CMS finalized the interim final rule in an April 27, 2012 final rule titled “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Changes in Provider and Supplier Enrollment, Ordering and Referring, and Documentation Requirements; and Changes in Provider Agreements” (
77 FR 25284
).
(b) Proposal To Require Providers and Suppliers That Are Covered Entities To Submit Documentation Relating to Part D 340B Claims (§§ 424.516(f)(4), 424.535(a)(10), and 428.203(c))
To inform policy development for this rulemaking, we reviewed and considered the comments received on the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule. In this feedback, many commenters suggested that we require covered entities and/or their contractors to report data to a 340B repository. We agree. To ensure robust data submissions in 2027 to determine if data submitted to the 340B repository could be used reliably in the future to remove 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations in accordance with section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act, we believe it necessary to transition from voluntary submission to requiring 340B provider participation in the 340B repository.
We therefore proposed at § 424.516(f)(4) that a provider or supplier that is a covered entity as defined at § 10.3 would be required to maintain and provide access to documentation as set forth at proposed § 428.203(c). We proposed this requirement in accordance with sections 1866(a)(1)(X) and 1842(h)(9) of the Act. As finalized, CMS would reserve the right to revoke, in accordance with existing § 424.535(a)(10), a currently enrolled provider or supplier's Medicare enrollment and any corresponding provider agreement or supplier agreement for failure to comply with the requirements for maintaining and providing access to documentation specified in proposed § 424.516(f)(4). Although we acknowledged that § 424.516(f) has historically set forth documentation requirements for providers and suppliers for their Part A and Part B services, the statutory authorities underlying that provision, sections 1842(h)(9) and 1866(a)(1)(X) of the Act, do not expressly limit documentation requirements to services furnished under Part A and Part B. Sections 1842(h)(9) and 1866(a)(1)(X) of the Act collectively set forth that providers and suppliers must maintain and provide access to documentation relating to “items or services written or ordered by the provider
under this title,
(
printed page 71304)
as specified by the Secretary” (emphasis added). Both sections 1842(h)(9) and 1866(a)(1)(X) of the Act fall under Title XVIII (that is, the Medicare statute), which inherently includes Part D. As such, requiring providers and suppliers to maintain and provide access to documentation related to covered Part D drugs written or ordered by a provider or supplier is consistent with sections 1866(a)(1)(X) and 1842(h)(9) of the Act. By transitioning from voluntary submission to mandatory participation in the 340B repository, CMS would be able to ensure more complete and reliable data submissions, thereby improving its ability to accurately assess potential future use of the 340B repository to exclude 340B units from Part D rebate calculations, consistent with its obligations under section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act.
At § 428.203(c), we proposed the documentation to which a 340B provider must provide access, as well as the timeframe within which such access must be provided, for the provider or supplier to fulfill their obligations set forth in the proposed § 424.516(f)(4). Proposed § 428.203(c)(1) would require that, beginning with claims with a date of service on or after January 1, 2027, a provider or supplier that is a covered entity as defined at § 10.3 must submit the data elements associated with each claim for a covered Part D drug billed to Medicare Part D for which such covered entity or its contractor(s) (such as contract pharmacies) dispensed units of a drug for which a manufacturer provides a discount under the 340B Program to such covered entity. This requirement would apply, for example, to claims for units of a drug covered under Part D and dispensed by contract pharmacies that the covered entity, its contractors, or its third-party administrators (TPAs) identify as 340B-eligible and for which the covered entity obtains a 340B discount, including through retrospective replenishment models. This requirement would also apply, for example, to claims for units of a drug covered under Part D and dispensed by the covered entity's in-house pharmacy.

For example, for claims with dates of service between October 1, 2027, through December 31, 2027, 340B providers would submit the data elements from Part D 340B claims to the 340B repository no later than March 31, 2028. Quarterly submissions are necessary so CMS has timely information to assess the reliability of the data for potential future use in removing 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations. In addition, quarterly submissions may minimize the burden on 340B providers by reducing the amount of data in each submission and the amount of quality assurance necessitated for each submission. Comment:
Many commenters supported CMS' proposal to require submissions from 340B providers to the 340B repository. Many commenters stated that mandating submissions from 340B providers to the 340B repository is an important step in advancing program integrity, ensuring robust submissions with complete and accurate data, and fulfilling the statutory requirement at section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act to exclude 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations.
Response:
We thank the commenters for the support.
Comment:
Some commenters urged CMS to shift to using data collected through the 340B repository in Part D inflation rebate calculations as soon as possible since, in their view, the 340B repository would provide the most comprehensive and accurate method for identifying and excluding 340B units. A few commenters stated that the 340B repository will provide more accurate data than the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology but did not specifically recommend that we use 340B repository data in Part D inflation rebate calculations now or in the future.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. As discussed elsewhere in this final rule, data submitted to the 340B repository will not be used in Part D inflation rebate calculations under this final rule. Before that data can be relied upon for that purpose, CMS must evaluate its completeness and representativeness, which requires the mandatory reporting we are finalizing here. We will continue to rely on the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology to exclude 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations while this evaluation is underway. Any future proposal to use 340B repository data for that purpose would be subject to separate notice-and-comment rulemaking.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that a mandatory reporting requirement is necessary because covered entities lack sufficient incentive to submit data voluntarily, and that a voluntary approach would result in low or unrepresentative participation that would limit CMS' ability to evaluate the repository's suitability for use in Part D inflation rebate calculations.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback and agree that requiring mandatory reporting allows us to avoid the methodological limitations that would result from building our evaluation on a data set shaped by which organizations chose to participate. Specifically, continuation of a voluntary reporting approach introduces a confounding factor into the data based on characteristics of organizations that choose to submit or not, which would limit our ability to evaluate the suitability of the data. To mitigate this limitation and support a robust analysis of 340B data submissions, we believe establishing a mandatory reporting requirement is necessary to help ensure sufficient and representative participation.
Comment:
A commenter stated that mandatory reporting is particularly important for biosimilar manufacturers, who often lack the market leverage available to reference product manufacturers to protect against duplicate discounts, and mandatory 340B claims reporting is therefore essential to ensuring that the statutory exclusion operates in practice, not merely in principle.
Response:
We thank the commenter for this feedback. We reiterate that the 340B repository will not be used in Part D inflation rebate calculations at this time. We will consider this feedback if we propose such a policy in future rulemaking.
Comment:
A couple of commenters supported mandatory reporting to the 340B repository because contract pharmacies generally do not know the 340B status of a Part D drug at the point of sale and should not be expected to identify or report 340B status through pharmacy claim submission processes.
Response:
We thank the commenters for this feedback and agree that reporting responsibility rests with 340B providers, not contract pharmacies. Sections 428.203(c) and 424.516(f)(4) apply to 340B providers, not to third-party entities such as contract pharmacies and TPAs. We recognize that contract pharmacies generally do not know a claim's 340B status at the point of sale, since that status is typically determined later through a covered entity's or its TPA's retrospective identification process. The reporting obligation therefore falls on the 340B provider, who may rely on data from TPAs and contract pharmacies to compile its submissions but remains responsible for the accuracy and completeness of the data submitted to the 340B repository. A 340B provider may arrange for a TPA or other vendor to submit on its behalf, but this does not shift the underlying reporting responsibility away from the covered entity.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that CMS has not provided sufficient explanation as to why it proposed to mandate reporting to the 340B repository even though it has not identified deficiencies with the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology. These commenters stated that this policy shift is significant, and CMS must explain why the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology finalized last
(
printed page 71306)
year is no longer sufficient. Some commenters stated that CMS does not explain why mandatory reporting must begin in 2027 since CMS is not yet using 340B repository data in Part D inflation rebate calculations, and that requiring reporting so soon undermines the purpose of the voluntary reporting period. A commenter recommended that CMS not finalize the proposal unless it can provide a reasoned explanation demonstrating why mandatory reporting is necessary and why less burdensome alternatives are inadequate to avoid arbitrary and capricious challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act. A commenter questioned the necessity of mandatory reporting since CMS already receives Part D claims data through existing PDE reporting mechanisms.
Response:
We thank the commenters for the feedback. We first note that, although CMS does receive Part D claims data through existing PDE reporting mechanisms, we do not currently receive information on the 340B status of all Part D claims through PDE reporting. In the current 340B landscape, only the 340B covered entity has visibility into all purchases under the 340B program and dispenses to individuals enrolled in Medicare Part D; thus, CMS believes there are no less burdensome alternative sources to obtain claim-level information on 340B dispenses to Part D enrollees from the 340B covered entity. Indeed, reporting to the 340B repository, whether submitted voluntarily in accordance with the submission periods established under the CY 2026 PFS final rule or, beginning in 2027, as required under this final rule, is structured to be minimally burdensome such that CMS can match the data elements stored in the 340B repository to PDE records for Part D rebatable drugs to test whether the 340B repository data could be used to identify 340B units in the future. The required data elements have not changed between the CY 2026 PFS final rule and the CY 2027 PFS final rule, meaning that the underlying data reporting tasks for the 340B covered entities are identical whether reporting is voluntary or mandatory.
Second, we note that, since publication of the CY 2026 PFS final rule, through engagement with a diverse range of interested parties, a consistent theme has emerged independent of the repository's launch: covered entities lack sufficient incentive to voluntarily report data, citing administrative burden without an offsetting benefit. We believe this feedback provides a reasonable basis for anticipating, prior to formally evaluating repository participation data, that voluntary reporting alone may not yield a data set that is sufficiently complete or representative of all providers and suppliers that are covered entities
.
We disagree with the commenter that CMS must find the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology deficient for CMS to propose mandatory reporting by 340B providers to the 340B repository. This is because mandatory reporting to the 340B repository is separate in authority and serves a distinct and independent purpose from the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology, which is to collect Part D 340B claims data from covered entities so that CMS can evaluate whether such data could satisfy the statutory requirement at section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act in the future. Voluntary reporting of 340B claims data to the 340B repository introduces a confounding factor based on the characteristics of the 340B providers that choose to participate, limiting CMS' ability to assess whether 340B repository data are sufficiently complete and representative of all 340B providers for this purpose. CMS is therefore adopting mandatory 340B claims data reporting to test a different data source for potential future use. This effort proceeds independent of whether the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology remains adequate for its current use; we will continue relying on that methodology to calculate Part D inflation rebates while this evaluation of 340B repository data is underway.
Third, we note that interested parties representing drug manufacturers and covered entities commented on the revised guidance for the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program and the CY 2025 PFS proposed rule recommending that we create a mechanism, such as a repository or a clearinghouse, through which covered entities would retrospectively submit data to us identifying 340B claims dispensed under Part D, and a couple of these commenters supported mandatory reporting to the 340B repository. Further, in comments on the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule, many commenters requested that we mandate covered entity reporting to the 340B repository so that CMS could—in the commenters' view—more quickly transition away from the Prescriber-Pharmacy Methodology and instead use 340B repository data in Part D inflation rebate calculations. Requiring participation in the 340B repository in this final rule is responsive to this feedback.
CMS has signaled its intent to move toward mandatory reporting over the course of several rulemaking cycles. In the CY 2025 PFS proposed rule (
89 FR 61971
), we solicited comments on potential authorities to require covered entities to submit data to a 340B repository. In response to comments received in support of such a requirement, we stated in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98293
) that we would consider comments received for use in future rulemaking and continue to explore requiring that covered entities and their contracted TPAs report to the 340B repository. In the CY 2026 PFS proposed and final rules (
90 FR 32642
,
49750
), we stated that we were actively considering options for mandatory reporting to the 340B repository in the near future and recommended that covered entities take advantage of the testing period to prepare for future policy development related to 340B repository reporting. Additionally, we noted in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49751
) that many commenters requested that CMS make reporting to the repository mandatory for covered entities and their contractors, stating that, without a mandatory requirement for submission to a 340B repository, the 340B repository would not be able to be used to fulfill the legal requirement to remove 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations. We agree with these commenters. As discussed earlier in this response, voluntary reporting introduces a confounding factor based on the characteristics of covered entities that choose to participate, which limits CMS' ability to assess whether 340B repository data are sufficiently complete and representative of all covered Part D drugs that are purchased under the 340B Program to support identification of 340B units for purposes of calculating Part D inflation rebates. We believe that continuation of voluntary reporting to the 340B repository could force us to delay our evaluation of the 340B repository data until an undetermined number of covered entities opt in—with no guarantee they ever would—or draw conclusions from an incomplete record of submissions. A mandatory requirement is therefore necessary to produce data of the completeness and representativeness needed to evaluate that use.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that CMS has not demonstrated clear statutory authority to compel reporting of Part D 340B data, and that the IRA charged CMS with calculating inflation rebate amounts but did not establish a corresponding requirement for 340B providers to report such data to CMS. These commenters stated that CMS' reliance on sections 1866(a)(1)(X) and 1842(h)(9) of the Act is unpersuasive, and that CMS has not sufficiently
(
printed page 71307)
explained how these statutory provisions authorize CMS to compel reporting of Part D 340B claim-level information that are not being used to support accurate processing of Medicare claims and payment. A few of these commenters stated that the most natural reading of section 6406(a) of the ACA is as an audit authority permitting the Secretary to obtain records when necessary, but it does not establish a prospective, permanent, nationwide authority to require routine submissions from 14,000 providers and suppliers. A commenter stated that CMS' proposal conflicts with
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation,” and the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995. A commenter asked CMS to explain how an enrollment documentation authority directed at the services a provider or supplier furnishes and bills reaches claims submitted by a different entity under a different part of the Medicare program (that is, Medicare Part D). By contrast, a couple of commenters stated that the proposed reporting requirement falls within CMS' statutory authority to establish documentation requirements for certain orders and referrals made by Medicare providers, which includes 340B claims. A few commenters asked CMS to confirm that the reporting obligation rests with 340B providers and not with authorized vendors such as contract pharmacies and TPAs, which are not enrolled parties subject to § 424.516(f)(4).
Response:
Section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act requires CMS to remove 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations beginning with plan year 2026, and we reiterate that data on which units dispensed under Part D and covered by Part D plan sponsors were purchased under the 340B Program is unavailable from the data sources specified at section 1860D-14B(d) of the Act (that is, information submitted by manufacturers, States, and Part D plan sponsors), and we do not currently have access to this data through other means. We believe that requiring 340B provider participation in the 340B repository is necessary to ensure robust data submissions in 2027 to determine if data submitted to the 340B repository could be used reliably in the future to remove 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations in accordance with section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act.
We agree with the commenters who stated that the reporting requirement falls within CMS' statutory authority. As we explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44012
), section 6406(a) of the ACA amended section 1842(h) of the Act by adding a new paragraph which establishes that the Secretary may revoke enrollment, for a period of not more than one year for each act, for a physician or supplier if such physician or supplier fails to maintain and, upon request of the Secretary, provide access to documentation relating to written orders or requests for payment for durable medical equipment, certifications for home health services, or referrals for other items or services written or ordered by such physician or supplier under Title XVIII of the Act, as specified by the Secretary. In addition, section 6406(b)(3) of the ACA amended section 1866(a)(1) of the Act to require that providers maintain and, upon request of the Secretary, provide access to documentation relating to written orders or requests for payment for durable medical equipment, certifications for home health services, or referrals for other items or services written or ordered by the provider, as specified by the Secretary. Although we acknowledged that §  424.516(f) has historically set forth documentation requirements for providers and suppliers for their Part A and Part B services, the statutory authorities underlying that provision, sections 1842(h)(9) and 1866(a)(1)(X) of the Act, do not expressly limit documentation requirements to services furnished under Part A and Part B. Sections 1842(h)(9) and 1866(a)(1)(X) of the Act collectively set forth that providers and suppliers must maintain and provide access to documentation relating to “items or services written or ordered by the provider
under this title,
as specified by the Secretary” (emphasis added). Both sections 1842(h)(9) and 1866(a)(1)(X) of the Act fall under Title XVIII (that is, the Medicare statute), which inherently includes Part D. As such, requiring providers and suppliers to maintain and provide access to documentation related to covered Part D drugs written or ordered by a provider or supplier is consistent with sections 1866(a)(1)(X) and 1842(h)(9) of the Act. By transitioning from voluntary submission to mandatory participation in the 340B repository, we will be able to ensure more complete and reliable data submissions, thereby improving our ability to accurately assess potential future use of the 340B repository to exclude 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations, consistent with our obligations under section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act. Finally, we affirm that the requirements at §§ 428.203(c) and 424.516(f)(4) apply to 340B providers and not to third-party entities such as contract pharmacies and TPAs.
Comment:
A few commenters requested that CMS affirm that the 340B repository and the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Program (“340B Rebate Pilot”) serve different purposes, and that the existence of the 340B repository does not diminish the need for a rebate model in the 340B Program. Some commenters stated that an expanded version of the 340B Rebate Pilot would offer the most efficient, accurate, and transparent path to identifying and excluding 340B claims from both the Part B and Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Programs and requested that HHS consider implementing a rebate model for all products.
Response:
We acknowledge that HRSA has announced the availability of a 340B Rebate Pilot, which would require covered entities to report an expanded set of data elements for selected drugs under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027 during their price applicability periods purchased at the 340B price to manufacturers.
[
236
]
CMS will coordinate with HRSA to reduce burden on covered entities as feasible. However, the 340B repository mandatory reporting requirement and the 340B Rebate Pilot are distinct in terms of legal basis, scope of drugs, recipient of collected data, and program purpose. The 340B repository mandatory reporting requirement is part of a distinct, comprehensive effort involving claims for all drugs dispensed under Part D and covered by Part D plan sponsors to assess use of the 340B repository to exclude 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations, whereas the 340B Rebate Pilot is at this time limited to selected drugs for initial price applicability years 2026 and 2027.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that the 340B repository requirement would be largely duplicative of information already being reported through other mechanisms, including the 340B Rebate Pilot, and recommended that CMS track duplicative reporting burdens and consider whether the Part D 340B claims data information needed can be obtained from existing data sources such as manufacturers, payers, or wholesalers. These commenters stated that the duplicative reporting requirements are wasteful, inefficient, and cause financial harm to covered entities. Many commenters stated that HHS should not impose two separate
(
printed page 71308)
and overlapping data submission requirements on covered entities under the 340B repository and the 340B Rebate Pilot and recommended that CMS and HRSA collaborate to unify reporting requirements. A commenter recommended that CMS only move forward with mandating participation in the 340B repository beginning in 2027 if HRSA delays implementation of the 340B Rebate Pilot until after implementation of the 340B repository since, in their view, the 340B repository would obviate the need for the 340B Rebate Pilot.
Response:
We disagree that our proposal for mandatory reporting to the 340B repository is largely duplicative of the 340B Rebate Pilot. As explained, there are key differences between these two initiatives to include the purpose of 340B reporting and underlying authority, scope of reported drugs, data elements, frequency of reporting, duration of reporting, and recipient of reported information. Duplication of reporting burden by a covered entity in CY 2027 to both the 340B repository and the 340B Rebate Pilot is limited to those drugs that are a selected drug in initial price applicability year 2026 and initial price applicability year 2027 during their price applicability period.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS use the information submitted to the 340B repository—or an expanded “neutral claims clearinghouse” version of the 340B repository that would collect data for Federal programs more broadly—in the administration of other Federal programs, including the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, so that covered entities need not submit data to multiple sources, including to the 340B Rebate Pilot and manufacturers. A commenter recommended that CMS consider how the 340B repository could be expanded to capture Part B 340B claims.
By contrast, some commenters recommended that the 340B repository be used only in the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program and that any expanded use be subject to notice-and-comment rulemaking. A commenter requested clarity on how 340B repository information will interact with other methods of identifying 340B units and asked which source will be used when data conflicts.
Response:
At this time, data submitted to the 340B repository will be used to begin testing usability of the data for the purpose of removing 340B units under the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program. As we stated in the revised collection of information (0938-1485) titled “Information Collection Request (ICR) for the Medicare Prescription Drug Inflation Rebate Program under sections 11101 and 11102 of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA)” (CMS-10930, OMB 0938-1485), CMS may also use the information collected by CMS from 340B providers to conduct other internal program analyses, such as those related to the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program. We note that this use is distinct from the external disclosure discussed in section III.F.3.c.2.c. of this final rule. Internal program analyses, including those related to the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, are conducted by CMS using data CMS already holds, and do not involve disseminating, distributing, or copying 340B repository data to manufacturers, Part D plan sponsors, or other parties outside the agency. If we were to decide to use data submitted to the 340B repository for purposes other than the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program and internal program analyses, we would undergo notice-and-comment rulemaking and provide interested parties an opportunity to comment before any such policy is finalized. We acknowledge the suggestion that we consider how to capture Part B 340B claims data but do not intend to expand the use of the 340B repository to collect Part B claims data at this time.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that the 340B Rebate Pilot and 340B repository remain distinct but that CMS explore how to use the data collected through the 340B Rebate Pilot to improve accuracy of and reduce burden in the 340B repository, such as using 340B Rebate Pilot data to validate 340B repository data or reduce duplicative reporting burdens on covered entities by establishing a mechanism through which 340B Rebate Pilot data are used to populate the 340B repository for participating drugs.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that CMS not move forward with mandatory participation in the 340B repository until the Administration takes action to stop what the commenters deemed to be unlawful denial of 340B pricing to covered entities that decline to submit data directly to drug manufacturers.
Response:
We note that the comments recommending CMS delay implementation of a mandatory 340B repository until the Administration ensures that 340B pricing is made available to covered entities is outside the scope of this final rule. We are implementing the reporting requirement at § 428.203(c) consistent with our obligations under section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act.
Comment:
A couple commenters stated that the reporting requirement is overinclusive because it would require submission of information relating to drugs that are not subject to Medicare Part D inflation rebates. The commenter stated that requiring 340B providers to report information relating to selected drugs under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program expands the reporting burden beyond what is necessary for the 340B repository's stated purpose.
Response:
We do not agree that the reporting requirement is overinclusive. Section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act requires CMS to remove 340B units from inflation rebate calculations for all Part D rebatable drugs. Because the status of a Part D rebatable drug can change over time (for example, a drug or biological may have average annual total costs below the applicable threshold set forth at § 428.101(b) in one applicable period but not another), we believe requiring 340B providers to submit data for all Part D 340B claims is less burdensome and will result in more complete data than if we were to require 340B providers to continually change the scope of drugs for which they are required to submit data. Additionally, we note that this final rule does not implement different or additional data requirements specific to selected drugs under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program. As we stated in the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98285
), the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program applies to selected drugs notwithstanding the status of the drug as a selected drug. The reporting requirement at § 428.203(c) therefore applies no differently to a Part D rebatable drug that is a selected drug than to a Part D rebatable drug that is not a selected drug.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern that CMS proposed to enforce the 340B repository reporting requirement through its Medicare enrollment authority, including that CMS would reserve the right to revoke a hospital's Medicare enrollment for noncompliance while simultaneously acknowledging that the data collected has not yet been tested nor would be used to calculate Part D inflation rebates at this time. These commenters stated that this enforcement approach could create substantial financial and patient-access consequences unrelated to the underlying reporting deficiency, and that loss of Medicare enrollment is an extraordinary sanction disproportionate to a reporting process CMS is using only
(
printed page 71309)
to evaluate the feasibility of a future alternative methodology. A few of these commenters also expressed concern that what they described as severe penalty could apply even if noncompliance was due to reporting by a TPA or other third-party and stated the challenges of bearing ultimate legal accountability across a multi-vendor ecosystem. A commenter stated that CMS has not built a sufficient record to justify using such a severe enforcement mechanism since, in their view, CMS significantly underestimated the burdens associated with reporting to the 340B repository. A commenter expressed concern that notice and appeal provisions of
42 CFR part 424, subpart P
appear designed to accommodate individual, discrete issues rather than an ongoing data reporting program. A commenter stated that CMS has not established a sufficiently clear procedural framework for imposing enforcement consequences.
Response:
We do not agree that the enforcement consequence for non-compliance is disproportionate to the reporting requirement. We note that, in accordance with §  424.535(a)(10)(ii), a provider or supplier that meets the revocation criteria specified in §  424.535(a)(10)(i) is subject to revocation for a period of not more than 1 year for each act of noncompliance. As we stated elsewhere in this section, continuation of a voluntary reporting approach, which introduces a confounding factor into the data based on characteristics of organizations which choose to submit or not, would present a methodological limitation in our evaluation of the suitability of the 340B repository data. To mitigate this limitation and avoid constraints on our ability to conduct a robust analysis of 340B data submissions, we believe that establishing a mandatory reporting requirement would help ensure sufficient participation and alleviate these concerns, consistent with our obligations under section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act. In response to the comment that CMS underestimated associated burdens, we refer readers to section V.B.5. of this final rule.
We also do not agree that we have not established a sufficiently clear procedural framework for enforcement. As we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44013
), we reserve the right to revoke, in accordance with existing §  424.535(a)(10), a currently enrolled provider or supplier's Medicare enrollment and any corresponding provider agreement or supplier agreement for failure to comply with the requirements for maintaining and providing access to documentation specified in proposed and finalized §  424.516(f)(4). The procedural framework previously established at existing §  424.535(a)(10) would apply no differently to failures to comply with the requirements specified in proposed and finalized §  424.516(f)(4).
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that, if CMS finalizes a mandatory reporting requirement, CMS establish a graduated compliance pathway—including a corrective-action process, a materiality threshold, technical assistance, a temporary safe harbor period as 340B providers transition systems to align with the requirement, and a permanent safe harbor for good-faith reporting errors, particularly when errors are due to third parties such as TPAs or contract pharmacies—before taking enforcement action, stating these safeguards would prevent disproportionate penalties for technical or inadvertent errors in complex claim-level submissions. Separately, a commenter stated that CMS should not impose Medicare enrollment sanctions without a separate finding of fraud, diversion, duplicate discounts, or improper billing. A commenter recommended that CMS tailor reporting expectations to scale with a hospital's actual capacity to comply, stating that applying a national standard disproportionately impacts small and rural hospitals. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS create a hardship exemption, with a commenter recommending that CMS exclude smaller 340B providers and another commenter recommending that CMS exempt Critical Access Hospitals, Sole Community Hospitals, Medicare Dependent Hospitals, rural referral centers, and low-volume covered entities from the mandatory reporting requirement.
In contrast, a few commenters recommended that CMS couple the mandatory reporting requirement with strong enforcement action, education, and auditing to ensure CMS is receiving complete and accurate data. These commenters stated that CMS should establish clear consequences for noncompliance, including penalties for inaccurate or incomplete reporting. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS suspend covered entities from the 340B Program for failure to comply with the reporting requirements. A commenter requested clarity on the consequences for non-reporting or misreporting but did not express preferences on types of enforcement actions. A commenter recommended that CMS ensure the reporting framework does not permit selective reporting by 340B providers that would reduce manufacturer inflation rebate liability for some products but not others.
Response:
We acknowledge commenters' concerns about consequence of non-compliance with the mandatory reporting requirement due to technical or inadvertent errors in claim-level submissions, including errors caused by third parties such as TPAs or contract pharmacies. We believe that allowing 340B providers to make corrections to previously submitted claims as outlined in the Medicare Part D Claims Data 340B Repository Companion Guide,
[
237
]
together with the existing enforcement framework at § 424.535(a)(10), distinguishes good-faith, correctable errors from conduct that would warrant enrollment revocation. We therefore do not believe a separate materiality threshold or permanent safe harbor is needed at this time. We also do not agree that revocation under § 424.535(a)(10) requires a separate finding of fraud, diversion, duplicate discounts, or improper billing; that authority addresses documentation failures independently of other violations.
We additionally emphasize our commitment to engaging with 340B providers to provide the education and resources necessary for them to adhere to their reporting obligations to ensure we are receiving complete and accurate data. Several resources related to the 340B repository are available on the CMS website, including Frequently Asked Questions, a Medicare Part D 340B Repository Companion Guide, and Medicare Part D 340B Repository Data Submission Template examples in Excel and CSV formats.
[
238
]
The Medicare Part D Claims Data 340B Repository Help Desk is also available to assist 340B providers.
[
239
]
The comment recommending that CMS suspend covered entities from the 340B Program for failure to comply with the reporting requirement is out of scope.
Comment:
A commenter stated that submitting data to the 340B repository would not be overly burdensome based on the data requirements and guidelines outlined in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule. Another commenter stated that they perform analogous reporting for manufacturers and therefore have established the internal processes needed to support a Federal reporting
(
printed page 71310)
requirement. A commenter stated that their health system could successfully submit Part D 340B claims data retrospectively on a quarterly basis. A couple of commenters supported the proposal to allow TPAs to transmit data to the 340B repository on behalf of 340B providers.
Conversely, many commenters noted concern that mandatory 340B repository submissions would create significant burdens for 340B providers, stating that implementing the requirement could require fees to software vendors and TPAs, additional staff time, and could divert resources away from patient care. A couple of commenters stated that the requirement would be particularly challenging for small and rural covered entities and recommended a hardship exemption or flexibilities for such entities. A few commenters described challenges of consolidating data and standardizing reporting across multiple contract pharmacies, TPAs and outpatient drug delivery settings (such as outpatient retail pharmacies and child site infusion clinics) with different operational and IT ecosystems.
A few commenters recommended that CMS engage with interested parties to test the 340B repository and identify ways to minimize reporting burdens before the 340B repository becomes mandatory, stating that interested parties' engagement will help identify operational challenges early and improve the accuracy and usability of the 340B repository over time. A commenter recommended that CMS work with interested parties to identify ways to improve the methodology for identifying Part D 340B drug units without adding additional reporting obligations.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters who stated that submitting data to the 340B repository would not be overly burdensome given the data requirements and guidelines outlined, that they already perform analogous reporting for manufacturers and have established internal processes that can support a Federal reporting requirement, and that permitting TPAs to transmit data to the 340B repository on behalf of 340B providers would ease compliance.
In developing the data elements for submission and process for voluntary submission to the 340B repository, we considered how to minimize burden on 340B providers. We are collecting the minimal number of data elements necessary to match 340B repository data to PDE records for Part D rebatable drugs, and we are providing quarterly submission deadlines and additional time for 340B providers to submit corrections to their Part D 340B data. We believe these decisions will lower burden on 340B providers to the extent possible. As we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44014
), we understand covered entities typically contract with vendors, such as TPAs, to determine 340B eligibility of claims using data submitted by covered entities and their contractors. We will allow covered entities that choose to submit data to the 340B repository to arrange for their TPAs or other vendors to submit certain data elements to the 340B repository on their behalf if they would like to do so. We note that there are no hardship exemptions or other reporting flexibilities for 340B providers that are small covered entities, rural covered entities, or both. We believe that permitting covered entities to rely on their TPAs or other vendors for data submission, as previously described, appropriately mitigates burden for all 340B providers, including small and rural covered entities, without the need for a separate exemption based on characteristics of a 340B provider.
Finally, we have engaged extensively with interested parties to develop the 340B repository in ways that minimize burden on 340B providers to the extent possible in an evolving 340B landscape. In addition to meeting with interested parties on specific issues, we have held broad discussions and technical calls open to all 340B entities and related parties to hear feedback and input on ways to minimize burden and share technical specifications in time for interested parties to participate in voluntary submissions this fall. We welcome continued feedback and remain committed to continued engagement with interested parties as we develop and test the 340B repository.
Comment:
A couple of commenters appreciated CMS' commitment to seeking public input through rulemaking before relying on 340B repository data for Part D inflation rebate calculations and recommended that CMS continue to seek public input through future rulemaking before adopting any methodology that relies on 340B repository data for such calculations.
Response:
We appreciate the support and affirm that any future proposal to use the data reported to the 340B repository to remove 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations would undergo notice-and-comment rulemaking, and we will continue to provide interested parties an opportunity to comment before any such policy is finalized.
Comment:
Many commenters urged CMS to delay mandatory reporting to the 340B repository, stating that the 340B repository has not yet launched and is not expected to become operational until Fall 2026, leaving insufficient time to identify problems, train staff, and validate submissions before mandatory reporting begins for claims with dates of service on or after January 1, 2027. Many commenters similarly urged CMS not to mandate reporting into an untested system, stating that the 3-month testing period in 2026 is insufficient to support a transition from voluntary to mandatory reporting and will not provide enough time to evaluate the quality and completeness of the data or fully assess the operational burden on covered entities. Many commenters opposed that the proposal to require 340B providers to report data would be used only for testing purposes, stating that the benefits of the proposal do not outweigh the costs to 340B providers since CMS will not yet be using the data in Part D inflation rebate calculations, and that CMS should delay mandatory reporting until it has assessed the feasibility of using voluntarily-reported data.
Many commenters recommended that CMS delay implementation of mandatory reporting by, for example, providing 340B providers a specific minimum period—such as at least 6 months, or sufficient time after publication of final technical specifications—to configure, test, and validate submission systems before mandatory reporting begins. Relatedly, many commenters recommended a phased-in approach rather than a single compliance date, so CMS could assess data quality and refine specifications collaboratively with 340B providers; suggestions included phasing in or simplifying reporting with technical assistance and a hardship exemption for smaller 340B providers and continuing voluntary reporting while evaluating participation and data quality before imposing any mandatory requirement.
Many commenters stated that the proposed compliance date would require covered entities to implement mandatory 340B repository reporting while simultaneously preparing for the 340B Rebate Pilot, also effective January 1, 2027, compounding financial and operational pressures and diverting resources from patient care, and recommended delaying implementation to July 1, 2027, or January 1, 2028 given these concurrent obligations.
Response:
We agree that 340B providers need adequate time following the 340B repository's launch to test workflows, train staff, and validate
(
printed page 71311)
submissions, and we recognize commenters' concerns that the originally proposed timeline could compress this preparation period, particularly given other data reporting obligations 340B providers face beginning in 2027.
As described in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44013
), we proposed at § 428.203(c) to require 340B providers to submit Part D 340B data to the 340B repository beginning in 2027, with the data elements and information set forth in proposed paragraphs (c)(1) and (2) of that section submitted on a quarterly basis as required under proposed paragraph (c)(3). Under this proposal, data for a given calendar quarter would be due within 1 calendar quarter following the close of that quarter, meaning that data for claims with dates of service in Q1 2027 would have been due by June 30, 2027. We also noted in the proposed rule that we expected the 340B repository to become operational for voluntary submissions in Fall 2026, consistent with the CY 2026 PFS final rule (

We are finalizing a delayed deadline of September 30, 2027, for 340B providers to submit data for claims with dates of service from January 1, 2027 through March 31, 2027. We note that this delay applies only to the deadline for the first mandatory quarterly submission. These deadlines are listed in Table B-F1. 91 FR 44012
through
44015
).

A few commenters stated that ADAPs are covered entities under
