Response:
We appreciate this input. We proposed at § 428.203(c) that providers and suppliers that are covered entities as defined under §  10.3 submit Part D 340B data to the 340B repository beginning in 2027. We recognize that
(
printed page 71312)
the documentation requirement we proposed and are finalizing at § 424.516(f)(4), as well as the enforcement mechanism we proposed and are finalizing in accordance with existing §  424.535(a)(10), relies on Medicare enrollment, and that this mechanism has no application to an ADAP that holds no such enrollment. However, we strongly encourage ADAP participation in the 340B repository. ADAPs are covered entities under the 340B Program, and although the mandatory reporting requirement finalized in this rule does not extend to ADAPs because ADAPs are not providers or suppliers enrolled in Medicare, we continue to strongly encourage ADAPs to submit their Part D 340B claims data to the 340B repository on the same basis as other covered entities. We acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding potential mismatches between ADAP rebate cycles and the proposed quarterly reporting timeline. As we outlined in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, data submitted to the 340B repository will not be used to exclude 340B units from inflation rebate calculations at this time. If we propose and finalize such a policy in the future, we would provide additional guidance to ADAPs at that time.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the data elements CMS proposed for the 340B repository, stating that the five proposed elements (date of service, prescription or service reference number, fill number, dispensing pharmacy NPI, and NDC-11) are appropriate.
Commenters stated that these elements did not present overly burdensome requirements or Protected Health Information (PHI) risks. Many commenters also supported the proposed quarterly submission timeline. These commenters stated that it was more efficient than the more frequent data demands covered entities currently face. Some commenters recommended that CMS instead align the 340B repository's data elements and reporting timeline with those required under the 340B Rebate Pilot. These commenters stated that this would improve efficiency and support future expansion of the 340B Rebate Pilot to the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program. These commenters recommended that CMS expand the data elements collected. Suggested additions included product serial number, prescribed date, quantity dispensed, bank identification number (BIN)/processor control number (PCN), prescriber identification number, and claims adjustment/paid date. These commenters stated that without common data elements, the 340B repository would have limited utility for cross-program validation. A few commenters recommended that CMS require more frequent submissions than the proposed quarterly timeline. These commenters stated that timelier data is critical to identifying 340B claims and administering the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program. A commenter stated that quarterly reporting may be sufficient for calculating Part D inflation rebate liability specifically. This commenter stated that quarterly reporting would not support other use cases requiring more timely identification of 340B claims.
Response:
We designed the 340B repository to assess whether covered entity-submitted data can reliably identify units of Part D rebatable drugs for which a manufacturer provided a 340B discount, to determine if such data could be used reliably in the future to remove 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations in accordance with section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act. We proposed the five required data elements (date of service, prescription or service reference number, fill number, dispensing pharmacy NPI, and NDC-11) because we determined these elements are necessary and sufficient to identify a unique PDE record. We agree with the commenters that stated requiring additional fields, such as product serial number and prescribed date, is not necessary. Based on our current review, we believe requiring these fields would impose burden on 340B providers without a corresponding benefit to the program.
We do not agree that we should, at this time, expand the required data elements or align them with the data fields required under 340B Rebate Pilot. The 340B repository serves a distinct purpose from 340B Rebate Pilot: the 340B repository exists to allow CMS to assess whether submitted data can support our statutory obligation under section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act to exclude 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations, not to facilitate manufacturer-level claims verification or cross-program reconciliation with the 340B Rebate Pilot. We intend to minimize burden on 340B providers while collecting the minimum elements necessary to match a submission to a PDE record to exclude 340B units from inflation rebate calculations, were the 340B repository to be used for such purpose in the future. We do not agree that we should require more frequent than quarterly submission of Part D 340B claims data at this time. Quarterly submissions provide CMS with timely information to assess the reliability of the data for potential future use in removing 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations. Quarterly submissions also minimize burden on 340B providers by reducing the amount of data and quality assurance required for each submission. Given the variety in the scope of provider types and organizations that participate in the 340B Program, the amount of preparation time needed to compile, certify, and submit complete and accurate claims data varies. The quarterly timeline provides 340B providers sufficient time to meet these requirements without imposing the additional burden that more frequent reporting would create.
Comment:
A couple of commenters recommended that CMS require 340B and non-340B claims indicators on Part D claims. One of these commenters stated that claims indicators would improve the effectiveness of the 340B repository because CMS lacks visibility into the full universe of 340B claims and therefore cannot reliably assess the extent of underreporting or identify gaps in 340B repository data. In contrast, a few commenters re-emphasized points made in their previous comments on the CY 2025 PFS proposed rule (which we summarized and responded to in the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98294
)) that adding 340B claims indicators to Part D claims would be infeasible due to operational challenges.
Response:
We note that 340B claims indicators are not currently required from CMS for Part D 340B claims and acknowledge feedback received on the CY 2025 PFS proposed rule that requiring such a claims indicator has the potential to pose operational challenges and increase pharmacy burden because 340B status may not be known at the point of sale and may not always be accurate. In this final rule, we maintain that reporting of a 340B claims indicator on Part D claims submitted by dispensing entities remains voluntary.
After consideration of the comments received, we are finalizing the proposal at § 428.203(c) to require providers and suppliers that are covered entities, as defined under § 10.3, to submit Part D 340B data to the 340B repository beginning in 2027, with modification. Specifically, at § 428.203(c)(1) we are finalizing without modification the five data elements proposed for each Part D 340B claim submitted to the 340B repository: (1) date of service, (2) prescription or service reference number, (3) fill number, (4) dispensing pharmacy National Provider Identifier (NPI), and (5) National Drug Code (NDC-11). At § 428.203(c)(2), we are finalizing, without modification, that
(
printed page 71313)
the 340B provider must submit its 340B ID and name as designated in the 340B OPAIS database. At § 428.203(c)(3), we are finalizing the requirement that 340B providers report data on a quarterly basis (though they may choose to submit more frequently) within 1 calendar quarter following the close of the relevant calendar quarter, with modification at § 428.203(c)(3)(i)(B) to delay the first mandatory reporting deadline by one quarter. We also made a minor technical modification to § 428.203(c)(3) to more precisely describe an applicable quarter as a “quarter of a calendar year” rather than a “calendar quarter.” We are finalizing § 428.203(c)(4) as proposed and adding new § 428.203(c)(5) to clarify the certification requirement; § 428.203(c)(4) and (5) are described in further detail in section F.3.c.2.c. of this final rule. We are also finalizing, with a conforming modification to reflect new § 428.203(c)(5), our proposal at § 424.516(f)(4) that such reporting would fulfill a 340B provider's obligation to provide access to documentation relating to covered Part D drugs written or ordered by such 340B provider to maintain enrollment in Medicare.
(c) Submitting Part D 340B Claims Data to the 340B Repository (§ 428.203(c))
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that we expect that the 340B repository will be operational by Fall 2026 for voluntary submissions from covered entities, as we adopted in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49748
). Since publication of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, the 340B repository launched on October 1, 2026, and 340B providers may now create an account and begin submitting Part D 340B data.
[
240
]
As we stated in the proposed rule, we proposed to require all 340B providers to submit certain data elements associated with Part D 340B claims beginning in 2027. We strongly encouraged 340B providers to begin submitting data to the 340B repository voluntarily in 2026 to test operational processes, as we proposed here to adopt the requirement that 340B providers submit data elements from their Part D 340B claims starting in 2027. The rest of this section proposed the form and manner by which, starting in 2027, under the proposed § 428.203(c), 340B providers would submit data to the 340B repository.
As stated in section III.F.3.c.b. of this final rule, under the 340B mandatory reporting proposal, the data elements and information set forth in paragraphs (c)(1) and (2) of § 428.203 would be submitted on a quarterly basis. We proposed here that we would rely upon the completeness and accuracy of the data submitted by 340B providers to the 340B repository, consistent with the 340B provider requirement to certify the accuracy of such submissions described later in this section, to consider all data elements received by the 340B repository to be associated with Part D 340B claims. That is, CMS would rely on the accuracy and completeness of the submitted, certified data to the 340B repository to verify the 340B status of a claim.
We solicited comments on this proposal. For ease of reference and organization, we summarize comments received and our responses at the end of this section III.F.3.c.2.c.
We also proposed, as part of every submission, to require 340B providers (or an individual or contractor with the delegated authority as an authorized representative of the 340B provider to perform the certification) to certify that the data elements from all claims submitted to the 340B repository are from verified 340B claims and, to the best of the 340B provider's knowledge, its submissions include all Part D 340B claims for the 340B provider at the time of submission for the relevant period. 340B providers or their authorized representative would be required to certify the completeness and accuracy of the data submitted and to certify that the submitter is authorized to submit on behalf of the 340B provider.
We solicited comments on this proposal. For ease of reference and organization, we summarize comments received and our responses at the end of this section III.F.3.c.2.c of this final rule.
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49750
), describing the proposal for voluntary data submission, we noted that we understand covered entities typically contract with vendors, such as 340B TPAs, to determine 340B-eligibility of claims using data submitted by covered entities and their contract pharmacies. We continue to acknowledge these contracts and, therefore, we proposed that 340B providers could arrange for TPAs or other vendors to submit the required data elements to the 340B repository on their behalf. 340B providers would ultimately be responsible for the accuracy of the data submitted to the 340B repository, even if a 340B provider has an arrangement with a vendor to submit on its behalf.
We solicited comments on this proposal. For ease of reference and organization, we summarize comments received and our responses at the end of this section III.F.3.c.2.c of this final rule.
In section III.F.3.c.b. of the proposed rule, we proposed to require that 340B providers report data on a quarterly basis. We separately proposed that 340B providers would have additional time to submit data to reflect a revision to the 340B determination of claims with dates of service throughout an applicable period. A revision could come in one of two forms: (1) resubmission of data for a claim that the 340B provider previously submitted to the 340B repository in error or with errors in the requested data fields, or (2) new submission of data for a claim for a drug that the 340B provider had previously determined was not purchased under the 340B Program but later identified was purchased under such program. In instances where the 340B provider submits Part D 340B claims data to the repository that is either (1) incomplete or (2) contains invalid data, we may inform the 340B provider of such error and request that the 340B provider resolve and resubmit the Part D 340B claims data to process the submission successfully. As noted in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49754
), we will provide details on the process and timing for covered entities to submit revised data to the 340B repository after the end of the reporting period in the future, and we anticipate that this same timing would apply to claims with dates of service in 2027. Specifically, at § 428.203(c)(4), we proposed that data elements and information submitted in accordance with paragraph (c)(3) of such section that is either incomplete or contains invalid data must be resubmitted at a later time in a form and manner specified by CMS.
We solicited comments on this proposal.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters supported CMS operating the 340B repository directly rather than through a third-party vendor, stating that, from a compliance and data-privacy standpoint, a neutral, government-operated platform is preferable to a vendor with commercial interests. These commenters recommended that CMS develop and operate the 340B repository itself, or, if it engages a contractor, ensure the contractor has no ownership, governance, or financial
(
printed page 71314)
relationship that could allow, or appear to allow, manufacturers, pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), Part D plan sponsors, or other interested parties to influence the 340B repository's operation or access its data, since covered entities should not have to submit sensitive claims-level information through systems controlled by parties with a financial interest in the 340B Program.
Some commenters urged CMS to collect only data necessary for Part D inflation rebate calculations and clarify the scope of permissible data use, access, and retention. These commenters recommended that CMS establish transparent policies governing which government agencies and contractors may access submitted data, how long it will be retained, and how it will eventually be destroyed; and limit use of the data to administration of the Medicare Part D Drug Inflation Rebate Program. A commenter recommended that CMS clarify data security and proprietary-information protections for claim-level 340B data, particularly where contract pharmacy relationships are involved.
Some commenters urged CMS to confirm that 340B repository data will not be shared with manufacturers on a claims-level basis and to retain this safeguard if CMS moves forward with the 340B repository. These commenters anticipated that manufacturers would request additional data elements or broader data sharing and urged CMS to reject such requests, stating that CMS has already determined the proposed data elements are sufficient to identify and exclude 340B units without manufacturer data sharing. Where manufacturer access to information is necessary for rebate calculation or verification, these commenters recommended that CMS provide only aggregate or otherwise limited data rather than access to individual claims, and, if CMS shares any data with manufacturers or other interested parties, explicitly conduct notice-and-comment rulemaking before doing so and prohibit its use for purposes unrelated to duplicate-discount prevention and prohibit further redisclosure. A commenter added that claims data submitted to the 340B repository is sensitive and proprietary, and recommended that CMS ensure manufacturers lack access to it and that strong data security standards be clearly set forth in user agreements. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS codify data protections from third parties into regulatory text.
In contrast, many commenters urged CMS to share 340B repository data with manufacturers to support validation of Part D (and, in one case, Part B) inflation rebate calculations, stating that manufacturers currently have no reliable way to confirm whether a claim was 340B-eligible, which limits their ability to verify rebate invoices, creates duplicate-discount risk, and prevents them from catching reporting anomalies, inconsistencies, and missing claims. A few commenters disputed CMS' confidentiality rationale for withholding this data, stating that the data elements do not constitute PHI, manufacturers already receive comparable claim-level data under the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and the 340B Rebate Pilot without it constituting PHI, and drew analogies to the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program and Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, where manufacturers receive utilization or claims data—and, in the Medicaid program, a statutory audit right—to validate payment obligations; a commenter urged CMS to extend this approach to Part B inflation rebates as well. A commenter recommended that CMS share 340B repository data with researchers, and a commenter recommended that CMS provide Part D plan sponsors with timely, preferably near real-time, access to 340B repository data related to their beneficiaries and pharmacy claims.
Response:
As we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44014
), we understand the importance of maintaining the confidentiality of data submitted to the 340B repository. Therefore, this data—irrespective of whether it is submitted to CMS directly from the 340B provider or from a vendor submitting on their behalf—will be for official use only and will not be disseminated, distributed, or copied to unauthorized persons, including manufacturers and Part D plan sponsors. We reaffirm our commitment to protecting sensitive and confidential data submitted by 340B providers and continue to acknowledge the importance of data security. The 340B repository will be designed to comply with all applicable Federal security laws, regulations, and HHS policies, including but not limited to those related to data protection and information security. Any third party that CMS engages to support the 340B repository will be required to follow protocols to address conflicts of interest. For example, CMS will implement safeguards such as firewalls or contractual limitations on usage of information to ensure that any third party supporting the 340B repository does not misuse information to which it obtains access in its role supporting the 340B repository. We decline to provide claim-level data, such as 340B repository data, to manufacturers regarding the 340B Program or other statutory exclusions of units from inflation rebate calculations as we do not believe this is necessary to operate the program at this time. First, we disagree with the premise that 340B repository data, if shared by CMS with manufacturers, could or should be used to verify manufacturers' rebate reports because 340B repository data is not relevant to Part D inflation rebate reports at this time since the current purpose of the 340B repository is to evaluate the completeness and accuracy of the data. In addition, section 1860D-14B(f) of the Act, codified at §  428.403(a)(1), precludes administrative or judicial review of the determination of units as set forth at §  428.203, the determination of whether a drug is a Part D rebatable drug as set forth at §  428.101, and the calculation of the rebate amount as set forth at §  428.201(a), inclusive of any reconciled rebate amount. As explained in the CY 2025 final rule (
89 FR 98307
), the Suggestion of Error process is limited to mathematical steps involved in determining the rebate amount, and the elements precluded from administrative or judicial review will not be considered in-scope for the Suggestion of Error process. Although we affirm that we will not share 340B repository data, we decline the suggestion to incorporate this detail into regulatory text as we do not believe such a step is necessary.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS has not adequately addressed the Privacy Act implications of the 340B repository and should consider issuing a public notice to members of the public describing its information collection before creating a system of records containing patient data. This commenter also stated that, in their view, the 340B repository constitutes a system of records, and CMS must therefore satisfy the Privacy Act's substantive limitations and notice requirements regarding information collection. The commenter stated that CMS has not demonstrated that the 340B repository satisfies this standard since CMS has stated that the purpose of the 340B repository is to test the data rather than use it in Part D inflation rebate calculations. Additionally, some commenters stated that several of the required data elements constitute PHI under HIPAA's Privacy Rule but did not specify which data elements. A commenter recommended that CMS clearly identify the legal authority supporting the
(
printed page 71315)
disclosure of PHI from covered entities to the 340B repository, explain how the proposal interacts with the HIPAA Privacy Rule, and provide 340B providers with operational guidance sufficient to ensure compliant disclosures. A commenter stated that its members have expressed general privacy concerns about submitting data to the 340B repository.
Response:
We appreciate this comment and acknowledge some of the required data elements may constitute PHI. In cases where a 340B provider is also a HIPAA covered entity and submits information that constitutes PHI, or is the business associate of a HIPAA covered entity
[
241
]
and submits information that constitutes PHI on the covered entity's behalf, disclosure of this PHI to the 340B repository must be for a purpose permitted by an applicable disclosure permission under the HIPAA Privacy Rule (
45 CFR part 160
and subparts A and E of part 164). For example, the HIPAA Privacy Rule allows HIPAA covered entities to disclose PHI without an individual's authorization when that disclosure is required by law and the disclosure complies with the requirements of that law (
45 CFR 164.512(a)
). CMS' use and disclosure of Part D data is governed by the Privacy Act of 1974, requiring that we establish and maintain a System of Records Notice (SORN). Per the Privacy Act of 1974, CMS intends to issue a SORN in the
Federal Register
for the 340B repository. (Currently, CMS does not have a standalone SORN issued specifically for the 340B repository.)
Comment:
A few commenters stated that new reporting requirements create a risk of good-faith technical errors arising from TPAs, contract pharmacies, or discrepancies between data sources. These commenters recommended that CMS define all required reporting elements, file specifications, and validation standards sufficiently in advance of the effective date. Many commenters recommended that CMS establish a defined timeline for correcting or revising 340B claims status after the reporting deadline. A few of these commenters recommended a hard cap of 45 to 90 days, stating that additional time would create administrative complexity and inaccurate inflation rebate calculations. By contrast, a few other commenters recommended adequate lead time, practical reconciliation tools, hardship exemptions, and a dispute process instead of fixed time frame for submission of corrections. A commenter noted that a change in 340B status of a Part D claim may occur months or even years after the initial dispense date with a consequence being that a 340B claim's status is never final. Several commenters recommended a reconciliation mechanism to adjust manufacturers' rebate liability whenever a claim's 340B status is revised after an invoice has been issued, stating that manufacturers should not pay inflation rebates on units later determined to be 340B units.
A few commenters recommended that CMS establish validation and audit processes rather than rely solely on self-reported data and that CMS require complete reporting of all Part D 340B claims, including contract pharmacy claims. These commenters stated that the 340B repository will only succeed if all eligible covered entities submit data, including data originating from contract pharmacies, since any covered entity that fails to report would result in an undercount of 340B units and inflated Part D inflation rebate invoices. Some commenters also recommended that CMS be transparent about its process for evaluating the 340B repository, including sharing its assessment results publicly in future rulemaking and consulting interested parties with experience in 340B claims validation, such as manufacturers. A commenter stated that adding another repository risks creating mismatched claim records and additional burden. By contrast, a few other commenters supported the 340B repository's design, which enables covered entities to leverage existing data and TPAs.
Response:
As we stated in the proposed rule, our 340B repository instructions already define the required data elements, specifications, and submission process in sufficient detail for 340B providers to prepare for the 2027 start date. Additionally, CMS has published technical specifications for the 340B repository on the CMS website.
[
242
]
As proposed, 340B providers would submit Part D 340B claims data quarterly, within one calendar quarter following the close of the applicable quarter (for example, data for the fourth quarter is due by March 31 of the following year). As discussed earlier in this final rule and detailed in Table B-F1, we are finalizing a delayed deadline of September 30, 2027 as the first deadline for mandatory submissions, which applies to data for claims with dates of service from January 1, 2027 through June 30, 2027.
As outlined in this final rule, a 340B provider may submit a revision to the repository in one of two forms: (1) resubmission of data for a claim(s) that the 340B provider previously submitted to the 340B repository in error or with errors in the requested data fields, or (2) new submission of data for a claim for a drug that the 340B provider had previously determined was not purchased under the 340B Program but later identified was purchased under such program. In instances where the 340B provider submits Part D 340B claims data to the repository that is either (1) incomplete or (2) contains invalid data (for example, if the NDC-11 field contains fewer than 11 characters), we will inform the 340B provider of such error and request that the 340B provider resolve and resubmit the Part D 340B claims data to process the submission successfully as soon as practically possible. CMS has provided instructions for how a 340B provider can resubmit a previously submitted claim in the Medicare Part D 340B Repository Companion Guide available to 340B providers on the CMS website. CMS will provide further instruction on the reporting deadline to submit corrections on 340B claims with dates of service in 2027 through future technical instruction. As we have outlined in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, data submitted to the 340B repository will not be used to calculate inflation rebates unless and until we propose and finalize a policy to use such data to exclude 340B units from inflation rebate calculations in the future. However, it is necessary that we establish a deadline to receive any and all corrections for submissions of 340B claims with dates of service in 2027, to allow CMS to assess the usability of 340B claims data submitted to the 340B repository. This correction process is separate from the quarterly deadlines for submitting 340B claims data, which are fixed.
(
printed page 71316)
We will consider all data elements received by the 340B repository to be associated with Part D 340B claims. 340B providers must report all Part D 340B claims, including contract pharmacy claims. The 340B repository does not independently verify the 340B status of a claim but rather serves to store these data. As described in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we intend to analyze the data submitted to the 340B repository to determine if it could be used reliably in the future to remove 340B units from Part D inflation rebate calculations in accordance with section 1860D-14B(b)(1)(B) of the Act. We will evaluate 340B repository data for: (1) data integrity, and (2) submission frequency and completeness across covered entity types and geographies, including through comparison to claims identified under the claims-based methodology adopted in the CY 2026 PFS final rule. In instances where a 340B provider submits data that is incomplete or contains invalid data, we will inform the 340B provider of the error and require resubmission in a form and manner specified by CMS. We intend to leverage existing processes and systems, including submission infrastructure designed to minimize reporting burden, whenever possible. We designed the 340B repository to let covered entities leverage existing data and TPAs, which we expect will minimize discrepancies with other reporting platforms.
Comment:
A few commenters supported requiring 340B providers to certify that repository submissions are complete, accurate, and include all Part D 340B claims for the relevant period. Another commenter also supported this certification requirement and recommended that CMS strengthen the policy by clarifying that 340B providers may face False Claims Act risk for improper certifications. A few commenters recommended that CMS qualify this certification standard to reflect reasonable diligence and good-faith reliance on available claims and internal 340B records, rather than an absolute guarantee, stating that 340B status is often refined through retrospective reconciliation and that a stricter standard could create compliance risk even for entities acting in good faith. One of these commenters noted that CMS should establish clear correction procedures and provide notice and opportunity to cure before imposing penalties. Another commenter recommended that CMS allow certification by any authorized representative with delegated oversight of the underlying data rather than limiting the role to a 340B provider's chief executive officer or chief financial officer.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback. We would rely upon the completeness and accuracy of the data submitted by 340B providers to the 340B repository, consistent with the 340B provider requirement to certify the accuracy of such submissions and would consider all data elements received by the 340B repository to be associated with Part D 340B claims. That is, CMS would rely on the accuracy and completeness of the submitted, certified data in the 340B repository to verify the 340B status of a claim. We note that 340B providers are required to certify that the data elements from all claims submitted to the 340B repository are from verified 340B claims and, to the best of the 340B provider's knowledge, its submission includes all Part D 340B claims for the 340B provider at the time of submission for the relevant period reflecting a reasonable level of diligence on behalf of the 340B provider. 340B providers may rely in good faith on available claims, TPA, contract pharmacy, and other internal 340B records. Claims data may require correction as additional information becomes available and a revision may take one of two forms: (1) resubmission of data for a claim previously submitted to the 340B repository in error or with errors in the requested data fields, or (2) new submission of data for a claim for a drug the covered entity had previously determined was not purchased under the 340B Program but later identified was purchased under such program. 340B providers may designate TPAs to submit data on their behalf, but the 340B provider remains responsible for the accuracy of that submission. In instances where a 340B provider submits Part D 340B claims data that is either incomplete or contains invalid data, we may inform the 340B provider of such error and request resolution and resubmission in order to process the submission successfully.

G. Medicare Shared Savings Program
1. Executive Summary and Background
a. Purpose
As of January 1, 2026, the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program) has 511 accountable care organizations (ACOs) with over 700,000 healthcare providers and organizations providing care to over 12.6 million assigned beneficiaries.
[
245
]
Eligible groups of providers and suppliers, such as physicians, hospitals, and other healthcare providers, may participate in the Shared Savings Program by forming or joining an ACO and in so doing agree to become accountable for the total cost and quality of care provided to an assigned population of Medicare FFS beneficiaries
[
246
]
(herein also referred to as “Original Medicare beneficiaries”). Under the Shared Savings Program, providers and suppliers that participate in an ACO continue to receive Original Medicare (OM) payments under Parts A and B,
[
247
]
and the ACO may be eligible to receive a shared savings payment if it meets specified quality and savings requirements, and in some instances may be required to share in losses if it increases healthcare spending.
As part of our effort to align spending and value in OM, we are focused on developing policies that would grow the number of healthcare providers and beneficiaries in accountable care relationships and grow savings to the Medicare Trust Funds. To achieve these goals, we proposed changes to the Shared Savings Program and sought comments on potential future policy developments in several requests for information, informed by the following strategic objectives:
Strengthen financial incentives to participate and drive savings while minimizing “gaming”
[
248
]
opportunities in the Shared Savings Program.
Grow participation in the Shared Savings Program through more meaningful participation and through beneficiary engagement, including beneficiary incentives.
Simplify Shared Savings Program requirements and reduce participant burden in the Shared Savings Program, including through advancing ACO use of digital quality measures.
More specifically, our changes to the Shared Savings Program's financial methodology will strengthen financial incentives for ACOs to participate in the program while mitigating selection issues and benchmark rebasing concerns. Our changes to the Shared Savings Program's beneficiary assignment methodology are expected to expand the population of Medicare FFS beneficiaries for which ACOs are accountable for quality and cost of care, while minimizing potential gaming opportunities in connection with the assignment methodology. The changes to the Shared Savings Program quality performance standard and other quality reporting requirements will support ACO advancement toward digital quality measurement and reduce participant burden. Our proposal to allow flexibility for Shared Savings Program ACOs to reduce or eliminate Part B cost sharing for eligible beneficiaries, and therefore expand availability of this flexibility beyond ACOs participating in the prepaid shared savings payment option (which we proposed to discontinue), is intended to increase beneficiary engagement. Our changes to simplify the Shared Savings Program Certified Electronic Health Record Technology (CEHRT) use requirements and beneficiary information notice requirements will reduce burden for ACOs. Other modifications to the Shared Savings Program regulations addressed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule included: proposed changes to the definition of primary care services for the purpose of determining beneficiary assignment, and proposed modifications to definitions of experienced and inexperienced with performance-based risk Medicare ACO initiatives used in determining an ACO's eligibility for participation options, and proposed changes to the methodology for determining quarterly payment amounts received by eligible ACOs participating under the Advance Investment Payment (AIP) option. Further, through the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we sought comment on specialty care in the Shared Savings Program. We provided a more detailed summary of the proposed changes to the Shared Savings Program and the topics on which we sought comment in a Request for Information (RFI) in section III.G.1.c. of the proposed rule.
We received public comments on these proposals. Our summary of the comments we received and our responses can be found in each section of III.G.

a. Modifications to the Shared Savings Program Assignment Methodology
(1) Background

Section 1899(c)(1) of the Act, as amended by the 21st Century Cures Act (
Pub. L. 114-255

Pub. L. 115-123

Section 425.402(b) of the Shared Savings Program regulations specifies the step-wise methodology we use to assign Medicare FFS beneficiaries to an ACO based on available claims information, for PY 2016 and subsequent PYs. In accordance with § 425.404(b), for PYs starting on January 1, 2019, and subsequent PYs, under the assignment methodology in § 425.402, we treat a service reported on an FQHC or RHC claim as a primary care service performed by a primary care physician.

(i) Use of ACO Participant List To Identify Primary Care Services Billed by ACO Professionals and CCNs Used in Assignment Calculations
As we described in the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69825
), under the Shared Savings Program, ACOs are accountable for the quality, cost, and overall care of the Medicare FFS beneficiaries that are assigned to the ACO (§ 425.100(a)). ACOs are formed by one or more “ACO participants,” which are responsible for managing and coordinating care for the assigned beneficiary population. The Shared Savings Program regulations define “ACO participant” at § 425.20 as an entity identified by a Medicare-enrolled billing Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) through which one or more “ACO providers/suppliers” (as defined at § 425.20) bill Medicare, that alone or together with one or more other ACO participants compose an ACO, and that is included on the list of ACO participants that is required under § 425.118 (herein “ACO participant list”). An “ACO provider/supplier” is an individual or entity that: (1) is a provider (as defined at § 400.202) or supplier (as defined at § 400.202); (2) is enrolled in Medicare; (3) bills for items and services furnished to Medicare FFS beneficiaries during the agreement period under a Medicare billing number assigned to the TIN of an ACO participant in accordance with applicable Medicare regulations; and (4) is included on the list of ACO providers/suppliers that is required under § 425.118 (herein “ACO provider/supplier list”).

More specifically, an ACO must submit a draft ACO participant list before the start of an agreement period and before each performance year thereafter. In accordance with § 425.118(a)(3), the ACO must certify the accuracy of its ACO participant list before the start of its agreement period and before each performance year thereafter. More generally, in accordance with § 425.102(a), an ACO may be formed from the following ACO participants or combinations of ACO participants: (1) ACO professionals in group practice arrangements; (2) networks of individual practices of ACO professionals; (3) partnerships or joint venture arrangements between hospitals and ACO professionals; (4) hospitals employing ACO professionals; (5) Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) that bill under Method II (as described in § 413.70(b)(3)); (6) RHCs; (7) FQHCs; and (8) teaching hospitals that have elected under § 415.160 to receive payment on a reasonable cost basis for the direct medical and surgical services of their physicians (herein referred to as electing teaching amendment (ETA) hospitals).
Under § 425.20, “ACO professional” is defined to mean an individual who is Medicare-enrolled and bills for items and services furnished to Medicare FFS beneficiaries under a Medicare billing number assigned to the TIN of an ACO participant in accordance with applicable Medicare regulations and who is either of the following: (1) a physician legally authorized to practice medicine and surgery by the State in which he or she performs such function or action; or (2) a practitioner who is a physician assistant (PA), a nurse practitioner (NP), or a clinical nurse specialist (CNS).

Under the claims-based assignment process we identify allowed charges for a beneficiary's primary care services received in an ACO (furnished by ACO professionals used in assignment billing through the TIN of an ACO participant or an FQHC, RHC, Method II CAH, or ETA hospital identified by a CCN enrolled under the TIN of an ACO participant), in any other ACO, or other individual practitioners, or groups of practitioners identified by Medicare-enrolled billing TINs or CCNs that are not participating in the Shared Savings Program. We use the ACO participant list certified by the ACO to identify ACO professionals used in assignment that are billing primary care services, and to identify CCNs enrolled under the TIN of an ACO participant, for purposes of performing claims-based assignment for the PY, and, if applicable, assignment for the ACO's benchmark years in the case of establishing or adjusting the ACO's historical benchmark under subpart G (see § 425.652(a)).
We use different approaches to identifying primary care services furnished by ACO professionals and CCNs enrolled under the TIN of an ACO participant. Because of the billing relationship between an ACO professional and an ACO participant, any claims for primary care services billed by an ACO professional through the TIN of an ACO participant would be used for assignment. (ii) Steps of the Claims-Based Assignment Process
In each step of the claims-based assignment process, we determine whether the allowed charges for a beneficiary's primary care services in an ACO are greater than allowed charges for the beneficiary's primary care services in any other ACO, or other individual practitioners, or groups of practitioners identified by Medicare-enrolled billing TINs or CCNs that are not participating in the Shared Savings Program (that is, a non-ACO individual or group TIN or non-ACO CCN). In doing so, we determine which ACO or non-ACO entity provided a beneficiary's plurality of allowed charges for primary care services for purposes of assignment. Herein, for brevity, we sometimes refer to this stage of the assignment process as “plurality competition”.

256

To follow is a summary of the steps used in the claims-based assignment methodology under § 425.402(b):
In accordance with § 425.402(b)(1), as a “pre-step” to the first and second step of the claims-based assignment process, CMS identifies all beneficiaries who had at least one primary care service during the applicable assignment window
[

with a physician who is an ACO professional in the ACO and who is a primary care physician as defined under § 425.20 or has one of the primary specialty designations specified in § 425.402(c). This pre-step is designed to satisfy the statutory requirement under section 1899(c)(1) of the Act that beneficiaries be assigned to an ACO based on their use of primary care services furnished by physicians participating in the ACO. Beneficiaries
(
printed page 71324)
who meet the pre-step requirement are then assigned to an ACO through either the first or second step of the assignment methodology specified in § 425.402(b)(3) and (b)(4).
As described in § 425.402(b)(2), for beneficiaries who meet the pre-step requirement under § 425.402(b)(1), CMS identifies all primary care services furnished by ACO professionals of that ACO who are primary care physicians as defined under § 425.20, non-physician ACO professionals, and physicians with specialty designations included in § 425.402(c) during the applicable assignment window. This provision reflects an operational step necessary to identify the sum of allowed charges for primary care services for a beneficiary received in an ACO (furnished by ACO professionals used in assignment billing through the TIN of an ACO participant or CCNs enrolled under the TIN of an ACO participant), as compared to any other ACO, non-ACO CCN, or non-ACO individual or group TIN, for determining the outcome of the plurality competition under step 1 and step 2 of the assignment methodology.
Under the first step of the assignment process, specified at § 425.402(b)(3), a beneficiary who is eligible for assignment and meets the pre-step requirement is assigned to an ACO if the allowed charges for primary care services furnished to the beneficiary during the assignment window by primary care physicians who are ACO professionals and non-physician ACO professionals in the ACO are greater than the allowed charges for primary care services furnished during the assignment window by primary care physicians, NPs, PAs, or CNSs who are ACO professionals in any other ACO, or not affiliated with any ACO and identified by a Medicare-enrolled billing TIN (that is, a non-ACO CCN, or non-ACO individual or group TIN).
The second step of the assignment methodology, specified at § 425.402(b)(4), applies to the remainder of the beneficiaries who are eligible for assignment and meet the pre-step requirement, who have not had a primary care service rendered during the assignment window by any primary care physician, NP, PA, or CNS, either inside or outside the ACO. The beneficiary will be assigned to an ACO if the allowed charges for primary care services furnished to the beneficiary during the assignment window by physicians who are ACO professionals with specialty designations specified in § 425.402(c) are greater than the allowed charges for primary care services furnished during the assignment window by physicians with such specialty designations who are ACO professionals in any other ACO, or who are unaffiliated with an ACO and are identified by a Medicare-enrolled billing TIN (that is, a non-ACO CCN, or non-ACO individual or group TIN).
For PY 2025 and subsequent PYs, as specified in § 425.402(b)(5), we employ a third step to assign eligible Medicare FFS beneficiaries who are not identified by the “pre-step” criterion specified under § 425.402(b)(1). In this step, we identify all beneficiaries who had at least one primary care service with a non-physician ACO professional in the ACO during the applicable assignment window, and had at least one primary care service with a physician who is an ACO professional in the ACO and who is a primary care physician or who has one of the primary specialty designations included in § 425.402(c) during the applicable expanded window for assignment (see § 425.402(b)(5)(i) through (ii)).

As described in § 425.402(b)(5)(iii), for a beneficiary meeting the aforementioned criteria in § 425.402(b)(5)(ii), we identify all primary care services furnished by ACO professionals in the ACO who are primary care physicians, non-physician ACO professionals, and physicians with specialty designations included in § 425.402(c) during the applicable expanded window for assignment. The identification of primary care services described in § 425.402(b)(5)(iii) serves as an operational step which is similar to the step described in § 425.402(b)(2). This operational step is necessary to identify the sum of allowed charges for primary care services for a beneficiary received in an ACO (furnished by ACO professionals used in assignment billing through the TIN of an ACO participant or CCNs enrolled under the TIN of an ACO participant), as compared to any other ACO, non-ACO CCN, or non-ACO individual or group TIN, for determining the outcome of the plurality competition under step 3.
In accordance with § 425.402(b)(5)(iv), a beneficiary identified in § 425.402(b)(5)(ii) who is eligible for assignment is assigned to an ACO if the allowed charges for primary care services furnished to the beneficiary by ACO professionals in the ACO who are primary care physicians, physicians with specialty designations included in § 425.402(c), or non-physician ACO professionals during the applicable expanded window for assignment are greater than the allowed charges for primary care services furnished by primary care physicians, physicians with specialty designations included in § 425.402(c), NPs, PAs, and CNSs who are ACO professionals in any other ACO, or not affiliated with any ACO and identified by a Medicare-enrolled billing TIN (that is, a non-ACO CCN, or non-ACO individual or group TIN).
As previously described, under § 425.402(b)(3), (b)(4), (b)(5)(iv), the plurality competition which occurs in each step of assignment compares allowed charges for primary care services furnished to a beneficiary by certain ACO professionals in an ACO with allowed charges for primary care services furnished by the same type of healthcare providers who are either (1) ACO professionals in any other ACO, or (2) not affiliated with any ACO and identified by a Medicare-enrolled billing TIN. Under the existing provisions, for purposes of plurality competition, we attribute to a non-ACO TIN the allowed charges for primary care services for a beneficiary furnished by an ACO professional that are billed through the non-ACO TIN. In determining the outcome of plurality competition for a beneficiary we consider both: (1) allowed charges for primary care services for the beneficiary received inside the ACO (furnished by an ACO professional or FQHC, RHC, Method II CAH or ETA hospital that has enrolled under the TIN of an ACO participant), and (2) allowed charges for primary care services for the same beneficiary being billed by the same ACO professional outside the ACO to a non-ACO TIN. As a result, a beneficiary may be identified as receiving the plurality of their primary care services outside an ACO based on a difference in the TIN to which the services are being billed by their healthcare provider who is an ACO professional used in assignment. Under these circumstances, when the plurality of allowed charges for primary care services is attributed to a non-ACO TIN, the ACO whose ACO professionals are furnishing services to the beneficiary would not be held accountable for the beneficiary's quality and cost of care.

(c) Overview of Assignment-Based Program Operations
Various Shared Savings Program operations are based on the ACO's assigned population, or consider the size of the ACO's assigned population, as described in prior rulemaking (see, for example,
88 FR 79137
through
79138
). To follow is a summary of these policies, including references to changes to Shared Savings Program policies elsewhere in section III.G. of this final rule.
Various aspects of the Shared Savings Program's financial methodology under subpart G depend on the size or composition of the ACO's assigned population, including calculating the ACO's benchmark and performance year expenditures, and adjusting and updating the ACO's benchmark. For each performance year, we determine whether the estimated average per capita Medicare Parts A and B FFS expenditures for Medicare FFS beneficiaries assigned to the ACO are above or below the ACO's updated benchmark, to determine whether the ACO qualifies for a shared savings payment or is responsible for sharing losses with CMS (as applicable) (§§ 425.605(a) and 425.610(a)). In computing an ACO's historical benchmark, we determine the per capita Parts A and B FFS expenditures for beneficiaries that would have been assigned to the ACO in any of the 3 most recent years prior to the start of the ACO's agreement period, in accordance with § 425.652(a) and (c). In benchmark calculations, the assigned population is the basis for determining the ACO's regional service area used in calculating the two-way blend of national and regional growth rates applied in trending and updating the ACO's benchmark (§ 425.652(a)(5)(iv)-(v), and (b)(2)), and the regional adjustment to the benchmark (§ 425.656). The assigned population is also used in calculating a proration factor applied in the prior savings adjustment (§ 425.658(b)(3)), and in determining an ACO's eligibility for and the amount of the population adjustment to the historical benchmark (§ 425.662(b)). The average prospective HCC risk scores for the ACO's assigned beneficiaries are used to risk adjust the ACO's benchmark expenditures (§§ 425.652(a)(3) and (10); 425.605(a)(1); 425.610(a)(2)), and other benchmark calculations (see, for example, § 425.656(b)(3) and (4) on calculating the regional adjustment, and § 425.660(b)(4) on calculating the ACPT component of the three-way blended benchmark update factor). As another example, as described in section III.G.5.e of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed to risk adjust the 5 percent cap on upward adjustments to the benchmark, based on average CMS-HCC risk scores for the ACO's assigned beneficiary population. In addition, we used the size of the ACO's assigned population in other financial calculations, including: determining the MSR/MLR threshold based on the ACO's number of assigned beneficiaries (§§ 425.605(b)(2)(i)(C) and 425.610(b)(1)(iii)); determining the eligibility of a low revenue ACO participating in the BASIC track for an opportunity to share in savings even if it does not meet the MSR (§ 425.605(h)); and determining the applicability of an alternative performance payment limit or loss recoupment limit for an ACO with fewer than 5,000 assigned beneficiaries in any benchmark year (§§ 425.605(i) and 425.610(l)).
The size of the ACO's assigned population is the basis for our determinations related to participation requirements and payment methodologies. For instance, we evaluate whether an ACO meets the requirement to have at least 5,000 assigned beneficiaries to be eligible to participate in the Shared Savings Program (§§ 425.110 and 425.600(h)(3)). We also use the ACO's number of assigned beneficiaries in repayment mechanism amount calculations (§ 425.204(f)), and in determining expenditures based on the ACO's assigned population when identifying if the ACO is a high revenue or low revenue ACO (as defined under § 425.20) for purposes of determining an ACO's eligibility for the Advance Investment Payment option (§ 425.630(b)(4)).
The ACO's assigned population informs the amount of quarterly advance investment payments (§ 425.630(b) and (f)) and prepaid shared savings (§ 425.640(f) and (h)) for eligible ACOs. Elsewhere in this final rule we are amending the quarterly advance investment payment calculation methodology (section III.G.7.) and discontinuing availability of the option for prepaid shared savings (section III.G.6.b.).
The assigned population is central to other programmatic areas, including quality and financial extreme and uncontrollable circumstances policies (see § 425.512(c)(1)(i); see also §§ 425.605(f)(1) through (2) and 425.610(i)(1) through (2)), and CMS's provision of beneficiary-identifiable data and aggregate reports to ACOs under subpart H.

(2) Revisions
(a) Exclude From Assignment Calculations Allowed Charges for Primary Care Services Billed Through a Non-ACO TIN by an ACO Professional Used in Assignment
As described in section III.G.2.a.(1)(a)(ii) of this final rule, in claims-based assignment calculations for a beneficiary we consider allowed charges for primary care services furnished by an ACO professional billed through an ACO participant TIN (that is, inside the ACO), and allowed charges for primary care services furnished by the same ACO professional billed through a non-ACO TIN (that is, outside the ACO). Under current assignment policies, it is possible that a beneficiary may not be assigned to an ACO, despite choosing to receive care from the same physician or non-physician practitioner, only because of a difference in the TIN through which the services are being billed.
We proposed to amend the Shared Savings Program assignment methodology to address the circumstance under which ACO professionals used in assignment bill primary care services for a beneficiary through an ACO participant TIN and non-ACO TIN. More specifically, we proposed to remove from assignment calculations for purposes of plurality competition in step 1 under § 425.402(b)(3), step 2 under § 425.402(b)(4), and step 3 under § 425.402(b)(5)(iv), allowed charges for a beneficiary's primary care services billed through a non-ACO TIN by an ACO professional used in assignment if that beneficiary also had primary care services billed by an NPI under an ACO TIN.
This change will only impact the determination of assignment under the Shared Savings Program, and will not change how assigned beneficiary expenditures are calculated under the Shared Savings Program's financial methodology, for a benchmark year (in accordance with § 425.652(a)) or performance year (in accordance with §§ 425.605(a) and 425.610(a)). We noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44025
), that under this proposal, assigned beneficiary expenditures for purposes of Shared Savings Program financial calculations would continue to include payment amounts for primary care services furnished to an assigned beneficiary billed through an ACO participant or non-ACO TIN, among other payment amounts.
We also noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44025
) that under this approach, ACO professionals may continue to bill under several different TINs, such as ACO participants in multiple ACOs or both ACO participants and non-ACO providers and suppliers. This change will not impact an ACO professional's ability to receive FFS payment for primary care services billed through an ACO participant or non-ACO TIN.
We provided the following hypothetical examples to illustrate the outcome of plurality competition under the current approach and the revised approach. In these illustrations, for simplicity, we assumed the beneficiary meets the assignment eligibility criteria and therefore could be assigned to an ACO based on the outcome of plurality competition.
As one example, consider a beneficiary for which ACO professionals used in assignment billed primary care services through an ACO participant in ACO A and a non-ACO TIN, and the sum of allowed charges for this beneficiary for these services is greater for the billings through the non-ACO TIN than through the ACO. For instance, ACO professionals billed primary care services through an ACO participant in ACO A, resulting in allowed charges of $100 for each of three services, totaling $300. For this same beneficiary, ACO professionals in
(
printed page 71328)
ACO A also billed primary care services to a non-ACO TIN, resulting in allowed charges of $100 for each of four services, totaling $400. Under our existing policy, we would determine that the non-ACO TIN provided the plurality of the beneficiary's primary care services, because it provided the greatest amount of allowed charges for the beneficiary, and as a result the beneficiary would not be assigned to ACO A. Under this approach, we will exclude from plurality competition the allowed charges of $400 which the ACO professionals in ACO A billed through the non-ACO TIN. As a result, under this approach, ACO A will be determined to have provided the plurality of allowed charges for primary care services for the beneficiary, and we will assign the beneficiary to ACO A.
As a second example, consider a beneficiary for which ACO professionals used in assignment billed primary care services through ACO participants in two different ACOs (ACO A and ACO B), and a non-ACO TIN, and the sum of allowed charges for this beneficiary for these services is greater for the billings through the non-ACO TIN than through either ACO. For instance, ACO professionals billed primary care services for the beneficiary through an ACO participant in ACO A, resulting in allowed charges of $100 for each of three services, totaling $300. These ACO professionals also billed primary care services for the beneficiary through an ACO participant in ACO B, resulting in allowed charges of $100 for each of two services, totaling $200. These same ACO professionals billed primary care services for the beneficiary to a non-ACO TIN, resulting in allowed charges of $100 for each of four services, totaling $400. Under our existing policy, we would determine that the non-ACO TIN provided the plurality of the beneficiary's primary care services, and as a result the beneficiary would not be assigned to an ACO. Under this approach, we will exclude from plurality competition the allowed charges of $400 which the ACO professionals in ACO A and ACO B billed through the non-ACO TIN. As a result, we will decide the outcome of plurality competition between ACO A ($300 in allowed charges) and ACO B ($200 in allowed charges), and determine that ACO A provided the plurality of allowed charges for primary care services for the beneficiary, and we will assign the beneficiary to ACO A.
As a third example, consider a beneficiary for which an ACO professional used in assignment billed primary care services through an ACO participant in ACO A and a non-ACO TIN, and for which other healthcare providers unaffiliated with an ACO are also billing primary care services for the beneficiary through a non-ACO TIN, and the sum of allowed charges for this beneficiary for these services is greater for the billings through the non-ACO TIN than the ACO. For instance, an ACO professional billed primary care services through an ACO participant in ACO A, resulting in allowed charges of $100 for each of three services, totaling $300. For this same beneficiary, an ACO professional in ACO A also billed primary care services to a non-ACO TIN, resulting in allowed charges of $100 for one service. Additionally, allowed charges of $100 for each of five services, totaling $500, were billed through the non-ACO TIN by a primary care physician who is unaffiliated with any ACO. Under our existing policy, we would determine that the non-ACO TIN provided the plurality of allowed charges for primary care services for the beneficiary, and as a result the beneficiary would not be assigned to ACO A. Under this approach, we will exclude from plurality competition the allowed charges of $100 which the ACO professional billed through the non-ACO TIN. In this hypothetical example, the outcome of plurality competition would not change under the approach, as we will still determine that the non-ACO TIN provided the plurality of allowed charges for primary care services for the beneficiary, and the beneficiary will not be assigned to ACO A.
We noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that if an ACO professional bills under ACO participants in multiple ACOs, but not to a non-ACO TIN, we do not anticipate the change will impact the outcome of the plurality competition (compared to our current approach).
As illustrated in the examples previously described, this approach will reduce the likelihood that we will determine the beneficiary's plurality of allowed charges for primary care services to be attributed to a non-ACO TIN or non-ACO CCN and increase the likelihood that a beneficiary is assigned to an ACO. Based on our simulations of this approach described in section III.G.2.a.(2)(c) of this final rule, we observed that nearly all ACOs (462 of 476 ACOs or 97 percent) would experience a relatively small increase in their assigned population (less than 1 percent growth). We observed the remaining 3 percent of ACOs would experience growth in their assigned population ranging from 4 percent to 12 percent. We also observed that on average the beneficiaries added to assignment with this proposed change have higher cost and higher risk scores. This latter point highlights that the existing assignment methodology includes vulnerabilities that could lead ACOs, ACO participants or their ACO professionals to avoid at-risk beneficiaries (as defined in § 425.20). We explore related considerations in the discussion that follows.
Shared Savings Program policies include certain safeguards against ACO avoidance of at-risk beneficiaries. Specifically, section 1899(d)(3) of the Act, and related regulations under § 425.316(b), authorize us to monitor for ACO avoidance of at-risk beneficiaries. If we discover that an ACO has engaged in the avoidance of at-risk beneficiaries, we can impose remedial action or terminate the ACO, in accordance with § 425.316(b)(2).
There may be multiple possible pathways for an ACO to engage in strategic patient risk selection.
[
270
]
In recent years, we have engaged in monitoring to identify potential patient risk selection behavior by ACOs. Our monitoring and compliance processes for identifying and addressing ACO avoidance of at-risk beneficiaries can be resource intensive. We believe that the change to determining the outcome of plurality competition within the assignment methodology will allow for a more efficient solution to mitigate a mechanism for ACOs, ACO participants, or their ACO professionals to avoid accountability for the quality and cost of care for high-cost at-risk beneficiaries. A pattern of billing by ACO professionals used in assignment resulting in a population of relatively higher costs beneficiaries not being assigned to the ACO could provide a mechanism for the ACO to achieve lower PY expenditures as compared to its historical benchmark, thereby potentially increasing its savings or decreasing its losses. An ACO avoiding assignment of high-cost beneficiaries under the Shared Savings Program reduces the cost effectiveness of coordinated care and shared savings initiatives, limiting savings for the Trust Funds, and potentially limiting improvements in quality of care and outcomes that could result for the patient. We are concerned that the provisions addressing avoidance of at-risk beneficiaries under section 1899(d)(3) of the Act and § 425.316(b), entail an ACO-specific analysis which
(
printed page 71329)
may not serve as an adequate deterrent against the aforementioned concerns about ACO professionals billing patterns for the care of the same beneficiaries resulting in differences in assignment outcomes that advantage the ACO's financial performance. In comparison, the approach to modifying plurality competition would result in a program-wide change which will be implemented with each assignment run, which we believe will largely resolve our concerns.
We believe the proposal to exclude from assignment calculations allowed charges for primary care services furnished by an ACO professional used in assignment billed through a non-ACO TIN offers a tailored approach to reduce the potential for ACO professionals' billing patterns, inside and outside the ACO for care of the same beneficiaries, to result in differences in assignment outcomes that advantage the ACO's financial performance. We recognize that the approach can result in assignment of beneficiaries for which ACO professionals may be billing a greater amount of primary care services through non-ACO TINs, compared to ACO participant TINs. We recognize there can be appropriate billings by ACO professionals through multiple different TINs (inside and outside the ACO) for services furnished to a beneficiary, such as a result of the physician or non-physician practitioner working in more than one practice location, or reflective of multiple employment arrangements. Nonetheless, we believe it is appropriate to assign the beneficiary to an ACO under such circumstances. We believe that beneficiaries added to ACOs' assigned populations under the proposed changes in assignment would benefit from better care coordination and quality improvement activities through ACOs participating under Shared Savings Program requirements, and the proposed changes to assignment are estimated to result in higher net Federal savings (as described in section III.G.2.a.(2)(c) of this final rule). These potential benefits outweigh potential concerns that this approach minimizes our consideration of billing arrangements of ACO professionals through non-ACO TINs.
We acknowledge a possibility that ACOs, ACO participants, or their ACO professionals, and non-ACO TINs may have relied on the existing program policy to structure arrangements in which ACO professionals bill inside and outside the ACO for the care of the same beneficiary. However, we do not believe any such reliance interests outweigh our concerns about the potential for ACOs and other providers/suppliers to exploit a vulnerability with the existing Shared Savings Program assignment methodology, and the potential benefits for beneficiaries and the Trust Funds of the modifications to the plurality competition, as we describe elsewhere in section III.G.2.a. of this final rule.
