We sought comment on the proposed change to the step-wise assignment methodology under which we would exclude allowed charges for primary care services billed through a non-ACO TIN by an ACO professional used in assignment, and related proposed changes to the Shared Savings Program regulations at § 425.402(b)(3) (applicable to step 1), (b)(4) (applicable to step 2), and (b)(5)(iv) (applicable to step 3), as revised and republished. We sought comment on the proposal to apply this approach in determining Shared Savings Program assignment for the PY starting on January 1, 2028, and subsequent PYs.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported our proposed policy to exclude allowable charges to non-ACO TINs by ACO professionals. In addition to the general support received from these commenters, many commenters included specific reasons for their support.
A commenter stated that the proposal will help mitigate unwarranted shared saving payments that result from large changes between ACOs' historical benchmark population and performance year populations. A few commenters noted that the proposed policy could benefit the most vulnerable (highest risk and costliest) beneficiaries that may be excluded from ACO assignment. Many commenters supported the policy citing that it advances the goal of connecting more Medicare beneficiaries with coordinated, accountable care. Many commenters supported the policy because it would ensure that assignment reflects the relationship with the provider responsible for their care. A commenter supported the policy and shared their belief that it protects ACOs from assigning beneficiaries based on care they received at facilities where ACOs do not have oversight. A couple of commenters acknowledged that ACOs may influence assignment to their advantage through billing to unaffiliated TINs and additionally recommend CMS extend the policy by routinely auditing ACOs' participant lists, publishing the amount of participant turn-over, and evaluating savings using fixed provider lists while using the current assignment rules.
Response:
We appreciate the comments in support of the proposal and the additional considerations they included. Many of the comments highlighted additional positive impacts that the policy may have on ACOs, providers, and beneficiaries, such as greater benefits for vulnerable populations, more accurate reflections of patient-provider relationships, and fewer unwarranted payments caused by changes between historical benchmark and performance year populations. These additional details provide further support and reasoning for implementing the policy change.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed the proposed policy. A commenter opposed being held accountable for beneficiaries that receive care provided by non-ACO TINs, as these non-ACO TINs may not have incentives to control cost and quality of care. Another commenter opposed any policy that disrupts genuine patient-physician relationships and expressed that CMS should provide sufficient assignment data to ACOs to identify and correct unusual results. Another commenter did not support the goal of expanding the number of beneficiaries in ACOs, but did not specify any reasons for this opposition.
Response:
We acknowledge the concerns with the proposed policy expressed in comments. CMS agrees with the concern that non-ACO TINs are less likely to control the cost and quality of care provided, however, the policy would only add beneficiaries to an ACO's assignment if the beneficiary also had primary care services billed under the ACO TIN. This proposed policy will work to address vulnerabilities within the current assignment methodology to ensure beneficiaries are not excluded from assignment due to avoidance, ultimately increasing the assigned population. CMS believes that in doing so, ACOs and their professionals that do have an incentive to control costs and quality will be held accountable for these beneficiaries.
With regard to the opposition to increasing the assigned population, we emphasize that the purpose of doing so through this policy is to provide a greater number of beneficiaries with access to the benefits of accountable care via the Shared Savings Program. For commenters concerned about disruption to genuine patient-physician relationships, we note that the policy does not prevent healthcare providers and patients from continuing existing relationships. Beneficiaries assigned to ACOs as a result of this policy would have received services from ACO professionals billing through their ACO TIN. Additionally, in regards for the request to provide sufficient assignment data to ACOs, we note that we will continue to provide ACOs with annual and quarterly reports, such as the Assignment List Report, Assignment Summary Report, and Beneficiary and Expenditure Utilization Report, and monthly Claim and Claim Line Feed Files that provide additional information related to each assigned beneficiary and the services they receive. We will also continue to monitor for opportunities to provide ACOs with additional assignment related data that can assist with better understanding of the relationships between providers and assigned beneficiaries. We believe the potential benefits of implementing the proposed policy on beneficiaries outweigh their concerns regarding adjustments to billing arrangements.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed their support for finalizing the policy, but recommended CMS provide continued monitoring and supporting data on expected beneficiary growth and characteristics. Many other commenters urged CMS to conduct further analysis of the policy's impact on participating ACOs prior to finalizing despite supporting the policy's goals in concept. Many commenters requested additional analysis and monitoring due to specific concerns about a negative financial impact based on the type of ACO, geographic location, or patient population, such as rural ACOs, ACOs that serve populations with higher needs, or the circumstances unique to nursing facilities and patients. Specifically, regarding long-term care, a commenter was concerned about situations where billing under different TINs occurs for legitimate purposes, such as for long-stay versus short-say patients in nursing facilities. Another commenter urged CMS to evaluate the impact on long-stay nursing facility patients to ensure they are not being assigned to an ACO based on historical primary care charges that no longer represents the delivery of their care. Some commenters requested analyses prior to finalizing or a delay in the
(
printed page 71331)
policy until more impacts were understood.
Response:
We appreciate comments with recommendations for further analysis to ensure the implementation of the proposed policy has the intended effect, without negatively impacting certain ACOs, providers, or beneficiary populations.
In updated simulations of PY 2025 data, we found similar results regarding the average number of added beneficiaries, and average impact on aggregate and per capita gross savings and losses as reported in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule. Specifically, we found that most ACOs (304 of 472 or 64 percent) would experience a small increase in their assigned population (less than 1 percent growth). Additionally, we found that nearly all ACOs (459 of 472 or 97 percent) would experience a relatively small increase in their assigned population (less than 5 percent growth). We observed the remaining 3 percent of ACOs would experience growth in their assigned population ranging from 6 percent to 43 percent.
We also compared financial performance of ACOs by different types of ACO characteristics. In PY 2025 simulations comparing rural ACOs to non-rural ACOs, we found that rural ACOs experienced a $17 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-4.69 percent), compared to non-rural ACOs that saw $24 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-4.09 percent). In comparing ACOs with a higher versus lower proportion of beneficiaries with Long-Term Institutionalized (LTI) Status, we found that these ACOs with higher proportion of beneficiaries with LTI status experienced $31 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-4.56 percent). ACOs with a lower proportion of beneficiaries with LTI Status experienced $21 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-3.98 percent) as a result of the policy. We also compared financial performance for ACOs that had a higher average Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) score among their beneficiaries. We found that these ACOs experienced $31 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-3.71 percent), while ACOs with lower average HCC scores experienced $21 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-4.42 percent). Although estimated impacts differed across these groups, differences between groups were relatively small and not statistically significant and therefore do not provide evidence that the policy would have different effects across the groups examined.
Given that we do not see statistically significant differences between the different types of ACOs and patient populations examined, and considering the policy's potential to provide safeguards against ACO avoidance of at-risk beneficiaries and the potential to increase beneficiaries assigned to ACOs improving beneficiary care coordination, CMS declines to delay implementation of this policy. CMS will continue to monitor the impact of the proposed policy on ACOs as additional performance data becomes available.
With respect to concerns about billing under multiple TINs for legitimate purposes, we note that the policy only impacts beneficiaries that are already seen at the ACO for primary care services. Therefore, it would only pull beneficiaries billed to the non-ACO TIN if they also had primary care services billed by an ACO professional to the ACO TIN. Similarly, with regards to impacts on long-stay nursing facility patients being assigned to an ACO based on historical primary care charges, we would not expect historical charges to have differing impacts under the existing assignment methodology compared to the proposed policy, and the proposed policy is intended to be incorporated throughout the window used for assignment.
Comment:
Many commenters urged CMS to implement guardrails or protections to reduce the possibility of unintended negative consequences. Specifically, some commenters asked for guardrails to protect against negative impacts on gross savings/losses, especially for the small number of ACOs that would experience a larger impact from this policy. Others asked for guardrails to ensure established relationships are not disrupted where billing patterns may reflect legitimate arrangements or needs, such as in rural areas.
Response:
We appreciate the concern for ACOs expressed in the comments, but we do not believe guardrails are needed at this time based on the relatively small impact observed in multiple performance years of our analysis which we believe would be outweighed by the potential benefits of this policy to strengthen safeguards against possible ACO avoidance of at-risk beneficiaries. Additionally, based on PY 2025 data we observed that most clinicians do not bill through multiple billing TINs/CCNs (81.9% of NPIs bill primary care services through a single TIN/CCN, and 87.5% of NPIs bill 95% or greater of the primary care services they provide through a single TIN/CCN).
Additionally, providers should continue to provide care for their patients as they normally would, and beneficiaries can continue to see the healthcare providers of their choice. This policy only impacts beneficiaries who receive healthcare from an ACO professional and also received care that was billed by the same ACO professional under a non-ACO TIN. Therefore, care relationships should not be disrupted. As reported previously, differential impacts on financial performance for rural ACOs or ACOs with a higher proportion of beneficiaries with high HCC scores were not statistically significant.
We will continue monitoring the impact of the proposed policy on ACOs for possible unintended consequences as additional performance data becomes available.

We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters expressed general support for the proposed change to assignment eligibility criteria. Many other supporting commenters cited the policy as a means of growing the Shared Savings Program and increasing beneficiaries in accountable care relationships.
A couple of commenters supported the policy emphasizing the importance of ensuring assignment policy accurately reflects beneficiaries that ACOs can manage. Another commenter stated that the proposed changes will contribute towards improved management and quality of care their ACO provides and emphasizes the importance of ensuring the Shared Savings Program beneficiaries are aligned with providers that meet the program goals. Another commenter expressed support, stating that improved consistency and clarity in beneficiary assignment standards will be especially helpful for organizations in long-term value-based payment arrangements.
A couple of commenters expressed their support of the policy and recommended that CMS provide supporting data regarding the expected impacts on assignment growth and beneficiary characteristics.
Response:
We appreciate comments in support of the proposed policy, which is intended to increase the Shared Savings Program assigned beneficiary population and improve symmetry between the definitions of the assigned and assignable populations. We appreciate that these comments recognize and support this intent, while also highlighting other potential beneficial impacts of the policy (for example, improving quality of care provided by ACOs, and consistency in assignment standards).
Comment:
We received several comments expressing opposition to the proposed assignment methodology. A commenter stated that ACO clinicians should not be required to assume the care, cost, and risk for patients who delay care until they are covered by Medicare. Another commenter does not support the goal of expanding the number of beneficiaries in ACOs.
Many comments expressed conceptual agreement with the policy and CMS' goals but cited various concerns. For example, a commenter warned that the policy could result in fewer beneficiaries in the Shared Savings Program if fewer ACOs decide to participate. Several commenters warned of an influx of hospice patients who transition to Traditional Medicare once they need the hospice benefit. A commenter expressed concern that ACOs do not have time to reach out to beneficiaries or engage them properly in care when they transition to Traditional Medicare mid-year. A commenter urged CMS to assess the impact of the interaction between this policy and recent changes to the enrollment pathways for dually-eligible special needs plans (D-SNPs), due to significant risk of beneficiaries transitioning in and out of Medicare Advantage while remaining assigned to an ACO. A commenter asked CMS to monitor the impact on beneficiaries in long-term care (LTC) who transition between FFS
(
printed page 71337)
Medicare and Medicare Advantage for any instability in their assignment population and to ensure that ACO and LTC providers have up-to-date information on these beneficiaries. Some commenters recommended that CMS implement guardrails to mitigate unintended negative consequences and adverse impacts on gross savings/losses, particularly for the small number of ACOs expected to experience larger impacts and those that serve populations with higher cost and higher risk.
Response:
We appreciate concerns raised in comments about decreased ACO participation in the Shared Savings Program. We acknowledge the commenter's suggestion that it is possible that a small decrease in the number of participating ACOs could occur, however, as a result of this policy we expect the overall number of assigned beneficiaries to increase, which is expected to increase savings and aligns with program goals, see discussion of program impacts in the Regulatory Impact Analysis in section VI.8.(a) of this final rule. CMS feels that this outweighs the possibility of fewer ACOs participating in the Shared Savings Program. We appreciate the comments concerning being held accountable for beneficiaries who are newly transitioning from Medicare Advantage and the potential complications, including, an influx of patients receiving hospice care, ACOs not having time to engage new beneficiaries in care, and changes to the dually-eligible special needs plans enrollment pathways. With respect to commenters' concerns about an increase in hospice beneficiaries or other special populations with high costs of care, the policy is intended to bring greater symmetry to program calculations between the assigned and assignable populations. This will allow for better comparison between factors based on assignable beneficiary expenditures. In other words, the assignable population already allows for beneficiaries who transition from Medicare Advantage mid-year and includes beneficiaries who joined Traditional Medicare in order to choose Medicare's hospice benefit or for other similar reasons. Therefore, any increases that ACOs see in assigned beneficiary populations under the proposed policy would align with populations already included in the assignable population, which would serve to improve symmetry in comparing expenditures to benchmarks. Additionally, the policy would be implemented in the same manner between benchmark and performance years, making changes as a result of the policy comparable. CMS believes that by improving alignment in the methodology used to determine the ACO-assigned and assignable populations, and symmetry in application of the policy in benchmark and performance years, ACOs will be fairly held accountable for care and expenditures that they have previously not been subject to. Financial impacts to ACOs are expected to be relatively modest, with average change in aggregate gross savings/losses of less than 1% based on PY 2025 simulations.
A similar line of reasoning applies to concerns about having time to reach out to beneficiaries newly transitioned from Medicare Advantage. The policy only brings in beneficiaries who would already be eligible for the assignable population and allows them to enter the assigned population, and some ACOs may already be aware of providing care for these beneficiaries before being assigned. Additionally, ACOs often have beneficiaries assigned to their ACO late in the performance year, and this policy likely only marginally increases this already existing circumstance.
In simulations of the policy using PY 2025 data, we found that ACOs with a higher proportion of beneficiaries with LTI status experienced $11 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-1.82 percent). ACOs with a lower proportion of beneficiaries with LTI Status that saw $15 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (-3.17 percent) as a result of the policy.
In simulations using PY 2025 data, ACOs with a higher proportion of beneficiaries with hospice status saw a $5 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (−1.05 percent) as an impact of the policy, while other ACOs had $17 lower average per capita gross savings/losses (−3.37 percent). Hospice status was determined by whether a beneficiary began hospice coverage during the benchmark or performance year.
Although estimated impacts of the policy differed across ACOs by proportions of beneficiaries with LTI status or with hospice status, these differences were not statistically significant and therefore do not provide evidence that the policy would have different effects across the groups examined.
With regard to the request that CMS implement guardrails to mitigate unintended negative consequences, while we appreciate the comments concerning the disproportionate impacts on ACOs that serve beneficiaries with higher risk, we believe this would add unnecessary additional complexity relative to the impacts and benefits from the proposed policy. In simulations of PY 2025 data, we compared ACOs whose assigned beneficiaries had higher average Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) scores. ACOs in the top quartile of HCC scores had a non-statistically significant impact on average gross savings/losses than ACOs with lower average HCC scores. Instead of guardrails we will continue monitoring the impact of the policy on ACOs for possible unintended negative consequences as performance data becomes available.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concerns that the Shared Savings Program risk adjustment isn't built to handle beneficiaries with incomplete or transitional Medicare enrollment histories, causing risk scores to potentially understate true expected costs. As a result, ACOs could be held accountable for higher-cost or higher-risk beneficiaries whose expenditures aren't fully captured in risk-adjusted benchmarks—whether the transition stems from mid-year Medicare Advantage-to-hospice disenrollment or from having under 12 months of traditional Medicare enrollment, such as those newly aging in or coming from Medicare Advantage.
Response:
We appreciate concerns raised in comments about risk adjustment not accounting for beneficiaries who have incomplete or transitional Medicare enrollment histories, or who have mid-year transitions from Medicare Advantage (MA). We disagree, however, that the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model, which is used in the Shared Savings Program for risk adjustment, is poorly suited to these populations or that it would systematically understate expected costs for ACOs. The CMS-HCC risk adjustment model is designed for and calibrated on claims and enrollment data taken from a sample of the national Medicare FFS population, including Medicare beneficiaries who are not enrolled in the Shared Savings Program.
[
283
]
Additionally, when calculating risk scores, we take all beneficiary data irrespective of the source, so diagnoses captured by MA organizations would still be reflected in the beneficiaries' risk scores for that year. When beneficiaries have 12 months of entitlement to Part A and less than 12 months of Part B enrollment during the data collection period, they do not receive the standard diagnosis-
(
printed page 71338)
based risk adjustment. Instead, CMS assigns risk using new enrollee's demographic factors, such as age, sex, and original reason for Medicare Entitlement. CMS uses the same model for Medicare Advantage risk adjustment and other Medicare payment purposes. Because the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model already reflects cost variation across the full range of Medicare FFS beneficiaries, the model already accounts for enrollment history and beneficiary transitions. Using one model across Medicare Advantage, the Shared Savings Program, and other Medicare payment contexts allows CMS to risk-adjust based on the same national standard for all beneficiaries. Modifying the model, or applying a different one, solely for ACO-assigned beneficiaries could create inconsistency in how CMS measures expected costs across the Medicare program and may undermine the comparability that a single, nationally calibrated model provides.

(c) Simulations To Understand the Potential Effect of Changes
In the CY 2027 proposed rule we performed separate simulations to understand the potential effect for each of the changes to the assignment methodology.
Using PY 2024 data we simulated the impact of the proposed approach to excluding from assignment calculations allowed charges for primary care services billed through a non-ACO TIN by an ACO professional used in assignment (described in section III.G.2.a.(2)(a) of this final rule). The simulation was performed using data for all 476 ACOs reconciled for PY 2024. For purposes of the simulation, we made multiple simplifying assumptions. This included treating all ACOs as if they were under preliminary prospective assignment with retrospective reconciliation for purposes of identifying the impact on assignment and simplicity of simulating benchmark assignment. Since the change is to plurality competition, we would anticipate a comparable impact if we performed the simulation using the off-set assignment window. For simulating financial impacts, we assumed all ACOs to be starting their first agreement period on January 1, 2024, to have benchmark years of BY 2021, 2022 and 2023, and applied an equal weight to each BY in benchmark calculations. In approximating the benchmark calculations under the simulations, we applied the benchmarking methodology applicable for ACOs entering an agreement period beginning on January 1, 2024 under §§ 425.652 through 425.660, with several exceptions. We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported expanding the definition of primary care services used for beneficiary assignment. Commenters supported adding Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment (SBIRT) services, Advance Care Planning (ACP) services, and Vaccine Adverse Effects Management, with several commenters expressly supporting the proposed HCPCS codes and recommending finalization for PY 2027 where the underlying codes are finalized for payment. Commenters stated that these services reflect prevention, care planning, behavioral health, patient engagement, care coordination, chronic disease intervention, and other longitudinal, relationship-based activities that are fundamental to comprehensive primary care. Several commenters stated that including these services would more accurately align beneficiary assignment with the clinicians and ACO participants furnishing meaningful primary care and would keep the assignment methodology aligned with Medicare billing codes and PFS policy. Some commenters noted that the descriptors for the proposed services are similar to services already included in the assignment methodology.
Commenters offered service-specific rationales. Several commenters stated that ACP is a core component of longitudinal primary care, particularly for seriously ill and medically complex beneficiaries, and that primary care's longitudinal relationships make it well suited for discussions of goals of care, advance directives, end-of-life preferences, and surrogate decision-making. Commenters also noted the roles of nurses, APRNs, clinical staff, family members, and surrogates in ACP and stated that ACP can help ensure that patients' care preferences are honored. Commenters supporting SBIRT stated that screening, brief intervention, and referral are core primary care and population health activities and can promote earlier identification and treatment of substance use disorders before more serious consequences occur. A commenter supporting Vaccine Adverse Effects Management stated that primary care is often the first and most consistent point of contact for patients with suspected vaccine adverse events and may provide symptom management, counseling, risk-benefit discussions, follow-up, and guidance regarding future immunizations.
Response:
We appreciate the comments in support of adding advance care planning; screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment; and vaccine adverse effects management codes to the definition of primary care services used for Shared Savings Program beneficiary assignment beginning in 2027, and agree that these services reflect prevention, care planning, behavioral health, patient engagement, care coordination, chronic disease intervention, and other longitudinal, relationship-based activities that are fundamental to comprehensive primary care which would keep the assignment methodology aligned with Medicare billing codes and PFS policy. We also agree that the proposed codes are similar to many already included in the definition of primary care services used for purposes of assignment. We also appreciate the service-specific rationale provided by commenters to support the inclusion of these services in the definition of primary care services used for purposes of assignment.
Comment:
A commenter generally supported the expanded definition but recommended delaying use of the Advanced Care Planning codes, GACP1 and GACP2, for assignment for at least one year to obtain claims experience and evaluate whether the codes strengthen assignment or inadvertently shift attribution away from established primary care relationships. Another
(
printed page 71344)
commenter urged CMS to review the assignment code set annually as coding and care delivery evolve, including consideration of remote therapeutic monitoring and advanced primary care management. Another commenter recommended monitoring the acuity and expenditure patterns of beneficiaries newly assigned through the added services and ensuring that benchmark and risk-adjustment methodologies reflect expected cost of care. Another commenter recommended monitoring whether the new service codes appropriately identify longitudinal primary care relationships and their effects on FQHCs and RHCs. A commenter supported the three proposed service categories but made clear that they recognize that CMS did not propose the addition of similar therapy evaluation codes because statutory practitioner classifications limit CMS's ability to add those services under current law. Another commenter supported G2011, G0396, GADV1, GACP1, and GACP2 but opposed adding G0397 stating that G0397 is more frequently associated with specialty care.
Response:
We acknowledge feedback in the comments. It is important for the definition of primary care services used for purposes of beneficiary assignment to remain in sync with billing and coding updates and changes and include appropriate new CPT and HCPCS codes as they are implemented. We believe that delaying the inclusion of new assignment codes or conducting multi-year testing of codes could result in beneficiaries not being assigned to an ACO based on primary care services that are provided by their primary care provider as utilization of these services is implemented. Implementing billing and coding updates and changes as they are finalized under the PFS is important for purposes of assignment to ensure that beneficiaries are assigned appropriately as services billed shifts from already existing CPT/HCPCS codes to new CPT/HCPCS codes. If the Shared Savings Program is out of sync with coding changes and updates, assignment of beneficiaries could be inaccurate. We also note that the step-wise assignment methodology maintains the statutory requirement to conduct claims-based beneficiary assignment based on beneficiaries' utilization of physician primary care services, recognizing the necessary and appropriate role of certain specialists in providing primary care services so we are not persuaded to delay implementation of these services.
We acknowledge the concerns about potential impact of unknown utilization and the suggestion to delay the addition of GACP1 and GACP2. Advance care planning (ACP) is a voluntary, face-to-face discussion between a practitioner and patient or their family member, caregiver, or surrogate (as appropriate) to discuss the patient's healthcare wishes if they become unable to make their own medical decisions.
[
292
]
The ACP HCPCS codes being finalized in this rule (see section II.G) are used to describe ACP services furnished by clinical staff under the direct supervision of the billing physician or other practitioner (and incidental to their professional services) and the existing CPT codes 99497 and 99498 would only be used to report time personally spent by the billing practitioner. Additionally, as explained in section II.G of this final rule, ACP services are a voluntary component of the annual wellness visit and can be billed together with CPT codes 99497 and 99498, if time thresholds by the billing practitioner and clinical staff are each met. Because annual wellness visits and other ACP services are currently included in the definition of primary care services used for purposes of assignment, we believe including the proposed ACP services (finalized as HCPCS codes G0572 and G0573) is critical to maintain consistency in the regulatory definition of primary care services used for purposes of assignment under § 425.400 regardless of future utilization.
We agree that monitoring the billing and utilization of the primary care service codes used for purposes of beneficiary assignment, and other codes, to ensure that the Shared Savings Program considers appropriate billing codes for purposes of beneficiary assignment is an important step in maintaining an accurate and effective assignment methodology. As we described in the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98095
), we will monitor the billing and utilization of the current primary care service codes used for purposes of beneficiary assignment, and other codes, to ensure that the Shared Savings Program considers appropriate billing codes for purposes of beneficiary assignment. If monitoring shows that the inclusion of service codes in the definition of primary care services used for beneficiary assignment is not appropriate, we will address that issue as needed.
With regard to the comment on statutory practitioner classifications, we confirm that therapy services are not included in the definition of primary care services used in assignment because therapists are not providers upon which assignment can be determined.
Regarding G0397 being more frequently furnished by specialists, we are not persuaded that this is a reason not to include this code for purposes of assignment in the Shared Savings Program. As we have previously explained in rulemaking (see, for example,
76 FR 67853
through
67855
; see also
80 FR 32748
and
32754
and
89 FR 98095
), the step-wise assignment methodology maintains the statutory requirement to conduct claims-based beneficiary assignment based on beneficiaries' utilization of physician primary care services, recognizing the necessary and appropriate role of certain specialists in providing primary care services, such as in areas with primary care physician shortages. Additionally, we noted in the June 2015 final rule (
80 FR 32750
), that we expect that specialist physicians often take the role of primary care physicians in the overall treatment of beneficiaries with certain chronic conditions, and such patterns are captured in step 2 in the current assignment methodology. Further, if services billed under these codes are provided by specialists not considered for purposes of beneficiary assignment, then the services will not be considered in beneficiary assignment.
Comment:
Another commenter supported CMS's proposed beneficiary assignment changes but stated that claims-based assignment alone has limitations in expanding accountable care relationships. The commenter recommended that Medicare beneficiaries also have a practical and accessible mechanism to affirmatively designate the clinician they trust to coordinate their care. The commenter viewed such a mechanism as complementary to CMS's efforts to expand beneficiary access to coordinated, accountable care in Original Medicare.
Response:
We believe this comment is referring to voluntary alignment and agree it is complementary to CMS's efforts to expand beneficiary access to coordinated, accountable care in Original Medicare. Under § 425.402(e) beneficiaries may voluntarily align themselves to an ACO at any time by logging into Medicare.gov and designating a provider or supplier who they believe to be responsible for coordinating their overall care. We are currently researching additional ways CMS can support beneficiary education
(
printed page 71345)
and enhance the accessibility of voluntary alignment.

As discussed in the CY 2025 PFS final rule, a quality performance benchmark is the performance rate a Shared Savings Program ACO must achieve to earn the corresponding quality points for each measure (
89 FR 98118
). Flat benchmarks assign a performance rate range to each decile. In flat benchmarks for non-inverse measures, any performance rate at or above 90 percent is treated as the top decile; any performance rate between 80 percent and 89.99 percent would be treated as the second highest decile, and so on. For inverse measures, this would be reversed—any performance rate at or below 10 percent would be treated as the top decile; any performance rate between 10.01 percent and 20 percent would be treated as the second highest decile, and so on. The number of measure achievement points received for each measure is determined based on where a Shared Savings Program ACO's performance rate is within the benchmark decile categories.
For non-inverse measures, better quality performance is indicated by a higher performance rate. For example, Controlling High Blood Pressure (Quality ID: 236) is a non-inverse measure that measures the percentage of patients 18 to 85 years of age who had a diagnosis of hypertension and whose blood pressure was adequately controlled (<140/90 mmHg) during the measurement period. Better quality performance on this measure is demonstrated by having a higher percentage of patients whose blood pressure was adequately controlled. Table B-G3 of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule lists the flat benchmarks for a non-inverse Medicare CQM under our proposals in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44043
). For example, if a Shared Savings Program ACO reports a non-inverse Medicare CQM in PY 2026 or a subsequent PY and earns a performance rate of 55.25 percent, then the Shared Savings Program ACO would score in the 6th decile on that measure.
For inverse measures, better quality performance is indicated by a lower performance rate. This is reflected in flat benchmark such that lower quality performance rates are found in higher deciles. For example, Diabetes: Glycemic Status Assessment Greater Than 9% (Quality ID: 001) is an inverse quality measure that measures the percentage of patients 18-75 years of age with diabetes who had a glycemic status assessment (hemoglobin A1c [HbA1c] or glucose management indicator [GMI]) greater than 9.0 percent
(
printed page 71353)
during the measurement period. Better quality performance on this measure is demonstrated by having a lower percentage of patients whose glycemic status assessment was greater than 9.0 percent. Table B-G4 of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule lists the flat benchmarks for an inverse Medicare CQM under our proposals discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44044
). For example, if a Shared Savings Program ACO reports an inverse Medicare CQM in PY 2026 or subsequent year and earns a performance rate of 12.25 percent, then the Shared Savings Program ACO would score in the 9th decile on that measure. Diabetes: Glycemic Status Assessment Greater Than 9% (Quality ID: 001) is the only inverse Medicare CQM in the APP Plus quality measure set.
There are scoring scenarios in which Shared Savings Program ACOs would earn higher measure achievement points under flat benchmarks compared to those they would earn under performance period benchmarks. Most notable are scenarios in which Shared Savings Program ACOs have a tight distribution of performance rates on a measure. For example, a non-inverse measure for which a performance rate of 90.00 percent is in the 8th decile. In this example, a Shared Savings Program ACO that reported a performance rate of 90.00 percent would be scored in the 8th decile when the hypothetical performance period benchmark is applied. Using the flat benchmarks described in Table B-G3 of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44043
), a Shared Savings Program ACO that reported a performance rate of 90.00 percent would be scored in the 10th decile, resulting in greater measure achievement points than under the hypothetical performance period benchmarks described in this example. For more details on the calculation of measure achievement points, we refer readers to the “APM Performance Pathway (APP) Toolkit” which is updated for each PY and posted in the QPP Resource Library.

We sought public comment on our proposals to score Shared Savings Program ACOs reporting Medicare CQMs using flat benchmarks for PY 2027 and subsequent years and to retroactively apply the flat benchmarks for Quality IDs: 001, 134, and 236 when reported via the Medicare CQMs collection type for PY 2026.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
All commenters supported our proposal to score Medicare CQMs using flat benchmarks for PY 2027 and subsequent years. Many commenters stated that extending the use of flat benchmarks to score Medicare CQMs provides increased predictability, transparency, and stability, and noted the advantage of consistency in a time of evolving quality reporting requirements and during the transition to digital quality measurement. A commenter supported the proposal and recommended that CMS maintain stable quality scoring methodologies during the transition to digital quality measurements. A commenter also noted that flat benchmarks appropriately reward high-quality performance while preserving opportunities for continued improvement.
Many commenters highlighted the limitations of performance-based or historical benchmarks for measures only used in the Shared Savings Program. Several commenters noted that performance-based or historical benchmarks can distort performance results when based only on Shared Savings Program ACOs. Another commenter stated that flat benchmarks prevent Shared Savings Program ACOs from being penalized due to comparisons to prior high performance and encourage participation from new ACOs. A commenter stated that flat benchmarks protect high performers from being scored against a moving target.
Several commenters stated that flat benchmarks enable ACOs to focus on improving quality of care and data infrastructure modernization rather than focusing on reporting infrastructure and its associated administrative burden. A commenter noted administrative burden when measures within the same measure set use different benchmark methodologies. A commenter stated that flat benchmarks better recognize long-term investments in care management, clinical integration, quality improvement programs, and population health capabilities.
Several comments noted that flat benchmarks can prevent scoring results that reflect methodology differences rather than actual changes in clinical performance. A commenter stated that flat benchmarks can address challenges that can arise when benchmark distributions produce counterintuitive results.
A few comments supported the proposal to extend the use of flat benchmarks and stated that, in the absence of flat benchmarks, Shared Savings Program ACOs that reported via the Medicare CQMs collection type would be evaluated using MIPS benchmarks.
Response:
We appreciate comments that support our proposal to score Medicare CQMs using flat benchmarks for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
Comment:
Some commenters supported our proposal to score Medicare CQMs using flat benchmarks and suggested that CMS should periodically reassess the appropriateness of flat benchmarks and evaluate whether observed performance changes reflect improvements in care or differences in data capture and reporting methods. A commenter encouraged CMS to monitor benchmark performance to ensure that benchmarks appropriately distinguish high performers while avoiding unintended consequences for organizations serving medically complex, rural, or socially at-risk populations.
Response:
We appreciate the supportive comments. We will continue to monitor ACOs' uptake of Medicare CQMs, the appropriateness of the flat benchmarks and how to assess quality of care improvements and differences as a result of using flat benchmarks.
Comment:
A commenter supported our proposals to score Medicare CQMs using flat benchmarks for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs and also retroactively for PY 2026 when Quality IDs 001, 134, and 236 are reported as Medicare CQMs, but requested that CMS ensure that high-performing organizations are not disadvantaged by changes in scoring methodology.

Higher percentage points would increase the likelihood that these Shared Savings Program ACOs would meet the quality performance standard for sharing in savings at the maximum rate under its track by achieving a quality score that is equivalent to or higher than the 40th percentile across all MIPS quality performance category
(

scores, excluding entities/providers eligible for facility-based scoring or the alternative quality performance standard to be eligible to share in savings at a lower rate that is scaled based on the ACO's quality performance. 89 FR 98118
and
98119

Comment:

Several commenters stated that the retroactive application of flat benchmarks improves benchmarking transparency, reduces reporting uncertainty, and promotes scoring consistency. Many of these commenters also noted that use of flat benchmarks provides the same scoring benefit to Shared Savings Program ACOs when reporting Shared Savings Program-specific measures. A few of these comments also stated that the retroactive application of the policy will reduce burden for ACOs.
A few commenters reported that maintaining consistent benchmarks is particularly important during the transition to digital quality measurement and other quality reporting transitions. A commenter also stated that this change enables ACOs to focus resources on quality improvement and that flat benchmarks support predictability by preventing scoring changes due to benchmark fluctuations.
Response:
We appreciate the support for our proposal to retroactively apply the flat benchmarks to score Quality IDs: 001, 134, and 236 when reported via the Medicare CQMs collection type for PY 2026.
Comment:
A commenter suggested that CMS provide additional justification regarding the retroactive use of flat benchmarks rather than the planned historical benchmarks for PY 2026. A commenter, while supportive of the proposal to use flat benchmarks to score Medicare CQMs, opposed the retroactive application of flat benchmarks to PY 2026. The commenter stated that the retroactive provision creates unpredictability and that Shared Savings Program ACOs should know the measure benchmarks prior to the start of the PY so that they can incorporate those standards into quality improvement strategies and appropriately direct clinical and operational resources.

We proposed that Quality IDs: 001, 134, and 236, if reported via the Medicare CQMs collection type for PY 2026 would be scored using flat benchmarks. We discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44042

We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that the evaluation of Shared Savings Program ACOs' PY 2026 quality performance, including the use of measure benchmarks to calculate quality scores, will occur in PY 2027. Retroactive application of flat benchmarks for Medicare CQMs for PY 2026 would enable the Shared Savings Program to better recognize the quality of care provided in PY 2026 and incentivize future improvements based on the evaluation of that care. We described that our simulated analysis of PY 2024 data showed that flat benchmarks were estimated to increase average quality scores by 11 percentage points, thus increasing the likelihood that Shared Savings Program ACOs would meet the quality performance standard for sharing in savings at the maximum rate under its track. This analysis also illustrated that the use of performance-based benchmarks, if flat benchmarks are not used, could lead to Shared Savings Program ACOs forgoing shared savings that might otherwise have been available for reinvestment. As such, applying flat benchmarks would afford the Shared Savings Program ACOs with increased shared savings the opportunity to devote greater resources to providing better quality of care to Medicare beneficiaries over time and improving care coordination that benefits the Medicare beneficiaries served by the Shared Savings Program ACOs. Additionally, we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44042

In response to the commenter's concern that the retroactive application of flat benchmarks to score the three Medicare CQMs in PY 2026 would create unpredictability and that Shared Savings Program ACOs should know the measure benchmarks prior to the start of the PY, we acknowledge the preference for Shared Savings Program ACOs to know the measure benchmarks prior to the start of the PY but note that the policy as finalized will ensure that Shared Savings Program ACOs know the measure benchmarks prior to the end of the PY 2026 and before the Shared Savings Program ACO is required to submit quality data for PY 2026. d. Addressing Shared Savings Program ACOs' Challenges With Meeting the MIPS Data Completeness Requirement
(1) Background
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44044
) we stated that requirements for data completeness are essential to ensure that data submitted on quality measures are sufficiently complete to accurately assess each Shared Savings Program ACO's quality performance. The data completeness requirement means that a Shared Savings Program ACO participant submitting measure data on a quality measure must submit data on at least a specific percentage of their patients that meet the measure's denominator criteria. Meeting the data completeness requirement ensures that the measure represents an appropriate percentage of the patient population applicable for a given quality measure. Robust data completeness requirements ensure the most accurate assessment of the performance of Shared Savings Program ACO participants.
In the CY 2017 Medicare Program; Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) and Alternative Payment Model (APM) Incentive Under the Physician Fee Schedule, and Criteria for Physician-Focused Payment Models (
81 FR 77125
), we established a data completeness threshold to ensure that data submitted on quality measures are complete enough to accurately assess each MIPS eligible clinician's quality performance. Additionally, in the CY 2020 PFS final rule (
84 FR 62568
,
62953
), we added a requirement at § 414.1340 that quality data would not be considered true, complete, or accurate if such data are submitted selectively such that the data are unrepresentative of a MIPS eligible clinician or group's performance. In the CY 2024 PFS final rule, we finalized that we would maintain the data completeness criteria threshold of 75 percent (
88 FR 79337
). Specifically, as finalized, the data completeness criteria for the quality performance category (§ 414.1340) state that MIPS eligible clinicians, groups, virtual groups, subgroups, and APM Entities submitting quality measure data on QCDR measures, MIPS CQMs, or eCQMs must submit data on at least 75 percent of the MIPS eligible clinician, group, virtual group, subgroup, and APM Entity's patients that meet the measure's denominator criteria, regardless of payer for MIPS payment years 2026 through 2030. In the CY 2024 PFS final rule, for APM Entities, specifically Shared Savings Program ACOs, we likewise established the data completeness criteria threshold of at least 75 percent for the Medicare CQMs aligned with the data completeness criteria threshold established for the eCQMs and MIPS CQMs collection types (
88 FR 79337
).
In the CY 2021 PFS final rule, we finalized modifications to the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements and quality performance standard for PY 2021 and subsequent PYs (
85 FR 84720
through
84743
) requiring Shared Savings Program ACOs to report quality data via the APP codified at § 414.1367. In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, we finalized that for PYs beginning on or after January 1, 2025, Shared Savings Program ACOs must submit quality data via the APP on the quality measures contained in the APP Plus quality measure set to satisfactorily report on behalf of the eligible clinicians who bill under the TIN of a Shared Savings Program ACO participant for purposes of the MIPS quality performance category of the Quality Payment Program (
89 FR 98568
).
For data completeness criteria pertaining to the quality performance category, we finalized in the CY 2025 PFS final rule that an APM Entity, specifically a Shared Savings Program ACO that meets reporting requirements under the APP, must meet the data completeness requirements established at § 414.1340(d)(1). Shared Savings Program ACOs reporting quality data on the APP Plus quality measure set meet the quality performance standard if they achieve a quality score that is equivalent to or higher than the 40th percentile across all MIPS quality performance category scores. If a Shared Savings Program ACO fails to meet data completeness on a measure in the APP Plus quality measure set, it will receive a 0/10 for the affected quality measure(s), resulting in a lower quality score used to determine eligibility for shared savings. For a Shared Savings Program ACO in the first PY of the ACO's first agreement period, the Shared Savings Program ACO must meet the MIPS data completeness requirement on all eCQMs/MIPS CQMs/Medicare CQMs in the APP Plus quality measure set and receive a MIPS quality performance category score. Shared Savings Program ACOs are eligible for the eCQM/MIPS CQM reporting incentive if they report all eCQMs/MIPS CQMs in the APP Plus quality measure set and meet data completeness requirements for all measures. Lastly, under the Complex Organization Adjustment, Shared Savings Program ACOs may receive one measure achievement point for each submitted eCQM that meets case minimum and data completeness requirements.

Shared Savings Program ACOs continue to express concerns related to the transition to dQM reporting including challenges with data aggregation, engagement of specialty practices, and patient matching. Shared Savings Program ACOs have shared with CMS that specialty electronic health record (EHR) systems are not designed to support the APP Plus quality measure set and that certain specialties may not be able to collect the needed data elements for quality reporting. Shared Savings Program ACOs noted that patients that are not managed by the Shared Savings Program ACO or do not have a primary care relationship with the Shared Savings Program ACO present data aggregation and patient deduplication challenges because specialists may not have quality reporting capabilities for the measures in the APP Plus quality measure set, which may not be part of specialists' clinical workflows. These challenges complicate a Shared Savings Program ACO's ability to meet the data completeness requirement. We have also received feedback that the MIPS data completeness requirement is a deterrent to specialist participation in Shared Savings Program ACOs. In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, some commenters stated that small independent practices and specialty practices are often unable to participate or continue to participate in the Shared Savings Program due to the technical and financial burden associated with the adoption of new technologies needed to meet reporting requirements (
89 FR 98105
). Several commenters requested that we consider adding exceptions or exclusions for small practices and certain specialties and/or altering data completeness requirements to address ongoing challenges and allow for Shared Savings Program ACOs to be successful in reporting eCQMs, MIPS CQMs, and Medicare CQMs (
89 FR 98105
).
With the sunset of the CMS Web Interface beginning in PY 2025 as finalized in the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65440
), Shared Savings Program ACOs are now required to report MIPS CQMs, eCQMs and/or Medicare CQMs and have reported difficulties with meeting the MIPS data completeness requirement. Shared Savings Program quality reporting data in PYs 2023 and 2024 indicates that Shared Savings Program ACOs have been slow to report eCQMs.
Since the CY 2021 PFS final rule was issued, Shared Savings Program ACOs and other interested parties have continued to express concerns about requiring Shared Savings Program ACOs to report all payer/all patient eCQMs/MIPS CQMs due to the cost of purchasing and implementing a system-wide infrastructure to aggregate data from multiple ACO participant taxpayer identification numbers (TINs) and varying electronic health record (EHR) systems (
86 FR 65257

86 FR 65259

In the CY 2023 PFS final rule, commenters expressed concerns regarding the requirement to report all payer/all patient eCQMs/MIPS CQMs beginning in PY 2025, such as issues related to meeting all payer data requirements, data completeness requirements, data aggregation and deduplication issues, and interoperability issues among different EHRs (
87 FR 69837
).
In light of these concerns, we proposed in the CY 2024 PFS proposed rule to establish the Medicare CQMs as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs to help ACOs build the infrastructure, skills, knowledge, and expertise necessary to aggregate patient data. We established the data completeness criteria threshold of at least 75 percent for the Medicare CQMs aligned with the data completeness criteria threshold established for eCQM and MIPS CQM collection types. We believed that the Medicare CQM collection type would address the concerns from ACOs regarding the capability of meeting the data completeness requirement for all payer data.
In the CY 2024 PFS final rule, many commenters also raised questions and concerns regarding how CMS will determine the appropriate Medicare CQM population for these measures (
88 FR 79102

Additionally, while the availability of the Medicare CQMs as a collection type assists with the transition from reporting eCQMs and/or MIPS CQMs to reporting dQMs, some commenters noted that reporting through the Medicare CQMs collection type will not inherently advance their capabilities to report on eCQMs. For instance, the commenters noted that the Medicare CQMs collection type does not address the adoption of CEHRT across Shared Savings Program ACO participants, processes to enable aggregation of quality measurement data across all Shared Savings Program ACO participants, the ability to assess data completeness, efficiently calculate quality measures outcomes, and the generation of a QRDA-III file (

and

To address these concerns, in the CY 2026 PFS final rule, we revised the definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQM” to align with our modifications to the stepwise assignment methodology and the approach to identifying the beneficiaries assignable to a Shared Savings Program ACO. We intended for the revised definition to reduce Shared Savings Program ACOs' burden in the patient matching necessary to report Medicare CQMs because the list of “beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs” would have greater overlap with the list of beneficiaries that are assignable to a Shared Savings Program ACO.
The Shared Savings Program continues to hear from Shared Savings Program ACOs and other interested parties about the challenges with reporting on all payer/all patient measures and meeting data management requirements given their muti-practice/multi EHR structure, the challenges to aggregate data with the health IT infrastructure in use by Shared Savings Program ACOs and current state of interoperability (

Section 1871(e)(1)(A) of the Act prohibits the Secretary from applying substantive changes in regulations retroactively before the effective date of the change except where the Secretary determines, as relevant here, that failure to apply the change retroactively would be contrary to the public interest. It is in the public interest to apply our proposed changes to § 425.508 “Incorporating quality reporting requirements related to the Quality Payment Program Beneficiary” beginning in PY 2026 because, absent the proposed changes, Shared Savings Program ACOs that generated savings while maintaining or improving quality of care may have difficulty meeting the quality reporting requirements at § 425.508(c). Based on the Shared Savings Program ACO public reporting requirements at § 425.308(b)(4)(ii), Shared Savings Program ACOs that generate shared savings must publicly report the total proportion of shared savings invested in infrastructure, redesigned care processes, and other resources required to support the triple aim of better health for populations, better care for individuals, and lower growth in expenditures, including the proportion distributed among Shared Savings Program ACO participants. If a Shared Savings Program ACO does not meet the quality reporting requirements, then that Shared Savings Program ACO would not be eligible to share in savings that could be used for quality improvement initiatives for the Medicare beneficiaries.
