The evaluation of Shared Savings Program ACOs' PY 2026 quality performance, including evaluation of MIPS data completeness, occurs in 2027. As such, retroactive application of the proposed reporting requirement for PY 2026 would be in the public interest and would afford Shared Savings Program ACOs that earn shared savings the opportunity to devote greater resources to providing better quality of care to Medicare beneficiaries over time and improving care coordination that benefits the Medicare beneficiaries served by Shared Savings Program ACOs, in accordance with ACO public reporting requirements at § 425.308(b)(4)(ii).
Additionally, Shared Savings Program ACOs that participated in the interviews discussed in section III.G.3.c of this final rule have also shared that some practices have closed due to financial challenges associated with the transition to digital quality measurement and have begun to remove practices that cannot meet digital reporting requirements from their organization. Practices that do not meet the quality reporting requirements and, therefore, do not earn shared savings, could experience financial instability. For these practices, the loss of shared savings would compound these challenges and may cause them to close or may negatively affect their ability to provide continuity of care, coordination of care, preventive care initiatives, and quality improvement initiatives for Medicare beneficiaries they serve. As a result, beneficiaries may experience challenges with accessing care, ineffective utilization of services, fragmented care, or duplicative tests or services, and ACOs may be slower to adopt digital quality measurement as a result. The proposed changes would allow Shared Savings Program ACOs to devote greater resources to improving care coordination so that they are better positioned to deliver the right care at the right time, all to the benefit of Medicare beneficiaries served by the Shared Savings Program ACO and Medicare Trust Funds.
We believe the proposed changes would have minimal impact on Shared Savings Program ACOs' existing processes because the Shared Savings Program ACO would continue to aggregate quality data and apply the measure specifications prior to the submission of quality data. Additionally, Shared Savings Program ACOs would benefit from the ability to meet the MIPS data completeness requirement, in the event they are unable to acquire data from a subset of their participant TINs, which may enable them to achieve a quality score equivalent to the 40th percentile MIPS quality performance category score to be eligible to earn maximum shared savings and, for ENHANCED track Shared Savings Program ACOs, avoid shared losses.
In alignment with the proposals described in this section, we proposed to revise the regulation text at § 425.508 as follows:
Under new paragraph (c)(1), we would specify that, for PYs beginning on or after January 1, 2026, ACOs may exclude one or more TINs of ACO participants from an ACO's submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data (as applicable) for each measure. We would specify that applicable exclusions may include:
++ Unforeseen circumstance(s) that are outside of the control of the ACO, such as the unexpected closure of a group or individual's practice that bills under the ACO participant TIN.
++ An ACO participant TIN has a CEHRT that is intended for specialty use and does not support the measure(s) included in the APP Plus quality measure set.
++ Other circumstances as determined by CMS.
Under new paragraph (c)(2), we would specify that ACOs may not exclude an ACO participant TIN from the ACO's quality data submission for each measure based on the following:
++ The demographics status of the beneficiaries who had an encounter during the performance year with an ACO participant TIN.
++ The health status of the beneficiaries who had an encounter during the performance year with an ACO participant TIN.
++ The estimated impact of the ACO participant TIN on the ACO's quality performance.
Under new paragraph (c)(3), we would specify that the ACO's submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data (as applicable) for each measure must include ACO participant TINs that represent at least 95 percent of the beneficiaries assigned to the ACO prior to the application of the measure specifications.
Under new paragraph (c)(4), we would specify that CMS retains the right to audit and validate eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data reported by an ACO and may request documentation from the ACO related to the exclusion of ACO participant TINs under paragraph § 425.508(c)(1). We would further note that failure to report quality measure data accurately, completely, and timely may result in compliance actions as described at §§ 425.216 and 425.218.
We sought public comments on our proposals to revise the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements at § 425.508 beginning in PY 2026. We also sought comment on other circumstances we should consider that would allow ACOs to exclude one or more TINs of ACO participants from their submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data for a measure.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Most commenters supported our proposals to revise the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements beginning in PY 2026. Many of these commenters noted that the policies address significant challenges and operational realities faced by ACOs. A commenter noted the policies acknowledge difficulties of obtaining quality data from all participant TINs, particularly in multi-specialty, multi-EHR environments while another noted that they recognize the variability of quality reporting capabilities among heterogeneous healthcare providers. Many commenters stated the policies will reduce burden and provide necessary flexibility while maintaining a meaningful MIPS data completeness threshold and while preserving accountability and the integrity of ACO-level quality results. A couple of commenters noted that the policies will reduce unnecessary reporting failures and protect ACOs against adverse reporting outcomes. A couple of commenters noted the policies will prevent them from being penalized for any future reporting issues outside their control. A commenter noted that this policy ensures health system-led ACOs that integrate information across multiple EHR platforms, provider/supplier organizations, and care settings have reasonable flexibility. The commenter noted that, in combination with other quality proposals, the policies will allow for investments in infrastructure needed to transition to dQMs and allow ACOs who report on behalf of a wide variety of EHRs to be successful. A commenter noted the policies will support practitioner participation and decrease the likelihood of practices being excluded from accountable care arrangements solely because of technology or data limitations. This commenter also stated that the policies would allow them to work toward more interoperable reporting options such as the eCQMs collection type instead of manual
(
printed page 71361)
options like the Medicare CQMs collection types.
A few commenters noted the flexibilities of the policies are particularly helpful to small and rural ACOs, that have limited resources and fewer administrative staff, and the policies avoid penalizing and help secure continued participation of these providers and suppliers. A commenter also noted the policies are important for physician-led ACOs that include independent practices using different EHR systems and another stated they protect independent, low-revenue practices from being penalized or forced into premature consolidation due to vendor EHR incompatibility or unexpected practice closures. A commenter noted the policies will support participating health centers who do not always have control over whether individual practitioners can report specific measures.
A few commenters supported the proposed exclusion criteria, including prohibiting exclusions based on beneficiary demographics, health status or potential impact on quality performance. A commenter agreed with the application of these exclusions at the TIN and individual-measure level and noted that the proposed safeguards ensure that exclusions address legitimate data-access and reporting barriers rather than being used to improve performance results selectively. Another commenter noted the safeguards appropriately protect program integrity. A couple of commenters agreed that reported data should continue to reflect the vast majority of ACO's' assigned beneficiaries.
Several commenters also supported applying the policies retroactively for PY 2026 to reduce burden and confusion during the upcoming reporting cycle. Lastly, some commenters were in support of the proposed quarterly reports, stating these reports will provide transparent and definitive data to ACOs to support implementation of these new flexibilities. Several comments supported the threshold but recommended that CMS monitor to ensure the threshold remains sufficient as implementation progresses, especially when measures shift to a fully digital environment. A comment appreciated the flexibility and encouraged CMS to avoid increases to the threshold that in their belief could create additional reporting burden for participating providers and suppliers.
Response:
We appreciate comments that support our proposal to revise the Shared Savings Program Quality reporting requirements beginning in PY 2026. We note that we will monitor the appropriateness of the 95 percent threshold throughout the implementation process.
Comment:
A commenter opposed the proposals to revise the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements and shared their belief that it is a new restriction for ACOs that is redundant, burdensome, and harmful to the participating practices that most need protection and encouragement. The commenter noted that the proposals are more restrictive than the 75 percent MIPS data completeness requirement and will disadvantage ACOs.
Response:
We believe the comment may be misinterpreting the proposed Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirement revision, and we wish to clarify our proposal. As stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44046
), current Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements at § 425.508(c) require that, for PYs beginning on or after January 1, 2025, Shared Savings Program ACOs must submit quality data on the APP Plus quality measure set to satisfactorily report on behalf of the eligible clinicians who bill under the TIN of a Shared Savings Program ACO participant for purposes of the MIPS quality performance category. In other words, Shared Savings Program ACOs must submit quality reporting data on all of their eligible clinicians who bill under a TIN of an ACO participant. Our proposals to revise the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements are intended to address concerns raised by Shared Savings Program ACOs regarding challenges meeting these requirements in situations where they are unable to obtain data from a Shared Savings Program ACO participant TIN. The proposals would allow ACOs the flexibility to exclude ACO participant TINs from their quality submission data based on the proposed criteria and still meet Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements, rather than impose additional restrictions or burden.
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44046
) that our proposal to require that the Shared Savings Program ACO's submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data (as applicable) for each measure must include Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs that represent at least 95 percent of the beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO prior to the application of the measure specifications is different than the MIPS data completeness requirement for the MIPS quality performance category described at § 414.1340(a) and (d) and proposed (e) (
91 FR 44046
). To further clarify the sequence of how the proposed 95 percent threshold interacts with the MIPS data completeness requirement, we note that the TIN exclusion would be applied by Shared Savings Program ACOs prior to the evaluation of the MIPS data completeness requirement. Under our proposal, a Shared Savings Program ACO would be able to exclude one or more Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs from a Shared Savings Program ACO's submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data (as applicable) for each measure prior to its submission of quality data to MIPS.
A Shared Savings Program ACO then would determine the denominator for a measure by applying the measure specifications using data from the remaining ACO participant TINs after the application of the TIN exclusion policy. MIPS data completeness would then be calculated based on that reported denominator. Additionally, Shared Savings Program ACOs would be required to meet the MIPS data completeness requirement (that is, the Shared Savings Program ACO must report on at least 75 percent of the APM Entity's applicable beneficiaries who meet the measure's denominator criteria for the respective PY) for each eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM for which the Shared Savings Program ACO submits data. MIPS data completeness is calculated based on the quality data submitted by a Shared Savings Program ACO and is assessed at the Shared Savings Program ACO-level.
Comment:
Many commenters suggested that CMS broaden the proposed second exclusion, which permits the exclusion of an ACO participant TIN that has CEHRT that is intended for specialty use and does not support the measure(s) included in the APP Plus quality measure set. Commenters recommended expanding this criterion to include an ACO participant TIN that has a CEHRT that does not support the measure(s) included in the APP Plus quality measure set, regardless of whether the CEHRT is intended for specialty use. The comment recommended that CMS broaden the proposed exclusion beyond “specialty-focused” EHR vendors to include any EHR vendor that is unable or unwilling to support required measures. Another commenter encouraged CMS to recognize ongoing interoperability challenges and continue investing in technical assistance, standardized data exchange, and
(
printed page 71362)
certified health IT capabilities so providers and suppliers can fully participate in quality reporting without relying on exclusion policies over the long term.
Response:
We appreciate the suggestions from comments but continue to believe the second exclusion should remain limited to the scenario described in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule in which an ACO participant TIN has a CEHRT that is intended for specialty use and, because of that focus, does not capture the data elements needed to report the APP Plus quality measure set. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we provided an example of an ophthalmology practice using an ophthalmology-focused EHR (
90 FR 44046
). In this case, the Shared Savings Program ACO cannot aggregate that participant TIN's data because the technology was never designed to capture the data elements needed to report the APP Plus quality measure set.
The suggestion to broaden this exclusion criterion is different in that it would extend the exclusion to any CEHRT, specialty-focused or not, that currently does not support the APP Plus quality measure set, for any reason, including business choices that are within the ACO's control, not an inherent mismatch between a specialty tool and the measure set. We disagree with broadening the exclusion on this basis. As described in section III.G.4. of this final rule, Shared Savings Program ACOs are required to have and use EHR technology that meets the definition of CEHRT (as defined at § 425.20) in one of the ways we are finalizing in § 425.507. Shared Savings Program ACOs also have multiple collection types available from which to choose and should choose the collection type that matches their data collection and reporting capabilities. Expanding the exclusion to cover any instance of vendor's non-support of the APP Plus quality measure set would allow Shared Savings Program ACOs to exclude data based on business choices within a Shared Savings Program ACO's control rather than genuine technical limitations and could reduce the completeness and comparability of quality data across ACOs.
We recognize, as another comment noted, that interoperability challenges persist. We note that interoperability is outside of the scope of our proposal and, as such, we are not addressing the comment's recommendations in this response. We are, therefore, finalizing the second exclusion criterion as proposed.
Comment:
Many commenters suggested revisions to the proposed third exclusion, which permits the exclusion of an ACO participant TIN based on other circumstances as determined by CMS. Several commenters requested that CMS clearly define the scope of this criterion and establish a transparent process for ACOs to request exclusions under this category. One of these commenters also recommended a defined review timeline. Another commenter recommended CMS expand the proposed third exclusion to include small practices whose EHR and/or billing vendors charge restrictive fees for data transmission. A couple of commenters recommended that CMS expand the third exclusion to allow CMS to change the 95 percent assigned beneficiary threshold on a case-by-case basis.
Response:
We note that the use of the proposed third exclusion described as “other circumstances as determined by CMS” is intended to address unforeseen circumstances that emerge during the PY. We would monitor implementation for recurring or systemic issues that are not adequately addressed by the specified exclusions and use those trends to inform ACOs when additional circumstances may warrant recognition under this provision ahead of the ACOs' quality reporting period.
We did not propose to establish a process for ACOs to request exclusions (
i.e.,
via the ACO-MS helpdesk, CMS regional office, or other means) or a review timeline under which an ACO may inform CMS of additional circumstances that may warrant an exclusion. We further clarify that there is no expectation that Shared Savings Program ACOs would need to submit a request to CMS to consider exclusions under § 425.508(c)(1)(iii) or that CMS will review such requests. Rather, CMS would identify and determine qualifying circumstances and communicate those determinations to ACOs, as appropriate. We are finalizing in this section of this final rule that CMS retains the right to audit and validate quality data for each measure reported by a Shared Savings Program ACO and may request documentation from the Shared Savings Program ACO related to the exclusion of Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs from the Shared Savings Program ACO's quality data submission. Shared Savings Program ACOs are required to maintain documentation on TIN exclusions for the purposes of auditing and validation. Shared Savings Program ACOs should review the descriptions of the applicable exclusions at § 425.508(c)(1) as finalized in this section of this final rule and are responsible for determining whether any of these exclusions apply and what documentation they need to maintain to substantiate an applicable exclusion.
We are also rejecting the recommendation to expand the third exclusion to include small practices whose EHR and/or billing vendors charge restrictive fees and note that ACOs can choose vendors that best meet their needs. We further note that we are not allowing ACOs to meet a threshold that is lower than the 95 percent threshold through this third exclusion as suggested in the comment since we are finalizing that the 95 percent threshold would apply to all ACOs. We refer readers to our responses later in this section of this final rule where we discuss our belief that the 95 percent beneficiary threshold remains appropriate as this policy is intended to address limited and unusual circumstances in which the ACO is unable to obtain data from an ACO participant TIN.
Comment:
A couple of commenters incorrectly stated that our proposed revisions to the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements allow Shared Savings Program ACOs to exclude low-volume TINs or those incapable of producing a QRDA file. A commenter requested that CMS add an exclusion for special-status (small volume) ACOs to align with the exclusions of the CEHRT use metrics. Another commenter stated that CMS should consider adding Promoting Interoperability exclusions and hardship exemptions to the applicable exclusions, as challenges with CEHRT can impede a TIN's ability to produce the necessary files for CQM reporting.
Response:
We appreciate suggestions on other circumstances that would allow ACOs to exclude one or more TINs of ACO participants from their submission of quality measure data. We clarify that the current criteria allow for the exclusion of these TINs if they meet applicable criteria. Specifically, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44046
), we stated that applicable exclusions may include the following: (i) unforeseen circumstance(s) that are outside of the control of the ACO, such as the unexpected closure of a group or individual's practice that bills under the ACO participant TIN; (ii) an ACO participant TIN has a CEHRT that is intended for specialty use and does not support the measure(s) included in the APP Plus quality measure set; and (iii) other circumstances as determined by CMS. We also stated that ACOs may not exclude an ACO participant TIN from the ACO's quality data submission for each measure based on the
(
printed page 71363)
demographics or health status of the beneficiaries who had an encounter during the performance year with an ACO participant TIN or based on the estimated impact of the ACO participant TIN on the ACO's quality performance.
Regarding the comment that our proposed revisions to the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements allow Shared Savings Program ACOs to exclude low-volume TINs or those incapable of producing a QRDA file, we note that under the proposed exclusions as described at § 425.508(c)(1) we did not propose to permit ACO participant TINs to be excluded solely based on volume or inability to produce a QRDA file. Low volume does not satisfy the applicable exclusion criteria at § 425.508(c)(1) as ACOs are expected to report on participant TINs, regardless of size. We did not propose to align an applicable exclusion with the criteria for the MIPS low volume threshold (as described at
42 CFR 414.1310(b)(1)(iii)
) and instead proposed to allow ACOs to exclude an ACO Participant TIN based on that TIN's contributions to the ACO's assigned beneficiary population. We believe that this approach more appropriately reflects the basis and scope of the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements. With respect to the suggestion that we allow Shared Savings Program ACOs to exclude TINs incapable of producing QRDA files, we encourage ACOs to evaluate all quality reporting options to determine which collection type is most appropriate based on the ACO's unique composition and technical infrastructure and note that QRDA files are not necessarily required for all reporting options. We are, therefore, not adding a new exclusion to permit ACOs participant TINs to be excluded solely based on volume or inability to produce a QRDA file.
Regarding the request that we add an exclusion for special-status (small volume) ACO to align with the exclusions of the CEHRT use metrics, we believe the comment may be referring to the MIPS Promoting Interoperability exclusion for small practices. We note that as discussed in paragraph (3) of the definition of “Small practice” at
42 CFR 414.1305
, beginning with the 2021 MIPS payment year, a small practice means a TIN consisting of 15 or fewer eligible clinicians during the MIPS determination period. We did not propose to include an exclusion for small practice because a small practice, as defined by MIPS, may contribute meaningfully to an ACO's assigned beneficiary population and, as such, should be included in an ACO's quality data submission, unless the small practice meets one of the other applicable exclusions as finalized in this section of this final rule. We do not believe a small practice exclusion is appropriate as ACOs are expected to aggregate data across TINs regardless of their practice size unless there are other circumstances outside the ACO's control.
Regarding the suggestion that we should consider adding Promoting Interoperability exclusions and hardship exemptions to the applicable exclusions at § 425.508(c)(1), we note that as described in section III.G.4. of this final rule, Shared Savings Program ACOs are required to have and use EHR technology that meets the definition of CEHRT (as defined at § 425.20) in one of the ways we are finalizing at § 425.507. We did not propose and are not finalizing a small practice exemption for the Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics.
Comment:
Several commenters requested CMS to clarify how Shared Savings Program ACOs and vendors would determine whether the submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data (as applicable) for each measure includes Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs that represent at least 95 percent of the beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO prior to the application of the measure specifications. A commenter asked if ACOs can exclude different TINs for different measures. Another commenter asked if threshold determination made earlier in the PY is treated as final, or whether an ACO must reassess and potentially adjust its TIN exclusions if beneficiary assignment changes between Quarter 3 and Quarter 4. A commenter suggested that CMS provide a specific list of the types of TINs that qualify for the proposed exclusions, which would allow ACOs to determine eligibility prospectively and reduce uncertainty and administrative burden during implementation. A commenter requested detailed reports by TIN to assist in the beneficiary and participant inventory process. Another requested information on data sources which could be used to identify beneficiaries and guidance on aggregation.
Response:
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44047
), we stated that, for Quarter 3 and Quarter 4 of each applicable PY beginning with PY 2026, we would provide Shared Savings Program ACOs with a new aggregate report that would contain the data necessary to determine how many beneficiaries would be represented by the TINs the ACO plans to report on. Specifically, the report would be at the beneficiary-TIN level and contain the number of beneficiaries that will be assigned to the ACO and demonstrate how the assigned beneficiaries are matched to the TIN(s). This would allow the Shared Savings Program ACO to have access to the data that is necessary to determine if the ACO's submission of eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data for each measure includes Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs sufficient to represent at least 95 percent of the beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO prior to the application of the measure specifications.
We also stated that the Quarter 3 report would be intended to provide Shared Savings Program ACOs with a preview of the necessary data, while the Quarter 4 report would be the definitive source for ACOs to determine whether the Shared Savings Program ACO meets the requirement that the data submitted for each measure must include Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs that represent at least 95 percent of the beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO prior to the application of the measure specifications. Regarding the recommendation that CMS provide a specific list of the types of TINs that qualify for the proposed exclusions, we note that ACOs must evaluate the ACO participant TINs based on the applicable exclusions to determine if any ACO participant TINs can be excluded while meeting the quality reporting requirements of § 422.508(c).
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 40446
) that since a Shared Savings Program ACO may encounter an unforeseen circumstance that may be specific to reporting a clinical quality measure(s), the Shared Savings Program ACO may exclude one or more Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs from the quality data submitted for only the impacted measure(s) for the applicable PY; specifically, if all requirements are met, Shared Savings Program ACOs could potentially exclude different ACO participant TINs for different impacted measures. A Shared Savings Program ACO would be required to meet the 95 percent requirement for each measure at the measure level. This means that the quality data submitted by the Shared Savings Program ACO for each measure in the APP Plus quality measure set must meet this requirement independent of the other measures in the APP Plus quality measure set.
As stated in this section of this final rule, we are finalizing our proposed revisions to the Shared Savings Program
(
printed page 71364)
quality reporting requirements beginning in PY 2026. After the release of this final rule, we will provide instructions to Shared Savings Program ACOs in future education and outreach materials on how to use the new aggregate report to determine the Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs that represent at least 95 percent of the beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO prior to the application of the measure specifications. These materials will also include examples of the 95 percent threshold calculations. We also encourage ACOs and their vendors to participate in our monthly QCDR and Qualified Registry support calls, Learning System Webinars and to submit questions to the QPP Service Center, as needed.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that CMS provide Shared Savings Program ACOs with the new aggregate reports that would contain the data necessary to determine how many beneficiaries would be represented by the TINs the ACO plans to report on early enough for ACOs to make informed decisions. A commenter stated that large ACOs require sufficient time to identify data gaps, determine TIN exclusions, implement corrective actions, and validate compliance with completeness requirements. This commenter recommended at least 90 days between release of the final report and quality reporting deadlines.
Response:
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44047
), we stated that we would provide ACOs with the new aggregate reports for Quarter 3 and Quarter 4 of each applicable PY beginning with PY 2026. We also stated that the Quarter 3 report would be intended to provide Shared Savings Program ACOs with a preview of the necessary data, while the Quarter 4 report would be the definitive source for ACOs to determine whether the Shared Savings Program ACO meets the requirement that the data submitted for each measure must include Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs that represent at least 95 percent of the beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO prior to the application of the measure specifications. We intend to provide this new information in the Quarter 3 and Quarter 4 reports package. For PY 2026, the Quarter 3 reports package is scheduled to be issued to ACOs in November 2026, and the Quarter 4 reports package is scheduled to be issued to ACOs in February 2027 after the conclusion of the applicable performance year. While the Quarter 4 report would not be issued within 90 days of the quality reporting deadline, we believe this timing is sufficient as this policy is intended to address limited and unusual circumstances in which the ACO is unable to obtain data from an ACO participant TIN. ACOs, regardless of size, should attempt to report data from all TINs, and this policy is intended to be a safeguard for situations outside an ACO's control.
Comment:
A few commenters suggested that the 95 percent requirement be revised to other thresholds, such as 80 percent, 85 percent, and 90 percent. A couple of the commenters noted that the 95 percent threshold is too narrow to accommodate the range of data-access failures, specialty CEHRT limitations, and other circumstances. Another commenter noted the 95 percent threshold creates operational challenges and recommends a 90 percent threshold with an attestation-based approach where Shared Savings Program ACOs would attest to reporting the full APP Plus quality measure set, for the participant TINs included in the quality submission, that the submitted data satisfies requirements and that the excluded TINs have been identified and documented per CMS requirements. A commenter recommended CMS consider a lower threshold or phase in approach for ACOs below a defined size. Another commenter recommended that particularly in the context of large multispecialty TINs, where it may be challenging to meet the 95 percent threshold criteria based on TIN-level exclusions, that CMS allow practice-, specialty-, or NPI-level exclusions or exceptions if the 95 percent threshold is met at the applicable level.
Response:
Regarding the proposed revisions to the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirements, we believe that the 95 percent beneficiary threshold remains appropriate as this policy is intended to address limited and unusual circumstances in which the ACO is unable to obtain data from an ACO participant TIN. Additionally, the 95 percent threshold ensures CMS still receives sufficient data to assess Shared Savings Program ACO quality in the applicable PY and over time. For these reasons, we also believe the 95 percent threshold is appropriate for ACOs of all sizes and reject the commenter's suggestion to consider a lower threshold or phase-in approach for ACOs below a defined size. Regarding the suggestion for an attestation-based approach, we refer to the section of this final rule where we finalize requirements for documentation on TIN exclusions for the purposes of auditing and validation (§ 422.508(c)(4)), which we believe minimize administrative burden compared to an attestation process. We are therefore rejecting the suggestion to add an attestation process. Regarding the suggestion to allow practice-, specialty-, or NPI-level exclusions, we did not propose to apply exclusions at these levels as the Shared Savings Program is a whole TIN program. For these reasons, we reject the suggestion to add practice-, specialty- and NPI-level exclusions.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern regarding the calculation of the 95 percent threshold for ACOs that select prospective beneficiary assignment and ACOs with more voluntarily aligned beneficiaries. Commenters stated the proposed approach would disadvantage ACOs under prospective assignment since the assignment window does not align with the PY. The commenters also shared their belief that the approach would also disadvantage ACOs with more voluntarily aligned beneficiaries who may not have a qualifying primary care encounter in the PY. These commenters noted ACOs could fall below the 95 percent threshold without excluding any TINs. These commenters recommended that CMS calculate the threshold by using the ACO's final assigned beneficiary population as the basis for both the numerator and denominator to acknowledge the beneficiaries ACOs are financially responsible for and create fairness across ACOs.
A commenter recommended calculating the threshold against the subset of assigned beneficiaries who have an eligible primary care encounter during the PY. Another commenter recommended proportional reductions to the assigned beneficiary percentage after TIN exclusions are applied. Another commenter noted that CMS should consider whether the 95 percent assigned-beneficiary threshold provides sufficient flexibility for large, multispecialty ACOs and suggested CMS should establish appropriate safe harbors for documented EHR and vendor limitations.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns expressed in the comments about how the 95 percent threshold calculation affects ACOs under prospective assignment and ACOs with higher shares of voluntarily aligned beneficiaries. We note that it is possible that ACOs may fall below the threshold without excluding data from any participant TINs. This scenario may be more likely to occur for prospective ACOs who may not be seeing some of their assigned beneficiaries in an eligible primary care encounter during
(
printed page 71365)
the PY. We further clarify that the 95 percent threshold requirement is only applicable if Shared Savings Program ACOs choose to exclude participant TINs under one of the applicable exclusions finalized in this section of this final rule. Shared Savings Program ACOs that choose not to exclude TINs would still meet the existing quality reporting requirements at § 425.508(c). However, ACOs have the option to choose their assignment type and can take into consideration these options weighed against the various Shared Savings Program requirements and how they want to operate as an ACO. Additionally, Shared Savings Program ACOs are expected to be accountable for the quality of care they provide to their assigned beneficiaries, so we believe the 95 percent threshold provides important flexibility to exclude participant TINs in limited circumstances, while otherwise ensuring that ACOs report quality data that reflect the care they provide. For these reasons, we also believe the current calculation of the threshold is appropriate and reject suggestions for alternative calculation methods.
Comment:
A few commenters requested clarity on the audit process such as timing and documentation needs. A commenter asked how the ACO is supposed to track, document and substantiate a TIN exclusion and whether CMS intends to review TIN exclusions prior to application and suggested that CMS provide a standard template or structured data fields for documenting each exclusion.
Response:
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44047
), we proposed to retain the right to audit and validate eCQM/MIPS CQM/Medicare CQM/Medicare eCQM data for each measure reported by a Shared Savings Program ACO. We further proposed that CMS may request documentation from the Shared Savings Program ACO related to the exclusion of Shared Savings Program ACO participant TINs from the Shared Savings Program ACO's quality data submission. We also proposed that failure to report quality measure data accurately, completely, and timely may result in compliance actions as described in §§ 425.216 and 425.218. We clarify that, to streamline implementation and minimize operational burden, we will not review TIN exclusions prior to their application and instead require the ACOs to maintain documentation on TIN exclusions for the purposes of auditing and validation. We clarify that we defer to Shared Savings Program ACOs to maintain the necessary documentation that would substantiate an applicable exclusion. Therefore, Shared Savings Program ACOs should review the descriptions of the applicable exclusions at § 425.508(c)(1) finalized in this section of this final rule and are responsible for determining whether any of these exclusions apply.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that the TIN exclusion policy does not address the PY 2026 mismatch between the Medicare CQM reporting population and the ACO's assigned population.
Response:
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44047
), we noted that, under the current definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” at § 425.20, beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs for PY 2026 are closely aligned with the Shared Savings Program ACO's assignable population rather than the ACO's assigned population (as finalized in section III.G.3.d.(4) of this final rule for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs). Since the TIN exclusion policy can be used by ACOs reporting the Medicare CQMs collection type, we believe the policy remains appropriate. For example, an ACO that chooses to report Medicare CQMs for PY 2026 could exclude ACO participant TIN(s) from the ACO's quality reporting as discussed in section III.G.3.d.(4) of this final rule prior to the application of the applicable measure specifications. This approach may address concerns that some ACOs have expressed about data aggregation and patient deduplication challenges for beneficiaries that do not have a primary care relationship with the ACO (
91 FR 44045
). We direct readers to section III.G.3.d.(4) of this final rule for further discussion of the revised definition of a beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQM for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.

(3) Shared Savings Program ACOs To Report Using the Medicare eCQMs Collection Type
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44048
), we stated that Shared Savings Program ACOs have expressed concerns regarding the difficulty for multi-TIN Shared Savings Program ACOs to aggregate and deduplicate patient-level data. Additional challenges persist with integration across multiple EHRs, and these challenges can be an impediment for some Shared Savings Program ACOs. In light of the concerns raised by Shared Savings Program ACOs and other interested parties related to reporting quality measures using the eCQMs collection type and our commitment to supporting Shared Savings Program ACOs in the transition to dQM reporting, for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, we proposed to establish the Medicare eCQMs for Accountable Care Organizations Participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare eCQMs) as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs reporting on the Medicare eCQMs (reporting quality data on beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs as proposed to be defined at § 425.20) within the APP Plus quality measure set. A Medicare eCQM is essentially an eCQM that is part of the APP Plus quality measure set and reported by a Shared Savings Program ACO on only the Shared Savings Program ACO's assigned beneficiaries, instead of its all payer/all patient population. That is, the Medicare eCQMs will generally follow the eCQM measure specifications; however, they will be reported on a different population and use a different identifier to distinguish that the submission is for a Medicare eCQM rather than for an eCQM.
In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, we noted the numerous benefits to using eCQMs, including their use of electronic standards that reduce reporting burden, and expressed intent to fully transition to digital quality measurement in CMS quality reporting and value-based purchasing programs (
89 FR 98106
). We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
) that we believe the addition of Medicare eCQMs would support our efforts to transition to dQMs by supporting Shared Savings Program ACOs that want to report eCQMs but are not able to operationally report on all patient/all payer data due to data aggregation challenges.
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
) that Medicare eCQMs would serve to address concerns which are discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44044
through
44046
) by defining a population of beneficiaries that exists within the all payer/all patient eCQM specifications and tethering that population to a Shared Savings Program ACO's assigned beneficiary population. Shared Savings Program ACOs have expressed challenges with quality data reporting as their list of eligible beneficiaries has often contained beneficiaries for whom the Shared Savings Program ACO is unable to identify a primary care relationship. Specifically, Medicare eCQMs would address the concern raised by Shared
(
printed page 71367)
Savings Program ACOs that for Shared Savings Program ACOs with a higher proportion of specialty practices and/or multiple EHRs, the broader all payer/all patient eligible population would capture beneficiaries with no primary care relationship to the Shared Savings Program ACO. We intend to allow Shared Savings Program ACOs to continue to report using the existing collection types to maintain stability of collection types during the transition to dQMs. If finalized, Medicare eCQMs would provide an additional optional collection type for reporting quality data for Shared Savings Program ACOs. Medicare eCQMs would provide ACOs the option to report electronically only on their assigned beneficiary population, easing the operational considerations as outlined in this section, and support those Shared Savings Program ACOs with the transition to dQMs. For these reasons, we believe that it is appropriate to establish Medicare eCQMs as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs only. We also anticipate that in the future, when FHIR-based reporting becomes mandatory, Shared Savings Program ACOs would be able to continue to use the FHIR-based digital specifications to report only on their assigned beneficiary population.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
), we encouraged ACOs to evaluate all quality reporting options to determine which collection type is most appropriate based on the ACO's unique composition and technical infrastructure. In addition to our proposal to allow ACOs the option to report quality data using the Medicare eCQMs collection type, for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, ACOs would have the option to report quality data using the all payer/all patient eCQMs/MIPS CQMs, and/or the Medicare CQMs collection types. Our long-term goal continues to be to support ACOs in the adoption of dQMs. We would monitor the reporting of quality data using the Medicare eCQMs collection type. To facilitate the reporting of Medicare eCQMs, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44155
), we proposed to amend the definition of “collection type” in § 414.1305 to include Medicare eCQMs as an available collection type in MIPS for ACOs that participate in the Shared Savings Program. Additionally, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (44049 and 44050), we proposed to establish MIPS data submission and data completeness criteria, in §§ 414.1335(a)(5) and 414.1340(e), respectively, pertaining to the Medicare eCQMs collection type for the MIPS quality performance category. We also proposed to define a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare eCQMs” at § 425.20 as a beneficiary identified for purposes of reporting Medicare eCQMs for Shared Savings Program ACOs participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare eCQMs), who is a beneficiary that is assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO under subpart E, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
).
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
), we proposed to revise § 414.1340(e) to establish the MIPS data completeness criteria threshold for the Medicare eCQMs collection type, in which Shared Savings Program ACOs that meet reporting requirements under the APP submitting quality measure data on Medicare eCQMs must submit data on at least 75 percent of the ACO's applicable beneficiaries eligible for the Medicare eCQM, as proposed to be defined at § 425.20, who meet the measure's denominator criteria for MIPS payment year 2029 and future MIPS payment years (PY 2027 and subsequent PYs).
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that to facilitate population-based activities related to improving health under the existing § 425.702(c)(1)(ii) and to aid Shared Savings Program ACOs in the process of patient matching and data aggregation necessary to report Medicare eCQMs, we would provide Shared Savings Program ACOs with a list of beneficiaries that are assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO and thus are eligible for Medicare eCQM reporting within the Shared Savings Program ACO (
91 FR 44049
). We anticipate that the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs would be shared with Shared Savings Program ACOs on a quarterly basis, beginning with Quarter 1 of PY 2027. We anticipate that the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs would be in the same format and delivery schedule as the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs that Shared Savings Program ACOs currently receive on a quarterly basis. The list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs would differ from the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs in that we would apply the eCQM specifications to generate the measure-specific indicators for the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs (unlike the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs which uses the Medicare CQM specifications to generate the measure-specific indicators). This new report would be delivered to Shared Savings Program ACOs via the Data Hub in the Shared Savings Program ACO Management System (
https://acoms.cms.gov
), but would not be included in the Shared Savings Program ACO's Quarterly Reports Package. The Quarter 4 list would include all beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs based on available claims data for encounters with dates of service from January 1 through December 31 and may be used as the final list for quality reporting. Like eCQMs, Medicare eCQMs would be reported end-to-end electronically. As such, we recognize that Shared Savings Program ACOs may have other technologically feasible means to identify beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs within the Shared Savings Program ACO or Shared Savings Program ACO participant TIN CEHRT. For this reason, we did not propose to require that Shared Savings Program ACOs use the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs to identify the universe of beneficiaries upon which the Shared Savings Program ACO would report Medicare eCQMs for an applicable PY; rather, the Quarter 4 list can be used as a resource to help Shared Savings Program ACOs identify beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQM reporting.

As part of our proposals for Shared Savings Program ACOs to report the Medicare eCQMs collection type for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, we proposed to revise the regulation text at §§ 425.20 and 425.512 as follows:
Under a new paragraph at § 425.20, we would define a beneficiary eligible for Medicare eCQMs as a beneficiary identified for purposes of reporting Medicare eCQMs for Shared Savings Program ACOs participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare eCQMs), who is a beneficiary that is assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO under subpart E of part 425.
Under § 425.512(a)(2)(iv), we would incorporate Medicare eCQMs into the existing quality performance standard policies for new Shared Savings Program ACOs. Under paragraph (a)(5)(iii)(C), we would also incorporate Medicare eCQMs into the existing policies that describe when a Shared Savings Program ACO would not meet the quality performance standard or the alternative quality performance standard.
We sought public comments on our proposals for Shared Savings Program ACOs to report the Medicare eCQMs collection type for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported our proposal to establish Medicare eCQMs as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
Commenters stated that they appreciated CMS' responsiveness to the challenges of multi-TIN data aggregation and all-payer population reporting. Many comments supported the additional flexibility a new collection type would provide and the reduction of burden provided by focusing on the ACOs' assigned beneficiary populations. A couple of comments expressed that the creation of the Medicare eCQMs collection type is an important interim step toward the transition to digital quality measurement and future all-payer models. A comment supported the Medicare eCQMs collection type as an option for ACOs that cannot readily aggregate data and encouraged CMS to treat this collection type as a foundation for outcome-based measures going forward and not only as a data aggregation solution.
Response:
We appreciate comments that support our proposal to establish Medicare eCQMs as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed the proposed effective date of the Medicare eCQMs collection type. A couple commenters stated that CMS should retain the existing three collection types and not add Medicare eCQMs as a fourth collection type for PY 2027. The comments noted that future inclusion of Medicare eCQMs should be done with appropriate lead time for implementation within EHRs. Another comment recommended that CMS delay implementation of the Medicare eCQMs collection type until the CY 2028 performance period to align the introduction of the Medicare eCQMs collection type with the start of the dQM transition period, or alternatively, prioritize finalizing and publishing dQM specifications rather than introducing an additional short-lived collection type for a single PY. A comment suggested CMS implement the Medicare eCQMs collection type after the necessary electronic workflows have been developed, tested, and made available.
Response:
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44048
and
44049
) that the Medicare eCQMs collection type was created to address concerns raised by Shared Savings Program ACOs and other interested parties related to reporting quality measures using the eCQMs collection type. We also stated that we believe the addition of Medicare eCQMs would support our efforts to transition to dQMs by supporting Shared Savings Program ACOs that want to report eCQMs but are not able to operationally report on all patient/all payer data due to data aggregation challenges.
We stated that we intend to allow Shared Savings Program ACOs to continue to report using the existing collection types to maintain stability of collection types during the transition to dQMs. Therefore, in addition to allowing ACOs the option to report quality data using the Medicare eCQMs collection type, for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, ACOs would have the option to report quality data using the all payer/all patient eCQMs/MIPS CQMs, and/or the Medicare CQMs collection types. Therefore, we believe that it is appropriate to establish the Medicare eCQMs collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs beginning in PY 2027 for those ACOs that could be ready and choose to report their quality data using this new collection type. We recognize that the Medicare eCQMs collection type may not be a suitable collection type for some ACOs at this time. Therefore, we encourage ACOs to evaluate all quality reporting options to determine which collection type is most appropriate based on the ACO's unique composition and technical infrastructure.
Regarding the comment that the Medicare eCQMs collection type would exist for a single PY, we note that we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44038
) that all quality reporting options for Shared Savings Program ACOs (that is, eCQMs, MIPS CQMs, Medicare CQMs, and Medicare eCQMs) would continue to be available during the 2-year transition period with FHIR-based reporting options that would begin in PY 2028. Therefore, at minimum, the Medicare eCQMs collection type would be available through PY 2029. Any changes to the availability of collection type quality reporting options would go through notice and comment rulemaking.

Comment:
A few commenters requested that CMS provide guidance in advance of when the Medicare eCQMs collection type becomes available. A commenter requested that CMS release updated QRDA III Implementation Guide specifications as early as possible to ensure vendors have sufficient development lead time. Another comment suggested CMS finalize quality specifications early enough for EHRs, registries, and ACOs to build and test before the PY. A commenter requested clarification regarding operational specifications for Medicare eCQMs, including whether they will differ from existing eCQM specifications, specifically regarding data extraction requirements, submission expectations, validation requirements, and audit processes.
Another commenter recommended that CMS identify, or commit to publishing, the specific technical specifications that will define the Medicare beneficiary-limited denominator for the Medicare eCQMs collection type. A couple of commenters noted concerns with QRDA I files and stated that without the ability to filter QRDA I files to a defined population, ACOs would need to extract large volumes of data and then filter down to an assigned beneficiary population. Response:
We acknowledge concerns related to the technical limitations of reporting Medicare eCQMs and recognize ACOs will have to develop these capabilities either in-house or through vendors. The Medicare eCQMs will follow the eCQM measure specifications; however, they will be reported on a different population. We will not be providing separate Medicare eCQM measure specifications. ACOs should use the eCQM measure specifications and report data on their assigned beneficiaries. The eCQM measure specifications for PY 2027 are available on the eCQI Resource Center website at
https://ecqi.healthit.gov/​
.
We also refer readers to
https://ecqi.healthit.gov/​ecqm-lifecycle
for an overview of the processes for measure use, continuing evaluation, and maintenance. The updated QRDA III Implementation Guide will be available after the release of this final rule.
ACOs will need to work in-house or with their vendors to determine the mechanism for identifying the beneficiary-limited denominator and any mechanism for which the CMS-provided beneficiary list is appropriately included in the ACO's application of the applicable measure specifications. If interoperability with specialty registries and infrastructure to filter QRDA I files is desired, ACOs will need to address this in-house or through vendors. Additional information on reporting Medicare eCQMs will be provided after the release of this final rule.
Comment:
A commenter noted that if CMS finalizes its proposal to introduce a distinguishing identifier for Medicare eCQM submissions, then implementing that identifier may require some development effort on the part of health IT vendors. The commenter noted that while they do not consider this to be a substantial burden, it is not without operational cost.
Response:
We appreciate the comment's concern. As stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44050
), to operationalize the reporting of the Medicare eCQMs collection type, specifically to distinguish between the submission of data for a Medicare eCQM from the submission of data for an eCQM to CMS, we will create and provide unique identifiers that are associated with each Medicare eCQM. These identifiers must be included in the submission files when reporting Medicare eCQMs beginning in PY 2027. Additional information on reporting Medicare eCQMs will be provided after the release of this final rule. We recognize that the Medicare eCQMs collection type may not be a suitable collection type for some ACOs at this time, and ACOs will have to develop capabilities either in-house or through vendors to report using the Medicare eCQMs collection type. Therefore, we encourage ACOs to evaluate all quality reporting options to determine which collection type is most appropriate based on the ACO's unique composition and technical infrastructure.
Comment:
A few comments recommended that CMS include Medicare eCQMs in the reporting incentive available for eCQMs and MIPS CQMs. A comment felt withholding the incentive from ACOs will slow uptake of the new collection type and the transition to digital quality measurement.
Response:
As stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44050
), we did not propose to add Medicare eCQMs to the eCQM/MIPS CQM reporting incentive described at § 425.512(a)(5)(i)(B)(2) for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs. We stated that the eCQM/MIPS CQM reporting incentive intends to provide an incentive to ACOs to report all payer/all patient eCQMs/MIPS CQMs while allowing them time to gauge their performance on the all payer/all patient eCQMs/MIPS CQMs. A Medicare eCQM is essentially an eCQM that is reported by a Shared Savings Program ACO on only the ACO's assigned beneficiaries, instead of its all payer/all patient population. Since Medicare eCQMs would include only the ACO's assigned beneficiaries, Medicare eCQMs are not a form of all payer/all patient reporting. As such, they are not included in the eCQM/MIPS CQM reporting incentive. In the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79105
), we declined to extend the reporting incentive to Medicare CQMs for the same reasons. We note that the alternative quality performance standard, which we finalized in the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
88 FR 69831
), would be applicable to ACOs that report Medicare eCQMs when those ACOs are otherwise eligible for scaled savings/losses.
Comment:
A commenter encouraged CMS to reconsider excluding Medicare eCQMs from the Complex Organization Adjustment noting that although Medicare eCQMs reduce the reporting population, they do not eliminate the complexity associated with electronic quality reporting, validation, submission, and ongoing quality improvement activities.
Response:
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
and
44050
), we stated that the Complex Organization Adjustment intends to account for the organizational complexities Shared Savings Program ACOs face when reporting all payer/all patient eCQMs. A Medicare eCQM is essentially an eCQM that is reported by a Shared Savings Program ACO on only the ACO's assigned beneficiaries, instead of its all payer/all patient population. Therefore, we believe that it is appropriate to not add Medicare eCQMs to the Complex Organization Adjustment.
Comment:
A couple of commenters encouraged CMS to maintain separate benchmarks for Medicare CQMs and Medicare eCQMs and noted that
(
printed page 71371)
separate benchmarks would better account for differences in data collections methodologies and support more appropriate performance assessment across reporting types. A commenter expressed concern that flat benchmarks would result in lower quality scores for Medicare eCQMs compared to Medicare CQMs and suggested that CMS use performance-period benchmarks for Medicare eCQMs until sufficient historical benchmark data are available to establish reliable historical benchmarks.
Response:
In the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98118
) regarding the use of flat benchmarks to score Medicare CQMs, we stated that flat benchmarks would allow ACOs with high scores to earn maximum or near maximum achievement points while allowing room for quality improvement and rewarding that improvement in subsequent years. Use of flat benchmarks also helps to ensure that ACOs with high-quality performance on a measure are not penalized as low performers. Like Medicare CQMs, the use of flat benchmarks to score Medicare eCQMs would also allow room for quality improvement while allowing ACOs with high scores to earn maximum or near maximum achievement points. Flat benchmarks would also mitigate the risk that MIPS would not be able to calculate performance period benchmarks for these measures in the APP Plus quality measure set, as MIPS benchmarking requires 20 submissions of at least 20 cases as the minimum standard for establishing a benchmark to reliably score measures (
81 FR 77277
). As stated at § 414.1380(b)(1)(ii), benchmarks are specific to each collection type. As such, Medicare CQMs and Medicare eCQMs will have separate flat benchmarks.
We are clarifying in this final rule that, for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, Table B-G5 lists the flat benchmarks for a non-inverse Medicare eCQM and Table B-G6 lists the flat benchmarks for an inverse Medicare eCQM. We believe the scales we are finalizing for Medicare CQMs in section III.G.3.c. of this final rule would also be appropriate for Medicare eCQMs since Medicare eCQMs will be a new collection type available to Shared Savings Program ACOs beginning in PY 2027 and, therefore, would not have data available to establish historical benchmarks and may not have enough submissions to establish a performance period benchmark.
We note that section 1899(b)(3)(C) of the Act directs that the Secretary shall establish quality performance standards to assess the quality of care furnished by ACOs and seek to improve the quality of care furnished by ACOs over time by specifying higher standards, new measures, or both for purposes of assessing such quality of care. Applying
(
printed page 71372)
flat benchmarks for a new collection type is consistent with our intent to improve quality of care furnished by ACOs over time. Medicare eCQMs are an optional collection type. Beginning in PY 2027, ACOs have the option to report quality data using multiple collection types, such as, eCQMs/MIPS CQMs/Medicare CQMs/Medicare eCQMs. We recognize that Medicare eCQMs may not be a suitable collection type for some ACOs. Therefore, we encourage ACOs to evaluate all quality reporting options to determine which collection type is most appropriate based on the ACO's unique composition and technical infrastructure. As stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
), we will monitor the reporting of quality data using the Medicare eCQMs collection type.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS apply benchmark changes prospectively rather than retroactively.
Response:
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44048
through
44050
), we proposed to establish the Medicare eCQMs as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs reporting the APP Plus quality measure set for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, and we also proposed that beginning with PY 2027, Medicare eCQMs would be scored using flat benchmarks. We are finalizing these policies as proposed, thus none of these policies will be applied retroactively.
Comment:
A commenter requested that Medicare eCQMs include a MIPS data completeness provision and that ACOs be required to submit data on at least 75 percent of applicable beneficiaries eligible for the measures.
Response:
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44049
), we proposed to revise § 414.1340(e) to establish the MIPS data completeness criteria threshold for the Medicare eCQMs collection type, in which Shared Savings Program ACOs that meet reporting requirements under the APP submitting quality measure data on Medicare eCQMs must submit data on at least 75 percent of the ACO's applicable beneficiaries eligible for the Medicare eCQM, as defined at § 425.20, who meet the measure's denominator criteria for MIPS payment year 2029 and future MIPS payment years (PY 2027 and subsequent PYs). We are finalizing the revisions to § 414.1340(e) as proposed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(d)(ii) of this final rule.
After consideration of public comments, in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(b) of this final rule, we are finalizing our proposal to establish Medicare eCQMs as a new collection type for Shared Savings Program ACOs reporting on the Medicare eCQMs (reporting quality data on beneficiaries eligible for Medicare eCQMs as finalized to be defined at § 425.20) within the APP Plus quality measure set.
To facilitate the reporting of Medicare eCQMs, in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(b) of this final rule, we are finalizing our proposal to amend the definition of “collection type” in § 414.1305 to include Medicare eCQMs as an available collection type in MIPS for ACOs that participate in the Shared Savings Program.
Additionally, we are finalizing our proposal to establish MIPS data submission and data completeness criteria, in §§ 414.1335(a)(5) and 414.1340(e), respectively, pertaining to the Medicare eCQMs collection type for the MIPS quality performance category, as discussed in sections IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(v) and IV.A.4.d.(1)(d)(ii), respectively, of this final rule.
We are also finalizing our proposal to define a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare eCQMs” at § 425.20 as a beneficiary identified for purposes of reporting Medicare eCQMs for Shared Savings Program ACOs participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare eCQMs), who is a beneficiary that is assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO under subpart E, in part 425.
In section IV.A.4.d.(1)(d)(ii) of this final rule, we are finalizing our proposal to revise § 414.1340(e) to establish the MIPS data completeness criteria threshold for the Medicare eCQMs collection type, in which Shared Savings Program ACOs that meet reporting requirements under the APP submitting quality measure data on Medicare eCQMs must submit data on at least 75 percent of the ACO's applicable beneficiaries eligible for the Medicare eCQM, as proposed to be defined at § 425.20, who meet the measure's denominator criteria for MIPS payment year 2029 and future MIPS payment years (PY 2027 and subsequent PYs).
We are finalizing in III.G.3.f of this final rule that, as proposed, there would be five eCQMs/MIPS CQMs/Medicare CQMs/Medicare eCQMs in the APP Plus quality measure set for Shared Savings Program ACOs for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
Diabetes: Glycemic Status Assessment Greater Than 9% (Quality ID: 001);
Breast Cancer Screening (Quality ID: 112);

Controlling High Blood Pressure (Quality ID: 236).
ACOs would have the option to report the five Medicare eCQMs, or a combination of eCQMs/MIPS CQMs/Medicare CQMs/Medicare eCQMs, to meet the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirement at § 425.510(b) and the quality performance standard at § 425.512(a)(5).
In section IV.B.1.c.(2) of this final rule and in the regulations at § 414.1380(b)(1)(ii)(G)(1), we are finalizing, as proposed, that beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, measures of the Medicare eCQMs collection type use flat benchmarks.
As part of finalizing our proposals for Shared Savings Program ACOs to report the Medicare eCQMs collection type for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, we are finalizing the proposed revisions to the regulation text at §§ 425.20 and 425.512 as follows:
Under a new paragraph at § 425.20, we are defining a beneficiary eligible for Medicare eCQMs as a beneficiary identified for purposes of reporting Medicare eCQMs for Shared Savings Program ACOs participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare eCQMs), who is a beneficiary that is assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO under subpart E of this part.
Under § 425.512(a)(2)(iv), we are incorporating Medicare eCQMs into the existing quality performance standard policies for new Shared Savings Program ACOs. Under paragraph (a)(5)(iii)(C), we would also incorporate Medicare eCQMs into the existing policies that describe when a Shared Savings Program ACO would not meet the quality performance standard or the alternative quality performance standard.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed for Shared Savings Program ACOs to report the Medicare eCQMs collection type for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
(4) Revising the Definition of a “Beneficiary Eligible for Medicare CQMs”
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44050
), we stated that in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49797
through
49803
), we finalized the revisions to the definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” at § 425.20 effective January 1, 2025. Specifically, beginning with PY 2025 and subsequent PYs, we revised the definition to require, in (1)(ii)(B) of the definition, “at least one primary care
(
printed page 71373)
service with a date of service during the applicable performance year from a Shared Savings Program ACO professional who is a primary care physician or who has one of the specialty designations included in § 425.402(c), or who is a physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist.” We stated that the revised definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” would reduce Shared Savings Program ACOs' burden in the patient matching necessary to report Medicare CQMs because the list of “beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs” would have greater overlap with the list of beneficiaries that are assignable to a Shared Savings Program ACO. We stated that we believed our revised definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” would substantially address Shared Savings Program ACOs' and interested parties' concerns by better aligning the definitions and clarifying which beneficiaries' data to use for quality data reporting through Medicare CQMs. In the CY 2026 PFS final rule, some commenters suggested that CMS require Medicare CQMs be reported for “attributed” beneficiaries only (
90 FR 49800
). In response, CMS noted that Medicare CQMs are designed to help Shared Savings Program ACOs address challenges with aggregating patient data required to report the all payer/all patient MIPS CQMs and eCQMs by defining a population of beneficiaries that is broader than the assigned population but exists within the all payer/all patient MIPS CQM specification.
We also stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44050
) that since the publication of the CY 2026 PFS final rule and implementation of the revised definition aligning with assignable beneficiaries, we have heard from Shared Savings Program ACOs and other interested parties that the current definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” continues to cause confusion regarding which beneficiaries to use for quality data reporting. Specifically, Shared Savings Program ACOs have inquired about the differences between the current list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs (which is broader than an ACO's assigned population) and the Shared Savings Program ACO's assigned and assignable populations. As discussed in the CY 2026 final rule, an analysis using PY 2024 data noted an average 85 percent overlap between a Shared Savings Program ACO's list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs and the list of beneficiaries assignable to the Shared Savings Program ACO (
90 FR 49799
). Moreover, we have heard from Shared Savings Program ACOs that the current definition aligning with assignable beneficiaries continues to create burden in patient matching, data aggregation and quality reporting for Shared Savings Program ACOs that elect to report Medicare CQMs. Lastly, Shared Savings Program ACOs have expressed that the current definition of “beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs” that aligns with assignable beneficiaries includes beneficiaries for whom the Shared Savings Program ACO does not readily have data.
Considering the concerns raised by Shared Savings Program ACOs and other interested parties with reporting Medicare CQMs, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44051
), we proposed to revise the definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” at § 425.20 for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, to align with the population of beneficiaries assigned to the ACO.
We also stated that we implemented Medicare CQMs in PY 2024 to help some Shared Savings Program ACOs build the infrastructure, skills, knowledge and expertise necessary to report all payer/all patient MIPS CQMs and eCQMs (
91 FR 44051
). The confusion that Shared Savings Program ACOs have expressed about the differences between the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs and a Shared Savings Program ACO's assigned populations have complicated the process for Shared Savings Program ACOs to meaningfully implement Medicare CQMs for this purpose. Our proposed revision would build upon the revisions finalized in the CY 2026 PFS final rule and further refine and align the definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” to correspond to a Shared Savings Program ACO's assigned beneficiary list to continue to address Shared Savings Program ACOs' challenges with patient data aggregation. The proposed change to the definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs intends to better support these Shared Savings Program ACOs in the transition to digital quality measurement and to eliminate an unintended barrier that Shared Savings Program ACOs have experienced in reporting Medicare CQMs, which have persisted after the revision of the definition in the CY 2026 PFS final rule to align with assignable beneficiaries.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44051
), we stated that the Shared Savings Program relies on primary care-based assignment, and the APP Plus quality measure set is primary care-based. Our proposals to use the Shared Savings Program ACO's assigned beneficiary population for the Medicare CQMs collection type beginning in PY 2027 would hold Shared Savings Program ACOs accountable for the quality of care for only the beneficiaries assigned to them and align with the voluntary risk they have undertaken to coordinate beneficiaries' care. Also, focusing on care provided by primary care providers would be a reasonable approach that addresses concerns with data aggregation and specialist participation. Similarly, we have heard from Shared Savings Program ACOs that the current definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” is a detriment to Shared Savings Program ACOs meeting the MIPS data completeness requirement described at § 414.1340. As such, the proposed change aims to support Shared Savings Program ACOs in meeting the MIPS data completeness requirement by tethering the universe of beneficiaries that a Shared Savings Program ACO is required to report on for Medicare CQMs to the universe of beneficiaries that have a primary care relationship with the Shared Savings Program ACO as demonstrated through the beneficiaries' assignment to the Shared Savings Program ACO. We anticipate that Shared Savings Program ACOs that choose to report Medicare CQMs would experience fewer barriers in aggregating the applicable numerator and denominator data for beneficiaries that are assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO and, as a result, would be better positioned to meet the MIPS data completeness requirement described at § 414.1340.
As stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44051
), in the CY 2024 PFS final rule, we finalized a new paragraph at § 425.702(c)(1)(iii) to share aggregate reports with Shared Savings Program ACOs with the aim of facilitating population-based activities related to the improvement of health through quality measurement using Medicare CQMs and to aid Shared Savings Program ACOs in the process of patient matching and data aggregation necessary to report Medicare CQMs (
88 FR 79099
). It was necessary at that time to revise the regulation text at § 425.702 because the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs, as finalized for PY 2024, was broader than the universe of beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO. As discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (91 FR

The sharing of aggregate reports for beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO is regulated at § 425.702(c)(1)(ii). As such, since the list of beneficiaries eligible for Medicare CQMs would align with the universe of beneficiaries assigned to the Shared Savings Program ACO under this proposal, it is appropriate to also propose to sunset the regulation at § 425.702(c)(1)(iii) beginning in PY 2027.
