Comment:
All commenters were supportive of our proposal to revise the definition of a “beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs” to align with the population of beneficiaries assigned to the ACO. A couple of commenters thanked CMS for being responsive to concerns from interested parties. A couple of commenters noted that the policy helps address ACOs' challenges with meeting the MIPS data completeness requirements by addressing long-standing quality reporting issues, alleviating the reporting burden, encouraging ACOs to remain in the program and addressing ACO concerns with data aggregation.
Some commenters noted that the policy focuses quality measurement on the population for whom the ACO is actually accountable which directly addresses previous concerns with assessing ACOs' quality based on patients not managed by the ACO for purposes of determining shared savings and losses and stated the policy aligns with the beneficiaries for whom ACOs are responsible under shared savings and shared loss calculations. Commenters noted that the revised definition would better reflect primary care relationships and is more clinically coherent. A commenter noted that the revised definition more accurately reflects ACO performance, strengthens the alignment between quality measurement and accountability, and reduces unnecessary reporting burden relative to measuring performance among beneficiaries outside of the ACO's attributed population which may introduce factors beyond the ACO's ability to influence. Response:
Section 1871(e)(1)(A)(ii) of the Act prohibits the Secretary from
(

e. Revising the Shared Savings Program Scoring Policy for Excluded APP Plus Measures and APP Plus Measures That Lack a Benchmark
(1) Background
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44052
and
44053
), we stated that in the CY 2024 PFS final rule given that the Shared Savings Program does not determine which quality measures are excluded and lack a benchmark and that Shared Savings Program ACOs do not have a choice of measures that they can report under the APP, we do not want to adversely impact shared savings determinations for events outside the Shared Savings Program ACOs' control, such as in the event a measure is excluded or does not have a benchmark (
88 FR 79122
and
79123
). Therefore, we finalized a scoring policy for excluded APP measures and APP measures that lack a benchmark at § 425.512(a)(7). We sought public comments on our proposed revisions to the Shared Savings Program scoring policy at § 425.512(a)(7).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A couple of comments supported our proposal to revise the scoring policy for excluded APP Plus measures and APP Plus measures that lack a benchmark. Specifically, comments supported our proposal to increase the number of measures from one measure to four or more measures that would need to be excluded from MIPS in a given performance year for the policy to apply. A comment noted how the revisions create a more balanced and predictable approach to quality scoring while reducing unnecessary complexity within the APP Plus quality measure set. The comment noted that these changes should improve consistency, reduce administrative burden, and allow ACOs to focus resources on quality improvement activities that directly benefit patients. A comment noted that the use of flat benchmarks to score Medicare CQMs and Medicare eCQMs mitigate the need for the scoring policy.
Response:
We appreciate comments that support our proposed revisions to the Shared Savings Program scoring policy at § 425.512(a)(7) for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, such that it would apply only if the Shared Savings Program ACO's MIPS quality performance category score is calculated on less than five measures for a given PY. We also appreciate comments that support our proposal that the current scoring policy at § 425.512(a)(7) would no longer apply when at least one of the required measures in the APP Plus quality measure set does not have a benchmark for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs.
In response to the comment that the use of flat benchmarks to score Medicare CQMs and Medicare eCQMs mitigates the need for the scoring policy, we note that there are still circumstances when a Medicare CQM or Medicare eCQM could be excluded, such as a measure that is submitted, if applicable, and impacted by significant changes or errors prior to the applicable data submission deadline as described at § 414.1380(b)(1)(vii)(A).
Comment:
A comment opposed the proposed revisions to the scoring policy for excluded APP Plus measures; specifically, the proposal to increase the measure threshold. The comment noted that reducing the APP Plus quality measure set to eight measures would increase the weight of each individual measure in an ACO's quality score.

Other comments conceptually agreed with the proposal but provided alternative suggestions for the measure threshold. Several comments expressed concerns that ACOs could lose scoring policy protections when one, two, or three ACO-reported measures are excluded, despite such exclusions being outside the ACO's control. The comments noted that, as proposed, a Shared Savings Program ACO could have three of five ACO-reported measures excluded and be scored based on the two administrative claims-based measures, CAHPS for MIPS survey, and the two remaining ACO-reported measures. A few comments further noted that ACO members have expressed challenges with the administrative claims' measures and the CAHPS for MIPS survey given ACOs do not receive performance data on them during the performance year to conduct improvement efforts in a timely fashion. The comments expressed it would not be appropriate to assess an ACO's quality score in this scenario.
Several comments suggested that CMS modify the proposal such that the measure exclusion component of the current policy would apply when three or more of the ACO-reported measures in the APP Plus quality measure set are excluded for a given performance year. A comment recommended CMS retain the existing one-measure trigger at § 425.512(a)(7) rather than raising it to four, citing that with a smaller measure set each measure carries proportionally more weight in an ACO's quality score.
Response:
Regarding comments that express concerns with potentially having the two administrative claims-based measures (Quality ID: 479 Hospital-Wide, 30-day, All Cause Unplanned Readmission (HWR) Rate for MIPS Eligible Clinician Groups, and Quality ID: 484 Clinician and Clinician Group Risk-standardized Hospital Admission Rates for Patients with Multiple Chronic Conditions) and Quality ID: 321 CAHPS for MIPS survey comprise additional weight in their quality scores and the challenges the comments expressed with these measures, we note that these measures are well-established aspects of assessing a Shared Savings Program ACO's quality performance. Specifically, in the CY 2021 PFS final rule (
85 FR 84726
), when establishing the APP quality measure set for Shared Savings Program ACOs, we explained that the measures included in the APP were selected because they align with the Meaningful Measures framework, focus on management of chronic health conditions that are high priority and highly prevalent among Medicare beneficiaries assigned to ACOs, and are broadly applicable to the primary care population and population health goals associated with the Shared Savings Program. We explained that the administrative claims-based measures promote effective communication and coordination of care and are appropriate measures of ACO quality performance (
85 FR 84726
). In addition, we stated that we continue to value the patient voice and believe it should play a significant role in quality scoring, and that inclusion of the CAHPS for MIPS survey measure preserves the relevance of patient experience in the assessment of ACO quality performance.
Accordingly, we continue to believe that the two administrative claims-based measures in the APP Plus quality measure set and the CAHPS for MIPS survey measure are well-established quality metrics that are appropriate to assess ACO's quality of care; therefore, these measures, along with the remaining two ACO-reported measures in the comments' scenario, would capture sufficient data to represent the ACO's quality performance. Furthermore, the scenarios described in the comments would be very rare and would necessitate that a large number of measures be excluded from MIPS in a given PY.
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44052
) that we believe that our proposed revisions to § 425.512(a)(7) would result in a more accurate assessment of Shared Savings Program ACOs' quality performance, as each measure in the five-measure minimum threshold would contribute a reasonable weight (20 percent) to the Shared Savings Program ACO's MIPS quality performance category score. However, if there are fewer than five measures available in a given PY, Shared Savings Program ACOs would not risk losing the ability to meet the quality performance standard to be eligible to earn maximum shared savings, and for Shared Savings Program ACOs in the ENHANCED track, avoid maximum shared losses, due to issues with the measures outside of their control, while allowing CMS to better evaluate ACOs' quality performance and appropriately determine shared savings eligibility based on quality of care.
In response to the suggestion from the comments that the exclusion component of the current policy be applied when three or more of the ACO-reported measures in the APP Plus quality measure set are excluded for a given performance year, we note that—while there are eight measures included in the APP Plus quality measure set for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs (as finalized in section III.G.f. of this final rule), we continue to believe that the less than five measure threshold for the application of this policy remains appropriate since it ensures that the ACO is otherwise scored on a sufficient number of quality measures that accurately reflect the ACO's quality performance. We further note that our intent is for this policy to function as a relief mechanism to address rare circumstances when four or more measures are excluded from the APP Plus quality measure set by MIPS. We disagree with, and are rejecting, the comments' suggestions to lower the threshold for the application of this policy to three or more measures since we do not believe that this suggestion would result in a more accurate assessment of the Shared Savings Program ACOs' quality performance.

4. Shared Savings Program Certified Electronic Health Record Technology (CEHRT) Use Requirements
a. Background
Section 1899(b)(3)(D) of the Act authorizes the Secretary to incorporate reporting requirements and incentive payments from section 1848 of the Act into the Shared Savings Program, such as requirements and incentive payments related to electronic prescribing and electronic health records. The statute also authorizes the Secretary to use alternative criteria for determining whether to make such incentive payments.
Section 1833(z)(2)(C)(iii)(II)(bb) of the Act (as amended by the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA)) generally requires Advanced Alternative Payment Models (Advanced APMs) to require the use of CEHRT. Under this authority, we have codified Advanced APM CEHRT use criteria at
42 CFR 414.1415(a)
. We have incorporated requirements related to the adoption and use of CEHRT in the Shared Savings Program regulations. We have adopted a definition of CEHRT in § 425.20 that cross references the
(
printed page 71383)
Quality Payment Program's definition of CEHRT (§ 414.1305).
For the Shared Savings Program, CMS updated the CEHRT definition in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79309
). Under paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition in § 414.1305, CEHRT currently means EHR technology (which could include multiple technologies) certified by the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) under the ONC Health IT Certification Program as meeting the 2015 Edition Base EHR definition, or subsequent Base EHR definition (set forth at
45 CFR 170.102
), and a designated set of health IT certification criteria adopted or updated in
45 CFR 170.315
that are determined applicable for the APM.
In the context of health IT, the secure exchange, access, and use of electronic health information supports better informed decision making and a more efficient healthcare system.
[
296

Interoperability (as defined at
45 CFR 170.102
) enables this secure exchange and access. To this end, CMS intends to utilize approaches based on the HL7® (Health Level 7) Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources® (FHIR)
[

standard to support the exchange of quality information, consistent with CMS' digital quality measurement initiatives, as described in the FHIR RFI in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule (
90 FR 32710
through
32715
). FHIR is a widely used application program interface (API)-focused standard used to represent and exchange health information maintained by the standards development organization HL7. ONC adopts the FHIR standard (currently FHIR R4) as well as FHIR implementation guides for different API use cases in
45 CFR 170.215
, and incorporates these standards into certification criteria for health IT.

Specifically, we codified that beginning with PY 2019, and in subsequent years, for ACOs in a track that did not meet the financial risk standard to be an Advanced APM (for example, ACOs participating under BASIC track Levels A through D), the ACO was required to certify that 50 percent of the ACO's eligible clinicians used CEHRT to document and communicate clinical care to their patients or other healthcare providers. For ACOs in a track that met the financial risk standard to be an Advanced APM (for example, ACOs participating under BASIC track Level E or the ENHANCED track), the ACO was required to certify that the percentage of eligible clinicians participating in the ACO that use CEHRT to document and communicate clinical care to their patients or other healthcare providers met or exceeded the threshold established under the Quality Payment Program at § 414.1415(a)(1). Under this requirement (§ 425.506(f)(2)), for PY 2019 through PY 2024, 75 percent of eligible clinicians were required to use CEHRT to document and communicate clinical care to their patients or healthcare providers (§ 414.1415(a)(1)(i)). ACOs have expressed confusion about MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category reporting requirements, exclusions, and exceptions. b. Simplifying Shared Savings Program CEHRT Use Requirements
As we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we believe that reducing burden for reporting CEHRT use will free ACO resources to focus on meaningful advancement toward digital exchange of health information, including digital quality measurement. As noted previously in this section, commenters on the Request for Information: Deregulation asked that we recognize ACO use of FHIR technologies and that we simplify Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. We believe that these suggestions would advance FHIR-based digital quality reporting by giving credit for incremental advances toward digital quality reporting (
91 FR 44059
).
We explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that, in response to the concerns and suggestions detailed previously in this section and in line with CMS' priorities to reduce burden and promote FHIR-based digital quality reporting and exchange of health information, we were proposing to sunset, beginning with PY 2027, the requirements at § 425.507(a) for Shared Savings Program ACO participants, ACO provider/suppliers, and ACO professionals that are MIPS eligible clinicians, Qualifying APM Participants, or Partial Qualifying APM Participants to report all MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category measures and requirements and to earn a performance category score for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category at the individual, group, virtual group, or APM entity level (
91 FR 44059
). Accordingly, we also proposed to sunset the associated exclusions that complement this requirement at § 425.507(b) (
91 FR 44059
). We proposed to replace the requirement in § 425.507(a) with different options for ACOs to meet CEHRT use requirements for the Shared Savings Program, described in further detail in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44059
).
We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that, as Shared Savings Program ACOs cover 12.6 million beneficiaries, served by over 700,000 participating clinicians and facilities,
[
301
]
we believe that a shift to FHIR-based digital quality reporting and exchange of health information at this scale would meaningfully advance care coordination and quality improvement. We expressed our further belief that reducing the burden of Shared Savings Program participation could lead to increased program participation from ACOs and ACO professionals, which would magnify the impact, moving even more clinicians toward meaningful use of EHR technology to improve care for beneficiaries (
91 FR 44059
).
We explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that, to encourage widespread adoption of FHIR-based transmission of clinical data, enable bi-directional exchange of clinical data across practices within ACOs, and support the capture of robust clinical quality information, we were proposing, in § 425.507(c), that for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs, to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement, ACOs would be required to perform at least one of three allowable activities (
91 FR 44059
). In summary, they are:
(1) Completely report at least one of the five ACO-reported measures in the APP Plus quality measure set through the eCQMs collection type or the proposed Medicare eCQMs collection type (discussed in section III.G.3.d.(3) of this final rule) using CEHRT; OR
(2) Attest to the ACO's use of FHIR capabilities to support reporting of at least one of the five ACO-reported measures in the APP Plus quality measure set using CEHRT (section IV.A.4.b.(2) of this final rule contains measures in the APP Plus quality measure set that are reportable by ACOs in PY 2027); OR
(3) Select and attest to one of the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use metrics, which are based on a subset of MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category measures, and which may be updated annually if there are changes.
We also proposed to sunset existing public reporting requirements at § 425.308(b)(9) and proposed to add a new section at § 425.308(b)(11), which would require ACOs to publicly report which of the allowable CEHRT use options proposed previously in this section they elected to perform to meet CEHRT use requirements for the Shared Savings Program for PY 2027 and subsequent PYs (
91 FR 44059
).
(1) Meeting Shared Savings Program CEHRT Use Requirement by Reporting at Least One ACO-Reported Measure Through the eCQMs or Medicare eCQMs Collection Types
As discussed earlier in this section, previous commenters have asked that CMS recognize efforts that ACOs are already undertaking to advance CEHRT use, without the need for additional reporting or attestation. Clinical quality measure reporting helps identify areas for potential care improvement, and use of CEHRT to report quality of care is a step toward bi-directional exchange of health information and digital quality measurement.

As discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44062

We also noted that an additional source of confusion is the requirement to report on behalf of all participants when an ACO reports at the APM entity level, including participants who would have been excluded or have received special status for reporting purposes when reporting at the individual or group level. We explained that, similarly, because QPs do not receive MIPS scores or payment adjustments, the requirement that QPs report the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category and earn a performance category score is a burden unique to the Shared Savings Program Promoting Interoperability requirements. ACOs have also reported incidents of practices included on the ACO's Participant Agreement closing throughout the year, which requires the ACO to report on behalf of groups with whom contact may be difficult. We noted that given this identified challenge, we no longer believe it is reasonable to require ACOs to report on every ACO provider and supplier in the ACO. We stated that we recognize and have been reminded by interested parties that participation in an ACO itself represents a commitment to coordinating care. (i) ACO Electronic Prescribing: An ACO could attest “Yes,” if, during the PY, at least one permissible prescription was written by at least one ACO provider or supplier in each of the ACO's participant TINs, and the prescription was transmitted electronically using CEHRT. In addition to the allowable exclusions from Shared Savings Program CEHRT use attestation discussed later in this section, ACOs choosing to attest to this metric would be permitted to exclude from their assessment any ACO participant TIN whose ACO providers and suppliers wrote fewer than 100 total permissible prescriptions during the PY. Similar to the MIPS e-Prescribing measure, a prescription would be defined as the authorization by an ACO provider or supplier to a pharmacist to dispense a drug that the pharmacist wouldn't dispense to the patient without such authorization. (6) No Impact on Current Shared Savings Program Quality or MIPS Scoring Policies or Process
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we stated that the proposed options for Shared Savings Program ACOs to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement will not change the existing scoring methodology for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. This means that, regardless of which of the three activities (or which option within their selected activity) ACOs choose to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT requirement, the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category reporting requirements for MIPS eligible clinicians participating in an ACO will remain unaffected. Additionally, an ACO performing any of the three CEHRT use requirement activities will not impact an ACO's quality score for purposes of determining the quality performance standard. For example, an ACO may choose to report an eCQM to meet the Shared Savings Program's ACO CEHRT use requirement; however, the eCQM will not necessarily be included in the MIPS quality performance category score as determined under § 414.1380. If an ACO reports multiple collection types for a given measure, including eCQMs, scoring is based on the highest scoring collection type which may not be eCQMs. Therefore, reporting the eCQM to meet the CEHRT use requirement may or may not contribute to the final quality performance score. In this example, even if the eCQM submission was not included in the ACO's MIPS quality performance category score as determined under § 414.1380, the ACO's complete reporting of the measure using the eCQMs collection type would satisfy the Shared Savings Program's CEHRT use requirement. Similarly, if an ACO uses FHIR technology to completely report a measure in the APP Plus measure set and attests to having done so, for the purpose of meeting the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement, the requirement will be met, regardless of whether that measure submission is used to calculate the ACO's MIPS quality performance category score under § 414.1380. By extension, in this example, an ACO's quality score for the purposes of determining shared savings as calculated under § 425.512 would be unaffected. The ACO's MIPS quality performance category score is an aggregate of the highest measure-level scores submitted by the ACO. However, submissions that do not contribute to an ACO's final MIPS quality performance category score are still eligible for purposes of meeting the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement (
91 FR 44066
).

c. Request for Information on Applying Electronic Prior Authorization Measures to Shared Savings Program ACOs
In section IV.A.4.d.(4) of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we included proposals on the use of electronic prior authorization measures in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Specifically, in that section of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, we proposed to (1) change the Electronic Prior Authorization measure from a required measure to a bonus measure for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year and a required measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year and (2) require a new measure, Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs, that requires requesting prior authorization for at least one prescription drug electronically using CEHRT (
91 FR 44066
). This measure would be required for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year.
We sought feedback on the use of electronic prior authorization by ACOs that participate in the Shared Savings Program. Specifically, we sought comment on the following potential future changes:
Requiring the use of specific FHIR-enabled Health IT Modules within CEHRT to complete at least one prior authorization request and determination for at least one medical item or service during the performance period or allowing it to be an option for meeting Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements beginning with the CY 2028 performance year.
Creating a new, ACO-specific electronic prior authorization measure to require use of specific FHIR-enabled health IT modules within CEHRT to complete at least one prior authorization request and determination for at least one prescription drug during the performance period, beginning with the CY 2028 performance year.
Considerations CMS should take into account, in developing electronic prior authorization measures to apply to Shared Savings Program ACOs.
We received public comments in response to our request for comment related to potential future policies for ACO use of electronic prior authorization and will take them into consideration for potential future rulemaking on this topic.
The following is a summary of the comments we received on our proposals related to Shared Savings Program CEHRT use and our responses.
Comment:
Most commenters expressed support for the three proposed new options for ACOs to meet CEHRT use requirements, and several of these commenters expressed strong support. Commenters stated that the proposals would simplify CEHRT requirements, provide ACOs with greater flexibility to meet those requirements, and reduce unnecessary burden on ACOs and their healthcare providers. Of the commenters who stated the proposals would reduce burden, several noted that the proposals account for operational complexities such as those related to having multiple participating health centers, diverse EHR environments, multiple TINs, or large clinically integrated networks. One of those commenters indicated that the proposed CEHRT requirements would reduce burden without weakening accountability, and several added that the simplified requirements would account for these complexities while maintaining an expectation for electronic health information exchange or meaningful connection to electronic quality measurement. A commenter praised the proposals as a meaningful step away from development of EHRs for measurement and reporting rather than clinician and patient needs, and several supported the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options' alignment with quality measurement initiatives and progress toward digital quality measurement.
A few commenters supported that two of the proposed policies allow ACO-level attestation instead of requiring ACOs to satisfy requirements they stated were designed primarily for individual clinicians or groups.
Some commenters specifically supported the proposed availability of multiple options to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, citing their belief that these varied pathways would accommodate different types of organizations or those with differing levels of technical readiness. Several commenters also expressed support for specific proposed options within those we proposed for ACOs to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. Several of these supported the option to leverage quality reporting through eCQMs or Medicare eCQMs collection types to also satisfy Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, and some commenters specifically expressed support for the FHIR attestation option.
A commenter supported the proposed CEHRT use metrics, stating their belief that bi-directional exchange across the practices and systems responsible for a population can improve coordination while reducing duplicative reporting. A commenter supported the inclusion of the Health Information Exchange attestation option as one of the three ACO CEHRT use metrics.
Several commenters also supported the proposed exclusions for Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics, which would allow qualifying participant TINs to be excluded under applicable special-status or hardship criteria without requiring advance CMS approval.
Several commenters specifically expressed support for the proposal to retire the current requirement that ACOs report the full set of MIPS Promoting Interoperability measures and activities, citing that they are burdensome, pose challenges for ACOs with differing compositions, systems, or capabilities, or that they served as a barrier to Shared Savings Program participation. Some of these commenters specifically expressed support for CMS' efforts to ensure that small, independent, or rural practices can participate in the Shared Savings Program, with one stating that the proposals restore trust, and another expressing appreciation for proposed movement away from requiring all Shared Savings Program ACO providers and suppliers to report MIPS promoting interoperability, including those in advanced APM tracks who would be otherwise exempt from MIPS.
Response:
We appreciate the statements in support of our proposals. We agree with commenters that the proposed options recognize operational complexities and the various compositions of ACOs and would reduce burden for ACO providers and suppliers and ACOs, align with the movement toward digital quality measurement, and promote better use of EHRs to meet provider and patient needs. We appreciate comments that the proposals remove an administrative obstacle for small practices to join ACOs.
(
printed page 71394)
Comment:
Several commenters who supported the proposals added recommendations about future implementation. Several of these commenters suggested that we align future CEHRT use requirements with other federal programs, including Innovation Center models such as ACO REACH, with one of these suggesting that ONC be the enforcement authority. The commenter suggested that alignment across programs would benefit organizations transitioning between value-based care models. A couple of commenters requested that CMS retain multiple pathways as proposed rather than narrowing them in the future or requiring ACOs to perform all three of the proposed pathways. These commenters suggested narrowing options or creating a cumulative requirement would preclude some organizations that exchange information interoperably from being able to meet the requirements or would recreate burden similar to our existing requirements.
A commenter suggested that future expansion of FHIR-based requirements should depend on demonstrated real-world readiness and reasonable implementation cost, and another recommended that CMS continue developing standards that integrate necessary data with appropriate safeguards. A couple of commenters addressed the future of the proposed FHIR attestation pathway, with one expressing hope that the FHIR attestation pathway would be “genuinely available” in practice and another encouraging CMS to keep the FHIR attestation pathway available on an ongoing basis.
A couple of commenters requested that CMS make the option for ACOs to attest that one ACO provider or supplier per participant TIN completed the activity required by the proposed CEHRT use metrics an initial requirement, rather than the endpoint.
Response:
We appreciate comments regarding future implementation of Shared Savings Program CEHRT use policies. With regard to the suggestion that we align future Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements with other federal reporting programs or Innovation Center models, with ONC serving as the enforcement authority, we agree with the value in alignment and note that we coordinate with ONC, which oversees the ONC Health IT Certification Program. We note that ONC directly regulates certified health IT and health IT developers as part of the ONC Health IT Certification Program rather than healthcare providers (unless the healthcare provider is also a developer of certified health IT). The Shared Savings Program currently aligns quality reporting requirements with MIPS, and we intend to maintain that alignment to the extent it is practicable. As we explained the CY 2021 PFS proposed rule, using a single methodology to measure quality performance under both the Shared Savings Program and MIPS would allow ACOs to better focus on increasing the value of healthcare, improving care, and engaging patients (
85 FR 50231
). We acknowledge that our proposed CEHRT use requirements do not fully align with MIPS. This is intentional and is based on our experience with ACO challenges in ensuring that all of their applicable ACO participants reported MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category requirements. The proposed ACO CEHRT use metric attestation option includes three metrics that align with three of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category measures. We do not believe that aligning with Innovation Center models' CEHRT use requirements is necessarily appropriate for the Shared Savings Program, as these models are testing innovative approaches to reducing costs and improving or maintaining quality for a time-limited period. We proposed CEHRT use options that we believe reflect concrete steps toward broader FHIR-based digital quality measurement and health information exchange. We believe that our proposals will meaningfully advance FHIR based exchange of health information with minimal burden to ACOs.
With regard to comments suggesting we retain multiple pathways for ACOs to meet CEHRT use requirements, we proposed three options to give ACOs more opportunities and flexibility to meet CEHRT requirements. Should we consider changes to this approach in the future, we would make any potential future changes to Shared Savings Program CEHRT use policies through notice and comment rulemaking.
We will continue to consider opportunities to align Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements with other CMS programs and implementation timelines and consider how best to preserve flexibility in implementation. With regard to the suggestions that future expansion of CEHRT use requirements be dependent on real world readiness and that we continue to integrate necessary data with safeguards, we appreciate the comments and will continue to monitor CEHRT use uptake and advancements to progress ACO CEHRT use along with broader CMS efforts.
With regard to the comments on the FHIR attestation option, as discussed in more detail later in this section, we are finalizing this option as proposed. The option will be available to ACOs in PY 2027. As we advance efforts and requirements for digital quality reporting via FHIR, we would propose any changes to available CEHRT use options through future notice and comment rulemaking to ensure these options align with other requirements for the Shared Savings Program. We will provide additional instructions for ACOs that choose to utilize that option in advance of the CEHRT use reporting period, which we stated we anticipate would follow the quality reporting window in the first quarter after the performance year (
91 FR 44061
). We will continue to consider opportunities to align Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements with other CMS programs and implementation timelines and consider how best to preserve flexibility in implementation.
With regard to the recommendation that the option for ACOs to attest that at least one ACO provider or supplier billing under each ACO participant TIN completed the action required by the proposed CEHRT use metrics serve as an initial threshold rather than the endpoint, we believe the requirements we are finalizing establish an appropriate standard for demonstrating ACO use of CEHRT at this time, while maintaining flexibility and limiting additional reporting and implementation burden. We are not adopting additional exchange or participation thresholds at this time.
Comment:
A commenter encouraged CMS to remove the Promoting Interoperability requirement altogether, stating that it creates administrative burden without added value, particularly for small practices that may choose to leave the program, and is unnecessary given ACOs' ongoing efforts to modernize and integrate EHR technology into their workflows.
Response:
We believe the commenter is referring to Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement. We disagree with the commenter's assertion that CEHRT use requirements are unnecessary for the Shared Savings Program. As stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, section 1833(z)(2)(C)(iii)(II)(bb) of the Act (as amended by the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA)) generally requires Advanced Alternative Payment Models (Advanced APMs) to require the use of CEHRT (
91 FR 44056
). In order for certain participation tracks of the Shared Savings Program (that is, BASIC Level E
(
printed page 71395)
and ENHANCED) to be Advanced APMs, they must require CEHRT use, and eliminating the CEHRT use requirement for the remainder of the Shared Savings Program would result in inconsistent CEHRT use requirements across Shared Savings Program participation tracks. We believe maintaining consistent CEHRT use requirements across tracks supports the program's goals of improving the quality and coordination of care for Medicare beneficiaries. Further, we believe that removing CEHRT use requirements from any track of the Shared Savings Program would not be consistent with our belief in the value of advancing interoperability to improve patient care. We believe, as we noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44056
), the secure exchange, access, and use of electronic health information supports better informed decision making and a more efficient healthcare system and that interoperability enables this secure exchange and access. For these reasons, we believe it is appropriate to retain CEHRT use requirements.
We recognize the commenter's concern regarding administrative burden associated with the existing requirements, particularly for small practices. We believe that the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements we are finalizing will reduce burden for ACOs, including those with small practices. We proposed multiple options for ACO-level reporting or attestation to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. Additionally, for ACOs electing to attest to Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics, the allowable exceptions for TINs comprised of ACO providers and suppliers with Shared Savings Program special statuses or those facing hardships are intended to provide greater flexibility for ACOs to meet the CEHRT use requirements. We believe these options appropriately balance the importance of CEHRT use in supporting coordinated, high-quality care with the need to reduce unnecessary reporting burden.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern regarding ACOs' ability to comply with new Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. A commenter recommended that CMS minimize documentation and audit burdens associated with CEHRT attestations. Another commenter recommended that minor documentation errors not threaten an ACO's shared savings eligibility if the ACO can otherwise demonstrate “substantive compliance.” Additionally, a commenter requested that we provide opportunities for CMS to cure isolated deficiencies of TINs that may impact an entire ACO's ability to meet the CEHRT use requirements. Some commenters requested that ACOs not be held accountable for ACO operational occurrences that may cause them to be out of compliance with the proposed changes. Similarly, a commenter recommended CMS ensure ACOs are not held accountable for technology infrastructure failure beyond their control.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding documentation burden and isolated deficiencies or circumstances outside an ACO's control that may affect its ability to comply with the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. We agree that compliance expectations should be clear and that ACOs should not be subject to unnecessary administrative burden. However, we are not establishing a separate cure process for individual TINs or adopting a blanket exception for minor documentation errors or operational circumstances. We do not believe such policies are necessary in light of the policies we are finalizing. We proposed multiple CEHRT use options for ACOs to meet Shared Savings Program requirements and included TIN-specific exclusions of which ACOs electing the ACO CEHRT use attestation option could avail themselves as appropriate. We would address any instances of noncompliance through the existing compliance framework at §§ 425.216 and 425.218 as appropriate. With regard to ACOs being found out of compliance due to circumstances beyond their control, we note that ACOs may elect the CEHRT use option among the three choices that best meets their ACO's needs to satisfy Shared Savings Program requirements. Further, for those electing to attest to one of three proposed ACO CEHRT use metrics, they may exclude certain participant TINs that meet specified special status criteria or experience circumstances that would allow them to request a MIPS Promoting Interoperability hardship exception (
91 FR 44064
). We believe these exclusions, together with the multiple options for meeting the CEHRT use requirements, provide appropriate flexibility for ACOs while maintaining accountability for meeting Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements and mitigating the negative impact of circumstances outside of an ACO's control on Shared Savings Program CEHRT use compliance.
Comment:
Many commenters requested guidance, additional information, technical assistance, or clarification from CMS. Several commenters requested that CMS confirm the documentation expectations clearly and in advance. Of these, a couple commenters expressed their belief that ACOs need to use this guidance to determine the best path for them. A commenter suggested CMS clarify in the final rule that the attestation is related to ACO CEHRT use and not a separate certification requirement for ACOs or their ACO participants. A commenter requested clear guidance on acceptable evidence of FHIR-enabled data exchange and quality reporting to promote consistent implementation across ACOs. A couple of commenters suggested CMS couple this proposal with ACO-level technical assistance, shared services models, and financial support, and a couple of commenters recommended that CMS clearly define the circumstances that qualify for exclusion. One of these commenters requested details about the documentation ACOs should maintain to support exclusion determinations, while the other stated that exclusion processes should be clear, objective, and administratively simple.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' recommendations regarding clear implementation expectations, documentation, technical assistance and financial support. We believe that the requirements described in this final rule provide ACOs with sufficient information to understand the available Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options, including applicable exclusions for ACOs electing the CEHRT use metric attestation option under § 425.507(c)(3), as discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44064
and
44065
). We fully described exclusions available to ACOs electing to attest to one of the three Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44064
and
44065
). In response to comments, we have also provided a summary table of certification criterion requirements for these Shared Savings Program CEHRT use metrics (Table B-G10). We intend to provide additional instructions for completing Shared Savings Program CEHRT use attestations in the ACO-MS system, for ACOs electing to attest that they used a Health IT Module certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria within
45 CFR 170.315
to obtain standardized data from a FHIR-based API to support their complete reporting of at least one measure in the APP Plus and ACOs electing to attest to one of the three proposed ACO CEHRT use metrics. We intend to provide summary or
(
printed page 71396)
illustrative materials to assist ACOs in complying with Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements and will continue to provide ACOs with technical assistance through existing channels.
With respect to documentation, we disagree that additional guidance is required related to documentation requirements. Existing policy at § 425.314(b)(1) includes the requirement that ACOs retain evidence sufficient to enable the audit, evaluation, investigation, and inspection of the ACO's compliance with program requirements. As discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, ACOs electing to attest that they used a Health IT Module certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria within
45 CFR 170.315
to obtain standardized data from a FHIR-based API to support their complete reporting of at least one measure in the APP Plus measure set would need to provide, on request, the CEHRT ID for the certified technology used, and ACOs electing to attest to one of the three proposed ACO CEHRT use metrics would need to provide, on request, the CEHRT ID for each of its participant TINs from which it attested that at least one ACO provider or supplier utilized CEHRT to meet the requirements of the metric. If ACOs electing to attest to one of the three Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics exclude a TIN based on the TIN meeting Shared Savings Program definition of “special status” or hardship, the ACO would be required maintain and provide on request adequate documentation to demonstrate that any TIN exclusions applied were appropriate (
91 FR 44065
and
66
). We believe these existing documentation requirements, together with the requirements and clarifications provided in this final rule, sufficiently establish CMS's expectations for demonstrating compliance.
We do not intend to provide financial support or establish shared services models for ACOs to implement the new Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options because the options are significantly less burdensome than our current CEHRT use policies. We confirm that the proposed CEHRT use option at § 425.507(c)(2), for ACOs to attest using FHIR to support reporting of a quality measure described in detail in section III.G.4.b.(2) of this final rule, is one option an ACO could select in order to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements and is not an additional certification requirement for ACOs or their ACO participants. We agree that the processes should be clear and as simple as possible.
Comment:
A commenter stated that ACOs should be free to select the pathway best suited to their circumstances and to change pathways between performance years without penalty.
Response:
We agree that ACOs should have the flexibility to select the pathway that best suits their circumstances and to change pathways between performance years. We did not propose limiting an ACO's ability to change its selected pathway between performance years to meet the CEHRT use requirements, nor are we finalizing any such limitation at this time.
Comment:
A couple of commenters requested clarification related to documentation of CEHRT identifiers. One of these commenters requested clarification in the final rule that the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options are an alternative, rather than an addition, to what they stated was the current practice of ACOs documenting that their practices are using CEHRT and another commenter requested that CMS confirm that, in addition to the three proposed CEHRT use options, direct verification using the CHPL would be considered to satisfy technology use verification requirements.
Response:
We appreciate comments requesting clarification. We wish to clarify that an ACO documenting that its practices use CEHRT would not meet or have met current Shared Saving Program CEHRT use requirements in § 425.507(a) and (b) or the proposed requirements in (c). The proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements described at section III.G.4.b. and that we are finalizing at section III.G.4.c. in this rule will replace existing Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, beginning with PY 2027.
Regarding the comment asking for confirmation that verification of CEHRT using the CHPL would satisfy Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, it would not. We are unsure whether the commenter may have been referring to existing MIPS requirements for documenting a CMS EHR Certification ID (also referred to as a CEHRT ID) obtained from the CHPL as part of MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category reporting. As we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, our proposed options for Shared Savings Program ACOs to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement will not change the existing scoring methodology for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category (
91 FR 44066
). The Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements are separate from and in addition to any MIPS requirements for documentation of CEHRT IDs.
We did not propose that verification or documentation of a CEHRT ID using the CHPL alone would satisfy Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, as it would not. ACOs may continue to use the CHPL to verify the certification status of health IT used by their ACO participant TINs. ACOs electing the option to attest to having used a Health IT Module certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria within
45 CFR 170.315
to obtain standardized data from a FHIR-based API to support the complete reporting of at least one measure in the APP Plus quality measure set (§ 425.507(c)(2)), or to attest to one of the three ACO CEHRT use metrics (§ 425.507(c)(3)) (that at least one ACO provider or supplier in each of the ACO's participating TINs performed the action described in the metric using EHR technology certified to the ONC Certification Criteria for Health IT (
45 CFR 170.315
) necessary to meet paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at
42 CFR 414.1305
) would be required to maintain documentation that the EHR technology meets the requirements of the CEHRT definition and other requirements in § 425.507(c)(1)-(3) as applicable and provide such documentation to CMS upon request. Likewise, ACOs that use CEHRT (as defined in paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305) that also supports the calculation and reporting of clinical quality measures by being certified to the ONC health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(c)(2)
and
(c)(3)
, to completely report at least one of the measures in the APP Plus quality measure set using the eCQMs or Medicare eCQMs collection types and meets the data completeness requirement at 42 CFR 414.1340 of this chapter for the applicable performance year (§ 425.507(c)(1)) would also be required to maintain documentation that the EHR technology meets the requirements of the CEHRT definition and other requirements in § 425.507(c)(1)-(3) as applicable and provide such documentation to CMS upon request.
Comment:
A commenter stated that they supported our proposal to eliminate the Promoting Interoperability measure category for ACOs.
Response:
We wish to clarify that we did not propose to eliminate the Promoting Interoperability Performance category, which is a part of MIPS. Rather, we proposed to sunset the
Shared Savings Program
requirement (§ 425.507(a)) that ACO providers and suppliers report all MIPS Promoting
(
printed page 71397)
Interoperability measures and requirements and publicly report on the number of MIPS eligible clinicians, QPs, and Partial QPs in the ACO who earned a MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category score (§ 425.308(b)(9)). As we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, regardless of which of the three proposed activities (or which option within their selected activity) ACOs choose to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement, the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category reporting requirements for MIPS eligible clinicians participating in an ACO would remain unaffected (
91 FR 44066
).
Comment:
A couple of commenters requested clarification regarding the proposed option for ACOs to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements through attesting to having used a FHIR-based API available in CEHRT to support measure data collection for complete reporting of a measure in the APP plus measure set. A commenter asked that CMS clarify that the FHIR-based attestation option is intended to become viable only once FHIR-based quality reporting capabilities are more broadly available and consider whether it is necessary to include this option for the CY 2027 performance period specifically, given that it is not currently operational for any ACO. Another commenter recommended we enumerate in the final rule which certification criteria other than
45 CFR 170.315(g)(10)
satisfy the attestation pathway at § 425.507(c)(2) and state what an ACO must be able to demonstrate for a Health IT Module to qualify as “supporting standardized API access.”
Response:
We wish to clarify commenters' potential misunderstanding of our proposal at § 425.507(c)(2). Under that provision, one option an ACO could elect in order to meet the Shared Savings Program's CEHRT use requirements would be for the ACO to completely report at least one measure in the APP Plus quality measure set and meet the data completeness requirement at § 414.1340 of this chapter for the applicable performance year using EHR technology that meets paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305 and attest that it used data collected from a FHIR-based API to support quality measurement using a Health IT module certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria in
45 CFR 170.315
supporting standardized API access. Meeting these requirements is separate from any future reporting of FHIR-based digital quality measures and so could be implemented by ACOs electing that option for PY 2027. ACOs would attest to meeting this requirement through ACO-MS, after the conclusion of annual quality reporting (
91 FR 44060
and
44061
). We appreciate the request for clarification on which criteria other than
45 CFR 170.315(g)(10)
would satisfy the requirement that the health IT module be certified to an unexpired criterion supporting standardized API access. At this time,
45 CFR 170.315(g)(10)
is the only unexpired criterion that would meet this requirement. The language was intended to preserve flexibility for ACOs to utilize any future ONC Health IT certification criteria that may support standardized API access or a potential future situation where
45 CFR 170.315(g)(10)
becomes expired and is replaced by a different criterion.
Comment:
A commenter requested clarification as to whether ACOs with a significant share of small-practice participants may satisfy the requirement at the ACO level rather than requiring uniform compliance across every participant TIN.
Response:
We appreciate the request for clarification. We believe the commenter may have been referring to the option for ACOs to attest that at least one ACO provider or supplier in each of its participant TINs completed a certain action. For ACOs electing this attestation option for the purpose of meeting Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, in order to attest “Yes,” those with a large proportion of small practices would still be required to ensure that at least one ACO provider or supplier in each of the ACO's participating TINs performed the action described in the Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metric using EHR technology certified to the ONC Certification Criteria for Health IT (
45 CFR 170.315
) necessary to meet paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305 to complete the action described in each metric.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS provide a transition period to ACOs or hold them harmless from compliance actions based on their not meeting the proposed CEHRT use requirements. Of these, several requested an extension of the enforcement discretion for at least one additional performance year, with most expressing concern that the timing for our proposal to replace existing Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements in PY 2027 does not allow ACOs sufficient development and/or implementation time. A couple of commenters requested CMS to treat every ACO as compliant in the first year, while another commenter requested a minimum 1-2-year transition for compliance.
Response:
We acknowledge the recommendations regarding a transition period. As discussed in section III.G.4.b. of this final rule, we are providing multiple options for ACOs to meet the CEHRT use requirements, allowing ACOs to select the option that best accommodates their organizational structure and technical capabilities. We believe these options significantly reduce burden on ACOs compared to our current CEHRT use requirements, while advancing ACOs toward digital quality measurement and health information exchange. We do not believe that an additional transition period is warranted because the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options at
42 CFR 425.507(c)
overlap with activities the ACO will already be doing to participate in the Shared Savings Program in PY 2027, including quality reporting. We are also finalizing an option for ACOs to attest to one of three Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics that are a subset of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability measures that ACOs are required to report for every ACO participant, ACO provider/supplier, and ACO professional under the current Shared Savings Program regulations at § 425.507(a). This subset of currently required MIPS Promoting Interoperability measures have also been simplified so that ACOs will only be required to attest that one ACO provider or supplier from each of the ACO's participant TINs has completed the action required by the metric. As the options under 425.507(c) allow ACOs to choose from multiple activities, including attesting to one of three simplified and lower-burden version of existing MIPS Promoting Interoperability measures, on which Shared Savings Program ACOs are currently required to report at 425.507(a), any ACO meeting the existing requirements should be able to attest that it met at least one of the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use metrics.
We disagree with comments that we should utilize our enforcement discretion for an additional year or guarantee compliance in the first year, in light of finalizing new options through which ACOs can meet CEHRT use requirements for PY 2027. We note that we finalized existing CEHRT use requirements in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79124
through
79132
), issued on November 2, 2023. Under the current policies, unless otherwise excluded, ACO participants, ACO provider/suppliers, and ACO
(
printed page 71398)
professionals who are MIPS eligible clinicians, Qualifying APM Participants (QP), or Partial QPs regardless of track, must report the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category measures and requirements to MIPS. We have exercised enforcement discretion for this requirement, for PY 2025 and PY 2026, due to challenges faced by ACOs including understanding the CEHRT requirements, determining which of their participants are excluded from the requirement, and aggregating data across providers. In contrast to the proposed policy at § 425.507(c), ACO providers/suppliers were required, under existing regulations at § 425.507(a), to report the full set of MIPS Promoting Interoperability measures and activities in PY 2025 and PY 2026. We believe the CEHRT use policies proposed to begin in PY 2027 allow for significantly greater flexibility, including for ACOs to choose to report one of three metrics that are parallel to three measures from the larger MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category activities currently required under existing Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements at § 425.507(a). ACOs electing to attest to one of these metrics would complete ACO-level attestations as finalized in section III.G.4.c. of this final rule. In addition, we proposed to allow ACOs electing to attest to one of the proposed metrics to exclude from their determination of whether one ACO provider or supplier from each of their participating TINs completed the action under a list of circumstances. Due to the simplification of the proposed CEHRT requirements, the multiple options for ACOs to meet CEHRT requirement for the Shared Savings Program, and the overlap between the proposed CEHRT use requirements and quality reporting, we believe that the need for enforcement discretion in PY 2027 is diminished. Accordingly, after consideration of the comments, we are not extending the period of enforcement discretion, nor delaying the effective date for retiring the existing CEHRT use requirements or for implementing the ones we are finalizing at section III.G.4.c. of this final rule beginning with PY 2027.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that CMS recognize standards and pathways outside of those we proposed. A commenter provided additional suggestions for CMS to include as options for ACOs to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, including recognition of standards-based health information exchange of health information with post-acute care, long-term care, or community partners, including for those that do not have CEHRT or that operate outside of a qualified health information network, making allowances for any technical failures these partners might experience. Another commenter recommended that we clarify that a contracted healthcare provider's technology status would not preclude an ACO from selecting any proposed CEHRT-use pathway, and another requested we add an option for meeting CEHRT requirements for the Shared Savings Program by reporting objective results for FHIR API performance for ACOs electing to report the Medicare eCQM pathway. A commenter also requested that CMS allow ACOs to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements by documenting efforts to exchange with partners that lack needed technology or connectivity.
Response:
We acknowledge the recommendations regarding additional options for meeting the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. We recognize the importance of supporting interoperability across the care continuum, including with post-acute care, long-term care, community-based and contracted healthcare providers that may face challenges adopting or using CEHRT. However, we believe the multiple options for meeting the CEHRT use requirements as finalized in section III.G.4.c. of this final rule provide ACOs with flexibility to accommodate differences in their organizational structures, existing health IT infrastructure and technical capabilities. Accordingly, we are not adopting additional options for meeting Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements at this time.
In response to commenters' concerns regarding exchange of health information with partners that may lack CEHRT, we believe that our Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options provide choices that do not require all of the healthcare providers with whom ACOs or ACO providers and suppliers exchange health information to have CEHRT. For example, for ACOs electing the option at § 425.507(c)(1), to use CEHRT meeting the requirements described in that section to completely report at least one of the measures in the APP Plus quality measure set using the eCQMs or Medicare eCQMs collection types and meet the data completeness requirement at § 414.1340 of this chapter for the applicable PY, it is the submitting EHR system that must be certified to ONC's regulations by the time eCQM data is generated for submission.
[
308
]
For ACOs electing the option at § 425.507(c)(2), to use EHR technology that meets paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305 and attest that they used data collected from FHIR-based API to support quality measurement using a Health IT module that has been certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria in
45 CFR 170.315
to support complete reporting of at least one of the five ACO-reported measures in the APP Plus quality measure set, there is also not a requirement that every system or organization with which the ACO exchanges health information must use CEHRT. Similarly, for ACOs electing the option in § 425.507(c)(3) to select and attest to the bi-directional HIE Shared Savings Program CEHRT use metric, attesting to that metric does not require that every system or organization with which the ACO provider or supplier exchanges information use certified health IT. Long-term and post-acute care settings can connect to a wide range of health information exchange entities that use a variety of methods to exchange information with ACO providers and suppliers in ACO participant TINs. As we explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, an ACO electing to attest to one of the three proposed CEHRT use metrics could consider an ACO provider or supplier in its participant TIN to have met the bi-directional HIE ACO CEHRT use metric's requirement if the ACO provider or supplier has, for at least one patient seen by the ACO provider or supplier, used EHR technology certified to the ONC Certification Criteria for Health IT (
45 CFR 170.315
) necessary to meet paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305 to support bi-directional exchange with an HIE that has the required functionality (
91 FR 44062
).
With regard to the suggestion that ACO documentation of efforts to exchange information with partners with limited technological capacity should be considered to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, we disagree. We note that CMS does not require that every system or organization with which the ACO provider or supplier exchanges information must use certified health IT. We believe the options we are finalizing in section III.G.4.c. of this final rule appropriately balance these considerations by providing ACOs with options to satisfy the CEHRT use requirement, which allow ACOs to select the option that best reflects their health IT infrastructure and capabilities.

printed page 71399)
We also note that, while we did not propose to allow ACOs to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements by documenting or reporting FHIR API performance, we did propose in
42 CFR 425.507(c)(2)
that ACOs could elect to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements by completely reporting at least one of the five ACO-reported measures in the APP Plus quality measure set and attesting to using CEHRT to support quality reporting using data collected from a FHIR-based API using a certified Health IT Module. While we do not believe that documentation of the FHIR-based API's performance should suffice as a demonstration of ACO CEHRT use, this option would allow an ACO that used a FHIR-based API to support complete reporting of an APP Plus quality measure using a Health IT Module that has been certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria in
45 CFR 170.315
supporting standardized API access to attest that it did so, in order to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements.
Comment:
A couple of commenters requested that CMS retain a public health data exchange option—for example, Immunization Registry Reporting or Electronic Case Reporting attestation, as one of the qualifying CEHRT-use activities under the revised Shared Savings Program requirement. These commenters noted this would align with the existing MIPS framework and support essential public health data exchange infrastructure.
Response:
We appreciate the recommendation to include public health data exchange, such as Immunization Registry Reporting or Electronic Case Reporting, as one of the ACO CEHRT use metrics that ACOs can use to meet the requirement under § 425.507(c)(3). While we agree that electronic public health data exchange supports broader interoperability goals and recognize the role of CEHRT in facilitating the electronic exchange of public health data, we believe that the multiple options we are finalizing provide ACOs sufficient flexibility to demonstrate CEHRT use while advancing interoperability. For example, consider an ACO provider or supplier that is a signatory to a Framework Agreement under the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA),
[
309
]
and exchanges immunization data with public health agencies for patients using TEFCA. That ACO could count that activity as part of meeting the requirement for that ACO provider or supplier's ACO participant TIN when determining whether one ACO provider or supplier from each of its ACO participant TINs has met the requirement for the proposed ACO Health Information Exchange (HIE) Bi-Directional Exchange metric. We discussed how a TEFCA Framework Agreement can help ACOs meet the requirement for the HIE metric in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44063
). Additionally, we note that public health agencies are potential participants in HIEs.
[
