]
Accordingly, we are not adopting the recommendation to include public health data exchange as an additional qualifying CEHRT use activity at this time. However, we will consider including public health data exchanged as part of bidirectional exchange via a health information network as an example, in future instructions, of an activity that could contribute to satisfying the requirements of the bi-directional HIE metric, for ACOs that elect to attest to it, to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement in
42 CFR 425.507(c)(3)
.
Comment:
A commenter recommended we add the MIPS Electronic Prior Authorization measure to the list of available metrics for Shared Savings Program CEHRT Use attestation for PY 2028 because omitting electronic prior authorization from the ACO CEHRT use metric list risks creating misalignment between payer obligations that take effect in 2027 and the incentives for ACOs to adopt ePA.
Response:
We appreciate the recommendation to add an ACO CEHRT use metric related to the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category Electronic Prior Authorization measure to the list of metrics available for CEHRT use attestation for PY 2028. We disagree that not proposing or finalizing an electronic prior authorization CEHRT use metric for Shared Savings Program ACOs for PY 2028 creates misalignment with MIPS. In section IV.B.1.d. of this final rule, MIPS is finalizing, as proposed, modifications to the Electronic Prior Authorization measure that make the measure optional for the CY 2027 performance period and required starting with the CY 2028 performance period. Additionally, in section IV.A.4.d.(4) of this final rule, MIPS is finalizing, as proposed, the adoption of the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drug measure, which will be a required measure starting with the CY2028 performance period. Further, the three Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics, of which ACOs could choose to attest to one in order to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements for PY 2027, align conceptually with the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category measures but have been revised to apply to ACOs. We proposed that we would make any future changes to the ACO CEHRT use metrics through notice and comment rulemaking. As we did not propose to include a metric around electronic prior authorization beginning with PY 2027, we are not accepting this suggestion but will consider it for potential future rulemaking.
Comment:
A couple of commenters requested that CMS monitor the uptake and results of these proposed requirements. Of these, a commenter requested monitoring of the FHIR attestation pathway specifically, and the other requested monitoring of whether the one provider or supplier participant TIN requirement in the CEHRT use metrics leads to meaningful exchange at scale.
Response:
We appreciate the suggestions and agree that there would be value in monitoring use of the FHIR attestation pathway as proposed in
42 CFR 425.507(c)(2)
. We intend to monitor ACOs' use of the available Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options including the FHIR attestation pathway. We appreciate the value in analyzing what activities lead to meaningful exchange of health information at scale, though we note that this option within the Shared Savings Program is only one factor in promoting increase in meaningful exchange of health information at scale. We do, however, believe that allowing ACOs to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements through our recognition of ACOs' concrete steps toward FHIR-based digital quality measurement and health information exchange, such as through the proposed attestation to using FHIR-based exchange to support quality measure data collection, provides a low-burden incentive for ACOs to invest in infrastructure and redesigned care processes to improve care for the beneficiaries they serve.
Comment:
We received several comments regarding movement toward interoperability in general, including ensuring our policies are meaningful and support ACOs' needs. Several
(
printed page 71400)
commenters recommended that CMS make sure our proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements support interoperability specific to the operations and needs of ACOs and their partners, including nursing facilities.
A few commenters addressed the proposed policies' specific requirements that ACOs use CEHRT, expressing concern about potential CEHRT cost and reliance on a particular vendor or other proprietary input.
A few commenters requested that CMS ensure that the CEHRT use requirements meaningfully lead to increased interoperability, with a commenter expressing their belief that the increased flexibility alone would not create interoperability and another recommending we ensure that the HIE CEHRT use metric assesses meaningful capability to exchange actionable data.
Several commenters addressed advancement of interoperability and digital reporting requirements across CMS programs and models, with one supporting CMS's efforts to advance interoperability, FHIR-based exchange, and digital quality measurement and reduce reporting burden but cautioning against creating a lower interoperability standard for value-based care programs that could conflict with Medicare's long-term interoperability goals.
Response:
We appreciate recommendations regarding meaningfulness and feasibility of the options for meeting Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. We agree that the policies should support ACOs' ability to coordinate care and improve care quality for their assigned beneficiaries, including through interoperability, and address ACOs' needs, and we believe that the additional flexibilities and exclusions we proposed address a redesign of care processes for high quality and efficient service delivery across the wide variety of ACO compositions and capabilities. With regard to supporting interoperability with partners including nursing facilities, we agree and believe that the flexibilities and the clarification, as discussed previously in this section, that the proposals do not require that every system or organization with which the ACO provider or supplier exchanges information must use certified health IT, in order to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements.
The proposed options do not require an ACO to use a specific EHR vendor or other proprietary input, and we believe that providing multiple options affords greater flexibility for ACOs and ACO participants with differing levels of health IT capabilities and resources. With regard to the comments suggesting we ensure the CEHRT use requirements are meaningful and that a lower bar is not set for interoperability in value-based care, we agree. We believe that the proposed options allow ACOs to demonstrate activities they have undertaken to use CEHRT to improve quality of care and service efficiency. We will continue to work to ensure advancement of interoperability within the Shared Savings Program, as interoperability advances in the larger Medicare program.
Comment:
Many commenters requested that CMS add or modify an exception for certain types of healthcare providers. Of these, many requested a small practice exception, a few suggested exceptions or additional support for rural practices or expansion of the types of facility-based providers eligible for exclusion, and a commenter suggested an exclusion for specialists. Several commenters noted that the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule will be finalized after ACOs will have had to make participation decisions for PY 2027, which some stated would limit ACOs' ability to comply, based on their inclusion of small practices. A commenter noted that small practices build capacity over time and should receive additional support from CMS, and several expressed their belief that a small practice exception would better align with our intent to increase small and independent practice participation in ACOs. Several commenters expressed their belief that a small practice exclusion would be more in line with the MIPS framework, with one stating our proposed policy would create a new CEHRT reporting requirement for practices that are currently excluded from MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category reporting.
Another commenter suggested that we add a time-limited exception for CEHRT use requirements for rural, small, or long-term/post-acute care when organizations demonstrate lack of access to technology or connectivity, and some commenters requested a rural health exemption, noting that adopting CEHRT for the first time may be prohibitive for them.
A few commenters expressed concern with ACOs' ability to influence facility-based practices' EHRs, and some of these requested we exclude additional types of facility-based practices from CEHRT use requirements, including for clinicians providing services in nursing facilities and assisted living facilities, who face similar challenges to those currently applicable for the exclusion.
Response:
We acknowledge the recommendations to add additional exclusions for Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. We wish to clarify that the exceptions we proposed are applicable to the option for ACOs to elect to attest to one of the Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics as proposed for
42 CFR 425.507(c)(3)
. We believe an additional small practice exclusion is unnecessary because ACO participation enables participating practices to leverage shared infrastructure, technology, data and care management capabilities that may be difficult for individual practices to develop or maintain on their own. Accordingly, small practices participating in an ACO should generally be positioned to meet the revised, less burdensome options for the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirement through the ACO's broader infrastructure and support.
The proposed policy also provides multiple options for ACOs to demonstrate CEHRT use, including the option at § 425.507(c)(2) to completely report at least one measure in the APP Plus quality measure set and meet the data completeness requirement at § 414.1340 for the applicable performance year using EHR technology that meets paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305 and attests that it used data collected from a FHIR-based API to support quality measurement using a Health IT Module certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria in
45 CFR 170.315
supporting standardized API access, if an ACO would prefer that option over attesting that each of its participating practices performed a certain CEHRT use activity. We recognize that small practices may face resource and implementation challenges and that some may currently qualify for flexibility under MIPS. We do not believe, however, that practice size alone warrants exclusion from the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements. Unlike the MIPS' Promoting Interoperability performance category, the CEHRT use policies proposed for the Shared Savings Program would not require practice-level reporting of Promoting Interoperability measures and activities (or the equivalent Shared Savings Program ACO CEHRT use metrics). ACOs could alternatively elect to: (1) Use CEHRT (as defined in paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305) that also supports the calculation and reporting of clinical quality measures by being certified to the ONC health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(c)(2)
and
(c)(3)
to completely report at least one of the measures in the APP Plus quality measure set using the
(
printed page 71401)
eCQMs or Medicare eCQMs collection types and meet the data completeness requirement at § 414.1340 of this chapter for the applicable PY; or (2) Completely report at least one measure in the APP Plus quality measure set and meet the data completeness requirement at § 414.1340 of this chapter for the applicable performance year using EHR technology that meets paragraph (3) of the CEHRT definition at § 414.1305 and attests that it used data collected from FHIR-based API to support quality measurement using a Health IT Module certified to an unexpired criterion or criteria in
45 CFR 170.315
supporting standardized API access, to satisfy the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements in § 425.507(c). We have also proposed to allow ACOs electing to attest to one of the three ACO-level CEHRT use metrics to exclude, from their assessment as to whether one ACO provider or supplier from each of their participating TINs met the metric, TINs comprised of ACO providers and suppliers meeting certain special statuses as well as hardships. ACO participant TINs that are small practices comprised of ACO providers and suppliers who meet the proposed hardship circumstances could be excluded by ACOs electing to attest to one of these metrics. We note that we have proposed multiple options for ACOs to satisfy Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements and have proposed exceptions to facilitate the ability of ACOs to meet them. Overall, the proposed requirements in § 425.507(c) result in a decreased burden for ACOs to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements compared to existing requirements under § 425.507(a). After consideration of these comments, we are not finalizing an exception for small practices.
We acknowledge the concerns regarding the timing of these requirements and their potential effect on ACO participation decisions and the inclusion of small and independent practices. However, we believe the options for demonstrating CEHRT use finalized in this rule provide ACOs flexibility in meeting the requirement while maintaining an appropriate minimum expectation for CEHRT use among ACO participants. We also believe that they represent a significant decrease in burden for ACOs as compared to the existing CEHRT use requirements.
With regard to the suggestion that specialists be excluded from the requirements, we disagree because we believe that specialists are an integral part of ACOs and that excluding them would decrease ACOs' ability to exchange health information to coordinate and improve care for the beneficiaries they serve.
Regarding the recommendation to expand CEHRT use exclusions to additional facility-based provider types, we did not propose to expand exclusions for ACOs electing to attest to one of three ACO CEHRT use metrics beyond those described in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44062
), which align with those available under MIPS. We will consider this suggestion for future rulemaking.
Regarding the suggestion that we add an additional exception for rural ACOs or practices, we believe ACOs that include participant TINs serving rural populations can meet the proposed CEHRT use requirements given the multiple options available and the exclusions for ACO participant TINs comprised solely of ACO providers and suppliers in rural and/or Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) circumstances available for ACOs electing to attest to one of the CEHRT use metrics. Specifically, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we discussed that ACOs would be permitted to apply exclusions for similar circumstances as the exclusions and exceptions under MIPS (
91 FR 44064
). We noted that an ACO would be permitted to exclude an ACO participant TIN that the ACO determines is comprised solely of ACO providers and/or suppliers who meet the Shared Savings Program definition of “special status” (
91 FR 44064
). We explained that the Shared Savings Program definitions of special statuses would be similar to the MIPS definitions at § 414.1305 except that they would not be limited to MIPS ECs, for the purpose of Shared Savings Program CEHRT use metric exceptions. We proposed to include as special statuses being located in a HPSA, defined as areas designated under section 332(a)(1)(A) of the Public Health Service Act or being located in a rural area, defined as ZIP codes designated as rural by the Federal Office of Rural Health Policy (FORHP) using the most recent FORHP Eligible ZIP Code file available as described in the definition of “Rural area” at § 414.1305.
Additionally, we want to clarify that, while most of the special statuses defined at § 414.1305 are aligned with the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category framework, this is not true for the statuses of “Located in a health professional shortage area (HPSA)” or “Rural area.” While these two statuses convey differential scoring under MIPS for the Improvement Activities domain, they do not have an impact on scoring for or qualify for reweighting of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category.
[
311
]
We proposed to allow ACOs electing to attest to one of the proposed metrics to exclude from their determination of whether one ACO provider or supplier from each of their participating TINs completed the action if the TIN is comprised entirely of ACO providers and suppliers meeting certain special statuses, including being located in a HPSA or rural area (as we further defined those in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule). Because we have not received comments opposing the HPSA and rural areas as special statuses as they relate to the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use metric attestation exclusions, and these exclusions are consistent with commenters' request that we offer special consideration for small or rural practices, we are finalizing these exclusions as proposed.
Overall, we believe the new proposed requirements and exclusions represent a decrease in burden for ACOs to meet the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements, and we will not be finalizing additional exclusions for § 425.507(c) at this time.
Comment:
Several commenters mentioned exceptions to Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements related to hardships or other situations. A commenter recommended that we maintain reasonable exclusions for variables outside the ACO's control, including technology limitations, vendor issues, cybersecurity incidents, and other circumstances. A commenter suggested hardship exclusions be aligned with MIPS, and another recommended that hardship and special-status exclusions should be simple and, wherever feasible, automatic.
Response:
We acknowledge the request for additional exclusions. We agree that providing certain exclusions is important, but we believe that additional exclusions are not necessary because the proposed policy provides multiple pathways for ACOs to demonstrate CEHRT use, enabling flexibility for a variety of ACOs to meet CEHRT requirements for the Shared Savings Program.
Regarding the suggestion that exceptions should be simple and automatic, we proposed that ACOs electing the option to attest to a Shared Savings Program CEHRT use metric would not be required to request
(
printed page 71402)
hardship exceptions for Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements but would be required to maintain documentation substantiating them to provide to CMS in the event of an audit. Similarly, ACOs would determine whether a participant TIN is comprised solely of ACO providers and suppliers meeting special status.
Regarding the suggestion that hardship exclusions align with MIPS, we note that we proposed to allow ACOs to exclude from CEHRT use metric attestation any TIN comprised solely of ACO providers and suppliers meeting hardship circumstances that parallel those available by request from MIPS (
91 FR 44064
and
44065
). We did not propose that ACOs or their ACO providers and suppliers would be required to request a hardship approval but rather, that they would need to maintain documentation to provide to CMS in the event of an audit.
Comment:
A commenter suggested we allow an ACO-level exclusion if a threshold proportion of its participating providers or suppliers meet an existing exclusion or reweighting criteria for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category.
Response:
We appreciate the recommendation regarding additional exclusions, but we do not agree that an ACO should be excluded from Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements if some proportion of its ACO providers or suppliers meet an existing exclusion or reweighting criteria. Unlike MIPS, which requires individual or group practice-level Promoting Interoperability performance category reporting, the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options would leverage eCQM or Medicare eCQM quality measure reporting or permit ACO-level attestation. Under our proposed policy, ACOs electing to attest to CEHRT use metrics would only need to attest that a single ACO provider or supplier in each ACO participant TIN performed the activity required by the metric.
Comment:
A couple of commenters expressed concerns about what they perceive to be unnecessary administrative burden and duplicative reporting.
Response:
We appreciate the input. We disagree that the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options would create duplicative reporting requirements. We proposed that Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements would be applicable at the ACO level. ACOs are not required to report Promoting Interoperability at the ACO level to MIPS, and the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT requirements do not require practice-level reporting. Therefore, we do not believe the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements impose a duplicate reporting requirement as compared to MIPS. We also wish to clarify that, for ACOs electing the option at § 425.507(c)(1), to meet Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements by using CEHRT that meets the requirements described in that section to completely report at least one of the measures in the APP Plus quality measure set using the eCQMs or Medicare eCQMs collection types and meet the data completeness requirement at § 414.1340 of this chapter for the applicable PY, would simultaneously contribute to the ACO's compliance with the CEHRT use requirement and the ACO's compliance with the requirements under §§ 425.508 and 425.510 to report quality data on the APP Plus quality measure set established under § 414.1367. This is intended to reduce administrative burden.
Comment:
A commenter requested that we ensure that the proposed CEHRT use changes would not adversely affect or weaken the data quality used for quality reporting requirements.
Response:
We appreciate the comment and agree that the new CEHRT use requirements should not diminish quality measurement data. The Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options we proposed would not impact quality measure reporting requirements. ACOs would still be required to capture data required to meet Shared Savings Program quality measure reporting requirements, regardless of which of the proposed Shared Savings Program CEHRT use options they elect.
Comment:
A commenter requested that CMS simplify the CEHRT use framework where possible, expressing their belief that multiple options create complexity.
Response:
We acknowledge the feedback. The multiple options are intended to give ACOs flexibility in being able to demonstrate use of CEHRT, and that may help them choose an option that takes into account their organizational structure, how they aggregate information across their ACOs and other ACO characteristics. Because we believe we have appropriately balanced any added complexity with the flexibility we believe to be beneficial to ACOs, we are not considering narrowing the proposed options at this time because this would limit flexibility for ACOs to demonstrate CEHRT use.
Comment:
Several commenters agreed with the proposed public reporting requirements and suggest finalizing as proposed. Some commenters specifically expressed support for sunsetting the current public reporting requirements and replacing them with reporting on the allowable CEHRT use activities attested to or performed. A commenter supported the straightforward public reporting requirement as proposed because it does not impose unnecessary reporting friction.
Response:
We appreciate the support. We agree that the proposed public reporting requirements (
91 FR 44065
and
44066
) are intended to simplify ACOs reporting to publicly demonstrate CEHRT use.
Comment:
A few commenters requested additional clarification regarding public reporting expectations, and one of these also suggested we evaluate whether CEHRT utilization data would provide meaningful information to beneficiaries.
Response:
We appreciate the recommendations. We agree that clear documentation and public reporting expectations are important and direct commenters to the proposed requirement in section III.G.4.b.(4) of this final rule, where we state our proposal for § 425.308 to require ACOs to publicly report which allowable CEHRT use activity in proposed § 425.507(c) the ACO has selected to perform to meet CEHRT use requirements for the Shared Savings Program. The Shared Savings Program will continue to provide public reporting guidance, including a template for ACOs to provide information they are required to report with ACOs, to facilitate their compliance with this public reporting requirement. We note that while one purpose for publicly reported information is to inform beneficiary choice and understanding, we also believe such information can be helpful to potential ACO participants. Beneficiaries and potential ACO participants may have an interest in how an ACO is advancing FHIR-based digital quality measurement and health information exchange. We also believe that public reporting can support program transparency and oversight by making information about how the program is executed in practice available to beneficiaries, participants, and other interested parties. We will continue to consider the benefit of public reporting of Shared Savings Program CEHRT use.
After considering public comments, we are finalizing the Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements as proposed and are finalizing the public
(

reporting requirement as proposed. Specifically, we are finalizing as proposed our requirements for meeting Medicare Shared Savings Program CEHRT use requirements at § 425.507 as follows:

5. Financial Methodology
a. Overview
As explained in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, the Shared Savings Program has demonstrated a strong track record of generating savings for Medicare while achieving high quality care for beneficiaries assigned to ACOs (
91 FR 44067
). For example, the Shared Savings Program has had eight consecutive years of generating savings for Medicare relative to benchmarks, with over $12 billion in total savings and a trend of increasing savings year-over-year between 2017 and 2024. As described in the CY 2026 PFS final rule Regulatory Impact Analysis (
90 FR 49975
through
49976
) and in the regulatory impact section of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, the Shared Savings Program has maintained a net savings percentage on total FFS spending of 0.5 percent (
91 FR 44067
). At the same time, ACOs in the Shared Savings Program have demonstrated higher quality relative to other physician groups, indicating that the Shared Savings Program is achieving savings while improving quality of care. For example, in PY 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs helped more patients improve markers of good health, such as controlled blood pressure, hemoglobin A1c control (an indicator for diabetes), and depression screening with a follow-up plan, compared to 2023.
[
312
]
In PY 2024, nearly all ACOs outperformed similar types of physician groups on quality measures. As described in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, based on an internal CMS analysis of 87 ACOs that participated continuously in the Shared Savings Program between 2014 and 2023, Shared Savings Program ACOs showed statistically significant and substantial improvement across 7 comparable CMS Web Interface quality measures used during that period where quality performance improved across a wide range of clinical practice areas including screening and preventive measures, control of health conditions such as hypertension and diabetes (
91 FR 44067
). ACOs have performed consistently better than comparable physician groups on the patient experience survey measure, Getting Timely Care, Appointments, and Information, for every year that the survey has been fielded since 2019 (
91 FR 44067
).
Based on the experience of the Shared Savings Program and as part of our effort to align spending and value in OM, we are focused on developing policies that would grow the number of healthcare providers and beneficiaries in accountable care relationships and grow savings to the Medicare Trust Funds while improving the quality of care for beneficiaries. To achieve these goals, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed several complementary modifications to the benchmarking and financial methodology under the Shared Savings Program to encourage new and sustained participation by ACOs in the program (

b. Summary of Statutory and Regulatory Background on Adjusting the Historical Benchmark
As discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, section 1899(d)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act addresses how ACO benchmarks are to be established, updated, and reset at the start of each agreement period under the Shared Savings Program (

This provision specifies that the Secretary shall estimate a benchmark for each agreement period for each ACO using the most recent available 3 years of per beneficiary expenditures for Parts A and B services for OM beneficiaries assigned to the ACO. In general, an ACO that meets or exceeds its minimum savings rate (MSR), and otherwise qualifies for a shared savings payment, shares in savings at a sharing rate specified by the ACO's participation track (and level, if applicable), not to exceed a performance payment limit (a percentage of the ACO's updated historical benchmark).

An ACO under a two-sided model that meets or exceeds its minimum loss rate (MLR) shares in losses at a shared loss rate

Under Levels A and B of the BASIC track (§ 425.605(d)(1)(i) and (ii)), ACOs may share in savings at a sharing rate of up to 40 percent, not to exceed 10 percent of the updated benchmark. Levels C, D, and E of the BASIC track (§ 425.605(d)(1)(iii), (iv) and (v)) each offer a sharing rate of up to 50 percent capped at 10 percent of the updated benchmark, with a fixed 30 percent loss sharing rate in each level's two-sided model. The loss recoupment limits increase across these levels. Under Level C (§ 425.605(d)(1)(iii)(D)), an ACO's shared losses may not exceed 2 percent of total Medicare Parts A and B
(
printed page 71407)

Under Level D (§ 425.605(d)(1)(iv)(D)), an ACO's shared losses may not exceed 4 percent of total Medicare Parts A and B FFS revenue of the ACO participants in the ACO capped at 2 percent of updated benchmark. Under Level E (§ 425.605(d)(1)(v)(D)), an ACO's shared losses may not exceed 8 percent of total Medicare Parts A and B FFS revenue of the ACO participants in the ACO capped at 4 percent of updated benchmark. Under Level E, the loss recoupment limit is the percentage of revenue specified in the revenue-based nominal amount standard under the Quality Payment Program (QPP) (

(b) Revisions
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule we stated that in 2020, the first full performance year under the glide path, 13.5 percent of ACOs in the Medicare Shared Savings Program participated under BASIC track Level E (
91 FR 44069
). As ACOs became more experienced and progressed through the glide path, participation in BASIC track Level E experienced modest increases, which peaked in PY 2023 at 27.2 percent. As of PY 2026, participation in BASIC track Level E decreased to 16 percent.
We discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that the disparity in sharing rates between the highest risk option under the BASIC track (BASIC track Level E) and the next highest risk option (ENHANCED track) has potentially disproportionately driven ACOs to take on the maximum risk allowed (
91 FR 44069
). For PY 2026, 58 percent of ACOs are participating in the ENHANCED track. This in part is likely a result of the 40 percent sharing rate in Levels A and B of the BASIC track and 50 percent sharing rate in Levels C, D, and E of the BASIC track, compared to the 75 percent sharing rate in the ENHANCED track. We noted that, based on current participation trends across the various risk tracks, we anticipate that the participation in BASIC track Level E may continue a downward trend as a percentage of total participation unless some action is taken (
91 FR 44070
). We stated that we believe that some ACOs cease longer term program participation in BASIC track Level E before they otherwise would because they transition to the ENHANCED track based on the incentives of the higher sharing rate, and this transition occurs before they're ready for the increased demands associated with the higher risk track (
91 FR 44070
). We added that decreased Shared Savings Program retention rates of ACOs that transition too quickly to the ENHANCED track, in combination with the decreased net savings rates associated with the ENHANCED track, ultimately result in decreased savings for the Medicare Trust Fund (
91 FR 44070
). Table B-G11 summarizes the distribution of ACO participation across the various risk tracks for PY 2022 through CY 2026.
As discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, while we still have the goal of ACOs transitioning to performance-based risk, we want to be conscious of long-term impacts to the Shared Savings Program related to participation, success, and growth (
91 FR 44070
). We stated that participation in the ENHANCED track is a positive, but we believe that some ACOs may be taking on additional risk more quickly than they otherwise would because the ENHANCED track offers a 50 percent increase in savings compared to BASIC track Level E, while both tracks include two-sided risk (
91 FR 44070
). We noted that, if ACOs progress to higher levels of risk before they are adequately prepared, they may take on too much risk with higher shared losses rates in the ENHANCED track, potentially resulting in program termination and a subsequent reduction in both program participation and care coordination for beneficiaries (
91 FR 44070
). We stated our belief that by reducing the savings percentage gap between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track, we may increase participation in BASIC track Level E as well as the Shared Savings Program and increase long-term success of ACOs, particularly those with less experience, with unique patient or provider populations, and low revenue ACOs (which tend to be small, rural and physician-only ACOs) (
91 FR 44070
).
Additionally, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule we shared a data analysis from the CMS Office of the Actuary of benchmark performance for cohorts of ACOs that participated in both PY 2022 and PY 2023 indicates that ACOs participating in the BASIC track generated 42 percent higher net savings for CMS as a percentage of their benchmark than ACOs transitioning to or continuing participation in the ENHANCED track, despite favorable regional adjustments likely inflating gross savings for ACOs under the ENHANCED track (
91 FR 44070

(

We stated that this is also largely due to the 50 percent differential in sharing rate currently present between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track, which resulted in ENHANCED track ACOs needing to generate twice the gross savings to equal the same net savings for the Trust Funds as ACOs participating under BASIC track Level E (

We stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that, as we seek to increase the percentage of Medicare beneficiaries in accountable care arrangements, we are balancing incentives and participation options to serve the dual purposes of sustaining participation by existing ACOs and increasing program growth, recognizing that ACOs vary in their composition of providers/suppliers, the needs of the populations they serve, and have varying degrees of efficiency relative to their region and experience with accountable care initiatives (

Comment:
Most commenters supported our proposal to increase the BASIC track Level E shared savings rate from 50 percent to 60 percent. A commenter conditionally supported the proposal, provided that the increase
(
printed page 71410)
meaningfully helps organizations, particularly those serving rural and low-resourced communities, sustain the substantial investments required for accountable care, including care coordination, workforce capacity, health information technology, data analytics, quality improvement, and population health management. Many supportive commenters shared their beliefs that the higher sharing rate would better align rewards with the accountability required under value-based payment arrangements, narrow the incentive gap between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track, and improve returns on the substantial infrastructure and operational investments needed to accept two-sided risk. Several commenters also stated that the proposal would make BASIC track Level E a more viable participation option for rural, low-revenue, and other ACOs that need additional time to build capacity before assuming the higher level of risk associated with the ENHANCED track, thereby supporting retention and continued participation. A few commenters further observed that smaller and physician-led ACOs can generate Medicare savings that increase over time, while another commenter stated that attracting high-cost ACOs to BASIC track Level E would preserve greater opportunities for Medicare to share in savings.
Response:
We appreciate the support. We agree that increasing the shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E may better align financial rewards with the accountability associated with two-sided risk, narrow the incentive gap between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track, and strengthen incentives for continued participation in the Shared Savings Program. We appreciate comments regarding the potential benefits for rural, low-revenue, and other ACOs, as well as the opportunity for ACOs to reinvest additional shared savings in care management, health equity, data and digital infrastructure, patient outreach, and clinician engagement. We recognize that ACOs may make substantial infrastructure and operational investments to participate in two-sided risk arrangements and that the increased sharing rate may strengthen the potential return on those investments.
Comment:
A couple of commenters opposed increasing the BASIC track Level E shared savings rate, arguing that larger shared savings payments based on potentially flawed benchmarks could increase participation and payouts without increasing gross savings, thereby reducing or reversing net Medicare savings.
Response:
We appreciate the comments regarding the potential effects of increasing the BASIC track Level E shared savings rate on the distinction between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track. We agree that the Shared Savings Program should maintain incentives for ACOs to progress to higher levels of downside risk. We believe that increasing the maximum shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E from 50 percent to 60 percent appropriately strengthens incentives for ACOs participating under two-sided risk while preserving a meaningful distinction from the ENHANCED track, which retains a higher shared savings rate and requires a greater level of downside risk.
Comment:
Many supportive commenters encouraged CMS to implement the proposed increase in the sharing rate alongside related benchmark reforms, stating that the combined changes would improve the financial return on the substantial infrastructure and organizational investments needed to accept two-sided risk. A commenter stated that the sharing rate increase and related changes could attract higher-cost ACOs to BASIC track Level E and preserve greater opportunities for Medicare to share in savings. Another commenter cautioned that CMS should preserve a meaningful financial advantage for ACOs that progress to the ENHANCED track and accept the highest level of downside risk, while maintaining incentives for organizations beginning the transition to value-based care.
Separately, a commenter remained neutral on the proposed changes to the BASIC track and regional adjustment, stating that the changes may meaningfully affect decisions between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track for lower-spending, community-based ACOs but would have limited effect on higher-spending ACOs whose per-beneficiary costs exceed their benchmarks. Another commenter requested that CMS finalize benchmark rebasing changes and balance the incentives between the BASIC Level E and ENHANCED tracks to avoid penalizing ACOs serving higher-risk populations.
Response:
We appreciate the recommendations regarding the interaction between the proposed increase in the BASIC track Level E shared savings rate and related benchmarking and track incentive policies. We agree that these policies should work together to provide appropriate incentives for ACOs to participate in two-sided risk arrangements while accounting for differences in organizational capacity and the populations they serve. As discussed elsewhere in section III.G. of this final rule, we are finalizing all proposed benchmarking policies after considering the comments received. We believe that the benchmarking policies we are finalizing are designed to ensure that shared savings payments reflect measurable performance against applicable benchmarks, and we will continue to monitor these benchmarking policies' effects on net Medicare savings. We also believe that increasing the maximum shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E from 50 percent to 60 percent improves the balance of incentives between BASIC track Level E and the ENHANCED track, while preserving the ENHANCED track's higher shared savings rate for ACOs that assume greater downside risk.
Comment:
Several supportive commenters requested flexibility for ACOs applying for a January 1, 2027 start date to revise their BASIC Level E or ENHANCED track selection after publication of the final rule. Collectively, the commenters explained that proposed changes to benchmarking, risk adjustment, and shared savings policies could invalidate actuarial analyses completed before the final rule and materially affect participation decisions. They offered several recommendations to support informed decision-making, including that CMS communicate the flexibility period promptly, provide at least 60 days for ACOs to reevaluate their track selections, incorporate complete 2025 reconciliation data, allow sufficient time for updated forecasting, avoid penalizing ACOs that need additional evaluation time, and provide technical guidance, data files, and modeling assumptions as early as possible. Another supportive commenter encouraged CMS to provide sufficient implementation timelines, information, and policy stability to allow ACOs to effectively plan for and implement the proposals. Rural ACOs in particular may face a disproportionate burden from needing to conduct additional actuarial analysis after key contracting activities have begun, according to a commenter, who argued that ACOs should not be expected to make significant risk-bearing decisions before the policies governing those decisions are finalized.
Response:
We appreciate comments regarding concerns around the timing of the final rule and the potential need for ACOs applying for a January 1, 2027 start date to update their actuarial analyses and reassess their track selections in light of finalized benchmarking, risk adjustment, and
(
printed page 71411)
shared savings policies. We recognize the importance of providing ACOs with timely information and sufficient opportunity to make informed participation decisions, particularly when those decisions involve assuming downside risk. CMS intends to offer ACOs an additional opportunity to update their risk track selection during the Phase 2 RFI period (November 12, 2026-November 17, 2026 at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time). CMS will communicate applicable procedures for revising track selections through established program guidance and application processes. We are unable to provide additional time for ACOs to reevaluate their track selection that would otherwise extend the Shared Savings Program application cycle and delay downstream program operations but will continue to provide relevant technical guidance, data, and modeling information, as appropriate, to support ACO decision-making. These operational considerations do not alter our determination that increasing the maximum shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E from 50 percent to 60 percent is appropriate.
Comment:
A few supportive commenters offered additional implementation considerations. A commenter requested that the 60 percent shared savings rate apply to all ACOs already in BASIC Level E agreements. Ongoing CMS transparency and monitoring of effects on participation, net savings, and the Medicare Trust Fund were also recommended. Commenters further encouraged us to continue evaluating whether rewards appropriately reflect the level of financial risk assumed. Regarding other participation options, a commenter recommended strengthening incentives in one-sided BASIC track Levels A and B to encourage ACO entry. Another supportive commenter requested that the increased rate apply to participation agreements beginning on or after January 1, 2024, suggesting that early renewal would force rebasing and loss of accumulated savings history for these ACOs.

We appreciate comments with recommendations regarding the scope and implementation of the policy. Section 1871(e)(1)(A) of the Act prohibits substantive regulatory changes from being applied retroactively unless the Secretary determines that failing to apply the changes retroactively would be contrary to the public interest. For purposes of the BASIC track Level E sharing rate policy, we do not believe that the policy rises to a level to satisfy the requirements for retroactive application of the rule. Maintaining that rate does not create comparable unanticipated harm or program disruption and therefore does not satisfy the public interest standard for retroactive application. Accordingly, the 60 percent maximum shared savings rate will apply only to ACOs participating in BASIC track Level E for agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027. We agree that continued monitoring and transparency are important and will assess the policy's effects on program participation, net savings, and the Medicare Trust Fund as additional performance data become available. We will also continue to evaluate whether the Shared Savings Program appropriately aligns potential rewards with the level of financial risk assumed across participation options.

(2) Reduce the Maximum Weight on the Regional Adjustment for ACOs Under the ENHANCED Track
(a) Background
In the June 2016 final rule (
81 FR 37962
through
37974
), we introduced a regional adjustment to ACOs' historical benchmarks to increase participation in the Shared Savings Program and recognize efficiency of providers/suppliers in their regional service area. To implement the regional adjustment, we also established a methodology for defining regional Medicare spending. We defined an ACO's “regional service area” at § 425.20 as the counties in which its assigned beneficiaries reside and calculated regional costs using county-Level Medicare fee-for-service expenditures for assignable beneficiaries in those counties (
81 FR 37958
). These county expenditures were then aggregated to estimate average per-capita spending in the ACO's region, which served as the basis for the regional adjustment applied when benchmarks were rebased (
81 FR 37957
and
37958
).
In the June 2016 final rule (
81 FR 37954
through
37991
), we finalized a Shared Savings Program benchmark rebasing methodology to include a regional adjustment to the historical benchmark. More specifically, we finalized that the regional adjustment would be calculated as a percentage of the difference between risk-adjusted average per capita expenditures in the ACO's regional service area and the ACO's rebased historical expenditures (
81 FR 37966
). We finalized that the regional adjustment would be applied for second or subsequent agreement periods, while benchmarks for an ACO's first agreement period would continue to be based solely on the ACO's historical spending and were not adjusted for regional expenditures (
81 FR 37973
).
To provide time for ACOs to anticipate and adapt to the regional adjustment being applied to historical benchmarks, we implemented a phased approach that gradually increased the weight applied to regional spending. The first time an ACO's benchmark was rebased using the regional adjustment, we applied 35 percent of the difference between regional spending and the ACO's rebased historical benchmark if the ACO's spending was below the regional average, and 25 percent if the ACO's spending was above the regional average. The second time the benchmark was rebased, CMS increased the weight to 70 percent for ACOs with spending below their regional average and 50 percent for those with spending
(
printed page 71412)
above the regional average. Beginning with the third rebasing and in subsequent agreement periods, the adjustment was set at 70 percent of the difference between regional and ACO spending for all ACOs, unless CMS established a different weight through future rulemaking (
81 FR 37971
through
37973
).
In the 2016 final rule, we also finalized that if we adjust an ACO's benchmark during the term of the agreement period due to changes in participating providers/suppliers, the agency would reassess whether the ACO's spending was above or below the regional average to determine the appropriate adjustment percentage (
81 FR 37964
). Together, these provisions increased the role of regional spending in benchmark calculations while providing a transition period intended to limit abrupt benchmark reductions for higher-spending ACOs.
In the December 2018 final rule (
83 FR 68018
), we revised the methodology to address concerns that the 2016 regional adjustment could inadvertently inflate benchmarks for low-spending ACOs while discouraging participation by high-spending ACOs relative to their region. Under the revised rule, we also applied the regional adjustment starting with the first agreement period. By design, the regional adjustment results in more generous benchmarks for ACOs that spend below their regions. In the December 2018 final rule (
83 FR 68018
), we noted that our initial experience with the regional adjustment found that 80 percent of ACOs that renewed for a second agreement period starting in 2017 received a positive adjustment. These ACOs saw their benchmarks increase by 1.8 percent, on average, when the adjustment was applied with the 35 percent weight, with several ACOs seeing increases of over 5 percent, and one over 7 percent. We also noted that for ACOs that renewed for a second agreement period starting in 2018, they showed a similar share of ACOs receiving a positive adjustment and one ACO seeing an adjustment of over 10 percent. We noted our concern that as the weight applied to the regional adjustment increases, benchmarks for the ACOs with the lowest spending relative to their region would become overly inflated to the point where they would need to do little to change their care practices to generate savings, which could reduce incentives for these ACOs to improve the efficiency of care provided to beneficiaries. To limit the influence of regional cost disparities, we reduced the maximum weight that could be applied to the regional adjustment in any agreement period from 70 percent to 50 percent. Additionally, we capped the total dollar impact of the regional adjustment at ±5 percent of national OM per capita expenditures for each beneficiary category (
83 FR 68017
through
68024
, and
42 CFR 425.603
).
In the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69915
through
69923
), we finalized additional policies to modify the regional adjustment to further support participation by high-cost or high-risk ACOs. We implemented a set of policies designed to mitigate the impact of negative regional adjustments on ACOs' benchmarks. First, we reduced the maximum negative adjustment from −5 percent to −1.5 percent of national OM per capita expenditures for Parts A and B services (based on benchmark year 3 for assignable beneficiaries). Second, we established an approach that gradually decreased the size of the negative regional adjustment for ACOs that have a higher proportion of dually eligible Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries or a higher weighted—average prospective Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk score (
87 FR 69923
). In the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69919
), we expressed our belief that by reducing the impact of negative regional adjustments, these policies would incentivize ACOs that serve high-cost beneficiaries to join or continue to participate in the Shared Savings Program.
Most recently, in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79185
through
79196
), we modified the regional adjustment policy further to prevent any ACO from receiving an adjustment that would cause its benchmark to be lower than it would have been in the absence of a regional adjustment.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule we stated, as part of CMS's effort to align spending and value in OM, we are focused on developing policies that would accelerate accountable care service delivery across a spectrum of risk-bearing options (
91 FR 44073
). To achieve this vision, we stated that our proposed change to the regional adjustment is informed by strategic objectives focused on strengthening financial incentives for ACOs to participate in the Shared Savings Program and driving savings for ACOs and the Trust Funds (
91 FR 44073
).
(b) Revisions
For the reasons discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed to reduce the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs participating in agreement periods under the ENHANCED track from 50 percent to 35 percent, while leaving the weights for ACOs with a higher spending than the regional average unchanged (
91 FR 44073
).
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we discussed that under the Shared Savings Program, an ACO's historical benchmark is adjusted to reflect differences between its own historical spending and average spending in its region—the regional adjustment (
91 FR 44073
). For ACOs with expenditures below their regional average, this adjustment is positive, increasing the ACO's benchmark and expanding savings opportunities available to the ACO. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule we shared an analysis of PY 2024 financial reconciliation data which indicates that ACOs in the ENHANCED track receive substantially larger positive regional adjustments on average than ACOs in BASIC track Level E ($304 versus $166 per beneficiary) (
91 FR 44073
). We stated that, taken together with observed differences in gross savings—where ENHANCED track ACOs achieve higher gross savings
[
319
]
per beneficiary than BASIC track Level E ACOs ($961 versus $714 in CY 2024)—this pattern suggests that more favorable benchmark adjustments may be contributing to the higher levels of observed gross savings for ENHANCED track ACOs (
91 FR 44073
). To assess whether the magnitude of the regional adjustment is associated with ACO performance, we calculated Pearson's correlations
[
320
]
between regional adjustment size and gross savings for ACOs reconciled in PY 2024.
[
321
]
Within the ENHANCED track, we noted that the larger regional adjustments are strongly associated with higher gross savings performance (r=0.691, n=59), a relationship that is not observed among BASIC track Level E ACOs (r=0.09, n=17) (
91 FR 44073
). We stated that the contrast between tracks raises the possibility that the scale of positive regional adjustments to the benchmark are partly driving performance rather than genuine efficiency gains (
91 FR 44073
). We noted that, while this is a descriptive finding, it is consistent with
(
printed page 71413)
our concern motivating the proposed reduction in the positive regional adjustment weight from 50 percent to 35 percent (
91 FR 44073
). Moreover, the average size of the adjustment has gone up—from $206 in PY 2020 to $344 in PY 2025, while the share of ACOs receiving a positive regional adjustment has remained mostly stable within a range between 70 and 86 percent over the same time period. We stated that this pattern suggests that, while the prevalence of regional adjustments has remained broadly unchanged, the financial impact of those adjustments has increased over time, amplifying the influence of regional adjustments on ACO benchmark calculations (
91 FR 44073
).
As discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, there is limited evidence suggesting that the ENHANCED track is generating additional Trust Funds savings relative to the BASIC track (
91 FR 44073
). First, the size of the regional adjustment may be contributing to higher gross savings performance in the ENHANCED track, which causes us to question whether those savings reflect genuine cost reduction. Second, lower spending ACOs (defined as those with historical expenditures below their regional average) in the ENHANCED track currently benefit from both a higher shared savings rate and larger regional adjustments on average. We stated that together these advantages may incentivize selection into the ENHANCED track independent of an ACO's capacity to achieve genuine cost savings to Medicare (
91 FR 44074
). We proposed to reduce the positive regional adjustment weight for these ACOs, paired with an increase in the shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E, which is designed to rebalance financial incentives across tracks and encourage ACOs to select their tracks based on their actual capacity to reduce costs rather than differences in financial advantages embedded in track design, thereby potentially improving Trust Funds net savings (
91 FR 44074
). We referred readers to the discussion in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44067
) and the data analysis described in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44068
through
44072
) for additional details.
We stated that we believe that a 35 percent positive regional adjustment would maintain consistency with the current schedule of weights used to calculate the regional adjustment, a structure with which ACOs are already familiar (
91 FR 44074
). We also stated that we believe this approach would minimize complexity by maintaining a single weight for lower-spending ENHANCED track ACOs for all participation years (
91 FR 44074
). We noted that, at the same time, it would preserve an appropriate balance between rewarding regional efficiencies demonstrated at the start of the agreement period and rewarding improvement relative to an ACO's past historical performance over time (
91 FR 44074
).
We proposed this change to be effective for agreement periods beginning on January 1, 2027, and in subsequent years (
91 FR 44074
). We stated that reducing the weight used in calculating the regional adjustment applied to ACOs considering participation in the ENHANCED track would reduce the contribution of baseline regional efficiency on historical benchmark calculations (
91 FR 44074
). And we stated that, as a result, it would put a stronger emphasis on rewarding improvement in the provision of coordinated care and lowering costs rather than baseline efficiency at entry to the agreement period (
91 FR 44074

91 FR 44076
through

We stated that one goal of this proposal—reducing the regional adjustment weight—is to encourage ACOs to select a diverse cross-section of participants so that ACOs' success is driven by operational efficiencies and clinical performance rather than passive capture of ACO participants with pre-existing regional efficiencies (
91 FR 44074

We added that more modest regional adjustment amounts could also result in ACOs opting for participation in BASIC track Level E instead of the ENHANCED track, and therefore result in the Trust Funds retaining a greater share of savings while still offering ACOs a long-term incentive for creating savings because of the proposed higher prior savings adjustments in future agreement periods (
91 FR 44074

In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we stated that under this proposal, the phase-in of weights used in the regional adjustment calculation for agreement periods beginning on January 1, 2027, and in subsequent years, as determined by an ACO's expenditures relative to their region, would change for ENHANCED track ACOs (

We sought comment on the proposal to reduce the maximum weight on the regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs under the ENHANCED track to a weight of 35 percent for agreement periods beginning on January 1, 2027, and in subsequent years. We stated that under this proposal, the weight for higher-spending ACOs, and for BASIC track ACOs that are lower spending would remain unchanged (
91 FR 44076
). We also sought comment on proposed technical and conforming changes to other provisions of § 425.656, and § 425.600.
The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters supported the proposal to reduce the maximum weight of the positive regional adjustment. A commenter stated that increasing the shared savings rate under BASIC track Level E while reducing the weight of the positive regional adjustment in the ENHANCED track may help attract more high-cost ACOs to the BASIC track, where Medicare has greater opportunities to share in savings. A commenter supported both the regional adjustment and prior savings adjustment proposals and recommended that the policies be considered in tandem rather than approved separately. Another commenter supported the changes if it helps community health centers (CHCs) enter, remain in, and succeed under the Shared Savings Program.
Response:
We appreciate the support of our proposal to reduce the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs participating under the ENHANCED track from 50 percent to 35 percent. The policy we are finalizing is limited in scope. It only applies to ENHANCED track ACOs that have lower spending than their regional service area, beginning with the second agreement period, where the ACO's benchmark is adjusted based on regional service area expenditures. It does not change the weights used for the regional adjustment for BASIC track ACOs, for ENHANCED track ACOs in their first agreement period (which weight remains at 35 percent), or for ACOs with higher spending than their region. It also does not change the negative regional adjustment or the cap on the regional adjustment. We agree with commenters that the interaction of benchmark policies and shared savings opportunities can influence ACO participation decisions. As a commenter observed, increasing the shared savings rate under BASIC track Level E while reducing the maximum weight of the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs under the ENHANCED track may improve the relative appeal of BASIC track Level E for certain ACOs. We believe these changes, when considered together, will better balance participation incentives across tracks and more closely align the financial opportunities available under each track with an ACO's capacity to reduce expenditures and assume performance-based risk. We also agree that moderating the magnitude of the positive regional adjustment under the ENHANCED track advances our goal of reducing differences in benchmark advantages that may influence ACO participation and track selection. While we agree with the commenter that described the revisions to the regional adjustment and the prior savings adjustment as complementing one another, we do not believe they are inextricably linked or that they must be adopted together. Each independently furthers program goals: the reduced maximum weight applied to the positive regional adjustment moderates benchmark advantages for lower-spending ENHANCED track ACOs, and the increased prior savings adjustment scaling factor mitigates the effects of rebasing for ACOs that have generated savings.

We appreciate comments in support of the proposal on the basis that it may support the participation of community health centers in the Shared Savings Program. We also appreciate comments supporting the proposal on the basis that it would improve the alignment of financial incentives within the Shared Savings Program and moderate benchmark advantages that may result from differences in spending relative to an ACO's regional service area. We continue to believe that regional expenditures are an important component of benchmarking methodology while recognizing the need to ensure that the magnitude of the regional adjustment does not create unintended participation incentives.
Comment:
A couple of commenters supported the proposal because it is consistent with their prior-year recommendations to mitigate selection effects and improve benchmark calculation but urged CMS to phase out the regional adjustment entirely to more fully address the effects of selective participation, noting this would also remove its influence on the prior savings adjustment and reduce program complexity. Some commenters further urged CMS to continue monitoring the selection effects of the regional adjustment, including its impact on the prior shared savings adjustment, as part of a broader effort to understand how the Shared Savings Program affects Medicare spending prior to applying risk adjustment and upward benchmark adjustments. Similarly, a commenter stated that regional benchmarks can reward preexisting efficiency without inducing additional savings and can attract already low-spending providers, and recommended that CMS reduce reliance on regional adjustments and evaluate changes in ACO composition as a program cost rather than as savings.
A couple of commenters supported the proposed reduction in the maximum weight of the positive regional adjustment for ENHANCED track ACOs but urged CMS to eliminate the regional adjustment across all tracks rather than reducing its weight for the ENHANCED track alone, stating the adjustment is asymmetrical because the benchmark increase for low-cost providers exceeds the reduction for high-cost providers and therefore rewards recruiting low-cost providers and beneficiaries over improving care. One of these commenters cited that 382 of 476 ACOs participating in 2024 received a positive regional adjustment and that the adjustment alone accounted for 2.1 percent of benchmark growth for ACOs beginning in 2024, and stated that higher benchmarks did not produce meaningful program growth. The commenter recommended that if CMS concludes additional support is needed to sustain rural and safety-net participation, it should provide that support directly rather than through a benchmark mechanism that rewards the exclusion of high-cost providers.
A commenter supported the proposed modifications, recognizing CMS's effort to place greater emphasis on an ACO's own performance and value-creation activities. The commenter recommended, however, that CMS consider a phased transition to the new methodology rather than an immediate change. The commenter stated that a gradual reduction of the regional adjustment factor would give organizations a predictable pathway to adapt their financial planning and care management strategies; and that a transition period would help maintain confidence in long-term program participation.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and recommendations. Several commenters recommended that we go beyond the proposed reduction and phase out or eliminate the regional adjustment, either for the ENHANCED track or across all tracks. The positive regional adjustment accounts for regional cost variation by making an ACO's benchmark less dependent on its own historical expenditures and more reflective of spending in its regional service area, which reduces disincentives for ACOs that are already efficient relative to their region to participate and continue lowering spending (
91 FR 44081
). Based on our experience with the program, we believe it is appropriate to rebalance rather than eliminate the adjustment by moderating the extent to which regional efficiency is reflected in benchmarks for lower-spending ENHANCED track ACOs.
Specifically, as discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44073
through
44074
), ENHANCED track ACOs on average receive larger positive regional adjustments than BASIC track ACOs while also benefiting from a higher shared savings rate. We noted that the proposed reduction in the positive regional adjustment weight for these ACOs, paired with an increase in the shared savings rate for BASIC track Level E, is intended to rebalance financial incentives across tracks and encourage ACOs to select their tracks based on their actual capacity to reduce costs rather than differences in financial advantages embedded in track design, thereby potentially improving Trust Funds net savings (
91 FR 44074
). We believe that reducing the maximum weight used in calculating the positive regional adjustment from 50 percent to 35 percent for lower-spending ENHANCED track ACOs, beginning in the second agreement period, meets the needs of the program by continuing to account for regional cost variation for these ACOs while better balancing financial incentives across tracks. We will monitor the impact of this change.
We appreciate the considerations commenters raised in support of a broader change, including the observation that the adjustment may influence the prior savings adjustment, that reliance on regional comparisons adds complexity to the benchmarking methodology, and that a substantial majority of ACOs participating in 2024 received a positive regional adjustment. We also acknowledge the concern that a regional comparison may recognize spending levels established before an ACO's participation in the program. As we explained in the December 2018 final rule, “by design, the regional adjustment results in more generous benchmarks for ACOs that spend below their regions,” and we stated at that time that we had concerns that the regional adjustment could have unintended consequences and adverse effects on ACO incentives and we would continue to monitor the regional adjustment for changes that may be needed in the future (
83 FR 68018
). The reduction we are finalizing moderates the magnitude of the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ACOs in the track where it is largest, and it does not rest on the conclusion that the adjustment lacks continuing value. Additionally, we are not in this rule substituting a direct form of support for rural or safety net ACOs in place of the regional adjustment.
We agree with commenters who urged us to continue monitoring the selection effects of the regional adjustment, including its interaction with the prior savings adjustment. Consistent with the commitments we made when the adjustment was established and refined (
81 FR 37962
;
83 FR 68023
), we will continue to monitor the effects of the regional adjustment on ACO participation, benchmark calculations, and expenditures, and will address any necessary refinements through future rulemaking. As part of that monitoring, we will consider the recommendation that we account for changes in ACO composition in assessing program savings. A commenter recommended that we phase in the reduced weight rather than apply it immediately. We address this recommendation together with other comments on implementation timing under section III.G.5.c.(2) of this final rule.

Comment:
Most commenters opposed the proposal to reduce the maximum weight of the positive regional adjustment from 50 percent to 35 percent, stating it would reduce the recognition provided to ACOs that maintain expenditures below those of their regional service areas. These commenters stated that reducing the maximum weight would weaken incentives for ACOs to enter or remain in the ENHANCED track, accept greater levels of performance-based risk, and continue investing in activities intended to improve quality and reduce expenditures. Several commenters stated that the proposal is inconsistent with the Shared Savings Program's objective of encouraging ACOs to assume greater risk and could discourage efficient, high-performing ACOs from continuing their participation under the ENHANCED track.
A few of these commenters also stated that reducing the adjustment could reduce resources available for reinvestment in care coordination, population health infrastructure, analytics, workforce, information technology, and other activities that support quality improvement and expenditure reductions. Among commenters who opposed this proposal, some expressed particular concern about the effects on smaller ACOs, including those with benchmarks that are more heavily weighted toward regional expenditure trends. A couple of commenters added that the change could undermine the longer-term transition toward regional, sustainable benchmarking.
Some commenters stated that reducing the maximum weight in the Shared Savings Program while the CMS Innovation Center's Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model retains a 50 percent positive regional adjustment would create inconsistent incentives across CMS accountable care programs and that efficient ENHANCED track ACOs might move to LEAD rather than remain in the Shared Savings Program. Some other commenters raised concerns about inconsistency across models, or about effects on continued participation, without predicting movement between programs. Commenters raising these concerns noted that CMS adopted the 50 percent positive regional adjustment in LEAD based on its application in the Shared Savings Program, that changing the adjustment is not a feature LEAD was intended to test, and that LEAD eliminates periodic rebasing during its 10-year performance period to provide a predictable opportunity to sustain savings and investment.
Response:
We appreciate comments expressing concerns that reducing the maximum weight of the positive regional adjustment could diminish the incentive provided to ACOs that maintain expenditures below those of their regional service areas, weaken incentives to accept greater levels of performance-based risk, or discourage participation in the ENHANCED track. We continue to believe that regional expenditures are an important component of the benchmarking methodology. The policy we are finalizing does not eliminate the positive regional adjustment or alter its fundamental role. Instead, it moderates the maximum weight applied to the positive regional adjustment for lower-spending ENHANCED track ACOs, beginning in the second agreement period when the ACO's benchmark is adjusted based on regional service area expenditures. ACOs with higher spending than their region, and all BASIC track ACOs, are unaffected by this policy change. Lower-spending ENHANCED track ACOs will continue to be eligible to receive a positive regional adjustment.
We recognize commenters' concerns that a reduced regional adjustment may lessen the financial benefit available to certain ACOs and could affect participation decisions, particularly for ACOs considering whether to participate under the ENHANCED track. We also recognize commenters' concerns that shared savings payments support continued investments in care coordination, population health management, analytics, workforce, and other activities intended to improve quality and reduce expenditures. In evaluating this proposal, we considered the importance of maintaining incentives for participation and performance while also ensuring that the financial opportunities available under the Shared Savings Program remain appropriately balanced across participation options. We believe that under the finalized policy, affected ACOs will continue to have ample opportunities to generate shared savings and to use these resources to continue to improve quality and reduce expenditures in future years.
As discussed elsewhere in sections III.G.5.c.(1) and III.G.5.d of this final rule, we are simultaneously increasing the shared savings rate under BASIC track Level E and increasing the prior savings adjustment scaling factor. Considered together, these policies will better align the financial opportunities available under the program with an ACO's capacity to reduce expenditures and assume performance-based risk. These changes will support continued participation in the Shared Savings Program while preserving greater potential rewards for ACOs that accept the higher levels of risk associated with participation under the ENHANCED track.
Using PY 2025 simulation data, we estimate that 144 of 249 ENHANCED-track ACOs (58 percent) would be impacted by the proposed reduction in the maximum positive regional adjustment weight (0.50 to 0.35). Of those, 141 experienced a benchmark reduction, with an average decrease of approximately $96 per beneficiary per year (0.82 percent of the historical benchmark). Individual benchmark reductions ranged from about $0.26 to $193 (0 percent to 1.79 percent of the historical benchmark). Three ACOs benefitted from this proposed reduction as it reduced the negative impact of enrollment groups that were higher spending than their region while the positive impact of other enrollment groups was subject to the cap under both weightings (0.50 and 0.35). We note, however, that these estimated benchmark reductions should be considered in the context of the rule as a whole, including other financial provisions that are expected to offset or mitigate these impacts for many ACOs.
We acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding the possible effects of the policy on smaller ACOs and other ACOs whose benchmarks may be more affected by regional expenditures. The revised maximum weight applies prospectively to agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, and does not alter the weights applicable to agreement periods already underway. As discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we are not modifying the negative regional adjustment weights, which will remain unchanged (
91 FR 44074
). In addition, the revised maximum positive regional adjustment weight applies only to lower-spending ENHANCED track ACOs beginning the second agreement period and no impact on BASIC track ACOs, ENHANCED track ACOs with higher spending than their region, or ENHANCED track ACOs in their first agreement period. We will continue to monitor participation, track selection, and program outcomes following implementation, including among smaller ACOs and ACOs currently participating under the ENHANCED track, and may consider refinements through future rulemaking.
We recognize the commenters' concerns that different maximum
(
