g. Reform the Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT) Component of the Benchmark Update Factor
(1) Background
As finalized in the December 2018 final rule (
83 FR 68024
through
68030
), we used our statutory authority under section 1899(i)(3) of the Act to adopt the policy under which we update the historical benchmark using a blend of national and regional growth rates, rather than the projected absolute amount of growth in national per capita expenditures for Parts A and B services under the original Medicare FFS program as required under section 1899(d)(1)(B)(ii) of the Act. In accordance with § 425.601(b), applicable for agreement periods beginning on or after July 1, 2019, and before January 1, 2024,
[
352
]
we update the historical benchmark for an ACO for each performance year using a blend of national and regional growth rates between BY3 and the performance year. To update the benchmark, we make separate calculations for expenditure categories for each of the following populations of beneficiaries based on Medicare enrollment type: ESRD, disabled, aged/dual eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, aged/non-dual eligible for Medicare and Medicaid (§ 425.601(b)(1)).
The national-regional blend is a weighted average of national FFS and regional growth rates between BY3 and the performance year for the applicable Medicare enrollment type (§ 425.601(b)(4)). The national growth rates are computed using CMS Office of the Actuary national Medicare expenditure data for BY3 and the performance year for assignable beneficiaries (as defined at § 425.20) identified for the 12-month calendar year corresponding to each year (§ 425.601(b)(2)). Regional growth rates are computed using expenditures for the ACO's regional service area for BY3 and the performance year (§ 425.601(b)(3)). To calculate regional expenditures, we determine the counties included in the ACO's regional service area based on the ACO's assigned beneficiary population for the year and determine the ACO's regional expenditures as specified under § 425.601(c) and (d) and § 425.601(b)(3)(i) and (ii).
As noted, the national and regional growth rates are blended together by taking a weighted average of the two. The weight assigned to the national component of the national-regional blend for a given Medicare enrollment type is calculated as the share of assignable beneficiaries in the ACO's regional service area that are assigned to the ACO for the applicable performance year (as calculated in § 425.601(a)(5)(v) and § 425.601(b)(4)(i)). The weight assigned to the regional component of the national-regional blend for a given Medicare enrollment type is equal to 1 minus the weight applied to the national growth rate (§ 425.601(b)(4)(ii)). Under this approach, as an ACO's penetration in its regional service area increases, the weight applied to the national component of the national-regional blend increases and the weight applied to the regional component decreases.
The national and regional growth rates are blended together by taking a weighted average of the two. Specifically, for each Medicare enrollment type, the national-regional blended growth rate is equal to the sum of the following: (1) the growth rate for national assignable FFS expenditures for BY3 to the performance year multiplied by the weight assigned to the national component; and (2) the average growth rate for regional FFS expenditures for BY3 to the performance year based on the ACO's regional service area multiplied by the weight assigned to the regional component (
87 FR 69881
). In accordance with § 425.601(a)(5), we also use blended national-regional growth rates to trend forward expenditures for each benchmark year (BY1 and BY2) to BY3 dollars, making separate calculations for each Medicare enrollment type.
We summarized commenters' concerns about using the blended national-regional growth rates for benchmarking in the CY 2023 PFS final
(
printed page 71460)
rule (
87 FR 69879
through
69881
). Specifically, ACOs and other interested parties expressed concerns regarding the dynamic under which an ACO that reduces costs for its own assigned beneficiaries also reduces its average regional costs, resulting in a relatively lower benchmark for the ACO under the blended national-regional growth rates used to trend and update the ACO's historical benchmark. As summarized in the CY 2022 PFS final rule, ACOs and other interested parties also have suggested that this dynamic particularly disadvantages ACOs with high market penetration in their regional service areas, which may tend to be ACOs operating in rural areas (
86 FR 65296
through
65299
).
In the CY 2023 PFS final rule, we implemented new policies effective beginning with performance year 2024 to address these concerns by incorporating a prospectively set projected administrative growth factor, a variant of the modified United States Per Capita Cost (USPCC) called the Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT), into a three-way blend with national and regional growth rates to update an ACO's historical benchmark for each performance year in the ACO's agreement period (
87 FR 69882
through
69898
). Incorporating this prospective trend in the update to the benchmark insulates a portion of the annual update from any savings occurring as a result of the actions of ACOs participating in the Shared Savings Program and helps to address the impact of increasing market penetration by ACOs in a regional service area on a growth factor that only uses blended national-regional rates. Under that methodology, because the ACPT is set prospectively at the outset of an agreement period, any savings generated by ACOs during the agreement period are not reflected in the ACPT. Accordingly, incorporation of the ACPT allows for benchmarks to increase beyond actual spending growth rates as ACOs slow spending growth. We noted that the use of the three-way blend to update ACOs' benchmarks should incentivize both greater savings by ACOs and greater program participation. We also noted that we believed that because incorporating the ACPT into the update would reduce the degree to which an ACO's savings negatively impact its benchmark through the regional trend component of the update, the ACPT would help to address the disproportionate impact of an ACO's savings on the benchmark update for ACOs with a high market share (
87 FR 69882
).
In addition, as discussed in the Regulatory Impact Analysis for the CY 2023 PFS proposed rule (
87 FR 46427
), we projected that this approach for use of an ACPT/national- regional three-way blended update factor, in combination with other proposed changes to the statutory payment model in the CY 2023 PFS proposed rule, as well as then-current policies established using the authority of section 1899(i)(3) of the Act (
87 FR 46403
through
46404

Since we have established the three-way blended update factor, we have continued to reexamine this projection to ensure that the requirement under section 1899(i)(3)(B) of the Act that an alternative payment model not result in additional program expenditures continues to be satisfied, and we have found continued compliance with section 1899(i)(3)(B) of the Act.
Under § 425.660, the three-way blend is calculated as the weighted average of the ACPT (one-third) and the existing national-regional blend (two-thirds) for use in updating an ACO's historical benchmark between BY3 and the performance year. As we described in the CY 2023 PFS final rule, we calculate the ACPT component of the blended annual update using an annualized growth rate based on 5-year projections in per capita spending as of the start of an ACO's agreement period as specified in § 425.660(b)(2)(ii). We use an annualized growth rate based on 5-year projections in per capita spending as of the start of an ACO's agreement period to align the ACPT with the 5-year agreement periods used under the Shared Savings Program. The CMS Office of the Actuary projects the ACPT, which is a modification of the FFS United States Per Capita Cost (USPCC) growth trend projections used annually for establishing Medicare Advantage rates. We set the ACPT growth factors for an ACO's entire 5-year agreement period near the start of the agreement period (
87 FR 46163
). The ACPT factors remain unchanged throughout the ACO's agreement period, providing a degree of certainty to ACOs.
Similar to the production of FFS USPCCs, for a given agreement period cohort (that is, ACOs with the same agreement period start date) and performance year, OACT produces two separate, modified USPCC values for ESRD and non-ESRD aged/disabled populations (as described in § 425.660(b)(2)). In the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69882
), we described the modified USPCC values as reflecting an exclusion of payments for indirect medical education (IME), disproportionate share hospitals (DSH), and supplemental payment for IHS/Tribal Hospitals and hospitals located in Puerto Rico, and including payments associated with hospice claims (
87 FR 69882
). Subsequently, for a given ACO and performance year, the two modified USPCCs serve as inputs into the calculation of four separate ACPT values, one for each of four Medicare enrollment types: ESRD, disabled, aged/dual eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, and aged/non-dual eligible for Medicare and Medicaid (
87 FR 69882
). In turn, each of these enrollment-type specific ACPT values is used to calculate an ACO's four enrollment-type specific three-way blended update factors (as described in § 425.652(b)(4)).
As we have previously noted (
87 FR 69896
), we expect in any year the ACPT could overestimate or underestimate the actual growth rate of expenditures of the national assignable population. In the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 69882-69888
), we included the following factors in the design of the three-way blended update factor to mitigate impacts in differences between the ACPT and the actual growth rate of expenditures for the national assignable population:
The ACPT is one-third of the three-way blended update factor; the remaining two-thirds of the blend are based on the national-regional trend, which reflects actual national and regional spending growth.
As part of the ACPT calculation, the ACPT is expressed as a flat dollar amount and is risk-adjusted, which may benefit low growth/low spending ACOs and ACOs serving medically complex populations.
We established a guardrail policy where, if an ACO generates losses for a performance year that meet or exceed its minimum loss rate (MLR) (for two-sided model ACOs) or negative minimum savings rate (MSR) (for one-sided model ACOs) under the three-way blended update factor, we will recalculate the ACO's updated benchmark using the two-way national-regional blended update factor. If the ACO generates a smaller amount of losses using the two-way blend, we will use this smaller amount to determine the ACO's responsibility for shared losses, if applicable.
If we determine that expenditure growth has differed significantly from projections made at the start of the agreement period due to unforeseen circumstances, such as an economic recession, pandemic, or other factors, a reduction in the weight placed on the ACPT may be considered. ). We stated that this would replace the current approach under which the modified USPCC annualized growth rates used to construct ACPT values are established on an agreement period-specific basis, as illustrated in Table B-G32 of the proposed rule (
91 FR 44105
). We noted that this proposal would not change the methodology by which CMS would calculate the modified USPCC annualized growth rates for any given performance year (
91 FR 44105
). We also noted that this proposal would only change the timing of the calculation and publicly reporting of modified USPCC annualized growth rates (
91 FR 44105
).
Specifically, for agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, and in subsequent years, we proposed that CMS would no longer calculate a fixed five-year schedule of annualized growth rates at the start of an ACO's agreement period (
91 FR 44105

91 FR 44105

This means that, although ACOs would no longer receive a five-year set of enrollment type-specific ACPT values near the beginning of the agreement period, they would still receive advance notice of the modified USPCC annualized growth rate used to calculate enrollment type-specific ACPT values for a given performance year in the year preceding that performance year. As illustrated in Table B-G33 of the proposed rule, in the late spring or early summer preceding the start of the first performance year of an agreement

period, an ACO would be able to review the performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates publicly reported, applicable to the first performance year (
91 FR 44105
through
44106

Then, during each subsequent performance year through the remainder of the agreement period, the ACO would receive a newly calculated set of ACPT values based on the performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates calculated and published in the summer preceding that performance year. For example, CMS will publicly report the PY 2028 ESRD and aged/disabled modified USPCC annualized growth rates in late spring or early summer 2027. These rates will be used to calculate PY 2028 enrollment type-specific ACO-level ACPT values (that is, PY1 values for ACOs entering agreement periods on January 1, 2028, and PY2 values for ACOs entering agreement periods on January 1, 2027). These ACO-level ACPT values will be provided to ACOs during PY 2028.
As illustrated in Table B-G34 of the proposed rule, under the current approach, modified USPCC annualized growth rates calculated on an agreement period basis may differ across agreement period cohorts (
91 FR 44106
).
As discussed in the proposed rule, establishing performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates would improve consistency across agreement periods by ensuring that, for a given performance year, the same modified USPCC annualized growth rates for that year would apply to all ACOs regardless of agreement period start date (
91 FR 44106
). For example, at reconciliation for PY 2028, the same modified USPCC annualized growth rates would apply to ACOs that entered agreement periods on January 1, 2027, and January 1, 2028. We noted that neither cohort of ACOs would face different modified USPCC annualized growth rates for that performance year solely because their agreement periods began in different years (
91 FR 44106
).
We stated that we continue to believe that the prospective character of the ACPT is an important feature that benefits ACOs by providing a degree of certainty regarding their annual benchmark updates (
91 FR 44106
). However, as we acknowledged in the
(
printed page 71463)
CY 2023 PFS final rule, establishing modified USPCC annualized growth rates at the start of an ACO's agreement period means that ACOs entering agreement periods in different years could be subject to higher or lower updates based on how projections differ across agreement periods. Thus, the current approach poses a tradeoff between long-term predictability (over a five-year agreement period) and inconsistency across agreement period cohorts. Under this approach, our goal is to thoughtfully recalibrate the balance of that tradeoff by forgoing some predictability in favor of greater consistency and, in turn, fairness across agreement period cohorts. Specifically, we noted that although ACOs would no longer receive a fixed five-year schedule of modified USPCC annualized growth rates near the beginning of the agreement period, they would receive advance notice of the modified USPCC annualized growth rates in the late spring or early summer of the year preceding a given performance year, thus preserving the ACPT's core design as a prospectively-set external factor that provides ACOs with a degree of certainty regarding their annual benchmark update, as originally intended, albeit on a shorter time horizon (1 year rather than 5 years) (
91 FR 44106
). We stated that, at the same time, applying a consistent modified USPCC annualized growth rate to all ACOs reconciled for a given performance year, regardless of their agreement period start date, would promote greater fairness by reducing the disparities that currently arise when different start dates result in different growth rates, which can advantage or disadvantage certain ACOs (
91 FR 44106
). Lastly, we noted that the approach may reduce operational complexity by ensuring that, in a given performance year, there is a single set of underlying modified USPCC annualized growth rates used to calculate ACPT values, rather than a unique set of modified USPCC annualized growth rates that are specific to each agreement period cohort of ACOs being reconciled for that performance year (

through

(b) Guardrail on the Difference Between the Modified USPCC Cumulative Growth Rate and the Actual Cumulative Growth Rate of Expenditures for the National Assignable Population for Agreement Periods Beginning on or After January 1, 2027
As discussed in the proposed rule, for agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, we proposed to establish a guardrail on instances in which the modified USPCC cumulative growth rates used to construct ACPT values differ substantially from observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures (
91 FR 44107
). Specifically, we proposed to establish a guardrail that would not allow the modified USPCC cumulative growth rate for each of the ESRD population and the Aged/Disabled population to be more than 1.0 percentage point below or 1.5 percentage points above the corresponding observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures for that population, respectively (where the percentage point thresholds are rounded to the nearest tenth of a percentage point) (
91 FR 44107
). We stated that we would apply the guardrail at reconciliation for a given performance year. Hereafter, we refer to the difference between the modified USPCC cumulative growth rate and observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures as “delta modified USPCC” (
91 FR 44107
).
We stated that establishing guardrail thresholds that are fixed over an agreement period, rather than thresholds that widen or narrow, acknowledges that the realized path of delta modified USPCC over an agreement period cannot be known in advance with sufficient certainty (
91 FR 44107
). That is, the extent to which delta modified USPCC widens or narrows over an agreement period depends on the extent to which projection errors in a given year offset the projection error that's accumulated over prior years. This is an outcome that can only be known at financial reconciliation for a given performance year. Therefore, whereas establishing thresholds that widen or narrow reflects a prospective assumption about the trajectory that delta modified USPCC will take over an agreement period, establishing fixed thresholds applies a consistent tolerance for delta modified USPCC to each performance year in recognition of the fact that delta modified USPCC may widen or narrow over an agreement period.
We stated that proposing to set the guardrail threshold levels asymmetrically at −1.0 percentage point and +1.5 percentage points, as opposed to a tighter, wider, or symmetrical guardrail range, primarily reflects a policy judgment about the appropriate approach to limit the effects of unusually large delta modified USPCC at financial reconciliation for a given performance year (
91 FR 44107
). The proposed threshold levels are not based on predictions of the path that delta modified USPCC will take over an agreement period (
91 FR 44107
). Rather, they establish the bounds within which delta modified USPCC would be addressed (
91 FR 44107
). In proposing these levels, we stated that we aim to balance several considerations: protection of ACOs from the financial consequences of unusually large cumulative under-projection (substantially negative delta modified USPCC); protection of the Medicare Trust Funds from the financial consequences of unusually large cumulative over-projection (substantially positive delta modified USPCC); and preservation of the original policy aims of the ACPT (that is, to allow for benchmarks to increase beyond actual spending growth even as ACOs slow spending growth) (
91 FR 44107
).
In proposing these levels, we stated that we also considered alternative approaches (
91 FR 44107
). For example, a tighter guardrail threshold would provide greater protection to ACOs and the Medicare Trust Funds from delta modified USPCC. However, we stated that it could also undermine the prospective design of the ACPT if it results in the frequent application of the guardrail (
91 FR 44107
). Conversely, we noted that a wider guardrail was also considered and such a guardrail could be applied less frequently than a tighter guardrail and, in turn, may preserve the prospective design of the ACPT to a greater degree, but the wider guardrail could also potentially expose the Medicare Trust Funds and ACOs to harms associated with substantially positive or substantially negative delta modified USPCC (
91 FR 44107
). We also considered a symmetrical guardrail that would apply equally in cases of both substantially positive and substantially negative delta modified USPCC (
91 FR 44107
). However, we noted that we believe that an asymmetric guardrail that imposes a tighter bound on substantially negative delta modified USPCC and a wider bound on substantially positive delta modified USPCC would more directly protect ACOs from the harms associated with substantially negative delta modified USPCC while still allowing ACOs to
(
printed page 71464)
benefit from modestly positive delta modified USPCC, consistent with the prospective design of the ACPT (
91 FR 44107
). Lastly, we stated that, while historical delta modified USPCC values have informed the reasonableness of the proposed thresholds, they have not determined the threshold levels themselves, as the path that delta modified USPCC takes over any agreement period cannot be known in advance and may differ across agreement periods (
91 FR 44107
). Taken together, the proposed threshold levels of −1.0 percentage point and +1.5 percentage points are best understood as reasonable policy calibrations that, we believe, strike an acceptable balance of the considerations discussed previously. We stated that we also believe that the guardrail as proposed would be consistent with the original policy aims of the ACPT, as well as program goals of predictability, fairness, and administrative feasibility (
91 FR 44107
). We sought comment on the proposed threshold levels, including whether a tighter guardrail, a wider guardrail, or a modification of any of the approaches discussed in this paragraph, would represent a better balance of the considerations discussed previously.
As discussed in the proposed rule, the following steps illustrate how the proposed guardrail on delta modified USPCC would operate in practice at reconciliation for a given performance year for agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027 (
91 FR 44107
through
44109
):
Step 1: Calculate the applicable delta modified USPCC values.
As illustrated in Table B-G35 of the proposed rule (
91 FR 44108
), at reconciliation for a given performance year, CMS would calculate two delta modified USPCC values for each agreement period cohort: one for the ESRD population, and one for the Aged/Disabled population. For a given population, delta modified USPCC would be equal to the modified USPCC cumulative growth rate minus the observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures. Because delta modified USPCC values are constructed at the agreement period cohort, performance year, and population levels, they apply uniformly to all ACOs within a given cohort for a given performance year.
Step 2: Determine whether each delta modified USPCC falls outside the guardrails.
As illustrated in Table B-G36 of the proposed rule (
91 FR 44108
), once calculated, each population-specific delta modified USPCC value would then be compared with the previously mentioned guardrail thresholds (−1.0 percentage point and +1.5 percentage points). If delta modified USPCC for either population falls within the guardrail thresholds (that is, greater than or equal to −1.0 percentage point and less than or equal to +1.5 percentage points), no guardrail adjustment would apply for a population, and the corresponding enrollment type-specific ACPT values initially calculated for that performance year would remain unchanged. If delta modified USPCC falls outside the guardrail thresholds (that is, less than −1.0 percentage point or greater than +1.5 percentage points) for one or both of the populations, a guardrail adjustment would apply.
(
printed page 71465)
Step 3. Calculate the guardrail-adjusted modified USPCC cumulative growth rate, as applicable.
As illustrated in Table B-G37 of the proposed rule (
91 FR 44108
), for a given population, if delta modified USPCC falls below the lower guardrail threshold, the applicable modified USPCC cumulative growth rate would be replaced with a guardrail-adjusted value equal to the observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures minus 1.0 percentage points. If delta modified USPCC falls above the upper guardrail threshold, the applicable modified USPCC cumulative growth rate would be replaced with a guardrail-adjusted value equal to the observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures plus 1.5 percentage points.
Step 4. Recompute ACPT values, as applicable.
If a guardrail adjustment applies (as determined in Step 2), the corresponding enrollment type-specific ACPT values initially calculated for that performance year would be recomputed using the guardrail-adjusted modified USPCC cumulative growth rate (calculated in Step 3) rather than the original modified USPCC cumulative growth rate. For the ESRD population, the guardrail-adjusted modified USPCC cumulative growth rate would be used to recompute ACPT values applicable to the ESRD enrollment type. For the Aged/Disabled population, the guardrail-adjusted modified USPCC cumulative growth rate would be used to recompute ACPT values applicable to the Disabled, Aged/Dual-Eligible, and Aged/Non-Dual-Eligible enrollment types. The recomputed ACPT values would then be used to construct the three-way blended update factors, updated historical benchmarks, and, in turn, shared savings and losses calculations for the applicable performance year.
The procedures described in the proposed rule would be applied at financial reconciliation for each performance year of an ACO's agreement period (
91 FR 44109
). The application of a guardrail on delta modified USPCC in a given performance year would affect only the ACO-level ACPT values and downstream shared savings and losses calculations applicable to that performance year. This is appropriate because delta modified USPCC is, by definition, a comparison of the cumulative modified USPCC growth rate to the cumulative observed growth in national assignable expenditures. Thus, the guardrail calculation of each performance year already accounts for projection error accumulated through prior years by construction. For example, in Table B-G38 of the proposed rule (
91 FR 44109
), the delta modified USPCC for PY3 reflects cumulative projection error through PY3. As a result, any guardrail adjustment applied in PY1 or PY2 would not need to be carried forward into PY3 because the cumulative structure of the guardrail calculation for PY3 would have incorporated the cumulative effect of projection errors from PY1 and PY2.
(
printed page 71466)

(c) Retroactive Guardrail on Substantially Negative Delta Modified USPCC for Agreement Periods Beginning on January 1, 2024, and Before January 1, 2027
As discussed in the proposed rule, for agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, we proposed to establish a guardrail on instances in which the modified USPCC cumulative growth rates used to construct ACPT values are substantially lower than observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures (
91 FR 44110
). Specifically, beginning at reconciliation for PY 2025 for ACOs currently in an agreement period, and for future performance years in their agreement periods, we proposed to establish a guardrail that would not allow the modified USPCC cumulative growth rate to be more than 1.0 percentage point below the corresponding observed cumulative growth in national assignable expenditures (where the percentage point threshold is rounded to the nearest tenth of a percentage point) (
91 FR 44110
). In other words, this proposed retroactive guardrail would be applied at reconciliation for any remaining performance years for agreement periods that began on January 1, 2024 (that is, PY 2025 through 2028), January 1, 2025 (that is, PY 2025 through 2029), and January 1, 2026 (that is, PY 2026 through 2030) (
91 FR 44110
).
We proposed to apply this proposal retroactively because it adjusts the methodology used in determining shared savings and losses for a performance year and for agreement periods that have already started (
91 FR 44110
). We stated that applying this proposal retroactively would either have no effect or a positive effect on an ACO's determinations of shared savings and losses, and no ACOs would be harmed by retroactively applying this proposed policy (
91 FR 44110
). Section 1871(e)(1)(A) of the Act prohibits substantive changes in regulations, manual instructions, interpretive rules, statements of policy, or guidelines of general applicability under Title XVIII of the Act from being applied retroactively to items and services furnished before the effective date of the change unless, as permitted under paragraph (ii), the Secretary determines that failing to apply the change retroactively would be contrary to the public interest. We stated that we believe it is appropriate to extend this retroactive applicability to PY 2025 for consistency with future performance years and for the reasons described in the subsequent paragraph (
91 FR 44110
).
As discussed in the proposed rule, failing to apply this proposed policy retroactively for agreement periods beginning on January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, would be contrary to the public interest (
91 FR 44110
). We acknowledged that some ACOs may feel unfairly punished by forcing them to assume financial risk when the modified USPCC is a substantial under-projection compared to actual growth, and no ACO would experience reduced shared savings or increased shared losses by retroactively applying this proposed policy (
91 FR 44110
). We stated that this is especially the case in comparison to ACOs with agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, that would be protected from financial risk if the delta modified USPCC is substantially negative simply because their agreement period would start after the potential implementation date of the proposed policy (
91 FR 44110
). A substantially negative delta modified USPCC would cause greater harm to ACOs with agreements starting January 1, 2024, January 1, 2025, or January 1, 2026, than for ACOs with agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027, especially because of the potential for these negative projection and mis-estimation errors to compound over multiple years. Specifically, for a given ACO, substantially negative delta modified USPCC would result in corresponding lower ACPT values, which would, in turn, potentially result in lower shared savings or greater shared losses than would occur for a similar ACO with an agreement period beginning on or after January 1, 2027. Such a consequence would be outside an ACO's control, potentially undermining both participation in and the sustainability of the Shared Savings Program and the public's faith in CMS as a fair partner. We noted that we are compelled to propose a retroactive remedy for a substantially negative delta modified USPCC because all ACOs covered by this proposed policy will either benefit from it or will be unaffected by it (
91 FR 44110
). Also, we stated that the proposed policy likely will not place additional administrative burden upon ACOs, CMS, or other interested parties (
91 FR 44110
).
We stated that ACOs participating in the Shared Savings Program and other ACOs that may be considering joining the Shared Savings Program may be less likely to join or continue to participate
(
printed page 71467)
in a program where applications of policy based on agreement period start date, which such ACOs may perceive to be arbitrary, can reduce shared savings or increase shared losses (
91 FR 44110
). Having more ACOs than what is typical terminating their participation in the Shared Savings Program could negatively affect the sustainability of the program. The Shared Savings Program financial methodology and the procedures we have utilized in the past to address projection errors in the ACPT provide a means to account for instances of substantially negative delta modified USPCC. However, we noted that these remedies to address projection errors under our current policies can only be used if an unforeseen circumstance occurs and we determine the negative effects of an under-projected delta modified USPCC to be substantial enough to affect ACOs (
91 FR 44110
). As a result, this can create uncertainty for ACOs on whether CMS would address projection errors with delta modified USPCC. The delta modified USPCC is a factor that directly affects whether an ACO receives shared savings, and ACOs can easily measure the impact of the delta modified USPCC on their shared savings. In recognition of the differing circumstances that could warrant accounting for errors, we have not established a set amount of difference between the modified USPCC and national expenditure trends that we consider to be a substantial enough under-projection to implement a remedy. This uncertainty can create challenges for ACOs to be able to plan what their benchmark could be and how they will achieve savings against such benchmark.
As discussed in the proposed rule, for some ACOs, the uncertainty in the difference between the modified USPCC and national expenditure trends may either discourage new ACOs from joining the Shared Savings Program or cause some ACOs to leave the program, which goes against our goal to encourage more ACOs to participate in the Shared Savings Program (
91 FR 44110
). We stated that if we do not remedy projection errors in update factors that directly affect the amount of shared savings earned by ACOs, this could cause a loss of faith by ACOs, healthcare providers, and the public in CMS's ability to effectively administer the Shared Savings Program, substantially reducing ACO and healthcare provider participation in the program (
91 FR 44110
). Reduced participation, in turn, would significantly diminish the savings to the Medicare Trust Funds, the quality of care improvements for Medicare beneficiaries resulting from ACO participants in the Shared Savings Program, and reduce the coordination of care performed for Medicare beneficiaries when obtaining items and services from ACO providers and suppliers. For these reasons, we stated that it would be contrary to the public interest for CMS to fail to retroactively apply our proposed policy mitigating this issue (
91 FR 44110
). With our proposed policy, we noted that ACOs will know the lower-bound limit on the difference between the modified USPCC and national expenditure trends for the duration of their entire agreement period and have more confidence participating in the Shared Savings Program (
91 FR 44110
through
44111
).

We sought public comment on the proposed reforms to the ACPT component of the benchmark update factor, described in section II.G.5.g of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule. The following is a summary of the comments we received on each of the proposals described in II.G.5.g.(2).(a), (b), (c), and (e), as well as the notice described in II.G.5.g.(2).(d) that reconciliation for PY 2025 will be delayed until after the release of the CY 2027 PFS final rule, and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters broadly supported one or more of the proposed ACPT reforms. Commenters emphasized their support due to the potential for greater benchmark accuracy and predictability; protection from projection error outside an ACO's control; greater consistency and fairness across agreement-period cohorts; improved financial planning and investment certainty; and support for continued or expanded Shared Savings Program participation. Some commenters highlighted the value of these protections particularly for smaller, rural, physician-led, safety-net, and high-needs ACOs. Many commenters recommended finalizing the package of annual performance-year rates, prospective guardrails, and retroactive downside protection; the specific combinations discussed varied by commenter.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support. We agree that the three ACPT reforms described previously operate together to preserve an external prospective trend while improving consistency across cohorts and limiting the consequences of substantial projection error for both ACOs and CMS.
Comment:
Many commenters supported calculating performance-year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates and applying the same rates for a given performance year regardless of agreement-period start date. These commenters stated that this approach would reduce differences attributable to agreement start dates, avoid reliance on projections that may become obsolete over a five-year period, improve operational simplicity and transparency, and reduce inequities across cohorts or incentives to time agreement entry. Some commenters also expected rates calculated closer to the performance year to better reflect current spending conditions.
A commenter noted that setting ACPT growth factors at the start of a five-year agreement period had provided certainty, while also emphasizing that subsequent divergence between projected and actual growth materially harmed ACOs. Other commenters favored annual, performance-year-specific rates because they would better reflect current conditions and apply consistently across agreement-period cohorts. Some commenters also recommended releasing the applicable ACPT rate before the beginning of each performance year, including through a summer release schedule, so that ACOs would have the rate in time for financial and operational planning. These comments distinguished advance publication from annual calculation because an annually determined rate would not provide the same planning value if it were not made available sufficiently before the performance year.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support for performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates. As described previously, CMS will publicly report the PY 2027 modified USPCC annualized growth rates in conjunction with the release of this final rule. For subsequent performance years, CMS will calculate and publicly report the modified USPCC annualized growth rates in late spring or early summer of the preceding calendar year. Our proposal will maintain the prospective character of the ACPT, which will provide ACOs with a degree of certainty regarding their annual benchmark updates, promote greater fairness among ACOs by having a consistent modified USPCC annualized growth rate apply to all ACOs reconciled for a given performance year, and reduce some of the operational complexity of calculating and applying the ACPT as part of the three-way blended growth factor. It is understandable that some ACOs may want additional advance knowledge of the prospective ACPT trend for a performance year, while others may find the advance notice prior to performance years (relative to how the ACPT was provided after the start of Performance Year 1 in agreement periods that started January 1, 2024 and 2025) may be useful to assist ACOs with their financial planning. Again, our goal is to recalibrate the balance of that tradeoff by forgoing some predictability in favor of greater consistency and, in turn, fairness across agreement period cohorts and eliminating disparate effects on the growth rates of historical benchmarks for ACOs because of when an ACO started its agreement period.
Comment:
Many commenters supported limiting the effect of divergence between projected and observed expenditure growth for agreement periods beginning in 2027. These commenters described the guardrails as preventing shared savings or losses from being driven by forecasting error unrelated to ACO performance, improving financial stability, and restoring confidence in the benchmarking methodology. Several commenters characterized the guardrails as a more durable response to under-projection than temporary adjustments to the ACPT's weight. Some specifically supported the asymmetric design because it could allow ACOs to share in more savings than losses while preserving room for the ACPT to mitigate benchmark ratcheting. Some commenters viewed the proposed approach as preserving a meaningful role for prospective trends while protecting ACOs and CMS from substantial projection errors.
Multiple commenters referenced estimates of substantial financial effects from under-projection. These estimates reflected different periods and formulations. Commenters cited estimated reductions in total ACO revenue of $154 million for PY 2024 and exceeding $700 million for PY 2025 as evidence of the need for a durable corrective mechanism.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support for our proposals to apply guardrails on delta modified USPCC. Regarding the asymmetric design, we previously stated that we believe that an asymmetric guardrail that imposes a tighter bound on substantially negative delta modified USPCC and a wider bound on substantially positive delta modified USPCC would more directly protect ACOs from the harms associated with substantially negative delta modified USPCC while still allowing ACOs to benefit from modestly positive delta modified USPCC, consistent with the prospective design of the ACPT. We believe that the proposed threshold levels are reasonable policy calibrations that strike an appropriate balance and are consistent with the original policy aims of the ACPT, as well as program goals of predictability, fairness, and administrative feasibility.
Comment:
Many commenters supported retroactive application of the lower-bound guardrail for eligible existing agreement-period cohorts. These commenters viewed retroactivity as correcting under-projection outside ACOs' control, preserving shared savings that otherwise could be reduced or eliminated, improving fairness and confidence in CMS as a program
(
printed page 71473)
partner, and supporting continued ACO participation and investment. A commenter supported CMS's stated approach to retroactive rulemaking, stating that significant risks from non-retroactive application can justify a retroactive remedy and strongly supporting application of the revised ACPT methodology to all agreement periods that include the ACPT.
Some commenters emphasized that smaller, rural, safety-net, independent-practice, and high-needs ACOs may be particularly vulnerable to benchmark volatility, citing factors such as smaller populations, concentrated costs, local market variation, and limited financial reserves. These commenters stated that protection against excessive under-projection could create a more stable environment for participation and investment.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support for the retroactive guardrail on substantially negative delta modified USPCC. We agree that applying this policy retroactively for agreement periods beginning on January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, would be appropriate to mitigate the effects of substantially negative delta modified USPCC outside an ACO's control, including undermining participation in and the sustainability of the Shared Savings Program, which would limit ACOs' ability to continue to provide coordinated care and improve the quality of care provided to assigned beneficiaries and weaken the public's faith in CMS as a fair partner. Accordingly, we believe it is appropriate to implement this policy retroactively, because not doing so would be contrary to the public interest.
Further, as we stated in the proposed rule (
91 FR 44110
), the retroactive guardrail is designed to ensure that ACOs in agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, would either benefit or be unaffected by its application. Preliminary analyses of PY 2025 financial reconciliation calculations indicate that applying the retroactive guardrail would produce favorable or unchanged financial outcomes across affected ACOs, consistent with the policy's design. At the program level, the analysis indicates that the guardrail would increase aggregate shared savings, modestly reduce aggregate shared losses, and result in favorable financial performance category transitions for some ACOs.
Comment:
A commenter acknowledged that establishing performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates could simplify the methodology, apply the same annual rates to all ACOs regardless of start date, and improve accuracy of projections by calculating them closer to the performance year. However, the commenter expressed concern that the approach would reduce predictability and make calculations more susceptible to annual abnormalities in expenditure growth. Accordingly, the commenter recommended that CMS not finalize the performance-year-specific growth-rate proposal pending additional analysis of the impacts and public comment, while strongly supporting guardrails if CMS proceeds. Another commenter stated that the proposal's financial effects and implementation were difficult to assess without clarification as to whether the ACPT adjustment would apply to all ACOs at once or only as ACOs renew their benchmarks. That commenter recommended delaying implementation until CMS provides additional analysis of financial effects across geographic regions for stakeholder review and engagement.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' recognition of our objective of improving benchmark predictability and limiting forecasting inaccuracies. While commenters requested additional analysis, clarification, or safeguards before we implement the performance-year-specific growth-rate proposal, we disagree that further delay is warranted. This policy addresses a structural inconsistency and operational complexity under the current methodology. Absent this policy, ACOs reconciled for the same performance year may receive different modified USPCC annualized growth rates solely because their agreement periods began in different years. A performance year-specific rate will eliminate that as a source of cross-cohort inconsistency. This policy will apply to agreement periods beginning on January 1, 2027, and in subsequent years. ACOs in existing agreement periods will continue to use agreement-period-specific rates, subject to the retroactive guardrail on substantially negative delta modified USPCC described previously.
We recognize that establishing performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates may produce different ACPT values, and therefore different financial effects, than retaining agreement period-specific rates. However, we do not believe that delaying finalization of the policy pending additional modeling is warranted. The primary purpose of the policy is to eliminate a structural source of cross-cohort inconsistency under the current methodology, in which the ACPT values applicable to ACOs being reconciled for the same performance year may be based on different modified USPCC annualized growth rates solely because their agreement periods began in different years. This policy will ensure that all ACOs covered by the policy that are being reconciled for the same performance year will receive adjustments based on the same modified USPCC annualized growth rates.
We also do not believe that calculating modified USPCC annualized growth rates on a performance-year-specific basis would necessarily make the ACPT more vulnerable to annual abnormalities in expenditure growth. Under either approach to calculating modified USPCC annualized growth rates (that is, on a performance year-specific basis or an agreement period-specific basis) the ACPT relies on projected annual expenditure growth and therefore may overestimate or underestimate observed growth. The principal difference between the existing methodology and our proposal for performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates is timing: under the current methodology, projected annualized growth rates may be established up to five years before the applicable performance year, whereas the proposed policy uses projections calculated closer to the year in which they apply. Calculating modified USPCC annualized growth rates on a performance year-specific basis may incorporate more current information, but timing alone does not necessarily establish or alter the trajectory of delta modified USPCC for a given ACO, and the guardrails separately limit the financial effects of substantial cumulative under- or over-projection at reconciliation. We will monitor the implementation effects of this policy across geographic regions, ACO types, and beneficiary populations and will consider future refinements if warranted.
Comment:
A commenter welcomed CMS's responsiveness to stakeholder concerns about the ACPT but cautioned against over-correcting the methodology and eliminating the gap between projected and observed spending growth that can preserve savings incentives. The commenter argued that an effective administrative benchmark should remain below counterfactual spending growth while exceeding actual spending growth, thereby retaining incentives for ACO participation. The commenter noted that this principle is recognized in the LEAD Model. The commenter did not recommend alternative numerical thresholds.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concern about preserving the wedge between projected and
(
printed page 71474)
observed spending growth to maintain savings opportunities and participation incentives. We interpret this concern as being related to whether the upper bound of the two-sided guardrail could constrain over-projection too much and diminish the ACPT's ability to mitigate the benchmark ratchet effect. As discussed previously, we selected an asymmetric guardrail with a wider upper bound to preserve greater room for modestly positive delta modified USPCC while limiting unusually large over-projection. We believe the +1.5 percentage point upper threshold balances protection of the Medicare Trust Funds from the financial consequences of unusually large cumulative over-projection and preservation of the core design feature of the ACPT as a prospectively-set external factor that allows benchmarks to increase beyond actual spending growth even as ACOs slow spending growth. We will monitor whether and the extent to which the finalized upper threshold constrains the wedge between projected and observed expenditure growth in a manner that materially weakens savings incentives. Based on our evaluation of implementation experience, we may consider future refinements if warranted, including additional adjustments or safeguards.
Comment:
Some commenters supported the proposed reforms while identifying remaining limitations in the ACPT's underlying design. These commenters identified several distinct limitations. Some commenters stated that under-projection could leave benchmarks below actual expenditure growth. A commenter estimated that the proposed 1.0 percentage point lower guardrail would provide less relief than reducing the ACPT's weight to zero. Other commenters cautioned that national trends may not reflect local spending or utilization patterns. These qualifications generally did not alter commenters' support for finalizing the proposed guardrails as an immediate improvement.
Commenters offered several longer-term methodological alternatives. Some commenters recommended replacing national trends with regional trends, particularly for smaller ACOs concentrated in one market; excluding ACO beneficiaries from reference trends to more directly address national and regional ratcheting; and explicitly accounting for major shifts in technology, policy, or clinical pricing that may affect ACOs unevenly. Other commenters supported the guardrails as an interim improvement but recommended eliminating the ACPT, returning to the prior benchmark trend methodology, or developing a more transparent and operationally straightforward alternative. These commenters viewed the need for guardrails, retrospective corrections, annual recalculation, and reconciliation adjustments as evidence of limitations in the ACPT's underlying design.
A commenter additionally requested alternatives that would allow rural providers with small Medicare Part B populations or limited financial reserves to continue transitioning from fee-for-service to advanced payment models without mandatory downside risk. The commenter linked this recommendation to rural providers' financial instability and to fragmented payment arrangements across Medicare and other payers. Although broader than the proposed ACPT mechanics, the recommendation reflects a distinct concern about whether benchmark reforms alone are sufficient to sustain rural participation.
Response:
We thank commenters who expressed support for the proposed reforms while identifying purported limitations in the ACPT's underlying design. As we developed the proposed reforms, we assessed whether reducing the weight of the ACPT component of the three-way blended update factor from one-third to zero would be preferable to implementing a retroactive guardrail on substantially negative delta modified USPCC. Based on that assessment, we determined that, from a harm-reduction standpoint, the retroactive guardrail is preferable because it is designed to have exclusively beneficial or neutral effects for all ACOs (increased or unchanged shared savings or decreased or unchanged shared losses), whereas eliminating the ACPT can potentially have harmful effects (increased shared losses or decreased shared savings). We arrived at this determination after comparing outcomes of both approaches (down-weighting to zero versus a retroactive guardrail) against the same status quo baseline; that is, one-third weight applied to the ACPT component of the three-way blended update factor and no guardrail on delta modified USPCC, independent of the performance year in question.
Relative to that baseline, eliminating the ACPT would mean that an ACO's updated benchmark would be based entirely on the two-way national-regional blended update factor rather than the three-way blended update factor. For many ACOs, this can result in higher benchmarks and therefore can be potentially beneficial. However, for ACOs where regional growth may be sufficiently below national growth, substituting the two-way national-regional blended update factor for the three-way blended update factor could result in lower benchmarks even in the presence of substantially negative delta modified USPCC. Stated another way, when a given ACO's ACPT is greater than its two-way national-regional blended update factor, eliminating the ACPT is not necessarily beneficial and could be harmful to the ACO's financial reconciliation results.
By contrast, compared to the same baseline, in the presence of substantially negative delta modified USPCC, the retroactive guardrail can only result in an increased benchmark, by construction. This is because, in the presence of substantially negative delta modified USPCC, the only component of the three-way blended update factor that can change is the ACPT, and it can only be made larger than it would otherwise be in the absence of the guardrail. Furthermore, because the retroactive guardrail design incorporates a benchmark-based loss-recoupment limit protection feature (as discussed regarding “Step 4. Recompute ACPT Values, as Applicable” in CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44112
)), there is no scenario in which an ACO could be rendered liable for greater shared losses than would otherwise occur in the absence of the retroactive guardrail. This benchmark-based loss recoupment limit protection feature will apply only to the retroactive guardrail on substantially negative delta modified USPCC for ACOs in agreement periods that began on or after January 1, 2024, and before January 1, 2027, beginning with reconciliation for PY 2025. It will not apply to agreement periods beginning on or after January 1, 2027.
More broadly, while we appreciate some commenters' views that the need for guardrails, retrospective corrections, annual recalculation, and reconciliation adjustments justifies the elimination of the ACPT entirely from the Shared Savings Program's financial reconciliation methodology, we disagree. Rather, for the reasons we discussed when we incorporated it into the financial methodology (
87 FR 69881
through
69899
), we continue to view the ACPT as an important tool for mitigating benchmark ratcheting and being a prospective measure of expenditure growth that makes benchmark updates more predictable. We view recent experience as evidence that the ACPT would benefit from refinement rather than elimination. Such refinements include safeguards against substantial delta modified USPCC, which may reflect projection error rather than ACO spending
(
printed page 71475)
performance, as well as performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates that ensure an ACO's agreement period start date does not determine the rate applicable at financial reconciliation for a given performance year.
Regarding other longer-term methodological alternatives, we appreciate commenters' suggestions to lengthen agreement periods, derive benchmarks from county rates, replace national trends with regional trends, exclude ACO beneficiaries from reference trends, and more explicitly account for major shifts in technology, policy, or clinical pricing that may affect ACOs unevenly. These recommendations would materially redesign the ACPT methodology or other aspects of the Shared Savings Program benchmark methodology beyond the scope of the proposed reforms. We will continue to monitor and consider whether implementation of these suggestions could be appropriate in the future, and we remain open to considering additional refinements through future rulemaking, if warranted.
We also appreciate the separate recommendation that CMS provide participation alternatives that would allow rural providers with small Medicare Part B populations or limited financial reserves to continue transitioning to advanced payment models without mandatory downside risk. That recommendation concerns Shared Savings Program participation and financial risk requirements more broadly than the ACPT methodology addressed by these proposals. Therefore, while we are not adopting such an alternative as part of these proposals, we will continue to consider the circumstances of rural providers, including the effects of beneficiary volume and participation requirements, in evaluating potential future program policies.
Comment:
A commenter supported the guardrail concept but recommended applying the methodology consistently across agreement periods. Specifically, the commenter recommended extending both the upper and lower guardrails to existing agreement periods rather than applying the two-sided guardrail only to agreement periods beginning in 2027 and applying only the lower guardrail retroactively. The commenter stated that this approach would treat similarly situated ACOs equitably and provide consistent protection against trend misestimation.
Separately, some commenters proposed different refinements to the guardrail design, including symmetrical guardrails, tighter thresholds, or alignment with approaches used in the LEAD model. These recommendations reflected differing views and did not establish consensus on a specific alternative.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' recommendations for consistent guardrails across agreement periods. We proposed a retroactive guardrail on substantially negative delta modified USPCC to protect ACOs in existing agreement periods from assuming financial risk when the modified USPCC is a substantial under-projection compared to actual growth, based on our observation of substantially negative delta modified USPCC occurring in both PY 2024 and PY 2025, affecting ACOs that entered agreement periods that began on January 1, 2024, and January 1, 2025. For those ACOs, failing to implement the retroactive guardrail at reconciliation for the remaining performance years of existing agreement periods, beginning with reconciliation for PY 2025, would potentially result in ACOs earning lower shared savings or incurring greater shared losses than would otherwise occur if the retroactive guardrail were applied and substantially negative delta modified USPCC were to persist.
Such consequences would be largely outside any given ACO's control and could potentially undermine both participation in and the sustainability of the Shared Savings Program and the public's faith in CMS as a fair partner. Specifically, over the course of an agreement period, if substantially negative delta modified USPCC persists and remains unconstrained, the adverse financial effects could either discourage new ACOs from joining the Shared Savings Program or cause some ACOs to leave the program. Reduced participation could significantly diminish savings to the Medicare Trust Funds, limit improvements in the quality of care provided to Medicare beneficiaries, and reduce the coordination of care for Medicare beneficiaries when obtaining items and services from ACO providers and suppliers. For these reasons, we believe it would be contrary to the public interest for CMS to fail to apply retroactively our proposed policy mitigating this issue. This rationale does not equivalently apply to a retroactive upper guardrail on substantially positive delta modified USPCC for existing agreement periods, which is effectively what the commenter is suggesting with the stated interest of treating ACOs across agreement periods equitably and providing consistent protection against trend misestimation. Thus, at this time, we do not believe that there is sufficient basis to apply a retroactive guardrail on substantially positive delta modified USPCC.
Separately, we appreciate commenters' suggestion that we consider other refinements to the guardrail design, such as symmetrical guardrails, tighter thresholds, or alignment with approaches used in other accountable care models (for example, the LEAD model). We have stated that the thresholds we have proposed represent a reasonable policy calibration that balances protecting ACOs and the Medicare Trust Funds from substantial misestimation of national expenditure growth on the one hand and preserving the prospective design objectives of the ACPT on the other. We remain open to considering future refinements to guardrail design features through rulemaking if warranted.

Response:
We thank commenters for raising concerns about the delayed PY 2025 financial reconciliation process and the potential effects on clinician compensation, provider distributions, cash flow, staffing, vendor commitments, and investments in care management and population health. Although we recognize these concerns, we continue to believe that it is appropriate to delay PY 2025 financial reconciliation until after the release of the CY 2027 PFS final rule. We made this decision based on a careful consideration of several factors unique to PY 2025, principally the observation of substantially negative delta modified USPCC affecting both the 2024 and 2025 agreement period cohorts for PY 2025, our determination that the proposed retroactive guardrail on substantially negative delta modified USPCC would be the most effective tool with which to protect affected ACOs from otherwise adverse financial consequences, and the practical need to finalize the retroactive guardrail in the CY 2027 PFS final rule before it could be implemented at reconciliation for PY 2025. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we provided ACOs with notice about our decision to delay PY 2025 financial reconciliation to allow them to plan accordingly as needed.
We also considered commenters' recommendations regarding provisional payments, provisional reconciliation results, and similar interim approaches, and suggestions that ACOs unaffected by the retroactive guardrail be reconciled separately and on an earlier schedule. While we appreciate the intent of these recommendations, we do not believe such approaches are operationally feasible under the circumstances, and the significant additional complexity these approaches would create would substantially increase the risk of creating errors in financial reconciliation calculations. Given the limited interval between finalization of this policy and completion of PY 2025 financial reconciliation, we do not believe that establishing provisional payment or interim reporting processes or conducting separate reconciliation cycles for different groups of ACOs, would provide sufficient additional benefit to justify the substantial added operational complexity, risk, and administrative burden associated with implementing them. As a result, CMS balanced these multiple perspectives and will be providing PY 2025 financial reconciliation and dissemination of Financial Reconciliation Settlement Reports shortly after the CY 2027 PFS final rule is released.
We also appreciate commenters' requests for timely information regarding ACPT calculations, guardrail implementation, and benchmark updates. Through published program specifications, CMS already publicly reports the methodologies used to calculate the ACPT. Further, with the finalization of performance year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates in this final rule, the published program specification will publicly report performance-year-specific modified USPCC annualized growth rates in the calendar year preceding the applicable performance year, beginning with the rates applicable to PY 2027. In addition, ACO-specific benchmark and reconciliation reports provide detailed information regarding benchmark calculations, including the components used to construct enrollment type-specific ACPT values. We believe these materials provide transparency regarding the calculation and application of the ACPT and associated guardrail policies and will continue to support ACOs' financial planning and operational decision-making.
Finally, we do not currently expect to delay financial reconciliation for future performance years. As stated previously, the circumstances that necessitated delaying PY 2025 financial reconciliation arose because the retroactive guardrail had not yet been finalized and therefore could not be incorporated into reconciliation calculations until finalization in the CY 2027 PFS final rule. With finalization of this policy, we expect the retroactive guardrail to be available for application in future performance years without requiring a similar delay, although CMS retains discretion to make operational decisions as warranted by future circumstances.

6. Beneficiary Engagement
a. Proposal To Allow ACOs To Reduce or Eliminate Part B Cost Sharing
(1) Background
We believe that ACOs play a key role in strengthening beneficiary engagement in their care; accordingly, we intend to continue expanding the tools available to ACOs to support this work. Improving beneficiary engagement allows the benefits of receiving care from healthcare providers who are part of an ACO to be more tangible and may ultimately result in improved quality and efficiency of care for beneficiaries, helping us meet our goals of improving beneficiary outcomes and reducing unnecessary spending.
As part of the effort to strengthen beneficiary engagement, in the CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, CMS finalized the prepaid shared savings option (
89 FR 98132
). This payment option is available to current Shared Savings Program ACOs with a history of earning shared savings and is intended to expand access to performance year savings that encourages investment in staffing, healthcare infrastructure, and additional services for beneficiaries. Under § 425.640(e)(1), ACOs participating in the prepaid shared savings option are required to spend a specific portion of the prepaid shared savings amount on direct beneficiary services, improving the quality of care beneficiaries receive. As discussed in section III.G.6. of the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, ACO interest in receiving prepaid shared savings has been limited, and we proposed to discontinue the participation option in future years. However, we believed a component of prepaid shared savings, providing ACOs the ability to reduce or eliminate cost sharing for certain Part B items and services, is a valuable tool to offer eligible ACOs. Cost sharing support for Part B items and services was offered in the ACO REACH model and allows ACO participants not to collect cost sharing amounts (in whole or in part) from eligible beneficiaries for eligible Part B items and services. In the ACO REACH model, ACOs and ACO participants enter into cost sharing support arrangements for the ACO to reimburse the ACO participant for beneficiary cost sharing amounts not collected. In the ACO REACH model, ACOs have wide flexibility to determine the beneficiaries and items and services that will be eligible for cost sharing support, but ACOs are prohibited from waiving Part B cost sharing support for items that may have a higher risk of fraud, waste, or abuse, such as durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, prescription drugs or supplies.
Part B cost sharing support is the third most used Beneficiary Engagement Incentive in the ACO REACH model with 41 percent of ACOs reporting that they had implemented it by 2025 or were planning to implement in 2026.

]
Additionally, interested parties have identified Part B cost sharing support as a valuable tool for ACOs to engage beneficiaries in their care.
[

In 2026, the standard Medicare Part B monthly premium is $202.90, with a $283 annual deductible.
[
360
]
After the deductible is met, beneficiaries generally pay 20 percent of the Medicare-approved amount for items and services, such as doctor visits and durable medical equipment, with no limit on out-of-pocket costs. While most beneficiaries have supplemental insurance that covers the 20 percent cost sharing, including Medigap plans, employer sponsored plans, and Medicaid, some beneficiaries do not. In 2023, 3.5 million Medicare FFS
(
printed page 71478)
beneficiaries (13 percent) lacked additional supplemental coverage.
[

]
These beneficiaries were more likely to have modest incomes (between $20,000 and $40,000 per person) compared to all Medicare FFS beneficiaries in 2023.
[

Beneficiaries with higher out of pocket costs receive less medical care than those with supplemental coverage.
[
363
]
While not all of this difference in care may be due to financial concerns, higher out of pocket costs may cause patients to skip or postpone necessary care and result in worsening health outcomes.
[
