We invited public comments on our proposals to make use of the revised OMB delineations as set forth in the July 21, 2023 OMB Bulletin No. 23-01 and the most recent modifications of the RUCA codes as discussed previously for CY 2027 for purposes of payment under the AFS.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposed update of the geographic delineations used for ambulance payment and also supported that the adoption of the revised OMB delineations and the updated RUCA codes would have no negative impacts on ambulance transports in super rural areas, as none of the current super rural areas would lose their status due to the proposed changes.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support.
Comment:
An initial commenter stated that it may be the case that some ZIP codes should have a more favorable geographic designation in this round, as well as in future modifications. To address this concern raised by the initial commenter, the initial commenter and some other commenters recommended CMS adopt two additional safeguards to protect beneficiary access to ground ambulance services. The first safeguard that the commenters suggested is to maintain current geographic designation
(
printed page 71505)
if there are 1,000 people per square mile or fewer in the ZIP code that would be redesignated. Those commenters stated that this safeguard would protect patients in low-population-density areas from potential access problems by ensuring their ZIP code's status remains unchanged.
The second safeguard that the commenters recommended is an appeals process where an ambulance provider or supplier could ask CMS for reconsideration of a ZIP code designation within a 1-year period after the changes in geographic delineations have been finalized.
Response:
None of the commenters provided specific examples of what ZIP codes should have a more favorable geographic designation. Further, we did not propose an additional methodology to preserve the current geographic designations for ZIP codes with a population density of 1,000 people per square mile or fewer. Implementing such a methodology would not be feasible given the complexities of identifying these areas at the ZIP code level. For instance, it is unclear how to account for ZIP codes that span multiple counties.
We believe that the most current OMB delineations, coupled with the updated RUCA codes more accurately reflect the urban and rural nature of areas across the county, and thus, we believe the use of the most current OMB delineations and RUCA codes under the AFS enhances the accuracy of AFS payments. Further, as discussed previously, we believe that our methodology of designating rural geographic areas by using OMB's delineations, and by using RUCA codes 4.0 and above to identify rural census tracts within MSAs, is appropriate for AFS payment purposes because it rectifies the limitations of broad county-level data, ensuring that isolated areas receive necessary higher reimbursement rates to cover higher structural operating costs.
We did not propose an appeals process where an ambulance provider or supplier could ask CMS for reconsideration of a ZIP code designation within a one-year period after the changes in geographic delineations have been finalized. If an ambulance provider or supplier has concerns about a ZIP code's delineation, they should contact OMB. If they have concerns about a ZIP code's RUCA code designation, they should contact HRSA.
Comment:
Some commenters urged CMS to reconsider designating as rural areas those census tracts that fall at RUCA levels 2 or 3 that are at least 400 square miles in area with a population density of no more than 35 people. A commenter recommended a reconsideration appeal process for ZIP codes containing census tracts that qualify as rural under RUCA 2 or 3 but do not receive a corresponding ZIP-level designation. The commenter further stated that they understand CMS's concern that it lacks an administrable method for translating tract-level RUCA 2 and 3 classifications into ZIP code designations. However, the commenter does not believe that concern is insurmountable. The commenter suggested that CMS allow a supplier or provider to petition for reconsideration by demonstrating, using HRSA's published criteria, that a majority of the census tracts or population within the ZIP code meets the RUCA 2 or 3 large-area or low-density rural criteria. Under this approach, the petitioner would provide the tract-to-ZIP crosswalk, and CMS would verify the analysis against the criteria already in use.
Response:
As we stated previously, we would not designate as rural areas those census tracts that fall at RUCA levels 2 or 3 that are at least 400 square miles in area with a population density of no more than 35 people. We have determined that it is not feasible to implement this guideline due to the complexities of identifying these areas at the ZIP code level. We do not have sufficient information available to identify the ZIP codes that fall in these specific census tracts.
Also, payment under the AFS is based on the ZIP codes; therefore, if the ZIP code is predominantly metropolitan but has some rural census tracts, we do not split the ZIP code areas to distinguish further granularity to provide different payments within the same ZIP code. We believe that payment for all ambulance transportation services at the ZIP code level provides for a more consistent and administratively feasible payment system. For example, if we were to pay based on ZIP codes for some areas and counties or census tracts for other areas, there are circumstances where ZIP codes cross county or census tract borders and where counties or census tracts cross ZIP code borders. Such overlaps in geographic designations would overly complicate our ability to appropriately assign ambulance transportation services to geographic areas for payment under the AFS.
Comment:
A commenter supports our proposal to classify census tracts with RUCA codes of 4.0 or higher as rural for AFS payment purposes. The commenter stated that this more granular methodology can identify rural communities that might otherwise be absorbed into a broader urban classification. However, the commenter stated that the RUCA methodology may not identify every ambulance operation that performs a predominantly rural function and recommends that CMS consider additional criteria for circumstances in which a pickup ZIP code's geographic classification does not accurately reflect the rural role of the ambulance provider or supplier or healthcare facility. The commenter stated that the potential criteria should include all of the following:
An ambulance provider or supplier -location standard that recognizes operations for which a majority of Medicare transports serve rural communities.
Recognition of hospitals and facilities holding a federal rural-related designation, even when their pickup ZIP codes are classified as urban.
Consideration of low transport volumes, extended travel distances, limited hospital access, and regional referral patterns.
Protection for air and ground medical bases serving broad rural, frontier, or medically underserved areas.
A defined process through which ambulance providers may request review of a classification that does not accurately reflect their service responsibilities.
According to the commenter, these additional criteria would complement, not replace, the proposed RUCA methodology. The commenter stated that this additional methodology would give CMS a way to address documented circumstances in which ZIP-code classification alone does not fully capture the rural nature of an ambulance operation or the population it serves. The commenter further recommended: (1). a predominantly rural provider-supplier location standard for air ambulance bases where at least 50% of Medicare transports originate in rural or super-rural pickup ZIP codes. (2). Qualifying bases should receive the rural ground and air ambulance adjustment for all Medicare transports. Alternatively, the commenter recommended CMS should establish a review process through which a provider or supplier may demonstrate that an operation functions as a predominantly rural regional resource.
The commenter also recommended a rural base exception for a ground and air ambulance transport originating from an urban-classified hospital or other pickup location when the responding aircraft is assigned to a rural or super-rural base where the transport should receive the rural air ambulance adjustment applicable to the base, recognizing that the base must maintain
(
printed page 71506)
the air and ground vehicles, clinical crews, equipment, communications systems, and 24/7 readiness required to serve its rural service area.
Response:
We did not propose an additional methodology or rural base exception. We believe that the most current OMB delineations, coupled with the updated RUCA codes more accurately reflect the urban and rural nature of areas across the county, and thus, we believe the use of the most current OMB delineations and RUCA codes under the AFS sufficiently enhances the accuracy of AFS payments. The payment for an ambulance transport is based on the ZIP code of the point of the ambulance pick-up.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS establish a five-year transition for ZIP codes that move from rural to urban under the new classifications. For these ZIP codes, the commenter stated that CMS should apply a five-year blended payment rate. According to the commenter, this approach would provide providers and suppliers and communities with a reasonable period to adjust to the payment changes and would be consistent with transition approaches CMS has used when other Medicare payment systems have adopted updated OMB delineations.
Response:
We did not propose a 5-year transition period for ZIP codes that move from rural to urban (1.40 percent of ZIP codes). We believe that it is important to use the most updated OMB delineations and updated RUCA codes based on the latest census data for AFS payment purposes because it directly impacts the accuracy, fairness, and statutory compliance of health care payment and funding allocation.
Comment:
A commenter supported the proposal to redesignate 12 ZIP codes in Puerto Rico from urban to rural and stated that these changes better reflect the operational reality of ambulance in the affected communities, where mountainous or coastal geography, limited road alternatives, extended response and transport times, and uneven access to appropriate receiving facilities materially increase the cost and complexity of service.
However, the commenter opposed the proposal to redesignate two ZIP codes, 00707 (Maunabo) and 00742 (Roosevelt Roads/Ceiba) from rural to urban. The commenter stated that these areas continue to present the access, travel-time, infrastructure, and destination constraints commonly associated with rural ambulance operations. The commenter further stated that the classification based on commuting patterns or broad statistical boundaries may not adequately capture prehospital realities. The commenter requested that these two ZIP codes: retain their rural designation pending an operational-access review that considers ambulance travel time, road connectivity, receiving facility capability, and unit cycle time.
Response:
ZIP codes 00707 and 00742 are listed under the San Juan-Bayamón-Caguas, PR CBSA with a RUCA code of 1, Metropolitan core: primary commuting flow is within an urban area (UA) of 50,000 or more people (metro UA). We designate rural census tracts in a Metropolitan Statistical Area (MSA) falling at or above RUCA level 4.0 as rural areas. HRSA also uses this methodology. We continue to believe that this HRSA guideline accurately identifies rural census tracts throughout the country and thus would be appropriate to apply for AFS payment purposes.
Comment:
A commenter supports the proposal to redesignate the 14 ZIP codes in Maine that will change their designation from urban to rural. However, the commenter opposes the proposal to redesignate the 15 ZIP codes that will change from rural to urban. The commenter also recommended that CMS reclassify the entirety of Penobscot County outside of the direct Bangor MSA as rural.
Response:
The 15 ZIP codes in Maine met the criteria to change their designations from rural to urban. Penobscot County is located in the Bangor MSA according to OMB's revised delineations. If an ambulance provider or supplier has an issue with a ZIP code's delineation, they should contact OMB. If an ambulance provider or supplier has an issue with a RUCA code designation of a ZIP code, they should contact HRSA.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposed changes to make use of the new OMB's revised delineations and the most recent modification of the RUCA codes to recognize levels of rurality in census tracts falling at or above RUCA code level 4.0 as rural areas for purposes of payment under the AFS.
I. Request for Information (RFI) on Duplicate Laboratory Testing, Imaging, and Result Sharing and Interoperability
1. Overview
Diagnostic imaging and laboratory testing are critical to determining a patient's course of treatment. Imaging data and test results are often siloed within the acquiring systems' electronic health record and inaccessible outside of those systems. Treating health care providers often do not even know of the existence of these siloed results. The inaccessibility of laboratory and imaging data due to siloing results in incomplete or delayed care management and duplicative testing, with concomitant increased costs (and in the case of duplicative diagnostic imaging, unnecessary radiation exposure).
2. Purpose of the RFI
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44139
through
44141
), we issued an RFI to gather input from interested parties—including clinicians, laboratories, imaging health care providers, health systems, payers, health IT developers, and other interested parties—to inform potential actions aimed at addressing the interoperability and duplicate testing concerns described earlier in this section.
3. Potential Mechanisms for Addressing Duplicative Payment
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44139
), we described several mechanisms we are exploring to address duplicate payment for diagnostic laboratory and image testing:
Clarifications to billing instructions to laboratories and imaging centers on parameters of duplicate laboratory or imaging tests;
Local Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC) edits that would result in non-payment or reductions in payment as applicable for duplicate laboratory or imaging tests;
Use of payment integrity levers to recoup payments from health care providers and suppliers who performed duplicate laboratory or imaging tests; and
Application of frequency limitations to certain tests where clinically appropriate.
We noted that frequency limitations are already in use in certain contexts. For example, a Local Coverage Decision (LCD) from a MAC limits testing for Vitamin D levels (L33996—Vitamin D Assay Testing), providing that once a beneficiary has been shown to be Vitamin D deficient, further testing is medically necessary only to ensure adequate replacement has been accomplished, with annual testing thereafter being appropriate depending on the indication and other mitigating factors. We stated that we believe there are likely other diagnostic laboratory tests that should similarly be subject to frequency limitations.
We also recognized that in some cases more frequent testing is clinically justified and therefore asked for input not only on which laboratory and
(
printed page 71507)
imaging tests should be subject to frequency limitations, but also on what exceptions should be permitted to ensure beneficiary access is not inappropriately restricted.
We asked how CMS can enforce these limitations without restricting beneficiary access to necessary care. Specifically, we asked how practitioners can communicate clinical justification for repeat testing in specific circumstances—for example, in cases of trauma, stroke, or evolving emergencies where repeat imaging may be clinically appropriate.
We also asked for input on the following questions:
Should CMS consider possible changes to payment policies when diagnostic tests are billed duplicatively; that is, additional imaging or diagnostic laboratory tests for the same condition? For example, is there a time period during which an image or laboratory test should automatically be considered “duplicate” and therefore subject to payment consequences? To which kinds of tests or subsets of tests should such policies apply?
We asked clinicians and payors, who have likely addressed or considered these or similar issues, to share their experience and perspective.
4. Laboratory and Imaging Interoperability
Section 4003 of the 21st Century Cures Act (
Pub. L. 114-255
) amended section 3000 of the PHSA to add a new paragraph (10) to include a statutory definition of “interoperability.” Interoperability is defined to mean, with respect to health information technology, such health information technology that—(A) enables the secure exchange of electronic health information with, and use of electronic health information from, other health information technology without special effort on the part of the user; (B) allows for complete access, exchange, and use of all electronically accessible health information for authorized use under applicable State or Federal law; and (C) does not constitute information blocking as defined in section 3022(a) of the Public Health Service Act.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44140
through
44141
), we described how several agencies within HHS have sought public input on interoperability for various health programs. We noted that CMS views duplicate imaging and laboratory testing as one of several use cases in which the lack of clinical interoperability causes non-trivial beneficiary harm and program integrity concerns. In recognition of that perspective, the broader department, and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) in particular, adopts standards that facilitate easier exchange of diagnostic clinical information and includes criteria in the ONC Health IT Certification Program that address the certification of health IT to exchange this information. In the January 30, 2026
Federal Register
(
91 FR 4054
), ONC published an RFI titled, “Request for Information: Diagnostic Imaging Interoperability Standards and Certification”. A summary of the efforts described in the January 2026 RFI (
91 FR 4055
), to build diagnostic imaging requirements into health IT certification, is available in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44140
).
Another example of HHS seeking public input on interoperability was in the Request for Information; Health Technology Ecosystem” which appeared in the May 16, 2025
Federal Register
(
90 FR 21034
) (hereinafter “Health Technology Ecosystem RFI”). The comments in response to the Health Technology Ecosystem RFI stated that the imaging exchange environment remains fragmented and unreliable, with ongoing dependence on CDs and DVDs and limited availability of modern, API-enabled tools that would allow patients and health care providers to access and share images seamlessly. Interested parties also raised privacy and security considerations that must be accounted for as exchange capabilities evolve. Other public feedback highlighted support for building on existing standards rather than creating entirely new exchange paradigms. Commenters explained that laboratory interoperability had similar patterns regarding data exchange, where challenges frequently stem from differing ordering workflows, variations in result reporting practices, local coding conventions, and inconsistent implementation of standards. These issues mirror broader interoperability challenges and reinforce the need for coordinated, standards-based approaches across diagnostic domains.
Other key information received in response to the Health Technology Ecosystem RFI:
The current system of fragmented patient portals is unworkable.
A unified, “one-stop shop” for health records is the universal goal.
API access must go beyond the USCDI data set to the full electronic health information (EHI).
Existing data access tools are insufficient.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44141
) we explained that based on this input, we believe CMS can help improve interoperability between laboratories and physicians, hospitals, and other care delivery organizations. Specifically, participation in a national interoperability network for exchanging diagnostic imaging and laboratory results in a standardized format remains top of mind for the Department. Such participation would allow physicians, hospitals, laboratories, and other care delivery organizations to more easily access relevant clinical data to prevent the duplicate imaging and testing discussed previously in this section. We noted that network participation alone may not solve the problem. Networks must resolve fundamental technical issues like authentication (for example, are you who you say you are?); authorization (for example, are you allowed to access the data?); and patient matching (for example, what records are associated with the individual in question?). Without a reliable way to match records across systems, even well-connected networks would return incomplete or incorrect results.
We also explained that we considered building on the existing Electronic Notifications Condition of Participation (CoP) at
42 CFR 482.24(d)
to require hospitals to participate in a national interoperability network. We stated that we believe that the relationship to patient health and safety is clear: timely and accurate information leads to coordinated, safer care and treatment decisions for patients. While we believe a CoP, for Medicare and Medicaid participating hospitals, would be an appropriate mechanism to drive interoperability, we also recognize that unlike other provider types the only statutorily available penalty for noncompliance with the hospital CoPs is termination from the Medicare program, as provided under section 1866(b)(2)(A) and (B) of the Act. We believe this would be overly burdensome. However, we stated that we will continue to monitor hospital advances in interoperability and may consider future rulemaking or look to other programs like the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program or the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting program (IQR) or both.
Building upon the RFIs noted previously, we asked for input on the following questions specific to diagnostic laboratory and imaging interoperability:
Because image exchange can involve substantial technical and operational costs, should HHS or CMS consider incentives to support adoption and implementation, and if so, what form should those incentives take?
(
printed page 71508)
Given variability in conformance to existing laboratory and imaging exchange standards, would interested parties find value in expanded conformance testing tools, certification approaches, or implementation guidance?
How should CMS account for cases in which repeat imaging occurs because prior imaging results were not available for timely, standards-based reuse? Should CMS consider payment, quality, or participation policies that create accountability for the initial imaging provider, furnishing entity, or facility when failure to make results reusable contributes to avoidable repeat imaging? Are there penalties or disincentives for non-compliance we should consider?
For laboratory interoperability specifically, what barriers continue to impede exchange despite the availability of established standards, and what policy levers could help address those barriers? Should we consider incentives to support laboratory adoption and implementation of health data standards?
Should CMS establish a minimum data standard for result shareability, for example, a United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI+) supplement for imaging and laboratory results, requiring all participating entities to deliver both a structured Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) R4 Diagnostic Report resource and a human-readable Portable Document Format/Archive (PDF/A) rendition to the ordering health care provider's designated endpoint as a condition of Medicare payment? How should CMS address health care providers who have not yet implemented FHIR-native workflows, especially in rural areas?
We received public comment on this RFI. Commenters from a variety of interested parties, including professional organizations, hospitals, physician offices and the public provided feedback.
Comment:
In general, commenters support CMS efforts to reduce costs associated with duplicative testing and imaging. However, some commenters do not support CMS denying Medicare payment for duplicative testing. These commenters noted that often times duplicate testing may be clinically necessary, and health care providers should not be penalized if access to prior results is not readily available. Some commenters expressed that improving laboratory and digital imaging interoperability should be addressed and recommend CMS work with interested parties and solicit feedback.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback.
IV. Updates to the Quality Payment Program
A. CY 2027 Modifications to the Quality Payment Program Reporting and Data Submission
1. Executive Summary
a. Overview
This section of this final rule outlines changes to the Quality Payment Program starting January 1, 2027, except as otherwise noted for specific provisions. We continue to move the Quality Payment Program forward, including focusing on alignment between the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) and Advanced Alternative Payment Model (Advanced APM) tracks of participation, alignment with broader CMS initiatives, and new options for clinicians to participate in more meaningful ways. We aim to achieve continuous improvement in the quality of health care services provided to Medicare beneficiaries and other patients through MIPS and Advanced APMs for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 payment year.
Authorized by the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA) (
Pub. L. 114-10
, April 16, 2015), the Quality Payment Program is a value-based payment program, by which clinicians are rewarded for providing high-value, high-quality care to their patients in a cost-efficient manner. There are two ways for clinicians who provide services under the Medicare program to participate in the Quality Payment Program: MIPS and Advanced APMs. The statutory requirements for the Quality Payment Program are set forth in section 1848(q) and (r) of the Act for MIPS and section 1833(z) of the Act for Advanced APMs.
For the MIPS participation track, MIPS eligible clinicians (defined at § 414.1305)
[
392
]
are subject to a MIPS payment adjustment (positive, neutral, or negative) based on their performance in four performance categories: quality, cost, improvement activities, and Promoting Interoperability. We assess each MIPS eligible clinician's performance according to established performance standards for the applicable measures and activities specified in each of these four performance categories during a performance period to compute a final composite performance score (a “final score” as defined at § 414.1305). In calculating the final score, we must apply different weights for the four performance categories, subject to certain exceptions, as set forth in section 1848(q)(5) of the Act and at
42 CFR 414.1380(c)(1)
. The weights of the performance categories in the final score for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year are as follows, unless a different scoring weight is assigned under
42 CFR 414.1380(c)(2)
: 30 percent for the quality performance category; 30 percent for the cost performance category; 25 percent for the Promoting Interoperability performance category; and 15 percent for the improvement activities performance category.
Once calculated, each MIPS eligible clinician's final score is compared to the performance threshold established in prior rulemaking for that performance period to calculate the MIPS payment adjustment as specified in section 1848(q)(6) of the Act, such that the MIPS eligible clinician will receive in the applicable MIPS payment year: (1) a positive adjustment, if their final score exceeds the performance threshold; (2) a neutral adjustment, if their final score meets the performance threshold; or (3) a negative adjustment, if their final score is below the performance threshold. In calculating the MIPS payment adjustment for a MIPS eligible clinician, we account for the scaling factor and budget neutrality requirements, as further specified in section 1848(q)(6) of the Act. We then apply the MIPS payment adjustment to amounts otherwise paid under Medicare Part B for covered professional services for the MIPS eligible clinician for the applicable MIPS payment year and payments for covered professional services could be increased, decreased, or not adjusted based on the MIPS eligible clinician's final score relative to the performance threshold.
Section 1848(q) of the Act sets forth other requirements applicable to MIPS, including opportunities for feedback, targeted review, and public reporting of MIPS-eligible clinicians' performance. Section 1848(r) of the Act sets forth more specific requirements for development of measures for the cost performance category under MIPS.
For the Advanced APM participation track, if an eligible clinician participates in an Advanced APM and achieves Qualifying APM Participant (QP) or Partial QP status, they are excluded from the MIPS reporting requirements and payment adjustment (though eligible clinicians who are Partial QPs
(
printed page 71509)
may elect to participate in MIPS and be subject to the MIPS reporting requirements and payment adjustment). In alignment with the application of QPP eligibility determinations, we are finalizing our proposal with modification to apply QP and Partial QP status to the TIN/NPI level. For eligible clinicians with QP and partial QP status at the individual level, we will apply partial QP status to all TIN reassignments for the NPI as codified at § 414.1425(d). Under current law, eligible clinicians who are QPs for the 2024 performance year/2026 payment year and beyond will receive an increased physician fee schedule update of 0.75 percent qualifying APM conversion factor. We note that, historically, QPs received a lump sum APM Incentive Payment in the corresponding payment year, calculated as a specified percentage of the QP's paid claims for covered professional services from the base year. Only legislation enacted by Congress can make changes to either the enhanced QP conversion factor updates or the APM Incentive Payment.
We plan to continue developing policies for the Quality Payment Program that more effectively reward high-quality of care for patients and increase opportunities for Advanced APM participation. We continue to implement MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs) to allow for a more cohesive participation experience by connecting activities and measures from the four MIPS performance categories that are relevant to a specialty, medical condition, or a particular population.
As we move into the 10th year of the Quality Payment Program, we will be implementing the updates set forth in this section of this final rule, encouraging continued improvement in clinicians' performance with each performance year and driving improved quality of health care through payment policy.
b. Summary of Major Proposals
(1) Transforming the Quality Payment Program
The Making America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative (
https://www.hhs.gov/​maha/​index.html
) represents a shift from the focus on chronic disease management and moves toward prevention and restoring foundational wellness. This initiative aims to address the root causes of poor health outcomes by reducing chronic disease rates, improving nutrition, promoting preventative care, and increasing transparency in health systems. This vision is supported by aligning policies in MIPS and APMs within the Quality Payment Program with the foundational pillars of MAHA. We are expanding the MVP portfolio to include Diabetic Disease and Hypertension MVPs that address the prevention of chronic illnesses and aim to reduce the incidence and impact of long-term conditions. In alignment with the goal of promoting preventive care and fostering a more proactive and holistic approach to health management, we are finalizing new improvement activities under the “Advancing Health and Wellness” subcategory within the improvement activities performance category. The improvement activities integrate concepts that address nutrition, implement lifestyle approaches to disease management, and support patient wellness to ensure a healthier future.
Through the policies described in this final rule, we intend to transform and simplify MIPS, promote the use of connected measures and activities, continue rewarding clinicians for providing high value care, and use data-driven information to help all clinicians improve care and engage patients. We are finalizing, with modification, our proposal to sunset the traditional MIPS reporting option. Specifically, we are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS by two years until the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. Therefore, beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, MVPs would be the only reporting option for MIPS eligible clinicians who do not participate in a MIPS APM. Traditional MIPS will remain available through the CY 2030 performance period/2032 MIPS payment year.
(a) Transforming MIPS: MVP Strategy
MVPs will improve value, reduce burden, and inform patient choice in selecting clinicians. To support our goal of phasing out traditional MIPS and transitioning eligible clinicians to MVP reporting, we are finalizing with modification policies supporting MVP only reporting for MIPS. The MVP reporting option offers aligned measures and activities across quality, cost, improvement activities, and Promoting Interoperability performance categories, focusing on specific specialties, conditions, or patient populations to make reporting more meaningful. Specifically, we proposed that beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians not reporting the APM Performance Pathway(APP), would be required to report the measures and activities in a selected MVP for MIPS. However, we have reconsidered the timeline for the full transition to MVP reporting and are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS reporting by two years to allow us to further refine MVP policies and provide additional time for clinicians to prepare for full MVP implementation.
Specifically, we are finalizing a policy to require that beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians not reporting the APP would be required to report the measures and activities in a selected MVP to meet MIPS reporting requirements. We are finalizing our proposal as proposed to include virtual groups in MVP reporting beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year to ensure all eligible clinicians can report MVPs.
(b) MIPS Value Pathways Development and Maintenance
To continue moving the healthcare community toward value-based, high-quality, safe, and cost-efficient care, we are finalizing as proposed three new MVPs around the following topics: Diabetic Disease, Hypertension, and Hospitalist.
We are also finalizing as proposed MVP maintenance updates to our MVP inventory that are aligned with the MVP development criteria and take into consideration feedback from interested parties we have received through the maintenance process. Additionally, we updated all the MVPs to include MIPS core measures. Finally, we are renaming the Rehabilitative Support for Musculoskeletal Care MVP to Rehabilitative Support MVP to better represent the measures and activities included in the MVP.

3. Transforming MIPS: MIPS Value Pathway (MVP) Strategy
We play a leading role in transitioning the Federal health care system from Original Medicare payment toward value-based payment, incentivizing higher quality of care over higher quantity of care. The Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) aims to drive value through the collection, assessment, and public reporting of data that informs and rewards the delivery of high-value care. We continue to focus on transforming health care delivery, driving higher value care, and increasing alignment with other CMS programs and initiatives to reduce burden. We intend to continue our efforts to align the Quality Payment Program with the broader aims of CMS to ensure patients receive the care they want and deserve by promoting
(
printed page 71512)
prevention, wellness, and chronic disease management. We are focused on achieving the best outcomes and safest care across the full care journey through innovation and collaboration. We are implementing meaningful improvements designed to strengthen healthcare delivery and advance patient outcomes. Through these efforts, we strive to create a healthcare system that not only responds to chronic disease but works proactively to prevent it.
In the CY 2022 PFS proposed rule and CY 2025 PFS final rule, we stated our intent to transform MIPS and obtain more meaningful, comparable performance data, and drive higher value care through MVPs (
86 FR 39356
and
89 FR 98346
) and that we intended to propose a full transition to MVP reporting along with the Alternative Payment Model (APM) Performance Pathway (APP) reporting to support movement towards value-based payment (
86 FR 65394
through
65396
,
87 FR 70034
, and
89 FR 98346
). As noted in the CY 2025 PFS proposed rule (
89 FR 62012
), robust MVP availability and clinician coverage would be a precursor to sunsetting traditional MIPS. Through this final rule and future rulemaking, we acknowledge that we will need to develop policies to support MVP reporting for all MIPS eligible clinicians by the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. We will continue engaging with interested parties, including specialists and specialty societies, to identify gaps and opportunities, and leveraging additional policy options, as needed.
In this section, we are finalizing with modification on our proposal to sunset traditional MIPS reporting. Specifically, we are finalizing with modification to require that beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians, not participating in a MIPS Alternative Payment Model (APM), would be required to report the measures and activities in a selected MVP. The MVP reporting option offers aligned measures and activities across the quality, cost, improvement activities, and Promoting Interoperability performance categories. MVPs focus on specific specialties, conditions, or patient populations to make reporting more meaningful. With increased MIPS eligible clinicians reporting MVPs, MVP comparative performance data may become valuable to patients and caregivers in evaluating clinician performance and making choices about their care. We are finalizing that MIPS eligible clinicians, not participating in a MIPS APM, would be required to report the measures and activities in a selected MVP beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. We are also finalizing to include virtual groups in MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year to ensure all MIPS eligible clinicians can report MVPs.

We noted that we created the MVP reporting option to improve value, reduce burden, and inform patient choice in selecting clinicians. We also stated the MVP framework will move MIPS forward on the path to value by offering a reporting option that connects measures and activities across MIPS performance categories, better informing and empowering patients to make decisions about their healthcare, and by helping clinicians to achieve better outcomes using robust and accessible healthcare data and interoperability (

We stated that if the proposal to phase out traditional MIPS reporting for MIPS eligible clinicians not participating in a MIPS APM is finalized, there would be two reporting options for MIPS: MVPs and the APP. The transition from clinicians selecting from a large inventory of measures and activities in traditional MIPS to reporting more clinically relevant measures and activities in MVPs represents a necessary progression in MIPS if we are to achieve our intended goals of connecting measures and activities across MIPS and providing meaningful data to inform and empower patients to make decisions about their healthcare. b. Background on Full MVP Implementation
The MVP framework was introduced in the CY 2020 PFS final rule (

through

In the CY 2022 PFS proposed rule, we noted our intent to sunset traditional MIPS in a future performance period and solicited public comments on: (1) the length of time MVP reporting should be voluntary; (2) the timing for when we should fully implement MVPs; and (3) sunsetting the traditional MIPS reporting option (

In the CY 2022 PFS final rule, we finalized that voluntary reporting of MVPs would start in the CY 2023 performance period/2025 MIPS payment year to allow time for MVP participants and third-party intermediaries to adapt to changes in policy, reporting requirements, and updates to their technology systems (

In the CY 2025 PFS proposed rule, we issued a Request for Information (RFI) on the development of a timeline for the full transition to MVPs beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year (

and
62012

(

We recognize that full MVP implementation may limit the choice of measures and activities compared to those currently afforded by policies in traditional MIPS. However, MVPs include a set of clinically relevant measures and activities that provide an opportunity for MIPS performance data to better reflect clinicians' scope of care.
With the full implementation of MVPs, clinicians who are not participating in a MIPS APM would be required to select an MVP relevant to their scope of care and further choose the quality measures and improvement activities within the selected MVP that reflect the care provided. Widescale adoption of MVPs, using a standardized connected set of measures and activities for a specialty or medical condition, may generate important and meaningful information for patients to be able to compare the performance of clinicians on the same or similar sets of measures. Additionally, we refer readers to section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule for details on the finalized MIPS core measure requirement for traditional MIPS and MVP reporting. The MIPS core measure requirement would further clarify how MVPs would emphasize and increase reporting on select quality measures that are most important to clinicians and patients and reflect the care that is central to an applicable specialty, medical condition, or episode of care.
