c. Update to the Timeline for Full MVP Implementation
As discussed previously in section IV.A.3.a. of this final rule, MVP reporting became available for clinicians beginning in the CY 2023 performance period/2025 MIPS payment year (
86 FR 65394
to 65396). In previous PFS rules, we stated our intention to fully transition to MVPs and to sunset traditional MIPS (
85 FR 50279
and
50284
,
86 FR 65394
through
65396
).
We are concerned that continuing to maintain the traditional MIPS reporting option may impede MVP adoption for MIPS eligible clinicians. Additionally, it may cause slow adoption which may delay the intended benefits of MVPs, including simplification of MIPS and improving comparable clinician performance data that helps to drive value and inform clinician selection by patients. In addition, the availability of two MIPS reporting options, MVPs and traditional MIPS, creates challenges for developing and refining MVP policies over time due to limited MVP reporting resulting from continued clinician
(
printed page 71514)
reliance on the traditional MIPS reporting option. However, in establishing the sunset date we are also cognizant of the need to provide ample time for clinicians to prepare for full MVP reporting. Therefore, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44147
), we proposed to phase out traditional MIPS reporting for MIPS eligible clinicians not participating in a MIPS APM beginning in the CY 2029 performance year/2031 MIPS payment year. Transitioning to MVP implementation alongside the option for MIPS APM participants to participate in MIPS through the APP would support efforts to transform MIPS for clinicians and patients who rely on program performance information. We noted that traditional MIPS reporting would be available to clinicians through the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. This proposed timeline would have provided a period of 6 years for voluntary MVP reporting, allowing clinicians time to engage in the development of the MVP inventory, update their systems and work processes to prepare for MVP reporting, and gain experience with MVP reporting. Clinicians would continue to be able to report through either traditional MIPS or via MVPs through the CY 2028 performance year/2030 MIPS payment year.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44147
), we proposed that beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, all MIPS eligible clinicians, with the exception of clinicians reporting through the APP, would report through an MVP. Specifically, we proposed to add under § 414.1365(a)(2) that beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, except for clinicians reporting under the APP pursuant to § 414.1367, all MIPS eligible clinicians must report through an MVP. We believed that the CY 2029 performance year/2031 MIPS payment year would be an appropriate timeline for full implementation of MVPs and would offer sufficient time for MIPS eligible clinicians and groups to prepare for required MVP reporting. However, we have reconsidered the timeline and determined that additional time is needed for us to further refine the MVP policies. For example, we require additional time to increase MVP availability and transition to digital reporting. The additional time would further allow eligible clinicians to successfully transition to full MVP implementation. Therefore, as noted in section IV.A.3.c. of this final rule, we are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS until the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. We considered setting a date for the sunset of traditional MIPS that is more than five years in the future but we are concerned that delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS that far would discourage clinicians and groups from undertaking the changes necessary to successfully report MVPs. Therefore, we believe that our finalized timeline of sunsetting traditional MIPS beginning with the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year strikes an appropriate balance between providing additional time for clinicians to prepare for the transition to full MVP implementation and setting a timeline for the transition that offers strong encouragement for clinicians and groups to begin reporting MVPs.
As discussed in section IV.A.4.a.(1) of this final rule, we continue developing new MVPs that are relevant and meaningful for MIPS eligible clinicians. We intend to explore a range of strategies for transitioning to full MVP reporting, including, but not limited to, proposing additional MVPs. We recognize that clinicians may currently lack applicable measures and may not have an applicable MVP or may be unable to report a sufficient number of measures in an MVP. However, for subspecialists without many applicable and available measures in the MIPS measure inventory, we are aware of the need to develop reporting options or explore alternatives to reporting MVPs by the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. For example, we may consider developing a process for clinicians to indicate at the time of MVP registration that no available MVP in the MVP inventory includes applicable and available measures and activities. Alternatively, we could consider expanding measure denominators as applicable to strengthen specialty coverage for clinicians with limited applicable measures. We could also consider policies that allow us to review available and applicable measures for clinicians in the selected MVP to reduce the denominator of the quality performance category to score the quality performance category with fewer than four measures.
We received public comments on this proposal to transition to MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, except for clinicians reporting under the APP. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposal to sunset traditional MIPS beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year. Several commenters stated that the transition to MVP reporting would move the program to better accountability and improved reporting of meaningful quality data. Several commenters stated that CMS's proposed timeline would provide adequate time for clinicians to transition to MVP reporting.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and agree that the full transition to MVP reporting will result in improved reporting of meaningful quality data. We note that we have reconsidered the timeline for the full transition to MVP reporting and are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS reporting by two years to allow us to further time to refine MVP policies. For example, we require additional time to increase MVP availability and transition to digital reporting. The additional time would further allow eligible clinicians to successfully transition to full MVP implementation. Therefore, traditional MIPS reporting will be available to clinicians through the CY 2030 performance period/2032 MIPS payment year. We considered a delay of one year, but as discussed in section IV.A.4.c. of this final rule we anticipate mandatory reporting of available FHIR-based digital quality measures (dQMs) would begin in the CY 2030 performance period/2032 MIPS payment year. Therefore, we decided that allowing an additional year of voluntary MVP reporting beyond the start of mandatory FHIR-based reporting of digital measures would better support clinicians who will be transitioning to FHIR-based digital reporting. Beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, clinicians will need to participate in MIPS through an MVP or the APP.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal to sunset traditional MIPS beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year and offered recommendations for ensuring a smooth transition. A few commenters recommended that CMS provide support by working with clinicians and other interested parties to monitor negative unintended consequences and providing technical assistance to clinicians, EHR vendors, and third-party intermediaries. A few commenters recommended that CMS focus on the health IT infrastructure necessary for reporting MVPs. A commenter urged CMS to maintain stability in the MVP framework during the transition.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support. We will consider the
(
printed page 71515)
recommendations for providing educational support as we plan communications and outreach activities to support the full transition to MVPs. We will continue to work with EHR vendors and third-party intermediaries and consider guidance for development of the health IT infrastructure necessary for reporting MVPs. We agree that it will be desirable to maintain stability in the MVP framework to the extent feasible as the transition to full MVP implementation proceeds and will take that goal into account in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters encouraged CMS to offer additional flexibility in MVP reporting. A few commenters recommended that CMS closely monitor participation and performance during the transition to mandatory reporting. A commenter recommended that CMS offer fiscal leniency in the first few years of mandatory MVP reporting similar to the flexibility offered during the initial implementation of MIPS.
Response:
We thank the commenters for these recommendations. We recognize that transitioning to mandatory MVP reporting may be a change for some eligible clinicians. We will monitor participation and performance data and may consider options in the future to provide flexibility in reporting requirements and scoring policies as feasible, consistent with the goals of full MVP implementation.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed opposition to the sunset of traditional MIPS and stated that MVPs should remain voluntary to maintain clinician flexibility to choose the measures and activities that are most relevant to their practice. A commenter suggested that if MVPs demonstrate greater value and better alignment with clinical practice, clinicians and groups will migrate toward them, decreasing the need for traditional MIPS.
Response:
We disagree with the commenters. We are concerned that maintaining traditional MIPS as a reporting option may hinder adoption of MVPs, delaying the benefits of simplification of MIPS and improving comparable clinician performance data. Although we agree that more clinicians and groups will begin reporting MVPs as they better understand the value of MVP participation, unless we establish a date for sunsetting traditional MIPS, clinicians will continue to rely on traditional MIPS, either instead of or in addition to MVPs. Maintaining both reporting options indefinitely would continue complexity in policies and operations and create challenges for evaluating the MVP performance and reporting experience and developing and refining MVP policies over time.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed concern that MVPs incorporate the fundamental flaws of MIPS, including siloed performance categories, comparison of unlike clinicians, and lack of linkage between quality and cost measures. A few commenters stated that MVPs cannot accurately assess clinician performance because they are based on certain specialties or are overly broad, instead of focusing on a specific health condition, procedure, or episode of care that would be treated by the same clinician.
Response:
We note that the MVP framework is built upon the statutory framework described in section 1848(q) of the Act, which requires us to include the four MIPS performance categories. However, because an MVP consists of a connected set of quality measures, cost measures, and improvement activities that are relevant to the MVP topic, clinicians would be able to choose measures and activities that are closely related. Furthermore, MVPs strengthen the relationship between the quality performance category and the cost performance category by scoring an MVP participant only on the cost measures in the MVP, which were selected because of their relevance to the MVP topic and the included quality measures. We anticipate that as more clinicians report MVPs and the measures and activities that are relevant to their scope of practice, scores will increasingly reflect comparisons of performance between similar clinicians. We note, however, that the statute requires that we compare all MIPS eligible clinicians to a single performance threshold. Regarding the commenters' concern that MVPs cannot accurately assess clinician performance because they are overly broad, we note that clinicians may choose the quality measures within an MVP that are most relevant to their scope of care provided. The MVP inventory finalized in Appendix 2 of this final rule does include several condition-focused MVPs such as Advancing Care for Heart Disease and Optimal Care for Kidney Health. However, it is not feasible to develop an MVP for every health condition, procedure or episode of care.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed the sunset of traditional MIPS and expressed concern that requiring MVP reporting would create burden for small, independent, and rural practices. A commenter expressed concern that requiring MVP reporting would accelerate practice closure and decrease patient access to local clinicians.
Response:
We note that MVP reporting requires clinicians in small, independent, and rural practices to report fewer quality measures when compared to the six quality measures that these clinicians are currently required to report in traditional MIPS. We are cognizant of the challenges small practices have faced in participating in MIPS and will continue to maintain existing flexibilities for small practices when MVPs are fully implemented.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS maintain the traditional MIPS reporting option because the existing inventory of available MVPs is not sufficiently aligned with the care furnished by specialists and subspecialists. The commenters stated that, at a minimum, the MVP inventory should include measures relevant to 100 percent of specialties. Several commenters disagreed with CMS' estimate that the current MVP inventory provides coverage for approximately 98 percent of specialists, citing specialties such as allergy and immunology and radiation oncology as lacking a relevant MVP. A commenter compared existing and proposed MVPs to existing specialty measure sets and stated that there were gaps in specialty coverage and clinical relevance. The commenters further noted that the existence of an MVP for a given specialty (for example, ophthalmology) does not necessarily ensure meaningful quality measurement for all clinicians within that specialty. The commenters shared their concern that due to the lack of relevant measure options, clinicians may be required to report measures that are not clinically relevant to their practice in order to satisfy reporting requirements. In addition, many commenters urged CMS to ensure that MVPs include adequate measure sets for subspecialties. Many commenters expressed concern that broad specialty-based or condition-based MVPs may not fairly assess highly subspecialized clinicians, and that gaps in cost and quality measures applicable to subspecialty care and nonphysician care reduce the clinical relevance of MVPs for some clinicians, including interventional cardiologists, neuro-ophthalmologists, orthopedic sports medicine specialists, otolaryngologists, and physical therapists. A commenter stated that low MVP adoption may indicate that MVPs do not yet provide sufficient clinical relevance or flexibility to replace traditional MIPS. A few commenters recommended that CMS should retain traditional MIPS until appropriate specialty pathways are
(
printed page 71516)
developed, tested, and shown not to create inequitable scoring or participation barriers.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' feedback and understand the concerns raised regarding the current availability and clinical relevance of MVPs for specialists, subspecialists, and other clinician types. The estimate that the current MVP inventory provides coverage for approximately 98 percent of clinicians reflects an assessment of the proportion of MIPS clinicians who self-reported a specialty designation that aligns with an MVP's identified target specialties. We acknowledge, however, that such alignment does not necessarily mean that the measures included in an MVP can be reported by every clinician within a specialty or subspecialty, nor does it ensure that all clinicians can meaningfully participate in a particular MVP. We will continue to work with interested parties to improve the clinical relevance, fairness, and usability of MVPs and to support clinicians in selecting the reporting option that is most appropriate for their practice. We encourage interested parties to submit potential new measures that will align with current goals and priorities during the annual Call for Measures which generally occurs in the spring of each year to fill identified gaps allowing meaningful and complete assessment of MIPS eligible clinician's performance within MIPS. To allow additional time for refinement of the MVP framework, as discussed in section IV.A.3.c. of this final rule, we are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS by two years, so that the traditional MIPS reporting option is available for clinicians through the CY 2030 performance period/2032 MIPS payment year.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern that the majority of the MVPs do not include a sufficient number of quality measures available through each collection type, limiting flexibility for clinicians to select and report measures within an MVP. The commenters recommended that MVPs include at least four quality measures under each collection type so that clinicians and group practices would not need to contract with multiple vendors to report an MVP. A few commenters noted that availability of a sufficient number of measures for each collection type would reduce reliance on QCDR measures. A few commenters also noted that including at least four measures for every collection type would enable third-party intermediaries and EHR vendors to support an MVP without being required to support every measure included in an MVP.
Response:
While we acknowledge the recommendation that each MVP include at least four quality measures under each collection type, we do not believe it is appropriate to establish a universal minimum across all collection types for every MVP at this time, as measure availability and feasibility may vary by specialty, clinical topic, and reporting mechanism. However, we will continue to consider opportunities to increase the number of measures available across collection types, as appropriate, in future MVP development and maintenance to ensure flexibility and choice of measures within MVPs. We will also continue to work with measure developers, third-party intermediaries, and EHR vendors to support more flexible reporting options over time.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS expand the MVP measures menu to include a sufficient number of eCQMs or dQMs to submit an MVP exclusively using an EHR. The commenters expressed concern that when an MVP does not include a sufficient number of eCQMs, it would add substantial burden to the practices because they must contract with thirdparty vendors to report other collection types. The commenters stated that electronic reporting options would help maintain existing workflows, reduce the burden of transitioning to MVPs and support broader efforts to advance digital health.
Response:
As discussed in section IV.A.4.c. of this final rule, it is our intent to transition to digital quality measurement across all CMS quality reporting programs. At the same time, we do not want to increase burden by requiring clinicians currently reporting eCQMs to report using multiple collection types. We note that we are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS reporting by two years, so that traditional MIPS reporting is available to clinicians through the CY 2030 performance period/2032 MIPS payment year. This additional time will allow us to continue to work with measure developers and interested parties to support the transition to more interoperable, digitally enabled reporting over time. As more eCQMs and dQMs become available, we will incorporate these into MVP measure sets, as appropriate, which would improve dQM alignment across CMS quality programs.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns that clinicians who could not report all four required quality measures would be unfairly penalized in an MVP-only reporting environment. A few commenters recommended that CMS establish a clear pathway for clinicians without an applicable MVP or who cannot meet the quality reporting requirement in an MVP. A few commenters recommended using the eligible measure applicability (EMA) process or a similar approach within the MVP framework to create a process that offered protections to clinicians from penalties and the right to appeal or request a reconsideration through processes such as targeted review. A few commenters also recommended automatic exemptions or exceptions for clinicians who do not have an applicable MVP available to report.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' concerns regarding clinicians who may be unable to report all four required quality measures in an MVP-only reporting environment, including clinicians for whom there may not be an applicable MVP. We will consider these comments as we continue to refine MVP policies and evaluate ways to support clinicians who may face limitations in meeting MVP reporting requirements. We will also take these recommendations into account as we consider future policy development related to measure applicability, exceptions, and other flexibilities, as appropriate.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern that the transition to MVP reporting would increase the operational burden for multispecialty groups with more than 15 clinicians as these groups would need to form subgroups and report multiple MVPs. The commenters noted that moving away from traditional MIPS reporting would significantly increase the number of quality measures required to be reported across subgroups within a group. A few commenters shared their concern that subgroup reporting would add operational complexity because they would need to configure and aggregate data at the subgroup level.
Response:
In the CY 2022 PFS final rule, we finalized a policy allowing MIPS eligible clinicians to participate as subgroups when reporting MVPs beginning with the CY 2023 performance period/2025 MIPS payment year (
86 FR 65392
through
65394
). We stated that the intent of these policies was to move away from large multispecialty groups reporting on a single set of measures that may not be relevant or meaningful to all specialists within the group. We have also heard consistently from interested parties over the prior years that data submitted at the large group level is not always representative of the clinicians who comprise the group. We note that our subgroup policies are flexible, including
(
printed page 71517)
no restrictions on the composition of subgroups other than the requirement that each subgroup include one clinician who is MIPS eligible at the individual level. We also did not establish a minimum number of subgroups that must be formed because we intend for groups to form subgroups and select MVPs in the manner that best represents the scope of care the group provides. We refer readers to regulations at §§  414.1305, 414.1318, and 414.1365 and the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65398
through
65405
), the CY 2023 PFS final rule (
87 FR 70038
through
70045
), the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79323
through
79328
, and CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49842
through
49846
) for additional details on previously finalized subgroup policies.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern that the transition would require groups to make significant changes to data collection, EHRs, clinician training, and workflows, and to monitor across multiple specialties billing under a single TIN. The commenters recommended that CMS maintain voluntary MVP participation and delay the sunset of traditional MIPS to give groups greater flexibility to update their infrastructure until the MVP framework is more fully developed and concerns related to specialty coverage and subgroup reporting burden for multispecialty group practices have been resolved.
Response:
We recognize that the transition from traditional MIPS to MVP reporting may present operational challenges for some practices, particularly those with multiple specialties and more complex reporting structures. We thank the commenters for the feedback regarding allowing practices additional time to update their infrastructure and workflows, and their recommendation that the sunset of traditional MIPS be delayed until the MVP framework is more fully developed, including with respect to specialty coverage and subgroup-related burden. As discussed previously in this section, we are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS, with MVP reporting required for clinicians not participating in a MIPS APM, beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. We will continue to consider these concerns, including the readiness of multispecialty groups and the operational implications of subgroup reporting, in future rulemaking as we further develop and refine the MVP framework.
Comment:
A few commenters requested guidance on how multispecialty groups should select the most appropriate MVPs such as those MVPs representing the highest volume of services provided by clinicians within the group or those applicable to the largest number of clinician specialty types in the group. A few commenters recommended that CMS provide guidance on the maximum number of MVPs a group would be required to report, stating that such guidance would reduce burden and help ensure that MVP reporting is operationally feasible for multispecialty group practices. A commenter recommended that CMS publish information on subgroup participation, measure applicability, and scoring before transitioning to MVP reporting so that group practices and third-party intermediaries would have sufficient time to configure their systems in advance of an MVP-only reporting environment.
Response:
Regarding the commenters' request for guidance on the maximum number of MVPs a multispecialty group may need to report, we are not establishing a policy at this time because reporting needs may vary based on the size, composition, and specialty mix of the group. As we continue to refine MVP policies, we will consider providing additional subregulatory education and guidance to support the understanding of subgroup participation, MVP selection, and scoring methodologies for clinicians, groups, and third-party intermediaries.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended that CMS establish a pathway for multispecialty groups to report on a single set of measures that appropriately captures multidisciplinary care, rather than requiring the formation of subgroups. A commenter recommended that CMS establish a group-level score so that clinicians who cannot be assigned to a subgroup would automatically receive the weighted average score of the subgroups within the group.
Response:
We acknowledge the commenters' recommendations to allow multispecialty groups to report on a single set of measures or establish a group-level score for clinicians who cannot readily be assigned to a subgroup. Although we recognize the potential benefit of these approaches in reducing administrative burden, we have concerns that such policies could undermine the relevance of reported measures for certain clinicians and specialties and introduce additional operational and methodological complexities. Therefore, we are not adopting these policies at this time.
Comment:
Many commenters stated that the transition to MVPs will require more time for practices to understand new requirements, develop their reporting infrastructure, and train clinicians. A few commenters stated that the low uptake of MVPs to date suggests there are significant barriers to MVP participation which cannot be addressed under the proposed timeframe. A few commenters expressed concern that transitioning to full MVP implementation on the proposed timeline would create administrative and technical burden. A few commenters stated that it is difficult for organizations to develop their internal processes when program requirements change frequently and that small rural practices are especially challenged. A few commenters recommended that CMS conduct pilot studies with small rural practices. A commenter expressed concern that CMS is expecting clinicians to prepare for MVPs, core measures, and modified scoring methodologies all at the same time.
Response:
We recognize that clinicians and groups will need sufficient time to develop and implement the processes needed to transition from traditional MIPS reporting to MVP reporting and appreciate the challenges and burden clinicians and groups may face in implementing the MVP-related policies being finalized in this final rule. Although we acknowledge that low uptake of MVPs to date may, to some extent, reflect barriers to participation, we believe the more significant factor is the continued availability of the traditional MIPS reporting option and, therefore, are finalizing a date for sunsetting traditional MIPS. We appreciate commenters' observations about the complexity for large, multi-specialty organizations in reporting multiple MVPs and note that our subgroup policies provide significant flexibility for a multispecialty group to implement MVP reporting in the manner that best fits its clinicians and scope of care. Similarly, we note that the flexibilities in place under traditional MIPS to assist small practices in participating will remain when the transition to full MVP reporting is accomplished. As discussed previously in this section, we are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS by two years, with required MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, partially to provide clinicians with additional time to prepare for an MVP only reporting environment.
Comment:
Many commenters urged CMS to continue traditional MIPS until measure and MVP gaps are filled and MVPs are improved. A few commenters stated that additional time is needed for
(
printed page 71518)
CMS, specialty societies, and registries to collaborate on measure and MVP development and testing. A commenter stated that CMS should develop a measure development plan for specialties that lack an applicable MVP and for subspecialties, clinical conditions and procedures that existing MVPs do not address. A commenter recommended that CMS delay the sunset of traditional MIPS until MVPs fully reflect the scope of patient care for large multispecialty groups. A commenter recommended that CMS consider delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS until scoring disparities between MVPs are resolved. A commenter stated that even if an Obesity Medicine MVP were developed and finalized for the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, there would be only one year of voluntary reporting of the MVP before it was mandatory under the proposed timeline.
Response:
We are committed to continued collaboration with specialty societies and other interested parties to develop additional MVPs, refine existing MVPs and fill measure gaps. We refer readers to the CMS Quality Measure Development Plan and the Measure Development Plan Annual Report at
https://www.cms.gov/​medicare/​quality/​value-based-programs/​quality-payment-program/​measure-development
for more information on measure development priorities. With respect to the concern expressed about having only one year of voluntary reporting for a new MVP introduced in the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, we note that our revised timeline for sunsetting traditional MIPS will provide three years of voluntary reporting for any new MVPs proposed and finalized for the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. With respect to delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS until MVPs fully reflect the scope of care for large multispecialty groups, we note that the MVPs in our inventory offer robust measure sets addressing top health priorities and the care provided to Medicare patients and provide clinicians with a method to report more specialty-specific, condition-based or more broad-based measures. We will continue to work with interested parties to improve the clinical relevance, fairness, and usability of MVPs and to support clinicians in selecting the reporting option that is most appropriate for their practice. We encourage interested parties to submit potential new measures that will align with current goals and priorities during the annual Call for Measures to fill identified gaps allowing meaningful and complete assessment of MIPS eligible clinician's performance within MIPS. Regarding scoring disparities between MVPs, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule we solicited feedback on MVP scoring issues in an RFI, including ensuring scoring fairness across MVPs (
91 FR 44206
). We may consider the feedback received in response to the MVP Scoring RFI in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that EHR vendors, registries, and other technology partners need more time to develop, test, and deploy MVP reporting infrastructure. A commenter stated that developing and testing automated reporting capabilities across multiple specialty-specific pathways requires substantial vendor investment and time.
Response:
We agree with the commenters that EHR vendors, registries, and other technology partners who support clinicians participating in the Quality Payment Program need sufficient time to develop and deploy the MVP reporting infrastructure. We anticipate the modified timeline we are finalizing in this final rule will provide sufficient time for technology partners to prepare for required MVP reporting.
Comment:
Many commenters urged CMS to prioritize the transition to digital quality measurement, ensuring a successful transition to dQM reporting and sufficient availability of dQMs for all MVPs and the Ambulatory Specialty Model before sunsetting traditional MIPS. A commenter stated that CMS should delay the sunset of traditional MIPS until FHIR-based dQM infrastructure is available, operational, broadly supported across CEHRT products, and tested for most MIPS measures.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback regarding prioritization of a successful transition to dQM reporting. We believe the modified timeline for sunsetting traditional MIPS that we are finalizing in this rule will allow clinicians and their technology partners to focus on the digital reporting transition and provide time for dQM infrastructure to become more widely available before MVP reporting requirements take effect. We note, however, conversion of existing quality measures to dQMs will require collaboration and active engagement with all measure stewards and interested parties.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended that CMS delay the transition to required MVP reporting. A few commenters recommended specific timelines of three to five years beyond the proposed timeline of sunsetting traditional MIPS beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year. A few commenters noted that providers already face significant regulatory demands, including the transition to digital quality measures. A commenter requested a delay in the sunset of traditional MIPS for small and independent practices.
Response:
We acknowledge the significant challenges clinician practices, including small and independent practices, may face in simultaneously navigating the transition to full MVP implementation and the transition to FHIR-based digital quality measures. We are therefore modifying our proposal to sunset traditional MIPS such that instead of beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, it will begin with the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, adding two more years of voluntary MVP reporting for all clinicians, including those in small and independent practices. With respect to commenters' recommendations to delay the sunset of traditional MIPS by three to five years, we believe that our finalized timeline of sunsetting traditional MIPS beginning with the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year strikes an appropriate balance between providing additional time for clinicians to prepare for the transition to full MVP implementation and setting a timeline for the transition that offers strong encouragement for clinicians and groups to begin reporting MVPs. We are concerned that setting a date for the sunset of traditional MIPS that is more than five years in the future will discourage clinicians and groups from undertaking the changes necessary to successfully report MVPs.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS needs more time to evaluate MVPs and the MVP reporting experience in order to demonstrate that MVPs are valid and beneficial before mandating MVP reporting. A few commenters recommended that the transition timeline should be based on readiness benchmarks instead of a predetermined date.
Response:
We thank commenters for their recommendations regarding readiness criteria and will consider the feedback as we further refine the MVP inventory and MVP reporting and scoring policies. We also urge clinicians to participate in voluntary MVP reporting prior to the transition to required MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. Voluntary MVP reporting, while traditional MIPS reporting is also available, would help clinicians gain experience and
(
printed page 71519)
determine any changes to their current workflows. Increased participation in MVP reporting would also provide us with additional data to further evaluate MVP performance and MVP reporting to allow us to further refine MVP policies before the transition to required MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed concerns regarding the MVP registration timeline, specifically noting that the current timeline to register ends before clinicians are aware of their final MIPS eligibility status. The commenters stated that this timeline could create unintended consequences as the clinicians who become subsequently MIPS eligible due to changes in licensure status or switching group practices may be unable to report an MVP. The commenters recommended that CMS align the MVP registration timeline with the timeline for release of final MIPS eligibility determinations. A commenter stated that extending the MVP registration deadline to December 31 of the applicable performance period would align with the timeframe for submitting MIPS Hardship Exception applications. Another commenter recommended that CMS establish an additional registration opportunity or an exception process for such clinicians. Another commenter questioned whether an MVP registration process would remain necessary in an MVP-only environment.
Response:
As we stated in the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65416
), we established the MVP registration process to enable MVP participants and us to accurately capture the MVP selection and determine subgroup participation ahead of MIPS data submission. We recognize that the registration requirement may involve additional nuances where final MIPS eligibility determinations change for reasons outside the control of the clinician or group practice. In light of our decision to delay the sunset of traditional MIPS by two years and transition to required MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, we will continue to consider feedback on these issues, including clinician experience with the MVP registration process and the role of registration as we move toward MVP-only reporting, in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that sunsetting traditional MIPS could result in removal of relevant MIPS quality measures that are not currently included in the existing MVPs. The commenters further noted that removing these measures would reduce the MIPS inventory of available quality measures, limit meaningful reporting options for specialists and discourage continued investment in quality measure development. A few commenters requested additional CMS guidance regarding the future of quality measures under the QCDR and MIPS CQM collection types that are currently not included in any MVP. A commenter recommended that CMS maintain the specialty-specific measurement infrastructure to support expansion of relevant quality measures for specialists and to enable meaningful participation in MVP reporting.
Response:
We acknowledge the concerns raised regarding the potential effect of sunsetting traditional MIPS on the continued availability of relevant quality measures, particularly for specialists. We recognize the importance of maintaining a robust inventory of quality measures that supports meaningful participation across specialties and encourages continued investment in quality measure development. We also recognize the value of specialty-specific measurement infrastructure, including measures reported through the QCDR and MIPS CQM collection types, in supporting clinically relevant quality reporting. As we continue to implement and refine MVP policies, we intend to consider the availability of relevant quality measures for specialists and the role of currently available MIPS quality measures that are not yet included in an MVP. We will also consider feedback on the QCDR and MIPS CQM measures as we consider future development of MVPs and related policies.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing with modification that beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, all MIPS eligible clinicians, with the exception of clinicians reporting through the APP, would report through an MVP. Specifically, we are finalizing to add under § 414.1365(a)(2) that beginning in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year, except for clinicians reporting through the APP pursuant to § 414.1367, all MIPS eligible clinicians must report through an MVP.
d. Include Virtual Groups in MVP Reporting
Section 1848(q)(5)(I) of the Act establishes the use of voluntary virtual groups for certain assessment purposes. The statute requires the establishment and implementation of a process that allows an individual MIPS eligible clinician or a group consisting of not more than 10 MIPS eligible clinicians to elect to form a virtual group with at least one other such individual MIPS eligible clinician for a performance period. As determined in statute, individual MIPS eligible clinicians and groups forming virtual groups are required to make such election prior to the start of the applicable performance period under MIPS and cannot change their election during the performance period.
In the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65394
), we finalized a delay in the availability of MVP reporting for virtual groups. We noted that there are several considerations, such as implementation burden for interested parties and us, value of MVP reporting for these clinicians versus burden, scoring policies, and other issues that must be addressed prior to allowing clinicians in virtual groups to participate in MVP reporting. Therefore, we did not include virtual groups in the previously finalized definition of an MVP participant at § 414.1305 (
86 FR 65392
through
65394
). However, to comply with the statute, full implementation of MVPs must include a pathway for virtual groups to participate. For this reason, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44148
), we proposed to allow virtual groups to participate in MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year. This approach would allow time for us to further refine participation criteria and address potential barriers for virtual groups to participate in MVP reporting.
To include virtual groups in MVP reporting, we proposed to revise the definition of an MVP participant at § 414.1305 to provide that, beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, MVP participant means an individual MIPS eligible clinician, single specialty group, multispecialty group that meets the requirements of a small practice, virtual group, subgroup, or APM Entity that is assessed on an MVP in accordance with § 414.1365 for all MIPS performance categories.
We considered including virtual groups in MVP reporting beginning in the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. We recognize that we would need to evaluate additional related policies before including virtual groups in MVP reporting. Under the current policy at § 414.1365(b), MVP participants must register during the performance period. We recognize that the inclusion of virtual groups in MVP reporting would therefore require these groups to register for MVP reporting, which would be an addition to the
(
printed page 71520)
existing registration requirement to form a virtual group prior to the performance period. We are exploring options to mitigate the need for virtual groups to register a second time for MVP reporting. Additionally, we noted that even with the proposed inclusion of virtual groups in MVP reporting, clinicians in virtual groups would be unable to participate as subgroups because the definition of a subgroup at § 414.1305 is limited to clinicians within a single TIN and therefore excludes virtual groups, which, by definition, are composed of clinicians across two or more TINs. Under § 414.1305, a subgroup is a subset of a group that includes at least one MIPS eligible clinician and is identified by the group TIN, a subgroup identifier, and each eligible clinician's NPI.
We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal to allow virtual groups to report MVPs beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
Several commenters urged CMS to take steps to minimize administrative burdens for virtual groups participating in MVP reporting. A few commenters recommended that CMS provide technical support and clear guidance on MVP reporting to virtual groups. A few commenters stated that CMS could streamline the registration process by combining virtual group registration and MVP registration.
Response:
We agree that clinicians interested in participating in MIPS as a virtual group may need additional guidance on MVP reporting and we will explore opportunities to provide appropriate communications and education materials. We may consider the suggestion to streamline the registration process as we further develop the process for MVP reporting by virtual groups.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns that virtual groups will need more time to prepare for MVP reporting and recommended that CMS should make MVP reporting available to virtual groups in the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year or delay mandatory MVP reporting for virtual groups until they have at least one year of voluntary MVP reporting experience.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback regarding virtual groups' readiness to report MVPs. We agree that virtual groups would likely benefit from an opportunity to report MVPs on a voluntary basis prior to the sunset of traditional MIPS. As noted in section IV.A.3.c. of this final rule, we are delaying the sunset of traditional MIPS until the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year. We note that allowing virtual groups to report MVPs beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year will provide two years for virtual groups to report MVPs on a voluntary basis and will allow us to further develop policies and operational details necessary to implement MVP reporting for virtual groups.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal to allow virtual groups to report MVPs beginning with the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year. Specifically, we are finalizing to revise the definition of an MVP participant at § 414.1305 to provide that, beginning in the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year, MVP participant means an individual MIPS eligible clinician, single specialty group, multispecialty group that meets the requirements of a small practice, virtual group, subgroup, or APM Entity that is assessed on an MVP in accordance with § 414.1365 for all MIPS performance categories.
4. QPP Reporting and Data Submission
a. CY 2027 MVP Development and Maintenance
(1) Development of New MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs)
The development of MVPs is informed by the framework established in prior rulemaking (
85 FR 84849
through

a. Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources®-Based Digital Quality Measurement in the Quality Payment Program and Other CMS Quality Programs—Request for Information
We are advancing quality measurement by transitioning existing quality measures and reporting processes to Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources® (FHIR®)-based digital approaches. Digital quality measures
[
393
]
(dQMs) use standardized, interoperable digital data from multiple sources, including electronic health records (EHRs), to enable more comprehensive and timely assessment of care while reducing reporting burden. We continue to collaborate with Federal partners to advance health information technology and digital quality measurement policy, interoperability standards, and quality measurement infrastructure to support the transition to FHIR-based digital quality reporting.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44143
), we discussed a phased transition to FHIR-based digital quality measurement across the Quality Payment Program and other clinician and hospital programs. Figure C-C1 reflects the phased 2-year transition timeline currently under consideration. The 2-year transition would begin in CY/FY 2028 when FHIR-based dQM reporting would coexist with existing CQM/eCQM options, followed by mandatory FHIR-based reporting for transitioned measures starting in CY/FY 2030. To support a seamless transition and implementation, we requested feedback on implementation timelines, readiness barriers, scoring and reporting requirements, and the technical assistance or flexibility needed, particularly for small and rural practices, and operationally complex organizations such as Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs).
We received many comments on this request for information (RFI) and appreciate the feedback which may inform future rulemaking. We did not propose any policies regarding the FHIR-based approaches in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, and we are not finalizing any policies regarding the FHIR-based approaches in this final rule; however, we are providing additional details on expected changes under a future transition to FHIR-based quality reporting. For example, in a FHIR-based reporting environment, a FHIR-based dQM may be reported using a measure specification and data requirements that differs from those used under existing CQM or eCQMs. This would be in addition to a change in the submission format that is used to submit an existing CQM or eCQM (for example, replacing Quality Reporting Document Architecture (QRDA) with FHIR). During the transition period, where we may have both dQM and existing CQM and eCQM versions of the same measures available, we intend to establish policies that address the fact that there are various specifications and data elements associated with each method of reporting. Part of these policy considerations would include addressing scoring and public reporting implications.
Additionally, the certification criteria and reporting specifications for FHIR-based dQM requirements may be different than those associated with current eCQM reporting. Any changes to certification criteria and associated changes to digital reporting of quality measures would need to go through notice-and-comment rulemaking by the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) and/or CMS as applicable. Depending on future policy and technical requirements, FHIR-based reporting could impact third-party
(
printed page 71527)
intermediaries, such as Qualified Clinical Data Registries (QCDRs) or qualified registries. However, we would continue to consider standards and other requirements applicable to such reporting options, including the extent to which ONC certification would be required and whether a third-party intermediary may transform data from other systems into the required FHIR-based specification.
Finally, we continue to focus on the broader objective of the digital transition and intend for all future reporting options, including those involving third-party intermediaries, to promote further adoption of FHIR-based standards rather than functioning solely as a conversion of existing measures into a FHIR format. We will continue to further clarify in future rulemaking the requirements applicable to clinicians, QCDRs, qualified registries, and others that may not use certified health IT.

(c) Modifying Quality Data Submission Criteria
(i) Designating MIPS Core Measures
In the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule (
90 FR 32702
), we published a Core Elements Request for Information (RFI) soliciting feedback on how to encourage MVP reporting on key quality measures, or “core” measures, that reflect the essential components of care. One goal of MIPS reporting, particularly with the transition to MVPs, is to provide patients with comparative clinician performance data so they can make the most informed decisions about their care. The number of MIPS quality measures available for clinicians to choose from in traditional MIPS reduces the standardization of performance data. While MVPs reduce the number of quality measures for clinicians to choose from, MVPs still provide a degree of measure choice that may not produce sufficient comparative performance data on standardized measures to support patient choice of care. In the Core Elements RFI in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule (
90 FR 37021
and
37022
), we sought feedback on a potential reporting requirement in which clinicians reporting an MVP would be required to select and report one quality measure from a subset of “core” quality measures in each MVP, which would count as one of the four quality measures required in MVP reporting. MVP reporting requirements for the other performance categories would be unchanged. MIPS core measures would be limited to measures that are most reflective of the care that is unique to each MVP's specialty or medical condition. In response to the Core Elements RFI in the CY 2026 PFS proposed rule (
90 FR 32702
), commenters shared concerns that MIPS core measures may not be applicable to their scope of care and that a MIPS core measure reporting requirement could add complexity to MVP reporting. We took this commenter feedback into consideration, as discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, in our proposal of the MIPS core measures policy and in our proposed modifications to the quality performance category data submission criteria for traditional MIPS and MVPs. Specifically, we proposed to designate certain measures as MIPS core measures. Traditional MIPS reporters would be required to report one MIPS core measure as one of their six required quality measures. MVP reporters would be required to report one MIPS core measure as one of their four required quality measures. Small practices would be exempt from this requirement.
As stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, one of the goals of implementing MIPS core measures is to provide patients with comparative clinician performance data. This will enable patients to make better assessments of the quality of care provided by requiring clinicians within a given specialty to report on a narrower group of measures. This will also emphasize and increase reporting on select quality measures that are the most reflective of the care central to an applicable specialty, medical condition, or episode of care. In developing the MIPS core measures policy, we evaluated several alternative approaches. First, when considering how to procure more robust comparative performance data, we considered mandating clinicians reporting an MVP be required to report the same MIPS quality measure. This approach was not consistent with section 1848(q)(2)(D)(i) of the Act, nor did it achieve intended policy goals of generating more comparative clinician performance data on key quality measures, since what matters most for high-quality care in one specialty may differ from another. Additionally, cross-cutting quality measures, while applicable to the majority of MIPS eligible clinicians, may not be applicable to all, especially bearing in mind subgroup reporting. Expanding upon this idea, we also examined the possibility of a uniform subset of quality measures that would be consistent across all MVPs, and from which clinicians would be required to report one to two quality measures. While having the same subset of measures provides better coverage of the variety of scopes of care provided by MIPS eligible clinicians, we remain concerned that a uniform subset of quality measures will not sufficiently account for the variety of MIPS eligible clinicians' scopes of care while meaningfully assessing quality performance.
In focusing on the goal of providing patients and clinicians with “comparative performance data,” particularly among clinicians practicing within the same clinical specialty or providing care to patients with a specific medical condition, we considered whether to use existing population health measures or to develop new administrative claims-based measures. While these approaches will allow for automatic capture of data, there are still constraints in applicability across MIPS eligible clinicians in addition to resources and feasibility. Given these findings, we determined that the most prudent way to capture meaningful comparative data and provide patients with better insight into the quality of care provided was to create a curated set of core quality measures for each MVP. The list of MIPS core measures was selected because we determined these measures were most reflective of the care central to a clinical specialty or medical condition and will be the measures that the MIPS eligible clinician will be required to report from within that MVP.
For each MVP, we proposed that from the list of MIPS quality measures already assigned to the MVP, we would designate at least one as a MIPS core measure that an MVP reporting clinician would be required to report as one of their four required quality measures because the quality measures within each MVP are measures that are clinically relevant to the MVP's specialty or medical condition, and the proposed MIPS core measures are intended to be most reflective of the care that is central to the MVP's specialty or medical condition. The selection process focused on existing MIPS quality measures and newly proposed quality measures for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year.
In determining which of the quality measures set forth in an MVP should be designated as a MIPS core measure, we proposed to select a minimum of three MIPS core measures per MVP and proposed to designate more than three measures as MIPS core measures if we determined more than three measures must be selected to reflect the care central to the subspecialties within that MVP.
We proposed that for CY 2027 and future years, selection of the MIPS core measures would be based on the following factors:
Whether the measure is an outcome-based measure;
Measure collection type availability and the clinician's ability to meet reporting requirements to the extent practicable. Qualified Clinical Data Registry (QCDR) measures were not considered for MIPS core measure selection to ensure MIPS core measures are broadly available and accessible for all eligible clinicians;
Measure adoption and current and historic performance rates for each measure, to be in alignment with section 1848(q)(3) of the Act, which states that the Secretary shall consider historical performance standards and opportunity for continued improvement in establishing performance standards; and
Whether the measure is most reflective of the care that is central to

We proposed that the MIPS core measure designation would apply to quality measures in both traditional MIPS and MVPs. Establishing a set of unified key quality measures across both reporting pathways promotes alignment, reduced reporting complexity for clinicians reporting both traditional MIPS and MVPs, and is operationally feasible. The proposed MIPS core measure inventory, in other words, the list of all measures from each MVP designated as a MIPS core measure in accordance with the above-mentioned factors, includes over 70 quality measures. These measures represent key aspects of care across a variety of specialties and medical conditions. The MIPS core measure inventory also overlaps with the MIPS quality measures currently designated as high priority measures. Given the proposed removal of the high priority designation for MIPS quality measures, the MIPS core measure inventory will not only support reporting within MVPs but will also be applicable to clinicians reporting via traditional MIPS. Additionally, it would provide sufficient data for benchmarking for the MIPS core measures once we phase out traditional MIPS reporting and transition to full implementation of MVP reporting, as detailed in section IV.A.3.c. of this final rule.
As detailed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule, we proposed that clinicians reporting through the traditional MIPS reporting option would select from the complete inventory of available MIPS core measures for the performance period. Whereas clinicians reporting through the MVP reporting option will select the applicable MIPS core measures from the core measures identified within their chosen MVP. As discussed in section IV.A.4.a.(2) of this final rule, we proposed to revise the format of the MVP tables in Appendix 3: MVP Inventory of this final rule to include MIPS core measures for each previously finalized MVP. We also added a MIPS core measure table to the newly proposed MVPs. Further, we proposed beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, to establish a MIPS core measure designation applicable to selected quality measures contained in the MIPS quality measure inventory and the MVP inventory found in the Appendices of this final rule.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the MIPS core measure proposals. A commenter stated that the MIPS core measure requirement is an improvement over the current outcome/high priority requirement for meeting the quality performance category.
Response:
We thank the commenters for supporting the MIPS core measure proposals.
Comment:
A commenter favored a small, clinically meaningful MIPS core measure inventory over a large menu of optional measures and urged CMS to ensure each specialty's MIPS core measures can be reported using data clinicians already captured (including remote monitoring and patient-reported outcomes), without requiring a separate abstraction workflow. A few commenters indicated that CMS should ensure that every MVP includes at least one broadly applicable and clinically relevant MIPS core measure. A commenter recommended expanding the MIPS core measure inventory or retaining a traditional reporting pathway, working with measure stewards to increase relevant measures, and providing a clear crosswalk between current high priority and proposed MIPS core measures. The commenter also requested that CMS explain the rationale for new MIPS core measures, clearly define core measure criteria, ensure appropriateness across specialties and subspecialties, and monitor implementation to support meaningful participation.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. As the goal of MIPS core measures is to focus clinician reporting on more relevant measures, we intentionally kept the MIPS core measure inventory smaller. The MIPS core measures we identified are a subset of measures within each MVP that represents care central to the MVP's clinical specialty or medical condition, and in many cases align with previously identified high-priority measures. These core measures represent the specific central care unique to and aligned with the clinical focus of an MVP. We did not prioritize selecting broadly applicable measures as MIPS core measures because they often do not meet these criteria for a core measure. In accordance with section 1848(q)(3) of the Act and as discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule, we focused selection of the MIPS core measures on several factors, including whether the measure is an outcome-based measure, measure collection type availability and the clinician's ability to meet reporting requirements to the extent practicable, measure adoption and current and historic performance rates for each measure, and whether the measure is most reflective of the care that is central to the clinical focus of the selected MVP, represents best practices essential to the MVP's specialty or medical condition, or addresses important areas for improving care.
However, not all MIPS core measures will be applicable to all clinicians reporting an MVP; therefore, we established an attestation process if a clinician does not have a MIPS core measure to report. Additionally, many of the selected MIPS core measures are available for reporting in more than one collection type, allowing clinicians to collect and submit quality measure data in the way that best suits their available health technology and clinical documentation processes. The capturing, reporting, and submission of MIPS core measure data is the same as other quality measures and doesn't require separate workflows. Clinicians can choose the most appropriate MIPS core measure for their scope of care and workflow. For MVPs that represent multiple clinician types, settings, or care scopes, we identified additional MIPS core measures ensuring measure availability for those clinicians who choose to report the MVP. We encourage commenters to reach out to measure developers/stewards to develop new measures that will align with current CMS goals and priorities, and fill identified gaps allowing meaningful and complete assessment of MIPS eligible clinician's performance within MIPS for submission during the annual Call for Measures (
https://mmshub-impl.cms.gov/​sites/​default/​files/​2026-MIPS-Annual-Call-for-Quality-Measures-Fact-Sheet.pdf

Comment:
A commenter supported the MIPS core measures proposal but is concerned that allowing multiple MIPS core measures within an MVP could create variation in reporting and limit meaningful performance comparisons. The commenter also noted this approach might unintentionally exclude sub-specialists whose care is not reflected in the broader MIPS core measures. The commenter asked CMS to monitor the MIPS core measures to ensure they support meaningful performance comparisons and subspecialty engagement. For future policy, the commenter urged CMS to work toward a single MIPS core measure per MVP that is meaningful for all participating specialties and subspecialties.
Response:
We thank the commenter for supporting the MIPS core measure proposals and for the suggestions to refine MIPS core measure implementation as we move forward. MVPs are structured in a manner that would not easily allow for identification of a single MIPS core measure, as while MVPs are more narrowly targeted than traditional MIPS, an individual MVP may also span multiple specialties or areas of care related to the MVP's clinical theme. Therefore, we identified a small subset of measures within each MVP that represents care central to the MVP's intent. Not all MIPS core measures will be applicable to all clinicians reporting an MVP; however, to the extent possible, we considered implementation factors such as collection type and setting/clinician type applicability. The intent of the selected set of MIPS core measures is to give a comparable data point for each of the represented specialties or subspecialties that will allow for improved comparison and monitoring across clinician specialties. We will incorporate this new monitoring opportunity in addition to the monitoring and performance comparisons which we already conduct within MIPS. While some MVPs, due to inventory constraints, include broadly applicable measures to ensure adequate coverage and reporting options for clinicians without a specialty specific measure, it is expected that clinicians that are able to report the specialty-specific MIPS core measures would do so, as appropriate, allowing for comparison across that measure's performance.

The norm will be to ensure appropriate coverage of all clinicians reporting the MVP, leading to a more complete data set of quality performance measures across clinicians reporting an MVP; therefore, multiple measures were selected for each MVP to allow flexibility in clinician choice and reduce the need for attestation. We encourage interested parties to submit potential new measures during the annual Call for Measures that will align with current CMS goals and priorities and fill any identified gaps, particularly for those subspecialties with limited measures, allowing meaningful and complete assessment of MIPS eligible clinicians' performance within MVPs.

Comment:
Many commenters expressed general concerns about the MIPS core measures policy. Of these commenters, a commenter stated a measure should not be designated as a MIPS core measure merely because it appears broadly relevant at the MVP level. The commenter stated that CMS should confirm that the measure: applies to the clinician's actual scope of practice; is reportable by the intended clinician type; has a benchmark with equitable scoring opportunity; can reasonably meet case minimum; and represents a meaningful aspect of care for the designated specialty or subspecialty. Another commenter stated that a quality measure must possess a benchmark to be classified as a MIPS core measure in an MVP.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. In designating core measures, we balanced choosing measures that most closely represent care central to the MVP topic, while ensuring the availability of the measure collection type and applicability of the setting/clinician type for clinicians that choose to report the MVP, in accordance with the factors we proposed for designation of MIPS core measures. We disagree that only measures with benchmarks should be considered, especially given the current ability to report as multi-specialty groups. Many critical quality actions are represented by specialty specific quality measures which may show low adoption as multispecialty groups focus on capturing data for the more broadly applicable measures. Additionally, we believe that as a designated MIPS core measure, there will be an increase in adoption for the selected measures, allowing for meaningful benchmark creation for quality measures that historically didn't meet reporting requirements. We appreciate the commenters' concern regarding reporting requirements and scoring opportunity and will continue to evaluate measure reporting and policies for future proposals, in addition to the 7-point cap removal policy for MIPS core measures finalized in section IV.B.1.b.(3)(c) of this final rule.
Comment:
A few commenters were concerned that the MIPS core measures policy would reduce flexibility and further restrict clinician's ability to select measures that meaningfully reflect their practice. The commenters were further concerned this policy will create a one-size-fits-all model and urged CMS to preserve measure choice, keep core requirements limited, and use broadly applicable measures within physicians' control. A commenter expressed that adding MIPS core measures would add another layer of complexity at a time when CMS is trying to streamline the program and added that physicians should have the flexibility to choose measures that are most relevant to their unique practice. Another commenter stated that MIPS core measures must be clinically relevant, feasible, and applicable across diverse practice settings and requested CMS maintain flexibility when no applicable MIPS core measure exists and regularly reevaluate MIPS core measures to reflect evolving clinical practice. Another commenter stated that surgeons must retain flexibility to select measures relevant to their practices and rather than requiring MIPS core measures, CMS should encourage development of additional measures for specific specialties.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback that this change in policy will modify reporting requirements. We note that clinicians will maintain the flexibility to choose the quality measures they report. The MIPS core measures policy will decrease complexity while also increasing flexibility. Reporting a MIPS core measure replaces the requirement to report an outcome/high priority measure, which may not be always best aligned with the MVP topic. For each MVP, we identified a small subset of measures that represent care central to the MVP's specialty or medical condition to continue to allow for flexibility and clinician choice. For some MVPs, such as the Surgical Care MVP, we determined more than three measures must be selected to reflect the care central to the subspecialties able to report the MVP. Additionally, the policy includes an option for self-attestation when the MIPS core measures are not appropriate or applicable to their scope of care, allowing clinicians to choose an alternate measure that is more relevant. We welcome feedback on all MIPS core measures and encourage commenters to submit this during the annual MVP maintenance review process. We also encourage interested parties to submit potential new measures that will align with current CMS goals and priorities and fill these identified gaps to allow meaningful and complete assessment of MIPS eligible clinician's performance within MIPS during the annual Call for Measures.

QCDR measures require additional resources for reporting and therefore may not be a feasible reporting option for some clinicians. As reporting a MIPS core measure is a criterion for meeting quality performance requirements, all measures need to be publicly available and free to use.

Comment:
Several commenters requested CMS further test the concept of MIPS core measures and urged CMS to delay finalizing MIPS core measures until clinicians have had sufficient time to transition to and gain experience with mandatory MVP reporting. Several commenters requested delaying the MIPS core measures requirement until the CY 2028 MIPS performance period to allow CMS time to refine the MIPS core measure definition and selection process and ensure EHR and registry vendors are ready to support MIPS core measures. Response:
As the MIPS core measures were chosen from quality measures already in MIPS, we do not agree that delaying implementation a year or two would result in meaningful information to change the MIPS core measures policy. Note that although we are finalizing our MIPS core measures policy for the CY 2027 performance period, we are delaying the sunsetting of traditional MIPS by 2 years, which means that MVP-only reporting will begin in the CY 2031 performance/2033 MIPS payment year period instead of the CY 2029 performance period as indicated under section IV.A.3.c. of this final rule.
