Comment:
A commenter stated it is critical that at least one of the MIPS core measures in an MVP be considered in relation to one or more of the cost measures.
Response:
During identification of MIPS core measures, we considered current and historical submission data to guide applicability and decision-making, working to include appropriate and available measures. Currently there are more specialty specific quality measures available, which are needed to cover as many specialties/subspecialties as possible, and there may not be a complimentary episode-based cost measure available. However, as the goal of MIPS core measures is to target performance data for specific quality actions central to the MVP intent, the link to cost is addressed at the MVP level, rather than to individual quality measures.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern for limited core measures available for specific specialties. Commenters stated that MIPS core measures add little value when a specialty already has a small, defined set of measures. A commenter stated the primary purpose of an MVP is to measure specialty-specific quality. The commenter stated that if there is only one MIPS core measure available, it does not help with the adoption of the use of MVPs for MIPS reporting. Another commenter stated that the current core set of measures does not meet CMS' stated goal of identifying measures “most reflective of the care that is unique to each MVP's specialty or medical condition.” Another commenter said that instead of mandating the reporting of MIPS core measures, CMS should focus its efforts on ensuring that each MVP offers a sufficient number of meaningful measures, including QCDR measures, that appropriately reflect the care delivered by the specialty or subspecialty. A commenter recommended that specialties with few available measures should be exempt from the MIPS core measure requirements. CMS should categorize each measure and report scores by category, which would be more meaningful to patients and avoid incomplete comparisons between clinicians.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their comment. In designating MIPS core measures, we balanced alignment of the measure with care central to the MVP topic, while ensuring measure availability for those clinicians who choose to report the MVP. The purpose of MIPS core measures is to capture data that best represents the care unique to the MVP topic, allowing for a targeted set of data that directly compares quality performance for essential care components that patients can readily understand and access for making care provider decisions. While MVPs allow for more meaningful comparisons of performance and connection of quality with cost, varied measure selection for reporting within the MVP leads to varied measure submissions across the MVP, even in MVPs with fewer measures and in cases where new measures are still being developed and may be added to MVPs that have fewer measures in the future. MIPS core measures will provide a more focused performance comparison point across those reporting the MVP. Alignment of MIPS core measures across MVPs was a secondary consideration as appropriate and applicable. MIPS core measures replace the outcome/high priority quality measure requirement while adding flexibility and designating more meaningful measures. Understanding that some clinicians, such as cardiovascular subspecialists, may be unable to report the selected MIPS core measures, we do allow attestation for cases in which a MIPS core measure is not available and applicable. We encourage interested parties to submit potential new measures that will align with current CMS goals and priorities, allowing MIPS eligible clinicians to maximize their potential performance within MIPS during the annual Call for Measures.
Currently, the measures within the MVP are bucketed into clinical groupings, which helps to guide measure reporting choice; however, these also do not always capture all clinicians' individual scope of care. Some MIPS core measures are broadly applicable, seeming to go against the goal of designating measures “most reflective of the care that is unique to each MVP's specialty or medical condition;” however, these are not mutually exclusive as the measure may represent a fundamental aspect of care that is unique and unifying across specialties and clinical care topics, such as shared decision-making and risk communication. Additionally, there are certain administration priorities aligned with such unifying concepts, representing important aspects of care that are widely comparable and an important data point for patients deciding on clinicians.

Given the implementation of the MIPS core measure designation in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule, which identifies a subset of measures that reflect the essential components of care specific to a given specialty, medical condition, or episode of care, we proposed to remove the high priority designation from the MIPS quality measure inventory and the MVP inventory. The new MIPS core measures intend to increase reporting on select quality measures that are most reflective of the care central to a particular specialty, medical condition or episode of care, while providing patients with more comparative clinician performance data. We considered maintaining the high priority designation since many of the new MIPS core measures are high priority measures. However, the high priority designation does not appropriately capture a measure's relevance to a specific clinical specialty, medical condition or episode of care. We identify and designate quality measures that reflect agency-wide priorities as high priority in our programs through a myriad of ways such as using the MIPS high priority definition, developing the Universal Foundation, and implementing the Core Quality Measures Collaborative (CQMC). However, the new MIPS core measure designations specifically represent key quality measures that reflect the measure's relevance to a specific clinical specialty, medical condition or episode of care for clinicians and patients for each MVP and essential best practices to the MVP's clinical topic. The significant overlap in the new MIPS core measures with the MIPS high priority measures means we will still largely capture agency-wide priorities but with a greater emphasis on supporting intended MIPS policy goals of providing robust quality measure data relevant to the scope of care for a specialty or medical condition. Additionally, maintaining the high priority measure designation can add complexity and confusion for clinicians given the overlap of the existing high priority measures and the new MIPS core measures. While we acknowledge the overlap in intended goals for high priority measures and MIPS core measures, we anticipate that the new MIPS core measures, with a selection emphasis on outcome-based measures, will provide a more targeted set of measures, focused on more meaningful improvement in the quality of care related to each MVP specialty or medical condition. Therefore, to implement the new MIPS core measure designation as described in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule, we proposed to remove the high priority designation from the MIPS quality measure and the MVP inventory in Appendices 1 and 3 of this final rule.

83 FR 59765
) at § 414.1330(c)(2), we revised the approach to remove quality measures to include considerations for retaining MIPS quality measures that otherwise meet the criteria for removal, including “whether the MIPS quality measure is designated as high priority or not.” To align with the removal of high priority designation from MIPS quality measures, we will no longer include the use of a high priority measure designation as one of the considerations for retaining a MIPS quality measure. Therefore, we proposed to update the existing quality measure retention consideration at § 414.1330(c)(2)(iv) to state that we will consider whether the quality measure is designated as high priority or not through the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal to remove the high priority designation for quality measures. A commenter added that it should be assumed that all measures remaining would be considered high priority and supported replacing outcome measures with MIPS core measures.

Response:
We thank the commenters for supporting the proposal to remove the high priority measure designation. As we move to a robust, streamlined quality measure inventory, we expect that each measure maintained would meet standards and criteria once associated with high priority measures, essentially resulting in a quality measure inventory that consists of high priority and MIPS core measures.
Comment:
A commenter believes that eliminating the high priority designation does not justify replacing it with a MIPS core measure requirement.
Response:
We thank the commenter for their comment but disagree. The overall goal of MVPs is to create a small, streamlined set of measures that are reflective of the care given. Identifying MIPS core measures allows for continued choice in measure selection while also supporting the goal of capturing comparable data across clinicians for patient use in care decision making. While we acknowledge the overlap in intended goals for high priority measures and MIPS core measures, we anticipate that the new MIPS core measures, with a selection emphasis on outcome-based measures, will provide a more targeted set of measures, focused on more meaningful improvement in the quality of care related to each MVP specialty or medical condition.
Comment:
A few commenters asked CMS to maintain the high priority/outcome designations. A commenter requested maintaining the requirement alongside the core measure designations and allow reporting of either a MIPS core measure or outcome/high priority measure to provide the flexibility needed for subspecialists to report on measures germane to their practice. A commenter believes the three MIPS core measures for its specialty were not a complete representation of the care provided by this specialty and asked for the high priority designation to remain. Another commenter expressed that eliminating these designations would devalue true patient outcome measures and conflict with CMS' goal of clinically relevant, evidence—based performance assessment. Another commenter stated that the high priority designation highlights core quality areas (patient outcomes, care coordination, safety, experience, and appropriate use) that are essential to primary care and expressed concern that removing this designation and its role in measure retention could lead to loss of important primary care measures.
Response:
The importance given to patient outcome measures remains regardless of the high priority designation. Currently, over 50 percent of the outcome and patient experience quality measures are designated as MIPS core measures, allowing for the continued reporting of previously selected measures. However, the distribution of outcome and patient experience quality measures across MVPs and within MVPs isn't consistent, leading to potential reporting inequities and inability to meet requirements, but more importantly, potentially missing key aspects of care unique to clinicians reporting an MVP. MIPS core measures, however, are specifically chosen from the MVP measure set to represent these key aspects of care, as opposed to choosing from a set of measures using a historical designation that does not serve the same purpose. While high priority was a consideration for retaining measures that met removal criteria, many of the other criteria found within

(B) Update for MIPS Core Measure Data Submission Requirements With Self-Attestation
In conjunction with the removal of the high priority designation for MIPS quality measures, and the new designation of MIPS core measures beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, we proposed to remove the current quality measure data submission requirement of one outcome measure (or, if an outcome measure is not available, one high priority measure) for traditional MIPS and MVPs and replace the requirement with a MIPS core measure data submission requirement to emphasize the reporting on the new MIPS core measures. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we stated the requirement to report an outcome measure (or, if an outcome measure is not available, one high priority measure) would no longer be necessary if the MIPS core measure selection policies were finalized, as the goals of that policy would be met by the new MIPS core measure reporting requirement. Specifically, we proposed that MIPS eligible clinicians reporting via traditional MIPS must submit data on at least six measures, including at least one MIPS core measure. Clinicians reporting a specialty measure set in traditional MIPS must report at least six measures and choose an applicable MIPS core measure, if available, within that specialty measure set. If the set contains fewer than six measures or fewer than six measures within the set apply, they must report on each measure that is applicable. Additionally, to be consistent with the existing reporting requirements for clinicians reporting a specialty measure set, as finalized in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77114
), if a specialty measure set does not contain a MIPS core measure, clinicians must still report on at least six measures within the specialty set. If the specialty set does not contain a MIPS core measure and contains fewer than six measures, or fewer than six measures within the set apply, they must report on each measure that is applicable within the specialty measure set. An MVP participant must select and report, if applicable, four quality measures, including at least one MIPS core measure. We noted in the proposed rule that clinicians submitting data for the quality performance category in traditional MIPS reporting would choose an applicable MIPS core measure from the full inventory of available MIPS core measures for the performance period. Clinicians reporting an MVP will choose an applicable MIPS core measure from those available in the selected MVP. Each MVP will include a minimum of three MIPS core measures for a clinician to select from. MVPs that encompass multiple specialties or subspecialties may include more than three MIPS core measures to ensure comprehensive coverage for the variety of clinicians reporting that MVP.
Since the new MIPS core measures are identified to reflect the care most central to a clinician specialty, medical condition, or episode of care within each MVP for clinicians and patients, we anticipated that clinicians can report the new MIPS core measures in the selected MVP. We acknowledged that due to the variety of clinician practices, specialties, and subspecialties reporting each MVP, there may be instances in which a clinician does not have an available and applicable MIPS core measure due to the limited inventory of the new MIPS core measures. If an individual eligible clinician, group, subgroup, or APM Entity does not have an available and applicable MIPS core measure that meets the numerator and denominator criteria as specified in the MIPS quality measure inventory for the applicable performance period, either in traditional MIPS or MVP reporting, we proposed to establish a MIPS core measure self-attestation process. Under this process, the clinician would be required in good faith to attest during the data submission period that there was not an available and applicable MIPS core measure for them to report. The clinician would then be required to choose another measure to report in place of the MIPS core measure. A clinician reporting via traditional MIPS can report any other applicable quality measure in the MIPS quality measure inventory. In MVP reporting, a clinician can report any other quality measure in the selected MVP. There may be instances in which a clinician attested to not having an applicable and available MIPS core measure, but new information or changing circumstances later made it so that the clinician does have an applicable and available MIPS core measure to report. To account for these cases, we would allow a clinician to attest that they do not have an applicable and available MIPS core measure and then submit a MIPS core measure. While we considered requiring clinicians without an available and applicable MIPS core measure to report an outcome or high priority measure, we determined that such a requirement would increase complexity for clinicians and would be unnecessary given that MVPs are already a collection of the key quality measures for a specialty, medical condition, or episode of care. We proposed that we would not penalize a MIPS eligible clinician who provides a self-attestation to not having a MIPS core measure to report. We noted in the proposed rule that we may monitor attestations received for the MIPS core measure requirement and may, in future years, conduct random reviews to verify that there were no available and applicable MIPS core measures for reporting. We refer readers to section IV.B.1.b.(1) of this final rule for details on the scoring policies for MIPS core measures.
For traditional MIPS reporting, we proposed at § 414.1335(a)(1)(i) that beginning in the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians, except as provided in paragraphs (a)(1)(ii) and (a)(1)(iii) of this section, submit data on at least six quality measures, including at least one MIPS core measure. If there is not an available and applicable MIPS core measure, a MIPS eligible clinician must attest to not having an available and applicable MIPS core measure and submit data on a separate MIPS quality measure. If fewer than six measures apply, then the MIPS eligible clinician, group, virtual group, or APM Entity must report on each measure that is applicable.
Additionally, we proposed at § 414.1335(a)(1)(ii) that beginning in the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, except as provided in paragraph (a)(1)(iii) of this section, a MIPS eligible clinician that reports on a specialty or subspecialty measure set, as designated in the MIPS final list of quality measures established by CMS through rulemaking, must submit data on at least six measures within that set, including at least one MIPS core measure. If there is not an available and applicable MIPS core measure, a MIPS eligible clinician must attest to not having an available and applicable MIPS core measure and submit data on a separate MIPS quality measure within that set. If the set contains fewer than six measures or if fewer than six measures within the set apply to the MIPS eligible clinician, report on each measure that is applicable.
For MVP reporting, we proposed at § 414.1365(c)(1) that, beginning in the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS
(

payment year, except as provided in paragraphs (c)(1)(i) and (c)(1)(ii) of this section, an MVP participant must select and report, if applicable, four quality measures, including one MIPS core measure available in the MVP, excluding the population health measure required under paragraph (c)(4)(ii). If there is not an available and applicable MIPS core measure, an MVP participant must attest to not having an available and applicable MIPS core measure and submit data on a separate MIPS quality measure within the MVP.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal to remove the requirement to report one outcome or high priority measure for traditional MIPS and MVP reporting. A commenter indicated this requirement has been problematic in mandatory MVPs where physicians have fewer measures to choose from and may be unable to identify a relevant outcome or high priority measure. A commenter expressed that replacing the outcome measure requirement with MIPS core measures will solve the issues with established quality measures not receiving benchmarks due to low participation, and clinicians unwilling to elect administrative claims measures (outside of the population health measures) that are available under certain MVPs because they are outcome measures. Another commenter agreed that many clinicians struggle to report outcome measures. Another commenter stated that removing the outcome measure requirement allows clinicians more flexibility to select measures relevant to their practice.
Response:
We thank the commenters for supporting the proposal to remove the requirement to report on one outcome or high priority measure for traditional MIPS and MVP reporting.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the attestation process for clinicians who have no applicable MIPS core measure to report. A commenter expressed that those with limited measures will also need to use eligible measure applicability (EMA) evaluation. The commenter recommended automatically linking attestation of no MIPS core measure with EMA evaluation to avoid separate processes. Another commenter strongly supported including a straightforward, transparent self-attestation process for physicians who cannot identify an applicable MIPS core measure, emphasizing that it should not create scoring disadvantages or added administrative burden. Another commenter urged CMS to expand flexibility in the attestation process, reduce administrative burden, closely monitor impacts before increasing reliance on MIPS core measures, and use high attestation rates to identify and fix gaps in the MIPS core measure set. Another commenter encouraged CMS to develop adequate guidance on the self-attestation and exemption processes associated with MIPS core measure reporting.
Response:
We thank the commenters for supporting the proposed attestation process. We appreciate the commenters' concerns and request for further flexibilities to requirements, such as linking EMA evaluation with the MIPS core measure attestation process or expanding the use of an attestation process for clinicians who are not able to meet program requirements and will continue to monitor the use of the MIPS core measure attestation pathway, MVP measure reporting trends, and interested parties' feedback to determine potential future refinements as we move toward the sunsetting of traditional MIPS. The self-attestation process is completed at the time of submission and is intended to replace the more involved processes associated with current outcome/high priority reporting requirements.
Comment:
A commenter requested CMS clarify whether an alternative measure selected, when there is not an available and applicable MIPS core measure, must come from the same MVP, from the broader MIPS quality inventory, or meet specific criteria such as eCQM availability, specialty relevance, denominator applicability, or alignment with the clinician's patient population. Another commenter requested that CMS finalize the MIPS core measure requirement with an exception of permitting an outcome measure of any collection type to satisfy the requirement within an MVP.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their suggestions. Clinicians who are unable to report one of the designated MIPS core measures may attest that an applicable core measure was not available to them and then select any other quality measure included within the MVP being reported. In selecting an alternative measure to meet the MIPS core measures requirement, the clinician would need to meet all reporting requirements, and it would be expected that the alternative measure be meaningful to their scope of care. We decline to allow an exception to report any outcome measure. Broadening the requirement to include additional outcome measures than originally identified would be counterintuitive to the goal of establishing a set of unified key quality measures.
Comment:
A few commenters requested clarification on the definition of “available and applicable” MIPS core measures. A commenter requested CMS define “applicable” for purposes of the MIPS core measure self-attestation so that a clinician whose relevant measures are all QCDR outcome measures may attest that no applicable MIPS core measure exists and report an outcome measure in its place. Another commenter requested CMS confirm in sub-regulatory guidance how “no applicable MIPS core measure” will be determined and audited for each MVP and specialty measure set.
Response:
Clinicians who are unable to report one of the designated MIPS core measures may attest that an applicable MIPS core measure was not available to them and then may select any other quality measure included within the MVP or specialty measure set being reported. There are no specific requirements for this alternative measure beyond current quality measure reporting requirements. As stated in the proposed rule clinicians, in good faith, can attest that they do not have a measure that is available or applicable to them. Additionally, as noted in the proposed rule, we may, in future years, conduct random reviews to verify that there were no available and applicable MIPS core measures for reporting. Measures that are available and applicable would be determined by the alignment of the measure with the clinician's case-mix, scope of care, and ability to implement. See section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule for details on the MIPS core measurement requirement for traditional MIPS and MVP reporting.
Comment:
A commenter opposed replacing the outcome/high priority measure requirement with a new MIPS core measure requirement. The commenter stated that practices have already built clinical workflows and EHR reporting modules around the outcome/high priority framework. Adding an entirely new structural requirement introduces administrative confusion and software re-engineering costs without providing a clear benefit to clinical quality or patient outcomes. Another commenter expressed concerned that mandatory MIPS core measure data submission will increase administrative burden and program volatility, contradicting CMS' goal of simplifying MIPS. The commenter urged CMS to avoid rigid requirements and prioritize stability, flexibility, and specialty—specific relevance in MIPS reporting. A commenter stated that
(
printed page 71537)
some MVPs do not have enough eCQMs to support full electronic measure submission, much less MIPS core measure reporting. Requiring CQMs or QCDR measures would create significant burden for organizations that currently report only eCQMs.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. The overall goal of MVPs is to create a small, streamlined set of measures that are reflective of the care given. Identifying MIPS core measures allows for continued choice in measure selection while also supporting the goal of capturing comparable data across clinicians for patient use in care decision making. We appreciate the feedback that this change in policy will modify reporting requirements, potentially requiring updates in systems and workflows. However, as the MIPS quality measure inventory is refined annually, this is an inherent circumstance required each year as applicable. Overall, the MIPS core measures policy will decrease complexity while also increasing flexibility. Reporting a MIPS core measure replaces the requirement to report an outcome/high priority measure, which is not always best aligned with the MVP topic. We recognize that the availability and applicability of MIPS core measures may vary, such as when no eCQM MIPS core measures are available in an MVP, which is why we are allowing for self-attestation in these circumstances. We are not requiring a clinician to report a MIPS core measure that is not available or applicable to the clinician. Clinicians who are unable to report one of the designated MIPS core measures may attest that an applicable MIPS core measure was not available to them and then select any other quality measure included within the MVP being reported. Additionally, we will continue to monitor the use of the MIPS core measure attestation pathway, MVP measure reporting trends, and feedback to determine potential future refinements as we move toward the sunsetting of traditional MIPS in the CY 2031 performance period/2033 MIPS payment year as indicated under section IV.A.3.c. of this final rule.

(C) Exempting Small Practices From MIPS Core Measure Reporting Requirement
We recognized that clinicians in small practices often face challenges in successfully participating in MIPS and MVP reporting due to limited financial, administrative, and health IT resources, when compared to medium and large practices. Historically, we have received feedback from small practices expressing concerns that meeting the MIPS reporting requirements can be challenging due to the limited resources of small practices, and we have implemented policies in MIPS to support clinicians in small practices to address these concerns. For example, in the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65412
), we finalized at § 414.1365(c)(1)(i) that the requirement to report four quality measures in an MVP does not apply to small practice clinicians reporting under the Medicare Part B claims collection type when the selected MVP contains fewer than four Medicare Part B claims-based quality measures. In addition, in MVPs, small practices reporting via Medicare Part B claims measures are currently exempt from the outcome/high priority reporting requirement if the MVP does not contain at least four Medicare Part B claims measures.
We considered several policy options for small practices with respect to reporting MIPS core measures. Initially, we considered whether to align the reporting requirements for small practices with the new MIPS core measure reporting requirements for clinicians in medium and large practices participating in traditional MIPS and MVP reporting. However, we anticipate that clinicians in small practices may continue to experience challenges with meeting the proposed MIPS core measure reporting requirement due to limited resources, difficulty reaching the case minimum requirement, and the limited inventory of MIPS core measures, particularly the limited inventory of new MIPS core measures available via the Medicare Part B claims collection type, which is only available to small practices. While we also considered exempting small practices from the proposed MIPS core measure reporting requirement only if the selected MVP does not contain at least one MIPS core measure available via the Medicare Part B claims collection type, we remained concerned that such a policy will further limit measure choice for clinicians in small practices and could lead to confusion and unfairness if some MVPs contained Medicare Part B claims MIPS core
(
printed page 71538)
measures and other MVPs did not. In recognition of these ongoing challenges, and to streamline reporting requirements for small practices while continuing to support clinicians in small practices, we wanted to provide flexibilities for clinicians in small practices to successfully report the MIPS quality performance category. Therefore, in both traditional MIPS and MVP reporting, we proposed that small practices, as defined under § 414.1305, be exempt from the MIPS core measure data submission requirement. Under this provision, clinicians in small practices will continue to report six quality measures for traditional MIPS or four quality measures as currently required for MVPs. It is important to note that while small practices are not required to report a MIPS core measure, they may choose to do so on a voluntary basis.
Specifically, we proposed at § 414.1335(a)(1)(iii) that beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians in small practices are not required to submit at least one MIPS core measure or attest to not having an available and applicable MIPS core measure. MIPS eligible clinicians in small practices must submit data on at least six measures, if applicable. Additionally, we proposed at § 414.1365(c)(1)(ii) that beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, an MVP participant that meets the requirements of a small practice is not required to submit at least one MIPS core measure or attest to not having an available and applicable MIPS core measure. Except as provided in paragraph (c)(1)(i) of this section, an MVP participant that meets the requirements of a small practice must select and report, if applicable, at least four quality measures included in the MVP, excluding the population health measure required under paragraph (c)(4)(ii) of this section.

(e) Addition of New Quality Measures
(i) Pre-Rulemaking Process
Prior to introducing a new MIPS quality measure in a proposed rule, we received public input on measures through the pre-rulemaking process (referred to as the Pre-Rulemaking Measure Review (PRMR)) established in accordance with section 1890A of the Act. Although section 1848(q)(2)(D)(viii) of the Act provides that the pre-rulemaking process under section 1890A of the Act is not required to apply to the selection of MIPS quality measures, we have found that the pre-rulemaking process provides a comprehensive review of measures from multi-interested party workgroups and have accordingly elected for such measures to be reviewed utilizing the PRMR process (
87 FR 70048
). Under the established PRMR process (additional information regarding the PRMR process is available at
https://p4qm.org/​PRMR
), CMS has contracted with a Consensus-Based Entity (CBE), which is responsible for convening a multi-interested party panel comprised of clinicians, patients, measure experts, and health information technology specialists to provide input on measures CMS is considering for use in Medicare.
The PRMR process begins with CMS' publication of measures under consideration for use in Medicare (the Measures Under Consideration (MUC) List). Each measure on the MUC List is reviewed by one of several committees convened by the CBE for the purpose of providing multi-interested party input to the Secretary. The PRMR process includes opportunities for public comments through a 21-day public comment period, as well as public listening sessions. The CBE posts the compiled comments and listening session inputs received during the public comment period and the listening sessions within 5 days of the close of the public comment period. More details regarding the PRMR process may be found in the PQM
(
printed page 71541)
Guidebook of Policies and Procedures for Pre-Rulemaking Measure Review and Measure Set Review (available at
https://p4qm.org/​sites/​default/​files/​2025-07/​OP2-PRMR-MSR-Final-Multi-Stakeholder-Group-Guidebook-of-Policies-and-Procedures-508_​1.pdf
).
Per the PQM Guidebook, the final vote of the multi-interested party committee convened by the CBE may result in the following disposition of a measure: The committee recommends that this measure be added to the CMS program or the committee does not recommend that this measure be added to the CMS program. A “does not recommend” voting result signals continued disagreement among the committee despite being presented with perspectives from public comments and committee member feedback and discussion and highlights the multi-faceted assessments of quality measures. There may be cases in which the CBE does not recommend a measure to move forward to the rulemaking process and eventual implementation but we go forth with proposing a measure. We note that section 1848(q)(2)(D)(iii)(v)(III) of the Act does not preclude the Secretary from proposing and implementing measures that are not endorsed by a CBE as long as the measure is evidence-based.

It is not feasible to implement the measure specifications.
A measure steward is no longer able to maintain the cost measure.

The availability of a more applicable measure, including a measure that applies across settings, applies across populations, or is more proximal in time to desired patient outcomes for the particular topic.

(3) Improvement Activities Performance Category
(a) Background
Section 1848(q)(2)(A)(iii) of the Act includes clinical practice improvement activities as a performance category under MIPS. We refer to this performance category as the improvement activities performance category. As required by section 1848(q)(2) and (5) of the Act, the four performance categories of MIPS are used in determining the MIPS final score for each MIPS eligible clinician. In general, MIPS eligible clinicians are evaluated under all four of the MIPS performance categories, including the improvement activities performance category.
Section 1848(q)(2)(C)(v)(III) defines the term “clinical practice improvement activities” as activities that relevant eligible professional organizations and other relevant interested parties identify as improving clinical practice or care delivery and that the Secretary determines, when effectively executed, is likely to result in improved outcomes.
Section 1848(q)(2)(B)(iii) of the Act provides that, for the improvement activities category, the Secretary shall specify subcategories of clinical practice improvement activities, including at least six subcategories as specified in section 1848(q)(2)(B)(iii)(I) through (VI) of the Act. These statutorily enumerated subcategories are: (1) expanded practice access (such as same day appointments for urgent needs and afterhours access to clinician advice); (2) population management (such as monitoring health conditions of individuals to provide timely health care interventions or participation in a qualified clinical data registry); (3) care coordination (such as timely communication of test results, timely exchange of clinical information to patients and other providers, and use of remote monitoring or telehealth); (4) beneficiary engagement (such as the establishment of care plans for individuals with complex care needs, beneficiary self-management assessment and training, and using shared decision-making mechanisms); (5) patient safety and practice assessment (such as through use of clinical or surgical checklists and practice assessments related to maintaining certification); and (6) participation in an alternative payment model, as defined in section 1833(z)(3)(C) of the Act (section 1848(q)(2)(B)(iii)(I) through (VI) of the Act).

(iii) Adopting New Improvement Activities
We are finalizing our proposal to add six new improvement activities beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. We are finalizing our proposal that IA_CC_20 (Use of Data to Improve Practice Workflows) and IA_CC_21 (Understand and Improve Diagnostic Performance) be included in the Care Coordination subcategory. We propose that IA_AHW_2 (Systematic Screening and Intervention for Nutrition and other Health-Impacting, Non-Clinical Issues), IA_AHW_3 (Advance Care Planning Conversations to Support Patient Wellness and Care Preferences), IA_AHW_4 (Clinician Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Improve Patient Care), and IA_AHW_5 (Lifestyle Approaches to Diabetes Remediation) would be included in the Advancing Health and Wellness subcategory.
The first new improvement activity, IA_CC_20, titled “Use of Data to Improve Practice Workflows,” would allow MIPS-eligible clinicians to improve integration of evidence-based guidelines into care by developing and refining clinical pathways and workflows. If gaps are identified through data, clinicians will update and implement changes, monitor adoption and outcomes, and reassess performance regularly.
The second new improvement activity, IA_CC_21, titled “Understand and Improve Diagnostic Performance,” supports clinicians in improving patient safety by reducing diagnostic safety events and miscommunication through standardized processes for tracking discrepancies, near-misses, and data accuracy. If issues are identified, teams would conduct root-cause analyses, implement corrective actions such as workflow changes or training, and monitor performance regularly to ensure improvement.
The third new improvement activity, IA_AHW_2, titled “Systematic Screening and Intervention for Nutrition and other Health-Impacting, Non-Clinical Issues,” would allow MIPS-eligible clinicians to implement standardized screening tools for nutrition, housing, transportation, and financial strain within clinical workflows. If needs are identified, clinicians would initiate referrals to appropriate community resources, track follow-up and resolution, and reassess screening processes and outcomes regularly to improve effectiveness. The fourth new improvement activity, IA_AHW_3, titled “Advance Care Planning Conversations to Support Patient Wellness and Care Preferences,” will allow MIPS-eligible clinicians to engage patients and caregivers in advance care planning and end-of-life discussions using structured communication tools while documenting goals of care, symptom management, and patient priorities. If care preferences or needs change, clinicians will update care preferences, coordinate across specialties, and reassess regularly to ensure alignment with the patient's goals and clinical status.
The fifth new activity, IA_AHW_4, titled “Clinician Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Improve Patient Care,” would allow MIPS-eligible clinicians to implement and participate in organizational initiatives that improve patient care through the responsible and transparent use of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical and operational workflows. Clinicians will establish policies for evaluating and monitoring AI tools or participate in
(
printed page 71546)
developing and refining AI-enabled resources, such as predictive analytics, clinical decision support, and risk-stratification models, to improve patient outcomes, care-team efficiency, and population health management. Examples may include using AI tools to summarize medical literature for clinical decision-making, assist with documentation (
e.g.,
AI-generated notes with clinician review), support population health management by identifying care gaps, determine patient eligibility for clinical trials, or generate draft responses to patient questions for clinician review.
The sixth new activity, IA_AHW_5, titled “Lifestyle Approaches to Diabetes Remediation,” engages clinicians in delivering structured, evidence-based lifestyle interventions for diabetes management, addressing nutrition, physical activity, sleep, stress, and behavior change through programs such as; Lifestyle Empowerment Approach for Diabetes Remission (LEADR) or the Diabetes Self-Management Education and Support (DSMES). Clinicians provide education and coaching, track patient progress, and adjust interventions as needed to improve health outcomes.

(4) MIPS Promoting Interoperability Performance Category
(a) Background
Section 1848(q)(2)(A)(iv) of the Act includes the meaningful use of certified electronic health record (EHR) technology (CEHRT) as a performance category under MIPS. We refer to this performance category as the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category (formerly the advancing care information performance category).
Section 1848(q)(2)(B)(iv) of the Act provides that the requirements established under section 1848(o)(2) of the Act for determining whether a MIPS eligible clinician is a meaningful EHR user also applies to our assessment of a MIPS eligible clinician's performance on measures and activities with respect to the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Section 1848(o)(2)(D) of the Act generally provides that the requirements for being a meaningful EHR user under section 1848(o)(2) of the Act continue to apply for purposes of MIPS.
Under section 1848(o)(2)(A) of the Act, a MIPS eligible clinician must meet three requirements related to the meaningful use of CEHRT during a performance period for a MIPS payment year. Specifically, under section 1848(o)(2)(A) of the Act, the MIPS eligible clinician must: (1) demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Secretary the use of CEHRT in a meaningful manner, which shall include the use of electronic prescribing as determined to be appropriate by the Secretary; (2) demonstrate to the satisfaction of the Secretary that their CEHRT is connected in a manner that provides, in accordance with law and standards applicable to the exchange of information, for electronic exchange of health information to improve the quality of care, such as promoting care coordination, and demonstrates (through a process specified by the Secretary), that they have not knowingly and willfully taken action (such as to disable functionality) to limit or restrict the compatibility or interoperability of the CEHRT; and (3) use CEHRT to submit information on clinical quality measures and such other measures as selected by the Secretary.

(b) Modifying the Definition of Certified Electronic Health Record Technology in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability Performance Category
(i) Background
In accordance with § 414.1375(b)(1), to earn a performance category score for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, a MIPS eligible clinician must be a meaningful EHR user for MIPS and use CEHRT during the performance period, as both terms are defined in § 414.1305. In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, we discussed previously finalized modifications related to the definition of CEHRT for the Quality Payment Program, including for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category at § 414.1305 (
89 FR 98414
and
98415
). Currently, we define CEHRT, for purposes of MIPS, as EHR technology (which could include multiple technologies) certified under the Office of National Coordinator for Health Information Technology's (ONC) Health Information Technology (IT) Certification Program that meets the Base EHR definition at
45 CFR 170.102
and certified as meeting additional ONC health IT certification criteria as adopted and updated in
45 CFR 170.315
as enumerated in paragraph (2)(i) of the definition of CEHRT at § 414.1305, including as necessary to report on applicable measures specified for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, Table C-G 8 (

and
44198
) outlined the measures for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year and the associated ONC health IT certification criteria set forth at
45 CFR 170.315
impacting the definition of CEHRT, as applicable.

(ii) Modifying the Definition of Certified Electronic Health Record Technology in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability Performance Category
Beginning with the CY 2019 performance period and subsequent performance periods, the definition of CEHRT for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category in § 414.1305 requires the use of EHR technology certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program that meets the 2015 Edition Base EHR definition or subsequent Base EHR definition (as defined at

We requested public comment on the proposal to modify the definition of CEHRT.
We received public comment on the proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposal to modify the definition of CEHRT in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category to align with the applicable ONC health IT certification criteria proposed for removal and revisions in the HTI-5 proposed rule. Several of such commenters supported that the modifications to the definition of CEHRT would ensure consistency and alignment between agencies. A few commenters supported that these modifications would remove outdated or duplicative requirements when functionalities have become embedded in the health IT infrastructure. A commenter indicated that streamlining the definition of CEHRT can reduce administrative burden while allowing CMS and ONC to focus certification requirements on capabilities that meaningfully advance interoperability and patient care.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters.
Comment:
Several commenters did not support the proposal to modify the definition of CEHRT in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category to align with the applicable ONC health IT certification criteria that are proposed to be removed and revised in the HTI-5 proposed rule. A few commenters did not support the proposal to remove the references in the definition of CEHRT to the health IT certification criteria for “automated numerator recording” at
45 CFR 170.315(g)(1)
and “automated measure calculation” at
45 CFR 170.315(g)
(2) from the definition of CEHRT. A few commenters opposed removing such health IT certification criteria because CMS still requires measures (such as “Provide Patients Electronic Access”) that depend on the capabilities associated with the health IT certification criteria. A few commenters stated that removal of these criteria without a clearly defined plan for measure calculation may introduce inconsistency, data errors, inaccurate scores, cost and administrative burden, and increased audit risk for MIPS eligible clinicians, particularly smaller and less resourced practices. A commenter requested that CMS coordinate closely with ONC to develop standardized calculation guidance, updated specifications, and a cohesive transition strategy. A commenter recommended that if CMS were to finalize removal of such health IT certification criteria, CMS should also remove the corresponding mandatory reporting requirements for MIPS eligible clinicians. Another commenter recommended that CMS should commit to not establishing future measures requiring numerator and denominator data.
Response:
Health IT developers seeking to support customers participating in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category will still need to support reporting of numerators and denominators for certain measures, including the Electronic Prescribing measure and Providing Patients Electronic Access to Their Health Information measure. However, ONC has stated that removing the health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(g)(1)
and
45 CFR 170.315(g)(2)
would reduce administrative burden for health IT developers associated with testing and certifying such functionality without impacting reporting requirements for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Thus, we do not agree with the concerns from commenters regarding potential burden from CMS continuing to require measures that require the capabilities associated with the “automated numerator recording” and “automated measure calculation” certification criteria.
In regard to concerns from commenters pertaining to calculation errors and accountability, we note that the proposed revisions to the definition of CEHRT do not affect current functionality; we have not proposed changes to measures with numerator and denominator calculations that would prompt configuration changes. Therefore, we recommend that MIPS eligible clinicians work closely with their vendors to ensure that current functionality is retained. Also, we note that MIPS eligible clinicians already have a responsibility to ensure the accuracy of their reported values. Using EHR technology certified to particular ONC health IT certification criteria is not sufficient to meet the responsibility to ensure accuracy of reported values due to the risk of local configuration errors.
Additionally, we note that while this functionality originally helped to ensure standardized approaches to reporting, health IT developers have gained time and experience with measures under the program since the certification criteria in §  170.315(g)(1) and §  170.315(g)(2) were added to the definition of CEHRT. We believe that health IT developers will continue to ensure that patients or actions included in a measure's numerator are recorded in a fashion that supports accurate calculation to meet CMS requirements without needing to
(
printed page 71556)
certify their health IT products to §  170.315(g)(1) or §  170.315(g)(2). MIPS eligible clinicians may continue to use a separate, non-certified system such as when supported by a qualified registry, a QCDR, or other third-party intermediary to calculate numerators and denominators and to generate reports on the measures. We will continue to work closely with ONC to ensure consistency in specifications and accuracy in reporting methodologies, and we intend to include details in this respect in future measure specification documents.
Lastly, we do not agree with commenters requesting CMS to remove measures that require numerator and denominator data or limit the addition of such measures in the future given that such measures assess important aspects of interoperability.
Comment:

(c) Removing ONC Direct Review and ONC-Authorized Certification Bodies (ACB) Surveillance Attestations
(i) Background
In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule, we finalized policies to support MIPS eligible clinicians in ONC health IT surveillance and direct review activities through requiring two attestations, specifically, the ONC Direct Review attestation and the ONC-Authorized Certification Bodies (ACB) Surveillance attestation (
81 FR 77019
through
77028
). The purpose of ONC surveillance and direct review is to provide greater assurance that health IT meets certification requirements not only in a controlled testing environment, but also when used by health care providers in actual production environments (
80 FR 62707
). When such attestations were finalized as requirements for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category (formerly the advancing care information performance category) in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule, we intended for the attestations to complement and strengthen recent updates to ONC's ability to perform surveillance and direct review activities.
Specifically, in October 2015, ONC finalized the 2015 Edition Health Information Technology (Health IT) Certification Criteria, 2015 Edition Base Electronic Health Record (EHR) Definition, and ONC Health IT Certification Program Modifications final rule, which added requirements for ONC-ACBs to conduct more frequent and more rigorous surveillance of certified technology and capabilities in the field (
80 FR 62707
). Additionally, in October 2016, ONC published the ONC Health IT Certification Program: Enhanced Oversight and Accountability final rule, which established regulatory processes to facilitate ONC's direct review and evaluation of the performance of certified health IT in certain circumstances (
81 FR 72406
through
72407
). In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule, we determined that surveillance and direct review activities provided greater assurance to health care providers that their certified EHR technology would perform in a manner that meets their expectations, but that such surveillance and direct review would not be effective unless health care providers cooperated with such activities, including by granting access to and assisting ONC-ACBs and ONC to observe the performance of production systems (
81 FR 77020
).
In § 414.1375(b)(3)(i)(A), we require an attestation that acknowledges the requirement to cooperate in good faith with ONC direct review of his or her health IT certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program if a request to assist in ONC direct review is received. A MIPS eligible clinician must attest that he or she, if requested, cooperated in good faith with ONC direct review of his or her health IT certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program as authorized by
45 CFR part 170, subpart E
, to the extent that such technology meets (or can be used to meet) the definition of CEHRT, including by permitting timely access to such technology and demonstrating its capabilities as implemented and used by the MIPS eligible clinician in the field. Also, we specified at § 414.1375(b)(3)(i)(B) an optional attestation that acknowledges the option to cooperate in good faith with ONC-ACB surveillance of his or her health IT certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program if a request to assist in ONC-ACB surveillance is received. A MIPS eligible clinician may attest that he or she, if requested, cooperated in good faith with ONC-ACB surveillance of his or her health IT certified under the ONC Health IT Certification Program as authorized by
45 CFR part 170, subpart E
, to the extent that such technology meets (or can be used to meet) the definition of CEHRT, including by permitting timely access to such technology and demonstrating its capabilities as implemented and used by the MIPS eligible clinician in the field.
The ONC Direct Review attestation is a required element of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Submitting a “Yes” response is the only means to fulfill the requirement of the attestation. If a MIPS eligible clinician submits a “No” response or does not submit any attestation for the ONC Direct Review attestation, the MIPS eligible clinician will receive a score of zero for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. The ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation is optional. A MIPS eligible clinician can submit a “Yes” or “No” response or not submit any attestation for the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation, which would not impact a MIPS eligible clinician's score for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we referred readers to the discussion regarding the scoring implications for the proposal to remove the required ONC Direct Review attestation and optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation (
91 FR 44191
).
(ii) Removing the ONC Direct Review and ONC-ACB Surveillance Attestations Beginning With the CY 2026 Performance Period/2028 MIPS Payment Year
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed to remove the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation in § 414.1375(b)(3)(i)(A) and (B), respectively, beginning with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year to reduce administrative burden (
91 FR 44172
). For the CY 2026 performance period, we noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that MIPS eligible clinicians would not be reporting on such attestations until the applicable submission period, which starts on January 1, 2027 (
91 FR 44172
). Given that the two attestations are reported during the applicable submission period, we determined that it would be feasible for CMS to implement and operationalize such modifications to the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category requirements prior to the start of the submission period associated with the CY 2026 performance period. As noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we continue to recognize the importance of ONC direct review and ONC-ACB surveillance activities and consider such mechanisms important for mitigating issues with health IT products that may pose serious risks to public health or safety, and we continue to collaborate with ONC to support the ONC Health IT Certification Program (
91 FR 44172
). As stated in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77020
), efforts to strengthen surveillance and direct review of certified health IT are critical to the success of HHS programs and initiatives that require the use of certified health IT to improve health care quality and the efficient delivery of care. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we noted that we do not anticipate a change in commitment from ONC and the ONC-ACBs toward such goals (
91 FR 44172
).
While ONC-ACB surveillance and ONC direct review activities remain important to being a user of certified health IT, we no longer consider the administrative step of attesting to cooperating and/or participating in such activities to be necessary. Since 2016 (1 year prior to the enactment of MACRA, in which the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category replaced the Medicare EHR Incentive
(
printed page 71559)
Program for eligible professionals), the ONC-ACB surveillance and ONC direct review activities and processes have become known to MIPS eligible clinicians and as a result, the value of participation has become evident without dependence on an ongoing need to conduct annual attestations. Therefore, the administrative burden associated with such attestations outweighs their value compared to when they were originally adopted.
The proposal to remove the required ONC Direct Review attestation and optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation aligns with the goals of reducing administrative burden while simultaneously focusing on high-value, outcome-oriented measures. Specifically, the removal of such attestations from the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category requirements provides an opportunity to reduce the number of discrete manual steps and reporting fields required for successful adherence to reporting requirements without diminishing the integrity or central goals of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Although we proposed to remove such attestations, we strongly encouraged MIPS eligible clinicians to continue participating in the surveillance and direct review processes when assistance is requested by ONC or an ONC-ACB. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we noted that CMS would continue to support surveillance and direct review activities, as appropriate (
91 FR 44172
).
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed to amend § 414.1375(b)(3)(i) by modifying the requirements to include a specific allotted timeframe (CY 2017 performance period/2019 MIPS payment year through CY 2025 performance period/2027 MIPS payment year) for requiring the reporting of attestations pertaining to the ONC Direct Review attestation and ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation (
91 FR 44172
). Specifically, we proposed to amend § 414.1375(b)(3)(i) as follows: “Supporting providers with the performance of CEHRT (SPPC). To engage in activities related to supporting providers with the performance of CEHRT beginning with the 2019 MIPS payment year through the 2027 MIPS payment year, the MIPS eligible clinician—. . .” We proposed to remove the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation beginning with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year to reduce burden. Additionally, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44172
) we noted that if the proposal to remove the ONC Direct Review attestation and ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation is finalized as proposed, for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians would not, in the case of the ONC Direct Review attestation, be required to report on such attestation, and in the case of the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation, have the option of reporting on such attestation during the applicable submission period (January 1, 2027, through March 1, 2027). We noted that the removal of such attestations would not affect a MIPS eligible clinician's score for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year, respectively. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44172
), we noted that the proposals to remove the ONC Direct Review attestation and optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation align with the same policies for the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program as proposed in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule (
91 FR 19621
through
19622
).
We requested public comment on this proposal.
We received public comment on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposal to remove the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation beginning with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year. Many of these commenters suggested that removal of these attestations would reduce burden and eliminate measures of limited value, and a few commenters noted that this reduced burden will allow more time and resources for MIPS eligible clinicians to dedicate to patient care and meaningful interoperability efforts. A commenter noted that this removal would align with the same finalized policy in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters.
Comment:
A few commenters provided recommendations about the removal of the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation beginning with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year. A few commenters recommended CMS maintain strong interoperability oversight, encourage voluntary cooperation with ONC review activities, give vendors time to update scoring tools, and clarify how third-party intermediaries should handle attestations already collected for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year without requiring retroactive changes.
Response:
We will continue to work with ONC to support direct review and surveillance activities. Please note that although we proposed to remove these attestations, we strongly encourage MIPS eligible clinicians to continue participating in these activities when requested. We recognize that MIPS eligible clinicians may have already been preparing to submit data for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year, which previously included the submission of an attestation for the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation. Also, we recognize that the proposal to removal the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year conflicts with the previously established policy that required MIPS eligible clinicians to submit an attestation for the required ONC Direct Review attestation and when applicable, the submission of an attestation for the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation. However, we believe that the removal of the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation starting with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year reduces the requirements and burden under MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. To facilitate understanding and minimize potential confusion regarding the requirements for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year, we intend to update the CY 2026 MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, disseminate a listserv announcing the reduction in requirements, and implement a technical function in the Quality Payment Program system alerting submitters that attestations pertaining to the ONC Direct Review attestation and ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation cannot be included in a submitted file for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year if the submission includes such attestations.
As finalized, these attestations would no longer be required for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year. We believe that the removal of the ONC Direct Review attestation and ONC-ACB Surveillance
(
printed page 71560)
attestation would not cause any harm or create undue burden for MIPS eligible clinicians who have already prepared for the submission of such attestations or already collected data for such attestations for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year. To prepare the submission file for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year that will be submitted to meet the reporting requirements, the file will need to exclude the ONC Direct Review attestation and ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation; otherwise, an alert will be prompted by the Quality Payment Program system indicating that a file submission cannot include the ONC Direct Review attestation and the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation, in which the file will need to be resubmitted without such attestations. For MIPS eligible clinicians who manually report data in the Quality Payment Program System, they will not be able to submit a response for the ONC Direct Review attestation or the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation given that the Quality Payment Program system will not include options to select the ONC Direct Review attestation or the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation.
Comment:
A commenter, while noting their support for removal, also shared their belief that removal will not meaningfully reduce compliance obligations and would require updating infrastructure to align with updated requirements.
Response:
CMS acknowledges there is burden in meeting these reporting requirements, and as a result, CMS decided to remove the burden associated with the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category measures. However, we recognize that some MIPS eligible clinicians may have already prepared for the submission of such attestations or already collected data for such attestations. To prepare the submission file for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year that will be submitted to meet the reporting requirements, the file will need to exclude the ONC Direct Review attestation and ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation; otherwise, an alert will be prompted by the Quality Payment Program system indicating that a file submission cannot include the ONC Direct Review attestation and the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation, in which the file will need to be resubmitted without such attestations. For MIPS eligible clinicians who manually report data in the Quality Payment Program System, they will not be able to submit a response for the ONC Direct Review attestation or the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation given that the Quality Payment Program system will not include options to select the ONC Direct Review attestation or the ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation.
Comment:
A commenter noted their support for the proposed removal of the ONC Direct Review and ONC-ACB Surveillance attestations but requested that CMS state the effective date for removal of the attestations, including identifying both the performance period affected and the submission period in which the change takes effect.
Response:
We appreciate the support from the commenter. The data submission period for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year is January 1, 2027, through March 31, 2027.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to remove the required ONC Direct Review attestation and the optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation in § 414.1375(b)(3)(i)(A) and (B), respectively, beginning with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year. We note that the finalized, as proposed, policy to remove the ONC Direct Review attestation and optional ONC-ACB Surveillance attestation aligns with the same finalized, as proposed, policy for the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program as proposed in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS final rule (
