However, as discussed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44172
through
44174
), we considered the ongoing applicability of the measure given its longstanding presence in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category and the established awareness of HIPAA Security Rule requirements among MIPS eligible clinicians. In the assessment of whether it remained appropriate to maintain the Security Risk Analysis measure in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, we considered the extent to which the measure continues to advance the measure's intended goals relative to the costs associated with the continued use of the measure. As asserted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44173
), we believe that such costs include not only the burden associated with reporting the requisite attestations, but also the costs associated with administering and maintaining the measure within the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Such costs may include, but are not limited to the following: clinician burden associated with information collection and submission; clinician burden associated with complying with overlapping programmatic and regulatory requirements, including the HIPAA Security Rule; and CMS resources associated with oversight, maintenance, education, and operational support for the measure. In the case of the Security Risk Analysis measure, due to the underlying security risk analysis and risk management activities are already required under the HIPAA Security Rule, we noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44173
) that it may be unnecessarily costly and of limited incremental benefit to retain this measure where its continued inclusion no longer meaningfully advances the objectives of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category beyond the separate regulatory requirements that already apply. For such reasons, we believe removal of the Security Risk Analysis measure at this juncture would balance the goals of reducing unnecessary administrative burden, maintaining a parsimonious and meaningful measure set, and preserving the focus of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category on high-value measures that more directly support program objectives. We rely on our federal partner, the HHS Office for Civil Rights, to administer and enforce compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule requirements that MIPS eligible clinicians may otherwise be subject to.
The proposal aligns with our goals of reducing administrative burden while simultaneously focusing on high-value, outcome-oriented measures. Specifically, the removal of the Security Risk Analysis measure from the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category provides an opportunity to reduce the number of discrete manual steps and reporting fields required for successful adherence to reporting requirements without diminishing the integrity or central goals of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Although we proposed to remove the Security Risk Analysis measure, we reminded MIPS eligible clinicians to continue to conduct security risk analysis and security risk management to safeguard ePHI as required under the HIPAA Security Rule (
91 FR 44173
). We anticipate that MIPS eligible clinicians will continue to conduct security risk analysis and security risk management activities to comply with the requirements pertaining to the security of ePHI that is created, received, used, or maintained by a covered entity or its business associate in accordance with the HIPAA Security Rule.
Retirement of the Security Risk Analysis measure from the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year would reduce burden by removing the attestation requirement and supporting a more parsimonious and outcomes-oriented measure set. Specifically, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed at § 414.1375(b)(2)(ii)(A) to specify a limited timeframe, through the 2028 MIPS payment year for which a MIPS eligible clinician would be required to report that they completed the actions included in the Security Risk Analysis measure during the year in which the performance period occurs (
91 FR 44174
).
We requested public comment on this proposal.
We received public comment on the proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposal to remove the Security Risk Analysis measure beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. Many of these commenters supported removal of the Security Risk Analysis measure because they believed it would reduce administrative burden and remove duplicative requirements as MIPS eligible clinicians are already bound by other privacy and security statutes and regulations such as the HIPAA Security Rule to perform security risk analysis. A few commenters also believed that removal of the Security Risk Analysis measure would allow providers to have more time and resources to focus on patient care and meaningful interoperability efforts. A commenter recommended that CMS continue
(
printed page 71562)
providing the `reminder' in QPP educational materials that MIPS eligible clinicians must safeguard electronic patient health information as required under the HIPAA Security Rule.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters. We will consider the feedback on communicating MIPS eligible clinicians' obligations to safeguard electronic patient health information.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended the removal of the Security Risk Analysis measure to be sooner than the proposed CY2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, but starting with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year to accelerate reduction of burden and program simplification.
Response:
We do not agree with the commenters suggestion to remove the Security Risk Analysis measure starting with the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year. With the CY 2026 performance period already underway, MIPS eligible clinicians are currently completing or have completed the actions required for the Security Risk Analysis measure given that requirements must be completed during the year in which the performance period occurs, unlike the ONC Direct Review and ONC-ACB Surveillance attestations, which do not always require specific actions to have already been completed during the performance period when attesting to participate in applicable ONC-related activities. Thus, we believe that removing the Security Risk Analysis measure starting with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year is appropriate.
Comment:
Many commenters requested clarification and confirmation that removing the Security Risk Analysis measure and relying on use of CEHRT does not remove clinicians' obligations to perform security risk analysis and risk management activities to support strong cybersecurity practices and meet obligations under the HIPAA Security Rule on emerging generative AI technologies. A commenter expressed the opinion that removing the measure does not meaningfully reduce MIPS eligible clinicians' burden.
Response:
We acknowledge that MIPS eligible clinicians will still need to meet the requirements in the HIPAA Security Rule. However, requiring MIPS eligible clinicians to report the Security Risk Analysis measure provides little incremental benefit compared to the associated costs and, therefore, we have decided to remove the requirement that MIPS eligible clinicians report the Security Risk Analysis measure. While MIPS eligible clinicians will continue to have the underlying obligation to assess security risk based on the requirements in the HIPAA Security Rule, we believe that removing the Security Risk Analysis measure from the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category reduces burden by eliminating MIPS-specific reporting and attestation requirements.
Comment:
A few commenters requested that CMS align requirements across other programs, coordinate with other agencies on security risk analysis including U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights and ONC, and monitor requirements of the HIPAA Security Rule.
Response:
We strive to align program requirements across applicable federal programs, if appropriate. Also, we intend to continue our efforts to coordinate with other CMS programs and federal offices and agencies involved in cybersecurity and security risk assessment and mitigation.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed the view that CMS should limit the year-to-year measure changes, which may create confusion and add administrative burden, and provide sufficient advance notice before changing or removing a security measure to allow MIPS eligible clinicians time to adjust their processes.
Response:
While we agree that minimizing annual measures updates provides stability to MIPS eligible clinicians, we must also balance stability with being responsive to emerging technologies, including generative AI and agentic tools integrated into EHRs that process ePHI, are posing new security concerns and must be continuously monitored. We will continue to work across federal programs and with other federal agencies and will, to the best of our ability, provide as much advance notice as possible before changes take effect.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed the proposal to remove the Security Risk Analysis measure due to increasing cybersecurity incidents in the healthcare industry, the delay in finalizing the new HIPAA Security Rule, and the lack of specificity in the HIPAA requirements around the frequency of performing a security risk analysis. A commenter shared a belief that the benefits of maintaining the Security Risk Analysis measure outweigh the burdens of reporting. Another commenter recommended revisiting removal once the HIPAA Security Rule is finalized and considering working with ONC to develop an alternative mechanism for MIPS eligible clinicians to report variations in expected operations of CEHRT to perform secure health information exchange, especially in the absence of ONC health IT certification criteria that validate functionality critical to CEHRT.
Response:
We are aware of emerging cybersecurity concerns and will rely on MIPS eligible clinicians meeting the requirements of the HIPAA Security Rule, without the additional MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category security analysis measure. Removal of the Security Risk Analysis measure from the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category does not remove the underlying security obligations applicable to MIPS eligible clinicians under the HIPAA Security Rule and such requirements continue to apply independent of MIPS requirements, regardless of whether updates to the HIPAA Security Rule are finalized. Additionally, while some commenters expressed concern that HIPAA does not provide specificity around the frequency of performing a security risk analysis, we note that risk analysis is an ongoing process and that retaining the MIPS measure would not address frequency as the measure is a simple annual attestation. We continue to believe that removing the measure reduces unnecessary MIPS reporting, documentation, and audit burden while preserving existing security obligations under HIPAA. We will continue to monitor to determine if additional requirements in this area are needed to supplement other federal regulatory requirements, and if necessary, will discuss in future rulemaking.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to remove the Security Risk Analysis measure beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year.

(e) Adopting a New Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs Measure Beginning With the CY 2028 Performance Period/2030 MIPS Payment Year
(i) Background
Under section 1848(o)(2)(A) of the Act, the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category assesses whether MIPS eligible clinicians use CEHRT in a meaningful manner. By statute, such demonstration includes the use of electronic prescribing as determined to be appropriate by the Secretary. The MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category has therefore included measures related to electronic prescribing since its inception (
75 FR 44337
; and
81 FR 77229
through
77237
). Separately from the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, we have also advanced the adoption of electronic prescribing through authority under section 1860D-4(e) of the Act, which requires that prescriptions for covered Medicare Part D drugs transmitted electronically comply with a uniform transaction standard specified by CMS. Under the same authority under section 1860D-4(e) of the Act, we also generally require that Schedule II, III, IV, and V controlled substances under Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage prescription drug plans be prescribed electronically in accordance with an electronic prescription drug program. That required standard includes transactions for the electronic prior authorization of Part D-covered drugs prescribed to Part D-eligible individuals (
85 FR 86827
through
86832
and
89 FR 51242
through
51247
).
Historically, the ONC Health IT Certification Program and the Part D Program have maintained complementary policies of aligning ONC health IT certification criteria and associated standards related to electronic prescribing, medication history, and electronic prior authorization for prescriptions (
89 FR 51257
). In successive rules supporting the ONC Health IT Certification Program, ONC has adopted the National Council for Prescription Drugs Program (NCPDP) SCRIPT standard as the required exchange standard for the electronic prescribing certification criterion at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
. In the “Medicare Program; Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Program; Health Information Technology Standards and Implementation Specifications” final rule (
89 FR 51242
through
51247
), the Part D Program finalized at §  423.160(b)(1) the requirement that Part D sponsors, prescribers and dispensers, when electronically transmitting prescriptions and prescription-related information for covered Part D drugs for Part D eligible individuals, must comply with the standard in
45 CFR 170.205(b)
. Taken in conjunction with the standards and expiration date adopted by ONC in the same rule (
89 FR 51258
through
51259
), § 423.160(b)(1) will require Part D sponsors, prescribers and dispensers to use NCPDP SCRIPT standard version 2023011, which ONC adopted at
45 CFR 170.205(b)(2)
, beginning January 1, 2028, and expire NCPDP SCRIPT standard version 2017071, which ONC previously adopted at
45 CFR 170.205(b)(1)
as of January 1, 2028. The NCPDP SCRIPT standard version 2023011 includes enhancements to support electronic prescribing and transmission of prescription-related and electronic prior authorization information.
On April 14, 2026, the “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges” (2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs) proposed rule was published and introduced proposals that require Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plans offered on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges (collectively “impacted payers”) to support certain exchange standards for the electronic prior authorization of prescription drugs (

through

(ii) Adopting Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs Measure
Across the healthcare industry, a majority of prior authorizations for prescription drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit remain a separate manual process outside of the EHR workflow, not connected to e-prescribing, and could cause major points of friction and delay in the prescribing and prior authorization workflow. In 2023, approximately 38 percent of prescription drug prior authorizations were fully electronic and 15 percent were fully manual, indicating continuing capacity for
(
printed page 71564)
improvement in the domain.
[
403
]
This current level of adoption of electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs contributes to a reliance on payer portals and manual processes, including processes based on phone, or fax, which are entirely outside the EHR and that may delay patients' access to needed medications, increase administrative complexity for clinicians and staff, and undermine the efficiency and clinical value of electronic prescribing. As more payers support standardized electronic prior authorization, we have determined that measuring the use of prior authorization for prescription drugs will be a valuable addition to our assessment of meaningful use of CEHRT under the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Standards-based electronic prior authorization should improve timeliness and transparency of medication access by facilitating information-gathering and tracking of prior authorization status within clinician EHR workflows to support care coordination and help close the prescriber-to-dispenser loop. Thus, we believe that incorporating electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs is an appropriate aspect of demonstrating meaningful use of CEHRT by MIPS eligible clinicians.
Action in this area is further supported by longstanding efforts to promote standards adoption for prescription-related transactions under the Part D Program and the ONC Health IT Certification Program. As previously noted, CMS and ONC have maintained complementary policies aligning electronic prescribing and prescription-related standards at
42 CFR 423.160(b)(1)
for Part D transactions and
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
for the ONC Health IT Certification Program. Health IT developers also have experience with the underlying transaction standards because of their use in Part D transactions. Therefore, we believe that MIPS eligible clinicians and their health IT vendors have a foundation to implement the functionality for a new measure and thus, we proposed the adoption of a new measure, Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44174
through
44176
).
We proposed to adopt the new measure, Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs, for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year (
91 FR 44176
). As noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we intend for the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure to be included in the Health Information Exchange objective for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category to emphasize the role of prior authorization in promoting care coordination and collocate the new measure in the same objective as the previously adopted Electronic Prior Authorization measure (
91 FR 44175
). The new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure aims to assess a MIPS eligible clinician's utilization of standards-based electronic prior authorization. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed for the specifications of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure to be as follows (
91 FR 44175
):
Measure Description:
For at least one prescription drug ordered by the MIPS eligible clinician during the performance period for which prior authorization is required, the prior authorization is requested electronically using CEHRT.
Reporting Requirements:
“Yes”/“No” response.
Exclusion:
Any MIPS eligible clinician who—
++ Does not prescribe drugs that require prior authorization during the applicable performance period;
++ Only prescribes drugs requiring prior authorization where the payer does not support the specified electronic prior authorization standard during the applicable performance period; or
++ Prescribes fewer than 100 permissible prescription drugs during the performance period.
We noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that the last exclusion matches an exclusion in the Electronic Prescribing measure (
91 FR 44175
). For this exclusion, “permissible prescriptions” means all drugs that meet the current definition of a prescription as ordered by a MIPS eligible clinician to dispense a drug that would not be dispensed without such order. “Permissible prescriptions” may include electronic prescriptions of controlled substances where creation of an electronic prescription for the medication is feasible using CEHRT and where allowable by state and local law. Additionally, for purposes of this exclusion, permissible prescriptions include any prescription, not only those requiring prior authorization. To successfully report this measure, MIPS eligible clinicians must submit a “Yes” response, in which they are affirmatively attesting to having requested prior authorization electronically using CEHRT for at least one prescription drug ordered by the MIPS eligible clinician during the performance period or (if applicable) claim an exclusion. We expect that once a MIPS eligible clinician has the capability of requesting prior authorization electronically, MIPS eligible clinician will do so more frequently, though we did not propose to measure frequency of use at this time with this initial version of the measure. The new measure will apply to prescription drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit, as functionally defined by whether prior authorization can be requested for the drug can be authorized using the NCPDP SCRIPT standard.
The proposal to use CEHRT for the measure would require use of health IT certified to the ONC health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
—“Electronic prescribing” and at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
—“Real-time prescription benefit” to support any electronic prior authorization requests used to satisfy this measure. Use of both “electronic prescribing” and “real-time prescription benefit” ONC health IT certification criteria ensures that MIPS eligible clinicians use standards-based capabilities within their health IT systems to successfully complete the measure. Beginning January 1, 2028, the specified standards within the certification criteria in
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
and
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
will be the same versions of the NCPDP SCRIPT Standard and NCPDP RTPB Standard, respectively, required for Medicare Part D sponsors and to be required for other impacted payers in the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule (
91 FR 19925
through
19927
). For purposes of the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, “requested electronically” means initiating and submitting an electronic prior authorization request from within CEHRT using health IT certified under
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
and
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
. Using health IT certified to the “real-time prescription benefit” ONC health IT certification criterion in
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
allows a MIPS eligible clinician to ascertain the patient-specific out-of-pocket cost of a prescription drug, the cost of suitable alternatives, compare prescription costs at different pharmacies, and learn whether prior authorization for a specific prescription drug is required.
The 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule also proposed that impacted payers support the NCPDP
(
printed page 71565)

91 FR 19925
and
19926
). We are not including this standard as part of required CEHRT for this measure at this juncture. However, we believe that the NCPDP F&B standard complements the NCPDP SCRIPT and RTPB standards certification criteria for Health IT Modules in
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
and
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)

We noted in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule that adoption of the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure is not contingent upon the finalization of the proposals in the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule (
91 FR 44176

91 FR 44176

Electronic prior authorization requests for prescription drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit, which would leverage the NCPDP SCRIPT Standard and NCPDP RTPB Standard, are often for those prescription drugs dispensed at a retail pharmacy. We recognize that other prescription drugs may be covered under a medical benefit and are usually administered or dispensed by a medical provider in a health care setting. Those drugs covered under a medical benefit generally use FHIR-based electronic prior authorization processes, such as those supported by the Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation guides finalized under ONC health IT certification criteria, and therefore, are not in scope for the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. A MIPS eligible clinician that only needs prior authorization for prescription drugs covered under a medical benefit and not a pharmacy benefit would be eligible to claim an exclusion for not ordering an applicable prescription drug during the performance period.
For purposes of the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, “one prescription drug ordered by the MIPS eligible clinician” includes a new prescription and, where applicable, a prescription renewal or refill request that generates a prior authorization requirement at the time of prescribing. A prescription drug “for which prior authorization is required” is one for which the applicable payer rules indicate a prior authorization requirement at the point of prescribing for the patient and plan. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we indicated that we believe the NCPDP F&B Standard would help inform MIPS eligible clinicians when a prior authorization is required or not, even if not a mandate of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. We recognized that coverage for certain prescription drugs may fall under either the pharmacy or medical benefit and would continue to consider future policies to reduce workflow fragmentation across prior authorization approaches (
91 FR 44176
). In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we requested public comment with a Request for Information (RFI) on the potential to expand the scope of the Electronic Prior Authorization measure to include prescription drugs covered under a medical benefit (
91 FR 44182
).
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed that the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure would require an attestation of “Yes” or “No” response from a MIPS eligible clinician (
91 FR 44175
and
44176

Beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, a MIPS eligible clinician would be required to submit a “Yes” response for the measure or claim an applicable exclusion in order to earn a score for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. If a MIPS eligible clinician submits a “No” response for the measure, fails to submit any attestation, or does not claim an applicable exclusion for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, the MIPS eligible clinician would receive a score of zero for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category (weighted at 25 percent of the MIPS final score), and would not be considered a meaningful EHR user for purposes of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category for an applicable performance period.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed that the measure would initially require an attestation of a “Yes” or “No” response to allow MIPS eligible clinicians to gain familiarity with electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs and measure reporting (
91 FR 44175
and
44176
). 91 FR 44176

We requested public comment on the proposal.
We received public comment on the proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposal to add the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure as a required measure in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. Several commenters highlighted the potential for standardized electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs to reduce administrative burden and delays and to improve patients' timely access to needed medications. A few commenters noted that electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs could improve care coordination, efficiency, and patient experience. A commenter noted that the new measure would align with the adoption of NCPDP SCRIPT standards supporting electronic prior authorization.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters regarding the proposal to establish the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. We agree with commenters that use of standards-based electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit has the potential to reduce administrative burden and delays, support more timely patient access to needed medications, and improve care coordination and workflow efficiency. We believe the proposed new measure would help advance adoption of interoperable electronic prior authorization capabilities among MIPS eligible clinicians and other entities involved in the prescription-drug prior authorization process.
Comment:
Many commenters did not support the proposal to establish the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure as a required measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. Several commenters expressed concern that the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure could become mandatory before standardized electronic prior authorization capabilities and workflows are sufficiently mature and have demonstrated meaningful value for MIPS eligible clinicians and patients. The commenters indicated that premature implementation of the
(
printed page 71566)
Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure could result in additional administrative and financial burden. A few commenters questioned the need for a mandatory measure, noting that MIPS eligible clinicians already have incentives to adopt electronic prior authorization due to its potential to streamline prior authorization workflows and reduce associated administrative burden.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback regarding the readiness of electronic prior authorization capabilities and workflows for prescription drugs, as well as the potential burden associated with implementing a new required measure. While we recognize the potential burden associated with the new required measure, we believe that the benefits of the measure outweigh the potential burdens and that finalizing, as proposed, to adopt the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure will advance use of standards-based electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit, which has the potential to reduce reliance on manual and portal-based processes and support more timely and transparent prior authorization workflows. Also, we believe that MIPS eligible clinicians and health IT vendors will have sufficient time to build an infrastructure, test, and prepare for the implementation of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure requirements during the entirety of CY 2027 and the permissibility of continuing preparation into CY 2028. We intend for the adoption of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure as a required measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year to strike an appropriate balance between providing stakeholders time to prepare for implementation and advancing broader adoption of electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs in a timely manner. The proposed start date allows a meaningful period for continued development, testing, and workflow integration while also supporting the objectives of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category to advance interoperable, standards-based electronic exchange.
MIPS eligible clinicians and health IT developers will have a foundation for implementation through the NCPDP SCRIPT and Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standards. CMS previously finalized requirements for Medicare Part D sponsors, prescribers, and dispensers to use specified NCPDP SCRIPT standards when electronically transmitting prescriptions, including for electronic prior authorization transactions, as well as requirements for Part D sponsors to implement a real-time benefit tool using the RTPB standard (
42 CFR 423.160
).
In addition, the measure includes an exclusion for MIPS eligible clinicians for whom no applicable payer supports the specified electronic prior authorization standard. The measure is structured as an attestation measure and merely requires a MIPS eligible clinician to electronically request prior authorization for one applicable prescription drug during the performance period to satisfy the measure. While MIPS eligible clinicians may already have business and clinical incentives to use electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs, we do not believe those incentives alone have been sufficient to drive widespread, consistent adoption of standards-based electronic prior authorization workflows and we believe that a measure under the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category will encourage further uptake.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended delaying or phasing implementation of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. Other commenters requested the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure be optional and eligible for bonus points for the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year to encourage early adoption and implementation experience and then transition the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure to be required beginning with CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment period or other future performance period. A few commenters noted that allowing for an optional reporting period prior to requiring the measure would be consistent with phased approaches used to introduce other Promoting Interoperability measures in previous years. Several commenters specifically requested delaying mandatory reporting until the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment period at the earliest. Commenters generally noted that a delayed or phased approach would provide additional time for payers, health IT developers, and MIPS eligible clinicians to implement and test electronic prior authorization capabilities, integrate them into clinical workflows, and gain implementation experience before mandatory measure reporting begins. A few commenters recommended that CMS consider the timing of payer implementation requirements when determining when to require the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, expressing concern that payers and health IT developers may not have sufficient time to implement and test the necessary capabilities. A commenter recommended that this new measure remains voluntary during the transition year if CMS finalizes policies to increase the performance threshold or require MVP participation in the same performance year.
Response:
We intend for the adoption of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure as a required measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year to strike an appropriate balance between providing stakeholders time to prepare for implementation and advancing broader adoption of electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs in a timely manner. The proposed start date allows a meaningful period for continued development, testing, and workflow integration while also supporting the objectives of the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category to advance interoperable, standards-based electronic exchange.
While we have previously used phased approaches (for example, establishing an initial optional reporting period prior to requiring a measure) when introducing new measures or policies, we do not believe an initial optional reporting period is necessary for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure and we note that an optional approach could lead to uneven adoption and slow progress toward more standardized use of electronic prior authorization processes for prescription drugs. Establishing the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure as required beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year will promote more consistent implementation across stakeholders and encourage movement away from manual prior authorization processes. We believe adoption of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure can incentivize adoption of practices that reduce inefficiency and potential delays in patient access to medications.
We do not believe it is necessary to delay implementation of the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure beyond the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year to align with payer compliance dates proposed in the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed
(
printed page 71567)
rule (
91 FR 19890
). We note the proposed October 1, 2027, compliance date for impacted payers to support electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs precedes the implementation of the new measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. However, adoption of this measure is not contingent on finalization of the proposals in the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule. The new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure promotes the use of existing electronic prior authorization workflows for prescription drugs, which are already supported through established standards and are not dependent on the FHIR-based Prior Authorization API requirements for medical items and services. CMS also has previously existing requirements for Part D sponsors, prescribers, and dispensers to use specified NCPDP SCRIPT standards for electronic prescription drug prior authorization (
42 CFR 423.160
). These requirements build upon previously established electronic prior authorization standards and provide a standards-based foundation for implementation of this measure.
Additionally, this measure is intended to align with the implementation of the Electronic Prior Authorization measure relating to medical services and items as it becomes a required measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. The simultaneous and in tandem implementation of the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure and the Electronic Prior Authorization measure as required measures will encourage expansive adoption of electronic prior authorization.
We note that the MIPS performance threshold has been finalized with no increases until CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year (
90 FR 49918
). Additionally, we refer readers to section IV.A.3.c. of this final rule for discussion of the proposed policy regarding the sunset of traditional MIPS, which has been finalized with a modification to delay implementation. Regardless, potential changes to the MIPS performance threshold, MVP participation policies and other policies, are separate policy topics that do not, in our view, justify making the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure optional.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concerns about ecosystem readiness to support the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. Several commenters noted that standardized electronic prior authorization capabilities and workflows for prescription drugs are not yet widely available or sufficiently mature, with functionality varying across payers, health IT developers, and clinical practice settings. Several commenters noted that MIPS eligible clinicians' ability to successfully use electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs depends on the readiness and functionality of payers, health IT developers, pharmacy benefit managers, pharmacies, and other entities outside of their control. Several commenters also stressed that availability of electronic prior authorization functionality alone does not automatically demonstrate readiness and highlighted the need for functionality to be fully operational, integrated into clinical workflows, and tested end-to-end across participating entities. Several commenters recommended that CMS assess and monitor payer, health IT developer, and MIPS eligible clinician readiness to inform implementation of the measure. Commenters also noted that inconsistent adoption across the ecosystem could require MIPS eligible clinicians to maintain multiple workflows. A few commenters additionally raised concerns about the affordability of available technology, implementation costs, and differences in readiness across practice settings (such as small, independent, rural, and safety-net practices). A commenter recommended that CMS accompany the measure with enforceable expectations for health insurance plans and pharmacy benefit managers such as response timeframes and patient protections.
Response:
We believe the previously established Medicare Part D requirements for use of specified NCPDP SCRIPT and RTPB standards for electronic prescribing and prescription-related transactions that support electronic prior authorization (
42 CFR 423.160
) provide a reasonable foundation for implementation beginning with the CY 2028 performance period. The measure's limited attestation requirement further supports implementation by requiring only one qualifying electronic prior authorization request during the performance period. Additionally, this measure, as proposed, includes exclusions that provide flexibility for MIPS eligible clinicians who may face challenges meeting the measure's requirements, including accommodation for where an applicable payer does not support the specified electronic prior authorization standard.
By requiring the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, we intend to promote coordinated readiness across stakeholders to ensure that workflows become operational. Establishing the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure will encourage continued progress toward broader implementation and workflow integration across the ecosystem. Over time, increased use of standardized electronic prior authorization has the potential to reduce reliance on fragmented and duplicative workflows and better support interoperability goals. We will continue to work to align with ONC and other agencies regarding requirements for health IT developers, health insurance plans, and pharmacy benefit managers. We intend to assess implementation experience, and broader industry progress as the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure is implemented, and we will consider whether future refinements are warranted through rulemaking.
Additionally, we acknowledge the concerns from commenters regarding the affordability of available technology, implementation costs, and the spectrum of readiness across practice settings such as small, independent, rural, and safety-net practices. We intend to monitor the availability of technology, implementation challenges, and readiness across various practice settings, including small, independent, rural, and safety-net practices.
Comment:
Several commenters emphasized the importance of aligning CEHRT requirements for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure with broader CMS and HHS interoperability and prior authorization policies, including aligning clinician and payer requirements around common underlying standards to support consistent implementation across clinicians, payers, and health IT developers. A few commenters recommended for CMS to maintain consistency across programs, including the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category and Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program, to minimize differences in measure requirements, specifications, and implementation timelines, and prevent clinicians from being subject to different electronic prior authorization requirements across programs. Some commenters specifically requested for the proposal to align with ONC-certified health IT and standards-based
(
printed page 71568)
functionality. A commenter requested that CMS finalize the underlying standards requirements in related rulemaking before adopting the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. A commenter recommended preserving established NCPDP standards for pharmacy-benefit transactions while promoting interoperability with emerging FHIR-based standards, emphasizing the importance of a coordinated approach that avoids disrupting established workflows as standards and program requirements evolve.
Response:
We agree with the comment regarding the alignment with ONC-certified health IT and applicable standards-based functionality as it is important to support successful implementation and to minimize avoidable differences in technical and operational expectations across the industry. We recognize the importance of promoting consistency across CMS programs, where appropriate, to reduce burden. The NCPDP SCRIPT and Real-Time Prescription Benefit standards supporting the health IT certification criteria specified for the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure align with standards required for Medicare Part D sponsors (
42 CFR 423.160
) and proposed for adoption by other impacted payers under the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs proposed rule (
91 FR 19925
through
19927
), supporting consistent standards-based electronic prior authorization capabilities across MIPS eligible clinicians, health IT developers, and payers.
However, we note that differences across programs may sometimes reflect distinct statutory authorities, program structures, or policy objectives. We agree that established standards, such as NCPDP standards, play an important role in current workflows and at the same time recognize the growing importance of newer approaches such as FHIR-based standards. We intend to continue seeking alignment across CMS programs and with broader federal interoperability efforts, to the extent feasible, as implementation proceeds.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended expanding or strengthening the proposed exclusions and other protections for MIPS eligible clinicians who are unable to successfully report the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure due to circumstances outside their control. A few commenters recommended that such protections account for circumstances in which required electronic prior authorization capabilities are unavailable, nonfunctional, or not operationally implemented or integrated due to payer or health IT developer readiness limitations. A few commenters also raised concerns about the burden and practical challenges associated with determining and documenting whether a MIPS eligible clinician qualifies for an exclusion and recommended simplifying this process, such as through standardized reasons for not being able to meet the measure successfully or CMS-provided information on payer support for applicable electronic prior authorization standards.
Response:
We note that the policies already available under the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, including existing exclusion policies where applicable, and the significant hardship exception for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, provide important safeguards for MIPS eligible clinicians who are unable to meet requirements due to circumstances beyond their control. These policies are intended to provide flexibility in cases where a MIPS eligible clinician cannot reasonably comply with the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category requirements. We do not believe it would be practical to base exclusions on a CMS-maintained list of payer support for applicable electronic prior authorization standards because payer readiness may vary over time and across products, markets, and vendors. We believe that the current MIPS exclusion framework provides a more consistent approach. We intend to assess implementation experience, payer and health IT readiness, technological advancements, and the availability of ONC-certified health IT as this measure is operationalized, including issues related to the availability and functionality of electronic prior authorization capabilities.
Comment:
Commenters provided mixed feedback on the proposed attestation based measure design for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. Several commenters supported the proposed attestation-based format for the initial measure design, noting that a percentage or frequency-based measure could potentially penalize MIPS eligible clinicians for payer limitations outside their control, particularly when their patient populations are covered by payers that do not yet fully support electronic prior authorization. Several commenters recommended that CMS transition to a numerator/denominator, performance-based approach as electronic prior authorization adoption and measure reporting capabilities mature. These commenters stated that a performance-based approach could better measure routine, integrated use of electronic prior authorization across applicable prescribing workflows. A commenter encouraged CMS to adopt numerator/denominator reporting as soon as feasible.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' feedback on the proposed Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure design. Beginning with an initial attestation based approach is appropriate because it allows MIPS eligible clinicians to gain familiarity with electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs and measure reporting while standardized data capture and reporting capabilities continue to develop. We also recognize that MIPS eligible clinicians may encounter variation in payer support for electronic prior authorization. The Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure includes an exclusion for MIPS eligible clinicians who only prescribe drugs requiring prior authorization from payers that do not support the specified electronic prior authorization standard during the applicable performance period.
As implementation of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure matures and more consistent data are available to support reliable performance measurement, we will continue to assess whether updating to a numerator/denominator-based approach is feasible and appropriate in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters requested additional clarification regarding the technical requirements for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. For example, commenters requested clarification regarding the technical capabilities and transactions that would satisfy the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, including whether conforming electronic prior authorization functionality delivered through a connected application would qualify and the minimum criteria for a qualifying electronic prior authorization transaction. Another commenter recommended clarifying the respective roles of NCPDP SCRIPT and Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standards in facilitating electronic prior authorization and specifying which certified health IT capabilities are necessary to satisfy the measure. A commenter requested clarification
(
printed page 71569)
distinguishing electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit from those covered under the medical benefit. Another commenter recommended that CMS develop standardized calculation guidance and testing tools to promote consistent measure implementation and reporting across health IT vendors. A commenter requested that CMS publish the complete specification for the measure.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback from commenters requesting clarification regarding the technical requirements for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure. To meet the measure, a MIPS eligible clinician must initiate and submit an electronic prior authorization request from within CEHRT using health IT certified to the “electronic prescribing” and “real-time prescription benefit” criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
and
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
. With regard to the request for clarification about electronic prior authorization functionality delivered through a connected application, we note that MIPS eligible clinicians adopt and use certified health IT from different health IT developers to meet the CEHRT definition, and may use applications connected to their primary EHR system as long as those applications are certified to the relevant ONC certification criteria required for the measure at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
and
(b)(4)
.
The Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB) functionality described in the certification criterion at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
may help a MIPS eligible clinician determine whether prior authorization is required for a particular prescription drug, but RTPB functionality alone does not satisfy the measure. The measure action requires the electronic submission of a prior authorization request using the applicable NCPDP SCRIPT transaction. Specifically, as we stated in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44176
), for purposes of the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, “requested electronically” means initiating and submitting an electronic prior authorization request from within CEHRT using health IT certified under
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
and
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
. Thus, we require the use of health IT certified to the ONC health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
—“Electronic prescribing” and at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
—“Real-time prescription benefit” to support any electronic prior authorization requests used to satisfy this measure.
Furthermore, we note that for every qualifying request, health IT certified to the RTPB functionality at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(4)
must be used to check for a coverage requirement and then use health IT certified to the ONC health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(b)(3)
—“Electronic prescribing” must be used to submit the request. We recognize that such actions may not be conducted in every circumstance in which a MIPS eligible clinician may seek prior authorization and note that the measure provides such flexibility as a result of requiring that for at least one prescription drug ordered by the MIPS eligible clinician during the performance period for which prior authorization is required, the prior authorization is requested electronically using CEHRT.
Regarding the commenter requesting clarification on distinguishing electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs covered under the pharmacy benefit from those covered under the medical benefit, we clarify that the electronic prior authorization processes outlined in this section of the final rule applies to prescription drugs covered under a pharmacy benefit and does not apply to prescription drugs covered under a medical benefit, which generally use different electronic prior authorization workflows.
We recognize the importance of clear implementation guidance regarding the technical capabilities and transactions that satisfy the measure. We will provide educational and guidance resources, as appropriate and feasible, to clarify implementation details. The measure specifications for the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription drugs measure will be available on the QPP website at
https://qpp.cms.gov/​reporting-requirements/​measures-activities/​explore
.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that when implementing the new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, CMS should require continued monitoring of denials, appeals, and treatment abandonment to measure whether patients are able to get needed care and medications in a timely manner.
Response:
The Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category is intended to assess whether MIPS eligible clinicians are using electronic prior authorization functionality for prescription drugs, rather than to measure payer decision-making, appeal outcomes, or patient medication adherence or abandonment. Data on denials, appeals, and treatment abandonment may not be consistently available to clinicians or captured in certified health IT in a standardized and reliable manner for purposes of MIPS reporting. In addition, these outcomes may be influenced by factors outside the clinician's control. Thus, we do not believe it is appropriate to require monitoring of denials, appeals, and treatment abandonment as a part of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure at this time.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to adopt the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year.

(ii) Modifying the Electronic Prior Authorization Measure for the CY 2027 Performance Period/2029 MIPS Payment Year
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed amendments to the Electronic Prior Authorization measure for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year by modifying the measure description (
91 FR 44176
through

91 FR 44176
through
44178
). When we adopted the
(

We requested public comment on this proposal.
We received public comment on the proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the modifications to the Electronic Prior Authorization measure for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. A commenter expressed the belief that the broader adoption of interoperable, standards based electronic prior authorization has the potential to reduce reliance on manual processes that disrupt clinical workflows and unnecessarily delay patient care. A few commenters supported CMS's efforts to clarify and update the measure, including the proposed change from requiring electronic prior authorization “using data from CEHRT” to “using CEHRT.” A few commenters indicated that the modified measure language would more clearly establish the role of certified health IT in successfully meeting the Electronic Prior Authorization measure and support alignment with standards-based electronic prior authorization capabilities.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters. We agree with commenters that the use of CEHRT and the alignment with ONC health IT certification criteria will help establish a consistent technical foundation for the measure, support broader adoption of standards-based electronic prior authorization, and improve interoperability across MIPS eligible clinicians, EHRs, health IT vendors, and payers.
Comment:
A few commenters raised concerns regarding changing the measure language from “using data from CEHRT” to “using CEHRT.” Commenters stated that electronic prior authorization workflows may rely on multiple systems, including EHRs, revenue cycle systems, payer portals, clearinghouses, and other connected applications. Commenters expressed concern that a narrow “using CEHRT” requirement could constrain practical software implementation options and increase burden. Commenters also noted that payer and health IT readiness to support standards-based electronic prior authorization remains variable, which could further limit the ability of MIPS eligible clinicians to satisfy the measure using CEHRT.
A few commenters recommended retaining the current “using data from CEHRT” language or clarifying that MIPS eligible clinicians may use conforming electronic prior authorization technology to meet the measure, whether embedded within CEHRT or provided through other systems or applications integrated into clinician workflows, such as revenue cycle systems, payer portals, and clearinghouses.
Response:
We acknowledge the concerns from commenters regarding the proposed change in the measure description from specifying “using data from CEHRT” to “using CEHRT.” We recognize that electronic prior authorization workflows may involve multiple systems, entities, and technology solutions. Our intent is not to prohibit the use of standards-based intermediaries or other interoperable tools that support the electronic prior authorization workflow. Rather, the measure is intended to ensure that MIPS eligible clinicians conduct the measure action using standards-based health IT functionality certified to ONC's electronic prior authorization certification criteria. We note that different types of health IT products may obtain certification under the ONC Health IT Certification program and that nothing prohibits eligible clinicians from using certified Health IT Modules from different health IT developers in assembling technology meeting the CEHRT definition to support participation in the Promoting Interoperability performance category. Moreover, our proposal does not prohibit intermediaries from supporting electronic prior authorization exchange in other ways separate from the capabilities reflected in the electronic prior authorization certification criteria. As discussed in sections IV.A.4.d.(4)(f)(v) and IV.B.1.d. of this final rule, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to make the Electronic Prior Authorization measure an optional measure and eligible for 10 bonus points for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, during which MIPS eligible clinicians may use one or more Health IT Modules certified to the applicable electronic prior authorization certification criteria, as necessary to fulfill the measure action. This final policy provides additional flexibility during initial implementation and assists in addressing concerns from commenters regarding implementation lead time, interface testing, and payer readiness.
Comment:
Several commenters requested clarification or modifications to the technical specifications for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure. A few commenters recommended that CMS more clearly define what constitutes a qualifying electronic prior authorization transaction. A commenter expressed concern that the proposed measure language could be interpreted inconsistently across implementers because it does not clearly distinguish among initiation of an electronic workflow, successful submission of a standards-based electronic prior authorization transaction, portal-based processes, and requested clarification regarding the acceptable source(s) for a request that can initiate the workflow for a qualifying electronic prior authorization transaction.
A few commenters specifically recommended that a successfully completed transaction count regardless of whether the payer determines that prior authorization is required and, for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, that a successfully submitted request count even if a payer response is not received. A commenter also requested that CMS clarify whether conforming electronic prior authorization functionality delivered through an application connected to CEHRT, rather than embedded within CEHRT itself, may satisfy the measure.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback from commenters, specifically the request for clarification regarding what constitutes a successful electronic prior authorization action for purposes of the
(
printed page 71572)
measure. For a prior authorization request for a medical item or service to qualify for the measure, the need for prior authorization must be established. Therefore, if a MIPS eligible clinician uses CEHRT to query a payer's Prior Authorization API and the payer responds that prior authorization is not required, the transaction would not satisfy the measure.
According to the Da Vinci IGs, the eligible clinician that queries a payer's Prior Authorization API will receive a response to the prior authorization request such as:
covered = not-covered
(that is
,
no coverage or possibility of coverage);
pa-needed = no-auth
(that is
,
service is covered and does not require prior authorization);
pa-needed = satisfied
(that is
,
prior authorization required, conditions evaluated, and authorization can be bypassed);
conditional
(that is, the payer cannot yet determine coverage, prior authorization, or documentation requirements); and
pa-needed = auth-needed
(that is
,
a prior authorization request is required, so the workflow can proceed through DTR and PAS until it is ultimately complete, having been approved or denied). To attest “Yes” for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, the electronic prior authorization request must result in a satisfied, approved, or denied request; submission of a request without receipt of a payer response would not be sufficient. For the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, a MIPS eligible clinician may use one or any subset of the Health IT Modules certified to the electronic prior authorization certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)
,
(32)
, and
(33)
, as necessary to complete a qualifying transaction. This approach accommodates variation in electronic prior authorization workflows based on the medical item or service and the payer's documentation requirements. A MIPS eligible clinician needs to only successfully complete one qualifying electronic prior authorization request for at least one medical item or service during the performance period to attest “Yes” for the measure. We will provide educational and guidance resources, as appropriate and feasible, to clarify qualifying workflows and implementation details.
With respect to the request for clarification about electronic prior authorization functionality delivered through an application connected to CEHRT, we recognize that electronic prior authorization workflows often involve multiple systems and entities, including EHRs, revenue cycle systems, payer systems, clearinghouses, health information exchanges, standards-based intermediaries, and other interoperable technology solutions.
