We received public comment on the proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for advancing the Electronic Prior Authorization measure toward a more complete, standards-
(
printed page 71573)
based electronic prior authorization workflow beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, including use of FHIR-enabled Health IT Modules certified to ONC's electronic prior authorization certification criteria. A few commenters suggested that alignment with standardized, certified electronic prior authorization capabilities would advance interoperability and electronic prior authorization adoption, support care coordination, and reduce administrative burden.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support. We agree that the proposed modifications will advance a more complete, standards-based electronic prior authorization workflow by requiring certified health IT functionality that enables a complete set of actions necessary to support robust electronic prior authorization. We believe this approach will support broader adoption and improve interoperability.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns with the modification to the Electronic Prior Authorization measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year to require completion of the specified electronic prior authorization workflow for at least one medical item or service, excluding drugs. A commenter expressed concerns that the measure holds clinicians accountable for the responsiveness of a payer to a prior authorization request, which is outside of the clinician's control. Several commenters noted that the proposed workflow includes electronic prior authorization functionality supported by the ONC certification criteria for determining coverage requirements, assembling required documentation, submitting the prior authorization request, and receiving a payer response. A few commenters stated that although MIPS eligible clinicians may need to have the capabilities supporting the complete electronic prior authorization workflow available, not every prior authorization request requires use of every capability. Commenters noted that, depending on the circumstances of a particular request, one or more steps may not be necessary to resolve the authorization. For example, an initial coverage requirements exchange may determine that prior authorization is not required or that additional documentation is unnecessary.
Several commenters, therefore, recommended that CMS not require every component of the specified workflow for a given request to satisfy the measure but instead allow MIPS eligible clinicians to use the certified electronic prior authorization capabilities necessary to successfully complete the particular request. Several commenters cautioned that requiring transactions that are not necessary to resolve a particular prior authorization request could add administrative burden to a process that electronic prior authorization is intended to streamline.
Response:
We recognize that individual prior authorization requests may not require every electronic prior authorization capability in all circumstances and that payers may not respond electronically to every prior authorization request made by clinicians. We note that to satisfy the Electronic Prior Authorization measure, a MIPS eligible clinician would attest “Yes” to completing the specified actions for at least one qualifying prior authorization request during the performance period. Successfully meeting the Electronic Prior Authorization measure does not require completion of the specified workflow for every prior authorization request. This approach appropriately advances adoption of the capabilities necessary to support robust, standards-based electronic prior authorization while limiting the reporting requirement to at least one qualifying request.
Comment:
Several commenters requested clarification regarding the proposed requirement, beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, for MIPS eligible clinicians to electronically request and receive coverage requirements, request and populate prior authorization documentation using templates and rules, submit the prior authorization request, and receive the payer response within the same qualifying prior authorization request. Commenters indicated that the actions necessary to complete a given prior authorization request may vary depending on the circumstances of the request and the payer's coverage and documentation requirements.
Several commenters therefore recommended that CMS allow MIPS eligible clinicians to complete only the electronic prior authorization actions necessary to resolve a given prior authorization request, rather than requiring each of the specified actions within the same request. A commenter specifically recommended that requesting and populating prior authorization documentation using templates and rules be required only when the payer requires additional documentation, noting that this action may not be necessary when the payer can complete the authorization without additional documentation.
Response:
We recognize that electronic prior authorization workflows may vary depending on the medical item or service and the payer's coverage and documentation requirements. However, the modifications to the Electronic Prior Authorization measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year are intended to advance the measure from the flexibility provided for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year toward a more complete electronic prior authorization workflow.
To satisfy the Electronic Prior Authorization measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, a MIPS eligible clinician must use CEHRT to electronically request and receive coverage requirements; request and populate prior authorization documentation using templates and rules; submit the prior authorization request; and receive the payer response through a provider Prior Authorization API, with each of these actions occurring within the same qualifying prior authorization request. We note that the Electronic Prior Authorization measure requires a MIPS eligible clinician to attest “Yes” based on at least one qualifying prior authorization request during the performance period; it does not require completion of the specified workflow for every prior authorization request. We recognize that only a subset of prior authorization requests may require the use of all capabilities and that clinicians will continue to conduct prior authorization requests that do not require the complete set of capabilities, consistent with the documentation needs associated with a given prior authorization request.
Accordingly, we disagree with recommendations from commenters that would require only those actions that may be necessary for a particular request, including the recommendation to require the documentation templates and rules action only when additional documentation is otherwise needed. Requiring the specified actions within at least one qualifying request will advance adoption of the capabilities necessary to support a complete, standards-based electronic prior authorization workflow. As noted previously, our intent is to pursue a stepwise expansion of electronic prior authorization capabilities in 2028. The revised measure would enable meeting this goal by ensuring eligible clinicians demonstrate the adoption of these
(
printed page 71574)
capabilities for at least one prior authorization.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns regarding whether MIPS eligible clinicians, payers, and health IT vendors would be sufficiently ready to support the proposed modifications to the Electronic Prior Authorization measure that begin with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. These commenters highlighted the variability in payer, EHR, and health IT vendor readiness as a particular concern given that MIPS eligible clinicians depend on them to support electronic prior authorization transactions. Commenters stated that successful implementation of standardized electronic prior authorization capabilities would require coordination, integration, and testing across MIPS eligible clinicians, health IT developers, payers, and other intermediaries.
A commenter stated that, based on discussions with electronic prior authorization stakeholders, only functionality for coverage requirements determination is expected to be available in the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, with end-to-end electronic prior authorization not expected to become available until at least the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. The commenter cautioned that availability of the technology does not necessarily equate to operational readiness, noting that EHR developers, payers, and intermediaries would need to test end-to-end functionality throughout CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year and that fully operational end-to-end electronic prior authorization may therefore not be realized until the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year at the earliest. Another commenter similarly noted that current implementation efforts are concentrated on coverage requirements discovery and that integrated use of the capabilities needed to support the complete electronic prior authorization workflow remains uncommon. Several commenters recommended that CMS monitor implementation and readiness of electronic prior authorization and adjust the measure requirements or implementation timeline, as needed, based on demonstrated readiness.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback from commenters. In regard to commenters' concerns about ecosystem readiness to support the proposed CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year requirement for MIPS eligible clinicians to use functionality represented by all three specified ONC electronic prior authorization certification criteria for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure. We recognize that successful implementation will require coordination among MIPS eligible clinicians, health IT developers, payers, and other partners, as well as time for development, certification, testing, integration, and workflow redesign. As discussed in sections IV.A.4.d.(4)(f)(v) and IV.B.1.d. of this final rule, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to make the Electronic Prior Authorization measure an optional measure and eligible for bonus points for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. As discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(4)(f)(v) of this final rule, we are also finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to modify the Electronic Prior Authorization measure by requiring a MIPS eligible clinician to use CEHRT to electronically request and receive coverage requirements, request and populate prior authorization documentation using templates and rules, submit the prior authorization request, and receive the payer response through a provider prior authorization API beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. We believe that such step-wise approach will allow participants additional time to gain implementation experience and advance operational readiness. We intend to assess implementation experience and coordinate with ONC and across CMS as standards, certified health IT capabilities, and payer-facing requirements continue to mature.
We further note that under the revised measure starting in the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, we would continue to require the completion of only one prior authorization request consistent with the use of capabilities identified in the revised measure language. Eligible clinicians and health IT developers that need a longer period during CY 2028 to adopt and deploy technology within clinical workflows could continue testing and rollout activities during the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year and successfully complete an action satisfying the measure at the end of the performance period. Additionally, this measure, as proposed, includes exclusions that provide flexibility for MIPS eligible clinicians who may face challenges meeting the measure's requirements, including accommodation for where an applicable payer does not support the specified electronic prior authorization standard.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to modify the Electronic Prior Authorization measure by requiring a MIPS eligible clinician to use CEHRT to electronically request and receive coverage requirements, request and populate prior authorization documentation using templates and rules, submit the prior authorization request, and receive the payer response through a provider prior authorization API beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year.

Consider an example, from the CY 2027 proposed rule, in which a patient is a Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollee who has stable coronary artery disease and new exertional dyspnea (feeling shortness of breath during physical exertion) (

When the cardiologist places an order for a TTE in the EHR, a Health IT Module certified to the “provider prior authorization API—coverage requirements discovery” criterion (

An embedded Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies (SMART) on FHIR app fetches the payer's specific documentation template and rules for oncology prior authorizations. For the PET-CT, the payer's documentation rules ask for the cancer staging information and previous imaging results; the immunotherapy, the payer's documentation rules require the patient's biomarker (for example, PD-L1 expression) status, prior treatment history, and recent lab results. Much of this information can be auto-populated because the embedded DTR app uses Clinical Quality Language (CQL) logic and FHIR queries to pull the patient's latest CT scan report and lab results from her medical record, and it confirms her cancer diagnosis and stage from the problem list. The oncologist answers a few additional questions (such as confirming the patient has no contraindications and that a required biomarker test was positive). By the end of this step, the EHR has compiled all necessary supporting documentation for the prior authorization, ensuring the request will be complete.

The EHR's certified Health IT Module ensures the request conforms to the required FHIR structure and sends it securely. Because all required information was provided up front and matched the plan's coverage criteria, the MA plan's system could potentially automatically adjudicate and approve the requests in near real-time. If that happened, the oncologist could now schedule the patient's therapy without delay, confident that the services are covered.

We received public comment on the proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed support for the proposal to update the Electronic Prior Authorization measure to require use of specific FHIR-enabled Health IT Modules certified to ONC health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)
,
(32)
, and/or (33) to support electronic prior authorization transactions for medical items and services, excluding drugs. The commenters supported alignment of the measure with the specified ONC health IT certification criteria, which are based on the HL7 Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), and Prior Authorization Support (PAS) implementation guides and support different aspects of an electronic prior authorization workflow. Commenters stated that use of standardized, certified functionality could support interoperable electronic prior authorization workflows and reduce administrative burden.
A commenter specifically supported requiring the complete electronic prior authorization workflow supported by CRD, DTR, and PAS. A few commenters also supported the proposed implementation flexibility provided under the proposed CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year measure specifications, under which MIPS eligible clinicians could use one or more certified Health IT Modules as necessary to support the applicable electronic prior authorization workflow.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters. We agree with commenters that aligning the Electronic Prior Authorization measure with ONC's electronic prior authorization certification criteria will promote use of standardized, interoperable functionality that supports electronic prior authorization workflows. Also, we
(
printed page 71577)
agree with commenters that allowing MIPS eligible clinicians, for the CY 2027 performance period/CY 2029 MIPS payment year, to use one or more certified Health IT Modules as necessary to complete a qualifying electronic prior authorization request provides appropriate implementation flexibility as these capabilities continue to mature and become integrated into clinical workflows.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns or requested clarification regarding the proposed requirement for MIPS eligible clinicians to use CEHRT that includes Health IT Modules certified to the ONC electronic prior authorization certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)
,
(32)
, and
(33)
. Commenters discussed the role of the three certification criteria as the technical foundation for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure, noting that the criteria correspond to the CRD, DTR, and PAS implementation guides and support different components of the electronic prior authorization workflow.
Several commenters requested clarification regarding how the certified functionality would be used or interpreted for purposes of satisfying the measure, including whether the measure may be satisfied using CRD, DTR, PAS, or a combination of these capabilities. A few commenters specifically recommended that a CRD response, indicating prior authorization is not required, should qualify as a successful transaction rather than requiring subsequent DTR or PAS functionality; the commenters noted that electronically determining prior authorization is not required provides useful information and can avoid unnecessary documentation, payer portal checks, phone calls, and other administrative processes. A commenter requested clarification regarding whether conforming electronic prior authorization functionality delivered through an application connected to CEHRT, rather than embedded within CEHRT itself, may satisfy the measure. Another commenter requested clarification regarding what constitutes a “decision or determination response,” including whether payer responses requiring further interaction outside the electronic workflow, such as a peer-to-peer review or referral to a delegated benefit manager, may satisfy the measure.
Response:
The ONC health IT certification criteria at
45 CFR 170.315(g)(31)
,
(32)
, and
(33)
support different components of an electronic prior authorization workflow, including coverage requirements discovery, documentation templates and rules, and prior authorization support. For the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, a MIPS eligible clinician could use one or more certified Health IT Modules, as necessary to complete a qualifying prior authorization request. Beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, clinicians would be required to use health IT that is certified to all three certification criteria to complete the actions specified in the measure within the same qualifying prior authorization request.
We disagree with commenters that a coverage requirement response indicating that prior authorization is not required should independently satisfy the Electronic Prior Authorization measure. A medical item or service that the payer determines does not require prior authorization is not within the scope of the measure because no prior authorization request is required or submitted. Although electronically determining whether prior authorization is required is an important component of the electronic prior authorization workflow, such a response would not satisfy the Electronic Prior Authorization measure for the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year due to the documentation and prior authorization submission actions specified in the measure would not occur.
With respect to how the certified functionality may be implemented, the intent is not to prohibit the use of applications, intermediaries, or other interoperable tools that are integrated with CEHRT and support the electronic prior authorization workflow. Rather, the Electronic Prior Authorization measure is intended to ensure that MIPS eligible clinicians have access to, and use, standards-based health IT functionality certified to ONC's electronic prior authorization health IT certification criteria to complete the required measure actions. Such approach supports a consistent technical foundation for electronic prior authorization within clinician workflows, while allowing Health IT Modules certified to the relevant criteria to be deployed in configurations that meet the operational needs of a MIPS eligible clinician.
Also, we clarify that receipt of a payer response does not require approval of the prior authorization request. A qualifying request may result in an approval or denial, provided that the MIPS eligible clinician completes the applicable measure requirements and receives the payer's decision or determination response through the provider Prior Authorization API. Where the payer's response indicates that additional documentation or other electronic action is needed before a decision can be made, the MIPS eligible clinician would need to complete the applicable workflow actions for the request to satisfy the measure. We will provide educational and guidance resources, as appropriate and feasible, to support consistent implementation and reporting.
Comment:
Several commenters raised concerns about ecosystem readiness to support the proposed use of FHIR-enabled Health IT Modules certified to the ONC health IT certification criteria for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure. Specific concerns included ongoing interoperability challenges, limited payer readiness to support FHIR-based prior authorization, and EHR developers that are still building, testing, and refining connectivity to payer Prior Authorization APIs at scale. A commenter requested further guidance on how clinicians and EHR developers would identify and connect to payer API endpoints and raised concerns that some payers may continue to rely on existing portal-based processes rather than transition to API-enabled exchange.
A few commenters specifically raised concerns about the maturity of the CRD, DTR, and PAS capabilities needed to support the proposed certified health IT requirements. Some commenters also recommended that CMS allow additional time for implementation of the certified health IT requirements and align implementation timelines with the availability and readiness of the required functionality.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns regarding the readiness of the health IT ecosystem to support standards-based electronic prior authorization. We recognize that successful implementation of the Electronic Prior Authorization measure depends on coordination among MIPS eligible clinicians, health IT developers, payers, intermediaries, and other partners, as well as on technical development, testing, workflow integration, training, and operational support.
The proposed phased approach appropriately balances these considerations with the goal of advancing interoperable electronic prior authorization. For the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, we are finalizing our proposal to make the Electronic Prior Authorization measure optional and eligible for bonus points, allowing MIPS eligible clinicians and their health IT developers additional flexibility to implement, test, and gain experience with certified electronic prior authorization capabilities before the measure would be required beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. For the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians could use one or more certified Health IT Modules, as necessary to complete a qualifying electronic prior authorization request.
We acknowledge commenters' concerns regarding the maturity of integrated CRD, DTR, and PAS capabilities and agree that ongoing coordination among CMS, ONC, payers, health IT developers, and clinicians will be important. We intend to assess implementation experience and consider recommendations from commenters as we develop educational and guidance resources, as appropriate and feasible. The measure is intended to advance the availability and use of standards-based, certified electronic prior authorization functionality through CEHRT, while supporting a transition away from fragmented and manual prior authorization processes.

Comment:

Many commenters expressed appreciation that making the Electronic Prior Authorization measure optional for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year would allow additional time and flexibility to ensure payer, health IT developer, and physician readiness, including testing and operationalizing electronic prior authorization workflows. A few commenters specifically supported making the measure eligible for bonus points during the CY 2027 performance period, noting that the incentive could encourage early adoption of electronic prior authorization. A commenter stated that the bonus opportunity would further strengthen incentives for clinicians to use electronic prior authorization tools associated with the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule.
A few commenters supported the phased implementation approach, noting its alignment with previously implemented Promoting Interoperability measures and the Electronic Prior Authorization measure proposed for the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program in the FY 2027 IPPS/LTCH PPS proposed rule. A few commenters also stated that optional reporting would provide time for practices to prepare for implementation of the modified measure requirements, particularly small, rural, and other under-resourced practices. A few commenters noted that the optional reporting approach could reduce reporting burden while providing practices additional time to implement evolving interoperability requirements.
Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters regarding the proposal to make the Electronic Prior Authorization measure optional and
(
printed page 71580)
eligible for bonus points for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. We agree with commenters that the phased approach would provide MIPS eligible clinicians, payers, and health IT developers additional flexibility and incentive implementation, testing, and operationalization of electronic prior authorization capabilities and workflows before the modified measure requirements would apply beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year.
Also, we agree with commenters that the optional reporting period may be particularly beneficial for small, rural, and other under-resourced practices by providing additional time to prepare for evolving interoperability requirements while encouraging early adoption of standards-based electronic prior authorization.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns about ecosystem readiness during the CY 2027 performance period to support the Electronic Prior Authorization measure. A few commenters noted that MIPS eligible clinicians depend on factors outside their control, including payer API readiness, availability of certified health IT, vendor implementation timelines, and integration of electronic prior authorization functionality into provider workflows. A few commenters also raised concerns about alignment between provider-side and payer standards and the resulting challenges for workflow integration across the industry.
Commenters noted that these dependencies may require additional implementation time and supported flexibility during the CY 2027 performance period to allow clinicians, payers, and health IT developers to gain experience and advance operational readiness. A few commenters specifically emphasized the need for additional flexibility for small, rural, and under-resourced practices as electronic prior authorization capabilities continue to mature.
Response:
We recognize that successful implementation of electronic prior authorization depends on alignment among MIPS eligible clinicians, health IT developers, and payers. We intend for the implementation of the Electronic Prior Authorization measure to encourage continued progress toward broader implementation and workflow integration across the ecosystem. With regard to concerns about readiness, we note that one year of reporting the Electronic Prior Authorization measure as an optional bonus measure provides sufficient time for MIPS eligible clinicians, including small, rural, and under-resource practices, to successfully deploy and test EHR upgrades by working with vendors, and to address any current challenges to electronic prior authorization implementation. The optional bonus year will also provide MIPS eligible clinicians with the opportunity to gain experience with and become familiar with the Electronic Prior Authorization measure without facing a penalty.
Comment:
A few commenters recommended extending the optional reporting period beyond the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year or delaying mandatory reporting until CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year or later, to allow adequate time for configuration, testing, training, and maturation of electronic prior authorization workflows across MIPS eligible clinicians, payers, EHR developers, and clearinghouses, and to allow practices and providers to become familiar with the Electronic Prior Authorization measure. Several commenters recommended that CMS assess payer, health IT developer, and MIPS eligible clinician readiness to inform implementation of the measure.
A few commenters also recommended aligning the implementation timeline for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure for medical items and services with the proposed Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, noting that aligned timelines could allow EHR implementation activities for the two measures to occur concurrently.
Response:
We appreciate feedback from commenters regarding the implementation timeline. We believe that making the measure an optional measure and eligible for 10 bonus points for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year provides appropriate implementation flexibility before the measure becomes required beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. We intend to assess implementation experience, payer and health IT readiness, technological advancements, and the availability of ONC-certified health IT as the measure is implemented. Also, we recognize the benefits of aligning implementation activities with the proposed Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, which is reflected in our final policies because the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure would also be required beginning in the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to modify the Electronic Prior Authorization measure to be an optional measure and eligible for 10 bonus points for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year.

Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal to require the Electronic Prior Authorization measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, with some commenters specifically supporting the phased approach of allowing optional reporting for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year before transitioning to mandatory reporting for the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. Response:
We appreciate the support from commenters. We agree with commenters that making the Electronic Prior Authorization measure optional for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year before requiring it beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year provides an appropriate phased approach to advance adoption of standards-based electronic prior authorization. We believe requiring the measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year will support MIPS eligible clinicians' use of the Prior Authorization APIs that applicable payers must implement and maintain, promote broader adoption and interoperability, and help reduce administrative burden. Comment:
Many commenters either opposed making the Electronic Prior Authorization measure mandatory beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year or recommended delaying mandatory reporting until the CY 2029 performance period/2031 MIPS payment year or later. A few commenters expressed concern that changing measure specifications for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure while making it a mandatory measure and adding a new Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure in the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year may add operational and technical burden for clinicians, specifically as a result of
(
printed page 71582)
having to update developer workflows. Several commenters recommended extending optional reporting of the Electronic Prior Authorization measure beyond the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. Several commenters requested that CMS use the period of optional reporting to evaluate real-world implementation and ecosystem readiness before transitioning to mandatory reporting. A commenter specifically recommended that CMS assess the number of impacted payers operating a conformant prior authorization API as a measure of ecosystem readiness. A few commenters noted that implementation challenges may be particularly significant for small, rural, and other resource constrained practices.
Response:
We recognize that successful implementation depends on coordination across the healthcare ecosystem, including the availability and deployment of certified health IT and payer support for electronic prior authorization transactions. However, we believe that making the Electronic Prior Authorization measure optional and eligible for bonus points for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year provides an appropriate transition to required reporting beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. The optional reporting year provides MIPS eligible clinicians, including small, rural, and other resource-constrained practices, an opportunity to gain experience with the measure, work with health IT developers to deploy and test necessary capabilities, and address implementation challenges without a negative effect on their Promoting Interoperability performance category score. Additionally, we believe the modifications to the Electronic Prior Authorization measure and the implementation of the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure are appropriate and necessary to advance more consistent electronic prior authorization processes across care settings. We expect these concurrent measure additions will promote greater standardization and interoperability over time, which would ultimately reduce manual processes, duplicative work, and administrative burden on clinicians.
We intend to assess implementation experience, payer and health IT readiness, technological advancements, and the availability of ONC-certified health IT as the measure is implemented. Requiring the measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year will support MIPS eligible clinicians' use of the Prior Authorization APIs that applicable payers must implement and maintain and advance broader adoption of standards-based electronic prior authorization.

We received public comment on the proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our response.
Comment:
Many commenters did not support the proposed scoring methodology for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure and expressed concerns regarding the scoring methodology for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, specifically, the provision that would consequently cause a MIPS eligible clinician to receive a score of zero for the entire Promoting Interoperability performance category if a MIPS eligible clinician attests “No” for the measure, fails to report the measure, or does not claim an applicable exclusion. The commenters described such consequence as disproportionate, particularly when successful reporting for the measure may depend on readiness factors that are outside the control of MIPS eligible clinicians. A few commenters supported the proposal to not assign points for the proposed Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, while a few commenters recommended changing the proposed scoring approach, including assigning points to the measure once it becomes required, in which the failure to meet the measure requirements would result in the loss of measure points rather than receiving a score of zero for the entire Promoting Interoperability performance category. A few commenters recommended that CMS make the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure optional and eligible for bonus points during the initial implementation of the measure to encourage early adoption.
Response:
We appreciate the feedback from commenters regarding the proposed scoring methodology for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year. We recognize that successful use of standards-based electronic prior authorization depends on coordination among MIPS eligible clinicians, payers, health IT developers, intermediaries, and other entities, and that some implementation challenges may be outside the control of individual MIPS eligible clinicians. However, we believe that requiring an attestation of a “Yes” response for meeting the measure requirements or allowing for an applicable exclusion to be claimed, which would result in the measure not being scored or contributing to the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category score beginning with the CY 2028 performance period/2030 MIPS payment year, is an appropriate scoring approach to encourage adoption of electronic prior authorization for prescription drugs, which provides valuable information in assessing meaningful use of CEHRT under the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. Additionally, as we aim to provide consistency and reduce complexity in scoring, such approach aligns with the scoring methodology for other required measures in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category in which a MIPS eligible clinician who does not affirmatively attest (submission of a “Yes” response) to meeting the requirements of a required measure or claim an applicable exclusion receives a score of zero for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category.
We intend to assess implementation experience, payer and health IT readiness, technological advancements, and the availability of ONC-certified health IT as the measure is implemented.
After consideration of public comment, we are finalizing, as proposed, the proposal to establish the scoring methodology for the Electronic Prior Authorization for Prescription Drugs measure, in which the measure would be included as a requirement under the Health Information Exchange objective. For MIPS eligible clinicians affirmatively attesting to meeting the Electronic Prior Authorization measure requirements or claiming an applicable exclusion, the measure will not affect the total score for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category. If a MIPS eligible clinician submits a “No” response for the attestation-based measure, fails to submit an attestation for the measure, or fails to claim an applicable exclusion, then the MIPS eligible clinician will receive a score of zero for the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category and will not be considered a meaningful EHR user for MIPS for the applicable performance period. B. MIPS Final Score Methodology
1. Performance Category Scores
a. Background
Sections 1848(q)(1)(A)(i) and (ii) and (5)(A) of the Act provide, in relevant part, that the Secretary shall develop a methodology for assessing the total performance of each MIPS eligible clinician according to certain specified performance standards and, using such methodology, provide for a final score for each MIPS eligible clinician. Section 1848(q)(2)(A)(i) of the Act requires us to use the quality performance category in determining each MIPS eligible clinician's final score, and section 1848(q)(2)(B)(i) of the Act describes the measures and activities that must be specified under the quality performance category. The statute does not specify the number of quality measures on which a MIPS eligible clinician must report, nor does it specify the amount or type of information that a MIPS eligible clinician must report on each quality measure.
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44198
through

Moreover, we proposed policies to modify the benchmarks for Medicare CQMs and apply flat benchmarks to Medicare eCQMs that are consistent with the proposed Medicare eCQM collection type in section III.G.3.d.(3) of this final rule. In this section, we also proposed policy to update scoring for the Electronic Prior Authorization measure in the Promoting Interoperability performance category. Lastly, we also included a request for information (RFI) on the future direction of MVP scoring policies. Specifically, we proposed to:
Establish a policy for scoring MIPS core measures;
Apply the defined topped out benchmark for certain topped out measures for clinicians impacted by limited measure choice;
Apply the defined topped out benchmark for topped out MIPS core measures;
Modify the publishing location of topped out measures impacted by limited measure choice and scored according to the defined topped out benchmark;
Modify the flat benchmarking methodology for the Medicare CQMs collection type;
Establish a flat benchmarking methodology for the Medicare eCQMs collection type;
Modify the Electronic Prior Authorization measure from a required measure to an optional measure under the Promoting Interoperability performance category for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year.
and

As discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule, clinicians who attest to not having an applicable and available MIPS core measure will still need to report enough measures to meet the required number of six quality measures in traditional MIPS or four quality measures in MVP

As discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule, there may be instances in which a clinician attested to not having an applicable and available MIPS core measure, but new information or changing circumstances later made it so that the clinician does have an applicable and available MIPS core measure to report. To account for these cases, if an attestation is submitted during data submission and a MIPS core measure is also reported, we will score the MIPS core measure as one of the six required quality measures in traditional MIPS reporting or one of the four required quality measures in MVP reporting. If a MIPS eligible clinician submits data for more than one MIPS core measure, we will use the highest scoring MIPS core measure as one of the six or four quality measures, and the remaining scored measures will consist of either the five highest scoring quality measures or the three highest scoring measures, as applicable, in traditional MIPS and MVP reporting.
In section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(ii) of this final rule, we are finalizing our proposal to remove the current quality measure data submission requirement of one outcome measure (or, if an outcome measure is not available, one high priority measure) for traditional MIPS and MVP reporting and replace the requirement with a MIPS core measure data submission requirement. As discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule, one of the factors considered for the MIPS core measure selection included an emphasis on whether the measure is an outcome-based measure. We refer readers to section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule for additional details on the designation of MIPS core measures. In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44199
and
44200
), we proposed to assign zero measure achievement points for one quality measure if clinicians reporting traditional MIPS or MVP do not submit a MIPS core measure and do not attest during data submission that they do not have an available and applicable MIPS core measure. This proposal is consistent with the existing rule under § 414.1380(b)(1)(i). Under the existing policy under § 414.1380(b)(1)(i), MIPS eligible clinicians who submit data in accordance with § 414.1325 on a greater number of measures than required under § 414.1335 are scored only on the measures with the greatest number of measure achievement points. Therefore, we did not propose any changes to the regulatory text for this proposal.
We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter supported the proposal to keep the scoring methodology consistent in the transition to MIPS core measures. A commenter supported using the highest scoring MIPS core measure for clinicians who submit more than one MIPS core measure.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that CMS not score zero points during the initial MIPS core measure implementation period to allow time for clinicians to update workflows to support the attestation and evaluate the applicability and burden associated with MIPS core measure reporting before incorporating such measures into scoring methodologies. A commenter requested that CMS provide information and notice as part of the annual performance feedback for clinicians who did not meet the MIPS core measure data submission requirement and are assigned zero measure achievement points.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' concerns that clinicians may need to assess the applicability of the MIPS core measures, update workflows, and become familiar with the process for indicating that a required MIPS core measure is not available or applicable. However, assigning zero measure achievement points when a required MIPS core measure is applicable, but the data submission requirement is not satisfied, is necessary to ensure that the MIPS core measure data submission requirement is meaningful and applied consistently across MIPS eligible clinicians. Additionally, we believe that clinician workflows will be able to support this policy because it is consistent with the existing policy under § 414.1380(b)(1) that MIPS eligible clinicians receive zero measure achievement points for each measure required under § 414.1335, on which no data is submitted in accordance with § 414.1325. As discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(i) of this final rule, the MIPS core measure inventory includes outcome measures or measures previously identified as high priority, and the MIPS core measure data submission requirement will replace the existing data submission requirement to report an outcome or high priority measure. Where a MIPS core measure is not available or applicable, clinicians may attest as such using the process defined in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule.
We also appreciate the commenters' interest in having an opportunity to evaluate the burden associated with MIPS core measure reporting and to gain experience with the applicable attestation requirements. We will continue to monitor implementation of the MIPS core measure data submission requirements, including clinician experience with the attestation process, reporting burden, and available submission and performance data. We refer readers to sections V.B.7.b.(1) and V.B.7.c.(1) for the discussion that we are not adjusting our burden estimates due to this policy.
Comment:
A few commenters did not support the proposal to assign zero achievement points if no MIPS core measure or attestation is submitted. A commenter expressed concern with the proposal since eCQM MIPS core measures are not available for every MVP.
Response:
Assigning zero measure achievement points when an applicable MIPS core measure is required but the data submission requirement is not satisfied is necessary to ensure that the MIPS core measure data submission requirement is meaningful and applied consistently across MIPS eligible clinicians. Without a scoring policy for not meeting the MIPS core measure data submission requirement, the requirement would have limited effect in promoting consistent reporting of MIPS core measures.
We recognize that the availability and applicability of MIPS core measures may vary, such as when no eCQM MIPS core measures are available in an MVP, which is why the data submission requirement as described in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule, does not require a clinician to report a MIPS core measure that is not available or applicable to the clinician. The clinician may attest to that circumstance and would not be assigned zero measure achievement points solely because the MIPS core measure was not available or applicable.
Comment:
A commenter requested confirmation that an attestation stating that no applicable MIPS core measure exists would not result in the assignment of zero achievement points. A commenter suggested that CMS should not assign zero achievement points for not reporting a MIPS core measure until CMS has established clear applicability guidance and provided clinicians with an opportunity to correct
(
printed page 71604)
a submission if a measure applicability determination is not accepted. A commenter requested that CMS ensure that MIPS core measure scoring reflects the diversity and complexity of practices while supporting meaningful comparisons across clinicians.
Response:
We agree that clear information regarding the applicability of MIPS core measures is important to support accurate reporting and scoring. As described in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule, when a MIPS core measure is not available or applicable, a MIPS eligible clinician may attest that the measure is not available or applicable. A MIPS eligible clinician who submits such an attestation that they do not have an available and applicable MIPS core measure would not be assigned zero measure achievement points for one quality measure in traditional MIPS or MVP as long as they report enough measures to meet the required number of six quality measures or a complete specialty measure set in traditional MIPS or four quality measures in MVP reporting. We recognize the importance of providing clinicians with sufficient information to understand the MIPS core measure data submission requirements, including the circumstances under which a MIPS core measure may be considered not available or applicable, as discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule. We will continue to provide guidance and resources, as appropriate, to support clinicians in understanding and satisfying these requirements. After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed to assign zero measure achievement points for one quality measure if clinicians reporting traditional MIPS or MVP do not submit a MIPS core measure and do not attest during data submission that they do not have an available and applicable MIPS core measure. A MIPS eligible clinician who submits an attestation that they do not have an available and applicable MIPS core measure would not be assigned zero measure achievement points for one quality measure in traditional MIPS or MVP reporting as long as they report enough measures to meet the required number of six quality measures or a complete specialty measure set in traditional MIPS or four quality measures in MVP reporting. This policy is consistent with the existing § 414.1380(b)(1)(i).
(2) Small Practice Scoring Exemption Clarification for MIPS Core Measures
Historically, we have heard from clinicians in small practices that they face unique challenges to successfully participate in MIPS. To further support clinicians in small practices, who often have limited resources to successfully participate in MIPS, we implemented policies to provide them with more flexibilities. For example, as described under § 414.1380(b)(1)(v)(C), beginning with the CY 2019 performance period/2021 MIPS payment year, MIPS eligible clinicians in small practices receive six measure bonus points if they submit data to MIPS on at least one quality measure. To continue the existing flexibilities and further support clinicians in small practices, we are finalizing in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(C) of this final rule, that small practice clinicians participating in both traditional MIPS and MVP reporting would be exempt from the MIPS core measure reporting requirement. Under this exemption, clinicians in small practices are not required to submit a MIPS core measure and will not need to attest during data submission if they do not have an available and applicable MIPS core measure. The existing regulation text under § 414.1380(b)(1)(i) states that MIPS eligible clinicians receive zero measure achievement points for each measure required under § 414.1335 for which no data is submitted in accordance with § 414.1325. Consistent with the existing regulation at § 414.1380(b)(1)(i) and given the finalization of the proposal to exempt small practices from the MIPS core measure requirement in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(C) of this final rule, we will not assign zero measure achievement points for one MIPS core measure if clinicians in small practices do not submit data for such measure in traditional MIPS and MVP reporting. If a small practice chooses to submit data on a MIPS core measure, we will include the MIPS core measure in the quality performance category score only if the MIPS core measure is one of the six highest scoring measures in traditional MIPS or one of the four highest scoring measures in MVP reporting, in accordance with the existing regulation under § 414.1380(b)(1)(i). We refer readers to Appendix 1: MIPS Quality Measures and Appendix 3: MVP Inventory of this final rule for details on the MIPS core measures inventory for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year.
We received public comments on the proposal that small practice clinicians participating in both traditional MIPS and MVP reporting would be exempt from the MIPS core measure reporting requirement. We refer readers to section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(C) of this final rule for discussion of the public comments received.

Topped out measures are measures for which measure performance is considered so high and unvarying that meaningful distinctions and improvements in performance can no longer be made (
81 FR 77136

Section 1848(q)(3)(B) of the Act requires that in establishing performance standards with respect to measures and activities, we consider, among other things, the opportunity for continued improvement. Topped out measures do not provide an opportunity for continued improvement, nor do payment adjustments based on topped out measures incentivize clinicians to improve their care. As a result, we finalized policies in the CY 2018 Quality Payment Program final rule (

Additionally, we established policies for the removal of topped out measures, such as establishing the topped out measure lifecycle, to continue to drive quality improvement in areas where such improvement is possible and necessary. through

We established at § 414.1380(b)(1)(iv)(B) that we will cap scoring for topped out measures at 7 measure achievement points in the second consecutive year that the measure benchmark is identified as topped out. If a measure has been identified as topped out for three consecutive years after being originally identified through the benchmarks, such measure may then be proposed for removal through notice-and-comment rulemaking (

In the CY 2025 PFS final rule, we finalized at § 414.1380(b)(1)(ii)(E) that beginning with the CY 2025 performance period/2027 MIPS payment year, we will annually publish a list in the

Measures included in the list are scored from 1 to 10 measure achievement points according to defined topped out measure benchmarks calculated from performance data in the baseline period, in which a performance rate of 97 percent corresponds to 10 percent of the performance threshold for the corresponding performance year.
In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (

We finalized that each specialty measure set and MVP is reviewed by collection type to identify if the prevalence of topped out measures within such a set of measures hinders a clinician's ability to successfully participate in the MIPS quality performance category. To make such a determination, we finalized a policy stating that we will analyze the ability of clinicians reporting the specialty measure sets and MVPs to reasonably achieve 75 percent of available quality achievement points based upon the measures available to them and program requirements. Specifically, at the collection type level, each measure is assigned points based upon the current benchmarking data: new measures receive 7 or 5 points based on year in the program, measures with benchmarks are given points based upon the highest decile achievable with a less than perfect score (less than 100 percent or greater than 0 percent for inverse measures), and measures with no available historic benchmark are given 0 points. All measure set points are added together to get an output of scoring potential; the Medicare Part B claims collection type measure sets have an additional 6 points added to the output to account for the small practice bonus. The sum of quality achievement points for each specialty measure set and MVP are then compared to the analysis threshold of 75 percent of available quality achievement points, based on the number of available measures. Any specialty measure sets or MVPs that are unable to meet or exceed the analysis threshold are flagged as “at-risk.” Additional factors that we take into consideration include whether the topped out measure is considered a cross-cutting measure or is a broadly applicable measure, which we consider to be a measure included in three or more specialty sets or MVPs. We also consider whether the specialty measure set or MVP contains more than ten measures, by collection type (

Comment:
Many commenters supported the proposed list of measures subject to the defined topped out measure benchmark for the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year. Commenters expressed their belief that the defined topped out measure benchmark will provide scoring relief for clinicians who feel compelled to report topped out measures with the 7-point scoring cap due to limited measure choice.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support.
Comment:
Several commenters suggested CMS expand the criteria for measures impacted by limited measure choice and apply the defined topped out measure benchmark to additional topped out measures, including measures that do not meet the previously finalized criteria for topped out measures impacted by limited measure choice. Several commenters suggested CMS apply the defined topped out measure benchmark to all topped out measures. Commenters cited their belief that limiting the application of the defined topped out measure benchmark to a subset of topped out measures impacted by limited measure choice adds complexity, creates inequitable scoring opportunities across specialties, and does not fairly reward high performance on topped out measures. A commenter recommended that QCDR measures should be included in the defined topped out measure benchmark policy.
Response:
The defined topped out measure benchmark is applied to measures impacted by limited measure choice, as determined by criteria finalized in the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98432
through

90 FR 49904
through
49908

We believe that encouraging clinicians to report non-topped out measures outweighs the complexity of only scoring some topped out measures using the defined topped out measure benchmark, and applying the defined topped out measure benchmark to all topped out measures may lead to increased reporting of topped out measures and increased quality performance category scores and the overall final scores. Because topped out measures do not provide an opportunity for continued improvement, nor do payment adjustments based on topped out measures incentivize clinicians to improve their care, we continue to believe the 7-point topped out measure scoring cap is appropriate. We will continue to monitor the impact of the topped out measure scoring cap and conduct future assessments to determine whether the criteria should be updated. In section IV.B.1.a.(3)(c) of this final rule, we are finalizing MIPS core measures in their second or more consecutive year of being topped out will also be scored using the defined topped out benchmark, which will provide additional scoring relief for clinicians reporting topped out MIPS core measures. There were 19 proposed MIPS core measures that are topped out and subject to the 7-point topped out measure scoring cap for the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year. 89 FR 98428
through
98435

(

to a benchmark calculated from performance data in the baseline period in which a performance rate of 97 percent corresponds to 10 percent of the performance threshold for the corresponding performance year.
The prevalence of topped out MIPS core measures, combined with the limited measure choice associated with MIPS core measures, could result in a clinician being compelled to report a topped out MIPS core measure as one of their six required quality measures in traditional MIPS or one of their four required quality measures in MVP reporting. Given the combination of limited measure choice and the 7-point scoring cap for topped out measures, we are concerned that the application of the 7-point scoring cap to topped out MIPS core measures would penalize clinicians for complying with the MIPS core measure reporting requirement. Therefore, we proposed in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44203
) that MIPS core measures in their second or more consecutive year of being topped out would not be subject to the 7-point topped out measure scoring cap, and instead the measures would be scored from 1 to 10 measure achievement points according to the defined topped out benchmark.
Subsequently, we proposed to create the scoring methodology for MIPS core measures that are topped out. Thus, we proposed to amend and codify at § 414.1380(b)(1)(ii) by establishing a new provision at § 414.1380(b)(1)(ii)(H), which would establish the scoring (1 to 10 measure achievement points) for MIPS core measures that have benchmarks identified as topped out for 2 or more consecutive years. Specifically, we proposed to establish and codify at § 414.1380(b)(1)(ii)(H), which would determine the following: Beginning in the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, MIPS core measures, which are required under § 414.1335(a)(1)(i) and (ii), for which the benchmark for the applicable collection type is identified as topped out for 2 or more consecutive years, are scored from 1 to 10 measure achievement points according to defined topped out measure benchmarks calculated from performance data in the baseline period in which a performance rate of 97 percent corresponds to 10 percent of the performance threshold for the corresponding performance year. Also, we proposed for MIPS core measures not to be subject to the 7-point topped out measure scoring cap. Specifically, we proposed to amend and codify at § 414.1380(b)(1)(iv) by establishing a new provision at § 414.1380(b)(1)(iv)(D), which would determine the following: Beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, MIPS core measures, which are required under § 414.1335(a)(1)(i) and (ii), are not subject to the 7 measure achievement point cap specified at § 414.1380(b)(1)(iv)(B).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed support for the proposal that MIPS core measures in their second or more consecutive year of being topped out would not be subject to the 7-point topped out measure scoring cap, and instead the measures would be scored from 1 to 10 measure achievement points according to the defined topped out benchmark. Commenters expressed their belief that the 7-point topped out scoring cap would unfairly limit scoring opportunities for MIPS core measures because of the MIPS core measure reporting requirement, as discussed in section IV.A.4.d.(1)(c)(iii)(B) of this final rule.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support.
Comment:
A few commenters requested clarification regarding whether the proposal to score MIPS core measures in their second or more consecutive year of being topped out according to the defined topped out benchmark would apply to all measures designated as MIPS core measures, even, for example, when reported via an MVP in which the measure is not a MIPS core measure for that MVP, but the measure is a MIPS core measure in another MVP. A commenter also requested clarification regarding whether the topped out MIPS core measure would be scored with the defined topped out measure benchmark if a clinician reports more than one MIPS core measure.
Response:
The defined topped out measure benchmark will be applied to all measures designated as MIPS core measures that are in their second or more consecutive year of being topped out. The defined topped out measure benchmark will be applied every time the measure is reported, even if the measure is not designated as a MIPS core measure in the MVP being reported, and even if a clinician has additionally reported other MIPS core measures.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern that scoring MIPS core measures in their second or more consecutive year of being topped out from 1 to 10 measure achievement points according to the defined topped out benchmark would not adequately address the scoring limitations of topped out MIPS core measures, citing their belief that the heavily skewed distribution of topped out measure performance limits a clinician's ability to earn a high score if their performance rate is below 100 percent.
Response:
The defined topped out measure benchmark, as described in the CY 2025 PFS final rule (
89 FR 98429
), is intended to address the heavily skewed performance distribution of topped out measures. Specifically, the defined topped out benchmark aims, for clinicians with limited measure availability, to continue to account for high performance without capping the scoring potential at 7 point for exceptional performers and offers better scoring opportunities for those performing higher than the median score in the distribution. . A performance rate of 97 percent corresponds to a score equivalent to 10 percent of the performance threshold. For example, if the performance threshold is 75, a performance rate of 97 percent would earn 7.5 measure achievement points. A clinician with a performance rate of 98-99 percent would earn 8-9 measure achievement points, which rewards clinicians with high performance.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing as proposed that MIPS core measures in their second or more consecutive year of being topped out would not be subject to the 7-point topped out measure scoring cap, and instead the measures would be scored from 1 to 10 measure achievement points according to the defined topped out benchmark.

https://qpp.cms.gov/​
).

2. Further Clarify in Regulation Text That Health IT Vendors Can Not Submit Data Beginning With the CY 2025 Performance Period/2027 MIPS Payment Year and That Preexisting Requirements for Health IT Vendors No Longer Apply
In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77377
through
77382
), we established the category of health IT vendors as a type of third-party intermediary in the Quality Payment Program. In the CY 2019 PFS final rule, we codified the definition of a health IT vendor as an entity that supports the health IT requirements on behalf of a MIPS eligible clinician (including obtaining data from a MIPS eligible clinician's Certified Electronic Health Record Technology (CEHRT) (
83 FR 59907
). In the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65541
), we finalized a reorganization of the regulatory text governing third-party intermediaries to improve clarity and readability. In that revised text, we established general requirements at § 414.1400(a), additional requirements for QCDRs and qualified registries at § 414.1400(b), and additional requirements for health IT vendors at § 414.1400(c).
The CY 2024 PFS final rule removed health IT vendors from the category of third-party intermediaries in the Quality Payment Program beginning in the CY 2025 performance period/2027 MIPS payment year at § 414.1400(a)(1)(iii) (
88 FR 79390
and
79391
). We noted that the removal of health IT vendors from the definition of third-party intermediary would not preclude the vendors from assisting MIPS eligible clinicians with reporting under the program by providing their technology for clinicians to directly report under MIPS. We also noted that removing the category of health IT vendor as a distinct type of third-party intermediary created a clearer distinction between (1) vendors that are submitting data to CMS for the purposes of MIPS and must meet the requirements of a qualified registry or QCDR, and (2) vendors that work with clinicians through the sale and support of health IT permitting the clinician or group to submit the data.
We recognize that § 414.1400(c)(1) outlines additional requirements for health IT vendors submitting data for the MIPS performance category beginning with the CY 2021 performance period/2023 MIPS payment year even though we removed the category of health IT vendors for the Quality Payment Program beginning in the CY 2025 performance period/2027 MIPS payment year at § 414.1400(a)(1)(iii). These requirements being left in the regulation text caused confusion for some organizations interested in serving as third-party intermediaries because it was not clear that these additional requirements for health IT vendors were no longer in place. If an organization that was previously under the health IT vendor category as a third-party intermediary would like to continue serving as a
(
printed page 71615)
third-party intermediary for the Quality Payment Program, they must meet the requirements to become a qualified registry or QCDR. Therefore, to reduce confusion and further clarify our existing policies, in the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule (
91 FR 44208
), we proposed to add at § 414.1400(c)(2) that beginning with the CY 2025 performance period/CY 2027 MIPS payment year, health IT vendors cannot submit MIPS data unless they meet the requirements for a qualified registry or QCDR. We also proposed to modify § 414.1400(c)(1) to clarify that the additional requirements for health IT vendors only apply for the CY 2021 performance period/CY 2023 MIPS payment year through the CY 2024 performance period/2026 MIPS payment year, when health IT vendors were still a separate type of third-party intermediaries.
We received a public comment on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comment we received and our response.
Comment:
A commenter expressed concern with the removal of the health IT vendor category from third-party intermediaries as finalized in the CY 2024 PFS final rule and suggested that this removal led to increased costs associated with transferring data from an electronic health record (EHR) to a QCDR or qualified registry.
Response:
As stated in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79391
), we finalized our proposal to remove the health IT vendor category given we observed many EHRs can self-nominate to serve as registries or QCDRs under our existing requirements and many others can also facilitate direct reporting of MIPS data by clinicians and groups. Further, as noted in the 2024 PFS proposed rule (
88 FR 52608
), a lack of self-nomination process has made it difficult to fully understand the nature of the health IT vendors and therefore made it difficult to properly identify and develop corrective action plans for those with data issues. We acknowledge the commenter's concern that removal of the health IT vendor category may have resulted in increased costs associated with transferring data from an EHR to a QCDR or qualified registry in their particular situation. However, the removal of this category did not preclude EHR vendors from supporting MIPS data submission or from self-nominating to become a QCDR or qualified registry, provided they meet the current requirements. Instead, this change in policy acknowledged that without a process to identify health IT vendors, we did not have a process to review them, approve them, or develop corrective actions to ensure data accuracy.
Additionally, although we finalized removal of the health IT vendor category in the CY 2024 PFS final rule, the corresponding requirements remained in the regulation text, causing confusion for some organizations interested in serving as third-party intermediaries because it was not clear that these additional requirements for health IT vendors were no longer applicable.
After consideration of the public comment, we are finalizing our proposal to clarify at § 414.1400(c)(2) that beginning with the CY 2025 performance period/CY 2027 MIPS payment year, health IT vendors cannot submit MIPS data as a third-party intermediary unless they meet the requirements for a qualified registry or QCDR. We are also finalizing our proposal to modify § 414.1400(c)(1) to clarify that the additional requirements for health IT vendors only apply for the CY 2021 performance period/CY 2023 MIPS payment year through the CY 2024 performance period/2026 MIPS payment year, when health IT vendors were still a separate type of third-party intermediary.
