We did not receive comments on our proposal to remove the term “clinicians and groups” from § 414.1400(b)(3)(iii). We received public comments on our proposal to require performance feedback at the level at which data was or will be submitted. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters opposed our proposal to require performance feedback at the level at which data was or will be submitted, expressing a concern that decisions about the level of reporting are often not made until long after the relevant performance period has started.
Response:
We recognize that the anticipated level of reporting may change during the performance period but would expect that the third—party intermediary provide feedback to the clinician or group at the level the clinician or group has indicated they intend to report at the time the feedback is provided. That is, we would expect that a third—party intermediary would provide feedback at the level the intermediary has on record for the clinician or group at the time feedback is issued. However, we believe that providing feedback at the applicable level of reporting is important to ensure the feedback is meaningful and useful to participants in understanding their performance. Accordingly, we believe this requirement balances the need to provide participants with relevant performance information while avoiding the unnecessary burden of requiring third-party intermediaries to provide feedback at every potential level of reporting.
Comment:
A few commenters suggested that the requirement to provide feedback at the level of reporting would require third-party intermediaries to provide performance feedback to participants at all potential levels of reporting and expressed concern that this much data would be confusing for participants and/or would increase administrative burden in the MIPS program.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' concerns that requiring feedback at the level of reporting could be interpreted as requiring third-party intermediaries to provide performance feedback at all potential levels of reporting, which could result in confusing information for participants or unnecessary burden. We clarify that this requirement is not intended to require third-party intermediaries to provide feedback at every potential level of reporting. Rather, third-party intermediaries would be required to provide feedback that is specific to the level at which the participant will report data for the purposes of MIPS (for example, providing information on the performance of an individual pulmonologist on measures contained in the Pulmonology Care MVP). We believe that providing feedback at the applicable level of reporting will ensure participants receive meaningful information regarding their performance without requiring third-party intermediaries to provide information at reporting levels that are not applicable to the participant.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing, as proposed, our proposal to add at § 414.1400(b)(3)(iii) that QCDRs and qualified registries must provide the performance feedback at the level at which the data was or will be submitted (for example, individual, group, virtual group, subgroup, APM entity). We are also finalizing, as proposed, our proposal to remove the term “clinicians and groups” in both places in this portion of the regulation.
b. Data Validation Requirements
(1) Background
Section 414.1400(b)(3)(v) outlines the requirements for a third-party intermediary's annual data validation audit. As finalized in the CY 2024 PFS final rule (
88 FR 79388
), specified at § 414.1400(b)(3)(v)(E), the QCDR or qualified registry must conduct each data validation audit using a sampling methodology that meets the following requirements: (1) Uses a sample size of at least 3 percent of a combination of individual clinicians, groups, virtual groups, subgroups and APM entities for which the QCDR or qualified registry will submit data to CMS, except that the sample size may be no fewer than a combination of 10 individual clinicians, groups, virtual groups, subgroups and APM entities, and no more than a combination of 50 individual clinicians, groups, virtual groups, subgroups and APM entities; and (2) Uses a sample that includes at least 25 percent of the patients of each individual clinician, group, virtual group, subgroup or APM entity in the sample, except that the sample for each individual clinician, group, virtual group, subgroup or APM entity must include a minimum of 5 patients and need not include more than 50 patients.
(2) Update Sampling Methodology for Data Validation Purposes
We noticed that recently certain third-party intermediaries are using less than the minimum sample size as required by § 414.1400(b)(3)(v)(E), which raises concern as to whether the data sample submitted is adequate. To ensure that our data remains true, accurate, and complete, we proposed the following updates (
91 FR 44209
):
If the third-party intermediary submits MIPS data to CMS for fewer than 10 Quality Payment Program participants, the data validation audit sample must include all Quality Payment Program participants. We proposed to modify the existing requirements at § 414.1400(b)(2)(v)(E)(1) and (2) that govern a QCDR or qualified registry's data validation audit sampling methodology. Specifically, we proposed at § 414.1400(b)(2)(v)(E)(1) that if the third-party intermediary submits MIPS data to CMS for fewer than 10 Quality Payment Program participants, the data validation audit sample must include all Quality Payment Program participants. If the third-party intermediary submits data for 10 or more Quality Payment Program participants, it must use a sample size of at least 3 percent of a combination of the individual MIPS eligible clinicians, groups, virtual groups, subgroups and APM entities for which the QCDR or qualified registry will submit data to CMS. The sample size may be no fewer than a combination of 10 individual clinicians, groups, virtual groups, subgroups, or APM entities, and no more than a combination of 50 individual clinicians, groups, virtual groups, subgroups and APM entities.
If there are fewer than 5 patient records from a Quality Payment Program participant, the patient record audit sample must include all patient records. We proposed at § 414.1400(b)(2)(v)(E)(2) that if there are fewer than 5 patient records, the patient record audit sample must include all patient records. If there are 5 or more patient records, the intermediary must use a sample that includes at least 25 percent of the patient records of the individual clinician, group, virtual group, subgroup, or APM entity in the sample, except that the sample for each individual clinician, group, virtual group, subgroup or APM entity must include a minimum of 5 patients and need not include more than 50 patients. These updates would help third-party intermediaries submit data that is true, accurate, and complete while meeting their submission requirements for data validation purposes.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
(
printed page 71617)
Comment:
A commenter supported both proposed updates to the data validation sampling strategy and suggested that high audit standards are an important element of high-quality data collection.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed the revised data validation sampling strategy and offered alternative suggestions in which third-party intermediaries would have more flexibility in demonstrating assurance of data accuracy which could be based on previous records of data compliance.
Response:
We understand the interest in having greater flexibility in demonstrating assurance of data accuracy which could be based on previous records of data compliance. However, we believe it is important to avoid any ambiguity in our data validation standards and to maintain clearly established data validation requirements that apply consistently across all third-party intermediaries. We believe these requirements are necessary to provide assurance that the data third-party intermediaries submit are true, accurate, and complete and that third-party intermediaries continue to meet submission requirements for data validation purposes.
Comment:
A commenter opposed the revised data validation sampling strategy as being unnecessarily complicated and duplicative of existing audits that CMS performs on MIPS eligible clinicians and suggested that these efforts undermine a statutory requirement to encourage the use of QCDRs to report quality measures.
Response:
Audits that may be performed on MIPS eligible clinicians have a different intent from the data validation requirements for third-party intermediaries. Clearly established data validation requirements are necessary to ensure that the data submitted by third-party intermediaries are true, accurate, and complete and consistent with the information recorded by the clinician in their medical records. Establishing these standards for third-party intermediaries protects clinicians who are interested in using them to facilitate reporting MIPS. The need to establish clear data validation requirements does not undermine the statutory requirement to encourage the use of QCDRs to report quality measures because the statutory requirement does not suggest that data quality be ignored in encouraging their use. Rather, establishing clear data validation requirements provides appropriate assurance regarding the accuracy and completeness of data submitted across all of our third-party intermediaries.

c. Require Submission of a Self-Nomination Plan for Third-Party Intermediaries That Do Not Submit Data for One Year
In the CY 2022 PFS final rule, we noted that we had identified several QCDRs and qualified registries that continued to self-nominate to become a third-party intermediary for MIPS but had not submitted data to CMS (
86 FR 65545
). We further noted as MIPS continues to mature, we wished to reduce the number of third-party intermediaries that self-nominate to become a CMS-approved third-party intermediary but do not actively participate in MIPS. Maintaining intermediaries who do not actively participate does not benefit MIPS, rather it creates interested parties' confusion by including these intermediaries in our qualified postings. We also noted that our goal was to decrease the operational burden on CMS and those third-party intermediaries that do not submit MIPS data to CMS (
86 FR 65546
).
Accordingly, we finalized requirements for approved QCDRs and qualified registries that have not submitted performance data to submit a participation plan as part of their self-nomination process. We finalized an incremental approach to addressing this issue. First, at § 414.1400(b)(3)(vii), we finalized a participation plan requirement, which requires a QCDR or qualified registry that was approved but did not submit data for any of the CY 2017 through 2020 performance periods/2019 through 2022 MIPS payment years to submit a participation plan in order to be approved for the CY 2023 performance period/2025 MIPS payment year (
86 FR 65545
and
65546
). Second, at § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii), we finalized that a QCDR or qualified registry that was approved but did not submit any MIPS data for either of the 2 years preceding the applicable self-nomination period must submit a participation plan in order for it to be approved for the CY 2024 performance period/2026 MIPS payment year or a future performance period/payment year (
86 FR 65546
).
While this policy has reduced the number of QCDRs and qualified registries that do not submit data, some QCDRs and qualified registries are still being listed on the qualified posting for as long as three years without submitting data. Maintaining these third-party intermediaries that do not actively participate does not benefit MIPS, rather it creates confusion for interested parties by including these third-party intermediaries in our qualified postings. We emphasize that our goal is to continue decreasing the operational burden on CMS and interested parties. CMS would decrease its operational burden by eliminating the need to screen these third-party intermediaries.
In an effort to avoid further confusion, reduce administrative burden for both CMS and interested parties, and ensure compliance, we proposed to reduce the timeframe available for a QCDR or qualified registry that was approved but did not submit any MIPS data to submit a participation plan. Currently, a QCDR
(
printed page 71618)
or qualified registry must submit a participation plan if they do not submit data for either of the 2 years preceding the applicable self-nomination period. We proposed to require a QCDR or qualified registry to submit a participation plan if they do not submit data for the year preceding the applicable self-nomination period. We proposed to redesignate and amend § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii) and add § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii)(A) and (B). Additionally, we also note that we encourage QCDRs and qualified registries to implement the participation plan at the beginning of the calendar year instead of waiting until the self-nomination period, which generally opens on July 1 and closes on September 1 of the year prior to the applicable MIPS performance period.
In summary, we specifically proposed to redesignate the existing text at § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii) to § 414.1400(b)(3)(vii)(B) and amend the text to reflect that this requirement applies from the CY 2024 performance period/2026 MIPS payment year through the CY 2026 performance period/2028 MIPS payment year (
91 FR 44209
). Additionally, we also proposed to add at § 414.1400(b)(3)(vii)(C) that beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, a QCDR or qualified registry that was approved but did not submit any MIPS data for the year preceding the applicable self-nomination period must submit a participation plan for CMS' approval. This participation plan must include the QCDR's and/or qualified registry's detailed plans about how the QCDR or qualified registry intends to encourage clinicians to submit MIPS data to CMS through the QCDR or qualified registry. We also proposed to redesignate the existing text at § 414.1400(b)(3)(vii) to at § 414.1400(b)(3)(vii)(A) and add the heading participation plan for third-party intermediary not submitting data at § 414.1400(b)(3)(vii).
We received a public comment on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comment we received and our response.
Comment:
A commenter opposed our proposed reduction in the timeframe available for a QCDR or qualified registry that was approved to submit data but did not do so. This commenter suggested that a one year gap in submitting is not evidence of a pattern of non-compliance and that requiring a participation plan after one year of not reporting would unduly increase administrative burden.
Response:
We acknowledge that while submitting a participation plan may impose some additional burden on a third-party intermediary that has not submitted data for one year, this limited burden is appropriate to demonstrate the third-party intermediary's intent to actively participate in the program. Additionally, we note that the purpose of this requirement is not to establish a pattern of non-compliance. Rather we intend to reduce the number of third-party intermediaries that self-nominate to become a CMS-approved third-party intermediary but do not actively participate in MIPS. Maintaining these intermediaries does not benefit MIPS, rather it creates confusion. Therefore, finalizing this proposal will reduce potential confusion, support more efficiency across CMS, and help ensure that CMS-approved third-party intermediaries intend to actively participate in MIPS.

d. Update Qualified Posting
Every year, CMS publishes a qualified posting on the Quality Payment Program website (
https://qpp.cms.gov/​
) containing a list of all CMS-approved third-party intermediaries that have self-nominated to submit data on behalf of MIPS eligible clinicians for the MIPS performance period. This list is updated to account for withdrawals, remedial action, or termination of third-party intermediaries. The qualified posting contains information about approved third-party intermediaries such as organization details, information about remedial action or termination, supported performance categories, specialty focus, a description of services they provide and associated costs, reporting options (MVP versus traditional MIPS) and participation options (individual clinician, group, subgroup, virtual group, APM entity) supported, and measures they are approved to support. MIPS eligible clinicians can refer to information in the qualified posting to identify and select a third-party intermediary.
In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77367
through
77369
and
77384
through
77385
), we established that QCDRs and qualified registries must sign a document that verifies their name, contact information, cost for MIPS eligible clinicians or groups to use the qualified registry, services provided, and the specialty-specific measure sets the qualified registry intends to report. As technology progressed, we no longer needed third-party intermediaries to sign a document and instead required an attestation. We became aware that this requirement was no longer consistent with our established policy in describing the manner in which the QCDR or qualified registry documents this information. To align with current processes, we finalized in the CY 2024 PFS final rule to add § 414.1400(b)(3)(xiv), which required that QCDRs and qualified registries attest that the information listed on the qualified posting is accurate (
88 FR 79385
). Additionally, we also finalized in the CY 2024 final rule, at § 414.1305, to define qualified posting as the document made available by CMS that lists QCDRs or qualified registries available for use by MIPS
(
printed page 71619)
eligible clinicians, groups, subgroups, virtual groups, and APM Entities (
88 FR 79385
). We noted that we had used the term qualified posting since the inception of the Quality Payment Program but had not previously defined the term.
We have recently been made aware that certain third-party intermediaries are making changes to the information they provided for their qualified posting after receiving CMS approval of the qualified posting. Examples of changes include updates to costs, services that are included in the initial cost, and other administrative changes. This creates an increased administrative burden for CMS, who must identify and rectify such changes, and it creates confusion amongst clinicians who contract with the third-party intermediary as to what they will pay for the cost of the third-party intermediary's services. Subsequently, we must make additional updates to the qualified posting, which increases the administrative burden on CMS. To reduce administrative burden for both clinicians and CMS, we proposed to update § 414.1400(b)(3)(xiv) by adding a requirement that changes to information (for example, cost, services included) on the qualified posting must be included and finalized during the qualified posting review period (
91 FR 44210
). We proposed specifying in regulatory text that third-party intermediaries will not be permitted to make changes after the qualified posting is publicly posted on the Quality Payment Program website (
https://qpp.cms.gov/​
).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters expressed general support for the goals associated with our proposal to not change information provided on the qualified posting following the qualified posting review period but suggested that in some cases external situations may alter what a third-party intermediary is able to provide and that it would be preferable to align that information with what is included on the qualified posting. Some of the commenters recommended a process for updating this information following the completion of the qualified posting review. A commenter requested that CMS remain flexible to accommodate the various differences in operating models across third-party intermediaries (for example., specialty society led QCDR vs. other QCDR entities).
Response:
We understand that there may be circumstances outside of a third-party intermediary's control that may affect the services or capabilities the third-party intermediary can provide after the qualified posting review period has concluded. However, having a defined review period during which third-party intermediaries, including those that may have different operating models, can review and request changes to their information as necessary can ensure that qualified postings are finalized in a timely manner. It also allows us to provide consistent information to clinicians and groups needing information on third-party intermediaries. Establishing an additional process to make changes after the qualified posting review would require us to continually review and update information, thereby creating uncertainty for interested parties relying on the qualified postings to identify third-party intermediaries and the services they offer. Therefore, we do not see a need to establish an additional process for updating information following the conclusion of the qualified posting review period.
Comment:
A commenter opposed our proposal stating their belief that it would increase administrative burden. The commenter suggested that this would require alignment of all business decisions by the third-party intermediary with the CMS qualified posting schedule and would discourage reporting through QCDRs.
Response:
Establishing a defined period during which a third-party intermediary may review and request changes to their information is necessary to ensure the qualified postings are accurate and the information posted can be finalized in a timely manner. While we aim to reduce administrative burden as much as possible, clinicians are using these third-party intermediaries to participate in MIPS and therefore need to know which third-party intermediaries are qualified and what services they offer so the clinician or group can select a third-party intermediary that meets their needs. As such, there are some deadlines and other requirements that the business entity may need to accommodate to facilitate reporting for MIPS eligible clinicians.
The designated review period gives third-party intermediaries an appropriate opportunity to verify the accuracy of their information and identify any necessary changes before the qualified postings are finalized. Accordingly, this approach balances the need to provide third-party intermediaries with an opportunity to review their information with the need to maintain accurate, consistent, and timely information for clinicians and groups seeking to identify a third-party intermediary for their MIPS reporting. Establishing a defined qualified posting review period should not discourage the use of QCDRs but should instead provide greater certainty regarding the information available on qualified postings.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal as proposed, to update § 414.1400(b)(3)(xiv) by adding a requirement that changes to information (for example, cost, services included) on the qualified posting must be included and finalized during the qualified posting review period. We are also finalizing our proposal as proposed, to specify in regulatory text that third-party intermediaries will not be permitted to make changes after the qualified posting is publicly posted on the Quality Payment Program website (
https://qpp.cms.gov/​
).
e. Update CMS Data Submission Requirements for Third-Party Intermediaries
In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule, we finalized at § 414.1400(b)(3)(x) and (b)(3)(x)(A) that a QCDR or a qualified registry must be able to submit to CMS data for at least six quality measures including at least one outcome measure and if no outcome measure is available, a QCDR or qualified registry must be able to submit to CMS results for at least one other high priority measure (
81 FR 77368
).
However, in CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we proposed to remove the high-priority designation from MIPS quality measures beginning in the CY 2027 performance period/CY 2029 MIPS payment year (
91 FR 44210
). Additionally, we also proposed to remove the requirement to report an outcome measure and require reporting a MIPS core measure. Under the new proposal, MIPS eligible clinicians participating through traditional MIPS must submit data on at least six measures, including at least one MIPS core measure.
To align third-party intermediaries' requirements with the MIPS core measure set and high priority designation for MIPS quality measures proposals, we proposed to revise § 414.1400(b)(3)(x)(B) to state that beginning in the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, a QCDR or qualified registry must be able to submit to CMS, data for at least six quality measures including at least one MIPS core measure (
91 FR 44210
). We also proposed to revise § 414.1400(b)(3)(x) and (b)(3)(x)(A) so that the requirement for a QCDR or
(
printed page 71620)
qualified registry to be able to submit an outcome measure and if the outcome measure is not available, then a high priority measure can be submitted, concludes with the CY 2026 performance period/CY 2028 MIPS payment year.
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters opposed our proposed update to require qualified registries and QCDRs to report on at least one core measure. These commenters generally expressed concern that a QCDR or qualified registry could capture data on a more specialized set of clinicians than would be part of a broader MVP such as a clinician providing echocardiography as part of a cardiology group and that requiring support for at least one core measure would reduce the availability of QCDRs for specialized clinicians.
Response:
Similar to our approach in establishing submission requirements for third-party intermediaries in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule, it is important to align requirements across third-party intermediaries where appropriate. The requirement to support at least one measure from the MIPS core measure set does not preclude a QCDR or qualified registry from continuing to support measures that are applicable to more specialized clinicians or clinical practice areas. Rather, this requirement establishes a minimum requirement for QCDRs and qualified registries while allowing them to continue to support the specialized measures and clinician populations they serve.
Comment:
A commenter suggested that CMS publish the MIPS core measure list on a timeline that precedes the self-nomination period for the applicable performance year in order to ensure that the third-party intermediary can demonstrate the capability to submit at least one MIPS core measure during the self-nomination period.
Response:
We note that the existing requirement is that a QCDR or qualified registry must be able to submit data to CMS for at least six quality measures, including at least one outcome measure or, if an outcome measure is not available, at least one other high-priority measure. Under the proposed policy, a QCDR or qualified registry would instead be required to be able to submit data to CMS for at least six quality measures, including at least one MIPS core measure. Consistent with the existing self-nomination process, QCDRs and qualified registries identify the measures they are capable of submitting based on the information available during the applicable self-nomination period. MIPS core measures will be cataloged and identified at the Quality Payment Program resource library (
https://qpp.cms.gov/​resources/​resource-library
). This same timeline would apply to the requirement to be able to submit at least one MIPS core measure. Identifying core measures for a particular MIPS performance period earlier than under the current timeline is not consistent with our overall review of the measure inventory on an annual basis which allows for updates to reflect changes in measure availability as close to the performance period as possible.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal as proposed, to revise § 414.1400(b)(3)(x)(B) to state that beginning in the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, a QCDR or qualified registry must be able to submit to CMS, data for at least six quality measures including at least one MIPS core measure. We are also finalizing our proposal to revise § 414.1400(b)(3)(x) and (b)(3)(x)(A) so that the requirement for a QCDR or qualified registry to be able to submit an outcome measure and if the outcome measure is not available, then a high priority measure can be submitted, concludes with the CY 2026 performance period/CY 2028 MIPS payment year.

b. Termination of a Third-Party Intermediary That Does Not Submit Data for 1 Year
In the CY 2023 PFS final rule, we established that we will terminate QCDRs and qualified registries that are required to submit participation plans during the applicable self-nomination period under § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii) because they did not submit any MIPS data for either of the 2 years preceding the applicable self-nomination period and continue to not submit MIPS data to CMS for the applicable performance period (
87 FR 70107
through
70108
). Timely termination of third-party intermediaries that are not submitting data is important to minimize unnecessary operational and administrative tasks for both CMS and third-party intermediaries. Maintaining third-party intermediaries that do not actively participate does not provide a benefit to the MIPS program, rather it creates confusion for interested parties by including these third-party intermediaries in our qualified postings (
86 FR 65545
).
In the CY 2027 PFS proposed rule, we noted that the policy for termination of third-party intermediaries not submitting data would be impacted by the proposed requirement to submit a participation plan for third-party intermediaries that do not submit data for one year (
91 FR 44211
). This proposed policy means that we would terminate QCDRs and qualified registries that were required to submit participation plans during the applicable self-nomination period under § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii) because they did not submit any MIPS data for 1 year (rather than 2 years) preceding the applicable self-nomination period and continue to not submit MIPS data to CMS for the applicable performance period. However, because the data submission period lasts for one year following the performance period, there is a delay in CMS being made aware of whether a third-party intermediary submitted data for a given year. Therefore, currently, CMS does not have a mechanism to acquire the necessary knowledge to appropriately terminate a third-party intermediary until the year after the applicable performance period.
Currently, if a third-party intermediary does not submit data for the performance period for which they submitted a self-nomination participation plan, they will be terminated. However, CMS does not become aware of the third-party intermediary's failure to submit data for a given MIPS performance period until the year following the performance period. For example, under the current policy, if a third-party intermediary self-nominated for the 2024 performance period and was required to submit a self-nomination participation plan but does not submit data for the 2024 performance period, CMS would not know the third-party intermediary did not submit MIPS data for the 2024 performance period until the end of the submission period in March 2025. Therefore, the third-party intermediary can continue to participate for the 2025 MIPS performance period as if they
(
printed page 71621)
were already approved and posted as a 2025 CMS-approved third-party intermediary. To shorten the timeline of when CMS is aware that the third-party intermediary does not submit any data and when CMS appropriately terminates the third-party intermediary, we proposed to update our policy such that CMS would request documentation that the third-party intermediary has contracted with Quality Payment Program's participants who will submit MIPS data for the given MIPS performance period. CMS's query for documentation would occur before the end of the calendar year for the given MIPS performance period. If the appropriate documentation cannot be provided by the date specified by CMS, the third-party intermediary would be terminated. This proposal would provide the information needed to terminate a third-party intermediary during the applicable performance period year instead of waiting until the following year.
Specifically, we proposed adding a new requirement for third-party intermediaries to submit documentation about intent to submit MIPS data and to terminate a third-party intermediary if they do not submit the appropriate documentation by the date specified by CMS (
91 FR 44211
). We also proposed to add at § 414.1400(e)(5)(ii) that beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, a QCDR or qualified registry that submits a participation plan as required under § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii), but does not submit MIPS data for the applicable performance period for which they self-nominated under § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii), will be queried by CMS before the end of the calendar year of the given MIPS performance period for documentation that they have contracted with Quality Payment Program participants who will submit data for the given MIPS performance period. If the appropriate documentation cannot be provided, the third-party intermediary would be terminated. We also proposed redesignating the existing text at § 414.1400(e)(5) to § 414.1400(e)(5)(i). We also proposed to add the heading “Termination for Third-party Intermediary not submitting data.” at § 414.1400(e)(5).
We received public comments on these proposals. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A few commenters opposed our proposal to update the requirements for submitting a participation plan after a year in which the QCDR or qualified registry did not submit data. The commenters supported the current policy requiring a submission plan after two years of failing to submit data but suggested that a single year in which the QCDR or qualified registry failed to submit data was not evidence of a pattern and that external circumstances may cause a QCDR or qualified registry to not report for a year. A commenter requested that if CMS were to finalize the policy, a process to demonstrate active engagement without submitting data should be developed.
Response:
We clarify that the purpose of this requirement is not to establish a pattern of non-compliance and understand that external circumstances may cause a QCDR or qualified registry to not report for a year. However, maintaining these intermediaries who do not actively participate in MIPS does not provide a benefit to the program and may create confusion across interested parties when these vendors continue to appear on our qualified postings despite not submitting MIPS data. A submission plan is a way to demonstrate active engagement in lieu of submission of data. Therefore, finalizing this proposal will reduce potential confusion, support more efficiency across CMS, and help ensure that CMS-approved third-party intermediaries intend to actively participate in MIPS.
Comment:
A commenter suggested that CMS clarify the documentation needed, the window within which the third-party intermediary must provide the documentation, and the criteria for approval in order to ensure that the third-party intermediary meets the submission requirements and avoids being terminated.
Response:
We clarify that required documents to self-nominate have not changed outside of what is already posted. Intermediaries can refer to the “2027-MIPS-QCDR-QualifiedRegistry-Self-Nomination-Fact-Sheet” included in the “2027 Self-Nomination Toolkit for QCDRs and Qualified Registries” posted in the QPP Resource Library. This resource includes the requirement of participation of at least 25 participants, verification and maintenance of clinician information such as Business Associate Agreements and consents (intermediaries have contracted with QPP participants who will submit data) for the given MIPS performance period.
If the third-party intermediary does not intend to submit data to CMS on behalf of any of their clients, they should notify CMS at the end of the performance period (December 31st) that they will not be sending any data for that performance period. If the submitter could produce an acceptable reason for no data submission, CMS would consider that documentation, but the termination clause would be executed unless adequate reasoning was provided. With respect to the window, CMS would expect documentation to show why no data will be submitted for that performance period and why the third-party intermediary believes that they will have clinicians and/or groups submitting data to them for reporting for the next MIPS performance period. This documentation is due to CMS by December 31st of the performance period. Finally, we note that we will provide additional technical guidance, as appropriate, at a later date.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing our proposal as proposed, to add a new requirement for third-party intermediaries to submit documentation about submitting MIPS data and to terminate a third-party intermediary if they do not submit the appropriate documentation by the date specified by CMS. We are also finalizing at § 414.1400(e)(5)(ii) that beginning with the CY 2027 performance period/2029 MIPS payment year, a QCDR or qualified registry that submits a participation plan as required under § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii), but does not submit MIPS data for the applicable performance period for which they self-nominated under § 414.1400(b)(3)(viii), will be queried by CMS before the end of the calendar year of the given MIPS performance period for documentation that they have contracted with Quality Payment Program participants who will submit data for the given MIPS performance period. If the appropriate documentation cannot be provided, the third-party intermediary would be terminated. Additionally, we are also finalizing our proposal as proposed, to redesignate the existing text at § 414.1400(e)(5) to § 414.1400(e)(5)(i). Finally, we are also finalizing as propose to add the heading “Termination for Third-party Intermediary not submitting data.” at § 414.1400(e)(5).

Commenters noted that disasters may disrupt clinical operations, and that it is essential for CMS to finalize this proposal to identify all affected clinicians and limit clinicians' need to apply for reweighting while experiencing a hardship.

We thank commenters for their support.

We agree that it is important to be as comprehensive as possible in identifying clinicians that are impacted by an EUC. (

through

Response:
We thank the commenters for their support

(
printed page 71624)

Additionally, before CMS can offer reweighting, CMS must consider the following in evaluating these requests: whether there is a written agreement between the MIPS eligible clinician and third-party intermediary; whether the MIPS eligible clinician knew or had reason to know of the issue with its third-party intermediary's submission of the clinician's data for the performance category(ies); whether the MIPS eligible clinician took reasonable efforts to correct the issue; and whether the issue between the MIPS eligible clinician and their third-party intermediary caused no data to be submitted for the performance category(ies) in accordance with applicable deadlines, which would also prohibit CMS from automatically applying reweighting.

In this section of the final rule, we are finalizing removal of the requirement that prevents public reporting of any performance data reported through a MIPS Value Pathway (MVP) on new improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability measures on the Compare Tools for the first year the new measures and activities are included in such MVP. 2. Remove the Public Reporting Requirements for the MIPS Value Pathway (MVP) Requirement at § 414.1395(c)(2)
In the CY 2022 PFS final rule (
86 FR 65550
through
65552
), we finalized a policy under which we would not publicly report any MVP data, or MIPS performance data reported through an MVP, on a new improvement activity or new Promoting Interoperability measure, objective, or activity for the first year the new activity or measure is included in an MVP. For example, if a new improvement activity is finalized for inclusion in MIPS and an MVP for the CY 2027 performance period/CY 2029 MIPS payment year, under the current regulatory framework, we would not publicly report the first year of data for MIPS eligible clinicians who report the new improvement activity through the MVP. The intent of this requirement was to encourage participation in the new MVP reporting framework and to provide participants with additional time to transition to MVPs before their performance on new Promoting Interoperability measures or improvement activities were publicly reported. However, we have determined that this requirement has not served as an effective incentive for MVP participation because most improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability measures included in MVPs are not considered new as of 2026 and would be publicly reported, as they have been included in MIPS for over a year.
Consistent with section 1848(q)(9)(A)(i)(II) of the Act, we finalized in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule a decision to make all measures, objectives, or activities under the MIPS quality, cost, improvement activities, and PI performance categories available for public reporting on the Compare tools
(
printed page 71625)
(
81 FR 77391
through
77396
), using a phased approach for new performance information facilitated by section 1848(q)(9)(A) and (D). In the CY 2018 PFS final rule (
82 FR 53825
through
53827
), we further finalized that the first year of data for new improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability measures would be publicly reported for MIPS eligible clinicians on the Compare tools if all other public reporting criteria established under § 414.1395(b) are met. Since we established § 414.1395(c)(2), the annual consumer testing conducted consistent with the requirements of § 414.1395(b) demonstrates that patients and caregivers find the new improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability information understandable and useful for their decision-making. Therefore, this information should be publicly reported. The purpose of the Compare Tools is to provide patients with timely, clear, and credible information on provider performance that is available for public reporting.
Since the adoption of the requirement to not publicly report the first year of new improvement activity or Promoting Interoperability measure information for clinicians who report through an MVP, we have observed that the policy does not apply to a sufficient number of MIPS eligible clinicians to encourage meaningful participation in MVPs. For example, during 2025, only four individual clinician's performance information would not have been publicly reported for new improvement activities included in MVPs, and CMS did not include any new Promoting Interoperability measures in MVPs for 2025. This represented less than 1 percent of clinicians reporting the new improvement activities for that performance period. Similarly, we observed that this requirement applied to less than 1 percent of MIPS eligible clinicians reporting new improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability information overall since MVPs became available as a reporting framework beginning with the CY 2023 performance period. There has not been a sufficient number of new Promoting Interoperability measures or improvement activities included in MVPs, and there is not enough data to continue supporting this requirement.
In the CY 2027 proposed rule, we proposed to remove the requirement at § 414.1395(c)(2) that we would not publicly report any MVP data on new improvement activity or Promoting Interoperability measure, objective, or activity for the first year in which it is included in an MVP. Upon the removal of this requirement, we would revert to the original policy finalized in the CY 2018 PFS final rule (
82 FR 53825
through
53827
) and would include all eligible performance information for new improvement activities and new Promoting Interoperability measures in public reporting on the Compare Tools beginning with the first year in which the measures and activities are included in the program.
We received public comments on this proposal. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported our proposal to remove the requirement that we will not publicly report any data on new improvement activities or Promoting Interoperability measures, objective, or activity during the first year in which it is included in an MVP. Several commenters agreed that this change will improve transparency in the quality of care. A commenter also noted that as MVP participation grows and stakeholders gain familiarity with the reporting framework, earlier public reporting is appropriate. Another commenter also discussed the low impact the first-year policy had on incentivizing MVP participation.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' support.
Comment:
Some commenters supported the proposal but discussed the need for CMS to remain attentive to risks to data quality and compliance arising from accelerated public reporting timeframes. Commenters also recommended that CMS continue to provide clinicians with sufficient opportunity to review and correct reported information to ensure that publicly displayed results accurately reflect clinician performance.
Response:
We appreciate the commenter's concern regarding data quality and compliance. We are required under sections 10331(a) and 10331(b) of the Affordable Care Act to include processes to ensure publicly reported data are valid, reliable, and accurate, and under section 1848(q)(9)(C) of the Act to provide clinicians with an opportunity to review information before it is publicly reported. Consistent with these requirements, we will continue to monitor data quality and maintain processes to assess, validate, and address potential data quality issues, and provide a 30-day preview period for clinicians and groups to review their performance information before it is public reported (
80 FR 71120
;
81 FR 77391
; § 414.1395(d)).
Comment:
Some commenters disagreed with the proposal. A few commenters stated that the first year allows clinicians needed time to adapt to new measures and activities before performance data are made public, and that removing the requirement may create unnecessary technical and workflow risks. A commenter also predicted that removing this requirement will increase hesitation for physicians to report MVPs.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' feedback regarding the time needed to adapt to new measures and activities, as well as potential workflow and technical challenges. These considerations can be addressed through clear guidance and education on any new improvement activity or Promoting Interoperability measure, objective, or activity. We have made this a priority since the beginning of MIPS and will continue to do so by providing a range of resources and support available through the Quality Payment Program website at
https://QPP.cms.gov
. We would also remind commenters of the nominal percentage of clinicians reporting new improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability measures overall since MVPs became available as a reporting option beginning with the CY 2023 performance period. Moreover, the limited reporting of new improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability measures suggests that the availability of such measures is not a significant driver of clinicians' decisions regarding MVP participation. Accordingly, we do not believe this policy is likely to materially influence clinicians' decisions to report MVPs.
Comment:
Two commenters recommended expanding the current requirement so that CMS would not publicly report any data on new improvement activities or Promoting Interoperability measure during the first 2 years in which it is included in an MVP.
Response:
Thank you for this recommendation. The primary concerns raised regarding the original proposal to remove the requirement to not publicly report MVP data on new improvement activities or Promoting Interoperability measures, objectives, or activities during its first year of availability to report focused on attributes of performance data from other performance categories, including measure attribution, calculation, risk adjustment methodologies, and benchmark development. Because individual MIPS eligible clinicians and groups simply attest to whether improvement activities and Promoting Interoperability measures were completed—and no calculation is involved at the measure or
(
printed page 71626)
activity level—we conclude that this does not provide a sufficient basis to postpone the public reporting of this information. Moreover, we believe that the recommendation to expand the initial public reporting grace period to 2 years would only further diminish transparency, particularly because this information continues to be meaningful to patients and supports their decision-making.
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing our proposal as proposed and removing the requirement at § 414.1395(c)(2) that we will not publicly report any MVP data on new improvement activities or Promoting Interoperability measures, objectives, or activities during the first year in which it is included in an MVP.
3. Request for Information: Star Rating Assignment Methodology for Administrative Claims Quality Measures
In the CY 2027 proposed rule, we issued an RFI to investigate potential improvements to the star rating methodology used to display administrative claims-based quality measure scores on clinician profile pages in the Medicare.gov Compare Tool. The option included in the RFI uses a standard deviation-based approach for the calculation of star rating cutoffs, reflecting the normally distributed nature of administrative claims-based measure scores. We requested feedback on whether this alternative method would be easily understood and more appropriate prior to public reporting of these scores. We appreciate the feedback we received in response to this comment solicitation and may consider this information for possible future rulemaking.
F. Advanced APMs
1. Overview
The Quality Payment Program provides incentives for eligible clinicians to engage in value-based, patient-centered care under Medicare Part B via MIPS and Advanced APMs. The structure of the Quality Payment Program enables us to advance accountability and encourage improvements in care. Our vision for increased clinician participation in Advanced APMs is aimed at integrating individuals' clinical needs across a spectrum of providers and settings to improve patient care and population health. In the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 50012
), we finalized an update to our methodology to add an individual-level calculation to Qualifying APM Participant (QP) determinations, as set forth in § 414.1425(b)(3) and (c)(3), for all eligible clinicians participating in an Advanced APM, such that each eligible clinician would receive both APM Entity-level calculation and an individual-level calculation. Second, we finalized a policy at §§ 414.1435 and 414.1305 to perform QP determinations using both an E/M services approach and a Covered Professional Services approach.
2. QP Determination
a. General
In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77439
through
77445
), we finalized our policy for QP determinations at § 414.1425. We perform QP determinations for eligible clinicians three times during the QP Performance Period using claims data for services furnished from January 1 through each of the respective QP determination snapshot dates. An eligible clinician can be determined to be a QP only if the eligible clinician appears on the Participation List on a snapshot date that we use to determine the APM Entity group and to make QP determinations as described at § 414.1425.
In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77433
through
77440
) we established a process to calculate Partial QP status at § 414.1425(d). While to date our Partial QP policies have impacted only a small number of eligible clinicians, and thus we have not focused our discussion on this specific policy, we note that any changes to QP determinations at § 414.1425 also would likely require conforming changes to the policies for Partial QPs for consistency across the program.
b. Applying QP Determinations at the TIN/NPI Level
When we initially established our policy in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule to make most QP determinations at the APM Entity level, we also specified that we would apply QP status at the NPI level (
81 FR 77440
). In other words, for a given eligible clinician (NPI), were one of their TIN/NPI relationships to be determined a QP, that QP status has applied all of their TIN/NPI relationships, both for purposes of being excluded from MIPS as well as for the application of QP financial incentives. Given the complexity of the program, we believed it was the best approach at the time to create one QP status result for a clinician at all of their billing organizations. However, we did not intend for the policy to create conflicting incentives to participation in Advanced APMs. We realized that an NPI being a QP at all of their TINs also meant that they would receive the financial incentives of QP status, at the time the APM Incentive Payment, across all of those TINs, irrespective of whether those TINs were participating with Advanced APMs. However, we believed that the significance of that incentive would serve to increase clinician participation in Advanced APMs, and that the application of the QP thresholds would ensure that the clinician was appropriately incented to try to increase their individual Advanced APM participation. Further, we also had finalized at § 414.1450(c)(1) that we would pay the entire APM Incentive Payment amount to the TIN associated with the QP's participation in the Advanced APM Entity through which QP status had been attained (
81 FR 77555
), and we believed that by directing the lump sum entirely to the TIN participating with the Advanced APM Entity, we would reward the clinician without also rewarding non-participating TINs.
Upon gaining early experience implementing the APM Incentive Payments, we learned that for a variety of reasons (clinician movement, changes to a practice's TINs), we were not always able to send payment to the TIN associated with the APM Entity. We revised § 414.1450(c) in the CY 2021 PFS (
88 FR 85035
) to establish a hierarchy we would apply when determining where to send the APM Incentive Payments, which still prioritized TINs participating in Advanced APMs but allowed for payment to be sent to other, non-participating TINs if that was the only place we could find the clinician active at the time of payment. Still, we were satisfied that our prioritization of the lump-sum APM Incentive Payment to TINs that had Advanced APM participation remained a protection against providing non-participating TINs significant windfalls.
However, section 1848(d)(1)(A) of the Act establishes that, beginning with payment year 2026, QPs will receive a higher qualifying conversion factor update than non-QPs on their covered professional services claims. While the APM Incentive Payment has been extended multiple times as described in section III.G.6.d. of this final rule, the implementation of the QP conversion factor means that a QP financial incentive goes directly to TINs in the form of claims payment. Particularly as the QP conversion factor grows and constitutes a larger proportion of the QP incentive structure over time, we are
(
printed page 71627)
concerned that a significant proportion of incentives paid for QP status will be paid to TINs that are not part of an Advanced APM, creating a disincentive for these TINs to join an Advanced APM and meaningfully engage in risk-bearing value-based care.
As such, we proposed adding new provisions at § 414.1425(c)(8) and (d)(5) to apply QP status and Partial QP status, respectively, strictly to an eligible clinician as such term is defined at § 414.1305, specifically as a TIN/NPI combination, and that meets the definition at § 414.1305 of Qualifying APM participant (QP) or Partial QP, respectively, by participating in an Advanced APM during the QP performance period. Under the proposal, QP status and Partial QP status would therefore only apply to the clinician at the TIN that is participating with the APM Entity in the Advanced APM. Therefore, the financial incentives in the form of both the APM Incentive Payment and the QP conversion factor would apply to the NPI's claims only with those TINs, as would the ability of a Partial QP to opt into or out of MIPS.
For an eligible clinician who is participating in multiple APM Entities, the proposal's effects would be based on how the clinician becomes a QP or Partial QP. Section 414.1435(h)(2) specifies that CMS assigns to the eligible clinician the score that results in the greater QP status. In accordance with this provision, if an eligible clinician attains QP status at the individual level from participation in multiple APM Entities, under the proposal we would assign the QP status at each of the clinician's TINs participating across those APM Entities. However, if, the eligible clinician did not attain QP status at the individual level and did attain QP status as part of a specific APM Entity-level determination, we would assign QP status to the clinician at only the TIN(s) that are associated with the APM Entity or Entities that collectively attained QP status. If the eligible clinician did not attain any QP status through any determination but did attain Partial QP status, this same preference for the highest status would apply for Partial QP status. As we explained in the proposed rule, this proposed approach would maintain the longstanding policy within QPP to give the clinician the highest possible outcome available to them.
We proposed to no longer apply QP determinations to a clinician as a whole and we recognized the possibility of this being perceived as introducing complexity into an eligible clinician's QPP experience, for example because under the proposal some eligible clinicians would be a QP with one TIN and participating in MIPS with another. In these cases, the eligible clinician's QP status would apply at each of their TINs under the proposal. For the clinicians who are not already participating in an Advanced APM across all of their TIN reassignments, we explained that CMS believes that this policy would provide a meaningful incentive to increase their participation in an Advanced APM. Participation in Advanced APMs across Original Medicare continues to grow and we expect this policy to support our progress.
As we noted in the proposed rule, our proposal aligns with MIPS, which already operates on a TIN/NPI basis, meaning that QPP internal operations and communications would be the same for all clinicians. Under our current policy, we receive a significant number of inquiries from billing organizations where clinicians have been excluded from MIPS as a result of QP status with another billing organization where that organization is participating in an Advanced APM. In these cases, organizations have made a significant investment to report MIPS but do not receive a MIPS final score and MIPS payment adjustment for these clinicians. Our proposed policy would ensure that these billing organizations are in control of how MIPS eligibility criteria apply to clinicians that have been reassigned to their organizations.
In addition to programmatic alignment, we explained in the proposed rule that our operational experience tells us that, when a TIN has any clinicians who are subject to MIPS, it most often simply reports on all of its clinicians, as including everybody is easier than removing clinicians before reporting. As such, we believe that in the relatively few situations where the proposal would result in an eligible clinician with QP status at one TIN being subject to MIPS at one or more other TINs, the TINs where the clinician is subject to MIPS in many cases already report data for that clinician, meaning that neither the clinician nor their MIPS-participating TIN(s) would bear any new burden as a consequence of the proposed policy. Further, as it was established at the outset, operational experience indicates that MIPS eligible clinicians' experience has not been significantly impaired by the TIN/NPI operation of that portion of the program.
Finally, in the proposed rule we recognized that this proposal would decrease the dollar value of the financial incentives available for affected QPs. However, we believe that assigning QP status at the TIN/NPI level will serve to prevent an increasing windfall for TINs that do not participate in Advanced APMs, particularly given that the higher qualifying conversion factor update that is now part of the physician fee schedule. This update is baked into the amount Medicare pays on claims and therefore always is paid to the TIN through which the service was furnished without regard to whether that TIN is part of the Advanced APM that conferred QP status to the clinician. We believe that this proposal would prevent waste and potential for abuse, and that these matters outweigh concerns around complexity or reduced incentives. Notably, under current law the QP conversion factor will increase each year relative to the non-QP conversion factor. In addition, because payment of the claims is made directly to the TINs through which the services were billed means that CMS has no mechanism of directing these incentives to Advanced APM participating TINs in the way we have done with the APM Incentive Payment. As such, while relatively few QPs would be affected by this proposal, CMS anticipates the amount of the resulting windfall flowing directly to non-participating TINs under the current framework will increase over time, with little benefit to the clinician and no benefit to the practices that are doing the work of Advanced APM participation.
With respect to Partial QP status, the proposal would maintain programmatic alignment within QPP and would provide for the application of the ability to opt out of MIPS at the TIN/NPI level. While there are not financial incentives for these eligible clinicians in the same manner that there are for QPs, we believe that applying the opt-out flexibility at the TIN/NPI level similarly confers the burden reduction of Partial QP status. In our proposal we limited the application of Partial QP status to only to those TINs that are affiliated with the APM Entity participating in the Advanced APM. However, based on comments discussed in this section we are modifying our proposal and finalizing a policy that extends Partial QP status to all TIN/NPI combinations for a given NPI.
We proposed amending § 414.1425(c) to add new paragraph (8) to apply QP status strictly to the eligible clinician as such term is defined at § 414.1305, specifically as a TIN/NPI combination, and that meets the definition of Qualifying APM participant (QP) as defined at § 414.1305 by participating in an Advanced APM during the QP performance period. We also proposed amending § 414.1425(d) to add new paragraph (5) to establish the same
(
printed page 71628)
policy with respect to the application of Partial QP status.
We sought public comments on this proposal.
We received several public comments on these proposals. Comments were a mix of support and opposition. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters opposed the proposal, citing administrative complexity for clinicians who bill under multiple TINs. Commentors noted that incentives for QPs are an important driver of Advanced APM participation, particularly for large organizations with multiple TINs. Commenters requested that we provide additional impact data.
Response:
We appreciate the substantial interested parties' input on this proposal. We acknowledge commenter concerns regarding administrative burden for clinicians who bill under multiple TINs. In an effort to understand the potential for increased burden we have investigated how this policy would have impacted historical participation in QPP. We started by modeling participation data from 2025. We were particularly concerned about instances where TIN/NPIs would be required to report to MIPS. However, we found that there would be very few instances where a TIN/NPI no longer had QP status but was also MIPS eligible at an individual level. Out of all the TIN/NPIs participating in an Advanced APM in 2025 only 1.1 percent would fall into the category of having lost QP status, while also being MIPS eligible at the individual level. In other words, the overwhelming majority of TIN/NPIs in advanced APMs have seen no change in reporting requirements. In order to further investigate MIPS reporting feasibility for this subgroup we looked at their MIPS reporting data for the 2025 performance year. We found that more than half of the TIN/NPIs, represented in the aforementioned 1.1 percent, already had MIPS participation data at the APM entity, group, or individual level.
We have noted in the CY 2026 PFS final rule (
90 FR 49994
) that, projecting future participation in Advanced APMs and the impact is difficult. We also continue to believe that the benefit of TIN/NPI-level application of QP status furthers the goal of increasing participation in Advanced APMs. In an effort to be responsive to interested parties' concerns we are finalizing a modification to our proposed policy as discussed in the comment and response below. Our modification will ensure that NPIs who are otherwise meaningfully participating, in Advanced APMs, above the Partial QP thresholds, can be afforded the choice to opt in or out of MIPS participation.
As commentors noted we would expect our policy to have a greater impact on large integrated systems which are often comprised of more than one TIN. We believe our policy provides an incentive structure that favors the inclusion of more providers in Advanced APMs, including specialists. Where the previous policy may have further promoted the creation of multiple TINs and the exclusion of some providers within a large organization from Advanced APM participation our policy seeks to correct the incentive structure.
Comment:
Several commenters noted potential issues for new TIN reassignment. Commentors noted that because there is a two-year delay between performance year and payment year our proposed policy may inhibit providers from joining new organizations or leaving their current organization.
Response:
We acknowledge commentor concern around new and changing TIN assignment. With the gap in timing between the QP performance period and payment year where we expect new TIN/NPI combinations will be created both as a part of an Advanced APM and not participating in an Advanced APM. We share this concern and plan to further clarify the application of the qualifying APM conversion factor to new TIN/NPI combinations in these scenarios in future rulemaking.
Comment:
Several commenters suggested that CMS' application of QP, and Partial QP status was inconsistent with the statutory provisions under section 1833(z) and 1848(q) of the Act.
Response:
We thank commenters for their comments. However, our application of QP status at the TIN/NPI level is consistent with our previous application of “qualifying APM participant” as defined in section 1833(z)(2) of the Act. When we established our policy in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule to apply QP status at the NPI level (
81 FR 77440
) we also considered applying QP and Partial QP status at the TIN/NPI level. We elected not to do so, in large part, to promote administrative simplicity as we developed the infrastructure to operate the new program. Some commentors had suggested we should apply QP status at the TIN/NPI level, and while we disagreed at that time and noted that we believed the most logical reading of the statute was to apply QP status at the NPI level, we did not dismiss the alternative of the TIN/NPI approach as legally barred. We also note that applying QP and Partial QP status at the TIN/NPI level is consistent with the definition of “Eligible professional” at section 1848(k)(3)(B) of the Act. Furthermore, we established in the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77439
through
77441
) and have consistently made QP determinations at the APM entity group level as defined at §  414.1305, which we note is a group of “eligible clinicians” as defined at §  414.1305 specifically as identified as a unique TIN and NPI combination. In other words, QP determinations have consistently considered TIN/NPI as the basis for participation in an Advanced APM.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal as more accurately targeting incentives to TINs that assume Advanced APM risk. Commenters on this subject included practices that have been adversely impacted by some of their clinicians having QP and Partial QP status and therefore not receiving the positive MIPS payment adjustment. Commentors noted that active enrollments often exist for TINs where the clinician is no longer rendering a large volume of services and that in these cases the action of another organization impacts the payment they receive through their TIN. Commenters who raised this perspective have indicated the financial impact of not receiving the MIPS adjustments for member clinicians who attained QP status elsewhere.
Response:
We appreciate the support for the proposed policy. Our aim is to balance program integrity and burden reduction. Applying QP status to the TINs participating in Advanced APMs ensures that organizations participating in these models are provided an earned incentive. We believe that this will result in a program where TINs are incentivized to participate in Advanced APMs. Furthermore, our policy aligns the application of QP and partial QP status at the TIN/NPI level with MIPS which for some TINs may reduce fragmentation within the program. In other words, when a group practice receives a MIPS payment adjustment based on their own performance and they are no longer impacted by the behavior of another group in QPP.
Comment:
Several commenters requested that the policy be delayed, or that CMS adopt an alternative approach that preserves QP or partial QP status at the NPI level while limiting the financial incentive to participating TINs. These commenters note return on investment in Advanced APM
(
printed page 71629)
participation, as well as MIPS relief afforded by QP and partial QP status, as key considerations. Some commenters expressed that providing TIN/NPI-level QP information for education would allow for practices to track and plan.
Response:
We appreciate commentor feedback. We recognize that commenters are in particular considering that the policy can lead to eligible clinicians being required to participate in MIPS with one or more TINs. However, we believe that delaying the implementation of the policy would extend the provision of the financial windfall described in this section without sufficient benefit to clinicians to be necessary. As proposed, the policy change is effective with the 2027 QP performance period, meaning that the first instance of MIPS reporting as a consequence of the policy would be in early 2028; further, while QPs are excluded from MIPS as clinicians, in significant numbers of cases, the QPs' other TINs (those that do not participate with Advanced APMs) already have MIPS reporting experience. We identified that when MIPS eligible TINs report for their practices, they commonly report for everyone, including clinicians who are QPs. As such, we do not believe that preparation for potential MIPS readiness warrants a delay. Further, we note that for TINs who are part of the APM Entities participating in Advanced APMs, the application of QP and Partial QP status at the TIN/NPI level would not increase burden or result in MIPS obligations. QP determinations always have involved the use of TIN/NPI-level data to form the numerator (APM Entity participation), so APM Entities and eligible clinicians who historically have attained QP status would not see that expectation change as a consequence of our proposed policy. Rather, the policy matches the resulting QP or partial QP status to the TIN/NPI combination(s) that were used in the determination itself. As such, TINs associated with participating APM Entities will not see changes in the QP or partial QP status results. The only thing that would change for these TINs is the amount of any APM Incentive Payment they might get in or after payment year 2029; we note that, under current law, there is no such incentive beyond payment year 2028.
The second suggestion made by these commenters was to continue applying QP and Partial QP status at the NPI level while limiting financial incentives to Advanced APM-participating TINs. This type of approach would stop the windfall we described in this section without leading to situations where MIPS participation is required for clinicians who have attained QP or Partial QP status. We recognize the appeal of such an approach, especially in cases where QP status or Partial QP status is earned at the individual level, signifying that the eligible clinician is individually and meaningfully participating in value-based care through one or more Advanced APM. As a result, we are modifying our proposed policy such that, in cases where QP or Partial QP status is attained at the individual level, the eligible clinician would be treated as a Partial QP across all of their TIN/NPI combinations. We believe that this modification preserves our goals with respect to program integrity and stopping wasteful spending without requiring eligible clinicians who are meeting or exceeding the Partial QP thresholds as individuals to also engage with MIPS. Notably, this approach also preserves the option for these clinicians to participate in MIPS, which we believe is important in light of supportive comments that we described earlier in this section.
Because Partial QP status means that reporting to MIPS is optional, this modification meets the preferences of both those commenters who are concerned about the burdens associated with MIPS reporting and those commenters who support the idea of having all of their clinicians participating in MIPS and receiving the attendant payment adjustments. Specifically, the modification would allow the TIN the choice of whether or not to participate in MIPS, allowing TINs to prioritize either MIPS adjustments or reduced burden, as they see fit.
We are finalizing the policy to amend § 414.1425(c) and (d) to add new subparagraphs that apply, respectively, QP status and Partial QP status at the TIN/NPI level, with a modification based on public comments that, for eligible clinicians whose QP or Partial QP status was determined at the individual level, we will apply Partial QP status to all TIN reassignments for the NPI as codified at § 414.1425(d), which will allow for the choice of whether or not to participate in MIPS for the applicable performance period.
3. APM Entity Terminations
a. Overview
In the CY 2017 Quality Payment Program final rule (
81 FR 77446
through
